### COMPLETE WORKS

# OF GIOVANNI
## PICO, COUNT OF MIRANDOLA
## AND CONCORDIA,
the prince, without controversy, of Theologians and Philosophers: A man, whether you consider his knowledge of languages or of things both human and divine, of admirable learning and talent.

->THESE ARE THE WORKS WHICH<-
->were most fortunately written by this author.<-

**Heptaplus** <note>The title is Greek for "sevenfold."</note>, concerning the six days' work of God the Creator from Genesis.
**Nine Hundred Conclusions**, publicly proposed at Rome, containing the principal points of Theology, and most of the subjects in which all the labor and study of philosophers is perceived. <note>Pico famously offered to pay the travel expenses of any scholar who would come to Rome to debate these 900 theses with him.</note>
**Apology** <note>original: "Apologia"</note> against those who attacked several of his Theological propositions.
**A Work on Being and the One**, in which many passages in Moses, Plato, and Aristotle are explained.
**On the Dignity of Man.** <note>This oration is celebrated today as a foundational text of Renaissance humanism, emphasizing human free will.</note>
**Rules or Precepts for the Instruction of a Christian Life**, by which, with help, a person may conquer the world and temptations.
<insert>NATIONAL LIBRARY OF ROME VITTORIO EMANUELE</insert>
**A Commentary on the Psalm, "Preserve me, O Lord"**, which is the 15th <note>Now usually numbered as Psalm 16.</note>.
**On the Kingdom of Christ and the Vanity of This World.**
**A Book of Letters.**
**Twelve Books of Disputations against Astrology.** <note>Pico was a fierce critic of judicial astrology—the idea that stars determine human fate—arguing instead for human agency.</note>
**Several Elegies.** <note>A form of classical poetry.</note>
**Three Books on Plato’s Symposium**, written in Italian.
**Also the Kabbalah of Johann Reuchlin**, which will be of great use to the reader for understanding certain passages of Pico. <note>Johann Reuchlin was a pioneering German humanist and Hebraist; Pico was deeply influenced by Jewish mystical traditions.</note>

<meta>This page continues from the general title page of Pico della Mirandola’s collected works. # The Judgment of Pope Alexander VI and a Defense of the Author's Works against the Slanders of Certain Detractors.

## ALEXANDER, SERVANT OF THE SERVANTS OF GOD, <note>original: "servus servorum dei" — a traditional title for the Pope emphasizing humility.</note> TO OUR BELOVED SON, THE NOBLE MAN GIOVANNI PICO, COUNT OF MIRANDOLA.

BELOVED son, Salutation and apostolic blessing. As far as God allows, we have looked out for the lives and reputations of all Catholics, especially those whom nobility of birth, literary discipline, and integrity of life and orthodox faith recommend. Indeed, some time ago, when you first brought yourself to the Roman Curia and our predecessor Pope Innocent VIII, you posted **Nine Hundred Conclusions** <note>The famous "900 Theses" Pico intended to debate in Rome.</note> in theology and other disciplines to be publicly disputed (as is the custom) with the permission of said predecessor. You offered to maintain these under the correction of the Apostolic See <note>The office of the Pope and the central administration of the Catholic Church.</note>. However, our predecessor understood from some people that among those conclusions were some contrary to our faith and religion—erroneous, scandalous, <term>ill-sounding</term> <note>original: "male sonantes" — a technical theological term for statements that might be technically true but are phrased in a way that suggests error.</note>, and suspect of unsound doctrine. At that time, wishing to protect the integrity of the faith so that the minds of the faithful (especially the simple folk who tend to flock to such public disputes) would not be corrupted, he commissioned several venerable brothers—then his, now our Bishops—and other professors of sacred theology and law. He commanded them by letter, in the form of a <term>brief</term> <note>A formal but less solemn papal letter.</note>, to examine the contents of said conclusions to see if any, by the force of their words, were dissonant from the Catholic faith or <term>tasted of heresy</term> <note>original: "haeresim saperent" — a legal category meaning something that strongly suggests heretical thinking without being a definitive heresy.</note>, or were so doubtful and ambiguous that they could be drawn toward an erroneous sense. They were to report back to our predecessor so that, having received their report on the faith, he might provide a timely remedy.

Those bishops and professors reported to our predecessor that certain conclusions seemed suspect to them and, as they asserted, tasted of heresy. You had nonetheless published these conclusions only for the sake of scholarly debate and under the correction of the Apostolic See, and you finally professed that you would hold them only as they were judged by our same predecessor, promising by oath that you would assent to whatever declaration he happened to make on the matter. 

Afterward, our predecessor received word that you had published another book, an **Apology** <note>original: "Apologeticum"</note>, in which you interpreted those same conclusions, declaring them in a better and Catholic sense and explaining your understanding of the sincere faith regarding them. Our predecessor, lest the aforementioned propositions should in any way corrupt the hearts of the faithful, forbade the reading of the booklet of the **Nine Hundred Conclusions**. However, he declared that you had incurred no stain on your reputation because of these things, as is contained more extensively in those letters, the contents of which we wish to be considered expressed here.

Truly, some people later suggested to our same predecessor that under the pretext of said *Apology*, you had contravened your aforementioned oath. He commanded you, then staying in France <note>original: "Gallis"</note>, to be summoned to the Curia. Having reverently accepted his commands, you set out on your journey to return to the Roman Curia. When you reached Italy, by the pleasure of that predecessor, you remained in the territory of Florence. In the meantime, these matters were brought to our notice. Having investigated the truth of the whole business, and especially based on the reports of our Venerable brother George, Bishop of Albano and Lisbon, and our beloved sons Giovanni Battista Orsini (Priest of the Title of Saints John and Paul) and Francesco (Deacon of Saint Eustachio), Cardinals of the Holy Roman Church—to whom we specifically committed the task of informing themselves accurately and reporting to us, along with our beloved son Paolo of Genoa, a professor of theology and of the Order of Saint Dominic and <term>Master of the Sacred Apostolic Palace</term> <note>The Pope’s chief theologian and the official responsible for the censorship of books.</note>—it was found that nothing else was done, processed, or attempted against you afterward. Furthermore, in that same *Apology*—which you wrote to relieve your mind in the eyes of everyone from any note of suspicion regarding the orthodox faith—you affirmed that you continually awaited the judgment and determination of our predecessor and the Apostolic See, to which you humbly submitted yourself. You have persisted in your aforementioned promise and oath, just as you intend to persist, and have now promised anew.

Therefore, embracing with fatherly affection your good and upright mind, your sincerity of faith, and your devotion and obedience toward us and the Apostolic See—and absolving you (whom Divine bounty has illustrated with various virtues) for your greater security from any guilt of perjury which you might have perhaps indirectly incurred by contravening said oath in any way—we, by our own motion and certain knowledge, extinguish the legal case against you. We declare that, persisting in your oath according to the form of our predecessor’s letters, you have incurred absolutely no stain on your reputation because of these matters. Furthermore, because of the publication of these declarations and the *Apology*, you have incurred no appearance or suspicion of heresy, nor any sinister mark, nor have you fallen into the crime of real or feigned relapse, nor have you in any way incurred the penalties or censures contained in the law against heretics or those suspected of heresy. 

By this same motion, knowledge, and authority, we decree and declare through these presents, strictly prohibiting and commanding in the name of holy obedience all local <term>ordinaries</term> <note>Local bishops or authorities with jurisdictional power.</note>, commissioners, and officials, including any inquisitors of heretical depravity, that they should not presume to molest or inquire after you in any way on the occasion of these matters. We decree as null and void anything attempted to the contrary by anyone, by whatever authority, whether knowingly or unknowingly, notwithstanding any apostolic constitutions or ordinances to the contrary.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter's, under the **Ring of the Fisherman** <note>original: "annulo piscatoris" — the signet ring used by the Pope to seal personal or less formal correspondence.</note>, on the 18th day of June, 1493, in the first year of our **Pontificate**.

->L. Podocataro<- <note>Ludovico Podocataro (1429–1504), a high-ranking churchman and secretary to Pope Alexander VI.</note>

<summary>This page contains a formal Papal Bull from Pope Alexander VI issued in 1493, which officially clears Giovanni Pico della Mirandola of all charges of heresy and perjury. It recognizes his "Apology" as a sincere explanation of his faith and restores his legal and religious standing.</summary>

# TO ANTON, ARCHBISHOP OF COLOGNE, PRINCE-ELECTOR <note>original: "VII VIRO" — literally 'one of the seven men,' referring to the seven Prince-Electors of the Holy Roman Empire who chose the Emperor.</note>, Johannes Herold sends greetings.

Since the surviving works of **GIOVANNI PICO** of Mirandola—those monuments of a truly divine genius—were being published to the great applause of learned men, I had every reason, **ANTON, Prince-Elector**, to illustrate them with a preface bearing your auspicious name. I did so with no less confidence that I could easily justify this gift to your Greatness (even though I am a stranger to you and this is the work of another’s labor) and to other illustrious men like yourself. Indeed, in this time of joy and eagerness throughout the German Republic—which I see everyone expressing openly at your accession to this highest dignity—I would consider it a shameful hesitation, full of vanity and folly, if I did not offer my congratulations at the first opportunity. I would otherwise seem to be like a detractor who grieves at another's glory or someone stripped of honor. For nothing is more effective for the health of the Republic than when a singular pursuit of wisdom by the elite is added to the power granted by the consensus of the whole. Indeed, it is a common saying that Republics are blessed when those who hold the highest power devote all their time to the business of learning and virtue. This has certainly happened for our Germany in these truly harsh and most difficult times; it has raised the nation with a great and nearly certain hope of its ancient authority and liberty, through the greatest and never-fading glory of your name, **ANTON, Prince-Elector**.

To say nothing of the gifts of fortune—all of which you possess in abundance, as much as the highest step of your dignity seems to require—you have the fame of the <term>SCHAUENBURG</term> <note>The House of Schauenburg and Holstein was a noble German dynasty; Anton von Schauenburg reigned as Archbishop from 1557 to 1558.</note> lineage, greatness of resources, and a heroic stature. With these many and great gifts, you are able to heal the disturbances of unruly fortune and the inconveniences of your people; indeed, you can ensure they are as happy as possible under your rule. I see everyone is most delighted by the fact that they have known you from your youth to be a most devoted student of all piety and philosophy. You are such by nature that even without the instructions of the wisest men, you have learned with the greatest care what the duties of a good man are. Having applied a purer doctrine of piety, you have cultivated all virtues, so that like some divine man sent from heaven, you have been received into the college of the Seven Electors among the arbiters of German affairs, succeeding your brother <note>Anton succeeded his brother, Adolf von Schauenburg, after the latter's death in 1556.</note>. Now that he has passed away, your holiness, prudence, and gravity shine forth like a light to consult for the human race, provide for the safety of all, and strike terror into savage and barbarian nations. 

For how much is 그 holy doctrine of Christian persuasion currently torn apart by loud arguments? In what infinite and various disputes is it not entangled? Certainly, it is nearly overwhelmed by the bitterest contentions, burning with rivalry. Yet everyone proclaims that, having accepted this dignity, your first priority is ancient piety, ensuring it is paid purely and chastely to the Divine Power. You strive uniquely to see that the system of religion handed down by the institutions of the Apostles and the Fathers is defended incorrupt and restored, as a true Bishop and master of sacred things.

Already, how many secret hatreds and bitter desires have been stirred up among the Germans? These have given rise to the most cruel dissensions, even among those most closely joined, to the point where, through the discords of powerful and famous men, the fortunes of every good person were consumed. By the force of the multitude, the stirring up of the common folk, and every kind of sedition, a cruel and destructive war was finally kindled in the Fatherland. In this war, no example of perfidy, treason, crime, disgrace, or calamity was missing; indeed, there was the present threat of total destruction and the unrestrained tyranny of barbarian nations. However, I hear by report and rumor that you are showing yourself to be a prince of the fatherland—gentle in authority, a leader in intellect, and most constant in greatness of soul—both in the assemblies of the nobles of this Holy Empire and in private meetings, seeking the councils by which the remains of such great and brotherly conflicts may be extinguished, and the wounds of lost liberty healed. You are restoring this very opinion people have of you upon a foundation of perpetual praise: namely, charity toward one's neighbor, without which nothing can be laudable and nothing can be Christian.

After your concern for divine affairs, they say the first of your cares is that equality be preserved in the matters and causes of your people. Following that, you see to it that the dignity of the social orders remains intact, and you provide mercifully and cheerfully for good studies and for the relief of the afflicted and miserable. And yet, since external matters are always preferred to domestic ones, amidst the immense and vast roar of a consenting people, we already feel that your kindly disposition of soul is being placed in the council of the heavenly ones. This is the disposition by which you yearn to help your brothers who are fighting for their religion, their children, and their hearths—those who are unworthily despoiled, slaughtered, and led away into captivity by the perpetual harassment and plundering of the Turks. This is especially vital since you yourself perceive that Germany, the citadel of the Christian world, can scarcely hold out much longer, despite the endurance of the present Emperor <term>FERDINAND</term> <note>Ferdinand I (1503–1564), Holy Roman Emperor, who faced the peak of the Ottoman threat in Europe.</note>, a father of his country fortified against all dangers, and the bravery of his most noble son of the same name. Although recently, under that famous Prince of youth—a commander of soldiers not by the offenses of war but by the victor’s discipline, enriched by no mere wages but by divine trophies—the borders of this eternal Empire have been rendered more secure from the incursions of the most savage tyrant and the foul slaughter of a perfidious race, and have been expanded by an ample vindication of the German name and ancestral virtue. This divinely given victory, won by the hands of brave men—this most joyful outcome of smiling Mars and war—one could pursue for the great good and immortal benefit of the Republic; to neglect or betray it would be to the detriment of the whole Christian world, as the situation itself declares that you [contribute] counsel and resources to this sacred war...

The letter praises Anton's wisdom and nobility while highlighting the dire political and religious state of Germany, specifically the threat of the Ottoman Turks and internal Christian discord.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Johannes Herold’s dedicatory letter to Anton von Schauenburg, the Archbishop-Elector of Cologne. Herold transitions from praising the Prince-Elector to a detailed biographical and intellectual appreciation of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, whose works he is publishing. He also references his own historical research on Germany and justifies the inclusion of Johann Reuchlin’s work on the Cabala in this edition.</meta>

# E P I S T L E .

A constant rumor flourishes that you show and offer everything—for your country, for your neighbor, and for Christ—as a true brother. Greetings, therefore, Prince **ANTON**, born for the good of the Commonwealth. Success to your virtue: reason itself persuades me to be carried away by my zeal for it, and integrity demands that I congratulate you. Therefore, so that I might testify how gladly my own agreement and my opinion of your immortality joins the congratulations of all ranks, I consider this edition of the books of **Pico**, offered to me by divine providence, to be the most certain proof of my goodwill.

For he who wrote these things was a most noble and most honored man, to whom wealth, protection, diligence, and the greatest distinction brought every kind of learning. Indeed, his devotion to piety and good literature was so great that, barely reaching his thirty-second year, he revealed and illustrated things that the Fathers of the Church investigated most acutely over many centuries; things which philosophers hid in many wraps of pretense; and things which the diversity of numbers and languages and the infinite variety of arts concealed in precepts, mysteries, and certain recondite oracles. He is certainly a brilliant and rich author; for in that single and modest-sized book which he titled *Heptaplus* <note>original: "Heptaplū"; a work by Pico providing a seven-fold mystical interpretation of the creation story in Genesis</note>, concerning God and the Nature of the universe, he cut through whatever the sects of all ages had established with a simple majesty of speech. Indeed, he said such great and distinguished things that those who held the greatest and most serious names among the doctors seem to have said nothing at all. 

Finally, who could deny that he is greater than any herald’s praise when one reads his **900 Conclusions**? I do not know if any who have been skilled in the sciences until now have attempted to explain them, but among those who exist today, I believe no one would wish to take up such a burden; to future men, undoubtedly, the pursuit of his genius and the infinite labor of the competition will seem heavy. He wished, however, to explain them all with more certain reasoning—as a subtle debater—had he not been obstructed. He certainly could have, since he defends the weightier Propositions so skillfully in his *Apology*, that free but modest oration, which was always for him a charming little conciliator of both studies and honorable souls. By these allurements he even showed the harmony of the greatest philosophers, Plato and Aristotle, in his book *On Being and the One* <note>original: "de Ente & Vno"</note>, while in his *Epistles* one may see a certain weight of sentiment and excellent holiness. 

The weight of the theologian he was to become is shown by his *Directing Rules*, in addition to that most weighty *Commentary on the 15th Psalm*; there, on a single small page, he expressed the entire instruction of a Christian man, which no one until now has been able to explain or prescribe more happily in many massive volumes. In adorning the human condition, he used an inimitable eloquence—for does it not equal the thunders of Pericles? Does it not express the persuasiveness of Cethegus? <note>Marcus Cornelius Cethegus was a Roman orator praised by Ennius for his "suada" or persuasive charm.</note> He would certainly have performed something even greater if he had flourished in life as he did in poetry, which is clear from his *Prayer to God* <note>original: "Depræcatoria ad Deū"</note> and that *Elegy* written to Benivieni. 

To sum up, our author here contends that no force of fate, no gift of fortune, no rising or setting of the stars can be placed before the order and sequence of providence flowing from eternity. Therefore, with an accurate and exquisite disputation, he does not so much attack that vain divination from the stars as he teaches the reason of the heavens and the certain courses and motions of the stars. The rest of his works in the vernacular <note>referring to Pico's writings in Italian</note> are of such a kind that they can greatly illustrate and adorn Plato’s *Symposium* <note>original: "Conuiuū Platonis"</note>. 

Since you have dedicated your mind to these studies from the earliest times of your youth, but have long been drawn away by the weight of business, I know you will return to them with a more burning love for the good in more tranquil times. Therefore, Prince **ANTON**, so that he might be at hand—an author whose precepts would be more pleasant to you and whose person more welcome—I wished to inscribe this **Pico** to your name until I myself might write something worthy of your greatness. For the works I have in hand, as they are of great importance for both business and leisure, require travel and the investigation of the nobler provinces of Germany, as well as the documents of antiquity preserved in the archives and libraries of the nobility—which you should not think is the least reason for this my writing to you. 

Relying on your clemency, I am persuaded that you will not deny me the descriptions of beautiful things (which I do not doubt exist with you) to adorn my *Commentaries on Flowering Germany* <note>original: "Effloreſcētis Germaniæ Cōmē tarios"; Herold's own historical and geographical project</note>. For the favor and great benevolence of **DANIEL**, Elector of Mainz <note>original: "DANIELIS VII uiri Moguntini"; Daniel Brendel von Homburg</note>—a man whose standing among the learned will live for those born after us—promises me the same; as does that singular zeal for good letters and the learned shown by your colleague **JOHANN**, Elector of Trier <note>original: "LAYEN IOANNIS VII uiri Treuirenfis"; Johann von der Leyen</note>, a unique example of innocence and integrity. This was indeed recently shown to me—or rather granted to the Commonwealth—by a man than whom I think I have seen none more worthy, a man whose existence in this state of affairs is a marvel: namely **WOLFGANG**, the restorer and true father of the Fulda fellowship. 

I am led into this greatest and, as I trust, most certain hope regarding you by the goodwill toward me of the most serious man **GERLACH von ISENBURG**. Because he was born of noble station and has performed the highest duties in sacred matters, he ought to have the greatest authority with you; yet he can recommend this cause of mine to you, Prince **ANTON**, for many reasons: for the sincerity of his character, the elegance of his judgment, the loyalty of his counsel, and the reverence with which he honors you. 

It remains for me to explain my plan regarding the *Cabala* <note>A tradition of Jewish mysticism. Renaissance humanists believed it contained ancient wisdom that supported Christian truths.</note> of **JOHANN REUCHLIN**, a most learned man, which we have added here to the works of **PICO**. Pico, who was learned and erudite in this truly divine art as in others, had proposed certain principles of this discipline, but was prevented by death and could not unfold the developments and furthest reaches of that science. However, **REUCHLIN**, being a man of excellent genius, restored and corrected what had been miserably vitiated and corrupted by the superstitions of the Rabbis and the portents of the philosophers, according to the judgment of all. Therefore, I thought these precepts, cultivated in all ages by the studies of the most pious and holy men, would not be unwelcome to you, and for that reason I saw to it that they were annexed to this work. 

Receive, I pray, Prince **ANTON**, my mind and will with the same frankness with which I offer this book to you, and persuade yourself that I wish to preserve perpetually that reverence of mine toward you, undertaken by a certain judgment of your virtues. May our Great God keep your Greatness safe for the Commonwealth for a long time. Basel, the 8th 

->day before the Calends of April. In the year from the birth of Christ<-
->1557.<-

<meta>This page transitions from Johannes Herold’s introductory letter to the formal biography of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, written by his nephew, Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola. The text shifts from the publisher’s dedication to a first-hand account of Pico's life, lineage, and character.</meta>

# The Life of Giovanni Pico of Mirandola and Concordia
## A most distinguished Prince, written by the illustrious Prince Gianfrancesco, son of Pico.

As I begin to write the life of Giovanni Pico, my uncle, I consider it my first duty to tell my readers not to suspect that I will speak in a flattering manner because I am his nephew or his student. Nothing here is granted to friendship, nothing to family, and nothing is repaid with fictional praise for the great favors he bestowed upon me. Indeed, my narrative is as far removed from adulation as was the necessity for it. I have been careful lest readers think me a liar or excessive in my praise; had I written down everything I felt about him, there might have been a risk that his own lofty virtues or those who assert them would be doubted. This can be seen by the following argument: since many works by the most learned men of our age—and indeed the most polished writings of the elite—have provided rich testimony to what I am about to say, both while he lived and after he exchanged this life for a better one, they have surpassed me in praising his character and his learning. I have ordered some of these to be added at the end of this book, after his own commentaries, so that trust might be placed in more reliable witnesses rather than just his kin.

Passing over his paternal lineage (though it is recorded that it took its origin from Emperor Constantine through his great-grandson Pico, from whom the name of the whole family is said to come), we shall begin with the time of his birth. I do this partly because he brought perhaps no less honor to the family than he received from it, and partly because I have chosen to reveal his own gifts of mind and the sequence of his life and death, which I either witnessed with my own eyes and ears or received from the most serious witnesses, setting aside his pedigree and the famous deeds of his ancestors.

In the year 1463 after the Virgin’s birth, while Pope Pius II <note>A humanist Pope known as Enea Silvio Piccolomini</note> presided over the Church and Frederick III held the reins of the Roman Empire, his mother Julia, of the noble Boiardo family, gave birth to him as her last child for his father, Gianfrancesco. She had already borne Galeotto, the eldest (from whom I was born), Antonio Maria, and two sisters. One of the sisters, then married to Leonello, gave birth to Alberto Pio, one of the princes of Carpi, and is now the wife of Prince Rodolfo Gonzaga; the other sister, after the death of her first husband Pino Ordelaffi, the Prince of Forlì, granted a second marriage to the Count of Monteagano.

A sign of no small importance appeared before his birth: a circular flame was seen to stand over the room of the mother as she was giving birth, and then soon vanished. This perhaps suggested to us that he who was being brought forth among mortals at that hour would be most similar to the perfection of a circular figure in his intellect, and that the excellence of his name was to be celebrated everywhere around the globe; that his mind, like a heavenly fire, would always seek the heights, and that his fiery eloquence, in harmony with his inflamed mind, would one day celebrate our God (who is a "consuming fire") <note>A reference to Hebrews 12:29</note> with all its strength, but would then be hidden from the sight of men, just as that flame vanished. Indeed, we read that unusual signs have sometimes preceded or followed the births of the most learned and holy men, as if divine will were setting those infants apart from the crowd of others and indicating they were born for great deeds. Thus—to omit others—a swarm of bees hovered over the mouth of the great Saint Ambrose; they entered his mouth, and then leaving and flying very high, they hid themselves among the clouds and escaped the sight of his father and the others present. Paulinus, making much of this omen, argued that it indicated the "honeycombs" of his writings, which would announce heavenly gifts and raise men's minds from the earth to heaven.

As for his appearance, he was of distinguished and noble form, tall and lofty in stature, with soft skin and a lovely face. On the whole, his complexion was fair, interspersed with a decent redness. He had gray-blue and alert eyes, yellow <note>often used for blond in Latin</note> and natural hair, and teeth that were white and even.

Under his mother’s care, he was brought to teachers and the liberal arts. He cultivated the study of the humanities <term>humanitatis: the study of classical literature, rhetoric, and history</term> with such an ardent spirit that, in a short time, he was rightfully placed among the leading poets and orators of that era. He was incredibly fast at learning, endowed with such a ready talent that he could recite poems once heard from a speaker in both forward and reverse order, to the great amazement of everyone. He possessed a most tenacious memory, which is usually the opposite for others; for it often happens by nature that those with quick minds do not have strong memories, while those who learn with effort become more tenacious in what they have grasped.

When he was fourteen years old, by the command of his mother—who vehemently desired him to be initiated into the sacred orders—he moved to Bologna to learn Canon Law <note>original: "iuris pōtificij"; the law of the Catholic Church</note>. After he had tasted this for two years, seeing that it relied on mere traditions, he turned elsewhere. Yet he did not leave without producing good fruit; for as a boy, and a very tender one at that, he compiled a certain "Epitome" or summary of the letters of the Popes, which they call the *Decretals*. In this work, he concluded all the opinions of those decrees more concisely than had ever been done—a work of no small weight even for seasoned professors. But as a curious explorer of the secrets of nature, leaving these well-trodden paths, he devoted himself entirely to the intellectual speculation of philosophy, both human and divine...

The narrative moves from his early education to his famous challenge in Rome and his subsequent conflict with church authorities.</meta>

-># GIOVANNI PICO<-

...brought forth <note>The Latin text begins mid-sentence: "didit," likely completing a word like "prodidit."</note> more quickly the grace to be attained. He traveled through the literary universities not only of Italy but also of France, most scrupulously seeking out the famous teachers of that time, in the manner of **Plato** and **Apollonius** <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a first-century philosopher known for his extensive travels in search of wisdom.</note>. He devoted such tireless labor to these studies that he was both a finished **Theologian** and a **Philosopher** while still a beardless youth—and was regarded as such. He had already spent seven years among those scholars when, eager for human praise and glory (for he did not yet burn with divine love, as will become clear), he moved to Rome.

There, desiring to show how much envy would later await him even from the highest doors, he proposed **Nine Hundred Questions** <note>Known as the *900 Theses*, Pico intended these to be debated by scholars from all over Europe.</note> on dialectics, mathematics, and natural and divine matters. These were drawn not only from Latin sources and excerpted from Greek records, but also unearthed from the mysteries of the **Hebrews**, the secrets of the **Chaldeans**, and investigated from the **Arabs**. He also interwove many questions regarding the ancient and obscure philosophy of **Pythagoras**, **Trismegistus**, and **Orpheus**, and much concerning the **Cabala**—that is, the <term>Secret Reception of Hebrew Teachings</term> <note>original: "Secreta Hebræorū dogmatū receptione." Pico was one of the first Christian scholars to study Jewish mystical texts.</note> (which among our own writers, **Origen** and **Hilary** most especially mention). He included much on **Natural Magic**, which he taught was separated by no small distance from impious and wicked magic; he proved this most elegantly through the testimony of many. Nor did he lack **seventy-two new dogmas** in Physics and Metaphysics, his own inventions and meditations, adapted to elucidate whatever philosophical questions might arise. To these, he added a new system of philosophizing through numbers, and he posted them all together in public places so they might be more easily publicized, promising that he would pay the expenses of any who had traveled to Rome from distant lands for the sake of the debate.

But due to the rivalry of detractors (which always seeks the heights, like fire), he was never able to ensure that a day for the debate was appointed. For this reason, he remained in Rome for a year, during which time those <term>fault-finders</term> <note>original: "vitiligatores," a term for those who make petty or malicious criticisms.</note> did not dare to attack him openly or with a free spirit, but rather attempted to prick him with tricks and "rabbit-holes" <note>Metaphorical for sneaky, underground maneuvers.</note> and to undermine him with hidden arrows, driven by the poisonous envy of a corrupted mind (so most believed). It was thought that he stirred up this spite primarily because many who had long brooded over literary business—perhaps out of ambition or greed—feared they would be discredited if this youth, bolstered by his ancestors' wealth and vast learning, like a fertile field in full bloom, did not fear to test his doctrine and intellect in the premier city of the world regarding natural and divine things, many of which had been inaccessible to our people for several centuries.

When they realized they could achieve nothing against his doctrine with honest "siege engines," they brought forth the "artillery of slander." They cried out that **thirteen** of the nine hundred questions were suspect regarding the true faith. Some joined them who attacked those questions as "unusual to their ears"—perhaps with piety, but perhaps with insufficient learning—under the zeal of faith and the pretext of religion. Nevertheless, not a few celebrated doctors of Theology had previously approved those very questions as pious and pure and had signed their names to them. Among their number was **Bonfrancesco, Bishop of Reggio** <note>Bonfrancesco Arlotti, a diplomat and scholar.</note>, a man distinguished by every kind of learning, the sharpest judgment, and gravity of character, who was then serving in Rome as the legate to the Pope for the **Duke of Ferrara**. However, those "babblers" attempted nothing against him, perhaps fearing they could not shake his reputation since he submitted whatever he treated to the correction of the Mother Church and the Pope.

But Pico, not enduring this damage to his reputation, published an ***Apologia*** <note>A formal written defense.</note>, certainly a varied and elegant work, filled with knowledge of things worth knowing. He labored over it in only twenty nights. In this edition, it was made clearer than light that his conclusions could indeed be accepted in a Catholic sense, and that those who had first barked at them should be convicted of insolence and ignorance. As a most Christian man, he committed the book itself and whatever he was to write in the future to the judgment of the Mother Church and its most holy leader. He was most convinced that this ought to be done either expressly or tacitly, as if he were quoting that saying of **Augustine**: *“I can err, but I cannot be a heretic,”* since one is a human trait, while the other is a trait of a perverse and obstinate will.

But when **Pope Innocent VIII** heard that through the publication of the *Apologia* those conclusions (which had previously been infested with slanders) had been interpreted in a Catholic sense and relieved of the mark of crime, he nevertheless forbade the reading of the little book of theses. This was because some to whom the examination of the conclusions had been entrusted reported that traps could be set for the faithful if some of those questions (which lay in a crude and unrefined state for the sake of debate) were to be circulated widely. All of this can be clearly seen in the decree—which they call a **Brief**—of **Pope Alexander VI**, under whom we now live. We have decided to hand this over to the printers along with the *Apologia* itself. 

Indeed, at the end of the *Apologia*, Pico had already done by his own reasoning what the Pope later provided by authority: he had begged friends and enemies, the learned and the unlearned, to read the *Apologia* but to pass over the unrefined book of conclusions without reading it. He did this because it contained many things he had undertaken to dispute not commonly in the streets, but in secret gathering among a few learned men as a **Scholastic exercise** in the manner of the academies. He had proposed many impious dogmas of the ancient philosophers—namely **Alexander**, **Averroes**, and many others—which he had always asserted, professed, and preached, both publicly and privately, to be as far from the paths of true and right philosophy as they were from the faith. Speaking in this way about that little book of nine hundred conclusions, he concluded his apologetic work: *"Therefore, let those who hate me not read them because they are mine; let those who love me not read them because from those things which are mine, they might think many things which are not ours."* But by the immense goodness of God, which brings [good] out of evil...

-># THE LIFE OF MIRANDOLA<-

### THE LIFE OF MIRANDOLA

...from these <note>The text begins mid-sentence, referring to the trials and slanders mentioned on the previous page.</note> he even drew out good. He judged the effect to be (as he reported to me) that the slander falsely brought against him by malevolent men served to correct true errors; it shone upon him like a most splendid radiance while he was wandering in the darkness, so that he could see how far he had stepped away from the path of truth. For previously, he had been both greedy for glory and kindled by vain love, moved by the charms of women. Indeed, many women, because of the beauty of his body and the grace of his face—to which were added his vast learning, riches, and noble birth—burned with love for him. Not shrinking from their devotion, and having for a short time neglected the way of life, he had drifted into delights. But awakened by that conflict <note>Referring to his legal troubles with the Roman Curia.</note>, he restrained his mind which had been dissolving in luxury and turned it toward Christ. He exchanged feminine flatteries for the joys of the heavenly fatherland. Neglecting the breeze of glory which he had once chased, he began to seek with his whole mind the glory of God and the utility of the Church, and so composed his character that from then on he could be approved even by the judgment of an enemy.

And when he learned that his glorious reputation had immediately begun to fly through both neighboring and remote lands, many of the philosophers who were considered most learned flocked to him as if to a "market of good arts" <note>original: "mercaturam bonarum artium," a quote from Cicero’s *De Senectute* describing a place where wisdom is traded or shared.</note>, either to stir up literary contests or, for those with a more upright mind, to hear and hold fast to the healthy teachings of right living. These teachings were sought all the more because they flowed from a man who was both most learned and most noble, who had once followed the devious paths of voluptuous softness. For it seems that for the purpose of instilling moral discipline into the minds of listeners, those things have the most weight which are both good by their own nature and proceed from a teacher who has converted to the paths of justice from the distorted and crooked path of lusts. 

He had once played with love in elegiac poetry, which, having composed in five books, he handed over to the flames for the sake of religion. He likewise wrote many things in Tuscan rhymes <note>meaning Italian poetry.</note>, which a similar fire consumed for the same reason. Then, embracing Sacred Scripture with the most burning zeal, he immediately offered in the temple of God, as if the first fruits of his harvest—being then in his twenty-eighth year—a work on the six days of <term>Genesis</term> and the day of rest titled the <term>Heptaplus</term> <note>From the Greek word for "sevenfold"; this work provides seven layers of interpretation for the creation story.</note>. This work was indeed perfect in its genius and elaborate in its industry, filled both with the sublime teachings of the philosophers and the deepest mysteries of our Christian theology. It was woven together with a sevenfold variety of narration, with a sevenfold number of chapters packed into each of the seven expositions, matching the name of the book perfectly. 

However, because of the things unearthed from the bosom of nature, the difficult unravelling of divine questions, the most hidden meanings of the prophet <note>referring to Moses, the traditional author of Genesis.</note>, and the elegance of the language, it does not present itself everywhere to those unrefined in philosophy and eloquence. Instead, the use of that precious and rare "furniture" is prepared for only a few. He himself, noticing this at the end of the preface to the work, made a not ungraceful mention of this matter. 

As soon as he tasted the sacred writings, he exulted with joy, finding that he had discovered not only true wisdom but also true eloquence. To omit many things, he brought forth many praises of the New Testament, saying that the letters of Paul surpassed the writings of all orators in eloquence. He specifically cited the late-night works of **Tully** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note> and even of **Demosthenes** himself, whom he called the primary craftsman of speaking. He said this not because Paul’s letters were branded with curling irons <note>A metaphor for artificial or overly-ornamented rhetorical style.</note>, or covered in dyes scraped from everywhere and packed with curls, but because they tasted of true, solid, and fragrant eloquence, supported by true sentiments and true art—to put it briefly, they were not deliberately stuffed with the "wealth of the Egyptians" <note>A common metaphor in Renaissance theology: using pagan philosophy and rhetoric (the "spoils of Egypt") to build the Christian faith (the "Tabernacle"). Pico is arguing that Scripture has its own inherent power without needing pagan decoration.</note>.

Furthermore, he proclaimed all the utterances of the Old Law to be full of the most consummate science and wisdom. Although others, especially **Augustine** in his book *On Christian Doctrine*, have clearly shown this, and **Tertullian**, **Eusebius Pamphili**, and **Cassiodorus** affirm it—namely, that the grammarians, rhetoricians, orators, and all the ancient philosophers drank the streams of their eloquence and learning from the fountains of the divine scriptures—he nonetheless pursued this gift with other reasons, part of which is worthwhile to see in the famous introductions of the *Heptaplus* and in the preface of the second exposition itself. 

Amidst so many constant unravellings of the divine law, in the second year after the publication of the *Heptaplus*, he also finished a small work titled <term>On Being and the One</term> <note>original: "De Ente & uno."</note>, divided into ten chapters. It was brief in body but ample in strength, sprinkled everywhere with the deepest teachings of the philosophers and theological meanings. In it, he showed that the "One" is not superior to "Being," but that they correspond to one another and are of equal scope. He reviewed the controversy held on this matter by the followers of **Plato** and **Aristotle**, asserting that those Academics <note>Platonists.</note> who contended otherwise had not grasped the true teaching of Plato. He intended to demonstrate that there was a completely common meaning between <term>Aristotle</term> and <term>Plato</term> regarding "the One" and "Being," as with other things in general, even if their words disagreed. In the final chapter of the work, he turned the entire disputation toward the instruction of life and the amendment of morals, no less ingeniously than religiously.

Against this work, **Antonio di Faenza** <note>original: "Antonius Fauentinus," a Scholastic philosopher.</note>, an otherwise excellent philosopher, brought forward several objections in four letters. Pico himself responded to three of them. As for the fourth, either because it was not faithfully delivered, or because he thought it could be answered from what he had already written, or for some other cause which must be believed to be just, he made no mention of it that I know of. After he departed from this life, I myself undertook the task of responding, so that no occasion would be given to the malevolent to bark or to the unlearned to believe something sinister. I took the greatest care to show that, from his preceding opinions, the answer had largely already been given. 

We have also seen several things by him concerning **Platonic** matters arranged in the vernacular tongue <note>Italian.</note>, in which many things serving to explain the theology of the ancients and many hidden meanings of the wise in enigmas and riddles are discovered. Perhaps, having found greater leisure, we will attempt to render these into Latin, lest the surpassing learning of such a great man concerning these... <margin>of these matters</margin> <note>The text ends with the catchword "dere," likely leading to "derelinquatur" (be left behind) or similar on the next page.</note>

-># OF GIOVANNI PICO<-

### THE BIOGRAPHY OF MIRANDOLA

...about the most accessible matters, and such as are brought before the eyes of the common people. So far, we have spoken of the completed works which he published before his death, like messengers and heralds of the magnificent works he had conceived and was working upon. For he had already illuminated the Old Testament with the torches of interpretation, and was prepared to perform the same service for the New Testament. He did not only bring forth the meanings that the literal sequence of the text could carry, but in those places which would bear three other senses <note>Pico is referring to the traditional "fourfold sense" of scripture: literal, allegorical, moral, and anagogical.</note> specific to divine eloquence, he built upon them. He compared the differing readings of our codices with Greek and Hebrew examples. But this was foremost in his mind, and settled deepest among all the projects he had conceived in the genre of commentary: that he would not bring forward the dogmas of others—since those were already held, read, and known—but would instead set forth his own discoveries and meditations. Thus, by his own powers rather than those of others, he would satisfy the starving souls of truth to the best of his ability.

After this, being powerful in the Hebrew tongue, he published a small book on the truth of Jerome's <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the primary translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> translation against the slanders of the Jews, as well as a defense for the seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> regarding the Psalms against the same people; he also wrote a book on the *True Calculation of Time*. Finally, he applied his mind to defeating the seven enemies of the Church. For whoever obeys neither Christ nor His Church is, by consequence, His enemy: either being impious, he receives no dogma of faith; or he serves false idols and worships demons under these images; or he observes the Mosaic law according to the ritual of the most lost Jews; or he follows the abominable Muhammad, enslaved to his detestable decrees; or, living a Christian life in hearing only but not in works or a sincere mind, he perverts the Gospel teachings; or, not consenting to the Catholic Church, he kicks back with an obstinate heart; or he receives the Gospel not with a chaste faith, but one adulterated and profaned by various superstitions; or, though he receives it with a solid, bright, and constant faith, he opposes it by his works. 

These seven, therefore, like leaders under whom the rest are contained as common soldiers, he had summoned to battle, intending to fight them with their own weapons. Against the impious philosophers—who, weighed down by the yoke of no religion and devoted to no deity, worship only natural reasons—he fought with those same reasons. He battled most strongly against the Hebrews with the sayings of the Old Testament and the specific authorities of the Jewish school. With the Muslims, relying on the Quran, he engaged in close combat. He prostrated the idol-worshippers with many wounds and not much force. Those ensnared in vain superstitions, especially those who worship divinatory astrology, he sharply rebuked with both true philosophy and the particular arguments of the astrologers themselves; he had already pursued their ravings in twelve books, and indeed most complete ones, out of the thirteen destined for this purpose. 

Finally, he examines individually Hydromancy <note>divination by water</note>, Geomancy <note>divination by earth/soil</note>, Pyromancy <note>divination by fire</note>, Haruspicina <term>Haruspicina: the ancient practice of divining the future by inspecting the entrails of sacrificed animals</term>, and other such vanities. But against the "prophesying" astrologers, he had explicitly declared a frontal assault <note>literally "a wedge-shaped battle formation"</note>, and with all his strength had aimed the battering ram, since other superstitions seek out supports for their errors in the futile and weightless dogmas of the astrologers—either weighing the moments of a birth chart or seeking "favorable" aspects such as hexagons or triangles in selecting hours, and other things of that sort which even a madman like Orestes <note>A mythological figure synonymous with madness.</note> would not approach. 

Not content with having fundamentally overturned all astrology, he wished to show to the astrologers of our time (who are mostly ignorant of the Greek language) that astrology, the vainest of all professions, was rendered even vainer (if that can be said) by perverse translations. While writing against them, as if doing something else, he translated the *Fruits of Ptolemy* (commonly called the *Centiloquium* <note>A collection of 100 astrological aphorisms traditionally attributed to Ptolemy.</note>) from Greek into Latin, and honored it with a most elegant exposition. In this book, he demonstrates that more errors (so to speak) are contained in that common translation than words—which, nevertheless, those lazy worshippers of the craft have always guarded in secret like a precious treasure. 

Against those who think wrongly concerning the faith of Christ and do not obey the command of Mother Church—whom we call by the more common name "Heretics"—he had attacked with an excellent rebuke using both the New Testament <note>original: "Nouo instrumento"</note> and reason. Nearly ninety heresies are publicly known; but he, having searched everything, found two hundred, which he proposed not only to eliminate and put to flight individually, but also to show from which part of improperly understood philosophy they had drawn or patched together their errors. 

Finally, he had vehemently attacked those Christians whose faith is seen without works. He had also diligently explored how it could be that men believe fire is placed in the center of the earth—where the bodies of the damned are to suffer perpetual punishment—and other such unthinkable torments of both soul and body, as well as the immense joys of the seen Godhead by which souls joined to bodies are blessed, and yet they are not obedient to the words of the Church which compel belief. Instead, they everywhere rave in vices and devote themselves to piling up riches; they fear nothing less than those punishments, and desire nothing less than the kingdom of God. He attempted to apply suitable help according to the quality of the diseases: namely, to cauterize foul diseases, naturally impure, with sharp and bitter medicines; but to cherish with gentle, soothing treatments those wounds which were infected with less malice or depravity and desired to be scarred over; and for those who had achieved health but feared a relapse, to prepare the most wholesome potions and celebrated antidotes. 

Many other works he had begun, from which it could be hoped that the study of philosophy as a whole would flourish again, with errors eliminated and barbarism driven out. Among these, the most important was the "Concord" of Plato and Aristotle, which he had already begun and was soon to complete, if life...

<meta>This page continues the biography of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, focusing on his intellectual project of reconciling disparate schools of philosophy and the state of his unfinished works at the time of his early death.</meta>

### THE BIOGRAPHY OF MIRANDOLA:

...had the Count survived for even a few more years—for he had so nourished Philosophy from its cradle <note>original: "ab incunabulis"</note> with the milk of study, and had brought it to such a maturity in our own times—that a philosopher of our age would have desired nothing more from Greek, Latin, or "barbarian" <note>This refers to non-Classical languages, particularly the medieval Scholastic Latin of the "barbarian" north, or perhaps Arabic and Hebrew.</note> manuscripts. He would have summoned the watery Thales, the fiery Heraclitus, and Democritus surrounded by his atoms; likewise, Orpheus, Pythagoras, and other ancients would have met in the Academy through his labor and favor. Finally, the princes of philosophy—namely Plato, cloaked in the veils of myths and mathematical coverings, and Aristotle, fortified by his theories of motion—would have joined hands to swear an oath of future friendship. Between Averroes and Avicenna <note>Two of the most influential Islamic philosophers of the Middle Ages.</note> also, and between Thomas Aquinas and Duns Scotus, who had long been in conflict, he would have obtained, if not a total peace, at least a truce in many matters. For in most of their controversies, if someone examines their differing words more closely, weighs them more exactly, and searches more scrupulously—shedding the "skin" of the text to penetrate the deepest hiding places and inner sanctums of the mind—they will find a unity of meaning within those disparate and conflicting words, without any ambiguity. The crowd of modern thinkers would have been both honored and corrected by him, partly according to their merits and partly for their faults.

<margin>—</margin>
Thus, entirely dedicated to God, he defended the Church with whatever weapons he could, and led Truth out from its hiding place in the "well of Democritus" <note>A classical proverb suggests that truth lies hidden at the bottom of a deep well.</note> (as they say). He utterly broke and cut down the unyielding grass of ignorance that suffocates the minds of many, along with the budding, ruinous weeds of error. But coming death rendered the labor of such great vigils and the birth of his refined nighttime studies almost vain. This was the primary reason why he left behind many commentaries that were, for the most part, only roughly sketched, unpolished, and incomplete: namely, that he wrote only for himself, not for us. For just as he possessed a swift genius for thinking, so too did he have a rapid hand in writing. Although he had previously drawn very beautiful letterforms, it happened that through the habit of excessive speed in composing, he was scarcely able to read what he himself had scribbled. He was accustomed to writing here and there, sometimes obliterating old notes with new ones; for that reason, he left behind some things that were worn out or erased, others that were merely jotted down in fragments. In short, everything was so confused and disordered that it might be thought of as a "forest" or a jumble of scraps <note>original: "sylvae aut farragines"</note>. From the seven-part book which he had titled *Against the Enemies of the Church*, that part which specifically attacks the divining astrologers and casters of horoscopes <term>genethliacos</term> was brought from the "anvil to the file" <note>A metaphor for moving from a rough draft to a polished final version.</note>. We have retrieved this work—not without great labor or moderate care—from a manuscript that was blotted and almost torn apart. In this work, he demonstrates himself to be a supreme philosopher, a supreme theologian, a supreme orator, and a most fierce defender of Christ's Church, endowed with the incomparable genius seen in all his commentaries. I also found among his papers some minor things not yet polished: an interpretation of the Lord's Prayer, and about fifty rules for living well—though these were far too brief and unexplained, which he surely would have expanded into many chapters had he lived. He also composed two "Deprecatory Prayers" to God, one in Tuscan rhythms <note>Written in Italian vernacular.</note> and the other in elegiac meter, with which he could soothe his mind with the song of the lyre when he was exhausted by heavier studies. Indeed, in the first years of his youth, he had so cultivated every kind of musical art that the melodies he devised and the harmonies he noted with their proper arrangements were considered famous. We also saw many other things in his chests, though disordered; from these, however, I believe something useful could be compiled, especially an explanation of the Psalms. But also about fifty letters published at various times—some personal, some doctrinal, some encouraging—emerged along with the *Oration* <note>The famous "Oration on the Dignity of Man."</note> which he would have delivered in Rome if the debate had taken place. This work does not merely smell of the most perceptive genius and abundant learning of a young man not yet twenty-four (as all his writings do), but it offers us the richest testimony of his most fertile eloquence. He used a style that is truly to be praised: always natural and noble rather than borrowed, and multiform according to the variety of the subjects. Although he may have exhausted "all of Isocrates’ box of perfumes" <note>A reference to the highly ornate and "sweet" rhetorical style of the Greek orator Isocrates.</note> (as they say), he nevertheless preserved the ornaments of purity and the decorum of majesty. Indeed, those celebrated styles of speaking—three of which Gellius describes and four of which Macrobius <note>Aulus Gellius and Macrobius were Roman authors who categorized different styles of rhetoric (e.g., the robust, the flowery, the plain).</note> details—can be gathered from his commentaries without effort. There is the copious style in which Cicero is said to rule; the brief style ascribed to Sallust; the dry style given to Fronto; and the rich and florid style in which Pliny and Symmachus were said to revel. Yet perhaps an orator with right judgment would easily find that this "copiousness" would not have been called "spineless" by Brutus, nor would Sallust have called it "immoderate." The dryness of Fronto is moistened, the brevity of Sallust is extended, and the florid richness of Pliny is carried into a wider field. Add to these the "milky fountain" of Livy—perhaps without his "Patavinity" <note>original: "Patavinitate." A famous ancient joke by Asinius Pollio, who claimed he could hear a "Paduan" (Patavium) regional accent in Livy's sophisticated Latin.</note>—with many little flowers of Apuleius added. But he did not exercise himself here in "borrowed" Greek philosophy, nor in "Attic Nights," nor in fictional "Saturnalia" <note>References to the titles of works by Gellius and Macrobius, implying Pico focused on substance over literary imitation.</note> manufactured to praise Virgil's *Aeneid*; he did not labor in Roman history, nor in mere history devoid of the deepest and most difficult speculations of nature. Rather, he sweated over the wonderful fabric of the world, in attacking the enemies of the holy Catholic Church, and was exhausted in eliminating the astrologers. He labored in examining theological questions and in the harmony of Aristotle and Plato; he brooded over the explanation of sacred speech; and he devoted his effort to warning and encouraging his friends. Indeed, he was so far from affecting this eloquence we speak of that he instead condemned those who, scrupulously seeking out "painted allurements," devoted all the strength of their genius to tracking down the origins of words. All of these things turned many people more readily toward admiration of him, because among those...

It highlights his rapid writing style, his defense of the Church against astrologers, and his rejection of shallow rhetorical imitation in favor of profound truth.</summary>

-># THE LIFE OF JOHN PICO<-

...letters for a long time and most diligently, even though they did not profess to decorate Latin literature with the **flowers of eloquence**. Let those who love antiquity too much endure this with a calm mind, for although these things are said concisely and briefly, they are perhaps all the more true because men more learned than I—such as Hermolao Barbaro, Battista the Carmelite <note>Original: "Baptista Carmelita," referring to the poet Battista Spagnoli of Mantua.</note>, Marsilio Ficino, Matteo Bosso, and many other most learned and eloquent men—have recorded them. He read through and excerpted from vast libraries of both Latin and Greek authors with incredible speed, and he never passed over any commentaries (if the opportunity was given) without reading them. He had acquired such a great knowledge of the ancient doctors of the Church that it is difficult to believe, even in one who had consumed his entire life solely in turning their pages. Regarding the more recent theologians who used that style commonly called **Parisian** <note>The "Parisian style" refers to the Scholastic method of rigorous, technical logic and questioning used at the University of Paris, often criticized by Renaissance humanists for its lack of elegance.</note>, so much judgment resided in him that if someone unexpectedly asked him to unravel an abstruse and poorly explained question from any of them, he opened it up with such fertility of mind and reported it with such skill that you would say he had all the sayings of that doctor before his eyes and ready at hand. He recognized all the "families" <note>The various "schools" of Scholastic thought, such as the Thomists, Scotists, and Albertists.</note> in the same way and had examined every notebook; yet you should not believe him so addicted to any one of them (as is the custom of our people) that he looked down on the others. For he was so instructed and so minded from his tender years that he sought the **truth** in them, and he venerated all of them with equal honor until that truth shone forth once found, stripped of any private affection.

What he felt about individuals who are generally considered more famous can be seen in the preface to his *Apology*, when he reported the properties and peculiar praises of the "barbarian," <note>In this context, "barbarian" refers to the medieval Scholastic philosophers whose Latin did not meet classical standards.</note> Greek, and Latin philosophers. However, whenever mention was made of those philosophers or theologians who wrote by debating in the French manner, he was accustomed to praise **Thomas Aquinas** above all others, as one resting on a more solid foundation of truth than the rest; he also calls him "the splendor of our theology" in his *Heptaplus* <note>Pico’s work on the seven days of creation.</note>. Having been asked about this very frequently, even by me, he gave the same answer. Nor should anyone be persuaded to the contrary by certain things contained in his *Apologetic* work which are to be disputed—otherwise being openly opposed to the opinions of Thomas—since he was then a very young man, eager for glory, and in that most celebrated city <note>Rome, where Pico famously proposed his 900 theses.</note> was hunting for fame by defending any side whatsoever in the manner of **Gorgias of Leontini** <note>A Greek Sophist famous for claiming he could speak on any subject.</note>. Furthermore, out of ten thousand propositions, the fact that he does not agree with—and even opposes—only three or four does not prove the contrary.

Moreover, he was most skilled in debating, and he bestowed frequent and most expensive labor upon literary "agonies" <note>Intellectual contests or formal debates.</note> while his mind was fervent. When he was the one raising objections, you could perceive the sharpness and vigilance of **Scotus**, the acrimony of **Francis** <note>Likely the Franciscan Francis of Mayrone.</note>, and the abundance and multitude of **Aureoli** <note>Petrus Aureoli, a 14th-century philosopher.</note>; nor were those "knots" missing, complicated by many turnings, supported not so much by tickling witticisms as by gravity. When he was the one responding, you would have seen the strength and power of **Thomas** and the breadth of **Albert**.

But he had long ago sent a "notice of divorce" <note>A metaphorical way of saying he had renounced or quit these activities.</note> to these conflicts, and day by day he hated that duty more and more. He declined it to such an extent that when **Ercole d'Este**, Duke of Ferrara, requested most earnestly through intermediaries and in person that he should not be reluctant to debate while the General Synod of the Friars Preachers <note>The Dominicans.</note> was being held in Ferrara, he long resisted obeying. However, with many entreaties, yielding to that prince whose love for him was no small thing, he complied. From this, it was debated whether he appeared more skillful or more eloquent, more learned or more refined. From the mouth of the debater, there always appeared such an alacrity of mind that he seemed to be arguing about a pleasant and peaceful matter rather than one that was slightly bitter and difficult; for this reason, the listeners who hung on his words were moved to a wonderful love for him. 

But a frequent adage of his was: **"That is the task of a dialectician, not a philosopher."** He also said that those disputations were beneficial which were practiced with a peaceful mind to track down and search for the truth in private places, with witnesses removed; but that those were most harmful which were done in public to show off learning or to catch the "breeze of the common people" and the applause of the unskilled. He judged it almost impossible for the desire for honor—by which those "forehead-striking" <note>Aggressive or theatrical debaters.</note> disputants are agitated—not to be linked by an inseparable bond to the desire for the infamy and confusion of the one with whom one disputes: a lethal wound to the soul and a deadly poison to charity. 

Nothing at all was hidden from him regarding the "little traps" and quibbles of the sophists and the **Suissetic trifles** <note>original: "suisseticas quisquilias," referring to the complex logical "Calculations" of Richard Swineshead, known as "The Calculator."</note> which are called "Calculations." These are mathematical commentaries applied to natural considerations with inventions that are, if I may say so, more morose than subtle. But even if he was learned in them and had read writings of that kind—which perhaps Italy does not know in full (for no path of literature could be found so trackless and inaccessible that it had not been abundantly explored by his step)—he nevertheless seemed to hate and detest them. In my judgment, he noticed that their common use served to prepare the infamy of companions and to undermine memory in replication, but contributed nothing or very little to finding the truth, to which he thought untiring labor should be devoted. 

But lest I follow this further and detain the reader, I will conclude briefly. One man has shone in eloquence but was dishonored by ignorance of the secrets of nature; another knew foreign languages but was not skilled in the universal decrees of the philosophers; another read the discoveries of the ancients but did not compose new doctrines; by another, the sciences of both divine and human things were sought only for the sake of men and human glory, not for the benefit of the Christian Republic. **But he indeed had embraced all these things with equal study**, so that they seemed to have flowed into him in troops and heaps. He was not like many who, not excelling in any one "wine," have a share of all; rather, he had progressed so far in all sciences that whichever of them you considered in him, you would think he had devoted himself to it alone.

<summary>This page describes Pico della Mirandola's vast intellectual range, his particular debt to Scholasticism and Thomas Aquinas despite his humanist leanings, and his growing conviction that private study of truth is superior to the vanity of public debate.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the biography of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, written by his nephew Gianfrancesco. Having established Pico’s mastery of Scholastic and ancient philosophy, the narrative now shifts to his personal character, his legendary memory, and his eventual renunciation of worldly wealth and titles in favor of a life of devotion.</meta>

## THE LIFE OF PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA.

...you would have judged that he had chosen a path entirely his own and peculiar to himself. These achievements were all the more wonderful because he attained them through the power of his own genius and a love for truth, almost without the help of a teacher. Indeed, we might say of him what Epicurus said of himself: **"That he had indeed been his own teacher."** <note>original: "Se sibi ipsum scilicet fuisse magistrum." Epicurus was famous for claiming to be self-taught (autodidaktos).</note> To produce such miraculous results in so short a space of time, I have found that five causes converged: an incredible natural talent, a most tenacious memory, ample wealth—which aided him in buying books in the Latin, Greek, and <term>barbarian</term> <note>In this context, "barbarian" refers to non-Classical languages, specifically Hebrew, Aramaic (Chaldean), and Arabic.</note> tongues (I recall from memory that he told me he had spent seven thousand gold coins up to that day in acquiring volumes of every kind of literature), a constant and tireless devotion to study, and finally, his contemplation of earthly matters. If that ancient age of the <term>Laconians</term> <note>The Spartans, known for their discipline and brief, pithy speech.</note> had produced him, he would have been called—if we believe Aristotle—a **divine man**.

But now it seems I must leave behind the virtues of his intellect and proceed to those excellent parts of his soul that concern his actions. His most upright character must be brought into the public view, so that his soul, set aflame for God, may be known; so that his wealth, bestowed upon the needy, may be praised; and so that those who have finally devoted themselves to the divine law may find an occasion to give the most abundant thanks to the Author of all good things. 

Three years before he died, in order to live in deep peace and put aside the cares of ruling—unconcerned with where the scepter of power might fall—he handed over all his ancestral lands which he possessed in Mirandola and Concordia (that is, a third part of them) to me, though I know not whether it was more a gift or a sale. This act was later confirmed by the Cæsarean generosity of **Maximilian Augustus** <note>Holy Roman Emperor Maximilian I.</note>, who is our king and immediate lord—for we have recognized no other for as many centuries as Mirandola and Concordia have stood, save for whoever sits successively upon the royal or imperial throne of the Romans. Whatever money he received from this transaction he partly distributed to the poor and partly spent on buying lands to support himself and his household. Specifically, he had acquired the estate of **Corbulas** in the territory of Ferrara for many thousands of gold coins. Likewise, he distributed many silver vessels and pieces of precious furniture for the use of the poor. He was content with a modest table, though it still retained something of his former elegance regarding the service and the silver. 

Every day at the appointed hours, he poured out prayers to God. He always gave money to the poor whenever he encountered them; and not content with that, he commissioned **Girolamo Benivieni** <note>A Florentine poet and close friend of Pico who became a follower of the radical preacher Savonarola.</note>, a Florentine citizen and man of letters—whom he loved dearly for his great charity and integrity of character—to use Pico's own money to constantly succor the needy and provide dowries for young women to be married. Pico instructed Benivieni to report back as soon as the money was spent so he could replenish it immediately. He delegated this duty so that he might more easily relieve the calamities and miseries of poor citizens through a faithful intermediary, which otherwise might have remained hidden from him.

He also frequently gave—and I think this should not be passed over in silence—alms from his own body. We know many people (to use the words of Jerome) who stretch out a hand to the needy but are overcome by the pleasures and allurements of the flesh. But Pico, especially on those days which represent the suffering and death of Christ for the sake of our salvation, would beat his own flesh in memory of that supreme benefit and in atonement for sins. With my own eyes (let all things return to the glory of God), I often saw the whip. 

His face was always cheerful and calm, and his nature was so mild that he testified—even while many were listening—that he had never felt himself to be disturbed. I recall him saying in conversation that he believed no event (even if things went most poorly) could move him to anger, unless perhaps he were to lose certain cabinets where his late-night labors and vigils <note>A reference to his intensive research and writing sessions often held at night.</note> were stored. But when he reflected that he labored for the Best and Greatest God and His Church, and that he had dedicated all his works, studies, and actions to them—and that this loss could not happen except by God’s command or permission—he felt confident that he would not be saddened. 

O happy mind, which could no longer be depressed by any adversity, nor (as will become clear) puffed up by any success! Certainly, his mastery of universal philosophy did not make him arrogant, nor did his knowledge of the Hebrew, Chaldean, and Arabic languages beyond Latin and Greek. Neither his great wealth, the nobility of his birth, nor the beauty and elegance of his body could draw him back into that soft and wide path of the many who live in sin. What, then, could be so admirable that it could pervert his mind? What, I ask, could be above a man who (to use the words of Seneca) was **above Fortune**? Whether she was swollen with favorable winds or humbled by adverse ones, he eventually despised her, so that his mind was joined to Christ and the citizens of the heavenly fatherland with a "spiritual glue." 

This is clearly perceived by this argument: while he saw many in our time (alas!) bidding and haggling for the offices and dignities of the Church—seeking, demanding, sighing for, and most strenuously buying them—he himself rejected these honors when they were offered by two kings through intermediaries. Most grave witnesses are present; I myself am a witness. He replied that he did not wish to be initiated into holy orders and turned them down. Another person promised he would give Pico secular dignities and large revenues if he would visit his king; seeing that no corner was left for him to hide in and all excuses were taken away, Pico gave him this response: so that the man would understand he did not seek dignities or riches, but rather had neglected them so that he might have leisure for God and his studies. At Ferrara, when certain friends and **Pandolfo Collenuccio of Pesaro** <note>A famous jurist, historian, and humanist.</note>—a man of sharp wit and wide reading with whom he was very close—had urged him to pursue the dignity of a Cardinal by whatever means...
