-># JOHN PICO#<-

<meta>catchword: perfect</meta>

...should be accepted, or certainly, if the Pope should offer it (as many thought would happen), it should be embraced. Pandulphus <note>Pandolfo Collenuccio, a scholar and diplomat who was a friend of Pico.</note> had tentatively explored this, as he was well aware that Pico preferred anything over being entangled in such honors. Pico himself, with his characteristic greatness of soul, immediately ordered a response by letter, citing the prophet:

> **"My thoughts are not your thoughts."** <note>original: "Non sunt cogitationes meæ cogitationes uestræ." A reference to Isaiah 55:8.</note>

He perhaps considered that regarding the goods of the Church—the greatest part of which is owed to the poor by hereditary right—it was not fitting to maintain magnificent displays. He kept before his eyes the examples of the holiest men, such as **Ambrose**, **Augustine**, and **Martin**, and others who fled the dignity of the Bishopric when it was offered and long refused that duty before undertaking it. Furthermore, he had read that the most holy **Celestine** <note>Pope Celestine V, who famously abdicated the papacy in 1294.</note> had abdicated not only from the Cardinalate itself but from the supreme power of the high papacy, shaking that burden from the shoulders of the entire Christian commonwealth. (A burden indeed, for while a great reward is prepared for those who undertake it, it should be embraced only by those who are unwilling and do so only for the sake of obedience and helping others).

This philosopher was fully persuaded that praise did not come from accumulating riches or seeking honors, but from refusing them. By rejecting shadowy glory, he sought to attain the true glory that always accompanies virtue like an inseparable companion and follower. He held human glory as almost nothing, often saying that fame benefits the living somewhat, but the dead not at all. We recognize that he valued his own learning only insofar as it served the utility of the Church and the elimination and exploding of contrary errors.

Indeed, we perceive that he reached such a goal of perfection that he cared little if his commentaries were published under his own name, provided that they brought the same benefit to humanity as they would have under the name of Pico. In his later years, he decided to be moved by no other books more than the **Old and New Testaments**, intending to spend the remainder of his life constantly poring over them. He would have done so, had not public utility spurred him on, seeing so many great things he had conceived and was laboring to produce—works that were not only requested by everyone but demanded even before they were mature. He valued the smallest spark of devotion toward God from a simple person or an old woman more than all his own knowledge of human and divine things.

In conversation, he very often warned his close friends to notice how much mortal things labor and falter; how frail and fleeting is this life we live, and how firm and stable is that which we shall be—whether we are thrust down to the depths or raised to the heavens. He urged them to turn and incite their minds to loving God, a work that outweighed any knowledge we could possess in this life. He followed this up most clearly in his book *On Being and the One*, where, turning in the midst of the argument to **Angelo Poliziano** <note>A famous Renaissance humanist and close friend of Pico.</note> (to whom he dedicated the book), he spoke these words:

> "But look, my Angelo, what madness holds us: while we are in the body, we can love God more than we can either speak of or know Him. By loving Him, we benefit ourselves more, labor less, and obey Him more. Yet we always prefer, through knowledge, never to find what we seek, rather than to possess through love that which, without love, would be found in vain."

That saying of **Saint Francis** was also frequently on his lips:

> **"A man knows only as much as he acts."** <note>original: "Tantum scit homo quantum operatur." A core Franciscan principle emphasizing that true knowledge is lived, not just intellectual.</note>

In his liberality alone did he exceed moderation. He was so far from applying any care to earthly matters that he was even stained by the blemish of negligence. We find he was often warned by friends not to despise riches entirely. They asserted that it brought him shame because it was widely rumored—whether true or false—that he provided his stewards with the opportunity for theft. Nevertheless, that mind, which was always fixed on contemplating and searching out the designs of all nature, could not easily lower itself to weigh these lowest and most abject things.

I remember when I was with him in **Ferrara**, a steward presented a small page seeking approval for expenses. Upon seeing this, Pico was struck with wonder and asked if the man expected him to apply his mind to something he had neglected in times past. His companion replied that he had not only requested but demanded that Pico undertake this duty, as he used to do out of habit. Yet Pico showed only as much care as he had before. Furthermore, when his primary steward interrupted him to ask for an audit of the money he had handled for many years—so that his own mind might be at ease—and brought the account books before him, we heard Pico reply with these words:

"I know that I could have been cheated by you very often, and still could be; therefore, there is no need for a discharge of these expenses. If I owe you, I will pay the money as soon as possible; if you owe me, pay it back now if you can, or in the future if you currently lack the means."

He always treated his friends with great indulgence, using encouraging words to lead them toward living well. I knew a man who, relying on Pico's learning and fame, spoke with him; when the conversation turned to morals, he was so moved by just two of Pico's words that he deserted the path of vice and reformed his character. The words were these: **"If we kept the death of Christ, suffered for love of us, before our eyes, we would likewise beware of our own end by contemplating it."** He showed an admirable modesty and kindness toward those who had won him over—not by their power or fortune, but by their character and learning. He was accustomed to love those who possessed even the smallest mastery of letters, or at least a sharp and industrious devotion to the liberal arts. For similarity is the cause of love; and toward a wise man, as **Apollonius** says in **Philostratus** <note>Referring to the *Life of Apollonius of Tyana* by the Greek writer Philostratus.</note>, there is a certain affinity. Knowledge also perfects a man, in that he is a man...

It also highlights his extreme financial negligence and generosity, viewing worldly wealth as a distraction from spiritual and philosophical contemplation.</summary>

-># THE LIFE OF MIRANDOLA#<-
<meta>catchword: most</meta>

# THE LIFE OF MIRANDOLA.

...attaining perfect goodness and being loved above other upright men is beyond doubt. Furthermore, nothing was more intolerable to him than (to use the words of *Horace*) "the proud thresholds of more powerful citizens," <note>original: "superba ciuium potentiorum limina." A reference to Horace’s Epodes, expressing a distaste for the anxieties of political life.</note> as well as the military service of this world and the bond of marriage. When asked in jest which burden would seem lighter to him—either military service or marriage—if he were forced by necessity or given a choice, he hesitated a little, nodding his head with a slight smile: "Marriage," he replied, for it did not have as much servitude or danger as the military. He loved liberty beyond measure, a trait suggested both by his natural temperament and his philosophical studies. For this reason, I believe he was mostly a wanderer and never chose a permanent home for himself, although he stayed often in *Florence* and sometimes in *Ferrara*. 

I believe he made the latter city a kind of home because it was there, after Bologna, that he first cultivated his literary studies, and its prince loved him wonderfully—being joined to him by a kind of kinship, since I myself was born from the prince's sister, *Bianca Maria d’Este*. <note>The author, Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola, notes his own lineage here; his mother was the sister of Ercole I d’Este, Duke of Ferrara.</note> Moreover, it was not too far from his homeland, as Ferrara is only thirty miles east of Mirandola. He loved and inhabited the other city, Florence, either for the pleasantness of the air, the sweetness of his many friends, or the refinement of the intellects there. Among these, he bound two to himself with a most particular literary love: *Angelo Poliziano*, <note>A renowned poet and classical scholar.</note> a man most learned in Greek and Latin and full of the flowers of various literatures, almost the protector of the Roman tongue; and the other, *Marsilio Ficino of Florence*, a man smelling of every kind of literature, but the greatest Platonist among those now living, whose efforts Pico used in claiming the works of the Academy <note>The Platonic Academy of Florence.</note> for himself.

He was not very fond of outward religious ceremony—we are not speaking of those things which the Church commands to be observed (for we saw him keep these before his eyes), but rather of those rituals which some people pursue and promote while neglecting the true worship of God, which must be "in spirit and in truth." <note>A reference to John 4:24.</note> Instead, he followed God with the most fervent internal affection. Sometimes that eagerness of soul would almost fade and fall away, only to take up strength again with even greater effort. I remember him burning with such love for God that when we were walking in a certain orchard in *Ferrara*, talking about the love of Christ along the long paths, he broke out into these words: 

"I tell you this, keep it hidden in your secret heart. <note>original: "Tibi hæc dixerim, in arcanis recondito."</note> Once I have finished and perfected certain scholarly works, I will give away the riches that remain to me to the poor; and, protected by the Crucifix, with bare and naked feet, wandering the world through castles and cities, I will preach Christ." 

I heard later that he changed this plan and decided to devote himself to the <term>Order of Preachers</term> <note>The Dominicans, known for their focus on preaching and scholarship.</note>; meanwhile, he hurried the publication of the works he had begun and started. 

But in the year of our redemption 1494, while he was completing his thirty-second year of age and staying in *Florence*, he was seized by a most treacherous fever. It raged so fiercely in his fluids and internal organs that it mocked every kind of medicine applied, forcing him to satisfy the debt of nature within thirteen days. But how he behaved in his illness—though I was far from him at that time—I shall not hesitate to relate what I received from the most reliable witnesses who were present. 

Such as this: when, after receiving the sacrament of the Eucharist, the image of Christ Crucified was offered to him so that he might take full draughts of love from the memory of that ineffable grace of our passion and salvation before he breathed out his soul—a most powerful defense against any adversity and a most strong bulwark against wicked demons—the elder priest soon asked him whether he firmly believed that this was the true image of the true God and true man. He asked if he believed that as God, He was begotten before time and the ages by God the Father Himself, to whom He is equal in all things; and that by the Holy Spirit, who is also God, and from the Father—which three are one—He was conceived in time, co-eternally remaining in the womb of Mary ever-virgin. He asked if he believed He had suffered hunger, thirst, labors, heat, and sleepless nights; and finally, to wash away our filth contracted from the seed of Adam and to unbar the gate of heaven, out of the greatest charity with which He embraced the human race, He had shed His most precious blood both spontaneously and most willingly on the altar of the cross. 

When these and other things of that kind were recited, Pico responded that he not only believed them but was certain of them. And likewise this: when *Alberto Pio*, <note>Pico’s nephew and a prominent prince and scholar.</note> his sister’s son—whom we mentioned at the beginning of this life as a young man conspicuous for his talent, study of the fine arts, and character—tried to make the approach of death more peaceful, Pico spoke to him. Just as Alexander of Aphrodisias and Themistius <note>Ancient commentators on Aristotle.</note> declared in their prefaces that strength against the fear of death is drawn from the contemplation of nature—an opinion later seized upon by *Averroes*—Pico replied that his mind was not set at peace merely by that reasoning, nor was it laid down without the pangs of death. Rather, he was comforted most by this: that an end was now being put to his offenses against his God, for he did not consider the brief time of his life to be enough to satisfy for his frequent offenses against God. 

And furthermore, it is known from several most proven witnesses of the college of the <term>Order of Preachers</term> and from *Alberto* himself, cited just before, that he revealed how the Queen of Heaven <note>The Virgin Mary.</note> came to him at night, smelling of a miraculous fragrance, and refreshed all his limbs crushed and contracted by that fever, promising that he would not yield entirely to death. He was found lying in his bed while ill with a cheerful and peaceful face, and even amidst the stings of death which he endured, he used to speak as if he saw the heavens opened to him, greeting all those who came to him and offered their help with the most charming...

-># IOANNIS PICI [OF GIOVANNI PICO]#<-

...accepted and embraced them with the most <note>The text begins mid-sentence, describing Pico's final interactions with his household.</note> kind speech. We have been informed that he also asked forgiveness from all his servants, if he had perhaps been troublesome to any of them. He had provided in a will made the previous year that some should be given food and clothing for as long as they lived, and others money according to their merits. He appointed the poor of the Florentine <term>xenodocheum<note>A charitable institution, specifically a hospital or hostel for the poor and sick; here referring to the Hospital of Santa Maria Nuova.</note></term> as heirs to those things which could not be moved; but for his movable goods, he named his brother Antonio Maria. 

How much grief his death caused the lowest and highest ranks of people is witnessed by the princes of Italy, its cities, and its peoples; witnessed by those kings we cited above; witnessed again by the kindness and grace of *Charles*, King of the *Gauls* [France], which should not be passed over in silence. When it was announced to him, as he was arriving in *Florence* to head for *Rome* and conquer the Kingdom of *Naples*, that Pico was suffering from a grave illness, he immediately sent two of his own physicians—who were still serving as ambassadors—to visit and help him. He also gave letters which we have seen and read, written in his own hand, full of humanity and those promises which both the benevolent mind of a magnanimous king and the noble virtues of the sick man demanded. For he was very well known to him by reputation and joined by a certain familiarity; for he had been honorably received by the King in France while visiting *Paris*. 

Indeed, He who made him an object of wonder to the whole world and to many ages while he lived, decreed that his death should be celebrated as no less famous and unprecedented. Therefore, I think those things should be related here which I heard with my own ears while I was in *Florence*—whither I had gone upon hearing of his illness, though not in time—at the sacred church called *Santa Reparata* <note>The old name for the Cathedral of Florence, the Duomo.</note>, listening to *Girolamo Savonarola* of *Ferrara*, of the *Order of Preachers* [Dominicans], a man most learned in theology, most distinguished, and most famous for his holiness, as he delivered sacred sermons to the Florentine people. 

But first, I intend to warn those ignorant of sacred letters, in the words of *Apuleius*, lest with "thick ears" and an obstinate heart they think those things are lies which seem new to the ear, or crude to the sight, or certainly difficult beyond the reach of thought; which, if they explored them a little more deeply, they would find not only evident in fact but also very easy to accomplish. 

He, therefore, declaiming from the pulpit, made known to all present what I am about to say. 

"A secret must be revealed to you, O *Florence*," <margin>.</margin> "which is as true as that proverb frequent among you, 'the Gospel of John.' <note>original: "Ioannis euangelium." A Florentine idiom used to denote an absolute, undeniable truth.</note> I would have remained silent, indeed, but I am compelled to speak, and He who can command me has ordered me to make these things public. I think none of you did not know *Giovanni Pico della Mirandola*; he was heaped with great benefits and great graces from God, and endowed with multifaceted learning; perhaps no mortal has possessed such a famous genius. The Church suffered a great loss in him. I would think, if his lifespan had been extended longer, he would have excelled all who died in the eight hundred years before him because of the monuments of writing he would have left behind. He used to converse with me and reveal secrets, from which I knew he was summoned by God to a religious life through internal voices. Desiring to comply with these inspirations, he had proposed more than once to obey. But, ungrateful for divine benefits, or called away by his senses, he shrank from the labors—for he was of a delicate temperament—or perhaps thinking that religion needed his work, he delayed the time. However, let me say this not as a certainty, but as something conjectured and presumed by me; on account of this, I threatened him for two years with a scourge if he should neglectfully perform the work God had proposed for him to accomplish. 

I confess I asked God repeatedly that, being struck a little, he might finally take up the path shown to him from on high. I did not seek this by which he was struck down [death]; I had not thought this. But it was decreed by God that he should leave this path, and lose part of the noble crown prepared for him in heaven, and not fully attain the fame and celebrity of name which he would have had to the highest degree if he had lived. But the most kind Judge behaved most mercifully toward him; and because of his alms, bestowed with a large and most lavish hand on the poor, and the prayers poured out most insistently to God, it has been brought about that neither does his soul yet exult in the bosom of the Father above the heavens, nor, being consigned to the depths, is it tortured by perpetual torments, but being committed for a time to the fire of **Purgatory** it pays temporary penalties. I would most gladly say this here: so that those who knew him, and especially those who were heaped with his benefits, might help him with their prayers." 

The man of God asserted these and many other things with a clear voice. He added that it was not hidden from him that preachers of the Word of God become worthy of eternal punishment if lies of this sort are mixed in. He also added that for some days these things had been known to him in general, but because of the words which the sick man had affirmed the *Virgin* had said, he had stood wavering and feared for a long time that he [Pico] had been deceived by the work of demons, since the *Virgin's* promise was frustrated by his death. Nevertheless, it became known to him that the deceased had been deceived by an <term>equivocation of death<note>Pico believed the Virgin promised he would not die (physical death), but Savonarola explains she meant he would be saved from the "second death" (eternal damnation).</note></term>, since she had spoken of the second and eternal death, but he had believed it was the first and temporary one. 

But if anyone should say this man either lied out of hypocrisy, or was mocked by a fantasy, or circumvented by the tricks of demons, he must—unless he thinks poorly of the faith or is of a disturbed mind—confess that God has revealed and can reveal in many ways to the living the happiness and misery of those who have poured out their souls. And in that same space of time, He makes those to whom these things are made public certain that they are not being mocked by visions or ghosts, but that the things they perceive and see with mind or eyes are true. Indeed, a man of such learning and authority, of such probity and prudence... whose [referring to Pico's works] short theorems on the philosophy of *Aristotle*, public warnings...

# THE LIFE OF GIOVANNI PICO

...of the state, the most famous interpretations of sacred speech, and predictions of future events—which almost all of Italy knows happened exactly—as well as his most holy way of life, have long provided the most proven evidence. No one but a malicious person would deny that in the principal temple of so celebrated a city, these things were pronounced to be held as true and unshakable to thousands of people to whom the truth was not yet known. Add to this that while I was inquiring somewhat into this business, I heard that a man who had been present at the sermon approached the preacher. To give more strength to what the preacher had published, the man reported that the deceased had appeared to him surrounded by fire and confessed that he was still paying the penalty for his ingratitude. <note>This refers to a famous sermon by Girolamo Savonarola, who claimed Pico was in Purgatory for delaying his entry into the Dominican Order.</note>

Moreover, a certain nun, famous for many noble prophecies—who had predicted many future things to Pico himself while he was alive which happened precisely—offered this one thing among others two years before he departed from this life: that at the time of the **lilies**, through the work and encouragement of Brother **Girolamo** (whom we mentioned), he would devote himself to the college of the Preaching Brothers <note>The Dominicans</note>. And at that same time, a certain Florentine family (which they call the **Pazzi**), then in exile, would return to their fatherland. 

Many who had heard this report wondered at this naming of "lilies," thinking she spoke of the springtime when lilies bloom. But it was discovered that this "lily" was the **King of the French** <note>Charles VIII, whose coat of arms featured the fleur-de-lis</note>, who uses such insignia. On the day before Pico took his religious vows—for he had so vowed before he died—and four days after that exiled family betook themselves to their home city, the King entered **Florence** with a great retinue, making his way through **Tuscany** to claim the Kingdom of **Naples** by force and arms. 

But before I finish, I think it not useless to say a few small things at the end of this work. For I seem to see "mastiffs barking at the shadow of the moon" at these revelations—men to whom a little bone must still be thrown (since they were perhaps not satisfied with the previous ones) lest they beat the air with useless barking. I see also that laughter is forced from the foolish. I see those who think themselves clever making light of this, who will perhaps contend that souls should not be tormented by fire because they did not disregard the healthy inspiration to enter religion, and that in our time no men are found inspired by the divine spirit who enjoy conversations with Christ. 

But if they considered that sins worthy not of death but of forgiveness are punished by <term>purgatory fire<note>The concept of Purgatory as a place of temporary purification for souls who died in a state of grace but still required penance.</note></term>, they would not wonder that even the just pay penalties. Also, if they were not ignorant that the servant who knows his master's will and does not fulfill it will be beaten many times (as the Truth <note>Referring to Christ in the Gospels</note> testifies), they would not think it unlikely that this man, who knew God's will and delayed fulfilling it, should suffer punishment even if he were free from every other guilt. On the other hand, I cannot sufficiently wonder at the crude and tasteless cunning of those who, while believing Christ died for men, do not believe he can easily speak to those same men. 

They also argue that mortals cannot become participants in the inspirations of the Virgin Mother, the angels, or the spirits of blessed men. It should truly be noticed by them that all lower things are governed by higher ones, as witnessed by **Dionysius the Areopagite** in his book *On the Celestial Hierarchy*. Separate minds of a lower grade and nature, to whom the care of men is entrusted, are illuminated by higher minds, which in turn draw divine mysteries either from the highest minds or from God himself. Men inspired by the divine spirit receive these same revelations when it is expedient to reveal them to the multitude of men. This is the sacred law of divinity: as we are taught by the same Dionysius in the book of the *Celestial Hierarchy*, that through the first things the following ones are raised to the most majestic light. 

They are undoubtedly ignorant of divine scripture and of an insolent and stubborn nature. For in those scriptures, one can see that divine future mysteries are revealed not only through good men, but sometimes through wicked men and false prophets. What prevents having faith in this man [Pico], who is so powerful in learning and so many virtues, and has already predicted many future things that have now occurred? And he testified to this not sleepily, but affirming it assertively. Add that the philosophy of **Aristotle** does not cry out against these things, and the **Platonic** views support them, though I have not accepted anything as a grave testimony unless it has the authority of divine scripture; but it is not absurd to cite these external things occasionally, so that the arrows of the malicious return upon the authors with greater force than they came. 

But we must now return to ourselves. We should not mourn so much that we have lost such a man, as give thanks to the King for whom all things live that we had him and still have him. Indeed, having completed the gift of mortal life, and having lived long with the inhabitants of **Kedar** <note>A biblical metaphor for living in a worldly or dark place of exile.</note>, whom he drenched with no small light, he is now entering the inaccessible and infinite light of the heavenly fatherland. 

->In his ineffable divinity, he will bring help to us daily<-
->and enjoy it without end.<-

# Paolo Giovio’s Eulogy 
## of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.

**Giovanni Pico della Mirandola** was deservedly called by the nickname "the Phoenix," <note>The phoenix is a mythical bird that is unique in the world and reborn from its own ashes; Giovio uses it here to describe Pico as a peerless, once-in-a-generation genius.</note> because the gods above bestowed upon him—beyond the nobility of his family—all the rarest gifts of both body and mind. Indeed, with the wonderful depth of a refined genius, a handsome face, the most distinguished manners, and an incomparable eloquence when he debated or wrote, he easily turned all the wise men of his age into admirers of himself. 

In a most weighty work, though not yet finished, he attacked the **Astrologers** <note>This refers to Pico’s *Disputationes adversus astrologiam divinatricem*, a massive critique of "divinatory" astrology that argued the stars do not control human destiny.</note> with such great learning and force, exposing the vanity of all divination, that he seems to have deterred the professors of those subtle disciplines from writing ever again. In the *Heptaplus* <note>original: *Heptaplus*, Pico’s seven-fold explanation of the seven days of Creation in Genesis.</note>, while he reveals the mysteries of Holy Scripture to us with a divine voice, and in his *Apology* <note>original: *Apologeticus*, a text Pico wrote to defend his 900 theses after they were challenged by a papal commission.</note>, he defends the decrees of his own genius proposed for debate with the gravest reasoning of all disciplines; in these, he seems to have surpassed even himself in learning and the excellence of his memory. 

He departed from life, worthy of Heaven, a young man of thirty-three years, on a day as celebrated as it was afterwards most mournful for Italy: the day on which **Charles VIII, King of France**, entered Florence. It was as if the grief for such a great death—even though

->the army of a foreign nation, adorned under banners in a parade,<-
->entered the city, and despite that unusual spectacle and<-
->the great joy of recovered liberty—was not in the least overcome.<-

<summary>A laudatory biography of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, highlighting his "Phoenix-like" uniqueness, his refutation of astrology, and his death in 1494 during the French invasion of Florence.</summary>

<meta>This page begins the "Heptaplus," Pico della Mirandola's esoteric commentary on the first chapters of Genesis. It follows the previous page's index, transitioning from a general reference tool to the formal dedication and introduction of the work to his patron, Lorenzo de' Medici ("the Magnificent"). The catchword "magnæ" anticipates the opening of the subsequent page.</meta>

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA Mirandola’s Preface to the Heptaplus, on the Sevenfold Explanation of the Six Days of Genesis, to Lorenzo de' Medici.
## Preface.

My emulation of your studies, Lorenzo de' Medici, has moved me to examine the secret books of Moses. Last winter, I observed that in whatever leisure you were granted from the affairs of state, you devoted your efforts nowhere more greatly or more willingly than to that reading. Then, a private reason also urged me: I have long been working on another project under your auspices—one that continues to grow in your name—in which I have attempted to defend the Davidic hymns <note>The Psalms of King David.</note> translated by the **Seventy interpreters** <note>The Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> and continually sung in the Church. In that work, I seek not only to protect them from every suspicion and slander but also to illuminate them with the torches of interpretation. For that task, I found no treatment more useful, none more fruitful, and none more consistent (or to speak more truly, more necessary) than the study of those books of Moses.

It has also happened during these days that I have been diligent in studying the creation of the world, specifically those celebrated works of the six days. Great reasons suggest that we should believe the secrets of all nature are contained within them. For even if I omit the fact that our prophet <note>Moses.</note>, filled with God and under the dictation of the celestial Spirit—the master of all truth—received all these things, have not the testimonies of our own people, his own people, and finally the gentiles shown him to be most deeply learned in human wisdom and in all doctrines and literature?

There exists among the Hebrews a book by that Solomon, surnamed the Wisest, titled *Wisdom* <note>original: "Sapientia"</note>—not the one now in circulation, which is the work of Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize Greek philosophy with Torah.</note>, but another composed in Jerusalem in what they call the more secret language. In this book, that man, who is considered an interpreter of the nature of things, confesses that he received all such learning from the inner chambers of the Mosaic law. Likewise, as far as our own authors are concerned, both Luke <note>Referring to Acts 7:22: "Moses was educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians."</note> and Philo, most weighty authorities, state that he was most learned in all the lore of the Egyptians. Moreover, all those Greeks who were considered more "divine"—Pythagoras, Plato, Empedocles, and Democritus—employed Egyptians as their teachers. That saying of the philosopher Numenius is well known: "What is Plato, but an **Attic Moses**?" <note>original: "Atticum Mosem"; meaning Moses speaking the dialect of Athens.</note> But even Hermippus the Pythagorean testifies that Pythagoras transferred many things from the Mosaic law into his own philosophy. 

But if Moses, meanwhile, appears in his books to be unpolished and common, rather than a philosopher or a theologian or...

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

...appears to be the craftsman of some great wisdom. Let us recall to our minds that it was a celebrated practice of the ancient sages either not to write about divine matters at all, or to write about them in a disguised manner. This is why they were called <term>mysteries</term> <note>From the Greek 'myein', meaning to shut the eyes or mouth; secret rites only for the initiated.</note>—for they are not mysteries if they are not hidden. This practice was observed by the Indians, by the Ethiopians (who were known by the epithet of the "Naked Ones" <note>original: "de nuditate cognomen"; referring to the Gymnosophists, ancient Indian or African philosophers who lived naked and practiced asceticism.</note>), and by the Egyptians. The Sphinxes placed before their temples suggested this very thing. 

Instructed by them, Pythagoras became a master of silence; nor did he commit anything to writing except for a very few things which, as he was dying, he entrusted to his daughter Dama. For the *Golden Verses* <note>A collection of moral exhortations traditionally attributed to Pythagoras.</note> that circulate are not by Pythagoras, as the common crowd and even the more learned are persuaded, but by **Philolaus** <note>A Greek Pythagorean philosopher and contemporary of Socrates.</note>. The Pythagoreans thereafter guarded this law of secrecy most religiously. Lysis complained that it was violated by Hipparchus. Finally, **Porphyry** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and biographer of Plotinus.</note> is the authority for the fact that the disciples of Ammonius—**Origen**, **Plotinus**, and **Herennius**—were sworn to this same secrecy. 

Our **Plato** so concealed his dogmas in the wrappings of riddles, the veil of fables, mathematical images, and the obscure signs of withdrawing meanings, that he himself said in his letters that no one would openly understand his opinion on divine matters from what he wrote; and he proved it to those who were less believing. Therefore, if for this reason we think the reading of Moses is common or "worn out" <note>original: "exculcatam"; meaning something trampled or trivialized by frequent use.</note> because it has nothing on the surface that is not vulgar or crude, let us by the same example condemn all the ancient philosophers for crudeness and ignorance, whom we otherwise venerate as the masters of all wisdom. 

Indeed, we see the same thing observed in the Church: **Jesus Christ**, the "image of God’s substance," did not write the Gospel, but preached it. He preached to the crowds in parables, but privately to a few disciples—to whom it was given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven—he spoke openly and without figures. Yet he did not tell even those few everything, because they were not capable of everything, and there were many things they could not carry until the coming Spirit taught all truth. 

If the disciples of the Lord, so few and chosen from among so many thousands, could not bear many things, then the whole Israelite crowd—the tailors, cooks, butchers, shepherds, servants, and maids, to all of whom the Law was handed over to be read—could not have carried the burden of all Mosaic, or rather divine, wisdom. Moses indeed, on the height of the mountain (that same mountain where the Lord often spoke to his disciples), illuminated by the light of the divine sun, shone wonderfully in his whole face. But because the people, with their blinking and night-owl eyes, could not bear the light, he spoke his words to them with a veiled face. 

Let us return to our own writers. **Matthew** wrote the Gospel first; and just as the prophet says he "hid the words of God in his heart so that he might not sin," so Matthew followed only the history of those things pertaining to the humanity of Christ, lest the memory of these deeds be lost to oblivion. This is why, in the mystical vision of **Ezekiel**, we understand Matthew through the figure of the **Man** <note>Refers to the Tetramorph: the four living creatures representing the Evangelists. Matthew is the Man, Mark the Lion, Luke the Ox, and John the Eagle.</note>. **John**, who revealed the secrets of divinity more than all others, was forced to speak what he had long kept silent many years after the Lord’s crucifixion, in order to abolish the heresy of the **Ebionites** <note>A Jewish Christian sect that regarded Jesus as a non-divine prophet.</note>, who claimed Christ was only a man and not also...

## Preface to the Heptaplus

He [Moses] affirmed God concerning the eternal generation of the Son, but did so in few words and obscurely. From that point, John began: "In the beginning was the Word" <note>John 1:1. Pico argues that Moses hinted at the Trinity, which the Gospel of John later made explicit.</note>. Paul denies "solid food" <note>original: "solidum cibum"; referring to 1 Corinthians 3:2.</note> to the Corinthians because they still live by the laws of the flesh, not the spirit, and he speaks wisdom only among the "perfect" <note>The "perfecti" or spiritually mature.</note>. Paul's disciple, **Dionysius the Areopagite** <note>A 5th-century Christian Neoplatonist whose writings were attributed to the Dionysius mentioned in Acts 17:34.</note>, writes that it was a holy and established practice in the churches that the more secret dogmas should not be communicated through letters, but only by voice to those who were properly initiated. I have pursued these things at length because many people, judging by the "rough bark" <note>An idiom for the literal surface level of a text.</note> of the words, despise and reject the Book of Moses as if it were something common and trivial. To them, nothing is less believable than that the book possesses something more divine in its hidden recesses than what it promises on its surface. 

But if this view has been sufficiently refuted, then it is easy to believe that wherever he [Moses] treats the nature or the craftsmanship of the entire world—that is, if in any part of his work he has buried treasures of all true philosophy, as if in a field—he has done so especially in this part [Genesis] where he philosophizes most deeply about how all things flow from God, and about the degree, number, and order of the parts of the world. For this reason, the ancient Hebrews made a decree (which **Jerome** <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century scholar and translator of the Vulgate.</note> also mentions) that no one should touch this account of the creation of the world unless they were of mature age.

Perhaps, therefore, I will seem to have done something worthwhile if, having lingered longer with more exact and laborious care—as far as my own weakness allowed—I have searched for the true understanding of the Mosaic text. When I saw that many Latins and Greeks had labored over its explanation, and that besides them there were almost innumerable Chaldean and Hebrew interpreters, both ancient and modern, I did not even dare to think of writing or commenting anything new on this matter. However, I remembered the caution in the Mosaic law that no one should reap their field so thoroughly and entirely that they leave nothing behind. Instead, they were to leave an untouched portion for the poor and the needy, who might gather sheaves and handfuls to satisfy their hunger <note>A reference to the practice of "gleaning" commanded in Leviticus 19:9.</note>. 

When this came to mind, I began to survey the Prophet's <note>Pico frequently refers to Moses as "the Prophet."</note> vast fields with keen eyes to see if the most learned interpreters—who were as much observers of the law as its explainers—had left some part untouched for us, the weaker ones, to reap. From this, I too might pluck even a few ears of grain to be placed on the altars of the Church as the first fruits of the harvest, so that I would not be cast out from the temple's privileges as if I were not a true Israelite or a guest without a contribution <note>original: "asymbolus"; a Greek term for one who attends a banquet without paying his share.</note>. The matter succeeded as I wished—not because I am capable of anything they were not, but because they knew, by the law's command, to leave a path for the industry of those who followed. Furthermore, the vastness and fertility of that field is so great that no amount of grain could ever match it. Even though almost infinite and powerful laborers have exerted all their strength upon it, we can still say that Gospel phrase: "The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few" <note>Matthew 9:37.</note>. 

Therefore, those things which the most holy men have written on this book—**Ambrose** and **Augustine**, and likewise **Strabus**, **Bede**, and **Remigius**, and from the more recent ones **Giles** and **Albert** <note>Albert the Great (Albertus Magnus).</note>; as well as among the Greeks, **Philo**, **Origen**, **Basil**, **Theo...** <note>The text likely continues with Theodoret or Theophylact on the following page.</note>

<page-num>4</page-num>

**Theodoret**, **Apollinarius**, **Didymus**, **Diodorus**, **Severus**, **Eusebius**, **Josephus**, **Gennadius**, and **Chrysostom** <note>These are early Christian Church Fathers and historians known for their biblical commentaries.</note> have written; these we will leave entirely untouched. It would be both rash and superfluous for a weak man to exert himself in that part of the field where the most robust minds have already exercised themselves. Likewise, regarding those things which **Jonathan**, **Onkelos**, or the ancient **Simeon** <note>Reference to the authors of the *Targums*, ancient Aramaic (Chaldean) translations and paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible.</note> handed down in Aramaic, or what the Hebrews—whether the ancients like **Eleazar**, **Abba**, **John**, **Nehunia**, **Isaac**, and **Joseph**, or the more recent like **Gersonides**, **Saadia**, **Abraham**, both **Moseses**, **Solomon**, and **Manaen** <note>A list of Jewish scholars and philosophers. "Both Moseses" refers to Moses Maimonides and Moses Nahmanides; "Solomon" refers to Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki).</note>—have composed, we shall make no mention at present. 

Instead, we shall bring forth, beyond all these, seven other interpretations of our own discovery and meditation. In these, we will first take care to overcome, if we can, three difficulties with which all those who have undertaken to explain this book seem to have had a great and difficult struggle. 

**The first difficulty** is to prevent anything from appearing to have been said by **Moses** <note>Pico regards Moses as the divinely inspired author of Genesis.</note> either insufficiently or with too little learning and wisdom. Some have freed themselves from this problem by saying that he did not speak of all things, nor bring forth grand and sublime matters, because he was speaking to a "rude people" <note>original: "rudi populo"; meaning unrefined or uneducated. A common medieval argument that Moses simplified science for the ancient Israelites.</note> who were not sufficiently capable of understanding everything. We can believe that the unlearned listeners were satisfied if the light of knowledge—which the wise would look into—was drawn over with coarser words, as if surrounded by a **horn shell** <note>original: "cornea testa"; an image of a translucent protective layer that softens bright light for weak eyes.</note>, so that the duller eyes would not be dazzled. He would therefore bring the light so that it might benefit healthy eyes, yet bring it included and veiled so as not to hurt those with sore eyes. For he neither should have, could have, nor would have wanted to help the learned any less than the unlearned.

**The second difficulty** is that the "tenor" <note>The consistent character or flow.</note> of the interpretation should be consistent with itself, fitting together and leading the whole series—as if by a single path—from the sense where it first begins back to that same purpose. We should not, for instance, introduce him speaking of **Ideas** <note>The Platonic forms or archetypes.</note> here, and then in the very next clause want him to deal with the **elements** or with **man**. This is an arbitrary and violent kind of exposition. Yet to avoid this in the explanation of this book has seemed to many—I will not say difficult and laborious—but truly impossible for everyone. Such is the perplexity, such is the ambiguity, such is the variety of the entire reading. See how much labor and how uneasy a task we have conceived in our mind (may we achieve it!): that we might interpret this entire creation of the world not by just one sense, but by a **sevenfold sense**, beginning a new work from the head each time in a perpetual and unmixed order of exposition, using nothing from the works of our predecessors.

**The third difficulty** turns on this: that the prophet [Moses]—or rather, let us say the Divine Spirit through the prophet—should not assert anything foreign, prodigious, or alien to the "nature of things" <note>original: "rerum natura"; the physical world as understood by science.</note> which is now perceived, nor to the truth which our own people have received as discovered by the better philosophers. 

Now, as to why seven interpretations are brought forth by us, by what reasoning they were undertaken, what our plan is, and what necessity drove us to them—and indeed, what this entirely new thing is that we are striving to bring—we shall make clear in the following chapter. In that chapter, we shall discuss him who treated this matter (that is, the creation of the world) most perfectly, in emulation of Nature itself, if...

...[the writer] will attempt to paint an idea of what he is about to write, then in the following pages he will prove that our prophet [Moses] fell short of that idea in no way, as if it were an archetype. Indeed, he achieved it in every respect, so much so that nothing else should be proposed to everyone as such an idea than the prophet himself. Added to this is the custom that when something festive or joyful happens to those we love or revere, we should not only congratulate them with words but also favor their happiness with some gift, so to speak, to bear witness to the joy of our soul toward them. Therefore, this study of ours comes to you at an opportune time: when your son **Giovanni** <note>The future Pope Leo X, who was made a Cardinal at the exceptionally young age of 13.</note> has been appointed to the supreme college of the Christian orders by the Supreme Pontiff **Innocent VIII** at an age younger than anyone before him—a distinction his character, which promises all good things for itself, and your own merits and authority, justly and deservedly demanded for him. It remains for us to hope that he shows himself worthy of this dignity. He will do so if he holds the same man as the model for his life—that is, the model of prudence and all virtue—whom he has as both a father and the author of his dignity. Farewell.

## lla Mirandola on the Heptaplus, concerning the work
### of the six days of Genesis, Preface to the Reader.

Antiquity depicts **three worlds**. The highest of all is the "ultra-mundane," which theologians call the **angelic** and philosophers call the **intellectual** world; **Plato** says in the *Phaedrus* that no one has sung of this world worthily enough. Next to this is the **celestial** world, and the last of all is the **sublunary** world—this one which we inhabit. 

This world is one of darkness, while that highest one is one of light; the heavens are tempered from both light and darkness. This world is characterized by its flowing and unstable substance through the **waters**; that highest world by the brightness of light and the loftiness of its place through **fire**. The heavens are of a middle nature, and for that reason, they are called <term>Shamayim</term> <note>original Hebrew: שמים</note> by the Hebrews, as if composed from <term>Esh</term> <note>fire; original Hebrew: אש</note> and <term>Mayim</term> <note>water; original Hebrew: מים</note>, which we have mentioned. 

In this world, there is the alternation of life and death; in that highest world, there is perpetual life and stable activity; in the heavens, there is stability of life but alternation of activities and positions. This world is constituted of the fleeting substance of bodies; that highest world of the nature of the divine mind; the heavens are composed of body, but incorruptible, and of mind, but bound to the body. The third world is moved by the second; the second...

<meta>This page continues Pico's introductory discussion from page 5. Having established that there are three worlds—the sublunary, the celestial, and the super-celestial—he now explains how Moses represented these three realms through the architecture of the Tabernacle in the wilderness.</meta>

->## Giovanni Pico della Mirandola<-

[The lower] world is ruled by the first, and furthermore, there are many differences between them which I do not intend to recount here, where we are merely skimming over these matters rather than flooding them with detail. However, I should not overlook the fact that these three worlds were most clearly represented by **Moses** in the construction of that admirable **Tabernacle** <note>The portable earthly dwelling place of Yahweh used by the Israelites, described in the Book of Exodus.</note> of his. For he divided the Tabernacle into three parts, each of which represents one of the three worlds we mentioned so perfectly that they could not be more expressly portrayed.

Indeed, the **first part** was protected by no roof or covering, but was open and exposed to rain, snow, sun, heat, and cold. This is a most evident image of our own **sublunary world** <term>sublunary world</term> <note>The region of the cosmos below the Moon, consisting of the four elements (earth, water, air, fire) and subject to change and decay.</note>. It is inhabited not only by men—the worldly and the pure, the sacred and the profane—but also by animals of every kind. Within it, due to the sacrifices and perpetual offerings, there was a constant succession of life and death. 

The **remaining two parts** were both covered and free from any outside harm, just as both the celestial and super-celestial worlds are incapable of receiving injury or insult. Both were also honored with the name of sanctity, yet in such a way that the more secret part was decorated with the title **Holy of Holies**, while the other was called the **Holy Place**. In the same way, although both the celestial and angelic worlds are holy—since above the moon, after the fall of Lucifer, neither stain nor sin exists or can exist—the angelic world is nevertheless considered far holier and more divine than the celestial. 

But why do we pursue these more remote similarities? For if the final part of the Tabernacle was common to men and beasts, the **second part**, which shone entirely with the splendor of gold, was illuminated by a **lampstand** <note>The Menorah.</note> distinguished by seven lamps. These, as all Latin, Greek, and Hebrew interpreters say, signify the **seven planets**. In the **third part**, the most sacred of all, were the winged **cherubim**. Do these not place the three worlds before our eyes? This world, which both beasts and men inhabit; the celestial world, in which the planets shine; and the super-celestial world, the dwelling place of the angels. 

From this, we are also reminded of an even higher **Gospel mystery**. Since the way to the super-celestial world and the company of angels has been opened for us through the cross and blood of **Christ**, therefore, as he died, the **veil of the temple was torn**. This was the veil that separated the Holy of Holies—which we said signifies the angelic world—from the other parts. This was a sign that the entrance to the Kingdom of God, and to God Himself (who "flies upon the cherubim"), is now open to man—an entrance that had been closed from the beginning by the laws of justice because of the sin of our first parent <note>Adam.</note>.

This is enough concerning the three worlds. In them, one must primarily and greatly observe—since nearly our entire intention depends on this—that these three worlds are **one world**. This is not only because they are all traced back to one principle and the same end, or because they are bound together by harmonious proportions and a certain natural kinship and an orderly series of steps, but because whatever exists in all the worlds at once is also contained within each one. There is not one among them in which all things that exist in the others are not present. I believe this was the opinion of **Anaxagoras** <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher (c. 500–428 BC) famous for the doctrine that "everything is in everything."</note>, if we think he was understood correctly, and later it was held by the Pythagoreans and Platonists. Truly, those things that are in the lower world are also in the higher ones, but in a [better]...

## *Preface to the Reader*

...of a higher mark, which are likewise seen in the higher worlds and are also visible in the lowest, but in a degenerate condition and with an adulterated nature, so to speak. Among us, heat is an elemental quality; in the celestial bodies, it is a heating power; in the angelic minds, it is the Idea of heat. Let me speak more clearly. Among us, fire is an element. The Sun is fire in heaven. In the ultra-mundane <note>Beyond the physical world.</note> region, there is the Seraphic <note>Referring to the Seraphim, the highest order of angels, whose name is derived from the Hebrew word for "burning."</note> fire of the intellect. But see how they differ: the elemental fire burns, the celestial gives life, and the super-celestial loves. There is water among us; there is water in the heavens, whose mover and mistress is the Moon, the vestibule of the heavens; there are also waters above the heaven, namely the Cherubic minds <note>Referring to the Cherubim, the second highest order of angels, associated with divine wisdom.</note>. But see the disparity of condition within the same nature: elemental moisture overwhelms the heat of life; celestial moisture nourishes it; super-celestial moisture understands.

In the first world <note>The super-celestial or angelic realm.</note>, God, the first unity, presides over nine orders of angels as if over so many spheres, and being himself immovable, he moves all things toward himself. In the middle world, that is, the celestial, the **Empyrean** <term>Empyrean</term> <note>The highest heaven, believed in medieval cosmology to be the dwelling place of God and composed of pure light or fire.</note> heaven likewise presides over nine celestial spheres as a leader over an army; and while each of these rolls with unceasing motion, the Empyrean remains unmoved, imaging God. There are also in the elemental world, after prime matter which is its foundation, nine spheres of corruptible forms:

*   **Three of bodies devoid of life**, which are the elements and mixed bodies, and between these a middle ground, which are mixed but imperfect, such as the impressions that occur in the heights <note>Phenomena like meteors or lightning.</note>.
*   **Three of a vegetable nature**, which is first divided into three kinds: herbs, shrubs, and trees.
*   **Three of the sensory soul**, which is either imperfect, such as in *Zoophytes* <term>Zoophytes</term> <note>literally "animal-plants"; organisms like sponges or corals that were thought to bridge the gap between the plant and animal kingdoms.</note>, or perfect but within the limits of irrational imagination, or what is highest among the brutes, which is even capable of human training—a middle ground between man and brute, just as the *Zoophyte* is a middle ground between brute and plant.

But regarding these matters, more than is necessary has been said; let us only add this: that the mutual containment of the worlds is indicated even in the sacred scriptures. For it is written in the Psalms:

> "Who creates the heavens in understanding" <note>original: "Qui creat cœlos in intellectu"</note>, and we read that the angels of God are "spirits and his ministers a flame of burning fire" <note>original: "spiritus esse & ministros eius flammã ignis urentis"</note>.

Hence, celestial titles are often given to divine things, and even earthly ones; now they are represented by stars, now by wheels and animals, and now by elements. Conversely, celestial names are often given to earthly things. For clearly, bound by the chains of concord, all these worlds grant to one another their names as well as their natures with mutual generosity. From this principle (if perhaps someone has not yet noticed this) the whole discipline of allegorical meaning has flowed. Nor could the ancient fathers have fittingly represented some things by other figures unless they were taught the secret friendships and affinities, so to speak, of all nature. Otherwise, there would be no reason why they should have represented one thing by a specific image rather than another. But being knowledgeable of all things and driven by that Spirit who not only knows all these things but made them, they represented the natures of one world most aptly through those things which they knew corresponded to them in the other worlds. Therefore, the same knowledge is needed (unless the same Spirit is also present) for those who wish to correctly interpret their figures and allegorical meanings...

# Of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

...preside. Besides the three worlds we have narrated, there is a fourth world in which all things found in the others are also found; this is man himself. For this reason, as Catholic doctors <note>Theologians and scholars of the Church, such as Thomas Aquinas or Jerome.</note> say in the Gospel, he is designated by the name of **every creature** <note>original: "omnis creaturę"; Pico refers to Mark 16:15, "Preach the gospel to every creature."</note>. For while the Gospel is to be preached to men, and not to animals or angels, Christ nevertheless commands it to be preached to "every creature." It is a common saying in the schools that man is a **microcosm** <term>microcosm</term> <note>Literally "little world"; the philosophical idea that the human being is a miniature reflection of the entire universe.</note>, in whom is seen a body mixed from the elements, a celestial spirit, the vegetative soul of plants, the senses of animals, reason, the angelic mind, and the likeness of God.

Therefore, if we establish these four worlds, it is believable that Moses, intending to speak sufficiently about the world, discussed all of them. And since a writer portrays nature accurately if he is skilled in nature—as we believe this man of ours <note>Moses, whom Pico regards as the ultimate divinely-inspired philosopher.</note> to be more than any other—it is believable that his teaching about them was arranged no differently than the Almighty God, the Craftsman, arranged the worlds themselves. Thus, this writing of Moses is a truly expressed image of the world, just as we read that it was commanded to him on the mountain where he learned these things, that he should "make everything according to the pattern seen on the mountain" <note>Exodus 25:40; Pico suggests that the text of Genesis mirrors the divine archetypes Moses witnessed on Mount Sinai.</note>.

First, therefore, since the greatest point of all is that (as we have shown) what is in all the worlds is contained in each individual one, Moses, as an emulator of nature, ought never to treat any of those worlds without treating all of them together at the same time, under the same words and the same context. From this, a fourfold exposition of the entire Mosaic reading immediately arises: first, we explain whatever is written there concerning the angelic and invisible world, making no mention of the others. In the second place, we explain everything concerning the celestial world; then concerning this sublunary and corruptible world; fourth, concerning the nature of man.

For if, for example, the intelligible realm is being discussed, since it contains all lower natures within itself, and since the scripture likewise warns us about the remaining worlds, we certainly can—nay, we must—interpret every small part in light of all of them. Again, just as natures, although they are mutually contained within each other in a mingled way, have nevertheless been allotted distinct, proper seats and certain peculiar laws; so also, if the letter of the text discusses the fourfold nature in the same sequence in individual parts of the present work, it must nevertheless be believed that in the first part, the first nature is dealt with more specifically, and then in the others in the same order. From this, the necessity of a fifth exposition also arises.

In addition, although these things are distinct, because there is no multitude that is not one, they are bound by a certain **discordant concord** <note>original: "discordi quadā cōcordia"; the idea that the universe’s harmony is composed of diverse and opposing elements.</note> and are tied together by multiform chains of connections. Since it is likely that Moses does this throughout the entire work, it calls us, even if unwillingly, to a sixth interpretation. In this, we will show that there are fifteen modes by which we can understand how one thing is related or joined to another; and since there are neither more nor fewer, they are all expressed so sufficiently and clearly by the prophet that **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher whose works on "Physics" were the standard scientific texts of the Renaissance.</note> never wrote anything more precisely about the nature of things.

Finally, just as the Sabbath—that is, rest—succeeds the six days of Genesis, it is fitting that we also, after the orders proceeding from God have been distributed, and their union, difference, covenants, and relations explained...

## Preface to the Reader: ❦

Now, in this seventh and, as I might call it, "sabbatical" <note>The word *sabbataria* refers to the Sabbath or the number seven; Pico's work, the *Heptaplus*, is divided into seven books, reflecting the seven days of creation.</note> exposition concerning the happiness of creatures and their return to God—which has been granted to man after his distance from Him due to the sin of our first parent, through the Mosaic and Christian law—let us touch upon a few points. We shall reveal those things which Moses most openly concealed in this present scripture, so that it may become clear that a most distinct prophecy is read here concerning the coming of Christ, the progress of the Church, and the calling of the Gentiles <note>The "Gentiles" refers to the non-Jewish nations being brought into the Christian faith.</note>. Truly, this book, if any other be such, is a **book sealed with seven seals** <note>original: "liber septem signaculis obsignatus"; a reference to the Book of Revelation 5:1.</note>, full of every doctrine and all mysteries. However, we shall not imitate those who, having at some time attempted to explain this creation of the world, heaped up here whatever has been disputed anywhere among philosophers and theologians concerning God, angels, matter, heaven, and the whole of nature. In this, the Hebrews **Isaac the Persian** and **Samuel the Ophite** <note>Medieval Jewish commentators whose works Pico studied in his pursuit of harmonizing Jewish and Christian thought.</note> sinned most greatly. Instead, we shall strive with all our might to declare only what the Mosaic letter intends, and what the context of the words either indicates or signifies.

Nor, if we show that the "firmament" signifies, for instance, the **eighth sphere** <term>eighth sphere</term> <note>In ancient astronomy, the sphere of the fixed stars, located beyond the seven spheres of the planets.</note>, will we immediately launch into a dispute about it—how it draws the other spheres along, how many signs it is divided into, how many images it contains, or whether it rotates in different directions by a simple motion, or rather by two or three. Or if in any place we say the human soul is indicated by some expression, we will not digress to explain everything written about the soul. Rather, we will briefly and even cursorily note only those things about each subject which the author seems to make express mention of. I said "briefly and even cursorily," because it is not the purpose of this work that those who have not learned these things elsewhere should learn them here for the first time, but that they may recognize that what they already know to be true is contained in the words of the prophet <note>Pico refers to Moses as a "prophet" because he believes Genesis contains prophetic secrets about the future.</note>. Thus, understanding how he has both included and concealed in a few words what they have read digested in immense volumes by theologians and philosophers, they may hear the lawgiver speaking with an **unveiled face** <note>original: "revelata facie"; a reference to Moses removing his veil to speak the words of God (Exodus 34:34).</note>.

But if anyone, perhaps moved by a spirit of "holy rusticity" <note>original: "sanctae rusticitatis"; a phrase used by St. Jerome to describe a simple, unlearned faith that is nevertheless pious.</note>, should not approve of these more deeply sought mysteries, and should instead desire a simpler exposition of the sacred context more suited to himself, I will bid him first to remember Paul's command: that neither should he who eats despise him who does not eat, nor should he who does not eat judge him who eats <note>A reference to Romans 14:3, here applied to "digesting" complex vs. simple interpretations of scripture.</note>. Then I shall address him not with my own words, but with those of **Augustine** in his own exposition of Genesis, in this manner:

> If you can grasp these things, do so; if you cannot yet, leave them for those who are more capable. But as for you, make progress while the Scripture does not abandon your weakness and walks with you more slowly, like a mother's gait. For it speaks in such a way as to mock the proud by its height, terrify the attentive by its depth, feed the great by its truth, and nourish the small by its kindness.

But let us return to ourselves and, beginning from this corruptible world which we inhabit, let us perform as much as we are able of what we have promised. Otherwise, even in great things, it is enough to have willed them; and as **Pomerius** <note>Likely Julianus Pomerius, a 5th-century priest. The quote "in great things, it is enough to have willed" is more famously attributed to the poet Propertius.</note> says, a great effort is progress in great things.

> <margin>X</margin> **I**n the beginning God created heaven and earth: but the earth was void and empty, and darkness was upon the face of the abyss, and the spirit of the Lord was moved over the waters. And God said, "Let there be light," and light was made. And God saw the light that it was good, and he divided the light from the darkness. And he called the light "Day" and the darkness "Night"; and there was made evening and morning, one day. God also said, "Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters." And God made the firmament, and divided the waters that were under the firmament from those that were above the firmament, and it was so. And God called the firmament "Heaven," and there was made evening and morning, the second day. But God said, "Let the waters that are under the heaven be gathered together into one place and let the dry land appear," and it was so. And God called the dry land "Earth," and the gathering together of the waters he called "Seas." And God saw that it was good, and he said, "Let the earth bring forth green herbs, such as may seed, and fruit trees yielding fruit after their kind, whose seed may be in itself upon the earth," and it was so. And the earth brought forth green herbs, such as yield seed after their kind, and trees yielding fruit, each having seed according to its species. And God saw that it was good, and there was made evening and morning, the third day. Then God said: "Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven to divide the day and the night, and let them be for signs and seasons, and for days and years, that they may shine in the firmament of heaven and illuminate the earth," and it was so. And God made two great lights: a greater light to rule the day, and a lesser light to rule the night. And the stars; and he set them in the firmament of heaven to shine upon the earth, and to rule over the day and the night, and to divide the light and the darkness. And God saw that it was good, and there was made evening and morning, the fourth day. God also said, "Let the waters produce the creeping thing of a living soul, and the flying creature above the earth under the firmament of heaven." And God created great whales and every living and moving soul which the waters had produced in their kinds, and every flying creature according to its kind. And God saw that it was good, and he blessed them, saying: "Increase and multiply, and fill the waters of the sea, and let the birds be multiplied upon the earth." And there was made evening and morning, the fifth day. God also said, "Let the earth produce the living soul in its kind: cattle and creeping things of the earth according to their species," and it was so. And God made the beasts of the earth according to their species, the cattle and every creeping thing of the earth in its kind. And God saw that it was good. And he said: "Let us make man in our image and likeness, and let him rule over the fish of the sea, and the fowls of the air, and the beasts of the whole earth, and every creeping thing that moves upon the earth." And God created man in his own image and likeness; in the image of God he created him. <note>Pico quotes the Latin Vulgate translation of Genesis 1:1–27. This serves as the "foundation stone" for the seven layers of interpretation he is about to provide.</note>

Thus far have we undertaken to explain Moses <note>In the Renaissance, Moses was viewed not just as a prophet, but as the supreme "theologian-philosopher" who encoded the secrets of the universe in the book of Genesis.</note>. Moreover, I have divided the entire exposition into seven books or treatises, rather to imitate Basil and Augustine <note>St. Basil the Great and St. Augustine both wrote famous "Hexamera"—commentaries on the six days of creation. Pico places himself in this prestigious tradition.</note> than because the attention of the reader is refreshed by this frequent distinction as if by a resting place. It is added that since there are seven expositions digested into seven books, and each book is divided into seven chapters, all things correspond to the seven days of creation. Likewise, it was done by us for a most fitting reason: that just as the seventh day according to Moses is the Sabbath and a day of rest, so any seventh chapter of ours is always directed toward Christ, who is both the end of the law <note>original: "finis est legis"; a reference to Romans 10:4, signifying that Christ fulfills the purpose of the Old Testament law.</note>, and is our Sabbath, our rest, and our happiness.

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MI-
## randola, regarding the elementary world, First 
## Book, of the First Exposition
### Chapter I.

**N**atural philosophers <note>In the Renaissance, "natural philosophy" was the study of the physical world and nature, the precursor to modern science.</note> who discuss the nature of corruptible things <note>Things subject to decay, change, and death, as opposed to eternal or celestial things.</note> generally establish that their principles consist of a raw matter, devoid of forms, which is indeed suitable for receiving all forms, yet by its own nature is deprived of them all. Therefore, besides matter, they also establish "privation" <note>A technical term in Aristotelian philosophy meaning the absence of a form that a thing should naturally have.</note> as a principle of natural things. <term>Averroes</term> <note>The influential 12th-century Andalusian philosopher Ibn Rushd, famous for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> added that matter is extended in a triple dimension—in length, breadth, and height—so that, naturally, physical things would not be said to arise from a non-physical subject. Then they bring forward the transforming cause, which he calls the "efficient" cause. By its power, matter is treated, so that what is potential becomes actual at some point, just as a mass of soft and indefinite wax is transformed into various figures by the movement and touch of the hand according to the will of the one handling it. Since, however, nature does nothing at random, but for the sake of attaining some good, the "final cause" <note>The purpose or goal for which something exists.</note> immediately introduces itself; and indeed the immediate goal of the acting cause is the "form" which it draws out from the womb of matter. For it acts and turns with this intention: that it might lead matter to the perfect state of form; hence form is established by <term>Aristotle</term> as the third principle. This form, however, cannot be led out from the bosom of matter unless the matter is first affected and prepared with suitable qualities. Around these qualities the whole labor of the craftsman and the whole duration of the action is spent: the species <note>The specific nature or "kind" of a thing.</note> itself shining forth in a single moment, as if the reward of the labor. The <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle, named for the covered walkways (peripatos) where they studied in Athens.</note> call the craftsman himself a "cause" rather than a "principle."

The divine <term>Platonists</term>, always mindful of divine things, wish us to be warned that although natural acting causes seem to us to be the only ones that act upon, form, and transform bodies, they are nevertheless not the primary causes of what is made, but rather the instruments of divine art which they obey and serve. Just as the hands of a builder—even if they themselves arrange, order, and transform all the material of a house, the wood, stones, and mortar, and nothing besides them seems to be that to which the building of the house is credited—we know, however, that they are an obedient and serving tool which, established in the mind of the architect, arranges bit by bit and unfolds the house he conceived in his mind into the unfeeling matter. From this it follows that they [the Platonists] add two causes: the "instrumental" <note>The tool used to do the work.</note> and the "exemplary" <note>The blueprint or model in the mind of the creator.</note>. This the Peripatetics do not deny; indeed, they confirm it, for among them there is that well-worn saying: *Every work of nature is a work of intelligence.* <note>original: "Omne opus naturæ opus eſſe intelligentiæ." This phrase suggests that nature operates according to a rational, divine plan.</note> These are the things which are said in common regarding things
