corruptible things, all of which Moses included in the work of the first day in such a way that the most esteemed philosophers have said nothing concerning them either more certain or more fit.

## CHAPTER TWO.

In the beginning, therefore, he established two causes: the agent and the matter—specifically, that which is in act <note>The state of being fully realized or functional.</note> and that which is in potential <note>The capacity or "raw material" to become something else.</note>. He calls the former "heaven" and the latter "earth." Our interpretation is supported first by the authority of the Stoics <note>A school of ancient Greek philosophy that viewed the universe as a living organism governed by reason.</note> who called the acting cause "heaven" and the material cause "earth," as Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a prolific Roman scholar.</note> writes, not to mention the Greeks. It is also supported by reason. For matter is the most lowly of all natures, just as the earth is of all elements; and they correspond in exactly the same proportion, as the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> prove: heaven is to the agent as earth is to matter.

But this earth—that is, matter—was "empty and void," as Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> translated it, or "invisible and unformed" as the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> has it. All these descriptions suit raw and unformed matter, which, being devoid of all forms, is rightly called empty and void, and is entirely unformed and invisible. However, the Hebrew words <term>Tohu</term> <note>original: תהו</note> and <term>Bohu</term> <note>original: בהו</note> which are read in this passage are explained differently by many Hebrews. They interpret *Tohu* as a "brute thing," stunned and astonished. This is referred by them to the dark and deformed face of matter for this reason: because focusing our attention on the knowledge of it leaves us astonished. Because of this, Aristotle said it is known by "analogy" and Plato said it is known by "bastard reasoning." <note>Pico refers to the difficulty of defining "prime matter," which has no qualities of its own. Plato in the *Timaeus* called the perception of matter a "spurious" or "bastard" reason because it is not based on direct observation or pure logic.</note>

Regarding *Bohu*, many explain it from the force of the word as the beginning or rudiment of form. For if we translate word for word, *Bohu* is as if we said "in it is he" or "something is in it." <note>Pico is referencing a Hebrew linguistic play: *Bo* (in it) and *Hu* (he/it).</note> If we follow this, we understand that besides the potentiality of the subject, there is a "begun form" within it. This was believed not only by Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus, a medieval scholar who sought to harmonize Aristotle with Christian thought.</note> and many Peripatetics, but also by the ancient Hebrews, as we clearly gather from the records of the ancient Simeon. <note>Likely referring to Rabbi Simeon bar Yochai, the traditional author of the Zohar, indicating Pico’s interest in Kabbalistic sources.</note>

But he declares how this "beginning" is to be understood by adding: "And darkness was over the face of the abyss." He calls the "abyss" the earth—that is, matter extended in a triple dimension into the highest depths. Over this is "darkness," which is <term>privation</term> <note>An Aristotelian term for the absence of a form that a thing is naturally supposed to have (like "blindness" is the privation of sight).</note>; a principle especially famous among the Peripatetics, for which no name is more fitting than "darkness." There is, however, a privation that differs from mere negation, as the Great Albertus most consistently maintains; it is this very "beginning of form" of which we speak, a matter on which that same philosopher argued copiously and subtly.

Furthermore, if the earth lies beneath the waters and is irrigated, from which it then brings forth what it eventually gives birth to, would the "waters" in this place not signify the accidental qualities and affections of matter? These, by their flowing and manageable nature, bear the likeness of waters. When matter is "moistened" by these, so to speak, it gives birth to form, which it brings into the light at the final moment of time. Over these waters, the "Spirit of the Lord"—that is, the power of the efficient cause, the organ and instrument of the Lord—is rightly said to be moved. Nor is it said to be moved over the "earth" because the agent does not reach or permeate the subject except through those intervening qualities; while it stirs and moves these, light arises... <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword indicates the next word is "arises" (oritur).</note>

He uses Hebrew etymology and Aristotelian physics to explain the "abyss" and "darkness" as the raw, unformed state of physical matter before it receives qualities.</summary>

light, that is, the beauty and elegance of form, the driver-out and router of the darkness we mentioned—that is, of <term>privation</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "privation" is the absence of a form or quality that a thing should naturally possess.</note>—and let it be so by the voice of God thus commanding, because natural causes do nothing that the order of divine art has not commanded. Then from evening and morning, one day is made. When a third substance, which we call the "composite" <note>A thing made of both matter and form.</note>, has leaped forth from the natures of potentiality and act, the reason is now clear according to this sense why he said "one day" and not "the first day." And deservedly He saw the light, because it was good. Since the nature of form is nothing other than a faint image and shadowy likeness of the First Good.

Thus far concerning corruptible substance in general, such as everything below the Moon, where we have seen both "heaven" and "earth"—that is, the nature that transforms and that which is transformed. We have seen the same "earth," that is, matter, empty of every specific substance and likewise void of every accidental form. And above it, <term>intrinsically</term> [intrinsecus], the deep abyss was spread out, with the darkness of privation sitting upon it—not indeed deep within it (for <term>privation</term> is not the essence of matter, as Aristotle <note>The influential Greek philosopher (384–322 BC) whose physical theories Pico is reconciling with the Bible.</note> proves), but occupying its outermost face. We likewise saw the Spirit of the Lord being carried over the "waters"—that is, the flowing dispositions of matter—as if present to the earth. This Spirit is the power of the acting cause, not as the principal cause, but as the Spirit of the Lord—that is, as the instrument of divine art, just as our vital spirit is the instrument of the soul. And immediately, as the Spirit handled those waters and pervaded the subject at the command of God the Craftsman, "light" arose—that is, the beauty and splendor of form.

### CHAPTER THREE.

<insert>S</insert>ince <note>original: "Quoniam"</note>, moreover, we descend in the correct order from common and general things to specific ones, as Aristotle proves, Moses—about to do the same thing—after speaking of those things common to all elementary things, divides the entire elementary substance into three parts on the second day. First, however, it must be understood that all material forms are designated by him here under the name of "waters," a term that could not be more fitting. For in this sphere of things that are born and die, while matter stands still like the bed of a sea, there is a perpetual and ceaseless ebb and flow of waves—the coming and going of forms that depart and arrive. <term>Generation</term> <note>original: "Generatio"—the process of coming into being.</note>, as Solomon <note>King Solomon, traditionally the author of Ecclesiastes.</note> says, passes away, and generation arrives, but the earth stands forever. For these forms are also called "generations" rather than "forms" by the Platonists <note>Followers of Plato; Pico frequently argues that Plato's wisdom originated from Moses.</note>—those imitators of Hebrew teaching—because they can more truly be said to be "becoming" than "being." For this same reason, it happened that the same name, "waters," which he used above to call the qualities and accidental forms of matter, he also used here for the material substances themselves; so that he might remind us—not of what Alexander <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a famous 2nd-century commentator on Aristotle.</note> believed, that the qualities themselves are the substantial forms of the elements—but of what the Platonists strongly confirm: that every species that exists in matter is to be referred to the condition of an accident rather than a true substance. That title [of substance] is legitimately claimed only by those things which stand by themselves, leaning upon themselves, and are true in their essence, unmixed with things...

<meta>This page continues Pico's First Exposition of Genesis. On the previous page, he interpreted the "Spirit of God moving over the waters" as the divine influence acting upon unformed matter. Here, he continues the metaphor of "water" and "sea" using Greek philosophy and mythology to explain the different layers of the physical world.</meta>

->Giovanni Pico della Mirandola<-

<note>original: "bus peregrinis"</note> ...in foreign and least adulterated names, Heraclitus <note>A Greek philosopher (c. 535–475 BC) known for his doctrine of change, famously saying one cannot step into the same river twice.</note> called the substance of sensible things the "sea." Among the poets, philosophers also veiled their wisdom in the coverings of myths: when, after the <term>Saturnine unity</term> <note>Referring to the "Golden Age" of Saturn, which Neoplatonists like Pico associated with the "Intelligible World"—a realm of perfect, unified ideas before the physical world was created.</note>—that is, the union of the intelligible world which enfolds all things within itself—they divided the sensible world into three parts. They assigned the celestial region to Jupiter and the subterranean region to Pluto. To Neptune, however, they assigned this middle region, namely that which extends from the Moon to the earth, which we are discussing now. They called Neptune the "lord of the sea"; among the Platonists, this same figure is understood as the power that presides over "generations" <note>The process of physical birth, growth, and change.</note>.

But let us return to Moses dividing the waters from the waters by means of the <term>firmament</term> <note>In ancient cosmology, the firmament was the "expanse" created by God to separate the waters above from the waters below.</note>. There is a threefold partition of <term>sublunary</term> <note>Literally "under the moon"; the realm of the four elements (earth, water, air, fire) where things are born and die.</note> bodies. Some are above the middle region of the air; these are the highest parts, namely, a portion of that same element and the purest fire, the whole of which is designated by the name "ether." There, the elements are pure, unmixed, and "legitimate." Others are below the very center of the air, which are the things among us; here there is no pure element (for no pure element can be perceived by the senses), but all things are composed of the drossy and thicker part of the mundane body. 

The intervening region of air is what is called here the "firmament," from which birds are introduced as flying "under the firmament of heaven." This is the region in which those sublime "impressions" appear: rains, snows, lightning, thunder, comets, and other things of that kind. See, then, how correctly this firmament—not only by its position but by the property of its nature—distinguishes and separates the higher elements from the lower ones, as if "waters from waters." Above it, the elements are pure; below it, they depart from elemental simplicity through a perfect mixing. In that middle space, they become mixed, but imperfectly and in a middle way, so that it may be most truly said to stand between the nature of the "mixed" and the "elements."

### CHAPTER FOUR

**B**ut let us see what Moses philosophizes further. He says: "Let the waters which are under the heaven be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear." The "dry land" is <term>matter</term>, as we have already established. Matter does not "appear," nor is it perceived, unless it is clothed in the beauty of <term>forms</term> <note>In Aristotelian thought, "matter" is the raw stuff, while "form" is what makes it a specific thing (like a tree or a stone). Matter without form is invisible and unknowable.</note>. But it does not even appear when clothed in the appearance of a [simple] element, because, as we have said and as the philosophers prove, a simple element can neither be seen nor touched, nor can it fall under any sense at all. 

Therefore, if the "earth" which was formerly invisible is to come into view, it is necessary that the "waters under the heaven"—that is, those below the middle region of the air—be "gathered into one place." This means they flow together into a common dregs of mixing according to certain laws, yet as if prescribed by shores, to coalesce into a single "form of mixture." This happens to the lower waters, as we have shown, but not to the higher ones, where there is either no mixture at all or only an imperfect one. And since the "vegetable soul" <note>The lowest level of "soul" or life-force, responsible for growth and nutrition in plants.</note> immediately follows the form of a mixture, what else should we expect from our philosopher but that, after that gathering of waters, he would immediately introduce "the earth fertile with herbs, shrubs, and trees"?

### CHAPTER FIVE

**A**lthough from here it seemed we should proceed in order to the animals, whose soul is most closely joined to the vegetable soul, nevertheless, since from animals...

<summary>Pico explains the "firmament" as a middle atmospheric region that separates pure elements from the complex mixtures of our world, and interprets the appearance of "dry land" as the point where raw matter takes on physical form.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's exposition of the physical world as described in Genesis. Having previously discussed the "waters" and the "sea" as metaphors for the material realm, he now moves through the layers of the atmosphere toward the creation of living things and, ultimately, man.</meta>

# Heptaplus.

We proceed toward man, in whom every discussion concerning the <term>corruptible world</term> <note>The physical realm below the heavens where things are born, change, and die, as opposed to the eternal, unchanging celestial realm.</note> reaches its end; for this reason, Moses interjected some things about those objects that occur in the firmament and with which he adorns it, just as the earth is adorned by those things produced within it: metals, plants, and living creatures. These, however, are those <term>impressions</term> <note>In Aristotelian meteorology, "impressions" (impressiones) referred to atmospheric phenomena like clouds, rain, wind, and meteors, thought to be formed by vapors rising into the air.</note> which occur on high, that is, in the middle region of the air. This region he called "above both the heaven and the firmament," but here he calls it the "firmament of heaven," so that we may know it is not that which is truly heaven, but that which lies beneath heaven. Wherefore Ennius <note>Quintus Ennius (c. 239–169 BC), often called the "father of Roman poetry."</note> in his *Achilles* called this part "the subject," because it is placed most closely under the heaven. That these secondary "stars," "constellations," and "heavenly bodies" are so named by the philosophers is too well known to need further proof, nor should it seem somewhat harsh to anyone that we explain here what is said about the stars. Since all the diversity of these things is traced back to two primary causes—heat and cold—we shall appropriately refer those which are hot by cause to the Sun, and those which are cold to the Moon. Nor do these things claim this title of "Sun," "Moon," and the "rest of the stars" for themselves only because they are to the lower heaven what the stars are to their own more divine heaven, or because they show themselves to men with a similar face, equally shining and flashing, but because some of them follow one star in heaven and some another, as if following a prince and leader. Whence they are also signs of those things which the stars, by which they were excited, are accustomed to portend for lower things. An argument for this is that they follow the motion of the stars, by whose power and influence they consist of terrestrial matter, that is, of a vaporous breath.

### CHAPTER SIX.

**N**ow follow the manifest things concerning the production of animals and of man. For after plants, those things are joined which feel and move, although the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras who held that even plants possessed a primitive or "dull" form of sensation or soul.</note> ascribe a "dull sense" even to plants, which we shall discuss in that <note>original: "concordia longioris fubfellij"</note> *Harmony* of ours, a work of a longer bench <note>Pico is likely referring to a larger planned work on the harmony between Plato and Aristotle that he never fully completed.</note>. These living creatures, however, which participate in motion and sense beyond all controversy, are distinguished here by Moses and in the *Timaeus* <note>A dialogue by Plato (c. 360 BC) that provides a creation myth for the universe.</note> into those that fly, those that live in the waters, and those that dwell on the land. Supreme over all and the prince is man, at whom the nature of the corruptible world, having progressed this far, comes to a halt and sounds the retreat.

### CHAPTER SEVEN.

**J**ust as man is the absolute completion of all lower things, so Christ is the absolute completion of all men. For if, as the philosophers say, from that which is most perfect in every genus, all perfection is derived to the others of the same order as if from a fountain: it is a doubt to no one that from Christ the man, the perfection of all goodness is derived into all men. To him alone, surely, was the Spirit given, not by measure, so that from his fullness we might all receive <note>A reference to the Gospel of John 1:16 and 3:34.</note>. See how undoubtedly this prerogative is owed to him as God and man, which even as he is man belongs to him by a peculiar and legitimate privilege.

<header>Of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s Exposition on the Celestial World</header>

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola
## Of the Exposition on the Celestial World
### The Second, Book II. Preface.

**L**et us press on from the elements to the heavens, from <term>corruptible bodies</term> <note>Physical things subject to change, decay, and death.</note> to those that are incorruptible, so that it may be clear to everyone that by the same words through which so much of nature was shown to us regarding elemental things, the most profound teachings concerning celestial things have also been included by the prophet <note>Pico refers to Moses, the traditional author of Genesis, as "the prophet."</note>. When we reflect on this within ourselves, there will be another reason ready at hand besides those we mentioned in the earlier prefaces. Why, for example, when Moses was about to speak of the <term>agent cause</term> <note>The "efficient cause" or the force that acts upon matter to create something.</note> and of matter, did he not call the one "agent" and the other "matter" in explicit words, but rather "heaven" and "earth"? And why did he call the "dispositions of matter" not "qualities" (as the philosophers say), but "waters"? And why did he call "form" "light" rather than "form"? Likewise, he named comets and thunderbolts and other things of that kind not by their specific names, but as "heavenly bodies" and "stars," and so on with the rest. In the beginnings [of this work], we cited the ancient custom of writing great physical and divine matters in a hidden and figurative way; furthermore, we cited the ignorance of the listeners, who, because they could not bear the brilliance of the Mosaic teaching, required him to speak to them with a "veiled face," lest those who were being undertaken for enlightenment be blinded by too much light. Now we have the occasion for a third reason: because, clearly, if he had used the terms "matter," "form," "qualities," and "agent cause," those terms could indeed serve for treatises on the corruptible world, but not for the others <note>Pico argues that Moses chose "water" and "earth" because those words can represent multiple levels of reality—physical, celestial, and angelic—simultaneously, whereas technical jargon is limited to one field.</note>. Therefore, this is the inconceivable and wonderful artistry of Moses—a truly divine and not human industry—to use such words and to arrange his discourse in such a way that the same words, the same context, and the same sequence of the entire scripture aptly fit the secrets of all the worlds and of all nature. This is why the book of Moses surpasses all the learning, eloquence, and genius of the nations. This is that new and hitherto untouched thing which we have attempted to bring forward: namely, to prove to our people by the thing itself that this was done by Moses. This is the idea, this is the model of the most perfect writer—not only because this kind of writing portrays and emulates nature (as we demonstrated above), but because, just as among angelic minds (according to the authority of <term>Dionysius</term> <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century theologian whose works on the celestial hierarchy were central to medieval and Renaissance thought.</note> and Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican theologian.</note>), that mind is supreme which, through the brilliance of our theology, understands through the fewest notions and forms those things which lower minds understand through many and various ones; so among scriptures, that one is supreme and holds the peak of all perfection which, in the fewest possible words, embraces all things as if they were one, both congruently and profoundly. But why do we delay any longer the prophet coming forward with his face revealed, to speak to us of celestial mysteries? Yet, before we hear him speaking, so that we may be more capable of receiving his words, it will be useful to say a few things first about the 
->tenth heaven.<-

<header>Heptaplus.</header>

## Heptaplus.

### CHAPTER ONE.

Beyond the nine spheres of the heavens—that is, the seven <term>Planets</term> <note>The Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note> and the eighth sphere, which they call "unmoving" <note>original: "inerrantẽ"; refers to the sphere of the fixed stars.</note>, and the ninth sphere, which was discovered by reason rather than the senses and is the first among moving bodies—it is believed that there is a tenth heaven that remains fixed and quiet, participating in no motion. This is not only believed by our own writers, most notably the younger ones like Strabo and Bede <note>Walahfrid Strabo (9th century) and the Venerable Bede (8th century), both significant medieval Christian scholars.</note>, but also by many of the Hebrews, as well as certain philosophers and mathematicians. From among these, it is enough to cite two: Abraham the Spaniard <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish polymath and astrologer.</note>, a most excellent astrologer, and Isaac the philosopher <note>Likely Isaac ibn Latif, a 13th-century philosopher who combined Kabbalistic and Aristotelian thought.</note>, both of whom attest to this. Indeed, this Isaac understands the tenth sphere to be designated by Ezekiel as the <term>Sapphire</term> <note>Referring to the vision in Ezekiel 1:26 of a throne like sapphire.</note> in the likeness of a throne; he suggests that the sapphire color signifies the brilliance of light, while the likeness of a throne signifies its immobility. 

He likewise understands the ten spheres to be symbolized by Zechariah through the golden <term>candelabrum</term> <note>The Menorah or seven-branched lampstand from Zechariah 4.</note> distinguished by seven lamps, with a bowl <note>original: "lampadem"; here meaning the reservoir of the lamp.</note> above its head, and then two olive trees above the bowl. For since the seven lamps indicate the seven Planets, and the bowl indicates the eighth circle shining with so many lights, he wants the ninth and tenth spheres to be indicated by the two olive trees, because oil flows from olives to the bowl and the lamps for the nourishment of the light. Therefore, by a likeness of reason, since the light of the heavens we see emanates from and is preserved by those highest spheres (for that which gives light also preserves it), the latter are rightly compared to olive trees, while the former are compared to lamps and bowls. 

But if two primary sources of the same water cannot be established, it is necessary that one of those two supreme spheres be the principle of all light. If this is referred to one of them, it must surely be the first—that is, the tenth—so that it is itself the <term>unity of lights</term>, and then the ninth sphere receives light through the entire essence of its substance. From there, in a third step, it comes to the Sun through full participation; then from the Sun, in a fourth and therefore final degree, it is distributed among all the stars in parts. 

Therefore, let us establish a tenth heaven above the nine heavens, which theologians call the <term>Empyrean</term> <note>Derived from the Greek "empyros" (in fire); the highest heaven in medieval cosmology, believed to be made of pure light or fire.</note>. Some have doubted whether its nature is corporeal or rather incorporeal. For perhaps it is fitting for unity, just as an analogy of nature corresponds to the number of celestial bodies, so it should not be of the same kind. But whatever is decided on this question, let it remain unshaken that the treasures of light are there, and whatever light is seen in bodies is derived from there as if from a first source into all others. Nor is it an obstacle if anyone wishes to believe—more stubbornly than truly—that it is not of a truly corporeal nature, since in the <term>theology of the Phoenicians</term> (as Julian the Emperor <note>original: "Iulianus Cæsar"; Julian the Apostate (r. 361–363), who wrote "Hymn to King Helios."</note> writes in his oration on the Sun) corporeal light emanates from an incorporeal nature. Therefore, this sphere presides over the nine heavens that follow it in sequence, like a leader to an army or <term>form to matter</term> <note>In Aristotelian terms, "form" gives identity and purpose to "matter."</note>; and bearing the type of the <term>Monad</term> <note>The number one; the principle of unity.</note>, it completes the <term>Denary</term> <note>The number ten; considered a number of perfection in Pythagorean thought.</note>.

### CHAPTER TWO.

Let us come to Moses, who, being about to speak of all things, has uniquely honored this sphere with the name of "Heaven" as if it were the first and principal one, just as—

<meta>This page continues the "Second Exposition" regarding the Celestial World. Pico is elaborating on the correspondence between the biblical text of Genesis and the structure of the cosmos, specifically interpreting the terms "earth," "deep," and "waters" as metaphors for different celestial spheres and the propagation of light.</meta>

<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

## Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

In a way, we are permitted to call the nine angelic choirs "Gods" because they participate in divinity. Hence that phrase: *God of gods* <note>original: "Deus Deorum"; a reference to Psalm 82:1 or 50:1.</note>. Yet when we speak of "God" in the absolute sense, we do not mean any of those angels, but we understand the indivisible Trinity presiding over them, just as the <term>Empyrean</term> <note>The highest, fiery heaven in medieval cosmology, often considered the abode of God and the angels.</note> heaven presides over the nine orbs subject to it. 

But he <note>Moses, as the presumed author of Genesis.</note> called the last eight spheres "Earth," and not without cause, but because the extremes of this number claim the name of "earth" for themselves. These are the Moon and the starry heaven <note>The sphere of the fixed stars, the eighth sphere.</note>, both of which we are compelled to call "earth" by the authority of the ancients and by reason. For in the <term>Academy</term> <note>Referring to the Platonic school of philosophy.</note>, it is most common to give the eighth sphere the name of earth. Likewise, Aristotle said the Moon was similar to the earth, imitating the <term>Pythagoreans</term> <note>Followers of Pythagoras who held mystical views on numbers and astronomy.</note>, who call it both a "celestial earth" and a "terrestrial heaven." 

But see what reasoning leads us to both. For if we look for the elements in the heavens, we establish the Moon as earth, the lowest and most ignoble of all the stars, just as the earth is the most opaque of all the elements—likewise, the Moon is similar to it in substance and in its spots. Then we call Mercury water, for it is a changeable and transformable star, which is why in Lucan <note>A Roman poet; Mercury was often associated with shifting states.</note> it is called an "arbiter" <note>original: "arbitrum."</note>. Venus is air, life-giving with its tempered heat; the Sun is fire for the most obvious reason. Then, in reverse order: Mars is fire; Jupiter is air, kindred to Venus in nature; Saturn is water, the "old man," naturally, of condemned coldness; this leaves the eighth sphere—the non-wandering one <note>The fixed stars.</note>—to be called "earth," as the very order of calculation requires. Correctly, therefore, he called "earth" this entire system which is enclosed by two "earths" on either side, and above which nothing is visible to us.

Then he adds, *And the earth was empty and void* <note>Genesis 1:2.</note>—empty, that is, of light, which had not yet been propagated to it from the first heaven, and empty of the other virtues for which light is the vehicle. Nor do we say this of ourselves, but the author himself declares what thing is "empty," adding, *And darkness was upon the face of the deep* <note>original: "tenebræ erāt super faciem abyssi"; Genesis 1:2.</note>, rightly calling it the "deep" <note>original: "abyssum."</note> because of such height, such a number of orbs, and such wondrous depth. 

But lest we believe that there is nothing in between the eighth sphere and the Empyrean seat—as many believed, following only the evidence of the senses—he reminded us of the intervening orb. He represented this through the "waters," and it is consistently called the <term>Crystalline Heaven</term> by more recent scholars. Over this was carried—or as the Hebrew truth has it, and as <term>Ephrem the Syrian</term> <note>A 4th-century theologian and writer.</note> translated—the Spirit of the Lord *was brooding* <note>original: "incubabat"; Pico highlights the Hebrew word *merachephet*, which suggests a bird warming its eggs, rather than just "moving" over the water.</note> over it. That is, the spiritual Olympus <note>A poetic term for the highest heaven.</note>, adhering most closely as the seat of the spirits of the Lord, was nourishing it with its life-giving light. 

And this was rightly done, so that what is adjacent to the source of light might drink in the light with its whole body and its whole mass; for this reason it is invisible to us, because it is not bounded by a more solid thickness. Therefore, the Empyrean, first "brooding" upon it, bestowed its light, which was soon derived into the remaining spheres (which we say were designated by "earth" and the "deep"), driving away the darkness at God's command; *and there was evening and morning, one day*, because through the reception of light and celestial influence, the lower heavens are joined in league with the first ones. 

In summary, then, on the first day, the eminence of the first heaven over the others and the derivation of light from it to them are indicated, and many properties of the ninth orb and the others are shown through the names of "water" and "earth."

In the previous page, he established that "Earth" can refer to the Moon or the Eighth Sphere. Here, he moves into the specific arrangement of the planets and the "waters."</meta>

# CHAPTER THREE.

Now, speaking more particularly about the moving orbs, he <note>Moses, as the author of Genesis.</note> teaches that the wandering sphere which we call the firmament <note>In this context, the eighth sphere of the fixed stars.</note> is in the middle of two waters. The reason for this statement is clear from what we have said: for both the ninth sphere and the planet Saturn, as we have explained, claim the name of "waters" for themselves. Therefore, the firmament was placed by God in the midst of the waters, and the waters that are under the heaven were gathered together into one place so that the dry land might appear—that is, the earth—and all this was provided for the well-being of living things.

Let us see what these words of Moses mean. The waters that are under heaven are the seven stars <note>The seven planets of the ancient cosmos: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon.</note> which are beneath the firmament that he called heaven, the first of which is Saturn. These waters are gathered into one place for this reason: because all the power of the planets is collected in the one Sun, which all philosophers and all mathematicians confirm with one voice. And if this gathering of waters is called the "sea," it will not be absurd here to say that this is that <term>Ocean</term> <note>The Greek deity and personification of the sea, here used as a metaphor for the Sun's vast influence.</note> who is called the father of Gods and men by those who have deemed the planets worthy of the name of gods.

But what else shall we call "Earth" than the Moon? It was so named by Aristotle and the <term>Pythagoreans</term> <note>Followers of the philosopher Pythagoras, known for their mathematical and mystical view of the universe.</note>. When she is entirely overwhelmed by the waves of the aforementioned sea <note>Referring to the "combust" state or the New Moon, when the Moon is so close to the Sun's light that it disappears from view.</note>, she is neither useful to us nor visible; but she is suitable for the needs of animals and ourselves when, moving away from that sea, she comes more and more into view. Then she is fertile, then she is fruitful, especially of those things which belong to the <term>vegetative nature</term> <note>The biological level of life concerned with growth and reproduction.</note>. Her gifts are growth, nutrition, and generation. For in these matters the power of the Moon is principal, as the <term>Chaldeans</term> <note>Ancient sages and astrologers of Babylon.</note> said. This is most clearly demonstrated here by Moses: for as soon as she appears, he makes her the parent of herbs, shrubs, and trees. See how he has indicated to us the nature of the Moon and the Sun in very few and figurative words.

But why is he silent about the rest? For we promised in our introduction that he would treat all things sufficiently and learnedly. Why, I ask, when he has made mention of the tenth, ninth, and eighth spheres, and likewise of Saturn, the Sun, and the Moon, has he not said a single word about the four that remain: Venus, Mercury, Jupiter, and Mars? You might perhaps say this was done because the unlearned people <note>original: "rudis populus"</note> only knew the Sun and the Moon. But I have deprived myself of this refuge, and I cannot turn there without blushing, for I have attested above that nothing was omitted by Moses that might lead to a perfect understanding of all the worlds. Another might say that he who has dealt with the Sun and Moon has dealt with the others, because these two hold the kingship of heaven; and while the power of the others is particular, these two stars prevail with a universal influence.

But even this does not satisfy us, and by the same reasoning he ought to have omitted Saturn, of whom we have nevertheless shown mention was made. I believe a deeper mystery of the ancient discipline of the Hebrews lies hidden. Among their dogmas concerning the heavens, this is the principal one: that Jupiter and Mars are enclosed by the Sun, while Venus and Mercury are enclosed by the Moon. If we weigh the natures of these stars, the reason for this opinion is not obscure, although they themselves offer no reason for their dogma. Jupiter is hot, Mars is hot, and the Sun is hot; but the heat of Mars is sharp and violent, that of Jupiter is beneficial, and in the Sun it is

# IOANNES PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

...is that sharp and violent nature of Mars; and we see the beneficial property of **Jupiter**, that is, a certain middle nature, so to speak, mixed and tempered from these. **Jupiter** is auspicious, **Mars** inauspicious; the **Sun** is partly good and partly bad—good in its radiation, but bad in its conjunctions <note>Original: "pocula." Literally "cups," here referring to the planet's direct influence or bodily presence as opposed to its rays.</note>. **Aries** is the house of Mars, **Cancer** the dignity of Jupiter; the Sun, having attained exaltation <note>Original: "sublimitatem."</note> in **Cancer** and dignity in **Aries**, shows a manifest kinship with both stars. Let us come to the **Moon**, which clearly participates in the "waters" of **Mercury**, and indicates how much affinity she has with **Venus**, especially from the fact that she is so exalted in **Taurus**, the domicile of Venus, that she is judged nowhere more auspicious or beneficial. Concerning the Empyrean heaven, therefore, the ninth sphere, the firmament, the star of **Saturn**, and concerning the **Sun** and **Moon** which embrace the rest, [Moses] has sufficiently spoken thus far, reminding us of this embrace by his very silence.

->### CHAPTER FOUR.<-

**I**t remained that after he had spoken of the nature of the stars, he should discuss their works and their office, declaring for what use they were founded and to what duty they were delegated by God. I know, however, that the discussion so far concerns the heaven as a luminous body, nothing yet of the intellect, nothing of the "mover" <note>The "motor" or soul that guides the celestial spheres in Aristotelian and Neoplatonic thought.</note>, as has been said so far by the prophet—which order *Timaeus* <note>The protagonist of Plato’s dialogue on the creation of the universe, which Pico often synchronizes with the Book of Genesis.</note> also follows: first fashioning the body, then applying a soul to the completed body. 

There are two manifest operations of the celestial bodies in the universe: **motion** and **illumination**. **Motion** is established as twofold: one of the whole world by which the heaven and the ether are revolved through the entire space of the universe in a perfect circuit within twenty-four hours; the other is the specific, multiplex, and varied motion of the stars, among which the principal is the motion of the **Sun**, which circles all the signs of the **Zodiac** in the space of twelve months. The former makes the day, whence it is called "diurnal"; the latter, however, makes the year. The motions of the remaining stars are completed through various intervals of time. 

Rightly and briefly, therefore, **Moses** reminded us of all these when he said: the stars were placed in the firmament for *days, years, and seasons*. He added *for signs*, which I pass over because it is sufficiently explained by other interpreters. He furthermore expressly indicated the remaining operation of the stars, which is **illumination**, when he said those bodies were ordained *so that they might shine in the heaven and illuminate the earth*. 

Although the opinions of the ancients differ as to what the celestial bodies influence in lower things, the words of **Moses** nevertheless fit any of them aptly. For if they influence nothing else but light—which **Aristotle** seems to have intended if we interpret his words religiously and not according to our own whim—nothing more fitting to the Mosaic sayings could be thought. If, besides light, they also influence heat, and nothing else besides, as **Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), the influential Andalusian Muslim philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.</note> the Arab and **Abraham the Jew** <note>Likely Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a polymath known for his biblical commentaries and astrological works.</note> maintain, it was enough to have spoken of light, from which these same authors confess that heat proceeds. Likewise, if many other and manifold powers are sent down from heaven, as appeared to **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian "Prince of Physicians" whose philosophical works were central to the Middle Ages.</note> and the **Babylonians**, the mention of light alone was not made rashly, since, as Avicenna himself writes, it is light alone which carries all other powers from heaven to us. Into these ministries, therefore, the bodies of the Moon, the Sun, and the stars are distributed.

## CHAPTER FIVE.

**I**t remained that he should make mention of both the signs that are visible in the **Zodiac**, and those which, though invisible to us, are far more effective in the **Crystalline** heaven <note>The Crystalline heaven was considered the ninth sphere in medieval cosmology, located above the firmament of fixed stars.</note>. For concerning these, nothing has been said until now. This, therefore, is what is meant by the "animals" which both the "waters" produced and the "earth" produced: namely, those waters which are above the heavens and the earth which is the firmament itself, as was proved above. For the signs which are seen in those two spheres alone are in the form of animals, such as those noted among us by the Egyptians and Indians, who were able to detect them more easily and correctly than our people, aided by the flatness of the ground and the serenity of the sky. Otherwise, the production of perishable animals that exist here on earth pertains no more to these two elements—earth and water—than to the others, namely fire and air. And because he gave the name of "waters" to the Crystalline sphere, he appropriately called the animals there "fishes"; conversely, those in the firmament, which he calls "earth," he called "cattle" and "beasts."

## CHAPTER SIX.

**H**itherto we have spoken of the bodily nature of the heavens. Now, being about to declare that they are endowed with a rational soul, he mentions **man** allegorically—not indeed that man who is perishable and earthly and whom we see, but the one by whom (as Plotinus says) that "man who sees" is ruled <note>Original: "is homo qui uidet." Pico is referencing the Neoplatonic idea that the inner, rational man governs the outer, sensing man.</note>. That very thing is the rational mind, which Timaeus <note>Referencing the narrator of Plato's dialogue, the *Timaeus*.</note> established from the same elements and in the same bowl <note>Original: "eadem patera." In Plato's *Timaeus* 41d, the Creator mixes the soul of the world and human souls in a metaphorical mixing bowl or crater.</note> from which he also established the soul of the heaven; thus, what is said concerning the mind of man is not incongruously transferred to the mind of the heaven as well. The sacred scriptures support our exposition, in which the entire angelic and rational nature is often designated by the term "man." This is most frequent in the prophets regarding good angels, and it is even written in the Gospel regarding the evil demon (who differs from them in nature not at all): "An enemy man has done this" <note>Original: "Inimicus homo hæc fecit." From the Parable of the Weeds in Matthew 13:28.</note>. Therefore, God added to the celestial machine a living and rational substance, a participant in intellect. For this reason, He willed that this [rational soul] should preside, in His image and likeness, over those living creatures we spoke of a little while ago—that is, over all the starry signs and planets. These turn at His nod and obey His word so perfectly that there is no delay, no defiance—something that does not happen in the same way with the brutish bodies of the elements. Nor will you easily find anything else over which the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> labor more than to prove that the celestial body in no way resists its "mover," just as our bodies resist us. Therefore, they experience neither boredom, nor difficulty, nor fatigue from perpetual motion as we do. This is the "dominion" which Moses touched upon, of the "celestial man" over the animals. It is also not without mystery that he created that man "male and female." For it is the prerogative of celestial souls that they perform both duties simultaneously: both contemplating and ruling the bodies, so that neither does the former clamor against the latter, nor the latter become an impediment to the former. Moreover, it was a custom used greatly by the ancients—which we observe even in the Orphic hymns—to designate these two powers in the same substance (of which one contemplates and the other presides over the body) by the names "male" and "female." This concludes the discussion concerning the celestial world.

### CHAPTER SEVEN.

<margin>n c 1</margin>
**T**his noble creature <note>Referring to the celestial spheres/heavens discussed in previous chapters.</note> is to be respected and celebrated by us. But if we have not forgotten the Platonic view—not to mention the theologians—of which we just made mention, that our temperate souls were formed by God the Maker in the same mixing bowl <term>crater: A reference to Plato’s Timaeus, where the Creator mixes the soul of the world and human souls in a "krater" or vessel</term>, and from the same elements as the celestial souls, let us see to it that we do not wish to be the servants of those whom nature intended us to be the brothers of. Nor should we measure our condition by this weak body. For man (as written in the *Alcibiades* <note>The Pseudo-Platonic dialogue *Alcibiades I*, which was a key text for Renaissance Neoplatonists in defining the essence of man as the soul.</note>) is not this fragile and earthly thing which we see, but is the soul, the intellect, which exceeds every circuit of heaven and every course of time. We must therefore take care not to do what many do: by giving more to heaven and attributing more to it than is necessary, we may rebel against both the will of the Maker and the order of the universe; and at the same time, while we strive to please the heaven itself—to which God's counsels and the world’s order are most dear—we may instead displease it. The Chaldaeans warn of this, saying: *Do not increase fate* <note>original: "Ne augeas fatum." A famous maxim from the Chaldaean Oracles, often cited by Pico to argue against deterministic astrology.</note>. Jeremiah proclaims this: *Do not fear,* he says, *the signs of heaven which the nations fear.* Our prophet <note>Likely referring to Moses, the presumed author of Genesis.</note> commands this elsewhere, warning that man, looking up at the Sun, Moon, and Stars, should take care not to worship those things which God created for the service of all nations. But if anyone does not accept this in the sense that those things serve us like ignoble and dead bodies, let us nevertheless understand that the author or mistress of our nature cannot be that substance whose even better part is found to be more ignoble than some part within us <note>Pico argues that the human intellect is superior to the physical matter of the stars.</note>. For in a work, nothing can or ought to be more perfect than those things which are in the maker. Let us therefore fear, love, and venerate Him. In whom, as Paul says, all things were created, whether visible or invisible. This is the "Principle" in which God made heaven and earth; moreover, this is Christ. For when He was asked who He was, being best aware of Himself, He replied: *I am the Principle who speaks to you* <note>original: "Ego principium qui loquor uobis." A common Latin Vulgate rendering of John 8:25.</note>. Therefore, let us not reshape the images of the stars in metals <note>A critique of the practice of making astrological talismans to draw down planetary influences.</note>, but rather the image of Him—that is, the Word of God—within our souls. We should not seek after the heavens, or the body, or fortune—which will not give them—but from the Lord of heaven, the Lord of all good things, to whom all power is given in

# On the Angelic and Invisible World,

## Preface to Book III of the Third Exposition.

So far, according to the strength of our wit, we have disputed the mysteries of Moses by revealing the celestial world. Now, however, "who will give me wings like a dove," "wings covered with silver and feathers shimmering with the yellow of gold," <note>Pico is quoting the Vulgate translation of Psalm 55:6 and Psalm 68:13 to describe his mystical ascent.</note> and I shall fly into the super-celestial region, where there is true rest, true peace, true tranquility: a peace, surely, which this visible and bodily world cannot give. Open my eyes, you spirits from beyond the world, and I shall contemplate the wonders of your city, which God has laid up for those who fear Him—wonders which "no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man." <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 2:9.</note> Since, however, many things concerning this angelic and invisible nature are handed down by the ancient Hebrews, and many also by Dionysius, <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century Christian Neoplatonist whose works on the celestial hierarchy were central to Renaissance theology.</note> my plan was to explain the words of Moses according to the doctrine of both families. But because the things said by the Hebrews (being unusual) could not easily be understood by our Latin people unless we started "from the twin egg" <term>ab gemino ovo: a Latin idiom meaning to start from the very beginning</term> and recounted most—indeed almost all—the dogmas of the ancient discipline of the Hebrew nation, I thought it should be deferred until we have written more extensively about these things elsewhere and made their opinions known to our people. There, we shall examine how much they harmonize with Egyptian monuments, how much with Platonic philosophy, and how much with Catholic truth. Wherever they agree with us, we shall bid the Hebrews stand in the ancient traditions of their fathers; wherever they disagree, we shall make an assault upon them with our battle-ready Catholic legions. Finally, whatever we find alien to the truth of the Gospel, we shall refute with all our might; whatever is holy and true, we shall transfer from the synagogue—as if from an unjust possessor—to ourselves, the legitimate Israelites. Meanwhile, following in the footsteps of Dionysius, or rather of Paul and Hierotheus <note>Hierotheus was the legendary teacher of Dionysius the Areopagite.</note> whom he followed, we shall attempt, despite our weakness, to bring light into the "darkness of the law" which the Spirit of God, the author of the law, made his "hiding place." <note>A reference to Psalm 18:11. Pico implies that the literal text of the Torah hides divine light in its "darkness."</note>

---

### CHAPTER ONE.

**W**hatever exists after unity is a number, perfected and completed by unity. Unity alone is altogether simple; being perfect in itself, it does not go out from itself but clings to itself in indivisible and solitary simplicity, because it is sufficient to itself, lacking nothing, full of its own riches. Since number is by its nature a multitude, it becomes simple by the benefit of unity, so far as it is capable of simplicity. However, the further any number is from unity, the greater the multitude into which it falls, and the more there is in it of dissimilarity, parts, and composition. Nevertheless, no number is so close to unity that it is not a multitude, possessing an accidental unity—one not by nature, but by composition. Let us transfer these things to divine matters in the Pythagorean manner. God alone, who is from no one, from whom are <meta>Catchword "sunt" (are) indicates the sentence continues on the next page.</meta>

<meta>This page continues Pico's philosophical commentary on the Book of Genesis, specifically examining the creation of the "Angelic World." He is currently explaining how the metaphysical properties of angels relate to the opening verses of the Bible.</meta>

<page-num>24</page-num>

in God, all things are an entirely simple and indivisible essence; whatever He has, He has from Himself. By the same reality that He exists, by that same reality He knows, He wills, is good, and is just. We cannot understand Him as being any thing other than the very act of *being* <note>Latin: "ipsum esse." Pico uses this Scholastic term to describe God as existence itself, rather than a thing that merely possesses existence.</note> which He is. Other things are not that *being* itself, but they exist by means of it. Therefore, an angel is not unity itself; otherwise, it would be God, or there would be many gods, which is a concept that cannot even be conceived. For what will be one if unity itself is not one? 

It remains, then, that an angel is a "number." <note>In the Pythagorean and Platonic tradition Pico follows, "number" refers to a composite of Unity (the divine) and Multiplicity (the created).</note> But if it is a number, it is, in another part of itself, a unified multiplicity. Every number is imperfect insofar as it is a multiplicity, but perfect insofar as it is one. Therefore, let us ascribe whatever is imperfect in the angel to the angelic multiplicity—which it has from the fact that it is a "number," that is, a creature—and let us ascribe whatever is perfect to the approaching unity, which it has from the fact that it is joined to God. 

We find a twofold imperfection in the angel: First, because it is not *being* itself, but only an essence to which *being* happens by participation so that it may exist. Second, because it is not the act of understanding itself, but it happens to it that it understands; for the angel is by its own nature an intellect capable of understanding. The second imperfection depends on the first, since that which does not exist of itself certainly does not understand of itself, since nothing can exist there where *being* itself is not. Both of these, therefore, happen to the angel insofar as it is a multiplicity. It remains for its perfection and completion to come from the unity descending from above. Now, God is that Unity, from whom being, life, and every perfection are derived unto the angel. 

Furthermore, just as the imperfection is twofold—like a double multiplicity—so let us understand a twofold approach of unity, so that both may be perfected. The first is that in which the essence is raw and formless, devoid of life and being; this is the "earth without form and void" <note>Genesis 1:2.</note> which God also created. You might not have believed (as some have believed) that the "forming" of essence belongs to the Craftsman <note>Pico uses "Opificem," a term for God as the Architect or Creator, common in Platonic philosophy.</note> but not the "creation" itself. Simultaneously with the earth, He created "heaven," that is, the act of that essence and the participated unity within the multiplicity—which is *being* itself. Thus, the creation of heaven and earth is, as it were, the same creation, seeing as it is a companion-embrace of two natures coming together toward the same thing by a similar bond. Nor do we speak out of harmony with the ancients when we call *being*—the participation in divinity—by the name "heaven," since Xenophanes called the archetypal world a "sphere," <note>Xenophanes of Colophon (c. 570–475 BC) was a Greek philosopher who famously described God as a single, eternal, and spherical being.</note> and the Saracens <note>A term used in the Renaissance to refer to Muslim scholars and philosophers.</note>—and indeed our own people—call God a "circle."

### CHAPTER TWO.

By these things we have said, the angel has now perfectly attained its nature and its intellectual property. Nevertheless, it does not yet have the means to fulfill its duties of understanding—namely, of contemplating—unless it is first clothed by God with "intelligible forms." <note>In Scholastic philosophy, an "intelligible form" is the mental concept or "image" that allows an intellect to actually perceive a truth.</note> Therefore, "darkness was still over the face of the abyss." The "abyss" is the intellectual property, penetrating and searching into all deep things. Over this, there is "darkness" until it is illuminated by the rays of spiritual notions by which it sees and looks upon all things. It is written, however, "over the face of the abyss," not "over the abyss," because the same place holds both darkness and light.

But light—that is, intelligible forms <term>intelligible forms: the mental concepts or "species" that exist in the mind of an angel</term>—occupies the "face," which refers to the outermost parts of the angelic intellect. These are accidental to it, for these qualities do not belong to its actual essence. What comes between them, before the darkness is driven away and light arises, the text immediately adds, saying: *and the spirit of the Lord moved over the waters.* <note>Latin: "et spiritus domini ferebatur super aquas." Pico is quoting Genesis 1:2.</note>

What could the Spirit of the Lord be, if not the spirit of love? For we would not call the spirit of knowledge the "Spirit of the Lord" in such a proper sense, since knowledge sometimes leads away from God, but love always leads toward God. Unless this spirit is carried over that abyss, light will not be made. For just as the eye will not be filled with light unless it is turned toward the sun, so the angel is not filled with spiritual light unless it is turned toward God. 

This movement of "conversion" <note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, "conversion" (conversio) is the process by which a created thing turns back toward its source, God, to receive its perfection.</note> is not, nor can it be anything else in angelic nature, than a movement of love. Therefore, the Spirit of the Lord was a loving spirit over the abyss—that is, over the angelic intellect—for love follows understanding. Through this movement and awakening, the angel's mind is turned toward God. *God said: Let there be light, and light was made*—light in the angel, namely, the light of intelligible forms. *And there was one day from evening and morning*, because as Averroës <note>original: "Auerrois." The 12th-century Andalusian philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> proves, a greater unity is formed from the intellect and the object of intellection than from matter and form. As he affirms, and as Moses the Egyptian <note>original: "Moses Aegyptius." Referring to Maimonides, the influential 12th-century Jewish philosopher.</note> also writes, this is found to be far truer in angels than in man. Leaving them aside, let this reason be sufficient for us: that the intelligible forms are joined to the angelic mind by an indivisible bond, not—as happens in the human intellect—in a wandering and temporary way, but united by everlasting ties.

# CHAPTER THREE.

We have seen the nature of the angel created by God, and that same nature turned toward God by the spirit of love, then illuminated by Him and perfected by the light of intelligible reasons. Let us see now in what order the angelic hosts are distinguished among themselves. 

We read that a *firmament was placed in the midst of the waters*, where three angelic hierarchies (for so we shall always call them by the accustomed name) are indicated to us. The first and last of these are designated by the "waters": the former by the super-celestial waters, the latter by those which are beneath the heavens; the middle one, dividing them, is called the "firmament." If we weigh the nature and duties of the three hierarchies, all these things could not be more in harmony with the doctrine of Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a theologian whose "Celestial Hierarchy" defined the nine choirs of angels.</note>. 

The highest hierarchy, since (as he writes) it is free for contemplation alone, is deservedly represented by the waters which are above the heavens—that is, set above every action concerning worldly things, whether celestial or earthly—and they praise God incessantly with a perennial sound. The middle order, however, since it is assigned to celestial duties, could not be more fittingly signified than by the firmament, that is, by the heavens. 

The lowest hierarchy, although by nature it is above every physical body and above the heavens, nevertheless cares for those things which are below the heavens. And since it is divided into Principalities, Archangels, and Angels, the operation of all these is only concerning those things which are beneath the Moon: the Principalities concern republics, kings, and princes (as we learn from Daniel), and the Archangels concern mysteries...

### CHAPTER FOUR ###

**W**hat it might mean, however, for the waters under the heaven to be gathered into one place, would perhaps be doubtful if Paul did not declare it to us. In his writings, regarding these angels who are sent to perform the duties of this world, we read that they are *all ministering spirits sent to serve for the sake of those who receive the inheritance of salvation.* <note>Latin: "omnes administratorios spiritus in ministeriū missos propter eos qui hæreditatem capiunt salutis." This is a reference to Hebrews 1:14.</note> From this we can understand these "waters under the heavens"—that is, the angelic armies—as being gathered together to one place: namely, for the procurement of the good and salvation of a single man. It is for this reason they are sent to us and appear to us, sometimes during rest, sometimes while we are awake, in various forms, places, and times.

How this opinion is to be understood we shall finally recognize once we turn our attention to how what Moses says is true—namely, that the waters were gathered into one place. For this is not true in the sense that waters are not found in distinct and separate places, since the Indian Sea is separated from the Hyrcanian, the Hyrcanian from the Adriatic, the Adriatic from the Euxine <note>The "Euxine" is the ancient name for the Black Sea.</note>, and furthermore, the very long flows of countless rivers, springs, and lakes are separated from each other by a great distance of locations. But the waters are said to be "gathered into one place" because these particular and divided collections of waters, whether of the sea or of rivers, all (as Solomon says) tend toward the primary sea and are united and come together in the one place of the ocean. <note>original: "omnes (ut inquit Salomon) ad primarium mare tendentes in unum oceani locum uniuntur & coëunt." Reference to Ecclesiastes 1:7: "All the rivers run into the sea, yet the sea is not full."</note>

We must understand in no different way these angels who care for sublunary things <term>sublunary: literally "under the moon," referring to the earthly realm which was believed to be subject to change and decay, unlike the eternal heavens</term>. For different angels preside over different physical things and other matters concerning man. For just as the Platonists believed, so also our own teachers have believed that various spiritual substances were set by God over the various things of this corruptible world. On this point, Augustine asserts that there is no visible thing among us which is not presided over by an angelic power, and that all bodies are constantly ruled through a rational spirit of life; this is a point which Gregory later confirmed. Origen likewise, in his commentaries on the book of Numbers, says that the world needs angels who preside over beasts and the births of animals, and also over the growth of shrubs, plantations, and other things. Being of this same opinion, Damascene <note>John of Damascus (c. 675–749 AD), a key monk and theologian in the Eastern Orthodox tradition.</note> believed that the angel who sinned was from among those of the most lowly rank who preside over the terrestrial order. 

But just as all these things beneath man are referred to man, so also all the care of the angels concerning these things is primarily a handmaid and servant to the labor and study of caring for human affairs. By aiding our weakness, they ensure—to the extent that we ourselves allow—that we live our lives piously and happily. Therefore, Moses immediately added what that "gathering of waters" intended: *that the earth might bring forth fruit, herbs, and plants, and trees.* <note>Genesis 1:11.</note> But what is this "earth" other than that about which it is written in the Gospel—

...in the Gospel, because some earth produces fruit a hundredfold, some sixtyfold, and some thirtyfold? <note>original: "fructum centesimum, alia sexagesimum, alia trigesimum." A reference to the Parable of the Sower in Matthew 13:8.</note> This is surely the earth of our soul, concerning which Paul spoke these words: *For the earth that drinks in the rain often falling on it and produces a crop useful to those for whom it is farmed receives the blessing of God. And let us hear the Father saying: *Behold, the smell of my son is as the smell of a full field which the Lord has blessed.* <note>Genesis 27:27.</note> Nor should anyone wonder that "heaven and earth" signify one thing to us on the first day, while "the firmament and the dry land" signify something else now. This is something we have also observed in the books of earlier writers, for both <term>Origen</term> and <term>Basil</term><note>Origen of Alexandria and Basil of Caesarea, prominent early Christian theologians who wrote extensively on the creation story (the Hexameron).</note> and many others maintain that in Moses' writing, "heaven and earth" on the first day are different from the "dry land" and "firmament" of the second day.

### CHAPTER FIVE

**T**he celestial virtues also favor this earth of ours. For the Sun, the Moon, and the stars are placed in the firmament to illuminate our earth. See how aptly these things correspond to the <term>Dionysian mysteries</term><note>Refers to the works of Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, whose "Celestial Hierarchy" defined the nine orders of angels. Pico uses "mysteries" to mean deep spiritual truths.</note>. We have already spoken of the lowest hierarchy, which is delegated to care for the things under the Moon—that is, human affairs. Now we treat the middle hierarchy, to which the administration of the heavens is entrusted. Nor should we similarly expect to hear of the third hierarchy, of which nothing more need be said beyond what has been stated: namely, that it is "above the heavens"—that is, above all movement of action and above the administration of all worldly things, being devoted solely to contemplation.

In this place, let us not think it forced or foreign to the Sacred Scriptures that he calls "the Sun and the Moon" not the stars we see, but the <term>angelic virtues</term> that are the rulers of the Sun and Moon. For even when Scripture calls a man a "son of God" through grace, it does not mean this fragile and falling man we see, but the one who rules this very man whom we see. And in the history of the Kings, we read (according to the Hebrew learning) that Solomon prayed in these words: *Hear, O heaven,* where he addresses not the physical sky, but God, the ruler and Lord of heaven and earth. So too in this place, when we hear of the Sun and the stars, let us understand them not as celestial bodies, but as the angels who preside over those bodies. Though they are themselves invisible, they illuminate an invisible earth—namely, the substance of our soul. 

Nor was it said haphazardly or in a common way that they were ordained "to illuminate." Rather, it was said so appropriately and so in harmony with what we have brought forward, that our exposition is most strongly proven here, if from nowhere else. For since (as Dionysius teaches) there are three angelic actions—<term>purgation</term>, <term>illumination</term>, and <term>perfection</term>—they are distributed such that the lowest order purges, the highest order perfects, and this middle order, which we are discussing now, illuminates. Therefore, the lower waters purge our earth, whence it comes into view as "clean"; the celestial powers...

<summary>Pico interprets the "earth" of Genesis as the human soul and explains how the middle rank of angels—symbolized by the Sun, Moon, and stars—acts to "illuminate" human reason and virtue.</summary>

->Ioan. Pici Mirandulæ<- <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</note>

...celestial beings illuminate. The <term>super-celestial beings</term><note>The highest ranks of angels or divine influences that exist beyond the physical heavens.</note> perfect and make us fruitful by a certain fiery and life-giving dew, often to such great happiness that the soul germinates not just healing herbs, but the Savior himself; thus, not just one single virtue, but Christ—the fullness of all virtues—is formed within us.

### CHAPTER SIX.

It follows that a multitude of inhabitants are produced from the elements: fish, birds, and beasts. Here, I would certainly have been held in great distress—more so than anywhere else in this whole work of ours—if <term>Isaiah</term><note>The biblical prophet; Pico refers to the vision of Seraphim in Isaiah 6.</note> were not at hand, in whose writings we read of the winged Seraphim. It is the same with <term>Ezekiel</term><note>The prophet Ezekiel describes "living creatures" with various faces (man, lion, ox, eagle) in Ezekiel 1.</note>, in whose writings (if we believe the Hebrew commentators) both "birds" and "beasts" also indicate spiritual substances to us. I would be lost if the ancient Hebrew scholars did not run to my aid, for they all maintain that the angelic multitude is hinted at by Moses in this passage. 

Let us say, therefore, following in their footsteps, that the Prophet Moses here refutes the error of the philosophers. These philosophers believed that there are indeed certain primary <term>intellectual substances</term><note>Pure minds or spirits without physical bodies; in this context, the primary angels.</note>, but they denied that each of them (as the theologians say) presides over a subsequent, numerous multitude, like generals presiding over legions. 

Therefore, when we think of the nine angelic orders, and that each order has been assigned its own leader, let us imagine in our minds that leader and prince as a "greatest sphere." Then, let us imagine the following army as the inhabitants and ornament of that sphere—just as we think of fish in the water, birds in the air, beasts on the land, and stars in the <term>eighth sphere</term><note>In the ancient model of the universe, this was the layer of the heavens containing the fixed stars.</note>. Then that saying of Daniel will be true: *ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him, and a thousand thousands ministered to him.* <note>original: "decies millia assistebant ei..." from Daniel 7:10.</note>

### CHAPTER SEVEN.

Lastly, he [Moses] mentions man. This is not because man is an angel, but because he is the end and boundary of the angelic world. In the same way, when Moses dealt with <term>corruptible nature</term><note>The physical world where things are born, age, and die.</note>, he also introduced man—not as a mere part of that nature, but as its principle and head. 

Thus it happens that the study of man pertains to three worlds: to the world that is his own, and to both "incorporeal extremes"—namely, the elemental world and the angelic world. Man is the middle point between these, such that he stands as the end of the one and the beginning of the other. 

But I see a trap prepared for our interpretation, since the text adds that man "rules over" the fish of the sea, the birds, and the beasts. For if those animals signify the angelic nature to us (as argued in the previous chapter), how can it be true that man rules over them? Both the philosophers know, and the Prophet testifies, that man is "lessened from the angels." <note>A reference to Psalm 8:5: "You have made him a little lower than the angels."</note> 

May He be present with us and break this trap, He who also crushed Satan under our feet: Jesus Christ, the firstborn of every creature. He certainly breaks the trap and unties every knot. For not only in Him—in whom the whole divinity dwelt bodily—was human nature so exalted that the man Christ, insofar as he is man (if we believe <term>Dionysius</term><note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential mystical theologian who wrote on the celestial hierarchies.</note>), teaches, illuminates, and perfects the angels. He was made (as Paul says) *so much better than the angels, as he has inherited a more excellent name than they.* <note>original: "tanto melior angelis effectus..." from Hebrews 1:4.</note> But also all of us, to whom power was given to become sons of God through grace (of which Christ is the giver), can be raised above angelic dignity.

<summary>Pico explains that the "animals" created in Genesis allegorically represent the vast hierarchies of angels. He further argues that although man is naturally lower than angels, through the grace of Christ, human nature is elevated to a position of leadership and dignity over the angelic realm.</summary>

# On the human world, that is, on the nature
### of man. The fourth exposition, Book IV. Introduction.

After we have sufficiently shown that the prophet <note>original: "propheta"; Pico refers to Moses as the author of Genesis.</note> treated all parts of the world—of every celestial, angelic, and corruptible nature—it remains (if we are mindful of our promise) to interpret the entire reading once again regarding man. We shall prove by this very fact that there is no passage in this entire work which does not embrace hidden meanings and the highest truths regarding the nature of man, just as it did regarding the three worlds discussed above. We will have performed a task no less worthwhile if we are diligent in explaining this fourth exposition than we were in the previous ones. For how useful and how necessary self-knowledge is for man (to say nothing of the <term>Delphic inscription</term><note>original: "literam delphicam"; referring to the famous Greek maxim "Know Thyself" (Gnothi Seauton) inscribed on the temple at Delphi.</note>), it was so demonstrated by **Plato** in the first *Alcibiades* that he left nothing for those who came after him to attempt to bring as if it were new on this matter. And indeed, the pursuit of that man is wicked and rash who, still ignorant of himself and still not knowing if he can know anything, yet boldly affects the knowledge of things that are so far from him. 

Let us therefore return into ourselves and let us see (as the Prophet says) what great things God has done for our soul. Lest perhaps, if the soul should be less diligent in recognizing itself, it should hear the Father saying in the *Song of Songs*: <note>original: "in Canticis"</note> "If you know not, O most beautiful of women, go forth and depart after the footsteps of your flocks." <note>Song of Solomon 1:8. Pico uses this to warn that the soul which does not know its own dignity falls to the level of animals.</note> You see what punishment for our ignorance awaits us. For we must depart from the Father, namely, an exile which disinheritance follows—and what could be more unhappy? We must also go out, specifically from ourselves. For the soul is not with itself if it does not see itself. But he who goes out from himself is torn away from himself—and what could be more bitter? Thirdly, we must go after the footsteps of our flocks, that is, after the tracks of the **brutes** which are within us (of which we shall say enough in the exposition)—and what could be more miserable? What more despicable and contemptible than to become the attendants of the beasts over which nature had appointed us leaders? Therefore, let us walk not after the footsteps of the brutes, but after those of **Moses**; let us enter into ourselves; let us enter the inner chambers of the soul with the Prophet himself opening the way for us, so that within ourselves we may happily recognize both all the worlds and the Father and our homeland.

---

### CHAPTER ONE.

Before we arrange the exposition more accurately according to the words and order of the prophet, it is necessary to say something beforehand about the nature of man, and to explain some terms in passing, so that the understanding of the entire meaning may then be clearer. Man consists of a body and a **rational soul**. The <term>rational soul</term><note>original: "Rationalis animus"; the part of the soul capable of logic and understanding, distinct from the animal soul.</note> is called "heaven." For **Aristotle** calls heaven a living being moved by itself, and our soul (as the **Platonists** prove) is a substance moving itself. Heaven is a circle, and the soul is likewise a circle; indeed, as **Plotinus** writes, heaven is a circle for the reason that its soul is a circle. Heaven is moved in a circuit...
