<meta>This page continues Book IV of the Heptaplus, where Pico della Mirandola provides a "microcosmic" interpretation of the Book of Genesis. Having established that man is a "fourth world" containing all the levels of the universe, he now maps specific psychological and physiological components—reason, spirit, and body—onto the first verses of the creation story. The previous page ended mid-sentence discussing how man's nature mirrors the cosmos; this page begins with the completion of that thought regarding the movement of the rational soul.</meta>

->Giovanni Pico della Mirandola<-

the rational soul, transferring itself from causes to effects, and again returning from effects back into causes, revolves in a circle of reasoning. And indeed, if these things had to be explained individually to those who have not read them elsewhere, we would now be interpreters of **Aristotle** and **Plato**, rather than of **Moses**. The body is called "earth," since it is of an earthy and heavy substance. For this reason, Moses writes that it was made from the ground <note>original: "humo"; Pico is playing on the Latin etymology where *homo* (man) is derived from *humus* (earth/ground).</note>, giving man his name. 

Truly, between the earthy body and the celestial substance of the soul, a middle link was necessary to couple such distant natures together. Assigned to this duty is that thin and spiritual "little body" <note>original: "corpusculum"</note> which both doctors and philosophers call the **spirit** <term>spirit (spiritus)</term><note>In Renaissance medicine and philosophy, "spirit" was a literal, subtle vapor that acted as a bridge between the immaterial soul and the physical flesh.</note>. Aristotle writes that this spirit is of a more divine nature than the elements and corresponds proportionately to the heavens; here it is called **light**. This name could not be more suited to the opinion of philosophers and doctors, for the common consensus of them all is that the spirit is a most lucid substance, and rejoices in, is nourished by, and is recreated by nothing more than by light. It follows that just as every power of the heavens (as **Avicenna** writes) is transferred to the earth by the vehicle of light, so every power of the soul—which we have called "heaven"—and all the power of life, namely motion and sense, passes and is poured into this earthy body (which we have called "earth") through the mediation of the lucid spirit. 

Let us descend now to the words of the prophet <note>Moses</note>, in whose writing we see first the creation of "heaven" and "earth"—the extremes, namely, of our substance: the rational power and the earthy body. Finally, since there is "light"—that is, the more lucid spirit—they are so united that from "evening" and "morning"—that is, from the nocturnal nature of the body and the morning nature of the soul—there is **one man**. And since (as we have shown) every vital and sensory power descends to our "earth" through this light, the earth was rightly "empty and void" <note>Genesis 1:2</note> before the birth of light. For the body could not participate in the benefits of life and motion from its "heaven" except through the messenger of light. Therefore, he immediately added the cause of that emptiness: because, naturally, darkness was still over it, as the light had not yet arisen.

### CHAPTER TWO.

**B**ut it still remains to be asked what this means: *And the Spirit of the Lord was moved over the waters.* <note>Genesis 1:2</note> He hands down here an indistinct and universal doctrine concerning the "waters," which is more clearly distinguished on the following day, when he teaches that some are "above the heavens" and others are "under the heavens." If we desire the true sense of all these things, let us consult nature itself, which our prophet (as we have often said) portrays and represents with the utmost precision. We have seen mention made of a threefold part of the human substance: namely, the rational, this mortal body, and the middle spirit. Two parts remain: for between the rational part by which we are men, and all that which is corporeal in us (whether it be thick or thin and spiritual), there is a middle **sensual part** which we share with the beasts. And since our communication with the angels is no less than our communication with the beasts, just as there is **sense** below reason (from which comes our commerce with the animals), so above reason there is **intelligence**, through which...

<summary>Pico allegorically identifies the "heaven," "earth," and "light" of Genesis as the human soul, body, and intermediary "spirit," explaining how they combine to form a single human being. He begins to analyze the "waters" of Genesis as representing the sensual and intellectual faculties that connect man to beasts and angels.</summary>

--- Page 66 ---
<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's microcosmic interpretation of Genesis in the Heptaplus. He is currently mapping the "waters" of the creation story onto the internal faculties of the human soul, specifically distinguishing between the rational intellect and the sensory powers.</meta>

->Heptaplus<-

we can say that of John: *Our fellowship is with the angels.* <note>original: "Societas nostra cum angelis est"; cf. 1 John 1:3.</note> You see what is below and what is above our reason. And if reason is called "heaven" (as we have proved), it is now manifest which are the **waters above the heavens** in us, and which are likewise the **waters below the heavens**. The name "waters" fits both the intellectual and the sensual parts, but for different reasons: the former because it is most permeable to the rays of divine illumination; the latter because it gasps for and delights in fleeting and flowing things. Moses sufficiently warns us of this diversity when he places these waters under the heaven, where all things are flowing and transient, and the others above the heaven, where there is the administration of pure and perpetual intelligence.

Therefore, when we read that on the first day the **Spirit of the Lord** <note>original: "spiritum Domini"</note> hovered over the waters, and since the waters are divided into two parts, we should certainly not take this as being said of those waters under the heaven, for over these it is not the Spirit of the Lord but rather the "heaven" <note>Here meaning the faculty of Reason.</note> that is carried. It remains, then, that this was said of those waters which are **above the heaven**. From this, a great dogma concerning the soul is unlocked for us. For the intellect which is in us is illuminated by a greater and indeed divine intellect—whether that be God (as some wish), or a mind close and kindred to man (as almost all the Greeks, the Arabs, and many of the Hebrews wish). This substance both the Jewish philosophers and **Abunafar Al-Farabi** <note>Also known as Alpharabius (c. 872–950 AD), a renowned philosopher of the Islamic Golden Age.</note>, in the book he wrote on principles, called the "Spirit of the Lord" in express words. Nor was it done without cause that Moses mentioned this thing—that is, the hovering of the Spirit over the waters—before he had established man from the bond of light, soul, and body. It was done lest we should happen to believe that this Spirit is not present to our intellect unless it were coupled to a body. This is what **Moses the Egyptian** <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent Jewish philosopher.</note>, **Abubacer the Arab** <note>Ibn Tufail (c. 1105–1185), author of the philosophical novel *Hayy ibn Yaqdhan*.</note>, and certain others falsely believed.

### CHAPTER THREE.

**I**t remains for us to explain what he means when he says the **waters which are under the heaven**—that is, the sensual powers which are under the rational part—are "gathered into one place." This is very clear to those not entirely unrefined in philosophy. For all the sensitive powers flow together toward the faculty which, from its actual function, we call the **common sense** <term>common sense (sensus communis)</term><note>In medieval and Renaissance psychology, this was an internal faculty that combined the data from the five external senses into a single coherent perception.</note>. This faculty, if we follow **Aristotle**, is located in the heart, just as rivers flow together into the sea. 

Nor would it be absurd to say that from that "sea," the five bodily senses which we see—hearing, sight, taste, touch, and smell—are spread out like five "Mediterranean seas" within the continent of the body. This was the clearly expressed opinion in **Plato's** *Theaetetus*. And since from the perfection of the sensitive powers—which we understand by this gathering toward their source—there comes to the body (which we call "earth") life, health, and nourishment, Moses rightly introduces the green and flowering earth immediately after that gathering of the waters. For the senses were provided by nature to all mortals to procure the life and safety of the body, so that through them they might recognize what is harmful and what is salutary; then, having recognized them through the appetite joined to the senses, they might reject the former and desire the latter; and finally, through the joined motive power, they might flee evils and pursue useful things.

<summary>Pico identifies the "waters above the heavens" as the human intellect illuminated by a divine Spirit and the "waters below" as the sensory faculties that gather into the "common sense." He argues that the intellect exists independently of the body, contrary to the views of Maimonides and Al-Farabi.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's Heptaplus, specifically his "microcosmic" interpretation where the days of creation represent the internal structure of the human being. Having previously discussed the "waters" as the sensory and intellectual faculties, he now moves to the "lights in the firmament" (Sun, Moon, and stars) and the "beasts" of the earth.</meta>

->Giovanni Pico della Mirandola<-

<note>original: "prosequantur"</note> ...pursue. The eye sees food, the nostrils smell it, the feet approach, the hands take it, and the palate experiences it. We say all these things so that we may recognize that the earth—which for a long time has signified the body to us—is aptly joined to the stability of the waters (that is, the sensory powers), representing a source of abundant happiness.

## CHAPTER FOUR

**B**ut truly, since our rational nature is distinguished by many strengths and powers, its bare substance has been discussed above. Now we must speak of its adornment and (so to speak) its royal furnishings. This is what Moses describes when he writes of the Moon, the Sun, and the stars being placed in the firmament. Indeed, the younger philosophers might perhaps interpret the **Sun** as the active intellect <note>original: "intellectum qui actu est"</note> and the **Moon** as the potential intellect <note>original: "eum qui est potentia"</note>. But since we have a great controversy with them on this matter, let us instead explain it this way: insofar as the soul turns toward the **upper waters**—that is, toward the Spirit of the Lord—it is called the **Sun** because it shines totally. However, insofar as it looks back toward the **lower waters**—that is, the sensory powers—from which it contracts some stain of infection, it takes the name of the **Moon**. 

The Greek Platonists would call the Sun, understood in this way, **discursive reason** <note>original: "διάνοιαν" (dianoia)</note>, and the Moon **opinion** <note>original: "δόξαν" (doxa)</note> according to the dogmas of their teaching. Furthermore, while we are wandering away from our true homeland, living in the night and darkness of this present life, we mostly use that part of ourselves which is turned toward the senses; hence we have more opinions than certain knowledge. But when the day of the future life dawns, turned away from the senses and toward divine things, we shall understand by that other, higher part. Thus it is rightly said that this Sun of ours rules the day, while the Moon rules the night. 

Likewise, because once we have stripped off this mortal garment, we shall behold by the single light of the Sun that which we now—in this most miserable night of the body—strive to see through many strengths and powers rather than actually seeing it. For this reason, the day shines with a single Sun, whereas the night, by contrast, gathers many stars as assistants to the less-powerful Moon—namely, the power of connecting and dividing, of reasoning, of defining, and all the rest.

## CHAPTER FIVE

**U**p to this point, we have dealt with the knowing powers of the soul. Now he transfers his attention to those whose work it is to desire—namely, the seats of anger and lust (that is, bodily desire). He designates these by the **beasts** and the irrational kind of living things, because these are common to us and the beasts, and (what is more unfortunate) they often drive us toward a brutal life. 

Hence comes that saying of the Chaldeans <note>Pico often refers to "Chaldean" oracles or ancient Middle Eastern wisdom</note>: *Beasts of the earth inhabit your vessel.* And in Plato’s *Republic*, we learn that we have various kinds of brutes within our own home, so that the Pythagorean paradox is not difficult to believe (if understood correctly): that wicked men migrate into brutes. For the brutes are inside us and so much within our own bowels that we do not have to travel far to "migrate" into them. Hence the fables of **Circe** <note>The enchantress from the Odyssey who turned men into swine</note>, and that saying of **Theocritus**: those whom the goddesses have looked upon—meaning with virtue and wisdom—cannot be undermined by Circe’s cups. But let us see...

<summary>Pico interprets the Sun and Moon as higher reason and sensory-bound opinion, and explains that the "beasts" of Genesis represent human passions and irrational desires that live within us.</summary>
<keywords>Sun and Moon, active and potential intellect, dianoia, doxa, rational soul, passions, Plato's Republic, Pythagoras, Circe, internal beasts</keywords>

--- Page 68 ---
<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's allegorical interpretation of the fifth and sixth days of creation. He moves from discussing the celestial bodies (the sun and moon of the soul) to the "living creatures" produced by the water and the earth, which he interprets as the various passions and drives within the human psyche.</meta>

->Heptaplus<-

...let us see how the reading of Moses <note>original: "Mosaica lectio"; referring to the text of Genesis</note> suggests the difference between these brute animals to us. Some are produced from the waters which are under the heavens, others from the earth. The waters, as we have said, signify the sensory part of the soul which is under the "heavens" <note>the heavens here representing the higher rational mind</note>, because it is subject to reason and serves it closely. The earth is this very earthly and fragile body by which we are surrounded. Let us consider, therefore, whether among the passions by which we are moved, some belong more to the body and others to the internal sense, which philosophers call the **imagination** <note>original: "phantasiam"</note>.

Those passions which drive us toward either food or sexual desire <note>original: "Venerem"</note> seem to me to regard the body. For these were given to us by God both for the protection of the body which we nourish, and for the procreation of children—in whom we survive even when we perish in our own selves. Yet we abuse these same gifts, attracted more than is proper by the bait of pleasure, making "provision for the flesh" (as Paul says) "in its desires." <note>A reference to Romans 13:14.</note> In his words, it should be noted that he did not say "make no provision for the flesh," but rather "not in its desires"; because, clearly, we must use these things for necessity, not for pleasure—and much less should our happiness be placed in them. 

Let us therefore understand these passions as the cattle and wild beasts, which are called the offspring of the earth rather than of the waters. This is because they are both satisfied and excited through the members of this thick, physical body, and were provided for us by God for its well-being—though they become the destruction of those who wither from gluttony or are dissolved by lust. 

On the other hand, let us refer to the waters—that is, the sense of imagination—those passions which can be called "spiritual" and the offspring of our thought rather than of our flesh. This is the kind of passion that calls us toward honors, toward anger, toward revenge, and other related emotions. These are necessary and useful for those who use them in moderation. For one must be angry, but within limits; and revenge is often a work of justice; and everyone must protect their own dignity, nor should those honors be refused which are obtained by honorable means. 

I say this so that we do not believe—along with the **Manichaeans** <note>A dualist sect that believed the physical world was created by an evil deity</note>—that because God created these "brutes" (which signify our sensory appetites) and blessed them, they are evil by their own nature or created by an evil principle rather than by the good God. All those things are therefore good and necessary for man; but we ourselves, by exceeding into ambition, fury, rage, and pride, make those things evil by our own fault which that Most High Creator had established as good.

# CHAPTER SIX

**V**iew, then, how accurately what follows agrees with what we have said: that man was made by God in His own image so that he might rule over the fish, the birds, and the beasts, which both the water and the earth had produced. Indeed, we were already discussing man above, but now for the first time we understand the "image of God" in him. 

From this comes his power and dominion over the brutes. For man was so established by nature that reason should rule the senses, and that every fury and appetite of both anger and lust should be restrained by its law. But once the image of God was wiped out by the stain of sin, we wretches began to serve our own beasts. Like the **Chaldean king** <note>original: "regi Chaldaeo"; referring to Nebuchadnezzar, who according to the Book of Daniel was humbled by God and lived like a wild animal</note>, we began to dwell among them, falling greedily upon the ground...

<summary>Pico allegorizes the animals of Genesis as human passions, distinguishing between bodily lusts (beasts of the earth) and psychological drives like ambition (creatures of the water). He argues that these are naturally good if ruled by reason, but sin causes man to lose his divine image and become a slave to these internal "beasts."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the conclusion of Book IV, where Pico reflects on the fall of man from his original dignity, and begins Book V of the Heptaplus. In Book V, Pico transitions from a general overview to a detailed, world-by-world exposition of the creation account in Genesis.</meta>

Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

...greedy for earthly things, forgotten of our fatherland, forgotten of our father, forgotten of our kingdom, and of the gifts given within us as a privilege of our former dignity. Surely "man, when he was in honor, did not understand, but was compared to the foolish beasts and made like unto them." <note>A quotation from Psalm 49:12 (Psalm 48 in the Vulgate). Pico is lamenting how humanity, by focusing only on the physical, loses its divine status.</note>

### CHAPTER SEVEN

**B**ut just as all [die] in the first Adam, who obeyed Satan more than God—whose sons according to the flesh, being deformed, we degenerate from man into brute animals—so in the last Adam, Jesus Christ, who fulfilled the will of the Father and by his blood defeated spiritual wickedness: whose sons we all are according to the spirit. Reformed through grace, we are reborn from man into the adoption of the sons of God, if only (as in Him, so in us) the prince of darkness and of this world finds nothing [of his own]. <note>Pico contrasts the biological descent from Adam (leading to "brutishness") with the spiritual rebirth through Christ.</note>

## Concerning all the worlds separately in
->their following order, the Fifth Exposition, Book V.<-
->Preface.<-

**J**ust as Moses—as we have already shown—discussed all the worlds together in every part of his text (the intellectual, the celestial, the elementary, and the human), imitating nature, or rather God, the craftsman of nature, who encompassed all worlds within each individual world; so, following the example of that same nature which distributed proper seats, proper rights, and peculiar laws to each, our prophet <note>referring to Moses as the author of Genesis</note> also, by a wonderful and truly divine mastery of art, arranged his writing so that although he discussed all things everywhere under the same appearance and the same veil of words, he nevertheless assigned individual parts of his work to the individual worlds in a following order. To show this, we shall begin to interpret the first small section concerning the first world—that is, the angelic—then subsequently the remaining sections concerning the rest, sagaciously observing in the words of Moses that golden Homeric chain <note>original: "auream illam Homericam catenam"; a classical metaphor for the "Great Chain of Being" that links the lowest physical matter to the highest divine spirit.</note> and the Platonic rings <note>A reference to Plato’s *Ion*, where divine inspiration is compared to a magnet passing its power through a series of iron rings.</note> suspended from the living power of the creator, as if from the true stone of the unconquered Hercules. <note>original: "lapide indomiti Herculis"; the "Stone of Hercules" was a common Renaissance term for the magnet or loadstone, symbolizing the attractive force of God.</note>

### CHAPTER ONE

**B**eing about to speak of the angelic nature, which is pure intellect, let us first conceive in the mind that minds are like certain eyes. For what the eye is in bodily things, that very thing is the mind in the spiritual genus. Although the eye, by the mixture of its innermost substance, possesses something of light, nevertheless, to perform the duty of vision, it requires external light in which it observes the colors and differences of things. Nor is it for that reason that its nature is not sight, even if it does not see except by the benefit of light. For even the ears—not to mention inanimate things—and all the other parts of the body are illuminated by light, yet they do not see. That, therefore, which has obtained the nature of seeing, and through the principle of its essence is sight, which having received [light]...

<meta>This page continues Pico's philosophical exposition in the Fifth Book of the Heptaplus, where he begins to interpret the first verses of Genesis as an allegory for the creation of the angelic or intellectual world.</meta>

### Heptaplus

...can see by the light. Let us consider these same things within intellects: intellects are the eyes, intelligible truth is the light, and the intellect itself, because it is intelligible, possesses something of light within its core. By this light it can see itself, but not in the same way as it sees other things. Indeed, it requires the forms of things, which it uses like certain rays of invisible light, through which intelligible truth is undoubtedly perceived. Nor should it be said for this reason—as we illustrated by the example of the eye—that those [intellects] are not intelligent by nature, or that they have obtained their intellectual property by accident, in the same condition as our own souls. From this reasoning comes the opinion of those who think the name of "intellect" is unworthy of God. For if we take the intellect to be like an eye which sees not of itself, but by participation in light, and since God is light (for truth is light), and since vision is the action by which the eye reaches the light, then God does not need this operation, as He is light itself. He is as much further removed from ignorance of all things than the angels are, as the nature of light is further from darkness than the eye is. 

But let us return to the angels. The eye—that is, the intellectual substance—is not entirely simple; otherwise, it would not be open to the composition of incoming light. Hence the common proverb that angels consist of "act" and "potency," <note>In Scholastic philosophy, "act" (actuality) is the completion or perfection of a thing, while "potency" (potentiality) is the capacity to receive that perfection.</note> although there is an anxious dispute over what that act is, what that potency is, and what the rationale of their composition might be. Likewise, there is debate over what <term>Averroes the Arab</term> <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd, 1126–1198) was an influential Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to medieval Western thought.</note> intended when he said that both intellects—the one in act and the one in potency—exist in all intellects below God. But for our purposes here, the common opinion suffices, however it may be understood. 

<term>Moses</term> <note>Pico identifies the author of Genesis as a prophet revealing deep philosophical secrets through the story of creation.</note> reveals all these things to us on the first day. For he divides the substance of the angel into "heaven" and "earth"—namely, the nature of act and the nature of potency. The same thing has different names just as it has different properties. For this reason, this same "act," insofar as it is the power granting sight to the eye and the consummation of potentiality, is called "heaven," because it stands in the same relation to potency as the heaven does to the earth. 

Conversely, insofar as it lacks light and cannot perform its own duty of intelligence by itself, it is represented by "the waters." <note>Pico interprets the "waters" of Genesis not as physical liquid, but as the receptive, fluid nature of the angelic mind before it is filled with divine ideas.</note> It is a body capable of light, yet by its own nature it is not at all luminous. There is also another reason for the comparison: this "act" of potentiality, which he calls "earth," is as close to it as water is to the earth. 

But let us now engage with the words of the prophet: *God created heaven and earth* <note>original: "Creavit Deus caelum et terram"</note>—the nature of act and the nature of potency, of which the angel consists. And *the earth*, that is, the potentiality, *was void and empty*—void of act and empty of light, which it does not receive except through the mediation of the waters. And since opposites occur around the same thing, and it pertains to the same subject to host both light and darkness, he added: *and darkness was upon the face of the abyss.* He did not say "upon the earth." For the "abyss" is nothing else (unless we misuse the word) than the depth of the waters. 

Over these waters *the spirit of the Lord was moved*—the spirit which is called the "Father of lights" by the apostle James <note>Referencing James 1:17, "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights."</note>—from whom, soon after, the light of intelligible forms arises over them, that is, over the angelic minds. Perhaps the <term>Saracens</term> <note>Pico uses this term to refer to Islamic philosophers/theologians, likely referring to their descriptions of the soul's journey or the creation of celestial beings.</note> also understood this when they said that the angels were led forth by God from darkness into light, and were filled with eternal joy. For pleasure follows understanding, and no pleasure is greater, none truer, and none more permanent.

### CHAPTER TWO. ###

**N**ext to this world <note>The "intelligible world" described on the previous page.</note> is the celestial world. Its first property is that it is the interval between both worlds: the <term>intelligible world</term>, of which we have just spoken, and this <term>sensible world</term> which we inhabit. We cannot more clearly indicate the essence of any middle nature than by expressing the extremes by which it is enclosed, since a middle nature is tempered by the extremes. Therefore, the greatest knowledge concerning the condition of the heaven is opened to us when [Scripture] says that the middle heaven is placed "between waters and waters" <note>original: "inter aquas & aquas"</note>—that is, between angelic and corruptible substances—not so much by reason of its physical position as by its essence. Moreover, we have already said that by "waters" we are to understand forms which are present, as it were, next to potentiality, and which perfect the essence. However, just as the "earth" of the angels is one thing and the "earth" of the elements another, because the potentiality in each is different, so too the nature of the "waters"—that is, of the forms—is different in each place. Between these truly lies the middle heaven; by the disposition of the Maker's providence, it has received on one side divine life, and on the other embodiment; on one side incorruptible substance, and on the other visible substance; on one side the firmness of essence, and on the other change of place; on one side whatever is simple and uniform, and on the other whatever is varied, mixed, and dissimilar.

### CHAPTER THREE. ###

**A**fter these things, he briefly reminds us of the integrity, position, and order of the elements through the "gathering of the waters into one place" and the laws prescribed for the sea so that it might not overwhelm the earth. For there is nothing that more clearly indicates that laws have been implanted in the elements by an intelligent cause—by which they are both ruled and held in their places—beyond the natural inclination of their corporeal and brute nature, than these barriers of the waters. By these, the ocean is restrained; though its impetus would carry it across the entire circuit of the earth (just as the whole of fire rests upon the whole of the air), yet, as if "admonished by the rod of a tutor," it draws back its foot and does not advance further than our safety and the life of all living creatures requires. This can be referred neither to the necessity of matter (which would rather incline all elements equally toward a spherical shape), nor to a "fortuitous collision of atoms" <note>A reference to the materialist philosophy of Epicurus.</note> such as Epicurus dreams of, nor to the "blind generative force of nature" <note>original: "uim fœminariam naturae." Pico refers here to Strato of Lampsacus, who argued that the world was governed by unconscious natural forces rather than a divine mind.</note> as Strato says, which is ignorant of any purpose. Instead, it must be referred to the final cause alone, which only a mind and intellectual providence can direct. For this reason, it happened that Moses, when about to treat the order of the elements, mentioned only this matter here, and why this is so often brought forward by the Prophets as the most powerful argument for divine power and wisdom. Hence in Proverbs: "when He fortified the depths with a certain law and circle"; <note>Proverbs 8:27</note> and elsewhere: "He who surrounded the sea with its boundary"; <note>Proverbs 8:29</note> and in Jeremiah: "Will you not fear me, says the Lord, who have placed the sand as a limit for the sea?" <note>Jeremiah 5:22</note> And also: "You have set a boundary which they shall not pass over, nor shall they cover the earth." <note>Psalm 104:9</note> Since, however, the entire constitution of the elements is being ordered—especially with the addition of those things which are alive—therefore, after the ordering and firmament of the earth and waters, he immediately added the command to the earth, that it should ger- <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "ger-" for "germinet" (germinate/sprout).</note>

# CHAPTER FOUR. #

**A**fter he dealt with the celestial and elementary sphere, and therefore with the entire integrity of the corporeal universe, it remained to speak of the inhabitants and citizens, so to speak, of this mundane city along with the celestial beings. These should be treated first, as if they were the senate and prefects of the city, and then the terrestrial beings, as if they were the common people and the populace. He first mentions the celestial beings, which God placed in the firmament to be <term>signs and seasons</term> <note>Genesis 1:14</note>, to shine in the sky and illuminate the earth. I speak of the Sun, the Moon, and the stars. At this point, the most profound questions ought to be treated—each of which would demand a full volume of its own—such as in what manner these stars exist in the firmament: whether they are its "nobler parts," as the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>The followers of Aristotle, who believed stars were concentrated parts of the celestial spheres.</note> feel, or whether they are like animals in their own spheres, as fish are in water or beasts are on the earth, which *Eusebius* and *Diodorus* maintain. Here also, the subject would demand a confrontation with the <term>genethliacs</term> <note>Astrologers who cast birth charts to predict the future.</note>, who confirm their science of divining by the stars and foreknowing future events from this passage, because *Moses* said the stars were placed by God as "signs." This science is not only sharply criticized by our own writers—such as *Basil*, who rightly called it "busy vanity," and by *Apollinaris*, *Cyril*, and *Diodorus*—but it is even rejected by the good Peripatetics, and was held in contempt by *Aristotle*. What is more, *Theodoret* is the authority for the fact that it was repudiated by *Pythagoras*, *Plato*, and all the *Stoics*. It might also seem to some that we should inquire here into the nature of the stars, their motion, their dominion, the spots on the Moon, and all the science of the stars. But if we were to descend into these matters, though they are beautiful and worthy of being known, we would perhaps hear that line of *Horace*:
> But now was not the place for these. <note>original: "Sed nunc non erat his locus." — Horace, Ars Poetica, line 19.</note>
Therefore, we defer these matters to the work we have destined for this purpose, in which, reconciling the <term>Platonists</term> with *Aristotle*, we have undertaken to treat and examine the whole of philosophy according to our strength.

# CHAPTER FIVE. #

**L**et us come, therefore, to *Moses*, who after he spoke of the celestial beings, mentions the terrestrial animals in a fitting order—those which inhabit either the waters, the earth, or the air (if indeed birds can be said to "inhabit" the air). Let no one here expect or demand from us a disputation on how the bodies of animals are formed from the elements, or what those <term>seminal reasons</term> <note>The "seeds" or latent potentiality implanted by God into nature to bring forth life.</note> are which were implanted by God into the natures of things; nor whether the life of "brutes" <note>Non-human animals, distinguished here by their lack of rational intellect.</note> is drawn out from the bosom of matter, or whether all life proceeds rather from a divine principle. The latter is most constantly asserted by *Plotinus*, whom our friend *Marsilio Ficino* will soon give to the public for the common good, to be read in Latin, illuminated by even longer arguments. Perhaps the Prophet <note>Pico refers to Moses as "the Prophet."</note> will seem to support this opinion in this passage, for after he said, "Let the waters bring forth the creeping thing with a living soul," he added afterward, "God created every living soul." Here, one should not merely observe that the waters bring them forth at God’s command, and then God Himself also produces them. But there is also this...

Then there are **cattle** (or beasts of burden), which, although they lack reason, are nonetheless capable of human discipline in some way; because they seem to participate in something of reason, they have been granted a middle condition between brutes and men.

### CHAPTER SIX.

**H**itherto we have dealt with the three worlds: the super-celestial, the celestial, and the sublunary <note>Pico’s cosmology divided the universe into the realm of God/Angels (super-celestial), the Stars/Planets (celestial), and the Earth (sublunary).</note>. Now we must deal with **Man**, of whom it is written: *Let us make man in our image*. Man is not so much a "fourth world," as if he were some new creature, but rather the complexity and the binding together of the three worlds we have already described. It is a custom often used by the kings and princes of the earth that, if they happen to have founded a magnificent and noble city, once the city is finished, they place their own image in the center of it, to be seen and admired by all. We see that God, the Prince of all, did exactly the same: once the entire machinery of the world was constructed, He placed man last of all in the center of it, formed after His own image and likeness.

But it is a difficult question why this privilege of being the "image of God" belongs to man. For if we reject the exploded insanity of *Melito* <note>Melito of Sardis (2nd century AD) was a bishop accused of "Anthropomorphism," the belief that God possesses a physical human body.</note>, who depicted God in a human form, and instead return to the nature of the reason and the mind—which, like God, is intelligent, invisible, and incorporeal—we would certainly prove from this that man is like God, especially in that part of the soul where the image of the Trinity is represented. 

However, we must recognize that these same qualities are found in the angels to a much greater degree than in us: they are more powerful, and they are mixed with less of the contrary nature (matter). Thus, they possess more similarity and kinship with the divine nature than we do. We are looking for something *peculiar* to man: something from which his own proper dignity and his unique status as the image of the divine substance might be found—a status shared with no other creature. What else can this be, other than that the substance of man (as some Greek interpreters also suggest) encompasses in itself the substances of all natures and the fullness of the entire universe? I say "in itself," because while angels and every intelligent creature contain all things in a certain way—being full of the forms and reasons of all things they know—man does so differently. For just as God is the "image" not only because He understands all things, but because He unites and collects in Himself the entire perfection of the true substance of things, so too does man—though in a different way, as we shall show; otherwise he would not be the image of God...

...image, but if he were God) he would summon and unite to the integrity of his own substance all the natures of the entire world. This we can say of no other creature, whether angelic, celestial, or perceptible to the senses. But there is this difference between God and man: God contains all things in Himself as the source of all; man contains all things in himself as the center of all. From this it happens that in God all things are of a better quality than in themselves, while in man, lower things are in a nobler condition, but higher things degenerate. 

Fire, water, air, and earth are present by the truest property of their nature in this thick and earthly body of man which we see. Besides these, there is another, more divine **spiritual body** <note>original: "spiritale aliud corpus diuinius". Pico refers to the "pneuma," a subtle substance that Renaissance thinkers believed connected the physical body to the immortal soul.</note> (as Aristotle says) which is proportional to the heavens. There is, moreover, in man the life of plants, performing for him all the same functions as for them: nourishing, growing, and reproducing. There is the sense of the beasts, both internal and external. There is a soul from heaven, excelling in reason. There is a participation in the **angelic mind**. There is the truly divine possession of all these natures flowing together into one, so that one might like to cry out that saying of Hermes: <note>original: "Mercury". Pico refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage thought to be the author of the Hermetic Corpus.</note> "**A great miracle, O Asclepius, is man**." 

Human nature can boast in this name above all, and by this it has come to pass that no created substance disdains to serve him. To him the earth and elements are ready and serve; for him the beasts are at hand and follow; for him the heavens fight; for him the angelic minds procure safety and good, if indeed it is true what Paul writes: *that they are all ministering spirits sent forth to serve for the sake of those who are destined for the inheritance of salvation.* <note>Hebrews 1:14</note> Nor should it seem a wonder to anyone that he is loved by all, in whom all things recognize something of their own—indeed, recognize themselves and all their own entirely.

### CHAPTER SEVEN.

**E**arthly things are enslaved to man, and heavenly things favor man, because he is the **bond and knot** of both celestial and terrestrial things. Neither can fail to have peace with him, provided he has peace with himself, for he is the one who ratifies the peace and treaties of both within himself. But let us take care, I pray, that being placed in such great dignity we do not fail to understand: let us always keep that truth before the eyes of our mind as a certain, explored, and indubitable truth: that just as all things favor us when we keep the law given to us, so if through sin and the transgression of the law we fall away from our course, we shall have all things adverse, hostile, and inimical. 

For it is reasonable that, just as we do injury not only to ourselves, but to the entire universe that we embrace within us, and to the author of the world Himself, the omnipotent God, we should also experience all things in the world—and God first of all—as most powerful avengers and most heavy punishers of the injury received. From this let us estimate what punishments and tortures await the transgressors of the divine law. These are they who (as the oracle said): **demons who wander with foot on earth and foot on sea, untiringly they are tamed under the lash of God** <note>original Greek: "δαίμονες οἳ φοιτῶσι ποδὶ χθόνα κὴ ποδὶ πόντον ἀκάματοι δαμάνανται ὑπὸ τῦ μασίγι θεόιο". This is a quote from the Chaldean Oracles, ancient mystical texts highly valued by Neoplatonists.</note>, that is, who proceed about the earth and about the sea, and are untiringly subdued under the whip of God; these the heavens, these the earth, these the unshaken justice of the whole worldly commonwealth...

strikes and pursues them. For they are guilty of violating the universe and wounding the divine majesty, whose image they have defiled with the foulest stain of iniquity. This is perhaps why, among the Prophets, whenever something is promulgated by God as either a command or a prohibition, heaven and earth are summoned as witnesses. This is because the transgression of that command violates them as well; having received a common insult, they too will participate in punishing the wicked while they serve as the ministers of God’s justice. It altogether exceeds every kind of madness to believe that someone placed in a city and decorated with the highest honors could be allowed to sin with impunity against the prince and the entire republic—which has deserved so well of him—rather than being immediately handed over to the <term>lictors</term> <note>Lictors were Roman civil servants who carried out the orders of magistrates, including the execution of punishments.</note> and the executioner to be tortured and tormented, or to be overwhelmed by the stones of the entire populace. 

In this republic of God, there are indeed executioners and lictors: the wicked demons. They are assigned to this most base ministry in punishment for their ancient crime. From this comes that saying of Paul: <note>original: "Tradidi illum Satanę in interitū carnis"</note> **"I have handed him over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh,"** and from this comes the name of the "avenging demon" found even in Orpheus, <note>Pico often cited Orpheus, the legendary Greek poet, believing that ancient "pagan" wisdom (Prisca Theologia) harmonized with Christian revelation.</note> if perhaps we find our own texts less convincing. 

But just as every creature hates and execrates the crimes of man, so too is his righteous life and conduct pleasing and acceptable to all. For all things—if I may put it this way—cannot fail to be admitted into the participation of both his good and his evil, since they are folded into him and joined with him by such a tight bond. From this comes that Gospel saying: **that all the angels exult with joy if a sinner repents.** From this also comes the clear reason for that mystery which was hidden for ages: that our nature, corrupted in the first Adam and cast down from its high state, should be restored through the cross of Christ. Indeed, for our sake, the Son of God became man and was fastened to the cross. For it was fitting that he who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature in whom all things were founded, should be coupled by an ineffable union to that creature who was made in the image of God—man—who is the bond of every creature and in whom all things are enclosed. Nor was it right, if the whole of nature was endangered through man’s fall, that its loss should be neglected or repaired by anyone other than the one through whom all nature had been instituted in the beginning.

[it] holds. <note>The syllable "ret" completes a word from the previous page, likely "tenet" (it holds/contains).</note> It is this second type of unity through which one creature is joined to another, and through which all the parts of the world finally become one world. The third and most principal type of all is that by which the whole universe is one with its Maker, just as an army is one with its leader. This threefold union is present in each thing through its own simple unity derived from that One which is both the first One and a Trinity—at once three and one—namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. For the power of the Father, producing all things, grants His unity to all; the wisdom of the Son, rightly ordering all things, unites and couples all things to one another; and the love of the Spirit, turning all things back toward God, joins the entire work to the Maker by the bond of charity. 

However, just as God is more inward to us than we are to ourselves, He is also more "one" with us than we are with ourselves. <note>Pico is drawing on a famous idea from Saint Augustine: that God is "more inward than my innermost self" (interior intimo meo).</note> Conversely, each thing is more tightly joined to itself than to other parts of the world. Thus, having been taught the order of universal charity, if we are willing to follow the divine law written on the tablets of nature, we will love God first—above ourselves and above all things; second, we will love ourselves; and third, we will love our neighbor. 

Our Prophet <note>Pico consistently refers to Moses as "the Prophet."</note> spoke sufficiently regarding that unity by which each thing is one with itself when he examined the nature of all things individually. Regarding that unity by which we are joined to God, it will be treated in the next discourse, where we shall discuss the summit of happiness. There remains that unity by which diverse parts are coupled together in a mutual covenant, which is what we must discuss at present.

## CHAPTER ONE.

Now that we have seen the distinct natures of things arranged in their separate stations (so to speak), we should not believe they become a single universe merely because individual things are contained by other individuals according to the condition of their nature. The Prophet also wished to indicate in his text how many and what kind of modes there were by which the natures of things were coupled together. He does this not only to call us to this curious understanding, but to instruct and demonstrate by what path and reason we can be coupled to those things that are better than ourselves. 

As I was thinking—before I approached the explanation of the words—about how many modes there were or could be imagined by which things might obtain either an affinity or a bond with each other, I ran through all the dogmas of the philosophers in which I have labored since boyhood. I encountered no more than fifteen genera. Approaching Moses thereafter, I saw these so clearly and so appropriately indicated by him that I believe no one could be better instructed in them anywhere else.

## CHAPTER TWO.

Immediately on the first day, he encompasses five modes—I know not whether more briefly or more clearly—by which something can be joined to another. For that which is joined to another is either its **essence**, or it is a **property of its essence**, or it exists within it as a **form in a subject**, or it touches it either as a **transformer** of that which is transformed, or as **art** acting upon the matter subject to it. Similarly, we read in Moses of five things compared and connected to one another: heaven, and earth, and emptiness... <note>original: "inanitatem"</note>

<summary>Pico defines three types of cosmic unity—internal, mutual, and divine—and begins an analysis of the fifteen ways things can be connected, identifying the first five in Moses's account of the first day of Creation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on the types of unity in the universe. The syllable "tem" at the very beginning of the page completes the word "unitatem" (unity) from the preceding sentence.</meta>

[unity], the abyss and darkness, the spirit of God and the waters, the light and bodies. First, the empty and void earth designates for us the first mode of conjunction, since earth—that is, <term>matter|the fundamental, formless "stuff" from which all things are made</term>—is empty unless it is filled with forms from elsewhere. The second mode is indicated by the darkness over the face of the abyss. For the abyss, by its own nature, is neither light nor dark; however, darkness follows its nature unless approaching light puts it to flight. In the same way, darkness and privation follow the formlessness and emptiness of matter, until the arrival of species <note>original: "species"; here meaning the specific forms or essences of things</note> expels them. The third mode is shown by light arising in bodies. For in them, light exists as a form within a subject. The fourth is heaven and earth, for heaven does not inhere in the earth as a form or an <term>accident|a non-essential quality, like the color of a shirt</term> exists in the thing it completes; rather, it is joined to it as an <term>efficient cause|the agent that brings something about</term> is joined to the thing that is acted upon and transformed. The example of the last mode is the spirit of the Lord, which is carried over the waters. For the wisdom of the Lord, the Artificer, and every spiritual nature—not being disconnected from commerce with the body—is understood to be joined to bodies in no other way than the art in the mind of an architect is joined to the cement, wood, and stones. 

But consider again this sequence of logic: the earth is empty of itself and possesses its own darkness, then it is joined most closely to light, through light to heaven, and through heaven to spiritual substance. But let us see how these things relate to us. The "earth" is the earthly body, void of life and empty of sense; over it is "darkness," death, torpor, inefficacy, immobility, and lack of sensation. "Light" is the life that nourishes, awakens, drives, and moves it, rendering it endowed with sense. "Heaven" is the soul, the source of that light, and the "spirit of God" is the intellect, the light of the divine face. Even more has been said on these matters here than was perhaps necessary.

---

->CHAPTER THREE<-

**L**et us examine what Moses intends in the following passages: we shall see ten other modes suggested by him, through which we may understand the mutual federation between things. For besides those we have mentioned, there are again these others which we shall enumerate. A thing is either a part of another, or an effect. If it is a part, it is either an inseparable part of its whole—in which way the Sun, Moon, and stars are in the <term>firmament|the sphere of the stars</term>—or it is a separable part, such as parts of water separated from the wholeness of their element, toward which they have flowed. If it is an effect, it either sprouts from an internal <term>seminal reason|the "seed-like" blueprint within nature that dictates growth</term>, just as plants sprout from the earth while remaining fixed to their parent and connected by natural bonds and ligaments; or it consists of and is fashioned from its own principles, like a mixture of elements. In this way, the bodies of animals are made from water and earth. Or, it has an extrinsic cause, which can be divided threefold into the efficient, the <term>exemplar|the model or pattern</term>, and the end <note>original: "finem"; the purpose or goal</note>. We have examples of these three from Moses: God creates and effects man (<term>efficient cause</term>); He creates him in His own image as if according to a model (<term>exemplary cause</term>); and the beasts are subject to man and are made for the sake of man as if for an end (<term>final cause</term>).

<summary>Pico explains how different parts of creation are connected, using the biblical "days" as metaphors for how matter receives form and how the human body relates to the soul and intellect. He also introduces ten specific ways that things in the universe are linked to one another, such as parts to a whole or effects to their causes.</summary>

### CHAPTER FOUR.

**W**e have spoken about the part and the effect, and by the same reasoning, about the whole and the cause. For these relations correspond to one another. But we have not yet fulfilled all the types of kinship <note>original: "cognationis"</note>. For regarding the cause, there remains this species of affinity <note>original: "affinitatis"</note>: that the secondary cause obeys and is joined to the primary. For example, when God produces, the waters produce; and these [the waters] indeed act first because they are the proximate causes, but they do so only at God's command, because the primary cause has a greater influence than the secondary. Similarly, there is a secondary <term>end|the purpose or goal for which something exists (its "telos")</term> attached and annexed to the principal one, which Moses wisely indicates by saying: the stars were placed so that they might shine in heaven and illuminate the earth. For the good of lower things is not the primary end of the heavenly bodies. Rather, they intend this first: that they shine for themselves; then, finally, that they illuminate us. For this reason, we read in Homer that both the Dawn and the Sun rise to bring light first to the immortals, and then to mortals. Besides all these, there is also a kinship between man and man, and lion and lion; and yet, one lion is neither a part nor an effect of another lion if it was not sired by it. The Prophet <note>Pico frequently refers to Moses as "the Prophet."</note> signifies this when he gathers and unites together the fish, the birds, and the beasts of the earth. There is one final type of affinity, which is that of a middle nature to the extremes. For man agrees with man, and animal with animal, because they share the same essence, whether specific or general. But a "middle" is not the same essence as the extremes; instead, it is tempered in some way from them, so that it differs from both while communicating with both. This was indicated to us by Moses when he places the firmament as a middle between the waters, dividing the waters above the heavens from the waters which are under the heaven. There, he sufficiently reveals the nature of the middle, just as we have abundantly declared in the preface of the first book and the second chapter of the fifth.

### CHAPTER FIVE.

**W**e are also reminded from this what we must do so that we may be united with better natures, in which the whole and the summit of our happiness is placed. For the first day also teaches us this: light first arose for the waters, with night driven away, only when the spirit of the Lord hovered over them. From this is signified that saying of James: *Every best gift is from above, from the Father of lights.* Not to mention our own [Christian] authors, Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who believed that human effort alone was not enough to reach the divine; ritual and divine aid were necessary.</note> confirms this so strongly that he wishes human nature to promise nothing to itself, even of a mediocre sort, unless it is aided by a greater power—that is, the divine divinity. If this is true, and approved not only by our people but also by the philosophers, then certainly all our zeal ought to be in this: that having turned toward the things above—which happens through sacred religion, through mysteries, through vows, through hymns, prayers, and supplications—we may seek strength from there for our weakness. This is why the Platonic and Pythagorean discussions, having begun with sacred prayers, end with them; Porphyry, Theodore, and all the Academics <note>Followers of the skeptical or later Platonic traditions.</note> confirm with one voice that nothing is more useful, or indeed more necessary, for man. We read that the Brahmans of India and the Magi of the Persians never attempted anything unless a prayer was first offered. I bring forward these testimonies of the Gentiles so that those who have been persuaded by an evil demon to believe the Gentiles rather [than...]

...than from the Church; or let them learn from those whom they trust that it is neither a laughable, nor a useless, nor an unworthy thing for a philosopher to devote effort—and indeed great and constant effort—to sacred prayers, to mysteries, to vows, and to hymns sung continually to God. If this practice benefits and suits any class of men most, it is especially useful and becoming for those who have given themselves to the study of letters and the leisure of contemplation. For nothing is more necessary for them than that they frequently turn the eyes of their mind toward divine things, purify them through integrity of life, and illuminate them more abundantly with light sought from above through the staff of prayer <note>original: "ferulam orationis"; Pico likely uses "staff" or "rod" to symbolize prayer as a support for the soul or a tool for discipline</note>. Being always mindful of their own weakness, they should say with the Apostle: *our sufficiency is from God* <note>2 Corinthians 3:5: "Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think any thing as of ourselves; but our sufficiency is of God."</note>.

### CHAPTER SIX.

**A**gain, let us examine what the arrangement of the water and the earth teaches us. Let us learn from the earth that we will not bring forth the fruit we are laboring to produce unless we repress and drive back the force of the fluid and falling matter that invades us, and unless we cast out from our dwellings the whirlpools and torrents of pleasures that rush in upon us. Let us learn from the waters, which were not considered fit for the procreation of fish until they were gathered into the unity of their entire element. For neither will we be able to bring into the light any offspring worthy of our divinity if we are torn apart and distracted by different things—if we are not carried toward a single intention with all our forces gathered together. There is also a deeper mystery contained here: just as it is the happiness of drops of water to reach the ocean where there is a fullness of waters, so too is it our happiness that the portion of intellectual light within us should one day be joined to the first Intellect of all and to the First Mind, where there is fullness and the entire universality of intelligence.

### CHAPTER SEVEN.

**B**ut the greatest lesson of all is that which the teaching of the firmament signifies to us. There we see that the lower waters cannot be enriched by any benefit from the upper waters except through the intervention of the sky, which is placed as a medium between them. In the same way, let us hold in our minds that the coupling of extremes can only happen through a nature that, because it is in the middle of the extremes, embraces both within itself. It joins those extremes together conveniently for this reason: because it first united them within itself through the property of its own nature. We are reminded here of that great sacrament <note>The word "sacramentum" here refers to a sacred mystery or a divine plan.</note> which is *folly to the Gentiles and a stumbling block to the Jews, but to us is the power and wisdom of God* <note>1 Corinthians 1:23-24</note>: that man cannot be joined to God except through Him who, having joined man to God in Himself, was made a true <term>Mediator|One who stands between two parties to reconcile them; here, Christ as both God and Man</term>. He is able to connect men to God in such a way that, just as in Him the Son of God put on man, so through Him men might become sons of God. If what we say is true—that extremes are not coupled to each other except through a medium, and that which has already united the extremes in itself is truly called a medium—then surely, if that ineffable dispensation occurs in Christ alone (so that the Word became flesh), then Christ alone is also He through whom flesh [can] [attain] to the Word...

# On the happiness which is eternal life,
## the Seventh Exposition, Book VII. Preface.

If we have completed our account of the ranks, order, and nature of the whole world in six expositions, as if in six days, it remains that in this seventh treatise—as if on the Sabbath <note>The Hebrew word for "rest" or "cessation"</note> of our commentary—we treat the Sabbath of the world and the rest of the creatures whose nature we established in the previous parts. That is to say, we shall treat their happiness (or to say it more correctly) let us listen to Moses, as a true prophet of all future things, treating it himself.

There is, however, a happiness (as the theologians proclaim) of one kind which we can attain through nature, and another which we can attain through grace. They call the former "natural" and the latter "supernatural." Concerning the first, that is, the natural happiness, enough has been said by Moses, since once the nature of things is known, we also know their natural happiness. It remains for him to teach concerning the second, showing himself to be a prophet rather than a teacher, because when Moses wrote, grace did not yet exist, but was destined to be.

But because I seem to see certain sciolists <note>smatterers or those with superficial knowledge</note>—or should I rather call them worthless idlers and scoundrels—who call themselves philosophers when they are nothing of the sort, immediately laughing at both grace and supernatural happiness as if these were empty names and old wives' tales, I wanted to make a brief discussion with them on this matter as a preface to the seventh book. This matter is both useful to everyone on its own and very necessary for the work we have undertaken, where we shall clearly prove that the opinion of the theologians stands firm and established, resting upon the deepest roots of philosophy.

I define happiness as follows: the return of each thing to its own beginning <note>original: "principium"; meaning both the starting point and the governing principle</note>. For happiness is the highest good; the highest good is that which all things seek; and that which all things seek is the very thing which is the beginning of all things—as Alexander of Aphrodisias <note>A celebrated commentator on Aristotle (c. 200 AD) who sought to explain the soul and intellect</note> testifies in his commentaries on philosophy, and the Greek interpreters in their works on Aristotle’s *Ethics*. Therefore, the same end of all things is that which is the beginning of all: the one God, omnipotent and blessed, the best of all things that can either exist or be imagined. Hence follow those two principal names for Him among the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras who believed numbers and ratios were the fundamental reality of the universe</note>: "the One" and "the Good." He is named the One because He is the beginning of all, just as unity is the beginning of all number; and He is named the Good because He is the end of all, the rest of all, and absolute happiness. We can already see, if we are a little more skillful, the reason for this twofold happiness.

<meta>This page continues the preface to Book VII of the Heptaplus, where Pico della Mirandola explores the nature of happiness (felicity). Having previously distinguished between natural and supernatural happiness, he now explains how every part of the created world—from inanimate elements to angels—attains its own version of natural happiness by participating in God's goodness.</meta>

-> ### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola <-

...ness. For happiness is the possession and attainment of this first good. Created things can attain this good in two ways: either in themselves, or in God Himself. For this good is both exalted above all things, dwelling in the depths of His own divinity, and also diffused through all things, found in everything—here more perfectly, there more imperfectly, according to the condition of the things that participate in it. Hence, as the poets write: *Jupiter is whatever you see, and all things are full of Jove.* <note>Pico quotes a famous line from the Roman poet Lucan, using the name of the king of the gods to represent the divine presence that permeates the entire universe.</note>

Therefore, since every nature possesses God in some way—because it has as much of God as it has of goodness (and all things that God made are good)—it follows that when a thing possesses its own nature, perfected in all its parts, it has attained itself and thus attained God within itself. And if the attainment of God, as we have proven, is happiness, then each thing is in some way happy within itself. This is **natural happiness**, which different things have received in greater or lesser degrees according to the diversity of their natures.

**Fire** is a thing lacking a soul, yet it participates in God in many ways. First, because it *is*, and everything that exists participates in God, who is Being itself. Likewise, because the form <note>In the philosophy of the time, "form" or "species" refers to the essential nature that makes a thing what it is.</note> and action of fire are definite, it is like God, who is the first form and first action. While fire produces fire, it imitates divine fecundity; while it keeps itself within the boundaries of its own sphere, it imitates justice; and while it serves us, it imitates beneficence, according to the measure of its nature. When fire acts in this way, having attained its own perfection, it is happy as far as it is capable of happiness.

**Plants** are happier, for they possess life in addition to being. **Animals** are happier still, for they have also been granted perception; as they find more perfection in themselves, they also find more of the divine. **Man** is in the best condition of all mortals; just as he excels others in nature, so he excels them in natural happiness. He is endowed with intelligence and **freedom of choice** <term>libertate arbitrij</term>—the primary gifts and those most conducive to happiness. 

The **angelic mind** is supreme among creatures, both in the nobility of its substance and in the attainment of its end, of which it is the greatest participant because it is both joined and closest to God. But truly, as we said above, through this kind of happiness, neither plants, nor beasts, nor man, nor angel reach God as the "Highest Good" in God Himself, but rather they reach Him within themselves.

For this reason, the definition of happiness varies step-by-step according to the capacity of different natures. This is why the philosophers, who spoke only of this kind of happiness, placed the happiness of each thing in the "best operation of its own nature." Regarding the angels—whom they call "minds" and "intellects"—even if they confessed that their highest perfection was to understand God, they nevertheless established that the knowledge of God which they possess is no different from the knowledge by which they know themselves. Thus, they understand only as much of God as the nature of God is represented within their own substance.

Regarding man, although different thinkers have held different views, they all remained within the narrow limits of human faculty. They determined human happiness to be either in the mere pursuit of truth (as the **Academics** <note>Followers of the skeptical tradition of Plato's Academy who believed certain knowledge was impossible and happiness lay in the search for truth.</note> held) or rather in its attainment through the study of philosophy (as **Al-Farabi** <note>An influential medieval Islamic philosopher (c. 872–950) known as the "Second Teacher."</note> said). 

**Averroes**, **Avicenna**, **Abubacher**, **Alexander**, and the **Platonists** <note>These are major figures of the Aristotelian and Neoplatonic traditions: Averroes and Avicenna were Persian/Islamic polymaths; Abubacher (Ibn Tufayl) was an Arabic philosopher; Alexander of Aphrodisias was a famous commentator on Aristotle.</note> seemed to grant something more: that our reason is joined to an "intellect that is in act," or some higher intellect that is nonetheless kin to us...

He argues that while philosophers like Al-Farabi and Averroes correctly identified this self-actualization, it remains limited to the creature's own capacity and falls short of supernatural union with God.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the preface to Book VII of the Heptaplus. In the previous section, Pico began distinguishing between the "natural happiness" described by ancient philosophers and the "supernatural happiness" revealed by theology. He continues here by arguing that while natural happiness is good, it is merely a shadow of the true union with God.</meta>

# Heptaplus

...confirming them as if in their own end; but neither do these [philosophers] lead man back to his beginning, nor to the highest good. I neither reject nor despise these arguments and opinions of theirs, if they profess to speak only of **natural happiness**. For it is certain that by such power, neither man nor angels can be raised higher than what they say. This is proven most strongly by this reasoning: since nothing striving by its own strength can rise above itself (otherwise it would be more powerful than itself), surely nothing striving by its own efforts toward happiness can attain anything greater or more perfect than its own nature. 

But let the philosophers tell me: if this is the only happiness in things, why do they themselves admit that among animals, only man is born for happiness? For why should others besides man also reach their own ends? We can say that the happiness of others is less than man’s, but how shall we defend the idea that there is none? Indeed, since other things below man never stray from the end established by nature, while man almost always goes astray, the human condition would seem the unhappiest of all, unless he could boast of some other privilege. 

Let us therefore listen to the holy theologians reminding us of our dignity, and to those divine goods offered to us by a most liberal Father; let us not, I pray, be cruel to our own souls and ungrateful toward God our Maker by rejecting them. We said above that the summit of happiness lies in the attainment of God, who is the highest good and the principle <note>In the philosophical tradition Pico followed, the "principle" refers to the source or origin from which all life flows and to which it seeks to return.</note> of all. But that attainment can happen in two ways: for we reach God either in the creatures in whom God participates, or in God Himself. 

We have shown, and will show, that created things cannot reach this latter [attainment] by their own powers, but only the former. Yet that former attainment, if we pay attention, is a shadow of happiness rather than true happiness, just as the creature in which one reaches God is not the highest goodness, but a thin shadow of the highest goodness—that is, the divine. Add to this that through it, things are restored to themselves rather than to God; they have achieved not a return to their own principle, but only this: that they do not depart from themselves. 

But **true and perfected happiness** carries and leads us back to beholding the face of God, which is all good, as He Himself said: and to perfect union with that principle from which we emanated. Angels can indeed be lifted up to this, but they cannot ascend to it by their own power. Wherefore Lucifer sinned, saying: *I will ascend into heaven.* <note>original: "Asscendam in coelum." A reference to Isaiah 14:13, interpreted as the prideful fall of the morning star.</note> Man cannot go toward this; he can be drawn. Whence Christ said of himself, who is happiness itself: *No one comes to me unless my Father has drawn him.* <note>original: "Nemo venit ad me nisi pater meus traxerit illum." A reference to John 6:44.</note> But beasts and those things below man can neither go nor be drawn to it. 

Therefore, only man and angel were made for that happiness which is true happiness. Steam can rise on high, but only if attracted by a ray of the sun; a stone and every bulky substance can neither admit the ray everywhere, nor be lifted into the heights by it. This ray, this divine power, this influence, we call <term>grace (gratia)</term>, because it makes both man and angel <term>pleasing (gratos)</term> to God. <note>Pico is playing on the Latin roots: "gratia" (grace) is the gift that makes the recipient "gratus" (pleasing or acceptable) to the giver.</note> But the philosophers have a manifest [proof] of this doctrine...
