<meta>This page continues Pico's argument from the preface to Book VII of the Heptaplus. Having established that human effort alone can only achieve "natural happiness," he now uses a physical analogy—linear versus circular motion—to explain the necessity of Divine Grace for reaching "supernatural happiness" or union with God.</meta>

### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

...an example found in physical bodies. For among bodies, some are moved in a straight line, while others are moved in a **circle**. Linear motion—by which the elements <note>The "elements" here refer to earth, water, air, and fire, which in ancient physics were thought to move naturally up or down to find their proper place.</note> are carried to their own proper places—symbolizes that happiness through which things are established in the perfection of their own nature. However, circular motion—through which a body is revolved back to the same point from which it departed—is the most perfect image of **true happiness**, through which the creature returns to that same beginning from which it first proceeded. 

But see how perfectly everything corresponds on both sides. Only immortal and incorruptible bodies move in a circle <note>In the cosmology of Pico's time, the "heavenly spheres" were thought to be made of an incorruptible fifth element (aether) and moved in perfect circles, unlike the changing world below.</note>. Similarly, only an immortal and eternal substance returns to God. The elements, to complete their own motions, require no force other than the impulse of heaviness or lightness implanted in them from their birth; in the same way, individual things are carried toward their natural happiness by their own impulse and their own power. 

But truly, although the celestial bodies are suited for circular motion, they are not sufficient on their own to complete this movement; rather, they have need of a **Divine Motor** <term>Divine Motor: Based on Aristotle’s "Unmoved Mover," this refers to the spiritual intelligence or power that keeps the heavens in motion.</term> to turn and revolve them. Finally, those bodies are so suited for perpetual revolution that they do not *create* that motion, but rather *receive* it. 

It happens to us and to the angels in no different a way. For we are such by nature that we cannot turn and reflect ourselves back, but we can be turned by the **motive power of grace** and be reflected back into God. Hence that saying: *those who are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God.* <note>original: "qui aguntur spiritu Dei, hi filij Dei sunt." (Romans 8:14)</note> He said "those who are **led**," not "those who lead." In this we differ from the heavens: they are moved by the necessity of nature, while we are moved according to our freedom. 

For the **Motive Spirit** knocks constantly at your soul. If you refuse to listen, you are left to yourself, to your body, to your weakness—wretched and unhappy. But if you admit Him, immediately, filled with God, you are carried back through the circle of religion to the Father and the Lord. There, you shall possess life forever in Him, in whom you were already life even before you were created. 

This is true happiness: that we may be one spirit with God, and that we may possess God in God’s presence, not in our own, *knowing even as we are known.* <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 13:12.</note> For He knew us not through us, but through Himself. So too shall we know Him through Himself and not through ourselves. This is the entire reward, this is **eternal life**, this is the wisdom which the wise of this world did not know: that we are brought back from all the imperfection of the "many" into unity through an unbreakable bond with Him who is **Unity itself**. For this happiness, Christ prayed to the Father in this manner:

-> "Father, just as I and you are one, make it so that these also may be one with us." <- <note>original: "Pater fac quemadmodum ego & tu unum sumus, ita & hi nobiscum unum sint." (John 17:21)</note>

Paul distinguished this happiness, saying: *I shall know not in part, but as it is*; and since he hoped for this, did he not rightly say:

-> "Who shall separate me from the love of Christ?" <- <note>original: "Quis me separabit à charitate Christi?" (Romans 8:35)</note>

And he desired to be dissolved so that he might become one with Christ. From this happiness the demon fell, because he wished to ascend to it by his own power, rather than be carried to it. Therefore, he lost that which he would have held had he remained. From this root it is known what the lot is of **infants** who have departed before being initiated <note>Referring to unbaptized infants. Pico suggests they remain in a "natural" state, neither suffering the pains of hell nor enjoying the supernatural vision of God.</note>. That is to say, they remain within themselves, neither stripped of their own natural goods nor enriched by divine ones. 

We, however, must fall to one side or the other: either to the highest misery or the highest happiness. For he who is the cause of his own failure to receive the **Motor** <gloss>the Holy Spirit or Divine Grace</gloss> not only makes himself immune to grace but also corrupts his own nature, the integrity of which depends upon...

<summary>Pico explains that while humans can reach "natural" perfection through their own efforts, "true happiness" (returning to God) requires the assistance of Divine Grace, much like the planets require a Divine Motor to move in circles.</summary>

...seeks the recognized spirit and does not refuse it; for undoubtedly, a nature cannot be right which, under the appearance of a greater proposed good, either rejects or despises it. Therefore, after Christ has been recognized, those who do not put on the following of Christ are deprived not only of their primary happiness <note>Supernatural union with God.</note>, but also of the second, that is, their natural right, because to be unwilling to receive grace can only belong to a corrupt and weakened nature. However, just as we who live under the Gospel receive Christ, the power and wisdom of God <note>original: "Christum Dei uirtutem & sapientiam"; a reference to 1 Corinthians 1:24.</note>, within ourselves because we love and hold onto Him as one already given to the human race, so too did the fathers under the Old Law receive Him, since they both believed in His future coming without doubt and hoped for it eagerly, desiring it most ardently. But just as they received Him not as one already present, but as one to come, so they did not experience the fruit of the indwelling spirit until after He arrived. After the ineffable sacrifice was completed on the altar of the cross, when Christ descended to them <note>A reference to the "Harrowing of Hell," where Christ was believed to have descended to Limbo to liberate the souls of the righteous patriarchs.</note>, they were whirled around by Him as their motor—as if in a sudden whirlwind—unto liberty, and were raised to the level of the highest happiness. Religion promotes, directs, and impels us toward this happiness, just as we use philosophy as a guide toward natural happiness. Because if nature is the basic training for grace, then surely philosophy is the beginning of religion; nor is it true philosophy that moves a man away from religion. Rightly, therefore, after we have philosophized about nature for six days with Moses, we shall speak on the seventh day about supernatural happiness, being at leisure for divine things.

### CHAPTER ONE

**T**wo natures (as we have shown) are capable of this supreme happiness: the angelic and the human. The former is called "heaven," the latter "earth," because angels inhabit heaven and we inhabit the earth. And of heaven, there is no need for him <note>Moses, the presumed author of Genesis.</note> to say more, because he is about to write a law not for angels, but for men. Descending, therefore, to men, he says:

->The earth was empty and void, and darkness was over the face of the abyss.<-

God does not create emptiness; He does not create darkness. But "the earth," he says, "was empty and darkness was there." He does not say these things were created, but that they *were*. Why this was said will become clear as soon as we recognize what this emptiness and these shadows are. Human nature, which is called "earth" when compared to the angels, was immediately from the beginning—because it sinned immediately—empty and void of **original justice** <term>Original Justice: The state of grace and harmony in which humans were believed to have been created before the Fall.</term>, and its "face"—that is, its reason—was veiled by the shadows of sin. God did not make these things, but rather the malice of man, who willfully deprived himself of those goods with which God had enriched him. In this way, the state of corrupt nature is described by the Prophet <note>Pico refers to Moses here as a Prophet.</note>; how it was then restored to its former dignity by God through Abraham, through Moses, through the Prophets, and finally through His only-begotten Son, and prepared for the highest happiness, will be demonstrated in what follows. Truly, even at the time when the waters were covered by darkness and infected—namely, marked by the ancient filth of the original stain <note>A reference to Original Sin.</note>—nevertheless, the **Spirit of the Lord** hovered over them. This is to be understood in two ways: both that men were ruled by the light of the Divine countenance which is "sealed upon us" <note>A reference to Psalm 4:6, implying the "light of nature" or innate reason.</note>—that is, by the light of natural intelligence—and also that the Divine...

...of providence, the human race was not forsaken; instead, "the spirit of the Lord hovered over the waters" <note>Genesis 1:2</note>, that spirit which (as the Apostle says) "intercedes for us with groanings that cannot be expressed" <note>original: "intercedit pro nobis gemitibus inenarrabilibus"; a reference to Romans 8:26.</note>. Even then, He was constantly considering how to purge those waters from the poisons with which the ancient serpent <note>A traditional title for Satan.</note> had infected them. And behold, He immediately commands light to arise, and light was made. This was **Abraham**, that most wise man and the first founder of the true religion. He was the first to fulfill the law of nature and to meditate upon the Divine Law. He was the first to persuade men to worship the one God against the influence of idols and the nations. He was the first who attempted both to dispel the darkness of error and to declare war against the evil demons (who are called "the princes of darkness"); for this reason, he is deservedly named "light." Because the disciples of the Lord all did the same, they were all called "the light of the world" <note>Matthew 5:14</note> by the Lord. This is the first light that shone upon the world, and it distinguished between the religion of demons and the religion of the true God, as if between light and darkness.

## CHAPTER TWO.

The Law followed after this light, and it is deservedly called by the name **the firmament**. Right at its beginning—precisely in the matter we are now treating—it announces to us "the works of God’s hands" (as David sang: "and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands" <note>Psalm 19:1</note>). The Law, therefore, was given to Moses through an angel and strengthened by the word of God. Even more than the previous light, it separated the nations from the Israelites—that is, it separated piety from impiety—just as it "distinguished the waters above the heavens from the waters that are under the heavens" <note>Genesis 1:7</note>. Now, the Jews are called "waters above the heavens" because they alone (as Jerome says) "do not fear the signs of heaven" <note>Jeremiah 10:2</note> which the nations fear. They alone do not worship the stars or the sky, but instead they recognize, worship, and venerate the Author and Lord of the stars and the sky. The nations, by the opposite reasoning, are the "waters under the heaven," since they both worship and serve demons (the inhabitants of the misty air, which is the region above the waters), and they make the visible sky, the stars, and the planets into their gods and masters.

## CHAPTER THREE.

However, it would have happened that, unless some greater power and mercy of God stood in the way, the "waters which are under the heavens"—that is, those serving idols—would have invaded and occupied the whole earth. Such was the infection of the entire world from the first stain <note>The Original Sin of Adam.</note>. Thus the empire of Satan the Avenger and his legal claim over us demanded it, for we were guilty of that ancient offense and almost liable to this kind of servitude. But the ever-beneficent and saving providence of God willed that one part of the earth (even if a small one, as far as the laws of justice allowed) should be free from the injury of the waters. This is **Judea**, called the "Promised Land," because it was promised by God to Abraham and his posterity. All the Prophets support this interpretation of ours, as in their writings the onslaught of the nations against the Israelites is so often compared to the incursions of waters and the sea. Hence that saying: "the floods have lifted up their voice," <note>Psalm 93:3</note> and "the wonderful surges of the sea," and that other: "their waters roared and were troubled," <note>Psalm 46:3</note> and "we will not fear while the earth is troubled, and the mountains are carried into the heart of the sea" <note>Psalm 46:2</note>—and certainly not otherwise...

In the same way that nations surrounded Judea—which was enclosed within the borders of a small region—so the ocean now surrounds on all sides this moderate portion of the earth which we inhabit. But also, in many places in the Christian scriptures, the nations are very clearly designated by "waters." For it is written: *the waters which you saw are the peoples* <note>original: "aquæ quas uidisti gentes sunt"; a reference to Revelation 17:15.</note>. And when the Lord Jesus made wine from water—which had run out in the house of the Pharisee <note>Pico here refers to the miracle at the Wedding at Cana, though he mentions a "Pharisee's house," perhaps conflating the setting with other Gospel scenes or following a specific allegorical tradition.</note>—it signified figuratively, as our writers say, that the waters (that is, the nations) were to be called to that faith. This faith would later fail among the Jews, where it had previously existed. Likewise, they teach in the mysteries <note>A reference to the liturgical practice of mixing water and wine in the Chalice during the Mass.</note> that water is mixed with wine for this reason: so that the waters—that is, the nations—may drink in the blood of Christ through the faith of the cross. 

Therefore, that part of the earth was claimed from the yoke of the waters by the providence of God, so that if the rest of the earth—overwhelmed by the waves of spiritual wickedness—was to be useless, deserted, and unfit for the fruits of true religion, at least this land might exist. Receiving the light brought forth on the first day <note>Representing Abraham.</note> and the dew of heaven established on the second <note>Representing the Law.</note>—that is, aided toward fertility by the doctrine of the Law—it would meanwhile sprout (as if they were herbs, plants, and trees) judgments, ceremonies, and good morals, until the fullness of time had come. Then it would bring forth that Savior whom Isaiah longed for in a most happy germination <note>A reference to Isaiah 45:8: "Let the earth open and bring forth salvation."</note>.

->CHAPTER FOUR.<-

**A**nd behold, now is the fullness of time. For if the number four is the fullness of numbers <note>A Pythagorean concept: 1+2+3+4 = 10, the "perfect" number containing all numerical possibilities.</note>, will not the fourth day also be the fullness of days? See, therefore, what the fourth day brings us. The heaven established on the second day—that is, the Law—was without Sun, Moon, and stars; it was capable of future light, certainly, but still dark, not yet illuminated by any distinguished light. 

The fourth day arrived, on which the **Sun**, the Lord of the firmament—that is, **Christ**, the Lord of the Law—and the **lunar Church**, the partner and bride of Christ, and the **Apostolic teachers** (who would instruct many in justice) would shine out in the firmament like stars for all eternity, calling the world to eternal life. The Sun does not destroy the firmament but perfects it, just as Christ came not to destroy the Law but to fulfill it. 

The light of the first day, most pious **Abraham**, saw the fourth day—which is the day of Christ—and was glad <note>Referring to John 8:56: "Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day."</note>. He saw the ray of his own light—that is, of true religion—which he had brought into the world through the Sun of Justice <note>A traditional title for Christ, from Malachi 4:2.</note>, the true light illuminating all men, to be spread most widely throughout the whole world. He saw Jesus Christ, the radiance of the Father's substance, shining upon those who sat in darkness and the shadow of death, and he saw the prince of darkness, the prince of this world, being cast out and being judged by the "folly" of men <note>Pico likely refers to the "folly of the Cross" (1 Cor 1:18) which overcomes the wisdom of the world.</note>. These things he saw and exulted; he saw the fourth day and was glad. This is the day the Lord has made; on which the Lord becomes man, on which God dwelt among us; let us also exult and be glad in it. 

I ask you, Christian brothers, to attend a little more diligently to how true and how solid the reasoning of our exposition is. From this, most powerful weapons will be supplied to you against the stony heart of the Hebrews, taken from their own armories <note>Pico suggests that by interpreting the Old Testament correctly, Christians can find arguments to convince Jewish scholars using their own traditions.</note>.

<meta>This page continues the "Fifth Exposition" of the Heptaplus, where Pico della Mirandola interprets the six days of Genesis as a timeline for human history. After discussing the first three days in the previous section, he now focuses on the Fourth Day—the creation of the sun, moon, and stars—as a prophecy for the arrival of the Messiah.</meta>

->### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola<-

We will prove this first from the testimonies of the Jews: that the coming of Christ is signaled to us through the works of the fourth day. Second, we will show that the Messiah is represented by no thing more fittingly than by the Sun. Finally, we will gather <term>through</term> <gloss>original: p̃, a scribal abbreviation for "per"</gloss> the most evident calculation of time that Christ will not come in the future, but that Jesus of Nazareth, son of the Virgin, was the Messiah promised to the Hebrews.

Among the decrees of the ancient Hebrew discipline, it is held that the six days of Genesis designate six thousand years of the world. Thus, the works described here on the first day are a prophecy of those things that were to happen in the first millennium of the world; likewise, the works of the second day represent what happened in the second millennium, and so on, always preserving the same order of succession in both cases. Even among the more recent scholars, Moses of Gerona <note>original: "Moses Gerundinensis"; also known as Nahmanides (1194–1270), a leading medieval Jewish scholar.</note>, a theologian of the highest renown among the Hebrews, attests to this opinion. Saint Jerome also mentions it in his exposition on that Psalm attributed to Moses <note>Psalm 90:4: "For a thousand years in your sight are like a day that has just gone by."</note>. This opinion seems to rest primarily on the foundation that "a thousand years are as one day before God," as the Prophet says. 

Therefore, if this doctrine is true, the fourth day is a prophecy of those things which were to occur in the fourth millennium of the world. Come now, let us show that Jesus appeared in the fourth millennium of the world, according to the Hebrew annals and the very calculation of years which they themselves approve. From Adam to the Flood, they count one thousand five hundred fifty-six years; from the Flood to Abraham, two hundred and ninety-two years; and thus from Adam to Abraham, one thousand eight hundred forty-eight years are collected. From the birth of Isaac to the fall of the second temple—which was after the death of Christ—they number approximately one thousand six hundred sixty years (for I am not cutting to the quick <note>An idiom meaning "being overly precise to the point of pain" or "splitting hairs." Pico is rounding the numbers for his argument.</note>). 

For they calculate four hundred and thirty years from Isaac to the departure from Egypt; almost as many from the departure to the temple that Solomon built; four hundred and ten years from Solomon to the desolation of the temple by the Babylonians; and four hundred and twenty years from the restoration of the temple under Ezra to this captivity under Titus. Therefore, if you collect all these together, you will calculate three thousand five hundred and eight years from the beginning of the world to Christ, according to the mind of the Hebrews themselves. 

Thus, Christ arrived in the very middle of the fourth millennium. Within that same millennium—as if within the boundaries of the fourth day—the light of the Sun (Christ) and the Moon (that is, the Church) shone upon the whole world. Furthermore, an innumerable multitude of martyrs, apostles, and doctors—all of whom flourished within five hundred years after Christ's death—illuminated the obscurity of the firmament (that is, the Law) and the shadows of our night. 

But the Hebrews will say: "Suppose Jesus did arrive during these times. You still do not have proof that he was the Christ, unless you show it was believed by our people that the Christ would come during those times." This is well put; they demand what is fair, and we can easily provide what they rightly ask. For there are manifest, well-known, and public oracles of Elijah circulated among them. Without any figure of speech and without a veil, he expressly says that the Messiah would come in the fourth millennium of the world. These oracles are not even <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword "ficta" on the next page suggests the word "fictitious."</note>

->### Heptaplus ###<-

Lest these things seem invented by me, or interpreted according to my own whim, I will bring forth the testimonies of the **Talmudists** <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law.</note> themselves, with whom we have this controversy. They make mention of these very things and, compelled by the truth itself, they confess that the time predicted by **Elijah** <note>Refers to a famous prophecy found in the Talmud (Sanhedrin 97a and Avodah Zarah 9a) attributed to the "School of Elijah."</note> for the coming of the Messiah has already passed. Two thousand void. Two thousand Law. Two thousand days of the Messiah, and because of our sins which are many, there have passed from them those [years] which have passed.

Thus they say. Come now, with these words placed before everyone’s eyes—since I can bring nothing either fabricated or arbitrary—let us discuss and examine the words of the oracle, and we shall immediately grasp the proposal. "The world is six thousand years," it says: which we may interpret thus: that after a cycle of six thousand years (as many of our own people have also believed), the consummation of the world will occur as a kind of Sabbath; or, if (which is more true) no one knows that day, let us take it in this sense: that concerning any further time, no prophecy is held in the Law. However, this does not pertain to the question at hand. Let us see what follows. *Two thousand void. Two thousand Law, then the Messiah.* He calls "void" (as all Hebrew interpreters say) the time before any Law was given by God to men. 

But I see the Jew mocking and saying: "If there are two thousand years before the Law, and two thousand of the Law before the Messiah's coming, then the Messiah does not come on the fourth day (while the fourth millennium is passing), but rather on the fifth day, because it would be after the fourth millennium." But indeed the response is easy, provided by the spirited truth. For what is said by Elijah—*Two thousand void, two thousand Law*—is not to be understood as if the world would be void for a full duration of two thousand years, and similarly that the Law would remain for exactly two thousand years; rather, it means that the time of the law of nature will reach into the second millennium, and the time of the [written] Law will reach into the fourth. But even before the second millennium is finished, there is the Law; and before the fourth passes away, the Messiah will be. 

I do not invent or dream up this exposition for myself; Elijah himself teaches it to me, and the Talmudists themselves teach it. This will soon be manifest to you, O Jewish asp <note>A harsh rhetorical flourish common in 15th-century polemics, comparing the opponent to a deaf adder that refuses to hear the truth (referencing Psalm 58).</note> (unless you close your ears). Elijah says *two thousand void, and two thousand Law.* Let us see in what sense the statement about the "void" was true, and from that, let us learn the method for explaining what is said about the Law. We take the beginning of the Law either from **Moses** or from **Abraham**. It cannot be taken from Moses, because the "void" would then have lasted more than two thousand and three hundred years, or thereabouts—for there are nearly that many years from **Adam** to Moses. Therefore, the beginning of the Law must be taken from Abraham, to whom the covenant of circumcision... <margin>circumcision</margin>

<meta>This page continues Pico's argument regarding the timing of the Messiah's arrival. circumcision—the root and foundation of the entire ancient law—occurred, yet if they consult their own histories from Adam to Abraham, they find that a full space of two thousand years had not elapsed, but only one thousand eight hundred and forty-eight years. From this it follows that the "fullness of the law" succeeded the "void" <note>Referring to the "two thousand years of void" (Tohu) mentioned on the previous page.</note> not after the second millennium, but within its boundaries. Therefore, by the same reasoning, the "evangelical fullness" <note>The arrival of the Gospel and the Messiah.</note> ought to succeed the "void of the law" not after the fourth millennium, but while the fourth was still passing. 

If they should attempt to deny this impudently and stubbornly, let them listen to their own **Talmudists** <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish law and tradition.</note> who greatly strengthen our opinion. For they themselves confess that even then, at the time they were writing, the time predicted by **Elijah** <note>The prophet Elijah; Pico refers to a prophecy in the Talmud (Sanhedrin 97a) regarding the ages of the world.</note> for the coming of the Messiah had already passed, and they attribute this to their own sins. But if the words of Elijah were to be understood as meaning that Christ was to come *after* the fourth millennium, the Talmudists would not have said, nor could they have said, that the time of the Messiah promised by the Prophets had already passed; for at the time when the Talmudic doctrine we have cited was written, four thousand years had not yet flowed from the beginning of the world. 

For as we have shown above, Jesus appeared three thousand five hundred and eight years after the beginning of the world according to the Hebrew reckoning. The **Jerusalem Talmud** (as they themselves hand down) was written three hundred years after the death of Christ, and the **Babylonian Talmud** one hundred years after the Jerusalem one. Therefore, both were composed within the limits of the fourth millennium, and yet they both confess and complain that the time spoken of by Elijah concerning the coming of Christ has passed. Where will they turn now, or what hiding places will they seek, to utterly flee from or avoid seeing our sun, which shines through the whole world even against their will? 

The Talmudists confess (even if they do not believe the ancient writers) that the times predicted by the prophets for the coming of Christ have passed. They confess it was believed by the Prophets that he would come during those very times in which we maintain Jesus arrived. Nor are their teachers entirely untruthful when they say the Messiah did not come because of their sins. For indeed, he did not "come" to them: those who did not recognize him. Nor is he the Messiah—that is, the **Redeemer**, the avenger of the worst captivity, the beneficent King, the rewarder of the land of promise (which is the heavenly Jerusalem)—except to those who have confessed him as the Messiah. 

But if he came unto his own and his own received him not, those who were once his own are his own no longer; instead, they come from the East and the West to lie down in the bosom of **Abraham**, while the "children of the love" <note>Pico is contrasting the "children of the promise" (Christians) with the biological descendants who rejected Jesus.</note> are cast out into the exterior darkness. From this, their persistent question is resolved: why would the Messiah be for the salvation of the Hebrews, yet Christ was for their destruction and ruin? For they are not "Hebrews" who not only fail to follow or worship the King and Lord promised to the Hebrews from the lineage of **David**, but who also—as if he were a thief, a sacrilegious man, and a profane person—affixed him to a cross with every injury and insult. If they were children of Abraham, they would stand firm in the institutions of Abraham, and they would celebrate his day—namely...

<summary>Pico uses Jewish chronology and the Talmud to argue that the Messiah was predicted to arrive during the fourth millennium, proving that Jesus's timing was correct. He concludes that those who rejected Jesus lost their status as the chosen people, resolving the paradox of why the Messiah's arrival coincided with the downfall of the Jewish state.</summary>

foreseeing that fourth [millennium], he rejoiced, so that they too, rejoicing, might receive Him upon His arrival. The Messiah brought peace to men, but not to all. For it was not said simply by the angels, "and on earth peace to men," but there was an addition: "to men of good will." <note>original: "hominibus bonæ uoluntatis"; a reference to the angelic hymn in Luke 2:14.</note> Certainly the same Sun which illuminates pure eyes blinds and darkens those that are sick and weak. And it is consistent with right reason that he who is a savior to the good should be harmful to the wicked; and he who blesses his friends, as one who is powerful and not ungrateful, should likewise strike down and scatter his enemies with lightning. If it had gone poorly for the Jews upon receiving Christ, He would not have been the Christ. But if it went poorly for them because they crucified Him, then He certainly was the Christ. For He who was nailed to the cross by His conquerors, and at that moment appeared most defeated, triumphed over them with such slaughter and calamity. <note>Pico refers to the Roman destruction of Jerusalem in 70 CE as a divine judgment for the Crucifixion.</note> Why then, you blind ones, do you wait for the Sun? The Sun is here and shines, but it shines in the darkness, and your darkness does not comprehend it. <note>A reference to the prologue of the Gospel of John (1:5).</note> The fourth day has passed, in which the Sun arose. He did not dissolve the law but fulfilled it, just as the Sun does not destroy the firmament, but adorns, perfects, and illuminates it. 

We have proven from the order of the fourth day and the time of Christ's arrival that the things said here are to be understood of Him. Let us prove the same from the similarity of the figure, because we can imagine Christ through no other thing more fittingly than through the Sun. For "He placed His tabernacle in the Sun," <note>original: "in Sole posuit tabernaculum suum"; Psalm 19:4. In the medieval tradition, this was often interpreted as the Incarnation.</note> and He came from the tribe of Judah, whose sign is the **Lion** <term>Leo (the Lion) is the zodiac sign traditionally ruled by the Sun in astrology.</term>, a solar animal; and since **Plato** <note>In Book VI of *The Republic*, Plato uses the Sun as an analogy for the Form of the Good.</note> in his *Republic* calls the Sun the "visible son of God," why should we not understand it to be an image of the invisible Son? If He is the true light illuminating every mind, He has a most expressive likeness in this Sun, which is the light of the world of images illuminating every body. But why do we seek other proofs? Let us ask the Sun itself, which, when the Moon stood in opposition during Christ’s suffering, failed [eclipsed], clearly showing us its natural sympathy for Him. Thus, by the best right—not to mention a deeper cause—we have called the day which the **mathematicians** <term>In the Renaissance, "mathematicians" often referred to astronomers and astrologers who calculated the movements of the heavens.</term> call the "Day of the Sun" [Sunday] the "Day of the Lord," and have devoted it entirely to His worship. We do this to show there is no reason why we should further worship the physical Sun (as the pagan nations once did) as the king and lord of heaven, now that the invisible Sun—co-eternal and co-equal with the Father, through whom both heaven and earth were created—has illuminated men sitting in the shadow of death.

### CHAPTER FIVE.

But now let us examine whether the works that follow the fourth day correspond to those things which are known to have happened after the arrival of Christ, so that we may finally accept this exposition of ours as true and stable, when we recognize that all things attest to and harmonize with it from every side. Let us see what happens after the fourth day. The waters bring forth fish and birds; the earth brings forth cattle and beasts of burden. Let us recall to mind what we said earlier was signified by the "waters," which, located under the heaven, were gathered into one place, and likewise by the "earth," which was made free from their flood.

-># Giovanni Pico della Mirandola #<-

We have said that the nations <note>Pico uses "nations" or "Gentiles" (gentes) interchangeably here to refer to non-Jewish peoples.</note> are symbolized by the waters, and the Israelites by the earth, which we have proven both with many testimonies from the Prophets and through the logic of resemblance. We saw that before the rising of the Sun, the sterile waters produced nothing that was good. The earth, however, was indeed fertile, but of meager fruit—mostly of grass and herbs. After the Sun, both the waters—with even greater fecundity than the earth—bring forth two kinds of living creatures: birds and fish. The earth, no longer content with trees and shrubs, produces both great cattle and beasts of burden. Do you not see, even without me speaking, that the word of the good Simeon has been fulfilled, so that this Sun of ours would be a **light for the revelation of the Gentiles and the glory of your people Israel**? <note>original: "lumen ad reuelationem gentium & gloriam plebis tuæ iſraël." This refers to the "Nunc Dimittis," the song of Simeon in Luke 2:32.</note> Do we not have before our eyes—even if we interpret nothing else—the calling of the Gentiles and the transformation of the terrestrial Jerusalem and the **shadowy synagogue** into the true church and the eternal and celestial city of God?

Before the rising of the Sun, the waters produce nothing. The earth produces something, but it is thin and meager. This is because before the advent of Christ, there was no sign of life among the Gentiles, no fruit of true religion. Among the Israelites, there was indeed some hope of life, and they knew the way of light in part, and they worshipped the true religion—but it was incipient and imperfect, until He came who is **the way, the truth, and the life.** <note>original: "uia, ueritas & uita." A reference to John 14:6.</note> 

And unless we return to this mystery, let someone offer me a reason why He divided the adornment and offspring of the earth in such a way that she produced some things before the Sun, and others after the Sun. Why, likewise, do the waters produce nothing before the sun, while the earth produces something? Why are two kinds of living creatures produced from the waters, while only one kind is produced from the earth? Why is the bird, an aerial animal, assigned to the waters? For (to deal with the first point) it is not enough to say, as some have, that herbs and plants were brought out of the earth before the making of the Sun lest they should seem to be created by its power. For by that same reasoning, the fish, the birds, and all the adornment of the elements ought much more to have been made before the Sun, lest they be believed to have been made by its power. 

Moses left this suspicion, therefore: that even if the light of the Sun was not necessary for producing plants, as they are more imperfect, it was nevertheless necessary for producing animals, which are more perfect. For it follows that if the more perfect things had come into the light without its help, then those which are less perfect could also be made without it. But the reasoning does not work in reverse: just because those things which are more ignoble were made without it—namely plants, the most lowly kind of living things—it does not follow that every kind of animal nature could be produced without its work intervening. Therefore, the intention of the author is more truly investigated from the source we have mentioned. 

Similarly, if anyone should speak of the living creatures related to the waters which dwell in the waters, he will see that one kind should rather have been referred to them, and two kinds to the earth, because the home of birds is the earth rather than the water; and beyond all controversy, if we consider the nature of the animal, a bird is either a terrestrial or an aerial animal, and is in no way aquatic. But hear the highest reasons of all, concerning Christ and the church...

...drawing the mysteries of the Church even from those who are unwilling. And indeed, if all things (as **Aristotle** says) harmonize with the truth, then all things must especially harmonize with **Christ**, who is Truth itself. It was not for nothing or without reason that he said so often to the Hebrews:
> *Search the scriptures; for they are they which testify of me* <note>original Latin: "Scrutemini scripturas, ipsę sunt quæ testimoniū perhibent de me"</note>, and asserted that so many things were predicted about him.
Indeed, he maintained that all things were contained in the Law, in the Psalms, and in the Prophets. But we are often blind in the presence of such great light, and unless he reveals them to us, we cannot consider the wonders of his law. Let us proceed, with his help, to the revelation of these mysteries and figures. 

Two kinds of animals are produced from the waters, and one from the earth, because there was a greater fullness of believers from the <term>Gentiles</term> <note>Non-Jewish nations, often referred to as "the nations" in biblical texts</note> than from the Jews. However, although the earth produces fewer in number, it produces more perfect living creatures than those the waters produce—namely, cattle and all four-footed animals. For even if more people believed from among the Pagans than from among the Hebrews, those from the Hebrews were more perfect, for from them came the **Apostles**, the founders of our entire religion.

Likewise, the water brings forth two different kinds and a double nature—birds and fish—while the earth brings forth only one kind. This is because from the **Gentiles**, some are transferred to Christ from the service of demons, while others come from the law of nature. Every **Hebrew** is simply a Hebrew because he was not permitted to live within the boundaries of nature alone; to him was given the Law of God, which was peculiar to him and not common to the rest of the nations. For *He has not dealt so with any nation, and his judgments he has not made manifest to them.*

The fish, therefore, signify to us those who came to us from the worship of demons. This is not only because the waters (as we showed above) represent the impiety of the Gentiles, but because **Jonathan the Chaldean** <note>Ionethes Chaldęus: Referring to the author of the Targum, the Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note> attests that in the sacred scriptures, wicked demons are often signified by these animals that live in the water. 

The birds signify those who are transferred to grace from the institutions of nature. The clear reason for this comes from what we wrote abundantly in the preface of this book concerning natural and supernatural happiness. For we showed that the heaven is the most expressive image of supernatural happiness, and that natural happiness is a certain secondary and imaginary thing rather than true happiness. Therefore, those who attain this by using the laws of nature are most fittingly denoted by birds—inhabitants not of the first and true heaven, but of the **air**, which by a certain secondary and imaginary reasoning also claims the name of "heaven" for itself. This is why they are so frequently called "fowls of the heaven" and "birds of heaven" in the divine scriptures. 

See, however, with what deep counsel it was arranged that the birds are referred to the water and not to the air. Because those who lived according to nature were nonetheless still counted as part of the "people of the Gentiles." Indeed, they were called Gentiles and lived among Gentiles—such as **Socrates** and many of the philosophers. For that reason, both groups were referred to the waters in common. 

But it is easy to show how well this exposition fits with the teachings of the Gospels and the Apostles. Since even the converts from the Hebrews—the Apostles—are referred to by **Paul** as "oxen" (land animals); and by our doctors in their commentaries on the Gospel...

<meta>This page continues Pico's allegorical reading of the Genesis creation days. On the previous page, he was distinguishing between the animals created from the water (Gentiles) and those from the earth (Jews), establishing why the Apostles were "fishers of men."</meta>

...in which the sellers are cast out of the temple, they are prefigured. And **Christ** calls the **Israelites** "sheep," but the **Apostles**, to whom the conversion of the <term>Gentiles</term> <note>The non-Jewish nations</note> was commanded, were called "fishermen" by the Lord. Their leader was **Peter**, who was to be a fisherman at **Rome**, the mistress of the Nations, as if over an ocean and the rest of the world. **Christ**, however, who said he was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of **Israel**, claimed for himself the name not of a fisherman, but rather of a shepherd.

### CHAPTER SIX.

The solution to the question that has long troubled interpreters of this book is also manifest from here: Why was it not said on the second day: *And God saw that it was good*? If we say what is usually said—that it was done because the work of the waters was not completed on that day, but on the third, when the waters under the heavens flowed together into one place—the answer does not seem fully satisfactory. For the proper work of the second day is not the arrangement of the waters, but the arrangement of the <term>firmament</term> <note>The "expanse" or sky created to separate the waters above from the waters below</note>, which was fixed in the middle place between the waters. On that day, both the making of the firmament (when God said, *let there be a firmament*) and the distinction of the waters (when He said, *and let it divide the waters from the waters*) were sufficiently completed. However, the collection of the waters called the "sea," the revealing of the dry land, and the production of plants belong to an entirely different kind of work; thus, they were finished on another day—the third—to which they belonged. 

Therefore, the reason must be sought in a deeper mystery. The firmament (as we showed above) prefigures the Law. Just as the firmament was unformed and not simply perfect until it was furnished with the **Sun**, **Moon**, and stars, so the Law was neither "bad"—as the **Manichaeans** <note>An ancient dualist sect that believed the material world was evil and that the God of the Old Testament was a lesser, malevolent deity</note> claim—nor was it "simply good" (that is, perfect) until **Christ** came, who fulfilled the Law. If the firmament had been evil, it would not have received the sun; if it had been good, it would not have needed the sun. 

But the firmament was good only insofar as it was capable of receiving the sun and the other stars, just as the Law was good only insofar as it was our <term>pedagogue</term> <note>A tutor or guardian; Pico uses the Pauline image of the Law leading people toward Christ</note> in **Christ**. **Moses** permitted many things because of the hardness of the people's hearts which the **Gospel** later did not permit. That we cannot call the Law "evil," as **Mani** <note>The founder of Manichaeism</note> believed, yet can call it "not good," is most clearly taught by the **Prophet**, through whom God, speaking of the **Hebrews**, says: *I gave them precepts that were not good* <note>original Latin: "Dedi eis præcepta non bona" — citing Ezekiel 20:25</note>. He did not say "evil precepts," but "precepts not good"—that is, not perfect, not absolute, not completed. This is confirmed by the ancient **Hebrew** doctors, who, interpreting that passage of **Ecclesiastes**, *Vanity of vanities and all is vanity* <note>original Latin: "Vanitas uanitatum & omnia uanitas"</note>, say: "Even the Law is vanity until the **Messiah** comes." And so much for these matters.

### CHAPTER SEVEN.

Since the supreme benefit of the Word made flesh <note>The Incarnation of Christ</note> was this: that through the sacrament of **Baptism**, through which the power of **Christ** is poured into us, we are re-...

<meta>This page concludes the sixth chapter of the seventh book, transitioning from the allegorical creation of man to a mystical analysis of the very first word of Genesis. It maintains the theme of the "Image of God" and begins the final technical section of the work.</meta>

...that we might be begotten as children of God, born not of blood but of God. Finally, Moses indicates this to us when, after the sun has risen and been shown to the world, and after the fertility of the waters and the earth, he makes man in the image of God—not a terrestrial man, but a celestial one. For with the <term>Gentiles</term> <note>Non-Jewish peoples</note> and Jews converted to Christ, this one thing remained: that through the most holy washing <note>The sacrament of Baptism</note>, conforming themselves to the Lord's cross, they might be reformed to the image of God. For if Baptism makes us children of God, and the Son is the image of the Father, is it not the power of the entire Trinity acting in baptism that says: *Let us make man in our image*? If, therefore, we are in the image of God, we are also children. If children, then we are heirs: heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ. But who are the children? It was written by Paul that we cry out, *Abba, Father*, in the Holy Spirit. Those, therefore, who live by the spirit, these are the children of God, these are the brothers of Christ, these are destined for the eternal inheritance, which they shall happily possess in the heavenly Jerusalem as a reward for both faith and a well-lived life.

## Exposition of the first word, that is,

### In the beginning.

Now we have come to the end <note>Original: "ad calcem," literally "to the heel," a metaphor for the finish line of a race</note> of the work, having run through the <term>septiform</term> <note>Sevenfold</note> exposition of the universal context. But I recognize that something still remains, untouched and undiscussed by us, which it seemed ought to have been explained in the first place: that is, what the first word of the Law <note>The Torah or Pentateuch</note> means, which is: *In the beginning* <note>Original: "In principio," translating the Hebrew "Bereshit"</note>. It was not recklessly or without cause that I wished to speak of this "beginning" at the end of the whole work. Nor am I going to dispute here about the Son of God, who is the Beginning through whom all things were made—for He is the wisdom of the Father. Nor will I prove that the ancient Hebrews felt the same as our people on this point—which we shall do elsewhere—but we intend, through another method of interpretation, to give readers a taste of Mosaical profundity. We shall not do this before we have deliberated a little on a certain doctrine of the older Jewish discipline, which is truly a <term>paradox</term> <note>A statement that seems contradictory or incredible but may be true; here Pico refers to the mystical Kabbalistic tradition</note>. It is the firm opinion of all the ancients, which they confirm with one voice as indubitable, that the complete knowledge of all arts, of all wisdom both divine and human, is included in the five books of the Mosaical law, but concealed and hidden in the very letters with which the words of the law are woven, in the manner we shall now declare. Let us take, for example's sake, the first small part of the book of Genesis—namely, from the start up to the place where it is written: *And God saw the light, that it was good*. That entire scripture is numbered as one hundred and three elements <note>Individual Hebrew letters</note>, which, arranged in the way the words are there constituted, present nothing but common and trivial things. This order of letters represents the husk, so to speak, of this text, hiding the inner marrow of the latent...

<meta>This page continues the exposition of the first word of Genesis, "Bereshit" (In the beginning). Pico is performing a Kabbalistic analysis by breaking down the single Hebrew word into multiple constituent words to reveal hidden theological and cosmological meanings. This page specifically links the structure of the human body to the structure of the universe.</meta>

->Heptaplus<-

of philosophy, mysteries regarding the whole of nature are revealed. *Ab* <note>Hebrew: אב</note> signifies the father. *Be-bar* <note>A combination of the prefix "Beth" and "Bar" (son)</note> signifies in the son and through the son (for the preposition *beth* signifies both). *Res* signifies the beginning. *Sabath* signifies rest and the end. *Bara* means he created. *Ros* means head. *Es* means fire. *Seth* means foundation. *Rab* means of the great. *Iish* means of man. *Berith* means by a covenant. *Tob* means in a good [way]. And if we weave the whole speech together in the following order, it will be thus: 

**The Father, in the Son and through the Son, the beginning and the end, or rest, created the head, the fire, and the foundation of the great man, by a good covenant.**

This entire sentence results from the first analysis and composition of that word <note>The word "Bereshit" (In the beginning)</note>. How deep and how full of all learning its meaning is cannot be clear to everyone immediately. But some things are immediately apparent to all Christians—though not all things are open to all people—which are signified to us through these voices: such as what it means for the Father to have created in the Son and through the Son. Likewise, what it means for the Son to be the beginning and the end of all things. For he is the Alpha and the Omega <note>Original: α & ω</note> (as John writes), and he called himself the "Beginning," and we have shown that he is the end of all things, so that they may be restored to their beginning. 

Other things are a little more obscure: namely, what those terms mean: "head," "fire," and "foundation of the great man"; what that "covenant" is, and for what reason it is called "good." For it is not immediately easy for everyone to see that the entire rationale, kinship, and likewise the happiness of the four worlds <note>Pico's system of the Intellectual, Celestial, Corruptible, and Human worlds</note> about which we are treating—and which we discussed last—are explained here. 

First, therefore, it should be noted that the World is called by Moses a "great man." For if man is a <term>microcosm</term> <note>Original: "paruus mundus," or small world</note>, then certainly the world is a <term>macrocosm</term> <note>Original: "magnus homo," or great man</note>. Taking this opportunity, Moses most aptly figures the three worlds—the intellectual, the celestial, and the corruptible—through the three parts of man. At the same time, he indicates by this figure not only that all worlds are contained within man, but he briefly declares which part of man corresponds to which world. 

Let us therefore imagine three parts in man: the highest is the head; then that which extends from the neck to the navel; and the third, which extends from the navel to the feet. For these are also distinguished and separated in the figure of man by a certain variety. But it is wonderful how beautifully, how precisely, and by the most exact reasoning they correspond in proportion to the three parts of the world. In the head is the brain, the source of cognition; in the breast is the heart, the source of the motion of life and heat; in the lowest part are the reproductive organs, the principle of generation. 

In the same way, in the world, the highest part—which is the angelic or <term>intellectual world</term>—is the source of cognition, because that nature was made for understanding. The middle part—which is the heavens—is the principle of life, motion, and heat, in which the sun rules like the heart in the breast. Below the Moon is that which is known to all as the principle of generation and corruption. You see how aptly all these parts of the world and of man agree with one another. Moses designated the first part by the proper name of the "head"; the second he called "fire," both because the heavens are judged to be so by many, and because in us this portion is the source of heat; the third he called "foundation"...

<summary>Pico uses Kabbalistic letter-permutation to extract a complex sentence from the word "Bereshit," then explains the "Macrocosm-Microcosm" analogy relating the human body to the three levels of the universe.</summary>
<keywords>Bereshit, Kabbalah, Macrocosm, Microcosm, Intellectual World, Celestial World, Sublunary World, Christology, Etymology</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the "Heptaplus," Pico's seven-fold narration of the creation of the world. The text finishes the Kabbalistic interpretation of the word "Bereshit" (In the beginning) by identifying the "foundation" (Seth) of the human body and the "covenant" (Berith) that binds the universe to God. It then transitions into a preface for Pico's "Apology," which he wrote to defend his "900 Theses" after thirteen of them were declared heretical or suspect by a papal commission.</meta>

...because through it (as is known to all) the entire human body is founded and sustained. He added, moreover, that he created these by a good covenant, because a covenant of peace and friendship has been sanctioned between them—by the kinship of their natures and mutual consent—through the law of God’s wisdom. This covenant is good because it is so directed and ordained toward God (who is goodness itself), so that just as the whole world is one within itself, it may also be one with its final author. Let us also imitate this most holy covenant of the world, so that through mutual charity we may be one with each other, and together, through true love of God, we may all happily become one with Him.

### ->END OF THE HEPTAPLUS.<-

### ->TO THE READER.<-

Out of those nine hundred Conclusions which we previously published, several of Pico's rivals—under the pretext of faith and zeal for religion—condemned thirteen propositions (though they had been approved by many good men). These propositions were marked with little stars <note>Original: stellulis; refers to the asterisks used to mark the controversial theses in the printed editions.</note> and their index number. When Pico perceived that his adversaries were not openly acting against his work, but that his reputation was being somewhat attacked, he published an *Apology* himself, in which he refutes the arguments of the slanderers. The sequence of the condemned propositions is as follows:

| | |
|---|---|
| 1 | **Concerning Christ's descent into hell.** |
| 2 | **Concerning the punishment for mortal sin.** |
| 3 | **Concerning the Adoration of the cross and images.** |
| 4 | **Whether an irrational nature can be assumed by God.** <note>This refers to a technical theological debate about whether God could, in theory, take the form of a non-human animal or object.</note> |
| 5 | **Concerning natural Magic and the Kabbalah of the Hebrews.** |
| 6 | **Concerning the sacrament of the Eucharist.** |
| 7 | **Concerning the Salvation of Origen.** <note>Origen was a 3rd-century theologian whose belief that all souls (and even the devil) might eventually be saved was highly controversial.</note> |
| 8 | **That believing is not within a man’s free power.** |
| 9 | **Concerning the accidents in the Sacrament.** <note><term>Accidents</term>: In Aristotelian philosophy, these are the physical properties (taste, smell, color) of the bread and wine that remain after the substance has changed into the body and blood of Christ.</note> |
| 10 | **Concerning the words of consecration.** |
| 11 | **Concerning the miracles of Christ.** |
| 12 | **Whether God understands.** <note>Pico argued that "understanding" is a human process of moving from premise to conclusion, and thus God's knowledge is more immediate than "understanding."</note> |
| 13 | **Concerning the hidden intelligence of the soul.** |

# OF GIOVANNI PICO
## of Mirandola, Illustrious Man, 900 Conclusions, 
### which he once presented in Rome 
### to be debated.

### GIOVANNI PICO OF MIRANDOLA 
### TO THE READER.

**R**egarding the nine hundred propositions listed here—Dialectical, Moral, Physical, Mathematical, Metaphysical, Theological, Magical, and Kabbalistic—comprising both his own views and those of the wise Chaldeans, Arabs, Hebrews, Greeks, Egyptians, and Latins, Giovanni Pico of Mirandola, Count of Concordia, will debate publicly. In reciting these, he has not sought the polish of the Roman tongue, but has instead imitated the style of speaking used by the most celebrated Parisian disputants <note>The "Parisian style" refers to the technical, often dry language of Scholasticism centered at the University of Paris, which focused on logic and precision over the elegant rhetoric favored by Renaissance Humanists.</note>, for the reason that almost all philosophers of our time utilize it. These dogmas to be debated are arranged as follows: those pertaining to specific nations or heresiarchs <note>Leaders of heretical movements.</note> are placed separately; those pertaining to the branches of philosophy are placed promiscuously <note>Meaning "mixed together" or "without a fixed order."</note>, as if all mixed together in a medley.

---

Conclusions according to the doctrine of the Latin philosophers and theologians: Albert the Great, Thomas Aquinas, Henry of Ghent, John Duns Scotus, Giles of Rome, and Francis of Mayronis.

-> ACCORDING TO ALBERT, XVI. <-
<note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280) was a Dominican friar and the teacher of Thomas Aquinas; he was known as the "Universal Doctor" for his vast knowledge of the natural sciences and philosophy.</note>

1 Intelligible species <term>species intelligibiles: the mental representations or "forms" that the mind uses to grasp universal concepts</term> are not necessary, and to posit them is not in accordance with the views of the good Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note>.
2 Even if all individuals of the human species were destroyed, this remains true: "Man is an animal."
3 This proposition is in the "fourth mode" of essential predication <note>A technical term in Scholastic logic regarding how a subject and predicate are naturally linked; the fourth mode refers to a cause being included in the definition of the effect.</note>: "A human is a human."
4 In every point of matter, there exist—by way of a potential beginning—the powers of the essences of all natural forms; these are co-eternal with matter according to the philosophers, but created together with it according to the Faith.
5 A form, in its intensifying or diminishing <note>The "intension and remission" of forms was a medieval theory explaining how qualities (like heat or grace) change in degree while remaining the same in essence.</note>, does not vary according to its essence, but according to its being.
6 The separated soul <note>The soul after death, separated from the body.</note> understands through species created together with it from the beginning of its existence; while it is in the body, it uses these either never or only rarely.
7 Sound is carried according to its real being as far as the beginning of the auditory nerve.
8 Light possesses nothing in the medium <note>The "medium" is the space between the object and the eye, such as air.</note> except an intentional being <term>esse intentionale: a mode of existence where a thing exists as a representation or image rather than as a physical object</term>.
9 The organ of hearing is the nerve expanded toward the cavity of hearing.
10 The proper object of the "common sense" <note>The internal sense that medieval philosophers believed integrated the data from the five external senses.</note> is magnitude, as Avicenna rightly said.
11 The rule stands <note>Original: "Status Stat." A technical shorthand in Scholastic debate meaning the established position remains.</note> that the species of which we are said to have a memory is totally lost.

12 The vegetative soul is not introduced before the sensitive, nor the sensitive before the rational, but all are introduced at once. <note>Pico is here siding with the view that the human soul is a single unit infused by God, rather than a series of souls—plant-like, then animal-like, then human—developing in stages.</note>
13 Although the sense concurs passively in the reception of the form <term>species: a mental image or likeness of an object</term>, it nonetheless concurs actively in judging the sensible object.
14 The mobile body is the subject of natural science. <note>In the Scholastic tradition, "Physics" or "Natural Science" was defined specifically as the study of physical things capable of change or motion.</note>
15 The consideration of the body (insofar as it is a body) belongs to the Metaphysician.
16 The relational potential of matter does not add a physical thing above matter, but only a conceptual relationship <term>ratio: a logical or reasoned distinction</term>.

## ACCORDING TO THOMAS [AQUINAS], 45 CONCLUSIONS.

1 If the Holy Spirit did not proceed from the Son, he would not be distinguished from the Son. <note>original: "Si spiritus à filio non procederet..." This refers to the Filioque, a core doctrine of Western Christianity stating that the Holy Spirit originates from both the Father and the Son.</note>
2 The temporal procession of the Holy Spirit is considered according to the gifts of "grace that makes one pleasing" <term>gratia gratum faciens: sanctifying grace that unites the soul to God</term>.
3 The existence of contingent things—those which are, will be, or have been—was therefore infallibly known by God from eternity, because it was presentially set before his eternity. <note>Pico defends the idea that God exists outside of time; therefore, he does not "foresee" the future so much as see all moments as "now," which preserves human free will.</note>
4 The contingency of future things (which could happen in one way or another) known by God stands together with the infallibility of divine knowledge.
5 Whatever contingent thing God knew was to be in the future, he necessarily knew that it would be in the future.
6 From divine goodness can be taken the reason for the predestination of some and the reprobation <note>exclusion from salvation</note> of others; and the divine will alone is the reason why he reproves some and elects others for glory.
7 Although God’s "consequent will" <note>the will of God that takes all human circumstances and choices into account</note> is always fulfilled, it does not necessarily impose necessity upon the things willed.
8 Neither can one who possesses grace (even by God’s absolute power) fail to be accepted by God for eternal life, nor can one who lacks it be accepted.
9 A work formed by a soul in the state of charity merits eternal glory "by worthiness" <term>de condigno: a merit that, by God's promise, establishes a just claim to a reward</term>.
10 The three divine persons could together sustain <term>suppositare: to act as the underlying person or subject</term> a single nature. <note>This refers to the possibility of all three persons of the Trinity being incarnated in one human nature.</note>
11 The moral and cardinal virtues will remain in the homeland <note>Heaven</note> after the resurrection.
12 Blessedness <note>supreme happiness or Beatitude</note> exists essentially in the act of the intellect. **Corollary:** Neither enjoyment nor any act of the will is essentially blessedness. <note>This is a classic Thomist position, arguing that our ultimate reward is *knowing* God (intellect) rather than just *loving* Him (will).</note>
13 The sacraments of the New Law are the cause of grace, not only as a necessary condition <note>sine qua non</note>, but also as the instrument through which it is given.
14 The true body of Christ is in heaven locally, and on the altar sacramentally.
15 The impassibility <note>the state of being unable to suffer or feel pain</note> of bodies after the resurrection will arise from the full dominion of the soul over the body.
16 Christ in the final judgment will judge not only in his human nature, but also according to his human nature.
17 Although it might be defended in some way that a creature can create, it is more rational to believe that the power of creating cannot be communicated to a creature.
18 *Aevum* <term>aevum: a mode of time for eternal beings like angels, midway between the "time" of humans and the "eternity" of God</term> exists subjectively in the more blessed angel.
19 There cannot be sin in the will unless there is a defect in the reason.

# Conclusions.

<margin>a</margin> 20 Not even through the power of God can the same body be in different places at the same time. <note>Thomas Aquinas argued that bilocation is a logical contradiction, as being in one place implies not being in another.</note>
21 There is no multiplication of angels under the same species. <note>According to Thomas, because angels have no matter, each individual angel is its own unique species, unlike humans who share one species but are many individuals.</note>
22 God is not seen in the heavenly homeland through a mental image <term>species: a likeness or representation of an object</term>, but God himself is applied to the intellect by his own essence, acting as the intelligible form.
<margin>b</margin> 23 "One," when considered as a transcendental property of being, adds nothing to "being" except the denial of division.
<margin>c</margin> 24 The subject and its proper attribute <term>passio: a property that necessarily flows from the essence of a thing</term> are really distinct from one another.
25 Form is generated only accidentally.
26 Matter designated by dimensions <term>materia signata: matter existing in space and time</term> is the principle of individuation. <note>This is a foundational Thomistic idea: what makes two humans different individuals, despite having the same human nature, is the specific "hunk" of matter they occupy.</note>
<margin>d</margin> 27 A quality remains numerically the same from the beginning of a change <term>alteratio: qualitative change</term> until the end.
28 All liberty resides essentially in the reason.
29 In substantial generation, there is a resolution all the way down to prime matter. <note>When one thing turns into another—like wood into ash—Thomas believed the old form disappears entirely, leaving only the "prime matter" to receive the new form.</note>
<margin>e</margin> 30 Being expresses ten immediate concepts <note>The ten Categories of Aristotle, such as Substance, Quality, and Quantity.</note> so unified among themselves that they do not belong to a single concept, but are related to a single one.
<margin>f</margin> 31 Essence and existence are really distinct in every created thing. <note>One of Thomas’s most famous doctrines: only in God are "what a thing is" and "that a thing is" the same.</note>
32 Contradictory statements can in no way be verified of the same thing when it is actually distinct outside the mind.
<margin>g</margin> 33 Matter expresses no positive act of being.
34 No moral virtue, except for justice, resides subjectively in the will.
35 This proposition, "Man is capable of laughter," does not belong to the second mode of essential predication <term>per se: a logical term for necessary truths</term>.
36 Two accidents differing only by number cannot exist in the same subject.
<margin>h</margin> 37 Heavy and light things are moved by no other mover than either the one that generated them or the one that removed an obstacle.
38 Heavy things are moved by themselves rather than from themselves.
39 The mental image <term>phantasm: a sensory image stored in the imagination</term> is a secondary and instrumental agent in the production of a concept <term>species intelligibilis: the refined mental form used by the intellect</term>.
<margin>i</margin> 40 The difficulty of understanding can arise both from the intellect itself and from the object being understood.
41 The powers of the soul are really distinct from the soul itself.
42 Essences <term>quiditates: "what-ness," the definition of a thing</term> in their particularity are not considered by the Metaphysician.
43 It implies a contradiction for matter to exist without form.
44 The idea of prime matter should not be placed in God.
45 The ideas of general categories <term>genera</term> should not be placed in God.

### ACCORDING TO FRANCIS [OF MEYRONNES], 8 CONCLUSIONS.

1 Therefore, this statement is false: "The Essence generates," because the essence is ultimately abstract, and "generates" is predicated formally. <note>Francis of Meyronnes was a follower of Duns Scotus; this explores technical Trinitarian logic regarding whether the divine nature itself "acts" or if only the Persons act.</note>
2 The divine essence can be seen without the Persons, and one Person can be seen without another.
3 The will cannot fail to enjoy an object of enjoyment once it is shown.
<margin>l</margin> 4 Being is predicated of God denominatively.
5 Essences <term>quiditates</term> possess their formal being from eternity from themselves, not from anything external.
6 No definition perfectly matches the thing defined.

7 A plurality of formalities is consistent with real identity. <note>This refers to the "formal distinction," a famous concept in Franciscan philosophy where things can be distinct in definition or "formality" while being the same actual thing in reality.</note>

## ACCORDING TO JOHN DUNS SCOTUS XXII.

1 Charity is not a habit distinct from the habit of grace, through which the Holy Spirit dwells in the soul.
2 The "idea" of a stone is nothing other than the stone produced by the divine intellect in its "intelligible being"—which is being in a qualified sense <term>secundum quid: in a certain respect, rather than absolutely</term>—existing in the divine mind just as the known exists in the knower.
3 Whoever says that the Persons in the Godhead are distinguished by absolute properties will not contradict Catholic truth.
4 In Christ there were two "beings" <note>original: "duo esse." This refers to Christ having both a divine and a human act of existence.</note>.
5 Practice is the operation of a power other than the intellect, naturally suited to be brought forth in conformity with right reason so that the action itself may be right.
6 Every individual is an individual through its own unique individual difference, which is called "thisness" <term>hecceitas: the property that makes a thing "this" specific thing and not another</term>.
7 "Being" is predicated of God and creatures univocally <note>meaning the word "being" has exactly the same meaning when applied to God and to a rock, a major departure from Thomas Aquinas who argued the terms were only "analogical."</note> in regards to their "whatness."
8 "Being" does not describe its own attributes <term>passiones: properties like "one," "true," or "good" that follow from being</term> and ultimate differences in terms of their essence.
9 In Christ there was no acquired knowledge. <note>Scotus argues Christ’s knowledge was infused or divine from the start, rather than learned through experience over time.</note>
10 Virtues are to be placed in the "higher appetite" <note>the Will</note>.
11 Grace resides subjectively in the will, not in the essence of the soul.
12 The body of Christ was, of itself, incapable of suffering.
13 By the absolute power of God, it is possible for original sin to be wiped away without the infusion of grace. <note>Scholastics distinguished between God's "ordained power" (how He chose to set up the world) and His "absolute power" (what He could theoretically do if He chose).</note>
14 After the passion of Christ, the ceremonies of the Old Law could be observed without sin.
15 Consecration [of the Eucharist] cannot occur through these words precisely—"This is my body"—unless the preceding words are also expressed, namely, "on the day before he suffered."
16 The relationship of a creature to God is really the same as its foundation, yet formally distinct by the nature of the thing.
17 Any other relationship is really distinct from its foundation.
18 Something can move itself from a state of potential power <term>actu uirtuali</term> to a state of actualized form <term>actu formalem</term>.
19 The act of understanding is caused by both the object and the intellect, acting as two partial agents to produce the result.
20 The act of understanding is caused in a nobler way by the intellect than by the object, no matter what the object is, provided it is not the "beatific" object <note>God as seen in heaven</note>.
21 Substance is not known through its own mental representation <term>species: a likeness or image in the mind</term>.
22 A habit produces an act as a partial efficient cause.

1 There is a light superior to the light of faith, in which theologians see the truths of theological science. <note>Henry of Ghent was known for his theory of "divine illumination," where God provides a special light to the mind to perceive certain truths.</note>
2 Fatherhood is the principle of generating in the Father. <note>Referring to the internal relations of the Trinity.</note>

3 Divine processions <note>In theology, "processions" refer to the ways the Persons of the Trinity (Son and Holy Spirit) originate from the Father.</note> are distinguished according to the intellect and the will.
4 This proposition is not to be granted: "the essence is the father of the son."

### ACCORDING TO GILES OF ROME XI.

1 The power of generating in the divine is neither the divine essence taken precisely and absolutely, nor a relation or property, nor something constituted from both, nor one of these including the other; rather, it is the essence with a "revealing mode" <note>original: "modo reuelatiuo." This likely refers to a "relational mode" (relatiuo) in Giles' technical vocabulary, describing how the divine essence acts as a parent.</note>.
2 Theology is neither practical nor speculative, but affective <note>Aegidius (Giles) argued that theology's goal is not just knowledge (speculative) or action (practical), but the love of God (affective).</note>.
3 God, under the aspect of "Glorifier," is the subject of theology.
4 The Father and the Son can be called not only two "breathers" <note>original: "spirantes."</note> but even two "spirators" <note>original: "spiratores." Both terms refer to the "breathing forth" or Spiration of the Holy Spirit.</note>.
5 Angels were not created in a state of grace.
6 An angel is obstinate and unrepentant because special divine impulses have been withdrawn from him.
7 A higher angel illuminates a lower one, not because he presents a luminous object to him, or because he divides and particularizes what is unified within himself for the other, but because he comforts and strengthens the intellect of the lower angel.
8 The sense of taste, as taste, perceives not only what can be tasted (flavor) but also moisture.
9 Heat, even if it were separated [from a body], could still generate fire.
10 For one science not to be subordinate to another, it is sufficient that it reduces its arguments to principles known through themselves within its own level of abstraction.
11 Given a vacuum, if something were to move within it, it would move in an instant. <note>This reflects the Aristotelian belief that resistance creates time in motion; without resistance, motion would be instantaneous.</note>

**C**onclusions according to the doctrine of the Arabs, who for the most part profess themselves to be Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note>: Averroes, Avicenna, Al-Farabi, Avempace, Isaac, Avenzoar, Moses, and Muhammad.

### ACCORDING TO AVERROES XLI.

1 Prophecy in dreams is possible through the illumination of the "agent intellect" <term>intellectus agens: the active force of the mind that makes thinking possible</term> upon our soul.
2 There is only one intellectual soul for all human beings. <note>This is Averroes' most controversial thesis: that all humans share a single, collective mind.</note>
3 The ultimate happiness of man occurs when the "agent intellect" is joined to the "possible intellect" <term>intellectus possibilis: the human capacity to receive knowledge</term>.

...as a form, which continuation both other Latin authors whom I have read, and especially John of Jandun <note>original: "Ioannes de Gandauo," a 14th-century philosopher and famous proponent of Averroism</note>, understood perversely and erroneously; he who not only in this, but in almost all philosophical inquiries, entirely corrupted and debased the doctrine of Averroes.
