->Corollary: the soul of the heaven first gives its sphere mobile and perfect being,<-
->before it gives it motion.<-

9 The heaven is a simple body, not composed of matter and form.

10 Three modes *per se* <note>meaning "of itself" or "essential"</note> are useful for demonstration: the first, the second, and the fourth.

11 In every demonstration, except for a simple demonstration <note>demonstration *simpliciter*, which shows the reason *why* something is</note>, circular reasoning can occur.

12 Heavy and light things move themselves accidentally by moving the medium essentially <note>per se</note>.

13 The heavens are not the same in genus but diverse in species, as Avicenna believed.

14 No science proves that its subject exists, nor a principal part of its subject.

15 Universals exist on the part of the thing only in potentiality, but in act through the operation of the soul <note>This addresses the "problem of universals," suggesting general concepts only become "real" through the mind's processing.</note>.

16 Indeterminate dimensions are co-eternal with matter, preceding any substantial form within it.

17 Any intelligence besides the first understands nothing except the first.

18 There is no way to prove that a simple abstract thing exists except through the way of the eternity of motion.

19 Whatever is within a genus is corruptible <note>subject to decay or change</note>.

20 The subject of metaphysics is being insofar as it is being <note>Aristotle's famous definition of "First Philosophy."</note>.

21 Definitions of natural substances mention matter only consecutively <note>as a necessary consequence of the form, rather than its primary definition</note>.

22 The demonstration in the seventh book of the *Physics*—that everything that is moved is moved by another—is a demonstration of a sign <note>an effect</note>, and in no way of a cause.

23 No active power which is merely neutral and indifferent to acting or not acting can be determined by itself to do the one or the other.

<header>Conclusions</header>

# Conclusions

24 One of two related terms is most appropriately defined through the other.

25 Aristotle's example in the second book of the *Metaphysics* concerning the night-owl <note>original: "nicticorax"; a bird of the night, often interpreted by medieval commentators as a bat, whose eyes are blinded by the sun</note> in relation to the sun does not denote impossibility, but difficulty; otherwise nature would have acted in vain <note>original: "otiose"; purposelessly</note>.

26 A necessary proposition, which is distinguished by Aristotle in the *Prior Analytics* from the possible and the found <note>original: "inuentam"; referring to an assertoric or *de inesse* proposition, which states a fact as it is found to be</note>, is that which consists of necessary terms.

27 For the arrangement of a necessary term, it is required that it be a term that is "one of itself" <term>per se one: a term representing a single, unified essence rather than a collection of accidental parts</term>.

28 When Aristotle said that from a necessary major premise and a "found" minor premise, a necessary conclusion is drawn, it must be understood regarding a minor premise that is found "of itself" <note>per se</note> but necessary "by accident" <note>per accidens</note>.

29 There can be no natural habitation for living things under the equinoctial line <note>the equator</note>.

30 In the heavens, there is a natural "right side," and this does not change, even though the parts of the world <note>the celestial spheres</note> change.

31 He who posits that the soul is a form of "complexion" <note>a physical mixture or balance of bodily humors</note> denies an efficient cause.

32 The metaphysical "One" signifies the privation of divisibility, not in act, but in aptitude.

33 The metaphysical "One" is the foundation of the arithmetical "one."

34 Number is found in abstract things exactly as it is found in material things.

35 The essence of each thing and its existence are really the same.

36 Quiddity <note>the "whatness" or defining nature of a thing</note> and essence are differentiated in every being except for the first <note>referring to God, the First Cause, in whom essence and existence are one</note>.

37 Substance is prior to accident, not only by nature but by time.

38 The physicist considers matter insofar as it is matter.

39 The essence of every intelligence <note>a celestial spirit or angel</note> is substantially "toward something" <note>referring to a relational property</note>.

40 Even if it were granted as an impossibility that a type of matter could be given which was not a principle of corruption <note>decay</note>, if the heaven were truly composed of such matter and form, it still could not be eternal.

41 The end <note>the goal or purpose</note> does not cause as a final cause according to its being as a concept, but according to its real being.

### ACCORDING TO AVICENNA XII <note>Twelve conclusions following the thought of the Persian philosopher Ibn Sina</note>

1 Besides the categorical and hypothetical syllogism, there exists a genus of "compositive" syllogisms.

2 Although in no syllogism that is actually or potentially categorical can a conclusion be drawn from two negative premises, this can nevertheless happen in a compositive syllogism: namely, that a conclusion is drawn from two negatives.

3 In the heavens, there is matter of the same nature as the matter of lower <note>earthly</note> things.

4 An intelligible notion cannot exist in the soul without actual intellection <note>the active process of thinking</note>.

5 It is possible for a human being to be generated from putrefaction <note>the medieval theory of spontaneous generation, where life arises from decaying matter without parents</note>.

6 The essence of a thing encompasses its own matter and form.

7 The first substance is prior to any substance having a relationship to...

<margin>8</margin> From a single entity, simple to the highest degree of simplicity, only one thing can proceed. <note>A fundamental Neoplatonic principle: the "One" or God is so simple that He can only have one immediate effect.</note>

# ACCORDING TO AL-FARABI
<note>Al-Farabi (c. 872–950) was a renowned philosopher of the Islamic Golden Age, known as the "Second Teacher" after Aristotle.</note>

<margin>1</margin> The "primary" element required in a demonstration is not what Aristotle defined in the first book of the *Posterior Analytics*, but should be defined thus: the primary is that which is more universal than the subject, yet in such a way that it is not predicated of the subject's genus.

<margin>2</margin> The definition of "genus" given by Porphyry <note>a 3rd-century philosopher whose "Isagoge" was the standard textbook on logic</note> is poor; it should be defined as follows: Genus is that which is the more universal of two universals.

<margin>3</margin> The highest good of man is perfection achieved through the speculative sciences.

<margin>4</margin> When Aristotle says that "all teaching and all learning" <note>the opening line of the *Posterior Analytics*</note> arise from pre-existing knowledge, the terms "teaching and learning" must be understood as knowledge obtained through definition and argumentation.

<margin>5</margin> The meaning of "being said of all" <note>original: "dici de omni"; a technical term in logic for a universal premise</note> according to Aristotle is this: that the predicate is said of the subject and of everything that is the subject, whether in act or in potentiality, specifically by a possibility of contingency and not of necessity.

<margin>6</margin> He who believes that "being said of all" is anything other than what was stated in the previous conclusion cannot defend Aristotle against Theophrastus <note>Aristotle's successor</note> regarding the rule that a necessary conclusion follows from a necessary major premise and a "found" <note>assertoric</note> minor premise.

<margin>7</margin> The "possible" which Aristotle defined in his book the *Prior Analytics* is common to both the potential and the "found" <note>the actual state of affairs</note>, as distinguished from the necessary.

<margin>8</margin> An accident <note>a non-essential quality, like 'redness'</note> cannot be understood even in the abstract without understanding the subject it belongs to.

<margin>9</margin> Species <note>the mental images or "likenesses" of things</note> exist in the medium <note>the air or space between the object and the eye</note> in a way that is midway between spiritual and material.

<margin>10</margin> Every "species" considered according to its spiritual existence is formally an act of knowledge.

<margin>11</margin> Dreaming is the actual knowledge of the "common sense" <term>common sense: the internal faculty that unites the data from the five individual senses</term> when it perceives a phantasm as if it were a physical object.

# ACCORDING TO ISAAC OF NARBONNE [4 CONCLUSIONS]
<note>Isaac of Narbonne, also known as Isaac Albalag, was a 13th-century Jewish Averroist philosopher.</note>

<margin>1</margin> To posit an "active intellect" <note>an external intellect that illuminates the human mind to allow for abstract thought</note> is not necessary.

<margin>2</margin> A "first intention" <note>a direct concept of a thing in the world, like 'cow' or 'tree'</note> is the quiddity <term>quiddity: the "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing</term> of a thing, reflecting objectively in the intellect.

-> ACCORDING TO ABUMARON THE BABYLONIAN <note>likely referring to Abu Bakr ibn al-Sa'igh, also known as Avempace, though Pico lists them separately on this page; or perhaps a specific tradition associated with Babylonian (Chaldean) learning</note> (4 conclusions) <-

1 The demonstration in the eighth book of the *Physics* brought forward by Aristotle to prove the First Mover proves something specific primarily.
2 The science of <term>metaphysics</term> <note>original: "metaphysica"; the branch of philosophy dealing with the first principles of things, including abstract concepts like being, knowing, and substance</note> is not a single science.

2 The representative images <note>original: "species"</note> of things are reducible to the same category as the things they represent.
3 Common sensibles <note>such as shape or motion</note> transmit their own distinct images to the senses, separate from the images of proper sensibles <note>such as color or sound</note>.
4 The sense of touch is not a single sense.
5 Whether a thing exists or not can be questioned by a specialist in a particular art.

1 In the heavens, there is matter of a different nature than the matter of inferior things.
2 Light and color do not differ essentially.

### ACCORDING TO SIMPLICIUS <note>Simplicius of Cilicia (c. 490–560 AD), one of the last great Neoplatonist philosophers who wrote extensive commentaries on Aristotle.</note> (9 conclusions)

1 To know its own act is not common to every external sense, but is special to human senses.
2 Aristotle, in the third book of *On the Soul*, deals only with the rational part of the soul.
3 When the soul returns perfectly into itself, then the <term>agent intellect</term> <note>original: "intellectus agens"; the active faculty of the mind that abstracts universal truths from sensory data</note> is liberated from the <term>possible intellect</term> <note>original: "intellectus possibilis"; the passive faculty of the mind that receives or "becomes" the thoughts processed by the agent intellect</note>.
4 The same rational part, as it goes out from itself, is called the possible intellect; but insofar as it is such that it can perfect itself as it is "possible," it is called the agent intellect.
5 The same rational part, as it goes outside itself and proceeds, is perfected by the <term>species</term> <note>original: "speciebus"; mental images or forms that represent objects of knowledge</note> which are in it; as it remains, it is called the intellect in habit <note>original: "intellectus in habitu"; the state where the mind possesses knowledge and can use it at will, even when not currently thinking about it</note>.
6 It can be known from the preceding why the agent intellect is sometimes likened to art, sometimes to habit, and sometimes to light.
7 The organ alone receives the affection <note>original: "passio"</note> produced by a sensible object, but the soul alone receives the sensation.
8 Just as light does not create colors as colors, but makes pre-existing colors that are potentially visible into actually visible ones, so the agent intellect does not create species as if they did not exist before, but makes pre-existing species that are potentially knowable into actually knowable ones.
9 When Aristotle says that we do not remember after death because the passive intellect is destroyed, he understands the "possible intellect" by the "passive intellect."

### ACCORDING TO ALEXANDER OF APHRODISEAS <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias (fl. 200 AD), a celebrated commentator on Aristotle whose interpretations often leaned toward a more materialistic or "naturalist" view of the soul.</note> (8 conclusions)

1 The rational soul is immortal. <note>This was a bold claim by Pico, as many Renaissance scholars argued that Alexander believed the individual soul died with the body.</note>
2 For every heavenly sphere, besides the soul that moves it as an efficient cause, there is a distinct <term>intelligence</term> that assists it and moves it as an end <note>a goal or purpose</note>; this intelligence is entirely distinct in substance from that soul.
3 According to Aristotle’s opinion, matter enters into no definition, not even a natural one.
4 God understands neither evils nor <term>privations</term> <note>original: "priuationes"; the absence or lack of a quality that should naturally be present</note>.
5 The number of abstract beings of which Aristotle treats in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics* is not the number of movers, but the number of intelligences, which are the ends <note>purposes</note> of motion.
6 When Aristotle says in the ninth book of the *Metaphysics* that separate and divine things are either totally known by us or totally unknown, this must be understood as referring to that knowledge belonging to those who have already reached the highest fulfillment <note>original: "actuationē"</note> of the intellect.
7 Just as the first intellect among all intellects understands itself first and other things secondarily, so the last intellect among all intellects understands other things first and itself secondarily.

# Conclusions.

8 The metaphysician and the <term>dialectician</term> <note>original: "dialecticus"; here referring to a philosopher who uses logical techniques to argue from probable opinions rather than certain demonstrations</note> debate about all things equally, but the former does so through <term>demonstration</term> <note>logical proof based on certain, necessary premises</note>, while the latter does so through probability.

->ACCORDING TO THEMISTIUS (5 conclusions)<-
<note>Themistius (c. 317–388 AD) was a statesman and philosopher who wrote "paraphrases" of Aristotle, attempting to make the texts more accessible.</note>

1 The <term>possible intellects</term> <note>original: "intellectus possibiles"; the capacity of the human mind to receive knowledge</note> which are only "illuminated" are many; the <term>agent intellects</term> <note>original: "agentes"; the active power of the mind that produces thought</note>, the participating, the illuminating, and the illuminated are also many; but the agent, illuminating intellect—being so great—is one.
2 The agent intellect that is "illuminating only" is, I believe, what is called *Maratron* <note>A reference to the archangel Metatron in the Jewish Kabbalistic tradition, whom Pico identifies here with the Aristotelian Agent Intellect.</note> in the <term>Cabala</term> <note>Jewish mystical tradition</note>, according to Themistius.
3 The science of the soul stands midway between the natural sciences <note>physics</note> and the divine sciences <note>metaphysics</note>.
4 Beyond the two types of demonstration that Aristotle posits, a third must be added: this occurs when one property is proven through another property that is <term>coeval</term> <note>original: "coæuam"; existing or originating at the same time or of equal standing</note> with it.
5 A proposition is "essential" <note>original: "per se"</note> when either the subject defines the predicate, or the predicate defines the subject, or both are defined by the same third term.

Conclusions according to the doctrine of the philosophers who are called Platonists: Plotinus the Egyptian, Porphyry the Tyrian, Iamblichus, Chalcidius, Proclus, Litius, and Adelard the Arab.

->ACCORDING TO PLOTINUS (15 conclusions)<-
<note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism. His philosophy focuses on the ascent of the soul to "The One."</note>

1 The first "intelligible" <note>an object that can be understood by the mind</note> is not outside the first intellect.
2 The soul does not descend entirely when it descends <note>into the physical body</note>. <note>Plotinus uniquely taught that a part of the human soul remains eternally in the divine realm.</note>
3 All life is immortal.
4 A soul that has sinned in either a terrestrial or an aerial body lives the life of a brute <note>an animal</note> after death.
5 The irrational soul is an <term>idol</term> <note>original: "idolum"; an image, shadow, or reflection</note> of the rational soul, depending on it just as light depends on the sun.
6 Being, life, and intellect coincide as the same thing.
7 The ultimate happiness of man occurs when our particular intellect is fully joined to the total and first intellect.
8 The <term>civil virtues</term> <note>practical virtues like justice or temperance used in social life</note> should not be called virtues in an absolute sense.
9 Likeness to the divine is not achieved through the virtues—even those of a purified soul—except as a <term>disposition</term> <note>original: "dispositiuè"; a preparation rather than the final cause</note>.
10 In the faculty of reason, there are likenesses and <term>species</term> <note>mental representations</note> of things, but in the intellect itself, the beings themselves exist.
11 It is a mark of perfected virtue to cut off even the <term>first motions</term> <note>original: "primos motus"; the initial, involuntary stirrings of emotion or desire</note>.
12 It is said improperly that the intellect "looks upon" or "contemplates" the <term>Ideas</term> <note>the eternal, divine forms of all things</note>. <note>Because the intellect is identical to the Ideas, it does not look at them as something external.</note>
13 Things that are necessary for an animal can be called "necessary," but not "good."
14 Just as accidental happiness requires conscious attention, substantial happiness is not only not lost by a lack of attention, but is actually strengthened.
15 A person who has already attained happiness is not hindered from it by <term>frenzy</term> <note>original: "phrenesim"; delirium or temporary madness</note> or <term>lethargy</term> <note>a state of profound unconsciousness</note>.

### ACCORDING TO ADELARD THE ARAB, 8 CONCLUSIONS.
<note>Pico likely refers to Adelard of Bath, a 12th-century scholar who translated many Arabic scientific works into Latin, though he labels him here as "the Arab" due to his sources.</note>

1 The <term>agent intellect</term> <note>original: "intellectus agens"; the active power of the mind that allows us to process information into thought</note> is nothing other than that part of the soul which remains above and does not fall <note>referring to the Neoplatonic idea that a portion of the human soul never fully descends into the physical body but stays in the divine realm</note>.
2 The soul possesses the <term>forms</term> <note>original: "species"; mental representations or archetypes</note> of things within itself, and is only awakened by external things.
3 To complete the preceding conclusion, which not only Adelard but all the <term>Moors</term> <note>original: "Mauri"; referring here to Islamic philosophers such as Averroes or Avicenna</note> maintain, I say that those forms exist actually and substantially in the part of the soul that does not fall, and are received anew and accidentally in the part that does fall.
4 The greater part of things made known in dreams are revealed either through the purification of the soul, or through "indenomination" <note>likely referring to a nameless or intuitive grasp of truth</note>, or through the pure revelation of the spirit.
5 What <term>Thabit the Chaldean</term> <note>original: "Tabet Chaldæus"; Thabit ibn Qurra, a 9th-century astronomer and philosopher</note> writes concerning sleeping on the liver in the revelation of dreams will be rightly understood if we harmonize this saying with the words of Plato in the *Timaeus*.
6 Because, as <term>Abdaia</term> <note>likely Obadiah, though the specific source is debated among scholars of Pico</note> said, seeing dreams is a power of the imagination, while understanding them is a power of the intellect; therefore, he who sees them for the most part does not understand them.
7 The soul is the source of motion and the governess of matter.
8 All the wise men of the Indians, Persians, Egyptians, and Chaldeans believed in the <term>transmigration</term> <note>original: "transcorporationem"; the passage of a soul into a new body after death</note> of souls.

### ACCORDING TO PORPHYRY, 12 CONCLUSIONS.
<note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) was a Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher and a student of Plotinus.</note>

1 According to Plato, we must understand the "Father" to be the cause that produces the entire effect from itself, and the "Maker" to be that which receives matter from another.
2 The <term>Architect of the World</term> <note>original: "Opifex mundi"</note> is the supermundane soul.
3 The <term>Exemplar</term> <note>the divine blueprint of the universe</note> is nothing other than the intellect of that Architect-soul itself.
4 Every soul participating in the <term>Vulcanian intellect</term> <note>referring to the divine fire or craftsmanship associated with the god Vulcan/Hephaestus</note> sows into the Moon.
5 From the preceding conclusion, I deduce why all <term>Teutons</term> <note>original: "Teuthones"; Germans</note> are of good physical stature and fair complexion.
6 From that same conclusion, I deduce why all Teutons are most reverent toward the Apostolic See.
7 Just as Apollo is the solar intellect, so Aesculapius <note>the god of healing</note> is the lunar intellect.
8 From the preceding conclusion, I deduce why the Moon in the <term>ascendant</term> <note>the zodiacal sign rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth</note> gives health to the newborn.
9 There are two kinds of evil demons: one kind consists of souls and substantial demons; the other consists of material powers and accidental demons.
10 Regarding the two kinds of demons mentioned in the preceding conclusion according to Porphyry, we believe they are nothing other than the "law of the members" and the "powers of this darkness" mentioned in the writings of <term>Paul</term> <note>a reference to the Apostle Paul, specifically Romans 7:23 and Ephesians 6:12</note>, although I do not believe they agree as to the "quiddity" <note>the essence or "what-ness"</note> and substance of these powers.

# Conclusions.

...that is, concerning that which truly is and is in no way generated, and concerning that which is truly generated and in no way being; regarding middle states nothing, of which one is being and generated, the other is generated and being. <note>Pico is here using ontological categories: "Being" refers to the eternal, unchanging divine realm, while "Generated" refers to the temporal, changing material world.</note>

12 God is everywhere because He is nowhere; the intellect is everywhere because it is nowhere; the soul is everywhere because it is nowhere. But God is everywhere and nowhere with respect to all things that come after Him. The intellect, however, is indeed in God, but is everywhere and nowhere with respect to those things which come after it. The soul is in the intellect and in God, but is everywhere and nowhere with respect to the body. <note>This "everywhere and nowhere" phrasing is a classic Neoplatonic paradox: spiritual substances are not confined to a specific physical location ("nowhere"), yet their power and presence extend to everything they govern ("everywhere").</note>

## ACCORDING TO IAMBLICHUS, 9 CONCLUSIONS.
<note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Syrian Neoplatonist who emphasized the importance of ritual and the hierarchy of divine beings.</note>

1 The speculative intellect is a <term>form</term> separated as to both its substance and its manner of acting; the practical intellect is separated as to its substance but joined as to its manner; the rational soul is joined according to substance but separated according to its manner; the irrational soul is joined according to both substance and manner.
2 The <term>Craftsman</term> <note>original: "Opifex"; the Demiurge or creator figure in Platonic thought</note> of the sensible world is the seventh member of the intellectual hierarchy.
3 Bodily nature exists in the intellect immovably; in the soul it is primarily mobile by its own power; in the animal it is mobile by its own power through participation; in the heavens it is moved in an orderly way from an outside source; below the Moon it is moved in a disorderly way from an outside source.
4 The elements are found twice in a celestial manner within the eight bodies of the heavens; one will find these if they proceed in a retrograde order in that double numbering.
5 Above this world, which the theologians call&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;, there is another, which they call&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;, and above this another, which they call. <note>The blank spaces appear in the original printed text; Pico likely intended to fill these with specific Greek terms for different celestial or super-celestial realms.</note>
6 When the soul is excellently assimilated to the intellect, a perfectly circular motion is created in its <term>vehicle</term> <note>original: "uehiculo"; the subtle, "astral" body that Neoplatonists believed carried the soul between the stars and the physical body</note>.
7 No power of the celestial stars is, insofar as it is in itself, malevolent. <note>Pico argues that the stars, being divine instruments, are inherently good, and any "evil" effects on Earth are due to the way they are received by material things.</note>
8 He who understands the final cause of floods and conflagrations will call these "purifications" <note>original: "purgationes"</note> rather than destructions.
9 When Plato says that the soul is placed in the middle of the world, it must be understood as the unparticipated soul, which he says is placed in the middle because it is equally present to all things, being freed from every specific perspective and particular habit.

## ACCORDING TO PROCLUS, 55 CONCLUSIONS.
<note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was the "successor" of the Platonic Academy in Athens and a massive influence on medieval and Renaissance philosophy.</note>

1 That which exists in intelligible terms as <term>limit and infinity</term>, exists in the intellectual realm as male and female; in the supramundane realm as identity and alterity, likeness and unlikeness; and in the soul as the circulation of the "Same" and the circulation of the "Other."
2 From the laws of Saturn are exempt those Gods who are "containing" and "perfecting"; from the laws of Jove, the Saturnian Gods; and from the Laws of Fate, every soul living intellectually. But all things obey the Law of <term>Adrastia</term> <note>original: "Adrastiæ"; a Greek name for the goddess of inevitable necessity or divine justice</note>.
3 The name "God" belongs simply and absolutely to the One alone, who is the God of gods; it belongs simply but not absolutely to any of the "supersubstantial" beings according to their essence; to any of the intellectual beings according to their participation; to divine souls according to their contact and union; to <term>daemons</term> <note>original: "dæmonibus"; here referring to guardian spirits or intermediaries, not evil entities</note> according to their likeness; and to human souls according to their dissimilarity.

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

4 The containing property belongs to the middle order of the second trinity, which in the *Phaedrus* is called the "celestial revolution." <note>original: "circumductus." In Plato's *Phaedrus*, this refers to the movement of the heavens where the soul glimpses true reality.</note>

5 In the intelligible realm <note>The highest level of reality, consisting of pure Being.</note> there is no number, but rather a multitude, and the paternal and maternal cause of numbers; however, in the intellectual realm <note>The level of the Mind or Intellect, which is more "divided" than pure Being.</note>, there is number according to essence and multitude according to communication.

6 That which is called "otherness" in the *Parmenides* is the same as the "supracelestial place" in the *Phaedrus*. <note>Pico is correlating concepts from two different Platonic dialogues to show they describe the same metaphysical reality.</note>

7 By the "one," "the many," "the whole," "parts," "finite," and "infinite," which we find in the *Parmenides*, understand them according to the order of the trinity of the intelligible-intellectual beings, following the triadic division of that order.

8 What is called the "back of heaven" in the *Phaedrus* is called the "One" in the *Parmenides*; what is called the "depth of heaven" there is here called "the whole"; what is called the "axis of heaven" there is here called "the limit."

9 Plato expresses the third order of the second trinity through three terms: the extremes, the perfect, and according to figure.

10 The intellectual gods have their unities from the first "One," their substances from the intelligible gods, their perfect, containing, and generative lives of divine things from the intelligible-intellectual gods, and their intellectual property from themselves.

11 Just as the intelligible gods produce all things uniformly, so the intelligible-intellectual gods produce them triadically <note>In groups of three.</note>, and the intellectual gods produce them by way of the <term>hebdomad</term> <note>A group of seven, a central concept in Procline Neoplatonism where the divine mind unfolds into seven powers.</note>.

12 Between the paternal gods at the extremes, Saturn and Jupiter, Rhea necessarily mediates through the property of fertile life. <note>In Neoplatonic allegory, Saturn represents the pure Mind, Jupiter the world-governing Mind, and Rhea the life-giving power that flows between them.</note>

13 The second trinity of the intellectual hebdomad is the trinity of the Curetes, whom theology calls the "undefiled gods." <note>The Curetes were mythical guardians; here they represent powers that keep the divine principles pure from material contamination.</note>

14 The characteristic of the Curetes is to render the work of the paternal trinity immaculate: the staying of the first, the proceeding of the second, and the illumination of the third. <note>This refers to the Neoplatonic cycle of "remaining, proceeding, and returning."</note>

15 Through the "slaughter of the gods," described tragically by the theologians, the seventh distributive unity of the intellectual hebdomad is designated. <note>This "slaughter" or dismemberment (like that of Dionysus) symbolizes the way divine unity is divided as it descends into the complexity of the world.</note>

16 The same goddess who is called Rhea when she coexists with Saturn at her highest peak, is called Ceres as she brings forth Jupiter and, together with Jupiter, the universal and partial orders of the gods.

17 Although the divine hierarchies are distinct as theology teaches, it must be understood nevertheless that "all things are in all things," each in its own manner. <note>A fundamental Neoplatonic maxim: every level of reality contains a version of all other levels.</note>

18 Just as the paternal property exists only in the intelligible realm, so the building or creative property exists only in the "younger gods" <note>A reference to Plato's *Timaeus*, where the supreme creator delegates the making of mortal things to lesser, "younger" gods.</note> who are both paternal and building; the creative property is found in the intelligible patterns, and the paternal is in the crafts.

19 Whatever operations belong either to the gods or to nature are twofold: immanent and transient. Through immanent operations, each thing contains itself and the principles within it; through transient operations, it turns itself toward external things.

20 After the intellectual hebdomad, the "supermundane" <note>Above the world.</note> gods are to be ranked immediately; they are exempt from the parts of the universe, uncoordinated with this world, and embrace it from all sides as its cause.

->**Conclusions.**<-

**21** It is the property of the **supramundane gods** <note>Gods that exist above the physical world but below the realm of pure Being. In Neoplatonism, they act as mediators.</note> to make beings like themselves and to bestow upon them that compassion and mutual communion which they possess due to their likeness to one another.

**22** Although the power of assimilation belongs to the **leader-gods** <note>Latin: *ducales*. These are the "hegemonic" deities who govern the celestial spheres.</note> mentioned in the previous conclusion, it is specifically attributed to the middle order of their trinity: the first order is immediately joined in substance to the **intellectual gods**, and the third mixes with the lower ranks.

**23** The **Jupiter** mentioned in the *Gorgias* <note>A dialogue by Plato.</note> is not the third universal creator among the intellectual gods, but the highest and first among the leader-gods.

**24** In the leader-trinity, **Jupiter** is the giver of substance, **Neptune** is the giver of life, and **Pluto** is the one who brings about the **return** <note>original: *conversivus*. This refers to the Neoplatonic concept of *epistrophe*, where a being turns back toward its divine source to find fulfillment.</note>.

**25** The work of the **craftsmanship** <note>Latin: *fabrica*. This refers to the Demiurge's act of building the universe.</note> is fourfold: the first fully adorns the universals of universals; the second adorns all things but in a particular way; the third according to things divided by their universal nature; the fourth weaves the parts particularly into the universals.

**26** **Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto**, who share the kingdom of **Saturn** <note>In Greek mythology, the three brothers divided the sky, sea, and underworld. Pico interprets this as a metaphysical distribution of power.</note>, do not receive that kingdom from Saturn except through the mediation of the **Creator Jupiter** <note>Here distinguishing between the higher "Demiurge" Jupiter and the "Leader" Jupiter.</note>.

**27** Under the first of the leader-trinity <note>Jupiter</note> is **substantial being**, every noble soul not subject to the world of change, the moving element of **fire**, and the highest part of the **air** which grows above the earth, and the **Eastern** part of the world.

**28** Under the second of the leader-trinity <note>Neptune</note> is **life and generation**, every soul entering into the world of change, the **wandering spheres** <note>The planets.</note>, **water**, and the lowest part of the **air** which lies beneath the "caves of Minerva," as well as earthquakes and the middle part of the earth around its center.

**29** Under the third of the same order <note>Pluto</note> is the **return** of specific divisions, the **purification of souls**, the sphere of active and passive elements, the **earth** along with terrestrial things surrounding **Tartarus** <note>The deep abyss of the underworld.</note>, and the **Western** part of the world.

**30** Although the entire second trinity of the supramundane gods is called **Proserpina**, her first unity is called **Diana** by the Greeks, the second **Persephone**, and the third **Minerva**. Among the barbarians <note>Pico often uses "barbarians" to refer to non-Greek sources like the Chaldeans or Egyptians.</note>, however, the first is called **Hecate** <note>original: *Mechate*, likely a scribe's error for Hecate.</note>, the second is **Soul**, and the third is **Virtue**.

**31** Following the previous conclusion, one of the sayings of **Zoroaster** <note>The legendary founder of the Magi; Pico refers to the *Chaldean Oracles* attributed to him.</note> can be explained according to the mind of **Proclus**, as it is read among the Greeks, although it is read and explained differently among the **Chaldeans**.

**32** The third trinity of the supramundane gods is called **Apollo**, and the power of **returning to the source** is attributed to him.

**33** The trinity of **Proserpina** is accompanied on its side by a **guardian and preservative trinity**.

**34** The **twelve gods** mentioned in the *Phaedrus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the soul and love.</note> are the gods intermediate between the supramundane and the mundane; they are the bond between them.

**35** The gods mentioned in the *Phaedrus* are to be distinguished into four trinities: **creative**, **guardian**, **vital**, and **returning**.

**36** There are four armies of **junior gods** <note>In Neoplatonism, these are the secondary deities who govern the material world, as described in Plato's *Timaeus*.</note>: the first lives from the first heaven down to the beginning of the air; the second from there to the middle of the air; the third from there to the earth.

**37** To each of these corresponds, in proportion, a fourfold army of angels, demons, and souls.

**38** In the **self-living being** <note>original: *per se uiuente*. A technical term for the Intelligible Living Being, the model for the universe.</note> there first appears the **fourfold nature** <note>original: *quaternitas*. The number four was considered sacred and foundational to the structure of the cosmos.</note> of the one being, the one-like being, and the being-like one.

**39** The **Craftsman** <note>original: *Opifex*. Referring to the Demiurge, the divine figure who fashions the physical universe according to a perfect model.</note>, looking toward the fourfold nature of the self-living being, fabricates the four principal parts of the world.

**40** Insofar as the Craftsman looks to the exemplar of the form of the "one" in the self-living being, he makes the first part of the worldly body.

**41** Insofar as the Craftsman sees the one of the essential one in the form of the "one," he makes the worldly **Gods** of that part; insofar as he sees the being of the essential one, he makes the **angels** in that same part; insofar as he sees the one of the being-like one, he makes the **demons** there; insofar as he sees the existence of the being-like one, he makes the **animals** in that same place.

**42** The Craftsman makes the other parts in proportion to the exemplars of their own forms, just as was said regarding the first part; there is no need to explain further, because anyone who knows the method of **reasoning by analogy** <note>original: *viam analogizandi*. A key method in Renaissance philosophy where one understands higher spiritual truths by looking at their reflections in lower, physical things.</note> will be able to deduce the rest for themselves.

**43** We ascend to the wise, beautiful, and good Lord through intellect, love, and faith.

**44** Just as the faith which is mere belief is below scientific knowledge, so the **faith which is true faith** <note>original: *ueræ fides*. Here Pico distinguishes between simple religious belief and a higher, mystical "faith" that represents a direct union with the Divine.</note> is beyond all substance, standing above knowledge and intellect, joining us immediately to God.

**45** Just as not every body participates in the soul, but only the perfect body, so not every soul participates in the intellect, but only the perfect soul; nevertheless, all things participate in the **One**.

**56** <note>This number appears as 56 in the original text, though it follows 45 and contextually should be 46.</note> Just as they follow the scope of causality, so according to the sublimity of their nature and rank, these things exceed one another in order: **soul, intellect, life, being, and the One.**

**47** Every middle order remains stable in the order that precedes it, and strengthens the order that follows it.

**48** Just as the first **trinity** <note>In this Neoplatonic context, "trinity" or "triad" refers to the grouping of divine principles: Remaining, Proceeding, and Returning.</note> after the "One" measures all things intelligibly and in the form of the **Finite**, so the second trinity is all things vitally, truly, and in the form of the **Infinite**; the third is everything according to the property of the mixture and in the form of **Beauty**.

**49** The first trinity only **remains**; the second remains and **proceeds**; the third, after the process, **returns** <note>original: *conuertit*. This describes the three-step movement of Neoplatonic reality: staying in the source, flowing out into creation, and turning back toward God.</note>.

**50** **Eternity** <note>original: *Aeuuum*. Often distinguished from "time"; it is the "duration" of things that do not change, like angels or ideas.</note> is above the "self-living animal" in the second and middle trinity.

**51** Just as the **intelligible things** are the causes of all species, so the **intellectual things** are the causes of the divisions according to the common genera: those above the world differing by species, and those within the world differing by the individual.

**52** By the **supracelestial place** <note>A term from Plato’s *Phaedrus* referring to the realm of pure forms above the heavens.</note> we are to understand that which belongs to the second trinity...

### ACCORDING TO THE MATHEMATICS OF PYTHAGORAS, 14.

**1** The One, Otherness, and That-which-is are the cause of numbers: the One for unified numbers, Otherness for generative numbers, and That-which-is for substantial numbers.

**2** In participated numbers, some are species of numbers, while others are the unions of those species.

**3** Where the point-like unity falls into the otherness of the <term>dyad</term> <note>original: *binarii*. The number two, representing the first departure from unity.</note>, there for the first time exists a triangle.

**4** He who understands the order of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 12, will hold the exact distribution of providence.

**5** Through the one, the three, and the seven, we know the power of the intellect in **Pallas** <note>The goddess Athena, representing divine wisdom.</note>: its unifying power of discernment, its causative power, and its beatific power.

**6** The triple proportion—Arithmetic, Geometric, and Harmonic—indicates to us the three daughters of **Themis** <note>The goddess of divine law and order.</note>, who exist as symbols of Judgment, Justice, and Peace.

**7** Through the secret of the straight, reflected, and refracted ray in the science of optics <note>original: *scientia perspectiva*.</note>, we are reminded of the triple nature: intellectual, animate, and corporeal.

**8** Reason has the proportion of an **octave** <note>original: *diapason*. A 2:1 ratio.</note> to desire.

**9** The spirited part of the soul <note>original: *irascibilis*. The part of the soul associated with anger and courage.</note> has the proportion of a **fifth** <note>original: *diapente*. A 3:2 ratio.</note> to desire.

**10** Reason has the proportion of a **fourth** <note>original: *diatessaron*. A 4:3 ratio.</note> to anger.

**11** The judgment of the senses should not be employed in Music, but that of the intellect alone.

**12** In numbering forms, we must not exceed the number forty.

**13** Any equilateral plane number symbolizes the soul.

**14** Any linear number symbolizes the gods.

### CHALDEAN THEOLOGIANS, 6 IN NUMBER.

**1** The principal order of separate things is not the first as the Egyptians think, but above it is the <term>fontal</term> order <note>original: *ordo fontalis*. An "original" or "source" order.</note>, which is unially exalted above all.

The catchword "2 Nos" from the bottom of page 79 leads into the second point on this page.</meta>

<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

**2** Fate is not the necessity of the primary <term>seminal power</term> <note>original: *potentiæ seminalis*. In Stoic and Neoplatonic thought, these are the formative "seeds" or principles that govern the development of the physical world.</note>, but is a rationally shared condition of living reasons, unswerving from things above and unavoidable by things below.

**3** The substantial qualities of visible things result not from a particular separate power, as the **Egyptians** believe, but dependently from the first receptacle of the fountain of lights through a living splendor.

**4** Partial souls <note>Individual souls, such as those of humans, as opposed to "World Souls."</note> are illuminated by intellectual splendor not immediately, as the **Egyptians** say, but through the mediation of "total" demonic souls. <note>In this context, "demonic" refers to *daimones*—intermediary spirits between gods and men—not "demons" in the modern evil sense.</note>

**5** Intelligible coordination is not within the intellectual coordination, as **Amasis the Egyptian** <note>Amasis II was a Pharaoh, but in the Renaissance, he was often cited as a source of ancient wisdom alongside Hermes Trismegistus.</note> said, but is hidden above every intellectual Hierarchy in the abyss of the primary unity and under the gloom of the primary darkness in an unparticipated way.

**6** Whatever is from the Moon upward is pure light, and that is the substance of the worldly spheres.

### *Ten Conclusions according to the ancient doctrine of Hermes Trismegistus the Egyptian.* <note>Mercurius Trismegistus, or "Thrice-Great Hermes," was believed by Renaissance scholars to be an ancient Egyptian priest and contemporary of Moses who anticipated Christian truths.</note>

**1** Wherever there is life, there is a soul; wherever there is a soul, there is a mind.

**2** Everything moved is corporeal; everything moving is incorporeal.

**3** The soul is in the body, the mind is in the soul, the <term>Word</term> <note>original: *uerbum*. This likely refers to the "Logos" or divine reason.</note> is in the mind, and the father of these is God.

**4** God is around all things and through all things; the mind is around the soul, the soul around the air, the air around matter.

**5** Nothing in the world is devoid of life.

**6** Nothing in the universe is subject to death or corruption.

->*Corollary: life is everywhere, providence is everywhere, immortality is everywhere.*<-

**7** God announces future things to man in six ways: through dreams, portents, birds, intestines, the spirit, and the **Sibyl**. <note>Pico is listing traditional forms of divination: oneiromancy (dreams), augury (birds), and haruspicy (intestines).</note>

**8** The True is that which is undisturbed, undetermined, uncolored, unshaped, unshaken, naked, clear, comprehensible by itself, unchangeable good, and entirely incorporeal.

**9** There are ten punishers within each person: ignorance, sadness, inconstancy, greed, injustice, lust, envy, fraud, anger, and malice.

**10** The deep contemplator will see that the ten punishers, about which the preceding conclusion according to **Hermes** spoke, correspond to the ten-fold evil coordination in the <term>Kabbalah</term> <note>original: *Cabala*. Jewish mystical tradition.</note> and its prefects, about which I have placed nothing in the Kabbalistic conclusions, because it is a secret.

### *Kabbalistic Conclusions, forty-seven in number, according to the secret doctrine of the wise Hebrew Kabbalists, whose memory may always be for good.*

**1** Just as man and the lower priest sacrifice the souls of irrational animals to God, so **Michael** the higher priest sacrifices the souls of rational animals. <note>In Kabbalistic thought, the Archangel Michael serves as a celestial High Priest who "sacrifices" the souls of the righteous to bring them into the presence of the Divine.</note>

# Conclusions.

**2** There are nine hierarchies of angels, whose names are <term>Cherubim</term>, <term>Seraphim</term>, <term>Chashmalim</term>, <term>Chayyot</term>, <term>Arelim</term>, <term>Tarshishim</term>, <term>Ophanim</term>, <term>Tafsarim</term>, and <term>Ishim</term>. <note>Pico provides a list of angelic ranks derived from Hebrew tradition, which differs slightly from the standard Christian hierarchy of Dionysius the Areopagite.</note>

**3** Although the <term>ineffable name</term> <note>original: *nomen ineffabile*. This refers to the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God (YHWH), which is not spoken aloud in Jewish tradition.</note> is an attribute of mercy, it must nonetheless not be denied that it contains an attribute of judgment.

**4** The sin of **Adam** was the "cutting off of the kingdom" from the other plants. <note>In Kabbalah, this refers to a spiritual separation where the final sphere (Malkuth or "Kingdom") is isolated from the higher divine energies, often called "cutting the shoots."</note>

**5** With the <term>tree of knowledge of good and evil</term>, in which the first man sinned, God created the world.

**6** The Great North <note>original: *Aquilo*. In mystical geography, the North is often associated with the attribute of Gevurah (Strength/Judgment) and the source of souls.</note> is the source of all souls simply, just as other "days" are the source of some souls and not all.

**7** When **Solomon** says in his prayer in the **Book of Kings**, "Hear, O heaven," by "heaven" we must understand the <term>green line</term> that circles the universe. <note>original: *lineam uiridem*. This refers to the *Kav* or the "Green Line" (Kav ha-Yaroq), a Kabbalistic concept representing the boundary of the created world.</note>

**8** Souls descend from the <term>third light</term> to the <term>fourth day</term>, and from there to the <term>fifth</term>; departing from there, they enter the night of the body.

**9** By the "six days of Genesis," we must understand the six extremities of the spiritual edifice proceeding from <term>In the Beginning</term> <note>original: *Bresith* (Bereshit). The first word of the Bible, interpreted here as a divine emanation.</note>, just as the Cedars proceed from **Lebanon**.

**10** It is more correctly said that **Paradise** is the whole edifice than that it is the tenth part, and in its center is placed the **Great Adam**, who is <term>Tipheret</term>. <note>Tipheret ("Beauty") is the central sphere or Sefirah in the Kabbalistic Tree of Life, representing harmony and the "ideal man."</note>

**11** It is said that a river goes out of **Eden** which is divided into four heads, to signify that from the <term>second numeration</term> proceeds the <term>third</term>, which is divided into the fourth, fifth, sixth, and tenth. <note>Pico is mapping the geography of Eden onto the Sefirot, the ten emanations of God.</note>

**12** It will be true that all things depend on fate, if by "fate" we understand the supreme fate.

**13** He who knows the mystery of the "gates of understanding" in the **Kabbalah** will know the mystery of the **Great Jubilee**. <note>In Jewish tradition, there are "Fifty Gates of Understanding"; the Jubilee year occurs every fifty years.</note>

**14** He who knows the southern attribute in the right-hand coordination will know why every journey of **Abraham** was always toward the south.

**15** Unless the letter *He* <note>The Hebrew letter ה.</note> had been added to the name of **Abraham**, **Abraham** would not have fathered children. <note>Refers to the biblical name change from Abram to Abraham (Genesis 17:5).</note>

**16** All [prophets] before **Moses** prophesied through the "one-horned doe." <note>original: *ceruam unicornem*. A cryptic reference to a lower level of prophetic vision compared to the direct "face to face" revelation given to Moses.</note>

**17** Wherever in Scripture mention is made of the love of male and female, it mystically designates for us the union of **Tipheret** and the **Assembly of Israel**, or **Beth** and **Tipheret**. <note>original: *Chienseth Israẽl*. This refers to the union between the male and female aspects of God (the Sefirot Tipheret and Malkuth).</note>

**18** For him who shall be joined with **Tipheret** at midnight, every generation will be prosperous for him.

**19** The letters of the name of the evil spirit <note>original: *cacodæmonis*.</note>, who is the prince of this world, are the same as those of the **three-lettered name of God** <note>original: *Triagrammaton*.</note>, and he who knows how to arrange the transposition will derive one from the other.

**20** When the light of the "non-shining mirror" becomes like the light of the "shining mirror," night will be like day, as **David** says. <note>In Kabbalah, the "shining mirror" (*aspaklaria*) represents the clear prophecy of Moses, while the "non-shining mirror" represents the veiled prophecy of others.</note>

**21** He who knows the attribute which is the secret of darkness will know why evil demons do more harm in the night than in the day.

**22** Although a multiple coordination of chariots occurs, nonetheless as far as pertains <meta>The text breaks off here; the catchword for the next page is "ad Phi", likely referring to "ad Philippenses" or a similar continuation.</meta>

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

Regarding the mystery of the <term>Phylacteries</term> <note>original: "philacteriorum." These are tefillin, small leather boxes containing Torah verses worn by Jewish people during morning prayers.</note>, two <term>chariots</term> <note>original: "currus." In Kabbalah, the "Chariot" (Merkavah) represents the structure of divine emanations or the throne of God.</note> are to be arranged, such that from the second, third, fourth, and fifth [emanations], one chariot is made, and these are the four phylacteries worn by the letter <term>Vau</term>. And from the sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth, a second chariot is made, and these are the phylacteries worn by the last <term>He</term>. <note>Vau and He are the third and fourth letters of the Tetragrammaton, the holy four-letter name of God. Pico is mapping these letters onto the Sefirot, or divine spheres.</note>

**23** Above the attribute of <term>Repentance</term> <note>original: "pœnitentiæ." Likely referring to the Sefirah of Binah (Understanding), which is the source of the "return" of the soul.</note>, the word "he said" <note>original: "dixit"</note> is not to be used.

**24** When **Job** said, "He who makes peace in his high places," he understood "water" to be the Southern [force] and "fire" to be the Northern, and their presiding officers, about whom nothing more is to be said.

**25** *Bresith* <note>original: "Bresith." The first word of the Bible, usually translated as "In the beginning."</note>—that is, "In the beginning he created"—is the same as if he had said, "In <term>Wisdom</term> <note>original: "sapiẽtia." Pico follows the Zohar in identifying the "Beginning" with the Sefirah of Chokmah (Wisdom).</note> he created."

**26** When **Onkelos the Chaldean** <note>original: "Anchelos Chaldæus." The 2nd-century translator of the Torah into Aramaic.</note> said *Becadmim*—that is, "with the eternals" or "through the eternals"—he understood the thirty-two paths of wisdom.

**27** Just as the gathering of waters is the <term>Righteous One</term> <note>original: "iustus." A reference to the Sefirah of Yesod (Foundation), which collects the divine flow before passing it to the world.</note>, so the "sea" toward which all rivers flow is the Divinity.

**28** By the "winged creature" that was created on the fifth day, we must understand the worldly angels who appear to men, not those who do not appear except in spirit.

**29** The name of God of four letters, which is composed of <term>Mem</term>, <term>Tzadi</term>, <term>Pe</term>, and <term>Tzadi</term> <note>original: "Mem, Sade, Pe, & Sade." A mystical permutation (Atbash or similar cipher) of a divine name.</note>, ought to be appropriated to the kingdom of **David**.

**30** No angel having six wings is ever transformed.

**31** <term>Circumcision</term> was given for liberation from the "unclean powers" <note>original: "uirtutibus immundis." In Kabbalistic thought, these are the *Klipot* (shells) that surround holiness.</note> that walk in a circuit.

**32** Circumcision occurs on the eighth day for this reason: because the eighth day is higher than the "universalized bride." <note>original: "sponsa uniuersalizata." This refers to Malkuth, the tenth Sefirah, which is associated with the Sabbath (the 7th day); the 8th day represents a step into the transcendent realm.</note>

**33** There are no letters in the whole Law which do not manifest secrets—whether in their forms, conjunctions, separations, twists, direction, defects, abundance, smallness, greatness, crowning, closure, opening, or the order of the ten <term>numerations</term> <note>original: "numerationum." Referring to the ten Sefirot.</note>.

**34** Whoever understands why it was said that **Moses** hid his face, and why **Hezekiah** turned his face to the wall, will know what the attitude and disposition of one who prays ought to be.

**35** No spiritual thing descending to lower realms operates without a <term>garment</term> <note>original: "indumento." A common mystical concept where divine light must be "clothed" in a form to be perceived or to act in the material world.</note>.

**36** The sin of **Sodom** was through the "truncation of the last plant." <note>original: "truncationem ultimæ plantæ." Repeating a theme from earlier conclusions, this refers to separating the lowest divine emanation from the higher ones, a symbolic "cutting of the shoots."</note>

**37** By the secret of "pre-dawn prayer," we should understand nothing other than the attribute of <term>Piety</term> <note>original: "pietatis." Referring to Chesed (Mercy/Lovingkindness).</note>.

**38** Just as outward fear is lower than love, so inward fear is higher than love.

**39** From the preceding conclusion, one understands why in **Genesis** **Abraham** is praised for fear, even though we know that through the attribute of piety he did everything out of love.

**40** Whenever we are ignorant of the attribute from which the influx comes regarding the petition we ask, we must recur to the <term>Lord of the Nose</term>. <note>original: "dominum naris." A technical term from the *Idra Rabba* (part of the Zohar) referring to the "Long Face" (Arich Anpin), a divine configuration characterized by infinite patience and mercy.</note>

# Conclusions

**41** Every good soul is a new soul coming from the east.

**42** Therefore **Joseph** was buried only in bones and not in body, because his bones were the virtues and hosts of the superior tree called <term>Sadich</term> <note>original: "Sadich." A transliteration of the Hebrew *Tzadik* (the Righteous), often associated with the Sefirah *Yesod* (Foundation) in Kabbalistic thought.</note> flowing into the superior earth.

**43** Therefore no one knows the tomb of **Moses**, because he was exalted into the superior <term>Jubilee</term> <note>original: "Iobel." In Kabbalistic symbolism, the Jubilee represents the fiftieth gate of understanding and the Sefirah *Binah*.</note>, and he sent his roots above the Jubilee.

**44** When the soul comprehends whatever it can comprehend, and joins itself to the superior soul, it will strip off its earthly garment, be uprooted from its place, and be joined with the divinity.

**45** The sages of Israel, after the cessation of prophecy through the Spirit, prophesied through the <term>Daughter of the Voice</term> <note>original: "filiam vocis." Known in Hebrew as *Bath Kol*, this refers to a divine echo or heavenly voice that provided guidance to the rabbis during the era of the Second Temple.</note>.

**46** No king of the earth is established on earth unless the celestial host is first humbled in heaven. <note>This reflects the "as above, so below" principle common in Renaissance thought, suggesting that earthly events are mirrored by or dependent on celestial shifts.</note>

**47** Through the word **Amen**, the order is explicitly held as to how the influx of the <term>numerations</term> <note>original: "numerationum." This refers to the *Sefirot*, the ten divine emanations or attributes of God in Kabbalah.</note> proceeds.

->Conclusions numbering five hundred, according to his own opinion, which are divided by a ten-fold division into Physical, Theological, Platonic, Mathematical, Dogmatizing Paradoxical, Conciliatory Paradoxical, Chaldean, Orphic, Magical, and Kabbalistic conclusions. In all of these, I state nothing assertively or even as probable, except insofar as the Holy Roman Church and its well-deserving head, the Supreme Pontiff **Innocent VIII**, judges it to be either true or probable; anyone who does not submit the judgment of their own mind to his judgment has no mind at all.<-

### Seventeen paradoxical conclusions according to his own opinion, first reconciling the sayings of Aristotle and Plato, and then of other doctors who seem to disagree the most.

**1** There is no question, whether natural or divine, in which **Aristotle** and **Plato** do not agree in sense and substance, even though they seem to disagree in words.

**2** Those who say that "innascibility" <note>A technical theological term for the property of the Father in the Trinity: the state of not being born or originated from another.</note> is a positive property constituting the Father in an incommunicable hypostatic being, do not differ at all from the opinion of the <term>Holy Doctor</term> <note>original: "sancti doctoris." This refers to St. Thomas Aquinas.</note>, from whom they seem to differ greatly according to their words.

**3** If the sixth notion—which is "inspirability"—is set aside, the <term>Thomists</term> and <term>Scotists</term> <note>The followers of Thomas Aquinas and Duns Scotus, respectively; two major and often conflicting schools of medieval Scholastic philosophy.</note> ought not to disagree, if they correctly look into the foundations of their own teachers.

**4** Concerning the subject of theology, **Thomas**, **Scotus**, and **Giles** <note>Giles of Rome (Aegidius Romanus), another influential medieval philosopher.</note> agree fundamentally and radically, even though in the branches and on the surface of their words, each of them seems to disagree with the others a great deal.

**5** Regarding that question: "Whether there is one being [esse] in Christ, or several beings," I say that **Scotus** and **Thomas** do not disagree.

**6** Concerning the "distinction from the nature of the thing" <note>The *distinctio formalis a parte rei*, a famous technicality in Scotist philosophy regarding how different qualities exist within a single object.</note>, the Thomists and Scotists ought not to disagree if they understand their teachers fundamentally.

Here, he continues his "reconciliation" of Thomas Aquinas and Duns Scotus, then transitions into his own original philosophical propositions (the "80 Conclusions").</meta>

->Giovanni Pico della Mirandola<-

**7** **Thomas** and **Scotus** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274) and John Duns Scotus (1266–1308) were the heads of the two dominant, and often conflicting, schools of medieval Scholasticism.</note> do not disagree on the distinction of attributes.

**8** In this specific point, stripped of its side-arguments, as to whether an angel could simply desire divine equality, **Thomas** and **Scotus** do not disagree.

**9** Regarding the matter of what is known first—the more universal or the less universal—**Thomas** and **Scotus** agree, even though they are thought to disagree most greatly on this. Concerning this, I propose the following three conclusions based on the mind of each.

**10** Regarding a thing conceived nominally <note>original: "nominaliter." Conceived by name or general reference rather than by its essential definition.</note>, the first concept that is held is the most universal concept.

**11** Regarding a thing conceived definitively, the first concept that is held<gloss>ur</gloss> is the concept of the thing itself: a concept that is proper and <term>convertible</term> <note>original: "conuertibilis." In logic, a term is convertible if it applies to exactly the same things as another term (e.g., "human" and "rational animal").</note>.

**12** In the most distinct knowledge, the last things known to us are the most universal predicates.

**13** The opinion of the **Commentator** <note>original: "commentatoris." This always refers to Averroes (Ibn Rushd), the 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational to Western universities.</note> regarding indeterminate dimensions in no way contradicts the principles and foundations of the doctrine of **Saint Thomas**.

**14** In the matter of the object of the intellect, **Thomas** and **Scotus** do not disagree as is believed, but rather agree.

**15** In the question regarding <term>free contingency</term> <note>original: "contingentia ad utrumlibet." This refers to the capacity for a cause to produce either of two opposite effects, essentially the basis of free will.</note> in the matter of chance and fortune, **Averroes** and **Avicenna** do not fundamentally or in reality disagree, although on the surface and in their words the opposite appears to be true.

**16** On whether the physicist receives the "composite body" from the metaphysician, **Averroes** and **Avicenna** cannot fundamentally disagree, even if they differ in words.

**17** Regarding the manner in which angels exist in a place, **Thomas** and **Scotus** do not differ.

### Philosophical conclusions according to my own opinion, numbering 80. Although these disagree with common philosophy, they do not shrink much from the common method of philosophizing.

**1** A universal <term>species</term> <note>original: "species." In this context, it refers to the mental image or "form" that allows us to recognize objects.</note> can be immediately abstracted from a species existing in the external senses.

**2** A <term>second intention</term> <note>original: "intentio secunda." A logical concept or "thought about a thought" (e.g., the concept of "species" or "genus"), as opposed to a "first intention" which is a thought about a real object (e.g., a "cat").</note> is a being of reason, existing in the manner of a qualitative form, arising from the operation of the intellect consecutively, not effectively.

**3** Neither the first intention nor the second intention exists subjectively anywhere.

**4** In the realm of bodies, one eventually reaches something that places other things corporally but is not itself corporally placed, and that is the **ultimate sphere** <note>The "ultimate sphere" or *Primum Mobile* was the outermost shell of the universe in the Aristotelian-Ptolemaic model, which contained everything else but was not contained by any further space.</note>. Just so, in the realm of intelligible things, one eventually reaches something that "places" things intelligibly but is in no way "placed," and that is **God**.

**Corollary.** One should not ask how the ultimate sphere is placed, but absolutely concede that it is not placed.

**5** The individual <note>original: "singulare." The specific, unique object (like a specific person) rather than the general category (humanity).</note> is not understood by the intellect—not according to truth, and not even according to the opinion of **Aristotle**, the **Commentator**, and **Thomas**.

**6** Although the intellect does not understand in a singular way, it is nevertheless because of the intellect that the individual is perfectly known.

# Conclusions.

**7** Any thing, whatever it may be, when established in the purity of its own being, is the intelligent subject, the intellect, and the thing understood. <note>Pico is drawing on a Neoplatonic and Aristotelian principle that at the highest level of reality—pure being—the act of thinking and the object of thought are identical.</note>

**8** From the preceding conclusion, one understands why matter is the principle of unknowability, and the agent intellect is the principle of knowability. <note>In this system, "matter" is formless and therefore cannot be "seen" by the mind, while the "agent intellect" provides the light of form that makes things understandable.</note>

**9** That is called an <term>immanent action</term> <note>original: "actio immanens." An action that stays within the person, such as thinking or feeling, rather than affecting an outside object.</note> which is not subjectively in that which is passively named by it; and by this, it is distinguished from a <term>transient action</term> <note>original: "transeunte." An action that "passes over" into an external thing, like a carpenter building a chair.</note>.

**10** Every other way of distinguishing besides the one mentioned in the preceding conclusion is insufficient for tellling an immanent action apart from a transient one.

**11** When **Averroes** <note>original: "Auenrois." The 12th-century Islamic philosopher Ibn Rushd, famous for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> says that there is no other means for proving an abstract substance besides the eternity of motion, he does not mean just any abstract substance, but that which is abstract from the body at the ultimate degree of abstraction.

**12** A thing does not possess its "corporeal being" from any substantial form or any degree of a substantial form.

**13** The six <term>transcendentals</term> <note>original: "transcedentia." In medieval logic, these were the most general concepts that apply to everything: Being, Thing, One, Something, True, and Good.</note> which the common doctrine posits were fabricated by the younger Latin thinkers; neither the Greek Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's school.</note> nor their leader **Aristotle** knew of them.

**14** According to **Aristotle**, it is necessary that the First Cause <note>The "Unmoved Mover" or God.</note> moves by necessity.

**15** According to **Aristotle**, it is impossible and entirely irrational for all things to happen by necessity, regardless of which cause that necessity is attributed to.

**16** The treatise on <term>suppositions</term> <note>original: "suppositionum." A technical branch of medieval logic dealing with how nouns refer to specific things in different contexts.</note> does not belong to the study of Logic.

**17** The world could not have existed from God from eternity through efficient causality—that is, a true efficiency which is the bringing of something from potentiality into act. <note>Pico is distinguishing between the Christian doctrine of "creation out of nothing" and the Aristotelian idea of an eternal world.</note>

**18** According to **Aristotle** and the **Commentator** [Averroes], the world could have been produced—and was in fact produced—from eternity by God through an efficiency that is a natural flow and an effectual consequence.

**19** Whoever denies that the heavens are ensouled—such that their mover is not merely their form—not only opposes **Aristotle** but destroys the foundations of all philosophy. <note>This refers to the ancient belief that the stars and planets are moved by celestial intelligences or souls.</note>

**20** In the acts of our intellect, there is no succession [of one thought after another] by reason of the sensitive and serving powers, as the moderns believe, but because the intellect itself is rational.

**21** Newly acquired knowledge arises from preceding knowledge as if from a starting point, and as if from an effective, partial, formal, and directive cause, and as if from a material predisposed cause.

**22** A <term>habit</term> <note>original: "habitus." In this context, a stable mental disposition or skill acquired through practice.</note> is "practical" when it is formally the thing that regulates a work of the reason that has been habituated.

**23** A habit possesses its practical or speculative nature from the object as it relates to the subject in which it exists; however, an intellect is called "practical" or "speculative" based on the end goal which the habituated person proposes for themselves.

**24** A practical habit is distinguished from a speculative one by its goals.

**25** <term>Praxis</term> <note>original: "Praxis." Action or practice, as opposed to "theoria" or contemplation.</note> is an operation which is not formally knowledge; it can be right or wrong, and it can be made right through a habit, acting as an effective partial cause of that correction by which the practitioner is trained.

**26.** Practical and theoretical knowledge are differences of an <term>accidental habit</term>. <note>In Scholastic philosophy, a "habit" is a stable disposition or skill. Pico is arguing that whether knowledge is "doing" (practical) or "thinking" (theoretical) is an external trait rather than an essential change in the nature of the knowledge itself.</note>

**27.** The theology of a **wayfarer** <note>original: "uiatoris." A "wayfarer" is a person currently living on earth, traveling toward God, as opposed to the "comprehensor" who has reached heaven.</note> as a wayfarer must be called simply practical.

**28.** That all medicine is practical is both a truth we assert and is consistent with the words and opinion of **Averroes** <note>original: "Auenrois." The 12th-century Islamic philosopher Ibn Rushd, whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to medieval university life.</note>.

**29.** Logic is practical.

**30.** The **common sense** <note>In medieval psychology, the "common sense" was a faculty in the brain that unified the data from the five individual senses into a single perception.</note> is not distinct from the senses of sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch.

**31.** <term>Intelligible species</term> <note>original: "species intelligibiles." These were thought to be abstract mental images that allowed the mind to understand physical objects.</note> abstracted from phantasms do not exist; we assert this both as truth and as the opinion of the **Commentator** <note>Averroes.</note> and **Albert the Great**.

**32.** In every question knowable through demonstration, it is necessary to know beforehand "what" the subject and its attribute are—understanding "what" not as a mere definition of a name, as other commentators understand it, but as the essence of the thing.

**33.** It is possible to reason backward from an effect to its cause without the "negotiation" <note>A technical term in logic for a specific type of argumentative process.</note> that **Walter Burley** <note>original: "Burleus." A 14th-century English logician.</note> dreams of.

**34.** Those who hold that there are <term>natural minima</term> <note>original: "minima naturalia." The theory that there is a smallest possible unit of a natural substance (a precursor to atomic theory).</note> in qualities do not therefore have to deny that the motion of change happens successively over time.

**35.** It is necessary to hold, according to **Averroes**, that the "form of a genus" is a different reality from the "form of a species"; the opposite view cannot stand with the principles of his teaching.

**36.** Aristotle's demonstration in the seventh book of the *Physics*—that "Everything that is moved is moved by another"—proves none of those things intended by **Thomas Aquinas**, **Duns Scotus**, **Giles of Rome** (whom **John of Jandun** follows), **Gratiadei**, **Walter Burley**, or others I have read. Rather, it proves only what the **Commentator** <note>Averroes.</note> best stated (though he was misunderstood by all the Latin commentators): that in anything moved, the mover is distinct from the thing moved, either by nature or by subject.

**37.** The demonstration in the seventh book of the *Physics* proves evidently that the heaven is not moved by itself, given that the principles of **Averroes** are indeed true and most firm.

**38.** The order of the books of natural philosophy handed down by **Aristotle** is this:
The *Physics*, *On the Heavens and the World*, *On Generation and Corruption*, *Meteorology*, *On Minerals*, *On Plants*, *On the Generation of Animals*, *On the Parts of Animals*, *On the Progression of Animals*, *On the Soul*, and then the books called the *Short Physical Treatises* <note>original: "parui naturales."</note>.

->**Corollary.** Those who call the book *On the Soul* the sixth book of natural philosophy are entirely out of harmony with Aristotle's mind.<-

**39.** Every way of upholding Aristotle's saying—that "Eastern winds are warmer than western ones"—is frivolous and void, except for the path of the **animation of the heaven**. <note>The medieval belief that the celestial spheres were moved by living intelligences or souls.</note>

**40.** Neither the reasons brought by Aristotle nor those by his commentators regarding the saltiness of the sea are sufficient; nor can any be assigned that is more sufficient (especially given **Mosaic truth** <note>A reference to the Biblical truth found in the writings of Moses (the Pentateuch).</note>) than the causality of that same universal providence which also worked the uncovering of the dry land.

**41.** No part of the heaven differs from another according to being luminous or non-luminous, but rather according to being more or less luminous.

<summary>Pico presents a series of academic propositions challenging standard Latin interpretations of Aristotle and Averroes, covering topics from the classification of sciences to the physics of the heavens and the saltiness of the sea.</summary>
