<header>Conclusions.</header>

# Conclusions.

**42** The method given by **Aristotle** <note>The famous Greek philosopher whose physics dominated medieval science.</note> regarding how lower things are heated by higher things does not appear to be correct in any way. <note>Pico is challenging the Aristotelian idea that the friction of rotating celestial spheres heats the Earth.</note>

**43** These two things stand together, and I believe both are true at once: that the reasoning of **Averroes** <note>The 12th-century Islamic philosopher Ibn Rushd.</note> in the final comment of the first book of the *Physics* against **Avicenna** <note>The 11th-century Persian philosopher Ibn Sina.</note> is conclusive, and yet despite this, Avicenna’s arguments for proving the **First Principle** <note>The First Principle is God, the primary cause of all existence.</note> are good and effective.

**44** If **Thomas** <note>St. Thomas Aquinas, the influential Dominican theologian.</note> says that the **Intelligences** <note>In medieval philosophy, these were non-material beings like angels or the movers of the celestial spheres.</note> are in a **genus** <note>A category of classification.</note> according to Aristotle, he contradicts himself no less than he contradicts Aristotle.

**45** If the unity of a genus exists not only in the mind of the one conceiving it but also in the thing being conceived, it is necessary that whatever things are in the same logical genus must also be in the same physical genus.

**46** Knowledge is actually a relative category, and the "knowable object" is related to it by <term>accidents</term>. <note>Accidents: non-essential properties of a thing, like color or size, as opposed to its essence.</note>

**47** Holding the common manner of the Doctors—namely, that something may be formally predicated of God—I state two closely related conclusions, of which this is the first: That God alone is a substance in such a way that He is in no way a "non-substance."

**48** Second: God is not in a genus for this reason—because He is substantially substance.

**49** To posit a difference between <term>limitateness</term> <note>original: "limitatem." The state of being bounded or limited.</note> and whiteness, or similar accidents, based on one being separable and the other inseparable from a certain subject, is a fiction.

**50** The difference that appears between the aforementioned accidents originates solely from the voluntary naming of things.

**51** According to **Averroes**, it is necessary to say that substance belongs to the intrinsic <term>quiddity</term> <note>Quiddity: the "what-ness" or essence of a thing.</note> of an accident; this opinion is most harmonious with both Aristotle and philosophy.

**52** The opinion that matter should not be included in the definition of natural substances is a view consistent with both Averroes and **Albert** <note>Albertus Magnus, the teacher of Thomas Aquinas.</note>.

**53** If **Thomas** says that there are accidents in the Intelligences according to Aristotle, he contradicts not only Aristotle but also himself.

**54** These propositions must be granted as entirely true: "primary matter becomes a donkey, an ox," and the like. <note>Pico is likely discussing the transformation of "primary matter"—the formless "stuff" of the universe—as it takes on the forms of different animals.</note>

**55** In a material composite, there are not two precise and distinct entities, but one single entity.

**56** I say that sound is caused not by the motion of air trapped between two bodies striking each other (as Aristotle and his commentators hold), but by the contact of such-and-such bodies producing such-and-such a sound.

**57** The arguments the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note> bring forward to prove that in essentially ordered causes one cannot go to infinity do not necessarily prove the falsehood of that position. <note>Pico is questioning the standard proof that there must be a "First Cause" because an infinite chain of causes is supposedly impossible.</note>

**58** The sensitive power of the **common sense**—just as it is not derived from the sensitive powers of the external senses (as stated in conclusion 30)—so neither is it derived from the sensitive powers... <note>Text continues on next page.</note>

<summary>In this series of numbered philosophical propositions, Pico della Mirandola critiques established Aristotelian and Thomistic views on the nature of God, the definition of substance, the physics of sound, and the hierarchy of causes.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle, Averroes, Thomas Aquinas, metaphysics, substance, primary matter, quiddity, physics of sound, first principle, scholasticism</keywords>

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

[58] <note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing a point from the previous page.</note> ...with the fictional <note>In the sense of "constructed" or "shaped" by the mind.</note> internal senses—the phantastic (or imaginative), the cogitative, and the memorative—I assert that they differ in subject (that is, in reality) and that this is the true opinion of both **Aristotle** and **Plato**.

**59** I say that all the qualities of the elements are symbols of different species.

**60** If a **fourth figure of syllogisms** <note>In logic, a syllogism is a form of reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two premises. Aristotle originally defined three "figures" or patterns; a fourth was later attributed to the physician Galen.</note> must be posited, it should be the one that **Galen** <note>A famous Greek physician and philosopher.</note> proposes, not the one childishly devised by **Francis of Mayrone** and **Peter of Mantua**; however, it is more correct to posit none at all.

**61** We must say, according to the doctrine of **Aristotle**, that the <term>metaphysician</term> <note>One who studies the fundamental nature of reality beyond the physical.</note> treats matter insofar as things are made from it <term>essentially</term> (*per se*), while the <term>physicist</term> treats it insofar as things are made from it <term>incidentally</term> (*per accidens*).

**62** An exclusive word added to one relative term does not exclude its correlate.

**63** It should not be granted that a part within a quantitative whole is in any way actually distinct from its whole.

**64** The opinion attributed to **Avicenna**—that "the One" which is interchangeable with "Being" is the same "One" that is the principle of number, and consequently that every single thing is "one" by an <term>intention</term> <note>In medieval logic, an "intention" is a mental concept or a way the mind identifies an object.</note> added to its essence—if not necessarily true, is nonetheless probable and will be defended by me.

**65** Although the intellective power in us is an <term>accident</term> <note>A property that is not essential to the existence of a thing; for example, being "tall" is an accident of a human.</note>, in **angels** it is a <term>substance</term> <note>The core essence or reality of a thing.</note>.

**66** Formality is an actuality suited to perfect the "possible intellect" by itself.

**67** If a mixture is created from the meeting of elements, in whatever way the elements are said to remain, the mixture will be made from elements in the mixture as if from matter digested by a spiritual, vaporous heat elevated from them.

**68** In all things below **God**, the matter is the same according to its essence, but different according to its being.

**69** The <term>quiddities</term> <note>The "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing.</note> of physical natures can be conceived through an adequate and proper concept without their accidents, whether they are considered by a metaphysician or a physicist.

**70** The organic body, which is the "matter" of the soul and is placed in its definition by **Aristotle**, is a body and is organic through a form that is essentially distinct from the soul that completes it.

**71** According to all philosophers, it must be said that **God** necessarily acts in whatever He does. <note>original: "Deum necessario agere quicquid agit." This was a highly controversial claim in the 15th century, as it seemed to limit God's free will.</note>

**72** He who doubts that a truer and more substantial unity is made from the "thing known" and the "knower" than from matter and material form is no philosopher.

**73** Holding the opinion on the intellective soul held by the **Commentator** <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd), known as "The Commentator" for his extensive work on Aristotle.</note>, it seems to me reasonable to hold that this soul is the subject of no accident; I shall defend this position as true, although whether he actually held this, I do not define.

**74** I say, following **Thomas** <note>St. Thomas Aquinas.</note>, that our happiness consists in the "reflective act" of the intellect.

**75** The definition of nature includes celestial things; and the word "and" is to be understood conjunctively, not disjunctively.

# Conclusions

**76** Just as any **Philosopher** has cause to say that the sensory powers are in the heart, so any **Physician** has cause to say they are in the brain. <note>This refers to the long-standing debate between the Aristotelian view (the heart as the seat of the soul) and the medical/Galenic view (the brain as the center of the nervous system).</note>

**77** What is stated by the common school of all Latin philosophers regarding the **first operation of the intellect** is an error; for there is no other operation of the rational part other than those two which they themselves designate as the second and third: namely, composition and discourse. <note>Scholastic philosophers usually divided logic into three parts: simple apprehension (1st), judgment/composition (2nd), and reasoning/discourse (3rd). Pico argues the first is not a distinct rational operation.</note>

**78** **Accidents** <note>Qualities that do not exist on their own, like "redness" or "size."</note> should in no way be called "beings," but rather "of a being."

**79** The **Six Principles** are absolute forms. <note>Pico likely refers to the "Book of Six Principles," a common medieval logic textbook that expanded on Aristotle's categories.</note>

**80** If there is any primary and non-causal language <note>A language not derived from others, but reflecting the nature of reality itself.</note>, it is evident from many conjectures that it is **Hebrew**.

## Seventy-one paradoxical conclusions according to my own opinion,
## introducing new dogmas into philosophy.

**1** Just as the being of properties is preceded by <term>quidditative being</term> <note>From the Latin *quidditas* or "whatness"—the essential nature of a thing.</note>, so quidditative being is preceded by **unial being**. <note>Pico uses the term "unial" to describe a level of existence characterized by absolute unity, prior to any division into specific types or essences.</note>

**2** We cannot say that anything is predicated of a thing taken in its most precise sense through what is properly called "predication." <note>To "predicate" is to assert a quality of a subject; Pico suggests that at the highest level of reality, things are so unified that they cannot be split into "subject" and "quality."</note>

**3** One who reaches a thing through its **definition** reaches the thing in its state of **alterity**. <note>Alterity means "otherness." Pico argues that defining something separates it from the whole, making it an "other."</note>

**4** Only he who reaches a thing in the precision of its **union** reaches the thing as it truly is.

**5** The more eminent a mode of knowledge is, the more imperfect and useless it becomes for an intellect that is disproportionate to it.

**6** Just as knowledge gained through **demonstration** <note>Logical proof.</note> is the most perfect knowledge for the common human state we experience here, so it is simply the most imperfect among all kinds of knowledge.

**7** Just as **God** is simply the knowledge of all being, so the **intellect** is the definition of all being, and the **soul** is the science of all being.

**8** If **theology** is treated theologically, it will treat that which is **unially one** as its primary subject, and everything else that exists according to its unial being as a secondary subject.

**9** True **metaphysics**, handed down metaphysically, treats whatever is a true form as its primary subject, and everything else according to its formal being as a secondary object, neglecting the demonstrative method.

**10** Just as with a **creature** the logic "it is a being, therefore it exists" does not hold, so in **God** the logic "He exists, therefore He is a being" does not hold. <note>original: "est ens, ergo est... est, ergo est ens." Pico is arguing that God is "beyond being" in the traditional sense.</note>

**11** The same thing in a creature is called "existence" (*esse*) by reason of its actuality, and "essence" (*essentia*) by reason of its determination.

**12** Just as an **angel** is necessarily composed of essence and existence, so the **soul** is necessarily composed of substance and accident.

**13** Contradictories are compatible within an intellectual nature. <note>This suggests that the higher mind can resolve or hold opposing truths simultaneously.</note>

**14** Although the preceding conclusion is true, it is nevertheless more properly said,

<meta>This page continues the "71 Paradoxical Conclusions" where Pico della Mirandola presents his own original philosophical system. Having previously discussed the nature of being, he now moves into the mechanics of the "intellectual nature" (the realm of pure thought and divine ideas) and redefines the fundamental categories of reality.</meta>

<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

**14** That in the intellectual nature there are no contradictories, except in the sense that they are compatible with one another.
**15** Contradictories coincide in the unial <term>unial: a state of being perfectly one or unified</term> nature.
**16** Aristotle reasonably established in his sciences the first principle: that one of two contradictories is said of anything, and never both at the same time. <note>This refers to the Law of Non-Contradiction, which Pico acknowledges as true for logic and the physical world, but not for the higher divine intellect.</note>
**17** In the intellect, there is "this" and "that," but "this" is not outside of "that."
**18** Therefore, the incompatibility of contradictories appears in the soul because the soul is the first quantity that places "part outside of part." <note>Pico suggests that the human soul experiences contradictions because it operates through extension and time, unlike the pure intellect.</note>
**19** Everything in the intellectual nature possesses from its own intelligible unity both the power to unite everything to itself, and the power to preserve its own property, immaculate and unmixed.
**20** The "self-ness" <term>ipseity: the quality of being oneself; individual identity</term> of each thing is most truly itself when all things are within it in such a way that all things within it are that very self.
**21** Through the aforementioned conclusions, one can understand the nature of Anaxagoras’s *homoeomeria* <note>original: "omiomeria"; the ancient Greek theory that every substance contains seeds of every other substance</note>, which the Craftsman Mind <note>the "Opifex," or Divine Intellect</note> distinguishes.
**22** Let no one wonder that Anaxagoras called the intellect "unmixed" even though it is "most mixed"; for the greatest mixture coincides with the greatest simplicity in the intellectual nature.
**23** Just as substantial forms in the second world <note>the celestial or psychic realm</note> exist in the manner of accidents <note>qualities that depend on a subject</note>, so accidental forms exist in the first world <note>the divine or intellectual realm</note> in the manner of substances.

**Corollary:** Just as in the first world there is not "white" but "whiteness," so in the second world there is not "fire" but "fiery."

**24** It cannot be said that in the intellect, the ideas of—for example—fire, water, and air are three separate ideas; rather, one must say they are a triad.
**25** Unless we destroy the intellectual nature, we cannot understand ideas to be counted as numbers, except through the permeation of the idea of "number" through the rest, just as each idea exists through all of them.
**26** From the preceding conclusions, it can be understood what the "formal number" is, which Pythagoras said was the principle of all things.
**27** Five primary categories <term>predicaments: the most basic classes or categories of things that exist</term> should be established: The One, substance, quantity, quality, and relation.
**28** The diversity of beings is more correctly reduced to the five mentioned above than to the ten that Archytas first and then Aristotle established, or the five that Plotinus establishes, or the four that the Stoics establish.
**29** The definition of the category of the "One" is the absolute cutting away <note>original: "praecisio"</note> from everything foreign.
**30** The definition of the category of "substance" is the united perfection of unparticipated substance.
**31** The definition of the category of "quantity" is the placing of part outside of part.
**32** The definition of the category of "quality" is the truth of naming through an inherent participation.
**33** The definition of the category of "relation" <note>original: "ad aliquid," literally "toward something"</note> is an imaginary being.
**34** There is no unparticipated formal predicate that cannot be partially predicated of an intelligence.

## Conclusions.

**§ 35** Just as it is truly said of the intellect alone that it is fire and that it is water, that it is motion and that it is rest, so it is truly said of the soul alone that it grows cold, that it grows warm, that it stands still, and that it moves.

**36** Just as the intellect of God multiplies unity, so the soul quantifies and extends the multitude of the intellect. <note>Pico argues that the soul acts as a bridge, taking the abstract, unified ideas of the divine mind and giving them "extension" or form in the physical world.</note>

**37** The first thing that can be understood coincides with the first intellect, and the first thing that can be known coincides with the first knower.

**38** In souls of a lower sort, reason acts by way of the senses; in more sublime souls, the senses act by way of reason.

**39** That marvelous saying of that barbarian <note>original: "barbari"; likely a reference to the ancient philosopher Petron of Himera or a figure from the Chaldean Oracles</note> companion of Nymphs and demons concerning **184** worlds arranged in a triangular figure with three units at the corners and one in the middle, will be most correctly understood if we understand it as the intellectual, animal, and seminal trinity proceeding from intelligible unity, and the calculation of the principal parts of the world through the first spherical number.

**40** That a soul can—through the purgative way <term>purgative way: a stage of spiritual purification where the soul is cleansed of earthly attachments</term> without any other study or investigation, but through only a modest and very easy comparison and attention toward the intelligible things it already possesses from above—acquire a perfect knowledge of all things that can be known; this must be conceded not only by Platonic philosophers, but even by those among the <term>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle</term> where it seems least likely: the followers of **Averroes**. <note>Averroes was a medieval Muslim philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to university learning; Pico suggests even these rigorous logicians must admit the power of spiritual intuition.</note>

**41** Just as the common sense <term>common sense: the faculty that binds together inputs from the five individual senses</term> functions in the cognition of accidental qualities and material quantity, so reason functions in the cognition of substantial qualities and formal quantity—maintaining the proportion that the former acts through the senses and the latter through reason.

**42** The infinity of God can be proven through "super-excellence" according to the state of the intellect and the path of **mystic theology**, and for proving this, every other path is ineffective.

**43** The act by which the angelic and rational nature is made blessed with ultimate happiness is neither an act of the intellect nor of the will, but is the union of the "unity" which exists in the <term>alterity: the state of being "other" or different; plurality</term> of the soul with the "Unity" which is without alterity. <note>Pico suggests that heaven is not just thinking about God or loving God, but a mystical merging of the soul's inner spark with the absolute One-ness of God.</note>

**44** **Aristotle**, in the book of *Metaphysics*, does not treat God except in the last chapter of the twelfth book, which begins: *It must also be considered in which way the universe possesses the good.*

**45** The order of the books of the *Metaphysics* following the books on *Physics*—in the way that Aristotle organized them—cannot be correct according to any process, whether it be investigative or analytical.

**46** Given any practical object, the operation that puts it into practice is nobler than the one that contemplates it, provided other things are equal.

**47** The text of Aristotle which says "every soul is immortal" can be better defended than the text which says "every soul is mortal." <note>Pico is navigating a fierce contemporary debate: many Renaissance scholars argued that Aristotle believed the individual soul died with the body; Pico disagrees.</note>

**48** Besides the three types of demonstration—"that it is," "why it is," and "simply"—which Aristotle and the Commentator <note>Averroes</note> establish, there is a fourth type of demon<insert>stration</insert> <meta>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page with "strationis" as indicated by the catchword.</meta>

<summary>Pico outlines how the human soul mediates between divine unity and physical plurality, asserting that spiritual purification can lead to total knowledge. He also critiques the structure of Aristotle's Metaphysics and argues for the immortality of the soul within the Peripatetic tradition.</summary>
<keywords>Averroes, Aristotle, mysticism, immortality of the soul, purgative way, metaphysics, alterity, common sense, celestial hierarchy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's paradoxical conclusions. It follows his discussion of the nature of the soul and the intellect, moving into the relationship between natural philosophy, the Hebrew language, and the internal workings of the rational soul.</meta>

...of demonstration, which can be called the demonstration of convertibility, which is stronger than all those previously mentioned.

<margin>☩ 12</margin>
**49** It is more improperly said of God that He is an intellect or an intelligent being, than of the rational soul that it is an angel.

**50** Matter alone is sufficient to account for that for whose sake Aristotle and other philosophers placed **privation** among the natural principles. <note>In Aristotelian physics, "privation" is the absence of a form that a subject should have; Pico argues this third principle is redundant if matter is properly understood.</note>

->Corollary: Privation is not to be placed among natural principles.<-

**51** There are three principles of natural things: matter, motion, and form.

**52** The science of God, man, and **prime matter** <term>prime matter: the most basic, formless reality that underlies all physical things</term> is one and the same; and he who possesses knowledge of one will also possess it of the others, while maintaining the proportion of extreme to extreme, of the middle to the extremes, and of the extremes to the middle.

**53** He who denies prime matter neither contradicts the senses nor denies physical reason.

**54** To prove that prime matter exists, the way of numbers or the way of universal philosophy provides more certainty than any physical reasoning in which the senses have an entrance.

**55** He who holds the order of the **Hebrew language** profoundly and radically, and knows how to maintain it proportionally in the sciences, will have the pattern and rule for perfectly discovering anything that can be known. <note>Pico believed the structure of Hebrew mirrored the structure of the universe, a key tenet of his Christian Kabbalah.</note>

**56** Beyond the distinction of the thing and the reason, a third distinction must be placed, which I call **inadequacy**. <note>original: "inadæquationis"; this is a technical term Pico uses to describe a distinction between things that are not entirely different but are not identical in their scope or perfection.</note>

**57** The species of enmity, which are multiplied from the wolf to the "estimative" power of the sheep, are species of substance, not of any accident. <note>The "estimative" power is the animal instinct that allows a sheep to sense a wolf is dangerous without prior experience.</note>

**58** **Formality** is the adequate object of the intellect.

**59** Wherever a nature is given that is composed of several natures actually remaining in it, one is always substantially nobler and the others are accidental.

<margin>☩ 31</margin>
**60** The soul understands nothing actually and distinctly except itself.

**61** The entire substance of the rational soul is the intellectual part.

**62** The soul always understands itself, and by understanding itself, it understands all beings in a certain way.

**63** Although there is an intellectual nature actually in the soul through which it corresponds with the angel (just as there is a rational nature through which it is distinguished from it), nothing is nevertheless intrinsic to the soul through which it could understand anything distinct from itself without its own specific **mental image**.

**64** The intellectual nature which is in the rational soul, above its rational nature, differs precisely from pure intellectual nature just as a part differs from the whole.

**65** Because the animal intellect differs from the intellectual intellect as a middle part, and not merely as a part, it is therefore more equalized to the intellectual totality.

**66** The soul can, through external informing, arrive at the point where it understands all things indivisibly through its own substantial form.

**67** To every series of souls, one pure intellect corresponds.

<summary>Pico presents a series of philosophical paradoxes regarding the nature of prime matter, the utility of the Hebrew language in systematic knowledge, and the self-reflexive nature of the human soul. He critiques traditional Aristotelian principles like "privation" and argues that the soul's primary object of understanding is itself.</summary>

<header>Conclusions.</header>

# Conclusions.

68 All celestial souls are one in the first intellect. <note>Pico is suggesting a Neoplatonic unity where individual souls find their source and singular identity within the "First Intellect" or Divine Mind.</note>
69 It is reasonable according to philosophy that every animate series be beatified <note>original: "beatificari"; to reach a state of supreme blessedness or ultimate happiness</note> in its own intellect; however, this is stated as a probability rather than an assertion.
70 Though there were three who said that all things are one—namely Xenophanes, Parmenides, and Melissus—whoever diligently scrutinizes their sayings will see that the "One" of Xenophanes is that which is simply one.
->The One of Parmenides is not "one" in an absolute sense as is commonly believed, but is "one being."<-
->The One of Melissus is a "one" that holds an extremal correspondence to the One of Xenophanes.<- <note>Xenophanes, Parmenides, and Melissus were Eleatic philosophers who argued that reality is a single, unchanging substance. Pico is distinguishing their subtle metaphysical differences.</note>
71 Empedocles, through "strife" and "friendship" <gloss>~</gloss> in the soul, understands nothing other than the powers in it that lead upward and downward <gloss>~</gloss>; these, I believe, are proportional in the science of the <term>Sephirot</term> to "Eternity" and "Beauty." <note>Empedocles (c. 490–430 BCE) proposed that Love (friendship) and Strife were the two forces moving the elements. Pico links this to the Kabbalistic Sephirot, specifically Netzach (Eternity/Victory) and Tiferet (Beauty/Harmony).</note>

## Twenty-nine conclusions in theology according to my own opinion, differing considerably from the common way of speaking among theologians.

<margin>✽ 1</margin> 1 He who says that an accident cannot exist unless it exists within a subject: such a person can still hold the sacrament of the Eucharist, even while holding that the substance of the bread does not remain, as the common way maintains. <note>In Scholastic theology, an "accident" is a property (like the taste or smell of bread) that usually requires a "substance" (the bread itself) to exist. Pico is arguing about how these properties persist after the bread has been consecrated into the Body of Christ.</note>
<margin>✽ 2</margin> 2 If the common way is maintained regarding the possibility of "supposition" <note>A technical term in logic and theology regarding how a term stands for a particular thing.</note> in respect to any creature whatsoever, I say that without the conversion of the bread into the body of Christ, or the annihilation of the "bread-ness" <gloss>original: "paneietatis"</gloss>, it is possible for the body of Christ to be on the altar according to the truth of the sacrament of the Eucharist. Let this be said speaking of what is possible, not of how things actually are.
3 We hold with theological truth that the ideal and formal reasons of things are found effectively from God, formally and primarily, in the first created mind.
**Corollary.** Where ideas exist "ideally," they do not exist "formally"; where they exist "formally," they do not exist "ideally."
4 If we posit that God knows creatures as a secondary object of His intuition, as is commonly posited, I say that the Father produces the Word <note>The second person of the Trinity</note> before He knows creatures.
5 The perfections of the Divine Attributes, whether in God or taken according to their own essence, do not signify diverse "reasons" <note>In this context, "reasons" (rationes) refers to distinct conceptual definitions.</note> that are directly and principally definable or describable.
6 The gaze of divine cognition is not formally terminated upon creatures as primary or secondary objects (as the common school of theologians says); rather, intuiting only Himself and nothing other than Himself, He knows all things primarily, secondarily, unitive-ly, and eminently—and more than equivalently.
**Corollary.** There is no multitude of things understood in God, nor do creatures, insofar as they are understood, add to the number alongside the divine essence as it is understood; rather, there is only the entirely one, most simple thing understood. <note>Pico is defending the absolute simplicity of God's mind, arguing that God doesn't have a "collection" of different ideas, but knows everything through His own singular essence.</note>

<summary>Pico synthesizes ancient Greek philosophy with Jewish Kabbalah and proposes radical theological shifts regarding the Eucharist and the simplicity of the Divine Mind. He specifically challenges the Scholastic "common way" by suggesting that God's knowledge does not consist of a multitude of distinct ideas.</summary>

## Of John Pico of Mirandola

7 The three transcendentals in which the image consists do not signify different rationalities in a direct sense, and are not primarily definable or describable. <note>The "transcendentals" in Scholastic philosophy are properties of being that transcend any specific category, usually identified as Truth, Goodness, and Unity.</note>

<margin>✠ 1</margin>
8 Christ did not truly, and in terms of real presence, descend to the underworld <note>original: "inferos"; often translated as hell or the place of the dead</note>, as Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent Scholastic theologian.</note> and the common path posit, but only in terms of his effect.

9 Although it seems probable to me, it must not be stubbornly asserted that the soul of Christ could not have descended into hell by some other mode unknown to us.

<margin>✠ 10</margin>
10 Those words, *This is my body* etc., which are spoken during the consecration, are held materially and not significatively. <note>Pico is suggesting that in the ritual of the Eucharist, the words perform the change through their utterance as a "material" act rather than simply pointing to a meaning.</note>

11 If the common path is held—that God is reached by an act of the intellect—I state the two following conclusions, the first of which is: those who see the Word by that act through which they reach the divine essence do not reach creatures except eminently and equivalently to formal cognition, an equivalence not of the act, but of the object.

12 The blessed have a twofold knowledge concerning creatures that reaches them formally: one of which is inferred from that by which they reach the Word, and the other according to which they contemplate the creature in the created thing itself.

<margin>✠ 4</margin>
13 I do not agree with the common opinion of theologians saying that God can assume <term>suppositare</term> any nature; rather, I concede this only regarding a rational nature. <note>The term "suppositare" refers to the "hypostatic union," the theological concept of God taking on a nature (like human nature in Christ). Pico argues God could only do this with rational beings, not animals or objects.</note>

<margin>✠ 3</margin>
14 Neither the cross of Christ nor any image is to be adored with the adoration of <term>latria</term>, even in the manner that Thomas posits. <note>"Latria" is the highest form of worship, reserved for God alone. Pico challenges the common view that the Cross, as a symbol of Christ, could receive this same level of worship.</note>

15 If Adam had not sinned, God would still have become incarnate, but he would not have been crucified.

16 In the same light in which John saw the *Apocalypse* <note>The Book of Revelation</note>, in that same light he did not understand the *Apocalypse*.

17 The first sin of the angel was a sin of omission, the second a sin of lust, and the third a sin of pride.

<margin>✠ 2</margin>
18 I say as a probability—and were it not for the common way of speaking among theologians, I would firmly assert the opposite—I assert however that this statement is probable in itself: that just as no one opines that something is exactly so just because they *want* to opine so, likewise no one believes something to be true exactly because they *want* to believe it is true.

->Corollary: It is not in a person's free power to believe an article of faith is true when it pleases them, and to believe it is false when it pleases them.<- <note>This was one of Pico's most controversial statements, suggesting that belief is a matter of the intellect's conviction rather than a choice of the will.</note>

19 Unless there were sayings of the saints which in the plain meaning of their speech seem to say the opposite, I would firmly assert this and the following conclusion; I assert, however, that they are probable and can be rationally defended: the first is that mortal sin is in itself a finite evil.

<margin>✠ 2</margin>
20 The second is that for a mortal sin of a finite time, an infinite punishment in terms of time is not owed, but only a finite one. <note>Pico is questioning the traditional doctrine of eternal damnation in Hell for sins committed during a short human life.</note>

21 Not every "will of God’s good pleasure" is efficacious. <note>Pico distinguishes between God's "will of sign" (what He commands) and His "will of good pleasure" (His internal desire), suggesting that not everything God wishes to happen necessarily comes to pass.</note>

The marginal marks indicate points that were condemned by the Church commission appointed by Pope Innocent VIII.</summary>

# Conclusions.

22 The saying of the Apostle <note>1 Timothy 2:4</note> stating, *God wills all men to be saved* <note>original: "Deus uult omnes homines saluos fieri"</note>, must be understood positively concerning the antecedent will of good pleasure.

23 Antecedent will may be described thus: God's antecedent will is that by which God gives someone natural or preliminary qualities by which they can achieve something, with which God is ready to cooperate if the other wills it, and he will not manifest the opposite to them by a command or counsel of execution, allowing them to act freely toward the pursuit of their own salvation.

24 Holding the common path of theologians—that happiness consists either in the intellect or in the will—I state two conclusions, the first of which is this: That the intellect would not arrive at happiness unless it were by an act of the will, which in this matter is more powerful than the act of the intellect itself.

25 The second conclusion is this: Although the act of the intellect formally touches the essence of the object of happiness, the fact that its act regarding that object is an act of "happiness" is formally derived from the act of the will. <note>Pico is weighing in on a major Medieval debate: whether our ultimate fulfillment comes from knowing God (intellect) or loving God (will).</note>

26 The Persons in the Godhead are distinguished by number.

27 The Personalities in the Godhead are primarily diverse.

28 Speaking theologically, I say that in the *aevum* <note>A Scholastic term for the duration of existence for celestial beings like angels, which sits between human "time" and divine "eternity."</note> there is no formally intrinsic continuous succession, but there is a terminative one; however, following the philosophers, I would speak otherwise.

29 It is more reasonable to believe that Origen is saved <note>original: "Originem esse saluum"</note>, than to believe that he is damned. <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–253) was a hugely influential but controversial Early Church Father. Pico’s defense of Origen's salvation was one of the points specifically condemned by the Church commission.</note>

->Conclusions according to his own opinion, numbering 62, on the doctrine of Plato, of which few are presented here because the first paradoxical conclusion takes the entire doctrine of Plato upon itself for discussion.<-

1 Through the triple numbers, which are placed by Plato in the <term>Timaeus</term> <note>Plato’s famous dialogue regarding the creation of the physical world.</note> in the triangle signifying the soul, we are warned how far we should proceed in the numbering of forms through the nature of that which is the first forming form. Truly, through the double numbers placed in the same location, we are warned how far, once the two extreme terms are placed, the middle terms must be coordinated through the nature of that which is the medium in the universe.

2 When it is asked by Plato whether the world was made according to a generated or ungenerated model, nothing else is asked but whether it was made according to "animal reasons" or intellectual "ideas."

3 Whoever knows the manner of illumination from the higher beings upon the middle ones will understand that the Platonists signify the same thing by the gathering of souls on Mount Ida as the Hebrews signify by the gathering of souls on Mount Sinai at the hearing of the Law. <note>Pico is practicing "syncretism," the attempt to show that different religions and philosophies are actually describing the same divine truths using different symbols.</note>

4 Whoever knows how the nature of a cause presupposes the nature of perfection will understand, according to Platonic doctrine, why <term>Pherecydes</term> <note>An early Greek thinker from the 6th century BCE, often cited as a teacher of Pythagoras.</note> said that Jove <note>The Roman name for the king of the gods, representing the Creator.</note> did not craft the world until he had been transformed into Love.

5 <term>Empedocles</term> <note>A Pre-Socratic philosopher who taught that the universe was moved by the opposing forces of Love and Strife.</note>, by the intelligible sphere contained by Venus, [means] nothing else

<meta>catchword: understand</meta>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s "Platonic Conclusions," a series of theses where he interprets the works of Plato and later Neoplatonists like Syrianus through his own syncretic lens. It follows a discussion on the nature of providence and the archetypal world.</meta>

-># Giovanni Pico della Mirandola<-

...he understands than the <term>archetypal world</term> <note>The world of ideal forms or divine ideas that serves as the blueprint for the physical universe.</note> contained by the order of the first providence remaining within itself.

6 Therefore, Love is said by Orpheus to be without eyes, because he is above the intellect. <note>Pico argues that divine love is "blind" not because it is lesser than sight, but because it transcends the logical distinctions of the intellect.</note>

7 When Plato says in the *Timaeus* that the soul is placed in the middle of the world, whatever other Platonists may say, I understand "the middle" to mean the Moon.

8 Within the scope of finite being, those five "genera" of Plato are correctly placed as transcendents: Being, Sameness, Otherness, Rest, and Motion. <note>Referencing the "Great Kinds" from Plato's *Sophist*.</note>

9 Speaking Platonically about the soul, I say that the soul lives a contemplative life with Saturn, a political and practical life with Jupiter, an irascible and ambitious life with Mars, a concupiscent and pleasurable life with Venus, and a vegetative life with dull sense with Mercury.

10 From the preceding conclusion, you have what the sleep-inducing wand of Mercury is. <note>The caduceus; here interpreted as the power that lulls the higher soul into the "sleep" of bodily, vegetative existence.</note>

11 The first <term>septenary</term> <note>A period of seven years</note> of human life is under Mercury, the second under Venus, the third under Mars, the fourth under Jupiter, the fifth under Saturn, and the remaining seven-year periods according to whichever planet was predominant in the preceding ones.

12 The Sun and Moon cooperate with the aforementioned lives as universal causes; and by appropriation, the Moon with Mercury and Saturn, the Sun with Venus and Mars, and both together with Jupiter.

13 If we follow the theology of Syrianus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonic philosopher who influenced Proclus</note>, it is reasonable that the priests of the <term>ecclesiastical hierarchy</term> <note>The earthly church structure</note> are proportioned to the upward-leading powers in the celestial hierarchy.

14 When we hear Plato calling Pallas <note>Athena</note> and Love "philosopher gods," let us understand it so that Love is a philosopher by reason of the path, and Pallas by reason of the goal.

15 By the logic of extremes and the middle, we can appropriately recognize that the levels of the universe can be divided into five: above being, truly being, not truly being, not truly not-being, and truly not-being.

16 By the terms "the thing itself," "truly such," and "always such," in Plato’s doctrine, we ought to understand the specific properties of the intellect, the soul, and the primary bodies.

17 If we follow the doctrine of Syrianus, it is appropriate, after the unity of total intellection (which is divided three ways: into substantial, potential, and operative), to place a trinity of partial intellection, namely, participated and imaginary.

18 Whatever other Platonists say about the distinction of the parts of the rational soul, I assert that if we <unclear>divide the rational part into three</unclear>, the same part is called "soul" as it is joined to the imagination [phantasy], "mind" as it is joined to the intellect, and "reason" as it relates to itself.

19 It is possible for that part of our rational soul which I call the "possible intellect" (according to the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note>) to reach a point where it discourses and operates without being joined to <term>phantasmata</term> <note>Mental images derived from the senses</note>.

20 Beauty is found more perfectly and truly in <term>intelligibles</term> <note>Things that can only be understood by the mind</note> than in <term>sensibles</term> <note>Things perceived by the five senses</note>.

# Conclusions.

21 When Plato says that Love was born from the union of **Penia** <note>original: "Peniæ"; the personification of Poverty</note> and **Porus** <note>original: "Porii"; the personification of Plenty or Resource</note> in the gardens of Jupiter, during the birth-feast of Venus while the gods were reclining, he means nothing other than that love—which is the desire for beauty—was first born in the **angelic mind** <note>In Neoplatonism, the "Angelic Mind" is the first created intellect, containing the archetypes of all things.</note> when the splendor of the <term>Ideas</term> <note>The eternal, perfect patterns of all things in the divine mind.</note> reflected within it, albeit imperfectly.

22 The Love of which Plato speaks in the *Symposium* can in no way exist in God. <note>Pico argues that because Love implies a desire for something one lacks, the absolute and perfect God cannot "love" in this specific Platonic sense.</note>

23 By the **double Venus** described in Plato’s *Symposium*, we ought to understand nothing other than **double beauty**: the sensible <note>Beauty perceived by the senses</note> and the intelligible <note>Beauty perceived by the intellect</note>.

24 The Love of which Plotinus speaks is not the "celestial love" described by Plato in the *Symposium*, but rather a true and immediate image of it.

25 We shall perfectly resolve the apparent conflict in the sayings of **Orpheus** and **Agathon**—the former saying Love is older than all the gods, the latter saying he is the youngest—if we look to the dual existence of the gods: the intelligible and the natural. <note>original: "Agotonis". Agathon is a character in the *Symposium*. Pico suggests Love is "oldest" as an abstract principle but "youngest" when manifested in the natural world.</note>

26 **Beauty** exists in God through its cause; in the total intellect truly, essentially, and totally; in a particular intellect truly, partially, and essentially; in the rational soul truly and through participation; in the visible accidents of the heavens <note>The stars and celestial movements</note> in an imaginary, essential, and total way; in the visible sub-celestial qualities in an imaginary, partial, and essential way; and in quantities in an imaginary way through participation.

27 When Plato says that everything which comes to be is produced by a cause, this must be referred "of itself" to what is "of itself," and "by accident" to what is "by accident." <note>A logical distinction: primary causes produce primary effects, while incidental causes produce incidental effects.</note>

28 When Plato said in the *Timaeus* that the soul is composed of **indivisible and divisible substance**, he signified the "animate intellect" by the indivisible substance, and "animate reason" by the divisible.

29 In the doctrine of Plato, it is not to be believed that the soul understands anything by looking at the <term>Ideas</term> except when it has reached that state which is the highest level of contemplative perfection.

->**Corollary.** They err who believe, according to Plato, that those things which<-
->we daily know and understand are known in the light of the Ideas.<-

30 The mode of knowing through the Ideas is that of which Plato said in the *Timaeus* "few men are participants, but indeed all the gods."

31 To interpret the **five births** in the fable of the *Critias* as the five forms of the body is entirely inappropriate.

32 By the "other life" mentioned in the *Epinomis*, we ought to understand the connection of the part with its whole; and I believe this is the same as what is called the **neutral age** <note>original: "seculum neutrum"</note> among the **Cabalists**.

33 How it is true—as stated in the *Epinomis*—that the science of **Arithmetic** contributes most to happiness among all the speculative sciences, can be understood through our conclusions on mathematics. <note>Pico viewed numbers as mystical keys to understanding the divine structure of reality.</note>

34 Regarding the "Heaven" in the *Epinomis* which Plato says is the cause of all goods for us: we should understand not the physical fitness of the sky, but Heaven itself as a **celestial animal** <note>In the sense of a living, ensouled being (Latin: *animal*).</note>.

<summary>In these theses, Pico interprets Platonic allegories on Love, Beauty, and the soul’s knowledge, reconciling them with Neoplatonic hierarchy and Kabbalistic concepts. He emphasizes that true knowledge of the "Ideas" is a rare, high contemplative state rather than an everyday occurrence.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Venus, Love, Angelic Mind, Ideas, Timaeus, Epinomis, Beauty, Agathon, Orpheus, Arithmetic, Kabbalah</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s "Platonic Conclusions," specifically focusing on technical interpretations of Plato's dialogues (*Symposium*, *Phaedrus*, *Philebus*) and reconciling them with Aristotelian physics, medieval scholasticism (Thomas Aquinas), and the "natural magic" tradition (Al-Kindi, Roger Bacon).</meta>

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

35 By the "kingdom of necessity" in Plato’s *Symposium*, we should understand nothing other than the superabundance of a different nature over the "nature of the same," and of the infinite over the limit. <note>original: "necessitatis regnum"; Pico is interpreting a passage in the *Symposium* (197b) regarding the rule of Necessity before the reign of Love.</note>

36 Through Plato’s demonstration in the *Phaedrus* regarding the immortality of the soul, immortality is proven and concluded neither for our souls (as Proclus, Hermias, and Syrianus believe), nor for every soul (as Plotinus and Numenius believe), nor for the world-soul alone (as Posidonius believes), but for any celestial soul whatsoever. <note>Pico is debating which "soul" Plato meant when he argued that "that which is always in motion is immortal."</note>

37 Time exists essentially in incorporeal things, and by participation in corporeal things.

38 Where time has its essential being, it exists entirely outside the soul.

39 Time derives its participated being from the soul: from the "first soul" by way of efficient causality, but from the "last soul" by way of objective consequence. <note>Pico distinguishes between how higher cosmic souls create the flow of time and how lower souls experience it as a sequence of events.</note>

40 The motion of the first heaven, and universally any motion—whether of place or of alteration—is measured by time only secondarily and accidentally.

41 Although an intellectual nature understands all things simultaneously, this is not through a virtual and unitive <term>containment</term> <note>original: "continentiam"; the capacity of a higher being to hold the powers of lower beings within itself</note>, but through the mutual penetration of forms and the inseparable communication of the whole participated—that is, formal—being.

42 Through Plato’s demonstration in the *Phaedrus* regarding the immortality of the soul, the eternity of the world is more firmly demonstrated than by any argument of Aristotle in the eighth book of the <term>Physics</term> <note>original: "Physicorum"; Aristotle's foundational work on the study of nature</note>.

43 Just as one human is seen and heard by another through the outward movement of the senses, so a demon is seen and heard by a human or by another demon through the inward movement of the senses.

44 Why a human being cannot help but be seen if they are present before someone with a properly functioning power of sight, while a demon is seen only when it wishes to be seen, can be understood from the manner in which each of them is perceived.

45 The "sense of nature," which Al-Kindi, Bacon, William of Auvergne, and certain others propose—and most especially all the Magi—is nothing other than the "sense of the vehicle" proposed by the Platonists. <note>The "vehicle" (pneuma) was believed by Neoplatonists to be a subtle, astral body that carries the soul; the "sense of nature" refers to a pre-conscious way of perceiving the natural world used in magic.</note>

46 When Plato says that "No one sins except unwillingly," it means nothing other than what Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the influential medieval theologian.</note> holds: namely, that there cannot be <term>sin</term> <note>original: "peccatū"</note> in the will unless there is a defect in the reason.

47 Providence exists "statuitive" <note>law-giving or decreeing</note> in God, "ordinative" <note>ordering</note> in intelligence, "executive" <note>acting out</note> in the soul, "denunciative" <note>announcing</note> in the heavens, and "terminative" <note>finalizing</note> in the whole universe.

48 Not only through the words of Plato in the *Epinomis* and the *Philebus*, in which dialogues Plato expressly places happiness in contemplation, but also through his words in the *Phaedrus* regarding the **amorous frenzy** <note>original: "furore amatorio"; a state of divine inspiration or "madness" described by Plato that elevates the soul.</note>, it is clear that according to Plato, happiness does not consist in the act of love; for frenzy is not happiness, but rather an impulse stirring, urging, and driving one toward happiness.

Pico concludes by arguing that happiness lies in contemplation rather than the impulse of love itself.</summary>

# Conclusions.

49 From that name by which they call the love of God, it is clear to those who pay careful attention that happiness does not consist in the act of love. <note>Pico argues that while love is a path to the divine, the ultimate state of "happiness" or "beatitude" involves a different faculty, likely the intellect or a state beyond action.</note>

50 This proposition in the *Phaedrus*: "Every soul has care for all that is inanimate" <note>original: *Omnis anima totius inanimati curam habet*</note>, is to be understood simply regarding any true soul.

51 From that saying of Plato in the *Phaedrus*, that unless the human soul had glimpsed those things which truly are, it would not have entered into this animal—if it is correctly understood, it will be understood that the opinion of Plotinus, which posits the transmigration of souls into brutes <note>non-human animals</note>, is not according to Plato's mind.

52 From the prayer of Socrates to Pan in the *Phaedrus*, Plato’s complete opinion on happiness is contained. <note>In this prayer, Socrates asks for inward beauty and for outward possessions to be in harmony with the soul.</note>

53 Cratylus's opinion on names is to be understood in this way: not that such *are* names, but that they *ought* to be such if they are to be correct. <note>Refers to the *Cratylus*, a dialogue about whether language is natural or conventional.</note>

54 For this reason, Socrates said in the *Cratylus* that he was "dreaming" about the Ideas, because we do not use the Ideas in this state <note>this earthly life</note>, but rather their closest or secondary images.

55 By "the one" in the *Sophist*, understand "the one in otherness."

56 That saying in the *Sophist*—"he who does not say 'one' says nothing"—is the same as what is said by Aristotle: "he who does not understand 'one' understands nothing."

57 Regarding that saying of Plato in the *Sophist* about images which he says are fashioned by "demonic machination" <note>original: *daemonica Machinatione*</note>: although it can be verified in many other ways, it is nevertheless appropriate to explain it by this: because those images hold a middle degree in being, they are proportioned to the demonic order. <note>In Neoplatonism, "demons" or "daemons" are intermediary spirits between gods and humans; Pico suggests these "images" occupy a similar middle ground in reality.</note>

58 That "hunt" of Socrates, mentioned in the *Protagoras*, can be conveniently described through six steps: the first is the being of external matter; the second is particular immaterial being; the third is universal being; the fourth is rational being; the fifth is particular intellectual being; the sixth is total intellectual being; in the seventh, as if on a Sabbath, one must rest from the hunt.

59 Regarding what is said in the *Euthydemus*—that happiness consists not in a habit but in an act—understand this as referring to a <term>reflexive act</term> <note>original: *actu reflexo*; an act of the mind turning back to contemplate itself or its source.</note>.

60 Through what is said in the *Laches*—that for whatever things there is knowledge, there is not one kind for past things, another for present, and another for future—this can be understood through the common saying among the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> that there is no knowledge except of the universal.

61 Regarding that saying of Plato in the *Gorgias*—"if the orator knows what is just, he is just"—I say this can be upheld absolutely on its own merits and not merely as an argument <term>against the person</term> <note>original: *ad hominem*</note>, if we understand that one follows from the other not formally, but by inference.

62 Although Plato's reasoning in the *Phaedo* via the "way of contraries" does not conclude absolutely, yet when explained by Cebes as an argument <term>against the person</term>, it does conclude something.

2 When Abucaten <note>Pico identifies "Abucaten" (Avempace or Ibn Bajjah) as the author of the influential *Book of Causes*, though modern scholars know it as an anonymous work based on Proclus.</note> says that every noble soul has three operations—divine, intellectual, and animal—it is to be understood that it has the first through the image of proportionality, the second through the formality of participation, and the third through the property of essentiality.

4 Although Abucaten says that Being, which is the first created thing, is above intelligence, you should not believe that it is distinct from intelligence according to its hypostasis <note>original: *hypostasim*; a technical term for the underlying substance or individual reality of a thing</note>.

5 When Abucaten said the first cause is superior to all description, he does not speak the truth so much because of what he first asserts—namely, that it has no cause before itself—as much as because of what he secondarily hints at: because it precedes every intelligible thing unially <note>original: *unialiter*; meaning in a completely unified or singular manner that transcends division</note>.

6 What Abucaten says, that intelligence is a substance that is not divided, is most true because of the indistinct penetration of intelligible things into one another within it.

7 From the preceding conclusion, one can grasp how we should understand the saying of Abucaten: that every intelligence is full of forms.

8 Through the final proposition of Abucaten we can understand what that division means which Plato made at the beginning of the treatise *Timaeus*, and we can know that the soul is not included under it except by way of an extreme combination. <note>The *Timaeus* is Plato's dialogue on the creation of the universe; Pico is linking Arabic Neoplatonism back to Greek foundations.</note>

9 From the third-to-last proposition of Abucaten it can be gathered that to decline more toward the senses than toward the intellect does not belong to the soul insofar as it is a soul, but insofar as it is "falling." <note>This refers to the Neoplatonic idea of the soul "descending" or falling into the material world.</note>

10 When Abucaten says that intelligence, insofar as it is divine, governs things, it is to be understood as a statuative <note>foundational or establishing</note> government, not an ordinative <note>arranging or sequencing</note> one, which belongs to it insofar as it is intelligence.

## Questions to which he promises he will respond through numbers.

1 Whether God exists.
2 Whether He is infinite.
3 Whether He is the cause of all things.
4 Whether He is most simple. <note>In medieval philosophy, "simplicity" means being entirely one, without any parts, components, or divisions.</note>
5 Whether He is intelligent.
<margin>6</margin>
6 How God understands.
7 Whether there is a nature superior to the intellectual nature.
8 Whether the quidditative <note>original: *quiditatiuum*; from *quidditas* or "whatness," meaning the essential nature or definition of a thing.</note> being of a thing is the most inward being that a thing has.
9 What can be predicated of humanity in its most precise abstraction, and what cannot.
10 How the elements are in the heavens.
<margin>t</margin>
11 What method ought to be held in the investigation of each and every knowable thing.
12 Whether above the nature of corporal things there is a rational, incorporeal nature.
13 Whether above the rational nature there is an intellectual nature.
14 Whether between the rational and intellectual nature there is some middle nature.
15 Whether between the intellectual nature and God there is some middle nature.
16 Whether in any nature contradictories are compatible with one another.
17 Whether in any nature contradictories coincide. <note>This refers to the "coincidence of opposites," a major theme in Renaissance philosophy (notably in Nicholas of Cusa), suggesting that in the divine or higher realms, logical contradictions are resolved.</note>

19 What is the number of years naturally owed to the life of a human.
20 How many principal degrees of the natures of the universe there are.
21 Whether corporal nature, as such, is active or only passive.

### Fifteen conclusions according to my own opinion on the understanding of the sayings of Zoroaster and his Chaldean interpreters.

1 What the Chaldean interpreters say regarding the first saying of Zoroaster, concerning the **ladder from the underworld to the first fire**, signifies nothing other than the series of natures in the universe, stretching in grades from the "non-grade" of matter to Him who is above every grade.

2 In the same place, I say that the interpreters understand nothing by "mysterious powers" other than **natural magic**.

3 What the interpreters say regarding the second saying of Zoroaster concerning the **double air, water, and earth**, means nothing else than that every element which can be divided into "pure" and "impure" has both rational and irrational inhabitants; however, that which is purely "pure" has only rational inhabitants.

4 In the same place, by the "roots of the earth," they can understand nothing other than **vegetative life**, consistent with the sayings of **Empedocles**, who posits that the soul can migrate even into plants.

5 From that saying of Zoroaster, *Ha Ha Hos, the earth weeps even for her children*, and following the exposition of Hosia the Chaldean, we have the expressed truth concerning **original sin**.

**6** The sayings of the Chaldean interpreters regarding the 11th aphorism on the dual intoxication of Bacchus and Silenus are perfectly understood through the sayings of the Kabbalists on the dual wine. <note>Pico is synchronizing Greek mythology (Bacchus/Silenus) with Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah), suggesting that the "intoxication" found in both refers to different levels of divine ecstasy or spiritual states.</note>

**7** What the interpreters say regarding the 14th aphorism is perfectly understood through what the Kabbalists say regarding the <term>death of the kiss</term>. <note>The "death of the kiss" (*mors osculi*) is a Kabbalistic concept referring to a mystical death where the soul leaves the body through an ecstatic union with the Divine.</note>

**9** From the preceding conclusion, you can understand something about the "garments of skins" that Adam made for himself, and about the skins that were in the Tabernacle. <note>Pico links the "skins" mentioned in the Chaldean oracles to the "garments of skin" in Genesis 3:21 and the leather coverings of the Hebrew Tabernacle in Exodus.</note>

**10** By "dog," Zoroaster <note>The "Zoroaster" Pico cites refers to the *Chaldean Oracles*, a text of late antiquity that Renaissance scholars believed was written by the ancient Persian sage.</note> means nothing other than the irrational part of the soul and its proportional parts; whoever carefully considers all the sayings of the expositors will see this is so, for they—just like Zoroaster—speak in riddles.

**11** That saying of Zoroaster, "Do not go out when the lictor passes," will be perfectly understood through that passage in Exodus, when the Israelites were prohibited from leaving their houses during the passage of the angel killing the firstborn of the Egyptians. <note>A "lictor" was a Roman officer who cleared the way for magistrates; here, Pico uses it to translate a term from the Oracles, equating it with the destroying angel of the Passover.</note>

**12** By the "Siren" in Zoroaster, you should understand nothing other than the rational part of the soul.

**13** By the "child" mentioned by the interpreters, nothing else is meant but the intellect.

**14** Regarding that saying of Zoroaster, "you shall sacrifice for three days yet, and no more," it appeared to me through the arithmetic of the higher <term>Merkhabah</term> <note>original: *merchiaue*; the Merkhabah, or "Chariot," refers to the highest form of Jewish mystical contemplation regarding the throne of God.</note> that those days of counting expressly predicted the coming of Christ.

**15** What is to be understood by the "goats" in Zoroaster is understood by whoever has read in the *Book of Bahir* what affinity goats and lambs have with spirits. <note>The *Sefer ha-Bahir* (Book of Brightness) is one of the earliest foundational texts of the Kabbalah.</note>

### Magical Conclusions, 26 in number, according to his own opinion.

**1** All Magic currently in use among the Moderns, and which the Church rightly exterminates, has no firmness, no foundation, and no truth, because it depends on the hands of the enemies of the first truth: those powers of darkness which pour the darkness of falsehood over ill-disposed intellects. <note>Pico begins this section by carefully distinguishing his "Natural Magic" from "Goetia" or demonic magic, which he condemns.</note>

**2** Natural Magic is lawful and not prohibited; regarding the universal theoretical foundations of this science, I set down the conclusions written below according to my own opinion.

**3** Magic is the practical part of natural science.

**4** From this conclusion and the 47th paradoxical conclusion, it follows that Magic is the most noble part of natural science.

**5** There is no power in heaven or on earth, whether existing as a seed or separated, which a Magician cannot actuate and unite. <note>Pico suggests that the Magician acts as a "midwife" to nature, bringing latent potential into active reality.</note>

**6** Whatever wonderful work is performed—be it magical, kabbalistic, or of any other kind—it must be referred most principally to God the Glorious.

...glorious and blessed, by whose grace he daily and liberally rains down the super-celestial waters of marvelous virtues upon contemplative men of good will. <note>This sentence fragment completes the thought from the previous page regarding divine grace and the contemplation of the "Chaldean" oracles.</note>

**7** The works of Christ could not have been performed either by way of Magic or by way of Kabbalah. <note>Pico clarifies here that while Magic and Kabbalah explain Christ's divinity, his miracles were not merely "magic tricks" or "kabbalistic operations" in a human sense.</note>

**8** The miracles of Christ are the most certain argument of his divinity, not by reason of the thing done, but by reason of the manner of doing it.

<margin>✾ s</margin>
**9** There is no science that more greatly certifies us of the divinity of Christ than Magic and Kabbalah. <note>This was one of Pico's most famous and dangerous claims. He argues that ancient Jewish and Hermetic wisdom actually supports Christian doctrine better than traditional logic.</note>

**10** What the magician does as a man through art, nature does naturally by making man.

**11** The wonders of the Magician’s art are not performed except through the union and activation of those things which are seminal and separate in nature.

**12** The form of all magic power comes from the soul of man standing, and not falling. <note>The "standing" soul refers to one that is spiritually upright and intellectually active, rather than "fallen" into material desires.</note>

**13** To perform Magic is nothing other than to marry the world. <note>original: "maritare mundum". This is Pico's poetic way of saying the magician unites the celestial influences of heaven with the objects of the earth.</note>

**14** If there is any nature immediate to us which is either simply rational, or rational to a high degree for the sake of well-being, it possesses Magic in the highest degree, and through participation in it, magic can be more perfect in men.

**15** No magical operation can have any efficacy unless it has an annexed work of Kabbalah, whether explicit or implicit.

**16** That nature which is the <term>Horizon of eternal time</term> <note>original: "Orizon temporis aeternalis"</note> is closest to the Magician, but below him.

**17** To that nature which is the <term>Horizon of time and eternity</term> belongs Magic proper; from there it must be sought through the proper methods known to the wise.

**18** To that nature which is the <term>Horizon of temporal eternity</term> is closest to the Magician, but above him; and to it belongs Kabbalah proper. <note>In Pico's Neoplatonic worldview, the "Horizon" represents a boundary or transition point between different levels of the cosmic hierarchy.</note>

**19** The reason voices and words have efficacy in a magical work is that the thing in which nature first exercises magic is the Voice of God.

**20** Any voice has power in Magic insofar as it is formed <gloss>is formed</gloss> by the voice of God.

**21** Non-meaningful voices have more power in Magic than meaningful ones; the reason for this conclusion can be understood by one who is deep, based on the preceding conclusion. <note>Pico is referring to "barbarous names"—incantations that seem like nonsense but were thought to hold primal power because they bypass human language to tap into divine resonance.</note>

**22** No names as signs—and insofar as they are names, taken individually and by themselves—can have power in a magical work unless they are Hebrew, or closely derived from it.

**23** Any number except the <term>ternary</term> <note>the number three</note> and the <term>denary</term> <note>the number ten</note> are material in Magic; these two are formal, and in Magical Arithmetic they are the "numbers of numbers."

**24** From the principles of the most secret philosophy, it is necessary to confess that characters and figures have more power in a magical work than any material quality could.

### *Thirty-one conclusions according to my own opinion on the way to understand the hymns of Orpheus according to Magic, that is, the secret wisdom of divine and natural things first discovered by me in them.*

**1** Just as it is not lawful to explain in public the secret Magic first drawn by us from the hymns of Orpheus, so it will be useful to have demonstrated it through the headings of aphorisms—by a certain hint, as will be done in the conclusions written below—in order to arouse the minds of contemplative men. <note>Pico claims to be the first to uncover a hidden system of "Natural Magic" within the ancient Greek poems attributed to the legendary musician Orpheus.</note>

**2** Nothing is more effective than the hymns of Orpheus in Natural Magic, if the proper music, the intention of the soul, and the other circumstances known to the wise are applied.

**3** The names of the gods sung by Orpheus are not the names of deceiving demons <note>original: "dæmonum"</note>, from whom evil and not good proceeds, but are the names of natural virtues and divine powers distributed throughout the world by the true God, primarily for the benefit of man, if he knows how to use them.

**4** Just as the hymns of David <note>the Psalms</note> wonderfully serve the work of Kabbalah, so the hymns of Orpheus serve the work of truly lawful and Natural Magic.

**5** The number of the hymns of Orpheus is equal to the number with which the Triune God created the world, counted under the form of the Pythagorean quaternary. <note>The "Pythagorean quaternary" or Tetractys refers to the number 4 (1+2+3+4=10). Pico is linking the total number of Orphic hymns to sacred numerology.</note>

**6** However much the property of natural or divine virtues is analogically the same, so too is the name the same, the hymn the same, and the work the same, provided the proportion is maintained; and whoever tries to explain this will see the correspondence.

**7** He who does not know how to perfectly intellectualize <note>to elevate from a physical to a spiritual understanding</note> sensible properties by way of secret analogy will understand nothing sound from the hymns of Orpheus.

**8** He who profoundly and intellectually understands the division of the Unity of Venus into a trinity of Graces, and of the Fatal Unity into a trinity of Fates <note>original: "Parcarum"</note>, and of the Saturnine Unity into a trinity of Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto, will see the proper way to proceed in Orphic theology. <note>Pico is explaining how a single divine "Unity" expresses itself as a "Trinity" of powers in various mythological frameworks.</note>

**9** The *Curetes* in Orpheus are the same as the *Powers* in Dionysius. <note>Pico synchronizes Greek mythology with Christian theology, identifying the Curetes (youthful guardians of Zeus) with the "Powers," one of the nine orders of angels described by Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite.</note>

**10** Let him who attempts the work of the preceding conclusion apply the work of Kabbalah according to what is appropriate to the "Fear of Isaac." <note>In Kabbalah, the "Fear of Isaac" refers to Gevurah (Strength/Judgment), the fifth Sephirah or divine attribute.</note>

**11** He will approach Palamon and Leucothea in vain who has not attracted Nereus; nor will he attract Nereus who has not worked around the primary animal trinity. <note>Pico uses these sea-deities as symbols for levels of natural or psychological forces.</note>

**12** Through the number eight of the maritime hymns, the property of corporeal nature is designated to us.

# Conclusions.

**13** Typhon <note>A monstrous giant in Greek mythology representing chaos</note> in Orpheus is the same as Zamael <note>Samael, often associated with the accuser or the angel of death</note> in the Kabbalah.

**14** If anyone works intellectually in the operation of the preceding conclusion, he will bind the north by the south; but if he works in a worldly manner through the whole, he will work judgment upon himself. <note>Pico is likely referring to the balancing of spiritual "directions" or forces (mercy vs. severity).</note>

**15** Night in Orpheus is the same as the Infinite <note>original: "Ensoph" (Ein Sof), the primordial, unknowable aspect of God</note> in the Kabbalah.

**16** From the preceding conclusion, one can explain more correctly than Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> what that saying of the theologian <note>Orpheus</note> means, which introduces the maker of the world consulting Night concerning the worldly craftsmanship.

**17** From these same sayings, it can be understood why in the *Symposium*, Diotima <note>The woman who teaches Socrates about love in Plato's dialogue</note> calls Poros the "son of Counsel," and Jesus in the sacred scriptures is named the "Angel of Great Counsel."

**18** The watery soul—as it generates lower things, contemplates higher things, and settles within itself—is sung by Orpheus in a triple hymn: of the Sea, of Neptune, and of the Ocean.

**19** No one will have anything firm in their work who has not attracted Vesta <note>Goddess of the hearth and stability</note>.

**20** Through the sevenfold hymns attributed to the Paternal Mind—those of the First-Born <note>original: "Prothogni"</note>, Pallas, Saturn, the lineage of Rhea, and the law of Bacchus—an intelligent and profound contemplator can conjecture something concerning the consummation of the age <note>The end of the world or a cosmic cycle</note>.

**21** There is no work of the preceding hymns without the work of Kabbalah, whose proper function is to put into practice every formal quantity, both continuous and discrete. <note>"Continuous and discrete quantity" refers to the mathematical and mystical study of geometry and numbers.</note>

**22** He who does not divide the Heroes into two types, the native and the adventitious, will often err.

**23** He who approaches Apollo will mediate the work through Bacchus of the Three-Year Festival <note>original: "Trietericum"</note> and will complete it through the ineffable name.

**24** No one will be intoxicated by any Bacchus <note>Dionysian ecstasy</note> who has not first been joined to his own Muse.

**25** Through the fourfold hymns attributed to the first worldly form, the nature of its formable self is designated for us.

**26** He who has perfectly returned into his soul will have equaled his own form to the first form.

**27** He who attempts the work of the preceding conclusion will approach the third Jupiter, as one who is living, not as one who gives life.

**28** In vain does one approach Nature and Proteus <note>The shape-shifting sea god</note> if one has not attracted Pan.

**29** Just as there is a particular animation after universal animation, so after universal providence there is a particular providence.

**30** From the preceding conclusion, it can be known why Ovid, in his curse against the Ibis, after invoking the name that rules the earth and the water, then invokes the Earth and Neptune. <note>Referring to Ovid’s poem *Ibis*, used here to show a sequence from universal to specific powers.</note>
