# Conclusions.

**11** <note>This thesis begins mid-sentence from the previous page</note> ...is not expressed by the Kabbalists, except through the separation of the soul from the body—not the body from the soul except by accident, as happens in the **death of the kiss** <note>original: "mors oſculi"; a Kabbalistic concept of a painless death where the soul leaves the body in a state of divine ecstasy</note>, regarding which it is written: *Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of His saints.* <note>Psalm 116:15</note>

**12** No one can work through pure Kabbalah who is not rationally intellectual.

**13** He who works in Kabbalah without the mixture of anything external—if he remains long in the work, he will die from *binsica* <note>original: "binſica," a Latinization of the Hebrew word for "kiss," referring to the death of the kiss mentioned in thesis 11</note>; and if he errs in the work or approaches it without being purified, he will be devoured by **Azazel** <note>In this context, a demonic force or the power of strict judgment</note> through the property of judgment.

**14** By the letter **Shin** <note>original: "Scin," the Hebrew letter ש</note>, which mediates <note>sits in the middle</note> in the name of **Jesus**, it is signified to us Kabbalistically that the world then rested perfectly, as if in its own perfection, when **Yod** was joined with **Vav**—which was achieved in Christ, who was the true Son of God and man. <note>Pico's famous argument that by inserting the letter Shin (representing the Word or Fire) into the four-letter Name of God, Y-H-V-H, it becomes the name of Jesus, Y-H-Sh-V-H.</note>

**15** Through the name **Yod, He, Vav, He** <note>the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter holy name of God</note>, which is the ineffable name that the Kabbalists say will be the name of the **Messiah**, it is clearly known that he will be God, the Son of God, made man through the Holy Spirit, and that after him, for the perfection of the human race, the **Paraclete** <note>The Holy Spirit as "Advocate" or "Comforter"</note> would descend upon men.

**16** From the mystery of the three letters in the word **Shabbat** <note>original: "Sciabat," the Sabbath</note>, we can interpret Kabbalistically that the world "Sabbathized" <note>reached its rest</note> when the Son of God became man, and that the ultimate future Sabbath will occur when men are regenerated in the Son of God.

**17** He who knows what the **purest wine** is among the Kabbalists will know why David said: *I shall be inebriated from the richness of Your house* <note>Psalm 36:8</note>; and what kind of drunkenness the ancient poet **Musaeus** <note>A legendary pre-Homeric Greek poet</note> said was happiness; and what the many **Bacchuses** signify in the works of **Orpheus**. <note>Pico is linking Jewish mysticism with Greek "pagan" mysteries, suggesting they all point to the same spiritual intoxication or divine ecstasy.</note>

**18** He who joins **Astrology** to Kabbalah will see that "Sabbathizing" <note>keeping the day of rest</note> and resting is more fitting after Christ on the **Lord’s Day** <note>Sunday</note> than on the day of the Sabbath <note>Saturday</note>.

**19** If we explain Kabbalistically that saying of the prophet, *They sold the righteous for silver*, it signifies nothing else to us than this: namely, that God the Redeemer was sold for silver. <note>Referencing the betrayal of Jesus for thirty pieces of silver as a fulfillment of Amos 2:6.</note>

**20** If the Kabbalists turn their interpretation to this word <note>the Hebrew word "Az" (אז)</note> which signifies **"then,"** they will be greatly illuminated regarding the mystery of the **Trinity**.

**21** He who joins the saying of the Kabbalists—who say that the numeration <note>Sephirah</note> called "the righteous" and "the redeemer" is also called **Ze** <note>Hebrew for "This" (זה)</note>—with the saying of the Talmudists—who say that **Isaac** went like *Ze* carrying his own cross—will see that what was prefigured in Isaac was fulfilled in Christ, who was the true God sold for silver. <note>Pico connects the "wood" Isaac carried for his own sacrifice (Genesis 22) to the Cross of Christ.</note>

**22** Through the sayings of the Kabbalists regarding the **redness of Esau**, and that saying found in the book **Bereshit Rabbah** <note>original: "Breſit Rhaba"; an ancient Jewish midrashic commentary on Genesis</note> that "Esau was red, and the Red One shall avenge him"—concerning whom it is said, *Why is your garment red?*—it is expressly held that Christ (concerning whom our doctors explain that same text) will be the one who takes vengeance on the unclean powers. <note>Pico identifies the "Red One" of Jewish prophecy with the blood-stained Christ of the Passion and the vengeful Christ of the Apocalypse.</note>

### Conclusions.

**35** If God is understood in himself as the infinite, as the One, and according to himself, we understand nothing to proceed from him. Instead, we understand a separation from all things, a total enclosure of himself within himself, and a profound and solitary withdrawal in the most remote recess of his divinity. We understand him as covering himself most inwardly in the abyss of his own darkness, in no way manifesting himself in the expansion and pouring out of his goodness and fountain-like splendor. <note>Pico is describing the "Ein Sof" (the Infinite), the state of God before the creation of the Sephirot or the universe, where God is hidden and undifferentiated.</note>

**36** From the preceding conclusion, it can be understood why it is said among the Kabbalists that God clothed himself in ten garments when he created the world. <note>These "ten garments" refer to the ten Sephirot, the divine attributes or emanations through which God acts in the world.</note>

**37** Whoever understands, in the coordination of the right side, the subordination of mercy to wisdom, will perfectly understand through the way of Kabbalah how Abraham in his day, through a straight line, saw the day of Christ and rejoiced. <note>Pico refers to John 8:56. In Kabbalah, the "right side" represents the pillar of Mercy (Chesed), which Pico associates with the Patriarch Abraham.</note>

**38** The effects that followed after the death of Christ ought to convince any Kabbalist that Jesus of Nazareth was the true Messiah.

**39** From this conclusion and the thirtieth one placed above, it follows that any Kabbalist must concede that when Jesus was asked who he was, he responded most correctly saying: "I am the beginning who speaks to you." <note>Pico is citing the Latin Vulgate translation of John 8:25 (Ego sum principium qui et loquor vobis).</note>

**40** The Kabbalists must inevitably concede that the true Messiah will purify men through water.

**41** It can be known in Kabbalah through the mystery of the <term>closed Mem</term> <note>original: "Mem clausum"; the Hebrew letter Mem normally has an open form (מ) and a closed form used at the end of words (ם). **42** It is known through the foundations of Kabbalah how rightly Jesus said: "Before Abraham was born, I am." <note>A reference to John 8:58.</note>

**43** Through the mystery of the two letters <term>Vau</term> and <term>Yod</term> <note>V (ו) and Y (י), the middle and first letters of the Divine Name YHWH</note>, it is known how the Messiah himself, as God, was the principle of himself as man.

**44** It is known from Kabbalah, through the mystery of the northern part, why God will judge the world by fire. <note>In Kabbalistic thought, the North (Zaphon) is associated with the attribute of Gevurah (Strength/Judgment) and the element of fire.</note>

**45** It is known most clearly in Kabbalah why the Son of God came with the water of baptism, and the Holy Spirit with fire.

**46** Through the eclipse of the Sun which happened at the death of Christ, it can be known according to the foundations of Kabbalah that then the Son of God and true Messiah suffered.

**47** Whoever knows the property of the North in Kabbalah will know why Satan promised Christ the kingdoms of the world if he would fall down and worship him. <note>The "North" or "Aquilo" was traditionally viewed as the seat of evil or the dwelling of Lucifer.</note>

For example, the Sun corresponds to Tiferet (the 6th Sephirah).</note>

# Conclusions

...to come from the ninefold group of nine numerations, which are below the first, which is the inaccessible abyss of the divinity. <note>This completes a sentence from the previous page regarding the emanations of the divine.</note>

**63** Just as Aristotle masked the more divine philosophy (which the ancient philosophers veiled under fables and allegories) under the appearance of philosophical speculation and obscured it with a brevity of words, so Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>The philosopher Maimonides (1138–1204)</note> in the book which is called by the Latins *The Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: "dux neutrorum"</note>, while appearing to walk with the philosophers through the superficial bark of his words, encompasses the mysteries of the <term>Kabbalah</term> <note>Jewish mystical tradition</note> through the hidden understandings of a deep sense.

**64** In the text, "Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one," <note>The Shema, Deuteronomy 6:4</note> it is more correct to understand a gathering from the lower to the higher, and from the higher to the lower, than a gathering from the lower to the higher twice.

**65** It is more correct that "Amen" signifies <term>Tiferet</term> <note>The Sephirah of "Beauty" or "Balance," associated with the heart and the sun</note> and the Kingdom <note>The Sephirah Malkhut, the lowest emanation representing the physical world</note>, as is shown through the way of number, than that it signifies the Kingdom alone, as some wish.

**66** I adapt our soul to the ten <term>Sephirot</term> <note>The ten emanations of God in Kabbalistic thought</note> in this way: through its unity it is with the first, through intellect with the second, through reason with the third, through the higher concupiscible <note>The faculty of desire or love</note> with the fourth, through the higher irascible <note>The faculty of spiritedness or righteous anger</note> with the fifth, through free will with the sixth; and through all this, as it turns toward higher things with the seventh, toward lower things with the eighth, and a mixture of both—rather through indifference or alternating attachment than simultaneous containment—with the ninth, and through the power by which it inhabits the first dwelling place, with the tenth.

**67** Through the saying of the <term>Kabbalists</term> that the Heavens are made of fire and water, he manifests to us both the theological truth concerning the <term>Sephirot</term> themselves, and the philosophical truth that the elements are in heaven only according to their active power.

**68** Whoever knows what the <term>denarius</term> <note>The number ten</note> is in formal arithmetic, and has known the nature of the first spherical number <note>A number whose powers end in the same digit, like 5 or 6; here used mystically</note>, will know that which I have not yet read in any Kabbalist, which is the foundation of the secret of the great <term>Jubilee</term> in the Kabbalah.

**69** From the foundation of the preceding conclusion, one can likewise know the secret of the fifty gates of understanding, and of the thousandth generation, and of the kingdom of all ages.

**70** Through the method of reading without points <note>Hebrew is written without vowels ("points"); Kabbalists believed the unvoweled Torah contained infinite meanings</note> in the Law, both the method of writing divine things and the unified containment through the indeterminate circuit of divine things are shown to us.

**71** Through what the Kabbalists say about Egypt, and as experience has attested, we must believe that the land of Egypt exists in an analogy and subordination of the property of power.

**72** Just as true <term>Astrology</term> teaches us to read in the book of God <note>The book of Nature/the Cosmos</note>, so Kabbalah teaches us to read in the book of the Law <note>The Torah</note>.

->THE END OF THE NINE HUNDRED CONCLUSIONS OF<-
->GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA.<-

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA TO LORENZO DE' MEDICI.

I have dedicated my **Apology** to you, Lorenzo de' Medici, as a matter which—I call God to witness—did not seem to me quite worthy of so great a man, but which is owed to you by that same right by which I realize I have long since owed you everything of mine. For you should be most fully persuaded that whatever I am, or am to be, is yours, Lorenzo, and shall always be so in the future. I say less than I would wish, and these words are altogether too cold to sufficiently express what I conceive—that is, with what love, what loyalty, and what respect I both honor you now and have honored you for many years. I am moved both by the many kindnesses you have bestowed upon me, which clearly testify to your most loving spirit, and by those same rare goods of yours—nay, goods peculiar to you—not so much of fortune as of the mind, which your own modesty does not permit me to recount at present.

I return to the *Apology*, which I pray you receive with a cheerful countenance. It is a small gift indeed, but truly a significant testimony of my loyalty and respect toward you for all time. If it should happen that you find a moment to touch upon this while resting from the great affairs with which you are always occupied, remember that this work was not so much a matter of choice as of necessity. The argument of the work had to be taken up by me based on the judgment of others rather than my own <note>Pico is explaining that he wrote this defense because his "900 Theses" were being investigated for heresy, not because he simply wished to write another book</note>. I have not addressed it to you so that you might recognize in me any excellence of talent or learning (which is not in me), but so that you may know (for I shall say it again) that I, whatever I am, am most devoted to your greatness.

# THE APOLOGY OF GIOVANNI PICO
## Count of Mirandola and Concordia.

When I had recently come to Rome to kiss the feet of the Supreme Pontiff Innocent VIII <note>Pope Innocent VIII, reigned 1484–1492</note>—whose name is most well-deserved due to the innocence of his life—according to custom, I did so that I might not depart from my usual practice of always composing or treating something regarding literary matters. I wished to perform a task to the best of my abilities that was worthy of the city of Rome, a grace to the Christian Prince <note>Referring to the Pope</note>, and useful to myself and to scholars. I proposed **nine hundred questions** concerning divine and natural matters, to which I was prepared to respond in a public assembly of the most learned men.

Hardly had they appeared in public when, among some who might have approved of at least my zeal for the liberal arts (if not my talent or learning), a manifold crowd of detractors arose. And although one could see the various distastes, the turned-up noses <note>original: "nasos" - a Latin idiom for sneering or scorn</note>, the censures, and altogether the differing judgments of every individual (as always happens when we attempt something new and non-trivial), there were roughly five principal objections which those whisperers <note>original: "summuffores," likely a variant of "susurrones," meaning those who mutter in secret</note> condemned in me. Some argued that philosophy and letters should be entirely shunned, even adding—so that they might seem like <term>pseudo-intellectuals</term> <note>original: "scioli" - those with a superficial or smattering of knowledge</note>—that Adam was cast out of Paradise because he wished to make himself equal to the gods through the knowledge of good and evil. To be banished...

# Apology.

->**K 4**<-

By a similar example, from the court of Christ, there are those who wish to know more than is proper. Others bark against not so much philosophy itself as this very manner of disputation and this custom of publicly debating letters, claiming it is for the display of talent and the ostentation of learning rather than for the acquisition of knowledge. Some call me bold and reckless—one who at this age, not yet twenty-four years old, did not hesitate to propose a disputation on the highest points of philosophy, the sublime mysteries of Christian theology, and unknown disciplines, in the most celebrated city <note>Rome</note> and in an ample assembly of the most learned men. Many accuse me not so much because it was in Rome or because I was a youth, but because I was to dispute about so great a number—that is, nine hundred questions—slandering it as a superfluous and ambitious act, and one beyond my strength. 

Of those, however, who profess the study of wisdom (that is, the study of Theology), there were some who, perhaps not content with lighter insults, no longer called me bold, reckless, or boastful, but proclaimed me a magician, an impious man, and a new leader of heresy <term>Heresiarch</term> <note>A founder of a heretical sect or a leader of heretics</note> in Christ’s church. 

I was for a long time (God is my witness) of a doubtful mind whether I should wash away these objections or rather pass them over in silence. Two things especially moved me to keep silent. First, because I, abhorring both contention and quarrels, have always loved peace of mind and the tranquility of a very quiet life which my studies provided me; nor have I ever hated any writing task more than one consisting of dispute and bitter altercation in any form. Indeed, I have never considered it the mark of a good man or a philosopher to either return or inflict an injury or insult. The second reason was this: that, being content with the judgment of the Supreme Pontiff <note>Pope Innocent VIII</note>—whose memory I must deservedly celebrate always—and of many in the most holy apostolic senate, whose kindness and most benevolent spirit toward me I can or should never forget, I seemed easily able to disregard both the hatred and the insults of wicked men. Indeed, regarding all other matters, I was of the opinion that I should judge those men unworthy of ever receiving a response. 

But regarding the one charge of heresy leveled against me, I feared that if I did this <note>remained silent</note>, I might seem to admit the crime by not refuting it. Moreover, **Ruffinus** <note>Tyrannius Rufinus, a 4th-century monk and theologian</note> writes most wisely: *“It is indeed glorious, after Christ's example, to endure injuries patiently; but he who bears or ignores a single mark of heresy is not a Christian.”* And our **Jerome** <note>St. Jerome, the scholar who translated the Bible into the Latin Vulgate</note>, with the greatest possible effort of mind, cries out with a clear voice: *“I do not want anyone to be patient under suspicion of heresy.”* 

Jerome, therefore, does not want me to be silent; he draws and drives an unwilling and idle man to write by all the authority he can. Therefore, if there are any who perhaps wish I would remain silent, let them know they have a controversy not with me, but with Jerome, who does not want me to keep silent. Who can fail to listen to Jerome without disgrace? Thus, at his persuasion—indeed, even his compulsion—I have undertaken a brief... <note>original: "ag..." completed by the catchword "gressus" on the next page, forming "aggressus," meaning "having undertaken"</note>

...I have proceeded to write this apology, not to tear down or accuse anyone, but to rightfully excuse myself from the greatest crime—that of impiety—which has been unjustly charged against me. This, I pray, my detractors may endure with the same spirit with which I have always endured their unfair offense. Let them permit, I say, that I—who was born a Christian of Christian parents, who bear the banner of Jesus Christ on my forehead, and who would willingly die for the faith of Christ—might exclaim with a voice like Paul’s, while they listen with an even mind: "I am no magician, no Jew, no Ishmaelite <note>original: "Ismaëlita"; historically used to refer to Muslims or those outside the Christian faith</note>, no heretic, but I worship Jesus, and I carry the cross of Jesus in my body, through whom the world is crucified to me, and I to the world." Finally, while I do not claim for myself, nor take away from others, titles of holiness, wisdom, or other such excellent labels, I ask that they do not take away this one thing—the defense of which I would even shed my blood: namely, that I may call myself a Christian.

If they grant me this, I do not write to them, for I have already obtained from them what our entire apology strives for. I write to others who believe or suspect me to be, or to have once been, a heretic. Although my principal purpose is to show that it is not I, but those who slander me as a heretic, who deviate from the orthodox and Catholic path; nevertheless, since I must write, we shall also say something about those things which were first objected against us, so that our detractors cannot abuse my silence as if it were a conscience of guilt.

Now, what many first found fault with was this: my very act of philosophizing. To them, I shall offer no response in this place, because it is my intention to defend the cause of philosophy separately in a specific work; and altogether, if it is shameful to devote oneself to letters and to cultivate the fine arts and disciplines, I would rather acknowledge this "fault" than beg for forgiveness. To those, also, who detest this manner of disputing and this practice of publicly debating about God, nature, and morals, I will not say much, since this crime (if it is a crime) is shared by me with great men—indeed, with the most approved philosophers of almost every age. It was a certainty to them that nothing was more useful for achieving the knowledge of truth they sought than to be frequently engaged in the exercise of disputation. 

Just as physical strength is made firmer through gymnastics, so in this literary wrestling ground <term>palaestra</term> <note>original: "palestra"; an ancient Greek or Roman wrestling school, used here as a metaphor for the intellectual arena</note>, the powers of the mind emerge far stronger and more vigorous. Nor would I believe that the Poets meant anything else by the "well-known arms of Pallas" <note>Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom, often depicted with a helmet, shield, and spear</note>, or the Hebrews when they say that "iron" is the symbol of the wise, than that these most honorable contests of this kind are absolutely necessary for attaining wisdom. Perhaps this is why the Chaldeans <note>Ancient Babylonian sages and astrologers</note> require in the horoscope <term>genesis</term> of one who is to be a philosopher that Mars should look upon Mercury with a trine aspect <note>An astrological alignment where planets are 120 degrees apart, suggesting a harmonious blend of Mars's drive/conflict and Mercury's intellect</note>, as if all philosophy would be sleepy and drowsy if you took away these encounters, these "wars." 

But as for these things, as I said, I prefer to defend myself with the authorities and precedents of great men rather than with arguments. It seems a greater task to satisfy those who—by their age, talent, and learning—are impa- <note>The word is cut off by the page break; likely "impatient" or "unmoved"</note>

<header>Defense.</header>

# Defense.

They say I am unequal to so great a responsibility, and that I have not, according to Horace, consulted "what my shoulders can bear and what they refuse." <note>A reference to Horace’s *Ars Poetica*, advising authors to choose subjects within their capabilities.</note> Truly, this is a difficult line of defense for me; for if I say I am equal to it, I seem immodest and full of myself, but if I admit I am unequal, I appear to undergo the mark of being reckless and ill-advised. I have fallen into grave difficulties, as I cannot promise what I cannot do without fault, nor fail to perform it without fault. And indeed, I could cite Job: "The spirit is in all people." <note>Job 32:8</note> And perhaps hear with Timothy: "Let no one despise your youth." <note>1 Timothy 4:12</note> But from my own conscience, I will say more truly that there is nothing great or singular in me. I do not deny that I am perhaps studious and eager for the noble arts, yet I neither claim nor arrogate the title of a "learned man" for myself. For as my friend Hermolaus <note>Hermolao Barbaro (1454–1493), a prominent Venetian humanist and scholar.</note> once wrote—that delight of the Roman tongue, the splendor and glory of our age—no one can fail to be unlearned who believes himself to be learned. 

Therefore, that I have placed such a great burden on my shoulders was not because I was unaware of my own weakness, but because I knew that in this kind of battle—that is, literary ones—it is a unique feature that "to be defeated is a gain." In these contests, even the weakest person not only can but should rightfully seek them out; for he who succumbs receives a benefit from the victor, not an injury. Indeed, he returns home wealthier (that is, more learned) and better prepared for future battles. Encouraged by this hope, I, a weak soldier, did not fear to decide on such a heavy battle with the strongest and most vigorous of all. Whether this was done rashly or not, one could certainly judge more rightly by the outcome of the battle than by my age.

It remains for me to answer those who are offended by the large number of things proposed, as if this burden rested on their shoulders and not rather on mine alone, where the entirety of the labor must be exhausted. It is truly indecent and overly peevish to wish to set a limit on another's industry and, as Cicero says, to desire "mediocrity" <note>Cicero often argued that in intellectual pursuits, excellence is preferable to a middle path.</note> in a matter that is better the greater it is. In such grand undertakings, it was necessary for me either to fail or to satisfy the requirement. If I satisfied it, I do not see why what is praiseworthy to perform in ten questions should be considered blameworthy to have performed in nine hundred. If I failed, they would have reason to accuse me if they hate me, or reason to excuse me if they love me; for in a matter so grave and so great, a young man of thin wit and meager learning failing should be worthy of pardon rather than accusation. Indeed, according to the Poet <note>A reference to Ovid or Propertius, common in humanist writing.</note>: "If strength fails, the daring is certainly praise," and "In great things, even to have willed is enough." 

But if in our own age many have been accustomed to imitate Gorgias of Leontini <note>A Greek Sophist famous for claiming he could speak on any subject offered to him.</note>—proposing to dispute not just about nine hundred things, but about all questions of all arts, and not without praise—why should I not be allowed, even without fault, to dispute about many things indeed, but things that are fixed and determined? But they say this is "superfluous" and "ambitious." I, however, contend that this was done by me not only in a non-superfluous way, but out of necessity. If they would consider my method of philosophizing, they would be forced to admit this, even against their will. For those who have devoted themselves to one of the families of philosophers—namely to Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas.</note> or Scotus <note>Duns Scotus.</note> (who are now most...

[in hand] favoring [me], they might indeed put their own learning to the test in the discussion of only a few questions. But I have so resolved myself that, **sworn to the words of no single master**, I might range through all the masters of philosophy, examine every page, and recognize every school of thought. Therefore, since I had to speak about all of them—lest, if I were the defender of a private dogma and had neglected the rest, I should seem bound to it—it was impossible (even if a few points from each were proposed) that there would not be very many points which were asserted about all of them at once. Nor should anyone condemn me for this, that **"Wherever the storm carries me, there I am driven as a guest."** <note>original: "Quocunque ferat tempestas, deferar hospes." A quote from Horace’s Epistles, emphasizing intellectual independence.</note>

For this was observed by all the ancients: that in unfolding every kind of writing, they passed over no commentaries without reading them and drawing from them what they could. This was especially true of Aristotle, who for that reason was called by Plato the **"Reader"** <note>original: "ἀναγνώστης" (*anagnostes*). Plato reportedly gave Aristotle this nickname because of his voracious appetite for books.</note>. And surely it is a mark of a narrow mind to have confined oneself within a single Porch <note>referring to the "Stoa" or Stoic school of philosophy</note> or a single Academy. Nor can anyone rightly select a path for themselves from among all the schools who has not first become familiarly acquainted with them all.

Furthermore, in every school there is something distinctive that is not shared with the others. And to begin now with our own thinkers—to whom philosophy last arrived—there is in **John Duns Scotus** something vigorous and analytical; in **Thomas Aquinas**, something solid and balanced; in **Giles of Rome**, something polished and precise; in **Francis of Meyronnes**, something sharp and keen; in **Albert the Great**, something ancient, ample, and grand; and in **Henry of Ghent** (as it has seemed to me), something always sublime and venerable. Among the Arabs, there is in **Averroes** something firm and unshakeable; in **Avempace** and **Al-Farabi**, something heavy and meditative; in **Avicenna**, something divine and Platonic. Among the Greeks, philosophy is generally clear and especially pure: in **Simplicius**, it is rich and abundant; in **Themistius**, elegant and concise; in **Alexander of Aphrodisias**, consistent and learned; in **Theophrastus**, seriously elaborated; and in **Ammonius**, smooth and pleasing.

And if you turn to the Platonists (to review a few), you will be delighted by the abundance of matter and the manifold religious devotion in **Porphyry**; in **Iamblichus**, you will venerate a more secret philosophy and the mysteries of the "barbarians" <note>Referring to the ancient wisdom traditions of the Egyptians and Chaldeans.</note>; in **Plotinus**, there is no single thing to admire, for he makes himself admirable in all things—speaking of divine things divinely and of human things far above the human level with a learned complexity of speech, which the persuasive Platonists themselves can hardly understand. I pass over the more recent ones: **Proclus**, luxuriating in his Asiatic fertility, and those who flowed from him—**Hermias**, **Damascius**, **Olympiodorus**, and several others—in all of whom that **"divine"** quality <note>original: "θειόν" (*theion*)</note>, the peculiar symbol of the Platonists, always shines forth.

Furthermore, if there is any sect that attacks truer dogmas and mocks good causes with the slander of its wit, it strengthens the truth rather than weakens it; like a flame shaken by movement, it rouses it rather than extinguishing it. Moved by this reasoning, I wished to bring forward the opinions not of just one school (as some would have liked), but of every kind of doctrine, so that by this comparison of many sects and this discussion of multifaceted philosophy, that **flash of truth** (which Plato mentions in his letters) might [shine forth] in our minds like a rising sun...

<header>Apology.</header>

# Apology.

...from on high, it might shine more brightly. What would it be if only the philosophy of the Latins—namely **Albert, Thomas, Scotus, Giles, Francis, and Henry** <note>These are the giants of medieval Scholasticism: Albert the Great, Thomas Aquinas, Duns Scotus, Giles of Rome, Francis of Mayrone, and Henry of Ghent.</note>—were treated, while the philosophers of the **Greeks and Arabs** were omitted, when all wisdom flowed from the barbarians to the Greeks, and from the Greeks to us? In this way, our fellow countrymen have always thought it sufficient, in their method of philosophizing, to rely on foreign discoveries and to cultivate the inventions of others. What would it be to have dealt with the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note> regarding natural things, unless the **Academy of the Platonists** was also summoned? Their doctrine, concerning divine matters, has always been held as the holiest among all philosophies (according to the testimony of **Augustine**); and now by me, for the first time as far as I know (may these words be free from envy), it has been brought forth into the public light for the test of debate after many centuries. What would it be to have treated the opinions of however many others there were, if, as if approaching a banquet of the wise without a contribution, we brought nothing of our own—nothing produced and worked out by our own talent? 

Truly, it is the mark of a narrow mind, as **Seneca** says, to know only from a commentary—as if the discoveries of our ancestors had closed off the path for our own industry, or as if the power of nature were exhausted in us, producing nothing from itself that might, if not demonstrate the truth, at least point to it from afar. For if a farmer hates sterility in his field, and a husband in his wife, surely the divine mind joined and associated with the soul will hate an unfertile soul all the more, since a far nobler offspring is desired from it. Therefore, not content with the common doctrines, I have added many things from the ancient theology of **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>original: "Mercurij Trimegiſti." A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a body of esoteric writings known as the Hermetica.</note>, many from the teachings of the **Chaldeans** and of **Pythagoras**, and many from the more secret mysteries of the **Hebrews** <note>This refers to the Kabbalah, which Pico was the first Christian scholar to promote as a tool for theology.</note>. I have also proposed for debate many things discovered and meditated upon by us concerning natural and divine matters. 

We have proposed, first, the **harmony of Plato and Aristotle**, believed in by many before this, but sufficiently proven by no one. **Boethius** <note>A 6th-century Roman philosopher who planned to translate and reconcile all of Plato and Aristotle but was executed before finishing.</note> among the Latins promised he would do this, but he is not found to have ever done what he always wished to do. **Simplicius** among the Greeks professed the same; would that he had fulfilled it as well as he promised! **Augustine** also writes in the *Against the Academics* that there were several who tried to prove the same thing with their very subtle discussions: namely, that the philosophy of Plato and Aristotle is the same. **John the Grammarian** <note>Also known as John Philoponus, a 6th-century commentator on Aristotle.</note> likewise says that Plato and Aristotle differ only among those who do not understand Plato's sayings, yet he left the proof of this to posterity. 

We have also added several points in which we assert that many opinions of **Scotus and Thomas**, and many of **Averroes and Avicenna** <note>The two most influential Islamic philosophers in the Latin West; Averroes was known as "The Commentator" on Aristotle.</note>, which are thought to be discordant, are actually in agreement. In the second place, we have set out seventy-two new dogmas in both physics and metaphysics which we ourselves have thought out. If someone holds these, they will be able, unless I am mistaken, to resolve any question proposed concerning natural and divine things by a far different reasoning than through that philosophy which is read in the schools and cultivated by the doctors of this age. Nor should anyone marvel that I, in my first years, in a tender age at which it was scarcely permitted (as some boast) to read the commentaries of others, wished to bring forth a new...

<page-num>120</page-num>
<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>
<meta>Catchword: [honored],</meta>

...to bring forward philosophy, rather than to either praise it if it is defended, or condemn it if it is rejected. Finally, since they are to judge these discoveries of ours and our writings, they should count not the years of the author, but rather their merits or demerits. 

There is also, besides that other philosophy, another new method of philosophizing through numbers which we have brought forward. It is indeed ancient, and was observed by the early Theologians—especially by **Pythagoras**, by **Aglaophemus**, by **Philolaus**, by **Plato**, and the earlier **Platonists**—but in this age, like other excellent things, it has so faded away through the negligence of those who followed that hardly any traces of it are found. 

**Plato** writes in the *Epinomis* <note>original: "Epimenide"; Pico likely refers to the *Epinomis*, a dialogue attributed to Plato that discusses the divine nature of mathematics.</note> that among all the liberal arts and contemplative sciences, the science of numbering is the foremost and most divine. Seeking likewise, "Why is man the wisest animal?" he responds, "Because he knows how to count." **Aristotle** also mentions this opinion in his *Problems*. **Abunasar** <note>The influential Persian philosopher Al-Farabi (c. 872–950).</note> writes that it was a saying of **Avenzoar the Babylonian** that "He knew all things who knew how to count." 

These things can in no way be true if, by the "art of numbering," they understood that art in which merchants today are primarily most skilled. **Plato** himself testifies to this, warning us with an uplifted voice that we should not understand this divine arithmetic to be the same as the arithmetic of merchants. Having explored this divine arithmetic (which is so highly extolled) through many sleepless nights, I have promised that I will publicly answer seventy-four questions, which are considered primary among physical and divine matters, through the use of numbers.

We have also proposed magical theorems, in which we indicate that **Magic** is twofold. One of these consists entirely of the work and authority of demons; this is, by my faith, a monstrous and cursed thing. The other is nothing else, when well-examined, than the absolute perfection of natural philosophy. When the Greeks mention both, they in no way deem the former worthy of the name of magic, calling it *goeteia* <note>original: γοητείαν; this refers to sorcery, witchcraft, or "low" magic involving spirits.</note>, while they call the latter by its own peculiar name, *mageia* <note>original: μαγείαν; derived from the Persian *magus*, implying the "high" wisdom of the priest-scientists.</note>, as if it were a perfect and supreme science. For as **Porphyry** says, in the language of the Persians, "Magus" means the same as what "interpreter and worshiper of divine things" means among us. 

There is, however, a great—indeed the greatest—disparity and dissimilarity between these arts. The former is condemned and cursed not only by the Christian religion, but by all laws and every well-ordered commonwealth. The latter, all wise men and all nations studious of celestial and divine things approve and embrace. The former is the most fraudulent of arts; the latter is a higher and holier philosophy. The former is useless and vain; the latter is firm, faithful, and solid. Whoever cultivated the former always concealed it, because it would bring shame and disgrace to the author; but from the latter, the highest literary renown and glory has been sought since ancient times, and almost always. No man who was a philosopher and eager for learning good arts was ever a student of the former; but to learn the latter, **Pythagoras, Empedocles, Democritus, and Plato** traveled across the sea. They preached it upon their return, and held it as primary among their secrets. As the former is supported by no reasons and no reliable authors, so the latter is honored by the most illustrious parents, as it were...

<page-num>121</page-num>
<header>Apologia.</header>
<sig>L</sig>

[Magic], being established, has two primary authors: *Zamolxis* <note>A legendary social and religious reformer of the Getae people, often associated with the teaching of the immortality of the soul.</note>, whom *Abaris the Hyperborean* imitated, and *Zoroaster*—not the one perhaps commonly believed, but that son of *Oromases*. If we ask *Plato* what each type of magic is, he will answer in the *Alcibiades* that the magic of *Zoroaster* is nothing other than the science of divine things, in which the sons of Persian kings were educated so that they might be taught to rule their own commonwealth according to the model of the commonwealth of the universe. He will answer in the *Charmides* that the magic of *Zamolxis* is the medicine of the soul, through which temperance is acquired for the soul, just as through medicine health is acquired for the body. 

In their footsteps later followed *Charondas*, *Damigeron*, *Apollonius*, *Hostanes*, and *Dardanus*. *Homer* followed them too; we will eventually prove in our *Poetic Theology* <note>A projected work by Pico that was never completed or has been lost, where he intended to explain the hidden philosophical meanings in ancient myths.</note> that he disguised this wisdom, as he did all other types of wisdom, under the wanderings of his *Ulysses*. *Eudoxus* and *Hermippus* followed; nearly all followed who have scrutinized the *Pythagorean* and *Platonic* mysteries. Among the more recent who have caught its scent, I find three: *Al-Kindi* the Arab <note>original: "Achindum"</note>, *Roger Bacon*, and *William of Paris* <note>William of Auvergne, the Bishop of Paris, who wrote extensively on the soul and the universe.</note>. And in our own time, I have seen *Antonio Cronico*—who, although very busy handling the greatest affairs, possesses such loftiness and elegance of mind that he has most beautifully touched upon this art, just as he has all other liberal arts. 

*Plotinus* also mentions it, where he demonstrates that the Magus is the servant of nature and not its creator. This very wise man approves and asserts this Magic, while so abhorring the other type that when he was called to the rites of evil demons, he said it was more proper for them to come to him than for him to go to them. And rightly so; for just as the former [evil magic] makes man subject and enslaved to wicked powers, so the latter [natural magic] makes him their prince and master. Finally, the former cannot claim the name of either art or science; the latter, full of the highest mysteries, embraces the deepest contemplation of the most secret things, and ultimately, the knowledge of all nature. 

This magic, calling forth into the light—as if from hiding places—the virtues scattered and sown in the world by the kindness of God, does not so much perform wonders as it diligently serves nature as she performs them. Having scrutinized more deeply the consensus of the universe (which the Greeks more significantly call <term>sympathy</term> <note>original: "$\sigma\upsilon\mu\pi\alpha\theta\epsilon\iota\alpha\nu$" (sympatheian). In Renaissance philosophy, this refers to the invisible web of connections linking all parts of the cosmos.</note>), and having gained insight into the mutual knowledge of natures, this magic applies to each thing its own native allurements—which the magicians call <term>charms</term> <note>original: "$\iota\upsilon\gamma\gamma\epsilon\varsigma$" (iynges). These were ritual "spinning wheels" or symbolic charms used in theurgy to draw down celestial influences.</note>. 

In the recesses of the world, in the womb of nature, and in the secret storehouses of God, it brings into public view the miracles hidden there, as if the magic itself were the creator. And just as the farmer marries elms to vines, so the Magus marries earth to heaven—that is, he marries lower things to the gifts and virtues of higher things. Consequently, just as that other [demonic] magic appears monstrous and harmful, this one appears divine and salutary. This is chiefly because the former, by enslaving man to the enemies of God, calls him away from God; but this one excites in him such admiration for the works of God that fervent charity, faith, and hope most certainly follow. For nothing promotes religion and the worship of God more than the constant contemplation of the wonders of God, which we grasp through this magic of which we speak...

# John Pico of Mirandola

...if we have well explored natural magic, being more ardently animated toward the worship and love of the Creator, we will be compelled to sing: *The heavens are full, all the earth is full of the majesty of your glory.* <note>original: "Pleni ſunt cœli plena eſt omnis terra maieſtate gloriæ tuæ." This is a liturgical refrain from the Sanctus, based on Isaiah 6:3.</note> And this is enough regarding Magic; I have said these things because there are many who—just as dogs always bark at strangers—so they themselves often condemn and hate what they do not understand.

I come now to those things which, unearthed from the ancient mysteries of the Hebrews, I have brought forward to confirm the most holy and Catholic faith. Lest these perhaps be thought of as fabricated trifles or old wives' tales by those to whom they are unknown, I want everyone to understand what and of what kind they are, from where they were sought, by which and by how famous authors they are confirmed, how recondite, how divine, and how necessary they are for our men to defend religion against the persistent slanders of the Hebrews.

Not only famous Hebrew doctors write of this, but also from among our own: Ezra, Hilary, and Origen <note>Pico cites these Church Fathers to provide Christian legitimacy to the idea of a secret oral tradition existing alongside written scripture.</note>. They write that Moses received from God on the mountain not only the Law—which he left for posterity inscribed in five books—but also a more secret and true explanation of the Law. It was commanded to him by God that he should indeed make the Law public to the people, but the interpretation of the Law he should neither commit to writing nor make common knowledge. Instead, he was to reveal it with a great religious duty of silence only to **Joshua, son of Nun** <note>original: "Ieſu Naue"</note>, and then he to others, the subsequent leaders of the priests who succeeded him.

And rightly so. For it was enough for the common people to recognize—through simple history—now the power of God, now his wrath against the wicked, his mercy toward the good, and his justice toward all; and through divine and salutary precepts to be instructed for living well and blessedly and for the worship of true religion. But to make public to the common folk the more secret mysteries, hidden under the "bark" of the Law and the rough covering of words—the secrets of the highest divinity—what else would that be but to *give what is holy to dogs and to scatter pearls among swine?*

Therefore, to keep these things hidden from the common people and communicate them only to the "perfect" (among whom alone Paul says he speaks wisdom), was not a matter of human counsel but of divine command. This custom the ancient philosophers also most holily observed. **Pythagoras** wrote nothing except a few small things which he entrusted to his daughter **Damo** as he was dying. The sphinxes carved into Egyptian temples warned of this: that mystical dogmas should be kept unviolated from the profane multitude through the "knots" of riddles. **Plato**, writing certain things to Dion about the highest substances, said: "I must speak through riddles, lest if the letter happens to reach the hands of others, what we write to you might be understood by them." **Aristotle** said that the books of his *First Philosophy* <note>Referring to the *Metaphysics*.</note>, in which he deals with divine things, were "both published and not published."

What more? **Origen** asserts that Jesus Christ, the master of life, revealed many things to his disciples which they were unwilling to write down, lest they become common to the masses. This is most strongly confirmed by **Dionysius the Areopagite**, who says that the more secret mysteries were transferred by the authors of our religion *from mind to mind, without writing, through the medium of the spoken word, not bodily, but more immaterially* <note>original Greek: ἐκ νοὸς εἰς νοῦν διαμέσου λόγου σωματικοῦ μὴ, ἀϋλοτέρου δὲ ὅμως γραφῆς ἐκτός</note>.

In this very same way, when by God's command that true interpretation of the Law...

# Apology

The interpretation divinely handed down to Moses was called **Kabbalah** <note>original: "Cabala"</note>, which among the Hebrews signifies the same as "reception" among us. It is called this because that doctrine was received from one person to another, as if by hereditary right, through a regular succession of revelations rather than through written records. However, after the Hebrews were restored from the Babylonian captivity through Cyrus, and the Temple was restored under Zerubbabel, they applied their minds to repairing the Law. Ezra, then the head of the Church, after amending the Book of Moses, clearly recognized that due to the exiles, massacres, flights, and captivity of the Israelite people, the custom instituted by the ancestors of handing down doctrine by hand <note>i.e., oral transmission</note> could not be preserved. He feared that the secrets of heavenly doctrine divinely granted to them would perish, for their memory could not last long without the intervention of commentaries. He therefore decided that the surviving wise men should be called together, and each should bring forward what he held in his memory concerning the mysteries of the Law. Notaries were employed to compile these into seventy volumes—for there were approximately that many wise men in the Sanhedrin <note>the supreme council of ancient Israel</note>. Regarding this matter, those who do not believe me should hear Ezra himself speaking thus:

> After forty days had passed, the Most High spoke, saying: "The first things you wrote, place in the open, so that the worthy and unworthy alike may read them. But the last seventy books you shall preserve, to hand them over to the wise among your people; for in these is the vein of understanding, the fountain of wisdom, and the river of knowledge." And so I did.

These are the words of Ezra, verbatim. These are the books of the science of **Kabbalah**, in which Ezra rightly pronounced with a clear voice that there is a "vein of understanding"—that is, an ineffable theology regarding the supersubstantial Deity; a "fountain of wisdom"—that is, an exact metaphysics concerning intelligible and angelic forms; and a "river of knowledge"—that is, a most firm philosophy concerning natural things. Pope Sixtus IV, who immediately preceded the current Pope Innocent VIII under whom we happily live, took the greatest care and zeal to ensure that these books were translated into Latin for the public benefit of our faith. By the time he passed away, three of them had reached the Latin world. Among the Hebrews of this time, these books are revered with such devotion that no one is permitted to touch them unless they are forty years old. When I had acquired these books for myself at no small expense, and had read them through with the utmost diligence and unwearied labor, I saw in them (God is my witness) a religion that is not so much Mosaic as it is Christian. There I found the mystery of the Trinity, there the incarnation of the Word, there the divinity of the Messiah; there I read about original sin, its expiation through Christ, the heavenly Jerusalem, the fall of the demons, the orders of angels, purgatories, and the punishments of hell—the same things we read daily in Paul and Dionysius, in Jerome and Augustine. In those matters which pertain to philosophy, you truly hear Pythagoras and Plato, whose decrees are so kindred to the Christian faith that our Augustine gives immense thanks to God that the books of the Platonists came into his hands. In short, there is hardly any point of controversy between us and the Hebrews concerning which, from these books...

## Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

the books of the Kabbalists can be so refuted and overwhelmed by their own arguments that not even a corner remains in which they might hide. I have a very weighty witness of this matter, Antonio Cronico, a most learned man, who with his own ears, when I was at a banquet with him, heard Dattilo the Hebrew, an expert in this science, descend "hand and foot" <note>original: *pedibus manibusque*; a Latin idiom meaning to commit oneself entirely or with all one's might</note> into the Christian opinion regarding the Trinity. 

And to review the remaining heads of my disputation, we have also brought forward our opinion on interpreting the poems of Orpheus and Zoroaster. Orpheus is read almost complete among the Greeks; Zoroaster is fragmentary among them, but more complete among the Chaldeans; both are believed to be the fathers and authors of ancient wisdom. For to say nothing of Zoroaster, of whom frequent mention is made among the Platonists <note>followers of the philosopher Plato</note> and always with the highest veneration, Iamblichus the Chaldean writes that Pythagoras took Orphic theology as a model according to which he shaped and formed his own philosophy. 

Indeed, they say the sayings of Pythagoras are called "sacred" for this reason: that they flowed from the institutions of Orpheus. From there came the secret doctrine of numbers and whatever great and sublime thing Greek philosophy possessed, as if it flowed from the first source. But such was the custom of the ancient theologians: Orpheus wove the mysteries of his dogmas into the coverings of fables and disguised them with a poetic veil, so that if someone reads his hymns, they would believe nothing lies beneath except the most trifling stories and pure nonsense. 

I wanted to say this so it might be known what labor was mine, what difficulty there was, to draw out the hidden meanings of secret philosophy from the affected knots of riddles and the hiding places of fables—especially in a matter so grave, so hidden, and so unexplored, and without the help or diligence of other interpreters. 

And yet my "dogs" <note>a metaphorical reference to his vocal critics</note> barked that I had accumulated some tiny and trivial things for the sake of showing off a large number of points—as if I had not brought forward many questions that are ambiguous and highly controversial, in which the principal academies clash, and which are entirely unknown and unattempted even by those who carp at my work and believe themselves to be the princes of philosophers. 

Indeed, I am so far from that fault that I took care to compress the disputation into as few headings as possible. If I had wanted, as others are accustomed, to divide it into its members and tear it apart, it would surely have grown to an innumerable number. And to say nothing of the rest, who does not know that one dogma of the nine hundred <term>nongentis</term>—namely, that the philosophies of Plato and Aristotle must be reconciled—I could have, without any suspicion of affected numbers, led into six hundred headings (if not more) by enumerating bit by bit all the points in which others think they disagree but I believe they agree? 

But why do I linger on these things any longer, and not rather come to that for whose sake this whole work was undertaken: to prove as clearly as light, beyond all controversy, that not only am I not impious, but that those who do not blush to say that I am or have ever been a heretic are themselves impious and heretical? I shall do this not with insults and outrages, but with the facts and reasons themselves, bringing into the open what I have said, what I have written, what I have felt, and likewise what those...

# DISPUTATION OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA ON THE DESCENT OF CHRIST INTO HELL.

**T**he first conclusion from those proposed by me in my disputation, which they have condemned, was this: **Christ did not descend into hell truly and regarding His real presence, as Thomas and the <term>common way</term> <note>In medieval theology, the "common way" (via communis) refers to the standard, widely accepted opinions taught in the schools, specifically those of Thomas Aquinas.</note> posit, but only regarding His effect.** Regarding this conclusion: First, I wish to declare my meaning—what my mind and opinion are concerning the manner of Christ’s descent—which it was my intention to explain in the proposed conclusion. I will show that this view is not only Catholic and believed and approved by many Catholic doctors, but also far more probable than its opposite. Second, I will declare how this proposition itself, by the virtue of its speech and according to the force of its words, is in no way to be judged heretical or "smacking of heresy" <note>original: "hæresim sapiens"; a technical legal term for a statement that sounds heretical even if not explicitly proven so</note> by learned men. Third, I will declare that they themselves err in the faith if they persist in the opinion that I cannot defend my conclusion from heresy, even in the sense permitted by the force of the words. Fourth and lastly, I will show in abundance that they can in no way excuse themselves from the fact that their condemnation was made recklessly.

However, before I explain the manner according to which I hold that Christ descended into hell, I wish to premise this: although we are bound to believe explicitly and in particular that Christ descended into hell as an article of faith handed down and promulgated to us by Philip <note>Pico refers to the tradition that each of the twelve Apostles contributed one clause to the Apostles' Creed; the article on the descent into hell was traditionally attributed to St. Philip.</note>—such that even my own protestation or one like it would not save someone who posited the opposite of this article—it does not seem, however, that every member of the faithful is bound to believe explicitly and in particular a *determined manner* of that descent. Rather, it seems to suffice for a Christian to believe that Christ descended into hell not according to His body, nor according to His body and soul together, but according to His soul alone. And he should believe this descent according to the soul happened in a way that was possible, fitting, expedient, and opportune. This is because a determined manner of that descent is not expressly found in, nor does it seem to be proven by, Holy Scripture, nor by any determination of the Universal Church, nor by special revelation from God, nor by the faithful report of the Apostles. Indeed, what is more, Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major Franciscan theologian whose views often rivaled those of Thomas Aquinas.</note>, who was no little exercised in the sacred letters, [says...]

Giovanni Pico della Mirandola
<meta>catchword: liter</meta>

[He] says that it is not held from Holy Scripture that Christ descended into hell, as Francis of Meyronnes <note>A 14th-century French Scholastic philosopher and follower of Duns Scotus</note> reports in the fourth book of his *Sentences*: how much less can we say that a certain and determined mode of Christ's descent is held from scripture. Whence there has also not been any doctor—whose condemnation on this article I have never read—to whom it seemed probable and defensible with the truth of the article that the soul of Christ was not presentially in hell. And all the authorities which both Francis in his fourth book and other theologians in their third bring forward, could seem to someone to be explained as a descent by effect <note>Meaning the power or results of his presence were felt there, rather than his soul literally occupying the space like a physical object</note>, just as much as by a real presence, even following the method of explaining scripture used by the very doctors who hold the opposite view. For it is read in Ecclesiasticus 24 <note>Now usually known as the Book of Sirach</note>: "I will penetrate all the lower parts of the earth." <note>original: "Penetrabo omnes inferiores partes terræ"</note> Thomas [Aquinas], explaining this in the third part of his *Summa*, says it must be understood as being by effect. Therefore, by a similar logic, someone might perhaps say the authorities could be explained as saying he "penetrated" to Limbo or to the Bosom of Abraham <note>A biblical term for the place of rest for the righteous dead before Christ's resurrection</note>: for "to penetrate" is the same as "to enter deeply and within," which is even more than "to descend." Therefore, if he had not only entered but even entered deeply and within the lower parts of the earth, it would be said not because he was really present there, but because he was there only by effect. So it could also be said that he was in the Bosom of Abraham, and entered the Bosom of Abraham, through effect alone, and not through real presence.

I do not say these things because I ever believed that Christ, existing presentially elsewhere, is said to have been in hell only because he worked something there—just as a King staying in his palace is said to be in another place of his province where he effectively works something through the authority of his power and his command. For that was never my opinion (as will soon be clear in the declaration of my opinion); rather, I firmly hold, and have held, and have always said both publicly and privately, that if Christ's soul was anywhere during those three days, it was in hell, and that it was truly present there. But I wanted to say these things for a fuller examination of this matter, so that we might see the truth of that saying of Augustine in his *Book of Heresies*: "Nothing is more difficult than to define what is or is not heretical." <note>original: "Nihil esse difficilius, quàm definire, hoc est hæreticum aut non hæreticum"</note> Thus, because of this, he says it happened that when two very famous writers, Epiphanius and Philastrius, wrote about heresies, they disagreed significantly in numbering them, for no other reason than because that <term>which</term> <note>original: "quod"</note> seemed heretical to one did not seem so to the other.

But now I come to manifest my opinion concerning the mode of Christ’s descent and to perfectly declare my conclusion: first, by putting forth its meaning in summary, and second, by explaining and proving it more broadly. The summary sense of my conclusion is this: Because Christ, according to his soul alone, descended to hell, and because it seems that being located or moved locally does not suit a soul (just as it does not suit any separated substance <note>In medieval philosophy, a "separated substance" is an entity without a physical body, such as an angel or a soul after death</note>) except by reason of its operation, I therefore say that to have descended into hell, or to have been in hell locally, seems not to have suited Christ except by reason of his operation: so that, although truly present...

# Apology

->L 4<-

[real]ly the soul of Christ was in hell, nevertheless its own substance was not the reason for its presence there, but only its operation <note>Latin: *operatio*. In Scholastic philosophy, this refers to the activity, power, or influence exerted by a being in a specific location</note>. So that these words may be more fully understood, it should be noted that there is a twofold opinion among those who posit that separated substances <note>Meaning spirits, like angels or human souls, that are not currently joined to a physical body</note> are not in a place except through a passing operation. 

For some say that by reason of its substance, no place is owed to an incorporeal substance, just as such a substance is never truly white or black; and so, according to them, it can be said not irrationally that it is not in a place and is nowhere, just as it is truly said to be neither hot nor cold. 

As for the authorities of Scripture which seem to give a place to angels—when they say they are in heaven, or are sent to this place or that—these must be understood in this way: not that they are actually "here" or "there," since they are not properly in a place, but that they are working here or there, or begin to work where they were not working before. And these people rely heavily on the words of Gregory of Nyssa <note>A 4th-century Greek bishop and theologian</note>, who says: "Where we ought to say the spirit works here, we say improperly <note>original: "abusive." In a rhetorical context, this means using a term in an unconventional or figurative way rather than a literal one</note> that it is here." 

And so this opinion holds that the substance of an angel or a separated soul can never be said to be present to this place or that, except in a negative sense of presence—that is, as "not distant." But if it is ever said to be or have been somewhere, that is to say it works or has worked somewhere. They add that this way of speaking is borrowed from corporeal things; because we see that physical things cannot act except where they are present (at least according to common opinion), we therefore conclude the same regarding incorporeal things: that where they work, and where their operation is found to be, there also their substance is locally present. 

They conclude finally that it is a coarseness of mind and a lack of imagination not to be able to understand that something can be a being and yet not be in a place. They say the argument of those who claim that "being" presupposes "working" is frivolous; for that proposition is true only in the sense that a non-being cannot work. For an agent must be "in act" <note>Actually existing or active</note>, according to the principle: "some moving species will always be reckoned." But it is not true in the sense that "working in a place" presupposes "being in a place," since it remains possible for the one working to be of such a nature that local presence or distance is no more owed to it than whiteness or blackness is. 

Therefore, those of this opinion would say that the soul of Christ, separated from his body, according to its substance was neither in hell nor outside of hell, but was truly nowhere. It is said to have been in hell because it operated in hell; and it is said to have been most principally in that part of hell where it most principally operated. 

Now, although many doctors hold this opinion about the way of being presentially in a place, I nevertheless do not hold it, nor did I follow it in my conclusion; rather, I held the one which I will immediately subjoin. 

There is, therefore, another opinion which says that a separated substance—such as an angel or a soul not united to a body—is indeed truly in a place. It is truly present locally in a <term>definitive</term> <note>Latin: *definitive*. A Scholastic term meaning the substance is "defined" or limited to a certain space, but without its parts occupying specific sub-sections of that space like a physical body does</note> way, just as a corporeal thing is present locally in a <term>commensurative</term> <note>Latin: *commensurative*. This describes how physical objects occupy space, where the size of the object "measures out" or matches the volume of the space it fills</note> way. And in this, this path agrees with the common view, which is the path of Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus, a hugely influential 13th-century Franciscan philosopher</note> and all the Scotists. But they disagree in this,

# John Pico della Mirandola

...what the **Scotists** <note>Followers of the philosopher John Duns Scotus</note> say: that the boundary and limitation of an essence, and finally the internal determination of its substance, is the reason a separated substance <note>A spirit, such as an angel or a soul, that exists apart from a physical body</note> exists in a place. 

However, this opinion, which I have followed, says in its conclusion: that just as a physical substance is in a place by measurement, yet the reason for its being in a place is not its "substantiality" but its **quantity** (which is external and foreign to the nature of its substance); so also, although an incorporeal substance is truly and definitely in a place and present locally, the reason for its being in a place is not its substance, but its **operation** <note>Latin: *operatio*. Here meaning the activity, power, or influence a spirit exerts on a specific location</note> passing from it to the outside. 

I judge that this opinion should be understood in this way, and so understood, I judge it not only not heretical, but even more probable than its opposite. This is because even if the finitude or limitation of a separated nature is the reason it is not everywhere—or the reason that if it is in one place, it is not simultaneously in another whole place—it is nevertheless not the reason for the separated substance's existence simply within that place. Rather, its **effect** or **operation** is the reason, taking "operation" to mean every relationship to a body or place that functions as an active or passive operation. This is distinct from the mere state of "being present" in a location. In saying this, I am speaking of the fact as it stands, without denying that there might be another possible way for a separated soul to descend or be located (as I say in the following conclusion), though that way is unknown to us.

Following this opinion in my conclusion, I say that **Christ was in hell only by effect**: because, since he was not there except according to his soul, it must be said according to this opinion that just as it does not suit a physical substance to be anywhere by measurement except through quantity, so it did not suit that soul to be in hell—where it is believed to have been—except through effect and operation. 

But just as the reason for the 
<margin>p.</margin>
<margin>i</margin>
presence of the souls of the **Holy Fathers** <note>The Old Testament righteous who died before Christ and were believed to be waiting in the "Limbo of the Fathers"</note> was a relationship to 그 place functioning as a passing operation (such as their detention and binding to that place until they were brought out by the Redeemer when the gate was opened), so the reason for the presence of Christ’s soul was the operation which he performed there. I will demonstrate below that this was my intention and that the words of my conclusion imply this. There I will declare that even by the strict meaning of the words and the force of the phrasing, the conclusion should not be judged heretical. 

As for which opinion is truer regarding the way separated substances exist in a place—namely, that of the Scotists or that of those whom I have followed—I do not determine. I say only this: that my opinion has been believed and held as most true by so many and such great Catholic masters and doctors, most celebrated for both their learning and holiness, that those who dare to judge the opinions of such proven doctors as heretical or "tasting of heresy" <note>original: *hæreſim ſapientę*. A technical inquisitorial term for a statement that sounds heretical even if not explicitly condemned</note> ought to be judged far more reckless than I, who prefer the authority of those ancient theologians over the determinations of the moderns.

# Defense

It can be seen that others follow this same opinion. The **Archbishop of Amalfi** <note>original: "Archiepiscopus Malphitensis"; likely referring to the theologian Landolfo Caracciolo</note> holds it in his second book. **John of Paris** <note>original: "Ioannes Parisiensis"; Jean Quidort, a prominent medieval philosopher</note> holds it in his *Correction of the Corruptor*. And why should I list more? I believe more than a hundred Catholic and most esteemed doctors have held this opinion, whose books are not only not rejected by the Church, but are celebrated and read publicly in all Christian **universities** <note>original: "gymnarijs"</note>. If anyone wishes to consult them, they will be able to see the foundations of this opinion and recognize its probability. I do not intend to do that here, as my only aim is to explain my proposed conclusions so that the simple-minded find no cause for scandal, nor detractors—if there be any—cause for slander.

However, for the sake of the exercise, I will bring forward certain arguments I have heard against this opinion.

**First**, one argues by the **Article of Paris 204** <note>Referring to the Condemnations of 1277, where the Bishop of Paris banned 219 philosophical propositions</note>, which says: "To say the substance of an angel is not in a place without operation <note>activity or influence</note> is an error."

**Second**, it is argued that it is possible for a **separated substance** <note>a spirit, such as an angel, existing apart from a body</note> to perform no operation toward the outside. This being the case, the question is: is it somewhere or nowhere? Or is it everywhere? It is not "nowhere," because even in that state it would be part of the universe; and it would be true to say that what is in the world is not "everywhere," because being everywhere is proper to God alone. Therefore, it must be "somewhere."

**Third**, because angels are said to be in the **empyrean heaven** <note>the highest part of heaven, thought to be composed of light or fire</note>, and yet they have no **transient operation** <note>an action that passes from the agent to an external object</note> toward that heaven.

Likewise, a certain **Master General** <note>likely the head of a religious order</note> insisted on two primary reasons:
1. Even if every external operation were removed, the essence of an angel is still finite; therefore, as such, it is still confined to a place.
2. If there seems to be a reason why an angel is denied a location, it is because it has no **extension** <note>physical size or dimensions</note>. But this is no obstacle, because even if a **point** <note>a mathematical point</note> were given separated from a line, it would still have a position <note>original: "situm"</note>, and yet a point has no extension.

To the first point, a multi-layered response is clear according to the aforementioned doctors. For there are some who, wishing to save the Article along with this position, say that the meaning of the Article is this: the opinion that a separated substance is not in a place *unless* through an operation that is an external local motion or a real alteration is an error. 

That this is the meaning of the Article is clear because **Article 77** says the following, as if explaining the former: "That if there were a separated substance that did not move a body in this world, it would not be contained in the universe: this is an error." See how, just as in the article cited by the objector it says it is an error for an angel to be in a place *only* through operation, so in this one it says it is an error to say a separated substance is not included in this universe except through the motion of a body. 

From this, it seems he understands the same thing by "operation" in Article 204 as he does by "motion" in Article 77. However, this position does not claim that an angel is in a place *only* by operation understood in that way, as will be clear in the response to the third point. Likewise, the **distinguished doctor** <note>original: "solennis doctor"</note> **Godfrey of Fontaines** <note>a famous secular cleric and philosopher at the University of Paris</note> says that these Articles are in need of great correction, because several are false and several contradict each other. Certainly, in this matter, it is necessary either that the Article be explained in the way just mentioned, or that there is a contradiction within the Articles themselves...
