He is currently navigating the "Articles of Paris"—a list of condemned philosophical propositions from 1277—which his critics used to claim that a spirit (like an angel) must be in a place by its very substance, rather than just by its activity.</meta>

<page-num>139</page-num>
# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

...is manifest. I prove it thus: There is **Article 218** <note>Referring to the Condemnations of 1277 issued by Etienne Tempier, Bishop of Paris</note>, which says that if it is understood that the substance of an angel is not the reason for its being in a place, then it is true to say that it is nowhere according to its substance. And **Henry** <note>Henry of Ghent (c. 1217–1293), a major scholastic theologian</note> testifies in his second *Quodlibet*, question 9, that all the masters of Theology gathered together agreed unanimously on this: **That the substance of an angel is not the reason for an angel being in a place.** He even says that he was among those masters who made this determination. 

**Henry** himself adds in the same passage that, by a similar reasoning, it is undoubtedly true that if an angel does not apply its power—namely through its intellect and will—to a place by operating within it, then simply its power of intellect and will is not the reason for it being in that place. This is because its power is no less "abstracted" <note>removed from physical matter</note> than its substance is. Therefore, it follows that one must either grant that the reason for it being in a place will be something acting by way of a <term>second act</term> <note>In scholastic philosophy, "first act" refers to what a thing is (its essence), while "second act" refers to what a thing does (its operation or activity)</note> passing into a body—whatever that may be, and this is exactly what the position I follow posits—or there will be a manifest contradiction within the Articles.

Wherefore **Henry** also confesses in the same place that he cannot understand how a **separated substance** <note>a spirit, such as an angel or a soul, that exists apart from a physical body</note> is in a place unless it acts upon something, or is acted upon by the place or by a thing existing in that place. However, **Giles** <note>Giles of Rome (Aegidius Romanus), a student of Thomas Aquinas</note> and many others say that one should not worry about those Articles, because they were made without summoning all the doctors of Paris, but rather at the request of certain chapters. 

Whatever the case may be regarding this, I wish to say two things: 

1. First, that **Article 218** supports our position no less than **Article 204** works against it. 
2. Second, that it is certain—and the Parisians themselves admit this—that those Articles do not bind all the faithful. Nor are we held to believe them except insofar as they rely on Holy Scripture or the determinations of the Universal Church. 

Hence the **English** are accustomed to say: *"Those articles do not cross the sea."* <note>A common medieval academic saying meaning that the local decrees of the Bishop of Paris had no legal authority at the University of Oxford</note> Therefore, if one may joke in so serious a matter, we can say: **"They do not cross the Alps."** <note>Meaning the Parisian decrees have no authority in Italy</note>

Wherefore, even if my conclusion were against a Parisian Article, those who condemned me should remember that they erred entirely in my condemnation. For they claimed my conclusion was against the **Apostles' Creed**, when they should have said it was against the **"Parisian Creed"**—although even this is false, as we have shown before.

It seems to me that the true understanding of those Articles is this: In **Article 204**, if it speaks of "operation" in the sense commonly accepted, it intends that even if all activity is excluded, the finiteness or limitation of the spirit's nature will be the reason why it is *not* everywhere, or why, if it is in one place, it is not simultaneously in another whole place. But in **Article 218**, I believe it is intended that the substance (or its finiteness) is not the reason for an angel being *simply* in a place. 

By explaining the Articles in this way, there is no contradiction between them. Understood thus, they are not only not against my position, but they totally confirm it on both counts, as is clear from the declaration of the position set forth above.

He is currently addressing the logical objections (or "inconveniences") raised by his critics, who argue that if an angel's substance is not tied to a place, it leads to absurd conclusions about the nature of the universe.</meta>

<page-num>131</page-num>

->**Apology**<-

...positioned. Regarding the second point, it is stated by many—granting that it is possible for an **incorporeal substance** <note>a being without a physical body, such as an angel or a soul</note> to exist without any activity passing to the outside—that once this is posited, the argument seems to bring forward three absurdities. 

The first absurdity is that, since the angel is a part of the universe, it would be improper for it not to be *in* the universe. To this, those thinkers would respond that the one arguing is using the word "part" in two different senses. For if by "part of the universe" he means something that has a fixed position in the world, they will say that an angel—neither when it is acting nor when it is not acting—can be said to be a "part of the universe" in that way. However, if he means a "part of all beings"—that is, one of the natures and entities that make up the universe—then they grant that it is indeed a part of the universe, and in fact one of the most noble. But from this, it does not seem to follow that it must have a physical site or a definition restricted to a place.

The second absurdity is that it could not be said to be everywhere, because being everywhere is a property belonging only to God. To this, it is said that being "everywhere" in the way theologians say God is everywhere—namely, through His essence, power, and presence—is indeed unique to Him, and can belong to no created nature. However, as for being "everywhere" by way of indifference <note>meaning the spirit is not naturally limited to one spot over another</note>, or being "everywhere" by lack of distance—that is, truly existing according to a substance that is not distant from any place—hear what **Henry of Ghent** <note>original: "Henricum"</note> says in his *Quodlibet* 7, question 9: 

"In a creature," he says, "two types of limitation can be understood. One is in its nature and essence, which is finite and contained within certain bounds; in this sense, only God is uncircumscribed and infinite in nature. The other limitation of nature can be understood as a limitation to a site, by which a thing is so finite and contained within certain limits that it must be 'somewhere'—neither nowhere nor everywhere—but 'here' such that it is not 'there.' Or, even if it is not determinately 'here' or 'there,' it is still under the requirement of being either 'here' or 'there' or 'somewhere.' This limitation belongs to the <term>category of 'where'</term> <note>original: "prædicamentum ubi"; one of Aristotle's ten categories used to describe how things exist</note>. I clearly see that every creature differs from God by that first limitation of essence. But as for why it is necessary for every creature to differ and stand apart from Him by the second limitation—namely, that He is everywhere while every creature is necessarily somewhere and not everywhere—I say that I am utterly ignorant of it." 

These are **Henry's** words to the letter; from these words, we see clearly enough that Henry cannot understand how that point which the critics bring forward as an "absurdity" is actually an absurdity at all.

The third absurdity is that, unless it is granted that the angel is somewhere, it must be granted that it is "nowhere." To this, hear the **Blessed Thomas** <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274)</note> in his commentary on the first book of the *Sentences*, distinction 37, responding thus: "I must say," he says, "that I do not consider it absurd that an angel can exist without a place, and not be in a place, when it has no operation concerning a place. Nor is it absurd that it be said then to be 'nowhere' or in no place. Nevertheless, this is not imaginable, because the **imagination** <note>the mental faculty that deals with physical images and space</note> does not transcend the **spatial continuum** <note>original: "continuum"; the physical, three-dimensional world</note>." These are **Thomas's** words to the letter. 

To the third point, I say that the critics' argument proceeds from an incomplete understanding of our position. For the position that says an incorporeal thing is located by its operation does not mean only that activity which is external...

He argues that being "nowhere" in a spatial sense is a logical possibility for non-physical beings, even if the human imagination struggles to conceive it.</summary>

These are the word-for-word words of Thomas. From these words, the response to the argument is clear: although angels do not perform an operation toward the **Empyrean heaven** <note>the highest part of the universe in medieval cosmology, believed to be the home of God and angels</note> that involves local motion or real alteration, they nonetheless have something that functions in the manner of a "passing operation," such as "presiding" or something similar. Regarding the fourth point, on which that **Master General** <note>likely referring to the head of a religious order who opposed Pico’s 900 Theses</note> leaned so heavily, if anything needs to be said, it could be made clear enough from the words of Henry <note>Henry of Ghent (c. 1217–1293), a prominent philosopher at the University of Paris</note> cited above in the solution to the second point. > Some say that an angel is in a place not **circumscriptively** <note>filling the space and bounded by it, like water in a glass</note> but **definitively** <note>being present at a spot without being physically contained by its dimensions</note>, because it is determined to a certain place such that it is in this place and not in another, since its essence is finite. Because it is a created thing, they say one must understand it to be determined to a specific place. But this is a very crude proof, because it proceeds from an **equivocation** <note>using the same word with two different meanings</note> of the word "limit." For when an angel’s essence is called "finite" [limited], "limit" is taken to mean the limit of essence and power (in the sense that a definition is called a boundary), and not the limit of dimension. A place, however, is called "finite" according to the three dimensions of quantity. A "limit" according to either definition has no common measure or proportion; thus, it is not necessary that what is finite in essence be limited by the boundaries of a place. <note>original: "Dicunt quidam quòd angelus non eſt in loco circũſcriptiuè ſed definitiuè..."</note>

These are the literal words of Thomas. From which it follows that, if Thomas is not lying, that Master is "crude," for he called his crude proof a "demonstration." Regarding the other argument about the **point** <note>a mathematical point in space</note>, I say it is even cruder than the first reasoning. For a point is a thing belonging to the category of **quantity**, having a position by its very nature. However, an **incorporeal thing** <note>a being without a physical body, like a spirit</note> is entirely abstracted from position. It is truly a great crudeness to imagine that the "indivisibility" of an incorporeal thing is the same as the "indivisibility" of a point. To make this even clearer to this Master, let him tell me, I ask: if there were a **separated unity** <note>the mathematical concept of "one" existing on its own, not as a physical object</note>, would it have a determined position? It is certainly clear it would not, since a "unity" is distinguished from a "point" by the fact that a point has position, while a unity does not. But it is manifest that an angel—and any incorporeal substance—is even more abstract than any quantity, whether continuous <note>like lines or shapes</note> or discrete <note>like numbers</note>. For **Metaphysics**, as is clear to everyone, deals with things more abstract than **Arithmetic**, which is one of...

> There are also many of the moderns who concede the conclusion of this argument, even though they know the logic is invalid. For we know from logic that an argument is invalid when it proceeds from the **denial of the antecedent to the denial of the consequent** <note>A logical fallacy where one assumes that if the first part of a "if/then" statement is false, the second part must also be false.</note>. Therefore, although it is true that "that which does not exist is nowhere," it does not follow from this that "that which exists is somewhere." And although this does not follow from what has been said, there are many who say that "everything that exists is in some place," using this reason: "Because everything that exists is a particular thing; a particular thing is 'here and now'; and what is 'here and now' is somewhere. Therefore, everything that exists is in a place." Furthermore, they argue: "Everything that exists has a definite essence because it is confined within its own limits; and what has a definite essence is defined in a place; and what is defined in a place is in some place."

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

## Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

we believe; for even the highest heaven is not defined, nor is it circumscribed by a place, because everything that is in a place is enclosed and contained by the place in which it exists. And an intelligence <note>In scholastic philosophy, an "intelligence" refers to a spiritual being like an angel or a detached mind.</note> by its own nature is not in a place, nor in any distinction of place. **Albert** <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), the teacher of Thomas Aquinas and a massive authority in medieval science and theology.</note> says these things literally, not approving that common distinction of "being in a place definitively and not circumscriptively" <note>Scholastics argued bodies are in place "circumscriptively" (occupying space), while souls/angels are there "definitively" (their power is limited to that area). Albert, and Pico, are questioning this technicality.</note>—a distinction which certain Masters nevertheless thought was an absolute sin to deny in any way.

Now, finally, it remains for me to show how the words of my conclusion are to be understood, and to declare that, according to the proper meaning of the words <note>original: "de uirtute sermonis," a technical legal and logical term meaning the literal, rigorous sense of a phrase.</note>, the conclusion itself is Catholic <note>Meaning "orthodox" or "in line with Church teaching."</note>. The conclusion states: <margin>The word *Li*—namely the adverb *ibi* [there] in Latin—refers to being in a place.</margin> **Christ did not truly and according to real presence (as Thomas and the common path posit) descend to hell, but only as to effect.**

Here it must be noted that the word *Li* <note>In medieval logic, "Li" was a technical term used to flag a word being discussed as a word—similar to modern quotation marks. Pico is explaining how his sentence should be parsed.</note> refers to "where," and the phrase "according to real presence" is held copulatively <note>Meaning A and B are joined together.</note>. Furthermore, the word "as"—when it says "as Thomas posits"—is held specifically and determinatively, as I will soon declare. From these points, it is clear that the aforementioned conclusion is a "negative copulative proposition," or a negation of a joined end-point placed before the joining conjunction.

Its meaning is this: *It is not the case* that Christ descended to hell truly and according to real presence *in the specific way that Thomas posits,* etc. Such a "negative copulative" is logically equivalent to an "affirmative disjunctive" made of contradicting parts: namely, "Christ did not descend truly to hell," **or** "He did not descend to hell according to real presence [as Thomas defines it]."

From this it follows that if someone tries to infer from my conclusion that "Christ did not truly descend to hell," they are arguing from a whole affirmative disjunctive to just one of its parts specifically. Such an argument fails "according to the consequent" <note>A logical fallacy where one assumes that because a complex statement is true, one specific part of it must be true in isolation.</note>. For an affirmative disjunctive is the result of its parts, not the cause of one specific part.

It follows further that the whole disjunctive should not be considered false just because one part of it is false. To use a similar example, this proposition is true: "Socrates is a man." But this one is false: "Socrates is a man, AND God is not God." If one were to argue from the latter, "Therefore, Socrates is not a man," it would be truly childish.

By the same logic, to argue from this negative copulative—"Christ did not truly, and according to real presence as Thomas posits, descend"—to the conclusion "Therefore Christ did not truly descend," is childish, and the mark of a man who knows nothing of logic, philosophy, or even theology.

Furthermore, I do not only intend for my conclusion NOT to mean that "Christ did not truly descend," but I do not even mean to say that "Christ or the soul of Christ was not present in hell by a real and true presence of his substance." I only intend to say that he was not there by a real presence **in the way that Thomas and the common path posit.**

Therefore, I said that the word "as" is held specifically and determinatively regarding "real presence." Thus, the argument does not hold: "He was not there really present *in the way that such a Doctor says*; therefore, he was not there really present at all." For the **Common Path**—that is, the way of **Scotus, Bonaventure,** and almost all the **Scotists** and almost all the **Nominalists** <note>These represent the major competing schools of medieval thought. Duns Scotus and Bonaventure often disagreed with Thomas Aquinas's more Aristotelian approach.</note>—holds that he was present there in such a way that his substance was—

<meta>The text cuts off mid-sentence; the catchword is "tia fue", leading into "substantia fuerit".</meta>

## Apologia.

[the substance] was the reason for his presence and locality. Because **Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the Dominican friar whose "Thomistic" philosophy became a cornerstone of Catholic teaching.</note> also seems to me to follow this opinion in this matter, I therefore said, "as **Thomas** and the **common path** <note>original: "communis uia," referring to the standard or mainstream school of thought among theologians.</note> posit." I call the "common path" of theologians that which is currently held in **Paris**, where the study of theology especially flourishes; for there, almost everyone proceeds in this matter concerning the presence of the soul in a place alongside the **Scotists** <note>Followers of John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), who often disagreed with the Thomists on technical metaphysical points.</note> and the **Nominalists** <note>A school of philosophy (led by figures like William of Ockham) that denied the existence of universal essences outside the mind.</note>. For this reason alone—that is, out of respect for the University of Paris—I did not wish to propose this conclusion of mine except as a "probable" one, even though I saw that it could be proposed "assertively" <note>In scholastic logic, "probable" means a well-supported opinion, whereas "assertive" means a definitive claim of truth.</note> according to the path of many most-proven doctors. 

That the term <term>as</term> <note>original: "Li ut." The word "Li" was a medieval convention used to point to a specific word as a linguistic object; "Li ut" means "the word 'as'."</note> can be held in the common way of speaking in a "determinative" sense is clear. For if someone says, "the divine attributes are not distinguished, **as Scotus says**," that proposition would have a double proper sense for everyone. One would be by taking the word "as" <note>original: "Li ut"</note> relatively; it would then be equivalent to saying "the attributes do not distinguish," which is what **Scotus** says, and the proposition would be false, even according to the **Thomists**, because they also concede that attributes are distinguished in some way. 

The other sense would be by taking the word "as" <note>original: "Li ut"</note> determinatively and specifically; it would then be equivalent to saying "the attributes are not distinguished in the *way* that **Scotus** says they are distinguished," and in that case, according to the **Thomists**, the proposition would be true. This is the case in any proposition where, after an opinion is recited, the authority of someone is joined by this word "as." 

Therefore, if this way of speaking—both proper and most common among all theologians—is conceded, it must also be conceded that in our proposition, where it is said "Christ did not descend, **as Thomas says**," the word "as" <note>original: "Li ut"</note> can be held relatively, giving the sense: "Christ did not descend, which is what **Thomas** says [of Christ's descent]." But it can also, just as well and just as properly, be held specifically, being equivalent to this: "Although Christ descended presentially, he did not descend presentially in the *way* that the **common path** says," and that is the sense I intend. 

But perhaps someone might still say: you do not escape, because you then add, "but only as to effect"; therefore you do not only exclude real presence in the way the **common path** posits it, but you simply exclude all real presence entirely, since you say "only as to effect." Thus, these people will say the proposition is not just negative and connective as you say (denying, for instance, presence in the manner of **Thomas**, etc.), but also affirmative—saying, namely, affirmatively, <unclear>that</unclear> Christ was in hell "only as to effect." 

But this objection is crude. For this word "but" is an adversative word, and by its power it brings in, through the things following it, an affirmative truth opposed to the statement which the upper part of the conclusion denies. If, therefore, as has been proven in the upper part, only the presence of the soul *through its substance* is denied—not "as to what" but "as to how" (that is, it is not denied that the substance was present, but that the substance was the *reason* for the presence)—so also in this last part, which posits...

the affirmative [statement] which precisely opposes that one—namely, that he was in hell through his effect—is to be understood not regarding the thing being located, but regarding the **reason for locating**. Briefly, the meaning (which can be clear even to the unlearned) is this: since his substance was finite, his substance was not the **reason for his locality** <note>original: "ratio localis." In medieval physics, this is the metaphysical "cause" or "reason" that allows a spirit to be assigned to a specific point in space.</note> in his state of penance; only his **effect** <note>The "effect" refers to his power or influence acting upon that place.</note> was such a reason for him.

Recapping briefly, therefore, I say: that Christ truly descended into hell, and that he was in hell through a real presence. But I say that he was not there truly and presently in the manner that **Thomas** and the **common path** posit—namely, that his substance was his reason for being in that place. Rather, I say his **operation** was that reason. Just how probable this opinion is, and how many Catholic and most excellent doctors have believed it, has already been made sufficiently clear above. We have also sufficiently explained that, by the **force of the words** <note>original: "de uirtute sermonis." A technical term in logic meaning the literal or strict interpretation of a statement.</note>, this should be judged as true and not heretical.

For we know that this statement is true: "Christ did not satisfy for us as God and man in the way **Arius** <note>Arius (c. 250–336) was a priest whose teachings—denying that Christ was of the same substance as God the Father—were declared heretical.</note> posits." For although it is true that he satisfied for us as God and man, it is nevertheless false if he is understood to exist as God and man in the specific way **Arius** posits. Likewise, although it is true that Christ was truly and presently in hell, it is nevertheless probable (and believed by many) that he was not there truly and presently in the way **Thomas** and the "common path" describe in the manner explained above.

But one **scruple** <note>A "scruple" (original: "scrupulus") here refers to a lingering intellectual doubt or a technical objection.</note> seems to remain: that this was not my intention when I set down the conclusion. For if **Thomas**, in the first book of the *Sentences* <note>original: "primo sententiarum." Referring to Aquinas's early commentary on Peter Lombard's *Sentences*, a standard theological textbook.</note>, holds this same path—that **operation** is the reason for an angel to be in a place—it would seem that my conclusion is true even according to **Thomas**. Therefore, when I say "not as **Thomas** posits," it would seem I have a different opinion about that descent than what I have stated. 

However, they would not have this scruple if they had considered my conclusions well. For I am of the opinion that **Thomas** felt differently on this matter regarding the **mode of being in a place** for **separated things** <note>original: "rerum separatarū," referring to spiritual beings like angels or human souls that exist apart from physical bodies.</note> at different times, and did not follow the same opinion everywhere. Therefore, although in the first book of the *Sentences* he seems to hold the path I follow, in his conclusion and elsewhere—such as in the fourth book of the *Sentences*, and especially in the **Third Part of the Summa** <note>The *Summa Theologiae*, Thomas Aquinas's most famous and mature work.</note> where he treats this descent, and by which his opinion should be judged rather than by his earlier writings—he seems to side with the opinion of the **Scotists** <note>Followers of John Duns Scotus.</note>. This view holds that he was there through his **essence** in such a way that his essence was the reason for his **locability** <note>The capacity of a thing to be placed in a specific location.</note>, and not his effect alone or his operation.

For **Thomas** says there that the soul of Christ was in other parts of hell through his **effect**, but in **Limbo** through his **essence**, etc. From this statement, I argue as follows: Wherever something is through that which is its reason for locability, it is there through its substance and real presence. Therefore, if **effect** was the reason for locability for the soul of Christ, then wherever he was through his effect, he was there through the real presence of his substance. But according to **Thomas**, he was in some places through his effect where he was *not* through his real presence; therefore, according to **Thomas**, effect was not his reason for locability. This moved me to probably believe that **Thomas**, in this article, walks with the **Scotists**. But whatever the case may be regarding the opinion of **Thomas**, it is nothing to...

# Apologia.

It is irrelevant to the matter, because to err in one's opinion of **Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the most influential Scholastic theologian.</note> is not to err in the faith, and often there are multiple opinions among the **Thomists** <note>Followers of the school of thought based on Aquinas.</note> regarding his actual opinion. It is enough that it evidently appears that when I proposed the conclusion, I believed this to be the opinion of Thomas, and that I am not now twisting the proposition to a meaning foreign to the one I held then. For it is most clearly evident that I believed this from the beginning, and that this was my judgment concerning the opinion of Thomas when I proposed the conclusions, because I proposed that conclusion: **that Thomas and Scotus do not differ regarding the manner of angels being in a place.** <note>Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308) was a major rival to the Thomist school; Pico is arguing that on this specific technical point, the two giants of medieval thought actually agreed.</note> Now, it is known that **Scotus** expressly says that even if all operation were excluded, a place is still owed to incorporeal substances; therefore, it was necessary for me to believe that Thomas was of this same judgment. And so, although I firmly held that **Christ** was truly and presentially in hell, and in this I agreed with Thomas and with all **Catholics**, nevertheless, because I thought Thomas believed his substance was the reason for his locatability and not his operation, I said in my conclusion: *not in the way that Thomas and the common path posit.*

Nor should it seem a marvel anywhere that Thomas follows one opinion in one place and another elsewhere. For in the first book of the **Sentences**, <note>The *Sentences* of Peter Lombard was the standard textbook of medieval theology; every great doctor wrote a commentary on it.</note> he follows the opinion of the **Commentator** <note>Averroes (1126–1198), the Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to University study.</note> regarding **things generated from putrefaction**, <note>Medieval biology held that some small creatures, like insects or worms, were spontaneously generated from rotting matter rather than born from parents.</note> which he then rejects in the seventh book of the **Metaphysics** and elsewhere. Likewise, in the second book of the *Sentences*, he follows the Commentator's opinion on the **matter of the heavens**, which he then rejects in the second book of **On the Heavens** and in the **Summa**. <note>The *Summa Theologiae*, Aquinas's most famous and mature work.</note> Likewise, in the fourth book [of the *Sentences*] and in the **Questions on Boethius's On the Trinity**, he holds the Commentator's path regarding **indeterminate dimensions**, and then in his own booklet (as is believed) and in many other places, he does not hold it. 

Likewise, in the first book of the *Sentences*, he says that by the same action the intelligible thing itself is understood and the act of understanding itself is understood. However, in the first part of the *Summa* and in the third book of the *Sentences*, he holds that a **reflexive action** <note>Thinking about one's own thinking.</note> differs from a direct one. Likewise, in his writings, he holds that the **soul of Christ**, insofar as it was joinable to the body, was like the soul of a **wayfarer**; <note>term: "viator" — a human soul currently living on earth, seeking God.</note> but insofar as it was joinable to the Word, it was like the soul of a **comprehensor**. <note>term: "comprehensor" — a soul that has already reached the "beatific vision" or the presence of God in heaven.</note> Yet in the *Summa*, he holds that the soul of Christ was totally and in all respects like the soul of a comprehensor, and that the fact that it did not transfer the gift of clarity and impassibility <note>The qualities of a "glorified" body that cannot suffer or die.</note> into the body was due to **divine dispensation**. <note>A special act or exception granted by God.</note>

He also feels one way about the **knowledge of Christ** in his writings and another way in the *Summa*, and so it is with many other things, as can be seen, in which he followed different opinions in different places. But if those men contend entirely that the opinion of "being in a place according to operation" also belongs to Thomas, they will have nothing further against me, except that my opinion on the manner of Christ's descent is all the more probable, and must be judged less heretical, insofar as it is true even according to the opinion of Saint Thomas. For this reason, I wonder all the more that my conclusion was condemned by these **Masters**, because before they judged that conclusion heretical, I myself expressed my intention regarding it to them...

<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

I had not only declared this in words, but had even dictated it to be written and noted down, saying: "Let no one understand me to say by this conclusion that the soul of **Christ** did not descend to the underworld, or that the soul of **Christ** was not in hell during the <term>three days</term> <note>The 'triduum,' referring to the period between Christ's death and his resurrection.</note>; indeed, I confess both. But I say that neither local motion nor being situated in a place is appropriate for any <term>separated substance</term> <note>A technical term for an intellect existing without a body, such as an angel or a human soul after death.</note>, such as the soul of **Christ** was then, except by reason of its operation." I pronounced these exact words and no others, word for word, for them to note down as a brief declaration of this conclusion. Since they nonetheless later judged it heretical, I do not see how they can now consider it Catholic. And to show briefly, by way of a summary argument, that those who believe my proposition cannot be defended from heresy are in error, I argue as follows: 

He who puts forward a conclusion that is heretical in itself can be accused of heresy, insofar as heresy exists in the intellect. But he who puts forward my aforementioned conclusion cannot be accused of heresy because of that position: therefore, the aforementioned conclusion is not heretical in itself. They themselves grant the first part of the argument; the second part I prove as follows. 

Whenever someone, by asserting everything from which a certain proposition (let’s call it 'A') necessarily follows, cannot be accused of heresy, then even the person asserting proposition 'A' itself cannot be accused. But someone asserting everything from which the position of my conclusion follows—in the manner in which it was proposed by me—cannot be accused of heresy: therefore, the person asserting the proposition itself, as I proposed it, cannot be accused. 

I prove the second part of this thus: 
The contradiction of this statement—*that the reason for being in a place (that is, 'here' or 'there') for separated substances, in the manner declared above, is operation and not the limitation of their nature*—is not <term>of the faith</term> <note>Meaning it is not a required dogma or an essential article of Catholic belief that one must accept to be a believer.</note>. 
And the contradiction of this statement—*that one may not argue from a combined statement to one of its parts*—is not of the faith. 
And the contradiction of this statement—*if someone, having put forward a negative or affirmative assertion, adds the authority of some doctrine with a proposition, such as "as it can be held," it can be understood as much in a definitive sense as in a relative one*—is not of the faith. For "in such a way" can be equivalent to "in the manner that," which similarly is not of the faith. 
And the contradiction of this statement—*that by the "common path" in theological matters we can appropriately understand the path commonly held in that university where, at the time of the speaker, the study of theology most flourishes*—is not of the faith. 
And the contradiction of this statement—*that at this time, the study of theology flourishes more at the **University of Paris** than elsewhere*—is not of the faith. 
And the contradiction of this statement—*that in the **University of Paris**, it is now commonly held that the limitation of nature is the reason for the locatability of a separated substance*—is not of the faith. 
And the contradiction of this statement—*that **Scotus** and the majority of the **Nominalists** <note>A school of philosophy that argued universal concepts are just names, not independent realities.</note> hold the aforementioned opinion, and that **Thomas** seems to hold it in the third part of his *Summa*, where he speaks of the descent of **Christ***—is not of the faith. 

Then it follows: If the contradictions of these statements are not "of the faith," it follows that to propose, believe, and dispute these statements is not in itself heretical or against the faith, nor are they [heretical] when taken disjunctively...

# Defense.

...asserting, holding, and disputing [these things] either **disjunctively** or **conjunctively** <note>This continues the logical argument from the previous page: whether one considers the parts of his statement separately or all together.</note> can be accused of heresy. But from these statements, when placed together and conjunctively, the positioning of my conclusion follows exactly as it stands: therefore, one asserting my conclusion exactly as it stands cannot be accused of heresy. The proofs of all the aforementioned points are found in what was written above. For concerning the first statement, it is clear that it is not only not heretical, but is even more rational than its opposite, and is believed and approved by many Catholic doctors. In the second statement, all **logicians** <term>dialectici</term> <note>Those trained in 'dialectics,' the medieval art of logical argument.</note> and all theologians who have ever known logic agree. So it is with all the other points; even if someone could doubt whether they are true or false, no one is so unrefined, so lacking in all learning, and so ignorant of the faith and those things pertaining to the faith, that they would say those things cannot be believed without heresy, and thus that their contradictions are matters of faith. Then, let it be further argued thus: 

Anyone who believes that this conclusion, "Christ," etc., cannot have a Catholic sense—based on the force of the words and according to proper, non-extorted usage—believes that the contradictory of one or more of the aforementioned seven statements is a matter of faith. But those who hold something to be a matter of faith which is *not* a matter of faith, have a wrong understanding of the faith. For this is against the word of the Lord in Deuteronomy 4: 
> You shall not add to the word that I speak to you, nor shall you take away from it. <note>original: "Non addetis ad uerbum quod ego loquor uobis, neque minuetis ab eo"</note>

Therefore, those who judge my conclusion poorly, as described above, have a wrong understanding of the faith. 

See, O **Supreme Pontiff**; see, O most august senators of the apostolic order <note>Referring to the College of Cardinals.</note>; see, O all of Rome, indeed all of Italy, and indeed the Church of Christians, how they are refuted in this first proposition! This was the one in which they were most heavily attacking me, and in which many seemed to have some handle—not so much for accusing me, as for excusing their own condemnation of me. Regarding my other conclusions, it will be clearer than light that they could not have had even the slightest occasion for condemning them as heresy. Now, regarding this first one where they were strongest, it has been seen what sort of thing it is, and whether it was condemned by them rightly or wrongly—especially since I have now explained to them the sense I intended by it, applied to the words of the conclusion without any abuse of terms or speech, and without distortion. 

And although this suffices for the defense of my conclusion, nevertheless, for a fuller discussion of this matter, I say that even interpreting the conclusion in the way they themselves interpreted it—namely, that Christ was in hell **only effectively** and not **presentially** <note>Meaning Christ's *power* reached hell to liberate souls, but his *actual presence* (soul) was not located there.</note>—it might still perhaps seem to some that it was a presumptuous act for them to determine that the conclusion was simply heretical. For it is a fact that **Durandus** <term>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain</term> <note>A famous 14th-century Dominican theologian known for his independent and often controversial views, though he remained an orthodox authority.</note>, a most great theologian of the Order of Preachers, who perhaps exceeds these present Masters in learning no less than I am exceeded by them, held that opinion to be probable and well-defensible alongside the truth of the Article of Faith. For thus it is written in the *Third Book of Sentences* <term>Sententiarum</term> <note>The 'Sentences' of Peter Lombard, the standard textbook for medieval theological study.</note>. ...it is argued, and it seems that Christ did not descend into hell according to his soul, because the same finite thing cannot be in different places at the same time; but the soul of Christ, since it was a finite creature, was immediately after death in paradise with the soul of the thief. To whom it was said in **Luke 23**: *Today you will be with me in paradise* <note>original: "Hodie mecum eris in paradiso"</note>; therefore, at least at that time, he could not have been in hell. Likewise, those things which Christ did and suffered in his assumed nature were ordained for human salvation, but for this, it would not have been necessary for Christ to have descended to the underworld, because through the passion which he endured in this world, he liberated us from all fault and punishment; therefore it seems that Christ did not descend to the underworld. 

In contrast is what is said in the **Creed** <note>The Apostles' Creed, the standard statement of Christian belief which includes the phrase "He descended into hell."</note>. *He descended into hell*. And the Apostle says in **Ephesians 4**: *But that he ascended, what is it, but that he also descended into the lower parts of the earth?* The **gloss** <gloss>a standard interpretive commentary used by medieval scholars</gloss> says, "that is, to the underworld." 

I respond that since it is an article [of faith] that Christ descended into the underworld, and it cannot be understood by reason of his divinity (according to which he is everywhere), nor by reason of his body (according to which he was in the tomb), it remains that it be understood by reason of his human nature under the premise of the soul, in which two things are to be seen. The first is by what mode the soul of Christ descended to hell. The second is to which hell he descended. 

Regarding the first, it must be known that since a **separated soul** <note>A soul that has been separated from the body by death but has not yet been reunited with it in the resurrection.</note> is neither a body nor a power within a body, it cannot be said that the soul of Christ descended to the underworld by that kind of motion or descent by which physical bodies are moved. The kind of motion by which **angels** are moved is not clearly evident; for angels are said to be moved from place to place insofar as they act successively in different places. A separated soul is not said to have any operation regarding a place or regarding a body existing in a place, because since by its nature it is determined to its own specific body, it cannot move nor act upon another except through the mediation of its own body; but it lacks that body while it is separated. Therefore, the soul cannot be moved from place to place by reason of the operation which it has regarding a place or a body existing there. 

Nevertheless, this notwithstanding, a separated soul can be said to have descended into hell in two ways. One way is according to **assignment** <term>deputationem</term> <note>The legal or divine designation of a soul to a particular state or location.</note>, and in this way the souls of the damned are said to descend to hell simply. This is because they are simply assigned so that, once they have resumed their bodies, they may be in hell; because of this, they are said to be where they are simply assigned. 

Moreover, the souls of the **Holy Fathers** <note>The righteous figures of the Old Testament, such as Abraham and David, who died before Christ.</note> are said to be in **Limbo** <term>lymbo</term> <note>From the Latin for 'edge' or 'border,' referring to the place where the righteous of the Old Testament waited for Christ's redemption.</note>, or to have descended to Limbo, because of an assignment that is not simple but conditional; for having resumed their bodies, they would remain there unless they were liberated by the Redeemer. However, the soul of Christ is not said to have descended to hell in this way—namely, by reason of assignment—because every such assignment is on account of a fault contracted or committed, which was not in Christ. 

In another way, a separated soul can be said to descend to hell according to its **effect**; and in this way, the soul of Christ can be said to descend to hell because of the twofold effect which he had upon those who were in hell. One effect was...

<summary>Pico addresses the theological puzzle of how Christ's soul could be in both Paradise and Hell simultaneously. He concludes that Christ's "descent" was not a physical movement, but rather occurred through the spiritual effects his presence had on those waiting in Limbo.</summary>

# Apologia

...the desire for the <term>divine vision</term> <note>Also known as the Beatific Vision, the ultimate direct communication of God to the individual soul.</note> which they lacked, toward which the passion of Christ acted as a form of merit; and because all merit depends principally on the act of the soul, this effect is attributed to the soul itself, as the primary principle of deserving. Likewise, by appropriation, just as Christ according to his soul was blessed, so according to that soul is he credited with being the cause of <term>beatitude</term> <note>The state of perfect happiness or spiritual walking with God.</note> in others. For it is fitting that a being in potentiality be brought to actuality by that which is already in actuality. 

According to some, there was another effect to which the soul of Christ related directly as an agent—namely, to illuminate the souls of the <term>patriarchs</term> <note>The holy figures of the Old Testament, such as Abraham and Moses, who died before Christ's resurrection.</note> who were in <term>limbo</term>, regarding the mysteries that fall under revelation. For according to **Dionysius** in the seventh chapter of *The Celestial Hierarchy* <note>A 5th-century work by Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a foundational text for medieval angelology and mysticism.</note>: Christ, according to his soul, has the task of teaching the angels; and by reason of this double effect, the soul of Christ can be said to have descended into hell. 

This is confirmed by a threefold reason. The first is because movement or descent belongs to a separated soul, not in the manner of the movement of bodies, but in the manner by which movement belongs to a spiritual substance. But for other spiritual substances—namely, God and the angels—it is not fitting to be moved from place to place by a movement that exists subjectively within them, but rather by the effect they have in other things. Therefore, in a similar way, it belongs to a separated soul, and it belonged to the soul of Christ. 

The second reason is as follows: Christ is said to have descended into hell so that he might illuminate the souls of the holy patriarchs to see God; but in the same instant in which Christ died, the holy patriarchs saw God. In that same instant, the soul of Christ could not have been in hell by physical movement; therefore, he did not descend there by a movement that was in the soul itself, but by the effect which he had in others. 

Likewise, just as in those three days the soul of Christ is said to have been in hell with the souls of the holy patriarchs, so in those three days (or part of them) he is said to have been in paradise with the soul of the thief, to whom it was said in **Luke 23**:
> Today you will be with me in paradise. <note>original: "Hodie mecum eris in paradiso"</note>

But this cannot be understood in terms of a location acquired through physical movement. Since those who discuss spirits say that when a spirit moves from place to place "definitively," the same spirit cannot be in multiple places at once, nor be moved by multiple movements tending toward multiple places simultaneously. Therefore, it must be understood according to its effect. 

But if someone should say that "Paradise" is spoken of in two ways—one way as a physical place, namely the <term>empyrean heaven</term> <note>The highest, most physical point of heaven in medieval cosmology, associated with fire and light.</note>, and in this sense the soul of Christ was not in paradise until after the Ascension; and in another way "Paradise" is called the vision of the divine essence, and thus the soul of Christ was in paradise from the moment of conception, and the soul of the thief on the very day of the passion—in this way it is not contradictory for the soul of Christ to have been simultaneously in "Paradise" so defined (that is, that it saw God) and to have been locally in hell. If it is said this way, I say it does not hold, because just as "Paradise" is spoken of in two ways, so is "Hell." In one way, Hell refers to a place corresponding to the interior of the earth; in another way, it refers to the lack of the divine vision. Therefore, just as the soul of the thief is not said to have been with the soul of Christ in paradise except that by the merit of Christ's passion...

<summary>Pico explains that Christ’s "Descent into Hell" was a spiritual action (an "effect") rather than a physical journey, allowing him to illuminate the souls in Limbo while simultaneously being in "Paradise" with the thief.</summary>

### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

...the soul of the thief saw God, so the soul of Christ is not said to have been with the souls of the chosen fathers in hell, except because their souls—which lacked the **divine vision** <note>The direct perception of God, which theologians believed was unavailable to the Old Testament righteous until Christ's sacrifice.</note> and thus were said to be in hell—were purged of this lack by the merit of this Passion. Therefore, both must be understood in terms of their effect, not in terms of place or local motion residing subjectively in the soul itself.

Although this has been said with probability and seems to sufficiently preserve the article of faith and the words of scripture, because divine power is not grasped by human reason, it must not be stubbornly asserted that the soul of Christ could not have descended to hell by some other way unknown to us.

To the first argument, it must be said that the same finite thing cannot be in several places at once definitively or circumscriptively <note>Technical terms in medieval physics: "definitive" presence refers to a spirit being where its power is acting, while "circumscriptive" refers to a physical body filling a space.</note>, and it is not in this way that the soul of Christ is placed in paradise and hell at the same time, but according to **effect**. Nothing prevents the same finite thing from being said to be in several places when the effects are compatible and simultaneously subject to the power of the same agent. Thus, Christ’s soul is said to have been in paradise and hell at the same time, because by its merit, the soul of the thief saw God—which is to be in paradise—and the souls of the fathers who lacked the divine vision—and were for this reason said to be in hell—were freed from this lack, and consequently from hell.

Indeed, according to one and the same effect—namely, the liberation of the fathers—the soul of Christ could be said to be in paradise and hell at once, by considering the "point from which" and "point to which" <note>original: "terminum a quo & ad quem"</note> of that effect. By reason of the lack of divine vision from which they were freed through the Passion of Christ, the soul of Christ could be said to have been in hell; by reason of the divine vision to which they were admitted, it could be said to be in paradise.

To the second, it must be said that by the very fact that we are freed from guilt and punishment through the Passion of Christ, Christ is said to have descended into hell, because by the merit of his Passion, some were rescued from the punishments of hell. For that descent is not considered according to local motion existing in the soul, but according to the effect it had on those being saved. Thus says <term>Durandus</term> <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain (c. 1275–1334), a philosopher and theologian who often disagreed with Thomas Aquinas.</note> word for word.

Since he is never found to have retracted such an opinion, if it is simply heretical and consequently against what has been determined by the <term>Church</term>, it follows that Durandus died a heretic. O distinguished <term>Order of Preachers</term> <note>The Dominican Order, known for its rigorous theological training.</note> and greatest splendor of our religion! Can you suffer your primary teacher—perhaps after <term>Thomas</term> <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas, the most influential Dominican theologian.</note>, or certainly among the first, whose books are daily kept, read, and honored in your schools, cloisters, and libraries—to now be pronounced a heretic?

Plead the cause of your doctor; I have pleaded mine. Indeed, O Church, plead your own cause, you who have permitted for so many years, and now permit, Durandus to be read publicly. Either through ignorance you never recognized such a foul heresy (according to these masters) in him, or through negligence and contempt for divine matters, you did not condemn it once recognized. But if they say there was no need for a new condemnation, since this opinion is among those already condemned, first it follows from this what I said above: namely, that Durandus [died a heretic...]

-> # Apologia. <-

...that he was a dead heretic. Secondly, it would mean that both Capreolus and Durandellus <note>Nicholas of Saint-Pourçain, often called Durandellus, a follower/commentator of Durandus.</note>, and many other doctors who recite the opinion of Durandus yet do not accuse it of heresy, were themselves ignorant and unrefined in the faith, not knowing how to discern a heretic from a non-heretic. Thirdly, let these fathers tell me: where have they read a condemnation of this opinion? I for my part, to confess of myself, do not remember ever reading it anywhere. Certainly, they can bring forth no determination of the **Councils** against Durandus, since not only was this opinion never condemned in the councils, but there was not even a mention of it in any of them.

Likewise, I do not know how they will be able to allege the words of **Sacred Scripture** against him—unless Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus, a major medieval philosopher-theologian.</note> is lying, who says (citing Franciscus <note>Likely Francis of Meyronnes, a student of Scotus.</note>) that concerning the very descent of Christ itself, let alone the *manner* of the descent, there is no express mention in the Gospel doctrine. This is clear from what we set forth at the beginning regarding the "manner," which Durandus would perhaps use to explain those authorities of Scripture that might seem to be against him.

Regarding the authorities of the **Saints** <note>Referring here to the "Church Fathers" like Augustine or Jerome.</note>, they could perhaps bring forward many who say that the soul of Christ was in hell during the three days <note>The *triduum*, the period between Christ's death and resurrection.</note> just as his body was in the tomb, and similar statements. And whatever the case may be regarding the "imagination" of Durandus—namely, the manner in which he himself would explain the aforementioned authorities, perhaps by saying this is said of the soul [as an agent] and not of the whole composite [the person], because he operated principally through the soul—whatever, I say, he himself might say (whose opinion I neither hold nor have ever held), I say this and firmly assert: **this consequence is not valid**: 

> "This opinion is against the sayings of Augustine, or Jerome, or Gregory, and so on for the other doctors of the Church; **therefore it is heretical**."

The truth of this statement of mine is believed by all good and subtle theologians, and so it shall be evidently proven by me. For however much the writings of the holy doctors, placed outside the **Canon of the Bible**, are to be handed down and read, and received with due reverence, nevertheless their sayings are not of such firm authority and immutability that it is not permitted to contradict them or to doubt them—unless they are otherwise proven evidently and expressly through Sacred Scripture, or it has been firmly determined by the Church itself, authorizing them, that they contain firm and indubitable truth.

Therefore, an opinion cannot be clearly convicted as heretical solely through the sayings of the saints outside the Canon of the Bible. For where there is no **infallible truth**, there is neither certain nor indubitable faith. Since certain faith rests upon infallible truth, indeed regarding such matters there is no infallible assent nor firm adherence; for where certain truth and indubitable faith are not present, one always assents with doubt and with the fear of the false. For as **Augustine** says in his letter to Jerome and in the eleventh book of *Against Faustus* (chapters 7 and 16): if Scripture does not contain ineffable truth and is found to be false in any part of itself, there remains in it no certain faith by which it may be firmly believed; and because of a falsehood found in one part of itself, the whole is held suspect, and thus faith would waver. Because, as Augustine says concerning Christian faith in chapter seven, Titus...

-> ## Giovanni Pico della Mirandola ## <-

<meta>catchword: is false</meta>

...faith would waver, if the authority of the sacred scriptures wavers. However, regarding the fact that there is no infallible truth in the sayings of the saints outside the canon of the Bible, three proofs occur to me for our present purpose. 

The first is because the doctors themselves doubt their own sayings, wondering whether they have erred in them or not. Thus Augustine, in the first book of <term>On the Trinity</term> <note>original: "De Trinitate"</note>, chapter 1, says: "I will not be annoyed to seek where I hesitate, nor will I be ashamed to correct myself where I err." And in chapter 2: "Therefore, let whoever reads this seek with me where he hesitates; where he recognizes his error, let him return to me; where he recognizes mine, let him call me back." From this comes Augustine’s book of <term>Retractions</term> <note>original: "Retractationum," a work where Augustine reviewed his life's writings and corrected his earlier mistakes</note>, in which he condemns and withdraws many things from what he had said previously. Hence also in the second book of *On the Trinity*: "I would rather be rebuked by anyone than be praised either by one who is erring or by one who is flattering; for the praiser who is erring confirms the error, while the flatterer entices one into error; but the just man will correct me in mercy and rebuke me, but the oil of the sinner shall not fatten my head" <note>A reference to Psalm 141:5, often used to describe the danger of being blinded by false praise.</note>. 

And as Guido the Carmelite <note>Guido de Terrena (c. 1270–1342), a philosopher and theologian who served as the Prior General of the Carmelite Order.</note> says in his book *On Heresies*: "Although Augustine speaks humbly in these sayings, he nonetheless speaks truthfully." Thus Augustine himself says to Vincentius: "I cannot nor should I deny that, just as in the works of the elders, so too in my many little works, there are many things which can be rebuked by a just judgment and without rashness." And in his book *On True Religion* he says: "Whatever error shall be found in my books is to be attributed to me alone; but whatever is true or well-explained, let that be attributed to God, the one rewarded and giver of all things." Therefore, the sayings of Augustine—that distinguished and divine doctor—may not always contain indubitable truth in all things, since he himself doubts whether he has erred regarding them. And what has been said of Augustine should be understood similarly regarding other Doctors.

The second proof is taken from the discord which exists among the authors themselves. For discord among writers is a testimony to falsehood, since it is necessary that at least one of those disagreeing says what is false, because one side of a contradiction is necessarily false. Therefore, Augustine, in the 16th book of <term>The City of God</term> <note>original: "De Civitate Dei"</note>, proves the truth of sacred scripture from the mutual harmony of its writers, in which all agree and no one disagrees with another—which bears witness to the indubitable and infallible truth of the sacred scriptures. 

For as <term>The Philosopher</term> <note>Referring to Aristotle, who was standardly called "The Philosopher" in medieval academic texts.</note> says in the first book of the <term>Ethics</term> <note>original: "ethicorum," referring to the Nicomachean Ethics</note>, "all things harmonize with the truth," which does not happen in other writings. For how great the discord is in the sayings of the saints outside the canonical scriptures, no one is ignorant, unless they have not read their books. Augustine disagrees with the other holy doctors concerning the understanding of the <term>six days of work</term> <note>The creation of the world in six days as described in Genesis.</note>, because others posit that God performed those six days of work according to a succession of time. Augustine disagrees with them, positing that all things were made at once, according to that text: "He who lives forever created all things together" <note>Sirach 18:1; Augustine argued for "simultaneous creation" rather than a chronological week.</note>. 

Driven by this, Augustine enumerates those six days not according to a succession of times, but according to the distinction of the angelic knowledge of things—both in their own kind and in the Word <note>Augustine's complex theory that the "days" of Genesis represent stages of angelic insight into God's creation.</note>. And yet, neither these men nor those men are called heretics; and it is certain that one of these opinions is false.

They similarly disagree regarding Paul's rebuke of Peter: was it concerning a mortal sin, or a venial sin on Peter's part? <note>This refers to the dispute in Galatians 2:11-14. Jerome argued the conflict was staged for the benefit of the audience, while Augustine insisted it was a real rebuke for a real error.</note> Likewise, they disagree on the cessation of the legal ceremonies <note>The "legalia" or Mosaic laws of the Old Testament.</note>, so that by contradicting one another, one necessarily says what is false: and yet, because of this, neither of them is considered a heretic.

Similarly, Bede, in his commentary on the first book of Kings, says that Samuel was a true priest, which Augustine expressly denies in the book *Questions on the New and Old Testaments*, saying that Samuel was not a priest since he was not of the sons of Aaron. And Jerome, in the first book *Against Jovinian*, says it must be recognized at the same time that Samuel was a Levite, not a priest nor a high priest; therefore he is not named among the priests, but among those who call upon the name of the Lord.

Therefore, the sayings of these men do not rely on infallible truth, since they contradict themselves, and one side is necessarily false—as is clear from the Philosopher <note>A standard title for Aristotle.</note> in the 4th book of the *Metaphysics*. Indeed, Augustine himself seems to oppose himself on this opinion; for in the book *Questions on the New and Old Testaments*, question 46, he says, "As we have said, Samuel was not a priest," and yet in book 12 *Against Faustus*, chapter 35, he says: "The priesthood was changed to Samuel when Eli was rejected, and the kingdom was changed to David when Saul was rejected." Here Augustine clearly says the priesthood was transferred to Samuel, so that Samuel was truly a priest, just as David was truly a king.

Regarding that same Samuel, as to whether he was raised from the dead, Augustine seems to disagree with himself. For in *Questions on the New and Old Testaments*, question 27, he holds that Samuel was not truly raised by the medium <note>original: "Pythonissam," referring to the Medium of Endor in 1 Samuel 28.</note>, but a demon appeared to Saul in the likeness of Samuel. Yet in the book *On the Care to be Taken for the Dead*, he posits that the soul of Samuel was truly stirred up by a demon and spoke to Saul through the magic art.

Jerome also, in that question of whether Salem was Jerusalem, seems to contradict himself in a certain letter of his whose title I do not remember; he also holds an opinion contrary to Augustine regarding the seventy translators <note>The authors of the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note>. Likewise, Gregory and Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential mystical theologian.</note> disagree concerning the orders of Angels. And Jerome alone opposes the others regarding the promotion of a twice-married man <term>bigamus<gloss>In canon law, a "bigamus" was a man who had been married twice (sequentially, such as a widower who remarried), which usually disqualified him from becoming a priest.</gloss></term>; for he himself holds and writes in his letter to Oceanus that a twice-married man, whether before baptism or after baptism, can be promoted [to the priesthood], provided he has not known more wives after baptism. The others contradict him, saying: that a twice-married man, whether before baptism or after baptism, cannot be promoted; and in this, the others are considered to have spoken better, as Augustine writes in *The Good of Marriage* and Ambrose in *On Duties*.

Likewise, Jerome, writing to Marcella on five questions, says that the saints who are found at the end of the world will not die but will be taken up alive. Augustine, however, in the book *The City of God*, affirms that everyone then will die. Likewise, Jerome, in his commentary on Matthew, says this statement from the Psalm: *Into all* <note>original: "In omnem [terram]" (Into all the earth). Jerome is likely discussing Psalm 19:4, "Their voice goes out into all the earth."</note>

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

**"Their sound has gone out into all the earth,"** <note>original: *in omnem terram exivit sonus eorum*; a quote from Psalm 19:4, often applied to the Apostles</note> and so forth; and also that saying of Christ, **"This Gospel shall be preached in the whole world,"** were fulfilled through the Apostles. Augustine, however, in his letter to Hesychius—with whom Origen agrees in his commentary on Matthew—holds that this has not yet been fulfilled. Likewise Jerome, in his commentary on the Epistle to Titus, holds that the angels existed and served God for many ages before the visible world was made; Ambrose also holds this in his *Hexameron* <note>original: *Exameron*; a series of homilies on the six days of creation</note>. Augustine, however, in his work on Genesis, holds that they were created at the same time as the empyrean heaven <note>The highest part of heaven, believed by medieval theologians to be the dwelling place of God and the angels</note>.

Likewise Jerome, in his prologue to the Book of Wisdom, holds that the book belongs to Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher</note> and is not to be counted among the Holy Scriptures. Augustine, however, in the third book of his *Retractations*, shows that he once held it was published by Jesus Son of Sirach <note>original: *Iesu Syrach*; the author of the book of Ecclesiasticus</note>, a view he retracts there; and although he does not explicitly state who published it, he nevertheless lists it among the sacred books in his work *On Christian Doctrine*.

Likewise Jerome, in his book of *Hebrew Questions*, says that before God made heaven and earth, He had already established Paradise, because of what is said: "God had planted a paradise from the beginning" <note>original: *a principio*; a reference to Genesis 2:8. Jerome interprets "from the beginning" as being prior to the creation of the world</note>. Augustine, however, in *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, explains "from the beginning" as meaning the third day.

Likewise Augustine, in the book *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, asserts that the entire denial of Peter took place in the courtyard of Annas, and that what was said thereafter, following Jesus being sent to Caiaphas, was spoken as a recapitulation. Jerome, however, in his commentary on Matthew, seems to argue that Peter denied Christ in the courtyard of Caiaphas, a view which Bede seems to agree with in his commentary on Luke.

Likewise Jerome, commenting on that passage of Habakkuk <note>original: *Abauch*</note>, "Your eyes are pure," denies that individual angels are set over individual physical creatures; but Augustine, in his *Eighty-Three Questions*, holds that they are, with whom Origen and John of Damascus <note>original: *Damascenus*</note> agree.

Likewise Jerome, on that passage of Jonah, "Take me up and cast me into the sea," says that it is permissible to die by one's own hand when one's chastity is at risk; but Augustine, in the book *The City of God*, affirms the opposite.

Finally, many such instances are found where the holy doctors <note>The "Church Fathers," the influential early teachers of the Church</note> wrote things contrary to one another while keeping the faith intact. But not all of them come to mind, especially to one in a hurry; nor could this work be elaborated by me with more exact diligence, because I wished to immediately counter the disease of unjust infamy <note>Pico is referring to the accusations of heresy brought against him by a papal commission</note> that was approaching. I intend to write on this matter at another time, with more leisure and care, and thus more things and perhaps better ones. Nevertheless, I will add one point that occurs to me now from Jerome’s letter to Augustine, where he says:

> "Do not wonder if, in your books and especially in your exposition of the Scriptures—which are most obscure—certain things seem to deviate from the straight line; and I say this not because I judge that there are things to be rebuked in your works, for I have never devoted effort to reading them, nor is there a great supply of these copies among us, except for the books of your *Soliloquies* and certain commentaries on the Psalms. If I wished to examine these, I would show—I will not say from myself, for I am nothing—but from the interpretations of the ancient Greeks, that they differ from the truth."

So said Jerome. Just as they disagreed among themselves, so too we may disagree with them in many things, while preserving the faith, the truth of Scripture, and the determination of the Holy Church. The third proof is taken from the special prerogative of Holy Scripture...

Hence Augustine, in an epistle to Jerome, speaks thus: "For I confess to your charity that I have learned to yield this fear and honor only to those books of Scripture which are now called canonical <term>canonical: the books officially recognized by the Church as the inspired Word of God</term>, so that I most firmly believe that none of their authors erred in writing. Or if I encounter anything in those writings that seems contrary to the truth, I will not hesitate to conclude nothing else than that either the manuscript is faulty, or the translator did not grasp the meaning, or I myself have failed to understand it. However, I read the writings of others in such a way that, no matter how great their holiness and learning may be, I do not consider a thing true simply because they thought so, but because they were able to persuade me—either through other passages of Holy Scripture or by probable, that is, evident reason—that it does not stray from the truth. Nevertheless, just as I want my reader to be devoted to me, I do not want my corrector to be devoted to himself. And as I say to the former, 'Do not be a slave to my writings as if they were canonical Scriptures,' but rather, 'In those [Scriptures], believe without hesitation even what you did not believe before you found it; but in these writings of mine, do not hold firmly to what you did not consider certain unless you have understood it to be certain,' so I say to the latter [the corrector], 'Do not correct my writings based on your own opinion or out of contention, but from divine reading or unshakable reason.'" And Augustine in the letter or book to Vincentius says: "Therefore, brother, do not gather or bring false accusations against the writings of lesser bishops—such as Hilary, Cyprian, or Agrippinus <note>Hilary of Poitiers, Cyprian of Carthage, and Agrippinus were highly respected early Christian leaders, but Augustine notes they are still "lesser" than the Apostles</note>—against so many, so clear, and so certain divine testimonies. And in the book *On One Baptism*: "Who does not know that the holy canonical Scripture of the Old and New Testament is contained within its own certain limits, and that it is placed so far above all the later letters of bishops that it is impossible to doubt whether whatever is established as written in it is true or right? # Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

...to depart from the sayings of the saints. For Robert Holcot says that the holy man Anselm was deceived in many things because of his ignorance of logic; and Ockham does not agree with Dionysius concerning the <term>hierarchical acts: the sacred duties or spiritual functions performed by different ranks of angels or clergy</term>; and Scotus, in the third book of the *Sentences* <note>The *Sentences* by Peter Lombard was the standard theological textbook of the Middle Ages; students and masters wrote "commentaries" on it to prove their expertise</note>, nearly destroys the entire argument of Anselm in the book *Why God Became Man*. And so you will often find the same regarding other doctors. I wished to bring these things up here, not so much because of the opinion of Durand <note>Durand of Saint-Pourçain was a theologian known for his independent and often controversial "modern" views</note>—which I neither hold nor have ever held—but because of what will soon be discussed at the beginning of the second question. From all these things I conclude that if there is no express determination of either Holy Scripture or the universal Church against the opinion of Durand, it is presumptuous to call it simply heretical; if, however, such a thing is found, let Durand patiently bear that mark.

But someone will say: "Granted that your meaning (which you declared you intended by that proposition) is Catholic; and granted that the force of the words allows it; can your proposition not also produce that sense of Durand's which you yourself detest? And therefore, did you not err in putting forward a conclusion that could cause scandal in the minds of the faithful?"

To this, I say first: there is one logic for things proposed for <term>disputation: a formal academic debate where a scholar defends a "thesis" against challengers</term>, and another for things intended to be read as doctrine in writing. For when something is proposed for dispute, the proposition is presented as brief, concise, and inexplicit, involving within itself multiple difficulties of both words and meanings, which are to be untangled in the heat of the debate itself. Otherwise, if everything were explained there, no room would be left for the disputation. Therefore, one who puts forward an ambiguous, obscure, or equivocal proposition for dispute is excused because he is going to distinguish and clarify it during the debate. But those who commit something to writing for the purpose of teaching do through writing what is done here through debating; for that reason, everything there ought to be clear, lucid, and settled.

Second, let these most severe censors consider that it is not only difficult, but nearly impossible, to so weigh and examine the words of every proposition one puts forward that there can be no ambiguity of meaning, and no erroneous opinion can be drawn from it. Indeed, I do not wish to claim for my propositions a quality that many Gospel and Apostolic propositions do not have; for many are to be found among them which have multiple interpretations and can be turned toward an erroneous sense—nay, which at first glance even seem to sound like heresy. From this, all heresies have sprouted: namely, while some did not look so much into the depth of meaning as they attended to what the "bark" or "shell" of the Gospel words sounded like. 

From this, Arius, hearing "The Father is greater than I" <note>John 14:28</note>, believed the Father to be greater than the Son and said the Son was a creature. From this, Helvidius, hearing that "Joseph knew not Mary until she brought forth her firstborn" <note>Matthew 1:25</note>, attending more to the grammatical force of that word "until" <note>original: *donec*</note>, doubted the perpetual virginity of Mary against the truth of the Gospel sense. From this, Marcion, reading that word of Paul, "But the law entered in that sin might abound" <note>Romans 5:20</note>, believed the law...
