...that the law of Moses was evil and came from an evil principle. Following the <term>Manichaean</term><note>A dualist religious movement that saw the world as a struggle between good/light and evil/darkness; they often rejected the Old Testament as the work of an evil deity</note> and <term>Basilides</term><note>An early Christian gnostic teacher in Alexandria</note> who, reading the passage *I once lived without the law* <note>original: "Ego aliquando sine lege vivebam," from Romans 7:9</note>, believed that the soul of **Paul** had once lived in another body. From this, **Eunomius**, hearing Christ responding to the Jews who were accusing Him because He called Himself the Son of God, noted that it was written: *I have said, ye are gods and all of you are children of the most High* <note>Psalm 82:6</note>. By attending to the thing said and to what was in the second response, rather than the intention and purpose of the respondent, he believed that Christ is called the Son of God in the same way that any holy person is called a son of God. Similarly, this proposition—*That day neither the Son knows* <note>Mark 13:32, a famous Christological difficulty</note>—was for many an occasion for believing that the Father understands more than the Son believes. If we interpret this according to the sense that the words commonly produce, it seems to suggest that, even though the truth of the hidden sense is otherwise. I could bring forward infinite similar propositions from the canon of the scriptures, and therefore **Hilary** <note>Saint Hilary of Poitiers, a 4th-century theologian known as the "Hammer of the Arians"</note> said well: *The understanding of things said must be assumed from the causes of the speaking, because the matter is not subject to the speech, but the speech to the matter.* And the <term>gloss</term><note>A standard marginal or interlinear commentary on a text</note> upon that text says: *We ought not always to understand things as the words seem to sound at first glance, especially where they are ambiguous, but we ought to return to the intention of the speaker.* And **Gregory** says: *Frequently, while the property of words is attended to, the sense of truth is lost.* And **Gregory** in the 26th book of his *Morals*: *One ought not to consider the words, but the will and the intention, because the intention ought not to serve the words, but the words the intention.* And **Jerome** testifies in his *Epistle to the Galatians*: *The Gospel is not in the words of the scriptures, but in the sense; not on the surface, but in the marrow; not in the leaves of the speeches, but in the root of reason.* For this reason, **Ockham** in his *Dialogue* falsifies this common proposition: *words are to be received not from the opinions of individuals, but from common usage,* especially in its second part. For he says: *That in ambiguous and multiple words, one must not recur to the common understanding, but rather to the intention of the speakers.* And so, while there is ambiguity in the doctrine of anyone speaking or writing, one must similarly recur to the intention of the speaker, so that he may explain himself and express the true sense which the force of the words allows. Nor is he to be rejected unless it can be proven <note>abbreviation for "that" or "which"</note> that such a true sense would be contrary to his other sayings, or would be irrelevant to his purpose. The same doctor says that even in simple speech one must recur to the intention of the speaker, and one must stand by his interpretation, unless it is established—either probably or by violent presumption—that he used such an ambiguous way of speaking to deceive or for some other evil end. From all these things, I conclude that I have not erred, who with a protestation probably put forward a multifaceted proposition to be declared during the dispute—which nevertheless can make no sense that some doctor, not rejected or not yet declared as such by the Church, has not held. Rather, those have erred who [condemn] a proposition having a Catholic sense which the force of [the words allows]...

Even if they had done so before my sense was declared, they might perhaps have erred more excusably; yet, because they are truly learned, they could have recognized on their own that the proposition has a double meaning. Observing this, they should not have simply condemned it, but rather interpreted it in its good sense. For **Augustine**, in his book *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, explaining that passage of **Matthew**: *Judge not, and you shall not be judged* <note>original: "Nolite iudicare & non iudicabimini"; Matthew 7:1</note>, says: "In this place, I believe nothing else is commanded except that we should interpret those deeds whose intent is doubtful in the better light." For concerning neutral deeds, which can be done with both a good and an evil intent, it is rash to judge, and especially to condemn. Therefore, what **Augustine** says regarding things that are *done*, let us likewise understand as being said regarding things that are *spoken*. Thus, applying **Augustine's** sentiment to theoretical matters, let us conclude: that in those sayings which can have both a good and a bad meaning, it is rash to judge, and especially to condemn.

## GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA’S DISPUTATION ON THE PUNISHMENT of mortal sin.

**I**t is, moreover, the second conclusion which those men condemned: *For a <term>mortal sin</term><note>In Catholic theology, a "mortal" or deadly sin is a grave offense that destroys divine charity in the soul; Pico is questioning the logic of its eternal punishment</note> of finite time, an infinite punishment according to time is not owed, but only a finite one.* And because while I placed the conclusion in my little book, these preceding words were added: *Unless they were the sayings of the saints, which in the manifest light of their speech seem to say the opposite, I would firmly assert the following conclusions; I assert, however, that they are probable, and can be reasonably defended.* The first of these is this: *Mortal sin is in itself a finite evil.* The second is this: *For a mortal sin of finite time, etc.* A certain Master <note>A Master of Theology, likely one of the inquisitors on the papal commission</note>, having a dispute with me concerning this conclusion, said: "What other testimony do we seek that your conclusion is heretical? Since you yourself manifestly say that it is against the sayings of the saints; for the logical consequence holds: 'It is against the sayings of the saints, therefore it is heretical.'" I showed him then, as I shall also show below, how my conclusion was in no way repugnant to the opinions of the saints, and how the words were to be understood. But even if it were the case that the conclusion was against the sayings of the saints, any person can see from what was said above regarding the first conclusion how much his "logical consequence" was worth, and how unworthy it was of a theologian as learned as he boasted himself to be. I know what I might say here regarding that Master: for he is the one who so often sent letters back to his home country promising, as it were, a trophy and a triumph over me. But I wish, as I promised from the beginning, to plead my case with reasons, not with insults. I come now to the conclusion: and because those Masters judged both the conclusion itself and the responses I gave them when they questioned me on this conclusion to be false, erroneous, and heretical, I wish first to declare that the conclusion itself is Catholic and in harmony with the sayings of almost all the doctors. I say...

...moreover, [it is] mine, because if you take it in a sense other than the one I intend through it, then it is no longer that conclusion of mine which I proposed. For a proposition is manifold—it contains many propositions—and so I wish to declare that my responses themselves are of such a nature, both concerning the conclusion itself and the responses, by always declaring that the power of the words allows for my meanings—that is, those which I intend through them. For the declaration of this conclusion, five points must be noted.

**First**, it should be noted that in sin, two things can be considered: a **turning toward a created good** <note>original: "conversio ad bonum creatum"; choosing a temporary, worldly pleasure over God</note> and a **turning away from the unchangeable and uncreated good** <note>original: "aversio à bono incommuntabili & increato"; rejecting God</note>. In the first way, sin is a finite evil, even according to all the doctors <note>the "doctors" are established authoritative theologians like Thomas Aquinas</note>; in the second way, sin is a finite evil according to the common path [of reasoning]. And because the turning toward a created good, which the sinner abuses by sinning, belongs to the intrinsic nature of the sin itself, it is therefore said that sin is **intrinsically a finite evil**. However, the turning away from the uncreated good makes it **extrinsically infinite**, because it is called an infinite evil only insofar as it is a turning away from an infinite good; thus, it only remains that it is an extrinsic and objective infinite evil.

**Second**, note that by **"time"** we can understand only the <term>time of the way</term> <note>original: "tempus viae"; the period of a person's life on earth during which they can still merit or sin</note>. In this way, it is certain that neither sin nor anything else pertaining to man can be infinite according to time, since the "time of the way" for any traveler is not only finite in duration but also brief. In another way, we can understand "time" as the time of both the "way" and the "end" <note>the "end" or *terminus* refers to the state after death, i.e., eternity</note>; this is how it is taken in the conclusion, and thus something in man can indeed last through infinite time, as is evident.

**Third**, note that <term>mortal sin</term> can be understood in two ways. In one way, as the **prohibited act** itself, or the omission of an act commanded by God. In another way, for the **guilt** <note>original: "reatus"; the state of being liable for punishment that remains after the sinful act is over</note> left behind from the aforesaid prohibited act or omission. This guilt is indeed called "sin" in many places of Holy Scripture, and by such "sin," someone is called a "sinner" even when the act of sin (spoken of in the first way) has ceased or passed away. From this third point, it is clear that it is reasonable to say that although in someone who is damned for a mortal sin, the sin itself for which they are damned eventually ends—in terms of the intrinsic entity of the act—the sin does not end in terms of the **guilt**. Indeed, if it ended in that way, eternal punishment would not be owed to them; thus the sin to which punishment is due is infinite—infinite according to time in respect to its guilt.

**Fourth**, it should be noted that **"to be owed"** <note>original: "deberi"</note> is understood in two ways, or can be understood in two ways when saying that some punishment is "owed" to a sin. In one way, something is said to be "owed" to someone which will eventually be rendered to them. In this sense, it is said reasonably and Catholically that for a sin of finite time—in terms of its intrinsic entity and its guilt—infinite punishment according to time is not "owed." It is in this way that the present conclusion is understood: that to a sin of finite time [punishment] is not owed, etc. For every sin to which [punishment] is "owed" in this way—that is, for which punishment will eventually be rendered—

...is infinite, in the manner previously stated, nor is anyone ever condemned unless the sin for which they are condemned is infinite in that same way—that is, in its duration. However, this conclusion also has another **Catholic sense**, namely this: that an infinite punishment is never "due" <note>original: "debetur"; Pico is distinguishing between what a sin deserves in theory and what is actually required to be paid out by God's justice</note> in the sense that it is actually rendered to someone for a specific duration, unless that person is **finally impenitent** <note>remaining unrepentant until the moment of death</note> and ceases to repent forever for the sin they committed or neglected during life. Thus, for a temporal sin <note>a sin committed in a limited moment of time</note>, an infinite punishment is "due" in the aforementioned way only if the sinner does not return to justice.

For just as repentance brings an end to sin in terms of its acceptance [by God], according to the saying: *At whatever hour the sinner shall groan [with regret], etc.* <note>A reference to Ezekiel 18:21–22, a common proof-text for the power of repentance</note>, so too does **impenitence** regarding a sin perpetuate that sin in its guilt and in its liability to infinite punishment. In this way, an infinite punishment is never "due" to anyone in that first sense unless they possess a sin that is infinite in its duration. 

For the vengeance which God seeks from the sinner is that the sinner should return spontaneously to the duty of obedience by grieving for their contempt; otherwise, the sinner will be tormented for as long as they choose to remain in that state.

In another way, it can be understood that something is "due" to someone because they are worthily or unworthily deserving of it, and that it will indeed be rendered to them if they die in that state. In this sense, for a **mortal sin** <note>a grave sin that causes the loss of divine grace</note> of a finite duration, an infinite punishment is "due." This is because whoever commits a mortal sin, even in the space of a single hour, is deserving of infinite punishment, and that punishment will be rendered to them if they finally depart [this life] in that state—even assuming they have no other sin that is infinite in duration. 

This distinction regarding the word **"due"** <note>original: "deberi"</note> is in frequent use among theologians. From this distinction, the **Doctors** <note>authoritative church theologians, such as Thomas Aquinas or Duns Scotus</note> say that for a person "foreknown" <note>original: "præscito"; someone God knows will eventually be damned</note>, eternal life is not "due" for a meritorious act performed while they are in a state of grace. This is because, using the first sense of "due," it will never actually be rendered to them. Similarly, it is said that for a person "predestined" <note>someone chosen by God for salvation</note>, eternal punishment is not "due" while they are in a state of mortal sin, because it will never be rendered to them, since that sin will be ended and they will not die in it, but rather in a state of grace.

From the preceding points, it is clear that my conclusion possesses a Catholic sense, even according to the customary way of speaking used by Catholic doctors. It should not have been condemned as heretical, false, or erroneous, since its opposite is actually more likely to be false and erroneous. Indeed, it was a mark of the **greatest ignorance** <note>original: "ruditatis aut maximæ"</note> to believe that by the aforementioned conclusion I intended to deny the eternal punishment of the damned. On the contrary, my conclusion provides an investigation into the *cause* for which the damned are punished eternally. I stated that this cause is the **perpetuation of guilt** in the soul of the sinner through their final impenitence and their perpetual failure to regret their sin. This opinion not only seems not to be heretical, but so Catholic that no one—if they are truly Catholic and practiced in the sacred scriptures—could rightly or reasonably deny it. 

Furthermore, that the proposition conveys this meaning by the very force of its terms is clear; for the proposition says: **An infinite punishment in duration is not due for a mortal sin of finite time.** In this proposition, I take "due" to mean that which will eventually be paid out—a usage which has already been shown above to be most common among the Doctors—and I take...

...sin as both offense and guilt, a usage that is not only imprecise or figurative, but frequent in the sacred scriptures. For after the <term>Master of the Sentences</term> <note>original: "Magister sententiarum"; this refers to Peter Lombard, whose work was the standard textbook for medieval theology students</note> inquires in his second book whether, once the act of sinning has passed, the sin remains in the one who sinned until they repent, he responds thus: "It must not be ignored that sins exist in someone in two ways—by the act itself and by the guilt—and they pass away in those same two ways." <term>Durandus</term> <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain, a prominent 14th-century philosopher and theologian</note> also says in the same place that the ending of a sin is understood in two ways: one way through the mere cessation of the act, and the other way through the forgiveness of the sin. Moreover, <term>Thomas</term> <note>Thomas Aquinas, the most influential of the Scholastic theologians</note> expressly states there that guilt is also sometimes called "sin," saying: "Guilt, standing as a mediator between the fault and the punishment, takes on the name of either extreme." <note>original: "Reatus medians inter culpam & poenam, sortitur nomen utriusque extremi"</note> 

But is sin not also understood as guilt in the following passage? *It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from sins.* <note>original: "Sancta ergo & salubris est cogitatio, pro defunctis exorare, ut à peccatis solvantur"; a reference to 2 Maccabees 12:46</note> For those deceased for whom we must pray so they may be loosed from sins are not in a state of sin—taking "sin" to mean mortal fault—nor are they loosed from such a sin after death; rather, they are loosed only from sin taken to mean the penalty or the <term>liability to punishment</term> <note>original: "reatu poenae"; the legal obligation to undergo punishment for a past act</note>. In this same way, sin is also understood here: *Redeem your sins with almsgiving* <note>original: "Peccata tua eleemosynis redime"; a reference to Daniel 4:24</note>; and so it is in many other passages of Scripture. 

Therefore, if the sense of my proposition is Catholic, and the usage of the terms in the proposition is Catholic and highly approved, why was there any reason to condemn this conclusion of mine as heretical? 

Now I come to my responses. First, I said that if someone persists in mortal sin only for a finite time, they will not be punished except for a finite time; this statement is proven true in three ways. 

**First**, when we take "mortal sin" to mean guilt, and not the act of commission or omission, as was said in the declaration of the conclusion. 

**Second**, it should be noted that in mortal sin, according to the rigors of logic, the term is understood <gloss>is understood</gloss> generally and not specifically. 

**Third**, because it is true that if the one who sinned persisted only for a finite time in a specific sin—for example, in the neglect of repenting for their sin—such that they eventually repented of it, they would not be punished for it except for a finite time. And that I intended these Catholic meanings, and nothing discordant with the faith, is clear from what I added in my response: I stated that it remains consistent with the truth of the conclusion that anyone departing this life in mortal sin will be punished forever. 

However, when I was further asked whether someone who sins with only one mortal sin for a finite time and dies unrepentant is punished forever? I answered: yes. But I said that such a person is not punished for that *act* alone; this was a truthful answer to the question asked. For even though it is true that if they had committed only that act, they would be punished eternally, once the question stipulates that this person "dies unrepentant," they are also punished for the <term>impenitence</term> <note>original: "impoenitentia"; the state of refusing to repent</note> itself—indeed, for infinite omissions of repentance, and for infinite other acts, whether total or partial, in which the damned person persists. For just as the damned person continuously wills evil, so they continuously sin and deserve punishment—not indeed...

Briefly recapitulating, my intention in this conclusion is this: it is certainly true that a mortal sin committed in finite time is worthy of <term>eternal punishment</term> <note>original: "pœna æterna"</note>. Nevertheless, while a mortal sin is finite in time—not only regarding its intrinsic, positive entity as an act prohibited by God (or the privative entity of omitting an act commanded by God), but also regarding its **imputation** <note>the theological assignment of the act to the person's account</note> or acceptance, and also the guilt and **stain** <note>original: "macula"; the lasting spiritual damage or "mark" left on the soul after the act of sinning</note> which is frequently called "sin" in many places in scripture and in the common speech of the Doctors. This state is so inherent to the nature of a sin to be punished eternally that if said imputation or stain does not remain, eternal punishment would never be owed to that sin, nor would it ever be paid.

Concerning such a sin, I say—provided it is finite in all the aforementioned ways, which occurs through repentance (at least concerning actual mortal sin)—that eternal punishment is *not* owed to it. By "owed," I mean it will eventually be returned or paid out to him. Thus we say that every man who is damned dies in the sin for which he is damned.

## GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA’S DISCOURSE ON THE
## Adoration of the Cross.

**T**he third conclusion which they condemned was this: Neither the cross of Christ, nor any image, is to be adored with the adoration of <term>latria</term> <note>original: "latriae"; in Catholic theology, this is the highest form of worship, strictly reserved for the Holy Trinity alone</note>, even in the manner that <term>Thomas</term> <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican friar and Doctor of the Church</note> posits. This conclusion, condemned by them, I believe to be not only Catholic, but even truer than its opposite, which is this: The cross of Christ and images are to be adored with *latria*, in the manner that Thomas posits. For the opinion of Thomas in this matter seems less reasonable to me than the opinion of <term>Durandus</term> <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain (c. 1275–1334), a theologian known for often disagreeing with Aquinas</note> and <term>Henry of Ghent</term>, <term>Johannes de Guarra</term>, <term>Robert Holcot</term>, <term>Petrus de Aquila</term>, and many others, whom I follow in this conclusion. So that this may become clear, I will first set forth the opinion of Thomas, which I do not hold, and then the opinion of the <term>Doctors</term> <note>recognized authoritative teachers of the Church</note> whom I follow. From these it will be evident that the determination of those <term>Masters</term> <note>the committee of theologians examining Pico’s work</note> regarding my conclusion—besides being neither right nor just—presupposes something entirely opposite to what I intend in my conclusion. Thomas says, therefore, that because (as <term>the Philosopher</term> <note>Aristotle</note> says in his book *On Memory and Reminiscence*) there is a twofold movement of the soul toward an image: one toward the image itself, insofar as it is a certain thing; the other toward the image insofar as it is the image of another. Between these two movements there is a difference, because the first movement, by which something moves toward the image as it is a certain thing, is distinct from the movement toward the thing of which it is an image. However, the second movement, which is toward the image insofar as it is an image, is one and the same as that which is toward the thing itself. Therefore, he concludes that although adoration is not owed to the image of Christ as a thing in itself, yet insofar as it is an image, the same reverence is owed to it as is owed to Christ himself, which is the adoration of *latria*. This is Thomas’s way of thinking, which rightly seems strange and dangerous to other Doctors; for the image itself, even as an image, is distinct from the thing imagined <note>original: "imaginato"; the subject depicted in the image</note>, because as such it is referred to the thing imagined as to something distinct from itself. Therefore, even if as such it were to <term>terminate</term> <note>original: "terminabit"; in this context, to be the final object or recipient of the act</note> the adoration of *latria*, it seems to follow that something other than God will be adored with *latria*, which is absurd. Nor can it be said, as <term>Capreolus</term> <note>Jean Capréolus (c. 1380–1444), the "Prince of Thomists," who defended Aquinas’s views</note> says (wishing to save Thomas's statement), that the image itself is not adored separately, but that the image and the thing imagined are one total object of adoration. For either the image itself—which is a created, relative being—is one part of this total object, or it is not. If it is not, then it should not be said that one total object is made from those two. For from such a statement it follows that each of them is a partial object, even if one of them is more principal. If it *is* a part, it follows that some created thing, belonging to the category of relation, will terminate the adoration of *latria* at least partially—to say which certainly seems poorly Catholic, the more so...

--- Page 190 ---
<meta>This page continues Pico’s refutation of the charge that he erroneously denied the adoration of the Cross. On the previous page, he began contrasting the view of Thomas Aquinas with his own preferred authorities, such as Durandus and Henry of Ghent.</meta>

<page-num>156</page-num>
<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

that not only can this not be said of a created thing, but even the persons within the Godhead, by reason of their personal property, are relatively not the formal object of adoration. However, the foundation used by **Thomas** seems insufficiently effective; for when the **Philosopher** <note>Aristotle, often referred to simply as "The Philosopher" in medieval scholarship</note> says that the movement of the soul toward the image and toward the thing represented is the same, he does not mean it in the sense that the soul declares the image, insofar as it is an image, to be identical with the original model—and thus that whatever is owed to one is also owed to the other. Rather, the Philosopher only intends this: that the act of remembering, by which the soul is moved toward an image in a recollective way, also terminates at the thing represented.

There is also another true sense, which is: because if I have a definitive concept of one relative term, I also understand the other. But that every movement of the soul, and especially of the will, is the same toward the image and the thing represented, the Philosopher in no way intends. This is clear from a similar case even according to the way of speaking used by Thomas himself. For he often says that the movement of the will is the same whether the will is carried toward the end <note>the ultimate goal</note> or toward those things which lead to the end when it desires them for the sake of that end; and yet it is also certain, according to him, that while that movement is "enjoyment" <note>original: "fruitio"</note> when it reaches the end, it is "use" <note>original: "usus"</note> and not enjoyment when it reaches those things which lead to the end.

Therefore, following the other doctors, it seems that it should by no means be said that we adore the image of Christ, even as it is an image, with the adoration of <term>latria</term> <note>the highest form of worship due to God alone</note>. This is because, as such, it is a created thing not united to the divinity, and what is more, as such it is a relative entity. For this reason, <term>Durandus</term> says that this proposition—*The Cross of Christ is adored with latria*—is false in its proper sense, but it has a true improper sense, which is this: Christ, as remembered through the cross, or as present in the cross (just as the thing represented is present in its image), is adored with the same adoration as if he were present in himself. And according to this sense I also concede this proposition: *The Cross is adored with the adoration of latria*. This is therefore what Durandus says: that it is adored "recollectively."

<term>Robert Holcot</term> intends the same opinion when he says: "It is a more proper way of speaking to say, 'We adore *before* the cross,' than to say, 'We adore the cross.'" Finally, <term>Henry of Ghent</term> and <term>Johannes de Guarra</term> intend the same opinion when they say that it is adored "incidentally" <note>original: "per accidens"</note>, and <term>Petrus de Aquila</term> says the same. However, that which Henry and Johannes de Guarra add further (who speak more fully on this matter) is this: they say that the honor which is owed in itself to the thing represented and remembered is owed to the image "incidentally" or "recollectively." Now, it is certain that there is nothing to which <term>latria</term> is owed in itself, except the Triune God, and Christ on account of the unity of his person—for an image of God cannot essentially exist. It remains that if there is any image to which <term>latria</term> is owed incidentally and recollectively, it would be the image of Christ.

But because such an image primarily represents Christ's humanity to us, and only secondarily his divinity, it seems that primarily there is owed to it incidentally such honor as is owed in itself to the humanity of Christ. Now, the humanity of Christ, taken by itself, is only adored with <term>hyperdulia</term> <note>original: "ὑπερδουλεία"; a level of veneration higher than that given to saints but lower than that given to God, often reserved for Christ's humanity or the Virgin Mary</note>; therefore, also to such an image, 

<meta>Catchword: primas (first)</meta>

<summary>Pico argues against Thomas Aquinas's view that images should receive the same worship (latria) as the thing they represent, siding instead with theologians who distinguish between the physical object and the divine reality it reminds the believer of.</summary>

<header>Defense.</header>
<sig>O</sig>

->Defense.<-

Primarily, and only by accident, the adoration of <gloss>hyperdulia <note>original: "ὑπερδουλίας"; a level of veneration higher than that given to saints but lower than the worship due to God alone</note></gloss> will be owed to an image. Secondarily, however, and also by accident, even the adoration of <term>latria <note>the highest form of worship, reserved for the Holy Trinity alone</note></term> will be owed to it, in the manner already described: because the image itself also secondarily represents and reminds us of the divinity of Christ. In this matter, **Henry of Ghent** is in agreement with **Francis of Meyronnes** and all the **Scotists** <note>followers of the philosopher John Duns Scotus</note>, who say that *latria* is not owed to the humanity of Christ itself. **Thomas Aquinas**, however, because he seems to hold the opposite view regarding the adoration of Christ's humanity, would perhaps also disagree with Henry in this case. Indeed, the opinion of Thomas—as Francis says in his third book—is somewhat dangerous; in this matter of adoration, his path does not seem to me to be very safe. For he went so far as to say in his *Commentary on the Sentences* <note>Book III of the "Sentences" of Peter Lombard, a standard theology textbook</note> that the Cross of Christ on which He hung, even as an inanimate thing, was owed some degree of adoration. Yet we know, according to all theology, that something which cannot be a subject capable of receiving holiness or virtue cannot be the endpoint of any adoration. Even **John Capreolus**, that great defender of Thomas, himself admits that this statement of Thomas’s cannot be defended. He has no other way to "save" Thomas’s reputation except by saying that Thomas himself seems to have felt differently later, in his *Summa Theologiae*.

From these points, it can be seen how "Catholic" <note>meaning orthodox or in line with universal Church teaching</note> my conclusion is, and how much more reasonable it is than its opposite, and more in harmony with the common path of the theologians. Briefly summarizing its meaning, I say that this proposition—"The Cross of Christ is adored"—can have two meanings. One is the "proper" sense: that the Cross of Christ—whether as a physical thing, an image, or as a partial or total object—is adored as the *endpoint* of the adoration. This is the sense Thomas intends, and it is the sense I deny. The other is the "improper" sense of the said proposition: that the Cross of Christ is adored—meaning Christ is adored *in it* as in a memorial of Him—as if He were present in Himself. I grant this second sense, and I pray with the Church, saying:

> Hail, O Cross, our only hope. <note>original: "O Crux aue spes unica"; a line from the hymn "Vexilla Regis"</note>

and,

> We adore your Cross, O Lord. <note>original: "Crucem tuam adoramus Domine"; a traditional antiphon</note>

Many things can now be made clear from what has been said. First, it is clear what I meant when I said elsewhere that, following the opinion of **Henry of Ghent** and **John of Guarra**, <term>hyperdulia</term> is owed to an image of the Crucified. This was to be understood by reason of that which is primarily brought to our memory, which is the humanity of Christ. I spoke of this in a truncated way because I was referring to those authors, whom I assumed these Masters <note>Pico's critics</note>—being veterans—had already read and re-read ten times over. Second, it is clear that they spoke falsely when they said I deny every mode of the adoration of *latria*. I expressly said in my conclusion that I deny the *mode of Thomas*. Even if I had not said that, but the proposition simply stood as "Neither the Cross nor any image is to be adored with *latria*," that proposition would still not deny every mode of *latria* by the virtue of its phrasing. For it is clear, according to good logic, that the negation or distribution of a "multiple term" <note>a word with multiple meanings or applications</note> does not negate or distribute it for every possible instance of every meaning. Otherwise, the proposition "Every dog is a star" <note>A classic medieval logical puzzle: "canis" in Latin means both the animal and the Dog Star, Sirius</note> would have to be simply accepted or simply denied.

He critiques Thomas Aquinas's view as potentially dangerous and aligns himself with the Scotist tradition and Henry of Ghent.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s defense against the condemnation of his thirteenth thesis. He is arguing that his denial of "latria" (the highest form of worship) for the Cross is logically and theologically sound, using the distinction between "proper" and "improper" meanings of words.</meta>

<page-num>158</page-num>
<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

Just as one does not say collectively <note>original: "copulativè"; a logical term meaning to join multiple subjects under one predicate</note> that "every dog—whether the celestial dog <note>the star Sirius</note>, the sea dog <note>a shark or seal</note>, and the barking dog—is a star," even though the term "dog" is applied to all of them individually; so it is with this negative statement: "The cross is not adored with the adoration of *latria*." <term>Latria <note>The highest form of worship, which Catholic theology reserves for God alone</note></term> is an equivocal term when applied to the Cross: it can mean adoration as a final goal <note>original: "per modum termini"</note> or adoration as a reminder <note>original: "per modum rememorativi"</note>. Thus, one does not deny every mode of adoration collectively, but rather each one individually.

Thirdly, it is clear that this proposition could have been stated even absolutely and without qualification: **"The Cross is not to be adored with the adoration of latria."** This is because, in its proper sense, the statement is true—or at least more probable than its opposite. The proper sense of a word should be prioritized according to the rigor of speech rather than an improper sense in which the statement would be false. For just as an <term>analogical term <note>A word that has a primary meaning and several related secondary meanings</note></term> stands for its most famous or primary meaning when used on its own, so too a statement that has both a proper and an improper sense should be understood according to its proper sense if no further specification is given.

Therefore, as I said, I could have stated the thesis without qualification, intending to clarify the sense in which I understood it during the actual debate. From this I infer that, while in a complex proposition it is perhaps better to do as I did—to specify the sense in which it is posed—there is nonetheless a greater defect in condemning a proposition "simply and without distinction" <note>original: "indistinctè & simpliciter"</note> when it is true in its proper sense, just because it is false in an improper sense. It is better to pose the proposition based on the truth of its proper meaning.

I wanted to note this here not only for this specific conclusion (in which I specifically reject the method of **Thomas Aquinas**), but also for my other conclusions. Although those others have a Catholic meaning—which I have always promised to clarify, as I am doing now—they were nevertheless condemned simply and without distinction. 

The truth is, however it may stand with my conclusion, my accusers cannot excuse their condemnation of it from error. I declare this evidently: their formal determination was as follows. Because he <note>Pico, referring to himself in the third person as viewed by the judges</note> "denies every mode of adoration of *latria* toward the Cross, according to the way of Catholic doctors and the prayer which the Universal Church offers to the Cross," they stated: "Therefore we say the aforesaid conclusion is scandalous, offensive to pious ears <note>original: "piarum aurium offensivam"; a standard ecclesiastical legal grade of censure for ideas that might shock the faithful</note>, and against the custom of the Universal Church." 

This was precisely their judgment. First, let them tell me: where does it appear to them that I deny *every* mode of adoration of *latria* toward the Cross according to the way of Catholic doctors? They certainly do not get this from my conclusion, in which I expressly and specifically say that I am rejecting the "mode of Thomas." Unless—and I cannot believe this—they have seen no other doctor and therefore imagine that the "mode of Thomas" is the *only* mode. 

Furthermore, they could not have taken this from my formal response, which claimed I denied every mode of *latria* according to the way of Catholic doctors. In that response, I expressly stated that I grant that mode which is granted by **John of Guara** (who was the teacher of **Duns Scotus**) and the solemn doctor **Henry of Ghent**. Unless, perhaps, they wish to say that both Henry and John are not Catholics.

...which necessarily follows from their own words. For since I told them that I follow Henry <note>Henry of Ghent (c. 1217–1293), a major Scholastic philosopher</note> and John <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), another pivotal theologian</note>, and they then say that I do not follow Catholic doctors, who would not infer from this that those whom I said I followed are not Catholic doctors? Who could bear this? Who could endure it with a calm mind? That Henry and John—such illustrious and excellent doctors, lights of the Church, bulwarks of the faith—should be rejected as non-Catholics, and consequently as heretics and infidels. I cannot help but be irritated at times, yet I believe I am in the right. Now let us attend to the second error. They say that "The conclusion is scandalous, and offensive to pious ears, and against the custom of the universal Church." O most damned judgment! Let them see how they cannot escape the snares: for either my conclusion denies only the mode of Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274). Pico argues that his disagreement is only with Thomas’s specific explanation of how images are worshipped</note>, in the manner explained above—and then it is clear my conclusion is not against the custom of the Church (as has been most extensively declared)—or, as they wish, it denies every mode of adoration and denies that images are to be adored in the customary form of the Church. In that case, the conclusion is not "scandalous" or "offensive to pious ears," but simply heretical. For according to Damascenus <note>John of Damascus (c. 675–749), who defended the use of icons</note>, the honor shown to an image according to the rite of the Church reaches the <term>prototype <note>original: "prototypon"; the original person or being represented by the image</note></term>. He who does not observe the Church’s manner in adoring images does not adore the thing imaged and represented (which is God) with <term>latria <note>The highest form of worship, reserved for God alone</note></term>. Therefore, whoever judges a conclusion that denies this as "scandalous" rather than "simply heretical" must himself be called simply a heretic.

## DISPUTATION OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA ON WHETHER
## AN IRRATIONAL NATURE CAN BE ASSUMED BY A DIVINE PERSON.

**T**he fourth conclusion condemned by these men is this: **I do not assent to the common opinion of theologians who say that God can assume any nature; rather, I grant this only regarding a rational nature.** Through this conclusion, I do not intend to deny that God *can* <term>assume <note>original: "suppositare"; a technical term for the Hypostatic Union, where a Divine Person takes on a created nature, as in the Incarnation</note></term> any nature. Rather, I only intend to deny a particular and explicit assent to this assertion. There is a great difference between these two intentions: "God can assume any nature" [as an assertion] and [my refusal to assent to it]. Even if this were possible according to the <term>absolute power of God <note>The theological concept that God can do anything that does not involve a logical contradiction, regardless of the laws of nature He established</note></term>, a proposition that, by the force of its words, only denies a positive, explicit assent to that specific saying does not disparage the omnipotence of God, nor does it savor of any heresy. The reason is this: Not every believer is bound to assent explicitly and in particular to all things possible according to the absolute omnipotence of God, or to profess these things explicitly. It is sufficient to believe some such things generally and implicitly, and to stubbornly disbelieve nothing. Therefore, it was not without a mystery <note>i.e., not without a deliberate reason or hidden purpose</note> that I did not phrase the conclusion in these terms: "God *cannot* assume any nature," but rather: "I do not assent to the opinion saying that God can assume any nature." From which conclusion, by the force of the words—

[...of the] operation, it cannot be inferred that God cannot do this. Nor can it be said that this is asserted by me in the conclusion; for it is not in the first part, which is negative, nor in the second, from which it only follows that a permissive act <note>original: "actus concessivus"</note> is held only regarding a rational nature <note>A nature capable of reason, such as a human or an angel.</note> distinctly—namely, and in particular. I therefore deny that there is a particular and explicit assent to this assertion in me: **God can assume the personhood of any nature.** And I can reasonably deny it, both because the opposite—even if it were true—is unknown to us in particular and explicitly, and it seems I am not obliged to believe it explicitly; and especially because it is not easy to falsify or disprove that assertion: "God cannot, etc.," as if it were derogatory to God's omnipotence.

This is especially confirmed by the authority of the solemn doctor, Henry of Ghent <note>c. 1217–1293, a hugely influential theologian at the University of Paris.</note>, who, after having held the opposite opinion—namely, that any nature could be assumed—later inclined toward this view: that only a rational nature can be assumed. For Henry writes as follows:

"Since there is no doubt about the possibility of the nature to be assumed—whether God can assume any assumable nature for you—therefore the entire difficulty of this question turns on the possibility of the nature being assumed. And there are two solemn positions on this matter. For the more common and solemn position, which I myself was once accustomed to assent to somewhat, says: 'That any nature subsisting in creatures can be assumed.' And these people hold that some nature is 'elevatable' <note>Capable of being raised to a union with the divine.</note> to which a corresponding power is not 'elevatable'—which does not seem to me to be something that can be reasonably posited. To understand this, it must be noted that God exists in creatures in two ways: one way naturally and in a manner fitting to nature; the other way voluntarily and in a manner exceeding the limits of nature.

In the first way, He exists through **indwelling** <term>illapsus<note>Literally a "flowing into"; the way God is naturally present in all things to keep them in existence.</note></term> in every nature. In the second way, He exists only in a nature assumed through **mutual indwelling** <term>circumincessio<note>A term describing the most intimate union between God and a created nature, specifically in the Incarnation.</note></term>. And although through 'indwelling' God is internal to every creature—and more internal than the creature is to itself or the form is to matter—nevertheless, through 'mutual indwelling,' He becomes most internal to every assumed nature, and more internal than He is in any nature through 'indwelling' alone. For through the intimacy of the 'mutual indwelling' of the assumed nature, the One assuming unites Himself ineffably and incomprehensibly to the assumed nature. Because of this, it is necessary for the assumed nature to lose its own 'being of subsistence' <note>Its independent existence as a separate individual thing.</note>, if it had one before the assumption; or, if it never had it, to enter into the 'being of subsistence' of the Nature into which it is assumed, so that there is the same **individual person** <term>suppositum<note>The "supposit" is the technical term for the "who" or the underlying subject that "owns" a nature; in Christ, the Divine Person is the supposit for both human and divine natures.</note></term> subsisting in a dual nature. For each of those natures, in their union, retains its own proper 'being of essence.'

Furthermore, through 'indwelling,' God is made internal to every creature naturally and in a manner fitting to nature, for two purposes: namely, for the 'first act' of nature, which is the stabilizing of being so that it persists; and for the 'second act' of nature, which is the operation to be produced so that it exists. For without that 'indwelling,' the creature cannot persist in being, nor call forth its own proper operation, because through 'indwelling' God preserves the creature in being and, by cooperating, [preserves] every action of its own..."

## Apologia.

He provides operation to it, as Gregory says in the 16th book of the *Moralia* <note>Gregory the Great (c. 540–604), a Pope and Doctor of the Church; his *Moralia in Job* was a standard medieval theological textbook.</note>, commenting on that passage of **Job 23**: *He is alone, are there not angels and men, heaven and earth?* Certainly there are. But it is one thing to be—namely, absolutely—and another thing to be principally. For these things exist, but principally they do not exist, because they do not subsist in themselves from the moment they were created. Indeed, all things were made from nothing, and their essence would tend back toward nothingness unless the hand of the ruling Creator held it. Behold the first of these statements; and the second follows: they would be able neither to subsist nor to move by themselves; they subsist only insofar as they have received that they ought to be; they move only insofar as they are disposed by a hidden instinct. The earth dries up, the sea is shaken, the air becomes fire, the sky grows dark, men are inflamed, the angelic virtues are moved—are these things agitated by their own instincts, and not rather by **divine impulses**? 

Through coinherence <term>circumincessio: typically a term for the mutual indwelling of the Trinity, but here used for the intimate union of two natures in Christ</term>, however, God is made intimate to a nature alone, which He assumes voluntarily, but in a supernatural manner. And this similarly applies to two things: namely, to the elevating of the nature to the **first act** <note>The "first act" refers to the basic existence or "being" of a thing.</note>, which is the being of the subsistence of the divine person <note>original: "suppositi"</note>; and to the power for the **second act**, namely, which is to operate—the beneficial act of understanding and willing. For without the said coinherence, a nature could not be elevated into the being of divine subsistence, nor perceive the difference of operations by seeing and loving the divine essence in a manner appropriate to a creature. 

But through coinherence, God raises the assumed nature to the divine being of subsistence, and promotes it to divine operation, as Damascene <note>John of Damascus (c. 675–749), an Eastern monk and theologian whose "On the Orthodox Faith" was highly influential.</note> says in Book 3, Chapter 16: *The flesh of the Lord is said to be deified,* and therefore shares in the divine <note>original: "communi diuiduali"</note>, not according to a transformation of nature, but according to the dispensation of the union, according to which the flesh is indivisibly united to God the Word. Through that mutual coinherence of the natures, the divine flesh was thus enriched with divine actions because of the most pure union with the Word. He uses "flesh" there to represent the whole of human nature. 

From these points, I argue: as God conducts Himself in every creature through a natural in-flowing <note>original: "illapsum naturalem"; refers to God's presence within all created things to sustain them in existence.</note> toward the two aforementioned actions that exceed the limits of nature (as is now clear from the words of Damascene), a similarity in some respect cannot be denied. For just as the in-flowing, by its nature, is meant to produce those two results in that which God flows into, so coinherence is meant, as much as is in itself, always to produce those two. But no nature is capable of receiving—nor can be capable of receiving—the in-flowing of God to receive in itself, in a manner appropriate to its nature, the first mentioned operation of God, unless it is also capable in itself of the second operation. This is because no creature can exist through substance to which some operation cannot belong through power, because according to the Philosopher <note>Aristotle (384–322 BC), often called simply "The Philosopher" by medieval scholars.</note> at the end of the 4th book of *Meteorology*: **All things are defined by their work**, and they exist for the sake of their operations; they exist only as long as they can perform their own proper operations, and when they cease to be able to perform their own proper operations, they simultaneously cease to be. For as Damascene says in the same place, Chapter 17: *An intellect that is foolish and deprived of knowledge will surely never exist; for if it is inoperable and immovable, it is non-existent.*

Through this, he clearly suggests that if it could not be elevated by means of the intellect, the very substance of the intellect would not be capable of being assumed, nor would man himself be, because he would not even be "man" according to what he stated previously. Since the soul is rational and intellectual—otherwise it is not man—how then was God made man if He had assumed a lifeless body or a soul *without mind* <note>original: "ἄνουν", which Pico glosses as "sine intellectu"</note>, that is, without an intellect? For this reason, although the argumentation of Augustine touched upon in the first reason does not hold in its logical form, it nevertheless does not fail in any specific subject matter, so that it follows: If this nature (namely, man's) can be elevated according to its essence, it must necessarily be simultaneously elevatable according to its power. Just as it follows: If the soul of Socrates <note>In medieval logic and philosophy, "Socrates" (often abbreviated as *Sortis*) was the standard example used for an individual human being.</note> is immortal, then the soul of every human is immortal. And if not the soul of every person, then not that of Socrates, because the same principle of immortality or mortality exists in all. And therefore such an argument, by reason of such matter, holds well, as if it held according to the form of the argument, which in truth holds by virtue of its form by having, namely, a view toward the common principle that belongs to any nature—for instance, the immortality of the soul. For that principle is the same in every soul. 

Let us therefore look at the possibility and impossibility of this "assumption." On one hand, as we have said, there is no doubt; but because it is unknown to us from the perspective of the one receiving <note>The "susceptible" nature, meaning the human nature that is being taken up or "assumed" by God.</note>, the understanding of the truth in the said question is difficult for us. Therefore, here is another position different from the one mentioned before; although it is less common, because it is more applicable to the mind—and though it might not seem so true because of its unfamiliarity—it is perhaps truer: namely, that no nature is capable of being assumed by God in the said manner, through coinherence, except for an intellectual nature. 

This pleases me more. Therefore, holding this opinion for the present, I say regarding the first point to the contrary: The incorporeal nature of the rational soul, or of an angel, and in man the nature of the body insofar as it is ordered toward the soul (as a thing to be perfected is ordered to its perfection), and in which the soul performs its intellectual operation more effectively—once every hindering accidental disposition is removed from it—than when it is separated <note>Pico is suggesting the soul acts more fully when united with a perfected body than when existing as a separate ghost-like entity.</note>, so that the whole composite of body and soul, with its intellective power, is the thing that is "susceptible." The body is susceptible through the mediation of the soul's substance, and in relation to that substance of the soul, insofar as it is an intellective power. Thus, that in which there is no intellective power is in no way capable of being assumed. And by "intellective power," I include everything in which the essence of the image <note>Referring to the *Imago Dei*, the "Image of God" described in Genesis, which theologians located in the human intellect and will.</note> principally consists, existing in the substance of the soul. ->### Defense<-

In all these things, the very image of God is, as it were, imprinted back onto its own prototype, just as the image on a **denarius** <note>A standard silver coin of the Roman world, here used as a metaphor for the human soul bearing God's "stamp."</note> relates to the figure from which its image was impressed. For this reason, **Damascene** <note>St. John Damascene (c. 675–749), a Syrian monk and Church Father known for his systematic "The Orthodox Faith."</note> says in the aforementioned chapter: *That which is "according to the image" is a willing thing in a willing reality; God the Word, having become fact, is man; the image of God exists according to the intellect.* For what is "according to the image" if not the intellect? Therefore, He left behind what was inferior and assumed what was better. He says this as if to say: this could not possibly have happened except by reason of the order which the nature has toward the intellect. He speaks here against those who proposed that a human body was assumed in Christ without a rational soul. He includes under the term "intellect" even the substance of the soul, and showing its power and potential even in the act of the **Assumption** <term>Assumption: In this context, the act of God "taking up" or uniting a created nature (humanity) to Himself.</term>, he adds: *For the intellect is in the middle between God and the flesh; the inhabitant of this intellect is the image of God. Therefore, intellect is mixed with intellect, acting as a medium between the purity of God and the coarseness of the flesh.*

By this "mixture," I mean a union through the **circumincession** <term>circumincessio: Also known as "coinherence," this refers to the mutual indwelling or complete interpenetration of the divine and human natures without them losing their distinct identities.</term> of the divine intellect with the human intellect. The human intellect—which exists through three powers: memory, intelligence, and will—is united to the soul. Through a certain circumincession, it is united to the Trinity of persons in the unity of the divine nature. Thus, in itself, the proximate cause—or the reason why something is "assumptible" by God—is the status of being the "image of God." This image exists only in an intellectual substance. Because of this, only an intellectual substance is capable of being received by Him.

According to this, in that glorious Assumption, the divine nature enters into the assumed nature through circumincession. The "image"—which is the intellectual nature being assumed—is intimately united to that which is in the divine nature itself. It is just as if one were to re-apply a seal to the wax in which the figure of that seal had already been impressed. The seal would re-enter all its own angles and grooves. In the same way, a seal could not be applied to something where its figure had not been previously impressed, but which only possessed some vague likeness. Such a likeness is merely a **trace of God** <note>original: "vestigium Dei." Medieval theologians distinguished between the "image" of God (found in humans) and the "trace" or "footprint" of God (found in animals, plants, and rocks).</note>, which exists in every non-intellectual creature. Therefore, no non-intellectual nature can be assumed by God except through the mediation of an intellectual nature in the manner described.

Regarding the second point—that an Assumption could be made to God because He contains the "reason of being" and "subsistence" found in the assumed nature—I say that this is true as a "con-cause." For if that were not the case, nothing could be assumed to God, just as one creature cannot be "assumed" into another. But this is not the *whole* cause. Although it may be the cause on the part of the one *assuming* (God), it is not the cause on the part of the *thing being assumed*. In the creature, the entire cause of "assumptibility" is the fact that it is an image of God. Through this alone is it capable of circumincession with God and of being elevated to that union in the divine essence, in the unity of the Person. 

Furthermore, there could be no **final cause** <term>final cause: The ultimate purpose or goal for which something is done.</term> for God to assume any nature other than an intellectual one. The assumption of a nature exists ultimately for the promotion and perfection of that nature in its elevation—a perfection which only an intellectual nature is capable of possessing. These are the words of **Henry** <note>Henry of Ghent (c. 1217–1293), a vastly influential Scholastic philosopher and theologian whose works Pico studied deeply.</note>, almost word-for-word. Therefore, it was not correctly determined...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's systematic defense of his theological propositions. Having previously discussed the necessity of the "intellect" in the union of God and man, he now defends his specific conclusion about the "force of the words" (literally, the logical implications of the terms used) against charges of heresy. He appeals to the authority of several famous medieval Scholastic thinkers to show that his position is within the bounds of orthodox debate.</meta>

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

my conclusion, concerning the **force of the words** <note>original: "de uirtute sermonis" — a technical term in Scholastic logic meaning the literal or strict meaning of a phrase.</note>, savors of heresy, which only denies the positive assent to the contradicting [opinion of] **Henry** <note>Henry of Ghent (c. 1217–1293), a major theologian whose works Pico frequently engaged with.</note>: a condemnation of whose opinion I have never read, nor do I believe they themselves have ever read. This I know, that neither **Scotus** <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), known as the "Subtle Doctor."</note>, nor **Godfrey** <note>Godfrey of Fontaines (c. 1250–1309), a prominent secular master at the University of Paris.</note>, nor **John of Warra** <note>Johannes de Warra (late 13th century), a Franciscan theologian.</note>, nor **Durandus** <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain (c. 1275–1334), a Dominican theologian known for his independent thought.</note>, nor **Thomas the Englishman** <note>Likely Thomas Jorz (d. 1310), a Dominican cardinal and theologian.</note>, nor **Robert of the Twisted-Neck** <note>original: "Robertus de Collotorto" — the nickname for Robert of Orford, a defender of Thomas Aquinas.</note>, nor **Bernard of Gannat** <note>A 14th-century French Dominican theologian.</note> (all of whom I have seen reciting the opinion of Henry) ever judged it to be heretical or to savor of heresy. So that they may not seem to have acted irrationally, I wish briefly to set down the second method by which Henry seems to protect his position. There are, however, two principal arguments against Henry.

The first argument stands in this: that in God is every **principle of substantiation** <term>principle of substantiation: the capacity to grant a thing its own independent existence or "substance."</term>, because He is the fullness of all being; therefore, it seems that he could **substantialize** and **supposit** <term>supposit: a technical term meaning to act as the underlying subject or "person" for a nature (in this case, God acting as the subject for a created nature).</term> any nature whatsoever. The second argument is this: because God, during the **three days** <note>original: "triduo" — the period between Christ's death and resurrection when His body lay in the tomb.</note>, "supposited" the body that was in the sepulcher—which nonetheless was not rational—and just as He "supposited" it for three days, He could have "supposited" it for as long a time as He wished. These are the two principal foundations of the opposing opinion, and Henry himself brings these very points against himself, as was seen in the recitation of his opinion.

To the first argument (as we have seen), he responds: that it is true that the fullness of all being is in God, and every principle of substantiation and "suppositing" is found most fully in Him, but this is not the total cause of the **assumptibility** <term>assumptibility: the quality of being able to be "taken up" or assumed into union with God.</term> of any nature, but is a co-cause. For unless there were one "assuming," He could not assume; but beyond this, something is required in the one being assumed through which it is "assumptible," and this is the **character of the image** <note>Pico is referring to the "Image of God" (Imago Dei) found in the human intellect.</note>, and finally the aptitude for supernatural elevation toward a beatific operation. Since this is found only in an intellectual nature, it seems fitting that only such a nature is "assumptible." For it seems reasonable that a nature which cannot be elevated to the **second act** <note>In Scholastic philosophy, the "first act" is the existence/form of a thing; the "second act" is its operation or functioning (e.g., the soul's ability to see God).</note> cannot also be elevated to the first. From this response, Henry seems to want to preserve the idea that nothing is taken away from divine omnipotence; for everything that they [the opponents] place in God, concluding that He is able to "supposit" in such a way, Henry also attributes to God. Nor does he deny that—by reason of what is required on the part of the one assuming—He could assume any nature most fully... [but] he says this is because the irrational nature itself is not "assumptible," not because of a defect in divine omnipotence, but rather because of the excellence of the divine nature and the deformed deficiency of the irrational nature.

Regarding the second argument, one may see that it can be answered in multiple ways. First is the response of Henry, who says: that He assumed the nature of that body insofar as it is ordered toward an intellectual soul; by reason of which ordering, even the body itself can be called "intellectual" in a ministerial—namely, a preparatory—sense. And so that it may be answered more completely, it must be said: that when it is said that nothing can be assumed by God except an intellectual nature, it is understood that nothing besides that can be assumed in such a way that it is the **primary thing assumed** and the total and adequate "assumptible." The body, however...

->Apologia.<-

# Apologia.

Likewise, in the three-day period <note>original: "triduo" — the three days between the Crucifixion and the Resurrection.</note>, it was not assumed in that way, as is evident, but only as a part of a rational nature, which was the total and primary thing assumed. Furthermore, someone might perhaps say that that body was not properly said to be "supposited" <note>original: "suppositari" — a technical term meaning to have its existence sustained by a person (the Divine Word) rather than existing as its own independent thing.</note> during those three days, because it is not a nature capable of being supposited by its own proper personhood. Whence, and consequently, it could be said—not improbably—that to terminate the dependency of the nature of that body is not the same as to "supposit" it; otherwise, everything that terminates the dependency or leaning of a part would "supposit" it, which is not said. And so, although the Word in those three days terminated that dependency of the body which the whole humanity would have terminated—by virtue of which the body in the three-day period communicated to Christ that property <note>original: "idioma" — in theology, this refers to the *communicatio idiomatum*, the sharing of attributes between the divine and human natures of Christ.</note> of lying in the tomb—nevertheless, it did not properly "supposit" the body in the same way it would "supposit" a human nature. The most evident sign of this is that the nature of that body did not communicate to Christ the attribute of "being a body" in those three days in the same way the human nature had communicated it to Him, and still communicates the attribute of "being a man" in a concrete sense.

And so the response is clear to the aforementioned objections against the opinion of **Henry** <note>Henry of Ghent (c. 1217–1293), a famous theologian whose views Pico is defending as at least "probable."</note>, who regarding other irrational natures seems to say essentially this: that the Word could not assume them through mutual indwelling <note>original: "circumincesasionem" — usually referring to the Trinity, here applied to the union of natures.</note> or sustain them through "suppositation," especially one having a final cause <note>A "final cause" is the ultimate purpose or goal of an action.</note>. For he himself says: "Nor could there be any purpose for the assumption of any nature other than an intellectual one, because assumption exists only for the promotion <note>elevation or improvement</note> of the assumed nature, which only an intellectual nature can have." Whence **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD).</note> says in his commentary on John: *The Word willed to be born from man, so that you might safely be born from God.* From this it seems that regarding any other nature which is not "born from God" through grace, God would be born as it in vain.

From these points it can be clear that I am not acting irrationally in not having an explicit act of contradicting this opinion in particular. And because these Masters <note>The papal commission investigating Pico's theses.</note> were also particularly insistent on this—that such conclusions should at least not be debated because of the "scandal" <note>In a theological sense, "scandal" means an obstacle that leads the simple-minded into error or loss of faith.</note> they cause—I want to say this about that conclusion: even if the opposite view were truer and more in accordance with the common way, nevertheless, if it were publicly debated, it would be much more scandalous among the common people and offensive to pious ears. For what unlearned or simple person would not be offended if he heard someone saying that it is possible for these propositions to be true: **God is a donkey** or **God is a piece of wood**? What if they also heard those things which many who follow the aforementioned opinion [of my opponents] concede: *God can be damned to hell; God could be tortured by the devil in hell; The devil can be God*? Although among many learned men, when speaking of God's **absolute power** <note>original: "potentia absoluta" — what God is capable of doing by logic alone, as opposed to what He has actually ordained to happen.</note>, these things cause no scandal, yet the common and simple people would certainly be much more offended than if they heard that a donkey cannot be united to the divine nature in a unity of person. This is stated in the manner I have declared in my conclusion—which those Fathers said "by the force of the words" <note>original: "ex ui sermonis" — strictly speaking or according to the literal logic of the terms.</note> derogated from divine omnipotence and thereby "savored of heresy." I know not what logic, or rather what theology, they are leaning upon. For let them tell me, I pray, whether he who says he does not assent to a certain proposition is speaking with rigor...

<summary>Pico defends his thesis that God cannot assume irrational natures (like animals) by arguing it is more respectful to God's dignity and less "scandalous" to the public than the alternative Scholastic view, which logically allows for the possibility of God becoming a donkey or being damned.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's rebuttal against the inquisitors who condemned his views on God’s omnipotence. He specifically addresses the logical distinction between "not holding a belief" and "holding an opposite belief," and then transitions into one of his most famous topics: the role of Magic and Cabala in proving Christ's divinity.</meta>

<page-num>166</page-num>
<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

...the opposite of that speech or conclusion, to which one does not assent. Let them say **whether this consequence is valid: "I do not assent to, or I do not have the assent of this conclusion: 'The Pope is sitting,' therefore I believe this: 'The Pope is not sitting.'"** Would not the first part be true in a person who is sleeping, or someone who had no mental act at all, while the second part could be false? Furthermore, if the present conclusion were to detract from divine omnipotence according to true theology, it would not merely "savor of heresy," but would have to be judged as heretical. Indeed, even a Catholic who is sleeping, or a small child who does not have the use of reason and does not hold the assent of this proposition—**"God can assume <note>original: "suppositare" — a technical term in medieval theology meaning to take a nature into a personal union, like the Incarnation.</note> any created nature"**—would be a heretic, or at least would err in faith. No one would say such a thing.

From these points, it is clear that their condemnation of these views was not correct. For this was formally their determination, considering the response of the proponent himself and the opinion, motives, and reasons of Henry <note>original: "Henrici" — referring to Henry of Ghent (c. 1217–1293), a famous theologian known as the "Solemn Doctor" (*Doctor Solemnis*).</note>, whose opinion the person posing the conclusion relies upon. It seemed to us that the aforementioned conclusion, by the literal force of the words <note>original: "ex ui sermonis" — a legal and logical term meaning the literal, outward meaning of a phrase regardless of the speaker's intent.</note>, detracts from divine omnipotence, and through this, it "savors of heresy" <note>original: "sapere hæresim" — a technical grade of ecclesiastical condemnation for a statement that sounds like heresy even if it isn't explicitly proven to be so.</note>.

First, they were deceived because when I said that I followed Henry in this, they did not understand that through the pronoun "this," I was denoting the conclusion itself about which they were asking for an explanation. In "this," therefore—that is, in the conclusion itself, which is to say in not assenting to this: **"God can [assume] any nature, etc."**—I said I followed Henry; I did not denote by "this" the opinion which says, "God cannot assume any nature." But they perhaps believed there was no difference between one statement and the other. However, if they are learned theologians, they ought to know that there is a difference between not explicitly believing something is possible by the power of God, and explicitly disbelieving it.

Second, they ought to remember that from their own words it follows that the famous Henry, who is called the "Solemn Doctor" for the excellence of his teaching, died a heretic. For, as was seen above, in his old age he declined toward this opinion and remained in it: that not every nature can be assumed by God.

Third, just as in the condemnation of the preceding conclusion, so too in this one, however things may stand with the conclusion, they are entirely in error. For if it is true, as they say, that the conclusion is against the omnipotence of God, then the conclusion is simply heretical, and not merely "savoring of heresy," as they claim.

Fourth and finally, they erred because even if Henry’s opinion were heretical, the conclusion by the force of the words would not be heretical at all, because the literal meaning does not imply that opinion, as has been most extensively declared. And yet, they specifically condemned it by the force of the words.
