# Defense

...there are sciences which, neither in their method of proceeding, nor in their principles, nor in their conclusions, rely on revealed truths; there is none that grants us greater certainty—in the manner that humanly discovered sciences are able to grant certainty—than that **Magic** <note>original: "Magia" — Pico consistently distinguishes "natural magic" (the study of nature’s hidden powers) from "goetia" or demonic sorcery.</note> about which the conclusions are posed there, which is a part of natural science; and that part of **Cabala**, which is a science and is not **revealed Theology**. Those Masters <note>The members of the papal commission investigating Pico's 900 theses.</note> said that my explanation was not relevant to the words of the aforementioned conclusion, and that the aforementioned conclusion, by the literal force of the words, was false, erroneous, and heretical. In their condemnation, I ask that we see individually how many things are to be condemned. First, let them tell me: how could my explanation be more relevant to the words of my conclusion? For what else is in that explanation but to explicitly declare the meaning of each individual term placed in the conclusion? For there, it is first explained what I understand by "science" when I say "no science"; and what I mean by "certify," what by **Magic**, and what by **Cabala**. I do not see what further remains to be explained.

Secondly, I wish to show that, by the literal force of the words, the conclusion is not only not false and heretical, but rather its opposite is false and, according to them, totally heretical. For the said conclusion is a negative one, which is explained disjunctively through three categorical statements like this: "No science not revealed, etc., other than **Magic** and **Cabala** certifies the divinity of Christ; OR **Magic** and **Cabala** do not certify it, etc.; OR **Magic** and **Cabala** certify us more regarding the Deity of Christ than any other non-revealed science." Now, this disjunction is true and Catholic because it has at least one true part. Thus it is now clear that, by the literal force of the words, it is not false. 

But it is also clear that its opposite, according to them, would be heretical. For the opposite of this—"No non-revealed science... certifies more..."—is this: "Some non-revealed science certifies us more regarding the Deity of Christ than **Magic** and **Cabala**." From this literal force of words, it follows that **Magic** and **Cabala** *do* certify the divinity of Christ—a claim which is regarded by them as heretical. And so it is clear that while they wish to condemn this negative statement—"No science certifies the divinity of Christ more than **Magic** and **Cabala**"—they are forced by their own judgment to hold this affirmative statement as Catholic: "**Magic** and **Cabala** certify us of the divinity of Christ."

However, how true the conclusion is in itself can certainly be demonstrated most evidently. For although there is no science invented by humans that can certify us of the divinity of Christ—because we only have certification of his divinity (as we said in the preceding conclusion) from the manner in which he performed miracles—and we only know that these miracles were performed by him, and performed in such a way, from the testimony of Scripture. Nevertheless, if human sciences can help us in this at all (just as they help in the knowledge of many supernatural truths), there is none that can help us more than the **Magic** and **Cabala** we have mentioned. For this purpose—so that the miracles of Christ may testify to his divinity for us—it is necessary to know first that they could not have been performed through natural power, but only through the power of God. Second, it is necessary to know that Christ held that power from himself and not...

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

...from elsewhere. In the first case, no human science can help us more than that by which we learn the powers and activities of natural agents, as well as their applications and proportions to one another and to their natural subjects—understanding what they can achieve by their own power and what they cannot. Among human sciences, this knowledge is best provided by that science which I call <term>Natural Magic</term> <note>original: "Magiam naturalem" — In the Renaissance, this referred to the study of the hidden "sympathies" and powers within nature, such as magnetism or herbal properties, rather than demonic sorcery.</note>, regarding which certain conclusions were set down, and that part of <term>Cabala</term> <note>original: "Cabala" — Pico was the first Christian scholar to combine Jewish mystical traditions with Western philosophy.</note> which concerns the powers of the celestial bodies. Through these, it is recognized that the works Christ performed could not have been done through natural powers. Therefore, among the conclusions on Magic, I placed this proposition: <term>The miracles of Christ</term> could not have been performed by Magic.

I offered this as a conclusion whose truth can be grasped from that science. Thus, it is clear that the judgment of those Masters <note>The members of the papal commission who condemned his work.</note> was not truly "masterful," especially since they condemn the proposition based on the "force of the words." Even if the sense I described were not the Catholic one, the statement would still not be worthy of condemnation in itself. By the literal force of the words, it does not imply that [heretical] sense, since it is a negative proposition to be explained disjunctively through three categorical statements, as was said above.

For a fuller declaration of this conclusion, it must first be understood that—as I said before—by this conclusion, I do not intend to compare Magic and Cabala to the revealed sciences. In this conclusion, I am not using the word "science" in a general sense, but specifically for a science that relies on revelation neither in its method of proceeding, nor in its principles, nor in its conclusions. Nor, in the present conclusion, am I speaking of the certainty of knowledge held through revelation in the aforementioned way, but of the certainty of knowledge discovered or acquired through demonstration—not from cause to effect (prior), but from effect to cause (posterior).

Specifically, I mean to say that if any science discovered by human effort and not through revelation can certify the divinity of Christ through his miracles, this is best achieved by the science through which we know the powers and activities of natural agents and their applications to one another and to their natural subjects. Through this, one learns what natural agents can do by their own power and what they cannot. Once this is known, and we subsequently see that the works of Christ exceed the degree and limit of those things which can be performed by natural agents, we necessarily conclude that they were performed by divine power. This is something we could not know if the former were not understood. For if the limits of the power and virtue of natural things are unknown, we might remain in doubt whether those same works that Christ performed could be done through natural means.

Since, therefore, such things are best known by that part of Cabala which deals with the powers of the celestial bodies, and that part of natural science which I now call "Natural Magic" (and many Catholic doctors have named it so, however others may wish to name it), I spoke not heretically, nor superstitiously, but scientifically, most truly, and in a Catholic manner when I said that we are aided by such Magic and Cabala in recognizing the divinity of Christ. Furthermore, the supreme theologian William, Bishop of Paris, <note>original: "Guilielmus Episcopus Parisiensis" — Referring to William of Auvergne (c. 1180–1249), a prominent philosopher-theologian at the University of Paris who wrote extensively on the "virtues" of the natural world.</note> also makes mention of this Natural Magic...

# Apology.

...of Paris <note>Refers to William of Auvergne (c. 1180–1249), Bishop of Paris and a prominent philosopher.</note>, a contemporary of Robert of Lincoln <note>Robert Grosseteste (c. 1175–1253), the scientist-bishop of Lincoln known for his work on optics and natural philosophy.</note>: who says that forbidden Magi are called "Magi" as if they were "evil-doers" <note>original: "mali"</note> because they perform evil deeds; but natural Magi are called "Magi" as if they were "great ones" <note>original: "magni"</note> because they perform great deeds. And because those critics could not tolerate this name of Magic, they shouted throughout the whole city that I was approving of <term>Necromancy</term> <note>original: "Necromantia" — In this period, this specifically meant "black magic" or sorcery involving demons, which Pico strictly rejected.</note>, which the whole Church condemned. I say again and yet again: this name "Magic" is an equivocal term <note>A word with multiple, distinct meanings.</note>, referring both to that which is called Necromancy—which is performed through pacts and covenants with demons—and to a branch of <term>practical natural science</term>. This latter branch teaches nothing other than how to perform wonderful works by means of natural virtues, through the application of these virtues to one another and to their natural subjects. The Church has never condemned this, nor can it condemn it; rather, many ecclesiastical and Catholic doctors have approved of and followed it. As I have said, William of Paris treats this in his work *On the Universe, Corporal and Spiritual*. He says that the forbidden Magic flourished most in Egypt, because the worship of demons thrived there; but this natural kind flourished in Ethiopia and India, because there is a great abundance of herbs and other natural things there which have efficacy in this natural Magic. And elsewhere in his book *On Laws*, he mentions the same science, asserting it to be a part of natural science. This <term>Natural Magic</term> a Catholic man, and the most holy <term>Albertus Magnus</term> <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a Doctor of the Church and patron saint of scientists who wrote extensively on the natural world.</note>, does not blush to say he followed, and that he discovered many things through experiments in it. And what more needs to be said? Let these Masters tell me: is that which I call "Natural Magic" a forbidden thing? Does it contain anything against the faith? They cannot say this, even if they wanted to. But they will say: "In this we rebuke you, that you call it 'Magic,' and by the ambiguity of the word, you cause a scandal in the minds of the faithful. Likewise, we hold from our Doctors that all Magic is forbidden. If all is forbidden, it follows that none is permitted; but you say that some is not forbidden, therefore you hold a view contradictory to the doctors of the church."

The ignorance of those speaking this way is truly marvelous. First, the assignment of names is not done by us now, but we use names and their meanings according to the custom of the ancients. If they, therefore, chose to call this branch of natural science "Magic," why do you want me to change the names? Do you want what they called Magic to be called Geometry or Arithmetic by me? I am not the first nor the latest to call this science Magic; many before me, both holy and learned men, did so. Let them be brought to court; let them be condemned, if it is a damnable thing to call this science by this name. However, we can easily understand that this naming was rightly established if we correctly consider Paul <note>Likely a reference to the Three Magi in the Bible or the broader concept of wisdom in the Pauline epistles.</note>. For this word <term>Magus</term> is neither Latin nor Greek, but Persian; and in the Persian language, it signifies the same as "wise man" <note>original: "sapiens"</note> does among us. Among the Persians, the wise men are the same as those called "philosophers" among the Greeks—a term first used by Pythagoras, whereas before they were called wise men. Indeed, among almost all different nations, their wise men were called by different names, such as the <term>Druids</term>...

<meta>This page continues Pico’s defense of his use of the word "Magic." On the previous page, he argued that "Magic" can refer to a legitimate natural science. Here, he provides historical and scriptural precedents for the word, distinguishing between its noble origins and its later corruption into sorcery.</meta>

<page-num>176</page-num>
<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

...[Drui]ds <note>The text begins with the suffix of "Druides," continuing from the previous page's list of wise men.</note> among the Gauls; prophets among the Hebrews; or the Sanhedrin, Pharisees, or <term>Cabalists</term> <note>original: "Cabalistæ" — Practitioners of Jewish mysticism, whom Pico studied deeply.</note>; among the Indians, the Gymnosophists; among the Egyptians, Priests; among the Greeks, philosophers; among the Persians, Magi; and so on with others. Just as royal dignity has specific names among different nations, such as the king of the Egyptians, who was first called Pharaoh and later Ptolemy; of the Persians, Artaxerxes; of the Romans, Caesar; of the Indians, Præstan—and there is one who is now called by our common people by the corrupted name "Prester John" <note>original: "Præsbyter Ioan" — A legendary Christian patriarch and king popular in medieval European lore, believed to rule a kingdom in the East.</note>; and so on for others.

Therefore, if Magic is the same as wisdom, they rightly wished to call this practical branch of natural science—which presupposes an exact and absolute knowledge of all natural things, like the peak and summit of all philosophy—by the specific and appropriate name "Magic" (that is, wisdom). Just as we say "Rome" for *the* city, "Virgil" for *the* poet, or "Aristotle" for *the* philosopher.

But if we shrink from this name "Magi" so much, then we will certainly not listen patiently to the Gospel when it says that "Magi came from the East to worship Christ." Those Magi were not <term>necromancers</term> <note>original: "Necromantes" — Sorcerers who summon the dead or demons.</note> or in league with demons; they did not come to worship the enemy of demons—indeed, their Lord, who would soon triumph over them—as such. Rather, they were wise men, learned in the science of celestial and earthly things, who worshipped and venerated the very Wisdom of the Father made visible in a human body.

Jerome <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420), a Doctor of the Church and translator of the Vulgate Bible.</note> makes this distinction very clear in his letter to Paulinus, in which he mentions Apollonius of Tyana <note>A 1st-century philosopher often compared to Jesus for his miracles; Pico uses him to show how "Magic" was often confused with "Philosophy."</note>, saying: "Apollonius of Tyana, whether he was a Magus as the common folk say, or a philosopher as the Pythagoreans say." In these words, Jerome expressly signifies that what is true philosophy is sometimes believed by the common people to be what they themselves call Magic.

Therefore, I am not to be blamed for calling this natural wisdom "Magic," following the proper and customary way of speaking used not only by the doctors of the Church but also by the Gospel itself. Nor should I have caused scandal to the faithful by the ambiguity of the word, because in my conclusions I did not use this name indistinctly or equivocally. Instead, to remove any occasion for a sinister opinion, I distinguished lawful Magic from the unlawful, and natural from superstitious, declaring what that natural kind is, what it can do, and what it cannot. I did this in such a way that even the simple and unlearned cannot suspect anything impious or erroneous in my conclusions regarding the faith. In those conclusions, while utterly rejecting and detesting forbidden Magic, I set down this first conclusion precisely in these words:

**"All Magic currently in use among modern people, which the Church rightly exterminates, has no stability, no truth, and no foundation, because it depends on the hand of the enemies of the first truth—those powers of darkness who pour the shadows of falsehood into poorly disposed minds."**

And after that conclusion, I place the second, which says: **"That natural Magic is lawful and not forbidden."** And I declare that I shall speak only of such things. This being done, what further suspicion can remain, or what scandal can be caused?

Here, he argues that clarifying the definition of magic—distinguishing the natural from the demonic—is a service to the Church and the unlearned, preventing common misunderstandings of the Bible and the works of great theologians like Albertus Magnus.</meta>

<page-num>171</page-num>
<header>Apology.</header>

By clarifying the ambiguity of this name "Magic"—distinguishing it so that I reject the superstitious and diabolical kind while approving the natural kind—I am not causing a scandal, but rather providing edification for the simple. For I have seen many people who, upon hearing that the Magi came to worship Christ, believe that the name "Magi" signifies nothing other than **necromancers** <term>necromancers</term> <note>original: "Necromantes" — Historically, those who claim to communicate with the dead, but used here by Pico to mean practitioners of black magic or sorcery.</note>. From this they take up the argument that Magic is not prohibited, nor is it against the faith of Christ, since practitioners of Magic were the first to worship Christ himself.

It is therefore useful to have taught the faithful that when they hear the word "Magus," they should not always understand it to mean a worshiper of demons. When they hear that among the Persians the Magi were held in the highest honor and reverence because of their learning and wisdom, they should know that these men were philosophers, not necromancers. For necromancers are destructive and harmful to the people—indeed, they are pestilential—and all nations have always cast them out, hated them, persecuted them, and detested them.

Similarly, when they read that **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and bishop who was one of the most influential medieval philosophers and scientists.</note> spent much time on the "experiment of magic," they should understand this to be natural magic, not the forbidden kind. This prevents them from devoting themselves to evil by following the example of such a great man, presuming that what was permitted to him is also permitted to them.

Therefore, my "Magic Conclusions" remove scandals from the minds of the faithful; they do not generate them. If ever they read in the works of the Doctors of the Church that "all magic is forbidden," they will immediately understand from the reasons for that prohibition that the Doctors speak only of that magic which involves commerce with demons, and that they intended nothing against natural magic.

Indeed, as **Hilary** <note>Saint Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367), a prominent theologian known for his work on the Trinity and biblical interpretation.</note> says, "the understanding of things said must be taken from the reasons for saying them." If people wish to return to the strict force of words, they can know from logic that the negation or distribution of a "multiple term" (a word with several meanings) does not negate or distribute that word for every possible meaning collectively. Therefore, since this term "Magic" is ambiguous, a general rule applied to it does not apply to every possible meaning at once. Rather, from the statement that "all magic is prohibited," it should be understood only that all species of **superstitious magic** are forbidden, as they all share one name and one underlying character. For many types are prohibited, and all these things are clear and lucid even to the moderately educated.

Therefore, my "Magic Conclusions" should in no way have been suspect to these Masters. For, as I said in my first conclusion, I refute all magic forbidden by the Church, damning and detesting it, and protesting that I speak only of natural magic. I declared this even more expressly through a specific conclusion, stating: *that by this Magic we perform nothing, except by activating or uniting natural virtues.* For this is what the eleventh of the Magic Conclusions says:

->The wonders of the magic art exist only through the union and activation of those things which are found in nature, sown as seeds and existing separately.<-

And this is the same as what I said in the 13th conclusion: ->To practice Magic is nothing other than to marry the world.<- <note>original: "maritare mundum" — One of Pico’s most famous phrases, describing the way a natural magician "marries" earthly materials to the spiritual and celestial influences of the heavens to produce effects.</note> The aforementioned specific—

## Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

the definition and restriction of my intention regarding my Magic conclusions, I intend for them to be applied to natural Magic. This applies to every particular conclusion; and so, when I speak of the activity of **characters and figures** in a Magic work, I am speaking of their true and natural activity. For it is clear that they possess such activity according to all philosophers, both in their action and in their manner of acting and being acted upon.

And although according to the **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>original: "peripateticos" — Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy, who generally prioritized material and physical qualities over mathematical abstractions.</note> they are of far less activity and power than material qualities are, nevertheless the **Pythagoreans** <term>Pythagoreans</term> <note>original: "Pythagorici" — Followers of Pythagoras who believed that numbers and mathematical ratios were the fundamental building blocks of reality.</note> (whose philosophy I call "more secret philosophy" in my 24th conclusion, because it is less known and less in use) would say that just as mathematical things are more formal than physical things, so they are also more actual. And just as they depend less on physical existence, so they also depend less on it in their operation.

And so, regarding what I said about their having greater power—even though the disagreement between the Pythagoreans and Peripatetics is indifferent to the faith—I did not state it as a truth in itself and an absolute truth, but as a consequence of the "secret philosophy" of the Pythagoreans, understood in the manner described above. It is also their opinion that among all mathematical things, numbers are both more formal and more actual; and among the odd numbers, the **number three** <note>original: "ternarium" — The triad. Pico notes it is the first "perfect" odd number because it has a beginning, middle, and end.</note>. Because it is the first odd number, and the first in any genus is the most perfect in that genus. And among even numbers, the **number ten** <note>original: "denarium" — The decad. In Pythagorean thought, 10 is the number of the universe, containing all other numbers within it.</note> which is "every number," as is evident; for from it we count further only by repetition. And this is what I intended by what I said concerning the three and the ten in natural Magic.

Moreover, Catholic doctors also attribute efficiency and power, both for good and for evil, to number. Hence **Hilary** <note>Saint Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367), a leading theologian and Bishop.</note> in his commentary on the Psalms, inquiring into the reason why the order of the Psalms is not according to history, but often a Psalm that was composed earlier is placed later in the order, says this:

"It must not be ignored that among the Hebrews the numbering of the Psalms is indistinct, and they were written down without any notation of order. For they do not mark there the first, or second, or third, or fiftieth, or hundredth, but without any prescription of order, they are mixed together into one. For **Ezra** <note>The biblical scribe and priest credited with reconstituting the Jewish community and scriptures after the Babylonian exile.</note>, as ancient traditions report, collected and restored them into one volume, unarranged and dispersed according to the diversity of authors and times. But the **70 elders** <term>70 elders</term> <note>original: "70. seniores" — Refers to the Septuagint, the legendary group of Jewish scholars who translated the Hebrew Bible into Greek in Alexandria.</note> remaining in the synagogue for the guardianship of the law and doctrine according to the tradition of Moses, after the care of translating the whole law from the Hebrew into the Greek language was mandated to them by King Ptolemy—understanding the powers of the Psalms through spiritual and celestial science—reduced them into number and order, assigning each to their respective numbers according to their efficiency, perfected by the perfection of the finished and efficient Psalms."

These are Hilary's words, verbatim. From these it is most clearly evident that number gives power and efficiency. **Jerome** <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420), best known for translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note> also, writing against **Jovinian** <note>A 4th-century monk whose views were declared heretical by Jerome and others.</note>, says that the number 20 is unlucky, for it was the number in which Jacob served, and Joseph was sold, and which Esau loved, receiving certain gifts in it.

...wisely, and in that same place he praises the **number ten** <term>denarius</term> <note>original: "denarium" — the number ten, considered a symbol of perfection and the Law (the Ten Commandments).</note>, saying that he has spoken of its praises quite often. And in the same book, chapter 7, he says that for this reason, on the second day of creation, it was not said, *and God saw that it was good*, because the **number two** <term>binarius</term> <note>original: "binarius" — the number two, which Pico notes was seen by some as a symbol of division or falling away from unity.</note> is evil; indeed, from the number two, he takes an argument against those who marry twice <note>original: "bigamos" — those who entered a second marriage after the death of a spouse, a practice debated in the early Church.</note>. For this reason, he says that all the unclean animals entered into Noah's ark in pairs, while the clean ones entered in groups of seven. You will find similar things a hundred times over in the writings of Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, Ambrose, Origen, Augustine, and others. Indeed, Rabanus <note>Rabanus Maurus (c. 780–856), a Benedictine abbot and scholar who wrote "On the Virtues of Numbers."</note>, a distinguished doctor of the Church, composed a specific book on the virtues of numbers. You will find that ecclesiastical doctors always observe the properties of these numbers everywhere—sometimes, if it may be said, even to the point of extreme curiosity. 

At one time, they refer the **number two** to the two Testaments, the two cherubim, the two precepts of charity <note>To love God and to love one's neighbor.</note>, the two primary ranks, or the two primary peoples. At another time, they contemplate the mystery of the **number three** <term>ternarius</term> in the substantial divinity [the Trinity], in the three days in the tomb, in the three theological virtues <note>Faith, Hope, and Charity.</note>, in the three eras of nature, law, and grace, and in the three states of perfection. Again, they maintain—not without mystery, but because of a hidden property of the number itself—that it was for the **number forty** that Moses, Elijah, and Christ fasted for 40 days; and that Christ ascended 40 days after his resurrection; and that he was in the underworld for 40 hours; and that after 40 days, Nineveh (which is a type and figure of this world) would be subverted; and that the Lord rained upon the earth for that same number of days and nights.

They likewise say it contains a great mystery <term>sacramentum</term> <note>In this context, "sacramentum" refers to a sacred mystery or hidden meaning rather than a ritual rite.</note> that the Holy Spirit descended in the **number fifty** <term>quinquagenarius</term>, in which there is the remission of sins. They also note that the Psalm *Have mercy on me, O God* <note>Psalm 50 in the Vulgate numbering (Psalm 51 in modern Bibles), the classic prayer of repentance.</note> is placed at that same number, a fact noted especially by Hilary and Origen. And the mysteries of the **Kabbalists** <term>Cabalistarum</term> <note>Followers of Kabbalah, a Jewish mystical tradition that Pico sought to synthesize with Christian theology.</note> agree with these things in every respect; they attribute the number fifty to the Holy Spirit. Among them, the Holy Spirit is also signified by fire, the same form and number of days in which he descended upon the apostles. 

Among the Kabbalists, the Holy Spirit is the third person, or property, in divine matters, proceeding from the first and the second. This second person is called **Wisdom**, and it proceeds from the first, differing from both only by the logic of its "procession" <note>A theological term describing how the Persons of the Trinity relate to one another without being separate beings.</note>—just as that which proceeds differs from those from whom it proceeds, while being one and the same with them in substance and essence. The Kabbalists say these things explicitly; and yet those Masters <note>Pico’s scholastic critics at the University of Paris and the papal commission.</note> detested these sayings—which I brought forward to use against the Jews—as if they were suspect regarding the faith. They also call this same third property **Penitence**, which agrees with what was just said: the same number is attributed to the Holy Spirit as is attributed to the sacrament of penance. From this we can gather that the "sin against the Holy Spirit" is properly a sin against penance, which is not forgiven in this age nor the next. But more on these things elsewhere. 

They also contemplate some secret property of the **number twelve** <term>duodenarius</term> in the twelve tribes of Israel, the twelve Apostles, and the twelve stones of the heavenly Jerusalem. They also believe, not without cause or chance, that into the **number ten**...

...happened to fall, both the precepts of the Law <note>The Ten Commandments.</note> and the ten strings of the psalter; and among the Hebrews, as is found in the <term>Midrash Tehillim</term> <note>original: "מדרש תהלים" — a traditional Jewish commentary on the Psalms.</note>, there are ten singers of the Psalms, who are Adam, Abraham, Melchizedek, Moses, Asaph, David, Solomon, and the three sons of Korah—although they are listed differently by our own [Christian] writers. There also correspond ten organs, that is, ten instruments or ten modes of music in which they were sung, named thus among the Hebrews: *Nezach, Neym, Mizmor, Shir, Tephillah, Berakhah, Hillel, Yedidiah, Ashrei, Hallelujah* <note>original: "נצח נעים מזמור שיר תפילה ברכה הלל ידידיה אשרי הללויה" — these terms refer to various musical and liturgical headings found in the Hebrew Bible, such as "Victory," "Psalm," "Song," "Prayer," "Blessing," "Praise," etc.</note>. I have observed that these are to be distinguished in this way: through the first, odes are sung; the second is the same as an organ; through the third, Psalms; through the fourth, songs; through the fifth, prayers; through the sixth, blessings; through the seventh, praises; through the eighth, thanksgivings; through the ninth, the happiness of someone; and through the last, the praises of God alone.

You might also add <term>Maskil</term> <note>original: "משכיל" — a Hebrew term meaning "instruction" or "contemplation," appearing in the titles of several Psalms.</note>, which are sung as contemplations; and *Hallelujah* would be like the <term>Ein Sof</term> <note>original: "eifoph" — a Hebrew Kabbalistic term meaning "The Infinite" or "Without End," referring to God in His essence.</note>, not being counted in the number with the others. They also add the ten days during which the Spirit descended after the ascension of Christ, and the ten curtains in the Temple, and countless and infinite similar things, always saying this: that nothing happens by chance, but God has arranged all things through His wisdom—just as in weight and measure, so also in number.

I shall remain silent on how many and how great are the things they observe in the **number nine** <term>novenario</term>, such as, besides the hierarchies of angels and the nine degrees of the beatitudes, even—according to Moses—the length in cubits of [the bed of] **Og of the herd of Bashan** <note>A giant king mentioned in Deuteronomy 3:11 whose iron bed was nine cubits long.</note>, who is a type [symbol] of the devil. They do not believe this to be accidental and without mystery, for they also observe that the Lord cried out at the ninth hour.

Do they not also consider the perfection of the **number four** <term>quaternarius</term> in the four Gospels, the four rivers of paradise, and the four living creatures of Ezekiel? And the **number six** <term>senarius</term> in the six days of the creation of the world, and in the six ages [of history]—whether the seventh age is the future life, as Augustine holds, or the eighth, as Jerome does. Indeed, even this is not overlooked: that the Lord suffered on the sixth day of the week <note>Friday.</note>. 

What of the **number seven** <term>septenario</term>? They would say it is worthy of great attention that on the seventh day the Lord rested; that there are seven gifts of the Holy Spirit; and in the Apocalypse [the Book of Revelation], there are seven seals of the book, seven horns, seven eyes, seven angels, seven churches, seven lampstands, seven stars; and also seven more wicked spirits, and seven iniquities in Solomon; and seven times a day the prophet David sings to God. Furthermore, we have seen the **number fourteen** observed by Matthew in such a way that, in order to retain it everywhere in the **Generations of Christ** <note>The genealogy of Jesus at the beginning of the Gospel of Matthew, which is structured into three sets of fourteen generations.</note>, he even omitted several generations.

I bring forward nothing here concerning physicians, astrologers, or philosophers—especially the Platonists and Pythagoreans—but only concerning our own ecclesiastical doctors. The issue at hand is whether believing that there are properties in numbers and certain natural virtues in any way contradicts the truth of the **Catholic faith**. Since we see that these things have been observed—as I said, perhaps even to the point of extreme curiosity—by Catholic authors, there is no further reason why we should doubt that such an opinion is not to be [rejected as heretical...]

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense of his "900 Theses." On the previous page, he was discussing the mystical properties of numbers and the Hebrew names for musical/liturgical headings. Here, he transitions from the power of names in natural magic to a passionate defense and explanation of the Kabbalah, correcting common misconceptions of his time.</meta>

...to be rejected. Since, therefore, in my conclusions I speak of figures and numbers, I do not speak in regard to their superstitious use through pacts and agreements with demons—for I have rejected all such things in my first conclusion—likewise, it is known to everyone that names possess a certain natural activity. Indeed, they do not have this natural activity merely as signs chosen by human whim <note>original: "ad placitum" — a technical term in linguistics meaning "by convention" or "arbitrarily," as opposed to having a natural, inherent meaning.</note>, but insofar as they are certain natural things in themselves. 

For this reason, I said that those names have power in **natural magic** <note>original: "Magia naturali" — Pico distinguishes "natural magic" (the science of natural forces) from "goetia" or demonic magic, which he condemns.</note>, not merely as signs, unless perhaps there are some names for which the meaning is natural. The Stoics make this claim about all names; the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note> oppose this, but Plato in the *Cratylus* agrees with it regarding those names which are "correctly imposed." 

**Origen** <note>An early Christian theologian (c. 185–253 AD) who studied Hebrew traditions.</note> holds this view regarding Hebrew names. He says that certain Hebrew names in the Holy Scriptures, such as *Hosanna*, *Sabaoth*, *Hallelujah*, and the like, were preserved as they were and not translated into another language, because in another language they would not have retained their natural meaning, and consequently, their power. And this was my only intention when I was comparing meaningful names to those without meaning, and Hebrew names to others, regarding their efficacy in **natural magic**.

I wish also to speak a bit more broadly about this **Kabbalah** <note>original: "Cabala" — derived from the Hebrew word meaning "reception" or "tradition."</note>, although we have already said much above in the first part of our Apology. But perhaps those matters will no more be understood by these "Masters" <note>A sarcastic reference to the conservative inquisitors and theologians attacking his work.</note> than a foreign tongue is understood by the learned. Therefore, we shall say something here in the **Parisian style** <note>original: "Parisiensi stylo" — referring to the rigorous, logical, and scholastic method of debate practiced at the University of Paris.</note> concerning this Kabbalah. 

For the name itself seems "horrendous" to these fathers, and to be feared for its very sound, so much so that there are perhaps some among them who suspect that **Kabbalists** are not men, but rather "goat-stags" <note>original: "hircoceruos" — a mythical creature, used here to mean something nonsensical or monstrous.</note> or centaurs, or something altogether monstrous. In fact, hear a ridiculous thing: once, when one of them was asked what this "Kabbalah" was, he replied that there was a certain treacherous and diabolical man named **"Kabbala,"** and that he had written many things against Christ, and therefore his followers were called "Kabbalists." Who, I ask, could keep from laughing at this? 

It should therefore be known that it is the opinion not only of Rabbi Eleazar, Rabbi Moses of Egypt <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent Jewish philosopher.</note>, Rabbi Simeon ben Lakish, Rabbi Ishmael, Rabbi Judah, and Rabbi Nachman <note>Nachmanides (1194–1270).</note>, and many others of the wise Hebrews, but also of our own Doctors <note>Christian theologians.</note> (as I will show below), that besides the Law which God gave to **Moses** on the mountain—and which he left written and contained in five books—there was also revealed to the same Moses by God himself a true exposition of the Law. This included the manifestation of all the mysteries and secrets which are contained under the "bark" <note>A common metaphor meaning the outer layer or literal sense of the text.</note> and rough face of the words of the Law. 

In short, Moses received a double Law on the mountain: the **literal** and the **spiritual**. The former he wrote down and communicated to the people by God’s command; but regarding the latter, God commanded him not to write it down, but to communicate it only to the wise men, who were seventy in number, whom Moses had chosen by God's command to guard it...

[...the] law, and likewise commanded them that they should not write it down, but should reveal it to their successors by word of mouth, and then those to others, and so on in a perpetual order. Because of this method of handing down that science through successive reception—that is, the receiving of words from one by another—the science itself was called the science of **Kabbalah** <term>Kabbalah: a Hebrew word meaning "reception" or "tradition"</term>, which is the same as the "science of reception," because among the Hebrews, **Kabbalah** means the same as what we call "reception." 

Later, these mysteries were committed to writing (at a time and for a reason to be discussed below), and those books were called the books of **Kabbalah**. In these books, many—indeed, almost all—things are found to be in harmony with our faith. For they were both handed down from the mouth of God and written by the Jews before the time of Christ, a period when they could not have been moved by any passion to corrupt or spoil the truth itself. From these books and the authors of this science, I have set forth many conclusions to confirm our faith against the Jews. When those certain Teachers <note>Referring to the ecclesiastical censors who challenged Pico’s 900 Theses.</note> perhaps had not well considered these conclusions, they said they were suspect in the faith and tasted of "Jewish perfidy." However, after they understood what **Kabbalah** actually was, many of them were ashamed of what they had said.

That the matter is as we have stated above—that God gave Moses, besides the literal law which he himself wrote, certain mysteries contained in the law—I have five witnesses from our own tradition: Ezra, Paul, Origen, Hilary, and the Gospel. 

First, we have this from the text of **4 Esdras 14** <note>An apocryphal book of the Bible highly regarded by Renaissance scholars for its mystical content.</note>, where the Lord, speaking, says:

> "Revealing, I was revealed <note>original: "Reuelans reuelatus sum"</note> over the bush, and I spoke to Moses when my people were serving in Egypt, and I sent him, and led them out of Egypt, and brought him up onto Mount Sinai. I kept him with me for many days, and I told him many wonders, and showed him the secrets of the times and the end; and I commanded him, saying: 'These words you shall make public, and these you shall hide.'"

Secondly, we have the authority of **Origen** <note>An early Christian theologian (c. 185–253 AD) who often looked for deeper, allegorical meanings in scripture.</note> (whose testimony is most valid in those matters in which he is accepted by the Church, for where he is good, no one is better). On that passage of Paul in **Romans 3**, *What advantage then is there, or what is the benefit of circumcision? Much in every way. Chiefly because the utterances of God were entrusted to them,* Origen says:

> "It must be considered that he did not say the 'letters' were entrusted, but the 'utterances' of God."

From this saying of Origen, you can see that besides the literal law, something else was handed down to the Jews, which Paul here calls "the utterances of God." For no one denies that the "letters"—that is, the literal law—were handed down to them, but this is not credited to them as a special prerogative, for the letter by itself kills; unless the life-giving spirit is present, it is entirely a dead thing in itself. But besides these letters, the "utterances of God" were handed down to them, in which they rightly glory. These are nothing other than what is called **Kabbalah** among the Hebrews—that is, the true sense of the law received from the mouth of God. 

For this reason, among the Hebrews it is sometimes called **The Oral Law** <note>original: "תורת בעל פה" (*Torah she-be-al peh*), meaning the "Law from the mouth."</note>, which is the same as "the law born from the mouth." Because of that successive reception, it was thereafter called **Kabbalah**. And that Moses communicated this science (already received from God) only to the seventy elders, **Hilary** <note>St. Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367 AD), a Doctor of the Church.</note> openly testifies, who...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense of the Kabbalah as a legitimate and ancient tradition. Having previously defined Kabbalah as "reception," he now provides historical and theological evidence from Christian Church Fathers to prove that Moses received a secret, oral revelation alongside the written Law.</meta>

-># Apologia<-

# Apologia.

In his exposition of the second Psalm, *Why did the nations rage*, etc. <note>Psalm 2:1</note>, he writes as follows:
> "Indeed, it was previously established by Moses that there should be seventy teachers in every synagogue. For although Moses committed the words of the Old Testament to writing, he had nonetheless separately imparted certain more hidden mysteries from the secrets of the Law to the seventy elders, who would thereafter remain as teachers. The Lord also makes mention of this teaching in the Gospels, saying: *The scribes and Pharisees have sat on the chair of Moses. All things, therefore, whatsoever they shall say to you, observe and do: but according to their works do ye not.* <note>Matthew 23:2-3</note> Their doctrine, however, remained for posterity."

These are the words of Hilary <note>Saint Hilary of Poitiers, a 4th-century bishop and Doctor of the Church</note> verbatim. Behold how Hilary expressly testifies that, besides the written Law, there was a certain other more secret doctrine which Moses imparted to those seventy wise men. Furthermore, that this more secret and truer exposition of the mysteries of the Law was not published to everyone everywhere, but was revealed by God specially to Moses, and by him only to the other seventy wise men, Origen <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian</note> also testifies in the previously cited place, saying:
> "Concerning Moses and the prophets and others like them, these things are to be understood as being said to those to whom the words of God were entrusted; add to this, if anyone among them was a wise and understanding listener and a wonderful counselor."

These are the words of Origen. By these "wonderful counselors," those are understood whom the Hebrews call the <term>Senedrim</term> <note>original: "Senedrim"; the Sanhedrin, the supreme judicial and administrative council of ancient Israel</note>, that is, those seventy elders whom Moses chose by the command of the Lord. The Cardinals in our Church seem to me to hold their place. 

According to the imitation of the number of those seventy elders (as we shall now declare), the mysteries of the <term>Kabbalah</term> <note>original: "Cabalæ"</note> were redacted into seventy principal books in the time of Ezra. For until the time of Ezra, nothing of this doctrine had been written; rather, as I have said, it was handed down only through successive reception, from which it took the name <term>Kabbalistic</term> <note>original: "Cabalisticē"; meaning "by way of tradition"</note>. After they were restored from the Babylonian captivity by Cyrus, and the temple was rebuilt under Zerubbabel, Ezra—who was the leader of the synagogue—at that time restored the written Law of Moses and corrected the Old Testament. He also wished that those secret words of God, which had not been written down until that time, should be put into writing. He did this because, due to the captivity of the nation, they could not maintain the old order of handing down that doctrine by hand <note>meaning through oral transmission from person to person</note>; and it was rightly to be feared that because of their dispersion, if the teachings were not found in writing, they might eventually perish.

Therefore, Ezra decreed that they should be written down, employing special notaries for this purpose. And because there were seventy elders or counselors among whom this doctrine resided, he ordered that all those secrets be redacted into seventy principal volumes, which, however, were still not to be shared except with the wise. This is what is read in the book of Ezra <note>2 Esdras 14:45-48, an apocryphal book</note> in these words:
> "When the forty days were ended, the Most High spoke, saying: The first things that you have written, publish openly, so that the worthy and the unworthy may read them; but you shall keep the last seventy books, so that you may hand them over to the wise among your people. For in these is the vein of understanding, the fountain of wisdom, and the river of knowledge. And so I did."

These were the words of Ezra <note>original: Esdras</note>, verbatim. Moreover, a broad and detailed mention of that Council—in which those seventy books were recorded—is found among the Hebrews in the book called *Seder Olam* <term>Seder Olam: Meaning "Order of the World," a 2nd-century CE Hebrew chronological work attributed to Yose ben Halafta.</term>, that is, the *Book of Ages*. In it are recorded those who sat in the council, and finally the deeds and order of the entire assembly. From all of this, it can be sufficiently clear that it is not a fabrication of mine that, besides the written Law, Moses also received a true exposition of the Law from God, and that this was thereafter revealed through a succession from Moses to the seventy elders, and from them to their other successors. 

Hence it received the name and was called **Kabbalistic** <note>original: Cabalistica</note>, and in the time of Ezra it was redacted into many books, which are called the books of **Kabbalah**. I have acquired these books for myself at great expense and have read through them diligently (for the Hebrews are not willing to share them with us Latins). Finding many things there—indeed, almost everything—in harmony with our faith, it seemed to me that Christians could have the means to strike down the Jews with their own weapons, since the authority of the Kabbalists (whom they hold in great honor and reverence) cannot be denied by them. 

Furthermore, it should be known that this exposition of the Bible corresponds to the method of interpreting the Bible which we call **Anagogical** <term>Anagogical: The highest level of interpretation, focusing on spiritual, heavenly, or future eternal realities.</term>. Just as we have a fourfold method of interpreting the Bible—literal, mystical or allegorical, tropological, and anagogical—so it is also among the Hebrews. 

1.  The literal sense is called **Peshat** <term>Peshat: The plain, direct meaning of the scriptural text.</term> among them, which is held by such men as Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator.</note>, Kimchi <note>original: Chemoy; likely referring to David Kimchi (Radak), a grammarian and biblical commentator.</note>, and their like. 
2.  The allegorical sense is called **Midrash** <term>Midrash: An interpretive method that goes beyond the literal sense to find legal, ethical, or homiletic truths.</term>, which is why you will often hear from them the *Midrash Ruth*, *Midrash Tehillim* (that is, the Midrash on the Psalms), and *Midrash Kohelet* (that is, the Midrash on Ecclesiastes), and so on for others. This is the method followed chiefly by the Talmudic doctors. 
3.  The tropological <note>The moral or ethical layer of meaning.</note> sense is called **Sekhel** <term>Sekhel: The "intellectual" or philosophical interpretation.</term>, followed by Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>original: Abnazara; a 12th-century Spanish polymath.</note> (wherever he does not explain literally), Levi ben Gershom <note>Also known as Gersonides (1288–1344).</note>, and many others, and above all by Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>Maimonides (1138–1204), the famous philosopher and jurist.</note>. 
4.  The anagogical sense is called **Kabbalah**. This is because that exposition, which is said to have been delivered to Moses by the mouth of God and received through succession in the manner described, almost always follows the Anagogical sense. 

This sense is the most sublime and divine of all, leading us upward from earthly things to heavenly ones, from things perceived by the senses to things perceived by the mind, from the temporal to the eternal, from the lowest to the highest, from the human to the divine, and from the physical to the spiritual. It is from this method that the strongest arguments against the Jews are found. The discord between them and us—as is most clear from the letters of Paul—depends chiefly on this: that they follow the "letter that kills," while we follow the "spirit that gives life." <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 3:6.</note> 

Let it suffice for now to have declared this with a single example. For when it is promised to them in the prophecies that the Messiah will deliver them from captivity and lead them into the Promised Land and into Jerusalem, and that they will rejoice and gather in the Temple, they understand these things literally. They believe the prophecy speaks of a worldly captivity, of the earthly land of Judea, and of a material city of Jerusalem and a physical Temple. Thus, they cannot believe that He has been... <meta>catchword: fuisse (has been)</meta>

# Apology

...that he was the Messiah, through whom they were cast out of that land of promise, the city was destroyed, and the temple was demolished. If they—along with the **Kabbalists**—would only wish to understand the Scripture by interpreting it **anagogically** <term>anagogical: A method of spiritual interpretation that seeks hidden, mystical meanings related to the soul's journey or the afterlife, rather than just the literal history.</term>, they would necessarily recognize and confess that those prophecies refer to the **heavenly Jerusalem**, to a **spiritual captivity**, and to the **heavenly land of the living**. They would see that he was the true Messiah, through whom almost the whole world was liberated from the hand of the demon, whom it previously served through idolatry. It is the firm opinion of the Kabbalists themselves that this liberation would be the chief effect of the Messiah's coming. 

This would be recognized in all other matters if the proofs of my **Kabbalistic conclusions** were examined—namely, that there is almost no article of faith in which the Jews are not compelled to agree with us through the authority of the Kabbalists. 

But immediately those "fathers" <note>Pico is likely referring to his critics and the papal commission investigating his theses.</note> rise up and ask: "Why then do all Jews not become Christians? And why did **Augustine**, **Jerome**, and other doctors of the Church make no mention of this teaching?" I marvel at the "wisdom" of these fathers, and I ask them to tell me: were the miracles of Christ true, or were they falsely fabricated by our people? If they say they were true, let them also tell me: why then did not all the Jews become Christians at that time? 

For even if we assume the Kabbalists write exactly the same things that **Augustine** <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 CE), one of the most influential Latin Church Fathers.</note> writes, there is no doubt that the miracles of the living Christ, performed daily before their eyes, were of greater power than the authority of any author, even if those authors were considered highly authentic among them. 

Furthermore, let them know that Jews are prohibited from reading those books <note>The books of the Kabbalah.</note> before they reach their fortieth year. And if they occasionally read them and still do not believe—just as they did not believe in Christ himself when they saw him—I say with **Origen** <note>Origen (c. 184–253 CE), an early Christian scholar who sought deeper meanings in the Bible.</note> that they have become like those who read and do not understand, who read and do not believe. For "their foolish heart has been darkened" <note>original: "Obscuratum est enim insipiens cor eorum." A quote from Romans 1:21.</note>. 

And just as **Paul** says concerning those "oracles of God"—which we declared above to be this Kabbalistic tradition—in this manner: *For what if some of them did not believe? Shall their unbelief make the faith of God without effect? God forbid. For God is true, but every man a liar* <note>original: "Quid enim si quidam illorum non crediderunt, nūquid incredulitas illorum fidem Dei euacuauit? absit. Est enim Deus uerax: omnis autem homo mendax." From Romans 3:3-4.</note>. 

So let us also say: what if many do not believe? Does their unbelief void the truth and nobility of this science? God forbid! Christians are most worthy of this science because, just as it is a **spiritual law** and not a fleshly one, so we are **spiritual Israelites**, not fleshly ones. This spiritual law belongs to him who, according to Paul, "sees in secret," not to him who only sees what is manifest <note>A reference to Romans 2:29, where Paul discusses being a Jew inwardly/spiritually.</note>. 

As for their claim that they wonder why the doctors of the Church never mentioned this doctrine, we have sufficiently shown above that **Hilary**, **Origen**, and **Ezra**—and alongside them **Paul** and the **Gospel**—made mention of this science. It should also be noted that you will never (or very rarely) find any doctor among our own—I speak of the ancients—who cites any Hebrew by name; rather, you will see them speak only in general terms: *"Thus say the Hebrews,"* or *"This is the opinion of the Hebrews."* Indeed, I do not recall finding this except once in Origen, who cites...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense of the study of Kabbalah. Having previously addressed why earlier Church Fathers did not explicitly name Kabbalistic sources, he now clarifies the distinction between different branches of Jewish thought—the Talmudic, the Philosophical, and the Kabbalistic—to prove that the "secret Hebrew wisdom" praised by the ancient Saints was, in fact, the Kabbalah.</meta>

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

...no patriarch was his contemporary; therefore, it is no wonder if you never hear the authors of the **Kabbalah** cited by them by name. However, we see that our own doctors rely so heavily on the testimony of the Hebrews that, as our **Jerome** says: when they wish to approve what they say—**Eusebius** especially, as well as **Origen**, **Clement**, and many others—they always refer back to the Hebrews, saying: *A Hebrew related to me*, or *I heard from a Hebrew*, or *This is the opinion of the Hebrews*. And **Jerome** himself even calls them "Masters," saying, *This is the opinion of the Masters.* There is no doubt that they mean the teachers of the **Kabbalah**. This can be demonstrated by clear reason, for the entire school of the Hebrews is divided into three sects: the **Philosophers**, the **Kabbalists**, and the **Talmudists**. 

It is not to be believed that the **Talmudists** were cited by our ancient doctors, both because **Clement** and many others who cite the Hebrews lived before the composition of the **Talmud** itself (which occurred more than 150 years after the death of Christ), and because the Talmudic doctrine is entirely against us, having been fabricated by the Hebrews while they were already fighting against Christians. Therefore, our doctors would not have paid such honor to that doctrine as to consider something firmly stated just because it was corroborated by the testimony of those Jews. 

Likewise, it is certain that they do not cite the **Philosophers**, because those who began to explain the Bible according to philosophy only began to do so recently. The first was **Rabbi Moses of Egypt** <note>original: "Rabbi Moyses de Aegypto," referring to Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the famous Jewish philosopher.</note>, who flourished while **Averroes of Cordoba** <note>The influential Islamic philosopher (1126–1198) whose commentaries on Aristotle dominated medieval thought.</note> was still alive; and not yet three hundred years have passed since the death of Averroes. 

It remains, therefore, that this "Hebrew doctrine"—to which Catholic doctors, by Jerome's testimony, defer so much and which they so highly approve—is that very doctrine which our own doctors confess and believe was revealed by **God to Moses**, and from Moses passed down through succession to other wise men. It is that which, from this method of "handing down," is called **Kabbalah** <term>Kabbalah: Derived from the Hebrew 'Qabbalah,' meaning 'reception' or 'tradition.' Pico defines it here as a divinely revealed oral tradition distinct from the written Law.</term>. I often see this designated by our authors by the phrase: *As the ancient tradition says.* This is the first and true Kabbalah, of which I believe I was the first among the Latins to make explicit mention. It is the one I use in my conclusions, which—since I set them down expressly against the Hebrews to confirm our faith—I do not know how those "Masters" <note>Pico's critics among the clergy.</note> could hold as suspicious regarding the faith. 

However, because this method of handing down through succession, which is called "Kabbalistic," seems to apply to every secret and mystical matter, the Hebrews have usurped the term so that they call every science held among them to be secret and hidden "**Kabbalah**." Every piece of knowledge obtained through an occult path is said to be held "by way of Kabbalah." In general, they have honored two sciences with this name. One is called the **art of combining** <term>ars combinandi: A method of manipulating Hebrew letters to uncover hidden names of God or mystical truths; Pico compares it to the system of Ramon Llull.</term>, which is a certain method of proceeding in the sciences; it is something similar to what is called among our people the **Art of Raymond** <note>Refers to the "Ars Magna" of Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), a system of logic using rotating charts to combine concepts.</note>, though perhaps they proceed in different ways. The other science concerns the powers of superior things that are above the moon, and...

Here it is enough to have shown that nothing is contained in them which is repugnant to the Catholic and orthodox faith.

## GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA’S DISPUTATION ON THE SACRAMENT OF THE
### Eucharist.

**S**i <note>The text begins with a decorative woodcut initial 'S'.</note> the common path is held regarding the possibility of **supposition** <term>suppositio: A technical term in scholastic logic and theology referring to the way a person (like the Word of God) can "take on" or "underlie" a nature or substance</term> with respect to any creature: I say that without the conversion of the substance of the bread into the body of Christ, or the annihilation of the "bread-ness," it is possible for the body of Christ to be on the altar according to the truth of the sacrament—let this be said speaking of what is *possible*, not of how things *actually are*. 

By this conclusion, I do not intend to say that the bread is not converted into the body of Christ, or that the body of Christ becomes present in the sacrament (as actually instituted by Christ) in some other way, or that the actual truth of that sacrament is the presence of Christ's body alongside the bread actually assumed or "supposited" by the Word. even to the sacrament itself, or rather even to the presence of the body of Christ together with the bread being assumed. Thus, perhaps it would not be necessary, by virtue of that assumption of the bread, that it should be the body of Christ which he already took from the Virgin along with the bread; yet it is possible that it could be on the altar together with the bread, if it were assumed by Christ. Therefore, in the present conclusion, I am speaking of a **possible sacrament**, and its **possible truth**, and the **possible presence** of Christ's body together with this bread that could be assumed. For this reason, I marvel that the present conclusion was condemned as erroneous on the grounds that the aforementioned things are false regarding the sacrament of the Eucharist as it is now instituted (which they claim I am speaking of), when I nevertheless explicitly profess in the conclusion to be speaking of a **possible sacrament** and its **possible truth**. Let them, therefore, consider the words of the conclusion more attentively before they condemn a conclusion that so explicitly refutes the sense which they condemn; indeed, let them consider that their own determination can hardly be defended from error. For if it were the case that the conclusion intended to uphold the truth of the sacrament according to the institution of Christ which the Church holds (as they say), then it would not only be erroneous, but simply heretical. If, however, the meaning of the conclusion is that which I have explained, it is not only not erroneous in faith, but rather it is erroneous to say the opposite. For there are many things which, as a statement of fact <note>original: "de sic esse"</note>, are heretical, but the opposite of which, regarding possibility, would be heretical. Just as saying the Father became incarnate as a statement of fact is heretical; however, to say the Father **could** be incarnate is not only not heretical, but it is heretical to say the opposite <note>Theologians argued that while only the Son became human, all three persons of the Trinity possess the power to do so; to deny God's power to do so would be a greater heresy.</note>. Let these things suffice for the declaration and defense of the conclusion.

But for the sake of scholastic exercise, leaving my conclusion aside, let us see whether this is true: *That the Body of Christ can be made present on the altar by another mode than the conversion of the bread into it—namely, through the **sustaining of bread-ness** <note>original: "substantiationem paneitatis"; Pico is coining a term for the hypothetical essence or "nature" of bread being supported by God's person.</note> in the divine **person** <term>supposito — the underlying substance or "hypostasis" that holds a nature; in Christology, the one Person of the Word holds the human nature.</term> together with the assumed humanity: so that there would be one person in three natures: namely, Divinity, Humanity, and Bread-ness. And by reason of the person, there would be a predication of each nature in its concrete form toward the person taken from the other nature, as well as a **communication of properties** <term>communicatio idiomatum — a theological rule where properties of one nature (like "dying") can be said of the Person ("God died") because the Person possesses both natures.</term>: God is bread and man, and vice-versa. And Christ as man is on the altar, just as Christ as bread is on the altar: and so on for similar cases.* And this would be done sacramentally or by the power of the sacrament, if a divine power were given for this purpose to the sacramental word. Nor should we concern ourselves with whether the word "This is my body" would suffice for this with the aforementioned power, or if something else would be required.

And first, it is argued for the affirmative side that this must be held, because **John of Damascus** <note>A 7th-8th century Church Father who wrote extensively on the Eucharist and the Incarnation.</note> seems to hold this as a fact: namely, that this sacrament exists through assumption. For he speaks thus: "Now having been asked how the bread is the body of Christ, and the wine and water the blood of Christ, I also say to you: the Holy Spirit comes upon them and performs this, which is beyond reason and understanding; for the bread and wine are **assumed**." And further down in the same place: "And just as in baptism, because it is the custom for men to be washed with water and anointed with oil, God joined...

water and the grace of the Holy Spirit, and made it the same bath of regeneration; so, because it is the custom for men to eat and drink bread and wine, God joined his divinity to them, and makes them his body and blood. <note>Pico is likely citing John of Damascus here, comparing the union of divinity with bread to the union of grace with the water of baptism.</note> And further on in the same chapter, speaking of this sacrament of the altar, he says: "Isaiah saw a coal; <note>original: "Carbonem uidit Esaias"</note> but a coal is not simple wood, but wood united with fire. So too the bread of communion is not simple bread, but united to divinity." Furthermore, Dionysius, in the third chapter of *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, calls this sacrament an "assumption." <note>original: "assumptionem"; referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite.</note> Therefore, what these doctors seem to say regarding how things actually *are*, can much more easily be held as a *possibility*.

Secondly, it is argued that—since according to Augustine's letter to Volusianus, in miraculous things, the whole reason for the deed is the power of the doer—to restrict this miraculous sacrament to a specific mode of defense that is not expressly required by the canon of Scripture or the determination of the Church is to restrict divine power to the capacity of our own understanding. This is dangerous and contrary to Augustine, who says in that same place: "If a reason is sought, it will not be a miracle; if an example is provided, it will not be unique; let us grant that God can do something that we confess we cannot investigate."

Thirdly, he argues that a position whose opposite is not evidently found in the sayings of the saints can much more easily be held as a possibility. But the opposite of this—namely, that as a matter of fact "bread-ness" <term>paneitas; a scholastic term for the essence or nature of being bread</term> remains on the altar substantiated by a divine <term>supposito; the underlying subject or personhood that "holds" a nature</term>—is not evidently found in the sayings of the saints. 

This is proven because of what Gregory says in his *Paschal Homily*: "The species and likeness of those things are the names of things that were before, namely bread and wine." Those who hold the opinion that they were "only" bread before, now explain that they are not "only" bread, because the body of Christ lies hidden there. Likewise, that saying of Ambrose: "That the power of God, which creates creatures from nothing, here changes those creatures." And other sayings which state that bread and wine do not remain after the consecration but are converted, are explained thus: that the bread which *was* bread does not remain, even though the same "bread-ness" exists; and this is because of the change in the underlying subject. For this word "bread" refers to a subject in the nature of bread-ness, and this does not remain. <note>Pico is making a technical distinction: the *nature* of bread might stay, but because it is now "owned" by the Divine Person of Christ rather than being its own thing, one can say the "bread" (as an independent entity) has ceased to be.</note> There is a great difference between saying that bread-ness remains hypostasized <note>originally: "hypostatizata"; meaning joined to a divine person</note> in a divine subject, and saying that bread-ness remains in its own subject; for in this second way, there would be no "communication of properties," <term>communicatio idiomatum; a theological term where the properties of two natures joined in one person are shared</term> which does occur in the first way. However, I believe these authorities are entirely against those who propose this as a matter of fact, and not merely as a possibility.

Fourthly, it is argued as follows: this opinion—as a matter of fact—is approved in the confession of Berengarius, <note>Berengarius of Tours (d. 1088) was a theologian who famously argued against the physical presence of Christ in the Eucharist but was forced to recant.</note> which was approved by Pope Nicholas in Rome before 114 bishops; therefore, it can much more easily be held as a possibility. He deduces the premise thus: because Berengarius confesses that after the consecration, there is not only a sacrament, but also the true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ on the altar, and that "sensually, not only sacramentally, but in truth, it is handled by the hands of priests, broken, and ground by the teeth of the faithful." These words seem unable to be taken plainly in a clear and ready sense, such as the words of a confession of faith ought to be...

In this way, it becomes the same body of Christ of both man and bread; thus it remains whole insofar as it is the body of the man, and is ground insofar as it is bread, just as Christ died and lived on the Cross—but he died as man, and lived as God. And that some have understood the words of the aforesaid confession in this way is clear from the Master of the Sentences <note>Peter Lombard, the standard medieval textbook author</note> in the 4th book, distinction 7. His words are these: "Others teach that the body of Christ is essentially broken and divided, and yet remains whole and incorruptible, which they assert they gather from the confession of Berengarius, who confessed before Pope Nicholas and several bishops that the bread and wine which are placed on the altar after the consecration are not only a sacrament, but also the true body and blood of Christ, and are sensibly <note>perceived by the senses</note>—not only in the sacrament, but also in truth—handled and broken by the hands of priests, and ground by the teeth of the faithful." Behold how the confession of Berengarius, heard and examined by the Church, maintains that the body of Christ is ground by the teeth of the faithful, not only in a sacramental sign, but in truth. If taken plainly, this would have truth through the communication of properties <term>communicationem idiomatum; a theological rule where properties of one nature (bread) can be attributed to the person (Christ) who has assumed that nature</term>, because it is ground by the teeth according to its bread-ness, yet remains whole according to its humanity.

But if someone wishes to explain the said confession by saying that the phrase <margin>**Book**</margin> "in truth, and not in the sacrament only" refers only to the immediate word—namely, being "handled by the hands of priests"—and that the subsequent words refer to the "species" <note>the outward appearances of bread, like color and taste</note> or to the external sacrament, under which the whole body of Christ is received while the species is broken and ground, it seems that the words of the confession are not being accepted plainly as they lie and plainly sound. For the words of a confession so examined ought to be accepted without violent exposition or extortion, according to the sense they openly present.

However, an argument is made to the opposite: that this opinion concerning the remaining of the substance of bread on the altar has been condemned by the Church; therefore it must be avoided as heretical. To this, those who hold this opinion respond: first, that it was condemned as a matter of "how things are" <note>the actual fact of the matter</note>, not as a matter of "what is possible." Second, that the condemned opinion differs from this one, which posits that the bread-ness remains hypostatized <note>made part of the divine person</note> by the Word-man. For the former condemned opinion posits multiple subjects <note>supposita</note> after the consecration—the man, Christ, and the bread. But this view posits one single subject in three natures, just as in divine things there is one nature in three subjects <note>referring to the Trinity</note>. That condemned view posits that the substance of bread remains after the consecration; but this view posits it remaining not by way of substance, but by way of accident <note>in the philosophical sense of something that belongs to a subject</note>, just as is the case with the assumed humanity. That view posits that bread and wine remain; but this view says no, but rather a different "bread," even though it is the same bread-ness. From that condemned view, it follows that the body of Christ cannot truly be on the altar under the sacrament, since the bread is changed in nothing; but from this view that does not follow, since it posits that the bread is changed, and even the bread-ness, as far as its mode of being is concerned. From that view, it is not verified that the bread "is" the body of Christ, since there are two subjects; but from this view it is verified, because of the unity of the subject which is one in two natures. From that view, it follows that whatever is in this sacrament is not to be worshipped with *latria* <term>latria; the highest form of worship reserved for God alone</term>, since there would be two subjects, Christ and the bread; but this view posits a single adoration
