## Second Argument
Secondly, it is argued that it can in no way be maintained that, through that manner <note>the theory of "substentification" or bread being assumed into Christ's person</note>, the body of Christ could be on the altar. For when it is asked, "Whether the body of Christ can be on the altar," etc., it is not understood as the "body" that Christ *is* (taking the word "body" as a general category <note>original: "genus"; here meaning a physical substance in general</note>), but it is understood as the body which is a *part* <note>a specific physical component of a human being</note>, and is not predicated of the man directly <note>original: "in recto"; a logical term meaning a direct definition, e.g., "Socrates is a man"</note>. 

Moreover, such a body that is a "part" does not share its properties <note>original: "idioma"; the specific characteristics of a nature</note> with a co-assumed nature, nor with the person, nor vice versa. For although God is man, and vice versa, yet God is not the "head of Christ," and vice versa. And although Christ as man is everywhere by reason of his person <note>the divine Word is omnipresent</note>, yet the head of Christ the man is not everywhere; because the parts of the assumed nature do not share their properties with the person, nor are they predicated of it, or vice versa. 

Therefore, even if "bread-ness" <note>original: "paneitas"; the essential substance of bread</note> were assumed by the Word together with "body-ness," it would still not be said that the body of Christ is bread, or that the body of Christ is on the altar simply because the bread is on the altar—although it might be said and verified that the bread is the "body" which Christ is, according to the sense where "body" is taken as a general category <note>genus</note>. 

That it is not taken otherwise in the question and in the sacrament appears: 
* First, because the "body" called a category <note>genus</note> is not called the "body of Christ" directly, just as "animal" or "man" which Christ is, is not called the "man of Christ" or "animal of Christ." 
* Second, because the form of words in which this sacrament was instituted is this: **This is my body**. It is clear that the truth of that word is not preserved regarding the "body" which is a category. For "animal," which is predicated of me directly, is not *my* animal, but the animal which I *am*. 
* Third, because if it had been consecrated during the three days of Christ's death <note>original: "triduo mortis"; the period between the Crucifixion and Resurrection</note>, there would have been on the altar not the "body-as-category," but the "body-as-part" only. For a "body" <note>in the general sense</note> is an animated <note>living</note> body, which he was not then. 

Therefore, the body of Christ, as it is asked here and as it is treated in the sacrament, is the "body-as-part" only, which is not predicated of bread, or God, or man; nor does it share the properties of the other natures. It would not, therefore, be true to say that the body of Christ was on the altar in the aforesaid manner, by reason of the bread or the person. 

Furthermore, granted that by reason of the said "substantification" <note>original: "substãtificationis"; the process of the substance of bread being sustained by the divine person</note> in one person, there is both bread and body: nevertheless, where the bread is on the altar, the body of Christ is not necessarily there; rather, the bread on the altar would be the body of Christ in heaven. Just as in the three days of death, the soul and body were sustained in the person <note>of the Word</note>, yet for this reason the soul was not in the tomb with the body, nor the body in hell with the soul. 

Furthermore, if this "sustaining" <note>original: "substentificatio"</note> existed, it would terminate at that point where we say the conversion of the bread terminates: but this is the body of Christ, at which the sustaining of a foreign nature cannot terminate; for this is proper only to the uncreated person <note>God the Word</note>, according to the common way. Therefore, the sustaining of "bread-ness" in the person of another nature cannot happen in this sacrament.

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

...[the bread] exists. If, however, it does not begin [to be there] when it previously was not, it follows that it will not be on the altar. Likewise, it is argued that although the "person" of the Word <note>original: "suppositum uerbi"; the divine person of the Son who takes on a nature</note> could assume "bread-ness" <note>original: "paneitatem"; the essential substance or "what-it-is-to-be-bread"</note> which he would create in the act of assuming it—just as we hold regarding the humanity of Christ—nevertheless, he cannot assume a "bread-ness" that already exists in its own right. This is because to do so would be to destroy the bread's own existence, not to assume it. Furthermore, it seems that such power cannot be granted to the Word regarding the union of "bread-ness" to the Word, because the assumption of "bread-ness" into the person of the Word is a matter of greater difficulty than creation itself. This is because the divine being is more "distant" from the nature of bread (to which it is said to be communicated in the act of assumption) than "being" is from "non-being." And yet, the power of creation cannot be communicated to a creature, whether by acting or cooperating. Therefore, neither can the power of assumption. This is confirmed by the authority of Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> in the third part [of the *Summa Theologiae*], who says that a creature cannot cooperate toward the [hypostatic] union. Furthermore, if that [theory] were granted, after receiving the sacrament, the priest would not be fasting, and it would not be a purely spiritual food there, but also a physical one, which is contrary to the dignity of the sacrament. Likewise, Christ would "let go" of something after he had assumed it into the unity of his person, because he would assume the "bread-ness," which he would then discard once the bread was converted into his limbs.

However, to these points, one might perhaps respond first by upholding the following statement: that without the conversion of the bread into the body of Christ, it is possible for the body of Christ to be on the altar in the manner mentioned above—namely, through the "subsistentification" <note>original: "subsistentificationē"; the process of making a nature exist or "subsist" within a divine person rather than on its own</note> of the "bread-ness" in the Word, alongside the humanity previously assumed from the body. This treats "body" as a general category <note>original: "genus"</note>, not as a mere part, and thus refers to the body which is Christ. This is derived from "corporeity," which is a nature and can be predicated directly <note>original: "in recto"; meaning one can say "Christ is this body"</note>. 

And when it is argued that a "body" as a general category would not be called the "body of Christ," it will be answered first: just as one says "a creature of salt" (meaning that which *is* salt) or "the Word of God" (meaning that which *is* God). For example, when it is said, "By the Word of the Lord," it means the Word who *is* God, "the heavens were established." We also say that the substance of matter remains through every natural transformation—that is, the substance which *is* matter. Similarly, it is said by our opponents that the "substance of the bread" is converted into the body of Christ—specifically the substance which *is* the bread, not just a part of the bread. Thus also [John] Damascene in Book 3, Chapter 17, takes the "flesh of Christ" (meaning the flesh which *is* Christ) as a general category, saying that the flesh of the Lord is said to be "deified" and consubstantial with God. 

And when it is argued that the form of the words would not be fitting—"This is my body" meaning "this body is a part of me"—it will be said that perhaps it would not be done through such a form of words. Perhaps a sacramental power would be divinely given to any word whatsoever; and perhaps also, whatever power God could give to any word, He could give to this word: "This is my body." Or, by his absolute power, He could even give it to a word with no meaning, because the power of God is not restricted to the literal signification of words. 

And when it is argued that, granting that the bread is the body and vice versa, it does not follow that where there is bread, there is the body on the altar, it will be said that, on the contrary, it *does* follow. This is because whatever is said of the predicate is also said of the subject. For just as, because God is man and God is everywhere, it follows that the man Christ is everywhere as God, and that God is enclosed in the cradles...

# Apologia:

...[morta]l, and is the Son of the Virgin, and flees the breast, just like the man Christ. It follows that if Christ the man is bread, and vice versa: if bread is on the altar, then Christ the man is also there—not only by that reason by which he is everywhere insofar as he is God, but because the bread is on the altar. For the properties <term>idiomata; the specific attributes or qualities of a nature</term> of the assumed nature are shared mainly on the side of the subject <note>the "subject" here refers to the person of the Word who "owns" the natures</note>, because in the subject, it is held to be the person <term>supposito; the individual substance or "person" that underlies the nature</term>. 

However, it is said "on the side of the subject" because on the side of the predicate <note>the "nature" being described</note>, they perhaps do not necessarily share properties with one another, because there it is held to be the nature itself. Therefore, perhaps it is not necessary that Christ be "man" everywhere, even though he is "God" everywhere, even though on the side of the subject, the man Christ is everywhere. 

Nor is the argument valid which is brought up concerning the soul and body during the three days <note>the *triduum*, the period between Christ's death and resurrection</note>, because they were not united in the "person" in such a way that they were predicated of the person, or of each other; since they were united as parts of a single nature <note>human nature</note>, and therefore it is not necessary for them to share properties with each other in the same way as those natures which are spoken of in relation to each other. It is certain, however, that if it does not follow by necessity, it follows at least as a possibility. 

As for what is said—that if there is a "sustention" <term>substentificatio; the act of making something exist or stay in being</term> of "bread-ness" <note>original: *paneitatis*; the essential quality of being bread</note>, it must end at that point where we say the conversion ends at the "body"—the response is that this has no necessity. Rather, we can say that the sustention occurs simply in the person <note>the Divine Word</note>, even though those who posit "conversion" <note>Transubstantiation</note> say that it ends at the "body" as a part. It could also perhaps be said, as will be discussed below: that the sustention can end at the body, not as "human," but as "united." It is as if the divine person has another nature to sustain within itself; insofar as it draws that nature to its own being, to whomever it communicates its own infinite being, it could also communicate to that same being the power to sustain another nature united to itself. More on this below. 

When, however, it is objected that according to this mode, the body of Christ would not *begin* to be on the altar, but rather something would begin to *be* the body of Christ (or Christ would begin to *be* a body), the answer would be: just as if "bread-ness" were added to Christ (who was already man), Christ the man would begin to be bread. Thus, he begins "accidentally" <note>per accidens; in a non-essential or secondary way</note> to be on the altar in a new way, which is appropriate to bread. According to this, Christ the man would begin to be on the altar visibly and as the food of the faithful by reason of the assumed "bread-ness," just as Christ as God began to be in the lap or womb of his mother in a new way by reason of the assumed humanity. 

Regarding what is said about the assumption of a pre-existing "bread-ness" into his own person: the response is that God can assume every nature capable of being assumed, even if it already existed in its own individual personhood. In the act of assuming it, He can deprive it of its own independent existence <note>original: *ratione suppositi*; its status as a self-standing individual</note> and draw it into His own being. For it is established that the Word could set aside the human nature, which would immediately have its own subsistence and the status of a "person," even though it does not have this while united to the Word; and it would be the same humanity in essence as was previously united. Therefore, in a similar way, He could assume a humanity (or bread-ness) previously existing in its own right, in the manner already stated; and it would be the same nature, now assumed, which was previously not assumed. When, however, it is argued that "power" <note>original: *uirtus*</note> cannot be conferred upon the Word for this purpose, perhaps it can, and perhaps it cannot. and if an inherent power cannot be given, because such...

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

...if power were created, perhaps an "assisting power" could be granted, because such a power would be uncreated rather than created. In this way, there would be an assumption of <term>bread-ness</term> <note>original: *paneitatis*; the essential "being" or substance of bread</note> <term>sacramentally</term> <note>original: *sacramentaliter*; through the functional power of the sacred rite</note> by the power of the Word, just as great men also posit that power is conferred upon the sacraments of the New Law. And perhaps, if power can be conferred—inhering in the sacramental word to convert the whole [substance] into the whole, and especially into something pre-existing without increasing it—it can also be conferred to achieve the aforementioned effect; for perhaps it will seem to some that this is of the same level of difficulty as that.

Regarding what is said about the breaking of the fast, one might respond that the rule about not breaking the "natural fast" follows the manner commonly proposed—namely, that the substance of the bread does not remain. But if we posit that the substance *does* remain, we would say something else; or perhaps it will be said that a priest is not called "fasting" after consumption because the substance of bread is absent, since <term>however much</term> <note>original: *quantūcunqꝫ*</note> the substance of bread might be absent, if a Jew or a Christian were to consume the sacramental species as physical food and with the intention of being nourished, he would break the fast. Instead, it is because the priest does not consume it as physical food, but as a sacrament, that the fast is not broken. It would be a similar case if the substance of the bread remained: he would still not break the natural fast, provided he did not consume it as physical food.

Furthermore, regarding the saying that "Christ does not let go of what he once assumed," this is said by presupposing that he is held to have assumed only human nature, just as in fact he assumed only that. However, he could assume another nature and then let it go. It can also be said that if <term>bread-ness</term> were assumed by the Word, it would never be let go by the Word of its own accord or on its own part; but "by accident"—from the condition of the assumed nature with its natural defects—He would let it go due to the corruption of the assumed nature, just as he let go of his humanity during the three days <note>The *triduum*, the three days between Christ's death and resurrection when his soul and body were separated.</note>. 

But let us inquire again by way of dispute: Can the Body, which is a part of being, be truly on the altar <term>without</term> <note>original: *absqꝫ*</note> the conversion of the bread into itself? It seems that it can. Just as color is sustained in a substance as in a subject through the mediation of another accident—for example, a surface—not because the surface is the subject of the color (since one accident is not the subject of another, because, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says, there is no "quality of a quality"), but because color does only exist in a subject in relation to a surface; so <term>bread-ness</term> can be sustained in the Word through the mediation of the Body. This is not because the Body is the immediate sustainer and giver-of-subsistence to the assumed <term>bread-ness</term> (the Word being the primary sustainer), but because the <term>bread-ness</term> is not given subsistence in the "person" <note>original: *supposito*; the individual divine person of Christ</note> of the Word except in relation to the Body of Christ as a part.

For God can place this order between "assumable" natures, even though they do not have that order in their own nature; just as he can take away from some things the natural order which they have among themselves—such as between heat and the act of heating, as seen in the **furnace of the Chaldeans** <note>A reference to the Biblical story in Daniel 3, where three youths were thrown into a furnace but the fire did not burn them.</note> and in many other cases. Therefore, just as color (because it exists in a substance in relation to a surface) is spoken of in terms of the surface in a concrete sense, by way of an accidental quality...

<summary>Pico argues that the "bread-ness" of the Eucharist can be assumed by the Word without breaking traditional rules of fasting or the permanence of the Incarnation. He uses Aristotelian metaphysics and the Biblical miracle of the fiery furnace to show that God can alter the natural relationship between substances and their properties.</summary>

...is, the surface is colored: thus <term>bread-ness</term> <note>original: *paneitas*; the essential "being" or substance of bread</note>, which is the substance, will be predicated of the body of Christ in the concrete, taken in the manner of a "substantial such," or by way of "whatness" <note>original: *per modum quid*; a term used to define the essential identity of a thing</note>, by saying: "The Son of God is bread," and vice-versa. Just as humanity is predicated of the <term>person</term> <note>original: *supposito*; the underlying individual subject of existence</note> in the "whatness," by saying: "The Son of God is man," and vice-versa. 

Therefore, just as because God is man and vice-versa, for that reason they communicate their <term>properties</term> <note>original: *idiomata*; the technical term *communicatio idiomatum* refers to the sharing of attributes between the divine and human natures in Christ</note> to one another—where God is, there is man—and similarly with a surface and whiteness, so it is with bread and the body: for if bread is on the altar, the body of Christ is on the altar. 

Perhaps it should be said otherwise: that assumed natures have the mode of an <term>accident</term> <note>original: *accidentis*; in philosophy, a property that does not exist by itself but only in a substance, like "redness" in an apple</note>, as the ancient theologians used to say, insofar as they come to a person already subsisting in act. They do not constitute the person, but are rather constituted in being through him. Therefore, just as among accidents one is found to be the subject of another (though not the ultimate one)—as we say the power of the soul is the subject of virtues and habits insofar as it is sustained by the soul, and similarly a surface is called the "subject" in a certain way with respect to color—so, although one assumed nature cannot by itself and primarily sustain another nature, nevertheless, insofar as it is united to the Word and sustained in it, it can sustain another in itself and have a mode as if it were a subject with respect to that other nature, which in turn has a mode like an accident with respect to it. 

This is only to the extent that one is sustained in the other as it is united to the Word and sustained by it. For if the Person does not give subsistence to the assumed nature except by reason of His own infinite being (to which He draws the nature united and associated with Himself), then to whatever nature He communicates His infinite being, He also communicates the power to sustain another nature united to it. Similarly, substance, insofar as it draws one accident to its own being—because an accident is not a "being" except because it belongs to a being—grants it enough so that it can sustain in itself and in its own being another accident coming to it (just as a specific act comes to a potential power). 

Therefore the Body, taken as the part united to and sustained by the Word in its own being (which is the being of the Word communicated to it), can sustain in itself the assumable nature of bread, which has the mode of an accident. For it is supposed that God gives to accidents the mode of substance; thus He can give to "bread-ness" the mode of an accident, sustaining it in another which will relate to it as if it were a subject. Nor does it differ, in this regard, whether it is perfect in its <term>species</term> <note>original: *specie*; the specific kind or category of a thing</note> or not, because sometimes the subject of an accident is "imperfect" in its species, such as a head or a hand. 

Just as God produces some creatures immediately and others by means of others, and as He terminates some creatures in Himself as their goal through others, so also the Word can terminate some creature in Himself as the sustaining subject by means of another. And just as creatures through which God produces are called "producers," and creatures through which He terminates them in Himself as their goal are called "ends" or "sub-ends," so a creature through which the Word gives subsistence to another in Himself will be said to "give subsistence." 

Therefore, by reason of such <term>giving of subsistence</term> <note>original: *substentificationis*</note> in the body of Christ, as in a "quasi-subject" and immediate support, it will be said in the concrete: "the bread is the body," and vice-versa. Just as the Son of God is...

<summary>Pico argues that the Body of Christ can act as a "subject" that sustains the "nature of bread" as an accident, similar to how the Divine Word sustains Christ's human nature. This metaphysical framework allows him to claim that "bread is the body" without requiring the bread's substance to be destroyed.</summary>

...man and vice versa. And they will communicate their <term>properties</term> <note>original: *idiomata*; the technical term *communicatio idiomatum* refers to the sharing of attributes between the divine and human natures in Christ</note> to one another in the manner aforesaid, just as a surface and a colored object do. For "bread" stands for the thing sustaining <term>bread-ness</term> <note>original: *paneitatem*; the essential "being" or substance of bread</note>, just as "white" stands for the thing sustaining whiteness. For as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the first book of the *Topics*: "A white thing is a body having such a color in such a way." John Damascene says in book 3, chapter 11: "God" is the one who has the divine nature, and "man" is the one who has the human nature, and so on for the rest. And just as it makes no difference to something being white whether the thing in which the whiteness is sustained is a "perfect species" <note>a complete, independent type of thing</note> or not, so it makes no difference to something being called "bread" whether that which is the "bread-ness" (as a subject in which the bread-ness is immediately sustained) is a perfect or imperfect species, or a nature or part of a nature.

On the contrary, because an assumed nature (or part of an assumed nature) does not have the character of a <term>person</term> <note>original: *suppositum*; the underlying individual subject of existence</note>, nor does it have the "being of subsistence" in itself; because although the "being of the Word" is communicated to it, nevertheless as it belongs to that nature, it is not the being of subsistence, but of "existence in another." Therefore, an assumed nature, insofar as it is united, cannot sustain another nature in itself, nor draw it to the person [suppositum], since it does not itself have the character of a person. 

But if this follows, would it not also follow that a surface cannot sustain color in itself, since the "being" (which is the "being of subsistence" regarding substance) is only "existence" when communicated to an <term>accident</term> <note>original: *accidenti*; a property like color that requires a substance to exist</note>? And thus the surface could not be the subject of color, because the surface itself is an accident. Should we say instead that the "being of the Word," as it belongs to the assumed humanity in relation to the Word, is "existence"; but as it belongs to that same humanity in relation to the "bread-ness," it is "sustaining"; and as it belongs to the nature last assumed, it is "existence" simply, as might be said of a surface.

But a further argument against the above is this: A nature is immediately united to the person [suppositum]; therefore it is not possible that "bread-ness" is united to the person of the Word by means of another nature, since no medium can fall between the nature and the person. But perhaps a nature is immediately united to its *own* person, but regarding a *foreign* person, in respect to which it has the mode of an accident, this is not necessary; rather, one can be united by means of the person, the other in the manner aforesaid. 

On the contrary, if the analogy of the surface holds, it would follow that just as a surface (separated from the substance) is the subject of color and is colored, so if the body were separated from the person [suppositum] of the Word, it could be as it were the subject of "bread-ness," and would still be called bread—which is absurd. This will not happen if we say, as Hilary <note>Saint Hilary of Poitiers, a 4th-century theologian</note> says, that to a surface separated from its substance can be granted "being" and a mode of being as a substance (by reason of which it was a subject for accidents), but to a separated humanity there cannot be granted the infinite being of the person of the Word (by reason of which it was able to sustain another substantial nature). 

And you should note that in all these inquiries, it was always presupposed that to <term>personize</term> <note>original: *suppositare*; to provide the individual personal foundation for</note> a foreign nature is a property of the infinite being. But a further argument is made: The Word assumed flesh by means of the soul, yet the soul is not for this reason predicated of the flesh or vice versa. Therefore, granted that the Word had assumed "bread-ness" by means of the body, not...

<header>Defense.</header>

## Defense.

Because of this, one thing would be said of the other. But perhaps it is not a perfect comparison, because the Word <note>The "Word" refers to the second person of the Trinity, Christ</note> is said to have assumed flesh through the medium of the soul, as if the soul were an intermediary in regards to its natural existence. Likewise, it happened through the medium of the soul in regards to the process of the "Assumption" <note>The "Assumption" here refers to the act of the Divine taking on a nature, not Mary’s Assumption</note>. However, he did not assume flesh through the soul as if the soul were first supported and then the soul in turn supported the flesh—as is said regarding humanity and "bread-ness"—but rather because he did not assume flesh except in relation to the human nature, of which the flesh is a part through the soul united to you. 

Again, it is argued on behalf of the [theologically] "false" position that it is more fitting to propose—even as a matter of fact—that the body of Christ is present on the altar through the **hypostatization of bread-ness** <note>original: *hypostatizationem paneitatis*; the idea that the "Person" of Christ takes the essence of bread into his own identity, similar to how he took on human nature</note> within the person of Christ as God, rather than through "conversion" <note>Conversion, or Transubstantiation, is the Catholic doctrine that the bread's substance is entirely changed into Christ's body</note>. For if that view is rejected, it is because it is considered unfitting as it goes against the decrees of the Church. But it is proven that this is not the case. For if this position were seen to be against Church decrees in any way, it would be seen most clearly in two points: namely, that the bread remains, and that the "accidents" <note>The physical properties like taste, smell, and color</note> would not be there without a subject. But this position claims neither of those things.

For it concedes that the bread does not "remain," because the "person" <note>original: *suppositum*; the independent subject of existence</note> of the bread does not remain. It can also be said that the accidents are there without a subject. For an accident depends on a substance only in regards to its existence—at least according to the common path—not according to its essence. Therefore, although the essence of the bread remains, since the "subsistence" of the bread (by which the accidents used to be sustained) ceases to be there, it follows that the accidents would subsist by themselves, unless we propose that they migrate from one subject to another.

Secondly, it is argued that this position is more fitting because more difficulties are removed by it. For here, there is only the difficulty concerning the union. One should propose as few things as possible in the articles of faith unless faith compels it, and the "Assumption" is a specific article of faith. Therefore, it is not necessary to multiply miracles and things to be believed beyond our reason without an evident and compelling necessity.

Thirdly, because the "appearances" are better preserved in this way. For it appears in this sacrament that there is bread and wine, which the theory of "Assumption" preserves, while "Conversion" does not. For we see someone nourished by the hosts just as they would be by true bread, and we see the hosts rot, and finally all the things happen to them which happen to the substance of bread. Therefore, if all these things can be preserved while truly maintaining that Christ’s body is on the altar—and that this bread (which, as Berengarius <note>Berengarius of Tours was an 11th-century theologian who argued against the physical change of the bread into flesh</note> says, is crushed by the teeth of the faithful) becomes the true body of Christ—it is better to adhere to this way than to the way of "Conversion," by which these things cannot be explained without a multiplication of miracles.

Fourthly, because Paul says in 1 Corinthians 10: "The bread which we break, is it not the participation in the body of the Lord?" <note>original: *Panis quẽ frãgimus, nonne participatio corporis Domini est?*</note>.

Fifthly, because Christ is sacramentally present where he is directly present by the power of the sacrament. But Christ would be more directly on the altar through "Assumption" than through "Conversion." This is because the "form" of this sacrament—which produces its effect more directly by what it signifies—produces that which it more properly signifies. This is the union through Assumption, by which the <term>properties</term> <note>original: *idiomata*; the technical term for the sharing of attributes between Christ's natures</note> are shared, so that this thing *is* that thing. This is what the formal words sound like: **This is my body** <note>original: *Hoc est corpus meũ*</note>. It does not sound like a union of conversion, because through conversion the bread is not Christ, nor vice versa; rather, the bread "becomes" Christ or is "converted" into Christ.

Sixthly, because that way of "Conversion" is intricate and has many difficulties, while this way is clear and easy.

He is arguing that the presence of Christ in the bread could potentially be explained through "Assumption" (the Divine Person taking the bread's nature into itself) rather than "Transubstantiation" (the bread's substance being destroyed and replaced). This was a highly technical debate in the 1480s involving Aristotelian logic and Catholic dogma.</meta>

<page-num>192</page-num>
<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>
<meta>catchword: tionem (conversion)</meta>

For we already believe in the **Assumption** <note>In this context, "Assumption" refers to the theological act of a divine person taking a nature into its own identity, similar to how the Word became flesh in the Incarnation.</note> through another article of faith. Furthermore, whenever things are limited within the same underlying subject <term>suppositum<gloss>The individual "person" or substance that acts as the foundation for various qualities; for example, "Socrates" is the subject in which "wisdom" and "whiteness" exist.</gloss></term>, wherever one is, the other is also. Just as wherever the musicianship of Socrates <note>original: *musica sortis*; "Sortis" was a standard medieval logic shorthand for the name Socrates.</note> is, there too is his whiteness. I say "limited" things, because if one were limited and the other unlimited, wherever the limited thing was, the unlimited would be, but not necessarily the other way around. 

But if bread were "assumed," the human body of Christ and the body of the bread would be one in their underlying subject, and both would be limited. Therefore, since the assumed bread would be on the altar, the body of Christ would consequently be there as well. Likewise, the "medium" is closer than the "extreme." If Christ were to assume bread or **bread-ness** <note>original: *paneitatem*; the essential nature that makes bread what it is.</note>, he would do this through the medium of his own corporeality <note>his physical body</note>, because a thing less worthy of being assumed is taken up through the medium of a thing more worthy, according to the fitness of the assumption. Therefore, since the subject of Christ who assumes the bread would be on the altar with the assumed bread, much more so would the body of Christ be there, as it would be the medium of that assumption.

Finally, it seems that the authorities of the Saints <note>The Church Fathers and established theologians.</note> regarding **conversion** can nonetheless be preserved while holding to the theory of "Assumption." Since "being" <term>esse<gloss>The act of existing or the state of being real.</gloss></term> differs from "essence" <term>essentia<gloss>The core nature of what a thing is, regardless of whether it currently exists.</gloss></term>, one can be assumed while the other is not. 

Hence, the Word is not "enfleshed" <note>Incarnate</note> in the same way it would be "enbreaded" <note>Impanate</note>. In that [Incarnation] assumption, the essence was taken up before it even had its own existence; thus, it never had an existence other than the divine existence communicated to it. Because of this, it was an Assumption without any "conversion" of the thing assumed into the one assuming it, or vice versa. This is why the Church says: *not by the conversion of the divinity into flesh* <note>original: "non conuersione diuinitatis in carnem"; a quote from the Athanasian Creed.</note> (nor, it follows, the reverse) *but by the assumption of humanity into God.* 

Pre-existing bread, however, has both "being" and "essence." The assumption of the bread into the humanity of the divine subject consumes the bread’s own independent existence <note>original: *subsistere*; its status as a standalone thing</note>—not through its total destruction <note>annihilation</note>, but through the assumption of its substantial essence. It is by this that the mystery is perfected. And so, all the authorities speaking of **transubstantiation** and **conversion** can be understood as referring to the bread's "being" (its independent existence) and not to its "essence" (its nature). And when authorities say that after the consecration the bread "does not remain" but rather "was" there, this is true regarding its "being," because it remains only regarding its "essence." 

From these points, it appears that the body of Christ can just as truly be present sacramentally on the altar through the assumption of "bread-ness" without conversion, just as it is now commonly held to be present through conversion. In fact, a clear distinction cannot be understood between these three terms—**assumption, conversion, and annihilation**—except by presupposing the perspective of this opinion:

1.  **Assumption:** That is assumed which, before having any independent existence as a subject, is taken up into the new existence of a divine subject.
2.  **Annihilation:** That is annihilated which simply ceases to exist. It is irrelevant to this definition whether something else succeeds it or not, because that is external to the thing which has ceased to be.
3.  **Conversion:** That is converted which, while remaining in its essence, loses its own independent "being" as a subject and passes into the "being" of another subject, truly becoming that subject. 

And this is the true definition of conversion, in which two things are understood in the thing being converted: namely, that it remains according to its essence (and thus differs from what is annihilated), and that it becomes another thing through...

...the condition of the subject, through which it differs from that which is not converted. And while it becomes something else, it relinquishes the nature of its own subject, and through this, it differs from what is assumed. However, holding to the common manner of conversion, the bread is not converted but annihilated; and those who wish to maintain that a conversion occurs, so that there is no annihilation, seem to satisfy the point more in words than in reality. Hence, many who follow that path have conceded that it is an annihilation, etc.

To the contrary, on behalf of the true side, it is argued that the opinion positing that the sacrament of the Eucharist is in fact performed through the **assumption of bread-ness** <note>original: *assumptionem panicitatis*; the theory that the Divine Word takes the nature of bread into its own person, rather than changing the bread into flesh.</note> is unfitting and irrational. First, Durand <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain (c. 1275–1334), a Dominican philosopher known for his independent and often "modernist" views.</note> argues thus: that it is ridiculous for one nature—nay, many—to be assumed every day by the divine subject and laid aside every day, which would be the case if the substance of the bread were assumed anew in this sacrament. For there would be as many assumptions as there are consecrations, and as many depositions <note>In this context, "deposition" refers to Christ "putting down" or leaving the nature of the bread after the sacrament is consumed or changed.</note> as there are receptions of the sacrament. But perhaps this "ridiculousness" does not demonstrate the falsehood of the underlying premise.

Secondly, it is argued that it seems impossible for such an assumption to take place by means of some created thing, as the aforementioned opinion posits. This is because that medium would act either in the capacity of the **efficient cause** <term>efficient cause<gloss>The primary agent or force that produces an effect or brings a change into being.</gloss></term> of such an assumption, or in the capacity of the terminating cause; but nothing created can relate to an assumption in either of these ways, therefore, etc. The minor premise is proved thus: that no created thing can be the efficient cause of such an assumption is clear, because such an assumption occurs when a thing loses its own natural mode of being and puts on another. It seems that no one can do this except the Author of nature, who alone instituted the natures of things, and thus He alone seems able to change them.

This argument of Durand’s perhaps shows that a created thing cannot be the principal efficient cause. By the same token, it seems that nothing created can terminate such an assumption, because something that is above nature and the entire course of nature cannot be attributed to any nature. This [act of assumption] consists of another nature subsisting—one which is born to subsist in itself—and perhaps this erroneous opinion set down above would believe it could avoid [this charge] through certain points already mentioned. For falsehood is not always easily convicted of its own falsity through evident reasons, so weak is the light of our intellect, being that which is lowest in the order of intellectual nature.

Furthermore, Durand argues as follows: whatever may be said of the position of such an assumption, it is nonetheless entirely unfitting that it should occur by means of the body as a part. For never does the "body," as it is understood as a part of human nature—positing only one form in man—refer to matter alone; rather, it necessarily refers to the **composite of matter and form** <term>matter and form<gloss>The Aristotelian concept that every physical object consists of "matter" (potentiality) and "form" (the essence that makes it a specific thing).</gloss></term> giving corporeal existence. It is necessary that the human body refers to the reality as a whole and not just a part, even though conceptually it can name a part, because the soul provides all the perfections that lower forms provide. And therefore, if the composite of matter and form (which is the soul) is considered insofar as it gives corporeal existence only, and is compared to the same composite insofar as it possesses through the soul not only corporeal existence but also sense, life, and reason: then the body in the first sense...

...which preceded. But Christ, in instituting this sacrament, spoke these words in **Luke 22**: *This is my body, which will be given for you* <note>original: "Hoc est corpus meum, quod pro uobis tradetur"</note> etc. And *this cup in my blood, which will be shed for you.* Therefore, it is that same body in number <note>In scholastic logic, "the same in number" refers to numerical identity—being the exact same thing rather than just the same kind of thing.</note> that was afterwards given to the Apostles in the sacrament to be eaten; but the body that was given to be crucified was not of the nature of bread, but was a body pertaining to the nature of humanity. Therefore, the body given to the Apostles in the sacrament of the altar was truly of the nature of humanity, and by equal reasoning, in our sacrament, it is the body of Christ pertaining to his humanity; it is not for you merely through a **communication of properties** <term>communicatio idiomatum; a theological doctrine explaining how the properties of both the divine and human natures are attributed to the one Person of Christ</term> arising from the **assumption of bread-ness** <note>original: "assumptione paneitatis"; the theory that the Word takes on the nature of bread.</note>.

If anyone should say that the relative pronoun refers to the same <term>subject</term> <note>original: "suppositum"; the individual substance or person that "underlies" the natures</note> and not the same nature—and thus it can truly be said, when the assumed bread is pointed to, *this is my body, which will be given for you*, because it is the same subject possessing both the assumed bread-ness and the body-ness later given up, and thus the same subject was first pointed out and then given up, even if according to one nature and then another—this is not valid. For when it is said, *This is my body*, "body" cannot be taken there for the subject possessing body-ness, but rather for the nature possessed, as is indicated by the possessive pronoun to which it is added when it is said, *My body*: that is, "that which I have." But perhaps this argument would have greater efficacy among **grammarians** than among **theologians**.

Furthermore, he argues thus: that the said "assumption" does not suffice for the body of Christ to be on the altar, neither really nor according to the communication of properties. Not really, indeed, because the assumption of two natures by one subject does not suffice for one nature to be where the other is. For if the subject of the Son had from the beginning assumed the humanity of Peter in Rome and of Paul in Judea, it would not follow that where Peter was, there Paul would be, and vice versa—except in regard to the subject, which is predicated of both, and of which both are predicated concretely. Similarly, granted that the subject of the Son has assumed both humanity and bread-ness, it does not necessarily follow that where the nature of bread is, there the nature of humanity must be. 

Nor, by reason of the subject, could it be said that where the bread is, there is the body of Christ because of the communication of properties; because according to that opinion, the name of the subject does not receive the predication of the assumed bread nor the parts of the body. For it is not true to say, according to those thinkers, that the Son of God is "bread" or a "body" which is a part. Therefore, by reason of a common subject, one cannot be predicated of the other so that it is said that "one is the other" or "one is where the other is." Nor is it like the tooth of an **Ethiopian** <note>A standard example in medieval logic used to discuss accidental properties (like the whiteness of a tooth) versus essential properties.</note> and its whiteness, because the tooth is called white, and the white thing is called a tooth. And where one is, the other is, because this is so through the fact that they are one in the subject, and consequently indistinct in subject and place. However, it cannot be said thus of the human body and the assumed bread-ness. And whatever may be the case regarding this argument, this is true: that just as it does not follow by necessity, it follows nevertheless as a possibility, etc. **Peter of Palude** <note>Petrus de Palude (c. 1275–1342), a prominent Dominican theologian and Archbishop.</note> however, argues thus: Either He would assume...

<summary>Pico argues against the theory of "Assumption" in the Eucharist, asserting that Christ's words "This is my body" require the actual presence of his human nature rather than just a shared subject with the bread. He uses scholastic logic to demonstrate that the presence of one assumed nature does not necessitate the presence of another at the same location.</summary>
<keywords>Eucharist, Assumption theory, transubstantiation, Luke 22, nature of bread, humanity of Christ, communication of properties, suppositum, Peter of Palude, scholastic logic</keywords>

--- Page 229 ---
<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate regarding the "Assumption" theory of the Eucharist. The text moves from the initial proposal of the theory to a rigorous philosophical critique, specifically addressing how physical properties (accidents) and the nature of "body" function in the sacrament.</meta>

<page-num>196</page-num>

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

...the substance of bread with its **accidents** <term>accidents; the outward, physical properties of a thing, such as color, taste, and size, as opposed to its inner essence</term>, or without them. It cannot be without them, because that is impossible; for something that cannot exist by itself, nor be sustained by any power—such as a "relation" or something of that kind—cannot be assumed by itself. Moreover, a physical substance cannot exist without **quantity** <note>In this context, "quantity" refers to physical extension or size.</note>, because quantity (or shape) is its own boundary and proper attribute. However, many would deny this. If, on the other hand, the bread is assumed with its accidents, then Christ would not be present on the altar **sacramentally**, but **locally** <note>"Locally" means occupying space in the way a physical object does, whereas "sacramentally" refers to a supernatural mode of presence that does not rely on physical dimensions.</note>, through the quantity associated with the substance assumed on the altar, and not moved from there—just as he was locally in the womb through the quantity associated with the humanity assumed there.

And perhaps this concludes that it is not in the sacramental manner that the **Thomists** <term>Thomists; followers of the theology of St. Thomas Aquinas</term> describe through **conversion** <note>The doctrine of Transubstantiation, where the bread "converts" into the Body.</note>. They say that Christ is not there through his own physical quantity, but through the quantity of the bread; yet if he were to assume the bread along with its nature, it would then seem that he is there through a quantity that is his own. The method of the Thomists, however, is not held by many. 

Secondly, **Peter** <note>Likely referring to the theologian Peter Paludanus or Peter Lombard.</note> argues that this cannot be understood as "body" in the sense of a general category (**genus**), but only as "body" in the sense of a specific **part**. This is because a general category is not predicated possessively of its inferior members, in the way a part is predicated of the whole. For example, I say "my humanity" and "my hand," but I do not say "my animal" or "my man" regarding myself. This is apparent in the consecration of the blood, where it is said: *This is the cup of my blood* <note>original: "Hic est calix sanguinis mei"</note>. "Blood" is not an ambiguous term referring to both a category and a part, like the word "body" is; rather, it is taken only for a part. 

Therefore, granted that the "body" which is Christ might be on the altar through "assumption" by the power of the sacrament, it would still not be the "Body of Christ" which is a **part** of him, except by **natural concomitance** <term>concomitance; the doctrine that because Christ is living, his Body, Blood, Soul, and Divinity are always found together</term>. This is because through "assumption," a union would not be made in the natures, but in the **Person** <note>original: "supposito"; the underlying subject or personhood of the Word.</note> only. Hence, that assumption would result in the bread being the "body" which is Christ, but not the "Body of Christ" specifically—just as currently the Divinity is not the Humanity. Enough has been said about this above regarding the body as a part and the body as a category.

Thirdly, he argues that just as the assumed human body of Christ was not allowed to decay or rot, neither in substance nor in quantity, so too the bread should not decay if it were assumed into Christ's person. However, perhaps this comparison does not strictly hold by necessity.

To the arguments for the opposite side, we respond to the authority of **John of Damascus** <note>An 8th-century Church Father often cited in Eucharistic debates.</note>. It is said: Just as it is certain that the water of baptism is not assumed into the unity of the divine Person, nor is the grace of the Holy Spirit united to it so as to make one single Person, similarly the bread and wine are not "assumed" into the divine Person. Nor is the Divinity joined to them in a unity of Person. Instead, just as the water is used there as the **permanent matter** of the sacrament, so the bread and wine are used as **transient matter**, because the matter of the sacrament is converted into the body of Christ. 

Consequently, it is said to be "united" to the Divinity in some way—not by an assumption where the nature of bread or wine remains, but through **transubstantiation** into the humanity previously assumed. This is clear from what follows, where it is said: *Just as naturally, through eating, bread, wine, and water are throughout changed into the body and blood of the one eating and drinking, and it does not become a different body than before, so also the bread, wine, and water of the offering, through change, and...* <note>original: "Quemadmodum naturaliter per comestionem, panis, & uinum, & aqua per totum, in corpus & sanguinem comedentis & bibentis transmutantur..."</note>

<summary>Pico critiques the theory of "Assumption" (impannation) by arguing that if the bread were joined to Christ's person without changing its nature, it would lead to logical absurdities regarding physical size and decay. He defends the Thomist view of transubstantiation using an analogy of digestion to explain how bread becomes Christ's body.</summary>

<header>Apology.</header>

# Apology.

...and the coming of the Holy Spirit, it supernaturally passes into the body and blood of the Lord, and therefore they are not two things, but one and the same. From these points, it appears that the intention of **Damascenus** <term>John of Damascus; an 8th-century Syrian monk and Church Father whose "Exposition of the Orthodox Faith" was a standard text in the Middle Ages</term> is not that the substance of the bread and the wine remain and are assumed by the divine **person** <term>supposito; the underlying "subject" or "person" that possesses a nature. In the Incarnation, the Divine Person of the Word assumed human nature</term>, but rather they pass into the body and blood of Christ, and are thus united to the divinity. 

However, they <note>The critics or opposing theologians</note> object, asking: "How can that which is annihilated—that is, truly ceases to be in itself—be united?" And they press the point using that analogy of the **burning coal** <note>A traditional analogy used to explain how two things coexist, like fire in wood or divinity in humanity.</note>, in which it is said that just as a coal is not simple wood, but wood united with fire, so the bread of communion is not simple bread, but bread united with divinity. But it is said that the coal and the fire are not the same in their underlying person; yet when the wood is consumed, it passes into something else. Thus, the bread of communion is not one in person with the divinity, but by its own ceasing it passes into the body of Christ, which is united to the divinity. 

But against this: for then the bread of communion would be compared to the fire (into which the wood has passed through its destruction), and not to the coal itself, in which the nature of the fire is found simultaneously with the preservation of the wooden nature. Seek the answer; and perhaps it is this: that the analogy does not hold true in all respects, and perhaps it would have been better if Damascenus had not proposed that analogy. 

And when the same Damascenus says that "God joined the divinity to the bread," it must be said that this is not through "assumption," but rather as food is joined to the one who is fed, because it is converted into him. Let that analogy be accepted between this conversion and that one, as far as it can apply. 

**St. Thomas** <term>Thomas Aquinas; the preeminent 13th-century Scholastic philosopher and theologian</term> in the fourth book <note>referring to Aquinas's "Commentary on the Sentences," Book 4, Distinction 11, Question 1</note> says that Damascenus's word is to be understood regarding the **outward appearances** <term>species; the physical properties of bread (like taste, smell, and color) that remain even after the substance of the bread is gone</term>, to which the body of Christ (already united to divinity) is joined in an ineffable way. He says this, and since this mode is ineffable <note>original: "ineffabilis"; meaning "unutterable" or "beyond description"</note>, one should not search further into it. 

In the third part of the *Summa* <note>Summa Theologiae, Question 75</note>, he says: "God joined his divinity—that is, his divine power—to the bread and wine, not so that they might remain in this sacrament, but so that they might from there create his body and blood." 

Regarding the authority of the **Apostle** <note>St. Paul, specifically referencing 1 Corinthians 10:16: "The bread that we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ?"</note>, it is said that his speech is figurative, both in terms of the subject and the predicate. For "bread" (the subject) stands for the sensible sacrament—namely, the appearances of bread—while "the body of Christ" is also taken figuratively. Hence, according to the **Gloss** <term>Gloss; the "Glossa Ordinaria," the standard medieval collection of biblical commentaries</term>, that statement does not imply that the substance of the bread or the appearances of the bread truly and realistically become Christ or the body of Christ, nor that "body of Christ" is predicated directly of the substance of the bread or the appearance of the bread. Rather, the sense is: the bread which we break in the sacrament—that is, the participation in the bread broken on the altar—is the participation in the divine body; that is, it makes us one with Christ. 

Let the **Masters** <note>The faculty of the University of Paris (the Sorbonne) who had condemned several of Pico's 900 Theses in 1487.</note> who were condemning my views remember that if the words of Damascenus and Paul in this matter were taken as they sound at first glance and on the surface, they could create a sense of faith that is erroneous for many. Furthermore, when it is said that this position regarding "assumption" <note>The theory that the bread remains and is "assumed" by Christ, similar to how he assumed human nature.</note> is followed by fewer difficulties, it must be said that in matters of faith, one should not always choose that which is followed by fewer difficul-

<meta>catchword: ties,</meta>

<summary>Pico defends his Eucharistic views by arguing that the writings of John of Damascus and St. Paul should be read figuratively rather than literally, supporting the doctrine of Transubstantiation over the "Assumption" theory. He warns his critics that a superficial reading of these authorities could lead to heresy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s defense of his eleventh thesis regarding the Eucharist. He is arguing that while the Church teaches "conversion" (transubstantiation), it is logically possible for God to have chosen "assumption" (impanation). He concludes this specific disputation by reconciling his views with Church tradition and the writings of Saint Thomas Aquinas and Peter de Palude.</meta>

<page-num>198</page-num>
<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

...authorities, but rather that which is more in harmony with Apostolic traditions and Ecclesiastical dogma, even if many difficulties occur. For it is necessary to **captivate the intellect** in obedience to faith, and to entrust oneself to the traditions of the fathers with the humility of obedience, as even **Plato** says well and most religiously in the *Timaeus* <note>original: "Timæo"; a Platonic dialogue often cited by Renaissance thinkers to show harmony between ancient philosophy and Christian humility.</note>. 

Likewise, someone might say that although that "assumption" <note>The theory that Christ "assumes" the nature of bread rather than replacing its substance.</note> would better preserve the appearance to the senses, nevertheless "conversion" <note>Transubstantiation; the total change of the bread's substance into Christ's body.</note> better preserves the appearance to the intellect—that is, the words of the Gospel, which it is better to preserve, because they cannot lie, just as senses can be deceived. 

But it is argued against this still for the opposing side: because if this were not through "assumption" (in such a way that it would be included in the article of the Incarnation, for the belief would be the same), it would be necessary for there to be a special article about this conversion, which nevertheless is not in the **Creed** <note>original: "symbolo"; referring to the Apostles' or Nicene Creed.</note>. Some say, like **Peter de Palude** <term>Petrus de Palude; a 14th-century Dominican theologian and Bishop known for his commentaries on the "Sentences"</term>, that the article on the Eucharist is perhaps a special one, contained under those words, "the communion of saints," etc. 

**Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> in the *Secunda Secundae* <term>The second part of the second book of Aquinas's Summa Theologica</term> says that in the sacrament of the Eucharist two things can be considered: 
1. One, namely, that it is a sacrament, and this has the same rationale as other effects of sanctifying grace. 
2. The other is that the body of Christ is miraculously contained there, and thus it is included under the article on **omnipotence**, just as all other miracles are attributed to omnipotence. 

In his commentary on the third book of the *Sentences*, however, he says that faith concerning the body of Christ, and all sacraments, and the "keys" <note>The power of the Church to forgive sins.</note>, and all things of this kind, is included in the article which concerns the effect of grace, which is "The Holy Catholic Church," etc. 

Regarding the confession of **Berengarius** <term>Berengarius of Tours (d. 1088); a theologian who originally denied the material change of the bread, later forced to recant</term>, it must be said, as the **gloss** <note>Standard marginal commentary on Canon Law or Scripture.</note> says there: "That unless you understand the words of Berengarius soundly, you will fall into a greater error than he himself had." Therefore **Peter de Palude** says: "When it is said the body of Christ is 'broken,' it must be explained: that is, it remains under the **species** <term>appearances; the outward qualities of the bread (color, taste) that remain after the substance has changed</term> which are broken, so long as it remains in any part whatsoever." 

Moreover, Peter adds these words: 
> "So I say, therefore, that God *could* assume bread and wine, just as He could convert them; and that He could have instituted words at the speaking of which an 'assumption' would follow, just as now at the speaking of these words a 'conversion' follows; yet He did not give this power to those words, nor could the meaning of the moderns <note>The contemporary Church teaching.</note> be preserved if there were an 'assumption' and not a 'conversion.'" 

Thus he says. These words are most effective for the truth of my conclusion, which is entirely about what is **possible**, not about how it actually is in reality. 

To the point that whenever there are two things limited to the same **underlying person** <term>supposito; the subject or personhood that holds a nature</term>, wherever one is, there is the other: it is said that this logic holds only for those things which are in a place by **accident** <note>Incidental properties</note>, but it is otherwise for those things which are in a place by themselves. When, however, it is said that these statements—namely, "the bread is the body of Christ" and "the body of Christ is the bread"—cannot be verified unless the bread remained, it must be said that it should be explained as: where the bread was, there the body of Christ becomes present. 

And let it suffice to have disputed about this question. From all of which I hold those things which are in harmony with the declaration of my conclusion explained above; those things which are discordant, I judge should be rejected and condemned.

<summary>Pico concludes his argument on the Eucharist by distinguishing between what is divinely possible and what the Church actually mandates as faith. He cites Aquinas and Peter de Palude to show that his exploration of the "possible" logic of the sacrament does not contradict the Creed or Church dogma.</summary>

# Apology:

## DISPUTATION OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA ON THE SALVATION
### of Origen.

**I**t is more reasonable to believe that **Origen** <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253 AD) was one of the most influential early Christian theologians, but his views on the pre-existence of souls and universal reconciliation later became subjects of intense controversy.</note> is saved, than to believe that he is damned. Those Masters <note>Referring to the members of the papal commission who examined Pico's 900 theses.</note> have said that this conclusion is rash and blameworthy, "smelling of heresy," <note>original: "hæresim sapiens"; a technical theological term for a statement that sounds heretical even if not explicitly condemned.</note> and against the determination of the universal Church. To speak of them more modestly, however, I wish to show that their judgment is not correct: and that this conclusion is not against the determination of the Church; and what is more, even if whatever they bring against me were true, it still cannot be said that this conclusion is heretical or smells of heresy. For a fuller declaration of this matter, there will be **seven articles**.

In the **first**, it will be seen whether Origen ever wrote or believed any heretical opinion concerning matters of faith.
In the **second**, assuming he did write them, whether he wrote dogmatically <note>Written as established, unchangeable truth.</note>, or with personal adherence, or merely as an inquiry. 
In the **third**, assuming he wrote with adherence, whether he adhered in such a way that he sinned mortally in writing them and could be called a heretic. 
In the **fourth**, assuming he wrote and erred in such a way, whether he ever repented for such things. 
In the **fifth**, assuming that neither his repentance nor his lack of repentance is certain, whether it is more reasonable to believe him damned or saved. 
In the **sixth**, what should be judged from the text of the decrees regarding what the Church has determined about Origen. 
In the **seventh**, how much the determination of the Church in this matter binds our "cruelty" <note>original: "crudelitatem nostram"; Pico is likely critiquing the harshness of those who are quick to condemn others to hell.</note>.

Regarding the matter of the first article, there was a bitter contention between **Rufinus** and **Jerome**. To them (as **Augustine** says, who deplores the dissension that arose between them), God had granted that, as the closest and most intimate of friends, they might together lick the honey of the Holy Scriptures. 

**Rufinus** is of the opinion that the heretical dogmas found in Origen's books were falsely inserted by heretics who corrupted his books, and were not from Origen’s own mind. **Jerome** feels the opposite. But let us see what probability each opinion holds, and it will perhaps appear that—saving the faith and the full satisfaction of all those things which we are bound to believe by the necessity of salvation—it can still be freely and probably believed that those principal heresies (from which Origen’s sin is convicted, and consequently his damnation) were not from Origen’s mind, but were falsely imposed upon him by faithless heretics corrupting his books. 

First, on this side, there is the authority of **Pamphilus the Martyr**, whose book is offered in defense of Origen. In this, that most glorious Martyr—using Origen’s own words from his books cited there—shows that he thought in a **Catholic** manner regarding those things for which he is accused of being a heretic. Jerome, however, denying that this book belongs to Pamphilus, says the following in his *Apology* written to Oceanus and Pammachius: 

*“If you say his books were violated by his enemies so that he would be defamed, why should I not be allowed to say that a volume was composed by his friends and followers under the name of Pamphilus, to protect him with the testimony of a Martyr?”*

<summary>Pico begins his defense of Origen's salvation, outlining a seven-point argument to challenge the commission's claim that Origen was a condemned heretic. He introduces the historical debate between Rufinus and Jerome regarding whether Origen's works were tampered with by later heretics.</summary>

...vindicate [Origen] from infamy. From these words it seems that it can be noted well enough that **Jerome** <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the translator of the Vulgate Bible, who became a fierce critic of Origen's theology later in life.</note> considers both possibilities probable. He suggests that just as **Rufinus** <note>Rufinus of Aquileia, once a friend of Jerome, who translated Origen's "On First Principles" into Latin and argued the text had been corrupted by heretics.</note> cannot be proven wrong in saying those books were not corrupted, so too he cannot be proven right in saying that the book in question belongs to **Pamphilus**. Jerome further adds: "And the very name *Apologetic* <note>original: "Apologetici"; referring to a work of defense.</note> reveals an excuse; for nothing is defended unless it is under accusation."

But someone might say: "Therefore, since Jerome titles this very treatise in which he writes these things an *Apology*—in which he defends himself, claiming he followed Origen's **teaching** <note>original: "doctrinam"</note> but not his **dogma**—he likewise shows himself to be guilty of a crime, since nothing is defended unless it is under accusation." If an excuse always presupposes a just accusation, then no one could ever be justly excused. 

But let us see what conjectures move Jerome to believe the book is not by Pamphilus. The first thing that moves Jerome is that the same things are read in the first of the six books that **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the "Father of Church History." Jerome distrusted him because of his perceived sympathies with Arianism.</note> wrote in favor of Origen. The second is that Eusebius himself, writing the *Life of Pamphilus*, said that Pamphilus wrote no work of his own. For Jerome says this in the first book *Against Rufinus*, addressed to Pammachius and Marcellus:

> "Eusebius, Bishop of Caesarea, once the standard-bearer of the **Arian faction** <note>Arianism was a major heresy that denied the full divinity of Christ. Jerome is using this to discredit Eusebius's defense of Origen.</note>, wrote six books on behalf of Origen—a very extensive and elaborate work—and with many testimonies he proved Origen to be a 'Catholic' according to himself; that is, according to us, an **Arian**. You are translating the first of these books under the name of the martyr [Pamphilus]."

And below he adds: 

> "If this is Pamphilus's book, which of the six will be the first of Eusebius's?"

And further:

> "Likewise Eusebius—the admirer, herald, and companion of Pamphilus—wrote three very elegant books containing the *Life of Pamphilus*. In the third of these, he says of Pamphilus: 'He himself wrote nothing at all of his own work, except for the letters he happened to send to friends.' To such an extent had this defender of Origen lowered himself in humility. And this admirer of Pamphilus says that Pamphilus produced nothing at all, not even a single discourse of his own; and he said this after Pamphilus had already been crowned with martyrdom, so that you might have no refuge in claiming Pamphilus wrote this after Eusebius’s books were published."

And below: 

> "What will the letters of Bishop **Theophilus** do? What will the letters of **Pope Anastasius** do, which pursue this heretic throughout the whole world, when your book, published under the name of Pamphilus, fights against their letters?"

And in the second book, Jerome writes thus:

> "When nearly ten years ago my friend **Dexter** <note>Flavius Lucius Dexter, a high-ranking Roman official and friend of Jerome.</note>, who served as Praetorian Prefect, asked me to weave for him an index of the authors of our religion, I placed among the other treatise-writers this book as having been published by Pamphilus, thinking it to be so, just as it had been spread about by you and your disciples. But since Eusebius himself says that Pamphilus wrote nothing except letters, etc., and since the first book of Eusebius’s six volumes contains the same things and in the same words as those which were forged by you under the name of Pamphilus, it is clear that you wanted to spread this book for this reason: so that under the persona of a martyr, you might bring forward a heresy. Indeed, even in this work which you pretend is by Pamphilus, you have distorted many things, so that it is one way in the Greek and another in the Latin."

<meta>This page continues the argument regarding whether the "Apology for Origen" was truly written by the martyr Pamphilus. # Apology.

-> **John Pico of Mirandola** <-

...the **doctrine** <note>original: "doctrinam"</note> of Origen, and did not follow his dogma. Jerome says this regarding the same book of Pamphilus: "It seems to have been a small work either of **Didymus** <note>Didymus the Blind (c. 313–398 AD), a prolific Alexandrian theologian and teacher who, despite his blindness, became a great scholar and defender of Origen's works.</note> or of some other person. Even if we concede, for the sake of argument, that it is by Pamphilus, it was not yet by the martyr—for he wrote it before he achieved martyrdom. And how, you might ask, was he worthy of martyrdom? Simply so that he might wipe away his error through martyrdom." These are Jerome's words, verbatim, in various places as cited, regarding this book of Pamphilus.

**Rufinus**, however, proving the book belongs to the martyr Pamphilus and serves as a defense of Origen, writes in his second book of invective against Jerome. After stating that it is easy to say of any work that it does not belong to the author to whom it is attributed, he says: "But let us suppose that this booklet is not by the martyr, but by any other member of the Church. Did he not use his own words, whoever that writer was, so that we should defer to the merits of the author? Regarding the volumes of Origen themselves, he provides examples; and what he thinks about individual points, he shows not through his own defensive words, but through the words of the very man who is accused. Therefore, the question of authorship is superfluous where the defense is of such a kind that it requires no external advocate." Thus speaks Rufinus.

To these things Jerome says, someone might perhaps respond on behalf of Rufinus. First, regarding the claim that **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the historian who co-authored a defense of Origen with Pamphilus while they were in prison.</note> wrote six books in which he proves Origen was an **Arian** <note>Arianism was a major 4th-century heresy that taught Jesus was a created being, not fully God. Jerome accused Eusebius of being an Arian and trying to claim Origen for that cause.</note>, and that the first of these was circulated under the name of Pamphilus: How can this stand? How could the book of Pamphilus be the first book of Eusebius, when they intend entirely different and conflicting things in those books? For through you, O Jerome, Eusebius tries in his books to prove that Origen was an Arian. In the book of Pamphilus, however, nothing else is attempted but to prove that Origen was *not* an Arian, but that whatever things confirming the heresy of Arius are found in his books were inserted by those Arians—of which kind Eusebius himself was, along with many others. 

Therefore, it is necessary that this book be entirely different from that one, as it pursues a completely different, even contrary, cause. Nor is it sufficient if someone says those parts pertaining to the Arian heresy were changed from Eusebius’s book. For regarding what pertains to other heresies, Jerome cannot say that Eusebius showed Origen’s books were corrupted in those matters; because Jerome himself, in his second book against Rufinus, says that except for what pertains to the Son and the Holy Spirit, in other dogmas Eusebius and Didymus most openly concede to Origen's sect. 

For this reason, it cannot be well understood how the same things read in the book of Pamphilus could be read in the first book of Eusebius—unless perhaps they were some general points about Origen not pertaining to the specific point of this conclusion being discussed. Nor does it seem so wondrous—as Jerome wonders—that Pamphilus and Eusebius wrote some similar things, since, as Jerome himself says, they were **companions** <note>original: "contubernales"; specifically referring to those who share a tent or living quarters, implying an extremely close intellectual and personal relationship.</note>. Eusebius could have either recounted things in his own books that he read in Pamphilus’s work, or, as happens every day, he could have discovered and thought them out for himself by a similar movement of the mind. And so much for the first book of Eusebius. As for what Jerome says—that Eusebius writes in the *Life of Pamphilus* that out of humility Pamphilus wrote nothing of his own work except letters:
