<meta>This page continues the debate between Jerome and Rufinus over the authorship of the 'Apology for Origen.' The previous page ended with Jerome's skepticism, and this page opens with Rufinus’s potential rebuttal to Jerome's reliance on Eusebius as a witness.</meta>

# John Pico of Mirandola

...and he adds that **Eusebius**—the defender of Origen and the praiser of Pamphilus—says this. Perhaps **Rufinus** would respond that this does not count for much against him. First, because that small treatise by **Pamphilus** tends toward the brevity of a letter rather than the magnitude of a full book. Second, because that brief *Apology for Origen* perhaps cannot rightly be called a "proper work" <note>original: "opus proprium"</note>, since Pamphilus does not establish dogma there. In fact, he does not treat any general question there at all, but deals briefly only with a particular man—that is, Origen—and whether his books were corrupted or not. Writing such a thing is not "founding" an original work, nor is he trying to elevate himself by avoiding the title of author or dogmatist out of humility. 

Third, it is possible that this book did not come to the notice of Eusebius, both on account of the book's small size and because of the author’s humility (which Jerome himself asserts); he wrote nothing great, and preferred to hide those thin and tiny things he did write rather than display them. Fourth, Rufinus says it is also possible that Eusebius, as a defender of the **Arian treachery** <note>original: "Arrianæ perfidiæ"; this refers to Arianism, a 4th-century belief that Jesus was a created being rather than co-equal with God</note>, might have wished not only to hide the book of the martyr—which deprived his own sect of Origen's testimony—but also to act through this indirect testimony so that posterity would believe it was not by Pamphilus. 

Therefore, what **Jerome** says to strengthen his reasoning—namely, that the "Defender of Origen" says Pamphilus wrote nothing, etc.—is actually against him rather than for him. Since Eusebius defended Origen not as a Catholic but as an Arian, he could justly be suspected in this matter, as I have said. But why is it necessary to labor over these things, or how can Jerome prove at all from Eusebius's testimony that the *Apology for Origen* is not by Pamphilus, when Eusebius himself says in the sixth book of his *Ecclesiastical History* that the *Apology for Origen* was written by the holy martyr Pamphilus? 

Moreover, when Jerome adds: "What will the letters of **Bishop Theophilus** do? What of **Pope Anastasius**?" <note>Theophilus of Alexandria and Pope Anastasius I were key figures who officially condemned Origenism in the late 4th century.</note> perhaps Rufinus would say that Pamphilus’s book does not fight against their primary intention. For their purpose was to root out from the world those worst heresies and poisonous dogmas, whoever's they might be, because this pertained to the faith, to the confirmation of religion, and the stability of the Church. These most religious pontiffs would have cared little whether those views belonged to Origen, as many believed, or did not. 

Indeed, it would perhaps have been desirable and most welcome to them if it could have been proven by certain and valid arguments that those heretical opinions were not believed by Origen. This would have worked for the faith, not against it; against the heretics, and not for the heretics, who relied not a little on the testimony of such a great man—so highly praised by Catholics—and who defended their error by his authority. Therefore, Pamphilus's book would only fight against those letters if the heresies they accused were excused within it. However, it does not do so if its entire effort is to ensure that the proponents of those heresies are deprived of such a good patron. If those letters pursue him <note>meaning Origen</note>, it is certain they do so only as the **heresiarch** <term>heresiarch: a leader or founder of a heretical sect</term> to whom those opinions were credited.

## Defense:

Regarding those points which **Jerome** brings forward in his second book, one might perhaps respond as follows. First, when he says that he himself at one time believed—and even wrote—that the work was the book of **Pamphilus**, before he had read in **Eusebius** that Pamphilus wrote nothing, and so on. Based on this statement of his, **Rufinus** would perhaps argue against him in this way: "If, O Jerome, you once both believed and wrote that the book you read was by Pamphilus, tell me, I ask you: what were you reading in it? Did you recognize it to be full of lies and heresies, or favors toward heresies? Or was it rather true, or likely to be true, and not at all harmful to the Catholic faith? If it was false and heretical, how could you be led to believe the author of the book was a **Catholic Martyr** <note>original: "catholicum Martyrem"; referring to Pamphilus of Caesarea, a revered figure whose reputation Jerome would not want to attack</note>, about whose testimony and words no one could suspect anything sinister without it being a disgrace? 

But if it was indeed Catholic—and ultimately worthy of a Christian martyr—why do you now condemn these same things and call them fabrications? Why do you say they were spread to introduce heresies? In short, why do you now judge as unworthy of a martyr that which you then judged worthy? For the things you read now are the same as what you read then. Even if we set aside the author’s title, let us consider the arguments themselves that are made there in defense of **Origen**. If they are bad, why did you then judge them to belong to a holy martyr? If they are good, why are they not accepted as good now, regardless of who wrote them? 

Furthermore, how can you say, O Jerome, that I distributed the book to introduce heresies? For in that book, nothing else is being attempted (as was also said above) except to ensure that heretics cannot strengthen their position using Origen's testimony. This serves to uproot heresy, not to spread it. 

Furthermore, this book is found not only in **Latin**, but in **Greek**. I, Rufinus, made the Latin version by translating from the Greek; but who published the Greek if not Pamphilus? Certainly not I, Rufinus—at least according to you, who accuses me of ignorance of Greek literature. I could not have written a book so well and so eloquently in Greek that it matched the style of **Eusebius**. If another author is put forward, Jerome responds that it is the work of **Didymus** <note>Didymus the Blind (c. 313–398), a famous theologian in Alexandria who was a teacher to both Jerome and Rufinus</note> or someone else. To this, Rufinus would press: Whoever that 'other' person is, it is no longer I, Rufinus, who will be held guilty of this crime. And if Didymus is a liar according to you, then your own teacher Didymus is a deceiver—he whom you, in your own books, called a 'seeing prophet' and 'the eye of the bride' <note>original: "prophetã uidentem, & oculum habentem sponsæ"; metaphors Jerome used to praise Didymus’s spiritual insight despite his physical blindness, referencing the Song of Songs</note> and an apostolic man. He is the liar, I say, who published the Greek version and falsely attributed it to Pamphilus—not I, who found the Greek under the title of Pamphilus and shared it with the Latins by translating it under that same author's title. Nor should it be a wonder to you that I believed Didymus in this matter, since you yourself believed him in the explanation of the Scriptures. 

As for what he says—that it is one way in Latin and another way in Greek—Rufinus would say: 'Why do you not bring forward the passages, O Jerome, that were badly translated? Is it so that I cannot defend myself against the blame? This is just like when **Augustine** wrote to you that certain parts of your translation from the **Hebrew** were condemned, yet he did not specify the passages; you said then that he did this so you would not be able to defend yourself or prove the truth of your translation.' Therefore, what [you said] to yourself...

-># Giovanni Pico della Mirandola<-

...if **Rufinus** were to speak, as it was permitted concerning **Augustine**, let it also be permitted for me to harbor suspicions about you, O **Jerome**. These things are said concerning the disagreement between **Jerome** and **Rufinus** over the book of **Pamphilus** <note>Pamphilus of Caesarea was a martyr whose library and research Origen had used; Jerome and Rufinus fought over whether a specific defense of Origen was written by Pamphilus or by Rufinus himself</note>, in which matter I—as in all others—always prefer the judgment of Jerome to the judgment of Rufinus.

The second point brought forward regarding the possibility of this <note>the possibility that Origen's works were tampered with</note> is that the books of **Origen** are corrupted; that is, we see this has similarly happened to many other books of Catholic doctors. For **Clement**, a disciple of the apostles, who was bishop of the Roman church after the Apostles and a martyr, published books called the *Recognitions* <note>original: "Recognitio"; a series of early Christian narratives once attributed to Pope Clement I</note>. In these, while the doctrine is set forth from the persona of **Peter** as if it were truly Apostolic, the dogma of **Eunomius** <note>A 4th-century bishop who taught that the Son was "created" and fundamentally different from the Father</note> is inserted in some places, so that one would believe no one else but Eunomius himself was disputing, saying that the Son of God was created out of nothing.

Likewise, in the writings of **Clement of Alexandria**, a priest of the church and a Catholic man, it is found written that the Son of God was created. And in the four books of **Dionysius**, bishop of the city of Alexandria, where he disputes against **Sabellius** <note>Sabellius taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were just different "modes" of one person; in over-correcting him, Dionysius was accused of leaning toward Arianism</note>, there is a confirmation of **Arian** dogma <note>The belief that Jesus was a created being, not co-eternal with God the Father</note>. 

And why is it necessary to bring forward only apostolic men? Since we know the **Gospels** themselves, and the very words of the apostles, have often been corrupted by heretics, as can be most clearly established by anyone from **Tertullian's** book *Against Marcion* <note>Marcion was a famous 2nd-century heretic who edited the Gospel of Luke and Paul's letters to remove Jewish influences</note>. Therefore, since this happened to their books, why could it not also have happened to the books of Origen? And in an altogether similar case, why is a similar excuse not accepted in every respect? This excuse seems even more acceptable regarding Origen's books because he himself, while still living, complains about this in his letters—as will be seen below—namely, that his books were being corrupted and depraved by heretics.

If **Jerome** considers this to be impossible, bringing forward the argument that in this way whatever is found in the books of anyone could be said by others to be corrupted, and that it is difficult for all copies to be spoiled: I do not know how he himself will be able to respond to the **Eunomians** when they prove their dogma by the testimony of **Clement**, the disciple of the apostles, in whose works it is found expressly written that the Son of God was created. For if Jerome himself flees to this defense—claiming the books of Clement were corrupted by those very heretics—they will argue using Jerome's own words that this is impossible. They will say the same thing: namely, that whatever is found in the books of anyone can be called corrupted by others, and that it is impossible for all copies to be corrupted.

Therefore, perhaps we must be careful lest, while we wish to make **Origen** an absolute heretic, we make the Apostles and the disciples of the Apostles heretics instead. For since no less detestable and cursed heresies, and no less impious dogmas, are found in their books than in the books of Origen, I do not see why they should not either be accused similarly or excused similarly. 

**Jerome**, however, responds concerning the corruption of the books of Clement and others with these words: "And how," you will ask, "are there several faulty things in their books?" If I respond that I do not know the causes of the faults, I will not immediately judge them to be heretics; for it is possible that they either erred simply, or wrote with another meaning, or that their writings were gradually corrupted by unskilled scribes, or in...

<summary>Pico argues that if Origen's works are condemned for heretical content, then revered figures like Clement of Rome and Dionysius must also be condemned, unless one accepts that heretics often corrupted early Christian texts. He challenges Jerome's refusal to accept this "corruption defense" for Origen by showing it would logically undermine the orthodoxy of many other Church Fathers.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's examination of the conflict between Jerome and Rufinus over the integrity of Origen’s writings. It focuses on Rufinus's argument that if other respected Church Fathers could have their works corrupted or be misunderstood, the same charity should be extended to Origen.</meta>

## Defense.

...innocently, and spoke less cautiously, and were unable to avoid the slander of perverse men. To this response of **Jerome**, **Rufinus** might perhaps reply in this way: if it is the case that you do not wish to judge those men as heretics immediately—even if you do not know the causes of the errors—simply because there are some faulty things in their books, then why do you immediately judge **Origen** a heretic when you see certain faults in his books, especially when you have read **Origen** himself contradicting those same points elsewhere? What is the cause of this great inconsistency? For you yourself have known, written, and preached that in **Origen** there was such sublimity of genius, such zeal for the faith, and such a great study of the Scriptures. Might you not then, with good reason, suspect that the fault lies in the manuscripts from various sources rather than in his own mind? 

Furthermore, just as it was possible—according to you—that those other men either erred simply, or wrote with a different meaning, or spoke innocently and less cautiously; why could it not similarly be that **Origen** either erred simply, or wrote with a different meaning (as **Didymus** <note>Didymus the Blind (c. 313–398), a prominent Alexandrian theologian who defended Origen</note> contends), or spoke certain things innocently and less cautiously which cannot avoid the slander of perverse men? And just as you say their writings could have been corrupted by unskilled copyists, why could the writings of **Origen** not similarly have been corrupted either by unskilled copyists or by treacherous heretics? The cause for the difference in treatment is not apparent at all.

**Rufinus** also reports that a book by **Hilary the Confessor** <note>Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367), a staunch defender of the Trinity against Arianism</note> was falsified by heretics after the **Council of Ariminum** <note>The Council of Rimini (359 AD), where many bishops were pressured into adopting a vaguely worded creed that favored the Arian heresy</note>. He claims that for this reason, when a question was raised against him in a council of bishops, **Hilary** ordered the book to be brought from his own house; yet, without his knowledge, a heretical version was being held in his own archives. He says that when it was brought forward and the author of the book was judged a heretic by everyone, **Hilary** left the council excommunicated. 

**Jerome** says this is false and a fiction created to slander **Hilary**, offering no other proof. But whether it be true or not, he cannot know for certain, nor does it pertain much to the defense of **Origen**. What is true is that **Rufinus**, about to recount this concerning **Hilary**, prefixes it with these words: "And so that nothing is clearly lacking for credibility, I will unravel events that are still within our memory, so that the truth of the testimony may be hidden from no one." Therefore, it was either true, or it was a great impudence on the part of **Rufinus** to weave an open lie and a new fable regarding a matter of such recent memory. But whether it be true or false, it does not seem to have been invented or recited to slander **Hilary**; rather, it slanders those who had corrupted **Hilary's** book, for he attests that **Hilary** was innocent of heresy, unjustly excommunicated, and craftily deceived.

After this, **Rufinus** recounts that a book by **Tertullian**, the title of which is *On the Trinity*, was being read in Constantinople by heretics of the **Macedonian faction** <note>Followers of Macedonius I of Constantinople, who denied the full divinity of the Holy Spirit</note> under the name of **Cyprian the Martyr**. **Jerome** says that the book is neither by **Tertullian**, nor is it said to be by **Cyprian**, but is by **Novatian** <note>An early Christian scholar and priest who was later considered a schismatic, though his work on the Trinity was highly regarded</note>. Neither of them offers anything else in their own favor, except that **Jerome** says the author's eloquence demonstrates the specific character of the style. Although in many cases it is often possible to detect a similar face and tenor of style; but these things have nothing to do with **Origen**...

<meta>This page continues the argument for the textual integrity of Origen’s works. Pico, following Rufinus, provides historical examples of how even orthodox fathers like Jerome and Athanasius had their writings tampered with by heretics to make them appear heterodox.</meta>

[...continued from previous page] generation. **Rufinus** himself shows that this same thing happened to **Jerome** which happened to the books of **Origen**. For he reports that when **Jerome** had been entrusted by **Damasus**, the bishop of the city of Rome, with the dictation of ecclesiastical letters, certain **Apollinarists** <note>Followers of Apollinaris of Laodicea, whose views on the nature of Christ were condemned as heretical</note> took a book by **Athanasius** <note>A 4th-century champion of orthodoxy against Arianism</note> where the phrase "the Lord's man" <note>original: "dominicus homo"—a term used to describe Christ's humanity that became a flashpoint in theological debates</note> had been written. They corrupted the text, erasing it and then re-writing it in such a way that it would not be thought a forgery of theirs, but rather an addition made by **Jerome**. And take note that **Jerome**, responding to **Rufinus** on this point, says: "My own little story is being thrust back at me." However, he does not deny that it happened, but at the end says: "It is possible, **Rufinus**, that even if you heard the truth from me, another who is ignorant of this matter might say to you that it was made up and fabricated."

A third point that makes it probable that **Origen's** books were corrupted is that he himself complained of this while he was still alive. For in the fourth book of **Origen**, there exists a letter of his to certain people in Alexandria, in which he complains in these words:

> But it seems no wonder to me if my doctrine is adulterated by enemies, and corrupted by such falsification as that by which the letter of the Apostle **Paul** was corrupted. For certain people composed a false letter under the name of **Paul**, so that they might throw the **Thessalonians** into confusion, as if the day of the Lord were at hand, and seduce them. Therefore, because of this letter, he said these things in the second letter which he wrote to the **Thessalonians**: *“We beg you, brothers, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our gathering together to him, that you be not quickly shaken in your mind or terrified, neither by spirit, nor by word, nor by letter as if sent by us, as though the day of the Lord were at hand. Let no one deceive you in any way.”* <note>2 Thessalonians 2:1-3</note> I see that certain things of this sort are happening to us. For a certain author of a heresy, when a dispute of ours had been held in the presence of many people, took the transcript from those who had copied the manuscript; he added what he wished, took away what he wished, and changed what seemed fit to him. Now he carries it about as if in our name, insulting us and displaying the things which he himself composed. Because of this, the indignant brothers who are in **Palestine** sent a man to me in **Athens** to receive the authentic copies from me. These had not even been re-read or reviewed by me before, but lay neglected such that they could scarcely be found. Nevertheless—and I speak with God as my witness—when I met that very man who had adulterated the book and asked why he had done this, he responded to me as if giving satisfaction: "Because I wished to more greatly adorn the dispute and to purge it." See with what sort of "purging" he purged our dispute! Truly, the same kind of purging with which **Marcion** <note>A 2nd-century figure who famously edited the New Testament to remove elements he considered too "Jewish"</note> purged the Gospels or the Apostle, or such as his successor **Apelles** did after him. For just as they subverted the truth of the Scriptures, so this man, by removing the things that were truly said, inserted false things for the purpose of accusing us.

These things are read word-for-word in **Origen's** letter. If heretics did not hesitate to corrupt his books while he was still alive, how much more must it be believed that they dared to do this after his death? Moreover, he complains of another certain heretic in **Ephesus** who contributed many false things as if they were his own, and this also appears in another of his letters.

<summary>Pico provides historical evidence that heretics frequently forged and altered the texts of Church Fathers, quoting a letter from Origen himself who complained that his theological debates were being "purged" and falsified by his enemies during his own lifetime.</summary>

It addresses the contradictions found in his works and provides testimonies from other Church Fathers regarding his orthodoxy.</meta>

<header>Defense.</header>

# Defense.

...regarding the complaint about the falsity of his books. The fourth point, which provides the greatest credibility to this matter—namely, that those heretical views are not **Origen's** but were inserted by heretics—is that **Origen** is found elsewhere to determine those same matters piously and catholically. From this, it follows that if those heretical views were truly **Origen's**, he would be contradicting himself. Moreover, one may see very many places where he acts catholically in the *Apology of Pamphilus*. This is why **Rufinus** says that one should not worry about the name of that book's author, since that defense, whoever it belongs to, is valid in itself, as it provides proof of **Origen's** catholic and orthodox dogma from his own words and sayings. By this, a certain saying of **Jerome** against **Rufinus** also seems to be answered. For when **Rufinus** said the same thing—namely, that **Origen** had determined those matters elsewhere piously and catholically—**Jerome** spoke against him thus: "Where is that confidence with which, with puffed-out cheeks <note>original: "inflatis buccis"—a metaphorical expression for speaking boastfully or pompously</note>, you very frequently proclaimed that you had corrected in the <term>Periarchon</term> <note>The Greek title "Peri Archon," translated as "On First Principles," Origen's most controversial theological work</note> those things you had read in other books of **Origen**, and that you had restored his own things to his own people, and not foreign things? From such a forest of books, you cannot produce even a shrub or a sprout." For **Rufinus** would perhaps respond that it was not necessary for him to produce sprouts from that forest, from which **Pamphilus** had already produced many entire trees. Indeed, **Pamphilus** recites those passages most copiously, and with that already presupposed, **Rufinus** acts in his own small book (which he adds to **Pamphilus's** book) to show where this came from: that contradictory things are found in the books of **Origen**; and he assigns that cause to the falsification by heretics.

The fifth point, which also does much to assert that these heresies are not from the mind of **Origen**, is that from the testimony of many to whom we are rightly bound to give credit, we hold that **Origen** felt catholically regarding the principal opinions in which he is said to have erred. For there are two principal heresies which are charged against **Origen**. The first is concerning the **Trinity**: namely, that he thought wrongly of the **Son**, and worse of the **Holy Spirit**. The second is concerning the salvation of the **Devil**: namely, that his punishment and the infernal torment would not be eternal, but that he would eventually be liberated from it. From this latter point, many other views attributed to him seem to depend: namely, that for the sake of the salvation of these demons who are to be saved, **Christ** must be crucified again in a more sublime element; and that all things are to be restored into one; and that the devil can repent; and that the punishment of the damned is not eternal. Regarding these two heresies, however, there seems to be evident proof that they were not from the mind of **Origen**. For regarding the **Trinity**, not only does **Didymus** <note>Didymus the Blind, a 4th-century Alexandrian theologian</note>—in whose teachership **Jerome** so greatly glories—say that **Origen** felt catholically (and proved this in his own published commentaries on <term>Periarchon</term>), but even **Athanasius**, the defender of the Council of Nicaea, in his own books against the **Arians**, called this man a witness to his faith with a clear voice. And we read that **Methodius** repented of having condemned **Origen**, and says that he was finally found to believe nothing wrongly concerning the **Holy Trinity**. Indeed, we have the words of **Origen** himself concerning the **Trinity**, differing in no way from the catholic faith; for upon that passage of **Paul** to the Ro-

...to the Romans. On the passage, *And the Spirit helps our weakness* <note>Romans 8:26</note>, he expressly holds that the Holy Spirit is not a creature; and regarding that verse, *He who did not spare even his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how has he not also with him given us all things?* <note>Romans 8:32</note> Origen, in explaining these words, says:

> For there is nothing, either of visible or invisible creation, that can be made equal to the Son; for in no way can the creature be compared to its Creator. And if the Creator himself has been given to us, how will not every creature be given to us with him?

And further down, upon that saying of **Paul**: *Who is over all, God blessed [forever]* <note>Romans 9:5</note>, Origen says the following:

> That **Christ** is one thing according to the flesh, and another according to the spirit: he already designated this in the earlier parts of this very letter, where he says: *Who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh, who was destined to be the Son of God in power, according to the spirit of sanctification* <note>Romans 1:3-4</note>. And how he is the Son of God according to the spirit, and the son of David according to the flesh, we have explained there more fully to the best of our ability. Therefore, him whom he called the Son of God there according to the spirit, here, as the doctrine proceeds in order for those making progress in the faith, he pronounces that he is himself the God who is over all. And I wonder how certain people—reading what the same Apostle said elsewhere: *One God the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things* <note>1 Corinthians 8:6</note>—deny that they ought to profess the Son of God <note>original: "filium Dei," referring to the Son's divinity</note>, lest they seem to profess and speak of two gods. And what will they do with this passage of the Apostle, in which **Christ**, "through whom are all things," is clearly described as being "God over all"? 

> But those who feel this way do not notice that, just as he said the Lord **Jesus Christ** is "one Lord" in such a way that God the Father is not thereby denied to be "Lord," so also he did not speak of God the Father as "one God" in such a way that the Son is not believed to be God. For the scripture is true which says: *Know that the Lord himself is God* <note>Psalm 100:3</note>. Both, however, are one God, because the beginning of divinity for the Son is none other than the Father; rather, the Son is the most pure emanation <note>original: "purissima manatio"</note> of that one paternal fountain, as Wisdom says <note>Wisdom 7:25</note>. Therefore, **Christ** is God over all—doubtless over all those things which we mentioned a little earlier: over principalities, and powers, and virtues, and every name that is named, not only in this age, but also in the future <note>Ephesians 1:21</note>. 

> But he who is over all has no one over himself. For he is not after the Father, but from the Father. This same thing, however, regarding the <term>Wisdom of God</term> <note>A title often applied to the Son or the Holy Spirit in early theology</note>, ought also to be understood concerning the Holy Spirit, where it is said: *The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world*, and *this which contains all things has knowledge of the voice* <note>Wisdom 1:7</note>. If, therefore, the Son of God is said to be over all, and the Holy Spirit is remembered to contain all things, and God the Father is he from whom all things come; then the nature of the **Trinity** and the one substance which is over all is thus evidently shown.

These are the words of Origen, verbatim. And elsewhere, upon that saying of **Paul**: *But how shall they preach, unless they are sent?* <note>Romans 10:15</note>, he says:

> For there are some who indeed announce and preach concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; but they do so not sincerely and not with integrity, as is the case with all the <term>heretics</term> <note>Those holding beliefs contrary to established Church dogma</note>, who indeed announce the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but do not announce them well nor faithfully.

# Defense.

For either they wrongly separate the Son from the Father, so that they call the Father one nature and the Son another <note>This refers to the Arian heresy, which claimed Jesus was a created being rather than being of the same substance as God the Father</note>, or they wrongly confuse them, so as to make God composed of three parts or merely a three-fold name <note>This refers to Sabellianism or Modalism, which claimed the Trinity is just three different names for the same person</note>. Those who speak well, however, announce good things; they will grant to each of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit their own properties, while confessing that there is no diversity in substance or nature. These are the words of ***Origen***. What could be more Catholic than these words? What could be expressed more clearly? It is necessary, therefore, that if something else is found written elsewhere in the books of Origen, it is not the work of Origen, but of heretics who, through the corruption of his books, wished to have Origen as a patron of their own error.

Regarding the second heresy <note>The belief in "Apocatastasis," or the eventual salvation of all beings, including the Devil</note>, there exists such evident testimony that, in my judgment, it can hardly be denied. For in his own letter, ***Origen*** himself—even according to the translation by **Jerome**, who mentions that letter—expressly denies that the Devil can ever be saved. He says that not even a madman could say such a thing. Furthermore, there still exists a dialogue between Origen and Candidus, a follower of the Valentinian dogma <note>Valentinianism was a major Gnostic movement in the early Church</note>; this Candidus objected to Origen with this same error, and Origen refutes it, denying that he holds such a view. And regarding that passage of **Paul**: *Have they stumbled so as to fall?* <note>Romans 11:11</note> ***Origen*** speaks thus: 

> Paul, looking upon this fall—of which **Christ** said: *I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven* <note>Luke 10:18</note>—denies that Israel has fallen. For their conversion will occur at the end of the age; then, when the fullness [of the Gentiles] has entered, all Israel will be saved. But for him who is said to have fallen from heaven, there will be no conversion even at the end of the age. 

These are the words of ***Origen***. 

Furthermore, that heresy which is attributed to him—that the Spirit does not understand the Son, and the Son does not understand the Father—is falsely attributed to him. This is clear from what he himself says regarding that passage of **Paul**: *O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God* <note>Romans 11:33</note>. For he says: 

> He calls this depth of God unsearchable to every creature; but he could not say these things of the Son and the Holy Spirit, because the Son says to the Father in the Gospel: *Father, all mine are yours, and yours are mine* <note>John 17:10</note>. And concerning the Holy Spirit, **Paul** himself pronounces, saying: *No man knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man which is in him; even so, no one has known the things that are in God except the Spirit of God* <note>1 Corinthians 2:11</note>. Therefore, when Paul says: *Who has known the mind of the Lord?*, he speaks of creatures, but he excepts the nature of the Trinity. 

These are the words of ***Origen***.

One heresy attributed to Origen seems to remain, namely in his opinions concerning the soul: that they were created from eternity and descend from heaven into bodies. And regarding the soul, ***Origen*** himself writes in his commentaries on the letter of **Paul** to Titus, saying that he can receive nothing definitive from ecclesiastical teaching except this: that all souls are of the same species, that they possess free will, that they are rational, that they are immortal, that they were created by God, and that they will have punishments for evil deeds and rewards for good ones. He says he only affirms these things about the soul. Because clear testimonies are held in the scriptures regarding these points, but in other questions concerning the soul, he says he says what seems more probable to him, and proceeds by way of inquiry rather than by way of determination <note>Origen often distinguishes between "dogma" (church teaching) and "speculation" (exploring possibilities where the church has not yet ruled)</note>, because nothing about those matters has been determined in the ecclesiastical...

-> # Giovanni Pico della Mirandola <-

be held as ecclesiastical <term>dogma</term> <note>dogma: an official, established doctrine of the Church</note>. However, regarding that which seemed more likely to ***Origen***—that souls were created in the heavens as living beings before they entered bodies—all are in harmonious agreement [that it was an open question]. Even ***Rufinus***, in his *Apology to Anastasius, Bishop of the city of Rome*, after he recounted three opinions concerning the soul, said this at the end: "I truly, though I have read each of these, testify before God that until the present I hold nothing certain or defined concerning this question, but I leave it to God to know what is true, and to whomever He himself deigns to reveal it. However, I do not deny that I have read each of these, and I confess I am still ignorant, except for this: that the Church clearly teaches that God is the creator of both souls and bodies." Also, in the book of ***Pamphilus*** <note>original: "libro Pamphili"; Pamphilus of Caesarea was a martyr who wrote a famous defense of Origen while in prison</note>, it is not denied that ***Origen*** adhered to that opinion, but it is written in his defense: "Now truly, since there is a diversity of opinion among churchmen, and some feel one thing about the soul and others another—and all feel differently—why should this man be accused more than the rest?" Then, after these words, the opinions about the soul that existed at that time are recited. Among these is the one now held by Catholics; and when it is shown that clear proofs for those opinions cannot be produced from the Holy Scriptures, and that great difficulties befall their authors, it is concluded at the end: "What we wish to show from all of this is that just as one does not rightly call those heretics who think any one of these opinions we explained above is true—because nothing certain or manifest seems to have been said about them in the Divine Scriptures, nor is it thought to be contained in the preaching of the church—so it is not just to blame this man for discussing what seemed more likely to him."

From all the above, I infer two propositions. The first is that if ***Origen*** felt "Catholically" <note>meaning: in accordance with the universal church</note> regarding both the Trinity and the salvation of demons—as seems more likely proven by the testimonies—we cannot prove his damnation on account of his erroneous opinion concerning the soul. This is because ***Origen*** was not bound in his own time to explicitly believe everything concerning the soul that we are now bound to believe; for these things were neither held clearly in Scripture, nor had they been determined by the Church at that time as they were later. Indeed, not only in the time of ***Origen***, but even in the time of ***Augustine*** (who lived 200 years after ***Origen***), nothing had yet been determined by the Catholics—that is, by the universal Church—concerning the soul. 

For ***Augustine*** himself was doubtful in his opinion on the soul, as is clear from his letter to ***Jerome***: specifically, whether souls are created individually for individuals (as <term>orthodox tradition</term> <note>orthodoxa traditio: the officially accepted teaching</note> now holds), from which opinion it seemed to ***Augustine*** that it would follow that God was unjust; or whether they come from that one soul which was made by God in Adam. Then, whether just as body is from body, so souls were propagated from soul. Do not believe that ***Augustine*** doubted this matter only in his youth; for in the first book of his *Retractations* <note>Retractationum: Augustine's late-life work where he revisited and corrected his earlier writings</note>, which was among his last, he still doubts this question. For he writes in the first book: "Without controversy, therefore, God is the kingly origin of the soul's happiness, who indeed did not beget the soul from Himself, but created it from no other thing, just as He created the body from the earth. For as for what pertains to its origin..."

...origin, how it happens in the body: whether it is from that one soul which was first created when man was made into a "living soul" <note>original: "animā uiuentem"; a reference to Genesis 2:7</note>, or whether individual souls are made for individuals in the same way, I did not know then, nor do I know yet. These are **Augustine’s** words exactly. From which it clearly appears, because of the aforementioned erroneous opinion about the soul, that **Origen** can in no way be called a heretic. 

The second proposition I state is this: That if it is true what **Thomas [Aquinas]** says in his *Quodlibets* <note>original: "quolibetis"; these were "open-topic" theological debates held at universities where masters answered difficult questions</note>—as will appear more broadly in the 7th article of this defense of **Origen**—he says that in good <term>Theology</term> <note>the study of divine nature and religious belief</note> we are not obligated by the necessity of salvation to believe not only the doctors of the church like **Jerome**, like **Augustine**, and similar figures, but not even the Church itself, except in those things which pertain to the <term>substance of faith</term> <note>the core, essential doctrines that define the Christian religion</note>. If we add that these [questions about the soul] pertain not at all to the substance of faith, whether **Origen** was the author of those heresies or someone else—provided we confess those heresies are indeed heresies, that is, impious teachings—it seems to follow that a faithful man and a true Christian is not bound by the necessity of salvation to follow **Jerome** in this question (even though the church leans more toward him) rather than **Athanasius**, **Didymus**, **Methodius**, or **Rufinus**. 

The faith of **Rufinus**, even in a time of perfected heretics in the holy Church of Alexandria, is said to have been proven by prisons and exiles. Indeed, one might rather believe the words of **Origen** himself, especially since in many other things which pertain even more to the substance of faith, we do not approve of **Jerome**. This is seen in the matter of ceremonies <note>referring to the famous dispute between Jerome and Augustine over whether converted Jews should still follow Mosaic Law</note>. Just as it is pious not to believe **Jerome** when he calls the commentaries of **Ambrose** on Luke "nonsense" <note>original: "nugas"</note>, and when he calls **Ambrose** himself now a "crow," now a "jackdaw" <note>original: "nunc coruum, nunc corniculam"; Jerome was notorious for his sharp-tongued insults of other scholars</note>; or when, in condemning **Ambrose's** book on the Holy Spirit, he says he saw "Latin things that were not good" taken from the Greeks; or when he taxes **Basil the Great** with pride; or when in the letters of **Augustine** he says he has read certain heretical things—so perhaps, in this case, he might rather wish those writings which show **Origen** to be <term>Catholic</term> <note>here used in its original sense of "universal" or "orthodox"</note> to be faked and corrupted, rather than admitting that the writings which prove him a heretic do not actually belong to him. 

It is neither impious, nor does it appear ruinous to the faith, to offer patronage to **Origen**; in fact, this seems rather to confirm the faith and take away testimony from the heretics, rather than weakening it, according to what is written in the book of **Pamphilus** in these words: 

"They ought to have considered how much matter for mockery, and how much [ammunition] they provide to heretics, when the heretics see those whom they think are the asserters and defenders of Christian <term>dogma</term> <note>official church teachings</note> being refuted and rejected by their own people; they rejoice as if at a civil war, seeing someone attacked whom they themselves could not defeat in a hostile manner."

There were also proven doctors of the Church, even later than **Jerome**, who held the opinion that those heresies did not come from the mind of **Origen**, but were falsely attributed to him by heretics. Whence **Haymo** <note>Haymo of Halberstadt, a 9th-century monk and scholar</note>, one of the noble and ancient doctors of the Church, in his book *On the Memory of Christian Affairs*, says this: 

"Therefore, concerning **Origen**, a man so illustrious, of the most abstinent and chaste life, of excellent doctrine, and of pure and lucid speech, I might say—saving the faith of the fathers—that he did not write these things at all, but they [were added] by heretics..."

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

... [forged] in order to obscure his illustrious name, were maliciously fabricated and written and titled with his name. These are his words exactly. These things were said regarding the first article to be examined and investigated, namely: whether those two opinions of **Origen** were heretical or not? In which matter, as in all others, I always place the judgment of the Church before the judgment and reasoning of all others.

Regarding the second article, it seems more reasonable that **Origen** should be excused for this reason: that if he wrote anything which is not accepted by Catholics, in writing those things, he proceeded neither dogmatically nor assertively, but always doubtfully and inquiringly. Therefore, just as in **Augustine’s** books *On Genesis*, there are many things which are not accepted, yet they are excused by us for that reason; because, as he himself says in his book of *Retractions*, more things in that book were sought than found. 

In the same way, there may be many things in the books of **Origen** to be reproved and condemned; but because he spoke not by determining a final answer, but by inquiring, he should not therefore be called a heretic. This is because <term>heresy</term> <note>a belief or opinion contrary to orthodox religious doctrine</note> properly means a dogma asserted against either the express truth of Scripture or the determination of the Church. 

That **Origen** always spoke in this way is clear from many places. For even after his disputation about the soul, he says: "Let these not be dogmas according to our opinion, but only sought after and cast forth, lest they seem entirely untouched." <note>original: "Hæc iuxta nostram sententiam non sint dogmata, sed quæsita tantum atq; proiecta, ne penitus intacta uiderentur."</note> And elsewhere, speaking of the resurrection, he says: "If these things are not contrary to the faith," etc. And further on: "A triple suspicion <note>in this context, 'conjecture' or 'possibility'</note> is therefore suggested to us concerning the end, from which the reader may inquire which is true and better." Then he joins three opinions about the resurrection. And in the preface to his books *On Genesis*, he says: "If anything profound should occur, it must indeed be spoken of, but not however affirmatively." And further on: "In great matters which are above us, we are not ignorant of our own ignorance." 

And on the second book of his commentary on the *Epistle to the Romans*: "Let these things be said by us on this condition: that if any have spoken better and more reasonably, those things should be held rather than these of ours." And in Book 4: "These things, brought forth as we were able in places so arduous and so difficult—if someone should perhaps consider the zeal of our mind, he will be able to embrace them; but if he wishes to note the weakness of our perception, we ask for pardon, and we freely yield to him who can discuss or explain these things better." And elsewhere: "Let him who reads prove which of these fits the Apostolic sense better, and let him hold that." And in Book 5: "These things in the meantime have been able to occur to us in the present place; but if anyone has perceived anything better, let it not be a burden to look back at those things once these have been omitted." 

And what more? Let the book *Periarchon* <note>Origen's most famous work, *On First Principles*, often referred to by its Greek title *Peri Archon*</note> be read; we will see that he proceeds in this order: that first he stated those things which seemed to him to be expressly determined in the scriptures, and in those he errs in nothing from the Church. Other things he says are doubtful to him, and he wishes to inquire about them, asserting concerning all of them that only that truth should be received which in no way opposes Apostolic and ecclesiastical dogmas. 

Regarding the third article, which is like a confirmation of the second, I say this proposition: that if there is someone having an erroneous opinion about matters of faith not yet determined by the Church, provided that in his will there is no ma- <meta>Catchword: ma- [malitia/malice]</meta>

On the preceding page, Pico argued that Origen’s controversial writings were intended as intellectual inquiries rather than definitive dogmas. Here, he develops the legal and theological argument that "heresy" requires not just an intellectual mistake, but a stubborn, malicious will—a quality he argues Origen did not possess.</meta>

<page-num>213</page-num>
<header>Defense.</header>
<sig>iij</sig>

## Defense.

[if there is no] stain [of the soul], but rather a firm intention to always believe in accordance with the Scripture and the Church, then that person neither commits a <term>mortal sin</term> <note>a grave sin that, according to Catholic teaching, leads to the soul's damnation if not repented</note>, nor should he properly be called a heretic. From this proposition, it follows as a corollary that it is possible for holding a certain opinion at one time to be a mortal sin, while it would not be so at another time. This is because one can believe something without <term>pertinacity</term> <note>willful, stubborn persistence in an error after being corrected</note> at one time, which at another time they could not believe without such stubbornness—for example, after a formal determination by the Church or a clarification of the Holy Scripture regarding the opposite of what was believed. This is attested by the consensus of all the Doctors of the Church, who say: that it is not precisely an error of the intellect that makes a man a heretic, but there must also be malice and perversity in the will. Therefore, **Augustine** used to say: *I can err, but I cannot be a heretic.* <note>original: "Errare possum hæreticus esse non possum"</note>

This is confirmed by the determination of the universal Church, which has <term>canonized</term> <note>officially declared as a saint</note> many who nevertheless persisted until death in erroneous opinions regarding the faith, which were later rejected by the Church as heretical. It is nowhere recorded that these men ever retracted those opinions. Such men were **Papias**, Bishop of Hierapolis, **Victorinus of Pettau**, **Irenaeus of Lyon**, the blessed **Cyprian**, and many others whom we know to have erred in faith and whose opinions were condemned as heretical. Yet, they are still held in the "canon" of saints. From this, it follows that we must necessarily say one of two things: either those men did not die in mortal sin, even though they died holding those erroneous opinions, or the Church erred in their canonization. 

If my critics say (as one of those attacking me has already said) that "perhaps those men were not properly canonized," then it is not I, but they themselves who are speaking against the determination of the universal Church. From this premise, I apply the argument to **Origen’s** case as follows: even granted that **Origen** held many and various erroneous opinions in faith, this fact alone—if there was no stain in his will—cannot in any way be an argument that his soul is damned. 

The argument is as follows: Either a great error in the intellect concerning matters of faith, provided there is no stain in the will, does not prevent a person’s salvation; or even the smallest error in any matter prevents it; or some errors prevent it and some do not. If even a great error does not prevent it, then even though **Origen** erred in many things, and even in fundamental ones, if his will was well-disposed and in no way stained, it did nothing to prevent his salvation. Thus, for those who wish to prove his damnation, it is not enough to show his errors and his perseverance in them; they must show that his perseverance was coupled with pertinacity, or negligence, or some other malice of the will. If even the smallest error were sufficient to condemn, then the error regarding the "rebaptizing of heretics" should have prevented the salvation of **Cyprian**, and the heresy of those called <term>Chiliasts</term> <note>from the Greek 'chilioi' (thousand); those who believe Christ will return to rule a physical kingdom on Earth for 1,000 years</note> should have prevented the salvation of **Papias**, who was the author of that heresy and died holding it. And if that were so, then they were wrongly canonized by the Church. If some errors prevent salvation and some do not, then let them say...

-> it is necessary <-

<summary>Pico argues that intellectual error alone does not make a heretic; there must be a "malice of will" or stubbornness. He supports this by pointing out that several canonized saints, like Cyprian and Papias, held views later deemed heretical but were saved because their intentions were pure.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s legalistic and theological defense of Origen. On the previous page, Pico established the principle that for an error to be a "mortal sin" or "heresy," it must involve "pertinacity"—a stubborn, malicious intent of the will—rather than a simple mistake of the mind. Here, he argues that Origen’s errors were intellectual, not moral, and compares Origen's situation to other early Church Fathers like Clement of Rome and Papias, who also held views that were later corrected but remained respected figures in the Church.</meta>

<page-num>214</page-num>
<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

It is necessary [to distinguish] which errors are those that hinder salvation and which are not. Where has such a distinction ever been found made by the Church? For example, to say that holding an error in matters pertaining to this or that article of faith is a <term>mortal sin</term> <note>a grave sin that severs one's relationship with God</note>—even if it is strictly a weakness or a defect of the intellect, and involves no perversity, negligence, <term>pertinacity</term> <note>stubborn persistence in an error after being corrected</note>, or any other malice in the will. Conversely, to hold an error in other matters is not a mortal sin unless there is a defect in the will. If such a distinction is not found made either by the Church or by the Doctors, and if it does not seem possible for it to be made, then it reasonably appears that the claim of certain people is invalid. They say there is one rule for **Cyprian** <note>a 3rd-century Bishop and Martyr</note> and **Papias** <note>an early Christian author who held millenarian views later rejected by the Church</note> and those like them, and another rule for **Origen**, because Origen erred in the principal [articles of faith]. For however great an error may be, provided it is only an error in the intellect and there is no malice in the will, it does not seem that the person erring in such a way sins mortally. 

Therefore, since we do not read that such malice existed in Origen’s will—even granting that he erred with a most grave error in the principal mysteries of the faith, an error rightly condemned by the Church—it cannot be proven that he himself is damned in his own soul. 

But if someone should say that there are many degrees of propositions to be believed, beyond those determined by the Church, and that even if there is no stubbornness, it is still a sign of pertinacity to assert things when the speaker is bound to hold and believe the opposite with <term>explicit faith</term> <note>a clear, conscious belief in a specific doctrine, as opposed to a general trust in the Church's teachings</note>; and that an error is not only blameworthy when it is mortal due to pertinacity, but also sometimes when it is blamed due to negligence in seeking the truth (which negligence is not pertinacity, at least not properly so-called), it seems a reasonable response can be made. 

First, Origen cannot be blamed for negligence in seeking the truth in this matter because, as **Jerome** <note>Saint Jerome, the translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible</note> well says, in the scrutiny of the Scriptures "he sweated by day and by night." 

Second, Origen erred in nothing that he was then bound to believe with explicit faith in such a way that one asserting the opposite—not dogmatically, but as it seemed more probable to him—could be called a heretic. I prove this evidently from a certain saying of the same Jerome cited above: for where Jerome says that even if faulty things are found in **Clement** <note>Clement of Rome, an early disciple of the Apostles</note> and others like him, he would not immediately judge them to be heretics for that reason. He adds a fourfold cause: 
1. The books could be corrupted. 
2. They may have written with a different meaning. 
3. They simply erred. 
4. They spoke with too little caution. 

In these words, we should notice that even if the book of Clement—in which he says the Son of God is a "creature"—is not corrupted, and even if the author intended no other meaning, Clement is still not to be judged a heretic immediately, because he could have "simply erred." What does it mean to have "simply erred" except to have erred from a defect of the intellect and an erroneous judgment of reason, and not from malice or perversity of the will? If this applies even to that heresy (that the Son is a creature) which is the greatest error, and which is also charged against Origen...

<summary>Pico argues that Origen’s theological errors were mistakes of the mind rather than sins of the heart, comparing him to Saint Clement and other early figures whose errors did not disqualify them from being considered holy. He highlights Jerome's defense of early writers who "simply erred" due to intellectual limits rather than malicious intent.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s defense of Origen’s salvation. On the previous page, he argued that intellectual errors made before a formal Church definition do not constitute mortal sin or heresy if the "will" remains pure. Here, he applies this to Origen, citing Saint Jerome’s testimony that Origen actually expressed regret for his more controversial writings.</meta>

<page-num>215</page-num>
<header>Apology. 215</header>

...born, one can simply err: because there was as yet no other determination of the Church regarding that matter, nor a more certain verification through a greater clarification of the scriptures. In such a state, an error eventually cannot be held against someone; and if at that time **Clement** <note>likely referring to Clement of Alexandria or Clement of Rome, early Church Fathers whose writings contained ideas later clarified by the Church</note> was not bound under penalty of mortal sin to believe with <term>explicit faith</term> <note>the clear, conscious belief in a specific dogma</note>, what can we say—that **Origen** was obligated to believe explicitly in those matters in which he is said to have erred? 

It must be noted, however, that because <term>heresy</term> <note>a belief or opinion contrary to orthodox religious doctrine</note> can exist both in words that are poorly and inordinately delivered (as **Augustine** says) and in the underlying meaning. Therefore, **Jerome**, giving a way to excuse one who has erred in either—whether jointly or separately—solely from a defect of the intellect and not of the will, says that such a person either "spoke less cautiously" (and this applies if heresy appears in the words), or "simply erred" (and this applies if the sense is heretical, produced by a simple and upright will but from a weak and wandering intellect). These words of Jerome are to be well noted and weighed, because in them a useful and healthy dogma concerning <term>heretical pertinacity</term> <note>the stubborn, willful persistence in error that makes one a formal heretic</note> is rightly founded.

Regarding the fourth article, certain people, saying that Origen repented, allege the "Pleas of Origen," but that book is considered <term>Apocryphal</term> <note>works of unknown authorship or doubtful authenticity, not accepted into the official canon</note>, as is held in the *Decrees* <note>referring to the Decretum Gratiani, a collection of Canon Law</note>, distinction 15. I, however, allege the testimony of Jerome himself—which cannot be considered apocryphal—who expressly witnesses that Origen repented of his errors. I do not bring this forward because it is strictly necessary for reasonably believing in Origen's salvation (as will be clear in the following article), but because these Masters have never stopped shouting: *"Show me that Origen erred, and then show me that he repented; you will never show this, you will never find it written that Origen repented of those things which he wrote."* 

Let these Reverend Fathers therefore hear Jerome himself, by whose authority they strike down Origen, in his *Apology to Pammachius and Oceanus*. In this work, Jerome shows that he followed Origen’s learning but not his dogma, and after reciting Origen's errors, he adds these words: 

> "Origen himself, in the letter which he wrote to **Fabian**, Bishop of the city of Rome, performs penance <note>original: "pœnitentiam agit"</note> for why he wrote such things, and he refers the causes of his rashness to **Ambrose** <note>referring to Origen’s wealthy patron, Ambrosius, not St. Ambrose of Milan</note>, because he brought into the public sphere things that had been produced in secret." 

These are Jerome's words, verbatim. What could be clearer? What more express? How can they now, or with what face can they say, that it is nowhere found that Origen repented? 

I will also mention, because it occurs to me, what happened to me these days regarding a similar purpose with two of those who were condemning this conclusion. For when I, in order to defend Origen against the charge of pertinacity, said to a certain man who was insisting heavily that Origen was damned in his soul for pertinacity by a determination of the Church, that I held from Greek histories that Origen’s dogmas were condemned many years after his death; and I had referred him—if he did not have the books at home—to the **Bishop of Trogir** <note>referring to a scholar-bishop from Trogir, modern-day Croatia</note>, a man no less outstanding in learning and character than in his dignity, at whose house I had seen a Greek book in which many things concerning the councils were collected. That good Father said: "Why do you refer me to the Greeks, when you know I do not know Greek letters..."

<summary>Pico argues that Origen's errors were intellectual "weakness" rather than "heretical stubbornness" and provides historical evidence from Saint Jerome that Origen formally repented in a letter to the Pope.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s narrative account of his debates with various theologians regarding the salvation of the early Church Father Origen. He transitions from abstract theological arguments to a specific, almost theatrical anecdote about a confrontation over historical sources.</meta>

# John Pico of Mirandola

...completely ignorant of literature? "Let us look," he said, "at the Latin ones. Do we not have the *Fasciculus temporum* <note>Latin: "A Little Bundle of Times," a very popular world chronicle written by Werner Rolevinck and printed in 1474</note>, which treats these matters most elegantly?" "Let that *Fasciculus* be brought forth," I said, though I added: "If you are preparing a fire for me as if for a heretic with this *Fasciculus* <note>Pico is making a pun on the book title; a "fasciculus" is a small bundle of wood or kindling used for burning heretics</note> placed beneath me, I will immediately drive you and your bundle to the devil <note>original: "in malam crucem," literally "to the bad cross," a Roman curse</note>. For there is no reliability in that book." He flared up as if I had blasphemed against the Trinity. "Do not flare up," I said, "let the bundle be brought, and do not think you can overcome me now as if my own defenses were untied." It was brought, and in it we read these things concerning **Origen**: "*Origen, an eminent doctor, and of incomparable holiness of life, most famous in the Church of God...*" and after a few words at the end it says: "*A great labyrinth is woven by various people concerning Samson, Solomon, Trajan, and this Origen: namely, whether they are saved or not? Since these things can be unknown without danger, and the Church has not been certified concerning them, they are to be committed totally to the Lord.*" Thus spoke the good *Fasciculus*. When these things were read, and he had heard that the Church was not "certified" regarding the damnation of Origen, it was a wonder how he turned pale; and while the authority of the most proven men could do nothing with him, this little *Fasciculus* alone could do so much that he changed his opinion on the spot. 

On the following day, another man addressed me more sharply, carrying a sufficiently large book in his hand: "How," he said, "or by what way at all do you dare to defend Origen from the punishment of eternal fire? Behold, I will show you a testimony you cannot contradict: One who says that Origen cannot be defended." "Produce your witnesses, venerable man," I said, "if you have them." "You [shall see]," he said. "Here is a certain great witness," and he added the name. I, however, wish to keep the name silent; whose speeches and preachings these are. Then I said: "What speeches are you bringing me? What nonsense?" "Nonsense?" he replied, now totally flaring up. "Nonsense," I said, "in which even regarding this matter, if he has a sermon about it (for heaven forbid that I should ever have read such things), unless some most express error is found, I am now willing to break Origen's head on **Ixion’s wheel** <note>In Greek mythology, Ixion was punished by being bound to a perpetually spinning fiery wheel; Pico is using a dramatic metaphor for absolute condemnation</note> along with you." 

Now impatient and boiling with bile, he opened the book and began to read, raging with a very loud voice: "*Wednesday, sermon 11, on the Origenists.*" Then, in the pursuit of what was written, he exclaimed at every single word: "Is this not an error?" And behold, while he was shouting thus to the **envy of Stentor** <note>Stentor was a Greek herald in the Iliad known for a voice as loud as fifty men</note>, he read these things written in the book: "*Finally, Jerome confesses that he himself read six thousand books of Origen.*" And when, having immediately read this through, he shouted again, "Is this not an error?" "Here," I said, "is an error, and indeed a great one; here is an open lie, here is express falsehood." And so that I might restrain the man on the spot, I ordered the letters of **Jerome** to be brought. Running immediately to the second book of his invective against **Rufinus** <note>Tyrannius Rufinus was an associate of Jerome who became his bitter rival during the Origenist controversy</note>, I showed him Jerome responding to Rufinus (who was claiming that **Pope Epiphanius** <note>Epiphanius of Salamis, a staunch anti-Origenist</note> boasted that he had read six thousand of Origen’s books) with these words: "*But concerning the six thousand books which you pretend were read by him, who will believe either that you are telling the truth, or that he could have lied? For if Origen had written six thousand books, it could have happened that a learned man, instructed in sacred letters from infancy, might have read the works of others out of curiosity and knowledge; but because he did not write them...*"

Pico is transitioning from a personal anecdote about a debate to a scholarly analysis of historical sources—specifically Jerome, Eusebius, and Rufinus—to prove that Origen's supposed errors were either youthful inquiries or unauthorized publications.</meta>

# Defense

->Defense.<-

...how he could have read them. Count the index of his books, which are contained in the third volume of Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the first great historian of the Christian Church</note>, in which he wrote the *Life of Pamphilus*, and I do not say six thousand, but you will not find even a third part: these are the words of **Jerome** <note>original: "hęc ad uerbũ Hieronymus"</note>. He blushed, and my case was saved. But let us now return to the proposal, concluding that either with **Rufinus** and others, whom we cited above in the first article, we must concede that **Origen** never sinned; or if we contend with **Jerome** that he did sin entirely, let us also know that we must concede with him that Origen repented of his sin in a personal book given to the Roman bishop.

However, after I have carefully weighed and examined these things with myself, especially what is said by Eusebius, Rufinus, and Jerome concerning Origen, I conjecture that Origen, laboring long in the deep study of the scriptures, was uncertain about many difficult and primary questions of theology, since it did not seem to him that he could certainly and indubitably assert anything else from the testimony of the scriptures. For this reason, regarding many mysteries of the faith, he perhaps said many things by way of inquiry and disputation in the earlier years of his life which the Catholic faith would not receive. Therefore Origen, who as he himself says, "was not ignorant of his own ignorance," and clearly recognized that he had not yet attained the truth of those questions, never wished—as Eusebius reports—to be recorded publicly by <term>stenographers</term> <note>original: "notarijs." These were shorthand writers who would record a preacher's spoken sermons for publication</note> for the things he preached in the Churches before the 40th year of his age.

Let us note, therefore, that Eusebius in the 26th chapter of the 6th book of his *Ecclesiastical History*, writes that Origen, in the third year of the Emperor Philip’s reign <note>Philip the Arab, reigned 244–249 AD</note> and under Pope Fabian, when he was already passing his 40th year, began to commit his words even to public writing. And let us also note what he says above in the 17th chapter: that under Pope Urban, who was succeeded by Pontianus—already before the time of Fabian—Origen's beginning of writing commentaries on the Holy Scriptures took place, with **Ambrose** <note>This is Origen’s friend and patron, not the famous Saint Ambrose of Milan</note> compelling him and forcing him by much weight of prayers and entreaties. This Ambrose, says Eusebius, seemed most worthy to have this duty bestowed upon him, and to whom Origen might open whatever secret and hidden things were covered in the sacred letters.

From these two passages of Eusebius, in which an apparent contradiction appears, it is evidently gathered that at the urging of Ambrose he dictated certain things in his earlier years, before he had yet discovered anything certain, to be communicated only to Ambrose privately and not to be published to the public, as he did not recognize them as being well-guarded or in harmony with apostolic truth. Ambrose, however, brought those things edited in secret into the public. Then, when the Catholic truth was discovered by Origen (now a man of sixty years), he began to write boldly and publicly because he wrote in a Catholic manner; and he was vehemently grieved that those things which he had written for the private use of Ambrose had already been published by him. Regarding these things, as I conjecture from the words of Jerome and Eusebius, in a letter of self-justification <note>original: "sui purgationem"</note> written to Fabian, the Bishop of Rome, he bore witness to the whole sequence of events and his own Catholic faith—narrating, namely, that he had not written the things found written by him earlier so that they might be published, as he himself was doubtful whether they were Catholic or not; but Ambro...

<summary>Pico argues that Origen's controversial writings were private, youthful inquiries published without his consent by his patron Ambrose. He reconciles conflicting historical accounts from Eusebius to show that Origen's mature, public works were orthodox and that he repented for any earlier errors.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s systematic defense of Origen, specifically addressing the historical accounts of Origen’s own repentance and the status of his controversial writings. Pico argues that Origen's errors were either youthful inquiries or works published without his consent by his patron, Ambrose.</meta>

<page-num>218</page-num>

## Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

...that he published those things. For this is what **Jerome** says: **Origen** himself, in the letter he wrote to **Fabian**, Bishop of the city of Rome, performed penance for having written such things, and he attributes the causes of this rashness to **Ambrose**, because he brought into public what had been produced in secret. Moreover, **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, the "Father of Church History"</note>, when recounting what he wrote after his sixtieth year—after he had counted the book *Against Celsus*, twenty-five books of *Commentaries on Matthew*, and twenty on the prophets—adds this: "He also wrote to **Fabian**, Bishop of the city of Rome, and to very many other leaders of the churches, concerning his own Catholic faith." These are his words. 

Let it be true, then, that before his sixtieth year **Origen** was doubtful concerning many mysteries of the faith; and let it be true that he shared many things in writing secretly with **Ambrose** which he then held not by firm adherence, but as a doubtful inquiry—things which are now not to be received by Catholics. Thus **Jerome** speaks the truth when he says that things found in many of Origen’s books are not Catholic, because they were truly dictated by him, though not as things believed, but rather as things sought after rather than discovered. Consequently, they should not be culpably attributed to **Origen**, to whom the Catholic truth was later revealed. We can also accept as true that many things in these works were devised by heretics, according to **Rufinus**, especially since **Origen** himself complained of this while he was still alive. 

Let it therefore be true, according to **Eusebius** in his *Ecclesiastical History* (approved as true by **Jerome**), that **Origen** does not hold as his own works—that is, those in which he says something definitively and with firm adherence—except those which he wrote after his sixtieth year. And let it be true, even according to **Jerome**, that he repented of those earlier writings rashly published by **Ambrose**, and consequently that he died a Catholic. Thus, not only according to **Rufinus**, **Pamphilus**, and **Eusebius**, but even according to **Jerome**, it is more reasonable to believe that he is saved than to believe that he is damned. 

Regarding the **fifth article**, I say this proposition: however gravely someone may sin mortally during their life, and even if it is certain that they sinned mortally, unless their <term>final impenitence</term> <note>The state of refusing to repent for one's sins up until the moment of death</note> is certain, it is rash to truly assert that the person is damned. The truth of this proposition is clear from the common opinion of all the **Doctors** <note>The "Doctors of the Church" or established theological authorities</note> who agree on this statement. From this proposition I infer two related conclusions. 

The first is this: simply because someone has sinned mortally in life, and we are not certain that they did not repent, we must not firmly judge that they are in hell. This is clear because the existence of a mortal sin does not, by itself, fulfill all the conditions from which eternal damnation follows; rather, beyond the sin, one must also establish and be certain of **final impenitence**. And I, who deny that it must be firmly believed that he is in hell, do not have to show you his repentance; but you, who assert that he is damned, must provide certainty of his impenitence. In support of this, the statement of **Henry of Hesse** <note>Heinrich von Langenstein (1325–1397), a prominent theologian and mathematician</note> carries great weight; in his exposition of the third chapter of the book of Genesis, he says these formal words: "Therefore, if the argument of certain people were effective, by which they persuade that someone is damned—as they do regarding **Solomon** <note>The biblical King Solomon, whose salvation was a common subject of medieval debate</note>—because his scripture...

<summary>Pico argues that Origen's controversial early works were unauthorized drafts and that Origen later recanted his errors, making it "more reasonable" to believe he was saved. He further asserts that no one can be declared damned unless there is absolute proof of their final refusal to repent.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s defense of Origen by addressing the theological uncertainty of any individual's damnation.
