# Apologia.

<margin>T 2</margin>
<meta>catchword: ctor,</meta>

...records the sin, and makes no mention of his righteousness or repentance, then the first man <note>Adam</note> would be proved condemned by his sin just like the first angel <note>Lucifer</note>. So says **Henry** <note>Henry of Ghent (c. 1217–1293), a prominent scholastic theologian</note>; for mention is never made of the repentance of **Adam**, but only of his sin. Similarly, in **Judges 8**, one reads of the sin of **Gideon**, but not of his repentance; and yet it is firmly believed by the Doctors of the Church that he was saved. You can also say that by this same argument, certain people were erroneously deceived into saying that **Moses** was damned, because his sin was read of at the **Waters of Contradiction** <note>The incident at Meribah (Numbers 20) where Moses struck the rock in anger</note>, and nothing was expressly held concerning his repentance. And yet God said to **Joshua**: "**Moses** my servant is dead." 

The second corollary proposition is this: No one can be certain that anyone is damned to hell, unless they have this by a special revelation from God, or from those to whom God is believed to have revealed it. The truth of this is clear from the preceding propositions, because no one can be certain of final repentance, or of impenitence, except for Him who knows the secrets of the heart, and to whom He has wished to reveal them. For since no one is as certain of another's state as he is of his own—for, "What pertains to a man, no one knows except the spirit of the man which is within him," as is said in **1 Corinthians 2**—and since a man cannot even be certain of himself, "whether he be worthy of hatred or love," as is said in **Ecclesiastes 9**, how much less can he be certain of another, unless he has a special revelation regarding this? 

Now, from this principal proposition and its corollaries, I infer for the purpose of my conclusion: even granted that **Origen**, in erring within those errors, sinned mortally, yet since we are uncertain of his final impenitence or repentance, to assert that he is damned is an altogether rash judgment and is to be rejected. Since, therefore, we can be certain neither of his salvation nor of his damnation, it is nevertheless pious and highly reasonable to believe—as I have said—that God saved him, a man of such great and immense knowledge. Concerning him, **Jerome** says in the preface to the **Song of Songs**:

> While he surpassed all others in other matters, in this work he surpassed himself.

And of him, that saying is verified:

> The king brought me into his chamber.

And elsewhere, wishing to imitate **Origen** in part, **Jerome** says that "no one except the unskilled denies he was the teacher of the churches after the Apostles." And elsewhere:

> **Origen** toiled with such great labor over the Scriptures that he justly received the name <term>Adamantius</term> <note>original: "Adamantius," a Greek name meaning "man of steel" or "unbreakable," referring to his tireless work</note>.

And after certain other things, he adds this:

> Who can ever read as much as he himself wrote? And for this toil, what reward did he receive? He was condemned by Bishop **Demetrius**, and—excepting the priests of **Palestine**, **Arabia**, **Phoenicia**, and **Achaia**—the city of **Rome** itself consented to his condemnation. It gathered a Senate against him, not because of the novelty of his dogmas, not because of heresy (as rabid dogs now falsely pretend against him), but because they could not bear the glory of his eloquence and knowledge. Why I have written this, and dictated it quickly but not cautiously by the flame of a poor lantern, you can understand if you consider the followers of **Epicurus** and **Aristippus** <note>Greek philosophers often associated here with those who prefer ease or worldly status over difficult spiritual truth</note>.

These are the words of **Jerome** verbatim. I ask you, O ingenious reader, to consider these words individually...

He then quotes Saint Jerome’s high praise of Origen to suggest that his condemnation was driven by professional envy rather than actual heresy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s defense of the Church Father Origen. Having previously argued that no one can be certain of another’s damnation without divine revelation, Pico now transitions to positive evidence for Origen’s sanctity by citing the high regard in which he was held by other Saints and his extreme physical suffering for the faith.</meta>

->**John Pico of Mirandola**<-

...n knows <note>continuing from the previous page: "...except for the spirit of the man which is within him."</note> [re]ader, attend diligently: and from these things, understand for yourself those things which I do not express. 

In the preface to his *Hebrew Questions*, speaking of this same **Origen**, **Jerome** says the following: "This one thing I say: I would wish, even with the envy attached to his name, to also have his knowledge of the Scriptures, regarding as worthless the images and shadows of ghosts, whose nature is said to terrify little children and chatter in dark corners." <note>original: "imagines umbrasque larvarum... in angulis garrire tenebrosis"</note> Furthermore, what **Jerome** proclaims about him—that he trampled on greed, that he castrated himself out of zeal for God <note>Origen is famously said to have taken Matthew 19:12 literally and castrated himself to avoid temptation while teaching women, an act later condemned as "zeal without knowledge."</note> (though not according to knowledge), that he labored by day and by night in the explanation of Scripture, which "those who explain shall have eternal life," as the **Wise Man** says <note>A reference to Sirach 24:31</note>. And as is written in the letter to **Vigilantius**: "He discussed the obscurities of the Prophets and revealed the greatest sacraments of both the New and the Old Testament." 

I pass over the fact that he was not only the son of a martyr, but he himself was very nearly worthy of the merit of martyrdom. For **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339), the first major historian of the Church.</note> says that even as a small boy, he burned with such a great fire for attaining martyrdom that he voluntarily threw himself into dangers. Then, in the time of the **Decian persecution** <note>A Roman persecution of Christians under Emperor Decius, c. 250 AD.</note>, he endured new crosses, new types of punishments, and torments unheard of in all ages. It reached the point that he was afflicted with "a thousand deaths" (as **Eusebius** says) so that he might not meet just the one he desired, while the persecutor worked with the greatest effort so that neither would death be granted to him, nor the pain cease. 

See how close he was to the glory of martyrdom, which many of his disciples achieved under his leadership and encouragement. I say again, he was truly close to the glory of martyrdom; indeed, he earned a merit almost equal to it. For **Augustine** also says in his book *On the Good of Marriage*: "The merit of martyrdom is not unequal in **John** <note>John the Evangelist, traditionally believed to have survived a vat of boiling oil and died of old age.</note>, who did not suffer, and in **Peter**, who did suffer." Note these words of **Augustine** well. Hence, just as **John**, although he did not pass by the sword, was nevertheless prepared to undergo martyrdom when he was cast into the vat of boiling oil, so too was **Origen**. Although he did not undergo death by martyrdom, he was nevertheless prepared—indeed, we have heard that he desired to undergo it—and he suffered torments (as **Eusebius** says) such that he underwent a thousand deaths for the sake of one. 

And this is what **Bernard** <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153)</note> says in a sermon on the **Holy Martyrs**: that there is a threefold martyrdom: a martyrdom of will only, a martyrdom of deed only, and a martyrdom of both deed and will. **John the Evangelist** suffered the martyrdom of will only, to whom it was said, along with his brother (in **Matthew 20**): "You shall drink of my cup." Therefore **Cyprian** says: "Among the servants of God, in whose hearts martyrdom is intended and in whose minds it is conceived, the soul devoted to good is crowned with God as judge. For it is one thing for the spirit to be lacking for martyrdom, and another for martyrdom to be lacking for the spirit." <note>Cyprian means that if you are willing to die but the opportunity never comes, you still get the crown; but if the opportunity comes and you lack the courage, you lose it.</note> 

If, therefore, the spirit was never lacking for the martyrdom of **Origen**, and he underwent a thousand deaths for one, how can we not believe him crowned by God the judge? If, that is, the martyr **Cyprian** does not lie. And if he is damned, who, I ask, damned him to the death of hell? Was it **Christ Jesus**, for whom he himself wished to die so many times? On the contrary, just as **Augustine** says of **Cyprian** himself, that the blood of martyrdom washed away in him every stain of heresy, so too regarding **Origen**: [the blood] shed by him—not so much upon the earth outwardly, as over his zeal for God and...

<summary>Pico argues for Origen's salvation by citing his immense physical suffering during the Decian persecution and the theological principle that the "will" for martyrdom is equivalent to the "deed." He uses testimonies from Saints Jerome, Augustine, Bernard, and Cyprian to suggest Origen was a martyr in spirit and thus surely redeemed.</summary>

# Apologia.

Let us piously believe that his heavenly soul, burning with charity, washed away every stain of heresy through the internal blood of martyrdom <note>Pico argues that Origen's suffering during the Decian persecution, though he did not die, functioned as a "baptism of blood" that purified his theological errors.</note>: saying with **David**, "Blessed is **Origen**," who, even if he sometimes "went into the council of the erring," yet "did not stand in the way of sinners" through impenitence, and "never sat in the seat of pestilence" <note>original: "in cathedra pestilentiæ"</note> through stubbornness; but "his will was in the law of the Lord, and in His law he meditated day and night." <note>Pico is paraphrasing Psalm 1:1-2 to defend Origen’s character.</note> Blessed is **Origen**, whose "iniquities are forgiven" through baptism, and whose "sins are covered" through penance, and to whom the "Lord did not impute sin" on account of his martyrdom. Finally, let us believe that such and so great a man—even if he sometimes erred in the mysteries of the faith from a defect of intellect, and not from any malice of the will—was not abandoned by the Lord in his final moments. Rather, we should believe that by the visitation of God’s most clement mercy, he was illuminated regarding the secrets of the faith (if he erred in any) and called back from an erroneous path to the way of salvation. 

And this is what I intended in my brief response when I said elsewhere: since he is not found to have been stubborn <note>Pico distinguishes between "error" (making a mistake) and "heresy" (stubbornly clinging to a mistake after correction).</note>, it is likely to believe that God saved him. That is, by visiting him with the visitation I mentioned, God most mercifully placed him in a state worthy of salvation, and, illuminating him regarding those secrets of the faith in which he erred, called him to a saving penance for them. Whether this was so or not, no one can know with certainty unless it has been revealed to him from above. But to believe it was so, rather than not, seems more harmonious and more reasonable to anyone considering the acts and life of **Origen**. For in doubtful matters, one must always reasonably adhere to the more favorable side. And let these things be said so that they may carry weight even if **Origen’s** penance were not established; however, we have very clearly shown above, from the testimony of the most blessed **Jerome**, that his penance is indeed established.

Regarding the **sixth article**, I say that it does not seem believable that the **Church** ever determined that **Origen’s** soul was damned to hell <note>original: "animam Origenis ad inferos esse damnatam"</note>. I prove the truth of this proposition by two reasons. The first reason is this: regarding a matter where one side or the other cannot be determined with certainty except by being rash, it should not be believed that a determination was made by the **Church**. But regarding this question—whether **Origen** is saved or damned—neither side can be determined except rashly, at least without a special revelation from God. Therefore, since such a revelation is not established, it should not be believed that a determination was made by the **Church** concerning this. The major premise <note>A term from formal logic referring to the first part of a syllogism.</note> is well-known, and its opposite would be injurious to the **Church**: namely, to believe that anything could be judged by her without consultation and rashly. The minor premise is clear from the articles mentioned above. It is confirmed because the **Church** could not be made certain of **Origen’s** damnation except through a special revelation made by God; but there is nowhere any mention that such a revelation was made; therefore, etc. 

The second reason is this: because if there is anything that persuades people that the **Church** determined **Origen’s** damnation, it is certain texts of the **Decrees** <note>Referring to the "Decretum Gratiani," the collection of canon law used in the Middle Ages.</note> which seem to suggest this to those interpreting them in a crude way <note>original: "groffo eos modo interpretantibus"</note>. Yet when these texts are rightly examined, they act against such people rather than for them;

<summary>Pico argues that Origen’s errors were intellectual mistakes rather than malicious heresy and suggests he was likely saved by God's mercy. He further asserts that the Church has never officially declared Origen damned, as such a judgment would require a divine revelation that hasn't occurred.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s legal defense of Origen. He specifically addresses various passages from Canon Law and papal decrees that critics used to argue that Origen was not only a heretic but was personally condemned to hell. Pico shifts from a theological defense of Origen's character to a technical, legal interpretation of what "damnation" means in ecclesiastical law.</meta>

->### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola<-

They put forward their case; these are nearly the exact texts they bring up. First, regarding **Distinction 15**, the chapter *Sancta Romana ecclesia*, as Pope **Gelasius** writes: "Likewise, we accept to be read some small works of **Origen**, which the blessed man **Jerome** does not reject. But all his other works we say are to be rejected along with their author." <note>This refers to the *Decretum Gelasianum*, an early medieval list of authorized and prohibited books. Pico notes that "rejected" (renuenda) is a specific technical term here.</note> Also, from **Question 24, question 3**, the chapter *Sane*: "Likewise, if someone looks back to the times of **Theophilus** of holy memory, or earlier, they will find **Origen** was anathematized after his death, which your Holiness also does." And **Julius**, the most religious man of ancient Rome, and the gloss on that passage says: "Since that man was condemned, are not his writings also?" as seen in the section **On Heretics**, the chapter *Fraternitatis*. There it is written: "Since **Celestine** and **Pelagius** were condemned in the **Synod of Ephesus**, how can their chapters be accepted, when their authors are condemned?" <note>Pico is citing standard works of Canon Law used by his opponents to prove that a condemned author means a condemned soul.</note>

From these authorities, some believe they can prove the damnation of **Origen's** soul to the underworld. I, however, say that nothing more is established by the preceding points except that the Church condemns the opinions and dogmas attributed to **Origen** as heretical, and condemns the man himself insofar as he was the one teaching those dogmas, and detests them. Regarding the damnation or salvation of his soul, the Church intends nothing at all.

That this is true is clear for many reasons. First, because it does not belong to the Church to damn or save the souls of men, as that belongs solely to Him who is the judge of the living and the dead. <note>Pico makes a sharp distinction between "Ecclesiastical Damnation" (excommunication or banning of books) and "Eternal Damnation" (God's judgment).</note> Therefore, it is ridiculous if one reads in the decrees, "We damn **Origen**," to interpret it as "we damn his soul with the damnation of hell." 

This is also evidently clear from the way **Gelasius** himself speaks, saying: "his other small works, we say, are to be rejected with their author." For this word "to reject" <note>original: "renuere"</note> can in no way imply what those critics intend. Rather, the Pope intends nothing other than this: that his works are not accepted as "Authentic" <term>Authentic: In this context, it means "officially authorized for teaching" or having the Church's stamp of approval.</term> in the Church, nor is he himself accepted as an approved Doctor of the Church whose words must be believed. 

Even if the Pope had not only said "We reject," but also "We damn," it would not help their case. For we are also accustomed to say: "**Scotus** damns **Thomas** in this point," or "**Herveus** damns **Scotus**," and so on with the rest. <note>Pico refers to the famous academic debates between followers of Duns Scotus, Thomas Aquinas, and Herveus Natalis. In a university setting, "damning" an opponent's argument meant proving it wrong, not sentencing them to hell.</note> In all such speech, we must understand the "damnation" of the doctrine, not the soul, according to the common and proper way of speaking.

Secondly, I argue against them from the very gloss they cite, which asks: "If the man himself is condemned, are his writings not also condemned?" I ask these people: if this logic holds—"**Origen** himself is condemned, therefore his writings are condemned"—how is the word "condemned" being used in the first part? If it is used to mean "not approved in his doctrine" and "not accepted as a teacher of dogma," then I have proven my point. But if it is understood as "damned in his soul to eternal hell," then the logic is worthless. 

For it is possible for many Doctors, whose writings are Catholic and are read daily as Catholic works, to be in hell; it is possible for someone to err in nothing regarding the faith and to feel correctly about all the articles of faith, and yet be in some other mortal sin and die in it. The damnation of a soul is entirely irrelevant to the condemnation of a doctrine, because the former depends on the malice of the will... 

<summary>Pico argues that Church decrees condemning Origen refer to his status as an unauthorized teacher and the errors in his books, rather than a divine judgment on his eternal soul. He highlights that the Church lacks the jurisdiction to pronounce on a person's salvation, which belongs to God alone.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's legal argument. He is responding to the claim that because Origen’s works were "rejected" by the Church, Origen himself must be in hell. Pico argues that the personal salvation of an author is separate from the orthodoxy of their writings.</meta>

# Apologia.

->### 223<-

attributed to them. This, however, is based on a lack of understanding. Therefore, the following logic is not valid: "This man is in paradise; therefore, his words are **orthodox**." <note>original: "catholica" — here meaning in accordance with universal Church doctrine.</note> For **Papias** is in paradise, as are **Irenaeus**, **Victorinus**, **Cyprian**, and many others, whose writings are nevertheless rejected as heretical in many points—writings which they are never recorded to have recanted.

I confirm this by the following statement, to which the gloss on the chapter *Fraternitatis* in the section **On Heretics** refers, where it is said: "If **Celestine** and **Pelagius** were condemned in the **Synod of Ephesus**, how can those chapters be accepted when their authors are condemned?" <note>The Synod of Ephesus (431 AD) was a major church council that addressed various heresies.</note> It is certain, however, that in that synod, **Celestine** and **Pelagius** were not condemned in themselves—that is, in their souls—but in their doctrine. This is true partly because, as stated above, the Church is neither accustomed to nor able to condemn men in that way, and partly because we must understand a judgment to apply to the matter that was originally questioned and disputed. In that synod, as is clear from the acts of the Council, the question was not: "Are the souls of **Celestine** and **Pelagius** in paradise or in hell?" but rather: "Are their sayings and dogmas orthodox or not?" Therefore, we must understand the judgment to be about the truth of those dogmas, and the approval or rejection of the authors only insofar as they were teachers of those specific dogmas.

Thirdly, it is foolish to say that the Church has determined that **Origen’s** soul is damned. Just as the Church is accustomed to **canonize** <term>Canonize: To officially declare a deceased person to be a saint in heaven.</term> certain people, it is not similarly accustomed to damn people—that is, to decree by a formal sentence that they are in hell. The reason it practices the former and not the latter is that to decree that someone is saved, we must be certain that they died in a state of grace. While we cannot have absolute certainty of this from the things they did during their life (since as long as one is "on the way," there is always room for merit or demerit and for changing one's purpose from one thing to another), we do have signs after death, such as **miracles** or something similar. However, it is not easy to find a sign after death by which we might be convinced of someone's damnation. 

Indeed, without a doubt, no other sign can be had except a special revelation regarding the matter. If such a revelation happened or had happened, then just as the Church testifies to miracles when it canonizes someone, it would also make mention of a special revelation if it were to damn someone, so as not to appear to have made such a decree rashly or without counsel. Yet the Church nowhere tells of such a thing regarding **Origen**. We must therefore understand that **Origen** was "damned" by the Church in the same way he appears to have deserved it based on what is recorded and testified about him. But nothing is recorded about him except that he erred in the mysteries of the faith. An absolute damnation of **Origen** himself does not follow from this error, but only a damnation of his writings and his doctrine, as is clear from the preceding arguments. 

Thus we must judge him to be "damned" by the Church in this sense and no other. Furthermore, we know that he was not **pertinacious** <note>In canon law, heresy requires "pertinacity," or stubborn persistence in error after being corrected by the Church.</note> against the Church’s determination in those opinions, because the councils in which those opinions were condemned took place long after **Origen’s** death.

<summary>Pico argues that the Church condemns Origen's writings but has no legal mechanism or divine revelation to declare his soul personally damned to hell. He notes that several Saints held views later deemed heretical and that Origen died long before his views were officially condemned, meaning he could not have been a "stubborn" heretic.</summary>

And whether he remained unrepentant of those errors, we can in no way know; indeed, we have proved above through **Jerome** <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD) was a contemporary critic of Origen who nonetheless respected his scholarship.</note> that he either did not write those things, or if he did write them, he repented. For the seventh article, I say that this proposition—namely, that according to the doctrine of **Saint Thomas**, any member of the faithful is not bound by the necessity of faith to believe that a person whom the church has judged and sentenced to be in hell is indeed in hell. The truth of this proposition is derived thus: because as much faith is to be given to the Church in the damnation of someone as is to be given in the canonization of saints. But **Thomas** says in the last article of his *Ninth Quodlibet* <note>A "Quodlibet" was a formal academic tournament where a theologian answered "any question" posed by the audience.</note> that we are not bound by the necessity of faith to believe that the saints canonized by the Church are in glory, but only by the **piety of faith**. <note>original: "pietate fidei" — a belief held out of reverence and respect for Church tradition rather than as an essential dogma required for salvation.</note> Therefore, we are also not necessarily bound to believe that those damned by the Church are in hell, but it is only to be believed so through piety. Now, **Thomas's** foundation is this: that we are only bound by the necessity of salvation to believe the Church in those matters which pertain to the substance of the faith, because in those things, the Holy Spirit, upon arriving, teaches it all truth. However, whether the soul of this or that person is in hell or in paradise pertains nothing to the substance of the faith; yet, because the honor we show to saints is a certain profession of faith by which we believe in the glory of the saints, therefore—although we are not bound to this by the necessity of salvation—it is still to be believed so through piety. From this proposition, I infer for the purpose of my conclusion that even if the Church had determined **Origen** to be damned, we would still not be bound by the necessity of Catholic faith to assent that it is so. From this it is clear that even if it were true (as they bring against me) that the Church had determined the opposite of my conclusion, it would still have been poorly judged by them that my conclusion "savors of heresy." <note>To "savor of heresy" was a specific legal category in the Inquisition for statements that sounded heretical even if they weren't explicitly condemned.</note> Let these Masters see, therefore, that it has not yet been correctly determined by them against my conclusion, even if the things they bring against me are true. And let them beware lest they institute new things to be believed for the faithful by their own authority and determine them to be "of the faith." Let them hear that prohibition of the Lord in the fourth chapter of **Deuteronomy**: *You shall not add to the word that I speak to you.* <note>Deuteronomy 4:2.</note> This saying condemns not only those who, by their own authority, add new things to be believed on top of previous ones, but also because they reject Catholic truth as if it were heretical.

### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA'S
### Disputation on the Freedom of Belief.

Just as no one opines precisely in such a way because he *wants* to opine so, likewise no one believes something to be true precisely because he *wants* to believe it so. From this conclusion, I infer this as a corollary: It is not in the free power of man to believe an article of faith to be true when it pleases him, and to believe it not to be true when it pleases him. These Masters have judged that this proposition, along with its corollary, was erroneous and "savored of heresy." I, however, consider the principal conclusion to be not only Catholic, but most true, and far...

...truer than its opposite; and I say the same regarding the corollary properly understood, whose meaning, if taken according to my intent, is not to be understood otherwise than as it follows from the principal conclusion, of which it is set forth as a corollary.

That the conclusion is not only Catholic but also most true is clear; for concerning its first part—which is that no one holds an opinion that something is so *precisely* because they wish to so opine—there is **Aristotle**, in the second book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "De Anima"</note>, text of the Commentary 253, where **Aristotle** establishes the difference between imagination and opinion. And this sentence of **Aristotle** is not only not rejected, but indeed is unanimously approved by all our theologians.

The second part of the conclusion—which is that no one believes something to be precisely true because they wish to believe it is true—is **Augustine's** in many places, who says this very often: that one cannot believe by <term>free choice</term> <note>original: "libero arbitrio"</note>, that is, by the mere command of the will, without the persuasion of reason or a motive. And my entire conclusion, in which this opinion is summarily held—that when some doubtful proposition is presented, for someone to believe or disbelieve it, the mere apprehension of the terms and the mere command of the will is not sufficient—is held by **Pierre d'Ailly**, **Henricus Haëta** <note>Likely Henry of Oyta (c. 1330–1397), a prominent theologian at the University of Vienna and Paris.</note>, and **Henry of Hesse**. And when I was in **Paris**, almost the entire **University of Paris** held it, along with many other Catholic doctors, so much so that they consider it true and its opposite impossible; indeed, I have not yet read a doctor contradicting this opinion.

Moreover, the corollary proposition is not to be understood and accepted otherwise than with the restriction or determination placed in the antecedent: specifically, that it is not in the free power of the will to believe an article of faith to be true whenever it pleases, and to believe it to be false when it pleases, so that it is not precisely because it pleases the will that the intellect should believe that it actually believes. Nor is such an understanding of one proposition through another linked to it unusual; indeed, in Holy Scripture, the meaning of the letter is often taken from what precedes or follows it, which ought especially to be done in our case.

Because, therefore, this statement—"it is not in our power," etc.—I do not put forward as a statement on its own or as a separate conclusion, but I set it forth as a corollary from the preceding one. If it does not please them to accept the understanding of the present corollary from its principal conclusion to which it is attached and linked, let them consider that something is said to be in "liberty" or in the "free power of the will" in two ways.

In one way: because once an apprehension is placed in the intellect, with no other act of the intellect required, it is within the <term>imperative power</term> <note>The "imperative power" refers to the will's ability to command or direct other faculties, like the intellect, to act.</note> of the will to perform that act. And thus it is denied in this conclusion that the act of believing is in the free power of man; nor is it necessary for every act of command, whether meritorious or demeritorious, to be in the power of man in such a way. For believing, the apprehension of the terms of an article [of faith] is not sufficient, but beyond that, persuasion or some probable reason is required, as was cited from **Augustine**.

In another way, something is said to be in the free power of the will, because...

# ## Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

...because, all other things being established which are required for that act to exist, the will can bring it into being or not bring it into being; nor is the will necessitated toward that act, even when all those other factors are present. And in this way, the act of believing an article of faith is within the <term>free power of the will</term> <note>original: "libera potestate uoluntatis"</note>. This is the understanding of the corollary proposition, and from what has been said, anyone who possesses an intellect can recognize that those Masters did not do well to say absolutely that the proposition was erroneous and "savored of heresy." 

Furthermore, that the opinion of those doctors whom I follow is probable and rational—namely, those who say that for the purpose of causing the <term>assent of faith</term> <note>The psychological moment when a person accepts a statement as true.</note>, the mere apprehension of the terms, combined with the command of the will, is not sufficient—can be clearly seen, not only by the authority of **Augustine** (who affirms this in many places, as I have said), but also by most effective reasons. 

And first, it is argued thus: It is not within the free power of a human being to hold an opinion that something is this way or that way simply when he wishes. Therefore, it is not within the free power of a human being to believe something is this way or that way simply when he wishes. The consequence is evident. Because, if that which seems more likely to be present is in fact not present, then [it follows for the lesser, etc.]. But it is a lesser thing to adhere to something with a <term>fear of the opposite</term> <note>original: "formidine ad oppositum"; in scholastic thought, "opinion" is a belief held while still acknowledging the possibility of being wrong, whereas "faith" or "knowledge" is held without this fear.</note> than to adhere to it without such fear. Therefore, the antecedent is expressed by **Aristotle** in the second book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "de Anima"</note>, in the text of commentary 153. And it is clear through experience: for anyone experiences within themselves that when a doubtful proposition is offered, if it is purely doubtful to them, they are inclined toward neither side to form an opinion by assent until some new "appearance" comes to them, either through a syllogistic reason, or through intuitive knowledge, or by the testimony of many, or by the authority of a speaker, or something similar.

Secondly, it is argued thus: It is not within the free power of a human being to make something appear true to his own intellect, or to make it appear not true. Therefore, it is not in the power of a human being to believe something to be true or not true in this or 그 way. The consequence holds: for it is a contradiction for someone to believe something and assent to it, while that thing does not appear to him to be true. The premise is proven because for this or that to "appear" such and such to the intellect is simply for this or that to be represented to the intellect in such a manner. And this cannot depend on the command of the will, because this representation precedes the act of the will. This is confirmed because something appearing a certain way to the intellect happens because the object being represented is such as it is; and the evidence, or whatever else makes it credible or not credible, is such as it is, and the intellect is such as it is. But to make the object be such, or the intellect be such, is not within the choice of the will. Therefore, making a thing appear this way or that way to the intellect is not under the command of the will.

Thirdly, it is argued thus: Whenever there is some power that is purely neutral and indifferent toward two opposite "second acts," it cannot move into either of them unless it is first determined by something which is a "first act," or which stands in the place of a first act with respect to the other of those second acts. But it is the case that the intellect is a power purely neutral and indifferent to the specification of any of its "second acts"; therefore, it cannot be determined to any such specification unless something else arrives which is either a first act...

# Apologia.

...the first act, or holding the place of a first act, with respect to such a determination. Then, under that reasoning, I assume this consequence: A mere act of the will cannot behave as a <term>first act</term> <note>The primary initiating cause of a motion or thought.</note> with respect to the <term>specification</term> <note>In scholastic logic, "specification" refers to what an act is (its content or truth-value), whereas "exercise" refers to whether the act happens at all.</note> of intellectual acts. Therefore, by the command of the will alone, the intellect cannot be determined toward such a specification; this consequence is well-known from the previously assumed reasoning. And the antecedent is clear from the common opinion of all **Doctors** <note>Authoritative church theologians.</note> consenting on this point: that although an act of the intellect depends on the will regarding its *exercise*, it does not do so regarding its *specification*.

These things having been established, I argue thus for the proposal: The act of assenting and the act of dissenting are acts having opposite specific characters. Therefore, the intellect cannot be determined to assent or non-assent by the command of the will. Therefore, the fact that someone believes an article of faith to be true through the intellect, or does not believe it, is not precisely because they so wish or do not wish to believe, but results from something else that determines the intellect—which is neutral in itself—to the specification of such an act.

Fourth, it is argued thus: A human being is not determined to believe something precisely by an act of the will if, when asked why they believed it, they do not assign it to a precise act of the will. But it is the case that if someone is asked why they believe the **Christian faith** <note>original: "Christianę fidei"</note> rather than the **Islamic faith** <note>original: "fidei Mahumetenum"</note>, they will not assign it precisely to an act of the will. Therefore, they were not inclined to believe by a precise act of the will. Moreover, that a mere act of the will is not assigned is clear from experience and from the sayings of our **Theologians**, by whom these eight reasons are commonly cited as to why we ought to believe the **Gospel** <note>original: "euāgelio"</note>: namely, **prophetic pronouncement**, the **harmony of the scriptures**, the **authority of the writers**, the **reasonableness of the contents**, the **unreasonableness of individual errors**, the **stability of the Church**, and the **clarity of miracles**.

Fifth, it is argued thus: Whenever any two people are determined to believe opposite things, and each of them is determined precisely by this—because they *want* to be so determined, while the judgment or persuasion of reason is entirely indifferent to it—it cannot be said that one is moved more reasonably to believe than the other. But given two people, one of whom wants to believe that *A* is true and the other does not want to believe it, we say that this one or that one wants it more **reasonably**, and the other more **irrationally**. Therefore, they do not determine their wanting this or that precisely because they want it so. 

The major premise of this reasoning is well-known because, as **Albert** says in the third book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "Albertus in 3. de Anima"</note>, when the will acts precisely because it wants to act so, it is likened to a **tyrant** <note>A ruler who acts on whim or "will" rather than on law or reason.</note>, in whose action the reason for the act is not sought, because his acting is not according to reason, but acting according to his whim. The minor premise is manifest: Because we say daily that **Muslims** <note>original: "Mahumetistas"</note> or **Jews** act irrationally in this, that they do not believe, and we act reasonably because we believe. But if the precise cause why I believe and he does not believe were precisely because I wanted to and he did not want to, each would be a tyrannical act of the will, and in neither would a greater or lesser reasonableness appear...

<summary>Pico argues that faith is not a blind choice of the will but requires intellectual "specification" based on evidence. He lists eight traditional reasons for Christian belief (like miracles and prophecy) to show that faith is a rational act rather than a "tyrannical" whim.</summary>

<keywords>will vs intellect, specification, exercise of the will, Albert the Great, reasons for faith, Islam, Judaism, rationality, Christian apologetics</keywords>

...fied; indeed, in neither case is there rationality, but mere power and a **tyrannical command of the will** <note>original: "imperium tyrannicum uoluntatis." Pico uses this provocative phrase to describe the will forcing the mind to accept a statement as true without any logical proof or "marks of truth."</note>. And from what has been said in this argument, the meaning of those brief words which I spoke in my response regarding the "tyrannical act of the will" will be clear to these **Masters** <note>The "Masters of Theology" or inquisitors who were examining Pico’s work.</note>. Many other reasons could be brought forward in favor of this opinion, but it is not my purpose here to treat these matters or to discuss the proposed questions in full, but only to show that my determination and conclusions are not heretical.

And although these points are sufficient for the defense of my conclusion, I also wish to say this: there was a certain **Doctor**—whose condemnation on this article I have never read—who held quite simply that the act of believing is not free. This was held assertively by **Robert Holcot** <note>A famous 14th-century English Dominican theologian known for his "subtle" logic.</note>, a most subtle Doctor of the Order of Preachers, in his first book on the *Sentences*. When it is argued against him that it would follow that the act of believing or not believing would not be **meritorious** or **demeritorious** <note>In theology, an act is "meritorious" if it earns a reward from God (like salvation).</note>, he says that this objection is null and frivolous. He argues that an act is not meritorious because it is free, but because it conforms to a law that promises a reward for that act, either to the one performing it or to another.

Consequently, he says that the act of believing is not meritorious because it is free, but because it conforms to the divine law, which promises such a reward—namely eternal life—to every believer. He adds that God could change this law and decree that whoever happens to fall over a **cornerstone** <note>A reference to a random or accidental event used as a logical hypothetical.</note> tomorrow by surprise shall be saved; in that case, that accident would be meritorious of eternal life. This is because our acts are not meritorious because they are free, but because they are accepted by God for eternal life. God can accept natural acts just as he accepts voluntary acts. Thus, He seems to have accepted the death of the **Innocents** <note>The "Holy Innocents," the infants killed by Herod in the Gospel of Matthew, who are considered martyrs despite being too young to choose faith.</note> for eternal life, in whom there was no use of free will. Nor does God act irrationally in doing this, because His will is the sufficient reason for all things that He decrees or ordains.

Therefore, Holcot concludes that if we take "to believe" to mean adhering with firm assent to those things whose truth is not evident to us except by the testimony of others—following the way **Augustine** defines it in his *Homily on John*, saying: *What is faith, except believing what you do not see?* <note>original: "Quid est fides, nisi credere quod non uides?"</note>—then such an act of believing is **not in the free power of man**.

However, if "to believe" is taken to mean assenting to whatever is revealed by God and witnessed by miracles, and *willing* to live and work according to them, then—because this "believing" includes both an act of the intellect and the will—he concedes that it is free. This follows the way Augustine defines it in the same *Homily*, saying: *To believe in God is to love by believing, to go to Him by believing, to adhere to Him and be incorporated into His members.* <note>original: "Credere in Deum, est credendo amare..." This describes "formed faith," which is faith animated by love (charity).</note> It is of this kind of belief that it was said: *Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.* But of the first kind of belief, it is said: *The demons believe, and they tremble.* The first [formed faith] is meritorious; the second [simple intellectual assent] is not meritorious. And when it is said that "faith exists only in those who will it," Holcot says this must be understood as **formed faith** <term>fide formata</term> <note>A technical term for faith that is "given form" or made alive by the presence of love/charity, as opposed to "unformed faith" which is mere intellectual agreement.</note>...

## GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, DISPUTATION ON THE
## accidents in the sacrament.

**W**hoever shall say that an **Accident** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" is a property (like color, smell, or shape) that cannot exist on its own but must exist in a "substance" (like bread or wood).</note> cannot exist unless it exists within the **Eucharist**, would be able to hold to the sacrament even while holding that the substance of the bread does not remain. Indeed, these **Masters** <note>The university theologians examining Pico’s work.</note> did not say that this conclusion was heretical, or that it smacked of heresy, but only that it was **erroneous**. If they had brought forward any reasons for this opinion of theirs, I would be able to either believe them or respond to them; but they have not brought forward any reasons that I have seen, neither in the condemnation of this conclusion nor in others.

I say, however, for the clarification of this conclusion, that by this statement I do not intend to say categorically and absolutely that an **Accident** cannot be without a **subject** <note>The "subject" is the underlying thing that possesses the qualities.</note>, or that in the sacrament they are in fact within a subject. On the contrary, I firmly hold with the Church that the sacramental accidents are, in fact, without a subject. Rather, I say: That he who would say that accidents cannot be without a subject, and who held—with **Thomas** <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas</note>—the real distinction of the bread's existence from its essence, could say that it does not contradict divine omnipotence to preserve the **existence** of the bread without its **essence**. Just as God preserves an act, whether substantial or accidental, without its own power, and consequently, in that "being" of the bread, he could make it the subject of the accidents while the substance of the bread does not remain. Regarding these accidents, the body of Christ could have a real presence just as it now has toward the accidents which are not situated in any subject. And whatever the case may be regarding the sacrament of the Eucharist as it was in fact instituted by Christ and believed by the Church—in which they hold in agreement that nothing of the bread remains, so much so that its reproduction would be a **creation**—nevertheless, by holding the aforementioned opinion of Thomas concerning the real distinction between essence and existence, and by taking the sacrament of the Eucharist in an extended sense... toward that which is, or can be, as it is taken in my conclusion, which is...

## Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

...modal and divided <note>Pico is using technical logic here. A "modal" proposition deals with necessity or possibility; a "divided" proposition separates the possibility from the specific state of the subject.</note>, the present conclusion is not only probable and not erroneous, but rather it is erroneous to say that there cannot be some sacrament of the Eucharist in which the **accidents** <term>Accidents: In Aristotelian philosophy, these are the external qualities of a thing (like color, smell, or texture) that usually cannot exist without a "subject" or "substance" to hold them.</term> would be in a subject. Nor do I know by what logic these **Masters** <note>The church authorities or inquisitors examining his work.</note> saw fit to condemn a "divided proposition of possibility" simply because of the falsehood of a "proposition of inherence" <note>An "inherence" proposition states that something is currently happening; a "possibility" proposition states that it *could* happen. Pico is accusing them of a logical blunder.</note> composed of the same terms. I am amazed that they do not know this is the **fallacy of the consequent** <term>Fallacy of the consequent: A logical error where one wrongly assumes that because a specific condition isn't met, the general possibility is also eliminated.</term>, arguing from the less broad to the more broad, while destroying the more broad.

It is as if someone were to say: "No man is in the house; therefore, no man **can** be in the house." For they argue in the same way in their condemnation of this proposition: "In no sacrament of the Eucharist that actually exists, or has been actually instituted by Christ, are the accidents in a subject; therefore, in no sacrament which is, or can be, or could be instituted by Christ, can the accidents exist without a subject."

From what has been said, it is clear how wrongly the present conclusion regarding **possibility** was condemned as erroneous by these fathers. They ought to remember that there have even been **Catholic doctors** <note>Respected theologians whose orthodoxy was not questioned.</note> who held that, in fact, the accidents in the sacrament of the altar are supported by the existence of the remaining substance. For there is one path of the theologians, as **Peter of Palud** <note>Petrus de Palude (c. 1275–1342), a prominent Dominican theologian and Archbishop.</note> reports in Book 4, Distinction 12, Question 3, who say that just as a **quality** <note>A type of accident, like "whiteness."</note> remains here naturally because its immediate subject remains—which is **quantity** <note>In this context, the physical dimensions or "extension" of the bread.</note>—even though its remote subject (the substance of the bread) is taken away; and thus the quality itself does not exist on its own, but inheres in the quantity.

So also, they say, quantity lacks its remote subject, which is the **essence** <term>Essence: The "whatness" of a thing; its internal nature.</term> of the substance, but it retains its own proper and near subject, which is the **being** <term>Being (Latin: *esse*): The actual act of existing, which Pico distinguishes here from the "essence" or nature of the thing.</term> of the substance, through which it is present in the substance. They argue this is possible because "being" can remain even if "essence" does not. Indeed, they say it is necessary for it to remain, considering the way "being" is defined here. They say it is clear that this is possible; for although essence is prior to being—from which it would seem that the prior can be separated from the posterior—and thus it would seem essence could exist without being more easily than the reverse; nevertheless, considering it from another side, essence relates to being as **potency relates to act**, and as **matter relates to form**. Because the "act" (being) depends less on the "potency" (essence) than the other way around, it seems more feasible for "being" to exist without "essence" than vice versa.

But God, in the **Incarnation of the Word** <note>The Christian doctrine of God becoming human in Jesus Christ.</note>, made the essence of humanity exist without its own independent "being" <note>Traditional theology held that Christ’s human nature did not have its own human "personhood" (being) but was sustained by the Divine person of the Son.</note>, as is said by many doctors. Therefore, He can much more easily do the opposite here: make the "being" of the substance of bread exist without its "essence." Thus, just as in the Incarnation the essence is assumed and remains while the [independent] being does not, so here, conversely, the essence can be changed and not remain, while the "being" is not changed and remains.

Secondly, they show that this is not only possible, but necessary: because nothing created can be converted into the **uncreated** <note>i.e., God.</note>, but one created thing can be converted into another when they share in matter and in genus; otherwise, they cannot. For example, an accident is not converted into a substance, nor into an accident of another category, according to common opinion. But the **essence** of bread agrees with the essence of Christ’s body in matter and genus; therefore, one can be converted into the other, even by nature, if the body were mortal. But the "being" of bread does not share in matter, nor in...

<summary>Pico defends his thesis on the Eucharist by arguing that it is logically possible for the physical properties of bread to remain supported by "being" even if the "essence" of bread is gone. He uses the logic of the Incarnation and the authority of Peter of Palud to show that his view, while not the standard rite, is not a heretical impossibility.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s technical defense regarding the metaphysics of the Eucharist. He is arguing against the "Masters" (the papal commission) who claimed that the "being" or existence (esse) of the bread must remain after consecration because it cannot be "converted" into the divine being of Christ. Pico is using Aristotelian logic and Scholastic theology to show that the bread's existence doesn't have to remain—it can be "annihilated" or "reduced to potentiality."</meta>

<page-num>231</page-num>
<header>Apologia.</header>
<sig>V 2</sig>

...nor in its genus with the substantial being of the body of Christ, since that [divine being] is uncreated and divine, belonging to the divine **person** <term>Person (suppositum): In theology, the "suppositum" is the individual subject or person. Pico is noting that in Christ, there is only one "person" (the Word), and therefore only one "act of being" (existence).</term>, whereas in Christ there is only one being of actual substantial existence. Therefore, [they argue] it is impossible for the "being" of the bread to be converted, and it is necessary for it to remain. I, however, am of the opinion that it is not necessary for it to remain; first, because even if it cannot be converted, it can nevertheless be annihilated, or it can be corrupted, yielding into the **potentiality of matter** <term>Potentiality of matter: The Aristotelian idea that when a thing is destroyed, it doesn't disappear into nothingness but returns to a "prime matter" that has the potential to become something else.</term>. Thus, just as the human nature [of Christ] could be assumed without assuming a separate "being" <note>original: "esse"</note>, but with that being remaining in the potentiality of matter, so the "being" of the essence can be converted—not by the "being" itself being converted, but by it being reduced into the potentiality of the essence. Though, to tell the truth, these "reductions" are more easily said than understood. 

Furthermore, although the "being" of the bread cannot be converted into uncreated being, it can nevertheless be converted into a created essence; for things that share in matter are mutually transmutable—granted that they may not share in "proximate matter," but only in "remote matter," just as an element can be converted into a living thing and vice versa. Now, the "being" of the bread and the essence of the body of Christ agree in **prime matter** <term>Prime matter: The most basic, formless substrate of all physical things.</term>, which is the remote potentiality of both, even if they do not agree in proximate matter. For matter is pure potentiality, while essence is potentiality joined with an act. Indeed, if that [the Masters'] reasoning were valid, it would conclude that of all the food which Christ ate before the Passion, only the essence was converted into him, and not the "being." But [that "being"] either remained, or was corrupted in some way other than by conversion, because the substantial being of Christ was uncreated before the Resurrection just as it was after. 

Likewise, some say that just as water—which by the **ordained power** <term>Ordained power (potentia ordinata): What God does according to the established laws of nature and the Church, as opposed to his "absolute power" to do anything that isn't a logical contradiction.</term> of God cannot be converted into the blood of Christ—is first converted into wine and then the whole is converted into blood, so too if "being" cannot by absolute power be converted into something of Christ, it is first by nature converted into its own essence, passing into it just as a **form** <term>Form: The organizing principle that makes matter into a specific thing (like "bread-ness").</term> yields into the potentiality of matter. And after that, the whole essence is converted into [Christ's] essence, and thus it is not necessary for the "being" to remain. And just as it seems erroneous to me to say that it is *necessary* for the being to remain, so it is no less erroneous to say that it *cannot* remain.

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA’S 
## Disputation on the Words of Consecration.

**T**hose words, *This is my body* <note>original: "Hoc est corpus"</note>, which are spoken in the consecration, are held **materially** and not **significatively** <term>Materially vs. Significatively: A "material" use of words is like a quotation or a formula (using the words as "objects"), whereas a "significative" use means the words are actually asserting a truth at the moment they are spoken.</term>. These Masters have said that this conclusion is scandalous and contrary to the common opinion of the holy Doctors, and that the opinion of the **glossator** <note>A "glossator" was a scholar who wrote explanatory notes (glosses) on legal or biblical texts. Pico is likely referring to the standard commentary on Canon Law.</term> is not held in this matter. 

I, however, say that their determination is scandalous and contrary to the common opinion of many doctors, and that the glossator’s opinion ought to be held in this matter rather than theirs. That this is so will be clearly evident once the meaning of the conclusion is understood. It must first be noted, therefore, that I do not intend for these words to have been taken "materially" when they were uttered by Christ, but only when they are uttered by a Gospel priest while consecrating. And for that reason I said in the conclusion: "The words which are spoken in the consecration," that is, which are now [spoken] by the one consecrating...

...are brought forward. It is certain, moreover, that the priest in the act of consecrating recites the aforementioned words of Christ, so that the prayer uttered by such a priest stands for the prayer uttered by Christ, taken **significatively** <term>Significatively (significative): Using a word to directly refer to its meaning or reality. Pico argues the priest doesn't do this; he isn't literally claiming he is Christ, but is quoting Christ.</term>. And such an opinion is not only not erroneous or scandalous, but rather the opposite opinion seems to be contrary to the form of consecration, in which the priest says those words **recitatively** <term>Recitatively (recitative): Using words as a quotation or a report of what someone else said. Pico’s point is that the priest is "playing a role" or quoting the Gospel.</term>. For the consecrating priest recites that Christ said to the apostles: *Take and eat, etc.* <note>original: "Accipite & manducate &c."</note>. The consecrating priest, however, neither speaks to the Apostles nor says to them "Take, etc." except recitatively. For he himself alone receives the sacrament, nor does he say to those standing by, "Take and eat, etc." Similarly, when he says, *This is my body* <note>original: "Hoc est corpus meum"</note>, that which is recited by the priest is that prayer: "This is my body," taken **materially** <term>Materially (materialiter): In Scholastic logic, using a word to refer to the word itself rather than what it represents.</term>, for a similar prayer composed of similar words uttered significatively by Christ. 

This is also evident through those words which are said before or after the consecration of the blood, namely: *Which shall be shed for you and for many, etc.* <note>original: "Qui pro uobis & pro multis effundetur &c."</note>. For these would be false if they were taken significatively, because the blood of Christ will not be shed from this time forward <note>Christ's sacrifice on the cross happened once; the Mass is a memorial, so "will be shed" in the future tense is a quotation of Christ's historical words at the Last Supper.</note>; therefore those words are taken only recitatively. What, after all, is a recitation but a voice uttered by another, for which the voice of the one reciting stands? And for that reason, this voice, being a recitation of another’s voice, is to be taken materially. Furthermore, if these words were taken significatively rather than recitatively, it would denote that the blood of Christ is shed for others and not for the one consecrating. When it is said, *Which shall be shed for you and for many*, it ought rather to be said, *Which for us, etc.* [if the priest were speaking for himself]. I do not say these things because I believe the opposite opinion cannot also be defended, but so that it may be clear that my conclusion is not only Catholic, but even more probable than its opposite. From these things it is clear that the present conclusion is not scandalous but probable, and the opinion of the **solemn glosser** <note>This refers to a standard legal commentator on the "Decretum" of Gratian, specifically the section "De Consecratione" (On Consecration).</note> in *De Consecratione*, distinction 2, chapter "Timore," is not to be rejected in this matter, but approved, just as it has never been rejected by the Church up until these times.

### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA’S Disputation on the Miracles of Christ.

**T**he miracles of Christ are the most certain argument of his divinity, not by reason of the thing done, but by reason of the manner of doing it. In explaining this conclusion, I said: because it is the firm knowledge of theologians that those miracles which Christ performed could be done by a pure human being through the power of God. For Christ says in John 14: *Amen I say to you, he who believes in me, the works that I do, he shall do, and greater than these shall he do.* Therefore, it is even unanimously concluded by the theologians themselves that that from which we can conclude Christ was God is not the thing itself that was done, but the **manner of doing** <note>Pico is arguing that the "miracle" (raising the dead) isn't the proof, because prophets did that too. The proof is that Christ did it by his own authority, whereas humans do it only as God's instruments.</note>: because he acted in such a way as those act who act by their own power and not by a power received from elsewhere. This is proper to God—namely, to act independently and not by another’s power—which manner of acting cannot be communicated to a creature...

<summary>Pico concludes his defense of the Eucharist by arguing that priests use "recitative" language (quoting Christ) during Mass. He then begins a new defense arguing that Christ's divinity is proven by His manner of performing miracles, not the miracles themselves.</summary>

...cannot be judged. Because, therefore, Christ performed many such acts—not by praying, nor clearly by asking, but by bidding and commanding, as one having power <note>A reference to Matthew 7:29: "For he taught them as one having authority."</note>—it is clear that he worked as God himself, and not as a man acting through the power of God. 

Having seen this declaration of mine, they said: "The conclusion can be drawn toward a bad sense, because it is contained among the **Magical** <term>Magical Conclusions: A specific section of Pico’s 900 Theses where he explored "Natural Magic," which he defined as the peak of natural philosophy, distinct from demonic sorcery.</term> theses, even granting that his declaration is true." 

Regarding this judgment of theirs, I wonder so much that I cannot wonder more. First, let them tell me: to anyone interpreting my words rightly and according to the correct and accustomed manner of speaking, can my conclusion have any sense other than the one I have stated? For what is clearer than these words? What is more expressive? *The miracles of Christ—not by reason of the thing done, but by reason of the manner of doing it—are the most certain argument of his divinity.* <note>original: "Miracula Christi non ratione rei factae, sed ratione modi faciendi, suae diuinitatis argumentum sunt certissimum."</note>

Second, let them tell me if this is the sentence of a righteous judge: "This conclusion, although it is true and Catholic, is nevertheless to be condemned because it can be drawn toward a bad sense." If so, then this must be condemned: *Christ cast out demons* <note>original: "Christus eiiciebat daemonia"</note>, because the Jews drew it toward a bad sense, saying: *That he cast out those demons in the name of Beelzebub, the prince of demons* <note>original: "Quòd in Belzabub principe dæmoniorum eiiciebat daemonia illa."</note>. And this must be condemned: *The Father is greater than I* <note>original: "Pater maior me est"</note>, because **Arius** <note>Arius (c. 250–336 AD) was a priest whose teachings led to the Arian heresy, which claimed that Jesus Christ was not co-eternal or co-equal with God the Father.</note> used it to conceive an inequality between the Son and the Father. And this must be condemned: *He did not know her until she brought forth her firstborn son* <note>original: "Non cognouit eam, donec peperit primogenitum filium suum"</note>, because **Helvidius** <note>Helvidius (c. 380 AD) argued against the perpetual virginity of Mary, using this verse from Matthew 1:25 as evidence.</note> used it to form a heresy against the perpetual virginity of Mary. And this must be condemned: *Neither does the Son know that day* <note>original: "Illam diem neq' filius nouit"</note>, because from it, some wish for the Father to know more than the Son knows. 

What more? Almost all **Gospel** <note>original: "Euangelicę"</note> propositions would have to be condemned, because they could be drawn to a bad sense by heretics. Why, then, should we condemn my proposition—placed in the same terms in which it is placed by many Catholic doctors—simply because some might be able to draw it toward a bad sense, even though it is true? Surely, if anyone interprets it poorly, it is *their* sense which is bad and to be condemned, not mine, which is holy and Catholic. 

Third, let them tell me: what is this "bad sense" that could be made of it? Let them speak if they know; but certainly there is no bad sense to be found, even if one wished to think of one. For if there were one, it would perhaps be this: that someone might suspect I wished to say that the same miracles Christ performed could be done through Magic in terms of the "thing done." But this suspicion is not allowed regarding my conclusion, because immediately before it, I placed another conclusion: *That the miracles of Christ could not be performed by way of Magic or **Kabbalah*** <term>Kabbalah: A tradition of Jewish mysticism. Pico was a pioneer of "Christian Kabbalah," believing that Jewish mystical texts could be used to prove the divinity of Christ.</term> <note>original: "Quòd miracula Christi non potuerunt fieri per uiam Magiæ uel Cabalæ."</note>. Any other bad sense that could be found or devised, I do not see; let them say it themselves if they can. 

Fourth, let them tell me what kind of logic this is, whether it holds in matter or in form: "It is among the **Magical** theses, therefore it is to be condemned." Truly, the form of this argument is similar to the one they used when they first tried to condemn the Magical conclusions. For they argued thus: "These conclusions are intricate and not understood by us. Therefore, they are to be condemned." O wonderful and unheard-of form of refutation! Let them be silent now, those who say that one cannot [decide/judge] regarding unknowns...

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

...judgment to be made, since it has already been decreed that those things which are most unknown are the most to be condemned. But let us return to the subject at hand. They say, "It is among the **Magical** [conclusions], therefore, it is to be condemned." Let them tell me themselves: Are magical conclusions good or bad? If they are bad, then these men have still judged poorly; for Christ hinted in the parable of the weeds <note>The Parable of the Tares (Matthew 13:24–30), where wheat and weeds are allowed to grow together until the harvest to avoid destroying the good crop.</note> that the wheat is not only not to be rejected because of the mixed-in weeds, but indeed, to save the wheat, he hinted that the weeds are not to be uprooted before the harvest. If they are good? Why then should they have felt the need to condemn a good conclusion placed among other good ones (if they themselves are good men)?

# A DISPUTATION BY GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA ON WHETHER GOD 
## understands.

**I**t is said more improperly of God that He is **intelligent**, or an **intellect**, than it is said of an angel that it is a **rational soul**. <note>original: "Magis impropriè dicitur de Deo, quod sit intelligens, uel intellectus, quàm de angelo, quod sit anima rationalis."</note> In declaring this conclusion, I said that the thesis relied on the manner of speaking used by Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential Christian mystic and theologian whose works Pico used to bridge Greek philosophy and Christian doctrine.</note>, who often says of God that He is neither intellect nor an intelligible thing. Similarly, I said my words should be understood in the same way one would accept the words of Dionysius. They said the conclusion was false and could be twisted toward a heretical meaning, and that my declaration did not satisfy them; I wonder not a little at this determination of theirs. I wonder, I say—if they are truly wise—that they say a conclusion is false which is not mine, but is a conclusion of Dionysius. And so that they may more clearly understand my mind, I will briefly explain the foundation of both the conclusion and the speech of Dionysius himself. 

It must therefore be noted that just as "reason" refers to the discursive knowledge <note>Knowledge gained through step-by-step logic or "running through" arguments, which is a human trait.</note> proper to humans—which reason would be said to be in God only in an improper sense—so similarly Dionysius says that <term>to understand</term> <note>original: "intelligere"</note> is the knowledge specific to an angel, caused by the angel and the angelic intellect, which informs the mind and changes it. He says such a way of "understanding" is not in God. Nor, by defining "to understand" in this way, can the conclusion be drawn to a bad sense, because Dionysius does not for that reason deny that God has knowledge of all things. Rather, God's knowledge is further removed from "intellection"—properly defined in the way mentioned above—than a human is from an angel. 

However, when it is said "God understands," the word "understand" is used generally for any kind of knowledge. Briefly, let them know this: through this conclusion, I do not intend to deny God's most perfect knowledge of all things, just as I do not deny any perfection in its simplest form. Indeed, I do not even intend to deny that God "understands" if we use the word "understand" in its common sense. But I deny that specific "understanding" which, according to Dionysius's way of speaking, refers to the kind of knowledge specific to an angel—just as "reason" refers to the knowledge specific to a human, which would also be improperly said to exist in God. 

But they say: "You say it is more improperly said of God that He is an intellect than of an angel that it is a rational soul. But this is false, because no one would ever say of an angel that it was a soul, yet it is said very often of God that He is an intellect; therefore, your comparison is a more improper way of speaking." I wonder at the learning of these men...

...of the holy fathers, and from a wide reading of sacred matters, who say that it is never said of an angel—neither properly nor improperly—that it is **rational**. But let them read Augustine in his book *On Music*, in his book *On True Religion*, in the *Acts against Fortunatum*, and in the book *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*: for in all these places, I remember that angels were called by the name of **souls** by Augustine. Although I have not seen everything, nor can I remember every place where I may have read in the holy Doctors that angels are called by this name; indeed, this is a matter which, when read, is often not considered worthy of much attention. 

However, when I said that it is more improperly said of God that He is **intellect**, I intended nothing else except that angelic knowledge—which claims the name of **intellectual knowledge** for itself—is further removed from the infinite knowledge of God (who knows all things through His essence) than it is from the **reasoning knowledge** <note>original: "noticia ratiocinatiua"</note> attributed to the rational soul or to man. If indeed it is inferred from this conclusion that God is "improperly" said to understand—just as a comparative term implies a positive one—let that inference be accepted only in this sense: God is not called **intellect** according to the proper or specific meaning of the word "understand," but according to a less proper common way, as was clear from the manner of speaking used by Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, whose "Apophatic" or negative theology argued that God is beyond all human names and categories.</note>.

### A DISPUTATION BY GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA ON THE HIDDEN
#### understanding of the soul.

**T**he soul understands nothing actually and distinctly except **itself**. In declaring this, I said that I was speaking about **hidden understanding** <term>intelligentia abdita: a concept from Augustine referring to a level of self-knowledge or mental activity that happens beneath the surface of conscious, sensory-based thought.</term>, which Augustine mentioned in his book *On the Trinity*, and Henry <note>Henry of Ghent (c. 1217–1293), a prominent Scholastic theologian.</note> in his *Quodlibeta*. These Masters <note>Pico's critics or the censors who examined his work.</note> said that my conclusion did not match the meaning of the Doctors I cited in my response; I do not know how they can say such a thing if they have actually seen those Doctors. 

And because this matter of **hidden understanding** is subtle and profound, I do not wish to explain it more broadly here, since they do not condemn the conclusion on other grounds. I wish only to say two things. **First**, that I do not intend to universally deny to the soul, in any state whatsoever, some distinct knowledge of things other than itself. For I grant that the soul of Christ understands other things actually and distinctly; and similarly, the souls of the blessed, through revelations or infused species <term>species infusas: in Scholastic philosophy, these are mental representations or "forms" of knowledge provided directly to the mind by God rather than through the senses.</term>. 

**Second**, I say that I am speaking of that **hidden understanding** which is without a *phantasm* <term>phantasm: a mental image or sensory impression. Pico is arguing that the soul can know itself directly, without needing to "picture" itself.</term> or the assistance of sense or imagination; and not just any such understanding, but a hidden understanding that is direct and permanent. Concerning this, I placed a conclusion next to this one, saying: *The soul always understands itself, and by understanding itself, it understands all beings in a certain way.* And so, in all my conclusions, there is always a certain **hidden connection** <note>original: "concatenatio"</note> which they perhaps do not notice. But returning to the point, I say: That the soul, through such a hidden, direct, and permanent understanding, understands nothing actually and distinctly except **itself**. From this it is clear that the present conclusion, understood in this way, was not to be vaguely condemned as erroneous, even if...
