...if in some sense it were not true. For in this way, many propositions of both the philosophers and the theologians, and even of Sacred Scripture, would be condemned. Such is that passage from **Habakkuk**, chapter 1:
> Your eyes are pure, so that you do not see evil, and do not look upon iniquities. <note>original: "Mundi sunt oculi tui, ne uideas malum, & ne despicias iniquitates." Habakkuk 1:13.</note>
And similarly that passage from **Matthew 25** concerning the foolish virgins:
> I do not know you.
For although the <term>vision of God</term> <note>original: "uisio Dei"</note>, or His knowledge, is a single and most simple thing, the aforementioned propositions—in respect to evil—would seem to universally deny such vision or knowledge even of God, because of the negation applied to the verb of "seeing" or "knowing." However, these are specifically explained by the Doctors of the Church as referring to the <term>approving knowledge of God</term> <note>original: "scientia Dei approbatiua" — the idea that God "knows" the righteous by favoring them, while "not knowing" the wicked in the sense of not granting them His grace.</note>, and the negation in them is not taken to deny every mode of God’s vision or knowledge. For that saying of the **Psalmist** is also true:
> My sins are not hidden from you. <note>Psalm 69:5 (Vulgate 68:6).</note>
If, therefore, many such passages are distinguished by expositors and Doctors and drawn toward a true meaning rather than being condemned, I do not know how my own thesis has deserved to be so simply condemned—even after it had been explained and declared to the "condemners" in the manner previously mentioned. 

Let these things, as they now stand, be dictated by me with a rushing pen; I shall write elsewhere with greater leisure and care, providing more, and perhaps better, arguments. This very work, such as it is, was composed during twenty nights <note>Pico famously claimed to have written this entire "Apologia" or defense in less than three weeks while under intense scrutiny from a papal commission.</note>. In publishing it, speed was more desirable to me than diligence; for it was necessary to provide my friends with something they might throw as a "sop to <term>Cerberus</term>" <note>original: "Cerbero offam obijcerent" — a classical reference to the three-headed dog guarding the underworld; Pico means throwing a distraction to his "barking" critics to quiet them.</note> against my barking enemies, and thus immediately meet the disease of unjust infamy that was coming upon me. 

Whatever I have written or shall write in the future, let it always be said with this preface: that only that shall be held as settled and holy which the <term>Supreme Pontiff</term> <note>The Pope.</note>, and all those whose judgment he approves, shall decree to be settled and holy. And would that he had already decreed something regarding these opinions of ours which have been called into doubt, through his wisdom and authority! Then this undertaking of mine would not have been necessary; for it would have been rash to defend what he had condemned, and superfluous to defend what he had approved. 

While, therefore, we cannot yet make use of the sentence of so great a judge, we have written these things so that my detractors might not have a reason to speak sinister things about the questions I proposed for dispute, nor the unlearned and simple have cause for suspicion. For it can happen that when someone less educated encounters them, reading this proposition—<term>Christ did not truly, and as far as real presence goes (as the common way posits), descend into hell</term>—he might immediately be offended by that word, **"Not truly,"** and believe the meaning of the proposition is that the <term>Article of Faith</term> concerning the descent of Christ is not true. Likewise, when he reads: <term>Infinite punishment is not owed to a mortal sin of finite time</term>, he might doubt whether I am leaning toward the <term>heresy</term> that the <term>punishment of Gehenna</term> <note>Hell.</note> is not eternal. And when he understands that I think well of <term>Origen’s salvation</term> <note>Origen (c. 185–253 AD) was a highly controversial Church Father whose eventual salvation was a major debate in the 15th century due to his theories on the eventual reconciliation of all souls to God.</note>, he might suspect that I love Origen's <term>dogmas</term> more than his life, character, learning, and repentance. It is the same with many other propositions, which perhaps might have on their first appearance...

<meta>This page continues Pico’s defensive argument from his "Apologia." -># Defense.<-

Because they may offend "holy rusticity" <note>original: "sanctam rusticitatem" — A term often used to describe the simple, uneducated, but devout faith of common people who might be confused by complex theological debate.</note>—that is, ears that are as pious as they are unlearned—I have for that reason written these things, intended to be read so that no one may think ill of us, or of the orthodox dogma of our holy religion. Therefore, I would not wish for our own people to read these original propositions themselves, which are raw, so to speak, and unexplained, unless they have first encountered this defense. For many things can be inferred from them that are as alien to the Catholic faith as they are to my own mind, especially by those of duller wit, and those who are unrefined and unaccustomed to the heights of learning.

I pray, therefore, I beseech, and I call to witness both friends and enemies, the pious and the impious, the learned and the unlearned, by the mercy <note>original: "uiscera Iesu Christi" — Literally "the bowels of Jesus Christ," a traditional expression for deep compassion or the heart of Christ.</note> of Jesus Christ our Lord, by the wondrous mystery of His descent into hell, by the eternal fire of the damned that is never extinguished (which is especially owed to heretics and the enemies of the most holy Roman Church), by the sacrament of the true and mystical body and blood, by the omnipotence of God, and by the reverence deservedly shown to the images of His Son and fellow-heirs: let them read what we are writing now without spite and without envy; but let them not read those prior things—that is, the propositions themselves—without their being narrated and explained. For when we proposed them for debate among the learned, we did not publish them to be read everywhere by everyone. 

For even in those theses there are many impious dogmas of the ancient philosophers, such as <term>Averroes</term> and <term>Alexander</term> <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd) and Alexander of Aphrodisias were influential commentators on Aristotle whose views, particularly regarding the mortality of the individual soul, were often condemned as heretical.</note> and many others. We have—even if we have at once professed, asserted, and preached, publicly and privately, that these are no less alien to true and right philosophy than to the faith—nevertheless undertaken to debate them in a <term>scholastic exercise</term>, according to the custom of the Universities <note>original: "Academiarum" — Referring here to the traditional methods of debate in medieval and Renaissance universities.</note>, in a private assembly among a few learned men. 

Truly, anyone who reads the booklet of propositions to be debated can be advised by its very title: while I distinguish what is said according to our own opinion from what is said according to the opinion of others, those views are not proposed by me as my own, or as true opinions, but as views believed by them. Thus, one might suspect that even if they are called the dogmas and inventions of others, they might still seem to me to be both true and probable. Therefore, let those who hate me not read them because they are ours; and let those who love me not read them because from them they might imagine many things to be my own which are not truly ours.

# Apologia.

<note>This paragraph is the conclusion of a point from the previous page, likely regarding the distinction between "natural" magic and "demonic" magic.</note>
...which either has a pact or communion in any way with demons, whether explicit or implicit, whether as a primary or secondary matter, whether preceding, accompanying, or following, or in any way whatsoever it occurs, is a prohibited thing, superstitious, and deservedly condemned by the Church.

22 That science, which is deservedly called "natural practical philosophy," and which is called <term>Natural Magic</term> <note>original: "Magia naturalis" — For Pico, this was not sorcery, but the study of the hidden powers of nature and how they could be used for good.</note> by William of Paris, by Bacon, and by all Greek authors, contains nothing in itself that is repugnant to the Catholic and orthodox faith. 23 There is no science—extending the name "science" to both revealed and non-revealed knowledge—that makes us certain of the divinity of Christ, other than the Evangelical doctrine and the science of Christian theology.

works of Christ that he was the master and author of true nature, who performed these deeds by his own power, which exceed the limits of all natural power, both celestial and earthly. those opinions, but they were falsely attributed to him by heretics (as <term>Rufinus</term>, Pamphilus, Methodius, Didymus, and Haymon maintain), or if he did believe them, he eventually repented of them at the end (as Jerome maintains), it is reasonable to believe well concerning the salvation of his soul, and we are not bound by the necessity of salvation to believe the opposite. <margin>∴</margin> 29 The act of believing is a free act. 30 The act of believing is not within the power of man in such a way that, when a purely doubtful proposition is presented, the intellect can adhere to one side rather than the other through the mere and sole command of the will. 31 He who believes this proposition—*It is not in the free power of the will to believe an article of faith is true when it pleases him, and to believe it is false when it pleases him*—allowing for the sense explained by the preceding conclusion, does not err in the faith. <margin>†</margin> 32 <term>Accidents</term> <note>The physical properties of a thing (like color or taste) as opposed to its "substance" or essence.</note>, in the Sacrament of the altar, exist in no subject. 33 It is possible, by the absolute power of God, for the existence of bread to remain without its essence, and for the <term>accidents</term> of bread to be subjected in that existence; and this is assuming a real distinction between essence and existence.

...remains in the sacrament of the Eucharist, sustained by Christ as God-man, but through conversion passes into the essence of the body of Christ. 36 If one holds with the common way <note>The "common way" (via communis) refers to the standard scholastic philosophical consensus of the time.</note> that God can assume any nature into his person <term>suppositare</term> <note>original: "suppositare" — a technical term in scholastic theology meaning to sustain a nature within a divine person or hypostasis.</note>, it is possible that Christ assumes the bread-ness <note>original: "paneitatem" — a scholastic term for the essential quality of being bread.</note> into the unity of the divine person. ## of Mirandola, on Being and the One to

### P R E F A C E.

YOU WERE RELATING to me in recent days what <term>Lorenzo de' Medici</term> <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent" (1449–1492), the de facto ruler of Florence and a patron of the Platonic Academy.</note> had discussed with you regarding being and the one, when he was disputing against <term>Aristotle</term>—whose <term>Ethics</term> you are publicly lecturing on this year—while leaning on the arguments of the <term>Platonists</term>. He is a man of such effective and multifaceted genius that he seems formed for all things. In him, I especially admire this: that although he is always most occupied in the <term>Republic</term> <note>Meaning the public affairs and governance of Florence.</note>, he is always either speaking of or meditating upon some literary matter. And since those who believe that Aristotle disagrees with <term>Plato</term> also disagree with me—who makes the philosophy of both concordant—you asked how Aristotle might be defended in this matter and how he might agree with his teacher, Plato. I said what came to my mind at the time, confirming what you had replied to Lorenzo during the dispute rather than bringing forward anything new. But this was not enough for you. For you demand that, although I intend to write more extensively on this in the very "Harmony of Plato and Aristotle" which I am still laboring to produce, I should nevertheless briefly outline for you in a short commentary those things I spoke to you in person about regarding this question, when perhaps <term>Domenico Benivieni</term> <note>A Florentine theologian and close friend of Pico and Savonarola.</note> was also present, a man most dear to both of us for his learning and integrity. Truly, how can I deny you anything, especially in a literary matter, being as you are nearly an inseparable companion? However, permit me, through you, the protector of the more polished tongue, to use certain words perhaps not yet granted the right of Latin citizenship <note>Pico is apologizing for using "Scholastic" Latin terms that might offend Poliziano's refined, humanist sensibilities.</note>. The very novelty of the subject and a certain necessity has wrung them out; do not look for the allure of a more elegant style. For as <term>Manlius</term> <note>Referring to Boethius (Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius). The quote is actually from the poet Manilius: "The matter itself refuses to be adorned, content to be taught."</note> says: *The matter itself refuses to be adorned, content to be taught.* These, therefore, if I remember correctly, were the things about which we were having our conversation.

### Chapter one, in which he relates the arguments of the Platonists, by which they wish to establish that "the One" is superior.

Aristotle says in many places that these things correspond to one another and are of equal scope: namely, the one and being, and likewise the true and the good—but more on these later. The <term>Academy</term> <note>The followers of Plato's school of thought.</note> resists this, for it pleases them that "the one" is prior to "being." When they say "prior," they want it to be understood as both simpler and more universal. For this reason, they say that <term>God</term> (whose simplicity is supreme) is indeed "the one," but is not "being." Likewise, they say that first of all, matter—namely, that crude and formless matter—is concluded within the boundaries of "the one," yet it is outside the limits of "being," as they would have it. Then there is that...

[They] argue that what is opposed to the **One** is not the same as what is opposed to **Being**. ### Chapter two, in which he inquires where Plato spoke about Being and the One, and shows that his words truly support the opinion that says the One and Being are equal, rather than those who wish the One to be superior to Being.

**T**hese are the reasons they rely upon. Before we dismantle them, it would not be out of place to bring into the light what may be found expressed by <term>Plato</term> on this question. I find Plato disputing about <term>Being</term> <note>original: "ente"</note> and <term>the One</term> <note>original: "uno"</note> in two places: namely, in the *Parmenides* and the *Sophist*. In both, the <term>Academics</term> <note>Refers here to the later Platonists/Neoplatonists who followed Plato's tradition.</note> contend that the One is placed by Plato above Being.

But I, concerning the *Parmenides* first, would say this: that in that entire dialogue nothing is actually asserted as a definitive doctrine; and even if it were asserted with the greatest possible force, nothing would be found clearly stated from which we could ascribe a dogma of this sort to Plato. Certainly, the book is not to be counted among the dogmatic ones, since it is entirely nothing other than a certain <term>dialectical exercise</term>. Our opinion is so far from being contradicted by the words of the dialogue themselves that no interpretations exist that are more arbitrary or violent than those brought forward by people who wished to interpret Plato’s *Parmenides* in a different sense.

But let us set aside all the interpreters and look at the sequence of the Dialogue itself: where it begins, where it leads, what it promises, and what it carries out. Furthermore, it goes like this: when the discussion moved from whether "all things are one" or "the things that exist are many," and <term>Socrates</term> had turned the conversation toward the <term>Ideas</term> <note>The abstract, perfect forms that Plato believed were the true reality.</note> and asked many things of <term>Parmenides</term> concerning them, Parmenides replied that he liked that impulse and the inclination of Socrates' mind toward defining the highest things. 

"But," he says, "collect yourself, and while you are young, exercise yourself more diligently in that faculty which seems useless to many—which they call <gloss>trifling</gloss> <note>original: "nugacitas" or "garrulitas"</note> or chatter—otherwise, the truth will escape you." 

It is admitted by everyone, as the following words manifest, that by these words he signifies <term>Dialectic</term> <note>The art of investigating or hunting for the truth through logical discussion.</note>. After this, when Socrates asks Parmenides, "What is the manner of this exercise?" Parmenides replies first that it is the one he had heard from <term>Zeno</term>; then, teaching more particularly about this matter, he warns that one must look around with sharp-sighted skill, not only at what follows if a certain thing *is*, but also what follows if it *is not*. Then one should see what follows concerning that which we suppose to "be" or "not be," both as it regards itself and as it regards other things, and likewise how other things regard themselves and that thing. When he had said many things to this effect, Socrates said: "You propose an arduous task, and I do not entirely understand you. But why do you not yourself propose something and treat it in that way which you approve, so that my understanding of this matter may become clearer?" Parmenides replies that this is laborious for him, an old man. Finally, Zeno says that Parmenides must do this, since he is in a gathering of only a few people; otherwise, he says it is hardly proper for such things to be treated in a large crowd by an old man, since very few would know how to handle such a treatment, and...

He emphasizes that the dialogue's primary purpose is training the mind to see both sides of an argument.</summary>

...that investigation is necessary for attaining the truth, even these words of <term>Zeno</term> <note>Zeno of Elea, a student of Parmenides known for his paradoxes.</note> provide full credit for what we have said. For the subject that <term>Parmenides</term> <note>An influential pre-Socratic philosopher who argued that reality is a single, unchanging "One."</note> is about to treat, if we believe Zeno, is of such a nature that it should not be discussed openly in a public gathering by an old man; yet if those [the <term>Academics</term>] want it to be about the divine orders and the first principle of all things, such a discussion would be more suitable for an old man, and less a cause for shame. But it is beyond all controversy—unless we wish to deceive ourselves—that the matter Parmenides was about to engage in was a <term>dialectical business</term> <note>A logical exercise or debate intended to test definitions, rather than a declaration of absolute truth.</note>, and <term>Socrates</term> had asked for nothing else from him. 

Zeno had judged such a task to be the duty of a youth rather than an old man. If we do not believe even these testimonies, let us run through the dialogue itself, and we will see that nowhere is anything affirmed; rather, everywhere it is only asked: "if this is so, what will follow?" and likewise "what if it is not so?" Here the Academics have seized an opportunity for their opinion regarding <term>Being</term> and <term>the One</term>, because in the first position he exercises himself with this problem: to see "if all things are one," what might follow. He responds that it would happen that the "One" which we assume to exist, if it is indivisible, would be infinite, would be nowhere, and after enumerating many things of that kind, he brings this up among others: namely, that it would follow that this "One" is not Being. 

Pay attention, however: even if this were not a dialectical exercise, but a dogma being handed down about Being and the One, consider how much difference there is between asserting that "the One is above Being" and asserting that "if all things are one, that One is not Being." Enough has been said of Parmenides. 

Truly, in the *Sophist* <note>One of Plato's later dialogues concerning the nature of being and non-being.</note>, he speaks in favor of the opinion that Being and the One are equal, rather than the One being superior to Being. For where he might explain that superiority, I cannot find. The former is signified in many ways, as through these words: *For considering it thus, you confess it is necessary that he who says something, says one thing.* And shortly after: *But he who does not say something, it is necessary that he says not even one thing—that is, he says nothing.* These are his words. Therefore, for him, "not one" and "nothing" are equal—or rather, the same—and likewise "one" and "something" are equal. After this, he likewise proves it cannot be said that "non-being" is "one," and thus concludes: *Being does not happen to non-being; therefore the One does not happen to non-being.* He speaks, moreover, of the One which he had said above was equal to that which is "something." He seems, therefore, to hold as granted that the One is Being. 

But so be it; let us grant that Plato affirmed this [the superiority of the One], which he certainly nowhere affirmed. Come, let us examine in what sense it could truly be said, first laying the foundations of the <term>Aristotelian</term> <note>Referring to the philosophy of Aristotle, who argued that Being and the One are different names for the same thing.</note> opinion itself in this manner:

### Chapter three, in which he declares how "Being" is understood by Aristotle, when he makes it equal to the "One" and encompassing all things.

**T**his word **Being** <note>original: "ens"</note>, about which there is doubt as to whether it is equal to **the One** <note>original: "uni"</note>, can be understood in two ways. The first is that when we say "Being," we understand everything that is "outside of nothing." This is how Aristotle used the term when he made Being equal to the One. Nor did he use the word thus without reason; for as it is truly said, we ought to think like the few, but speak like the many. We think and hold opinions for ourselves, but we speak to others—that is, to the multitude—and therefore we speak so that we may be understood. Now the common people, and whoever is of the ordinary sort, understand "Being" in such a way that it includes everything...

### John Pico of Mirandola

...let that be called <term>being</term> <note>original: "ens"</note> which does not lack the act of <term>being</term> <note>original: "esse"</note>, and about which it cannot truly be said that it is "nothing." But we also find that those who were considered the wisest among the very people who hold the opposite view used this expression in this way. For <term>Parmenides</term> the Pythagorean, when he said that the <term>One</term> is that which is, he understood it to be <term>God</term>. This is true if we believe <term>Simplicius</term> <note>A 6th-century philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.</note> and many others who wish to defend Parmenides against those who misrepresent him—as if he had said that all things are simply one. For they respond with one voice that Parmenides never believed there was no division, multitude, or plurality in things. Indeed, he openly admits this elsewhere in his own poems. But when he said "the <term>One</term> is that which is," he <term>judged</term> that the title of "being" truly fits that which is, and that what truly possesses the act of <term>being</term> is <term>only the One</term>, and that <term>One</term> is God. Therefore, if we believe Parmenides and his defenders (even the Platonists), the <term>One</term> cannot be above <term>being</term> unless it were above God; and Parmenides is so far from denying that God <term>is being</term> that he grants the true title of "being" to God alone. 

And so, the solution to the first argument of the Platonists occurs to us in passing. Even <term>Dionysius the Areopagite</term> <note>A Christian theologian (Pseudo-Dionysius) often cited by Neoplatonists to support the idea of a "One" beyond "Being."</note>, whom those who argue against us claim as a supporter of their opinion, will not deny that it was truly said by God to <term>Moses</term>: "I am who I am," which we read in Greek as <note>original: "ἐγὼ εἰμὶ ὁ ὤν"</note> "I am the one who is," that is, I am <term>being</term>. Furthermore, since they say that "nothing" or <term>non-being</term> is the opposite of "being," just as "multitude" is the opposite of the "one," they must necessarily concede that what is not <term>being</term> <term>is</term> nothing or <term>non-being</term>. Just as that which is not <term>one</term> is many or a multitude. Therefore, if they follow the same rule of speech, they must admit either that God is nothing (which the ears themselves dread to hear) or that He <term>is being</term>. 

In this way, when <term>being</term> is accepted as that <term>first</term> axiom and universal premise we establish about any thing—that it must necessarily be said either to exist or not to exist, and that of no thing can both be said or thought at the same time—then, since there is nothing outside of all things except "nothing" itself, if <term>being</term> understood in this way excludes only "nothing" from itself, it must undoubtedly encompass all things. Therefore, the <term>One</term> cannot encompass more than "being" unless it encompasses "nothing" itself, which Plato denies in the <term>Sophist</term> <note>Plato’s dialogue exploring the nature of "being" and "non-being."</note>. When he says that <term>non-being</term> or "nothing" <term>cannot</term> be called <term>one</term>, it follows that if the "One" does not encompass fewer things (as they themselves wish), then <term>being</term> and the <term>One</term> are equal.

We have explained one of these ways in which we said <term>being</term> could be understood; those who use it, just as they can use it correctly, affirm <term>most truly</term> that nothing is more common than being. It remains for us to explain the other way, according to which it will nonetheless be <term>manifest</term> that it can truly be said that there is something placed above the eminence of being. 

Of names, some are <term>concrete</term>, others are <term>abstract</term>. <term>Concrete</term> names are: hot, shining, white, man. <term>Abstract</term> names are: heat, light, whiteness, humanity. Moreover, their power and difference is this: that what is called <term>abstract</term> denotes that which is such of itself, and not from another. A <term>concrete</term> name, on the contrary, signifies that which is such not of itself, but by the benefit of another. Thus, a "shining thing" shines by light. A <term>white thing</term> is <term>white</term> by whiteness. And a man is a man by humanity. Where...

X 3
<meta>catchword: you accept</meta>

# On Being and the One.

Indeed, nothing participates in itself, nor can the same condition exist in the same thing both by itself and by the participation of another. It follows that what is called "abstract" cannot be named by its concrete form; for this reason, it is not properly said that "whiteness is white" or "blackness is black." <note>Pico is using a grammatical argument common in Scholastic philosophy: a property (the abstract "whiteness") cannot "possess" itself as if it were an object (the concrete "white thing").</note> Indeed, anyone who would make such claims would be ridiculous—not because whiteness is black or heat is cold, but because whiteness is so far removed from blackness, and heat from cold, that whatever things are white are white by *that* whiteness, and whatever things are hot are hot by participation in *this* heat. 

Therefore, we deny that a certain property exists in a thing for two reasons: either because the thing simply does not have it (as when we say "black is not white"), or because the thing possesses that property in a more excellent way and through a more perfect reason than our speech can signify. For instance, when we deny that whiteness is "white," it is not because it is black, but because it is not merely white by *having* whiteness (which is what the word "white" implies); rather, it is whiteness itself. 

Let us come to our own subject: <term>Being</term> <note>original: "ens"</note> has the appearance of a concrete noun. For "a being" and "that which is" mean the same thing. The abstract form of this word appears to be <term>to be</term> <note>original: "esse"; the act of existence itself.</note>, so that "a being" is said of that which participates in "to be." Just as "shining" is said of that which participates in light, and "seeing" is said of that in which the act of "to see" exists. 

If, therefore, we look at this exact meaning of "being," we shall deny that "to be" itself is "a being"—not only because it is not (and is thus "nothing"), but because it *is* to such a degree that it is the very act of <term>to be</term> itself. It exists by itself and from itself, and by participation in it, all things exist. Just as we would deny that heat itself is "hot," not because it lacks heat, but because it is the very essence of heat. Such a one is God, who is the fullness of the totality of <term>to be</term>, who alone exists from Himself, and from whom alone—with no intermediary standing between—all things have proceeded into existence. 

For this reason, we shall truly say that God is not "being," but rather <term>super-being</term> <note>original: "super ens"; being that transcends the category of being.</note> and something higher than "being." This is God himself, and since the name of "the One" is given to Him, it follows that we must admit that "the One" is above "being." We call God "the One" at that point, not so much stating *what* He is, but rather *how* He is all things that He is, and how other things come from Him. For God is called "One," says <term>Dionysius</term> <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-6th century Christian Neoplatonist.</note>, because He is all things uniquely. Again, He is called "One" because He is the principle of all things that exist, just as "unity" is the principle of all numbers. 

Wherefore, if—as the <term>Academics</term> <note>The followers of the Platonic school.</note> wish—Plato affirms in the first part of the *Parmenides* that "the One" is superior to "being," that "One" will be nothing other than God. Even they admit this by common consent, asserting that Plato is there treating the first principle of all things. 

<margin>vi.</margin> But someone might say that, at least in this regard, <term>Aristotle</term> will be at odds with Plato, because Aristotle never treats "being" in such a way that it is subordinate to "the One" or excludes God, as Plato does. Those who say this have not read Aristotle; for he himself does this, and far more clearly than Plato. For in the sixth book of his *First Philosophy* <note>Known today as Aristotle's *Metaphysics*.</note>, he says that "being" is divided into <term>being through itself</term> and <term>being by accident</term>. Since "being through itself" is divided into ten categories, there is no doubt among good interpreters that God is not contained under this "being," since He is neither "being by accident" nor is He contained under any of the ten categories into which "being through itself" is divided. Likewise, the division is common among the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle's school.</note> which says that "being" is divided into substance and accident; and since this is so...

<summary>Pico explains that God can be called "above being" not because He lacks existence, but because He is the pure act of "to be" itself, rather than a thing that merely "has" being. He argues that both Plato and Aristotle agree that God transcends the standard categories of existence.</summary>

Having established that God can be described as both "Being" and "above Being," Pico now addresses the specific divine titles of "the One" and "the Good."</meta>

<meta>catchword: imper-</meta>

we accept "being" so that God is above being, and is not contained under being, just as Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican theologian.</note> teaches in the first book of his commentaries on the *Theological Sentences*. I will also add this: certain Platonists boast wrongly, as if they possess a mystery unknown to Aristotle, when they say that there are two proper names for God—namely, "the One" and "the Good"—and that thus "the Good" and "the One" exist before "Being." For just as we have shown that it does not escape the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>The followers of Aristotle, named for the covered walkways (peripatos) where they studied.</note> how God can be understood as being above "being," we can also show that Aristotle gave these two primary names of "the Good" and "the One" to God. For in the twelfth book of his *First Philosophy* <note>The work we now call Aristotle's *Metaphysics*.</note>, after he disputed concerning the whole of being and separate minds, he finally asks (as if having turned, after all other things, to investigate the properties of God alone) whether, besides the good that exists in the universe of beings (as if in an army), there is some "Separate Good," like a leader of this army. And he determines that this is so: that God is the Good. Consequently, in the same chapter, he proves God's unity as a testimony to this, citing after strong arguments that line from <term>Homer</term> <note>Iliad, II.204.</note>: "Let there be one leader, one king" <note>original: "εἰς κοίρανος ἔστω εἰς βασιλεύς"</note>. Where, then, is Aristotle mistaken? Where is he discordant with Plato? Where is he profane? Where does he think of God less honorably than is fitting?

### Chapter five, in which he declares for what reason the Peripatetics ascribe
### many things to God which the Platonists deny of Him, and he teaches
### by what means we ascend through four stages to the darkness which God inhabits.

**L**et us now resolve the arguments of the Platonists by which they contend—not in the way we agree with, but absolutely—against Aristotle that "the One" is superior to "Being." Although the first argument has been sufficiently resolved by the previous points—in which it was said that God is "the One" but not "Being"—it will nevertheless be worth the effort to digress further to show why certain things are truly affirmed and truly denied of God, not only by different schools such as the Platonists and Peripatetics, but often by the same author. God is all things, and He is all things most eminently and most perfectly. This would not be possible unless He enclosed the perfections of all things within Himself in such a way that He rejects from Himself whatever pertains to imperfection in things. We can define whatever has the character of the "imperfect" in these existing things under two headings. The first is when something in a thing is less than perfect within the <term>genus</term> <note>A category or class of things.</note> of that thing. The second is when a thing is perfect in its own kind, but is therefore not *simply* perfect, because it possesses the perfection of only one kind, and there are many kinds outside of it, honored with their own perfections, which are not included in that thing. An example of the first: sensory knowledge is imperfect not only because it is only knowledge and not desire, but because it is an imperfect form of knowledge. This is both because it requires a brute and bodily organ, and because it only touches the surface of things and does not penetrate to the innermost part, that is, to the <term>substance</term>. Likewise human knowledge, which is called "rational," is an imperfect knowledge because it is wandering, uncertain, shifting, and laborious. Add to this the intellectual knowledge of divine minds, which theologians call <term>angels</term>, and even this [is imperfect]...

He begins an explanation of "negative theology," distinguishing between different types of imperfection in created things to explain how God transcends all categories.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's argument regarding the divine names. Having established that Aristotle identifies God with "the Good" and "the One," Pico now examines why human concepts of "life" and "knowledge" are inadequate descriptors of God unless they are stripped of their limitations and unified into a single, simple essence.</meta>

<page-num>247</page-num>
<header>On Being and the One</header>

# On Being and the One

Knowledge is imperfect. Or at least for this reason: that it seeks outside itself what it does not fully possess within itself—namely, the light of truth which it needs and by which it is perfected. Consider life. The life that is in plants—indeed, which is in every body—is not imperfect only because it is life alone and not knowledge, but because it is not pure life. Rather, it is a certain "vivification" <note>The act of giving or sustaining life.</note> derived from the soul into the body, always flowing, always mixed with death, and finally more deserving to be called death than life. For we begin to die, in case you did not know, at the very moment we begin to live, and death stretches out alongside life; and then for the first time we cease to die, when we are released from "this body of death" <note>A reference to Romans 7:24: "Who will deliver me from this body of death?"</note> through the death of the flesh. 

But neither is the life of angels perfect; for unless the eternally life-giving ray of divine light cherished it, it would all collapse into nothingness. The same reasoning applies to all other things. Therefore, when you represent God as knowing and God as living, pay attention first to this: that the life and knowledge ascribed to Him must be understood as free from all these defects. 

But this is not enough. For there remains another imperfection, of which this is the example: Conceive of a most perfect life, which is entirely life, and pure life, having nothing mortal, nothing mixed with death, which needs nothing outside itself to remain stable and permanent. Conceive likewise of a knowledge by which all things are known both simultaneously and most perfectly. Add this also: that the knower knows all these things in himself, so that he does not seek the truth he knows outside himself, but he himself is that very truth. Yet each of these, although most perfect in its own kind and such that it could not exist outside of God, if taken in this way and distinguished from one another, is unworthy of God. 

For God is an all-encompassing and infinite perfection; but He is not called all-encompassing and infinite merely because He contains all particular and infinite perfections within Himself. For then He would not be <term>most simple</term> <note>In medieval theology, "simplicity" means God is not made of parts; His essence, His existence, His power, and His will are all one and the same.</note>, nor would the things in Him be infinite; rather, He would be a single infinite thing collected from many things that are infinite in number but finite in perfection—a thought that is profane to speak or think regarding God. 

But truly, if life were a most perfect life indeed, but only life and not knowledge; and likewise if desire or will were a most perfect will, but only will and not life nor knowledge; and if other similar things were placed in God, it would clearly follow that the divine life is of finite perfection. This is because it would possess the perfection of life, but it would not possess that of knowledge or desire. 

Let us, therefore, remove from "life" not only what makes it an imperfect life, but also what makes it "life only"; and let us do the same for "knowledge" and the other names by which we call God. Then, what remains from all of these will necessarily be what we want God to be understood as: namely, the One, most perfect, infinite, and most simple. And since life is a certain kind of being, wisdom is likewise a certain kind of being, and justice as well—certainly, if you strip away the condition of particularity and boundaries from these, what remains will not be *this* or *that* being, but Being itself, simply Being, universal Being, not a predication—

<page-num>248</page-num>
<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

...not by its universality, but by its perfection. Similarly, wisdom is a certain kind of good, because it is specifically *this* good—namely, wisdom—and it is not that other good which is justice. Remove, as Augustine <note>St. Augustine (354–430 AD), the influential North African bishop and theologian whose works shaped much of Western Christianity.</note> says, the "this" and remove the "that." That is, remove the particular limitation by which wisdom is a good in such a way that it is only wisdom and not the good of justice; and likewise, that justice has the goodness of justice in such a way that it does not possess the goodness of wisdom. Then, in a riddle <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 13:12: "For now we see through a glass, darkly [in an enigma/riddle], but then face to face."</note>, you will see the face of God: which is every good, the Good itself, simply the Good, the Good of every good. 

In the same way that life is a certain kind of being, so it is a certain kind of "one," for it is a single perfection; likewise, wisdom is a single perfection. Cast aside the particularity, and what remains is not "this" or "that" one, but the One itself and the simply One. Therefore, since God is He who—as we said from the beginning—is everything once the imperfection of all things is removed, then surely when you have set aside from all things both the imperfection found beneath their class and the particularity of their specific kind, that which remains is God. God, therefore, is Being itself, Unity itself, and similarly the Good itself and the Truth itself. 

We have now advanced two stages, ascending toward the darkness <note>original: *caligine*. This refers to "Divine Darkness," a state where God is so bright He becomes invisible to human reason, like a sun that blinds the eyes.</note> which God inhabits, purging from the divine names every stain that comes from the imperfection of the things we name. There yet remain two stages: one of which proves the deficiency of names, while the other accuses the weakness of our own intelligence. 

These names—"being," "truth," "one," "good"—speak of something concrete and, as it were, participated in. Therefore, we say again that God is *above* being, *above* truth, *above* one, and *above* good. This is because His very existence is Truth itself, Unity itself, and Goodness itself. Yet we are still in the light; but God "made darkness his secret place." <note>A reference to Psalm 18:11.</note> Therefore, we have not yet reached God. For as long as we understand and comprehend what we say about God, we are said to remain in the light. We speak and think of things far smaller than God, just as the capacity of our intelligence is smaller than His infinite divinity. Ascending, therefore, to the fourth stage, let us enter the light of ignorance; and, blinded by the darkness of divine splendor, let us cry out with the prophet:

-> I have failed in your courts, O Lord. <note>original: *Defeci in atrijs tuis Domine.* Based on Psalm 84:2 (or 73:26), expressing the soul's exhaustion when trying to reach the heights of God.</note> <-

Saying this one last thing about God: that He is, in a way that is intelligible and inexpressible, above everything most perfect that we can either speak of or conceive. Then, we place Him most eminently even above that very unity, goodness, and truth which we had conceived—even above Being itself. 

Looking toward this, Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A 5th-century Christian Neoplatonist author. Pico viewed him as the ultimate authority on "mystical theology," the study of God through what He is *not* rather than what He *is*.</note>—after all he had written in his *Symbolic Theology*, his *Theological Institutions*, and his works *On the Divine Names* and *On Mystical Theology*—finally, at the end of that same book, as one who was already in the darkness and speaking of God as holily as he could, cried out (after certain other matters pertaining to the same subject): 

"Neither is He truth, nor kingdom, nor wisdom, nor the One, nor unity, nor deity, nor goodness; nor is He spirit, so far as we can know; nor is He the name of 'son' or 'father,' nor is He any other thing from among those which..."

# On Being and the One. 249

[God is none] of those things which are known to us or to any other in the world; he is none of the things which are not, nor any of the things which are. Nor do the things that exist know him as he is, nor does he know existing things as they exist. There is no discourse of him, no name, no knowledge. He is neither darkness nor light, neither error nor truth. There is absolutely no way to affirm or deny anything about him. These are the words, verbatim, of that **divine man** <note>original: "uir ille diuinus." Pico is referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century Christian mystic whose writings heavily influenced medieval theology by emphasizing that God is beyond all human understanding.</note>. Let us gather what we have said, and we shall see that in the **first stage** we learn that God is not a body—as the **Epicureans** <note>Ancient followers of Epicurus who believed the world was made of atoms and that the gods, if they existed, were material beings who did not interfere in human affairs.</note> thought—nor the form of a body, as those believe who assert that God is the soul of the heavens or of the universe. This was the view of the **Egyptians**, as **Plutarch** <note>A Greek philosopher and biographer (c. 46–119 AD).</note> writes, and of **Varro**, the Roman theologian <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a Roman scholar whose works on religion were often cited by St. Augustine.</note>. This belief provided great fuel for idolatry for both, as we shall declare elsewhere. Indeed, some among the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle, named for the covered walkways (peripatoi) where they walked while discussing philosophy.</note> are so dull-witted that they confirm this to be the true opinion of **Aristotle**. See how far these men fall short of a true knowledge of God! They rest in their prison as if in the goal-line <note>original: "in calce." A metaphor for the end of a race, suggesting they think they have finished their journey when they haven't even started.</note>, believing they have reached the heights of God when, still lying on the ground, they have not yet moved a foot toward him. For in that case, God would be neither a perfect life, nor a perfect being, nor even a perfect intellect. We have attacked this profane opinion at length in the **fifth decade** <note>original: "quinta decas." This refers to a section of Pico's larger project on the "Concord of Plato and Aristotle," much of which is now lost.</note> of our *Concord*.

We learn in the **second stage**—which few attain correctly, and in which we are more likely to be deceived if we deviate even slightly from true understanding—that God is neither life, nor intellect, nor an intelligible object <note>term: intelligible object <gloss>something that can be understood by the mind, as opposed to something felt by the senses.</gloss></note>, but something better and more excellent than all these. For all these names speak of a particular perfection, none of which exists in God. Looking to this, both **Dionysius** and the later **Platonists** deny that there is life, intellect, wisdom, or similar things in God. However, because God, through his own unique perfection—which is his infinite divinity, which is himself—unites and collects within himself the total perfection of these things (which in us are many and divided), he is not just one of those many things, but the **One** who exists before those many things. 

Therefore, certain others, especially the **Peripatetics**—whom the **Parisian theologians** <note>The Scholastic scholars at the University of Paris, the premier center for theology in the Middle Ages.</note> imitate in almost everything as far as they are able—concede that all these things are in God. In saying and believing this, we not only speak and believe correctly, but we also agree with those who deny those attributes, provided that we always keep before our eyes the words of **Aurelius Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo.</note>: that the wisdom of God is no more "wisdom" than it is "justice," and the justice of God is no more "justice" than it is "wisdom." Likewise, life is no more "life" in him than it is "knowledge," and knowledge is no more "knowledge" than it is "life." For all these things are in God as one—not through confusion or mixing, or a mutual penetration of distinct things, but through a simple, supreme, ineffable, and **font-like unity** <note>original: "fontalem unitatem." This suggests that God is the "fountain" or source from which all these different qualities flow out.</note>. In this unity, every act, every form, and every perfection is enclosed—like an eminent leader in the innermost treasures of divine infinity. Thus, God is above all and beyond all things in an excellent way; yet he is not only intimate to all things, but more "one" with all things than they are with themselves. Truly, words fail, and are far less than what is even conceived.

<meta>catchword: Chapter</meta>

But see, my dear Angelo <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the brilliant humanist poet and scholar who was Pico's close friend and the dedicatee of this work.</note>, what madness holds us! While we are in the body, we are able to love God more than we can either speak of Him or know Him. By loving Him, we benefit ourselves more, we labor less, and we obey Him more. Yet we always prefer, through searching by means of knowledge, never to find what we seek, rather than to possess it through love. For if He were not loved, He would be found in vain. But let us return to our subject.

It is now clearly evident to you how God is sometimes called Mind, Intellect, Life, and Wisdom, and yet at other times is placed above all these things. Both claims are proven to be both true and consistent. Nor does Plato disagree with Aristotle because he—in the sixth book of the *Republic*—places God, whom he there calls the <term>idea of the good</term> <note>original: "ideam boni." In Plato’s philosophy, the Form of the Good is the ultimate source of reality and knowledge, transcending even Being itself.</note>, above the intellect and the things that can be understood (the intelligibles), granting to the former the power to understand, and to the latter the quality of being understood. 

Aristotle, however, often calls God intellect, the one who understands, and the object of understanding. For even **Dionysius the Areopagite** <note>A 5th-century author whose works were believed in the Renaissance to have been written by a convert of St. Paul; he is the father of "negative theology," which describes God by what He is not.</note>, while saying the same thing as Plato, will not deny—along with Aristotle—that God is not ignorant of Himself and of other things. Therefore, if He understands Himself, He is both an intellect and an object of understanding, for He who knows Himself necessarily knows and is known. Yet, if we take these perfections as specific attributes (as I have said), or if by "intellect" we mean a nature that tends toward an object of understanding as if toward something outside itself, Aristotle would most certainly deny that God is an intellect or an object of understanding, just as the Platonists do.

In the **third stage**, as we drew nearer to the darkness <note>In mystical theology, "divine darkness" refers to the overwhelming light of God that blinds human reason; the closer one gets to God, the less the rational mind can "see."</note>, a greater light shone upon us. We do not impiously imagine God to be something imperfect or "maimed"—as He would be if He were called a body, or the soul of a body, or a living being composed of them. Nor do we imagine Him as some particular kind of thing, however perfect—as if we were making Him wise according to human wisdom by calling Him life, or mind, or reason. Instead, we recognize that He is better even than the names used for universal concepts that encompass everything: namely, the "True" and the "Good." 

In the **fourth stage**, we knew Him to be not only above those things, but above every name that can be formed and every notion that can be conceived by us. Then, for the first time, we "knew" Him in a certain way when we realized we did not know Him at all. From this, it can be gathered that God is not only that "than which nothing greater can be thought" (as **Anselm** <note>St. Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109), famous for the "ontological argument," which defines God as the greatest conceivable being.</note> says), but that He is that which is infinitely greater than everything that *can* be thought. As the Prophet **David** truly said according to the Hebrew text: *Silence is praise to You* <note>original: "Tibi silentium laus." A reference to Psalm 65:1. While the Latin Bible says "A hymn becomes you," Pico follows the Hebrew reading where "silence" is the highest praise for an infinite God.</note>. 

Let us say these things as a solution to the first argument. From here, a great window is opened for a proper understanding of the books of Dionysius titled <term>mystical theology</term> <note>A treatise by Pseudo-Dionysius explaining how the soul unites with God by moving beyond all senses and intellect.</note> and <term>divine names</term> <note>A work by Pseudo-Dionysius exploring how human names for God (like "Good" or "Beautiful") are only metaphors for a reality that exceeds them.</note>. In these, one must take care that we do not make the things he wrote smaller than they are—for they are very great—

# On Being and the One

<meta>catchword: Chapter</meta>

## Chapter six, in which he resolves the second argument of the Platonists concerning the first [principle], namely matter.

The objection they raise regarding <term>primary matter</term> <note>The underlying, formless "stuff" that Aristotle and Plato believed was the foundation of all physical things.</note> is frivolous. For insofar as it is <term>being</term> <note>original: "ens"</note>, to that extent it is <term>one</term> <note>original: "unum"</note>. In fact, if they wish to follow Plato’s words exactly, they must concede that matter possesses less of the nature of the <term>one</term> than it does of <term>being</term>. For Plato does not wish for matter to be absolutely nothing; otherwise, how could it be the "receptacle of forms," how could it be the "nurse," how could it be a "certain nature" and all the other things he confirms it to be in the <term>Timaeus</term>? <note>One of Plato's most famous dialogues, describing the creation of the universe.</note> It is not, therefore, nothing—that is, it is not entirely devoid of <term>being</term>, if we believe Plato. Yet, he calls this same matter in the <term>Philebus</term> <note>Another Platonic dialogue focused on pleasure and the nature of the "Good."</note> not only "multitude" (which, as they claim, is opposed to the one just as nothing is opposed to being), but "the infinite." Now, if a multitude is finite, it does not entirely escape the logic of the <term>one</term>, because insofar as it is finite, it is <term>one</term> [unit]. But an infinite multitude no more possesses the nature of the <term>one</term> than it possesses boundaries or limits. Therefore, according to Plato, primary matter is more accurately called <term>being</term> than it is called <term>one</term>. They argue the opposite in order to prove that the <term>one</term> is superior to being, claiming it is not <term>being</term> and yet it is <term>one</term>. 

**Iamblichus** <note>A Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who had a massive influence on later Platonic thought.</note>, likewise a Platonist, in the book he wrote on the Pythagorean sect, calls primary matter "duality," because the first duality is a multitude and the root of all other multitudes. Therefore, according to him—who is so great among the Platonists that he is called "divine"—primary matter is not only not <term>one</term>, but it is multitude itself; it is the very root of all the multitude found in things. I have said these things by throwing their own arguments back at them. For the rest, matter is not entirely devoid of unity, just as it is not devoid of existence. I shall pass over the arguments regarding whether its unity is affirmative or negative, or how it receives its exact unity from the same source as its being—namely, from <term>form</term>. All these things are well known to anyone who has taken even a short stroll with <term>Aristotle</term>. <note>A playful way of saying anyone with even a basic education in Aristotelian philosophy.</note>

## Chapter seven, in which he resolves the third argument of the Platonists concerning multitude, and shows that for those who say the One is more common than Being, they must concede something that Plato denies.

They are greatly mistaken in their third argument. For multitude is not opposed to the one in the same way that non-being is opposed to being. The latter have a "contradictory" opposition <note>Where one must be true and the other false, like "alive" and "not alive."</note>, while the former have either a "privative" or "contrary" opposition—a matter discussed at length by the followers of Aristotle in the tenth book of the <term>First Philosophy</term>. <note>The *Metaphysics*, which Aristotle referred to as "First Philosophy."</note> 

But let those called Platonists see what ruins they fall into when they say the <term>one</term> is superior to being. It is certain that whenever two categories are related such that one is more "common" (broader) than the other, it is possible for something to escape the scope of the lower category while remaining within the scope of the higher. This is exactly why one is called "more common." A ready example: because "animal" is more common than "man," it is possible for something to be "not a man" while still being an "animal." By the same logic, if the <term>one</term> were more common than <term>being</term>, it would be possible for something to be "non-being" or "nothing" and yet still be <term>one</term>. Thus, the <term>one</term> would be predicated of "non-being"—a claim that Plato expressly refutes in the <term>Sophist</term>. <note>A dialogue where Plato explores the nature of "Being" and "Not-being." Pico is using Plato's own logic to argue that Being and the One must be the same size.</note>

<summary>Pico argues against the Neoplatonic view that "the One" is a broader category than "Being" by analyzing the nature of primary matter and the logical relationship between categories. He concludes that for Plato and Aristotle alike, everything that exists is "one" and everything that is "one" exists.</summary>
<keywords>Primary Matter, The One, Being, Plato, Aristotle, Timaeus, Philebus, Iamblichus, Sophist, Metaphysics, Duality, Multitude</keywords>

->Giovanni Pico della Mirandola<-

# Chapter eight, in which he explains how these four—namely Being, the One, the True, and the Good—exist in all things that come after God.

The most true opinion is that there are four concepts that encompass all things: <term>Being</term>, the <term>One</term>, the <term>True</term>, and the <term>Good</term>. <note>In medieval philosophy, these are known as "transcendentals"—properties that belong to everything that exists, regardless of what category of thing it is.</note> These are held as such if we accept that their opposites are "nothing," "divided," "false," and "evil." Two others were added to these four by later followers of <term>Avicenna</term>: <note>An influential Persian philosopher (980–1037 AD) whose interpretations of Aristotle shaped much of later European thought.</note> namely, "Something" and "Thing." Avicenna frequently interrupted the philosophy of Aristotle in many places, which led to great wars being fought between him and <term>Averroes</term>; <note>An Andalusian philosopher (1126–1198 AD) known as "The Commentator" for his strict adherence to Aristotle; he often criticized Avicenna for deviating from Aristotle's original meaning.</note> however, as far as this matter is concerned, the disagreement is over a small thing. For these later thinkers divide what is understood under the "One" into "the One" and "Something"—a view not far removed from Plato, who in the *Sophist* <note>One of Plato’s complex dialogues exploring the nature of being and non-being.</note> enumerates "Something" among these most universal terms. They also divide what is contained under "Being" into "Being" and "Thing," but we shall discuss these elsewhere. To proceed with what we have begun, these four exist differently in God than they do in those things that come after God, since God possesses them of Himself, while other things have them from Him.

Let us first see how they reside in created things. Everything after God has an <term>efficient cause</term>, an <term>exemplar cause</term>, and a <term>final cause</term>; for all things are *from Him, through Him, and toward Him.* <note>A reference to Romans 11:36, here used to align Christian theology with Aristotelian causality: God as the Maker (Efficient), the Model (Exemplar), and the Goal (Final).</note> Therefore, if we consider things as they are established by God as the **efficient cause**, they are called **beings** <note>original: "entia"</note>, because by that efficient cause they participate in existence. If we consider them in relation to their **exemplar**—which we call the "Idea" according to which God fashioned them—if they match and correspond to it, they are called **true**. For an image of Hercules is called a "true" image if it conforms to the real Hercules. If we consider them as they tend toward Him as their **ultimate end**, they are called **good**. But if each thing is taken absolutely according to itself, it is named **one**.

There is, however, an order here: first, each thing is conceived under the rationale of "being," since an agent makes a thing exist before that thing is "something" in itself; otherwise, the thing would not originate from the agent according to the whole of what it is. Thus it follows that there is nothing after God which we can conceive without understanding that it is a **being from another**, a **finite being**, and a **participated being**. The "One" succeeds "Being." Third is "Truth," because after a thing exists in itself, it must be seen whether it is such as the exemplar to which it was formed; if it is found to be similar, it remains for it to turn itself through "Goodness" toward that exemplar as toward something related and kindred.

Who cannot see that these four are equal in their scope? Grant that something exists, and certainly it is also **one**. For he who does not say "one" says nothing (as Plato says in the *Sophist*). Whatever it is, it is undivided in itself and divided from other things which are not itself. When we say this, we understand the "One"; or to use Plato's words, it is *the same as itself and different from others,* which he confirms in that same dialogue belongs to every single thing. It is also necessarily **true**. For if it is a man, it is certainly a "true" man. It is the same as saying "this is not true gold" and "this is not gold"; for when you say it is not true gold, you mean it appears to be gold and is something similar to gold, but it is not gold. For this reason, <term>Aurelius Augustine</term> <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational Christian theologian.</note> defining in his *Soliloquies* what is "true" or "truth," says: *it is that which is.* This should not be taken to mean that "Being" and "True" are the exact same concept; rather, although they are the same in reality, they differ in reason... 

<meta>Catchword: [in] reason</meta>

<summary>Pico explains that Being, the One, the True, and the Good are universal properties of all things, derived from God's roles as Creator, Model, and Final Goal. He argues that these terms are co-extensive, meaning anything that truly exists must also be one, true, and good.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument from page 252 regarding how the four "transcendental" properties—Being, Unity, Truth, and Goodness—relate to one another and to God. Pico is specifically defending the idea that these concepts are interchangeable in reality, even if our minds define them differently.</meta>

<page-num>253</page-num>
->On Being and the One.<-

...name and definition are different; for this reason, one ought not to be defined by the other. However, **Augustine** <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), one of the most influential Latin Church Fathers.</note> wanted to express this: that a thing is called "true" when it is that which it is called and said to be. For example, gold is then "true gold" when it is gold, and it is nothing other than gold. This is therefore what he meant when he said, *Truth is that which is* <note>original: "verum est id quod est"</note>, a definition which some people, through lack of attention, have wrongly criticized.

In the same way, a thing is also "good," because whatever exists, insofar as it exists, is good. In my opinion, **Olympiodorus** <note>An Alexandrian Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 495–570 AD) known for his commentaries on Plato and Aristotle.</note> wanders far astray, believing he can prove that the "Good" and "Being" are different things because we desire the Good absolutely. He argues that we do not desire "to be" absolutely, but rather "to be well"; therefore, it is possible that if we are in a bad state, we might desire not to exist. 

To set aside for a moment the question of whether those who are in a bad and miserable state can truly or naturally desire not to exist, Olympiodorus fails to notice that just as "being" is manifold, so too is goodness. For first, there is the **natural being** of things—such as for a man to be a man, a lion to be a lion, or a stone to be a stone—and a natural goodness follows this being indivisibly. There are other forms of "being" that can be called <term>adventitious</term> <note>From the Latin "advenire" (to come to); in philosophy, this refers to qualities that are added to a thing rather than being part of its essential nature.</note>, such as for a man to be wise, to be beautiful, or to be healthy. Just as wisdom and beauty are "beings" distinct from "humanity," so too are they distinct "goods." For the goodness by which a man is a man is one thing, and the goodness of wisdom—by which he is no longer just a man, but turns out to be a *wise* man—is another, just as the one and the other are different kinds of "being" and are spoken of as such.

Therefore, just as all things seek the Good, so all things seek Being. First, they seek that goodness which follows their natural being, because this is the foundation for all subsequent goodnesses that may come to them; without that first being, the others cannot stand. For how can one be "happy" if one does not exist at all? To be sure, that first goodness they receive when they first exist is not enough for them; they also desire to reach those remaining goods that might complete and adorn that first one. 

And just as we truly say that they seek other "goodnesses" beyond the first, so we can truly say they desire other "beings" beyond the first—because **to be happy** is one kind of being, and **to be a man** is another. Even if one were to grant that a person might not want "to be" unless they were "to be happy," it would not follow (as Olympiodorus thinks) that the Good and Being are different things. Rather, it follows that the "being of a man" is one thing, and the "being of happiness" is another; likewise, the goodness of being a man is one thing, and the goodness of happiness is another. A man does not want the first (being a man) unless he also has the second (happiness). 

I will leave aside for now whether something is called "good" absolutely and "being" absolutely for the same reason—or whether that which is called "being" is simply such a "good," and what is called "good" is simply such a "being." This is not the place to dispute everything. We were saying truly, therefore, that everything which exists is good to the extent that it exists. For **God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good.** <note>A reference to Genesis 1:31.</note> And why not? They are from a good craftsman, who imprints his own likeness upon everything that comes from him. 

In the **entity** of things, therefore, we can admire the power of God as the Producer; in their **truth**, we can venerate the wisdom of the Creator as the Architect; in their **goodness**, we can proclaim the generosity of the Lover; and in their **unity**, we can embrace the unique simplicity, so to speak, of the Founder. This unity joins each thing to itself, all things to one another, and finally all things back to Him.

...[God] has united all things to Himself, calling each thing to the love of itself, to the love of others, and finally to the love of God. Let us also examine whether the opposites of these properties are equally similar in their scope; what we have said above shows that "the false" and "nothing" are the same thing. If we were to say that **Evil** and **Nothing** differ, philosophers and theologians alike would protest. For this reason, to "do evil" is to "do nothing," and it is commonly said that evil does not have an **efficient cause**, but rather a **deficient** one. <note>An "efficient cause" is the agent that brings something into being. Pico follows St. Augustine’s view that evil is not a "thing" created by an agent, but a lack or "deficiency" of goodness and being.</note> This refutes the insanity of those who proposed two [foundational] principles—one of good and one of evil—as if there were some active principle of evil. 

Furthermore, to divide a thing is the same as to destroy it; we cannot take away the natural unity of a thing without the thing itself ceasing to exist in its integrity. For a "whole" is not merely its parts, but that **oneness** which springs forth from the parts, as **Aristotle** teaches in the eighth book of his *First Philosophy*. <note>Aristotle’s "First Philosophy" is the work now known as the *Metaphysics*. In Book 8 (Eta), he argues that a definition or a house is more than just a list of ingredients or bricks; it is the "form" or "unity" that organizes them.</note> Therefore, if you divide a whole into parts, the parts indeed remain, but the "whole" that was divided does not remain; it ceases to exist in **act**, and remains only in **potential**, just as the parts (which were previously only potential) then begin to exist in **act**. <note>To exist in "act" means to be fully realized and functioning; to exist in "potential" means to have the possibility of existing but not being currently realized.</note> For when they were in the whole, the parts did not have their own distinct unity in act; they only obtain this when they are separated from the whole and subsist by themselves.

### Chapter nine in which he declares how those four are in God.

**E**xamine once again how these four properties exist in God. They do not exist in Him in relation to a cause, for He has no cause; He is the cause of all things and is caused by none. These properties can be considered in God in two ways: either insofar as He is the cause of others (a distinction that does not apply to created things in the present context, since God can exist without being a cause, whereas other things cannot exist without Him), or they are conceived in Him primarily. Thus, we first conceive of God as the **totality of every act**, the fullness of Being itself. **Unity** follows this understanding so closely that no opposite can even be imagined. 

See how far those wander who imagine multiple first principles or multiple gods! Immediately, He is also "the truest"; for what could appear "to be" and yet not be He who is **Being itself**? It certainly follows that He is **Truth itself**. But He will also be **Goodness itself**. For as **Plato** writes in the *Philebus*, there are three conditions of the Good: that it be **perfect**, **sufficient**, and **desirable**. <note>In Plato's dialogue *Philebus* (20d), Socrates argues that the Good must be complete and sought by all who recognize it.</note> That which we conceive of in this way will be **perfect**, because nothing will be lacking to Him who is all things; it will be **sufficient**, because to those who possess Him, nothing will be lacking, for in Him they will find all things; and it will be **desirable**, because from Him and in Him are all things that can be desired for any reason. 

God, therefore, is the fullest **entity**, indivisible **unity**, most solid **truth**, and most blessed **goodness**. This, if I am not mistaken, is that **Tetraktys** <note>original: "τετρακτύς". The Tetraktys (the number four) was a sacred symbol for the Pythagoreans, representing the organization of the universe.</note>—that is, the "Quaternary"—by which **Pythagoras** used to swear, calling it the "principle of ever-flowing nature." For we have demonstrated that these four, which are one, are God, the "being" of all things. Furthermore, we swear by things that are holy, firm, and divine; and what is firmer, holier, or more divine than these? However, if we assign these four titles to God insofar as He is the **cause** of things, the entire order is inverted. For first, He will be "One," because...
