...understands Himself, rather than being understood as a cause. Second, He will be **Good**. Third, **True**. Fourth, **Being**. For the cause called the "final cause" <note>The "final cause" is the purpose or goal for which something is done.</note> is prior to the "exemplary cause," and the exemplary is prior to the "efficient cause." <note>The "exemplary cause" is the internal blueprint or idea of a thing; the "efficient cause" is the actual agent or force that builds it.</note> For first, we desire to have something by which we may be protected from the harm of storms; then, we conceive the **idea** of a house in our mind; finally, we form it in matter by building it from the outside. Therefore, if—as we defined in the previous chapter—the **Good** relates to the final cause, the **True** to the exemplary, and **Being** to the efficient, then God, as He is the cause, will first possess the character of the Good, then the True, and finally of Being. We touch upon all these matters here briefly, though they are otherwise teeming with many great questions.

### Chapter ten, in which he turns the entire discussion toward the conduct of life and the improvement of morals.

**B**ut we must take care lest we dispute for the sake of others rather than ourselves, and lest, while searching out the highest things, we live in a lowly—that is, unworthy—condition, we to whom it has been granted by heaven that we may investigate the very reasons of heavenly things. Instead, we must constantly meditate on this: that our mind, to which even divine things are accessible, cannot be from mortal seed, nor will it be happy anywhere except in the possession of divine things. The more it raises and inflames itself toward the divine, having set aside the care for earthly things, the more it approaches happiness while it travels here as a guest and a pilgrim. 

This present discussion seems to warn us above all that if we wish to be happy, we must imitate God, the happiest of all, by possessing **unity**, **truth**, and **goodness** within ourselves. Ambition disturbs the peace of **unity**; it seizes the soul that should cling to itself and drags it outward, tearing and ripping it into diverse pieces. Who would not lose the splendor and light of **truth** in the mud and darkness of pleasures? Greed—that most thieving of desires—steals **goodness** from us. For it is the peculiar trait of goodness to communicate to others the goods that you possess. For this reason, when **Plato** asked why God created the world, he answered himself: "He was good." <note>A reference to Plato's *Timaeus*, where he argues the Creator made the world because He was good and lacked any grudging spirit.</note> 

These are those three: the **pride of life**, the **lust of the flesh**, and the **lust of the eyes**, which, as **John** writes, are of the world and are not of the Father, who is unity itself, truth itself, and goodness itself. <note>original: "superbia uitæ, concupiscentia carnis, & concupiscentia oculorum." Pico cites the First Epistle of John 2:16, mapping these three biblical vices onto the loss of Unity, Truth, and Goodness.</note> Let us flee from here, therefore—that is, from the world which is steeped in malice—and let us fly to the Father, where there is unifying peace, the truest light, and the best pleasure. 

But who will give us wings so that we may fly there? The love of things that are above. Who will take them away? The lust for things upon the earth. If we pursue this lust, we suffer the loss of unity, truth, and goodness. For we are not **one** if we do not bind together our base senses and our reason (which looks toward heavenly things) by a covenant of virtue. Instead, there are two princes within us, reigning as if by turns: while now we follow God through the "law of the mind," and now we follow **Baal** <note>Baal here represents false idols or base physical desires, contrasting with the "law of the mind" described by St. Paul in Romans 7.</note> through the "law of the flesh," our kingdom, divided against itself, is surely laid waste. If we are "one" in such a way that reason is enslaved to the senses and only the "law of the members" rules, this unity will be false; for we will not be true, since we will be called and appear to be men—that is, animals living by reason—and yet...

## ANTONIO OF FAENZA <note>Antonio Faventino (or Antonio da Faenza) was a contemporary philosopher who challenged Pico’s reconciliation of Plato and Aristotle.</note> AGAINST THE TREATISE
### On Being and the One. First Objections.

**I**f any treatise deserves to be titled *On Being and the One*, it is necessary that it explain the nature and properties of being and the one. However, in this little work which recently came into my hands, and which is titled *On Being and the One*, several matters are treated that are almost foreign to the title and inscription. For the author’s primary purpose is to dispute whether, according to Plato, "being" <term>ens (that which is)</term> and "the one" <term>unum (unity)</term> follow each other mutually, or whether—as the Academics <note>Followers of Plato's Academy, specifically the later Neoplatonists who believed the "One" was superior to "Being."</note> think—the One is more universal than Being. But this is not to treat "On Being and the One" generally, but rather the mutual convertibility <note>A logical term meaning two words refer to the same reality and can be swapped, like "human" and "rational animal."</note> of being and the one; and even then, not absolutely, but only according to Plato. For if some philosopher were to discuss only the question of whether the soul is immortal, he would not be disputing "On the Soul" in its entirety, but rather a treatise would be held "On the Immortality of the Soul" alone. 

Furthermore, the author of the work says that the Academics judge that God, according to Plato, is not truly and properly "being," which I wonder at greatly. For if he means all Academics or Platonists, as his phrasing seems to signify (otherwise he would not pronounce absolutely that the Academics feel this), it perhaps lacks truth. For Themistius <note>A 4th-century philosopher and statesman known for his paraphrases of Aristotle.</note>, a not ignoble author among the Platonists, testifies that according to Plato’s opinion, the "Idea"—which is the principle of things—is truly and properly "being" and "one." The Platonists, either all or most, do not think the Idea is one thing and the Craftsman God another. 

Continuing, he says: "If it can be defended in any way that according to Plato the 'one' is more universal than 'being,' it must be judged thus: the words which he calls 'concrete' <note>Pico uses "concrete" in a scholastic sense to mean a noun that implies a quality, like "white thing" versus the abstract "whiteness."</note>—by a name not very Latin—such as 'white,' 'shining,' and 'being,' signify something foreign to their essence, by which those who possess the quality obtain the name. For whiteness is one thing, and a white thing is another; humanity is one thing, and a man is another; therefore, that will be called 'being' (*ens*) in which the 'act of being' (*esse*) is one thing, and that which 'subsists' is another." 

God, therefore, who is "Being" (*esse*) itself, could not be considered "a being" (*ens*), but rather "The One," because from that position he contains and encloses all things. But does not this kind of defense hold together poorly? For by the same reasoning that "white," and "man," and "being" signify something foreign to their pure essence, wouldn't the words "one," and "blessed," and "God," and many similar things also signify something foreign?

<summary>Pico concludes his ethical argument that human life is only "real" when aligned with Truth and Goodness. The page then introduces Antonio Faventino’s critique, which argues that Pico's title is misleading and his interpretation of Plato and the "Academics" is flawed.</summary>
<keywords>Pico della Mirandola, Antonio Faventino, Neoplatonism, Being vs. One, Scholasticism, logic, Themistius, God as Esse, convertibility</keywords>

# On Being and the One.

...is necessary. Therefore God, who is unity, and blessedness simultaneously, and deity, will neither be able to be called "one," nor "blessed," nor "God" at all. How, then, is He not "being" <term>ens (that which exists)</term> but only "the one"? Furthermore, a thing is called "being" because it *is*; just as it is impossible for someone who sits not to be "sitting," it is impossible for Him who truly and properly *is* not to be "being." For God Himself said: "I am who I am." <note>A reference to Exodus 3:14, the traditional scriptural proof that God's essence is Being itself.</note>

It seems even more admirable <note>In this context, "admirable" carries the sense of "surprising" or "astonishing."</note> that the author not only tries to defend the idea that God is not "being" according to Plato, but even tries to drag Aristotle himself into that same opinion. For he says that in the fifth book of the *Metaphysics*, Aristotle divides "being" into <term>ens per se (being in itself)</term> and <term>ens per accidens (being by accident)</term>. He then divides "being in itself" into the ten <term>predicaments (the Categories)</term>. In no genus, however, can God be placed—as the author believes the Blessed Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas.</note> has demonstrated. 

Therefore, if God is not "being" in Himself, nor "being" by accident (as is evident according to Aristotle), he concludes God will not be "being" at all. Furthermore, "being" is separated into <term>substance</term> and <term>accident</term> according to the most common division. God is not an accident, nor is He a substance, for the author says "substance" is a genus. God, however, exceeds the limits of any genus. 

But for my part, I do not see by what reason the author of this work is led to ascribe this Platonic opinion to our Aristotle—if indeed it even is the opinion of Plato. For the division of "being" into "being in itself" and "being by accident" is a division of *complex* being <note>In medieval logic, "complex" refers to propositions or sentences rather than simple terms.</note>, as the Blessed Thomas—to whom the author grants much authority—subtly writes in that passage. This is manifest from examples: for "being by accident," according to Aristotle, is threefold. Either an accident is predicated of a subject, or a subject of an accident, or an accident of an accident—all of which pertain to the *complexion* <note>The joining of terms in a statement.</note> of a sentence. 

In the same way, things are called "beings in themselves" in which something is predicated that pertains either to substance, or to quantity, or to another genus, provided that what is predicated belongs to the subject through itself—such as "white" belongs to Socrates <note>Socrates is a standard example in logic texts.</note>, though not to "man," "animal," or "horse" generally. 

Furthermore, the division of "being" into substance and accident also embraces God. For this division is made through affirmation and negation: for "substance" is that which relies on nothing else but is through itself, while "accident" is that which is in another (namely, in a substance). There is no middle ground between these two, as the Blessed Thomas thinks, since no middle can be imagined between "having" a substance and "not having" it. Therefore, "substance," when it is opposed to "accident" in this way, will not be a genus, even if God is contained in no genus. 

Moreover, it is not the undisputed opinion of Aristotle that God is contained in no genus through Himself. For there are some followers of Aristotle who think that God *is* placed in a category through Himself. I even think that the distinguished philosopher Boethius held that view, and I could show, if necessary, that this is clearly gathered from the words of Boethius as well as Augustine. 

Again, the author says that the negation of "the one" is "the divided." This he proves by the fact that a thing is destroyed when it is torn apart and divided. But how can "the divided" be opposed to "the one" as a negation? For there is a contradiction between affirmation and negation: yet a <term>Chimera</term> <note>A mythological monster, used here as a logical placeholder for something that does not exist.</note> is neither "one" nor "divided." Nor is the idea that "the diameter of a circle is commensurable" <note>An example of a logical impossibility or a false mathematical statement.</note> either "one" or "di[vided]..."

<summary>Antonio of Faenza critiques Pico della Mirandola's claim that Aristotle and Plato agree that God is above "Being." Antonio argues that Pico misinterprets Aristotle's categories and logical divisions, asserting that God must be considered "Being" to avoid logical contradictions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the critique by Antonio of Faenza against Pico della Mirandola’s "On Being and the One," concluding a point about the nature of falsehood and evil before transitioning to Pico's polite and scholarly response.</meta>

<page-num>258</page-num>
<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

seen. He also considers falsehood to be the negation of truth, which, though it might be defended in some way, is nevertheless a contrary rather than a negation, as the Blessed Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican friar and philosopher.</note> shows. For a chimera <note>A mythical creature; in medieval logic, it was often used as an example of a "non-being" or something that cannot exist.</note> is neither true nor false, unless we utterly misuse the word. For the "true" is that which *is*—that is, as he explains, that which is what it appears and is said to be; therefore the "false" will be that which *is not* what it appears and is said to be, such as a false coin. Therefore, nothing happens to be false except what appears to be something other than what it is. 

Between that which appears to be what it is, and that which is not what it appears to be, there is no contradiction; therefore truth and falsehood do not oppose each other by any opposition of affirmation and negation. He also thinks evil is the negation of good; but Aristotle <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BC).</note> affirms in the *Categories* <term>predicamentis (Aristotle's work on the classification of things)</term> that good and evil are genera <term>genera (classes or categories)</term> of contraries, whereas a negation cannot be a genus. Furthermore, good, by the very reason that it is good, is to be sought, while evil is to be avoided. Seeking and avoiding are themselves contraries, just as gathering and separating are; therefore good and evil will be contraries—as Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 477–524 AD), a Roman senator and philosopher who translated Aristotle.</note> also asserts in his commentary on the *Categories*, no matter what others may have said about it.

## GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA TO ANTONIO OF FAEN-
## za, Greetings. Response to the first objections.

**I** read your questions against that little book I recently published, *On Being and the One*, with as much pleasure as the charity and freedom of spirit with which they were written by you. I owe you much for this service. If we either offered this to friends more freely or demanded it from them more willingly, we would certainly be far more learned and better than we are. 

But this deadly persuasion has seized the minds of men: that we think we do not please those whom our errors do not please, and we interpret the free judgment of friends as either hatred or moodiness, while we interpret flattery as love and natural kindness. So it happens that while we prefer to be praised even when undeserving, rather than be corrected when we deserve it, we are always laughed at and never deserve praise. 

See how far we err. For almost all praise is always useless, and often harmful. Since if it is true, what utility does it bring? If it is false, it surely makes those of us who are praised insane, and those who praise us ridiculous. Reproof is certainly always useful; if it is just, it leads to knowledge; if less just, it rouses us to the defense of the truth. Finally, what else is being corrected than becoming better through another's labor? Or what else is a book made to shine by a friend’s file <note>The "file" (original: *lima*) is a classic metaphor for the process of editing and refining a literary work.</note> than you profiting from his vigils while you sleep? 

I cannot, therefore, as I was saying, help but owe you much—you, who have freely indicated to me what you thought about those things in my book that pleased you less. I recognized in your writings, besides benevolence, that dexterity of wit already known to me for a long time; and I immediately began, not as a father <note>Meaning he did not look at his book with parental bias toward his "child."</note> but as a judge, to examine more severely whatever you had noted, as these things had already come under suspicion of falsehood for me because of your testimony. But while thinking in this way...

Several points occurred to me by which those claims might be defended and vindicated from fault; these I have wanted to write to you freely, so that I might not embrace that very virtue of liberty less than I praise it in you. Thus, if I do not imitate your judgment in censuring those points, I might at least imitate your freedom in defending them. You say, "The book is not correctly titled *On Being and the One* <note>original: "De ente & uno"</note> since you do not treat the nature of being and the one, nor all their properties, but only the conversion <term>conversion (the metaphysical principle that "Being" and "One" are interchangeable and refer to the same reality)</term> of the two." To me, Antonio, it usually seems that two "vestibules," as it were, are set before books: the Title and the Preface. The Title is a shortened Preface; the Preface is an expanded and explained Title. The title promises a treatise on being and the one. The preface explains what is to be treated concerning being and the one. If this were done in the title itself, it is to be feared that the title of the book would become a book itself. This could be defended by the precedent of a thousand authors whose titles would be subject to the same verbal hair-splitting. But this is not a question of such weight that either I or you should occupy ourselves with it any longer. 

Furthermore, you marvel that I said the Platonists <note>Followers of the philosophy of Plato (c. 427–347 BC), particularly the later Neoplatonists who emphasized a mystical hierarchy of reality.</note> believed that God is not properly "being." Do not marvel at me, but at those whom I—like you—do not approve of in the assertion of this dogma. Yet, that they felt this way (which seems almost incredible to you) and left it in writing for posterity is very well known to all who have read the Platonic works. Syrianus, Proclus, Plotinus, <note>Major Neoplatonist philosophers: Syrianus (5th c. AD), Proclus (412–485 AD), and Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD), the latter being the founder of the school.</note> and finally all the extant interpreters of Plato confirm this with one voice. 

But, you say, Themistius <note>A 4th-century AD philosopher and rhetorician known for his paraphrases of Aristotle.</note>—no ignoble figure among the Platonists—asserts that according to Plato’s opinion, the Idea is truly and properly "being" and "one." Moreover, all or most Platonists think the Idea is nothing other than God, the craftsman of things. Therefore, if the Idea is properly called being, God himself will also properly be called being. You argue this quite ingeniously, but consider whether you do so with enough expertise. For those men—namely Proclus and Plotinus—confess that the Idea is and is called "being," but they contend that just as God is above beings, so He is above Ideas. For Plotinus placed all the Ideas in that Mind which is closest to God—which he calls the "first being," "the first intelligible," and "the first life"—so that God is not the "bosom" of the Ideas but their source, not their receptacle but their principle. 

Proclus makes not just one, but many intermediate orders of minds between God and the Ideas; emulating the fullness of these Ideas, he called the "animal-in-itself" <note>A Platonic term from the *Timaeus* referring to the eternal model of all living things.</note> in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s famous dialogue on the creation of the universe.</note> by that name. I pass over Syrianus, Amelius, Iamblichus, and many others who feel the same. These are the rudiments and, as it were, the cradle-teachings <term>incunabula (the earliest stages or origins of a doctrine)</term> of that doctrine which is considered Platonic. Even if someone were to grant you that the Idea and God are the same in reality, you would not deny that they are different in "reason" <note>A Scholastic distinction: things may be the same object (*in re*) but perceived as different concepts (*in ratione*).</note>. This distinction is more than enough to show that God, insofar as He is the exemplar <note>The perfect pattern or "blueprint" of a thing in the mind of God.</note> of a man, a horse, or a lion, can truly be called "being"; but insofar as He looks to nothing outside Himself and has no relation to created things, but remains solitary in the secret recess of His own divinity, He exceeds every designation of "being." As Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist whose works, like *The Divine Names*, argued that God is beyond all human language and categories.</note> says, there is neither a name nor an opinion of Him. Therefore, it is most manifest even among the leaders of the Academy <note>The school founded by Plato.</note> that God cannot properly be called "being." And if someone grants that the Idea and God are the same in reality, it does not immediately follow that if the Idea is being, God must also be called properly being. 

Let us pass to other things, among which this displeases you most: that I said...

...that there is a certain way of speaking which, if we follow it, we will be able to say truly that the <term>One</term> <note>original: "unum"; in Neoplatonic thought, the ultimate, simple source of all reality, often placed above existence itself.</note> is higher than being. In this way, we can grant the name of "One" to God, even if we do not grant Him the name of "being." This is because <term>Being</term> <note>original: "ens"</note> has the character of a "concrete name" (as we may speak in Latin), and it signifies that which participates in existence from another. This cannot be said of God, who is Being itself. By the same reasoning, you might say, He could not be called "One" either, because <term>the One</term> is also surely a concrete name, just as <term>Being</term> is. 

I both saw this question when I was writing and I resolved it. For as soon as I proved that <term>Being</term> cannot be predicated of God—because it signifies that which is not from itself but exists by participating in another—I added to which God, of course, the name of "the One" is given. It follows from this that we must admit the One is above Being. Immediately after this, meeting your objection, I added: we call God "One" at that point not so much to declare *what* He is, but rather *how* He is all things that He is, and in what way all things are from Him. For <term>Dionysius</term> <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist whose writings were highly influential in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> says that God is called "One" because He is all things uniquely; and again, He is called "One" because He is the principle of all things that exist, just as <term>Unity</term> is the principle of all numbers. 

These were my words there, verbatim. If, therefore, when we call God "One," we wish to declare *what* He is, I admit with you that He cannot be called "One" for the same reason that He cannot be called "Being"—because both are, of course, concrete names. Indeed, I was the first to openly assert this to you in that same book through these words: *These names—<term>Being</term>, <term>True</term>, <term>One</term>, <term>Good</term>—being concrete, what do they say? They suggest something that participates.* Wherefore we say again that God is above being, above truth, above oneness, above goodness, because He is existence itself, truth itself, unity itself, and goodness itself. Those were my words there. 

It did not escape me, therefore, while I was writing, that <term>Being</term> and <term>the One</term> are equally concrete, and by reason of that concreteness, either neither or both should be equally removed from God. But as I had cautioned above, when we call God "One" but not "Being," we are signifying not what God *is*, but how He is that which He is—namely, because He is all things in the most primary and simple way. This "way" of being can in no way be indicated or figured through the name of "Being," but it can be through the symbol and title of "Unity." For beings relate to one another like numbers, as <term>Aristotle</term> writes, and of numbers, <term>Unity</term> is both the most primary and the most simple. 

You add that you marvel that I wish to defend the idea that God is not "being," not only according to <term>Plato</term>, but even according to <term>Aristotle</term>. But if you have run through the book more attentively, I am primarily acting in this whole work to show that God both *is* and is properly called <term>Being</term>, not only from the doctrine of <term>Aristotle</term>, but also <term>Plato</term>; consequently, the One is not higher than Being. However, lest those who said God is not Being but "above Being" should seem entirely insane—among whom, if <term>Plato</term> and <term>Aristotle</term> are not included, certainly <term>Dionysius the Areopagite</term> is, who is greater than both—I attempted to prove that there is a certain way of speaking which, if followed, makes it not inconsistent with the truth that God is greater than the name of "Being," which the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note> even occasionally use...

...to be used, and although you shrink from it so much, you cannot deny it unless you deny the authority of those to whom, even in your own opinion, the first place in that school is due. For who does not know that the division of <term>being</term> <note>original: "ens"; the most general category of anything that exists.</note> into <term>substance</term> <note>original: "substantia"; that which exists in itself (like a tree or a person).</note> and <term>accident</term> <note>original: "accidens"; a quality that exists only in something else (like the "brownness" of the tree).</note> is frequent among the followers of Aristotle? Yet when being is so divided, it is the opinion of your own **Thomas Aquinas** that God is not "being" but "above being." Regarding this, you used to say: <note>original: "Thomam aufer, mutus fiet Aristoteles"</note> "Take away Thomas, and Aristotle becomes mute." The words of Thomas are roughly these: **God is neither an accident, nor can He properly be called a substance,** both because substance is called substance because it "stands under" or subsists, and because substance indicates a "quiddity" <note>An "essence" or "what-ness" of a thing.</note> which is different from its actual existence. Therefore, that division of being into substance and accident is a division of *created* being; these are his words. 

Moreover, when **Aristotle** says the "first philosopher" <note>What we now call a Metaphysician.</note> treats of being insofar as it is being and the causes and principles of being, there are many among the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy.</note> who maintain that God is not placed by Aristotle among "beings" there, but among the *causes* of being. However, that God can also be called "being" in another proper sense of the word, I not only did not deny, but I asserted and confirmed it with many reasons in the third chapter of that same work. I do not know why you, who are always an imitator of illustrious authors, now defect from the most famous Peripatetics to follow those who place God under a "genus" <note>A general classification or category.</note>; I have no doubt that **Boethius** would in no way wish to be numbered among them.

Lastly, you contend that "the divided" is not the negation of "the one," nor "the false" the negation of "the true," nor "the evil" the negation of "the good." Indeed, I know that the controversy concerning these opposites is not an easy one among great authors, and for that reason I ended the book in which these were briefly discussed with this closing statement: *All these things we touch upon here briefly, otherwise a thicket of many and great questions.* However, nothing you object moves me to doubt that the opinion I followed is less probable or true. 

You say a <term>Chimera</term> <note>A mythical beast made of parts from different animals; used in philosophy to represent an impossible or non-existent thing.</note> is neither "one" nor "divided." But I say that the Chimera which we conceive in the mind does not exist precisely because the parts of which we understand it to consist are, in your own view of the nature of things, divided rather than united. And just as that thing does not exist whose parts (from which it would be constituted if it did exist) are divided, so too it not only does not exist, but it is impossible for it to exist if its parts are neither united nor able to be united by the power of nature.

For this reason, we not only say a chimera does not exist, but we believe it is impossible for it to be, because it is not believable that the brute animals from which we imagine it would ever come together into a single animal composition. Again, you insist that because a **diagonal** <note>Referring to the mathematical proof that the diagonal of a square is "incommensurable" with its side (it cannot be expressed as a simple ratio).</note> is not commensurable, it is neither "one" nor "divided." In my opinion, you are mistaken. For by the same reason that something is false, it is necessarily divided in itself. For something is detected as false insofar as it fights with itself and includes a contradiction. And what else is it to include a contradiction than to be divided within oneself? **Every truth is therefore one**, because it is consistent and harmonious with itself; **every falsehood is divided**, because it fights with itself and does not cohere...

<page-num>262</page-num>

<meta>catchword: and in</meta>

...is occurring. Many have believed that the **false** is a negation of the **true**—a fact which is certainly not hidden from you—and the arguments you bring forward do not stand in the way. For, as I said, we call "false" that which is not what it seems to be, just as **false gold** is that which *appears* to be gold, yet is not actually gold. Although false gold is not only "not gold" but is also "something else" than gold, it happens to be something other than gold only insofar as it is false; it is false specifically because it is not the gold it appears to be. Therefore, gold is false when it does not match the <term>idea</term> <note>In this philosophical context, an "idea" is the perfect mental blueprint or essential definition of a thing.</note> of gold. But because it *does* match the idea of copper or silver, it is not "entirely" false, but only false in a limited sense: it is "false gold," just as it is not "entirely" a non-entity. For even if it is not that which is gold, it is nevertheless something else—say, copper, lead, or silver.

However, that which corresponds to *no* idea at all is entirely and absolutely false, just as it is also entirely "non-being," such as that which we call a **chimera**. <note>A mythological creature composed of parts from different animals; in philosophy, it is often used as the standard example of an impossible object that cannot exist in reality.</note> See, therefore, how they proceed at an equal pace: non-being, the divided, and the false; and thus every chimera can rightly be called false, and every false thing can rightly be called divided. Truly, **evil** does not oppose the **good** as a contrary opposite, as you judge and as **Albertus** <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a teacher of Thomas Aquinas and a primary authority on Aristotle.</note> teaches when explaining the *Categories* of **Aristotle**, and as your **Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274).</note> teaches most extensively in the first question of his work *On Evil*; all of which, I believe, have long been very well known to you. Farewell.

## TADINO SENDS GREETINGS. Second Objections

How much I have loved you and always honored you, most excellent man, you yourself are witness; you can easily recall, if you wish, my diligent and exceptional devotion toward you. But if you now either doubt that you are loved by Antonio, your old friend and <term>compatriot</term>, <note>original: "compatre"; this can refer to a literal godfather relationship or a very close, quasi-familial bond between friends.</note> or if you do not believe it at all, then by Hercules, you remember very little of my respect for you. For how could it be that I—who loved and honored you when you were barely initiated into philosophy—would not love and admire you now, when you are so distinguished in learning and integrity? Would that everyone you have lived familiarly with had embraced you with a benevolence equal to that with which your "compatriot" has always followed his Pico! 

But now let us come to our business: You say that your short book <term>On Being and the One</term> <note>original: "de ente & uno"; Pico's most famous metaphysical work, which attempted to reconcile Plato and Aristotle.</note> was appropriately titled. You argue that although the title of the work is brief, and promises a treatise on "being" and "the one," the Preface (which is an expanded title) explains what kind of treatise it promises: namely, the **mutual conversion** <note>A technical term in Scholastic logic meaning two terms are interchangeable; e.g., everything that is "one" is also a "being."</note> of being and the one. By the same reasoning, if a book were published in which only the **immortality of the soul** was asserted by the author, it could rightly be titled *A Book on the Soul*. For the author, entering into the discussion, might soon propose the question, asking whether the soul is immortal or not. This true objection was almost entirely explained in my previous letter, but in my judgment, you responded with nothing. <meta>catchword: who</meta>

# On Being and the One.

And if at the beginning of the work the author should promise that he will take many things from geometry, the booklet could be titled "On Geometry," even though it might actually concern motions; but let us omit these things as they are frivolous. I have written on this opinion in another booklet. No one, I say, has said that the **Platonists** feel differently unless all or most of them feel that way. If indeed **Themistius** <note>Themistius (c. 317–387 AD) was a statesman and philosopher who wrote influential paraphrases of Aristotle, often attempting to harmonize Aristotelian and Platonic thought.</note>, who is not ignoble among the Platonists, affirms according to Plato’s opinion that the <term>Idea</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, an Idea or Form is the eternal, perfect blueprint of a thing.</note> which is the principle of things is truly and properly **being** in an absolute sense, it should not have been declared that the Platonists—following Plato—judge that God is not truly and properly being; for the **Idea is God**. 

You, however, respond that the Idea is one thing and God is another; and that even if it were granted that the Idea is God, it would not necessarily follow from this that God is properly and truly "being," because God and the Idea, even if they do not differ in reality, differ nevertheless in <term>reason</term> <note>A "difference in reason" (distinctio rationis) is a conceptual or logical distinction made by the mind, even if the things themselves are identical in reality.</note>. But I would not wish to dispute in this place whether the Platonists believe God is one thing and the Idea another, since that question is far removed from our purpose—even though many authors, both Greek and Latin, place the Ideas of Plato within God. 

I seem to have done enough for my purpose by following Plato and showing that a certain Platonist (and by no means an ignoble one!) asserts that, according to Plato, the Idea—and therefore God—is truly and properly **being**. Nor does the distinction in "reason" to which you flee do anything to help you in this matter. For an **Idea** is relative <note>It is "relative" because it is an Idea *of* something else (like the Idea of a Circle).</note>, while **God** is an absolute reality. If, therefore, God is truly and properly "being" in that part where He refers outward <note>i.e., as an Idea or archetype for created things.</note>, how much more ought He to be considered "being" by that reason through which He is God and exists in His own nature? For why is the Idea, in that respect where it is an Idea, truly and properly being? No reason, I say, can be assigned unless it is said to be truly and properly being for the very reason that it truly and properly **is**. Therefore, God will be truly and properly "being" to a greater degree by that reason through which He is God: "I am," He said, "who I am." <note>original: "ego sum qui sum" — A reference to the divine name revealed to Moses in Exodus 3:14.</note> 

Furthermore, an objection was raised in this manner: if the Platonists can be rightly defended when they say God is not truly and properly "being," but rather "the One," because the name "being" <note>original: "ens"</note> is a <term>concrete</term> <note>In medieval logic, a "concrete" term (like "white" or "human") implies a subject possessing a quality, whereas an "abstract" term (like "whiteness" or "humanity") refers to the quality itself. Pico's opponent argues that "Being" implies a subject that *has* existence, which they feel is beneath God's simplicity.</note> name which signifies something different from that which "is," while He is "the One" because He is all things uniquely—by that same logic, it can be concluded that God is not "the One," for "one" is also a concrete name. Indeed, He would be neither "blessed" nor "God," for both of those words are concrete. 

You, however, respond that one does not call God "the One" as if the substance of God were shown by the name of "the One," but rather to explain *how* He is that which He is. But I ask: to what end is this? For the objection is not yet solved. You say God is not "being," but "the One," because the name of being is concrete. If, therefore, "the One" is also concrete, must it not be concluded by the same reasoning that God is not "the One," nor "God" (which is a name pertaining to substance, just like "being")? 

Furthermore, if He is "the One" because He is uniquely that which He is, why should He not also be called "being"? For by being "one" He is all things that He is—namely, wisdom, and goodness, and power. For He is not called "One" because He is the *only* one; therefore, by the same reasoning, He can be called "being," even though He is not the *only* being, for He is "being" in the highest degree. Furthermore, that argument has not yet been resolved which was stated thus: God is truly and properly being, for He said: "I am..." 

<summary>Pico argues against the Neo-Platonic idea that God is "beyond Being," asserting instead that God is Being in its highest sense. He critiques the linguistic argument that "Being" is too concrete a term for God, noting that if "Being" is rejected on those grounds, names like "the One" or "God" must also be rejected.</summary>

## Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

...who I am. Again, I wondered why you would defend, according to <term>Aristotle</term> <note>Aristotle (384–322 BC), the Greek philosopher whose logical and metaphysical works formed the basis of medieval university education.</note>, that God is sometimes not at all to be judged by the name of <term>being</term> <note>original: "entis." In this context, "being" refers to the most general nature of anything that exists.</note>, because He would not be a "being through itself," nor a "being by accident," nor a <term>substance</term>, nor an <term>accident</term> <note>In Aristotelian logic, a "substance" is a thing that exists in itself (like a man or a tree), while an "accident" is a quality that exists only in a substance (like "tallness" or "whiteness").</note>. For I have shown that God is neither a being through itself <note>in the limited, created sense</note> nor a being by accident, and that no middle ground can be imagined between <term>substance</term> and <term>accident</term>. You, however, give no answer to the first objection. Against the second, you allege only one interpreter of Aristotle, that is, the Blessed Thomas <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent Scholastic theologian and philosopher.</note>, who says that God is not properly a <term>substance</term> because He "stands under" <note>The word "substance" literally means "that which stands under" (sub-stantia).</note> no accident, and the essence of God is not something other than God himself.

But see, O most excellent man, whether Thomas might actually bear witness against you? For if the division of <term>being</term> into <term>substance</term> and <term>accident</term> is, according to the Blessed Thomas, a division of *created* <term>being</term> (as you report), how can it be ignored that there is something that is *uncreated* being, which is God? By what reasoning, then, can you maintain—according to the interpretation of Saint Thomas—that <term>Aristotle</term> thinks God is not properly and truly being? 

Furthermore, although Saint Thomas seems in a certain place to deny that God is properly a <term>substance</term>, imitating the **Master of the Sentences** <note>Peter Lombard (c. 1096–1160), whose book "The Sentences" was the standard textbook of theology. He argued that God is beyond the category of substance because He has no changing qualities.</note> on the grounds that He "stands under" no accident, it is nonetheless not false what I wrote in the previous letter: that there is no middle ground between <term>substance</term> and <term>accident</term>. The Blessed Thomas proves this in many places with effective arguments, and you have not solved a single one of those points written to you. If, therefore, he sometimes denies that God is a <term>substance</term>, the very words you bring forward clearly reveal the man's mind: for <term>substance</term> can be spoken of in many ways, which he himself explains more broadly in the first part <note>Likely referring to the "Prima Pars" of Aquinas's "Summa Theologica."</note>.

For sometimes "substance" is properly so called because it "stands under" accidents; by this reasoning, he denies that God is a <term>substance</term>. Nor does he say this simply and absolutely, but says He is not *properly* a substance because He stands under no accident. Yet <term>substance</term> is sometimes said to be that which exists through itself and does not need a "substantive" <note>i.e., it does not need another subject to exist in.</note>, in which way Thomas sometimes, and indeed frequently, uses the name of <term>substance</term>. In this way, however, no middle ground can be imagined between <term>substance</term> and <term>accident</term>, for it is a division of both through affirmation and negation.

As for the fact that, led by no necessity but by my own will, I affirmed from the opinion of <term>Boethius</term> <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 477–524 AD), a philosopher who translated and commented on Aristotle's logic.</note> and <term>Augustine</term> <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), whose "On the Trinity" explored how Aristotelian categories apply to God.</note> that God is placed through Himself in a <term>category</term> <note>original: "prædicamento." The ten Categories of Aristotle are the fundamental ways in which things can be described.</note>, I did not say it because I do not highly value, venerate, or approve of Saint Thomas. Rather, I said it because the authority of Saint Thomas alone is not sufficient to demonstrate that either Aristotle or the Aristotelians judge that God is by no means placed in a <term>category</term>. Nor do I, for that reason, desert the best authors for those who are wicked or common; on the contrary, I follow and approve of the best. Do you make Saint Thomas either the equal or the superior of either <term>Boethius</term> or <term>Augustine</term>? 

I indeed have read them all in the past and read them daily, nor do I think anyone is of a vigorous mind who either remains ignorant of or neglects those things devised by our **Englishmen**, I mean **Swineshead** <note>Richard Swineshead (fl. c. 1340–1354), known as "The Calculator," was an Oxford mathematician and philosopher famous for his extremely complex logical and physical calculations.</note> and those like him. Indeed, I do not approve of and admire everything written by them, and—by Hercules—I am often accustomed to weaken quite a few things based on the opinion of <term>Aristotle</term> and approved authors; but I cannot...

He reconciles the views of Thomas Aquinas with those of Augustine and Boethius, arguing that while God lacks accidents, He remains the ultimate "substance" as He exists through Himself.</summary>

...I cannot but wonder at the great subtlety of men and the very sharp reasons in physical matters, which <term>Aristotle</term> <note>Aristotle (384–322 BC), the foundational Greek philosopher for medieval logic.</note> himself, if he rose from the dead, would admire and extol in a marvelous way—approving their subtlety in many cases, even if not their truth. You defend, moreover, that the <term>negation</term> <note>A logical term meaning the denial or opposite of a statement.</note> of the "one" is the "divided." For you say a **Chimera** <note>A mythical creature made of parts from different animals; in logic, it is often used to represent something that is "impossible" because its parts cannot naturally exist together.</note> is divided because the parts of which it would consist, if it existed, are divided from each other and cannot be united. But you think a **commensurable diameter** <note>In geometry, the diameter (or diagonal) of a square cannot be measured by the same unit as its side; thus, a "commensurable" one is a mathematical impossibility.</note> is divided because it is divided from itself and is dissonant. These are the words you use: *For a thing is found to be false insofar as it fights with itself and includes a contradiction.* What else is it to include a contradiction than to be divided within itself?

Therefore, every true thing is "one," because it is consistent and harmonious with itself; every false thing is "divided," because it fights with itself and does not cohere. But see how you can sustain your position. For if something is "one" because it is harmonious with itself, then the "false" and the "impossible" themselves will be "one" and "true." I would not say this or that specific false thing—such as that a **Chimera** exists or that a **stag flies** <note>original: "cervum volare." A standard example in medieval logic for a false or impossible proposition.</note>—but I mean the very nature of the "false" and "impossible" itself. I shall prove this nature is "one" and "true." 

According to your dogma, the Chimera is divided because its parts are always divided from each other, and because it is divided from itself; for a Chimera is not a Chimera <note>Pico is pointing out a logical trap: if a thing "fights with itself," it cannot even be defined as itself.</note>, and by the same reason, a commensurable diameter is divided, for neither of these can be understood otherwise than as disagreeing with itself and fighting with itself. But if you look at the "false" itself separately, the false is false, and the impossible is impossible; neither, therefore, fights with itself, and neither is dissonant from itself. By the same reasoning, the dead by no means fight with themselves. For those who are already dead, are dead; therefore, any of these is "one" and "true," if a thing is "one" because it is undivided from itself.

Moreover, how is it true that everything false contains a <term>contradiction</term>? Are there not many false things that could be true either by the power of nature or of man? You also try to defend the definition of the "true" that you previously set down, and you say that the **true** is that which seems to be what it is, and the **false** is that which seems to be what it is not. Now, for this reason, you think it follows that the "false" is not the negation of the "true." But to my argument—if I may say so with your permission—you have so far responded with nothing. 

The argument is this: If the "true" is what seems to be what it is, and the "false" is what seems to be what it is not, then since there is no contradiction between "seeming to be what it is" and "seeming to be what it is not," the "false" will not be the negation of the "true." For if there were no man in the nature of things, nor God, <term>Socrates</term> <note>The famous Greek philosopher, used here as a standard placeholder name in logical examples.</note> would not exist; he would not, therefore, seem to be what he was, nor what he was not; he would be neither true nor false, but he would be <term>non-being</term> <note>original: "non ens." Something that has no existence at all.</note>. Therefore, "non-being" and "false" sometimes disagree. Even the **Blessed Thomas** <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the highly influential Catholic theologian.</note>, whom you do not oppose, declares that the true and the false are contraries to each other if they are referred to the mind, upon which your theory of the true and false depends. *True and false estimations,* he says, *are contraries to one another,* just as Aristotle says. Finally, you deny that good and evil are contraries to each other...

<summary>Pico critiques his opponent's definitions of truth and unity, arguing that if "unity" is merely self-consistency, then even "falsehood" could be considered "one." He uses logical paradoxes like the Chimera and mathematical impossibilities to show that truth and falsehood must be defined by their relationship to existence (being), not just internal consistency.</summary>

...therefore you respond to the reason by which it was proved they are contraries, nor do you explain how evil is a negation of the good. For I have said this: no negation—especially one that encompasses things that do not belong to a <term>genus</term> <note>A general category or "family" in logic within which specific types, or species, are organized.</note>—can exist. You also say that <term>Albert</term> <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a dominant medieval scholar and teacher of Thomas Aquinas.</note>, who I judge carries weight with you, denies that good and evil are mutually contrary, and that <term>St. Thomas</term> <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican theologian and philosopher.</note> feels the same in the first question on *Evil*; yet you do not respond to how <term>Boethius</term> <note>Boethius (c. 477–524 AD), whose commentaries on logic were standard textbooks for centuries.</note> either spoke the truth or lied when he said in his commentary on the *Categories* that good and evil are mutually contrary—not in the way that white and black or hot and cold are (which are all true qualities), but in the way that healthy and sick, strong and weak, rare and dense, beautiful and ugly, and many similar things are. Nor does St. Thomas deny this, but that most eminent man, in the first question on *Evil* regarding the solution to the second argument, shows how good and evil, even if they oppose one another by the opposition of <term>privation and habit</term> <note>A logical distinction: a "habit" is the presence of a quality (like sight), while "privation" is its absence where it should naturally be (like blindness).</note>, are nonetheless usually counted among contraries; he confirms this by the authority of <term>Simplicius</term> <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist commentator on Aristotle.</note>. 

Therefore, our objections, which were devised solely for the investigation of truth and our mutual charity, do not yet seem to me to be entirely weakened. I ask and beseech you, therefore, that with that same love with which you attempted to open the truth of Platonic doctrine to your <term>Angelo Poliziano</term> <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), a famous Renaissance humanist and close friend of Pico.</note>, the most learned man of our age, you might also untie the knots and difficulties of our weakness with the same zeal. I, for my part, am meanwhile entangled in many readings and the duty of practicing medicine; but you, who are entirely free for contemplation and are able to strive through four stages into the <term>deep darkness of God</term> <note>A reference to "apophatic" or negative theology, where God is described as a "divine darkness" because His light is too bright for the human mind to grasp.</note>, will rescue the light from the shadows with little or no labor. Farewell, and remember us. 

From Ferrara, May 22, 1491.

### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA TO ANTONIO CITTADINI, GREETINGS. Response to the second objections.

**E**ither my previous letter was far too brief, or certainly more obscure than it should have been in solving your questions regarding that little book I recently published, **On Being and Unity**. For you repeat the same questions and doubt the same things about them. Indeed, I will not deny that in the first letter certain things were omitted to which no answer was given, lest I waste words on trivial matters; some things were treated briefly by me, as I believed the matters should be indicated rather than explained to a man who is a philosopher. 

Now, since you demand this of me, we shall track down even every little detail; and through the individual chapters of your questions, I shall bid you remember those things which we wrote before, and I shall rouse you, where necessary, to a deeper understanding of them. Furthermore, since you have not yet touched the Platonic commentaries, nor the Greek <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>The followers of Aristotle, named for the "covered walkways" where they studied.</note> due to your ignorance of the Greek language, I shall lead you by the hand through the lines and decrees of the Latins.

<header>On Being and the One.</header>
<sig>Z 2</sig>
<meta>Catchword: and to be</meta>

# On Being and the One.

...especially <term>Thomas</term> <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the Dominican theologian who synthesized Aristotelian philosophy with Christian doctrine.</note>, who is more familiar to you, in order to perceive the meanings of the <term>Platonists</term> <note>Followers of Plato, who often argued that the ultimate principle—the "One"—is superior to even the category of "Being."</note> which are treated in my book. Now, that which troubles you first is by what reasoning the Platonists place God above <term>Being</term> <note>original: "ens". In metaphysics, "Being" refers to the most general category of anything that exists.</note>. For if God (you say) truly is, He is certainly truly and properly called Being, just as someone who has been sitting for a long time is truly said to be "sitting" because they sit. You add that insofar as He is an <term>Idea</term> <note>In Platonic thought, Ideas are the perfect, eternal patterns of which all earthly things are mere shadows.</note>, He is Being; much more so insofar as He is God, He might perhaps become and be called Being. But even if not all Platonists grant that the Idea and God are the same, you say it is enough to oppose me if even a single person like <term>Themistius</term> <note>Themistius (c. 317–388 AD), a Greek philosopher and statesman who wrote extensive commentaries on Aristotle.</note> did not say what I have ascribed to the Platonists in common.

Likewise, you cannot understand how I say God is called "the One," since by this we signify not *what* He is, but *how* He is that which He is. For if He is "One" (you say) because He is uniquely all things, why should He not also be called "Being," since by one existence He is all that He is? For He is not called "One" simply because He alone becomes one. Therefore, He could equally be called Being, even though He alone is not Being. These are the primary things from which you cannot extricate yourself, but in a few words—and as I promised—I shall remove every scrap of doubt from you using even those things known to you.

You know that in the works of Thomas, the <term>essence</term> <note>The "what-ness" of a thing; the definition that makes a horse a horse.</note> of a thing is one thing, and its <term>existence</term> <note>The "that-ness" of a thing; the fact that it actually exists in reality.</note> is another. The existence of a thing is that by which the thing is—that is, it exists. Essence is that by which a thing attains a certain species, such as that of a horse, or a stone, or a shrub. Therefore, what is called "essence" is also called <term>quiddity</term> <note>A technical term in Scholastic philosophy derived from the Latin "quid," meaning "what." It refers to the "what-it-is-ness" of a thing.</note> by more recent thinkers, because from the notion of essence, we know *what* a thing is. 

Therefore, as <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BC) whose logic dominated medieval education.</note> teaches in the second book of the *Posterior Analytics*, there is one question when we ask, for example, "Does a rose exist?" and another when we want to know "What is a rose?" The first question certainly regards the thing's **existence**. The second regards its **essence**, or to use the words of the more recent scholars, its **quiddity**. Again, remember that according to the opinion of Thomas, all things below God which exist in act are composed of essence and "being" (for so he calls existence). God Himself is neither composed of essence and existence, nor is He again an essence, but He is pure existence itself, from which subsequently all other existence of created things is derived, being communicated to created essences. 

Add to this that by this word which is **Being** (<term>ens</term>), essence is mostly indicated; however, by this word which is **is** (<term>est</term>), existence is indicated, not essence. The same Thomas teaches you this in the first question of his work *On Evil*, where he says that when we say this or that is "a being," the question being answered is "what is the thing?" (which, as we said above, pertains to the essence of the thing). But when we say "this is" or "is not," the seeker of whether the thing exists is satisfied, which question, as we were saying, belongs to existence. 

Now, I believe, the entire opinion of the Platonists and the solution to your objection is open to you. For if God is **existence** but not **essence**, just as we truly say God "is," so we truly deny that God is "Being." Nor can I help but marvel at you, that even if you have not read the Platonic works, yet being frequent in the reading of Thomas, you insist so much on this argument: "God is, therefore He is Being," when Thomas himself says, word for word, that these do not mutually follow...

<summary>Pico explains the metaphysical distinction between essence (quiddity) and existence to resolve why God can be said "to be" while simultaneously being "above Being" in Platonic thought. He relies on Thomas Aquinas's distinction to show that God is pure existence rather than a categorized essence.</summary>
<keywords>Being, the One, essence, existence, quiddity, Thomas Aquinas, Platonists, Aristotle, God, metaphysics</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Pico's argument that "Being" and "to be" address different metaphysical questions, responding to the interlocutor's confusion over Platonic terminology.</meta>

<page-num>268</page-num>
<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>
<meta>catchword: unity</meta>

...and "to be" is "being," but that they pertain to entirely different and unrelated questions. However, what need is there here for the authority of <term>Thomas</term>? <note>Thomas Aquinas, whose work Pico frequently reconciles with Platonic thought.</note> Who is so foolish as to doubt whether God exists? And again, who is so foolish as to presume to know—even in the smallest part—*what* God is? Since, therefore, knowing *whether* God is and knowing *what* God is are entirely different things, there will also be a vast difference between the statement "God is" <note>original: "Deus est"—referring to His existence.</note> and the statement "God is <term>Being</term>." <note>original: "Deus est ens"—referring to His essence or what He is.</note> For the former asserts that God exists (of which nothing is more certain), while the latter dares to pronounce something about what God is (of which nothing is more uncertain).

For this reason, when you recently asked during our dispute what God was, our most learned friend <term>Poliziano</term> <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), a brilliant humanist scholar and close friend of Pico.</note> very rightly answered you in the spirit of the poet <term>Simonides</term> <note>A Greek lyric poet who, when asked by Hiero of Syracuse to define God, kept asking for more time to think, eventually concluding that the more he meditated, the more obscure the subject became.</note> that he did not know what He was.

The example you bring forward about a "sitting person" is far removed from this purpose. The statements "to be a sitting person" and "to sit" do not vary in the same way that "to be" and "Being" do. For I answer the same question when I say "<term>Socrates</term> sits" as I do when I say "he is a sitting person"—namely, the question of someone inquiring about Socrates's posture. Just as when we say "Socrates is white" and "Socrates is whitened," we satisfy the same question: "What is Socrates like?" But the same logic does not apply between "Being" and "is." One of these—to hammer home the same point—reveals *what* a thing is to those who ask, while the other reveals *whether* it is.

From this it is also clear that if God is called "Being" insofar as He is an <term>Idea</term>, <note>In the hierarchy of Platonic forms, an "Idea" is a perfect archetype that possesses being.</note> it does not follow that He retains the title of "Being" when He is conceived as He is in Himself, absolute. For just as He takes on the character of an Idea, so too does He take on the character of an <term>Essence</term>; yet as He is understood in Himself, above all essence and relationship to created things, He is greater than the name "Being." For the fact that He is not called "Being" is not due to a deficiency, as you believe, but to <term>eminence</term>. <note>Pico is explaining "negative theology": God is so far above our categories that "Being" is too small a word for Him.</note> This is why the <term>Platonists</term> pronounce Him to be "above Being" rather than "not-Being."

I do not know why you so stubbornly insist on counting <term>Themistius</term> among their number. If you ask the ancients, they will all answer that he is a <term>Peripatetic</term> <note>A follower of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note>—he is "Themistius," not a Platonist. If you were to ask the man himself, I think he would call himself a "paraphrast" and a follower of Aristotle, not of Plato. But perhaps (allow me to joke) you drag him into the <term>Academy</term> <note>Plato’s school in Athens; here used to mean the Platonic tradition.</note> against his will just so you don't appear entirely ignorant of Platonic and Greek matters—you who have at least read Themistius in the Latin translation provided by our friend <term>Hermolaus</term>. <note>Ermolao Barbaro (1454–1493), who translated Themistius's commentaries on Aristotle into Latin.</note>

But let Themistius be a Platonist, and let him be entirely correct: we have already declared abundantly in this and the previous letter that what he says in no way contradicts our view. This is because the Platonists will say some things about God insofar as He is God, and other things insofar as He is an Idea.

Let us come to the point of why God is called "the One," even though He is not called "Being." Recall what I wrote to you in my first letter. When the Platonists call God "the One," they are not stating *what* He is, but *how* He is that which He is—though they may not understand this well enough themselves. I will speak more clearly: if you ask an Academic man <note>A follower of the skeptical or Platonic tradition of the Academy.</note> what God is, he answers not only that he cannot tell you what He is, but that you have no right to ask—that such a question is unworthy of Him. Since He is above all essence and above everything that can be understood, this alone can be asserted of Him: that He is...

<summary>Pico distinguishes between knowing that God exists ("is") and knowing His nature ("Being"), arguing that God is "above Being" due to His supreme excellence. He also disputes the classification of the philosopher Themistius as a Platonist, attributing the confusion to recent Latin translations.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's philosophical defense of why "the One" is a more appropriate name for God than "Being," addressing technical objections regarding Aristotelian categories and the nature of contradiction.</meta>

<page-num>269</page-num>
->On Being and the One.<-
->Z 3<-
<meta>catchword: because</meta>

# On Being and the One.

...most similar to unity, because just as unity is the principle of all numbers, so is God the principle of all things that exist. Just as unity contains within its own individual simplicity all numbers, both even and odd—though it is itself neither even nor odd—so too God closes and contains all things within His impartible <note>Indivisible or unable to be partitioned.</note> infinity. Do you not see what this means? That by the name "the One," we do not indicate *what* God is, but rather *how* He is that which He is? Finally, if we say: "God is like unity," which is what we mean to signify when we give Him the name of "the One," we shall certainly be speaking the truth. But if we say: "God is like <term>Being</term>," <note>original: "ens"</note> we would surely make our listeners laugh. But why say more on a matter already clear? For either these words are enough, or I do not know what words could be enough. Furthermore, it is gathered from this why God is under no <term>genus</term>; <note>A "genus" is a general class or category in logic (like "animal" or "substance"). Pico argues God is beyond all such classifications.</note> for the genera of things are their <term>essences</term>, <note>original: "essentiae"</note> but God is neither an essence nor does He possess an essence. For this reason, since "being" is sometimes understood by the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> to encompass only the ten genera, it is manifest that God is not contained under the name of "being," a term which even the followers of <term>Aristotle</term> sometimes use in this way.

But you insist that <term>Thomas</term> <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Scholastic theologian.</note> and others of that same school often use "substance" and "being" in such a way that God is called both substance and being. As if I were either ignorant of this—which everyone knows—or as if it were not enough for my point that they *sometimes* act otherwise. For I said that they were accustomed to use those terms in that manner not always, but only on occasion.

Let us move on to the objections you raise concerning the opposition between "the one" and "the divided." Truly, I think you are testing me with childish quibbles. For if you say "the false" is divided, then surely "the false" is not "the false." For the false is not divided from itself, because the false *is* the false. Likewise, you say that dead men do not fight with one another at all, for they are dead who are already dead. Furthermore, <term>Antony</term>, <note>Presumably Pico’s interlocutor in this correspondence.</note> when I said that things which are false "fight with themselves": if this "fight" must be with a fist or a weapon, I admit that even dead men do not fight among themselves, nor do false things. But just as "the false" is indeed "the false," so too the fact that "the false is false" is not false, but true; therefore it is not divided, but one.

You add, speaking as a doctor, that it is false that "the false" includes a contradiction. Your reason is that there are many false things which, by the power of either nature or man, could truly come to be. But consider this: everything that is false, as long as it remains false, includes a contradiction. But just as some things are false in such a way that they *could* become true, while others are so false that they can *never* be true, so too some things are so contradictory to themselves and so much at war with themselves that they can never return to friendship and concord. Others hate one another in such a way that they can nevertheless return to favor. This will be clear by example: for a "man to be a lion" is always false, because it always includes a contradiction; and just as it can never be reduced to unity, so can it never be reduced to truth. But that "I am sitting" is neither true nor false <note>Pico means as a standalone abstract proposition without context.</note>. If, however, you add that "I am sitting while I stand," you immediately bring in both falsehood and contradiction. For "me sitting while I stand" includes a contradiction, and as soon as it ceases to be false—such as when I actually begin to sit—it immediately returns from division to unity. As for the other things you object to regarding the opposition of the false and the true, they have already been resolved in my previous letter. For you say that if it is true, as it seems...

<summary>Pico argues that God is better described as "the One" than as "Being" because God transcends all categories and essences. He also defends his logical definitions of truth as unity and falsehood as a form of self-contradiction or division.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's philosophical defense of why "the One" is a more appropriate name for God than "Being," specifically refuting arguments that equate "evil" or "falsehood" with a positive existence that could stand as a "contrary" to "good" or "truth."</meta>

<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>
<meta>catchword: contradiction</meta>

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

[...that which] is, while the false is that which seems to be, but is not. Since there is no <term>contradiction</term> <note>In logic, a contradiction exists between "being" and "not-being," where one must be true and the other false.</note> between "seeming to be what is" and "seeming to be what is not," the false will not be a simple negation of the true. However, I do not define the nature of the false as simply "seeming to be something which is not." Rather, I maintain that its nature lies in the fact that it *is not* that which it is said to be. For instance, "false gold" is called false precisely because it is not gold; and as far as the definition of "false" is concerned, it is accidental whether it appears to be gold or appears to be something other than gold. 

As for your claim that I have not untied the knot of your argument—the one by which you prove that good and evil are <term>contraries</term> <note>original: "contraria." In formal logic, "contraries" are opposites that can both be false (like black and white), whereas "contradictories" cannot (like being and non-being).</note>—I will say frankly: I did not think a solution was needed where there was no knot to begin with. Your argument was this: "The good is to be sought, while the evil is to be avoided. Seeking and avoiding are contrary motions. Therefore, good and evil are contraries." To me, your reasoning seems so powerful and effective that it would prove not only that good and evil are contraries (about which someone might perhaps doubt), but it would even prove that <term>Being</term> and <term>Non-being</term> are contraries—even though everyone knows they are <term>contradictories</term>. For by your logic, we would conclude: "Being is to be sought, Non-being is to be avoided. Seeking and avoiding are contrary motions. Therefore, Being and Non-being are contraries." So, you must either grant me that Being and Non-being are contraries, or I shall not grant you that good and evil are contraries. 

Or perhaps you will say another argument must be resolved. You might ask: "Non-being is not a <term>genus</term>; <note>A "genus" is a general category of things that exist.</note> so how can evil be 'nothing,' when <term>Aristotle</term> says in the *Categories* <note>original: "Prædicamentis." This is Aristotle’s famous work on the classifications of reality.</note> that good and evil are the 'genera of contraries'?" All the interpreters of Aristotle are full of solutions to this question. I referred you to them in my previous letter so that I wouldn't involve us both in unnecessary work. 

To pass over the fact that <term>Simplicius</term> <note>A 6th-century philosopher and famous commentator on Aristotle.</note> is satisfied that Aristotle was speaking there in the manner of the <term>Pythagoreans</term>, <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who believed the universe was organized into two columns of opposites (The Ten Opposites).</note> who established two orders of things (one contained under "the good" and the other under "the evil"), or that Aristotle often uses examples in his logical commentaries based on others' opinions rather than his own—I will give you the answer you could have read in Simplicius: Good and evil are called "genera of contraries" because one side of a pair of contraries always has the quality of "evil" or "deficiency." For example, "black" is considered a deficiency when compared to "white," and "bitter" when compared to "sweet." In this way, all contraries are reduced to "good" and "evil," insofar as every defect has the nature of evil. This is why, in the first book of the *Lectures on Physics*, <note>original: "physicæ auscultationis," referring to Aristotle's "Physics."</note> it is said that contraries are always compared to one another according to the ratio of "better" and "worse." 

I will skip over the many other solutions offered by <term>Porphyry</term> <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a famous introduction to Aristotle's logic.</note> and more recent scholars. But I cannot wonder enough at your claim that <term>Thomas Aquinas</term> <note>The influential 13th-century theologian and philosopher.</note> descends to the opinion that good and evil are opposed as contraries. You even add that he confirms this by the authority of Simplicius. And yet, he opposes your very opinion with all his might throughout the entire first question of his work *On Evil*. <note>original: "de malo."</note> For what else does he aim for in that disputation, if not to prove that evil is "nothing"? If evil is nothing, it cannot be a contrary to the good—since both parts of a pair of contraries must, by nature, be "something." Indeed, this is the very point that Thomas confirms there using the authority of Simplicius.

<summary>Pico refutes the idea that evil is a positive "contrary" to good, arguing instead that evil is a "nothing" or a deficiency. He uses logical proofs to show that if evil were a positive contrary, one would have to absurdly conclude that non-existence is a contrary to existence.</summary>

[He] confirms [this]. See how far you wander, you who believe that this opinion is confirmed by the testimony of <term>Simplicius</term> <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.</note>, when in fact it is weakened by that very testimony. Perhaps you would not have fallen into this error if you had at some point actually read the book of Simplicius himself; in his work, there is never any mention of an opposition of <term>contraries</term> <note>In formal logic, "contraries" are opposites that exist on the same level of reality, like hot and cold. Pico argues evil is not a contrary but a "nothingness."</note> between good and evil. 

But if you should object to me by citing <term>ophthalmia</term> <note>A general historical term for inflammation of the eye.</note> and sickness—conditions in which <term>Thomas</term> <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican theologian and philosopher.</note> seems to acknowledge a contrariety—I bid you to look more closely at his words. For he does not say that these things are contraries, but rather that since they are <term>privations</term> <note>A "privation" is the absence of a quality that should normally be present (like blindness being the absence of sight), rather than a "thing" in itself.</note>, they are nevertheless sometimes *called* contraries. If you pay attention to why he wishes this to be done, you will see how entirely the nature of evil itself is ignorant of the properties of a contrary. For he allows these things to obtain the name of "contrary" in some way only insofar as they do not possess the full character of evil, but still retain something of the goodness which they have not yet lost. 

Therefore, they are in some way contraries only insofar as they are in some way not entirely evil. But if I were to set before you death or blindness, and ask whether these are "true evils" according to the opinion of Thomas, and again whether they oppose one another by that "species of contrariety" you describe, I do not see at all what you would answer. For if these are evils—and in that very passage where you bring forth Thomas’s testimony for your side—he would maintain with great assertiveness that these can in no way be contraries by that very species of contrariety which you bring into the discussion. With what mind, then, do you affirm that according to the opinion of Thomas, good is opposed to evil by some opposition of contrariety? Certainly, you ought to have considered this: that what is granted concerning certain "imperfect" evils (on account of the mixture of goodness they still retain) must not be transferred to the unmixed and absolute nature of evil itself. 

->Farewell.<-
