Thomas <note>The syllable "mas" from the previous page completes the name "Thomas."</note> would protest against this opinion; for in the First Part <note>Referring to the *Summa Theologiae*.</note>, in the *Summa contra Gentiles*, in the *Disputed Questions*, in the small book *On Being and Essence*, in the commentaries on Aristotle—in all places, finally, where the matter requires it—he holds and proves that God is essence, nor is there any need to cite the man’s words in a matter so clear. Unless you take pleasure in it, I will recount more than is necessary. <gloss>c</gloss> Furthermore, in your own small book *On Being and the One*, unless it has slipped your mind, you previously said that according to the <term>Platonists</term> <note>Followers of Plato who often argued that God (The One) is "beyond being."</note>, God is not "being" precisely because God's <term>to be</term> <note>Latin: *esse*, the act of existing.</note> is not different from His <term>essence</term> <note>Latin: *essentia*, what a thing is.</note>. How is it then that now, following and defending these same Platonists, you deny that God is essence? <gloss>d</gloss> Likewise, tell me from what passage of Saint Thomas you gathered that the word "being" <note>original: *ens*</note> mostly signifies essence and not also "to be" <note>original: *esse*</note>? Since in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics* and the first question of *On Truth*, and elsewhere, he says that "being" <note>*ens*</note> is so called because it *is* [exists], but "thing" <note>*res*</note> is so called because it is an essence or possesses essence. <gloss>e</gloss> Likewise, tell me where in Thomas you could have learned that the question "what is it?" <note>Latin: *quid est*</note> is rationally answered by saying "it is a being"? For it is absurd to ask "what is it?" unless it is known that the thing *is* [exists], as Aristotle in the second book of the *Posterior Analytics* and Thomas openly testify. By "to be" <note>*esse*</note>, however, I understand the way substances and <term>accidents</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "accidents" are qualities (like color or size) that exist only within a substance.</note> "are," in both of which there is essence, not the way <term>privations</term> <note>The absence of a required quality.</note> and negations "are," in which Thomas seems to deny that what is usually answered to the question "what is it?" can be found, whether that be <gloss>f</gloss> true or false, which is omitted for the present. <gloss>g</gloss> However, the words of Thomas in the first question of *On Evil*, which if I am not mistaken provided you the occasion for error, and which you also seem to hint at, are these: "Being" is spoken of in two ways. In one way, insofar as it signifies the nature of the ten <term>categories</term> <note>original: *generum*. The ten "predicaments" or classes of things defined by Aristotle.</note>, and in this way neither evil nor any privation is a being, nor anything. In another way, according to how one answers the question "is it?" <note>Latin: *an est*</note>, and in this way evil "is," just as blindness "is"; yet evil is not "something," because "to be something" signifies not only that which answers the question "is it?", but also that which answers the question "what is it?" <note>Latin: *quid est*</note>. But I pray, revisit the words of such a great philosopher more carefully, for they bear judgment against you, which is shown thus <gloss>h</gloss>: Thomas openly says that "being" and "something" are spoken of in two ways. One way, that it has the nature of some category. The other way, that it answers the question "is it?". Now, "God" is the answer to the question "is there a God?", and the response is not a lie; therefore, God is a being. But if we must proceed further, let us say this, departing in no way from Thomas: that to the question "is it?", the answer "it is a being" is rightly given; therefore, that which is the answer to the question of whether a thing truly and properly *is*, is truly and properly a being. For just as that which "is" simply relates to that which "is" simply, so does that which truly and properly "is" relate to that which truly and properly "is." To one asking whether God truly and properly *is*, the answer "God [is]" is rationally given; therefore, God is truly and properly a being. <gloss>i</gloss> Furthermore, Thomas <gloss>k</gloss> calls "something" and "being," according to the first way, that which is given as an answer to the question "what is it?". To one asking "what is it that preserves and moves the world, that raises the dead?", the answer "God" is rationally given. Therefore, in both the first way and the second, God is a being and something.

# On Being and the One. 273

...furthermore, will you dare, according to Thomas, to deny that God is good and is one? Since, therefore, the good, being, and the one are <term>mutually convertible</term> <note>original: *mutuo convertantur*; a Scholastic principle meaning these terms refer to the same reality but signify different aspects of it.</note>, how can it be said or imagined, according to Thomas, that God is not being? You, however, seem to argue from these words (unless I am mistaken) in this way: "being" is said in one way as signifying the nature of the <term>ten categories</term> <note>original: *decem generum*; Aristotle’s classification of all things into substance and nine accidents.</note>. But God is in no category, as Thomas himself also testifies; therefore, God is neither being nor essence. 

But you ought to have noticed (allow me to joke) that if your reasoning is effective in showing that God is not "being" in the first sense—for though He is in no category, nothing prevents Him from truly and properly existing in the nature of things—then the question "does He exist?" can be answered truthfully. How then could it be unknown that He is "being" in the other sense? 

Furthermore, your reasoning has no force, for the meaning of Thomas’s words is of this kind: "Being" is said in one way as signifying the nature of the ten categories—that is, it signifies <term>substance and accident</term> <note>Substance is what exists in itself; accident is what exists in another, like a color or a shape.</note>, and absolutely all positive things contained in the ten categories, either by themselves (as species and genera) or as certain principles, whether <gloss>a</gloss> limited or not—such as primary matter and "fortune" in the category of substance, and God, and all substantial differences. In this way, certainly, negations and privations cannot belong to a category. 

In another way, "being" is used for that which can answer the question "does it exist?" <note>original: *an est*</note>, whether it be a true and positive being or not. Hence, adding an example, he says: "and thus evil is, just as blindness is"—that is, in this sense, evil is a "being" just as blindness is a "being." For in Thomas’s usage, there is no difference whether one says "it is" or "it is being." 

But as for what he subjoins—that "to be" does not only signify something, etc.—he does not intend that if someone asks "what is the Moon?" or "what is thunder?", it would be a reasonable answer to say "it is being" or "it is something," as you seem to have thought. <gloss>o</gloss> For such a solution is ridiculous. Rather, it is like this: "to be" signifies something, especially according to the first way; it is that which can be reasonably answered to the question "what is it?"—for instance, it signifies being a substance, or an accident, or an animal, or a color, or something of this sort which might rightly be answered to one asking "what is it?" 

Blindness and evil, however, are none of these. That St. Thomas does not wish the first part of the division to be interpreted with your meaning, he explains himself in the *First Part, Question 48, Article 2*, where it is asked whether evil is in things. For responding to the second argument <gloss>q</gloss> he says this: "As it says in the sixth book of the *Metaphysics*, 'being' is said in two ways. In one way, according to which it signifies the entity of a thing as it is divided into the <term>ten predicaments</term> <note>Another term for the ten categories of Aristotle.</note>, and in this way it is convertible with 'thing'; and in this way, no privation is being, and thus neither is evil. In another way, 'being' is said as signifying the truth of a proposition, which consists in composition, the indicator of which is this word 'is'; and this is the 'being' that answers the question 'does it exist?' and thus we say that blindness 'is' in the eye, or any other privation. And in this way even evil may be called a being." These are Thomas’s words. 

You see, therefore, how he declares the first member of the division to be convertible with "thing." <gloss>r</gloss> And he does not deny that God is a "thing," nor whatever is good; for every good, both in that argument and in the first question on <meta>catchword: evil</meta>

If, therefore, an Idea is *being*, this will be because the existence of the Idea is distinct from the Idea. But the existence of an Idea cannot be located or imagined outside of God, if God is the Idea as was granted; therefore, it is necessary that there be composition in God." 

You say, moreover, that God is called "The One" by the Platonists because He is similar to unity, which, though it contains all numbers in potentiality—namely even and odd—is itself neither even nor odd. <gloss>y</gloss> By Hercules, what a subtle reason for naming! Aside from the fact that God cannot be similar to things (as Cicero and Thomas say)—for the model of the world is not similar to the world, nor is a man similar to a painting—no other cause can stand. 

For when a name is changed from one thing to another because of similarity or analogy, it is customary to call it by the proper name of that same thing. For we call a statue that imitates a man a "man," not "human-like." We also call a <term>topic</term> <note>original: *locum*; in logic, a 'place' or 'topic' from which arguments are drawn.</note>, which is a distinction of propositions or a "maximal proposition," a "place" based on the analogy of a physical place; we do not call it "place-like." Therefore, if God received His name from unity because of similarity, He should not be called "one" but rather "Unity" itself. <gloss>A</gloss> 

Furthermore, if every <term>concrete name</term> <note>A name that signifies both a quality and the subject possessing it, like "white" or "man," as opposed to "whiteness" or "humanity."</note> signifies one thing and another, why do the Platonists call God "the similar" rather than "Similarity" itself? <gloss>B</gloss> 

Furthermore, if matter is "one" according to the Platonists, as you write, and the unity of matter is not one thing and the matter another (which I don't think you would deny), by what reasoning can "one" be defended? For it is not similar to unity; otherwise, it would also be similar to God. 

Furthermore, you also previously said God is "one" because He is uniquely all things; but now <gloss>C</gloss> you seem to approve of the reasoning of the Platonists rather than that of Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist whose writings on the "Divine Names" were highly influential.</note>, perhaps having cast aside the former. If you still hold it, it remains for you to answer the arguments that have been written. 

For the <gloss>a</gloss> root upon which you rely to solve my objections is not true—namely, that God is neither *being* nor *essence*—as I have now fully declared. But now let us come to the definition of "truth" provided by you. You said in your earlier pamphlet that "truth" is defined by Augustine in this way: "Truth is that which is." And lest the definition of truth and being seem to be the same, you say it ought to be added in this way: "Truth is that which is that which it is said to be." <gloss>b</gloss> I...

Therefore, I opposed the definition in this way: that which is said to "be" seems to signify nothing other than to be that which it is called. Moreover, for a thing to be called by this name or that is for it to appear as this or that; wherefore it finally seemed to be concluded that to "be" that which is said is nothing other than to be what it appears to be. Since, therefore, there is no contradiction in appearing to be what one is, or appearing to be what one is not, I was proving that falsehood is not the negation of truth, provided the definition held firm.

But because you have now explained your definition more clearly, there will be no shortage of many more points that seem to disprove your formal definition. For you say, **Truth is that which is said.** <gloss>e</gloss> <note>original: "Verum est id quod dicitur." Pico is critiquing a specific Scholastic or Platonic definition here.</note> This means: truth is that which is, namely that which it is itself; for instance, gold is "true" gold because it is gold. But against this is the fact that if God did not exist and gold remained, gold would still be what it is, and it would be "true" [gold], yet it would not actually exist <note>In Pico's logic, "truth" requires a relationship to a divine Idea; without God, the thing might exist physically but lacks the "truth" of its archetype.</note>, since it would correspond to no <term>Idea</term> <note>In this context, an "Idea" is the divine blueprint or archetype in the mind of God.</note>. For you say later that things are "true" because they correspond and respond to Ideas.

If the true definition of a human is a **rational animal**, it is a contradiction to think that if God did not exist and a human were a **rational animal**, that the human would not be a human. Nor can that point be answered which was said elsewhere—namely the contradiction—that it is impossible for God not to exist while gold exists; for there is no such contradiction, as theologians, philosophers, and <term>dialecticians</term> <note>Logic experts who analyze arguments.</note> themselves openly confess. For it can be imagined that gold exists even if God does not exist, nor any first cause or first being at all. For those who judge that there are infinite worlds, or that the heavens are infinitely multiple, or many similar things, do not for that reason deny that the gold seen with the eyes and handled with the hands exists. 

Furthermore, whether there is a contradiction or not, the reasoning is not yet resolved. For I say this: If God did not exist, and gold were gold, it would be gold, but it would not be "true." Therefore, the formal definition of the "true" is not simply "to be that which it is." Just as it would not be a formal definition of a human if I said: if God did not exist and a human were a rational animal, he would not therefore be a human. For nothing can be deprived of its own definition, nor can a definition apply to anyone to whom the defined name cannot be fitted.

Furthermore, you cannot deny that gold is gold by nature prior to its corresponding to the Idea of God <gloss>f</gloss>, for the absolute is prior to the revealed. Therefore, even if gold is gold, it cannot be "true" unless, beyond the nature of gold, some likeness is added by which it responds to its exemplar—whether that likeness is something different from the gold itself or not, which is a question of its own.

Furthermore, you seem to posit a definition of <term>Being</term> <note>Latin: "ens." The most general category of anything that exists.</note> in this way: "Being is that which is." Otherwise, you would not say that the definition of Augustine <note>St. Augustine (354–430 AD), a foundational Church Father.</note> must be completed in this way: "Truth is that which is itself," lest if we only said "that which is" <gloss>g</gloss>, the definition of the "true" and of "being" should appear to be the same. 

If, therefore, the definition of being is "that which is," then by that same reasoning by which being is that which is, it is also itself and being. Therefore, by the same reasoning that something is a "being," it must also be "true," which is utterly false. Furthermore, if the true is that which it is <gloss>h</gloss>: **blindness** will be true, as will **death**, and **falsehood**, and altogether **non-being**. For blindness is blindness, and death is death, and falsehood is falsehood, and even non-being is non-being; any of these would be "true" in no...

If, therefore, God did not exist, then "God does not exist" would be neither false nor a contradiction. If, then, a falsehood is a negation of the true (as you posit), it would be "true" that God does not exist, if God were not to exist.

...it does not agree, nor does that whose definition it is. And if neither the one nor the other agrees simply, then it is not the case that every falsehood is simply "divided" <note>In scholastic logic, "division" is the opposite of "unity." Pico is arguing whether a false statement is internally "divided" or broken.</note>, for that cannot be granted. For every falsehood is simply and absolutely **non-being**. Since both are interchanged, by that same reasoning it is simply divided—if, that is, "divided" and "non-being" coincide. <margin>1</margin> Furthermore, every true thing is simply "one"; therefore, every false thing is simply "divided." For one is the negation of the other. Moreover, if I demonstrate that every falsehood is absolutely divided, what reason was there for you not to dare to state simply and absolutely that every falsehood is divided, but only when there is an opposition? 

We demonstrate the "division" of the false in this way: "Socrates is sitting" is false <note>Assuming Socrates is actually standing.</note>, but for "Socrates to be sitting" is not "Socrates sitting"; therefore, it is divided from itself. For if "Socrates sitting" is "Socrates sitting," and a "sitting Socrates" is a "sitting Socrates," both are joined <term>conjugated</term> <note>Referring to the logical connection between a subject and its properties.</note>. If, however, a "sitting Socrates" is "Socrates," then by a simple conversion, "Socrates is Socrates," and therefore "sitting is sitting," and therefore "he sits"—which is false. 

By the same reasoning, I will prove that a **chimera** <note>A mythological creature (lion-goat-snake) used by logicians to represent a "non-being" or an impossible concept.</note> is not a chimera, nor is "being a chimera" the same as "being a chimera." For if a chimera *is*, then a chimera is an animal. We understand a chimera to be an animal consisting of a goat and a stag <note>original: "animal ex hirco constans & ceruo"</note>, or something of this sort. But if it is an animal, it can live and die—which we do not agree upon, for we posit that a chimera can in no way be produced by nature, just as a "golden mountain" cannot be generated. Furthermore, if a chimera is some kind of animal, then an animal is a chimera; but no animal is a chimera. For every animal exists, and lives, and is simply a **being** and a "something." That which is *not*, is not an animal, except <term>equivocally</term> <note>i.e., using the same word for two different things, like a "drawn animal" vs. a "living animal."</note>. 

Therefore, a chimera is not a chimera by the same reasoning, nor is "to be a chimera" the same as "to be a chimera." For if "to be generated" is "to be moved," then generation is motion; therefore, if generation is not motion, then "to be generated" is not "to be moved." By equal reasoning, if "to be a chimera" is "to be a chimera," then a chimera is a chimera. For both are joined; yet, a chimera is *not* a chimera, as has already been proven; therefore, "to be a chimera" is not "to be a chimera." 

Furthermore, no chimera is a chimera; therefore, it is *true* that no chimera is a chimera; therefore, it is *false* that any chimera is a chimera. By the same reasoning, it will be shown that a **vacuum** is not a vacuum because it does not exist, nor is **blindness** blindness if nothing is blind. Nevertheless, "non-being" is always "non-being," for "not to be non-being" is true, just as "not to be a chimera" is both true and necessary. 

Why then was it necessary to fear that you might be refuted if you had stated simply and absolutely that every falsehood is divided in itself? There was no need to take refuge in contradiction. Next, you frankly confess that my argument—by which I proved that **Good** and **Evil** are contraries to each other—was not "dissolved" <note>meaning "refuted" or "untied."</note>, but you say it was not dissolved because there was no "knot" <note>original: "nodus"</note> in it. A clever excuse indeed! <margin>m</margin> But it is a wonder that if there was no "knot," how you were able to "untie" it. ...but evil is to be avoided. To seek and to avoid are contraries to one another, just as gathering and separating are. You might say it this way: "Being, by the very reason that it is being, is something to be desired (that is, the proper nature of being is to be desired), and non-being, by its own nature, is something to be avoided; therefore, they are contraries." You would be assembling a fine argument! Indeed, by this very form we have demonstrated that hot and cold, and white and black, are contraries. For the nature of the hot is to separate things of different kinds <term>heterogeneous</term>, while the nature of the cold is to bring them together; likewise, the nature of white is to disperse the sight, while that of black is to concentrate it. 

When you responded to my argument in person, you said that the proper nature of the good is not that it is "something to be sought"—though this is granted by all philosophers, especially the Latins, and Aristotle says in the *Ethics*, Book 1: "They have correctly defined the good by saying it is that which all things desire." <note>A foundational principle in Aristotelian philosophy.</note> This statement of yours seemed marvelous <note>Meaning "strange" or "astonishing" in this context.</note> to those listening. For if God is not "good" <note>In the sense of having "good" as a property.</note> and is certainly not "evil," how then can it be defended that evil is merely the negation of the good, if a middle ground is granted? 

Furthermore, if evil is the negation of the good, then "evil" and "not-good" are the same thing, for there is only one unique negation for one thing. It follows then: "It is not-good, therefore it is evil." Thus, an affirmation could be gathered from a negation. Furthermore, it does not even follow if evil is either a privation <note>A lack of something that should naturally be there, like blindness is a privation of sight.</note> or something "deprived." If it is something deprived, it is a subject, and therefore it is also a "being" and "good." If it is a privation, then it exists within a subject. But whatever exists is, in some way, a being and a good; therefore, it is not "not-good." 

Furthermore, you deny the truth of what Aristotle says in the *Categories*: namely, that good and evil are "genera of contraries" <note>This means they are the broad categories under which other opposites fall.</note>, something which neither Boethius nor the Latin commentators dare to deny. <note>Small circular reference mark</note> You, however, having set aside the Latin interpreters, flee only to Simplicius <note>A 6th-century Greek philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.</note>, who says that good and evil are "genera of contraries" in this sense: that of any two contraries, one is always "good" (meaning it is better) and the other is "evil" (meaning it is worse). Thomas Aquinas also reports this from Simplicius. But if one may oppose Simplicius, the counter-argument is what Aristotle says in the same place: not only is good the contrary to evil, but sometimes an evil is the contrary to another evil. <note>For example, the vice of cowardice is the contrary of the vice of recklessness; both are "evils" compared to the virtue of courage.</note> Indeed, if Aristotle calls that which is "better" the good, and that which is "worse" the evil, then the good will always be the contrary to the evil. Furthermore, if the good and evil which Aristotle says are "genera of contraries" are actually "better" and "worse," then good and evil would be placed in the category of *relatives*, among which are "better" and "worse." Yet Aristotle says that good and evil are not *in* a genus, but are themselves *genera*. <note>P-shaped reference mark</note> Finally, you wonder that I affirm—even following the opinion of Thomas—that good and evil are contraries, and that...

...cannot explain <note>The text begins mid-word, likely completing "claro" or "lucidius" (more clearly) from the previous page.</note> unless as it has been stated. Therefore, <term>Thomas [Aquinas]</term> <note>The influential 13th-century theologian.</note>—who says that <term>Simplicius</term> says those things are properly called <term>contraries</term> of which each is "something else"—when he explains the reason why "healthy" and "sick" are numbered among contraries, and not also "blind" and "seeing," must necessarily gather this from Simplicius, which <term>Aristotle</term> explains, which: 

> "whether it be true or false, is a matter of no importance in which one should wander."

But since in your last letter you think to call <term>evil</term> a <term>negation</term> <note>A simple "not," whereas "privation" is the lack of a quality something *ought* to have.</note> of good, you seem to be asking about an evil that is entirely evil; in the same way, I want to question you about the <term>false</term> as divided from the one <term>true</term> thing. **s** Whether you think a <term>chimera</term> <note>A mythical beast used here as a logical example of a "non-thing" or an impossible creature.</note> is entirely a **non-being**: If you deny it, you must necessarily contradict yourself, because you said before that a chimera is entirely a non-being and false. If, however, you grant it to be entirely a non-being, I shall proceed in this way: "non-being" and "entirely evil" are equivalent. A chimera, however, is entirely a non-being; therefore, it is also entirely evil. But this cannot be, for a chimera being [what it is] does not involve a logical contradiction. Therefore, it can be created by God. Now, whatever can exist, its existence is a good; therefore, that which can **t** be created can be good. But the potential for good is itself good; therefore, a chimera is not entirely evil. **u** Furthermore, a chimera can be understood both by God and by us; it can therefore exist within our mind and soul. Therefore, in whatever way it can exist, that which in any way can exist also participates in goodness in some way; therefore, a chimera is not entirely evil. 

Furthermore, nothing can be evil unless it is something to be avoided; but nothing can be fled or avoided unless it is known, either by the one who flees or by God who inserted the natural instinct for flight. It is therefore necessary that every evil can be known in some way; but knowledge is a certain good, and therefore the ability to be known is also a good, for the potential for a good is itself a good. **x** Furthermore, Aristotle in the 4th book of the *Metaphysics* says that negations and <term>privations</term> are in some way beings; indeed, he says that even "non-being" itself is in some way a "being," the sign of which (he says) is that we say "non-being **is** non-being." But whatever is a being in some way is also good in some way. A chimera, therefore—in which the term "non-being" is a true description—is in some way a being and is good. **z** Furthermore, evil is a privation of good, but every privation is a negation of a form in a subject naturally suited to possess that form and state. Therefore, nothing can be evil which is not capable of and suited for good; but the capacity and aptitude for good is itself good. Therefore, evil cannot be entirely evil, whence **y** <term>Augustine</term> <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), who famously argued that evil has no independent existence but is a corruption of good.</note> says that evil is always rooted in the good. 

***** Furthermore, if evil is a privation of good (as you say), how can it be a negation of good? For the opposition between privation and possession is one thing, and the opposition between affirmation and negation is quite another. 

Furthermore, it is your responsibility to show that the argument you previously made is valid, by which you proved from Aristotle and Thomas that God is not a "being" (*ens*); for I have weakened both of your points. Nor is it enough to say, "I know that sometimes the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> call God a 'being,' but I also know that among those same men God is sometimes not included under the name of 'being'." **A** Show me, I ask, in what place either Aristotle or the Aristotelians do not consider God under the name of "being"? **B** Moreover, if there is time, explain how you defend that God "is" and is "One," yet God is "not God." For if the word is understood, it is necessary that a certain description be formed by the mind, which being given, it follows immediately that God is God; for not even the poet <term>Simonides</term> <note>A Greek poet who, when asked by Hiero of Syracuse to define God, kept asking for more time because the more he thought about it, the more difficult the answer became.</note> would have asked for more time to respond...

He challenges his opponent to prove that God should not be classified as a "being" (ens) according to Aristotelian thought.</summary>

For "God" is that about which one asks what can or should be declared; it is not that which is declared about something else. Let us come, then, to your gold, which you are entirely unwilling to lose, even if God were to be lost. It is impossible for anything to exist if "Being" <note>original: *esse*; the act of existing</note> itself does not exist. It is therefore impossible for gold to exist if God does not exist. Furthermore, if God does not exist, then the infinite exists; if the infinite exists, then nothing exists, because if the infinite is, the finite is not. But even if the infinite is, then the infinite is not, because the infinite destroys itself, just as other things do which contain a contradiction. If nothing exists, then gold does not exist. I believe these points are sufficient for you, however ingenious a man you may be. **Farewell.**

### ANTONIO CITTADINO TO GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA
### Greetings. The Fourth Objections.

**I**t was not said that God is not <term>being</term> <note>Latin: *ens*; that which exists</note> because being in God stands for His essence, but because "to be" is not distinct from <term>essence</term> <note>Latin: *essentia*; the "what-it-is" of a thing</note>, which is a very different matter. Otherwise, the very "being" of a stone, which stands for its essence, would be neither a "being" nor a "good." For the "being" of a stone is not its essence <note>Cittadino is critiquing the idea that a thing's existence and its nature are the same</note>, but is itself for itself, both its own "to be" and its own essence. If one cannot ask "what they are" regarding negations and privations, then since they *do* exist, it is not enough to simply know that the thing being questioned exists in order to form the question "What is it?" Rather, one must know more: both that it is, and *what* it is. Therefore, to someone asking "What is it?", is it not ridiculous and irrational to answer "being" or "something"? This is true whether "being" is taken in the first or second sense. For if one asks what "sin" is, the question concerns the word rather than the thing itself. If something is a "being," then according to your position, it is a "being" because its "being" is factually different from its essence. You say that "humanity" is one thing, "man" is another; "white" or "whiteness" is one thing, a "white object" is another. Therefore, if an "Idea" is a being, it will be a being because the "being" of the Idea is different from the Idea itself. But an Idea is God. Therefore, the "being" of the Idea is something other than God. If so, there is a factual composition <note>A mixture of different parts, rather than being perfectly simple and unified</note> in God, not just a conceptual one. According to the definition of derivatives <note>words derived from a root noun, like "brave" from "bravery"</note>, "the one" is derived from "unity." However, God, according to your...

### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

...according to your position, God is called "one" by a similarity to unity; therefore, the predication <note>The act of declaring or attributing a quality to a subject</note> by which the Platonists say "God is one" does not actually concern the substance of God. Furthermore, when we say "God is one," you think that what is signified is not *what* He is, but *how* He is. But a "mode" <note>A way of being or a temporary state</note> belongs to the category of <term>accidents</term> <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that a thing has, but which is not essential to its nature—like the color of a shirt.</note>; therefore, the term "one" as applied to God is not substantive, nor does it concern the actual thing. It is irrelevant whether I have not studied the Platonic sect or am ignorant of the Greek language, for that knowledge alone is not enough to defend the teachings of the Academics <note>The "Academics" refers here to the followers of Plato's Academy.</note>. If God did not exist, and gold did exist, he says that gold would be gold, and gold would also be "not-gold"; therefore, it would be gold. 

If, then, the definition of truth is established, truth will fit no <term>Idea</term> <note>Referring to the Platonic "Forms"—the perfect, abstract patterns of all things.</note>. If the statement "Socrates is sitting" is neither true nor false because it is not a necessary fact, I will certainly defend the view that a true affirmation or negation is not found in just anything; for in some things, neither one nor the other holds a necessary truth. If good and evil exist in things, but truth and falsehood exist in the soul, where is your opposition between affirmation and negation? For a negation <term>posits</term> <note>Places or establishes as a fact</note> nothing. How is a chimera <note>A mythical beast; used in logic to represent something that can be imagined but has no physical reality.</note> also both in real things and in the soul, if it is entirely a non-being and a falsehood? Especially since you think that non-being and evil are interchangeable terms. 

If it is true that "blindness is blindness," who cannot see that blindness is "true"? For they are the same thing; by the mere fact that blindness is established, the fact that "blindness is blindness" is also established, and if it is taken away, the fact is taken away. By the same reasoning, "Socrates" and "Socrates being Socrates" are the same thing, and both are produced by the same act of generation; and by itself, God and "God being God" are also the same, for both are eternal and represent the primary truth. 

If everything false is simply "divided" <note>Separated from reality or internal consistency</note>, as you do not deny has been proven, it should not have been said that a falsehood is divided only under this one condition—that is, as long as it is false. For if every human is simply and absolutely <term>risible</term> <note>original: "risibilis"; a technical term in logic meaning "capable of laughter." It was the classic example of a property that belongs uniquely to humans.</note>, one does not need to add a contradiction that restricts it by saying, "every human is capable of laughter as long as he is a human." Nor should a restriction be added just because not all false things are equally divided, or equally false; for not all beings are equally good, yet all things are absolutely good. 

How one concludes that good and evil are contraries—provided that "seeking" and "fleeing" are contraries—will be easily established if the logic of contrary motions has been sufficiently understood by you. Why are you surprised if I say the Latins do not deny Aristotle, whom Simplicius <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist who wrote famous commentaries on Aristotle.</note> denies, but Boethius <note>A 6th-century philosopher who sought to reconcile Plato and Aristotle; Pico views him as a primary authority.</note> does not? Does it follow that I am either failing to imitate Boethius or that I am praising the Barbarians? <note>Pico famously defended the medieval "Barbarian" philosophers (like Thomas Aquinas) for their rigorous logic, even if their Latin style was unpolished.</note> It is a wonder you even call me a man! Indeed, I would call you "wonderful" for thinking that while I imitate Boethius, I simultaneously despise him and follow the "Barbarians," just because I have set Simplicius aside for the moment. 

If good and evil are contraries, you wish to prove that a chimera is something that exists in the nature of things; but if it were understood in what sense I called good and evil contraries (which you either do not yet wish to, or cannot, understand), you would have proven nothing regarding the chimera. You are greatly surprised that I call certain <term>privations</term> <note>The absence of a quality that should normally be present, like blindness being the privation of sight.</note> "half-full," and you prove they do not exist in this way: "Evil is nothing, therefore it is not a 'half-full' privation." But I, following your own argument, shall say this: sickness...

<note>This section begins mid-sentence, discussing the nature of evil.</note> ...is evil, therefore it is nothing; it is not, then, a semi-complete <term>privation</term> <note>In philosophy, a "privation" is the absence of a quality that should normally be present, like blindness is the absence of sight.</note>. However, sickness is a certain kind of privation; therefore, it is not a semi-complete privation of either health or some particular good, but rather a full and perfect one—which is impossible. Therefore, imperfect privations are "semi-complete," such as sickness, rarity, ugliness, or blindness (which is a perfect privation of sight, but an imperfect privation of the good, for it does not take away the entirety of the good that exists within the one who sees). 

If it is true, as you write, that every evil leaves something of the good behind, then the <term>chimera</term> <note>A mythical beast often used by philosophers to represent something that can be imagined but has no real existence.</note>—which is entirely non-being and evil—retains something of the good. If, however, it preserves something of the good, then it is not entirely evil, nor is it entirely non-being. Even though the power by which it could be created and exist resides in God, and the concept by which it can be understood resides in the mind, this does not prevent the chimera from being "good" and "being" in potential. For the potential of God and the potential of the chimera are different in their reasoning; nor do we deny that the **Antichrist** is good in potential, since the power by which he is able to exist is partly in matter, in the heavens, and in man. 

Furthermore, how could a chimera exist if, in the meantime, all thought and power of God were excluded? It would be entirely non-being and evil. For in order to be "non-being," it certainly cannot be "evil": for evil is a privation that exists within a subject <note>A "subject" is the underlying thing that possesses qualities, like a body being the subject for the quality of health.</note>, and that subject must necessarily participate in goodness; otherwise, it could not be a subject at all. That which is entirely non-existent cannot act as a subject. 

You have not yet disproven what was said by me, even though you confirm it with the authority of **Simplicius** <note>A 6th-century commentator on Aristotle.</note>, except that you claim Simplicius does not say it—but there was no reason to boast about that. For I did not say that **Aristotle** believed that every single being exists either through itself or by <term>accident</term> <note>Something that happens by chance or is a non-essential property.</note>, nor did I falsely attribute anything to **Blessed Thomas** <note>St. Thomas Aquinas.</note> regarding this. Although every privation is a certain kind of negation, it is not yet established that there isn't one type of opposition between affirmation and negation, and another between privation and habit <note>In this context, "habit" refers to the presence of a quality, the opposite of privation.</note>. Nor is it necessary that if evil is the privation of good, "evil" and "not-good" must be interchangeable.

As for your defense, by which you wish to maintain that "God is not God," I consider it consistent with neither the truth nor with **Blessed Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential Christian Neoplatonist.</note>. Blessed Dionysius never denied that God is God; rather, as Blessed Thomas interprets him, no name can completely explain the nature of God, nor does he think for any other reason that affirmations about the gods are "incompatible." 

But you say that the name of God, if it has a description, has the nature of a subject, but not of a <term>predicate</term> <note>In logic, the "subject" is what the sentence is about, and the "predicate" is what is said about the subject. Pico is debating whether we can truly "say" anything about God.</note>. Yet even if this is granted, the argument stands. For let *A* be the "definition of the name," and let it be said in this way: "God is," for *A*—the definition of anything—is predicated of that of which it is the definition; therefore, by a simple conversion, "*A* is God," and thus "**God is God**." 

Likewise, you say that when it is asked whether God is something other than God or not, one must know what is conceived by the name "God." Whatever is given, you say, "I will say that God is something else," for He is above everything that can be conceived. But does not such a solution contradict itself? For if you confess a proposition of this kind—namely, that "God is above that which can be conceived"—are you not openly affirming something about God? Let the definition of the name, therefore, be that very statement: "that which is above all that can be conceived," and the argument will still hold force. Furthermore, it follows that God is above all...

...everything that can be conceived; therefore, God cannot be conceived, for otherwise he would be above himself. Thus, he could neither be loved nor worshipped. ->Antonio of Faenza, distinguished philosopher, Greetings.<-

**A**lthough by the death of my uncle Giovanni Pico, all the eagerness and hope of my studies—which had been placed almost entirely in him—has withered away, I had nonetheless hoped while he lived that the study of philosophy might be restored to its pristine purity, yet enriched with great resources, and that the Christian faith, with errors utterly eliminated and heresies driven out, might be fortified like a mighty tower against its enemies. Yet I was not so struck down in spirit that I did not labor with all my might to ensure that those nocturnal labors <note>original: "lucubrationes," referring to scholarly work done by lamplight late at night.</note> and unfinished works, which flowed from that man so admirable in every branch of letters, would not utterly perish. 

Therefore, looking out for myself and for our people, I hastened to Florence by the quickest possible routes and took every care I could so that whatever had been noted down by him—though unpolished and unexamined—might be committed into our power. Our efforts were not entirely in vain; for even if the accounts were not yet open nor the heir known, the chests were nevertheless opened so that we might inspect and turn over all the commentaries. We saw in those scattered paper volumes the man's incredible zeal, his all-encompassing reading, and concepts admirable beyond the grasp of the human mind. Truly, however, in the arrangement of his writings there was a lack of care that cannot be praised; everything was scattered and dissipated here and there—but more on this another time. While we were unrolling these works with diligent care, his short work *Of Being and the One*—published nearly four years before his death—fell into my hands, along with three letters written to him by you and his responses to them. Because of the novelty of the matter, I did not merely read them through, but drank them in...

## On Being and the One

...but, as they say, having almost swallowed <note>original: "devoratis"; meaning he had suppressed or ignored the rumors initially.</note> these objections (for I had recognized through rumor that this had happened, but I did not yet have enough certainty about how much weight it carried), I began to think and deliberate with myself whether I should give that work to the printers to be published along with the other works I had compiled and judged worthy of publication, making no mention of your objections. Or whether it would be more advisable if it went out into the public at once attacked by these obstacles on one side and fortified with defenses <note>original: "propugnaculis"; literally "bulwarks" or "ramparts," referring here to intellectual defenses.</note> on the other. After a long discussion of the matter, the latter opinion finally settled in my mind. Indeed, it would seem to bear marks of infamy when encountering learned men if the work did not just fear its accusers, but—like one lacking confidence in his conscience—did not rightly dare to summon them to judgment. Similarly, it seemed appropriate that it should go accompanied by responses, as if with witnesses to defend the cause of innocence.

I did not doubt that our decision would be praised by honest men, since I would have had to either allow my deceased uncle <note>The author here is Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola, referring to his famous uncle Giovanni Pico.</note>—a man who truly deserved much from me—to be deprived in some part of the fame of his celebrated learning by not publishing such a book, or, if it went forth alone, to always leave an opening for the most wicked detractors to bring accusations, not having called to court the arguments that had been prepared through several letters on both sides, both by objecting and by repelling. 

But when some letters were presented by our Christopher Saxolus <note>A physician and citizen of Modena who moved in the Picos' intellectual circle.</note>, both a citizen and a physician, in which it was signified to us that you had forged a fourth letter on this matter which had lacked a response (as you claimed), the matter was called into question again. Once more I was made to be of a wavering opinion, thinking the judgment already delivered had to be weighed more exactly when a final accuser pressed the case and there was no one to act as an advocate <note>original: "patrocinaretur"; legal terminology for someone defending a client in court.</note>. Then a certain itch <note>original: "titillatio"; a stirring or prompting of the spirit.</note> to take up the defense entered my mind, though it was not immediately clear where I should turn to maintain silence. 

On one hand, the man's modesty and kindness toward everyone moved my mind, as did the skill and sharpness of his talent in unraveling and dissolving difficult knots and inexplicable riddles <note>original: "scirpis"; literally "rushes," used metaphorically for intricate problems or puzzles.</note> even on the spot. Thus, I began to think that your last letter had perhaps not been safely delivered; from that, I thought it likely that he *had* written back, but if your letters were indeed delivered to a faithful messenger, they were lost on the journey either by the negligence of the couriers (as often happens) or by some other accident. 

Finally, in the explanations of your earlier questions, it occurred to me that you had often complained of the same things being repeated and often doubted the same points. For that reason, I immediately ran through the main points of your entire controversy to see if, perhaps in the first responses, something could be found by which I might show that the requirements of the fourth letter had been sufficiently met in part before it was even written. The matter succeeded according to my wish, and I found so many things supporting the opposite view that I have answered the objections of the last letter as much as possible, if not in words, then in substance, so that you can recognize the knots of those letters opened in large part by the solutions to your previous questions. We have added many things sought as testimony even from great authors, all of which I would wish you to think were done by me for no other reason than to guard against the unrefined and insolent critics of philosophy and the malevolent...

Otherwise, my dear Anthony, I would have most gladly omitted the work I have undertaken from the very beginning. I would have done so both to avoid appearing to enter into controversies (which I abhor, even if I were pleading a most just cause) and to ensure I did not deviate from the true path of philosophy. 

I began to travel this path after my time with horses and arms <note>Gianfrancesco had a military and political career before fully dedicating himself to the philosophical and religious legacy of his uncle.</note>—though I have caught the scent of a few "little flowers" of literature since I was a boy—under the guidance of my uncle Giovanni Pico and our friend Giovanni Mainardi <note>Giovanni Mainardi (1462–1536) was a celebrated physician and a close member of the Pico circle.</note>, following my interactions with great leaders. This was at a time when the knowledge of nature was being directed not toward sweating through literary contests, but toward recognizing the Founder of nature itself. Philosophical meditations should, of their own accord, always invite us to investigate the deepest meanings of the divine oracles. This is the end of all studies; by these, the way to heaven is revealed to us—provided, however, that we do not cultivate them for the sake of capturing our own glory, but so that we can both know our God more easily and love Him more fervently, and thus more readily follow what He has commanded to be done and flee what He has taught us to avoid. 

Here then is the reason for this burden I have undertaken and the explanation of the business with you. It is most just, as it seems; therefore, it should be borne by you with an even mind. Indeed, I might even have thought I could use these writings of ours as messengers to confirm the goodwill between us, which was so auspiciously contracted in Ferrara. For when I arrived there in recent days, and you deigned to visit me out of your kindness, we spoke of literature and of the death of my uncle and his many works that were begun but not finished. Having perceived my intention to respond to you and to untie your arguments, you showed yourself to be so far from being offended that you even praised what I was going to do. 

But as we now approach the business itself, let us first apply our hands to dissolving the first objection. It is of this sort: It was not said that God is not "being" <term>ens; the philosophical concept of a thing that exists</term> because "to be" <term>esse; the act of existing</term> in God stands for His essence, but because His "to be" is not different from His essence—which is a very different thing. Otherwise, the "to be" of a stone, which stands for its essence, would be neither a being nor good. For the "to be" of a stone is not its essence, but is itself both its "to be" and its essence. 

To this we shall respond very easily. But first, I will ask you to remember the things written by Pico himself for the sake of this matter, lest he should seem to have uttered conflicting words. In that commentary *On Being and the One* <note>Giovanni Pico's famous 1491 treatise *De Ente et Uno*, which attempted to reconcile Plato and Aristotle.</note> (which he also mentioned in the responses to your objections), he not only did not approve of Amelius, Iamblichus, Syrianus <note>These were Neoplatonist philosophers who argued that the ultimate Principle (The One) is "beyond being."</note>, and many other Platonists who said God is not "being," but throughout the entire treatise he principally worked to show—not only from the teaching of Aristotle but also from that of Plato—that God both is, and is properly called, "being." But he also showed there is a certain way of speaking which, if followed, makes it not inconsistent with the truth to say that God is greater than the name "being." # On Being and the One

...account might be taken of authority and of Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent scholastic theologian.</note>, lest—to use his own words—those most learned and holy men should seem to be entirely insane who said that God is not "being," but rather "above being" <note>original: *super ens*. This Neoplatonic idea suggests God transcends the category of "being" entirely.</note>. One of these men repeated this opinion a thousand times, while the other occasionally adopted it. But let us return to our own points. Since it has been said in this way that God is not "being" for this reason, we assert that what was put forward is that "existence" <term>esse [to be]</term> in God stands in place of "essence" <term>essentia [what a thing is]</term>. You object to this, claiming it was asserted not for this reason but for that one—namely, that existence is simply not distinct from essence—thinking these two are entirely different. I, however, contend that the one is an opening and clarification of the other. 

For when it is said that God is not "being" because in Him existence is not something separated from essence, nothing else is being asserted than that in God, existence serves as His essence. Nor by this statement—namely, that existence in God is not something other than His essence—are we told that essence exists in God [as a separate category], as is clearly seen through the words of the one against whom you argued. For [my] uncle <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note> refuted your objection, which concerned this very matter, saying: "For the Platonists, when they say this, do not mean that essence and existence exist in God [as two things], but that they do not differ in Him." Rather, existence in God holds the place that essence holds in other things, so that for Him there is nothing other than existence itself in place of essence.

As for your belief that it is entirely incongruous that the "existence" of a stone cannot be called "being" and "good," you will perhaps change your mind if you consider what is said by Thomas Aquinas (whom we have called upon as a sort of judge of this controversy) in the first part of the *Summa*, Question 45, Article 4. There you will openly recognize that the "existence" itself which falls into the composition of an essence should be called neither "being" nor "created," since he pronounces that all non-subsistent forms and accidents, and other things of that kind, can be called "co-existent" and "con-created" rather than "created" and "beings." 

Wherefore, by his followers—most notably Capreolus <note>Jean Capréolus (c. 1380–1444), known as the 'Prince of Thomists,' a major defender of Aquinas’s thought.</note>—the question is raised regarding the distinction between being and essence: whether the "existence" of created things should be included in the number of true beings or of created things. If it does not receive the name "being," then without doubt it does not receive the name "good," since "being" and "good" follow one another and are reciprocal in the same scope <note>A core medieval principle: whatever has being is good, and whatever is good has being.</note>. 

In the second place, you argue in this manner: if in negations and privations <note>A 'privation' is the absence of a quality that should be present, like blindness being the privation of sight.</note> one cannot ask "what they are," since they *are*, it is not enough to form the question "what is it?" simply to know that the thing asked about exists; rather, one must know both that it exists and *what* it is. Therefore, to one asking "what is it?", the answer "being" or "something" is given ridiculously and irrationally, whether "being" is taken in the first or second sense. But if it is asked "what is sin?", the question concerns the word rather than the thing. 

To this objection, we respond that he [Giovanni Pico] never said that in privations and negations one cannot ask what they were, but rather that "what" <note>original: *quid*</note> could not be answered. He put this forward for the sake of Thomas, whom he cited—addressing you who doubted this in previous letters, whether it was true or false—with these words: "You must admit it is true unless you abandon your Thomas." We find this also asserted by Aegidius Romanus <note>Giles of Rome (c. 1243–1316), a student of Aquinas and a major philosopher in his own right.</note> in the second book of his commentaries on the theological *Sentences*. For it is enough to form the question "what is it?" to know that the thing...

...about which existence one inquires, nor is it necessary for the person who is about to track down what a thing is to know that the thing "is" or is "something" in the first way, but only in the second way—that is, simply that it exists. 

But if you were to contend that you understood that a question can be formed to which an affirmative and correct answer can be given: First, if you think that a question cannot be correctly formed unless the thing being asked about is of such a nature that an answer can be returned to that question through it, I do not agree with you. For it is the opinion of **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BC), whose logical works formed the basis of medieval education.</note> that one can inquire whether a centaur exists or not, even though a centaur is not the kind of thing that can provide an answer to the question "does it exist?" since it is a mere fable, a mere figment of the imagination. 

Similarly, I also oppose you if you believe that the person asking this must already know [the essence]; for (as we have shown) the person who correctly inquires into *what* a thing is does not need to know more than the fact that it *is*. Therefore, if someone knows that a thing is "something," it is not ridiculous to answer that it is "something" to someone who does not know and is inquiring about it. 

As for the fact that we are not accustomed to teaching those who ask "what a thing is" that it is merely a "being" <term>ens [a thing that exists]</term> or "something" (so that we might answer more fully), this happens because, having already established that it is something, they would still be searching for what *kind* of being it might be. We therefore satisfy not only their explicit request but also their desire for discovery, by dissolving their conceived but unuttered questions by anticipating them with our answers. 

However, those words of yours—that if it is asked "what is sin?", the question concerns the word rather than the thing—which were part of your objection against you, seem to have brought little weight to the response. For when you had previously argued from the opinion of **Thomas** <note>St. Thomas Aquinas.</note>—namely, that "being" <term>ens</term> is used in the first way for that which answers the question "what is it?", and that to someone asking what it is that preserves and moves the world, "God" is reasonably answered (from which you concluded that God is "being" and "something" in the first way)—he replied: "See how much you are mistaken; evil, according to Thomas, is not the kind of thing that allows us to answer someone asking what it is by saying 'it is something' or 'it is a being.'" And yet, to someone asking "what is sin?", we can answer "it is evil." 

Therefore, your response does not help you at all—namely, that if it is asked "what is sin?", the question is of the name rather than the thing. For the question "What is it that governs the world?" is no more a question of a name (although there is a different reasoning here and there) than "What is sin?", since He who governs the world—namely God—does not have a <term>quiddity</term> <note>quidditas: a scholastic term for the "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing.</note>, as the more recent thinkers say. This is confirmed most clearly by everyone except those who place Him within a "category" <note>Aristotelian categories (like substance, quality, quantity). Most theologians argued God is "beyond category."</note>. 

And as the most holy **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-6th century mystical theologian who argued God is "beyond being."</note> says—the prince of our theology after the Apostles—He has neither a name nor a definition. Furthermore, this response of yours does not even harmonize with what you said before; previously you said that evil itself is not "nothing" but is "something positive," but now you confess that a question is formed only regarding its name. 

You oppose for a third time with these words: If something is "being" <term>ens</term>, then according to your position it is "being" because its "existence" <term>esse</term> is, in reality, something different from its "essence" <term>essentia</term>. You say that **humanity** is one thing, a **human** another; **whiteness** <term>albedo</term> is one thing, and a **white thing** <term>res alba</term> another. Therefore, if an **Idea** <note>Referring to Platonic Ideas or Forms.</note> is "being," it will be "being" for the reason that the existence of the Idea is different from...

<header>On Being and the One.</header>

# On Being and the One.

...idea. For an Idea is God; therefore, the existence of the Idea would be something other than God, and consequently, there would be a composition in God according to the thing itself <note>original: "secundum rem"; referring to a real, ontological division as opposed to a mental distinction</note> and not just according to reason <note>original: "secundum rationem"; a conceptual distinction made by the mind for the sake of analysis</note>. To these points, we say that an answer has already been provided. For since you argued using nearly the same means as you now use in your third letter, he responded that this composition of being and essence in divine matters exists according to reason, and not according to reality. Therefore, we deny the first proposition of this hypothetical syllogism which you bring forward; for even if in created things essence differs from being <note>original: "esse"</note>, it does not necessarily follow from this that whatever can in any way be called "being" <term>ens [a thing that exists]</term> must be composed of essence and being (or existence) as if from parts. Thus, Ideas—which are the models of created things—do not possess an essence and existence that are distinct in reality. Rather, this "composition" is something we create when we consider an Idea as a model-cause of the essence and being (or existence) found in created things. We apply this same composition and distinction even to the simplest things; and we call it "according to reason" when our intellect has fashioned it. The **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle</note> use this common distinction very frequently—one which, as he says, was repeated by **Antipater** <note>Antipater of Tarsus, a Stoic philosopher</note>, mentioned by **Posidonius** <note>A Stoic philosopher and polymath</note>, and recorded in the letters of **Seneca** <note>The Roman Stoic philosopher and statesman</note>. For that reason, we can say in this way that an Idea is "composed" of essence and existence according to reason, and we can call it "being"—namely, by considering it as the model for creatures which *are* composed of essence and being (which differ in reality). However, we do not place this composition in God when we contemplate Him not as the model for others, but as He who enjoys Himself in the innermost sanctuary of His own divinity.

Fourthly, you say that according to the definition of denominatives <note>A grammatical term for a word derived from another, like "just" from "justice"</note>, "one" <note>original: "unus"</note> is a denominative from "unity" <note>original: "unitate"</note>. But according to your position, God is called "one" from a likeness to unity; therefore, this predication (by which the **Platonists** say "God is One") does not pertain to the substance of God. Furthermore, when we say "God is One," you think that what is signified is not *what* He is, but *how* He is. But a "mode" <note>A specific quality or manner of being</note> belongs to the category of accidents <note>Non-essential qualities that can change without destroying the thing itself</note>; therefore, the word "one" in God is not substantive. You suggest that I have either not learned the Platonic sect or am ignorant of the Greek language—but that is not enough to defend the discipline of the **Academics** <note>The followers of Plato's Academy</note>. But the response is easy: since it has been said by the Platonists that the "One" predicated of God is substantive and not merely denominative, it has been correctly asserted. And again, since it was affirmed that He is called "One" because He is similar to Unity, this is not incongruous; nor can it be said on that account that the term is not substantive. For even if a name is adapted to someone from a property or likeness of some thing, it does not necessarily follow that the name is not substantive, provided it is accepted as a substantive name—one which signifies not by way of an adjective <note>original: "per modum adiacentis"; literally "by way of lying adjacent," describing an attribute</note>, but as something standing by itself. Indeed, it is so clear that the "One" predicated of God is understood not as something inherent but as something standing [independently] that it needs no proof. You have, therefore, the property from which the name is taken; applying it does not take away its status as a substantive. For your **Thomas** <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican theologian</note>—or rather, ours—since in [other] places...

<meta>This page continues the defense of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s metaphysical arguments, likely written by his nephew Gianfrancesco Pico or a close associate. It addresses specific logical objections raised by Antonio Cittadini regarding the names we give to God and the relationship between God and existence.</meta>

->Giovanni Pico della Mirandola<-

In other places, and especially in the first part, he notes that the thing which a name is meant to signify differs from the property from which the name is derived. <gloss>it is derived</gloss> For example: he explains that this name "stone" <note>original: "lapis"</note> is used to signify that substance which is called by that name, but it is derived from a related property—namely, that it "hurts the foot" <note>A common medieval folk etymology for the Latin *lapis*: *laedere* (to hurt) + *pes* (foot).</note>. From this, he teaches in another place that it was adopted by the Grammarians to write that a name denotes "substance with quality," which **John Duns Scotus** <note>A hugely influential 13th-century philosopher and theologian known as the "Subtle Doctor."</note> also affirms in his book of commentaries on the *Sentences*. Therefore, my dear **Antonio**, when we speak of God, we speak truly and we speak as if using a "substantive" name <note>A noun that stands for a thing’s essence, rather than an "adjective" which describes a quality.</note>, because we both conceive and predicate Him through the "mode of standing" <note>original: "per modum stantis"; a grammatical pun on "substantive," suggesting God is the ultimate underlying reality that "stands" or remains.</note>. 

Furthermore, when we say a name is applied to God based on a likeness to unity and its properties, we approach the truth as much as is permitted to us. We use a fitting term to indicate that divine nature, even though it remains utterly beyond description <note>original: "ineffabilem"</note> above all created things; for God is the principle of all things that exist, just as "one" is the principle of all numbers. From these words, you will also find the solution to your other argument concerning the "mode" <term>mode [the specific way a thing exists or is expressed]</term>, which you claim can only belong to the category of accidents. Specifically, in this statement: "God is one," the way in which God is one is signified, and yet the word "one" remains substantive when applied to God. 

If you consider from what source the name begins and to what thing it is attributed for the purpose of denoting it, you can also recognize the solution to your doubt quite briefly from the words of my uncle <note>The author is referring to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note>, when he says: "How can you say I follow the reasoning of the **Platonists** rather than that of **Dionysius** <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian mystic who synthesized Christian thought with Neoplatonic philosophy.</note>, since you have never actually read either Dionysius or the Platonists—though you boast of it with a loud voice?" You should know that for the Platonists, the "Deity-type" <note>original: "Deitypum"; the divine model or archetype</note> is unity, and for Dionysius, God is "uniquely all things." One could not ask for a more direct solution. For when he says the "Deity-type" is unity, he refers to likeness and mode; but when he says God is "uniquely all things," he refers to the substance, though it has been asserted that these are ultimately the same thing. Indeed, in the Greek language (which he knew well), the abstract and the concrete can sometimes be signified by the same word.

Regarding the solution to your fifth doubt, many words are not needed. He says: "If God did not exist and gold existed, gold would be gold and it would not be gold." You add these words: "Therefore, it would be gold. But if the definition of truth remains, it will be a truth that fits no Idea." I beg you, add these few words which follow from his own: "How can there be a truth that fits no Idea?" What am I saying? An impossibility, of course, gives birth to an impossibility <note>original: "impossibile scilicet impossibile parit"</note>; and therefore it is no wonder if, from your premise, you make whatever you wish follow from the impossibility. For if God did not exist and gold did exist, it would be a truth fitting no Idea because an impossibility is sired by an impossibility—a point on which not only the logicians but also the theologians agree. For if you ask the Carmelite **John Baconthorpe** <note>An English philosopher (d. 1348) known as the "Prince of the Averroists."</note> whether it is possible for gold to exist and God not to exist, he will answer you in his first book on the *Sentences* that no thing whatsoever, of any kind, can be understood unless God is understood first. Since God is involved in the understanding of all things, you can conclude for yourself whether this is beyond all controversy...

# On Being and the One

Bb 4

among novice logicians <term>dialecticians; those who study the art of formal logic</term> it might be stated that it is impossible for "gold to exist" and "God not to exist." But we will speak of this again at the end of the work. If you later consult the **Cardinal of Cambrai** <note>Pierre d'Ailly (1351–1420), a famous theologian and philosopher.</note>, you will hear a man practiced in all philosophy say in the first book of his commentaries on the *Sentences* that a contradiction follows from any impossibility. 

In the sixth place, you said that if the statement "Socrates is sitting" were neither true nor false—as he [Pico] had asserted because it was not a necessary state—then you could defend the idea that it is not true that either a negation or an affirmation must hold in every case, since in such instances neither one nor the other possesses necessary truth. 

Solving this objection, we respond that this statement—namely, the truth or falsehood of "Socrates is sitting"—is not necessarily determined in itself; however, it does not follow from this that the affirmation is not true or the negation is not true for any given instance. Nevertheless, if you understand it in the way he teaches, you could also deny that in every case an affirmation or negation is "true" in the sense that one part is *necessarily* true. For he says that "I am sitting" is always either true or false, because I am always either sitting or not sitting; but when it is said that "me sitting" is neither true nor false, it means that this proposition does not determine truth or falsehood for itself by its own nature, as necessary propositions <note>Such as "2+2=4" or "God exists," which are true by definition and cannot be otherwise.</note> do. But since it can be true when I am sitting, and false when I am not sitting, the proposition is indeterminate in itself toward both possibilities.

Furthermore, you press against some of his words regarding good and evil, truth and falsehood, which he had proposed exist in things and in the soul in this way: "If good and evil are in things, and truth and falsehood are in the soul, where is your opposition of affirmation and negation?" For a negation posits nothing. How is even a **Chimera** <note>A mythological beast; in logic, it represents a concept that is "non-being" because it cannot exist in reality.</note> in things and in the soul? If it is altogether non-being, and false because it is non-being, then you might think evil and being are mutually convertible <note>A scholastic principle where "being" and "good" are seen as the same thing; therefore, evil is a "lack" of being.</note>. 

But I beg you to pay attention and notice that evil and good are pronounced to be "in things" for the same reason that truth and falsehood are considered "concerning the soul." For truth and falsehood are not in the things themselves, as **Aristotle** writes in the sixth book of *First Philosophy* <note>The *Metaphysics*.</note>, but in the mind. It does not follow from this that a thing which is altogether evil is a "true thing." Indeed, the truth and falsehood of which Aristotle makes mention in that place are "complex" <note>Propositions or statements, rather than simple objects.</note>. Nor does it follow that if good and evil are in things, they cannot be opposed contradictorily. This is because the "evil" which is said to be in things is not called "in things" so that it is understood to be a real thing itself, but because it is considered regarding the things themselves—that is, insofar as it deprives things of their perfections and causes them to be "not good." 

The **Chimera**, however, is not in things itself, because it is altogether non-being and altogether evil. Yet if it were possible for nature to produce it, it would be a thing, and it would be good. It is "false" insofar as it is nothing at all existing and fits no Idea <note>Platonic Ideas or divine archetypes.</note>. Nor do we affirm that the Chimera itself is in the soul, but rather the *notion* of the Chimera is there. That notion, as a certain "thing," is both good and true; it is only "false" insofar as it represents a Chimera, since the Chimera itself is both nothing and evil.

After this, you believed you could prove that **blindness** is true, which he had denied; and if he had neither denied nor conceded that "blindness is blindness" is true, but...

<meta>This page continues the technical defense of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's metaphysics against the objections of Antonio Cittadini. It specifically addresses the logical distinction between a "thing" (like blindness or Socrates) and the "truth of a proposition" about that thing.</meta>
