-> # Giovanni Pico della Mirandola <-

...had said they were far different. And you argued in this way: if "blindness being blindness" is true, and who would not see that blindness is true, for they are the same. For if only blindness is established, then this fact—that blindness is blindness—is established; and if it is taken away, the fact is taken away. By the same reasoning, "Socrates" and "Socrates being Socrates" are the same, and both are generated by the same generation. Likewise, God himself and "God being God" are the same, for both are eternal and the first truth. 

But I, my Antonio, contend on the contrary and deny that those things which you assert are the same. For when one of those things you assert is established, the other is not necessarily established. For if only blindness were established, with no intellect considering it, blindness would indeed exist, but this statement "blindness is blindness" would not exist <note>This is a classic distinction in medieval logic: a thing (like a stone or blindness) can exist in reality, but a "proposition" or "truth" about that thing requires a mind to formulate it.</note>. For this reason, the argument concerning God and the generation of Socrates is also dissolved. For Socrates is generated by himself, but the fact "that Socrates is Socrates" is not, since <term>complexes</term> <note>In logic, a "complex" refers to a proposition or sentence made of multiple parts, whereas a "simple" is a single word or concept.</note> are not generated. 

Even if I were to grant you that they are the same, we still say that what you were concluding does not follow because of the different <term>mode of signifying</term>—namely, in a complex and incomplex way. For this argumentation would be of no value: "blindness" and "blindness being blindness" are the same; but this [the latter] is true, therefore the former [blindness itself] is also true. By that same logic, it would follow that "this is complex, therefore the other is also complex," which is absurd, since "blindness" is a simple name, not a complex one. Or, if an enunciation is something else, then "blindness being true" is one thing, and "it is true that blindness is blindness" is another. 

And although these points would suffice for my uncle's defense, nevertheless, lest you believe that more ways of defending and protecting him are lacking, and so that a more complete response may reach you, I would have you know that I could have spoken according to the opinion of **Gregory of Rimini** <note>Gregory of Rimini (c. 1300–1358) was a major scholastic theologian known for his strict readings of St. Augustine.</note>. Even if by establishing blindness alone, the fact that "blindness is blindness" were established, it does not therefore follow necessarily that they are the same. For he denies this consequence and many of this kind: "if everything else but God is excluded, God exists; therefore, God is the fact that God exists." 

The **Cardinal of Cambrai** <note>Pierre d'Ailly, a prominent logician mentioned on the previous page.</note> also denies all statements in which something is predicated of an <term>infinitive phrase</term> <note>original: "oratione infinitiva"</note> taken significatively; he asserts they are both false and inconsistent, as can be seen in his first book on the *Sentences*. 

Next, you complain that "the false" should not have been pronounced as "divided" with this condition—that is, "as long as it is false"—and you explain it in these words: "If every false thing is simply divided—which you do not deny has been proven—then it should not have been said that a certain false thing is divided only with this condition, namely, 'as long as it is false.'" For if every man is simply and absolutely <term>capable of laughter</term> <note>original: "risibilis"; a standard logical example used to define human nature.</note>, it is not necessary to add a condition by which you restrict it, saying: "Every man is capable of laughter as long as he is a man." Nor should the restriction have been added because not all false things are equally divided or false; for not all beings are equally good, yet all are absolutely good. 

But weigh his words carefully, by which you will be able to cast away every scruple and doubt. He says "every false thing is divided," yet not every false thing is "equally false," because not being "equally divided" follows when things are not equally false...

<meta>This page continues a rebuttal against Antonio Cittadini regarding Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s work "On Being and the One." The previous page discussed the logical distinction between a thing’s existence and the truth of a statement about that thing. This page focuses on the relationship between truth, goodness, and being, as well as the technical definition of "contraries" in Aristotelian philosophy.</meta>

<page-num>297</page-num>

-> ### On Being and the One ### <-

...are not necessarily and always false, and those which are always and necessarily false. Rightly, therefore, Antonio, was that phrasing "as long as" added, regarding those things which are not always and necessarily false among the things that are false. For if they can become true and be united either by the work of nature or an artisan—as you yourself said in your second objections—nevertheless, **as long as they are divided, they are false.** However, those things which can never return into friendship <note>The author uses "friendship" metaphorically to mean "harmony" or "logical consistency."</note> are always false, as is abundantly seen in the response to the second objection. Nor does the comparison between beings and **risibility** <term>risibilitas</term> <note>In medieval logic, "risibility" (the ability to laugh) was the standard example of a "property"—something that is not part of a human's essence but belongs only and always to humans.</note> support you in the least.

For beings are always and absolutely good; and although they are not equally good—some participating in the nature of "the good" more than others—nevertheless they are always and necessarily good. For insofar as they are beings, they are good, nor can they become "non-beings" and "non-good" unless they are reduced to nothingness. But a "false" and "divided" thing (which consists in a complex statement) can conveniently become "undivided" and "true." Therefore, the comparison does not fit. For although not all false things are equally divided, they are nonetheless divided insofar as they are false, not united, and not true. 

Furthermore, this objection should have troubled us very little. For who would doubt that it can be said of a human (who is absolutely and always capable of laughter) that he will be capable of laughter under this condition: "as long as he is a human"? Would learned men disapprove of this phrasing: **"A human is capable of laughter as long as he is a human"**?

The tenth chapter of your objections brings nothing else against him except that what you said could have been easily established if the logic of contrary motions had been sufficiently understood by him. But he—unless he has forgotten—complained that you did not prove what you said so often followed: namely, that from the contrariety of "pursuing" and "fleeing," the contrariety of "good" and "evil" is inferred. 

<margin>He asks: by what reasoning is the good to be sought and the evil to be fled?</margin>

Even if "fleeing" and "seeking" are contraries, how do you prove from this that good and evil are contraries? This is what you had to prove, yet you have never said a single word to prove it, nor do you do so now. He denies this—namely, the form of your argument—perhaps for this reason: because "seeking" and "fleeing" are not properly **contrary motions** from which one can conclude that their endpoints are contraries. Indeed, even Aristotle himself assigns a certain contrariety of changes in the sixth book of the *Physics* <note>original: "Physica auſcultatio"</note> whose endpoints are not contraries, but **contradictories**—namely "being" and "non-being"—since generation proceeds from non-being to being, while corruption falls from being into non-being. 

You, however, have treated this contrariety of good and evil yet again, but brought forward no other proof. Do not doubt that he has carefully examined the logic of contrary motions "from his very fingernails" <note>An idiom meaning "thoroughly" or "from his youth."</note> as they say. On the contrary, he has quite often not only repelled your arguments against him regarding this contrariety, but even acted against you when, in his second letter, he deduced that your proof implies not only that good and evil are contraries, but that **contradictories are contraries.** Secondly, he turned your own weapons against you in this way: "Good and evil, according to you, are contraries, and each of two contraries is something..."

<summary>This page defends the idea that all existence (being) is inherently good and argues that the logical relationship between "seeking" and "fleeing" does not automatically prove that good and evil are "contraries" in a formal Aristotelian sense.</summary>

something positive, and according to you non-being is good, therefore according to you non-being is something positive; and "something" and "being" are interchangeable <term>convertuntur</term> <note>In scholastic logic, terms are "convertible" if they refer to the same thing under different aspects, such as "Being" and "Good."</note>; therefore, according to you, non-being is something positive. When you had said in your third letter that he [Pico] fled to Simplicius <note>Simplicius of Cilicia, a 6th-century Neoplatonist and influential commentator on Aristotle.</note> while abandoning the Latin interpreters regarding the opposition of good and evil, he replied as if in wonder: why would you—who usually claim to be a follower of Boëthius <note>An influential Roman philosopher who translated Greek logic into Latin.</note> and a mocker of the "Barbarians" <note>A term used by humanists for medieval scholastic philosophers whom they considered to have poor Latin style.</note>—now mock those who follow the Greek interpreters while setting aside the Latins? He was very aptly suggesting that you feel wrongly if you believe Greek philosophers are not to be held in high esteem, whom Boëthius (whom you value so highly) always held in the greatest honor and used as both teachers and guides. To these points, you reply that it is not a matter worthy of wonder, although you said the Latins do not deny Aristotle, whom Simplicius does not deny, and so on.

But it does not seem to me that Simplicius denies Aristotle when he interprets him correctly, nor does it appear that the Latin interpreters deviate from Simplicius’s opinion when they embrace it with their whole minds and carry it out in their works. If he [Pico] marveled that you denied that the Latin expositors follow Simplicius, perhaps he would have fallen into a greater stupor if he had understood you to say that the Latins do not deny Aristotle, while Simplicius (you claimed) did deny him. Furthermore, Simplicius and those who followed him clearly illuminate Aristotle’s mind when he said that good and evil are contraries for this reason: that one of the contraries always has the character of evil and deficiency. For this reason, in the first book of the *Physics* <note>original: "Physicæ Auscultationis"</note>, he taught that contraries are always compared to one another according to the logic of the "better" and the "worse." 

He also imitated the Pythagoreans, who established two orders of things, one of which was contained under the "good" and the other under the "evil." In his books on reasoning, he frequently used external examples. This exposition, as your own Thomas [Aquinas] says—who is not only a Latin, but the preeminent one among the Latins—he not only reports but also approves. To him, we also add Aegidius [of Rome] in his commentary on the second book of the *Sentences* <note>A standard medieval theological textbook by Peter Lombard.</note> and many others, namely Burley <note>Walter Burley, a 14th-century English logician.</note> and Cecco d’Ascoli <note>original: "Aesculanum"</note>, who feel the same way. Moreover, John [Duns] Scotus, in explaining Aristotle’s *Categories*, supports this opinion of ours, saying: "If 'good' is taken insofar as it is interchangeable with 'being,' then 'evil' is nothing <note>original: "malum esse nihil"</note>, and thus it is not contrary to the good." For since each of two contraries is beyond dispute something positive, it is necessary that what is "nothing" in the nature of things—which is what evil is—cannot be declared a contrary. 

And although you have denied that evil is nothing, appealing to Thomas [Aquinas], he himself not only fails to support your opinion but abundantly opposes it, as my uncle <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note> showed sufficiently in his third letter. Nevertheless, we do not think it would be off the mark to briefly touch upon a few things in passing in favor of my uncle’s opinion, and to show that not only was Thomas of the opinion that evil was "nothing," but that many other illustrious philosophers and theologians descended into this view with "hands and feet" <note>An idiom meaning "with total agreement" or "wholeheartedly."</note>. We find that Augustine, in discussing the customs of the Manicheans <note>A dualistic religious movement that Augustine famously converted from; they believed evil was a physical substance or power.</note>, said that no nature is evil.

<summary>Gianfrancesco Pico defends his uncle's metaphysical position that evil is not a positive substance (it is "nothing") by citing a consensus of Greek and Latin authorities, including Aristotle, Simplicius, Thomas Aquinas, and Duns Scotus.</summary>

## On Being and the One

...and a little after, lest there be any ambiguity about what he understood regarding "nature," he added: <note>original: "Et ipsa natura nihil est aliud quàm id quod intelligit in suo genere aliquid esse."</note> *And nature itself is nothing other than that which it understands to be something in its own genus.* We have seen that Giles of Rome <note>Aegidius Romanus (c. 1243–1316), a celebrated theologian and student of Thomas Aquinas.</note> left written in the first book of his commentaries on the *Sentences* <note>The "Sentences" of Peter Lombard was the standard textbook of medieval theology.</note> that evil, insofar as it is evil, is a pure privation and not "something," and it can be pronounced to be "something" only in that way in which "nothing" itself can be said to be "something," since both can be designated by a name. 

In the second book of those same commentaries, he affirms that evil does not have—to use his words—a <term>quiddity</term> <note>From the Latin "quidditas," meaning the "whatness" or essential nature of a thing.</note>, and for that reason the question "What is it?" cannot be answered; it is nothing other than a name. He likewise interprets the words of Aristotle concerning the opposition of evil and good according to my uncle's mind, and he agrees with the dogmas of Simplicius and other upright interpreters of Aristotle. Namely, he pronounces that they [good and evil] are not themselves <term>genera</term> <note>In logic, a "genus" is a broad category or class of things.</note>, but rather the genera of other contraries ought more properly to be called so, since one has the character of a positive thing while the other does not. He argues that none of the contraries, according to themselves, are "non-being," but are instead some nature and existence. 

Gregory of Rimini <note>Gregorius Ariminensis (c. 1300–1358), a major scholastic philosopher known for his rigor.</note> testifies to this same thing in his commentaries on the second book of the *Sentences*, namely that evil itself is not—to use his own speech—any <term>entity</term>, but a pure privation. Robert Holkot <note>Robertus Olchot (c. 1290–1349), an English Dominican philosopher and theologian.</note>, a man of the most sharp intellect, felt this same way in the first question of his commentaries on the second book of the theological *Sentences*. Many others have judged this same thing, whom to bring forward now while I am writing might perhaps bring boredom to you as you read later. It will be enough for the present business to have enumerated these most important ones, especially since it will be necessary to speak of this again when other objections are to be dissolved, whenever mention of evil is made in those places. 

But to return to where we digressed. You seem to cite only Boethius <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose works served as a bridge between Classical Greek thought and the Latin Middle Ages.</note> out of all the Latins to stand in judgment against Simplicius and the other illustrious interpreters. If you deign to count him as the only one among the Latins, he will be "one of the Latin expositors," not "the Latin expositors" [plural] who would seem to support your opinion. Add to this that not even he, if his mind is properly scrutinized, cries out against our view. He neither ponders this question exactly nor investigates it with final judgment, but only declares what the words of Aristotle, strictly and narrowly grasped, demand. This habit was most familiar to him in his first editions, as he left the various opinions of the Greek interpreters for the second edition, to be examined scrupulously and anxiously. 

Furthermore, I think he not only proved but demonstrated that whenever it is granted that good and evil are contraries, it can immediately be pronounced without any controversy that a Chimera <note>A mythological creature used in philosophy as a standard example of a "non-being" or an impossible thing.</note> is something in the nature of things. Responding only this to his arguments against you: namely, that it was not perceived by him by what reasoning you called good and evil contraries; and you bring nothing else for yourself. Therefore, I shall do nothing against you except to say that he both saw and perceived everything you had written, and when he pleased, he reviewed many things you had said about contraries. For my plan in this business is [to treat] your latest objections against <margin>my uncle</margin>...

<summary>Gianfrancesco Pico cites several medieval authorities, including Giles of Rome and Robert Holkot, to argue that evil is a privation of good rather than a positive existence. He challenges his opponent's reliance on Boethius, suggesting that a deeper reading of Boethius actually aligns with the Greek commentators and his uncle's philosophy.</summary>

### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

[...] to resolve [the arguments regarding] the uncle, while passing over in silence those to which he himself had already responded in some way. Nevertheless, if anything seems to you not to have been fully clarified by him, and which you both desire and demand that I open up, I will attempt to satisfy your longing. Through these efforts, I will wander through your arguments, both by dismantling and responding to them as best I can; for he did not judge it inconsistent if every tiny detail of your words lacked a response. He admits in his first letters that certain things were omitted to which no response was given, lest he waste words on trivial matters; and certain things were treated lightly, as he deemed that for a man who is a philosopher, things ought to be indicated rather than explained. I would wish you to interpret these words in such a way that it was not worthwhile for you—a noble philosopher—to bring up certain matters whose controversies are well known even to "Gregorian" philosophers <note>The term "Gregorian" here likely refers to advanced or venerable scholars, perhaps referencing the followers of a specific master or simply a synonym for "venerable."</note> against a man most celebrated in both learning and fame, who was holding a discourse on the highest matters, and who would not descend to discuss these lowest things without a loss to the concepts he had formed regarding the most difficult speculations. Concerning this contradiction, however, we shall say something in the following response when we speak of "semi-full" <note>The Latin *semiplena* refers to a partial or incomplete state. In this context, it describes a "partial" lack of a quality.</note> privations.

You wonder, furthermore, that he was amazed that "semi-full" privations were being imagined by you; I think he turned this into admiration not so much at that time, but after you proved you were attempting it again (if indeed your last objections were seen by him). He had said against you: **evil is nothing, therefore it is not a semi-full privation.** But you pursue his argument in this way: *Sickness is evil, therefore it is nothing, therefore it is not a semi-full privation; but sickness is a certain privation, therefore it is not a semi-full privation of either health or some good, but rather a full and perfect one, which is impossible; therefore, imperfect privations are semi-full, such as sickness, scarcity, ugliness, and blindness of sight—the latter being a perfect privation of good, but these others imperfect.* These are your words verbatim. 

But I, my dear Antonio, would say freely that these words of yours either do nothing against him, and so that you may see this more clearly, I will review them one by one. You say first, from his own words: *evil is nothing, therefore it is not a semi-full privation.* You are walking on the right path. Again: *sickness is evil, therefore it is nothing, therefore it is not a semi-full privation.* Up to this point you are also proceeding correctly, because sickness, insofar as it is evil, is to that extent "nothing." Again you say: *but sickness is a certain privation, therefore not of health etc.* all the way to the end, by which words, in my judgment—if you will pardon my saying so—a falsehood is built up, which we shall strive to show. For blindness is not only a "perfect privation of sight" as you say, but it can also be called a "perfect privation of good," because it takes away that entire good which it is naturally meant to take away—namely, sight. 

Ophthalmia <note>A historical term for severe inflammation of the eye or conjunctivitis.</note> does not do this, although even that destroys the good which it is naturally meant to take away; yet regarding that which it is not fit to destroy, it can in no way be called a privation, whether you call it semi-full or full. For <term>Privation</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, a "privation" is not just the absence of something, but the absence of a quality in an entity that should naturally possess it (like blindness in an eye, rather than "blindness" in a stone).</note> is considered either absolutely—namely, as it relates to a "habit" <note>The Latin *habitus* refers to the possession of a positive quality or state, the opposite of privation.</note> in general—or as it is restricted to a certain and limited genus of being: for instance, to the health of the entire body, to the eye, to beauty, and other things of that kind. In the first way, it is accepted...

<summary>Gianfrancesco Pico defends his uncle's brevity in philosophical debate and refutes Antonio Cittadini's argument that sickness is a "semi-full" privation of good, arguing instead that privations must be defined by what they specifically take away.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola’s detailed rebuttal of Antonio Cittadini’s critiques. It focuses on the nature of evil as a "privation" (a lack of something that should be there) and whether such a lack can be considered "full" or "partial."</meta>

-> # On Being and the One <-

...taking up the <term>habit <note>In Scholastic philosophy, a "habit" (*habitus*) is a stable quality or disposition of a subject, such as health in a body or sight in an eye.</note></term>, it does not deprive some particular thing, because an all-encompassing privation, as Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential Christian theologian and philosopher whose works, like *On the Divine Names*, were foundational for medieval thought.</note> says in his book *On the Divine Names*, is entirely lacking in power. Taken in the second way, which Dionysius calls "singular," it distinguishes it against the universal; it deprives that habit which it regards, and in this way a habit of this kind—to which a full privation is opposed—is not "semi-full" <note>The debate here concerns whether an evil like blindness is a "partial" lack of good or a "complete" lack of the specific good (sight) it opposes.</note> of some other thing. For who would dare to say that blindness is a semi-full privation of a man, or of some other good that might be in a man? Therefore, an absolute privation regards an absolute habit, and a proper and particular privation regards a proper and particular habit, and it does not exceed its limits. 

Wherefore sickness is a full privation, not semi-full, whether you ascribe it to the whole body or to a particular limb. For a fever is the perfect <note>Here, "perfect" means "complete" or "total."</note> privation of that temperature which it is born to corrupt. Even <term>ophthalmia <note>A general historical term for severe inflammation of the eye.</note></term>, even if it is not a privation of the whole good that is in the eye, is nevertheless a perfect and proper privation of some specific good, because it destroys all that good which it is born to destroy—even if it does not take away the sight while it destroys the perfect health of the eye, and insofar as the inflammation does nothing else. Ugliness also, because it takes away all that good which it can take away—namely, the perfect composition of parts which is called beauty—is a perfect privation; and so you should consider it in the rest of these cases. 

We might also say this in excess: blindness, insofar as it is blindness, is an evil; insofar as it is an evil, it is nothing; insofar as it is nothing, it is not a semi-full privation, because if it were semi-full, it would leave behind something positive, which evil does not do. Furthermore, no privation in itself actually deprives all good; therefore [by your logic] all privations would be semi-full privations, which goes against your own argument, because you contend that some are full and some are semi-full. This is an excellent and necessary connection, and what we have assumed we prove by this argument: since no good would ever be found if some total and universal privation were discovered in the nature of things, as we suggested a little earlier from the words of Dionysius. For evil deprives a particular good, since evil is in the good, and a universal evil would destroy a universal good—if indeed such a thing could be found, which is impossible. And thus conclude that one always finds not semi-full, but full privations of their own proper habits.

To the fourteenth objection, which contains several questions, I respond individually. First, that not every evil leaves something of the good, unless you understand it in some subject which the evil itself does not regard, or you take that subject whose habit is destroyed by the evil itself. Nor did he <note>Referring to the author's uncle, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note> assert that which you impose upon him and seize upon for your hypothesis. For he abundantly testified that some evil is found which takes away entirely every good born from it, since in the response to the second letter he reminded you of this, writing in this manner: 

> "Certainly you ought to have considered this: that what is conceded concerning certain imperfect evils—on account of that admixture of goodness which they still retain—is not to be transferred to the unmixed and absolute nature of evil itself." 

And so that you may perceive the truth more clearly, it will not be [tiresome...] <note>original: "pigebit", completed from the catchword on the bottom of the page.</note>

<summary>Gianfrancesco Pico argues that evil is a "full" privation of a specific good (like sight or health), even if it doesn't destroy the entire being. He uses examples like blindness and fever to show that an evil completely removes the specific "habit" it opposes.</summary>

...it will be necessary to explain the force of the distinction: that evil can be considered in two ways. First, it can be considered absolutely and under the proper definition of evil—that is, insofar as it is nothing. Second, it can be considered insofar as it is a privation of a certain good—that is, a particular evil. Evil accepted in this [second] manner leaves behind at least something of a good subject; but the other kind of evil—which is entirely non-being and nothing—does not do this. We call the <term>chimera <note>In Scholastic logic, the "chimera" is the standard example of an impossible object or a "being of reason" (*ens rationis*) that has no existence in reality.</note></term> such a thing, since it does not relate to any subject or habit.

And for this reason, it is called "entirely evil" by its very self and its absolute, unmixed nature. This evil, I say—to use the words of Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, *On the Divine Names*.</note> in his book *On the Divine Names*—is "in no way, nowhere, and a non-existing nothing," because it lacks a subject. As for the chimera, even if it could be called "good in potency" <note>Potential existence rather than actual existence.</note> because of the power to produce it which exists in God, it still cannot be designated as either a "being" or a "good." For if this connection—namely, "something is good in potency, therefore it is good"—were to have any force, the blow would turn back upon its author. I should think it would lead him to admit that all things which ought to be created by God (rather than being made by the force of nature), and even those things which have been corrupted, would be "something" and yet "not something" at the same time.

For if, according to him, they were both beings and goods by the power of the Creator, then they would necessarily be "something," since "something" and "good" are <term>convertible <note>In Medieval and Renaissance philosophy, the "transcendentals" (Being, One, Good, True) are "convertible," meaning they refer to the same reality under different aspects; whatever has being is also, in some sense, good.</note></term> and share the exact same scope. I shall argue that it cannot be "something" in this way: nothing can be made out of nothing; before it is created, a chimera (according to you) cannot exist unless it is created; it is therefore created out of nothing; therefore, before it was created out of nothing, it was not "something." Therefore, a thing cannot be designated as "absolutely good" merely because of the power of goodness that exists in the Creator; otherwise—to use the language of us logicians—a fallacy of <term>*secundum quid ad simpliciter* <note>Latin: "from a qualified statement to an absolute one." A logical fallacy where one assumes that what is true under certain conditions is true universally. Here, Pico argues that being "good in the power of God" is not the same as being "good" in reality.</note></term> would be committed.

I deliberately set aside those arguments which might be brought against that opinion concerning—if I may put it this way—eternal <term>quiddities <note>The "whatness" or essence of a thing that exists independently of whether the thing actually exists in the world.</note></term> and objective potency, even if your own opinion could perhaps be weakened by those very same reasons. For it is enough for our purpose if we have proved that a chimera cannot be called "good." Furthermore, imitating <term>Averroes <note>Ibn Rushd, the 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to Renaissance philosophy.</note></term> in this matter, we can say that "being in potency" is not "being," just as he said in his commentaries on the fourth book of the *Metaphysics* (section fifteen): "that which is not in act is not a being." 

Regarding the point you add—namely, that a chimera is a "being" because, although that power of producing a chimera exists in God, the power of God and the power of the chimera are distinct by different reasons—I respond: First, that I can deny that the power of God and the power of producing a chimera are different in their reasoning. Second, even if it were freely granted to you that those powers were different, what would your argument then prove? Since a chimera can in no way be called a "being" on account of a power to produce it that exists in God. For that power is so far from being able to be declared a "chimera" or anything intrinsic to a chimera, that they are actually separated by an infinite distance. You further add that, once the power of God and our own thought are excluded, the chimera is not "evil," since evil is a privation which consists in a subject participating in goodness. To this, I would like to respond with the same distinction as a little while ago: since the chimera does not regard any subject...

<summary>Pico argues that a "chimera" (an impossible non-being) cannot be considered a "being" or "good" simply because God has the power to create it, as potential existence is not the same as actual existence. He uses authorities like Dionysius and Averroes to maintain that evil is either a lack of good in a subject or absolute nothingness.</summary>

...but would be absolutely evil, even if the notion of it which we conceive—that is, the very concept of the <term>chimera <note>A standard example in Scholastic logic of an impossible thing that exists only as a thought, not in reality.</note></term> that we carry in the mind—is something, and thus can be called "good." Likewise, you say you did not claim Aristotle believed every being whatsoever exists either <term>by itself <note>Latin: *per se*. Something that exists by its own nature or definition.</note></term> or <term>by accident <note>Latin: *per accidens*. Something that exists only as a property or a coincidental feature of another thing.</note></term>, nor did you attribute anything false to Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent Scholastic theologian.</note> because of it. Indeed, even if so many things have been said on this matter by the man we are defending <note>Gianfrancesco is defending his uncle, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note> that it seems unnecessary for me to speak further, and although I once proposed not to retract matters he had already discussed, I will say these things as an extra measure for my uncle’s sake. Specifically, I point out that Simplicius, whom you have frequently summoned as a witness for your side, has more often given testimony against you—a fact my uncle mentions more than once in his responses. 

Again, I would like to know if you have undertaken to defend the view that, according to the mind of Aristotle, not every being is either by accident or by itself. For in the fifth book of his *First Philosophy* <note>Referring to Aristotle's *Metaphysics*, specifically Book 5 (Delta), which functions as a philosophical dictionary.</note>, he divides being into being by itself and being by accident. Ultimately, these are divided into <term>substance <note>What a thing is in its essence.</note></term> and <term>accidents <note>Qualities like color or size that belong to a substance.</note></term>, which were contained in the first branch of the division, since being "by itself" is partitioned into ten <term>categories <note>The ten "genera" or classifications of all things according to Aristotle.</note></term>, of which one is substance and the others are accidents. I would now most gladly be taught by you what kind of being that would be which is neither "by itself" nor "by accident." 

But if perhaps you were to say that the division into being "by itself" and "by accident" is a classification of <term>complex being <note>In Scholastic logic, "complex" usually refers to propositions or sentences (e.g., "The man is tall"), whereas "incomplex" refers to single terms (e.g., "man").</note></term>, as you put forward in your first objections, I would not hesitate to respond that you cannot truly show this. You cannot support your opinion by any statement of Aristotle’s nor by suitable reason, since in that passage Aristotle divides being "by itself" into ten categories, of which one is substance and nine are accidents. No one believes these would be "complex beings," since they are distinguished in opposition to complex things. And in that same place, <term>Averroes <note>The 12th-century Islamic philosopher and "Great Commentator" on Aristotle.</note></term> says that being "by itself" is divided through words that signify the categories. But a single word is not a "complex being." Also in the sixth book of the *Metaphysics*, the same Averroes says that the primary division of being is into "by itself" and "by accident." It could not be the primary division if a division of complex being preceded it; nor is it found in Thomas’s commentary on the fifth book of the *Metaphysics* that complex being is divided in the way you asserted. 

Truly, it cannot be believed—when being is first divided into being "by itself" and "by accident," and the "by itself" is then subdivided into ten categories which we have shown to be "incomplex"—that a division of complex being is being provided in that passage. This is because that which is divided must necessarily be predicated of the parts that divide it. Even if these points pertain little to the business at hand, let them be said, as your dogma seems to me at first glance to be consistent neither with the views of the Aristotelian interpreters nor with reason. But if by chance you prove the contrary, it will be most welcome to have learned something from a philosopher as serious as I certainly judge you to be. 

Furthermore, he <note>Referring to Giovanni Pico.</note> said that evil is a <term>privation <note>The absence of a good that should be present (e.g., blindness is the privation of sight).</note></term> insofar as privation was formally a negation. You oppose this, saying it is not established that there is one kind of opposition between affirmation and negation, and another between privation and <term>habit <note>Latin: *habitus*. The state or quality that a privation lacks (e.g., sight is the habit, blindness is the privation).</note></term>...

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

[if] evil were the <term>privation <note>A philosophical term meaning the absence of a quality that should naturally be present, like blindness is the privation of sight.</note></term> of good, then "evil" and "non-good" must necessarily be <term>convertible <note>In logic, terms are "convertible" if they can be swapped without changing the truth of a statement (e.g., "every human is a rational animal" and "every rational animal is a human").</note></term>. To those people, I would like to respond that the opposition of privation is one thing, and the opposition of negation is another; and that he did not put forward that specific opposite, but nevertheless it follows that if evil is opposed to good through privation, "evil" and "non-good" must be convertible. For privation, as <term>Albert the Great <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a dominant figure in medieval science and philosophy.</note></term> says in the first book of the *Physics*, is not something "of itself" or "by itself" insofar as it is a privation, because its state is "not-being." Furthermore, it was asserted by <term>Aristotle <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BC) whose logic and metaphysics formed the basis of medieval education.</note></term> in his *First Philosophy* <note>The work now commonly known as the *Metaphysics*.</note> that privations belong to the category of non-beings, since privation by its nature is the other extreme of a contradiction. Therefore, since evil is a privation of good, and consequently a non-being insofar as it is evil, then "evil" and "non-good" are also convertible. For "evil" and "nothing," as has been proven, are the same thing; likewise "nothing" and "non-being" are the same non-being; and similarly "non-good" is the same, because "being" and "good" are the same. For this reason, my uncle <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note> said most correctly that negation is a privation only to the extent that privation is formally a negation. For even if they differ in this—that one of them (namely, contradiction) has no middle ground, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> says in the first book of the *Posterior Analytics*, while the other has one in a certain way, since it occurs simultaneously with its opposite around the same subject—yet as far as the present proposal is concerned, they would be the same. This is because privation by itself is a negation and a non-being, and it establishes nothing, as <term>Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274).</note></term> proves in many places, most especially in his *Treatise on the Four Opposites*. If indeed non-beings are evil, and evil things are non-good, from these points you can gather that "evil" and "good" are entirely convertible [in their opposites], and you should not believe that illustrious men have been lacking who asserted this. Hear Aristotle saying that "good" is spoken of equally with "being." Therefore, by the rule of contradictories, add "evil" to "non-being." Hear the most celebrated theologian <term>Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury <note>Anselm (1033–1109), famous for his "ontological argument" for God's existence.</note></term>, uttering these words in his book *On the Fall of the Devil*: <note>original: "Malum non est aliud quàm non bonum"</note> "Evil is nothing other than non-good," from which it is most firmly concluded that "evil" and "non-good" follow from one another.

In the seventeenth place, there would have been no controversies between you and him if you had considered that little book *On Being and the One* more diligently, and if you had called to memory whatever was written in it concerning those levels, and concerning that very <term>darkness <note>Latin: *caligine*. A reference to "mystical darkness" or the "divine gloom," a concept from negative theology where God is so bright/pure He appears as darkness to the limited human mind.</note></term> which those who contemplate are granted to reach. You would have seen that in those first three levels, something can be stated about God; in the fourth, not at all. There, the window of understanding to the books of <term>Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-6th century philosopher who wrote on the "Divine Names" and "Mystical Theology."</note></term> was opened, by which you could most conveniently be moved regarding this matter. For he neither denies, nor could he deny, that this statement is true: "God is God," in the way that we are able to both conceive and speak of God—namely, when we are situated in those first three levels. But he only denies that any <term>predicate <note>The part of a sentence that describes or makes a claim about the subject.</note></term> can truly explain the nature of God, specifically in that fourth level of darkness. All rightly-thinking philosophers (to say nothing of the theologians) would also affirm this. However, since this name "God," which performs the office of the predicate in this proposition "God is God," not only fails to explain and declare the divine essence and nature, but is also surpassed by it infinitely, he denied that it could be [truly] affirmed of God.

<summary>Gianfrancesco Pico defends his uncle’s logical and theological positions, arguing that evil is merely the privation of good and therefore non-existent. He also explains the levels of mystical contemplation, noting that while we can name God in lower stages of understanding, His true essence surpasses all human language and predicates in the highest stage of "divine darkness."</summary>

investigated <note>The Latin text here begins mid-word, likely "investigavit."</note>, attending to that fourth degree of darkness <note>A reference to the "divine darkness" in mystical theology, where the soul moves beyond light and understanding to encounter God.</note>. Come then, let us examine the words themselves which will testify to the man’s mind; afterward, we shall bring forward several points so that it may be seen more clearly whether and how God can be spoken of by us. Then we shall show that your arguments against his words—even as they lie apprehended—conclude nothing. He <insert>Giovanni Pico</insert> had said that "God is" can be stated in different ways, and likewise that God, according to the opinion of **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-6th century philosopher whose works on "negative theology" argued that God is beyond all human descriptions.</note>, is greater than every naming, even this naming of "God," just as was held in the book on **Mystical Theology**.

He had said in another place that when you conceive by this word "God" only that which is signified by the noun, this word does not have the nature of a <term>predicate <note>In logic, the part of a sentence that says something about the subject (e.g., in "The sky is blue," "blue" is the predicate).</note></term>, but of a subject, when it is the thing about which it is asked: "What can or should be stated of it?" rather than that which is stated about something else. For this reason, it was unknown neither to **Simonides** <note>A Greek poet who, when asked by King Hiero of Syracuse to define God, repeatedly asked for more time, eventually concluding that the longer he meditated, the more obscure the subject became.</note> nor to the Tyrant consulting him. When you likewise asked whether, if God could not be called "God," he would be something other than God, he would ask you what you conceived through this word "God" which you stated of God. If you conceived nothing, you would not err, because you would be saying nothing; if you conceived something, he would say that God is something other than what you conceive, and you would be explaining what you conceived through this word "God," since He would be above everything that can be conceived by us. These are his words. 

I believed it was clear to you from those words that they provide the truest resolution of your doubts on this matter. You, however, contend that **Dionysius** does not deny that "God is God." Read, I pray, **Dionysius** in the last chapter of the book on **Mystical Theology**, and the first letter to Gaius, and it will be plain to you that God is greater than every naming. Read also the same author in the second chapter of the **Celestial Hierarchy**, and you will understand that this divine man teaches us that the underlying likeness of divine truth transcends all things and all life; that no light expresses this, and that every speech, every mind, and every reason is, without any comparison, inferior to the likeness of Him. From these things, I would think you could weigh the mind of my uncle: namely, that "God is God" cannot be truly said in such a way that the name "God" acts as a predicate. By this, we attempt to explain what we try to conceive through the subject—not that it could not be said in some way that "God is God," just as it is said "God is good" or "God is wise." 

Other <term>predications <note>The act of making a statement or attribution about a subject.</note></term> are also allowed, with which the sacred books are filled, in which something is stated about God in some way; but His nature is not explained, since He is infinitely distant from those concepts, just as that uncle of mine taught quite clearly in the fifth chapter of the book **On Being and the One**. He did not speak upon those words of **Dionysius** which are brought forward by **Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Scholastic theologian.</note> as you supposed, but upon those which were cited just a little before. Furthermore, **Damascenus** <note>John of Damascus (c. 675–749), a Syrian monk and Church Father.</note> writes in the first book of the sentences of his theology that there are certain things said affirmatively of God that have the power of a "super-excellent negation." For example, if we speak of "darkness" in God, we do not mean darkness but rather the absence of light. But we say he is "above light" and "is light" when darkness is absent; a sentiment which the most learned and devoted of the **Parisians** <note>Likely referring to the faculty or the famous mystical theologians of the University of Paris, such as Jean Gerson.</note>...

The Chancellor, treating the subject, says: "Therefore, whatever we say affirmatively about God includes some negation." And a little later: "For this reason, he says that **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a foundational figure in Christian mysticism who argued that we learn more about God by saying what He is *not* than what He is.</note> denies God is a being, but affirms Him to be **above being** <note>original: "super ens"</note>." **Giles of Rome** <note>A 13th-century theologian and student of Thomas Aquinas.</note> says in the first book of his *Sentences* that God is wise, but not in the way that we understand wisdom. Hence he says this is the reason why **Averroes** <note>The famous Islamic philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.</note>, in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics*, pronounces that these <term>predications <note>Statements or attributes assigned to a subject in logic.</note></term> we attribute to God are similar to mathematical propositions. In their manner, the things we understand are in actual objects, but not in the same way that we understand them; for example, when we understand a line that exists in physical matter, we do not understand it by the same logic as the matter it is in. But why should I delay you with many words when I can make you more certain of this truth we assert with only a few? Namely, that you may know that whatever we predicate of God signifies something far different from what we conceive and express.

Jesus Christ himself—the power, wisdom, and truth of God, as witnessed in the Gospel of John—says: "God is spirit." Yet **Dionysius**, in his book on *Mystical Theology*, speaking of God and contemplating the ineffable deity while removing many of the predicates that we attribute to Him, says: "Neither is He spirit, as far as we can know." See then, that Dionysius does not want "spirit" to be predicated of God in the way that we can know spirit. Through these final words, he teaches the reader that it is true that God is spirit, so that he might agree with the Gospel of Christ, and yet He is not spirit in the way we understand spirit, lest we believe that the nature of God can be truly expressed by us through any name.

Indeed, how great the authority of Dionysius is, and how his most sacred doctrines are praised and celebrated without reserve by all the theologians who have attended the **schools of Paris** <note>original: "Parisiorum gymnasia," referring to the University of Paris, the center of medieval theology.</note>. Although I thought this was not hidden from you, since your uncle <note>original: "patruus," referring to Giovanni Pico’s nephew and biographer, Gianfrancesco Pico, or a similar family relation.</note> hinted in the responses to your objections that you did not very willingly admit Dionysius’s sayings during the dispute, I would have you know that he was that most faithful disciple of **Paul the Apostle** in the faith of Christ. By Paul's help, God willed that Dionysius leave behind the errors of the pagans to recognize and follow the truth, and be granted the crown of martyrdom for the faith of Christ. **Gregory** <note>Pope Gregory the Great.</note> and **Pope Martin** said great things about his teaching in the synod celebrated at Rome against the heretics. **John of Damascus** and many others have extolled him with the highest praise. His books, hidden by heretics for a long time, were unknown to the minds of the faithful. There was also a saying by **Constantine the Philosopher** <note>Likely Saint Cyril, the "Apostle to the Slavs," who was known as Constantine the Philosopher.</note>, who had committed all his books to memory, that if Dionysius had been available to the many Fathers who fought great wars with the heretics and enemies of the holy Catholic Church, they would have achieved triumph over their enemies much faster and more easily (which they only did later, slowly and with great, exhausting labors).

But when you intend to prove that God can be called "God" because of the logic of the name which is predicated of the name, I say that you labor in vain (my dear Antonius). For you do not express anything about God, but about this name "God." To help you understand this more clearly, I will explain it more broadly. For...

<meta>This page continues the exploration of "negative theology"—the idea that God is so beyond human understanding that we can only describe Him by what He is not. The previous page discussed how our words for God are more like mathematical symbols than direct descriptions.</meta>

<page-num>307</page-num>
->### On Being and the One<-
<center>Cc 4</center>

I will ask you what you conceive by the word "water" according to the meaning of the name. If you conceive nothing, you do not err (to use the words of **Porphyry** <note>original: "parrui." Likely a reference to the Neoplatonist philosopher Porphyry, who wrote extensively on logic and categories.</note>). If you conceive something, I ask again: if you conceive it as that about which something can be stated—if you take it in this way—you also do not err, because that concept will again occupy the role of the **subject** rather than the **predicate** <note>In logic, the "subject" is what we are talking about, and the "predicate" is what we say about it. Pico is arguing that even when we think we are defining God, we are really just setting up a subject for a sentence we cannot finish.</note>. But if you were to conceive that which is stated about Him, you would stray far off, since God Himself is infinitely greater than everything you can conceive. Even the Platonist **Apuleius** <note>A 2nd-century philosopher and author. While famous for his novel *The Golden Ass*, he was also a noted commentator on Plato.</note>, in his book *On the Teachings of Plato*, calls Him "unspoken" and "unnameable." The words of **Plato** himself on this matter were rendered into Latin by Apuleius as follows: *To find God is indeed not easy; to understand Him is impossible.* Therefore, let us say that all affirmations about God are improper, since He infinitely exceeds whatever we might wish not only to say, but even to conceive. 

Furthermore, we are not only limited while held in this earthly prison of ignorance and misery; even when we are established in heaven in the very enjoyment of God—by which we are perfectly blessed—the power will not be granted to us to **comprehend** God, but only to **apprehend** Him (to use the technical terms of our theologians <note>In medieval theology, to "comprehend" means to understand something fully and exhaustively, while to "apprehend" means to reach out and touch or know a part of something without fully grasping its entirety.</note>). 

In addition, you believe these two statements conflict with one another: "God is above that which can be conceived" and "nothing can be affirmed about God." You say that if the definition of the name is "that which is above what can be conceived," then your argument will hold weight. But this is resolved: for when it is said that proper affirmations cannot be applied to God, it is understood that no predicate can be found that represents God’s nature in its entirety. This phrase, "above that which can be conceived," means nothing else than that God cannot be fully conceived and that what God is cannot be known. Therefore, these words speak not only of what God is, but also that what He is cannot be known. Thus, they possess the force of denying rather than affirming. 

But even if they were to affirm, your argument would still not hold weight. Consider some other thing unknown to us that someone might desire to know: if we responded to the inquirer regarding its **essence** <note>The fundamental nature or "what-ness" of a thing.</note> by saying, "It is that which we do not know, which we are not acquainted with, which we have not yet conceived in our mind nor can conceive," would his request not seem satisfied? Through this teaching, he could not state anything affirmatively about that thing, but only negatively—unless perhaps someone were found who could explain to others what that thing was, which, being entirely unknown to men and above the reach of all thought, could not be known or conceived even by itself. 

And thus both **Simonides** <note>An ancient Greek poet. Legend says that when the tyrant Hiero asked him "What is God?", Simonides kept asking for more time to think, eventually concluding that the more he thought about it, the more obscure the answer became.</note> and the **Tyrant** <note>Hiero I of Syracuse.</note> consulting him knew that the name of God represented something of the highest degree; yet one of them desired to know what God was, while the other denied that he knew. Furthermore, you use this logical connection: "God is above all that can be conceived, therefore God cannot be conceived (otherwise He would be above Himself); therefore He cannot be loved or worshipped." I respond that God can be fully conceived as He is by Himself alone, and by no other intellect. It does not follow from this that He cannot be loved or worshipped. For we conceive that there is such a great deity, endowed with omnipotence, infinitely surpassing all creatures in every kind of virtue...

<summary>Pico argues that God’s nature is "unnameable" and "unspoken," asserting that humans can only "apprehend" (touch) but never "comprehend" (fully grasp) the Divine. He defends the use of negative theology, explaining that saying God is "above all thought" is a way of acknowledging human limitation rather than making a full affirmation.</summary>

<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

...so that we cannot conceive it except through our affections <note>The "affections" (affectibus) refer to the emotional and spiritual inclinations of the heart, as opposed to cold intellectual reasoning.</note>; and having been stirred up and warmed by this wonder, we burn with love for Him. We conceive of His effects, and that He is the supreme good, and we wonder at, worship, and love Him. For once those things which God has made are perfectly known—to use the words of **Themistius** <note>A 4th-century Greek philosopher and statesman who provided influential commentaries on Aristotle.</note>—He turns the minds and mouths of all toward the admiration and praise of Himself. We likewise read those things which have been revealed from heaven, and, being endowed with His grace, we conceive through faith that which we cannot fully conceive by nature: namely, that we ought to love Him above all things. This is so that finally, when the riddle of this flesh <note>original: "carnis enigmate." A reference to the biblical idea that in this life we see "through a glass, darkly," but in the next, "face to face."</note> is broken, we may be able to contemplate Him as He is, with the greatest joy of both the inner and outer man, which is our ultimate happiness. 

Furthermore, for us to love something, there is no need for it to be perfectly seen, known, or conceived by us. It is enough if we know that it exists, or that it is of a certain nature, even if that knowledge is confused and obscure; this can come either from faith or from observing His effects. Thus, even a modest preceding knowledge—of whatever sort it may be—is enough for us to love such a thing. For we can love any thing at all, unless we are entirely lacking in knowledge of it; as **Gregory** <note>St. Gregory the Great, a 6th-century Pope and influential theologian.</note> says: *from the things the soul knows, it learns to love the things it does not know.* **Thomas** <note>St. Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century Dominican friar and "Angelic Doctor" of the Church.</note> also proves in the *Prima Secundae* <note>Part of Aquinas's *Summa Theologiae*.</note> that it is possible to love something perfectly even if it is not perfectly known, and he proposes God as an example among other things. 

Finally, you say that my uncle <note>Gianfrancesco is likely referring to his famous uncle, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note> thought the power of gold was so great that, whether we wished it or not, in reality or in the soul, it would by necessity pull God along with it. But, my dear Antony, I would believe he was not merely of the opinion, but was made certain, that this is not the *power* of gold, but its *impotence*—since gold could neither exist nor be understood if God were removed. And although I could refer you to **John Baconthorpe** <note>original: "Ioannem de Bacchone." A 14th-century English Carmelite philosopher known as the "Resolute Doctor."</note>, whom we mentioned in the resolution of the fifth objection, I will say more. Even if you, while recounting my uncle's arguments in which he asserted that "God is not" and "gold is" were contradictory statements, said you did not wish to respond (lest you seem to be groping in the dark in a matter clearer than light), my intention is to show that it was worthwhile for you to undertake the task of dissolving those arguments if you were able. If not, you should at least put your hand to the work or frankly admit that his assertions were true. 

The arguments of my uncle are these, which I will soon explain: It is impossible for anything to be if it is not <term>Being itself</term> <note>original: "ipsum esse." A technical term in Scholastic philosophy meaning the pure act of existing, which is the definition of God's essence.</note>. But God is **Being itself**; therefore, it is impossible for gold to be if God is not. Furthermore, if God is not, then there is an "infinite." If there is an infinite, there is nothing; for if there is an infinite, there is no finite, since the infinite destroys itself, just like other things that contain a contradiction. If "nothing" is, then gold is not. 

It is impossible for anything to exist if it is not Being itself, which is God, and so on. Since Being itself, which is God (as no one denies), does not exist <note>This is a "reductio ad absurdum" argument: if we assume God (the source of existence) doesn't exist, then nothing else can either.</note>, by whose <term>participation</term> <note>original: "participatu." The philosophical concept that all created things exist only by "sharing" in the existence of the Creator.</note> not only are all things what they are, but they also depend on Him and are preserved at every moment—as not only all theologians, especially **Thomas**, teach most abundantly, but as was also asserted by **Plato** in the *Timaeus*—it is impossible for gold to be, because it exists only by the grace of His being and by participation in Him.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s philosophy, moving from how we love God through His effects to a logical proof of His necessity. It argues that without God as a "Limit" or "First Cause," the universe would collapse into nothingness.</meta>

<page-num>309</page-num>

# ->On Being and the One.<-

Furthermore, if God is not, then the infinite exists. All beings besides God are finite and contained within certain limits; there is no doubt that they have and possess this limited nature by the work and grace of God. For this reason, the followers of Plato say that he called God the **Limit** in the <term>Philebus</term> <note>A Socratic dialogue by Plato focusing on the nature of pleasure and the "good life," where the concepts of "Limit" and the "Unlimited" are central.</note>, because He limits all things by forms distributed everywhere like measures. But the <term>Book of Wisdom</term> <note>Also known as the Wisdom of Solomon, a book of the Bible (Deuterocanonical) famous for the phrase "You have ordered all things in measure, and number, and weight" (11:20).</note> also says that all things were established by Him in weight, number, and measure. 

If, therefore, God—for whose sake all beings are finite—did not exist, nothing would be finite; thus, everything would be infinite. If something is infinite, it is nothing, because if it is infinite, it is not finite; the infinite destroys itself <note>In this scholastic logic, the "infinite" (unbounded chaos) is a contradiction in terms for created things; if a thing has no boundaries or definition, it ceases to be a specific "thing" at all.</note>, just as other things do that contain a contradiction. Since it has been proven that there is some "One" from which all things receive their being, and that they are finite, it follows that if that One were removed, nothing would exist and nothing would be finite. For if something is "infinite"—that is, not bounded and limited by that First One, by whose help all things both exist and are bounded and limited—it follows that the infinite does not exist. Therefore, the infinite destroys itself, since saying that something is infinite (in the sense used here) is saying nothing else than that it is nothing; for if a thing is neither finite nor God, it is beyond controversy that it is nothing at all. 

These are the things, Antonio, which I have brought forward to explain my uncle’s <note>Referring to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note> opinion, which perhaps contains other dogmas as well; for it is not for everyone to reach the heights of what he had conceived. But because I think other meanings also lie hidden under the "bark" <note>original: "uerborum cortice." A common medieval metaphor where the literal words are the "bark" or "husk" and the spiritual/intellectual meaning is the "fruit" or "pith."</note> of the words, I am moved by those words of his with which he ended his response. Specifically: "I believe these things are sufficient for you, as ingenious a man as you are; but let us leave aside the inaccessible, and let us hold to what we have written while performing the duty of an interpreter." Since these words are satisfactory, they shall also close my response, though I will first bring forward certain points that both strengthen my uncle’s opinion and clarify and confirm my own interpretation of his words. 

For if the First fails, it is necessary that all those things which proceed from it perish, as is gathered from the eighth book of <term>Aristotle's</term> <term>Physics</term>. Moreover, God—as the same philosopher witnesses—is the "First Truth" from which all other true things come; therefore, if God is removed, it is necessary that all true things perish. But if true things tend toward nothingness, beings are likewise not saved from destruction, since truth and being travel in the same circle <note>A reference to the transcendental properties of being: in Scholasticism, "Being" and "Truth" are "convertible," meaning they refer to the same reality from different perspectives.</note>. Likewise, if He who communicates both being and life to things is removed, who would not see that those very things would utterly perish? 

Moreover, it is the opinion of <term>Aristotle</term> in the first book of <term>On the Heavens</term> that God bestows existence upon things themselves, adding that this is communicated to some more clearly and to others more obscurely. Furthermore, whatever is governed by the art of the First Cause falls down if that cause perishes. That this whole machine <note>original: "machinam." A common term for the structured universe or "cosmos."</note> of the universe is governed and ruled by the First Cause is testified by <term>Auerroes</term> <note>Ibn Rushd, the medieval Andalusian philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational to Western university study.</note> in the second book of <term>Metaphysics</term> <note>original: "primæ Philosophię." Aristotle called Metaphysics "First Philosophy."</note>, under which rule no one can doubt that even gold is contained and included. 

I could bring many other things into the midst from the sacred books, such as many things from the Gospel itself, many from the most sacred dogmas of the Apostle Paul, and many from others; for instance, from <term>Gregory</term> <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604).</note>, who said that all things would fall into nothingness unless they were preserved by the Almighty God. Also from <term>Augustine</term> in his literal commentary on Genesis, and from <term>St. Thomas</term> [Aquinas], and from <term>John [Duns] Scotus</term> in his treatise on...

<summary>The author argues that God is the essential "Limit" (Terminus) that prevents the universe from dissolving into the nothingness of the infinite. He supports this by citing a wide array of authorities, including Plato, Aristotle, Averroes, and the Church Fathers, to prove that all existence depends on the First Cause.</summary>

the first principle; however, I deliberately pass over these points, since it is enough to have proven it through the natural reasons you seemed to demand and through the teachings of the pagan philosophers—something you by no means believed could be proven by him. Therefore, given all these things we have stated, I would think it beyond controversy for those of good intellect that all my uncle's <note>Gianfrancesco Pico is here defending his famous uncle, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note> opinions have been sufficiently defended, perhaps even in your own judgment. 

Nevertheless, I have written these things not to clash with you; indeed, I wrote them reluctantly, as our friend **Giovanni Mainardi** <note>A noted physician and scholar from Ferrara who was a close associate of the Pico family.</note> and **Christopher Saxolus of Mirandola** <note>A physician and citizen of Mirandola who had been a student of the person Gianfrancesco is addressing.</note>, our fellow citizen and physician and formerly your student, can testify. If it should please you to put my feelings toward you to the test, you will find that my deeds outweigh my words.

->TO HIS ILLUSTRIOUS PRINCE AND SINGULAR LORD,<-
->Count Giovanni Francesco, Antonio of Faenza sends greetings.<-

**I** have read the defenses sent to me regarding your uncle’s writings. In them, I clearly perceived great learning and an admirable sharpness of mind, and I was wonderfully delighted by your findings. This is not only because I see that the liberal arts will at last have excellent guardians and patrons by whom they may be rescued from darkness and barbarism, but even more so because I easily promise myself something great and grand from you, if you continue to philosophize. Posterity will see that I have told no lie, provided you live; may God only grant you a longer life. 

As for what concerns me, I certainly shall not disparage what you have written with such subtlety and precision in defense of your uncle. For even if your uncle were still alive, I would not have prolonged the dispute already begun any further, just as I clearly testified to him in my last opposition; he replied through a messenger that he too would write nothing more. Therefore, let those who read these things be the judges of the cause. 

If you have decided that these well-considered reflections should be given to the printers, let it be done while keeping the honor of a friend safe and intact, as you promised. There are indeed some words in your booklet that have something of a sting—and not a small one—which you can easily moderate if you wish, without changing the meaning of the matter. If you do this, as I hope, it will be appreciated. I feel I have protected my own case sufficiently and could have easily continued to do so daily. But let there now be a limit to this dispute. Furthermore, illustrious Count, I wish you to believe that I am yours and always shall be, to be employed at your discretion. Farewell. From Ferrara, on the 
->16th day of December, 1495.<-

<page-num>311</page-num>
<header>To Antonio of Faenza, philosopher.</header>

## To Antonio of Faenza, philosopher.

->GIANFRANCESCO PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA<-
->sends his best greetings to the distinguished philosopher Antonio of Faenza.<-

**Y**our wishes have been fully satisfied. My promises to you have also been fulfilled, as I have removed from my writings every word that seemed to carry even a slight sting <note>original: "aculei," literally "little needles" or "stings." Gianfrancesco is referring to his edits to remove insulting language from his philosophical critique.</note>. We must forgive the impulse of the mind if, by chance, I acted more sharply than was proper. Something must be granted to a just defense—and it must be granted all the more because it is a common vice among those who use their commentaries to either accuse someone or excuse themselves and their friends, to pursue those to whom they write with insults, to attack them with slanders, to provoke them with shames, and to commit other such acts foreign to the duty of a good man. From these things (I call upon you as my witness and judge), we have entirely abstained. At your request, we have removed at most ten somewhat sharp words (though without changing the meaning), for I would not want you to believe I had any other plan in working out this little commentary than to defend my uncle Pico <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), the famous Renaissance philosopher known for his "900 Theses."</note> without causing you offense. Indeed, I would have much preferred if no dispute had ever occurred between you, so that the path to writing on this matter had been closed to me and every occasion for it removed. For the business of letters can only be conducted with the greatest difficulty when it is placed in the context of a dispute, even when all due honor is shown to those to whom one speaks. Furthermore, this duty can hardly be performed without a certain swelling of the spirit <note>A reference to intellectual pride or arrogance.</note>, which must be greatly avoided. As for what you say regarding the protection of your cause, I say the same regarding mine. But enough of this controversy. Let those who read it be the judges (as you rightly wrote), provided they are learned and impartial—or, if they are held too ardently by love for either of us, let that love not cast a veil over their eyes.

Otherwise, you attribute much to me, perhaps more than I deserve, and you promise great things for me if I continue to pursue philosophy. But I fear, my dear Antonio, that I may entirely restrain myself or perhaps even cease from this study of philosophy you mention. Let me tell you how I feel about this matter: namely, that this pursuit brings much harm and little benefit to those of us who desire it too much. I do not say this to condemn or disparage the many truths, or at least the likenesses of truth, that we acquire for ourselves by philosophizing. Rather, I blame the common use—or, to speak more significantly, the abuse—of it. Unless we strive greatly to avoid this and examine our thoughts constantly and with the utmost diligence, ambition, the poison of the Christian soul, creeps into the heart. This later gives birth to a deadly pride, from which it often happens that the lovers of this wisdom in which we are daily engaged—swollen and puffed up by fleeting glory—entirely neglect that Wisdom which was begotten, yet is eternal <note>A theological reference to Christ as the Eternal Wisdom (Logos), contrasting it with secular or human philosophy.</note>, and from which all this flowing and temporary knowledge is derived.

But let us see, I pray, from what source we are carried away in spirit, and why we value ourselves too much. For how small is our knowledge? Since we possess only the smallest understanding of natural things, and those very things of which we are ignorant—which are both many and great—seem to cry out <note>original catchword: "clament" (they cry out).</note> silently...

<meta>catchword: cry out</meta>

He then pivots to a skeptical view of secular philosophy, warning that it often leads to pride and distracts from divine wisdom.</summary>
