<header>Letter of Gianfrancesco of Mirandola</header>

...they cry out in vain—namely, and falsely—that we either profess to be or consider ourselves learned. Without a doubt, even a coarse man, a farmer with little skill or one entirely ignorant of letters, could ask many things—even about things placed right before our eyes—for which an otherwise great <term>philosopher</term> <note>original: "philosophus"</note> would be unable to give a certain explanation. In perceiving those very substances which are entirely separated from sensible matter, how far do we actually proceed in our knowledge? We see them only with the bleary and nocturnal eyes of the mind. But what shall we say of divine matters? To know these—or rather, to even track them down—we direct our sight, gasping and anxious, yet blind and dim, covered by the thickest of clouds. Furthermore, have we not received this knowledge of ours either from books or from a teacher? What need is there, then, to boast that we have learned the things of others, swallowing meditations as if from someone narrating a history? But it is a history of nature, one placed amid bitter altercations through diverse studies and tossed about by various opinions, and for that reason, it is uncertain. This is revealed most clearly by the very name of "opinion." If we indeed obtain some small bit of knowledge by our own efforts, what else is it, I ask, than a certain uncertainty, wrapped in a thousand coverings and entangled in a thousand deceits? I would pursue this matter by being angry at those who value these studies more than is appropriate, if I had not treated this subject specifically in a long inquiry and dedicated a special book to it. For these reasons, I have decided to turn myself to studying those books whose propositions are already established and whose axioms <note>original: "dignitates," referring to self-evident principles in logic</note> and conclusions are gathered by an infallible <term>syllogism</term> <note>a form of logical reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</note> and which render the mind purified (if we take care for it). 

But let there now be an end to this literary conflict, and even to this <term>epistle</term>. But see how different the effect of our controversy has been compared to others: after a <term>disputation</term> <note>a formal academic debate</note> is finished—whether conducted by voice or in writing—hatreds and grudges are often practiced between those whose minds were discordant; they plot fraudulent wars, and slanders against honor and fame flow forth from here and there. You, however, and our Pico were "spiritual brothers" <term>compatres</term> <note>original: "compatres," literally "co-fathers" or godparents; Gianfrancesco notes they are "bound by a spiritual knot."</note> before the debate began. Nevertheless, the original concord of your minds was not dissolved because of this. As for me, I was known to you only by name while my uncle was alive, nor were you known to me; this defense has brought it about that a certain treaty of friendship has been struck between us. See to it that this remains stable while we live, and strive so that it may endure eternally after this death we expect, by living rightly and piously; I shall also strive to do the same in whatever way I can. Meanwhile, do not be reluctant to experience the love with which I regard you. Perhaps I shall perform what you have asked more abundantly than I promised at the conclusion of my defense. 

->For there is nothing so difficult that I would not do for the sake of more readily earning the favor of you (a truly most serious <term>philosopher</term>).<-

->From the Castle of Mirandola, January 4, 1496.<-

<meta>This page serves as the introduction to the famous "Oration on the Dignity of Man." It transitions from Gianfrancesco Pico’s personal correspondence to his editorial preface for his uncle Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s works, followed by the opening lines of the Oration itself.</meta>

<page-num>313</page-num>
<header>on the dignity of man.</header>

### ->THE ARGUMENT<-
### ->of Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola, regarding the<-
### ->Oration and Letters of his uncle, Giovanni Pico, etc.<-

Accept, Reader, these scholarly works <note>original: "lucubrationes," literally "works produced by candlelight," implying late-night study</note> of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola—works of a lighter focus which perhaps he himself would not have published while living, nor would we have, had we not been stirred by the frequent encouragements of distinguished men. You will first read a most elegant oration, dictated indeed with youthful eagerness, but which has often been admired by the more learned for its height of doctrine and eloquence. Let it not trouble you if many things are seen at its conclusion which were also inserted in the preface of his *Apology*, since he published the latter to the world, but always kept the former at home, sharing it only with friends. You will see many of the secret teachings of the ancients, previously hidden in the wrappings of riddles and fables, most ingeniously unlocked; and you will see that effort, through both strength and oratorical charms, show how the **poetic theology** <note>A humanist concept suggesting that ancient myths contained hidden theological truths compatible with Christianity.</note> of the ancient sages served the mysteries of our own theology. Furthermore, by untying certain knots in both, he invites men to the **literary arenas** <note>original: "literarias palæstras," referring to the public philosophical debates common in the Renaissance.</note>. For at that time he was most frequently engaged in these, which he later left behind as mere playful battles and preludes to more serious studies, turning his mind to the completion of those works which we have already released, and those we shall release in the future. You will also read several letters (for it would be most laborious to collect them all), some of a personal nature, written both in his tender youth and more mature years; others, written after he dedicated his whole heart to God, filled with most holy advice. You will find that the former taste most richly of both learning and eloquence, while you will perceive that the latter savor abundantly of both, and beyond these, breathe most fruitfully of the love of Christ.

# ->ORATION<-
# ->on the<-
# ->DIGNITY OF MAN,<-
# ->by Giovanni Pico della Mirandola,<-
# ->Count of Concordia.<-

I HAVE READ, Most Venerable Fathers, in the records of the Arabs, that when **Abdala the Saracen** <note>Likely referring to Abd-Allah, though the specific source is debated; Pico uses "Saracen" as a general term for Islamic scholars.</note> was asked what was to be seen as most wonderful on this, so to speak, world-stage, he replied that nothing is seen as more wonderful than man. Matching this sentiment is that famous saying of **Hermes** <note>Refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary figure to whom the "Hermetic" writings on magic and philosophy were attributed.</note> to Asclepius: "A great miracle, O Asclepius, is man." When I began to think about the reason for these sayings, those many things which are brought forward by many people concerning the excellence of human nature did not fully satisfy me: that man is the intermediary between creatures, familiar with the gods above, the king of those below...

--- Page 347 ---
<meta>This page contains the most famous passage from Pico della Mirandola’s "Oration on the Dignity of Man." It moves from traditional medieval praises of man to Pico’s revolutionary Renaissance argument: that man’s unique dignity lies in his total freedom to define his own nature.</meta>

<page-num>314</page-num>
<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>
<meta>Catchword: minis (the start of the word "humanity" on the following page)</meta>

...[man is] the interpreter of nature by the sharp inquiry of his reason, by the light of his intelligence; the interface between stable eternity and flowing time; and (as the Persians say) the bond, or rather the marriage-hymn of the world; a little lower than the angels, according to the testimony of David <note>original: "teste Dauide," referring to Psalm 8:5.</note>. These are great things, to be sure, but they are not the primary ones—that is, those which rightfully claim the privilege of the highest admiration. For why should we not admire the angels themselves and the most blessed choirs of heaven more? At last, I seemed to understand why man is the most fortunate creature and thus worthy of all admiration, and what exactly that condition is which he has been allotted in the sequence of the universe, an enviable one not only to the beasts, but even to the stars and the minds beyond this world. A thing beyond belief and marvelous. And why not? For it is for this reason that man is rightly called and considered a great miracle and a truly wonderful animal.

But hear what this condition is, Fathers, and grant me this attention with kind ears, according to your humanity. Now the highest Father, God the Architect, had already built this world-house of divinity which we see—this most august temple—according to the laws of secret wisdom. He had adorned the super-celestial region with minds; He had animated the ethereal spheres with eternal souls; He had filled the excrement-filled and drossy parts of the lower world with a crowd of animals of every kind. But with the work completed, the Craftsman desired that there be someone to weigh the reason of such a great work, to love its beauty, and to admire its vastness. Therefore, with all things already finished (as Moses and Timaeus <note>referencing the Book of Genesis and Plato’s dialogue on the creation of the universe</note> testify), He finally thought about producing man. 

But there was nothing left in the archetypes <note>the original patterns or ideas in the mind of God</note> from which He might fashion a new offspring, nor in His treasures was there anything He might bestow as an inheritance upon a new son, nor in the benches of the whole world was there a place where this contemplator of the universe might sit. Everything was already full; all things had been distributed into the highest, middle, and lowest orders. But it was not in the nature of the Father’s power to fail in His final birth, as if exhausted. It was not in the nature of His wisdom to have wavered in a necessary matter for lack of a plan. It was not in the nature of His beneficent love that he who was to praise divine liberality in others should be forced to condemn it in himself. 

Finally, the best of craftsmen decreed that he to whom nothing could be given as his own should share in common whatever had been private to each individual. Therefore, He took man, a work of indeterminate image <note>original: "indiscretæ opus imaginis," meaning man has no fixed species or pre-set mold</note>, and having placed him in the center of the world, addressed him thus: 

"Neither a fixed seat, nor a form of your own, nor any peculiar gift have we given you, O Adam, so that whatever seat, whatever form, and whatever gifts you yourself shall desire, these you may have and possess according to your wish and your own judgment. The nature of all other things is limited and constrained within the laws prescribed by us. You, constrained by no limits, shall define your nature for yourself according to your own free will, in whose hand I have placed you. I have set you in the center of the world, so that from there you might more easily gaze upon whatever is in the world. We have made you neither heavenly nor earthly, neither mortal nor immortal, so that as if you were your own voluntary and honorary sculptor and maker, you may fashion yourself into whatever form you prefer. You will be able to degenerate into the lower things, which are brutes; you will be able to be reborn into the higher things, which are divine, according to the judgment of your soul." 

O the supreme liberality of God the Father! O the supreme and wonderful...

<summary>This page contains the philosophical "heart" of the Oration, where Pico describes God's creation of Adam as a being with no fixed nature, granted the free will to choose his own place in the hierarchy of existence.</summary>
<keywords>human dignity, free will, creation of man, Adam, Great Chain of Being, Renaissance philosophy, Platonism, architect of the world</keywords>

--- Page 348 ---
<meta>This page continues the core argument of Pico’s Oration: the unique "chameleon-like" nature of humanity. While other beings have fixed natures (beasts are born as beasts, angels remain as angels), humans are defined by their freedom to choose their own form and destiny.</meta>

<page-num>315</page-num>
# On the Dignity of Man

...humanity's happiness. To whom it is granted to have whatever he chooses, to be whatever he desires. Brute beasts, as soon as they are born, bring with them from their mother's womb—as <term>Lucilius</term><note>Gaius Lucilius was an early Roman satirist; Pico suggests that animals are born fully formed with their traits.</note> says—everything they will ever possess. The highest spirits <note>referring to angels</note> were from the beginning, or soon after, what they will remain for all eternity. At man's birth, the Father planted seeds of every kind and germs of every way of life. Whatever seeds each person cultivates will grow and bear fruit in him. If they are vegetative, he will become a plant. If they are sensual, he will become like a beast. If they are rational, he will turn out to be a heavenly creature. If they are intellectual, he will be an angel and a son of God. And if, not content with the lot of any creature, he withdraws into the center of his own unity, he becomes one spirit with God—in the solitary darkness of the Father who is set above all things—and he will surpass everything else. 

Who would not admire this <term>chameleon</term> of ours? Or who would admire anything else more? Not without reason did <term>Asclepius of Athens</term> say that man, because of this shifting and self-transforming nature, was symbolized by <term>Proteus</term> <note>A sea god in Greek mythology capable of changing his shape at will.</note> in the ancient mysteries. This is the source of the transformations celebrated among the Hebrews and the <term>Pythagoreans</term>. For the more secret theology of the Hebrews transforms the holy <term>Enoch</term> into the angel of the divine presence (whom they call the *Angel of the Shekhinah* <note>original: "מלאך השכינה", a reference to Jewish mystical traditions where the patriarch Enoch is transformed into the archangel Metatron.</note>), and transforms others into various other names. And the Pythagoreans deform wicked men into brute animals, and—if <term>Empedocles</term> is believed—even into plants. Following them, <term>Muhammad</term> often had this saying on his lips: "He who turns away from divine law becomes a beast." 

And rightly so. For it is not the bark that makes the plant, but its mindless and unfeeling nature; nor is it the hide that makes the beast, but its brutish and sensual soul; nor is it the circular body that makes the heavens, but right reason; nor is it the separation from the body that makes an angel, but spiritual intelligence. If you see someone dedicated to his belly, crawling on the ground like a serpent, it is a shrub you are looking at, not a man. If you see someone blinded by the empty illusions of his imagination, as if by <term>Calypso</term> <note>The nymph in the Odyssey who detained Odysseus; here representing the entrapment of the senses.</note>, and enslaved by the senses through some soothing lure, it is a beast you see, not a man. If you see a philosopher discerning all things by right reason, revere him; he is a heavenly creature, not an earthly one. If you see a pure contemplator, oblivious to the body, withdrawn into the inner sanctuary of the mind, this is neither an earthly nor a heavenly creature; he is a more august divinity, clothed in human flesh. 

Who would not admire man? He is, not without merit, designated in the sacred <term>Mosaic</term> <note>Referring to the books of Moses (the Pentateuch).</note> and Christian writings by the names "all flesh" or "every creature," since he shapes, crafts, and transforms himself into the appearance of all flesh and the character of every creature. For this reason, <term>Evantes the Persian</term>, in his explanation of Chaldean theology, writes that man has no native image of his own, but many external and foreign ones. Hence that saying of the <term>Chaldeans</term>: *Man is an animal of a varied, multiform, and fickle nature* <note>original: "אנוש הוא שוני' וכמה טבעית בעלחי'", a Hebrew/Aramaic phrase Pico interprets as describing man's fluid nature.</note>. 

But what is the purpose of all this? It is so that we may understand that, since we were born with the condition that we are whatever we want to be, we must take the greatest care that it not be said of us that, though we were in a place of honor, we did not realize it and became like beasts and foolish cattle. But let us rather follow the word of the prophet <term>Asaph</term>: "You are gods, and sons [of the Most High]."

<sig>Dd 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: of the Most High (excelsi)</meta>

<summary>Pico argues that humanity possesses no fixed nature, but instead functions like a chameleon, capable of ascending to divinity or descending to a bestial state based on free will. He draws on Hebrew, Pythagorean, Islamic, and Persian traditions to illustrate this unique "protean" capacity of the human soul.</summary>
<keywords>free will, human dignity, chameleon, Proteus, Enoch, Metatron, Shekhinah, Muhammad, Chaldean theology, Asaph, metamorphosis</keywords>

--- Page 349 ---
<meta>This page continues the central argument of Pico's "Oration on the Dignity of Man." Having established that humans have the unique freedom to choose their own nature, Pico now exhorts his readers to "sacred ambition"—to reject mediocrity and strive for the highest spiritual states, modeled after the angelic hierarchy.</meta>

<page-num>316</page-num>
<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

all of us who are high-born, let us not abuse the most indulgent liberality of the Father, who gave us free choice, lest we turn what was intended as a life-saving gift into something harmful. Let a certain sacred ambition invade our souls, so that, not content with mediocre things, we long for the highest, and strive with all our strength to achieve them—since we can, if we will. Let us disdain earthly things, disregard celestial ones, and finally, setting aside whatever belongs to the world, let us fly to the super-mundane court nearest to the most eminent divinity. There, as the sacred mysteries teach, the **Seraphim**, **Cherubim**, and **Thrones** <note>These are the three highest orders in the traditional medieval hierarchy of angels. Pico uses them as symbols for Love, Knowledge, and Justice.</note> hold the primary places; let us, impatient of being second and not knowing how to yield to them, emulate their dignity and glory. We shall be in no way inferior to them, if we will it.

But by what means, or what are we to do? Let us see what they do, what life they live. If we live that life (and we can), we will have already equaled their lot. The **Seraph** burns with the fire of charity <note>original: "charitatis," meaning divine, selfless love.</note>. The **Cherub** shines with the splendor of intelligence. The **Throne** stands firm with the steadfastness of judgment. Therefore, if devoted to the active life, we take up the care of lower things with a right examination, we shall be strengthened by the stable solidity of the **Thrones**. If, resting from actions, meditating on the Creator in the creation, and the creation in the Creator, we are occupied in the leisure of contemplation, we shall flash everywhere with **Cherubic** light. If by charity we burn for the Creator alone, we shall suddenly be inflamed into the **Seraphic** image by His fire—that fire which is all-consuming. 

God, the judge of the ages, sits upon the **Throne**—that is, the just judge. He flies above the **Cherub**—that is, the contemplator—and cherishes him, as if by brooding over him. For the Spirit of the Lord is carried over the waters—those, I mean, which are above the heavens, which in the Book of Job praise the Lord with dawn hymns. He who is a **Seraph**—that is, a lover—is in God, and God in him; indeed, God and he are one. Great is the power of the **Thrones**, which we attain by judging; supreme is the height of the **Seraphim**, which we attain by loving. 

But how can anyone either judge or love what is unknown? <term>Moses</term> loved the God whom he saw, and as a judge administered to the people those things which he, as a contemplator, had first seen on the mountain. Therefore, the middle **Cherub** prepares us with his light and equally illuminates us for the judgment of the **Thrones** and with **Seraphic** fire. This is the knot of the primary minds, the <term>Palladian order</term> <note>Referring to Pallas Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom; Pico uses this to describe the order of philosophers and seekers of wisdom.</note>, the presiding force of contemplative philosophy; this we must first emulate, desire, and indeed comprehend, so that from there we may be snatched up to the heights of love and descend well-instructed and prepared for the duties of action. 

But truly, it is worth the effort—if our life is to be formed according to the model of the **Cherubic** life—to have before our eyes and ready at hand what that life is, of what quality it is, and what their actions and works are. Since it is not permitted for us to achieve this through ourselves—we who are flesh and savor the things of the earth—let us go to the ancient fathers, who can provide us with the most abundant and certain faith regarding these matters, since they are familiar and related to them. Let us consult the **Apostle Paul**, the "vessel of election," <note>A traditional title for St. Paul, referring to God choosing him to spread the Gospel.</note> to see what he saw the armies of the **Cherubim** doing when he was lifted up to the third heaven. He will certainly answer, through the interpretation of <term>Dionysius</term> <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century author whose writings on the "Celestial Hierarchy" were the foundation of medieval angelology.</note>, that they are purged, then illuminated, and finally perfected. 

<meta>catchword: perfected.</meta>

<summary>Pico argues that humans should emulate the three highest angelic orders—Thrones, Cherubim, and Seraphim—representing Justice, Contemplation, and Love. He identifies contemplation (the Cherubic path) as the essential middle step that prepares the soul to either act with justice or ascend to divine love.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s exhortation to emulate the angelic orders. Having previously discussed the Seraphim (Love) and the Thrones (Judgment), he now focuses on the Cherubim (Knowledge/Intelligence) and the practical steps of spiritual ascent through the metaphor of Jacob's Ladder.</meta>

# On the Dignity of Man.

<margin>ci.</margin>Therefore, we too, emulating the Cherubic life on earth—by restraining the impulses of our passions through moral science <note>In the Renaissance, "moral science" or moral philosophy was the study of ethics and the regulation of human behavior.</note>, by dispelling the darkness of reason through dialectic <note>The art of logical argument and investigation of truth.</note>, as if washing away the filth of ignorance and vice—let us purge the soul, lest either the passions run wild recklessly, or an imprudent reason sometimes goes astray. Then, let us drench the well-ordered and purified soul with the light of natural philosophy, so that finally we may perfect it with the knowledge of divine things.

And lest we be satisfied with our own efforts, let us consult the patriarch Jacob, whose image shines sculpted on the throne of glory. This most wise father will advise us—he who sleeps in the lower world and watches in the upper world. But he will advise us through a figure (for in this way all things were revealed to them) that there are scales <note>Jacob’s Ladder, as described in Genesis 28:12.</note> stretched from the lowest ground to the heights of heaven, divided by a series of many steps, with the Lord sitting at the summit, and the contemplating angels ascending and descending them in alternating turns.

If we, who aspire to the angelic life, must do this same thing, I ask: who would touch the Lord's ladder with either a filthy foot or poorly cleaned hands? As the mysteries hold, it is a sacrilege for the impure to touch what is pure. But what are these "feet"? What are these "hands"? Surely the "foot" of the soul is that most contemptible part by which it rests upon the soil of matter as if on the ground—I mean the nourishing and feeding power, the fuel of lust, and the teacher of voluptuous softness. Why should we not call the "hands" of the soul its anger, which, as the defender of desire, fights on its behalf and, like a predator, seizes its prey under the dust and sun? To prevent the soul from being devoured by these hands and feet—that is, the entire sensual part in which the lure of the body sits, which holds the soul by the neck (as they say) <note>original: "obtorto collo," a classical idiom meaning to drag someone by force or against their will.</note>—let us wash these away with moral philosophy as if with a living river, lest we be cast back from the ladder as profane and polluted.

But even this will not be enough if we wish to be companions to the angels running to and fro on Jacob's ladder, unless we have first been well-fitted and instructed to be promoted rightly from step to step, never to wander from the path of the ladder, and to undertake reciprocal journeys. When we have achieved this through the art of speech or reasoning <note>original: "artem sermocinalem siue rationariam," referring to logic and rhetoric.</note>, we will then be animated by the Cherubic spirit. We shall philosophize through the steps of the ladder—that is, the degrees of nature—pervading all things from center to center. Now we shall descend, tearing the "One" apart into a "multitude" like Osiris by Titanic force <note>Pico references the Egyptian myth of Osiris being dismembered by the Titans/Typhon, which Neoplatonists used as a metaphor for the divine Unity descending into the many forms of the physical world.</note>; now we shall ascend, gathering the multitude like the limbs of Osiris into one by Phoebean force <note>original: "ui Phœbea," referring to Apollo (the Sun), symbolizing the intellectual light that brings unity and harmony.</note>, until, finally resting in the bosom of the Father who is above the ladder, we shall be perfected in theological happiness.

Let us also consult the just Job, who entered into a covenant of life with God before he himself was brought forth into life. As to what the highest God most desires among those ten hundred thousand who assist Him, Job will surely answer: "Peace." This is according to what is read in his book: "He who makes peace in the high places" <note>Job 25:2.</note>. And since the middle order interprets the commands of the highest order to the lower ones, let the philosopher Empedocles <note>A Greek Pre-Socratic philosopher who taught that the universe is governed by the two opposing forces of Love (attraction) and Strife (repulsion).</note> interpret for us the words of Job the theologian. He points out a double nature situated in our souls: by one, we are raised upward to heavenly things; by the other, we are thrust downward to the lower regions, through strife...

Having introduced the image of Jacob’s Ladder, he now explains how different branches of philosophy—moral, dialectical, and natural—serve to pacify the internal conflicts of the human spirit before it can reach the divine peace of Theology.</meta>

# John Pico della Mirandola
<meta>catchword: in herself</meta>

...[unity] and friendship, or war and peace, as his poems <note>Pico refers to the Greek philosopher Empedocles, who proposed that Love and Strife are the fundamental forces of the universe.</note> testify to us, in which he complains that through strife and discord, in a state like madness, he is tossed about on the deep, a fugitive from the gods. Truly, Fathers, there is a manifold discord within us; we have grave and internal domestic struggles, and more than "civil wars." If we wish to avoid these, if we strive for that peace which lifts us so high that we are placed among the Lord's exalted ones, philosophy alone will completely restrain and calm these struggles within us.

**Moral philosophy** first—if our human nature <note>original: "noster homo," literally "our man," referring to the lower, sensory or earthly nature of the human being.</note> seeks even a truce from enemies—will crush the unbridled raids of the manifold beast <note>A common metaphor for the diverse and chaotic desires of the lower soul.</note> and the lion's <note>Representing the spirited or angry part of the soul.</note> quarrels, rages, and outbursts. Then, if we take better counsel for ourselves and desire the security of perpetual peace, she will be present and generously fulfill our prayers. For once both beasts are slain—as if by the ritual of the sacrificed sow <note>original: "icta porca." Pico refers to an ancient Roman custom where a pig was sacrificed to seal a treaty; here, it symbolizes the sacrifice of lower instincts to secure internal peace.</note>—she will establish an inviolable treaty of most holy peace between the flesh and the spirit.

**Dialectic** will calm the turmoils of reason as it struggles between conflicting arguments and the anxiously rioting traps of syllogisms. **Natural philosophy** will calm the disputes and disagreements of opinion which vex, distract, and tear apart the restless soul from every side. But it will calm them in such a way that it bids us remember that nature, according to **Heraclitus** <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who famously argued that "war is the father of all things."</note>, was born from war, which is why **Homer** called it "strife." Therefore, natural philosophy cannot provide us with true rest and solid peace in herself; this is the duty and privilege of her mistress, most holy **Theology**.

Philosophy will show the way and lead as a companion to Theology, who, seeing us hastening from afar, will cry out: "Come to me, you who have labored; come and I will refresh you; come to me and I will give you peace which the world and nature cannot give you." <note>Pico blends the words of Christ from the Gospel of Matthew 11:28 and the Gospel of John 14:27.</note> So gently called, so kindly invited, flying with winged feet like earthly **Mercuries** <note>Mercury was the messenger of the gods and the patron of eloquence and hermetic wisdom.</note>, into the embraces of our most blessed mother, we shall enjoy the longed-for peace: most holy peace, an indivisible bond, a unanimous friendship, by which all souls do not merely agree in one mind which is above all minds, but in an ineffable way become utterly one.

This is that friendship which the **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of Pythagoras, for whom "friendship" (amicitia) was a cosmic principle of harmony.</note> say is the end of all philosophy. This is the peace which God makes in his high places, which the angels descending to earth announced to men of good will, so that through it men themselves, ascending into heaven, might become angels. Let us wish for this peace for our friends, for our age, for every house we enter, and for our soul, so that through it the soul may become the house of God. After it has shaken off its filth through moral philosophy and dialectic, and adorned itself with manifold philosophy as if with courtly splendor, and crowned the tops of its gates with theological garlands, let the **King of Glory** descend; and coming with the Father, let Him make His home there.

If the soul shows itself worthy of such a great guest—such is His immense mercy—it will receive the beautiful guest, surrounded by the variety of many sciences like a golden wedding gown, not as a guest now, but as a bridegroom. So that she may never be parted from him, she will desire to be parted from her own people and her father's house; indeed, forgetting herself, in herself...

->de hominis dignitate.<-

# On the Dignity of Man

The soul will desire to die in herself that she may live in her spouse, in whose sight the death of his saints is truly precious—that death, I say, if it should be called death, which is the fullness of life, the meditation upon which the wise have said is the study of philosophy. Let us also summon Moses himself, who was diminished only a little from the fountain-like fullness of the holy and ineffable intelligence, from which the angels are inebriated with their nectar. We shall hear the venerable judge proclaiming laws to us who dwell in the desert solitude of this body: 
> Those who are still polluted and in need of moral [purification] should dwell with the common people outside the tabernacle under the open sky, like Thessalian priests <note>original: "Thessali sacerdotes." Pico refers to ancient rituals of purification, suggesting those who are not yet "composed" in character must remain outside the sacred space.</note> cleansing themselves in the meantime. Let those who have already composed their conduct, being received into the sanctuary, not yet touch the sacred objects, but first as diligent Levites in the service of dialectics <note>original: "dialectico famulatu." Here, dialectics is the logical training required to serve higher wisdom.</note>, let them minister to the holy things of Philosophy.

Then, once they too are admitted to these things, let them contemplate in the priesthood of philosophy now the multicolored royal ornament—that is, the starry decoration of the court of the highest God—now the heavenly candelabrum distinguished by seven lights, and now the elements made of skins <note>original: "pellicea elementa." This refers to the "garments of skin" from Genesis, interpreted by Neoplatonists as the material world or the physical body that veils the spirit.</note>, so that at last, through the merits of theological sublimity, being received into the inner recesses of the temple, with no veil of an image intervening, we may enjoy the glory of the divinity. Moses certainly commands these things to us, and by commanding he admonishes, excites, and exhorts us that through philosophy we should prepare a way for ourselves toward future heavenly glory while we are able. Yet, it is not only the Mosaic or Christian mysteries, but also the Theology of the ancients that shows us the benefits and dignity of these liberal arts about which I have come to dispute. For what else do the stages of initiation observed in the secrets of the Greeks mean? To those first purified through those arts we called "purifying" <note>original: "februales artes." Referring to the Roman month of purification, Februarius, and the rites of cleansing.</note>, namely moral philosophy and dialectics, the reception of the mysteries was granted. And what else can this be but the interpretation of a more secret nature through philosophy? Then finally, to those so prepared, came that <term>vision <gloss>epopteia</gloss></term> <note>original: "ἐποπτεία," the highest stage of initiation in the Eleusinian Mysteries, signifying a direct sight of the sacred.</note>, that is, the inspection of divine things through the light of Theology. Who would not desire to be initiated into such rites? Who would not desire, setting aside all human things, despising the goods of fortune, and neglecting the body, to become a guest of the Gods while still dwelling on earth, and, soaked in the nectar of eternity, to be gifted with the prize of immortality though still a mortal animal? Who would not wish to be so breathed upon by those Socratic frenzies <note>original: "Socraticis furoribus." In Plato's *Phaedrus*, these are types of divine inspiration—poetic, religious, prophetic, and erotic—that lift the soul.</note> sung by Plato in the <term>*Phaedrus*</term>, so that by the rowing of wings and feet, fleeing quickly from here—that is, from the world which is set in wickedness—he might be carried in a most swift course to the heavenly Jerusalem? We shall be driven, Fathers, we shall be driven by the Socratic frenzies, which so place us outside our own minds that they place our mind and our very selves in God. We shall be driven by them indeed, if we have first driven ourselves to do what is in us; for if the powers of the passions are so tuned to their proper scales through the due proportions that they sound together in an unshaken harmony, and if reason has moved itself in a measured progression through dialectics, then, stirred by the frenzy of the Muses, we shall drink in the heavenly harmony with our innermost ears. Then Bacchus, the leader of the Muses...

->Giovanni Pico della Mirandola<-

...in His mysteries—that is, the visible signs of nature—showing the invisible things of God to us as we philosophize, He will inebriate us from the abundance of the house of God, in which, like Moses, we shall be entirely faithful. As most sacred Theology approaches, she will animate us with a double frenzy. For, raised to her most eminent height of contemplation, measuring from there with an indivisible eternity <note>original: "insectili aevo." A philosophical term for eternity, which unlike time, cannot be cut or divided into past, present, and future.</note> those things which are, which will be, and which have been, and gazing upon the primeval beauty, we shall be the winged lovers of those things, like the prophets of Phoebus <note>Phoebus is another name for Apollo, the Greek god of prophecy, music, and healing.</note>. Finally, stirred by an ineffable charity as if by a divine sting, and like burning Seraphim <note>The Seraphim are the highest order of angels in Christian theology, characterized by their "burning" love for God.</note> placed outside ourselves, full of divine power, we shall no longer be ourselves, but we shall be He Himself who made us. 

If anyone examines the significance and the hidden mysteries of the sacred names of Apollo, they show clearly enough that this God is no less a philosopher than a prophet. Since Ammonius <note>Likely referring to Ammonius Hermiae, a Neoplatonic philosopher who wrote on the harmony of different philosophical schools.</note> has sufficiently followed this path, there is no reason for me to treat it differently now. But let the three Delphic precepts <note>These were famous maxims inscribed on the Temple of Apollo at Delphi.</note> enter your minds, Fathers—precepts exceedingly necessary for those who are about to enter the most holy and august temple of the true Apollo (who illuminates every soul coming into this world). You will see that they warn us of nothing else than that we should embrace with all our strength this three-part philosophy about which we are currently disputing. 

For that saying, <term>Nothing in excess</term> <note>original Greek: "μηδὲν ἄγαν."</note>, rightly prescribes the norm and rule for all virtues through the principle of the "mean," which is the subject of moral philosophy. Then that saying, <term>Know thyself</term> <note>original Greek: "γνῶθι σεαυτόν."</note>, rouses and exhorts us to the knowledge of all nature, of which the nature of man is the connector and, as it were, the link <note>original: "Cynnus." A term Pico uses to describe man as the "middle point" or "bridge" between the material and divine worlds.</note>. For he who knows himself, knows all things in himself, as Zoroaster first wrote, and later Plato in the *Alcibiades*. 

Finally, illuminated by this knowledge through natural philosophy, and now close to God, saying "Thou art" <note>original: "ε" (ei), the Greek word for "you are." This was a traditional salutation at the temple of Apollo, acknowledging the eternal existence of the Divine.</note> as a theological greeting, we shall then address the true Apollo familiarly and thus happily. 

Let us also consult Pythagoras, the wisest man, who was considered wise chiefly because he never thought himself worthy of the name "wise" <note>Pythagoras is credited with coining the term "philosopher," meaning "lover of wisdom," rather than "sophist" or "wise man."</note>. He will first command us "not to sit upon a bushel" <note>A symbolic Pythagorean "symbolon" or riddle. Pico interprets it as a warning against intellectual laziness.</note>; that is, we should not lose the rational part of the soul—by which she measures, judges, and examines all things—by letting it fall into idle sloth. Instead, we must direct and stir it up constantly through the practice and rules of dialectics <note>In this context, dialectics refers to the art of logical reasoning and debate used to uncover truth.</note>. 

Then he will point out two things we must especially avoid: "not to urinate toward the sun," and "not to cut our nails during a sacrifice." But after we have, through moral philosophy, "urinated out" the flowing desires of overflowing pleasures, and "cut away" the parings of our nails—as if they were the sharp protrusions of anger and the stings of our passions—then at last we may begin to take part in the sacred mysteries of Bacchus <note>Bacchus (Dionysus) represents the ecstatic, inspired state of the soul in union with God.</note> which we mentioned, and to dedicate ourselves to our contemplation, of which the Sun is rightly called the father and leader. 

Finally, he will advise us to "feed the cock"; that is, to nourish the divine part of our soul with the knowledge of divine things as if with solid food and heavenly ambrosia. This is the cock at whose sight the lion—that is, all earthly power—trembles and feels awe. This is that cock to whom we read in the Book of Job that understanding was given. When this cock crows, the wandering man...

<meta>This page continues Pico’s synthesis of various ancient traditions—Greek, Chaldean, and Hebrew—to describe the soul's journey toward the divine. Having just discussed the Greek god Apollo, he now moves to the symbolism of the "cock" of Socrates and the winged soul of Zoroaster.</meta>

<page-num>321</page-num>

### ->On the Dignity of Man<-

...man comes to his senses. This is the cock which, in the twilight of morning, sings in harmony with the morning stars as they praise God daily. When Socrates was dying, hoping that he would join the divinity of his own soul to the divinity of the greater world, he said that he owed this cock to Aesculapius <note>original: "Aesculapio." The Greek god of healing. Socrates' famous last words were "Crito, we owe a cock to Asclepius," often interpreted as thanks for death "curing" the soul of the body’s illness.</note>—that is, to the physician of souls—for he was now placed beyond all danger of disease. Let us also review the monuments of the Chaldeans <note>Pico often refers to the "Chaldeans" when discussing the ancient Babylonian or Persian wisdom traditions, particularly the Zoroastrian Oracles.</note>, and we shall see (if they are to be believed) that the path to happiness is open to mortals through these same arts. The Chaldean interpreters write that it was a saying of Zoroaster that the soul is winged, and when its wings fall off, it is carried headlong into the body; then, as those wings grow back, it flies back up to the heavens. When his disciples asked him by what means they might obtain winged souls with well-feathered plumes, he said: "You must water the wings with the waters of life." When they asked again where they might seek these waters, he answered them through a parable (which was the man’s custom) that the paradise of God is washed and watered by four rivers; from that same place, you should draw your saving waters. The name of the one from the north is *Pischon*, which denotes rightness; the one from the west is *Dichon*, which signifies expiation <note>The Hebrew name usually spelled Gihon; Pico links it to the concept of atonement or cleansing.</note>; the one from the east is *Chiddekel*, which sounds like light; and the one from the south is *Perath*, which we can interpret as piety.

Pay attention and diligently consider, Fathers, what these dogmas of Zoroaster mean: surely they mean nothing else than that we should use moral science <note>Ethics</note> to wash away the filth of our eyes as if by the northern waves of the Pischon; then use dialectic <note>Logic</note> as if by a northern rule <note>original: "amufsi." A carpenter's tool for ensuring a straight line.</note> to direct our sight toward what is right. Then, in the contemplation of nature, we should accustom ourselves to endure the still-weak light of truth, like the cradle of the rising sun, until at last, through theological piety and the most sacred worship of God, we may—like heavenly eagles—bravely endure the most brilliant radiance of the midday sun. These are perhaps those "morning, midday, and evening" levels of knowledge first sung by David and later explained more widely by Augustine. This is that midday light which inflames the Seraphim to their limit and likewise illuminates the Cherubim. This is the region toward which the ancient father Abraham was always traveling. This is the place where, as both the teachings of the Cabalists <note>Followers of Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical tradition.</note> and the Moors <note>Likely referring to Islamic philosophers such as Averroes or Avicenna.</note> have handed down, there is no place for unclean spirits. 

And if it is permitted to bring some of the more secret mysteries into the public, even under a riddle: after the sudden fall from heaven turned our man’s head dizzy, and—according to Jeremiah—death entered through the windows and badly affected the liver and the heart, let us call upon Raphael, the heavenly physician. Let him free us through moral philosophy and dialectic as if with healthy medicines. Then, once we are restored to good health, the "Strength of God," Gabriel, shall dwell within us; he will lead us through the miracles of nature and point out the power and virtue of God everywhere. Finally, he will hand us over to the high priest Michael, who will distinguish those who have completed their service in the ranks of philosophy with the priesthood of Theology, as if with a crown of precious stones. 

These, most worshipful Fathers, are the things which have not only encouraged but compelled me to the study of philosophy. I certainly would not have said these things if I were not responding to those who are accustomed to condemn the study of philosophy, especially in leading men, or in those of even modest fortune...

...they live, they are accustomed to condemn. For now, this whole pursuit of philosophy (which is the misfortune of our age) is held in contempt and insult, rather than in honor and glory. Indeed, this fatal and monstrous persuasion has invaded almost everyone's minds: that one should philosophize either not at all or only for a few things, as if having before one's eyes and in one's hands the causes of things, the ways of nature, the reason of the universe, the counsels of God, and the mysteries of heaven and earth—all thoroughly explored—were nothing at all, unless one could hunt for some favor or acquire some profit for oneself. To our sorrow, it has come to this: that no men are now considered wise except those who turn the study of wisdom into a mercenary trade. Thus, we see the chaste Pallas <note>The goddess of wisdom, Athena, also known as Pallas Athena.</note>, dwelling among men by the gift of the gods, cast out, driven off, and hissed at. She has no one to love her or favor her, unless she, as if prostituting herself and receiving a paltry wage for her deflowered virginity, brings back ill-gotten copper to her lover’s money-box. 

I say all these things not without the greatest pain and indignation—not against the princes of our time, but against the philosophers, who both believe and preach that one should not philosophize because no rewards or prizes are established for philosophers, as if they do not show by this very fact that they are not philosophers. Since their whole life is placed either in gain or in ambition, they do not embrace the knowledge of truth for its own sake. 

I will grant myself this, and I will not blush to praise myself in this regard: that I have never philosophized for any other reason than to be a philosopher; nor from my studies and late-night labors have I either hoped for or sought any other reward or fruit than the cultivation of my soul and the knowledge of the truth I have always so greatly desired. I have always been so greedy and loving of this truth that, leaving behind all care for private and public affairs, I have given myself over entirely to the leisure of contemplation. From this pursuit, no slanders of the envious nor any curses from the enemies of wisdom have been able—nor will they be able in the future—to deter me. Philosophy herself has taught me to depend upon my own conscience rather than on external judgments, and always to think not so much of whether I might hear ill spoken of me, but whether I myself say or do anything ill. 

Indeed, I was not unaware, most worshipful Fathers <note>Pico is addressing the assembly of scholars and Church officials gathered in Rome for his proposed debate.</note>, that this very disputation of mine would be as welcome and pleasant to all of you who favor the good arts and have deigned to honor it with your most majestic presence, as it would be heavy and troublesome to many others. I know there is no lack of those who have condemned my undertaking before now, and who condemn it currently on many counts. Thus, those things which are done well and holily toward virtue are accustomed to have no fewer—I will not say more—barking critics <note>original: "oblatratores." Literally "barkers," suggesting critics who snap like dogs at things they do not understand.</note> than those things done wickedly and wrongly toward vice.

There are, moreover, those who do not approve of this whole genre of disputing <term>disputandi</term> <note>Formal public debates used in medieval and Renaissance universities to test logical and theological arguments.</note> and this practice of debating literature in public, asserting that it is intended more for a display of wit and a boast of learning than for the acquisition of knowledge. There are others who do not disapprove of this kind of exercise, but in no way approve of it in me, because I, at this age—being only in my twenty-fourth year—[have dared to propose a debate] on the sublime [mysteries] of Christian

<meta>Following his lament on the previous page that philosophy has become a mercenary trade, Pico now turns to a personal defense. He addresses the critics who have attacked his plan to hold a massive public debate in Rome on nine hundred different philosophical and theological topics.</meta>

-> ### ON THE DIGNITY OF MAN ### <-

...mysteries of theology, concerning the most sublime topics of philosophy, and regarding unknown disciplines, in a most celebrated city, in a most distinguished assembly of the most learned men, and before the Apostolic Senate <note>The "Apostolic Senate" refers to the College of Cardinals and the high-ranking officials of the Papal court in Rome, where Pico intended to hold his debate.</note>, I have dared to propose a disputation. Some, while granting me the right to dispute, are unwilling to grant that I should dispute on nine hundred questions, slandering the project as being as superfluous and ambitious as it is beyond my strength. I would have yielded at once to their objections if the philosophy I profess had so taught me; and I would not be answering now, according to her teaching, if I believed this discussion established between us were for the purpose of brawling and quarreling. Therefore, let all intent of disparaging and provoking—and that malice which Plato writes is always absent from the divine choir <note>A reference to Plato's *Phaedrus*, where he suggests that envy has no place in the company of the gods.</note>—be banished from our minds, and let us determine in a friendly manner whether I ought to dispute, and indeed, whether I should dispute on so many questions.

First, to those who slander this custom of public disputation, I shall not say much, since this "fault"—if it is judged a fault—is shared with me not only by all of you, most excellent teachers (who have often performed this duty with the highest praise and glory), but also by Plato, by Aristotle, and by the most esteemed philosophers of every age. For them, it was certain that nothing was more effective for achieving that knowledge of truth which they sought than to be very frequent in the exercise of disputation. For just as the strengths of the body are made firmer through gymnastics, so without doubt, in this literary wrestling-ground <note>Pico uses the term <term>literaria palæstra</term>, referring to the ancient Greek wrestling school, to describe intellectual debate as a form of "mental athletics."</note>, the powers of the mind become far stronger and more vigorous. 

Nor would I believe that either the Poets, by the celebrated arms of Pallas <note>Pallas is another name for Athena, the goddess of wisdom; her "arms" or armor symbolize the defensive and offensive power of the intellect.</note>, or the Hebrews, when they say that "iron" <note>original: בַּרְזֶל (*barzel*)</note> is the symbol of the wise, meant to signify anything to us other than that these most honorable contests of this kind are utterly necessary for attaining wisdom. For this reason, it happens that the Chaldeans <note>Ancient Babylonian astrologers and sages.</note>, in the horoscope of one who is to be a philosopher, require that Mars should behold Mercury in a trine aspect <note>In astrology, a "trine" is a favorable 120-degree angle. Pico is suggesting that the "warrior" energy of Mars must support the "intellectual" energy of Mercury for a philosopher to be effective.</note>; as if to say, if you remove these encounters and these battles, all philosophy will become sleepy and sluggish.

But truly, with those who say I am unequal to this task, the method of my defense is more difficult. For if I say I am equal to it, I may be seen as immodest and thinking too much of myself; if I confess I am unequal, I risk being branded as reckless and ill-advised. See the straits into which I have fallen, and the position I am in: I cannot promise what I am able to do without fault, yet I cannot fail to perform it without fault. Perhaps I could cite that passage from Job: "the spirit is in all men" <note>A reference to Job 32:8: "But it is the spirit in a person, the breath of the Almighty, that gives them understanding."</note>; and with Timothy: "Let no one despise your youth" <note>1 Timothy 4:12.</note>. But I shall say this more truly from my own conscience: there is nothing in us that is great or singular. Though I do not deny that I am perhaps studious and eager for the good arts, nevertheless, I neither take nor claim for myself the name of "learned." 

Therefore, if I have placed such a heavy burden on my shoulders, it was not because I was unaware of my own weakness. Rather, it was because I knew that it is a peculiar feature of these kinds of battles—that is, literary ones—that in them, there is profit in being defeated.

<summary>Pico defends his plan to debate 900 theses in Rome, arguing that intellectual conflict is essential for sharpening the mind and attaining truth, much like physical exercise strengthens the body.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s defense of his 900 Theses. Having previously established the precedent of public disputation, he now addresses specific criticisms regarding the massive number of topics he proposed and his refusal to adhere to a single school of philosophy.</meta>

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola #

From this it follows that even the weakest man not only should not refuse these debates, but should seek them out of his own accord. Since the one who is defeated receives a benefit from the victor rather than an injury, for he returns home richer—that is, more learned—and better equipped for future battles. Animated by this hope, I, a weak soldier, have not feared to decide upon so grave a battle with the strongest and most energetic men of all. Whether this was done recklessly or rightly, one can certainly judge better from the outcome of the battle than from my youth. It remains for me, in the third place, to respond to those who are offended by the large number of proposed topics, as if this burden rested on their shoulders, and as if it were not I alone who had to endure <note>original: "exanclandus" - a term meaning to drain or exhaust, often used for grueling labor.</note> whatever labor there might be. It is truly unseemly and far too irritable to wish to set a limit on another person’s industry. And as Cicero says, in a matter which is the better the greater it is, it is wrong to desire mediocrity. In such grand undertakings, it was entirely necessary for me either to fail or to satisfy the requirements. If I satisfy them, I do not see why what is considered praiseworthy in performing ten questions should be judged blameworthy in performing nine hundred. If I fail, those who hate me will have a reason to accuse me, and those who love me will have a reason to excuse me. For in a matter so grave and so great, undertaken with thin talent and meager learning, it will be more worthy of pardon than accusation for a young man to have fallen short. Indeed, as the Poet <note>A reference to Ovid, who wrote that in great undertakings, the will is enough even if the strength fails.</note> says: "If strength fails, boldness will certainly be a merit; in great things, it is enough even to have willed them." Furthermore, if in our own age many have followed Gorgias of Leontini <note>Gorgias (c. 483–375 BCE) was a Greek Sophist famous for claiming he could answer any question on any subject.</note> by offering to debate—not without praise—not only nine hundred questions but all questions regarding all the arts, why should it not be permitted for me, at least without blame, to dispute on many questions, but nevertheless on certain and determined ones?

But they say this is superfluous and ambitious. I, however, contend that this was done by me not only in a way that was not superfluous, but in a way that was necessary. If they would consider with me the method of practicing philosophy, they would be forced to admit this, even against their will. For those who have devoted themselves to any one of the families of philosophers—favoring, for instance, Thomas <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary figure of the Dominican school of Scholasticism.</note> or Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), the primary figure of the Franciscan school of Scholasticism.</note>, who are now most frequently in people’s hands—can indeed put their learning to the test in the discussion of only a few questions. But I have so trained myself that, having sworn loyalty to the words of no master <note>A famous phrase from Horace: "nullius addictus iurare in verba magistri."</note>, I have poured myself through all the masters of philosophy, examined every page, and come to know every "family." Therefore, since I had to speak regarding all of them, I could not propose only a few things about each without appearing to be bound to one, while neglecting the rest as a defender of a private dogma. Even if only a few things were proposed about each, the total number of things asserted about all of them together could not help but be very large. Nor should anyone condemn me for this: "wherever the storm carries me, I am driven as a guest." <note>Another reference to Horace (*Epistles* 1.1.15), describing a philosophical traveler who does not stay in one school.</note> For it was observed by all the ancients that, in turning over every kind of writer, they passed over no commentaries they could possibly read. This was especially true of Aristotle, who for that reason was called by Plato "the Reader" <note>original: "ἀναγνώστης" (anagnōstēs)</note>. And surely it is a mark of a narrow mind to have confined oneself within only one "Porch" <note>The "Porch" refers to the Stoa, the meeting place of the Stoic philosophers.</note> or Academy. Nor can one choose from all...

<meta>This page continues Pico’s defense of his philosophical eclecticism. He argues that he has chosen not to limit himself to one school of thought because every major thinker, from the Scholastics to the Arabs and the Greeks, offers a unique and necessary perspective on the truth.</meta>

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola #

-> ON THE DIGNITY OF MAN <-

[...it is impossible for anyone] to have correctly chosen a private path for themselves who has not first become familiarly acquainted with them all. Add to this that in every family of thought there is something distinctive that is not held in common with the rest. 

And so, to begin with our own thinkers, to whom philosophy most recently arrived: In **John Duns Scotus** <note>Johannes Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a hugely influential Franciscan scholastic known as the "Subtle Doctor."</note>, there is something vigorous and analytical. In **Thomas Aquinas**, something solid and consistent. In **Giles of Rome** <note>Aegidius Romanus (c. 1243–1316), a student of Aquinas known for his precision.</note>, something polished and exact. In **Francis of Mayrone** <note>Franciscus de Mayronis (c. 1280–1328), a student of Scotus known for his "acute" distinctions.</note>, something sharp and acute. In **Albert the Great**, something ancient, ample, and grand. In **Henry of Ghent**, as it has seemed to me, something always sublime and venerable. 

Among the Arabs: In **Averroes**, something firm and unshakeable. In **Avempace** and **Al-Farabi**, something grave and meditated. In **Avicenna**, something divine and Platonic. 

Among the Greeks, philosophy is, in general, clear and especially pure. In **Simplicius**, it is rich and copious. In **Themistius**, elegant and concise. In **Alexander of Aphrodisias**, consistent and learned. In **Theophrastus**, weightily elaborated. In **Ammonius**, unknotted <note>original: "enodis" - meaning clear or without knots/difficulties.</note> and gracious. 

And if you turn to the **Platonists**, to review but a few: In **Porphyry**, you will be delighted by the abundance of matter and a multifaceted religion. In **Iamblichus**, you will venerate a more secret philosophy and the mysteries of the "barbarians" <note>Referring to the ancient Egyptians, Chaldeans, and Assyrians whose wisdom Iamblichus defended.</note>. In **Plotinus**, there is nothing in particular to admire because he offers himself as admirable in every way; the sweating Platonists can barely understand him as he speaks of divine things divinely, and of human things in a learned, indirect style far above the reach of man. I pass over the more recent ones: **Proclus**, luxuriating in Asiatic fertility, and those who flowed from him, **Damascius**, **Olympiodorus**, and many others, in all of whom that <term>theion</term> <note>original Greek: θεῖον</note>—that is, the "divine"—which is the peculiar symbol of the Platonists, always shines forth. 

Furthermore, if there is any sect that attacks truer doctrines and mocks good causes with clever slander, it strengthens the truth rather than weakening it; like a flame fanned by movement, it excites the fire rather than extinguishing it. Moved by this reason, I wished to bring into the open the opinions not of just one school (as some would prefer), but of every kind of doctrine. I did this so that through this comparison of many sects and the multifaceted discussion of philosophy, that "splendor of truth" which **Plato** mentions in his letters might shine more clearly upon our minds, like the Sun rising from on high. 

What would it be if only the philosophy of the Latins—namely Albert, Thomas, Scotus, Giles, Francis, and Henry—were treated, while the philosophers of the Greeks and Arabs were omitted? Especially since all wisdom flowed from the "Barbarians" <note>Pico uses this term for the non-Greco-Roman ancients, such as the Hebrews and Egyptians, whom he believed were the original sources of wisdom.</note> to the Greeks, and from the Greeks to us. Thus, our own thinkers have always considered it enough, in their way of philosophizing, to stand upon foreign discoveries and to cultivate the ideas of others. What would it be to have dealt with the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note> regarding natural things, unless the **Academy of the Platonists** was also summoned? Their doctrine regarding divine matters has always been held as the most sacred among all philosophies (as **Augustine** witnesses), and is now brought by me into the public light for examination in debate for the first time in many centuries—as far as I know (may I say so without giving offense). 

What would it be to have treated the opinions of others, however many there were, if we—approaching the symposium of the wise like <term>asymboli</term> <note>A Greek term for guests who contribute nothing to a communal feast or potluck; Pico means a "freeloader" of wisdom.</note>—brought nothing of our own, nothing produced and elaborated by our own talent? Truly, it is ignoble...

He argues that truth is best discovered by comparing all schools of thought and that he must contribute his own original ideas rather than merely repeating others.</summary>

<page-num>326</page-num>
<header>Ioan Picus Mirandula</header>

(as **Seneca** says) to know only from a commentary, as if the discoveries of our ancestors had closed off the path for our own industry, and as if the power of nature were exhausted in us—unable to produce anything of itself that might, if not demonstrate the truth, at least point to it from afar. For if a farmer hates a barren field, and a husband a barren wife, surely the divine mind, joined and associated with the soul, will hate it all the more the more it is unfruitful, since a far more noble offspring is desired from it. Therefore, not content with the common doctrines, I have added much concerning the ancient theology of **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the "Hermetica," texts on philosophy, magic, and religion thought in the Renaissance to be of great antiquity.</note>, much from the teachings of the **Chaldeans** <note>Referring to the "Chaldean Oracles," a set of mystical texts Pico attributed to ancient Babylonian sages.</note> and of **Pythagoras**, and much from the more secret mysteries of the **Hebrews** <note>This refers to the Kabbalah, which Pico was among the first Christian scholars to study and integrate into Western philosophy.</note>; I have also proposed for debate many things discovered and meditated upon by ourselves concerning natural and divine matters. 

We have proposed, first of all, the harmony of **Plato** and **Aristotle**, believed in by many before this but sufficiently proven by no one. **Boethius** <note>A 6th-century philosopher who intended to translate and reconcile all of Plato and Aristotle, though he died before finishing.</note> promised he would do this among the Latins, but he is never found to have done what he always wished to do. **Simplicius** among the Greeks professed the same; would that he had fulfilled it as well as he promised. **Augustine** also writes in *The Academics* that there were several who attempted to prove the same with their most subtle disputations—namely, that the philosophy of Plato and Aristotle is one and the same. Likewise, **John the Grammarian** <note>Also known as John Philoponus, a 6th-century commentator who argued that those who see conflict between Plato and Aristotle simply do not understand Plato.</note>, while he says that Plato differs from Aristotle only for those who do not understand Plato's words, nevertheless left the proof of this to posterity.

Furthermore, we have added several passages in which we assert that the opinions of **Duns Scotus** and **Thomas Aquinas**, and those of **Averroes** and **Avicenna**, which are thought to be in disagreement, are in fact in harmony. In the second place, we have set out things we ourselves have thought out in both Aristotelian and Platonic philosophy, as well as seventy-two new physical and metaphysical dogmas. If anyone holds these, they will be able (unless I am mistaken, which will soon be clear to me) to resolve any proposed question regarding natural and divine things by a far different method than the philosophy that is taught in the schools and cultivated by the doctors of this age.

Nor should anyone wonder, my Fathers, that in my first years, in a tender age <note>Pico was only 23 when he prepared these theses for debate.</note> during which it was scarcely permitted (as some boast) to even read the commentaries of others, I should wish to bring forth a new philosophy. Rather, one should either praise it if it is defended, or condemn it if it is refuted. And finally, when you are to judge these discoveries of ours and our writings, you should not count the years of the author, but rather their merits or demerits.

There is, moreover, besides that one, another new method of philosophizing through numbers that we have introduced. It is ancient indeed, and observed by the ancient theologians—especially by **Pythagoras**, by **Aglaophemus**, by **Philolaus**, by **Plato**, and the earlier **Platonists**. But in this age, like other noble things, it has so faded through the neglect of those who followed that hardly any traces of it are found.

**Plato** writes in the *Epinomis* <note>A dialogue traditionally attributed to Plato or his student Philip of Opus.</note> that among all the liberal arts and contemplative sciences, the most principal and especially divine is the science of numbering. Seeking also why man is the wisest animal, he answers: because he knows how to count. **Aristotle** also mentions this opinion...

<meta>On the previous page, Pico discussed his synthesis of various philosophical traditions, including the harmony between Plato and Aristotle. Here, he moves into the specifics of his "900 Conclusions," focusing on the symbolic power of numbers and the true definition of magic as the peak of natural philosophy.</meta>

<page-num>327</page-num>
<header>On the dignity of man.</header>

->On the dignity of man.<-

In his problems, **Abu Ma'shar** <note>original: "Abumafar"; a famous 9th-century Persian astrologer known in the West as Albumasar.</note> writes that it was a saying of **Avenzoar the Babylonian** that "he knew all things who knew how to count." This could in no way be true if, by the art of numbering, they understood that art in which merchants are now most skilled. **Plato** himself testifies to this, warning us with a raised voice not to think that this divine arithmetic is the same as the arithmetic of merchants. Having explored this highly extolled arithmetic through many nights of study, and being about to put it to the test, I have publicly promised to answer seventy-four questions—which are considered primary among physical and divine matters—through the use of numbers.

We have also proposed theorems on **Magic**, in which we have indicated that magic is twofold. One type consists entirely of the work and authority of demons; this is, by God, an execrable and monstrous thing. The other, when well-examined, is nothing other than the absolute perfection of natural philosophy. The Greeks, when they mention both, refusing to grant the first the name of "magic," call it <term>sorcery</term> <note>original: "γοητείαν" (goeteia); often associated with black magic or "low" magic involving spirits.</note>. The latter they call by its own peculiar name, <term>magic</term> <note>original: "μαγείαν" (mageia); which Pico views as "high" or "natural" magic.</note>, as if it were a perfect and supreme wisdom. For as **Porphyry** <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> says, in the language of the Persians, a "magus" means the same as what we call an "interpreter and worshiper of divine things."

Moreover, Fathers, there is a great—indeed, a maximum—disparity and unlikeness between these two. The first is condemned and execrated not only by the Christian religion, but by all laws and every well-ordered Republic. The second is approved and embraced by all wise men and all nations studious of celestial and divine things. The first is the most fraudulent of arts; the second is a higher and holier philosophy. The first is vain and hollow; the second is firm, faithful, and solid. Whoever practiced the first always tried to hide it, because it would bring ignominy and reproach upon the author; but from the second, the highest brilliance and glory of letters was sought in antiquity, and almost always. No philosopher or man eager to learn the good arts was ever a student of the first; but to learn the second, **Pythagoras**, **Empedocles**, **Democritus**, and **Plato** traveled across the seas, and having returned, they preached it and held it as a chief secret in their mysteries. Just as the first is proved by no rational arguments, so it is backed by no certain authors; the second, honored by the most illustrious "parents" as it were, has two primary authors: **Zalmoxis** <note>original: "Xamolfidem"; a legendary social and religious reformer of the Thracians.</note>, whom **Abaris the Hyperborean** imitated, and **Zoroaster**—not the one you perhaps think of, but the son of **Oromasius**.

If we ask **Plato** in his *Alcibiades* what the magic of each is, he will answer that the magic of **Zoroaster** is nothing other than the science of divine things, in which the kings of the Persians educated their sons, so that they might be taught to rule their own Republic according to the model of the Republic of the world. In the *Charmides*, he will answer that the magic of **Zalmoxis** is the medicine of the soul, through which temperance is produced in the soul, just as health is produced in the body through medicine. In their footsteps later followed **Corandas**, **Damigeron**, **Apollonius**, **Ostanes**, and **Dardanus**. **Homer** also persisted in this, and we shall one day prove in our *Poetic Theology* <note>A planned work by Pico that was either lost or never completed, intended to explain the philosophical truths hidden in ancient myths.</note> that he disguised this wisdom, like all others, under the wanderings of his **Ulysses**. **Eudoxus** and **Hermippus** also followed in this path.
