<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

Almost all who have thoroughly investigated the Pythagorean and Platonic mysteries have persisted in this view. Among the more recent thinkers who have caught a scent of it, I find three: **Al-Kindi** <note>original: "Alchindum Arabem"; a 9th-century polymath known as the "Philosopher of the Arabs."</note> the Arab, **Roger Bacon**, and **William of Auvergne** <note>original: "Guilielmum Parisiensem"; the 13th-century Bishop of Paris and philosopher.</note>. **Plotinus** also mentions it where he demonstrates that the Magus is a servant of nature and not its creator. This wisest of men approves and affirms this magic, while so abhorring the other [demonic magic] that when he was called to the rites of evil demons, he said it was more fitting for them to come to him than for him to go to them—and rightly so. For just as that first type makes man a subject and a slave to wicked powers, so this natural magic makes him their prince and lord. Finally, that first type cannot claim for itself the name of either art or science; but this one is full of the highest mysteries, involving the deepest contemplation of the most secret things, and ultimately encompassing the knowledge of all nature. 

This magic, calling out into the light from their hiding places the virtues scattered and sown in the world by the grace of God, does not so much perform miracles as it diligently serves nature as she performs them. Having scrutinized more deeply the consensus of the universe, which the Greeks more expressively call <term>sympathy</term> <note>original: "$\sigma\upsilon\mu\pi\alpha\theta\epsilon\iota\alpha\nu$" (sympatheian); the concept that all parts of the universe are interconnected and affect one another.</note>, and having a clear perspective on the mutual knowledge of natures, it applies to each thing its own native charms—which the Magi call <term>iynxes</term> <note>original: "$\iota\upsilon\gamma\gamma\epsilon\varsigma$"; originally a type of bird used in love spells, in Neoplatonism these represented the cosmic links or "charms" that bind the world together.</note>. Thus, it brings into the public view the miracles lying hidden in the recesses of the world, in the lap of nature, and in the secret storehouses of God, as if she herself were the creator. And just as the farmer weds elms to vines, so the Magus weds earth to heaven—that is, he marries the lower things to the gifts and virtues of the higher. 

From this, it appears that while the former magic is as monstrous and harmful as the latter is divine and salutary. This is chiefly because the former, by enslaving man to the enemies of God, calls him away from God; but this natural magic excites in him an admiration for the works of God, which is most certainly followed by willing charity, faith, and hope. For nothing promotes religion and the worship of God more than the constant contemplation of God's wonders. Once we have well-explored these through this natural magic of which we speak, we are more ardently inspired to the worship and love of the Creator, and we are compelled to sing: 

> The heavens are full, and all the earth is full of the majesty of Your glory. <note>original: "Pleni sunt cœli, plena est omnis terra maiestate gloriæ tuæ"; a liturgical reference to Isaiah 6:3.</note>

And this is enough regarding magic, about which I have spoken because I know there are many who, like dogs always barking at strangers, often condemn and hate what they do not understand. 

I come now to those things which, having been unearthed from the ancient mysteries of the **Hebrews**, I have brought forward to confirm the holy and Catholic faith. Lest these things be thought of as inventions, trifles, or the fables of storytellers by those to whom they are unknown, I want everyone to understand what and of what sort they are, from where they are sought, by which and how famous the authors who confirm them are, and how recondite, how divine, and how necessary they are for our people to defend religion against the persistent slanders of the Hebrews. Not only famous Hebrew doctors write of this, but also from our own tradition **Ezra** <note>original: "Hesdras"; refers to the biblical scribe or the apocryphal Fourth Book of Ezra.</note>, **Hilary**, and **Origen** write that **Moses** received on the mountain from God not only the Law, which he left to posterity inscribed in five books, but also a more secret and true explanation of the Law. ### On the dignity of man.

...with God so that he might indeed publish the law to the people, yet he neither committed the interpretation of the law to writing nor made it public. Instead, he revealed it only to Joshua <note>original: "Iesu Naue"; this is the Latin form for Joshua, son of Nun, who succeeded Moses.</note>, and he in turn to the other succeeding high priests, under a strict religious vow of silence. It was sufficient to recognize, through simple history, now the power of God, now his wrath against the wicked, his mercy toward the good, and his justice toward all, and to be instructed by divine and salvific precepts toward living well and happily, and in the worship of true religion. 

But to make public to the common people the more secret mysteries, the secrets of the highest divinity hidden under the <term>shell of the law</term> <note>original: "sub cortice legis"; a metaphor common in medieval thought where the "bark" or "shell" is the literal text, and the "nut" or "fruit" is the hidden spiritual meaning.</note> and the unrefined pretext of words—what else was that than to give what is holy to dogs and to scatter pearls among swine? Therefore, it was not by human counsel but by divine command to keep these things hidden from the common crowd and to communicate them only to the perfect, among whom alone Paul says he speaks wisdom. 

The ancient philosophers most sacredly observed this custom. Pythagoras wrote nothing except a few brief things which he entrusted to his daughter Dama at his death. The Sphinxes carved on Egyptian temples warned that mystical dogmas should be kept inviolate from the profane multitude by means of the knots of enigmas. Plato, writing certain things to Dionysius about the supreme substances, said: "I must speak in enigmas, lest if the letter should perchance fall into the hands of others, what we write to you may be understood by others." Aristotle said that his books of *Metaphysics*, in which he treats of divine matters, were "published and not published." 

What more? Origen asserts that Jesus Christ, the teacher of life, revealed many things to his disciples which they were unwilling to write down, lest they should become common to the crowd. This is most strongly confirmed by Dionysius the Areopagite, who says that the more secret mysteries were transferred by the authors of our religion <term>from mind to mind through the intervening word</term> <note>original Greek: "ἐκ νοὸς εἰς νοῦν διὰ μέσου λόγου" (ek noos eis noun dia mesou logou); referring to oral transmission without writing.</note>, without letters. 

In this very same way, when that true interpretation of the law, divinely handed down to Moses, was revealed by God’s command, it was called <term>Cabala</term> <note>Pico is transliterating the Hebrew word "Kabbalah," which literally means "reception."</note>, which is the same among the Hebrews as "reception" is among us. It is called so, of course, because one person received that doctrine from another, not through written records but by the regular succession of revelations, as if by a hereditary right. 

However, after the Hebrews were restored from the Babylonian captivity through Cyrus, and after the temple was restored under Zerubbabel, they applied their minds to repairing the Law. Ezra, then the head of the Church, after amending the book of Moses, clearly recognized that through the exiles, slaughters, flights, and captivity of the Israelite people, the custom established by the ancestors of handing down the doctrine by hand could not be preserved. He saw that the secrets of the heavenly doctrine divinely granted to him would perish, for their memory could not endure for long without the intervention of commentaries. He therefore decreed that the wise men who then remained should be called together, and each should bring into the open what he remembered concerning the mysteries of the Law; and with scribes employed, these were reduced into seventy volumes (for there were approximately that many wise men in the <term>Sanhedrin</term> <note>original: "Finedrio"; Pico's Latinization of the Hebrew "Sanhedrin," the supreme council or court of the ancient Israelites.</note>). 

Concerning this matter, do not believe me alone, Fathers; hear Ezra himself speaking thus: 

> After forty days had passed, the Most High spoke, saying: The first things you wrote, publish openly...

...lest both the worthy and the unworthy read them; but you shall preserve the final seventy books to hand over to the wise among your people. For in these is the vein of understanding, the fountain of wisdom, and the river of knowledge. And so I did." These are the words of Ezra <note>original: "Esdras"; Pico is citing the apocryphal book 2 Esdras (or 4 Ezra) 14:45–47, which was often used to justify the existence of a secret Jewish tradition.</note> word for word. These are the books of the science of the <term>Kabbalah</term> <note>From the Hebrew "Qabbalah," meaning "received tradition." Pico was the first major Christian scholar to attempt to synthesize this Jewish mystical system with Christian theology.</note>. In these books, Ezra clearly pronounced with a loud voice that there was a "vein of understanding"—that is, an ineffable theology of the <term>supersubstantial deity</term> <note>original: "supersubstantiali deitate"; a term from mystical theology referring to God as existing beyond all categories of "being" or "substance."</note>—a "fountain of wisdom"—that is, an exact metaphysics of intelligible and angelic forms—and a "river of knowledge"—that is, a most firm philosophy concerning natural things.

Pope Sixtus IV, who immediately preceded our current Pope, Innocent VIII <note>Innocent VIII reigned from 1484 to 1492; this confirms the Oration's composition in late 1486.</note>, under whom we live so happily, took the greatest care and zeal to ensure that these books were translated into Latin for the public benefit of our faith. By the time he passed away, three of them had already reached Latin readers. Among the Hebrews of this time, these books are revered with such great religious awe that no one is permitted to touch them unless they are forty years old. 

When I had purchased these books for myself at no small expense, and had read through them with the greatest diligence and untiring labor, I saw in them (God is my witness) a religion that was not so much Mosaic as it was Christian. There I found the mystery of the Trinity, there the incarnation of the Word, there the divinity of the Messiah; there I read of original sin, of its expiation through Christ, of the heavenly Jerusalem, of the fall of the demons, of the orders of the angels, of purgatories, and the punishments of hell. I read the same things there that we read every day in the works of Paul and Dionysius <note>Referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century Christian mystic whom Pico believed was a direct disciple of St. Paul.</note>, in Jerome and Augustine. 

Truly, in those parts that pertain to philosophy, you may clearly hear Pythagoras and Plato, whose doctrines are so closely related to the Christian faith that our Augustine gives immense thanks to God that the books of the Platonists came into his hands. In short, there is almost no point of controversy between us and the Hebrews about which they cannot be so refuted and convinced by the books of the Kabbalists that not even a corner remains in which they might hide. I have a most weighty witness of this fact in Antonius Chronicus <note>Antonio Vinciguerra, a Venetian diplomat and scholar.</note>, a most learned man, who with his own ears (when I was with him at a banquet) heard a Jew named Dactylus, skilled in this science, fully and completely agree <note>original: "pedibus manibusq; descendere," literally "to descend with hands and feet," an idiom for total agreement.</note> with the Christian view on the Trinity.

But to return to reviewing the main points of my debate: I have also brought forward my own opinion on interpreting the poems of Orpheus and Zoroaster. Orpheus is read among the Greeks in an almost complete state; Zoroaster is read among them in a fragmented state, but more fully among the Chaldeans. Both are believed to be the fathers and authors of ancient wisdom. I shall pass over Zoroaster, of whom mention is frequently made among the Platonists, and always with the highest veneration. Iamblichus the Chaldean writes that Pythagoras held Orphic theology as the model according to which he shaped and formed his own philosophy. Indeed, they say the sayings of Pythagoras are called "sacred" only because they flowed from the teachings of Orpheus; from there, the secret doctrine of numbers and whatever great and sublime things Greek philosophy possessed flowed as if from a primary source. But that...

<meta>On the previous page, Pico discussed the mystical and secret Jewish tradition of the Kabbalah, which he claimed was preserved by Ezra and later translated into Latin under Pope Sixtus IV. He now concludes his defense of his broad, multi-disciplinary approach by comparing his method to the ancient theologians who hid their wisdom in myths.</meta>

<page-num>331</page-num>
<header>on the dignity of man.</header>

It was the custom of the ancient theologians—just as Orpheus wove the mysteries of his teachings into the coverings of fables and concealed them with a poetic veil—that if anyone were to read his hymns, they would believe nothing lay beneath them except the most unadulterated trifles and nonsense. I wanted to say this so that it might be understood how great a labor was mine, and what difficulty I faced, to extract the hidden secrets of philosophy from the affected knots of enigmas and the hiding places of fables—especially since I was aided by no work or diligence of other interpreters in a matter so grave, so hidden, and so unexplored. And yet my "dogs" <note>original: "canes mei"; Pico refers to his critics and detractors who "barked" against his project.</note> have barked that I have accumulated only certain small and trivial things for a show of numbers, as if I had not brought forward all those questions which are most ambiguous and highly controversial, over which the principal <term>academies</term> <note>referring to the major schools of thought, such as the followers of Plato, Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas, and Duns Scotus.</note> fight. It is as if I have not brought many things—entirely unknown and unattempted—to these very men who carp at my work and believe themselves to be the princes of philosophers.

Indeed, I am so far from that fault that I have taken care to compress the disputation into as few headings as I possibly could. If I had wished (as others are accustomed) to divide it into its own members and tear it into pieces, it would surely have grown into an innumerable number. To say nothing of the rest, who is there who does not know that one single teaching out of my nine hundred <note>Pico's famous "900 Theses," which he intended to defend in a public debate in Rome.</note>—namely, that concerning the reconciliation of the philosophies of Plato and Aristotle—I could have developed into six hundred headings (if not more) without any suspicion of "affected numbers," by enumerating one by one all the points in which others think they disagree but I think they agree? But certainly (for I will speak, though neither modestly nor according to my usual character), I will say it because my envious detractors and critics compel me: I wished, by this meeting of mine, to give proof not so much that I knew many things, but that I knew things which many do not know. 

And so that this may now become clear to you in reality, most venerable Fathers, and so that my speech may no longer delay your desire, most excellent doctors—whom I see with great pleasure standing ready and girded to await the battle—let us now join hands <note>original: "conferamus manus"; a metaphor for engaging in the formal intellectual combat of a disputation.</note>, as if at the sound of the trumpet <note>original: "classico"; the Roman signal for battle.</note>, and may it be happy and auspicious.

# THE TWELVE RULES OF GIOVANNI PICO
## DELLA MIRANDOLA,

->partly encouraging, partly directing<-
->man in the Spiritual struggle.<-

1 If the path of virtue seems hard to a person, because we must continually fight against the **flesh** <term>flesh</term> <note>In this context, "flesh" (Latin: *caro*) refers not just to the body, but to worldly impulses and physical desires that distract from spiritual goals.</note>, the devil, and the world, let him remember that whatever life he chooses—even one following the ways of the world—he must still suffer many adversities, sorrows, inconveniences, and hardships.

2 Let him remember that in the affairs of the world, one struggles longer, more laboriously, and more fruitlessly; in those worldly pursuits, labor is the only end of labor, followed at last by eternal punishment.

3 Let him remember that it is foolish to believe that heaven can be reached except through this kind of struggle, just as our head, Christ, did not ascend into heaven except by the cross; nor should the condition of the servant be better than the condition of the master.

4 Let him remember that this struggle is not only to be endured with patience, but to be desired—even if no reward were to come to us from it—solely so that we may be conformed to Christ our God and Lord. Every time you resist a temptation and do violence to one of your senses, think of which part of Christ's cross you are being made to resemble. For example, when you resist gluttony and afflict your sense of taste, remember him being given **gall and vinegar** <note>original: "felle potatū & aceto"; a reference to the wine mixed with gall offered to Jesus during the Crucifixion (Matthew 27:34).</note> to drink. When you pull back your hands from stealing something that pleases you, think of his hands nailed to the wood of the cross. If you resist pride, remember him, who though he was in the form of God, took the form of a servant for you and humbled himself even to death on the cross. When you are tempted by anger, remember him who was God and the most just of all men, yet when he saw himself treated like a thief and mocked, spat upon, scourged, and afflicted with every insult, and counted among criminals, he never showed any sign of anger or indignation; instead, bearing all things most patiently, he answered everyone with the greatest gentleness. Thus, by running through every circumstance, you will find there is no passion that does not, in some part, make you conformed to Christ.

5 Do not trust in these twelve weapons <note>Pico is referring to his other famous short work, "The Twelve Weapons of the Spiritual Battle," which usually accompanies these rules.</note>, nor in any other human remedy, but in the sole power of Jesus Christ, who said: *Have confidence, I have overcome the world* <note>John 16:33</note>; and elsewhere: *The prince of this world is cast out* <note>John 12:31</note>. Therefore, let us trust in his power alone both to conquer the world and to overcome the devil; for this reason, we must always seek his help through prayer and through the prayers of his saints.

6 Remember, when you have conquered one temptation, another is always to be expected, because the Devil **always circles seeking whom he may devour** <note>original: "semper circuit quem deuoret"; a reference to 1 Peter 5:8.</note>. Therefore, it is necessary to always serve in fear, and to say with the prophet, *I will stand upon my watch* <note>Habakkuk 2:1</note>.

<summary>This page outlines the first six of Pico della Mirandola's twelve rules for spiritual life, emphasizing that the struggle for virtue is necessary and that believers should find strength by identifying their personal hardships with the suffering of Christ.</summary>
<keywords>Pico della Mirandola, spiritual warfare, imitation of Christ, virtue, temptation, twelve rules, Christian asceticism</keywords>

<header>Directing Rules.</header>

# Directing Rules.

7 So that you are not only not defeated by the devil when he tempts you, but that you actually defeat him: this happens when you not only refrain from sinning, but take the very thing he used to tempt you as an opportunity for some good. For example, if he offers you one of your own good works as a temptation toward **vain glory** <term>vain glory</term> <note>original: "uanam gloriam"; the sin of seeking personal acclaim or pride for one's own spiritual achievements rather than giving credit to God.</note>, you should immediately think of it not as your own work, but as a gift from God. Humble yourself and judge how little gratitude you have shown God for His blessings.

8 When you fight, fight as if you are already winning and about to possess perpetual peace; perhaps God will grant you this through His grace, and the devil, confused by your victory, will not return. But once you have won, behave as if you are about to fight again immediately. Thus, in the struggle, you should always be mindful of victory, and in victory, always be mindful of the struggle.

9 Although you may feel yourself well-fortified and prepared on all sides, you must still always flee from the occasions of sin. For as the Wise One says: *He who loves danger will perish in it.* <note>A reference to Sirach 3:27 in the Bible.</note>

10 Always confront temptations at their very beginning, and **dash the infants of Babylon against the rock** <note>original: "allidas paruulos Babylonis ad petram"; a metaphorical interpretation of Psalm 137:9. In medieval theology, the "infants of Babylon" represented the very first stirrings of sinful thoughts, and the "Rock" was Christ. One must destroy bad thoughts while they are small before they grow into powerful habits.</note>. Now, the Rock is Christ. For **medicine is prepared too late** <note>original: "sero medicina paratur"; a reference to a famous line by the Roman poet Ovid: "Sero medicina paratur, cum mala per longas convaluere moras" (Medicine is prepared too late when the disease has grown strong through long delays).</note> when the illness has already taken hold.

11 Remember that although the struggle of temptation may seem like a conflict in the heat of the moment, it is far sweeter to conquer a temptation than to give in to the sin toward which you lean. Many are deceived in this, because they do not compare the sweetness of victory with the "sweetness" of sin. Instead, they compare only the pain of the struggle to the pleasure of the sin. Yet a person who has experienced a thousand times what it is to yield to temptation ought to try, at least once, to see what it is like to conquer temptation.

12 Because you are tempted, do not believe yourself to be abandoned by God, or less pleasing to Him, or less righteous and perfect. Remember that after Paul had seen the divine essence, he suffered a **temptation of the flesh** <note>original: "tentationem carnis"; often referred to as Paul's "thorn in the flesh" (2 Corinthians 12:7).</note>. God allowed him to be tempted so that he would not be tempted by pride. In this, a person should realize that even Paul—who was a **chosen vessel** <term>chosen vessel</term> <note>original: "uas electionis"; a traditional title for the Apostle Paul based on Acts 9:15.</note> and caught up even to the third heaven—was still in danger of becoming proud of his virtues. As he says of himself: *Lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, there was given to me a thorn in my flesh to buffet me.* Therefore, above all other temptations, a person must most strongly fortify themselves against the temptation of pride, for pride is the root of all evils. The only remedy against it is to always remember that God humbled Himself for us even unto the cross, and that death—even against our will—will humble us so far as to make us **food for worms**. <note>original: "esca uermium"; a common *memento mori* theme in Renaissance thought, reminding the reader of the physical reality of decay to combat ego.</note>

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA ON THE TWELVE
## conditions of a lover.

1 To love only one, and to despise all things for the sake of that one.
2 To consider anyone unhappy who is not with the beloved.
3 To endure all things, even death, in order to be with him.
4 To adorn oneself so as to please him.
5 To be with him however one can; if not in reality, then at least in thought.
6 To love all things that pertain to him: all his friends, his house, his clothes, and his images.
7 To desire his praise, and to be unable to endure any dishonor toward him.
8 To believe all the highest things about him, and likewise to desire that everyone else believe them too.
9 To wish even to suffer some discomfort for his sake, and for that discomfort to be sweet.
10 To weep with him often; if he is absent, out of grief; if he is present, out of joy.
11 To always languish and always burn with desire for him.
12 To serve him, thinking nothing of a reward or payment.

We are usually led to this <note>that is, to the twelfth condition: serving without thought of reward</note> especially for three reasons. The first is when the service itself is desirable for its own sake. The second is when the one whom we serve is, in himself, profoundly good and lovable—as we are accustomed to say, "We serve him because of his virtues." The third is when that person, before you even began, bestowed many benefits upon you. All three of these are found in God: for through His service, nothing is newly received that is not for our own good, both regarding the soul and the body; because to serve Him is nothing other than to move toward Him—that is, toward the **highest good** <term>highest good</term> <note>original Latin: "summum bonum"; a philosophical term referring to the ultimate goal or supreme value from which all other goods flow.</note>. Likewise, He is the best, the most beautiful, and the wisest, possessing all the qualities that usually move us to love someone and serve them freely. Furthermore, He has bestowed the greatest benefits upon us, since He created us from nothing and redeemed us from hell through the blood of His own Son.

# GIOVANNI PICO
## della Mirandola’s Commentary on 
## Psalm 15.

->Preserve me, O Lord.<-
<note>In the Vulgate Bible used by Pico, this is Psalm 15; in most modern English Bibles, it is Psalm 16.</note>

If anyone who has reached a state of perfection wishes to examine his own condition, he faces one particular danger: that he might become proud of his own virtue. Therefore, David, speaking in the persona of a righteous man, begins his description of that state with this word: *Preserve me.* When correctly considered, this removes every occasion for **pride** <term>pride</term> <note>original: "superbia"; considered in medieval theology to be the root of all sins, specifically the desire to be independent of God.</note>. For he who is able to acquire something by his own power is also able to preserve it for himself by his own power. Therefore, he who asks to be preserved by God...

It explores the nature of true prayer and the definition of a "righteous state" through the lens of one's ultimate priorities.</meta>

<page-num>335</page-num>
<header>Directing Rules.</header>

...to be preserved in a state of virtue signifies by this that he did not acquire that virtue from himself at the beginning. However, he who remembers that he obtained virtue not by his own power, but by the power of God, cannot be proud of it, but is rather humbled before God. This is according to that word of the Apostle <note>Saint Paul, in 1 Corinthians 4:7</note>: "What do you have that you have not received? And if you have received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?" <note>original: "Quid habes quòd non accepisti? & si accepisti quid gloriaris? quasi non acceperis?"</note> There are therefore two phrases which we should always have in our mouths: one, namely, "Have mercy on me, O God" <note>original: "Miserere mei Deus"</note> when we remember our sins; the other is, "Preserve me, O God" <note>original: "Conserua me Deus"</note> specifically when we remember our virtues.

->Because I have hoped in you.<-
<note>original: "Quoniam speraui in te." From Psalm 16:1</note>

This is the one thing that makes us obtain from God what we ask: specifically when we hope that we will obtain it. And if we observe these two conditions—that we never ask anything from God except those things which are beneficial for our salvation, and that we ask for what we seek ardently, with firm hope that God will hear us—our prayers will never be in vain. Therefore, when we do not obtain what we ask, it is either because that thing is harmful to us—for "we do not know what we should ask for," as Christ says <note>This sentiment appears in Romans 8:26 and Matthew 20:22</note>—and Jesus said: "Whatever you ask in my name will be given to you" <note>John 14:13</note>. For this name "Jesus" signifies "Savior"; and therefore, nothing is asked in the name of Jesus unless it is for the salvation of the one asking. Or, He does not hear us because even if we ask for good things, we do not ask well—that is, with little hope. For he who hopes timidly asks coldly. Therefore, James said: "But let him ask in faith, with no doubting" <note>James 1:6; original: "Postulet autem in fide nihil hæsitans"</note>.

->I said to the Lord: You are my God.<-
<note>original: "Dixi domino Deus meus es tu." Psalm 16:2</note>

After he has fortified himself against pride, he begins to describe his own state. The entire state of the righteous <term>status iusti</term> <note>the spiritual standing or "rank" of a person living in accordance with divine law</note> consists in this phrase: "I said to the Lord: You are my God." Although this phrase seems common to almost everyone, there are few who can truly say it. For a person considers as "God" whatever they hold as their supreme good; and we hold that as the supreme good which, if we possess it alone even when all else is lacking, we think ourselves happy. And if that one thing is missing, even if we have all other good things, we think ourselves miserable. Thus, the greedy person says to money: "You are my God." Because even if he lacks honor, health, virtue, and friends, as long as he has money, he is content; and if he has all those other goods we mentioned but lacks money, he thinks himself unhappy. Likewise, the glutton says this to his excess, the incontinent to his lust, and the ambitious to power or glory: "You are my God." See, therefore, how few can say, "I said to the Lord: You are my God," because only he can do so for whom God alone is sufficient—so much so that if all the kingdoms of the world and all heavenly and earthly goods were offered to him, he would not offend God even once to obtain them. In this saying, therefore, the entire state of the righteous man consists.

->Because you have no need of my goods.<-
<note>original: "Quoniam bonorum meorum non eges." Psalm 16:2</note>

He gives the reason for his proposal—specifically, why he says to the Lord alone: "You are my God." The reason is that God alone does not need our goods. For there is no creature who...

<header>Directing Rules</header>

...[God] does not need other creatures, though they, being more imperfect than Him, do need others. As philosophers and theologians prove, if those [creatures] did not exist, these [others] would not exist, because when one part of the universe is destroyed, the whole universe is destroyed. When the whole is destroyed, all parts are destroyed. All creatures are parts of one single universe; God Himself is not a part of this universe, but its <term>principle</term> <note>The "principle" or "first cause" is the source from which all other things begin or are created.</note>, depending on nothing from it. For God gained nothing by creating the world, and He would lose nothing if the entire world were annihilated. God alone, therefore, does not lack our goods. We should be ashamed to hold any being as God who stands in need of our goods, as every creature does. Furthermore, we should not hold anything as "God"—that is, as the <term>highest good</term> <note>original: "summum bonum." The ultimate, perfect source of happiness.</note>—except that in which the highest good resides. In no creature is every good found; therefore, we ought to say to the Lord alone: "You are my God."

->To the saints who are in His earth.<-
<note>original: "Sanctis qui sunt in terra eius." From Psalm 16:3.</note>

After God, we must love most those who are most closely joined to God, such as the <term>angels</term> and the <term>blessed</term> <note>The "blessed" (beati) refers to the souls of the righteous currently in heaven.</note> in the heavenly homeland. Therefore, after he said to the Lord: "You are my God," he adds that God:

->Has made wonderful His desires.<-
<note>original: "Mirificauit uoluntates suas." A variation of Psalm 16:3.</note>

This means He made His loves and His desires wonderful toward the saints who are in His earth—that is, in the heavenly homeland, which is called the "earth of God" and the "land of the living." And truly, if we consider how great the happiness of that homeland is, how great the misery of this world, and how great the goodness and clarity of those citizens, we will always desire to depart from here so that we may live there. When we meditate on these and similar things, we must always take care that our meditations are not fruitless. Instead, from every meditation, we should always acquire some <term>virtue</term>. 

For instance, from this meditation on the goodness of that higher homeland, we should acquire this virtue: that we not only bear death bravely and patiently when our hour comes, or if we must face it for the faith of Christ, but that we even voluntarily long for it. We should desire, in other words, to depart from this valley of miseries so that we may reign in that happy homeland with God and His saints. When the righteous man has described his own state, which is focused entirely on God and divine matters, he also looks down from on high at the state of evil men and says:

->Their infirmities have been multiplied.<-
<note>original: "Multiplicatæ sunt infirmitates eorum." From Psalm 16:4.</note>

By "infirmities," he means <term>idols</term>, and the Hebrew text reads this way. Just as a good person has one God whom he worships, so the evil have many gods and idols. This is because they have many pleasures, many vain desires, and various passions which they serve. They seek many pleasures specifically because they find none that can satisfy them, and therefore "the wicked walk in a circle." <note>A common medieval reference to Psalm 12:8, suggesting the aimless, repetitive nature of sin.</note> And he adds: "Afterward they hurried," <note>original: "Post accelerauerunt."</note> because they rush headlong and thoughtlessly after their desires. From this we are taught that we should run no less quickly toward virtues than they run toward vice; nor [should we serve] our Lord less...

<summary>This page explains God's total independence from His creation and contrasts the singular focus of the righteous on the "heavenly homeland" with the scattered, restless idolatry of the wicked.</summary>
<keywords>God's self-sufficiency, highest good, heavenly homeland, saints, angels, meditation, idols, virtue vs vice</keywords>

<page-num>337</page-num>
# Directing Rules

...that we should serve Him more diligently than the wicked serve their own lord, the devil. The just man, considering the state of the wicked, firmly resolves—as we always ought to do—that he has no desire to follow them, and says:

->I will not gather their assemblies of blood: nor will I be<-
->mindful of their names with my lips.<-
<note>original: "Non congregabo conventicula eorum de sanguinibus: nec memor ero nominum eorum per labia mea." Psalm 16:4.</note>

He speaks of "blood" both because idolaters used to gather the blood of their victims to perform their ceremonies, and because the entire life of the wicked—having abandoned reason—follows <term>sensuality</term> <note>In this context, "sensuality" refers to the lower, physical nature of humans, which was thought to be governed by the blood and physical humors rather than the soul.</note>, which is seated in the blood. He stated, moreover, that he not only refuses to sacrifice to idols, but will not even name them. This shows that a perfect person must abstain not only from unlawful pleasures, but even from lawful ones, so that he may be carried more fully toward heaven and be more purely free for the contemplation of divine things. And because someone might believe it is foolishness to deprive oneself of every pleasure, he adds:

->The Lord is the portion of my inheritance.<-
<note>original: "Dominus pars haereditatis meae." Psalm 16:5.</note>

It is as if he says: "Do not wonder if I leave all other things behind to possess God, in whom all other good things are ultimately possessed." This ought to be the voice of every good Christian: "The Lord is the portion of my inheritance." For we Christians, to whom God Himself is promised as an inheritance, should be ashamed to desire anything besides Him. And because it might seem like <term>presumption</term> <note>The sin of "presumption" involves overestimating one's own abilities or assuming God's grace without effort.</note> for anyone to dare promise this for themselves, he adds:

->It is You who restores my inheritance to me.<-
<note>original: "Tu es qui restituis haereditatem meam mihi." Psalm 16:5.</note>

It is as if he says: "Lord my God, I know well that since I am nothing in respect to You, I cannot by my own strength ascend to possess You; rather, it is You who draws me to Yourself through Your grace, and it is You who gives Yourself to me to be possessed." Then, the just man considers how great this happiness is, that God has fallen to him as an inheritance; he adds:

->The measuring lines have fallen for me in pleasant places.<-
<note>original: "Funes ceciderunt mihi in praeclaris." Psalm 16:6. "Funes" (ropes or cords) refers to the tools used to survey and divide land into portions.</note>

For in ancient times, portions and lots of land were divided by measuring cords. And since there are many who, although called to this happiness—as all Christians are—nevertheless treat it as nothing (often trading it for a trivial pleasure), he adds:

->My inheritance is excellent to me.<-
<note>original: "Haereditas mea praeclara est mihi." Psalm 16:6.</note>

It is as if he says: "Just as the inheritance is excellent in itself, so do I regard it as excellent." Everything else, in respect to it, I regard as <term>refuse</term> <note>A reference to the Apostle Paul in Philippians 3:8: "I count all things but loss... and do count them but dung (refuse), that I may win Christ."</note>, as Paul used to say. However, to have this light of the intellect so that a person may recognize the happiness given to him by God is itself a gift of God, and therefore he adds:

->I will bless the Lord, who has granted me understanding.<-
<note>original: "Benedicam dominum, qui tribuit intellectum." Psalm 16:7.</note>

Furthermore, because a person often judges that he should serve God according to reason, yet sensuality and the flesh rebel, a person is only "perfect" when not only his soul but also his flesh is carried toward God, according to the saying: "My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God." Therefore he adds...

<summary>This page provides a moral commentary on Psalm 16, emphasizing the rejection of worldly "blood" (sensuality) and the embrace of God as a spiritual inheritance through divine grace. It explains that true perfection is reached when both reason and physical nature are aligned in the service of God.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's line-by-line spiritual commentary on Psalm 15 (Psalm 16 in modern numbering). The previous page discussed choosing God as one's sole inheritance over worldly idols; here, the focus shifts to the internal discipline of the believer and the ultimate hope of the Resurrection.</meta>

<page-num>338</page-num>
<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

-> And even until the night my kidneys have rebuked me. <-
<note>original: "Et usque ad noctem increpuerunt me renes mei." In biblical anatomy, the "kidneys" (or reins) were considered the seat of human emotions and base desires.</note>

That is, the kidneys themselves—in which the greatest inclination toward <term>concupiscence</term> <note>Strong desire or lust, often specifically referring to physical or worldly longing that distracts from spiritual goals.</note> usually resides—do not merely incline me toward evil, but rather "rebuke" me. That is to say, they pull me back even until the night; they go so far as to voluntarily afflict their own body. For "night" is often used to designate affliction. He then shows the root of such a great deprivation <note>In this context, "privation" refers to the act of denying oneself worldly pleasures or "privating" the senses.</note> and says:

-> I set God always in my sight. <-
<note>original: "Providebam Deum semper in conspectu meo."</note>

For if anyone kept God always before their eyes as a rule for all their actions, and in every deed sought neither personal profit, nor glory, nor pleasure, but only to please God, they would quickly become perfect. And because the one who acts in this way prospers in all things, he therefore says:

-> He is at my right hand so that I may not be moved. <-
<note>original: "Ipse a dextris est mihi ne commouear." To be at the "right hand" is a position of protection and strength.</note>

He then shows how great the happiness of the just man is, because he will be happy for eternity in both soul and body; therefore, because of these things, he adds:

-> My heart has been glad. <-
<note>original: "Lætatum est cor meum."</note>

That is, my soul is joyful, knowing that heaven is prepared for it after death.

-> And my flesh shall rest in hope. <-
<note>original: "Et caro mea requiescet in spe."</note>

That is, although the flesh itself does not rejoice as if it were to receive its final state immediately after death, it nevertheless rests in the grave with this hope: that it will rise again on the Day of Judgment along with its soul, immortal and most splendid. He declares all of this in the following verse; for because he had said that the soul was glad, he adds the reason:

-> Because you will not leave my soul in hell. <-
<note>original: "Quia non derelinquet animam in inferno." In this context, "hell" (inferno) refers to the abode of the dead, or Sheol, rather than a place of eternal punishment.</note>

And because he had said that the flesh rested in hope, he adds the reason, saying:

-> Nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption. <-
<note>original: "Nec dabis sanctum tuum videre corruptionem."</note>

Because even that which was corruptible shall rise incorruptible. And because Christ was the first to enter Paradise and opened the way of life to us, and was the first to rise—and his resurrection is the cause of our own resurrection—therefore these things we have said concerning the resurrection are understood principally to refer to Christ, as Peter the Apostle declared. Secondarily, they can be understood as referring to us, insofar as we are members of Christ. He alone did not see corruption, because his body did not rot in the tomb. Therefore, because the way of living well leads us to the perpetual life of the soul and body, he adds:

-> You have made the ways of life known to me. <-
<note>original: "Notas mihi fecisti vias vitæ."</note>

And because the total happiness of this life consists in the open vision and enjoyment of God, he adds:

-> You will fill me with joy with your face. <-
<note>original: "Adimplebis me læticia cum vultu tuo."</note>

And because this happiness shall endure for eternity, he adds:

-> Delights are at your right hand forever. <-
<note>original: "Delectationes in dextera tua usque in finem."</note>

He says "at your right hand" because our happiness is completed in the vision and enjoyment of the humanity of Christ, who sits at the right hand of majesty on high.

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA
## Prayer of Petition to God.

> **O** nurturing God, to be revered for your supreme majesty,
> You who truly possess one divinity in a threefold power.
> To whom, above the flaming walls of the high world,
> The blessed crowd of the angelic choir serves.
> <note>The "flaming walls of the world" (flammantia moenia mundi) is a classical phrase borrowed from the Roman poet Lucretius, here adapted to describe the boundary between the physical heavens and the dwelling of God.</note>
> Whose almighty right hand once created this 
> Immense work, visible to our eyes.
> You who spin the heavens, who guide the globe with a nod,
> From whose command the hurled lightning bolts fall.
> Spare the wretched, I pray; wash away our filth, I pray,
> Lest just punishment for that fury drive us on.
> But if our debts are weighed on an equal scale,
> And if the standard of your judgment be severe,
> Who could endure the horrific lash of the living 
> Avenger, and withstand his heavy blows?
> The <term>Fabric of the world</term> itself will not withstand your angry right hand—
> <note>original: "Machina." Pico uses the "Machine of the World" to describe the universe as a complex, divinely designed structure.</note>
> That Fabric which is not destined to perish until the final day.
> What mind is not condemned by the origin of the first fault?
> <note>A reference to "Original Sin" (prima culpa), the theological concept that all humanity shares in the fall of Adam.</note>
> Or what soul is not made guilty by its own crime?
> Or certainly, you are he whose very nature is always to spare,
> And who holds justice with equal piety,
> Who returns rewards far greater than merits,
> Just as you return punishments lighter than the sins committed.
> For your mercy is greater than our faults,
> And to give to the unworthy is a thing more worthy of God.
> Although they are worthy enough, if he deigns to love them—
> He who himself makes those worthy whom he found unworthy.
> Pitying, I pray: look upon your own with a peaceful countenance,
> Whether you prefer them to be servants, or rather to be the accused.
> Indeed, the accused, if you look at the crimes of our life—
> The work of an excessively ungrateful mind.
> Or if instead you see your own gifts in us—
> Gifts ennobled by the highest blessings.
> We are those whom nature once made your servants,
> And whom holy <term>grace</term> soon after made your children.
> <note>In Christian theology, "Grace" is the free gift of God's favor that elevates a person from a mere creature (servant) to an adopted child of God.</note>
> But (alas) the indulgence of such a great lot weighs down the wretched:
> Those whom grace made children, guilt has made the accused.

> [He] made them guilty, but let <term>grace</term> conquer the fault,

### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, TO GIOVANNI FRANCESCO
### his nephew by his brother, Greetings in Him who is true salvation.

**D**eparting as you are from me, it is no wonder, my son, that many opportunities for evil were immediately offered to you which might disturb you and oppose the purpose of living well which you have seized; nor is it something to grieve over or be terrified by. How much more of a miracle would it be if, to you alone among mortals, a path to heaven lay open without sweat—as if now, for the first time, the deceitful world and the evil demon had ceased to be, or as if you were not still in the flesh. For the flesh lusts against the spirit and (unless we look out vigilantly for our Salvation) deforms us with seductive Circean drunken cups into the monstrous forms of beasts.
<note>original: "circeis... poculis." In Greek mythology, the sorceress Circe turned men into pigs using a drugged drink. Pico uses this as a metaphor for how physical temptations can strip a human of their reason and dignity.</note>
But James also affirms in his writing that you should rejoice: *Rejoice, brothers, when you fall into various temptations*;
<note>A reference to the Epistle of James 1:2.</note>
and not without merit, for what hope of glory can there be if there is no hope of victory? Or what place can there be for victory where there is no battle? He is called to the crown who is challenged to the fight, and especially to that fight in which no one can be conquered against his will; nor [is there] for us any other strength to conquer...

# Letters

there is [nothing more] needed than that we ourselves wish to conquer. Great is the <term>happiness of a Christian</term><note>original: "Christiani felicitas." In Pico's philosophy, this is not just an emotion but a state of being in harmony with God's will.</note>, when victory is placed within his own judgment, and the rewards to come are greater than every wish and every expectation of the victor. Tell me, I pray, most dear son<note>Pico is writing to his nephew, Gianfrancesco, but uses the paternal "son" to denote his role as a spiritual mentor.</note>, is there anything in this life among those things for which desire agitates earthly minds, for the obtaining of which many labors must not first be undergone, and many unworthy and miserable things tolerated? A merchant thinks he has done well for himself if, after a ten-year voyage, after a thousand inconveniences and a thousand risks to his life, he has acquired an estate slightly more abundant. Concerning the <term>warfare of the world</term><note>original: "militia sæculi." This refers to the active, secular life and the struggle for status, rather than literal military service.</note> there is nothing I need write to you, for experience itself has taught and continues to teach you enough of its miseries. In deserving the favor of princes, in reconciling the friendships of equals, in seeking honors—what a mass of troubles, how much anxiety, how much worry I can learn from you rather than teach you; for I, content with my books and my little leisure, have learned since childhood to live within my lot, and (as much as I am able) dwelling within myself, I sigh for or aim for nothing outside of myself. 

Therefore, we barely attain these earthly things—fleeting, uncertain, base, and common also to the beasts—even while sweating and panting; yet toward the heavenly and divine things, which *no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor heart imagined*, we are dragged by the Divine like drowsy and sleepy people, and almost against our will—as if God could not reign or those heavenly citizens could not be blessed without us. 

Certainly, if earthly happiness were provided to us while we were idle, someone shirking labor might prefer to serve the world rather than God. But if we are fatigued no less in the <term>way of God</term>—indeed, far more in the <term>way of sinners</term> (whence comes that cry of the damned: *We have grown weary in the way of iniquity*<note>A quotation from the biblical Book of Wisdom 5:7.</note>)—it cannot but be the height of madness to be unwilling to labor where one goes from labor to a reward, rather than where one goes from labor to punishment. 

I set aside how great is that peace, how great the happiness of the soul, to be conscious of no wrong in oneself and to turn pale at no fault<note>A reference to the Roman poet Horace: "nulla pallescere culpa."</note>—which undoubtedly far outweighs all pleasures that can be possessed or hoped for in life. For what is desirable in the pleasures of the world? While they are sought, they exhaust us; when they are acquired, they stupefy us; when they are lost, they torture us. Do you doubt, my son, that the minds of the impious are agitated by perpetual cares? It is the word of God, who can neither be deceived nor deceive: *The heart of the wicked is like a boiling sea that cannot rest*<note>A quotation from the Book of Isaiah 57:20.</note>. For nothing is safe for them, nothing is peaceful; all things threaten fear, all things threaten cares, all things threaten death. 

Shall we then envy these people? Shall we emulate them? And, forgetting our own dignity, forgetting our homeland and our heavenly father, shall we—though we were born free—voluntarily make ourselves slaves to these things? And living miserably along with them, and dying more miserably, shall we at last be afflicted by <term>eternal fires</term>? O blind minds of men, O blind breasts! Who does not see, clearer than light itself, that all these things are truer than truth itself? And yet we do not do the things we know ought to be done, but we still hesitate, not desiring to pluck our foot from the mire. There will occur to you, my son (do not doubt it), in these [matters...]

<meta>This page continues Pico’s letter of spiritual advice to his nephew, Gianfrancesco. Having previously discussed the vanity of worldly labor, Pico now warns about the corrupting influence of society and the "insanity" of living as though the Gospel were not true.</meta>

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

...especially in the places where you live, there are countless obstacles every hour which deter you from your proposed goal of living a holy and good life and (unless you are careful) drive you headlong into ruin. But among all these things, the most deadly plague is to dwell day and night among those whose life is not only an enticement to sin in every respect, but is entirely focused on the destruction of virtue. Under the devil as their commander, under the banners of death, and under the <term>wages of Gehenna</term><note>original: "stipendijs gehennæ." Gehenna is a biblical term for the place of fiery punishment or Hell.</note>, they wage war against heaven, against the Lord, and against his Christ. You, however, must cry out with the prophet:
> Let us break their bonds asunder, and cast away their yoke from us.<note>original: "Dirumpamus uincula eorum..." Psalm 2:3.</note>

For these are those whom God has handed over to shameful passions and to a depraved mind, so that they do those things which are not fitting. They are full of all iniquity, full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, and malice. They are detractors, hateful to God, insolent, proud, boastful, inventors of evil, foolish, disorderly, without affection, without loyalty, and without mercy. Though they see the justice of God every day, they still do not understand that those who do such things are worthy of death—not only those who do them, but also those who consent to the doers. Therefore, my son, do not wish to please those to whom virtue itself is displeasing. Instead, let that saying of the Apostle always be before your eyes:
> It is necessary to please God rather than men;<note>original: "Oportet Deo magis placere..." Acts 5:29.</note>

and that other:
> If I were to please men, I would not be a servant of Christ.<note>original: "Si hominibus placerem..." Galatians 1:10.</note>

Let a certain <term>holy ambition</term><note>original: "sancta quædam ambitio." Pico often uses the language of worldly competition to describe the pursuit of spiritual excellence.</note> take hold of you, and disdain to have those as the masters of your life who rather stand in need of you as a teacher. For it is far more becoming that they, by living well with you, should begin to be men, than that you, through the abandonment of your good purpose, should wish to shamefully <term>become like a beast</term><note>original: "obbrutescere." This reflects Pico’s famous philosophical theme that humans have no fixed nature and can ascend to the divine or descend to the level of beasts based on their choices.</note> with them. 

<margin>—</margin>

I am seized (God is my witness) at times by a kind of ecstasy and stupor when I begin to consider the pursuits of men, or (to speak more significantly) their mere insanities. I know not whether to think on them or to grieve; whether to marvel or to weep. For it is surely a great insanity not to believe the Gospel, whose truth the blood of martyrs cries out, the apostolic voices echo, miracles prove, reason confirms, the world witnesses, the elements speak, and the demons confess. 

But it is a far greater insanity if you do not doubt the truth of the Gospel, yet live as if you did not doubt its falsehood. For if those things are true—that it is very difficult for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven—why do we pant for the daily accumulation of riches? And if it is true that we must seek the glory which comes from God and not that which is from men, why do we always hang upon the judgments of men? There is no one who cares to please God. And if there is firm faith in us that the time will come when the Lord shall say:
> Depart, you cursed ones, into the eternal fire,<note>original: "Ite maledicti..." Matthew 25:41.</note>

and again:
> Come, you blessed ones, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world;<note>original: "Venite benedicti..." Matthew 25:34.</note>

why is there nothing we fear less than hell, or hope for less than the kingdom of God? What else can we say except that many are Christians in name, but very few in reality? You, however, my son, strive to enter through the <term>narrow gate</term><note>A reference to Matthew 7:13, suggesting the path to salvation is difficult and few find it.</note>. Do not pay attention to what the many are doing, but look to what must be done; the law of nature itself, reason itself, and God himself will show you. For neither...

<summary>Pico warns his nephew against the corrupting influence of wicked companions and characterizes the disconnect between Christian belief and worldly behavior as a form of "insanity." He urges a "holy ambition" to please God rather than seeking human approval.</summary>

# Letters

Either your glory will be less if you are fortunate alongside only a few, or your punishment will be lighter if you are wretched among many. There will be, however, two especially present remedies for you against the world and Satan, by which—as if with two wings—you may be lifted high out of this vale of tears: namely, <term>Almsgiving</term><note>original: "Eleemosyna." The practice of giving money or food to the poor as a spiritual act.</note> and <term>Prayer</term><note>original: "oratio."</note>. For what can we do without God's help? Or how will He help us if He is not called upon? But He certainly will not hear you when you call if you did not first listen to the poor man calling to you. For it is not fitting that God should not despise you, a man, when you first, as a man, despised another man. It is written: *With the measure you use, it will be measured back to you,* and elsewhere: *Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.* 

When I invite you to prayer, however, I do not invite you to that which consists of many words, but to that which speaks to God in the secret retreat of the mind, in the depths of the soul, with the very movement of the heart. In the <note>Pico refers here to "brightest darkness" (lucidissima tenebra), a concept from mystical theology suggesting that God's light is so intense it appears as darkness to the human mind.</note> brightest darkness of contemplation, prayer does not merely present the mind to the Father, but unites it in certain ineffable ways that only those who have experienced them can know. I do not care how long your prayer is, but how effective, how burning it is—interrupted by sighs rather than continuing in a perpetual series of words or spread out in a rhythmic chant. If your salvation is dear to your heart, if you wish to be safe from the devil's snares, from the storms of the world, and from the traps of enemies—if you desire to be pleasing to God and finally to be happy—let no day pass in which you do not approach your God at least once through prayer. Prostrate before Him with the humble affection of a pious mind, cry out not from the edge of your lips, but from your innermost depths, as the prophet did:

> Remember not the sins of my youth and my ignorances, but according to Your mercy remember me, for Your goodness' sake, O Lord.<note>Psalm 25:7 (Vulgate 24:7).</note>

Both the Spirit who intercedes for us and necessity itself will suggest to you every hour what you should ask of your God. <term>Sacred Reading</term><note>original: "sacra lectio." The meditative study of scripture, often called Lectio Divina.</note> will also suggest it to you; I ask you again and again that you always have this in your hands, setting aside the fables and trifles of the poets. You can do nothing more pleasing to God or more useful to yourself than to never cease turning the pages of the sacred letters by night and by day. For there lies hidden in them a certain heavenly power, living and effective, which transforms the mind of the reader—provided he handles them purely and humbly—into divine love by a certain wonderful power. 

But I have now exceeded the limits of a letter, drawn along by the subject itself and by a wonderful charity with which I have always followed you, especially from that hour when I was informed of your most holy purpose <note>Pico refers to his nephew’s decision to commit to a more devout, religious life.</note>. Finally, I wish you to be reminded of this (of which I spoke with you often when you were here with me): never forget these two things—that the Son of God died for you, and that you also, even if you live long, will soon die. With these "twin spurs"—one of fear, the other of love—urge your horse through the short course of this momentary life toward the rewards of eternal happiness. We neither should nor can set any other goal for ourselves than to enjoy the infinite good without end, in the perpetual peace of the <note>The "twofold man" refers to the harmony of both body and soul in the afterlife.</note> twofold man. 

Farewell, and fear God. 
Ferrara, May 15, 1492.

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA to GIAN-
## francesco Pico, his nephew, greetings.

**Y**ou are happy, my son, when God grants you not only the grace to live well, but that while living well, you are spoken of poorly by the wicked—precisely because you live well. For it is equal praise to be praised by the praiseworthy and to be disapproved of by the wicked. But I do not call you happy because this slander is glorious for you, but because the Lord Jesus—who is truthful, or rather, is Truth itself—affirms that our reward shall be abundant in heaven when men curse us and say all kinds of evil against us, lying for His sake. 

If you do not know it, this is an <term>Apostolic dignity</term><note>Pico suggests that being slandered for one's faith elevates a person to the same rank of honor as the original Apostles.</note>: to be considered worthy of being defamed by the impious for the sake of the Gospel's name. We read in the writings of <note>referring to the Acts of the Apostles, traditionally attributed to Luke the Evangelist (Acts 5:41)</note> Luke that the Apostles left the presence of the council rejoicing, because they were considered worthy to suffer insults for the name of Jesus. Let us also rejoice, therefore, if we are worthy of such great glory before God, so that His glory may be made manifest in our disgrace. And if we suffer anything harsh or troublesome from the world, let those most sweet words of the Lord console us: *If the world hates you, know that it hated me before it hated you.* 

If the world hated Him through whom the world was made, shall we—the most <term>worthless little men</term><note>original: "homuntiones." A diminutive, humbling term for humans in comparison to the Divine.</note>, and if we weigh our own shames, most worthy of every possible insult—suffer it poorly if someone detracts or curses us? Shall we ourselves begin to act badly just so that someone might stop speaking ill of us? Let us rather receive these curses eagerly; and if it is not our lot to be so happy as to endure lashes, chains, prisons, or the sword for the sake of virtue and truth as our <term>heroes</term><note>original: "heroes nostri." Pico refers to the early Christian martyrs as the "heroes" of the faith.</note> once did, let us consider it a job well done if we suffer at least the taunts, slanders, and hatred of wicked men. Otherwise, if every opportunity for merit is taken away from us, no hope of a reward would remain. 

If men praise you for living well, then your virtue, insofar as it is virtue, makes you like Christ; but insofar as it is praised, it makes you unlike Him, who received the death of the cross as the reward for His virtue from men. Because of this, as the <note>The Apostle Paul, in his letter to the Philippians 2:9.</note> Apostle says, *God exalted Him and gave Him the name which is above every name.* It is therefore more desirable to be crucified by the world so that you may be exalted by God, than to be exalted by the world so that you may be judged by God. For the former crucifies unto life, while the latter exalts unto a fall; the former exalts unto glory, while the latter judges unto <term>Gehenna</term><note>original: "gehennam." A term for hell or a place of spiritual punishment.</note>. 

Finally, if the world applauds you, it is hardly possible for virtue—which, being directed entirely upward, ought to have God alone as the one it seeks to please—not to incline itself for a little while toward the favor of the men applauding it. And even if it does not lose its integrity, it loses something of its reward; for when a reward begins to be paid on earth, where all things are meager, it will be less in heaven, where all things are immense. Happy are the insults that keep us safe, so that the flower of justice is not [withered] by the pestilential breath of vainglory...

->Letters.<-

...by a breath <note>Continuing the thought from the previous page: "lest our virtue wither by a breath [flatu]."</note>, or lest the rewards of eternity be diminished for us by the vain endorsement of popular rumors. Let us embrace these insults, my son, and as faithful servants, let us take pride with a most holy ambition in the shame of the Lord's cross alone. 

> "We preach," says **Paul**, "Christ crucified: a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles, but to us, the power and wisdom of God." 

That wisdom of the world is foolishness before God, and that "foolishness" of Christ is what overcomes the wisdom of the world, through which it pleased God to save those who believe. If you do not doubt that those who disparage your virtue are insane, and call the Christian life—which is wisdom—madness, then consider how great your own madness would be to be moved from a right way of life by the judgment of the insane. Every error should be removed by correction, not increased by imitation. Let them whinny, bark, and bay; you continue the journey you have begun without fear. Consider how much you owe to God because of their wickedness and misery, for He has enlightened you as you sat in the <term>shadow of death</term><note>A biblical metaphor for a state of sin or ignorance (see Psalm 23 and Luke 1:79).</note>, and having transferred you from the assembly of those who wander here and there in the thickest darkness, raving without a guide, He has joined you to the children of light. Let that most sweet voice of the Lord sound in your ears always: 

> "Let the dead bury their own dead; you, follow me." 

For they are dead who do not live for God, and in this span of temporary death, they most laboriously acquire eternal death for themselves. If you were to ask them where they are going, to what they direct their studies, works, and cares—finally, what end they have set for themselves in the attainment of which they will be happy—they will either have nothing at all to answer, or they will speak words that are self-contradictory and conflicting, like the ravings of madmen. For they themselves do not know what they are doing, but like those who float in rivers, they are carried along by the force of a poorly adopted habit, as if by the rush of a torrent. Blinded by wickedness on one side and spurred on toward evil by <term>Satan</term><note>original: "satanae"</note> on the other, they rush headlong into every crime—blind leaders of the blind—until an unforeseen death overtakes them, and it is said to them: 

> "Friend, this night they will demand your soul from you; and these things you have prepared, whose will they be?" 

Then they will envy those whom they once despised, and praise those they mocked; they will wish to imitate those whom they cannot, whom they preferred to persecute when they could have followed them. Therefore, my dearest son, <term>stop up your ears with wax</term><note>A classical reference to Odysseus (Ulysses), who plugged his sailors' ears with wax to avoid the deadly song of the Sirens; here, Pico applies it to ignoring the "song" of worldly critics.</note>, and holding as nothing whatever men say or think about you, look only to the judgment of God. He will render to each according to his works in His revelation from heaven with the angels of His power, in a flame of fire taking vengeance on those who did not know God, nor obeyed His Gospel. They shall suffer the punishment (as the Apostle says) of eternal destruction away from the face of the Lord and from the glory of His power, when He comes to be glorified in His saints and to be marveled at in all who have believed. It is written: 

> "Do not fear those who can kill the body, but Him who can cast the soul into <term>hell</term><note>original: "gehennam"</note>." 

How much less are these people to be feared by you, who can harm neither your body nor your soul. If they disparage you now while you are living according to reason, they will disparage you no less if you were to abandon virtue and be overwhelmed by vices.

...not because vice displeases them, but because the vice of disparagement always pleases them. Flee, if your health and salvation are dear to your heart; flee as much as you can from their company. Returning to yourself, pray often in secret to the most merciful Father, crying out with the Prophet:

> To you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul. My God, in you I trust, let me not be ashamed, even if my enemies mock me; for indeed everyone who hopes in you shall not be confounded. Let those be confounded who act wickedly without cause. Show me your ways, O Lord, and teach me your paths. Guide me in your truth and teach me, for you are God my Savior, and in you I will hope all the day. <note>original: "Ad te domine leuaui animam meam..." — This is a translation of Psalm 25 (Psalm 24 in the Vulgate numbering).</note>

Likewise, see that you reflect always upon imminent death, and that our life is but a <term>point</term><note>A common philosophical concept suggesting that human life is an infinitesimal moment compared to eternity.</note>, and even less than a point. Consider then how evil is the <term>ancient enemy</term><note>A traditional epithet for the Devil.</note> who promises us the kingdoms of the world so that he may snatch from us the kingdoms of heaven; how false are the pleasures that embrace us only to strangle us; how deceitful are the honors that raise us up only to throw us down afterward; how lethal are the riches which poison us the more they feed us. Consider how brief, uncertain, shadowy, false, and imaginary is everything that these things can provide us, even if they flow to us according to our every wish. On the other hand, consider how great are the things promised and prepared for those who, despising present things, sigh for that <term>fatherland</term><note>A reference to the "Heavenly Jerusalem" or the afterlife.</note> whose king is Divinity, whose law is charity, and whose measure is eternity. Occupy your mind with these and similar thoughts, which may rouse the sleeper, kindle the lukewarm, confirm the wavering, and provide wings of divine love to one striving for heaven. Thus, when you come to us—which we all expect with great desire—we may see you not only as the person we want, but in the state we desire. Farewell, and love God, whom you once began to fear. Bigus <note>Ludovico Pittorio (1454–1525), known as "Bigus," a poet and friend of Pico.</note> greets you. From Ferrara, July 2, 1492.

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, to his nephew
### GIOVAN FRANCESCO, sends many greetings.

**Y**our letter was most welcome to me, not only because I had heard nothing from you for a long time, but also because it indicated things to me that gave me wonderful delight—since these same things are pleasing to you, and I do not doubt they are most pleasing to God. You also should have no doubt that if you continue on the path you have begun, your reward will be abundant in heaven. I have not yet fully determined whether I must go to Rome or not. And as far as I can gather by conjecture, I believe it is more likely that I will have to go there; you know the reason <note>Pico was likely referring to his ongoing legal and theological disputes with the Church regarding his "900 Theses," which required him to deal with the Roman authorities.</note>. As soon as I am certain of this, I will let you know, so that if you happen to come here (which I would otherwise desire most greatly), you do not find me gone, or find that you must return to your homeland immediately as I go south. Meanwhile, you can stay at home, unless you feel otherwise. But also remember that you have a wife, to whom you owe your body no less than you owe your soul to God. Her desire must be satisfied in some part, and you must consider what she either desires or could desire based on her physical condition and age, and what she does not ask for out of modesty and virtue. For why should one be ashamed...

## GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA TO Philip Beroaldo, Greetings.

**I** received from you, most learned Beroaldo, a letter both loving and erudite, along with many verses that without a doubt challenge antiquity itself; it was a most welcome gift to me. Therefore, thanks to you, I have spent my leisure hours well in a noble pursuit, and I could not have taken pleasure in anything more joyfully or honorably. Truly, I would act as an exceedingly ungrateful man if I wished to repay your excellent works with my own worst ones, and exchange the <term>poisons of a Suffenus</term><note>original: "catullianis salibus suffeni uenena" — An allusion to the Roman poet Catullus, who mocked a bad poet named Suffenus. Pico is modestly comparing his own poetry to Suffenus's "poisonous" bad writing.</note> for your Catullian wit. For I am no better than he in poetry, unless I excel in this: that I recognize myself to be a Suffenus and I see <term>what is in the bag on my back</term><note>An allusion to Aesop’s fable where people see the faults of others in the bag hanging in front, but are blind to their own faults in the bag on their back.</note>. Yet you demand this: namely, that I give you something from my own writings; and you demand it in such a way that you seem to make a claim, and appear unlikely to take a rejection calmly. Therefore, even if it costs whatever reputation I have with you, it must be done. You have, then, two letters: one to Lorenzo de' Medici, the other to Ermolao [Barbaro] concerning the style of speaking used by philosophers. To these I have added certain short verses which slipped out from me during these days while I was busy with other things. You shall read these in such a way that you remember I have applied only a hurried care and leftover time to these <term>more human studies</term><note>original: "humanioribus his studijs" — Referring to the *studia humanitatis* or the humanities (grammar, rhetoric, poetry), which Pico views as secondary to his primary focus on philosophy.</note>, as one who has devoted his primary labor and, as they say, his **serious lamps** <note>A metaphor for late-night, intense scholarly study.</note> to the philosophers. Among them, I hope I have made such progress as you have among the orators and poets, among whom (I speak from the heart) I see no reason why you should not rightly claim the first place. Your friend Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano, the renowned scholar and close friend to both Pico and Lorenzo de' Medici.</note> is yours; he loves you as much as anyone can. You can promise yourself anything from me that is within my power. Farewell.
