# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA TO LOREN-
## zo de' Medici, many greetings.

**I** have read, Lorenzo de' Medici, your <term>verses</term><note>original: "Rhythmos"; referring here to poems written in the Italian vernacular rather than Latin.</note> which the vernacular Muses suggested to you during your tender youth. I recognized in them the legitimate offspring of the Muses and the Graces, but I did not recognize the work of a "tender age." For who would not perceive the Graces dancing to the beat in your verses and the rhythmic joining of your lines? Who would not hear the Muses singing in your melodious and modulated style of speaking? Who would recognize a mere youth in such unforced charm, cheerful wit, honeyed pleasantries, and suitable allurements—all with a marvelous clarity, prudent arrangement, and the most serious meanings unearthed from the very depths of philosophy? 

I know certainly that I am not "on the white list"<note>A Roman idiom meaning to be among the select few or experts.</note> nor one who should climb so high—that is, to the judgment of such matters. But I wish it could be said without the suspicion of flattery what I truly feel about them: I would certainly say there is no one among the ancient writers whom you have not surpassed by a long distance in this genre of writing. Lest you think this is said merely to please you, I will bring you my reasons for this opinion. 

Among your people, there are two especially celebrated poets of the <term>Florentine language</term><note>The Tuscan dialect of Italian, which was becoming the literary standard.</note>: Francesco Petrarch and Dante Alighieri. Concerning them, I might preface by saying that among the learned, there are those who find substance lacking in Petrarch and refined words lacking in Dante. <note>original: "qui res in Francisco, verba in Dante desiderent." This was a common Renaissance debate: whether a poet prioritized "res" (matter/thought) or "verba" (style/vocabulary).</note> In you, however, anyone with a mind and ears will find neither missing; in your work, one cannot tell whether the matter is more illustrated by the speech, or the words by the sentiments. 

But let us weigh the merits of each one individually, as if on a small scale. Indeed, if Petrarch were to come back to life, who doubts that he would voluntarily <note>original: "herbā tibi daturū"; a classical idiom meaning "to yield the palm of victory" or admit defeat.</note> concede the victory to you regarding the meaning? For you are always sharp, serious, and subtle; he, however, snatching thoughts mostly from common sources, colors them with words, making ordinary things extraordinary through his style. 

In this style, let us see what he offers you, and what you offer him. In certain parts, he might appear sweeter. But to me, his sweetness happens to be (if I may say so) sweetly and pleasantly austere. He is flowing and smooth; you grip the soul with majesty and a certain vivid light of speech. In him, there is an ambitious and excessive diligence; in you, a diligence that is neglected rather than affected. He is tender and soft; you are masculine and muscular. He is fluid and melodious; you are concise, full, firm, and modulated. He is perhaps more charming; you are certainly more ample and elevated. He is more painted, but you are more vigorous. In him, there is much you might cut away; in you, there is nothing redundant and nothing short. 

But perhaps I am a bit bold to say that anything should be removed from him. It is certainly so, and so it seems to many whose judgment I trust. For in my own view, one can often see him erring as the <term>Asiatics</term><note>The "Asiatic" style in rhetoric was criticized by classicists for being overly flowery, wordy, and structurally weak.</note> used to err—that is, stuffing in words as if to fill up cracks, and using full and elegant terms not to decorate, but to prop up the poem like <term>flute players</term><note>original: "tibicines"; a reference to the supports used in building, metaphorically applied to "filler" words used to maintain poetic meter.</note> so that the song does not limp. In you, every word is no less necessary for the matter than it is pleasing for the ornament; thus, whoever would take from you would mutilate the work, while whoever would take from him would merely prune and clean it. Even if we grant (which I never will) that what he wrote is more charming and more polished than yours, it was easy for a man to excel when he did not have to struggle and fight with the weight of the thoughts themselves. But those of yours...
<margin>those</margin>

<summary>Pico della Mirandola praises Lorenzo de' Medici's Italian poetry, arguing that Lorenzo surpasses Petrarch and Dante by masterfully combining philosophical depth with vigorous stylistic refinement.</summary>

<meta>catchword: exupes (exsuperare)</meta>

Those sharp, subtle, and—to use a single word—**Laurentian** insights can hardly be described; they reject the <term>curling-irons</term><note>original: "calamistros"; a Roman metaphor for overly artificial or "frilly" rhetorical style.</note> and do not willingly admit those "cosmetics" of speech. If that writer whom we read as soft, polished, and pleasant <note>Pico is referring to Petrarch here, as established on the previous page.</note> had been required to handle such themes, we would instead read him as thorny, neglected, and disagreeable. Indeed, one can see that whenever he attempts anything sharp, complex, or knotted, he fails as much in his style as he rises in his thought. 

But when he shows off his "furniture" of words—his ointments, curls, and flowers—Castritius <note>A Roman teacher of rhetoric mentioned by Aulus Gellius.</note> would often remind him (as he reminded Gracchus) not to be deceived by a well-rounded sound and the flow of the lines. Instead, we should inspect what lies beneath: what seat it occupies, what firmament supports it, and what foundation the words have. If you were to do this, you would see there at times the <term>void of Epicurus</term><note>Epicurus taught that the universe consisted of atoms and "the void" (empty space). Pico is suggesting Petrarch’s words are sometimes empty of substance.</note>—either no meaning beneath them at all, or something cold and trivial. In that department, although it is the most important, even if you do not grant him superiority, I see no reason at all why he should be superior to you in the grace of speaking. For your words could not be more illustrious, and their arrangement is so fitting that they could not be more tightly joined, flow more smoothly, or fall into a more musical rhythm in any way. 

But let us now weigh **Dante** alongside you. Perhaps more people will raise a controversy about him; for there are many who, when comparing writers, do not so much weigh their merits as count their years. They command others to read the ancients with reverence, yet they themselves cannot read their contemporaries without envy. Certainly, as far as style is concerned, I think no one will deny you the first prize. Dante is sometimes so rough, harsh, and scrawny that he seems quite crude and unpolished; even his own <term>goldsmiths</term><note>original: "aurarij"; meaning the commentators or dedicated fans who "gilded" Dante's reputation.</note> admit this. But they cast the blame entirely upon his age and that century. You are altogether more refined in speech, while he is not "grander." 

But, they will say, he is grander and more sublime in his meanings. I ask you: what wonder is it if, in a philosophical matter, the very nature of the philosophers compelled him and even voluntarily supplied him with thoughts? If the subject is God, the soul, or the blessed, he brings forward what **Thomas** <note>St. Thomas Aquinas.</note> or **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo.</note> wrote about them. He was as frequent and diligent in handling and meditating upon these things as you are in conducting the greatest public and private affairs. It was not so much a matter of great renown for Dante to have done this, as it would have been a disgrace not to have done it. 

Yet it was, without a doubt, the work of a supreme genius—which you yourself perform—to make philosophical those things which are about love. You take things that are austere in their own severity and, by introducing a certain charm, make them wittily lovable. In your words, the serious matters of the philosophers are so mixed with the playfulness of lovers that the latter gain dignity and the former gain cheerfulness and grace. Through this union, both have retained what was their own and shared themselves with one another so mutually that each part possesses individually what previously both had only when together. 

But this is not as admirable as what moved me most: these ideas are introduced by you in such a way that they do not seem "introduced," but rather dug out from the very bosom of the subject matter itself. As you irrigate the soil, they seem to bloom from it, so that they appear native and not foreign, necessary and not acquired, entirely genuine and not grafted on. This is what I cannot sufficiently admire, and why you seem to me to surpass Dante...

<summary>Pico della Mirandola argues that Lorenzo de' Medici's poetry is superior to Petrarch's in substance and Dante's in style. He particularly praises Lorenzo for seamlessly blending deep philosophical truths with themes of love.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s comparison of Lorenzo de’ Medici’s poetry and commentary to the works of Dante and Petrarch, moving into a discussion of Lorenzo’s philosophical depth.</meta>

<page-num>350</page-num>
<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

...to have surpassed. For even if he <note>Referring to Dante Alighieri.</note> flies sublime, he is raised by wings of matter; you, though matter resists and pulls you down, are raised on high by the wings of genius, and you are raised in such a way that you do not depart from matter, but rather lift it up along with you—doing as much for matter as Dante’s subject matter did for him. Now one may see what the difference is between you, Francesco <note>Petrarch (Francesco Petrarca).</note>, and Dante. Regarding them, I would add this: Francesco sometimes does not live up to his promises; he has something that entices at first glance, but further on he does not satisfy. Dante has something that occasionally offends upon encounter, but he pleases more as he persuades the inner mind. Your works have no less to hold the reader in the end than they have to capture them at the first front. Add to this that they composed their poems in seclusion, in the shade, and in the greatest tranquility of study; you sang yours amidst tumults, the noise of the court, the shouts of the forum, the greatest cares, and the most turbulent storms, while most heavily occupied. For them, the Muses were an ordinary and principal business; for you, they are a game and a certain relaxation from cares. For them, they were the ultimate exhaustion; for you, weary as you are, they are leisure. In short, by relaxing your mind, you reached a point which they, perhaps, did not reach even while straining every nerve of their souls.

But what shall I say of my paraphrase? <note>Pico is referring to Lorenzo’s own commentary on his sonnets, the "Comento sopra alcuni de' suoi sonetti." He calls it "mine" as a gesture of deep affection and intellectual kinship.</note> For why should I not call it mine? Either by the right of this title which is mine, or finally, why not mine, since even if I venerate it as yours, I love it as my own. I truly admire it, and you in it, from which I gather how far I was from a true appreciation of your verses. In those verses, things that were greatest and most illustrious—which I had not looked into with my <term>owl-eyes</term><note>original: "noctuinis oculis"; a metaphor for being blind to obvious truths or unable to see in the light of genius.</note>—I then saw as revealed by you, who alone both could and should have done so; you owed it to yourself and to us, lest you should defraud yourself of much glory and us of much pleasure. 

I read it (God is my witness), greatest Lorenzo, not so much for delight as for doctrine. For how much is there from Aristotle—namely from the *Physics*, from the books *On the Soul*, *On Ethics*, *On the Heavens*, from the *Problems*—and how much from Plato’s *Protagoras*, from the *Republic*, from the *Laws*, from the *Symposium*? All these things, although I have read them elsewhere in those authors’ own works, I nevertheless read in your work as if they were new, as if they were better and transformed by you into I know not what new appearance, so that they seem to be yours and not theirs, and in reading them I seem to learn something. This is the greatest evidence that you know these things not so much from a commentary as from yourself. For many are accustomed to have more <gloss>sophistry</gloss><note>original: "σοφισια" (sophisia); Pico uses the Greek here to denote a superficial or performative cleverness.</note> in their letters than actual work; when they are about to write something, they keep philosophers as if they were "technical advisors" suggesting certain dogmas to be thrust into their books so that they might appear to be philosophers. But you may easily catch these people. For you see that those things are neither rightly arranged, nor coherent, and are not explained by the authors, but rather entangled. And men who are otherwise eloquent appear like infants when speaking of such things. 

But who does not see that you do not hold these ideas on loan, but as things over which you have right and power to turn, act, and handle according to your will? These things you have attained (O happy genius!) in the heat of the Republic and in an active life—things which we, not the disciples but the "tenants" of the philosophers, follow rather than attain in our shaded and <term>sedentary life</term><note>original: "sellularia"; literally "sitting in a chair," referring to the inactive life of a professional scholar.</note>. But what shall I say of the most sweet style of your paraphrase? It seems to me entirely like that of Caesar in the Roman tongue, for it is a speech not manufactured...

Pico highlights Lorenzo's mastery of Plato and Aristotle, noting that he integrates their ideas so naturally that they become his own.</summary>

...not gilded, not entirely superficial, but upright by its own nature, pure, and well-proportioned; not running on haphazardly, but keeping its rhythm; neither excessive nor meager, neither playful nor unpleasant; sweetly serious, seriously lovable; words chosen and not strained, illustrious but not fake, necessary but not sought after, not merely explaining the matter, but placing it before the eyes themselves. Furthermore, how you always remember your own character, how the seeds and traces of that famous prudence of yours are scattered everywhere—these things I, along with many others, [value] as far better than anything else. But I have seen two principal things besides these, which perhaps not many see, even those with sharper eyes. The first is how it <note>Referring to Lorenzo’s writing or his commentary on his own poetry.</note> hides its riches to avoid envy, keeps its flowers in its lap and does not flaunt them; it does not shoot up into plants but sinks to its knees to appear smaller. The other quality I cannot quite see—for I am not so skillful—but I see there is something I might most significantly call "Laurentian" <note>original: "Laurentianum"; implying a style unique to Lorenzo de' Medici.</note>. For if anyone sees Lorenzo’s gifts, genius, and excellence, they would see the whole Lorenzo graphically portrayed. But perhaps I have said too many things, even against my will, as the sentiment of my mind draws me sideways (as they say) into words. I will not omit to urge you as much as I possibly can to steal a little leisure sometime from governing the Republic <note>Lorenzo de' Medici was the de facto ruler of the Florentine Republic.</note> to devote to completing the paraphrase <note>The "Comento," Lorenzo’s philosophical commentary on his own sonnets.</note>, to the honor of yourself and our native tongue, and for the future use and pleasure of your citizens and all of us. At Florence, on the Ides of July, 1484.

### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA TO
### his friend Hermolao Barbaro, greetings. <note>The "S." in the heading stands for "Salutem," the standard Latin greeting.</note>

**I**, for my part, my dear Hermolao, can neither remain silent about what I feel concerning you, nor fail to feel those things which are due to one in whom all things are found, individually, in the highest degree. But I wish that my mind’s capacity were such that I could feel about you according to your merits; I wish I had such power of speech that I might one day express what I always feel. I know that the concepts I have formed of you sink infinitely below the heights of your learning. You should also know that whatever we say is far less than what we conceive; you should know that words are as lacking to the mind as the mind is lacking to the reality of things. And yet, do you believe me to be so bold as to hope I can imitate your works, though I cannot even estimate their greatness? All may admire you, but as few can imitate you as can find fault with you. And would that I had such good fortune that what I write might in some part reflect my Hermolao. For, to say nothing of the rest, your very style—to which you yourself are so little partial—it is marvelous how much it affects me, how much it delights me: it is so learned, weighty, well-composed, scholarly, refined, and ingenious. In it, nothing is commonplace, nothing is trivial, whether you look at the words or the thoughts. Our friend Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the famous humanist scholar and poet.</note> and I often read whatever letters of yours we have, whether addressed to others or to ourselves; the following parts always vie with the preceding ones, and new Graces <note>The "Gratiæ" or Charites, goddesses of charm, beauty, and creativity.</note> blossom fruitfully as we read, so that in a sort of perpetual acclaim we have no room to catch our breath. But it is wonderful to say how you persuade, and how you drive the reader’s mind wherever you wish. I have experienced this both at all other times and [especially] in this...

<meta>This page marks the beginning of a famous letter from Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to the humanist scholar Hermolao Barbaro, written in June 1485. It responds to Barbaro's criticisms of the "Barbarian" (Scholastic) philosophers.</meta>

<page-num>352</page-num>
# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola #

...your most recent letter to me, in which you attack these **"Barbarian" philosophers** <note>The "Barbarians" refers to the Scholastic thinkers of the Middle Ages, whom Renaissance Humanists criticized for their technical, unpolished Latin.</note>, whom you say are commonly held to be sordid, rude, and uncultured; men who did not truly live while they were alive, and who certainly do not live now that they are dead—or if they do live now, they live only in punishment and disgrace. I was so moved by this, and so ashamed and weary of my own studies—for I have already spent six years among them—that I wished I had done nothing at all rather than to have labored so hard on something so worthless. I have wasted, I say, my best years, and such long nights of study upon **Thomas [Aquinas]**, **John [Duns] Scotus**, upon **Albert [the Great]**, and upon **Averroes** <note>These are the giants of Scholasticism and Islamic philosophy whose works formed the core of the university curriculum Pico studied.</note>, in which I might perhaps have become something of note in the world of fine literature. I thought to myself, to console my spirit, that if any of those men were to return to life now, they—being otherwise quite argumentative men—might have something to say to defend their cause with some degree of reason. Finally, it occurred to me that one of them, perhaps a bit more eloquent than the rest, might defend his own "barbarism" in a way that is as little "barbaric" as possible, perhaps in this manner:

"We lived as famous men, O **Hermolaus**, and we shall live hereafter, not in the schools of grammarians and schoolmasters, but in the circles of philosophers and the assemblies of the wise. There, the discussion and debate are not about the mother of **Andromache**, nor the children of **Niobe** <note>References to Greek mythology; Pico is contrasting "frivolous" literary trivia with "serious" philosophical inquiry.</note>, and light trifles of that sort, but about the fundamental principles of human and divine things. In meditating, inquiring into, and untying these knots, we were so subtle, sharp, and keen, that we may perhaps have seemed at times too anxious and fussy—if indeed anyone can be too fussy or curious in the pursuit of truth. And if anyone should charge us with dullness or slowness, come now, I pray you, let whoever he is step forward and engage us; he will find that these 'Barbarians' had **Mercury** <note>Mercury was the god of eloquence and wit; the Scholastic argues that their brilliance was internal and intellectual, even if their speech was plain.</note> not on their tongue, but in their heart. They did not lack wisdom, even if they lacked eloquence. To have failed to join eloquence with wisdom is perhaps so far from being a fault that to have joined them might even be a sin. For who would not condemn and detest curls and makeup on a virtuous maiden?

There is such a conflict between the duty of the orator and that of the philosopher that they could not be more opposed to one another. For what else is the rhetorician’s office than to lie, to deceive, to circumvent, and to perform sleight-of-hand? For it is your power, as you say, to be able to turn black into white or white into black at your whim; to be able to raise up, cast down, amplify, or diminish whatever you wish by speaking; and finally, to transform things themselves—by the almost magical power of eloquence which you boast of—into whatever face and habit you please. Thus, things do not appear as they are by their own nature, but as you wish them to be—not that they actually become so, but they appear so to the audience even though they are not. Is this entire thing anything other than pure lying, pure imposture, and pure trickery? Since it always either exceeds the nature of the thing by increasing it or falls short by diminishing it, and by holding out a deceptive harmony of words—like masks and phantoms—it mocks the minds of the listeners with flattery. Shall there be any affinity between such a man and a philosopher, whose entire study is occupied with knowing the truth and demonstrating it to others? Add to this that we can have no trust in you who seek after such elegance and charms, as if you lacked confidence in the facts themselves..."

<meta>This page continues the imaginary speech Pico has written for a "Barbarian" (Scholastic) philosopher defending their technical, unpolished style against the elegant rhetoric of the Humanists.</meta>

<page-num>353</page-num>
### Letters. ###

...we do not seek to draw men into our opinion with such allurements. For this reason, it is better to read sacred matters written in a rustic rather than an elegant style; for nothing is more unbecoming or harmful, in any subject where the search for truth is at stake, than that whole elaborate style of speaking. This belongs to the legal disputes of the courts, not to natural or heavenly inquiries. It belongs not to those in the Academy, but to those engaged in that sort of Republic where actions and words are weighed on a popular scale—a place where flowers far outweigh the fruit. Do you not know that saying: "Not all things suit all people with the same thread"? <note>A variation of the Latin proverb *non omnia omnibus cupiunda*, suggesting that different styles suit different professions.</note> Eloquence is an elegant thing (we admit this), full of charm and pleasure, but in a philosopher, it is neither fitting nor welcome. Who would not approve of a delicate gait, expressive hands, and playful eyes in an actor or a dancer? But in a citizen or a philosopher, who would not disapprove, argue against, and loathe them? If we see a girl who is charming and witty in her ways, we praise her and shower her with kisses. But we would condemn and shun these same traits in a matron. Therefore, we are not the fools, but rather those inept men who perform "Bacchanals" <note>Wild, drunken festivals in honor of Bacchus; here used to describe overly dramatic or festive rhetoric.</note> at the feet of your "Eloquence," who dishonor the gravity and chastity of philosophical matters with trifles and curling-irons, as it were. Truly, what **Synesius** <note>Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–414 AD), a Greek bishop and philosopher.</note> said of a young man can be aptly said of a speech: **"A well-coiffed speech is always an effeminate one."** <note>original: "comatam orationem semper cinœdam." This is a harsh critique implying that ornate prose lacks "masculine" intellectual vigor.</note> Therefore, we prefer our own speech to be "hairy," tangled, and rough, rather than beautifully coiffed with the stain—or even the suspicion—of impurity. 

And even if there were nothing else, this is most true: nothing is further from the philosopher's purpose in any matter than that which tastes of luxury or pride. **Socrates** used to say that **Sicyonian shoes** <note>term: <term>Sicyonian shoes</term> (calceos Sicionios). Famous luxury footwear from the Greek city of Sicyon, known for being soft and comfortable but considered decadent.</note> were well-made and fit the foot perfectly, but they did not suit Socrates at all. The logic of civic dress and philosophical dress is not the same, just as it is not the same for the dining table or for speech. The philosopher uses these things only for necessity; the civic man uses them also for grace. If the latter neglects grace, he is not "civic"; but if the former affects it, he will not be a philosopher. If **Pythagoras** could live without food, he would spare even his enemies; <note>This likely refers to Pythagoras's legendary asceticism and his refusal to kill animals for food.</note> if he could explain his thoughts with a look, or at least with less effort than speech requires, he would not speak at all. So far is he from polishing and adorning his tongue, for we must be careful that a reader is not lured by a "medicated skin" <note>A metaphor for makeup or cosmetic enhancement of the text.</note> and lingers upon the surface, failing to reach the marrow and the blood—which we have often seen to be corrupted beneath a face painted with white lead. We have seen, I say, in all these people, that it has become their habit—since there is nothing inside them that is not empty and vain—to detain the reader at the first appearance with various modulations and harmonies. If a philosopher should do this, **Musonius** <note>Gaius Musonius Rufus, a Stoic philosopher of the 1st century AD.</note> will cry out that it is not a philosopher speaking, but a flute-player piping. 

Therefore, let it not be held against us as a vice that we did not do what it would have been a vice to do. We seek *what* we should write, not *how* we should write it—or rather, the "how" we seek is to write without pomp or any floral display of speech. We do not want our writing to be delightful, charming, or witty, but rather useful, grave, and reverent; so that it achieves majesty from its ruggedness <note>original: "horrore," implying a bristling or unpolished austerity that commands respect.</note> rather than grace from its softness. We do not expect the applause of the theater, because...

--- Page 387 ---
<meta>This page continues Pico's rhetorical defense of the "Barbarian" (Scholastic) philosophers against the Humanist critique of their unrefined Latin style. Pico argues that the beauty of philosophy lies in its internal truth, not its external elegance.</meta>

<page-num>354</page-num>
<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

...whether a smooth or rhythmic cadence soothes the ears, [judging] that this part is false or that part is charming. Instead, we look for the silence of the few, born of admiration—those who look deeper into something, either unearthed from the inner sanctuaries of nature or brought down to men from the court of heaven. We seek a point so well argued that there is no room to challenge it, or so well defended that there is no room to attack it. Let them admire us, moreover, for being keen in inquiry, circumspect in exploration, subtle in contemplation, grave in judgment, complex in binding arguments, and fluent in unraveling them. Let them admire in us a brevity of style, pregnant with many and great matters, with the deepest meanings—full of questions and full of solutions—hidden beneath plain words. How fit we are, how well-equipped to remove ambiguities, to smooth away difficulties, to unfold what is entangled, and to both weaken falsehoods and confirm truths with soul-swaying <term>syllogisms</term> <note>A form of logical reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two given or assumed premises.</note>.

With these titles, O **Hermolaus** <note>Hermolaus Barbarus (1454–1493), the famous Venetian scholar to whom this letter is addressed.</note>, we have hitherto defended—and do not doubt we shall hereafter defend—our memory from oblivion. If, as you say, we are commonly held to be filthy, rude, and uncultured, this is a glory to us, not an insult. We did not write for the common crowd, but for you and your peers. No differently than the ancients used the coverings of their riddles and fables to keep ignorant men away from the mysteries, we too have made it a custom to frighten them away from our feasts—which they could not help but pollute—with a somewhat bitter crust of words. 

Those who wish to hide treasures, if they cannot put them away in secret, are accustomed to cover them with scraps or rubble so that passersby do not discover them, unless they are judged worthy of that gift by the owners themselves. The aim of philosophers is similar: to hide their affairs from the common people. Since it is fitting that they are not only unapproved by the crowd but not even understood by them, it cannot be but disgraceful for their writings to have anything theatrical, plausible, or popular that would seem to adapt itself to the judgment of the multitude. 

But would you like me to fashion an image of our discourse? It is the very same as the **Silenus-statues** <note>In Plato’s *Symposium*, Alcibiades compares the philosopher Socrates to these statues: they were ugly and grotesque on the outside but contained beautiful golden images of gods within.</note> of our **Alcibiades**; for their images had a shaggy, foul, and despicable face, but inside they were full of gems and rare, precious furnishings. Thus, if you look from the outside, you see a wild beast; if you look within, you recognize a divinity. 

But, you will say, the ears cannot bear the texture—now harsh, now gaping, always discordant. They cannot bear "barbarian" names that are terrifying even in their sound. O, how delicate you are! When you approach flute-players or harpers, place yourself in your ears; but when you approach philosophers, call yourself away from the senses. Return to yourself, into the inner chambers of the soul and the recesses of the mind. Take up those ears of the **Tyanean** <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a 1st-century Neopythagorean philosopher said to possess divine perception.</note>, with which—since he was not entirely in his body—he heard not the earthly **Marsyas** <note>A satyr who challenged the god Apollo to a musical contest and was flayed for his hubris; he represents earthly, sensual music.</note>, but the heavenly **Apollo** <note>The god of music, order, and logic.</note> tempering the melody of the universe in ineffable ways with a divine lyre. If you taste the words of philosophers with these ears, they will seem honeyed to you, even to the envy of **Nestor** <note>An elderly king in the *Iliad* known for speech that flowed "sweeter than honey."</note>. But let us leave these things, which soar far too high. Truly, it is more fastidious to find fault with a less polished style in a philosopher disputing with the utmost subtlety...

<page-num>355</page-num>
<header>Letters.</header>
<sig>Gg 4</sig>
<meta>catchword: nor</meta>

# Letters.

...this [rejection of our style] does not come from a delicate stomach so much as from an insolent one. It is no different than if someone, while **Socrates** <note>The famous Greek philosopher who prioritized moral truth over physical appearance.</note> was teaching about ethics, were to take offense at either a loose shoe or an untidy toga, or were to be irritably annoyed by a poorly cut fingernail. **Tullius** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman statesman and master of Latin eloquence.</note> does not require eloquence in a philosopher, but rather that he satisfy the requirements of the subject and the doctrine. As a man who was as wise as he was learned, he knew that it is our task to compose the mind rather than the diction, and to ensure that reason—not speech—does not go astray. He knew that it is our concern to dwell <term>in the truth of the word</term> <note>original: ἐν ἀλήθεια λόγου (en alētheia logou)</note>, and not in <term>the wisdom of poetry</term> <note>original: ποιήσεως σοφία (poiēseōs sophia)</note>. It is praiseworthy for us to have the **Muses** <note>The Greek goddesses of inspiration in the arts and sciences.</note> in our hearts and not just on our lips, lest our voice sound too harsh through anger, or too weak through lust—in short, lest there be any discord from that genuine harmony by which a tempered soul is measured.

Because **Plato** understood that this harmony is often corrupted by theatrical displays and by poets, he banished all poets from his Republic. He left the governing of it to philosophers, whom he would surely soon condemn to exile as well if they were to imitate the poets through a wantonness of discourse. But **Lucretius** <note>A Roman poet and philosopher known for explaining Epicureanism through verse.</note> will insist that even if philosophical commentaries do not lack the pleasantness of speech in themselves, yet the austerity of the subjects must be disguised by its use. Just as wormwood <note>A bitter plant used in medicine; here a metaphor for difficult truths.</note> dispels diseases by its own power, yet it is smeared with honey so that the unsuspecting age of children may be tricked. Perhaps you had to do this, O Lucretius, if you were writing your works for children or for the common crowd; it was certainly necessary for you, who offered not just wormwood, but the most unmixed poisons to drink. 

But we must follow a far different reasoning—we who, as we said before, seek not to entice the common crowd, but to frighten them away. We do not offer bitter wormwood, but nectar. Yet **Lactantius** <note>Lactantius (c. 250–c. 325), an early Christian author known as the "Christian Cicero" for his polished style.</note> will argue that it is well established that truth flows more powerfully into the minds of listeners—even the elderly—when it is both equipped with its own strength and adorned with the light of speech. If you had been as well-versed in the **Sacred Scriptures** as you were in fictitious lawsuits, O **Firmianus** <note>Lactantius’s full name was Lucius Caelius Firmianus Lactantius.</note>, you would not have said this. Perhaps you would have confirmed our positions no less effectively than you destroyed those of others. 

Tell me, I pray, what moves and persuades more strongly than the reading of the Sacred Scriptures? They do not merely move or persuade; they compel, they agitate, they exert force. You read words that are rough and rustic, but they are alive, they are animate, they are fiery, they are stinging, penetrating to the very depths of the spirit, transforming the whole man by a miraculous power. **Alcibiades** <note>A prominent Athenian statesman and student of Socrates.</note> says that he was not moved at all by the elaborate and brilliant speeches of **Pericles**, but he was moved by the naked and simple words of **Socrates**. He adds that even if they are unpolished, one is seized by a frenzy, placed outside of oneself, and whether one wants to or not, one must do what Socrates has commanded. 

But why do I waste words on a settled matter? If the listener is not a fool, what else can he expect from a disguised speech but a trap? Three things above all create persuasion: the life of the speaker, the truth of the matter, and the sobriety of the speech. These, O Lactantius, are what will win trust for a philosopher—if he is good, if he is truthful, if he seeks that kind of <unclear>speaking</unclear> which flows not from the pleasant groves of the Muses, but from that "dreadful cave" in which **Heraclitus** <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who lived in isolation and was known for his "obscure" and deep sayings.</note> said truth lies hidden. But someone will say: "Come now, friend, let us examine these things, setting aside our dispute. **Wisdom** is something inherently reverend and divine..."

<summary>Pico argues that true philosophy relies on internal reason and the "sober" truth of the matter rather than external literary polish. He uses the examples of Socrates and the Bible to show that simple, unadorned language can be more transformative and persuasive than sophisticated rhetoric.</summary>
<keywords>Scholasticism vs Humanism, rhetoric, Socrates, Cicero, Plato, Lucretius, Lactantius, Sacred Scripture, persuasion, truth, style, philosophy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense of the "Barbarian" philosophers. Having previously argued that truth is more important than eloquence, he now addresses the specific charge that the Scholastic philosophers write in "bad Latin."</meta>

<page-num>356</page-num>

-> # Giovanni Pico della Mirandola <-

nor does it <note>Philosophy</note> need any exotic ornament. But what envy is it that brings us here? Who denies that things which are decent in themselves become even more decent if they are adorned? I, my friend, deny this in most cases; for there are so many things whose splendor you would erase rather than illuminate if you added anything to them. They are, in fact, in such an excellent state by their own nature that they cannot be changed from it except for the worse. A marble house does not accept a painting; if you were to apply a plaster coating over it, you would subtract from its dignity and its beauty. It is no different with wisdom and the subjects treated by philosophers; they are not made clearer by a <term>plasterer's coating</term> <note>original: tectorio; Pico uses this as a metaphor for flowery rhetorical embellishment.</note> but are instead obscured. What more can I say? Is it not common knowledge that beautiful forms are made ugly by <term>white lead</term>? <note>original: cerussa; a toxic lead-based cosmetic used in the Renaissance to whiten the skin, here symbolizing artificiality.</note> In general, whatever beauty you impose on top of something hides what it found there; it shows off only what it brings with it. Therefore, if that which was there before is superior to what is added, then whatever that thing is, it has suffered a loss, not a gain.

For this reason, philosophy presents itself naked and visible from all sides; it longs to come entirely before the eyes and under judgment. It knows it has within itself that which allows it to please entirely from every angle. To the extent you would wish to add to it, to that same extent you would wish to diminish its form and its praise. It wishes to be held as something sincere and unmixed; whatever you mix in, you will have infected, adulterated, and turned into something else. It stands upon an <term>untouchable and indivisible point</term>. <note>A metaphysical concept suggesting that truth is a singular, precise point that cannot be altered without becoming untruth.</note> For this reason, one must not play with tropes or words, nor luxuriate too much, nor wanton with metaphors, nor be daring with invented terms in a matter so serious and of such great consequence, in which to subtract, add, or change anything would be a disgrace.

"But," you will say, "come now, we grant you that it is not your task to speak with ornament; but surely it is your duty—which you do not fulfill—to speak at least in *Latin*. Even if you do not explain matters with flowery words, you should at least use proper ones. I do not demand an elegant oration from you, but I do not want a filthy one. I do not want it perfumed, but neither should it be <term>goatish</term>. <note>original: hircosam; a Latin idiom meaning foul-smelling or uncouth.</note> Let it not be exquisite, but let it not be neglected. We do not ask that it delight us, but we complain that it offends us."

Very well; now you are indeed coming over to our side. But please, let us investigate what this "Latinity" is which you say philosophers alone owe and do not pay. If, in speaking, one should happen to say (for example) that a man is "produced" by the sun, our people <note>The Scholastic philosophers.</note> would say the man is <term>caused</term>. <note>original: causari; a technical scholastic term for the act of being brought into existence by a cause.</note> You will immediately cry out: "This is not Latin!" Up to this point, you are correct; it is not said in the Roman fashion. But this is even truer: therefore, it is not "right"? The argument is flawed. An Arab will say the same thing, an Egyptian will say it; they will not say it in Latin, but they will nonetheless say it correctly. For names of things consist either by will or by nature. If they are established by chance—that is, by a community of men coming to the same opinion and decreeing what each thing should be called—then among them it is called correctly. What prevents these philosophers whom you call "Barbarians" from having conspired into one norm of speaking, which is held as sacred among them as the Roman norm is among you? There is no reason why you should not call it "correct," even if you call it your own. If this imposition of names is entirely arbitrary, then if you do not wish to dignify it with the name "Roman," call it "Gallic," "British," "Spanish," or what the common people usually call the **Parisian style**. <note>Referring to the University of Paris, the premier center for Scholastic philosophy in the Middle Ages.</note> When they speak to you, it will happen that they are mostly laughed at and mostly not understood; the same thing will happen to you when you speak among them.

<meta>The catchword "Αναγκαι" is Greek for "Necessities" or "Necessary things."</meta>

<summary>Pico defends the "ugly" technical language of Scholasticism by arguing that truth needs no rhetorical makeup and that language is a matter of social convention rather than inherent "Latin" purity.</summary>

## Letters.

"Anacharsis commits a <term>solecism</term> <note>original: σολοικίζει; a grammatical error or impropriety in speech. Anacharsis was a Scythian philosopher famous for his plain, "barbaric" wisdom.</note> among the Athenians, but the Athenians do so among the Scythians." That is, Anacharsis makes a solecism among the Athenians, and the Athenians do so among the Scythians. But if the correctness of names depends on the nature of things, should we not consult the rhetoricians—or rather the philosophers, who alone have looked into and explored the nature of all things—concerning this correctness? Perhaps reason accepts things which the ears reject as being a bit harsh, because they are more closely related to the facts. But why was it necessary for those men to invent a new language, and, though born among Latins, not to speak in Latin? O Hermolaus, while they were reading the laws of fate in the heavens and the order of the universe, and studying the cycles of birth and death in the elements, the powers of simple things, and the temperaments of mixtures, could they not, I ask, at the same time note down the properties, laws, and observances of the Roman tongue in Cicero, in Pliny, and in Apuleius? They were seeking what was repellent or accepted in nature; meanwhile, they did not care what was accepted by the Romans. 

But indeed, I now place you in a better position: I grant you that eloquence and wisdom have conspired together in a mutual bond. The philosophers separated wisdom from eloquence; the historians, rhetoricians, and poets separated eloquence from wisdom—something Philostratus <note>A Greek scholar of the Roman imperial period who wrote on the lives of Sophists.</note> laments. You do not doubt that the latter will live with celebrated fame, while the former live only for punishment and insult. See what you are doing! Cicero prefers an unpolished wisdom to a foolish loquacity. In money, we do not ask what mint struck it, but of what material it consists. Nor is there anyone who would not rather have pure gold under a **German mark** <note>original: nota Teutonum; Pico is defending the "German" or Scholastic thinkers against the "Roman" or Italian humanists.</note> than counterfeit gold under a **Roman symbol**. Those who create a divorce between the heart and the tongue are in error; but those who are entirely tongue and have no heart, are they not merely—as Cato says—"funeral glossaries"? <note>original: mortuaria glosaria; a collection of dead words, or words used only at funerals.</note> We can perhaps live without a tongue (though not comfortably), but without a heart we cannot live at all. He is not "human" who is unfamiliar with more refined literature; but he is not a "man" who is devoid of philosophy. The most "infantile" wisdom can be of benefit, but an unwise eloquence is like a sword in a madman's hand—it can hardly fail to do great harm. 

"Therefore," you will say, "even statues are commended not for their figure but for their material; and if Choerilus had sung the same things as Homer, or Maevius the same as Virgil, then the former would be received among the poets just as the latter are." Do you not see the disparity in your comparison? We too assert that a thing is judged by its <term>form</term> <note>original: specie; in philosophical terms, the "species" or essence that makes a thing what it is.</note> and not by its subject matter. For it is by its form that a thing is what it is. But one form is to be received among philosophers, and another among poets. Let Lucretius <note>A Roman poet and Epicurean philosopher known for his elegant Latin verse.</note> write about nature, about God, and about providence; let one of our own write about the same things; let **John the Scot** <note>original: Ioannes Scotus; likely referring to the Scholastic Duns Scotus, whose Latin was considered "barbaric" by Humanists.</note> write, and indeed in verse, so that he might be even more "inept." Lucretius will say that the principles of things are atoms and the void, that God is corporeal and ignorant of our affairs, and that all things are carried along blindly by the chance collision of little bodies—but he will say these things in Latin and with elegance. John will say that things which exist in nature are constituted by their matter and form; that God is a separate mind, knowing all things and providing for all. And he will say that God is not moved in the least from His own peace, despite seeing and governing all things, even the lowest. But what is usually said...

<summary>Pico della Mirandola defends the "Barbarian" philosophers, arguing that the pursuit of truth (wisdom) is superior to the pursuit of style (eloquence). He compares the elegant but "false" philosophy of Lucretius with the "clumsy" but true philosophy of the Scholastics like Duns Scotus.</summary>

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

it is customary <note>original: "κατιοντα μὴ καλιναι"; likely a corrupted Greek proverb meaning "not to revile those who speak plainly" or "not to call things by their names."</note>. But someone will say he speaks tastelessly, rudely, and not in Latin words. I ask, who would call into doubt which is the better poet, or which the better philosopher? It is beyond all controversy that Scotus <note>Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major medieval Scholastic philosopher often criticized by Renaissance humanists for his "barbaric" Latin style.</note> philosophizes more correctly than that other one speaks ornately. But see how they differ: this one has a tasteless mouth, that one a deficient mind; this one does not know the decrees of the grammarians—not to say the poets—while that one knows nothing of the decrees of God and nature. This one, though most speechless in his manner of expression, perceives things that cannot be sufficiently praised in speech; the other, while most eloquent in his talk, utters abominable things. These are the arguments they might perhaps bring forward, my dearest Ermolao, in defense of their own "barbarism"—or perhaps arguments that are much better in their subtlety. I do not entirely agree with their opinions, nor do I think any noble or liberal person should. But I have willingly exercised myself in this "infamous" subject—much like those who write praises of a quartan fever—both to test my wits and with this intention: just as Glaucon <note>A character in Plato’s *Republic* who argues in favor of injustice to provoke Socrates into a better defense of justice.</note> in Plato praises injustice, not from his own judgment, but to stimulate Socrates to the praise of justice, so I might hear the cause of eloquence pleaded by you. For a short time, I have attacked eloquence with a somewhat license-taking spirit, against my own feeling and nature, as if I thought it should be neglected or held second to the "barbarous" thinkers. If I really thought so, I would not have almost entirely defected from them to eloquence—as I have recently done—to Greek literature, and to your never-sufficiently-praised Themistius <note>Themistius was a 4th-century philosopher; Ermolao Barbaro had recently published a Latin translation of his commentaries on Aristotle.</note>. Although I will say freely what I feel: certain little grammarians turn my stomach. When they have grasped two origins of words, they show themselves off so much, they sell themselves so much, they carry themselves about so boastfully, that they think philosophers should be held as nothing compared to themselves. "We do not want these philosophies of yours," they say. And what wonder? Neither do the dogs of Phalerum <note>original: "nec Phaleranum canes"; a proverbial expression suggesting that those without refined taste do not appreciate quality.</note>. But let us close the letter with this conclusion: If those "Barbarians" earned some glory and a name for themselves through the knowledge of things alone, it is not easy to say what place or what praises you should claim for yourself—you who are the most eloquent among philosophers, and among the eloquent, let me say it in Greek, the <term>most philosophical</term> <note>original: "φιλοσοφώτατος" (philosophōtatos).</note>. Florence, June 3rd, 1485.

**G**reetings, most beloved Father. Regarding Apollonius of Tyana <note>A 1st-century Greek philosopher and miracle-worker whose life was often compared to that of Jesus.</note>, I feel nothing more than what you feel; I shall write back to you more on this matter when there is leisure, and perhaps with things that will not be unpleasing to you. Concerning the variation of our translation from the Hebrew text in the third chapter of the book of Genesis, where it treats of Eve and the serpent: this is indeed what I think. In the Hebrew it is as you write: "he shall crush your head" <note>Genesis 3:15. This verse, known as the "Protoevangelium," was a point of major debate between those using the Hebrew text and the Latin Vulgate.</note>, and it refers to the seed of Eve of whom it had said, "I will put enmity between your seed and her seed." However, the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> and Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> translated it as "she shall crush your head." In both cases, however, the meaning is the same. For when it is said "he shall crush," it regards not so much the person of Eve herself as the posterity of Eve, since one is said to do that which one does in one's own seed. But as to why they preferred to translate it as "she" rather than "he," I believe this was...

## GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA TO ALDUS
-> To Manutius, greetings. <-

**I** am sending the Homer that you desired, though later than you wished and I owed. I am so distracted by business, my dear Aldus, that there is no space to even catch my breath. I have (as you know) long since devoted myself to the service of letters. They, by their own command, demand such a severe burden of reading and dictating that I can scarcely recover my health. As for what you write that you will do, equip yourself for philosophy, but on this condition: that you remember there is no philosophy that can call us away from the truth of the mysteries. Philosophy seeks the truth, Theology finds it, religion possesses it. Farewell. Florence, the 11th day of February, 1490, the year of grace.

## GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA TO ERMOLAO
-> To Barbaro, Patriarch of Aquileia, greetings. <-

**I** hear that you have been elected Patriarch of Aquileia. I congratulate those people for having such an excellent shepherd, the whole church for such a most vigorous soldier, and you for the opportunity given to illustrate and amplify your virtue. There are roughly three ways of living: the civil, the contemplative, and the religious. In the first, we require prudence; in the second, learning; in the third—which is like the summit of the whole life—besides those two, we also require holiness. Before this, your city has experienced you as most diligent and prudent in managing the Republic and handling great affairs, and all scholars love and admire you as a patron and champion of the liberal arts. As for what remains, we know for a certainty that you will do it, and we rejoice seriously in this: namely, that the Church shall owe no less to you in the future than your city and literature have owed to you until now.

In recent days, my brother Antonio came here on his way home; I asked what Ermolao is doing. "This is what he is doing," he said: "he loves you, praises you, carries you to the heavens—before me, before others, before the Pope himself—and he does this so constantly and so strongly as if he had nothing else to do." Likewise, the friends I have in your area sometimes write to me, one especially

... Cosimo de' Pazzi <note>Cosimo de' Pazzi (1466–1513) was an archbishop and humanist scholar from the famous Florentine family.</note>, a man (to embrace his praises all at once) worthy of your singular love; indeed, as often as he writes, he writes of your favors toward me, of your love, and of a certain wonderful disposition of mind, so that you always feel and speak of me in the most honorable way. Oh, this unheard-of kindness of yours! You never think you have said enough in favor of men, and if you are such toward me—so that you might make me more your own and obligate me further—you are, as they say, "doing what has already been done," <note>original: "actum... agis" — a Latin idiom meaning to labor in vain or do something redundant; here, Pico means he is already fully devoted to his friend.</note> for I cannot owe you more or love you more. Farewell, and I ask you now to praise me moderately, provided that you love me immoderately. Poliziano greets you, who is always true and always immoderate in loving and praising you. Florence, the last day of July, 1490.

### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA to Jerome, Greetings.

Unless our Angelo <note>Referring to Angelo Poliziano, the scholar mentioned in the previous letter.</note> were writing to you, I would have written more, but I do not want my **magpies** <note>original: "picas meas" — a play on his own name, "Pico," which means magpie in Latin.</note> to chatter over his **muses**, nor do I wish to impertinently disturb your pleasure. But if he has bestowed a benefit who has refrained from an injury he could have inflicted, you cannot help but credit me for a benefit in this brevity of my letter—for which you will be most beautifully rewarded if you return very long letters to me in exchange for these very short ones. For nothing is more pleasing to us than your letters; I pray you do not deprive me of them. Otherwise, if you remain silent, I shall return like for like. For then I shall especially not be silent, for in that way I shall have retaliated against you quite handsomely. Farewell, and give many greetings in my name to our Ermolao <note>Ermolao Barbaro (1454–1493), a prominent Venetian humanist and diplomat known for his work on Aristotle.</note>, the delight of the Roman tongue.

### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA to his nephew, Giovanni Francesco Pico, Greetings.

The reason I have not responded to your letters until now was this: there fell into my hands certain **Hebrew books** in which I have now been diligent day and night for a solid week, so much so that they have nearly blinded me. For the man who brought the books here, a certain **Sicilian Jew**, is to depart from here in twenty days. Therefore, until I have extricated myself from them, do not expect even a syllable from me; for I cannot depart from them for a moment, lest they should perhaps depart before I have thoroughly examined them all. When I am free from this care, I will overwhelm you with letters, though you know I have a very occupied mind. If, however, you are ever going to do anything for my sake, see to it by whatever means you can that the Prince of Mirandola <note>original: "Burri princeps" — referring to the ruler of the Pico family's territory.</note> does not require my presence there; for it would disturb all my studies, to which you know how devoted I am, and indeed I care for nothing besides them. It is not quite clear to me whether it would be more troublesome to displease him or myself. Farewell, and fear God, and think daily upon the fact that you are going to die. Ferrara, May 30, 1492.

-> ## GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA to MARSI- <-
-> ## LIO FICINO, Greetings. <-

Those who plead with many words for what they desire from friends do an injury to friendship, as if friendship itself were not capable of what the lure of speech can achieve. Therefore, I shall deal with you simply, as is required by the benevolence that has long existed between us. At this time, Iamblichus the Platonist <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher. Pico was deeply interested in his works on theurgy and divine mysteries.</note> is very necessary for my studies. If you send this book to me, you will bind me to you in eternal obligation. It will remain here for twenty days, or a month at most, and then it will be returned immediately by courier. In the meantime, use my library and all my things as your own. Farewell.

-> ## GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA to ANGE- <-
-> ## LO POLIZIANO, Greetings. <-

My **Loves** <note>original: "amores mei" — Pico refers here to his own collection of love poems. In his later years, Pico famously attempted to suppress or burn these youthful works, but here he discusses them playfully with Poliziano.</note> declare they were never received more politely or cheerfully than these past days at your house; and as they have confessed like friends, while they congratulate themselves most highly, they also owe much to you. For who would not wish to die by that sword of yours? <note>A metaphor for Poliziano’s sharp critical eye or brilliant wit.</note> Yet they grieve that it was done more indulgently than was proper, and they have come to this point: they doubt whether you, blinded by love for me, have become blinded toward my "Loves." Indeed, they doubt so much that they do not trust enough in their own case against your judgment, which is otherwise most grave. They trust, nonetheless, and now they claim themselves from their bonds; they do not know how to stay at home, and they demand freedom and the public eye instead.

But what shall I say of the charm of your Epictetus? <note>Poliziano had recently translated the *Enchiridion* (Manual) of the Stoic philosopher Epictetus from Greek into Latin, dedicating it to Lorenzo de' Medici.</note> Oh, what a humorous thing, worthy of a laugh from Cato! <note>Cato the Elder was the Roman archetype of sternness; a "Catonian laugh" is one that breaks even the most serious man.</note> He was hardly at the threshold when, opening the folds of his robe, he said: "Behold the daggers <note>original: "obelos" — the obelus (÷) was a proofreading mark used to denote suspected or spurious text. Pico personifies the book as a warrior armed with editorial marks.</note>, behold the arrows! If you do not know Greek, behold me, ready to strike back if any of you should be so bold." Who could have restrained their laughter when that Stoic man joked so charmingly? We certainly held back our weapons, both because he threatened to return the injury, and because his skin had grown so thick <note>original: "occaluerat" — referring to the toughened skin of an old man or, metaphorically, the resilience of Stoic philosophy.</note> that it would not admit such light strikes. 

Therefore, we received the old man with the veneration we owed him. When he finally sat down with us, he began to philosophize about ethics, and that indeed in Latin—not so much because he was among Latins (for there were those in that gathering who knew Greek), but because he himself tasted more clearly in Latin through your benefit. Nor was his effort wasted, since he did not stop speaking until he had turned us from Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school.</note> into Stoics. And we all approved of that <term>apatheia</term> <note>original: "ἀπάθειαν" — a Stoic term for a state of mind where one is not disturbed by passions or external events; "imperturbability."</note>. Now one might see men who were a little while ago delicate, now made the most tolerant of all things, who can indeed be provoked by others, but harmed only by ourselves; who never struggle against fate, and who wish for things that are not ours to happen exactly as God wills. We shall never blame nor accuse them; we shall grieve for nothing, demand nothing, and we shall not know how to be enslaved or conquered. Let us philosophize in deed, not in speech; and since we are novices, let us observe ourselves as adversaries. Let us neglect the opinion of others about us and other things of that external sort, rather than rejecting them. Let us care for the day as travelers do an inn; finally, let us possess things, not be possessed by them. Let us love silence, lest anything be vomited up that is not [concocted/digested]...

...digested. Let others rarely laugh at us, and let us never provoke laughter in others. And to sum it up in a word: let us have abundantly learned the whole of Epictetus—both to endure adversity and to abstain from pleasures <note>This refers to the famous Stoic motto "Bear and Forbear" (Greek: *Anéchou kaì apéchou*). Epictetus was a Greek Stoic philosopher whose "Handbook" Pico was studying intensely at this time.</note>. See how point by point we have modeled our life after your Epictetus; see how quickly we did so, lest even in this part we should not be Stoics, who want us to be warned that a man is failing as long as he is not progressing. While I have admired this in others, I have admired it most of all in myself. Although I have always spent my time in the Lyceum or the Academy <note>The Lyceum and the Academy were the schools of Aristotle and Plato, respectively. Pico is noting that his background was in traditional metaphysics, not in the "Portico" (the Stoa), which was the home of Stoic philosophy.</note>, never in the Portico, I was so overcome by the speech of the old man <note>The "old man" refers to Epictetus.</note> that I have moved over to his opinion not just with my feet, but with my hands and my whole body too. I am sending you the index of the Greek books which are staying here with me, along with the Manual <note>original: "Manualis" — referring to Epictetus’s *Enchiridion* or Handbook.</note> of the letter, as your letters requested. I likewise desire an index of yours. Give greetings in my name to Lorenzo the Younger <note>Lorenzo di Pierfrancesco de' Medici (1463–1503), a cousin of Lorenzo the Magnificent and a patron of the arts.</note>, to whom I was going to write, but shame deterred me lest I seem to compel the man with letters. Farewell.

->GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA TO THOMAS MEDIUS, GREETINGS.<-

**T**he fact that you have dedicated your little story—and a festive and elegant one at that—to my name, was proof to me of both your learning and your singular goodwill toward me. Both are weighty reasons that urge and impel me to love you. I do not know which is greater; for just as in love (as the proverb goes) it is a disgrace not to have returned the favor, so too it is a sign of either a boorish or truly wicked character not to have loved a most praiseworthy man, even if you are not provoked to do so. See, therefore, how you not only call but draw me into friendship with "twin ropes" (as they say), since there is nothing in that little story that does not smell of learning and talent. You could not have deserved better of me than to look after me so friendlily and generously with the dedication of this excellent little story to my name. So far am I from neglecting or criticizing its subject matter that I even approve of it most highly. For it has always been my opinion—and I think no learned person will object to it—that it takes a sharper talent to write these jests and little stories, provided it is done with erudition and elegance (as you yourself have most abundantly achieved), than to have discussed the gravest matters even in an ornate style. Indeed, since we judge it much more laborious to have fashioned a beautiful statue out of mud than out of bronze or gold, why should it not likewise be something remarkable to have spoken on humble rather than sublime material? It is certainly a matter of more work, and therefore even more praiseworthy: the dignity of the subject matter serves as a "pimp" <note>original: "lenocinatur" — in a rhetorical context, this means the natural importance of a "serious" subject makes the writer's job easier by providing inherent interest, whereas "humble" subjects require more skill to make appealing.</note> for the work of the former. These [writers of light works] produce whatever worth they bring entirely from the writer's own storehouse <note>The abbreviation on *depromit* indicates *depromitur*, meaning "is drawn forth".</note>. The material itself contributes nothing, as if providing no share of the feast. Nature diligently assists the former; the latter certainly struggle against nature. Even if this is so, I will not deny that among these humble subjects I mentioned, some surpass others in a marvelous way, and there are even some of that kind so lowly and tasteless that they cannot be sufficiently raised or skillfully seasoned by any force or majesty of words. This defect can never be present in those things which are repaired by the charming wit of jests. But truly, I think those should be placed in the front seats which have mixed in with the charm of wit...

<sig>Hh 2</sig>

...of ages and persons, for they possess all those qualities which belong to the comic poets, and which you have most beautifully imitated in that little play which you gave to me. What sharpness of wit is there! What a timely and ingenious blending of salt <note>original: "salium" — a common Latin metaphor for wit or humor.</note>! How it delights, how charming, how complete it is in every part; and if any section appeared a little sordid or weaker due to the lowly nature of the subject matter, it raises itself up by the light and dignity of the speech, assuming brilliance and strength. It is indeed (to speak briefly) a work that clearly demonstrates it proceeded from a most learned man. 

But among all other things, that exquisite and suitable portrayal of character, ages, and persons is especially dear to my heart, in which I see from afar your unique wisdom—and no small amount of it—as if from a watchtower. I wish you could see what laughter that eighty-year-old prelate provokes in me, who, however else things may go, continually rolls this stone <note>A reference to the Myth of Sisyphus; here used to describe a persistent, obsessive habit.</note>: to scrape together money from somewhere—a vice that has always been kin and familiar to the elderly. What shall I say of our parasite, who, by pretending, extorts a Saliaric banquet <note>original: "coenam Saliarem" — a proverbially sumptuous and expensive feast, named after the Roman Salii priests.</note> from a most stingy old man, and who—to put it so—most singularly milks a pumice stone <note>original: "pumicem emungit" — a humorous metaphor for getting something out of a person who is extremely stingy or has nothing to give, similar to the English phrase "squeezing blood from a stone."</note>? 

There is no word in that little play, my Thomas, which does not claim for itself some peculiar prize; but it is not my place to report everything I have scented, nor do I have the nose to scent everything. Let this be certain to you: that no matter has ever occurred to me more pleasing or joyful; and therefore I have received the work within these walls, and yourself within my soul. You have, my Thomas, what (even if you had to ask for it) should have been sought from me: a mutual friendship which you yourself (as befits a most excellent man) have inaugurated with the Muses. It remains that whenever you find my affairs—however small they are—or my efforts worthy, you should make trial of my goodwill toward you. Nor shall I (if any occasion is given) omit that kind of duty toward you which you yourself performed first toward me in the vestibule of friendship. Farewell.

### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, COUNT OF CONCORDIA
### to his dear Niccolò Leoniceno, greetings.

**I** would have conversed with you much more often and at greater length through letters, my sweetest Niccolò, if your location had been known to me either by messenger, letter, or rumor. Indeed, I have anxiously inquired after this from many people, but received a doubtful response from all. At last, in recent days, the letters of Antonio of Faenza <note>Antonio Cittadini of Faenza, a contemporary philosopher and physician.</note>, a most serious philosopher, to Tommaso Frignano fell into my hands; from these I learned that you are in Florence, which was then most pleasing to me. As soon as I understood this, I sent a letter to you in Florence by courier. The journey was in vain, for he did not find you there, which grieved me exceedingly. Today Thomas indicated that you have departed from Florence and are in Bologna; I immediately ordered these letters to be brought to you. In them, I shall not strive to disclose my benevolence or singular love for you at great length, for you should not doubt my goodwill toward you even a tiny bit, unless [you think] me forgotten (which is not in my nature) both of your outstanding virtue and of your services toward me...

...you might think. I have composed a long poem about it; the house will be sweet to you, and the poem not unpleasing. Farewell once more.

### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA TO ANGE-
### lo Poliziano, Greetings.

**B**ecause you praised me so much in your last letter, I owe you as much as I am distant from actually deserving that praise. For that which is given freely is owed to the giver, not that which is paid as a debt. Therefore, I myself owe you everything you write about me, since there is nothing of the sort in me. That you should feel you owe me this in no way was entirely due to your kindness and singular goodwill toward me. For the rest, if you examine me, you will find nothing but what is thin, humble, and narrow. We are novices and mere recruits <term>tyrunculi</term> <note>A 'tyro' was a newly enlisted soldier in Rome; Pico uses the diminutive to emphasize his intellectual youth and lack of experience.</note> who have only just moved a foot out of the shadows of ignorance; we have advanced almost nowhere. It is a kind treatment of us if we are even counted among the ranks of scholars. The name of "learned" belongs to something else, something peculiar to you and those like you; such grand things do not suit me, since of those things which are foremost in literary studies, I have nothing that is not only unprobed, but which I have not even seen except through a lattice <note>original: "per transennam" — a common Latin idiom meaning to see something only partially or in passing, as if through a screen or window-blind.</note>.

I will certainly strive (as I am doing now) to become at some time such as you now proclaim me to be—and which you either judge me to be, or certainly wish me to be. Meanwhile, I will imitate you, Angelo, you who excuse yourself to the Greeks because you are Latin, and to the Latins because you "Greekize." I shall use a similar refuge: to prove myself to the poets and rhetoricians because I am said to philosophize; and to the philosophers because I act the rhetorician and cultivate the Muses. Yet it happens far differently for me than for you. Indeed, while I wish to sit on two chairs (as they say) <note>original: "geminis sellis sedere" — a proverb similar to 'falling between two stools,' meaning to attempt two things at once and risk failing at both.</note>, I am excluded from both, and it ends up (to speak briefly) that I am neither poet, nor rhetorician, nor philosopher. You, however, so fulfill both roles that it is not quite clear which you are more; you who so beautifully embrace both the Greek and our own Minerva <note>A metaphor for the wisdom and literary traditions of both languages.</note> like a swan of both tongues, so that what is foreign and what is native cannot easily be discerned. For to say nothing of your Latin (in which you yield the first place to no one), who would believe—as was said of the Emperor Hadrian—that a Roman man could speak so well in Greek? You...

<page-num>365</page-num>
# Letters.

...our friend Emmanuel <note>likely Emmanuel Adramyttenos, a Greek scholar who worked with Pico and Poliziano</note> remarked while he was reading yours that Athens itself was not so Attic <note>original: "Atticas Athenas" — 'Attic' refers to the purest, most elegant style of Greek speech and thought, centered in ancient Athens.</note>. You are the one, my dear Angelo (let all flattery be set aside), to whom only one or two of our own—if I may not say none—should be compared. For if there were more such men, this age would have no reason to envy antiquity. Apply yourself, I pray, and rescue literature from its decay as much as you can, lest that splendor of the Roman tongue completely fade away through the injury of time; always forge something new that may help and illuminate the cause of Latin. And those works you have at home, see that they finally come forth for the common benefit of scholars. Indeed, just as I love you yourself, I love and long for all your works; all the more so because I have set you before me as a model to be shaped by, even if you are the sort of man whom all ought to follow, yet few can actually overtake. Farewell.

### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, TO HIS DEAR PAOLO
->Cortesi, Greetings.<-

**Y**ou think rightly, Paolo. Let us send letters frequently, so that we who are divided by distances of place may at least be joined by the exchange of letters. It is customary to ease the longing for those who are absent if you perhaps have a statue or an image of them at home. To me, indeed, there seems to be this difference between a portrait and a letter: the latter portrays the mind, while the former portrays the body. The portrait outlines only the outward appearance, but the letter clearly expresses and shapes even the innermost parts. The image represents, as it were, the cloak and garment of a friend; the letter represents the true friend to us. The image imitates the colors and form of the flesh as best it can, but the letter imitates thoughts, plans, sorrows, joys, cares, and finally all the affections. And those secrets of the soul which one hardly speaks even to oneself when present, one most faithfully transmits to an absent friend. This, in short, is a living and effective thing; that is a dead and mute image. Let us, then, exchange these images of our souls in turn—you indeed sending those golden and silver ones of which you are capable, while I send ones of bronze or clay. In this way, we shall be beyond all injury of places and times, just as the power of the mind itself knows neither the distances of space nor the delays of time. 

But truly, how great is my debt to you, most dutiful Paolo, you who first called me to this duty, especially with such a letter that it held and delighted me so much that I do not remember being more delighted by any reading for many days now. For it is full of eloquence, full of graces, full of love and benevolence—perhaps you expected me to say, full of my own praises. Indeed, I was going to say that as well, for I am not so iron-hearted, or—if this can be said to be greater—so much a philosopher, that I am not delighted by the praises of friends. If they are true, they recommend me to myself; if false, they recommend to me the love and goodwill of the friends. I will easily obtain permission from my philosophy, therefore, to read your letters frequently and with pleasure, even in those parts where they praise me. But it is not so easy to appear sufficiently polite or not ungrateful in repaying this duty of letters, for an imperious mistress <note>Philosophy, to whom Pico dedicated his life's work.</note> so distracts me, so demands her daily task, and finally so occupies me entirely, that hardly anything of myself is left even for my own use. But such is your kindness that you would prefer even poor letters when we write...

### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, TO TROILO Malvezzi, Greetings.

**Y**our little book on lots <note>original: "de sortibus" — This likely refers to a treatise on divination or the casting of lots, a subject of great interest to Renaissance thinkers investigating the boundaries between fate, chance, and divine will</note> has filled me with as much pleasure as usually fills one who has happened upon the best of luck.
