Farewell, and love me. Ferrara, May 19, 1492.

### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, TO TADdeo Ugolino, Greetings.

**I** held your most welcome letters, full of love, faithfulness, and charity, as very dear, not only because you remember me, but because in them you kindly advise me that I should remember myself—that is, my virtuous studies and the need to uphold the expectation I have given. Indeed, being conscious of my own weakness, I would not dare to promise anything even mediocre about myself; but He from whom every good thing comes, the most merciful Father of Lights <note>A biblical reference to James 1:17, "the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change"</note>, as He has given until now the reason why men might hope for something from us, so He will give in the future, so that we may not hold such a well-conceived opinion in vain. I am hurrying to Rome where we shall put our studies to the test <note>original: "periculum... faciemus" — Pico refers here to his planned public defense of his 900 "Theses" in Rome, an event that was eventually forbidden by the Pope</note>, or even do so at some risk. If we succeed in anything, it is a gift of God; to Him be the praise and thanks. If we fail in anything, it is our own frailty; let it be imputed to us. For the rest, I am yours, as one who, on account of the integrity of your life and character, would hardly yield the first place in loving you even to our friend Girolamo <note>likely referring to the famous friar Girolamo Savonarola, a close friend of Pico</note>. Farewell, from La Fratta <note>a town in the Veneto region, now Fratta Polesine</note>.

### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, TO TOMMASO MEDIO, Greetings.

**I** do not remember ever being more solidly delighted than recently while I was reading your *Epyrota* <note>a Latin comedy written by Tommaso Medio in 1483, modeled on the ancient Roman style</note>, a little play undoubtedly most witty, challenging even the ancient comedies with both the festive nature of its plot and the erudition of its style. For what should I say of these modern ones, which are plainly foolish and witless, and which clearly reveal the childishness <note>original: "infantiam" — literally 'infancy,' used here to mean a lack of rhetorical and literary skill</note> of their authors? It was truly worthy to be dedicated by name to Hermolao Barbaro <note>a brilliant Venetian scholar and diplomat known for his massive commentary on Pliny the Elder</note>, though I know not whether he is more yours than mine; I consider that all learned men owe as much to him alone as they hardly owe to antiquity itself. That you did not deprive me of it in the least, you did in accordance with your benevolence toward me, which has been most clearly seen before now. Nor is there anything of mine of such value that, if I had sent it to you as a sort of exchange, I would think the favor had been abundantly returned. I am now waiting with open mouth for the new comedy which you promise me. Nor is there anything I desire more than that, except for your own arrival to visit us. Whom unless [you come] within ten days from here...

that I would have to depart, as I think you have learned from our friend Sita, I certainly would have obtained it from you by entreating; for it is possible to gather this from what you wrote. What delight will there be in our intimacy, what in our living together, what in the very sound of our voices on the road—voices which surely possess a hidden energy <note>original: "latitantem energiam" — an inner power or force of spirit that Pico believes is more effective in speech than in writing</note> that affects the soul more deeply and delights it with wondrous movements, far outweighing any writings. ->**GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, TO MARSILIO**<-
->**Ficino, Greetings.**<-

**Y**ou could not have asked for your Latin Muhammad <note>likely a Latin translation of the Quran or a work attributed to Muhammad</note> back at a more opportune time than now, when I hope very soon to hear Muhammad himself speaking in his native tongue. For after I kept watch over the Hebrew language day and night for an entire month, I turned myself completely to the study of Arabic and Chaldean <note>In the Renaissance, "Chaldean" usually referred to Aramaic or Syriac, the languages associated with the Kabbalah and ancient magical oracles</note>. I had no fear that I would make less progress in them than I did in Hebrew, in which I can now—not yet with praise, certainly, but without fault—dictate a letter. See what the impulse of the soul can do; see what labor and diligence can achieve, even where the strength is somewhat weak. Moreover, certain books in both languages, which came into my hands not by chance or accident, but surely by the counsel of God and the favor of the divine power toward my studies, have encouraged me and even compelled me while I was doing other things to learn the letters of the Arabs and Chaldeans. Hear the titles, and you will give up your security <note>original: "vadimonium deferes" — a legal metaphor meaning "you will drop your case" or "surrender," implying Ficino will be so impressed he will abandon his current thoughts to listen</note>. These are Chaldean books—if they are books and not treasures! They include the oracles of the father Ezra, of Zoroaster, and of Melchior the Magi, in which those parts which are circulated among the Greeks as corrupted and mutilated are read as whole and complete. Then there is an interpretation of the Chaldean sages—brief and rugged, to be sure, but full of mysteries. There is likewise a small book on the dogmas of Chaldean theology, then of the Persians, Greeks, and Chaldeans in that divine and most rich commentary. See, Marsilio, what unexpected blessings have crept into my lap! Why should I not think that I have now obtained a horn of plenty? But what of the Arabic works? Among which are the letters of Muhammad of Toledo <note>possibly referring to the 12th-century translation efforts in Toledo</note>, and Abulgalem <note>likely Abu al-Qasim, an Arabic philosopher</note>, who heard Averroes, and (what will touch you more) many works of a certain Adelandus <note>possibly a corruption of a name like Al-Farabi or a Neoplatonic commentator</note>, who philosophized in Egypt under Ammonius, the teacher of Plotinus, which...

I am a Pythagorean, among whom nothing is more sacred than friendship; and if there is anything that can either weaken or diminish it between us, as they say, let it vanish into the West Winds. Farewell, and love me, who am yours just as I once was. From Fratta.

### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA TO GIROLAMO DONATO, GREETINGS.

**F**or a long time now, such is my negligence, I have written nothing to you; that alone was the cause of this silence of ours. I will allow myself to be judged by you on this charge—negligence, that is—for otherwise I am neither a forgetful man nor a deserter of friendships, which I establish as not temporary but entirely perpetual toward friends of such talent as Donato possesses.

### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA TO HIS ERMOLAO, GREETINGS.

**I** sent a letter to you in recent days via our friend Sita; I do not know if it was delivered. Regarding the commentaries on Aristotle which you requested, I have no doubt you learned from the same man why you have not received them. They will come as soon as I return to my library, for I have come here at present to explore the libraries of others. Nor is there any reason for me to regret it, for I have found so many things here, both Greek and Latin, pertaining to the more refined letters <term>humaniores literas</term> <note>The "studia humanitatis" or liberal arts</note> and learned philosophy; indeed, on this very day that I was giving this letter, there fell into my hands a fragment of Apuleius *On Interpretation*. It is a learned work, and one you would clearly recognize as being by Apuleius, but it is mutilated and crippled. I would gladly know from you whether a complete version is held there, or anywhere that you know of—although when you publish those works of yours that are now under the hammer <note>A metaphor for being currently edited or "forged" into final shape</note>, there will no longer be any reason for us to long for Apuleius. 

Regarding my studies, I have nothing to write to you except that I am assiduously occupied with "Ermolao," and the greatest part of my nights I spend keeping watch over your *Themistius* <note>Ermolao Barbaro published a famous translation of the ancient commentator Themistius</note>. I have recently turned aside from Aristotle into the Academy <note>The school of Plato</note>, but not as a deserter (as that man says), but as an explorer. I seem, however (I shall tell you, Ermolao, what I feel), to see two things in Plato...

## GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA TO BROTHER BAPTIST OF MANTUA, CARMELITE, GREETINGS.

Greetings, best of fathers. For some time I have not written to you, but in the meantime I have read those divine and most holy poems of yours which you have written, in which there is such majesty of matter and such splendor of eloquence that the words and the sentiments seem to vie with one another to claim the prize. Happy are you who can achieve such things with the best of intentions; happy are we to whom it is given not only to read what you have written, but also to love you, to see you, and to speak with you. 

Here is a rich subject for me, one that would fill a proper volume and not just a letter, if either my own weakness or your modesty would allow me to wander into praises of your poetry. I shall say only this one thing: I am so delighted by the reading of your verses that almost daily, whenever boredom or fatigue takes hold of me, I am accustomed to withdraw into them as if into a garden. From this, such a great pleasure always arises in my soul that it desires nothing more than to be fatigued again, so that it may be refreshed again. 

I miss the *Life of Apollonius* by Philostratus <note>A 3rd-century biography of the Neopythagorean philosopher Apollonius of Tyana</note>, if you are finished with it; and see to it that I may eventually have a copy of the philosopher Zacharias, whom you said you obtained in Rome. Furthermore, [send me] an index of your library in Bologna, if that can be done for your convenience. Farewell.

## GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA TO C. P. <note>Possibly a high-ranking church official or "Cardinal P."</note>, GREETINGS.

I have long questioned within myself whether I should deal with you through silence or through letters. Searching for a justification for both, as I judged first in one direction and then in the other, was the reason why I have remained silent with you until this time. For it seemed no less impudent than troublesome to interrupt with these lighter trifles the ears of a man who is, above all, most busy; and there was nothing at all worthy of you for me to write. 

On the other hand, if I did not venerate a man of such distinguished dignity as yourself—who has deserved the best from me—through letters when I could not do so in person, I was undoubtedly failing in my duty. When my mind had fluctuated between these thoughts for a long time, devotion finally conquered shame, and persuaded me that I should rather undergo the mark of being a bit bold and rash than that of a forgetful or negligent man. 

Receive, therefore, C.P., with that cheerful and open brow with which you always received me when I was there, these letters of mine—unpolished and disorganized as they are—as a most serious testimony of my loyalty toward you and of a truly dedicated will. By these letters, I wish this one thing above all to be signaled to you: that there is nothing I desire more than that some occasion be given to me by which I might leave a clear witness with you...

->GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA TO BALTHASAR<-
->MILLIAVACCA, GREETINGS.<-

**Y**ou will wonder, and quite rightly, that my reply to your letter comes much later than you perhaps desired, and as your letters themselves deservedly required. Briefly hear how this happened. A man, truly honest but previously unknown to me, was going to you around the same days I received your letter. He said he was doing business in Milan <note>original: "Mediolani"</note>. I thought this a favorable opportunity to send my letter to you by a faithful messenger—something I especially desired—without delay. But I was frustrated by fortune <note>original: "Austrum perculi", literally "I struck the south wind," a Latin proverb for a plan that has gone awry.</note>; for when he had postponed his departure for a month by procrastinating, he finally left, but without my knowledge. Since I had already grown comfortable in the hope of a certain messenger, a negligent forgetfulness of the letter almost crept over me. Now, finally, when your letter to me fell into my hands, it immediately woke me as if I were sleeping and reminded me of the time I had let pass without fulfilling my duty. I grieved (God is my witness) no small amount, and I grieve still. I do not wish to say these things to excuse myself, but rather to accuse myself; I will easily allow myself to be condemned for negligence and called by you to whatever punishment you prefer. 

Now to your letter. I received no small pleasure from the letters themselves and from the Greek books which you so liberally and kindly made available to me—not so much because their use would do much for my studies, but because we have laid the foundations of a perpetual friendship between us. I value this friendship more than the entire library of either Sammonicus <note>The OCR reads "Sunandiij," likely a transcription error for "Sammonici," referring to the legendary 62,000-volume library of the Roman scholar Quintus Serenus Sammonicus.</note> or Ptolemy <note>Refers to the Great Library of Alexandria, founded by the Ptolemaic dynasty.</note>. For I am so far from neglecting the friendships of learned men that nothing is more a matter of care or heart to me. I know what place you claim for yourself among learned men, since your letter was to me a most evident proof of your teaching, erudition, and humanity. Therefore, if I did not love you very much, I would surely have forgotten myself and would be acting far differently than I am accustomed. I love you, therefore, uniquely, although I have never seen you. I love you so from my heart that I love few others more, so that while your arrival here could certainly add to our familiarity, it could not add to my love. Yet if anything can be added, it will all be added by your coming here. This you promised of your own accord in your letter, and we seek it so ardently that we desire it with impatience. If you can provide me with John the Grammarian <note>original: "Ioannem Grammaticum." This refers to John Philoponus, a 6th-century Christian philosopher and commentator on Aristotle whose works were highly sought after by Renaissance humanists.</note> on the *Physics* and Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*, you will bind me to you in eternal service. For I do not have them here, and I am in great expectation of them. **Farewell.**

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA TO JACOBUS FELTRINUS, GREETINGS. <note>original: "IACObo Feltrino, S." - The "S" stands for "Salutem," a standard Latin greeting.</note>

**Y**our letters have delighted me now more than ever before, for through them I have learned that you hold such an opinion of me that I could not have imagined anything better in my wildest dreams. One thing alone disturbed me: since you noted nothing <note>Meaning he offered no corrections or criticisms.</note> in those things I wrote to you, you made me suspect that you did not think everything was even worthy of notice. For I would have believed that many things had pleased you only if you had indicated that some things had displeased you. Thus it happens that I do not sufficiently trust your testimony in my case—otherwise most highly valued—for you love everything of ours just as we do; and since by your innate easy-going nature you praise everyone, this happens to you especially regarding my affairs, for everything that is in me has flowed from your own source. Indeed, I do not stop, nor shall I stop, trying to emulate you and stand in your footsteps; would that I might one day catch up to you. But I grieve that the distance between our locations prevents me from hearing you in person as you weightily discuss the highest points of philosophy, as is your custom. Even if those same things you say can be sent by letters—which I would most greatly wish to obtain from you—nonetheless, the <term>living voice: "viva vox," the idea that spoken instruction is more powerful than written text</term> has a certain something that more deeply affects and shapes a student. **Farewell.**

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA TO HIERONYMUS DONATUS, GREETINGS. <note>Hieronymus Donatus (Girolamo Donà, c. 1457–1511) was a Venetian diplomat, humanist, and theologian.</note>

**I** received your letters, truly both sweet and learned, by which I was delighted just as I once was by your company when I was in Padua <note>original: "Patauj"</note>, as often as the opportunity of enjoying it was offered to me. Indeed, I was always both eager and most hungry for your company, even beyond what you might think. For it was not hidden from me how sweet, how pleasant was the genius of Donà, how overflowing and stuffed on every side with all good disciplines and every virtue. But it is certainly so, my dear Girolamo: it very often happens to me that the free and ready ability to obtain that which we most desire makes us lazy and negligent; for while we hope that what we neglect today can be done quite conveniently tomorrow, it finally happens that from this sluggish procrastination of ours, a year flows away while we are blinking. But since the matter has turned out this way, you have done quite beautifully to rouse me with your letter while I was sleeping through this kind of duty; I shall use this duty toward you more often in the future, and I would most greatly wish that you be asked to do the same. Regarding your poems, they were with me for several days while I was in Padua, and I remember being greatly delighted by the charm of the little book and the most elegant composition of the verses; but if I am not mistaken, they were returned to Ramusio <note>likely Girolamo Ramusio, a physician and humanist in the same circles</note> before I departed from there. Concerning other things which belong either to me or are mine, consider it settled that you may use them as your own, or else you will certainly be doing an injustice to both me and our friendship. **Farewell.**

### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA TO ANGELO, GREETINGS. <note>original: "ANGELO, S." — Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494) was a brilliant poet and scholar, and one of Pico’s closest intellectual companions.</note>

<margin>—</margin>**S**ince I have arranged my slender Muses <note>A common metaphor for one’s own poetry.</note>—with which I trifled regarding my loves as much as my age then permitted—into five small books, I am sending you the first of them, intending to send the rest soon. In this one matter, I wish to experience you as a friend, not a flatterer. For they come to you under the condition that they be corrected and <term>beaten: "vapulent," a schoolroom metaphor for being struck or corrected</term>, so that they may pay the price for their errors with both the fingernail and with <term>obelisks: "obœliscis," the mark (— or ÷) used by ancient critics to denote doubtful or incorrect passages in a text</term>. Therefore, present yourself to them as a fair judge, not an unfair one; that is, be severe, not indulgent. For what is greater unfairness than to deceive a friend who promises himself everything from you? I am not of such a delicate temperament that I would be offended by another’s erasures, nor do I seem so much a "little book" <note>An idiom suggesting he identifies too closely with his own writing.</note> to myself that I would either ignore or accuse my censor. Indeed, perhaps neither you nor anyone else would believe how much these works of mine fail to satisfy me, and how much I fear that—even in those parts which please me more—I might be, as that fellow says, a <term>Suffenus: a character from the poet Catullus, used to describe a man who is charming but a terrible, self-deluded poet</term>. Surely we are all deceived, and we do not see the <note>original: "manticam quæ in tergo est" — "the knapsack on the back." This refers to Aesop’s fable where people carry their own faults in a bag behind them, visible only to others.</note> knapsack on our back. Therefore, do not deny your effort in this honorable and noble matter to a man who is your greatest friend, especially one who entreats it with such great zeal and from the heart. If I were the kind of person who could return the favor to you in a matter of this kind, I would not keep silent about that Greek proverb: that Lysippus used the work of Apelles, and Apelles that of Lysippus, in turn. <note>Lysippus was a sculptor and Apelles a painter; Pico suggests that even the greatest masters improved through mutual critique.</note> Farewell.

### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA to Angelo Poliziano, Greetings.

<margin>|</margin>**W**hen I was in Florence in previous years, I left with you those love elegies which, as often happens for the sake of exercising the mind, I had fashioned when I was almost a boy. They were indeed tasteless, unlearned, and trivial, such as would easily reveal the author's age and ignorance. You, however, approved of them—not according to the merit of the work, but out of your own kindness, or perhaps too indulgently—and for that very reason, to prove that you had approved them, you asked for copies. Certainly, you were not unaware that such things are sharp incentives for the minds of youths toward virtue; enticed by the desire for praise, having tasted a little glory, they soon strive to taste it more deeply. For just as strength lies flat and cold in the face of despair, there is no one who doubts that it is raised up and set on fire by hope. But now the protection of my age is being taken away; errors that were previously signed off on will now be turned into a vice against me, because I, now more mature in years, have neither cleaned them up better nor deleted them. Therefore, whatever poems of mine are in your possession, if you love me, either send them back to me, or tear them up, or commit them to the fire. All those works, more highly polished, along with many others which have fallen from me during my leisure since I departed from there, will shortly be submitted to your <term>file: "limæ," referring to the "labor limae" or the painstaking process of polishing a literary work</term>. Meanwhile, let those which cannot live without injury to a friend be condemned by a <term>capital vote: "capitali calculo," a reference to the black pebble used in ancient courts to vote for a death sentence</term>. Furthermore, I would very much like you to send me your *Epictetus*, and those things of Homer which you have translated to this day; likewise what you have composed about Giuliano de' Medici in the native tongue <note>Italian (Tuscan).</note>, and whatever else you have composed in the Latin tongue. I ask this of you as one who asks most urgently, and I desire it as one who is most impatient; there is no reason for you to refuse because they might perhaps...

->GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA TO Marsilio<-
->Ficino, Greetings.<-

**I**t has always been my judgment, most learned Marsilio, that in no matter should we work more diligently than to ensure that we do not in any way degenerate through sloth or indolence from the nobility of the soul—by which, on the testimony of <term>Trismegistus: Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical Egyptian sage and supposed author of the Hermetic corpus</term>, we are considered next after Jove <note>Pico uses "Jove" as a humanist synonym for God</note>—and this has always been my primary aim: to acquire the cultivation of the soul and the disciplines of the liberal arts from wherever I could. This plan of mine, though I have held it most steadfastly since childhood, was nevertheless greatly stirred and inflamed by your encouragements when I was with you in previous years; never have I devoted myself more ardently to letters than from that day to this. For three years now, Marsilio, I have been occupied among the <term>Peripatetics: the followers of Aristotle, named for the covered walkway (peripatos) where they studied</term>, nor have I omitted anything within my power so that I might be admitted into the <term>Aristotelian: relating to the philosophy of Aristotle</term> household as one not unworthy of their family. Although I have not achieved this in abundance—since I am barely in the vestibule—I have nonetheless proceeded so far that I would not hesitate to claim for myself the name of a "student," even if not of a "learned and erudite man," which my age does not yet allow. But because it has always been your opinion, and that of the most learned men, that he who <term>mixes Academic teachings with Peripatetic ones: Pico's famous project of "syncretism," aiming to prove that the philosophies of Plato (the Academy) and Aristotle (the Peripatetics) were fundamentally in agreement</term> will hold both sects more rightly and more richly, I thought I should undertake this province: that now, to the best of my intellectual strength and with the greatest possible assiduity and diligence, I might compare <term>Plato: the Greek philosopher known for his theory of Forms and the immortality of the soul</term> with <term>Aristotle: Plato's student who emphasized empirical observation and logic</term>, and in turn, through alternating studies, Aristotle with Plato. But just as I needed you as an advisor before, so now I need you as a helper. It will be a mark of your kindness and goodwill toward me not to fail my purpose—especially one so honorable and noble. I believe this would be most fully accomplished by you if you were to send me your book on the <term>immortality of souls: Marsilio Ficino’s "Platonic Theology on the Immortality of Souls," his most important philosophical work</term>. With this as a sort of guide, I am confident I will make progress in <term>Platonic: relating to the philosophy of Plato</term> discipline as I desire. For who would not promise themselves the greatest things in that kind of learning from <term>Ficino: Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the central figure of the Florentine Renaissance and translator of Plato's works</term>, in whom (if the opinion of the <term>Pythagoreans: followers of Pythagoras who believed in the transmigration of souls</term> were true) I would believe Plato had lived again? Only do not fail me—a request I would press upon you with more words if the very principle of honor, which you value so highly, did not itself demand this of you. For if <term>our Cicero: Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman statesman and orator</term>, and <term>Chilo the wise: Chilo of Sparta, one of the Seven Sages of Greece</term>, and <term>Theophrastus: the successor to Aristotle in the Peripatetic school</term>, the gravest philosopher, thought that for the benefit of friends one should deviate somewhat from the path, would it not be a disgrace to have failed a most dear friend in so honorable a request? See to it, therefore, that what I have long pursued by your encouragement, I may finally achieve by your help. For I have no one else besides you who can assist me in this matter, since—just like many other beautiful and noble things—the care for <term>Platonic: relating to Plato</term> matters has completely faded away among the men of our age. Farewell.

## GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA to his dear HER-
## molaus, greetings.

**N**ot because I have anything worthy of you to write about do I write, but only so that you might write back; otherwise, I have no reason for writing, nor any subject. Indeed, I have always condemned the opinion of those who feel that one must write to friends as if this were a debt to be paid to friendship. For this whole business of writing and constantly sending letters belongs to a friendship that is weak and somewhat chilly, which does not stand firm supported by its own strength but seeks support from elsewhere to stay upright. But for that friendship which has already taken deep root in the very recesses of the soul, why, I ask you, should it need the props of letters? I will therefore send these words of mine to you, Hermolaus Barbarus, for this reason alone: to entice yours, which I desire most greatly, to come to me. You, in turn, lest they be missed by me in vain, shall return yours as abundantly as possible. For just as it is a mark of a weak soul to use letters as "props" <note>original: "tibicines," literally flute-players or architectural supports used to hold up a sagging wall</note> for friendship so it does not waver, so it is a sign of singular generosity and benevolence to show oneself easy and kind to friends. Farewell, and if it is no trouble to you, please send me Ptolemy’s *Harmonics* <note>original: "musicam Ptolemaei," referring to the work on music theory by the 2nd-century scholar Claudius Ptolemy</note>, which will stay here for just a few days. For what would I not boldly ask of you, to whom I have long since vowed and dedicated all my things?

---

## GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA to Her-
## molaus, greetings.

**I** have never pleased myself more, nor been more indebted to myself, than at this time when I have called forth such sweet, such learned letters, so very like yourself, with one letter of my own. But if the facts that you were away from Padua while I was there, and that I missed your company for two years, were the reason you wrote this to me, I cannot help but find that circumstance pleasant now; so abundantly have your letters not only fulfilled my every wish but even exceeded them. For to say nothing of the elegance, charm, erudition, and sweetness of the letter—the reading of which is a great reward in itself—how much do you think I value the fact that you give yourself to me as a friend so lovingly, so kindly, and so truly from the heart? And how much do I value that you so liberally promise your help in honoring me in every way—something I would not dare to hope for? This kind of service I should not merely receive, but even seek out; I confess this frankly and would not blush to say it to your face. For not even the Stoics themselves, as you know, approve of <term>apatheia: (Greek: ἀπάθειαν) the Stoic ideal of a soul free from emotional disturbance or passion</term>, nor among these, which the Greeks call <term>pathe: (Greek: πάθη) passions or emotions</term>, can any affection be more praiseworthy or more honorable than that—if indeed it is among them—which is called the desire for a name and glory. Truly, this can be provided to me by no one more richly than by yourself, in whom all virtues vie to claim the prize for themselves; and there is certainly no one to whom I would more gladly be indebted. Therefore, this promise of yours is as pleasing and desirable to me as it is honorable, and I rejoice in it most especially because it provides proof of your extraordinary love and most affectionate goodwill toward me. I have at last what I have desired for a long time, so that now I seriously triumph...

...pho <note>Likely the conclusion of a name, perhaps "Rodulpho" (Rodolfo Agricola) or a similar correspondent.</note>. I have, I say, Ermolao Barbaro <note>Hermolaus Barbarus (1454–1493), a prominent Venetian humanist and diplomat.</note>, the darling of the Latin language and an illustrious storehouse of all the liberal arts, who is not only well-disposed toward me, but is my dearest friend. You likewise have Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, so devoted to you and so zealous for your studies that no one could be more devoted or more zealous. ### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, ETC.

**N**othing was sweeter to me while you were here among us than your company, and nothing was more useful; such is the sweetness of your character and such is your learning. See, moreover, how sweet and how pleasing you were to me while I enjoyed your presence, since now while you are away, nothing is sweeter to me than the memory of you. But surely, if the soul is the seat of friendship, and if we are essentially our souls—as <term>Plato and Aristotle</term><note>The two pillars of Greek philosophy; Pico famously attempted to reconcile their differing systems into a single harmony.</note> write—there is no reason why any distance of place or long intervals of time should be able to create a rift between us. I was thinking just now whether there might be any other way I could manage to be with you, and nothing came to mind except that my nocturnal labor on the <term>seven-fold explanation of the six days of Genesis</term><note>original: "septiformi in sex dies geneseos enarratione." This refers to Pico's work *Heptaplus* (1489), a mystical and philosophical commentary on the creation story in the Bible.</note> should come to you. For if we give birth to books as if they were children, and the greatest part of the father is in the son, I too shall come to you in that which I have begotten. Receive, therefore, my little son as he comes to you, just as you used to receive me, cheerfully and gladly. I know it will please you because you love me. I know also it will displease you for the same reason. For it is the nature of such devotion to look closely into the errors of those we love so that we may correct them, and once they are looked into, to indulge them lightly so that we do not cause distress.

### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA to F. B., C. TH. <note>Likely "Fratri Barbaro, Canonico Tarvisino"—referring to Ermolao Barbaro, who held the title of Canon of Treviso.</note>

**G**reetings, most beloved father. Here is for you the <term>Apollonius</term><note>Likely referring to the *Life of Apollonius of Tyana* by Philostratus, a popular text among humanists for its depiction of a wandering sage.</note> whom, if I did not owe him to your virtue and your favors toward me, I would certainly owe him because of this letter in which you demand him—such is the love and such is the kindness in your words. For it is a mark of the highest love to call me to that place where you have already arrived—namely, to the <term>purification of the soul</term><note>original: "purgationem animi." A Neoplatonic concept where the soul is cleansed of material distractions to achieve "true happiness" or union with the divine.</note>, which is to say, to true happiness—and it is a mark of the highest kindness to encourage me as if I were an equal, though you could dictate the law to me as if to a son. But would that it might happen through experience at some point that we could philosophize together piously in some retreat; you will see that for me, nothing is more important than to join piety with wisdom. You will see that I am most firmly convinced that there is no wisdom which should erase the image of eternal wisdom within us and make us like the "senseless beasts." I have as a witness my housemate <term>Angelo</term><note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the famous poet and scholar who lived and worked closely with Pico.</note>, that I set down as profit for my studies every day only as much as I emerge from them better equipped and stronger for the struggle of purifying the soul. This all-encompassing handling of various disciplines, and whatever literature can promise us, only colors the skin; it is like a face painted with cosmetics, it does not make us truly more beautiful. But we cannot hope for a sound, firm, and robust mind from anywhere else than from integrity of life, from character, and finally, from divine religion. You therefore compel me, though I am already willing (so to speak)...

->GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, to<-
->Ermolao Barbaro, greetings.<-

**W**hen I was deliberating which of the schools of Italy I should choose as my seat for the study of philosophy, although many things called me to Padua, I sought to go there most willingly so that my love for you—which I had long nurtured in my heart—might become known to you through our mutual acquaintance. I was in Padua for two years; yet, who would believe it? I neither saw Ermolao, nor knew him except by his reputation from long before. It often happens that while we neglect an offered opportunity through some lazy procrastination, it slips through our fingers like something slippery. I have regretted this matter vehemently, and I still regret it—and all the more so because that learning of yours in all things, which I previously knew only by rumor, I have now recognized with these eyes and these ears. For I have heard the "Roman" <term>Themistius</term><note>Themistius was a 4th-century Greek philosopher; Pico refers to him as "Roman" because Ermolao Barbaro had recently translated his works into elegant Latin</note> discoursing from your very mouth on the nature of the soul, the first principles of things, and the science of reasoning. Good God, what learning! What richness of expression! What brilliance! What purity of speech! O most illustrious man, O living image of antiquity! It was my frequent prayer that the writings of <term>Varro</term><note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BCE), ancient Rome's greatest scholar, whose works on "divine and human things" were largely lost</note> on divine and human matters might someday come back to life, so that there would be someone from whom we might learn the principles of physics in Latin. Indeed, you, reflecting both him and all the most approved authors, have presented yourself to us, so that nothing else remains for us to desire, except that by translating other Greek works, you may both win for yourself more abundant praise and deserve even better of natural history and of all students. All these words, most learned Ermolao, look toward nothing else but that you may understand that I am your dearest friend; your virtues so kindle me to love and respect you that I would yield to no one, not even among your own kin, in my love for you. Let this letter sanction a treaty of friendship between us, so that we may henceforth engage in a most honorable contest of mutual affection.

---

->GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, to<-
->Andrea Corneo of Urbino, greetings.<-

**I** received your most recent letter on the <term>Ides of October</term><note>October 15th</note>. The ones you write that you sent earlier did not arrive; I would have replied immediately had I received them, as I am quite diligent in writing and, whether by study or by nature, I am not one to slack in this duty. However, there was no reason for you to fear that our friendship could be weakened by even a long silence; I am a constant friend, not a temporary one. A friendship is not firm enough if it requires these exchanges of letters like <term>supports</term><note>The Latin 'tibicines' refers to structural props or pillars used to hold up a sagging building</note> which (to use a word from <term>Plautus</term><note>A famous Roman comic playwright</note>) prop up something that is wobbling and rather weak. But as for those matters...

The letter is a famous defense of the "contemplative life" of study against the "active life" of politics and courtly service, which Corneo had apparently urged Pico to join.</meta>

<page-num>377</page-num>
<header>Letters.</header>
<sig>Ii 3</sig>

# Letters.

I come to what you write. You urge me toward an active and civic life, saying that I have philosophized for so long in vain—and even to my shame and disgrace, as it were—unless I finally sweat in the wrestling-ground of doing and managing affairs. And indeed, my dear Andrea, I would have lost both the "oil and the labor" <note>original: "oleum operamque"; a Latin idiom meaning to waste time and effort, derived from the oil used by athletes and scholars</note> of my studies if I were now so inclined that I could agree or assent to you on this point. This is that fatal and monstrous persuasion that has invaded the minds of men: either that the studies of philosophy should not be touched by leading men, or should be tasted only with the tip of the lips <note>i.e., superficially</note> more for a display of wit than for the cultivation of the soul, or even as an idle pastime. They hold that decree of <term>Neoptolemus</term> <note>a reference to a line from a lost play by Ennius, often cited by Cicero: "One must philosophize, but only a little, for to do so completely is not pleasing."</note> as absolute: either one should not philosophize at all, or only a little. Now those sayings of the wise are accepted as trifles and mere fables—that firm and solid happiness lies in the goods of the soul, and these external things of the body or of fortune concern us little or not at all.

But you will say: "I want you to embrace **Martha** in such a way that you do not meanwhile desert **Mary**." <note>A common medieval and Renaissance trope: Martha represents the active life of work, while Mary represents the contemplative life of prayer and study (Luke 10:38–42).</note> On this point, I do not oppose you, nor do I condemn or accuse those who do so. But it is far from the case that moving from the contemplative life to the civic life is not an error, or that *not* moving should be considered a disgrace or entirely marked with the note of fault or crime. Shall it then be counted as a vice if someone seeks and pursues virtue perpetually for the sake of virtue itself, seeking nothing outside of it? Because, while searching out divine mysteries and the designs of nature, he enjoys this leisure, despising and neglecting other things, since those things can sufficiently fulfill the prayers of their followers? Therefore, will it be ignoble, or not entirely befitting a prince, to make the study of wisdom something not done for hire? Who could calmly endure or hear such things? Certainly, he has never truly philosophized who philosophized only so that he might one day be able—or unwilling—to stop philosophizing. That man practiced commerce, not philosophy.

You write that the time is approaching for me to devote myself to one of the great princes of Italy. You do not yet know the opinion those who philosophize have of themselves—who, according to **Horace**, think themselves "kings of kings" <note>Horace, *Epistles* 1.1.106–107. Pico refers to the Stoic paradox that only the wise man is truly a king.</note>. They do not know how to endure the whims of others or to serve; they dwell with themselves, and content with the tranquility of their own minds, they are sufficient unto themselves. They seek nothing outside themselves. Things that are honored among the common crowd are dishonored among them; and they neglect and despise everything for which human lust thirsts or ambition sighs. This must be done without doubt by all, but especially by those on whom fortune has so smiled that they can live not only elegantly and comfortably, but even splendidly. Great fortunes truly uplift and show off a man, but like a wild and bucking horse, they often throw the rider; certainly, they always trouble and vex rather than carry him. That desirable **golden mediocrity** <note>original: "Aurea... mediocritas"; the famous "Golden Mean" of Horace, advocating for a middle path between extremes.</note> should be sought, which might carry us like a hand more evenly, and, patient of command, truly serve us rather than dominate us.

Persisting in this opinion, I prefer my little cell, my studies, the delights of my books, and my peace of mind to royal courts, public business, your hunting parties, and the favors of the court. Nor do I expect such fruits from this literary leisure of mine that I should be tossed and fluctuate in the heat and tumult of public affairs; but rather that what births...

at last, I might give birth to offspring <note>i.e., intellectual works or books</note> and—may it be happy and auspicious—give something to the public; if not profound learning, then at least something that smells of talent and diligence. And so that you do not believe that anything has been relaxed in our industry and labor, know that after much work devoted to constant and tireless late-night studies, I have learned the **Hebrew** and **Chaldaic** <note>original: "Chaldaicam"; Pico refers to Aramaic, which was then commonly called Chaldaic</note> languages, and have now also applied my hands to overcoming the difficulties of **Arabic**. These are things I have always judged, and still judge, to be worthy of a leading man. But let me say this as truly as I say it severely: indeed, I so cherish and venerate those most excellent princes—and especially the high-spirited **Ludovico, Duke of Bari** <note>Ludovico Sforza, known as "il Moro," the powerful regent and later Duke of Milan</note>—more than any other prince of Italy. I understand that I owe him much for many reasons, and there is nothing so heavy, nothing so arduous, that I would not do (if the opportunity were given to me) for the sake of deserving that man's favor. But such is their greatness, and my insignificance, that while I cannot help but need them, they can in no way need either my work or my arrival there. I shall set out for **Rome** very soon to spend the winter there, unless some sudden event or new turn of fortune draws me elsewhere. From there, perhaps, you will hear what your Pico has accomplished in this life of shadows and of sitting <note>original: "umbratili & sellularia"; terms used to describe the quiet, sedentary life of a scholar compared to the "sunlit" life of a public official</note> while in contemplation; or what at last—I shall say it, though it may sound rather arrogant—what, I say, he needs from the work of others in literary matters, since you promise him an abundance of learned men if he were to come to you. At Rome, and wherever on earth I may be, those princes will have someone they can command, whom they may turn at their will like a **hand-mill** <note>original: "trusatilem... mola"; a reference to the Roman playwright Plautus, who was famously said to have worked at a grain mill to support himself</note>, as Plautus says. 

As for what you write regarding **marriage** <note>original: "re uxoria"</note>, I do not think it was said rashly or for no reason; but I am **Davus, not Oedipus** <note>a famous Latin proverb from Terence’s play "The Andrian," meaning "I am a simple servant, not a solver of riddles"</note>, nor if I were could I wish to be. Whatever that matter is, if it seems right, explain it more broadly; if not, then be **Harpocrates** <note>the Greek god of silence</note>. As things present themselves, I take counsel in arms. There is no reason for you to desire my **Tuscan rhymes** <note>original: "Rhythmos meos Hetruscos"; referring to his early Italian poetry or sonnets</note>; we have long since sent a message of farewell to those love-trifles, as we are meditating on other things. But I also wish to warn you of this: if you are about to publish your **Laura** <note>likely a reference to a poetic work by Corneo</note>, suppress it for a few more days; for perhaps a little later our people will read things about love (see what I am saying!) which they have not yet read, and you will be able to note many things that will greatly serve your purpose. 

Regarding **Alibrana**, although he is not worthy of me speaking about him, I will say this: he, having been well-treated, has returned poor thanks to his master. There is no reason for him to cast or derive the cause of his flight upon anyone other than himself, since he owes my household—which he cannot deny—almost no less than he owes me. But it is not the first time now, as you know, that he has either broken faith or mocked his master. I know what he has said against me and about me since he fled, but **the elephant does not care about the gnat** <note>original: "non curat culicem elephas"; a proverb meaning a great man is not bothered by the insults of an insignificant person</note>. And I am willing to forgive you whatever that frivolous man has done wrong before now, but let him not abuse my patience in the future, lest I be forced to eventually show myself to him as he has undeservedly shown himself to me. 

That you have excused that friend of yours, whose love affair turned out badly, to our friend **Floriano**, you have done out of duty. He indeed has means from history, from the poets, and even from philosophy itself, by which to clear himself of the mark of a crime; he has...

whence he might protect himself with the precedents of great men, especially David and Solomon—not to mention Aristotle, who, while he often fell desperately in love with certain courtesans, remembered nothing of his own moral precepts when he performed sacred rites to his beloved woman as if she were **Ceres of Eleusis** <note>original: "Cereri Eleusinæ"; referring to the Eleusinian Mysteries, Pico alludes to a legend where the philosopher Aristotle was so besotted by a woman that he worshipped her or allowed her to dominate him.</note>. But he does not merely embrace or love these defenses and, as it were, ramparts for his misdeed, but rather he hates, rejects, and refuses them; he laments his loss, he does not plead against his guilt; he grieves that he has sinned, he does not defend it. And to me, indeed, he seems worthy of excuse for this very reason: that he offers no excuse for himself. Nothing is weaker than man; nothing is more powerful than love. Even that invincible and unshaken mind of **Jerome** <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), known for his asceticism and Latin translation of the Bible.</note>, while it clung entirely to heaven, was yet haunted by choirs of girls. What plague could infest him, whom love will not subdue? If love could do this in the desert, on the ground with bruised limbs, in the midst of weeks of fasting, what could it not do among feathers, in the shade, and in every abundance of delights? Added to this is the fact that he has now fallen for the first time, being otherwise unaccustomed to and ignorant of such a ruin. One can only complain of **Neptune** <note>The Roman god of the sea; used here as a metaphor for the "storm" of passion or bad luck.</note> if they have suffered shipwreck only once. If he should stumble over the same stone again, let no one stretch out a hand, let no one take pity. Now, he cannot rightly be denied an excuse, since he regrets the deed so much that he does not even consider himself worthy of the favor of an excuse. But enough of this, since your friend makes such a memory of this kind; he desires not only that it be recorded in letters in some way, but that his subsequent life should cause it to be entirely obliterated. Farewell. Christopher was not present when I received yours. You will commend me in no common way to your Lord and to the entire **Borromeo family** <note>A powerful and influential noble family from Milan, later famous for Saint Charles Borromeo.</note>, whom I have always loved, and now love very much. At Perugia. October 15, 1484. The year of grace.

->GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA to his<-
->Jacopo Antiquario, Greeting.<-

**A**mong the pleasures I used to take most especially from the company of **Poliziano** <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the preeminent humanist scholar and poet of the Medici circle.</note> when I was in Florence—a man who is, in my opinion, the most learned of all in our age—it was no small delight that he would immediately give me your letters to him to read as soon as he received them, for they were always serious and elegant. In those letters, I was greatly delighted by a certain singular wisdom, for which you are commended by the most prudent men even in the handling of great matters and business; and by the refinement and sobriety of your speech. Furthermore, because in some of them you made honorable mention of us, not only did your letters please me, but in them I also pleased myself—my conscience, yielding to the testimony of such a great man, was somewhat disguising what it felt; as if it were betraying itself, it was deceived without much of a fight and almost willingly. Thus, I was indebted to you on a double count: first for your virtue, and second for the favor, or rather the benefit, so often bestowed upon us. I thought more than once of giving you thanks through a letter, lest perhaps I be thought ungrateful or unrefined toward you. But since you and our Poliziano [shared] a certain most beautiful [exchange of] letters...

...so that you might carry out your business, I did not want the intrusive **Magpie** <note>original: "Pica"; a pun on the author's name, Pico, which means "magpie" in Latin. He is humorously suggesting his own writing is mere chatter compared to his friend's work.</note> to squawk at the Muses, or like a harsh-voiced goose, to disturb the swans as they harmonize with one another. Besides, I knew my mind was open to you through our friend **Poliziano** <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), a famous poet and scholar who was Pico's closest intellectual companion.</note>; being conscious of my own lack of eloquence <note>original: "infantiæ meæ"; literally "my infancy," but used here to mean his lack of skill in public speaking or polished rhetoric.</note>, I used him as a most eloquent interpreter. 

Now, your letters have been sent to us by him—those you recently gave to **Riccius** <note>Pietro Riccio (1474–1507), known as Crinitus, a student of Poliziano and a humanist scholar.</note>, a gifted young man—in which you attribute so much to me that I would not even dare to wish for it, let alone believe I deserve it. The greatness of your kindness has broken my silence—I know not if it was discourteous, but it was certainly not out of pride—and I could not fail to give you immortal thanks. This is not because you overwhelm me with immoderate praise (which I do not recognize as true), but because you love me so much that your judgment, otherwise constant and robust, has nonetheless wavered under the weight of that love. 

I therefore owe you more than I can pay, or than you can easily believe; nor is there anything so arduous or difficult that I would not do for your dignity as readily as for my own safety. You who possessed me through Poliziano until now, will now—with the situation unchanged—simply make clear the name of Pico which lay beneath your accounts. Farewell. From the Ferrarese countryside, June 28, 1494.

### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA SENDS GREETINGS TO ANDREA CORNEO

**M**y prayers have been fully and abundantly satisfied, dearest Andrea. Since I learned from your letters to our dearest **Christopher** <note>Likely Christopher Persona or Christopher Landino, both prominent scholars in Pico's circle.</note> that you are living there in both comfort and dignity. This has always been my greatest wish: for you to be well and happy; and I have nothing greater to say regarding your merits, for I never doubted this would happen. One thing was always certain to me: as long as your tongue survived you, wherever in the world you might be, you would be held in high esteem. 

I know (and this is said without flattery) the nobility of your spirit, which will endure nothing lowly or common. I know your virtues, learning, character, and wisdom, all of which will easily lead you wherever you aim. I only fear for your health, which has been oppressed by so many illnesses from your youth until this day—as you used to tell me—weakened more than broken, so much so that even your health has moved your intellect, so that it knows not how to be defeated, but fights strenuously against the blows of fortune with a certain perpetual solidity. 

I beg you, take no less account of your health than of your fortunes, for where life fails, fortunes are nothing. As for the fact that you speak honorably of me to everyone, you do so out of your humanity and long-standing benevolence toward me, and for that, I owe you as much as anyone can owe. But I fear you are **unravelling your own web** <note>A classical idiom (referring to Penelope's web) meaning to undo one's own work or labor in vain.</note> when you call into public view my "ineptitudes" and the "trifles" that flowed from me in my younger years. For all those things are inept and quite unlearned; even if one judges them most kindly, they certainly are not the sort of things that can sustain the high opinion those men may have conceived of me through your speech. Whatever they may be, I thought they should be sent, so that you might [have control] of my whole reputation...

### -> GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA to R. C. C. S. <-

<margin>x</margin>
**O**ur friend Matthew <note>Likely Matteo Bosso (1427–1502), a regular correspondent of Pico and a member of the Augustinian Canons.</note>, a most dutiful man, has given me many greetings in your name, and has most clearly declared with what love and goodwill you regard me. Furthermore, he promised on your behalf your zeal and your labor, should it ever happen that I might use them. Would that I were equal to such kindness, most kind Father. For I have always desired and hoped to be received into your protection and to be numbered among your people. But to have you come forward of your own accord to meet me as I approached—so kindly, with such friendly and liberal promises—and calling me to your friendship (if I may call it that, though you yourself allow it), has surpassed all my hope and every wish. For what a great thing it is to be invited by one by whom it would have been enough simply not to be excluded! Although you have done something worthy of yourself, even if not of me; for by my own merits I might not have been admitted, yet by your kindness I could not help but be invited. Therefore, how much I rejoice for myself, or how much I owe you, I cannot explain, for I cannot even conceive of it. 

Certainly, I owe you all the more because you owe me nothing at all. Nor are those things so grand or so numerous which Matthew and my other friends have reported, for they were judging me by their affection rather than by their judgment. But such as I am, or however great, permit me also to be among all those who honor and admire your virtues—to say nothing of your other qualities—through which one may see in you that which both surpasses antiquity and cannot be surpassed by posterity. I might say this with merit, since in you nothing is lacking that consists of honor, or wisdom, or learning. One thing alone ought to be desired by all: that through you eventually, according to the wish of Plato <note>Refers to the "Philosopher King" ideal in Plato’s *Republic*, where the state is best governed when power and wisdom are united in one person.</note>, the highest power might be joined with the highest wisdom. 

But these things come from God; meanwhile I ask and request this of you: that you provide me an occasion—not for returning the favor, for there is no room for that given your greatness and my own meager status—but for testifying to my spirit toward you, and my faith and respect. You will find Giovanni Pico a man dedicated and devoted to you beyond all expectation. You cannot promise yourself more than this, but you can have all those things, whatever they may be, which are in him. When you yourself use them, you will bring something of your own splendor to them; they will become great when they begin to be yours, for while they are mine, they cannot be great. Farewell.

->**GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA to his friend**<-
->**ALESSANDRO CORTESI, Greetings <note>The letter "S." stands for "Salutem," the standard Latin greeting.</note>**<-

**Y**our letters were most welcome to me. You sent them recently, not as you suppose, as a stranger to a stranger, but as a friend—and an old one at that—to a friend; not even as one unknown to another who is known. For as you write, you knew me before, and you deemed me worthy of your love. I, likewise, have very often heard of your learning and virtue, both from many others and especially from our friend <term>Poliziano</term> <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), a leading humanist scholar and poet in the circle of Lorenzo de' Medici.</note>, in whose judgment who would not trust? He created in me a faith in your integrity, just as he can create in you a faith in my long-established goodwill. And although that goodwill was already very great, know that through your letter such a heap of it has been added as few could even conceive in their minds. For what could be sweeter than that letter? What more scholarly? How learned it is, how lovable, most generously agreeing with our friend <term>Puccio</term> <note>Puccio Pucci (1437–1494), a Florentine diplomat and close associate of the Medici.</note> who speaks of me more as a friend than with strict truth. Truly, nothing more pleasing could reach me from you, nor anything more honorable than your opinion of me. For all these things, I give you the greatest possible thanks, and I confess that whatever I am, or whatever is in me, I owe to my Alessandro. I am sending you the letter of mine to <term>Lorenzo de' Medici</term> <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent," the de facto ruler of Florence and patron of the arts.</note> which you requested. Farewell.

---

->**GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA to**<-
->**DOMENICO BENIVIENI, Greetings.**<-

**G**reetings, my Domenico, chosen perhaps in the Lord. Your letters were welcome to me, but it was more welcome that I learned—both in person from your brother while he was here, and through letters from our friend <term>Pietro Antonio</term>—that you are of a firmer bodily condition and a better stomach. If you care for all of us, if you care for letters, then care for your health. I have always been anxious about it, not only because I love you (for I love you vehemently), <gloss>but also</gloss> because I love the letters <note>Here "letters" refers to literature, learning, and scholarship.</note> which I believe and certainly know are endangered along with you. If your brother reported anything to you regarding my goodwill, you should have the fullest faith in it; if he said anything in praise of me, believe him as little as the amount that he loves me is great. There is no reason for you to wonder at our "little commentary"; when we wished to be idle and do nothing at all, we did that, relaxing our mind rather <gloss>than</gloss> straining it. It is entirely a prelude to the commentaries we are meditating on <term>Plato’s Symposium</term> <note>The *Symposium* is Plato’s dialogue on the nature of love. Pico's "little commentary" refers to his *Commento*, written in Italian, on a poem by Girolamo Benivieni.</note>. There will be something in those that you at least will love and praise, you who love and praise everything of ours. Regarding the council and the questions, I think your brother has reported them; you already know why I wrote that I am working for you. I will most gladly do what you ask of me when I understand that you have been restored to your former and longed-for health from that bodily weakness from which you have suffered until now. I pray and wish for this for you with the same spirit with which you pray and wish for the health of my soul. Farewell, from <term>Fratta</term> <note>Likely Fratta Polesine, where Pico stayed while preparing his 900 Theses for the planned Roman debate.</note>, November 10, 1486.

There is nothing left for me to write, except that you should commend me in no ordinary way to Hermolao <note>Hermolao Barbaro (1454–1493), a prominent Venetian scholar and diplomat.</note> whenever you see the man. Let that learned and serious man <term>Giacomo of Volterra</term> <note>Iacobus Volateranus, also known as Giacomo Gherardi (1434–1516), a papal diplomat and humanist scholar.</note> understand that he is vehemently loved by me; if I obtain from him the letters of Symmachus <note>Quintus Aurelius Symmachus (c. 340–402), a Roman statesman whose letters were prized as models of style by Renaissance humanists.</note> for a few days—only, that is, until they are transcribed—he will bind me to him by a perpetual favor. Farewell. 1489.

## GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, to BATTISTA
### Guarini, his teacher, Greetings.

**W**hy do you furrow your brow? Is it because I have addressed you as "teacher" against your instructions, and therefore done you an injustice? If you are not a teacher, I am not bound by your instructions. If you are a teacher, I rightly call you teacher. But why do you refuse a student whom you praise so highly? These things contradict each other, unless perhaps one belongs to love and the other to judgment; and while you proclaim his praises out of benevolence, you fear his errors out of conscience, lest they cause you shame—errors which you, as a praiser, might perhaps not acknowledge, but as a teacher, you could not. 

But I beg you, accept me into a partnership of learning on this condition: that I admit you into a partnership of our little glory, if there shall be any, while I alone would bear the blows. But why do I delay the heat of my joy with cold jokes? That joy which I conceived from your letter, from your so serious and so honorable praise—now at last my <term>Heptaplus</term> <note>Pico's *Heptaplus* (published 1489) is a mystical, sevenfold interpretation of the six days of creation in Genesis.</note> smiles upon me; now it is pleasing to me, since under your public proclamation, as if behind the shield of Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom; her shield (the aegis) offered divine protection.</note>, it now shows itself invulnerable to rivals. 

You urge me toward other writings of this kind, which you would do in vain, were it not that while you subscribe to me with such full approval <note>original: "plena cera"; literally "full wax," referring to a wax tablet fully written upon, implying complete endorsement.</note>, you have made me far bolder for writing than I was before by instilling sparks of good hope. For I trust myself so much by your judgment that, although I have taken up the burden of explaining the whole Old Testament—a task for which I am entirely unequal—I shall nevertheless bear it far more strongly than usual. As for the books, I might perhaps satisfy you better if I had an index of those books which are with you, since many could serve your purpose, though you might not lack them. To <term>Lorenzo de' Medici</term>, your aforementioned virtue has made you most highly recommended. Nor is there ever a mention between us of the learned men of this age without your name being much on our lips...

### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA to ANTONIO PICIMANNO, Greetings.

**N**othing in my entire life has been more pleasant to me than these letters I recently received from you, full of love, duty, and kindness. As I hope to be happy, I am not deceiving you—unless perhaps that day was even more pleasant when you and <term>Grimani</term> <note>Likely Domenico Grimani (1461–1523), a Venetian nobleman and scholar who later became a Cardinal and a great patron of the arts.</note> (I know not whether he is more yours or mine) met me as friends and greeted me with honor. For although you took on roles, as if borrowing a mask, and presented yourselves to me not as you were but under some witty fiction of names, nonetheless your most sweet character, your singular learning, your lovely gravity, and your noble modesty—your very nature, your face, and your most charming speech—revealed the true and open Grimani and Picimanno to me. Therefore, even if I could be deceived by the names themselves, I could not be cheated of the pleasure I owed to you. You were able to disguise your names, but you could not disguise your <term>virtue</term> <note>In the Renaissance sense, "virtue" (Latin: virtus) refers to excellence, talent, and moral intellectual power.</note>, which betrays itself by its own brilliance and knows not how to remain hidden. That serious discussion on <term>physics</term> <note>original: "rebus physicis"; in this period, "physics" referred to natural philosophy or the study of the workings of the natural world.</note>, those sharp and intricate arguments, those most refined judgments—whom else could they signal to me but your very selves? I was silently congratulating myself while I listened to you, thinking how fertile our age had been to produce not just one Grimani and one Picimanno, as I thought, but two of each. However, as soon as our Poliziano indicated to me who you actually were, I began to congratulate my own judgment no less than my era; for I seemed to have recognized in you everything that I had learned was in those men (that is, in you) by the consistent testimony of everyone. But see how your praises lead me astray and draw me away from your letter to yourselves—though that letter also calls me to the same place, even against my will. But I shall restrain myself, lest I seem to want to repay your praises with a "mutual service," for you have heaped so many upon me. Whether these come from a leaning of the soul or from your judgment, I know not whether they bring me greater honor or greater pleasure.
<margin>—</margin>
I owe you very much, my dear Picimanno, for your spirit toward me. But please, if ever a trial of me occurs—that is, of my goodwill toward you—you will find a man so loving and studious of your virtue that I would not yield even to your Grimani himself in the first place of loving you.
<margin>— i</margin>
Farewell. July 9, 1489.

<header>Letters.</header>

than that I have learned you love literature and (what is more important) that you are a student of sacred matters and of the law. And since I felt I could satisfy you in some part regarding those things you requested, so that I might auspiciously begin our friendship from here, I wanted to signify to you what I thought. I would certainly have done so far more richly if I had those friends of all men here—I mean my books—which I might consult; but they have already preceded their master to Rome like forerunners, and I myself, already wearing my traveling hat and boots <note>original: "petafatus iam & caligatus" — a classical idiom for being ready for a journey.</note> and prepared for departure, wrote this to you as familiarly as I did hastily.

Regarding what you ask about Josephus, you should know that the true Josephus is not found among the Hebrews. Instead, there is an epitome of Josephus—that is, a certain brief summary—in which there are many fabrications. Many Hebrews have confessed to me that what is read there concerning the ten tribes (who did not return home after the Babylonian captivity) is spurious and adulterated; wherefore no credit at all should be given to their Josephus. In the Greek Josephus, I know there are certain things that make mention of Christ both faithfully and honorably, but I would not assert they are entirely the same as those read in the Latin codices unless I were recently reading the Greek copy, of which I have no supply here.

And to come to those things you desire regarding the letters of the Chaldeans and Hebrews: I have often inquired of <term>Mithridates</term> <note>Flavius Mithridates, a Jewish convert and humanist scholar who taught Pico Hebrew, Arabic, and Aramaic.</note> and many Hebrews about those things read in Jerome’s <term>Galeato Prologue</term> <note>The "Helmeted Preface" (Prologus Galeatus) is St. Jerome’s famous introduction to the Books of Kings, where he discusses the Hebrew alphabet and canon.</note>, where he writes that the characters of the Samaritans and Hebrews were once the same, but that Ezra, after the restoration of the temple under Zerubbabel, invented other letters which are now in use. They all declare themselves ignorant of this change, and (what is more significant) they take it as certain that both Moses and all the ancient Patriarchs used the same characters in Hebrew literature that we use now. 

To this opinion—as it now occurs to me—the science of <term>Kabbalah</term> <note>Pico was a pioneer in "Christian Kabbalah," attempting to harmonize Jewish mystical tradition with Christian theology.</note> gives the greatest credit. Its writers, who were in the synod with Ezra himself, both wish and prove that Moses concealed divine mysteries under those very letter characters and shapes in which we now have the Law written; this could in no way be the case if Moses had used characters other than those we use now. 

Yet, as to how I might be able to defend Jerome’s statement, I have this one thing which I recently read in the commentaries on the book which our ancient father Abraham published concerning Creation <note>Refers to the *Sefer Yetzirah* (Book of Formation), traditionally attributed to the patriarch Abraham.</note>. While the authors interpret those thirty-two "gates" <note>The "32 Paths of Wisdom" in the *Sefer Yetzirah*.</note> which he mentions, they say that number is composed of ten numerations <note>The *Sephirot*, or divine emanations.</note> and twenty-two letters. They say the remaining letters—which are *mem*, *tzade*, *pe*, *kaph*, and *nun*, which are double letters <note>Pico refers to the *Sophit* or final forms of these five Hebrew letters, which take a different shape at the end of a word.</note> whose characters are ך ם ן ף ץ—were added by the "bishops" or the "perfect ones." Perhaps Jerome understood this; his testimony ought to be held by everyone in all matters, and it is indeed held by me as most holy.

The Chaldean alphabet which you seek, you would not have obtained from Mithridates, nor through him—even though you can obtain it from me, from whom you can obtain everything. For he would not teach me the Chaldean language by any means unless [he were] sworn...

I had previously sworn, and indeed in <note>original: "conceptis uerbis" — a legalistic phrase meaning a formal or prescribed oath</note> formal words, that I would not hand that over to anyone. # TESTIMONIES OF MOST CELEBRATED MEN,
## regarding the life, teaching, and commentaries of Giovanni Pico della
## Mirandola, collected from various places.

## TWO LETTERS OF BROTHER BAPTISTA MANTUANUS,
### Most learned and eloquent Carmelite theologian, to Giovanni
### Francesco Pico della Mirandola, Count of Concor-
### dia, concerning the death of Giovanni
### Pico, his uncle.

**I**llustrious Lord, having recently heard of the death of your uncle Giovanni Pico, a most famous and learned man, I was so struck with grief in my soul that neither my feet nor my mind could perform their proper duty. I nearly complained against both God and nature for taking such a light from the world so soon, and for cutting down such an ornament of Italy and such a glory of our age—as if they envied the goods of the earthly Republic and had no regard for us. They cut him down, I say, while he was still growing, while he was flourishing, and while he was feeding everyone with the most copious fertility of his talent. But remembering the sentiment of <note>Saint Paul (Romans 11:33)</note> Paul, who says, "the judgments of God are a great abyss," I restrained myself, lest I should think ill of God and His works with impious rashness. In the passing of this man, literary studies, the knowledge of things, and the integrity of morals have suffered a great eclipse.

For there was (as you know) in your uncle such a holiness of life joined with a mastery of languages and a knowledge of things human and divine, that I seemed to see <term>Jerome</term> and <term>Augustine</term> <note>Two of the most influential "Church Fathers" and scholars of the early Christian church.</note> brought back to life in one and the same man. And would that he had finished that work *On the Harmony of Plato and Aristotle* before he departed. For its title promised the whole of ancient philosophy and the opening of the most hidden things most worthy of being known. All his short works, both those he finished and those he left imperfect, must be sought out with all zeal and diligence; for since they flowed from such a happy talent, they cannot fail to be most worthy of being read, loved, and revered by all posterity. I would urge you to this duty, were I not certain that you are already sufficiently persuaded and moved to it. This immortal honor was lacking to your family: that alongside your most ancient nobility, your abundance of wealth and resources, and your glory in military affairs, there should also be placed such an excellence of wisdom, so that all things which are worthy of the highest praise among mortals might flow together into your house.
