->Giovanni Pico, learned in the heavens, the elements, and God,<-
->Died sanctified while still a young man.<-

**I**llustrious Count Giovanni Francesco, the most honorable delay of your response had made me believe that my letters had perished on the road; and while I was deciding to send you new ones for that reason, and had already begun to write them out, yours—most longed for, most refined, and most pleasant—arrived on the following night. I believe that because I had thought of him during the day, as I slept toward dawn—the time when dreams are usually seen to be true—an image of your uncle, already deceased, appeared to come to me and to discuss many things with me about the nature of angels, and the species, names, and duties of airy, earthly, and even aquatic spirits, with the greatest pleasure for both of us. And when I asked him why he stammered (for he seemed to be stammering), he replied that it was a sign of the imperfect and incomplete discourse which he had long ago begun concerning the nature of things and philosophy <note>Pico died young, leaving many of his most ambitious projects, like his work against astrology and his reconciliation of Plato and Aristotle, unfinished.</note>. I seemed to be inflamed with a desire for inquiring about many occult matters which are marvelous and unknown to us mortals, and I know not how it happened that this first occurred to me: namely, what use amulets and corals and other things of that kind were to infants, which are tied around the necks of little children. He replied that there is sometimes some virtue in these, and that this pertains to <term>natural magic</term> <note>original: "magia naturalis" — In the Renaissance, this referred to the use of natural properties of herbs, stones, and stars for healing or knowledge, distinct from "black" or demonic magic.</note>, but that for the most part they are condemned customs and superstitions. With these things said, he vanished, and I, having woken up, thought for a long time about what we had discussed in the dream, because they seemed not to be empty but to have some weight. I write this, however, not because I place any faith in dreams, for that is foreign both to my profession and to my nature, but because I cannot wonder enough at the manner in which it happens that those who sleep debate, teach, learn, and often do things that are impossible, or certainly difficult, for those who are awake. Our souls certainly possess some touch of divinity, and if we lived holily and piously, and if our minds were not spun around by so many tangles of business, we would have great commerce with <term>separated spirits</term> <note>original: "spiritus separati" — spirits that exist without physical bodies, such as angels or souls after death.</note>. But enough of these things for now. That you wish, as you write, to compose a life of your uncle, I both praise and urge and beseech you to do it more promptly; for that duty is most fitting for you, and must be undertaken by you for many reasons, for you are very strong in both style and eloquence, which is a gift of nature, industry, and a singular gift of God. Likewise, because you are of his clan and a very close relative to such a marvelous man, it follows that you cannot help but be a partaker in his glory. Nor should you allow in any way that his most bright...

[noble] family of yours should lose any of such great ornament and splendor. To this is added that his life ought to be better known to no one than to you, since you had long ago proposed to yourself that it should be imitated—and indeed most wisely, for he was an outstanding exemplar of holiness and religion, in whom the light of all wisdom was apparent. I will say to you, therefore, what Christ said to the Apostles: "Gather the fragments, lest they perish" <note>original: "Colligite fragmenta ne pereant"; a reference to John 6:12, here applied to the urgent need to collect and preserve Pico’s scattered writings after his sudden death.</note>; and this must be done all the more studiously as it will be more profitable for us who survive and for future generations.

<margin>/</margin> Doubtless, even if I see that he is more to be congratulated—who, after such a short voyage, amassed so much spiritual wealth and so happily reached the harbor—I cannot, however, help but grieve with you over the loss of such a great man. The death of <term>Giorgio Merula</term> <note>An Italian humanist (c. 1430–1494) known for his classical scholarship and historical works.</note>, first a fellow student and later my teacher (for we served together under Gregorio Tifernate), affected me with sadness; but he was already aged and, with old age weighing him down, was now infirm and had completed his duty. The lamentable passing of <term>Ermolao</term> <note>Ermolao Barbaro (1454–1493), a brilliant Venetian scholar and diplomat who died of the plague.</note> and <term>Poliziano</term> <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the renowned poet and scholar closely associated with the Medici in Florence.</note>, two illustrious men, brought heavy heartache to me and all the learned; but this wound sits deeper, and the Republic of Letters has suffered a far greater loss in our Pico. The fields of eloquence mourn; the studies of the mathematical arts have fallen; all philosophy, and the highest speculations of metaphysics and theology, which he had already begun to expand and illuminate, will henceforth fall silent.

But I refrain now, lest I indulge too much in just grief. We must take more care that we emerge like him, both in the study and practice of the sciences and in integrity of character and religion, so that, enriched by a similar trade as his, we may one day arrive where he now rejoices to have reached. I will come as soon as I can, so that I may see and venerate the immortal remains of his divine genius that are in your possession. In the meantime, devote your efforts to writing his life, and love me. May your Lordship fare well, to whom I commend myself. From Mantua, January 3, 1495. Brother Baptista Mantuanus, Carmelite.

#### ERMOLAO BARBARO TO GIOVANNI PICO
#### della Mirandola, sends greetings.

**Y**ou indeed, Pico, owe me nothing at all, either in the name of silence or any duty of mine toward you, so much so that your letters were a cause of great blushing for me. You would apologize to me for my own negligence as if it were yours, when on the contrary, this goodness, brilliance, and fairness of your mind ought to have been redeemed by me from you first at any price. You acknowledge the fault of another when you could certainly either avoid it or share it; you are anxious in a mutual transgression, you who could have been secure both by a counter-accusation and even by a better cause. Either both are guilty, or you are not. Otherwise, as far as you are concerned, you have already cleared yourself; it remains for me to make satisfaction as well. ...to dedicate yourself, in which you have made such progress that it is difficult to know to which part of philosophy you have applied more effort: to that which contains the speculative and the instruments <note>original: "spectativas & instrumenta"; referring to theoretical philosophy and the logical "tools" or methods of inquiry.</note>, or to that which embraces the dogmatic and the instructional <note>original: "dogmaticen paraeneticenque"; referring to the study of established doctrines and the art of moral guidance or exhortation.</note>. It is altogether a supreme achievement, greater than human capacity, which you owe either to your own genius or certainly to your Maker, having attained at such a tender age what would be shameless to even hope for in extreme old age. These things are not yours, Pico; they belong to nature, they belong to God—although if anything is yours, these are yours most of all. See how much less your own they can be called: the nobility of fortune, health, and beauty—goods in which you yield to no one, just as you do not in those things which are more truly yours.

I urge you to turn your mind here; turn this over day and night: what a name you must give to Him who has enriched you so far that you will never be able to repay or even calculate what you possess. Think how much He can do, who willed that you should be capable of these things; how much He loves you, who chose you for Himself out of so many thousands—you who, though almost a boy, would surpass old men, and who, not yet a youth <note>original: "ephoebus"; a Greek term for a young man reaching maturity.</note>, would turn the circles of learned men into admiration of your doctrine. Unless you see this, unless you value it, I affirm to you right now, and I proclaim with a free voice, that you are not as great as you truly are. What I have long promised myself about you, and what I still promise, is immense and infinite; but neither speech nor praise can keep up with my preconceived opinion. I act as those are wont to do who, the more they admire someone and wish to explain what they feel, the less they achieve what they want; so that although they conceive something great in their mind, words nevertheless fail them, and they seem to have been able to struggle rather than to speak. 

Therefore, do not listen to these things which I write about you and bring out to the world, but rather understand those things which I speak about you alone and in silence within myself—as much greater, by Hercules, as thought is than this speech. Greet <term>Marsilio</term> <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the influential Neoplatonist philosopher and head of the Platonic Academy in Florence.</note> and your Salviati. There is no need for you to labor regarding <term>Poliziano</term> <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), a brilliant humanist poet and scholar who was a close friend of both Pico and Lorenzo de' Medici.</note>, because shortly (as I hear) he will be with me, than which nothing more pleasant could happen to me in this entire embassy. That a library there <note>The Laurentian Library in Florence, one of the most important collections of the Renaissance.</note> is being built up daily, larger and more ornate, makes me more joyful than I can say. Letters <note>Meaning literature and classical learning.</note> owe much to the Florentines, and among the Florentines to the Medici, and among the Medici to **Lorenzo**, who fosters this ancestral glory of his family with no less care than he does the republic, which he has the right of administering and establishing. Farewell. At Milan, on the Kalends of January [January 1], 1487.

### To Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

<note>The text begins mid-word, continuing "praedicatione" from the previous page.</note> ...proclamation, I am less able to depart from the subject in which I currently find myself. Yet I do not seem immoderate to anyone, for there is so much praise in it and so little limit to it, that there is no longer any room for ambition or flattery. I have read his *Apology* <note>Pico's *Apologia*, written in 1487 to defend his 900 theses against charges of heresy.</note>, and in it I wonder: why does he grant me so much, who deserve so little? Why does he announce me with such an honorable preface—me, an ordinary witness, not to say one of the common herd? Especially in that work, than which nothing is more subtle, more powerful, or more acute; however, it is better that I defer my judgment for a little while until I have read the whole thing clearly. 

As for your desire to know what I am doing, what else can I say but that I am studying? My public duties <note>Barbaro served as an ambassador for the Venetian Republic.</note> do indeed take something away from my application—or rather, from my time, but not from my application. For I press on more sharply and exact my required task more severely; because this public occupation has taken away my constant devotion, the more business has been added to me, the more greed and eagerness for study it has struck into me. Therefore, all those holidays which a private man would give to his health, I distribute to public service; thus, what I lose for one reason and what departs from me, I gather back by another means. 

I believe I have written to you elsewhere, or told those who might have heard it from me, that the "instrument" of Aristotle <note>original: "instrumentum Aristotelis"; a reference to the *Organon*, Aristotle's collected works on logic.</note>—for that is what the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> usually call his logic—as well as the eight books on *Natural Philosophy* <note>original: "auscultatione physica"; referring to Aristotle's *Physics*.</note> and his three books on *Rhetoric* were translated by me into Latin some time ago. My *Dioscorides* <note>Barbaro’s translation and massive commentary on the Greek herbalist Dioscorides, titled *Corollarium*.</note> is now finished; I am currently putting the finishing touches on it. It is ready; it is my daughter’s dowry <note>A humanist metaphor where the scholar’s book is treated as a child, and its publication is its "marriage" or entry into the world.</note>, and it will soon be settled. 

Then, relieved of that burden, I shall apply myself entirely to Aristotle. Unless God calls me elsewhere, he will go forth completed within about two years from the publication of the *Dioscorides*—at least the works on logic, and with them the commentaries which I have already finished on the *Posterior Analytics*. After these are released, I shall enter upon the natural and divine works. Likewise, the *Rhetoric* and *Poetics*, partly with commentaries and partly with annotations, as I am equipping all the volumes of that philosopher to the best of my ability. For there are also some things in the *Problems* and the *History of Animals* that lack clarity and light; I am prepared to glide past those with the light of a brief and cursory note. I intend to attempt nothing new for the rest of my life; for I must restrain this greed, or rather this audacity of my intellect, lest while it wishes to be considered correctable and fertile—that is, industrious and ambitious—I experience more truly every day what is commonly said: that to embrace everything is to grasp nothing. 

Farewell. Milan.
October 21, 1488. <note>original: "12. Calen. Nouembris. 1488."</note>

Nor can I pass over the fact that you conduct yourself as a middle ground between the new and old theologians, such that you do not hate the simple majesty of the latter, nor are you carried away by the ambitious subtlety of the former. Thus it happens that while you are able to imitate the one and avoid the other, you have plucked the best of both kinds—which is what we hope you will also do in your commentary on the Davidic poem <note>The Psalms of David</note>. Farewell. Venice, the day before the Nones of September, 1489.

### ERMOLAO BARBARO to GIOVANNI PICO della Mirandola, Greetings.

**S**alutations, most kind Mirandola. Indeed, I proclaim your name everywhere so gladly that I do nothing with greater pleasure—not only because (as Plato says) nothing is more pleasant to hear than the truth, but also because, as Panaemo says, it is much more pleasant to speak the truth than to hear it. It happens that with no effort (as we find in Aeschylus, Menander, and Euripides), the truth often comes forth even when not sought; it is frequently expressed even by a most unwilling man, through no questioning but by its own force alone. This is that "tyranny" which you, following your own candor, interpret as kindness and goodness. And by Hercules, you are already so great that whoever does not praise you detracts from their own judgment and reputation. Those who favor and desire your fame are acting in their own interest, consulting their own reasons, and redeeming their own reputation. There are many names in your daily ledger that you do not know; your creditors are in your debt. Many follow the counsel of Prodicus: they give so that they may receive; "one hand scratches the other," as Epicharmus sang <note>A common Greek proverb for mutual favors</note>. Surely, the less you owe your creditors—that is, your praisers—the more you owe to yourself, who make them your creditors whether they like it or not. O unheard-of kind of debt: to be the creditors of a debt, and not the debtor! But I am too busy to play with you any longer. But you, how relaxed you are, good gods, that you allow anyone to be at leisure! I pray you have borne with me this far; I do not ask that you admit some longer joke, only a brief little yawn <note>A metaphor for a brief moment of rest or distraction</note>. Farewell, along with my dear Poliziano.

->Rome, on the Ides of August.<-
->1490.<-

# ERMOLAO BARBARO, VENETIAN AMBASSADOR,
## Patriarch of Aquileia, to Giovanni Pico, Greetings.

<margin>—</margin>**I**t is well, it is perfectly fitting, that you who love me so much should congratulate me so greatly on the Patriarchate of Aquileia, and that you should grant and prophesy for me things much greater than I could ever hope for, even if I were most ambitious, or deserve, even if I were most modest. I know your piety toward me; I see how much you value me. I recognize the power of your love; I have nothing more precious. Would that it might one day be permitted for me to live with you, to philosophize together on nature, on God, and on holy conduct. How much I desire this, and how much of an addition to my favorable circumstances I judge it would be if this happened, I can neither express, nor would I wish to do so in this place even if I could. I implore you, if you have ever judged me worthy of your goodwill, that I might be held by you in that same rank and place—or even a better one if possible—as Ermolao and as a priest; so that you might more closely cherish and hold dearer the one whom you loved as a secular man of the world <note>original: "paganum seculi," here referring to his life before taking high ecclesiastical office</note> now that he has become a soldier of Christ. As for me, I am as unable to stop proclaiming, admiring, and extolling you and your most brilliant virtues, as you are <margin>/</margin> unable to stop increasing them. If I agree with you or lie to you, may I be an object of contempt to all learned men; for a long time now, amazement regarding you and your achievements has held me. * Now there is the stupor and ecstasy of knowledge. Read these words patiently, and let your heart not be exalted, nor your eyes raised high; for why should you be pleased with yourself, you who know that these goods which you possess are not yours, nor are they from your own private savings <note>original: "peculio," a Roman legal term for property held by someone under another's authority, used here to mean Pico's innate talents versus God's gifts</note>, but are granted from elsewhere and belong to the Lord. Forgive me: the north wind of truth and the west wind of charity <note>The "Aquilo" (North wind) and "Favonius" (West wind) are used here as metaphors for the divine or intellectual forces driving his praise</note> have seized me and carried me away.
->Farewell. Rome, the day before the Calends of April.<- <note>March 31, 1491</note>

# LETTER FROM BROTHER BAPTISTA THE CARMELITE TO GIOVANNI
## Francesco Pico.

**I**llustrious Count and Lord: I have read the *Apologia* <note>Pico’s defense of his 900 theses, which had been challenged by a papal commission</note>, or rather the prologue to the *Apologia*, of your most learned and eloquent uncle. I read it with as much pleasure of mind as it is supported by truth, as it shines with brilliance, and as much as the love and reverence with which I have always followed its author. But in reading it, while I desired to quench my thirst, another thirst grew: the desire, namely, of seeing the rest. When I obtain this through the gift of your favor, I shall consider myself to have attained a great part of happiness. Your uncle, Giovanni Pico, has in my judgment surpassed the philosophers of every age of ours. He has done so chiefly for these reasons: that while others consume their lifetimes only in the dogmas of Aristotle and the Peripatetics <note>The traditional school of Aristotelian philosophy</note>, he himself, with Herculean audacity, has scrutinized the sects and families of all philosophers, both ancient and modern, with a marvelous vigor of intellect. Furthermore, while the moderns <note>original: "neotericis," referring to the Scholastic philosophers whose Latin was often considered "barbaric" by Humanists</note> pursue no flower of oratory, he has so joined philosophy with eloquence that he may be said to have restored the ancient and true Academy <note>The school of Plato, emphasizing both deep thought and beautiful expression</note>. These things are worthy of all the greater admiration because he ascended to such a height of virtue and glory with such swift study and in so few years. Nor does he seem to have sought knowledge, as others do, by labor and study and many late-night oil-burnings <note>original: "lucubrationibus," work done by candlelight</note>, but rather to have grasped the whole of it at once...

# MATTEO VERO, CANON 
# Regular, to Roberto Salviati, sends greetings.

**T**he interpretation of the Six Days in which God created all things, written by our Giovanni of Mirandola <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), the famous Renaissance philosopher</note>, which you sent to me as a gift, inscribed and titled by him as the <term>Heptaplus</term> <note>From the Greek 'hepta' (seven), referring to Pico's sevenfold explanation of the creation story in Genesis</note>, is indeed of such a nature that it cannot easily be grasped and understood by someone merely skimming through it. Nevertheless, the beginning of the work so inflamed and drew me in that, eager for the end and never catching my breath, I did not so much taste it as certainly devour it; it is something to be chewed over later with sharper study and by the light of a longer-burning lamp. This Giovanni of ours seemed to me not only to be well-versed and wise in all philosophy and whatever is contained within the laws of nature, but even to raise himself above human things, to fly through the heights, and to have turned secret mysteries and heavenly sacraments toward mystical meanings and allegories. These are things that those of our time who are considered wise and learned scarcely notice or pass over entirely untouched. He explains here the most difficult and celestial matters, and, as far as the subject allows, opens them up more brilliantly than the sun, reveals them, and illuminates them. What is truly miraculous is that, while still a young man living in the secular world, he joins himself closely to the ranks of Dionysius, Hilary, Damascene, Augustine, Ambrose, Jerome, and the other most holy and rare men of old. All posterity will admire him once envy has grown quiet and the slow passage of time has established his authority. What should we suppose God will finally give to him if a life matches such a mind? For even now, with his first beard <note>A common expression for youth or early manhood</note>, he is already most learned in Latin and equally in Greek letters—a feat for which antiquity marveled at Origen and Jerome—and he is not ignorant of Hebrew. Furthermore, in sacred matters he is capable of so much that it is scarcely credible that anyone else could be so capable. Truly, whatever delights we expect next are from the psalms and songs of David, which he has been treating, interpreting, and explaining for some time now, having researched with infinite labor what all the Latin, Greek, and Hebrew writers have left written about them. I am glad that, to complete this business, he has chosen for himself the leisure of our <term>Fiesole monastery</term> <note>The Badia Fiesolana, a monastery near Florence where Pico often studied under the patronage of the Medici</note> at this time; it is a true happiness to see and hear him. And so, my dear Roberto, I give you as many thanks as I possibly can for having taken such care to see such a work printed so diligently and correctly—firstly, because it pertains to the common good and the praise of your noble soul, and secondly, because you gifted it to me immediately. In order that I may appear grateful to you in whatever way I can, behold, accept something of mine,

### FROM A LETTER OF ERMOLAO BARBARO
### to Giovanni Pico.

**O** your brilliant and clearly divine genius, Pico! For although the things you write yourself are of the highest quality, you nevertheless express and shape the inferior works of others so skillfully that they seem to be your own—which is to say, excellent. For I consider it a greater feat to humble oneself and descend to a lower style than to strive for the heights; while the latter may be more honorable, the former is certainly more laborious and requires greater effort. Therefore, whether you truly believe my works are worthy of the effort you spend imitating them, or whether you do this to put me in your debt, I am deeply beholden to you in either case. I shall return the favor someday—I will not say "when I am able" (for I shall never be able), but when you yourself or your family think me capable. For so great is the goodness and kindness of your whole family that you are accustomed to counting as a favor even that which is not one. Wherefore, it will be to my advantage if I leave both the manner and the time for repayment to you, so that in the settling of our accounts, any error or deception proceeds entirely from you, not from me.

As for what you wrote so skillfully regarding the plan of your studies, and your wish to share it with me, it has brought me the greatest pleasure. I have congratulated this century for possessing a man of such great learning that he knows almost everything, and of such great diligence that he seems to know nothing at all <note>Barbaro is praising Pico’s humility despite his vast knowledge.</note>. I see that you are an extraordinary Poet and a most eminent Orator. I perceive that you have become a Philosopher, first an Aristotelian, and now a Platonic one. I see that you have not only learned but drunk deeply of Greek literature—the only thing that could have been found wanting in you, and without which you would have been nothing. You have done this with such ease and speed that you yourself no longer remember that you were once ignorant of Greek, nor could you persuade others of it. I say the same of my friend Girolamo Donato <note>Girolamo Donato (c. 1457–1511) was a Venetian diplomat, scholar, and close associate of the humanists mentioned here.</note>, and I proclaim it as much with pleasure as with truth. I would urge you to use these letters as naturally and familiarly as you do Latin, but you do not need the spurs, and so forth.

### FROM ANOTHER LETTER BY THE SAME TO THE SAME.

**T**hen, when I myself, in a certain corner of one of my letters to you—as if doing something else entirely and in passing—attacked those philosophers whom we call "barbarians," <note>The "barbarians" refers to the medieval Scholastic philosophers (like Thomas Aquinas or Duns Scotus), whose technical Latin was despised by Renaissance humanists like Barbaro.</note> and wrote that you too had become hostile to them and sent them a notice of divorce; you took this opportunity to send us a long and ancient dispute between us regarding the style of those philosophers. It was a work of many thousands of lines, elegant, erudite, and elaborate—perfected with such speed that, had I not known the most perfect resources of your genius, I would have believed you had this argument ready for a long time, so that you could produce it at the first opportunity. But to make the matter even more witty and pleasant for me, you—a most delightful, most kind, and most "Latin" man—defend the barbarians against me, Barbaro <note>A pun on his own name: Hermolao "Barbaro" attacking the "barbarians," while the refined Pico defends them.</note>. You acted as if you were an enemy standing for an enemy, a companion against a companion, and yourself against yourself, and so forth.

### FROM THE SAME LETTER, A LITTLE LATER BELOW.

**N**ow, if there is anyone in that flock who can grasp the things you have said, which are presented with such elegance—dazzling the eyes of those who approach with so many lights and so many ornaments. Add to this so many stimulating <note>The Latin "prurientes" suggests sentences that "itch" or "tickle" the intellect or ears, provoking a reaction.</note> maxims, so many stories and examples of more remote learning, used like little flowers and altogether <gloss>*</gloss> to which, if there are any among them who are slightly less than asses—I was about to say **unrefined** <note>original: "ἄμουσοι" (amousoi); literally "without the Muses," meaning uncultured or lacking in education.</note>—they only twitch their ears, while the rest flee, reject it, loathe it, and so forth.

**G**reetings. I have received Pico's book on the *Interpretation of the Seven Days*, <note>This refers to Pico’s *Heptaplus* (1489), a sevenfold narration of the six days of creation in Genesis.</note> a copy of which Jacobo Volaterrano, <note>Giacomo Gherardi of Volterra (1434–1516), a humanist and papal diplomat.</note> the envoy of the Supreme Pontiff, had also sent to me not long ago. I have run through the work as much as was permitted amidst the heat and the dust. It is an offspring worthy of a divine and admirable genius; certainly, the harvest and material of the work do not demand a hurried or makeshift judgment. But it can be said at once that it is nearly a miracle that Pico, the most learned, most eloquent, and most Christian, has achieved all this at his age. I owe you a great deal.

**I**t does not escape me, nor did it ever escape me while you were spending your life in Padua, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, how great was the excellence of your genius and how great your eloquence; you have indicated this more clearly through many things always, but especially through this, your most learned interpretation of Moses. For, to speak of myself, you have not only confirmed every opinion—and the highest one at that—which I had long ago conceived of you, but you have also nourished it in a wonderful way, increased it, and even raised it to the very peak. Indeed, I have been so delighted in reading this work of yours that I believe nothing more excellent or more worthy can be held, which ought to be read or heard by everyone. For while many things in this most brilliant work of yours are recognized as worthy of praise—which, whether joined together or even individually, would have great power—this seems most prominent: that you have spoken like a divine being, not a human, with (as the saying goes) a divine mouth. Furthermore, you have attained such facility in interpreting the enigmas of Moses that Jesus Christ seems to have granted it to you alone (who otherwise deserve well of Him), and to no one else. For I am not ignorant that this is a gift of some celestial nature rather than one comparable to any lower nature; indeed, it is impossible for any human genius to run through three languages <note>The "three languages" of sacred scholarship: Latin, Greek, and Hebrew.</note> during these few years of yours, let alone to be sufficiently skilled in them as you are skilled. Then, also being thoroughly acquainted with them, to equally untie and interpret such abstruse and such hidden meanings of Moses; and finally, to speak and write what you have undertaken not in an uncultivated or barbaric way, but in the Roman and Latin tongue. For it happens to few "whom impartial Jupiter has loved" <note>A reference to Virgil’s *Aeneid* (6.129), referring to those of extraordinary merit or divine favor.</note> to write as you have written. Wherefore posterity has commended you as a second Jerome, <note>St. Jerome was the model of the trilingual scholar in the Renaissance, having translated the Bible into Latin from Hebrew and Greek.</note> most skilled in the three languages. Accordingly, I congratulate you that you have rendered your name eternal and everlasting; for by this most useful labor of yours, all students of literature will owe you as much for giving it to all to read as they owe to Plato and Aristotle.

## GIROLAMO DONATO TO ROBERTO
## Salviati, Greetings.

**I** have been provoked by you in love with great charms: a little while ago by the sweetest gift of the *Heptaplus*, <note>Pico's sevenfold account of the creation of the world.</note> then by your most kind and elegant recent letter. Either of these could have been enough to encompass all the requirements of friendship. To this was added our friend Seraticus, <note>Likely Girolamo Seratico, a contemporary scholar.</note> a man as upright in letters and character as he is refined; for his sake also, I must love you exceedingly. Regarding how much I owe your kindness, I prefer to be conscious of it myself rather than write it to you. Pico’s benevolence toward me, already perceived before, will earn a more grateful judgment in my eyes through the trust of your testimony. I know how much value I should place on being loved and praised by that man in whom the rewards of learning and character have converged with the highest glory of our age. It is more fitting to admire his *Heptaplus* than to judge it. This style of writing delights me wonderfully, because I see no richer harvest of doctrine and erudition from anywhere else than from the Sacred Scriptures; but that boldness is a happy one. Among the very few, including my Pico—bid him health in my name as much as you can. I am most dear to myself for this very reason: that I love him vehemently. You, my Salviati, will promise yourself as much from me as is fitting to be provided by a most friendly and well-wishing man. Farewell. Milan, October 25, 1489.

## BATTISTA GUARINO TO THE MOST LEARNED PRINCE
## Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Greetings.

**O**ur Pictorius, <note>Likely a messenger or minor humanist associate.</note> with his own rather quick step, brought your little gift to me in recent days. Oh, why did I say "little gift" on account of the number of pages? Rather, it is a greatest gift, on account of the broad and manifold knowledge and the eloquence of your book. What point is there in me writing much about it, since it has already achieved such a consensus of opinion from all who are in the registry of judgment, so that it neither grows by praise nor is diminished by blame? I shall finish in one word: from your (since you wish it so) teacher, I have been made your disciple; and so, beware of calling me by any other name hereafter. Throughout the halcyon days <note>original: "halcedonia"; a metaphor for a period of peace and scholarly leisure.</note> of our lecture hall, I read through everything and re-read it; I learned many things additionally and learned most things thoroughly. Previously, I loved you as much as anyone could; now, because of this gift, I love you even more—that is, beyond my strength—and I look up to your genius. Do so, my Pico: continue by these monuments to deserve well of other literary men and especially of students of sacred philosophy (which is to be considered the true and genuine philosophy), and to rescue yourself from the customs of this devouring age. Know, however, that the greatest things are expected from you, as from one in whom refined humanity...

## CRISTOFORO LANDINO TO ROBER-
## to Salviati, Greetings.

**H**ow grateful and how pleasant your most excellent gift has been to me, I am confident I could not express even with a second *Iliad*, given the magnitude of the thing. For what could more suitably come from you—a man as generous as you are learned—or what could be brought more expectantly to me—one most greedy for literature—than that *Heptaplus* <note>Pico's famous work, a seven-fold commentary on the six days of Creation in Genesis.</note> by our friend Pico? He is easily the leader in all literature and doctrines in our age, and this work is wonderfully written. For although we see this subject treated learnedly, distinctly, and eloquently by almost infinite Hebrew authors, many Arabs, and not a few Greeks and Latins—so much so that I believed not a single word could be added—he nevertheless began the whole matter with an almost new argument. Arriving by a path unused by others at things that seemed well-worn and common to everyone, he described them in such a way that even the most learned admire them as if they were new and unheard of. 

Therefore, for me, who has never yet stepped beyond the borders of Tuscany, to be carried through all regions and tracts of the earth without being delivered by a horse or carried by beasts of burden, but led by the perpetual vehicle of his reason, he has transported me with no effort. Leaving the continent behind, I was carried through all the seas by his narration—as if in a chariot of Neptune—not by the dolphins of Arion, <note>In Greek myth, the poet Arion was rescued from the sea by music-loving dolphins.</note> much less by human ships. These things could indeed seem great and incredible to all. 

Yet there are other things greater and worthy of more admiration. For, raised up from the waters—I know not whether on the feathers of swans or the wings of Daedalus and Pegasus <note>References to flight in Greek mythology: Daedalus escaped Crete on wax wings; Pegasus was the winged horse.</note>—I have traveled through the whole air and the whole ether to the very highest summit of corruptible things. He was not only leading me but carrying me up in a state of perpetual and extreme wonder; a thing truly worthy of note, to have traversed this lower and elemental world. 

But it was a much greater thing to have reached the heavenly realm: to have first penetrated the orb of the Moon, then Mercury, and then Venus; to have seen the rays of the Sun, felt the heat of Mars, and finally recognized both the health-giving rays of Jupiter and the heavy rays of Saturn. Then, at last, I observed that eighth sphere <note>The sphere of the fixed stars, beyond the seven planetary spheres in the traditional geocentric model of the universe.</note> shining with burning stars, and saw all these heavens rotating not with a simple and uniform motion, but with a triple and threefold movement. How these things affect our senses...

knows how to fail? Moreover, he gave me the third world <note>Pico’s *Heptaplus* describes three worlds: the elementary (earthly), the celestial (stars), and the supercelestial (angels/divine). Landino refers here to the highest, divine realm.</note> to fly forth into, in such a way that with all my senses lulled to sleep (for they hinder rather than help this kind of inspection), I might travel through these vast spaces with the mind alone—for by that alone are they traversed—and I would have certainly seen and perceived them clearly. But the sharpness of my sight, like **an owl blinded by the rays of the sun** <note>original: "noctua ad solis radios cæcutiens." A common classical metaphor for the human intellect's struggle to perceive divine truths.</note>, could not sustain such great splendor; wherefore, whatever remained hidden from me or escaped my eyes in this kind of pilgrimage—or to speak more truly, this **return to the homeland**—found the fault not in the guide himself, but easily in the one to whom it was being shown. For the divine genius of **Giovanni Pico della Mirandola** both promises and provides a demonstration of everything.

What is there then, my dear Robert, that I should not confess I owe to you? For I have been enriched by you with such a great gift; as soon as I began to taste it, such a greed was stirred up in me, and such a love for feasting arose from the sweetness of this food, that impatient of any delay, I did not order it to be chewed slowly, but like a most ravenous young ox, I devoured the whole solid mass. But when, through continuous reading, I had completed the entire work, I began to act like that same beast: gathering it into my stomach and then calling it back to my mouth, I ruminated on it more diligently. Then, truly, a wonderful sweetness appeared; then a stupor fell upon me such as never before. 

But you will say, "did you not already admire the man’s learning?" Indeed, I used to admire how he was so well-versed in all disciplines that he seemed to excel in each one individually. No topic escaped him when disputing in **physics** <term>natural philosophy</term>, none in **mathematics**; but in **metaphysics** and in every kind of **theology**—whether you seek that which was stirred up by **Mercury** <note>Landino refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of "Hermetic" wisdom.</note> and brought to perfection by **Plato**, or our own **Christian** theology, which is the most excellent and true of all—these ages of ours, and even several preceding ones, have seen nothing more learned than him. But do not think—a vice many of us have struggled with—that he has separated eloquence from wisdom. Does he not describe everything most weightily, most abundantly, and furthermore, most ornately, so that by his own best right he can now be counted among those ancient orators? These things I have admired about him until now, to such an extent that I thought nothing could be added to such a combination.

<margin>/</margin> However, having read his ***Heptaplus*** <note>Pico's "Seven-fold" commentary on the six days of Creation.</note> through, I have now begun to wonder *why* I used to admire those earlier things so much. Wherefore, I would believe it happened neither rashly nor by some chance, but by God’s command, that this divine man emerged distinguished by these three names. For **Giovanni** <note>the name John, or Ioannes</note> is interpreted as "the grace of the Lord," or "one in whom there is grace," or "one to whom a gift has been made by God." Who does not see that he could not have attained the learning he has reached without the special and greatest grace of God? In the name **Pico**, however, we know there is such hardness of the beak and such strength of the head <note>Landino is punning on the Latin word "picus," which means "woodpecker."</note> that you can find no wood so bony (so to speak) nor so stony that this bird does not pierce it, and skillfully hollow out a hiding place for its retreat and a nest for its brood. In the same way, nothing in all the disciplines of human genius is so difficult to know that he has not penetrated even its hardest parts by striking them, and there he has nested, hatched his chicks, and brought them forth. Since everything in this man is to be wondered at, who would not also call him **Mirandola**? <note>Landino puns on the name of Pico's home, Mirandola, linking it to the Latin "mirari," to wonder or admire.</note>

<summary>Cristoforo Landino praises Pico della Mirandola’s "Heptaplus," using a series of metaphors to describe his intellectual awe, including a ravenous ox ruminating on knowledge and a woodpecker drilling into difficult truths. He argues that Pico’s very names—Giovanni (Grace), Pico (Woodpecker), and Mirandola (Wonder)—prophetically describe his divine genius.</summary>

...thought to call him? Therefore, just as I congratulate you, who enjoy his friendship constantly, so I grieve for myself—I say for myself, who consider myself unhappy in this regard, because due to my many and necessary occupations, I am not permitted to stick to him night and day as I most ardently desire. For if it were permitted, I would never depart from his side—I do not say from the side of an old man, but of a young man, a young man, I say, in whom all wisdom and all learning is aged and venerable. 

But you, to whom fortune has offered far greater leisure, and to whom nature has granted an excellent wit—which your subsequent long exercise and frequent practice in all the liberal arts has increased and polished—enjoy this good thing that has fallen to you from heaven. Drink from this most fertile spring, or rather this immense ocean, and drink as much as can be enough to quench not only your present thirst but every future one. Therefore, reflect, calculate, and debate with yourself how very few mortals such a great good has ever happened to. That famous **Alexander the Great** <note>The King of Macedon, famously tutored by Aristotle.</note> boasted that he had lived in the times of so great a philosopher as **Aristotle**. But to you, by your most happy lot, it has been given to live familiarly with both **Aristotle and Plato** <note>The two giants of Greek philosophy. Pico was famous for his project of "syncretism," attempting to prove that the teachings of Plato and Aristotle—and many other traditions—were ultimately in agreement.</note> at once—and such an Aristotle and Plato that in them, beyond the ancient doctrine of the **Academics** <note>Followers of Plato.</note> and **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note>, we see shining back **Paul**, our **John**, **Dionysius**, **Augustine**, **Jerome**, **Thomas**, and other lights of this kind <note>Landino lists the key figures of Christian theology: the Apostles Paul and John, Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, the Church Fathers Augustine and Jerome, and the Scholastic giant Thomas Aquinas. He argues Pico has synthesized all their wisdom.</note>. Therefore, from these things, best Roberto, conclude how much you ought to love yourself, or love him for this; for fortune has offered this to you, and you by your prudence have seen to it that you have made yourself exceptionally familiar to this man. Farewell. November 22nd <note>original: "10. Calendas Decembris." This is the Roman way of dating: the 10th day before the Kalends (the 1st) of December.</note>.

->ALESSANDRO CORTESI TO HIS PICO, GREETINGS.<-

**I** have taken no greater pleasure in my whole life than recently from your letters; and although I had believed the very highest things of you, you have nevertheless (I confess) surpassed my expectation. You have surpassed it in such a way that I now think the boundaries of your glory are narrow, even if they are spread far and wide. Let us speak more openly and far from the flattery from which illustrious minds have always shrunk: What is there in you that is not extraordinary? What is not worthy of admiration? Individual qualities could honor anyone; but in you, all have been brought together equally; you alone (if I may say so) have stolen all the **Graces** <note>original: "ueneres." Referring to the Charites or Graces, the personifications of charm, beauty, and creativity in Greek mythology.</note> from everyone else. 

And although your ancestors reached a height that none but those born from them could easily attain, you have nevertheless emerged so great that you seem to return more grace to them than you received. While old age brings authority to others, youth exalts your dignity—a dignity which others gain through time, but which you have overcome with invincible virtue. In my judgment, you are placed beyond all the risks of talent; and even if I search for Greek praises, I find no one to whom I may deservedly compare you. In short, one may believe that someone equal to you once existed, but it is not possible to see such a person at this time. Let all the ingenious forgive me: all are far surpassed by Pico alone, whom the kindness of nature has so cherished that it must seem to nature herself that such a great abundance of all praises has been crowded into one man. ...are you **blushing**? Or do you think I am lying? Indeed, I would yield the point if you attributed it to love, which is painted as blind. But I have witnesses more reliable than my dear **Poliziano** <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the preeminent poet and scholar of the Medici circle.</note>—who is deceived only in my case—and if he, as I hear, increases his riches of gold no less than his riches of speech every day, I congratulate him on that as much as I thank him. May he possess a **horn of plenty** <note>A "cornucopia," symbolizing endless abundance.</note>, since he is mindful neither of his guest nor of our old friendship. Concerning **Puccio** <note>Puccio Pucci, a Florentine political figure and friend to scholars.</note>, that most affectionate of men, I shall write elsewhere; who would not wish to be indebted to him? But I delay you too long as you lean over your deeper studies. And I see **Marsilio Ficino** <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the leader of the Platonic Academy in Florence and the most influential philosopher of the age.</note>, the prince of philosophers in our time, laughing at these trifles. Why shouldn't he laugh? He who values all mortal things no less than he despices them.

O, would that someone might place me in your academy, and cover me with the great shade of its branches! Especially since **Mars alone holds this sky** <note>A reference to Virgil’s *Georgics* (1.506-508), describing a world at war where the "honor due to the plow" is gone, and sickles are forged into swords.</note>, no honor is given to the plow; the fields grow rough with the farmers led away, and the curved sickles are turned into rigid swords. But we are content with this **Cato** <note>Likely a reference to a local person of strict moral character, or perhaps a literary allusion to Cato the Elder.</note>. You, meanwhile, gather from these scraps the fruit of my love, and do not think it a small thing to be loved by me, but return the favor. For this hope of mutual affection, in which I rest entirely, can soothe my longing for you. May you be happy, **Prince of the Latin Youth** <note>A classicizing title of honor frequently bestowed upon Pico for his unmatched intellectual potential.</note>, and be mindful of me. 

Live well. December 26th. From Gradoli, **faster than asparagus is cooked** <note>A favorite idiom of the Emperor Augustus, meaning "extremely quickly."</note>. Regarding the panegyric letter to **Lorenzo de' Medici** <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent," the de facto ruler of Florence and patron of the arts.</note>, I will write what I think when I am permitted, when I am in Rome. I have almost unlearned my letters in such a retreat, as you can see; and unless the desire to contract and confirm our goodwill compelled me, I would not abuse your kindness and gentleness to such an extent. For now, take it in good part. Likewise, my <term>provision for the road</term> <note>original Greek: ἐφόδιον (ephodion), meaning travel supplies or a parting gift.</note> is honey. Farewell again.

->GIROLAMO DONATO TO HIS GIOVANNI<-
->Pico, Greetings.<-

<initial>T</initial>he parts that should have been mine, you have taken all for yourself, most learned Pico, by accusing yourself of negligence toward me, and seeking an excuse in that very crime of which I am most guilty toward you. It seems too little to you to excel others in genius and erudition, unless you also surpass—not only others, but yourself—in modesty and kindness. But indeed, I pray you so embrace the gifts of these virtues that you leave some occasion for us also to perform our duty; lest while you claim all these roles for yourself, we be considered unrefined and uncivil. 

In this matter—such is my impudence—I no longer excuse my negligence, but rather I accuse your kindness, because you write that you have established not a temporary friendship with me, but a perpetual one. I understand that I owe you very much for this reason, and indeed you seem to have defined friendship correctly for me; for when it is temporary, it can no longer be friendship. Know this: that I have set this friendship apart in the choice of my own honors. For what can happen to me that is more distinguished than not only to be praised, but even to be loved by such a great man? Our **Hermolao** <note>Ermolao Barbaro (1454–1493), a brilliant Venetian scholar and diplomat.</note>, who by his incredible tranquility of learning and his <term>love of labor</term> <note>original Greek: φιλοπονίᾳ (philoponia); referring to his legendary diligence in study.</note> in his studies...

### FILIPPO BEROALDO TO GIOVANNI PICO
### of Mirandola, Greetings.

**W**hile I was about to dine at the house of **Mino Rossi** <note>A prominent Bolognese senator and patron of the arts.</note>, who is most refined in literary studies and the greatest ornament of our local senate, I was reading the plays of **Plautus** <note>A Roman playwright (c. 254–184 BC) known for his "salted" or sharp-witted comedies.</note>, which overflow with the most sophisticated wit. Just then, your letter was delivered to me—certainly a most literary, polished, and refined letter. Immediately setting aside that comic charm, we began to read your most delightful writings with haste. Good gods, how much beauty, how much learning, how much majesty we found to be within them! Great fame had preceded **Giovanni Pico**, but he was found to be even greater; nothing worn out, nothing trivial resonates in your writings. Your matter fits your words, and your words fit your matter perfectly; you speak in Latin and purely so, using a style that is splendid and magnificent. You possess a way of speaking full of pleasantness and integrity, a most copious "furniture" of the best words, and thoughts that are frequent and well-rounded. You bring forth the feelings of your mind so clearly and elegantly that the immortal gods seem to have given to you alone what they have given to very few: namely, to think the best things and to say the best things. Moreover, you embrace this no less in verse than in prose. **Livy** and **Homer** write almost by divine inspiration, yet the gods did not grant all things to one man; hence it is that we often read of some who flourished by being excellent in eloquence, and others endowed with learning, but very few who stood out as both eloquent and learned at the same time.

From this, the two peaks of the Roman language, **Terentius Varro** and **Marcus Tullius Cicero**, are cited; from the former, the knowledge of things was sought, and from the latter, the mastery of words. The former is called "most learned in every respect" by Terentianus, and the latter "most eloquent" by everyone. **Virgil**, as **Seneca** so excellently says, was abandoned by that felicity of talent when it came to prose; Cicero wrote poems with no charm and no wit, the Muses being—it is clear—unwilling and resistant. But you are indeed both most learned and most eloquent. You are powerful in prose and in verse; you write things worth reading, you are skilled...

...to be written. You may deservedly be called a foster-son of the Muses, you who have not—as many do—drunk only one or another musical mixing bowl, but like a second Apuleius <note>original: "alter Apuleius"; Beroaldo references the Roman author Apuleius who, in his *Florida*, famously described drinking from different bowls of the Muses (poetry, geometry, music, etc.).</note> have drained every bowl, and especially that clear and nectar-like bowl of philosophy, which so very few touch even with the tips of their lips, and which they hardly greet from the threshold. O great fruitfulness of mind! O most blessed abundance of immortal talent, which has forged such great virtues in Pico della Mirandola while still a boy, still a youth, poured in so many yoked disciplines, and implanted such great gifts of the soul; he who is a mere recruit in age, is a veteran in erudition. Proceed, most learned man, where you have begun; ensure that as your years increase, your knowledge grows, your talent matures, and your memory becomes more vigorous and better supported. You who in your youth are the glory of our age and an example of virtue, what shall you be in your old age? Papinian <note>A celebrated 3rd-century Roman jurist.</note> is called by Spartianus <note>One of the legendary authors of the *Augustan History*.</note> a sanctuary of justice and a treasury of legal learning. You shall be called by us a sanctuary of the liberal arts; you shall be a treasury for us whenever anything hidden in the more private depths of literature is encountered—indeed, to speak more truly, you are already a treasury now. All things, even the most profound in literature, are at your hand; all things occur to you readily. That "circle of learning" <note>original: "orbis ille doctrinae"; a translation of the Greek *enkyklios paideia*, the origin of the word "encyclopedia."</note> which is praised by the learned seems to be in your service. Both Greek and Latin letters serve you as handmaidens. It is permitted for you to refresh your talent now with this meditation, now with that, for the one <margin>✓</margin> is the seasoning of the other. And just as varied and rotated seeds restore and refresh the lands, so the change of studies restores and delights the mind. It is permitted for you to gladden your talent with the sweeter studies of poetry whenever it grows weary from the more austere dogmas of philosophy. You, finally, stand at the citadel and the very summit of the good arts, while we sweat at the very first slope. You have ascended the narrow path of virtue with the step of a climber; we attempt to ascend with the pace of a tortoise or an ant, and we toil on rugged paths, repeatedly slipping, repeatedly nodding, and stumbling. I write what I feel, I feel what I write; my pen accords with my mind. I am moved by an incredible desire to visit you along with Poliziano, a desire I shall satisfy within a very few days; for Minus Roscius <note>A friend and likely a student or associate of Beroaldo.</note>, who is most loving of all men of letters and who pursues us both especially with a wonderful love, is coming there this Easter holiday to fulfill his vows. I shall accompany the man; then it will be possible to join right hands in turn and enjoy mutual conversation. Then I, a common man of letters and a simple teacher of grammar <note>original: "grammatista"; Beroaldo uses this modestly to contrast his status with Pico's "literatissimus" (most learned) status.</note>, will approach you most learned men, speak to you, and greet you; then I, who seem wise here, will perhaps whisper there, or sound out like a goose honking among swans <note>original: "anfer inter olores"; a classical trope for an inferior poet or speaker in the company of greats.</note>. Meanwhile,

->farewell, sanctuary of letters, and love me in return, and<-
->greet the most missed Poliziano in my name.<-

# BARTOLOMEO DELLA FONTE TO ROBERTO SALVIATI.

**G**reetings. Indeed, Robert, if ever I read your Pico with the greatest pleasure, I did so last night for two reasons: both because it was sent by you, a most dear friend, and because I love the author of the work for his own sake—a man whom I thought it would be a disgrace not to have read until now. Since I have finally obtained through your kindness what I most desired, I both give you thanks for such a gift and heartily congratulate him for publishing so great a work, which ought to be celebrated by all of Christendom. In it, I am truly uncertain whether to marvel more at the discovery of so many great things, or at such incredible order amidst such variety, or at such great elegance of speech in such laborious descriptions. For why should I mention those things in the <term>Heptaplus</term> <note>Pico's *Heptaplus* (1489) is a seven-fold mystical commentary on the seven days of Genesis.</note> which most recommend the authors of works: that there is no wordiness, no swelling pride, and a singular modesty in all things, free from any suspicion of envy. I only wish I could have returned a similar gift for this most sweet and welcome favor of yours, so that you might see my affection for you more clearly. But, as I was able, I have sent to you before anyone else the speech I recently delivered at Buda to King Matthias Corvinus. <note>Matthias Corvinus (r. 1458–1490) was the King of Hungary and a famous patron of humanist scholars.</note> When you have read it yourself, you shall also give it to your friend Pico to read. Among all those of our age whose writings I have seen so far, I judge him to be the most outstanding in every branch of learning. Farewell, and love me in return, as you do.

# BATTISTA GUARINI TO THE MOST LEARNED PRINCE
->To Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Greetings.<-

**I** do not yet concede that the dispute ought to be decided in your favor, for I can easily <term>turn back your own clever arguments against you</term>. <note>original: "ἀντιστρέφοντα"; a Greek rhetorical term for an argument that can be reversed to prove the opposite point.</note> If I am your teacher, why do you not obey me? If I am not, why do you call me teacher? Nor do I refuse this name because I look down on you as a student—for I assert that you are my own teacher—but because I both venerate and proclaim your learning. I am conscious that in your work, neither my own talents, nor the mark of my <term>crossing-out pen</term>, nor my little wax corrections, nor finally my <term>obelisk</term> or <term>asterisk</term> <note>These were traditional marks used by editors to denote suspect or noteworthy passages in a text.</note> have contributed much. But we seem to have fallen into a new kind of legal case, while you strive to claim for me that possession which I am trying to grant to you. What cause of the rhetoricians ever had a plaintiff or defendant of this kind? My dear Pico, I shall never <term>hand over the herb</term> to you <note>original: "herbam porrigam"; a classical idiom meaning to concede defeat or surrender.</note> in this battle unless we first settle it with good grace: that since you will not succumb otherwise, each of us shall be judged as both teacher and student to the other in equal measure. But jests aside, let us move to serious matters. Both your *Heptaplus* and you yourself can rightly be pleased with your work, since you have won every vote <note>original: "omnes puncta"; literally 'every point,' referencing a poet winning all the votes of the judges.</note> of learned men so thoroughly that not even a hidden corner of envy appears on the page. It is to be hoped that the same will be more easily granted to you in your remaining writings, especially when experience is added, which is usually held to be the best master in writing. As for me, I rejoice exceedingly that I am on the lips of Lorenzo—a man praised and to be praised by everyone and everywhere—especially with the added <term>vote</term> of Poliziano. <note>Guarini refers here to Lorenzo de' Medici (the Magnificent) and the famous scholar Angelo Poliziano.</note> I so embrace Poliziano's copious and secret reading of manifold disciplines that I am filled with admiration...

### FROM THE LETTER OF ERMOLAO TO GIOVANNI
### Pico.

Although I love these letters of yours because they flow, because they are not affected, and because they do not just ignore care—I would say—but reject it; that is, they do not admit to being composed by design, and they exclude any such thing that tries to creep in. Thus, traces of diligence are indeed deep within them, but suppressed and, in a way, repudiated. I am not so skillful that I can look deep into your genius and estimate its magnitude and fertility. I seem to see—and perhaps I am not mistaken—where you are aiming and likewise where you will end up. And indeed, a little further on: Nothing is more noble than that natural talent of yours, nothing more delightful <note>The original reads 'rifibilius,' likely a printer's error for 'festivius' (more festive/delightful) or 'risibilius' (more laughable/humorous).</note>, and—to put it a bit more harshly—nothing is more productive, if indeed "talent" is the right word. It has produced fruits that should not be looked down upon even by those of mature age and well-practiced learning. Come now, how great a spirit—as I hear—is in your poetry! What happiness, what sinews, and finally what nobility and splendor in every act, especially in literature. What of when you act the philosopher? What memory, what subtlety, what speed of mind, harmonizing with the vigor of your whole body! But I am carried away into your praises against my will—or rather, quite willingly—for each person desires most that which turns them toward itself even when they are unwilling and reluctant. You will be given—if that is your ambition—praise from those who are little learned. Indeed, a time more suited for this duty will be given. Now I come to this and the rest.

### FROM THE LETTER OF ERMOLAO TO GIOVANNI
### Pico.

I have congratulated this century for having a man of such great learning that he knows almost nothing not at all, and of such great care that he seems to know nothing [of his own effort] at all <note>A humanist paradox: Pico knows everything, but his mastery is so complete it appears effortless, as if he hadn't had to "study" it at all.</note>. I see that you are an excellent poet, an most eminent orator (either already or soon to be), and I notice you have become a philosopher—first an Aristotelian, and now also a Platonic one. I see that you have not just learned but "drunk in" Greek literature—which was the only thing that could be missed in you, and without which you would have achieved nothing. You did this with such ease and speed that neither you can remember, nor can you persuade others, that you were ever ignorant of Greek letters. This is something I declare about my friend Girolamo Donà <note>Hieronymus Donatus (c. 1457–1511), a Venetian diplomat, scholar, and friend to Barbaro.</note> no less gladly than truly. I would urge you and the rest...

# Letters.

### FROM THE LETTER OF JACOPO ANTIQUARI <note>Jacopo Antiquari (1444–1523) was a secretary to the Dukes of Milan and a patron of humanist scholars.</note> TO Angelo Poliziano.

Do not, therefore, keep us wasting away in expectation for the offspring of your long incubation, but since you have accepted Pico as a guarantor for the security of your name—one whose whole life is full of glories, and by whom I hope with all my prayers you will be received into the flock of friends—I, who always adore his footsteps, urge you to send out whatever is born at home from the "flock of fattened birds" <note>original: "altilium cohorte"; a metaphorical way of referring to refined, finished literary works prepared for the public.</note> to be gazed upon, read, and learned by heart. You will hold all those who are led by any image of virtue or harmony captivated by your strings. **Farewell.**

### ANGELO POLIZIANO to his friend GIOVANNI PICO della Mirandola, Greetings.

I have burned almost always (too shamelessly, perhaps, but I burned nonetheless) with a desire for perpetual fame, so much so that any surviving glory seemed as nothing in comparison. But since the things I was writing barely promised even the antiquity of a name, you appeared, Pico, who could provide what I could not; namely, by the dedication of your *Commentary on Being and the One* <note>original: "Commentario, de uno & ente"; Pico's famous work attempting to reconcile the philosophies of Plato and Aristotle.</note> (for so you titled it). In this work, you bring the streams flowing through the Lyceum <note>Aristotle’s school of philosophy.</note> and the Academy <note>Plato’s school of philosophy.</note> back to a single head, and you join our own theology with a philosophy that is more one than it is a pair. Why then should I seek the herb of Glaucus <note>original: "Glauci gramen"; in Greek mythology, the fisherman Glaucus became immortal after eating a magical herb.</note> to live forever through you? Yet, together with you, posterity will one day tell that there was once a certain Poliziano whom even Pico himself—the light of all learning—valued so highly that he did not hesitate to dedicate to him his most beautiful book on the most profound matters. I therefore give you thanks for this immortality—eternal thanks. **Farewell.**

### MARSILIO FICINO OF FLORENCE to GERMAIN de Ganay <note>A French high official and patron of the arts who served as President of the Parlement of Paris.</note>, President of Paris, his warmest greetings.

You wish to be more certain about the death of Pico della Mirandola, which seems to you still uncertain, but you surely wish to grieve more heavily, Germain. For since you have grieved heavily until now over this ambiguous loss, once you are made certain, I think you will soon grieve most heavily indeed. Perhaps it was better to mourn a doubtful loss than to be tortured by a certain one. Alas, what do you ask, my most longed-for Germain? I myself would rather remain in doubt, and I cannot at this moment make you more certain without tears. This past November, on the very day that Charles, the great King of the Franks <note>Charles VIII of France, who entered Florence on November 17, 1494.</note>, entered our city of Florence, our Mirandola left us. He affected the learned with almost as much grief as the King meanwhile brought joy to the city; thus the provident spirit of the place compensated for the groan of the scholars with the joy of the people. In place of the extinguished light of philosophy, he meanwhile lit a royal light, so that Florence might not seem darker on that day. The light of Mirandola was extinguished to the earth, but restored to heaven; for Pico migrated from this shadow of life with such a cheerful confidence that he seemed, without a doubt, to be returning from a kind of exile to his heavenly fatherland. You desire to know, moreover, what Pico once... <margin>Pico once</margin>

# Letters.

### [Continuation of the Letter to Gianfrancesco Pico]

...[Pi-]co <note>The text begins mid-word, referring to Pico della Mirandola.</note> once composed, or what he was recently composing: the *Hexameron* <note>A work on the six days of creation.</note>, the *Apologia* <note>Pico's defense of his controversial 900 theses.</note>, and the work he wrote *On the One and Being* <note>original: "de uno & ente"; Pico's attempt to reconcile the philosophies of Plato and Aristotle.</note>, as well as several letters. Whatever he had composed concerning love while his youth was still glowing, he later condemned with a more mature judgment and wished to be utterly destroyed; it cannot be published without doing him an injury. Indeed, I know the final will of this pious man. For in age, Pico was a son to me; in intimacy, a brother; and in love, truly a second self. 

He worked daily on three things: the harmony of Aristotle with Plato, commentaries on the sacred words [Scripture], and refutations of the astrologers. All these were argued as eloquently as they were subtly, but however brilliant they were in style, they were sketched out in such new and obscure characters <note>Pico was notorious for a personal shorthand or "cipher" handwriting that made his unfinished drafts nearly illegible to others.</note> that they could scarcely be read even by him. Therefore, they have neither been completed or revised by him, nor can they be transcribed by others, unless they perhaps possess the gift of prophecy. For if they could perhaps be transcribed, we would not long for our Pico so much, as if he were merely absent, nor would we ever suspect him to be extinguished. 

But his pious nephew Gianfrancesco, excelling in letters and intellect, strives daily to rescue them from the shadows into the light, and is writing the life and deeds of his uncle. Finally, accept this epigram of ours concerning him: "The high priests show the more secret mysteries very rarely to eyes and immediately hide them away again; thus did God show to mortals that divine philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, mature in his thirtieth year."

Furthermore, so that you may know the rest of the loss to literature that occurred this autumn in Florence: our Angelo Poliziano <note>One of the greatest poets and scholars of the Renaissance.</note>, most learned in the Latin and Greek languages, departed from life this past September, before the death of Pico, in the fortieth year of his age. He had long since published his *Miscellanea*, the *Sylvae*, and certain *Declamations*, and several letters—all of them composed with sharp wit and elegance. Every day he also noted down many things necessary for elegance in uncertain characters, just like Pico, so that in both men a grave loss to literature has occurred. 

**March 23, 1494.**

->MARSILIO FICINO THE FLORENTINE, TO GIOVANNI<-
->Francesco Mirandola, Count of Concordia, Greetings.<-

**I** sent a brief letter regarding the death and praises of Pico to France after your departure. However, his long and singular praises may be gathered here and there from my many writings over a long time, especially from the later books of my letters—for twelve are now printed—from the preface to *Plotinus*, from the book *On the Sun*, and from the commentaries on the *Timaeus* and *Parmenides*. 

Receive this epitaph for him: "The high priests show the more secret mysteries very rarely to eyes and immediately hide them away again; thus did God show to mortals that divine philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, mature in his thirtieth year." Let the epitaph end here. God seems to have given Giovanni Pico all the most abundant goods of mind, body, and fortune, if only He had granted a longer span of life. But it is not right to accuse Providence in this matter; for if God had already brought him to the summit, beyond the powers of nature, in a very short time, he perhaps could not have progressed to anything better. Yet the flux of nature does not permit one to remain in the same state; therefore, toward the worse...

->BACCIO UGOLINI SENDS GREETINGS TO ROBERTO SALVIATI.<-

**R**ightly do the learned love you, Roberto, whom you have always cultivated with a certain marvelous passion; and all students love you, whom you help not only with effort but also with expense, so that they may more conveniently make progress. I, truly, although I am to be numbered neither among the learned nor even the studious, nevertheless confess that I owe you much, because through you, even to those of us further away, a copy has been provided of that most divine work recently published by Pico Mirandola—a man truly to be admired above all who are and all who have been, whom my Poliziano, another miracle of our age, rightly calls no longer "Pico" <note>original: "Picum"; a pun on Pico’s name, which means 'woodpecker' in Latin.</note>, but his own Phoenix, nesting in the sacred Laurel <note>original: "Lauro"; a reference to Lorenzo de' Medici, whose name shares a root with the laurel tree.</note> of the Medici. Among these, it fell to me, through your friend Victorius Caianus—a man of much humor and sprinkled with much sweetness and wit—to obtain this desired gift. This zeal of yours toward famous men, this dutiful liberality toward all lovers of virtue—he who does not praise it and pursue it with more grateful affection is discordant with all humanity, and that...

### JUNIANUS MAIUS SENDS GREETINGS TO ROBERTO SALVIATI <note>Junianus Maius (Giuniano Maio) was a Neapolitan humanist and grammarian; Roberto Salviati was a Florentine patron and friend to the circle of Pico and Ficino.</note>

**B**ecause you have seen to it that the divine work of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola was printed with no less care than he composed it, I think that much gratitude is owed both to your diligence and to his divine learning. To you, because you did not allow such a sublime work to hide in the forgetfulness of shadows—you who, with one effort, consulted both the immortality of your friend and the common utility of all. To him, however, because he was undeterred by the authority or sanctity of the ancients who recounted these same things, and without following the footsteps of others, he illuminated those same matters with his own particular light. For as soon as such a profound work, removed from the knowledge of many, reached my hands, I began to read it more diligently. It brought pleasure not only with admiration, but it even lifted the contemplating mind to such a height of sublimity that I have never seen or heard anything more admirable or more clearly explained. 

Indeed, his genius surpasses the sharpness of others; he is skilled in an incredible investigation of the sciences and already possesses a knowledge of all things beyond what is believable—especially at this age where, having just barely passed adolescence, he has attained such a knowledge of things as has not been permitted even to the most learned and those advanced in age. Therefore, I shall never fear to call him the sacred dwelling-place of all good arts and sciences, and the miracle of our age—especially when I read more accurately the hidden meanings of the work <note>This refers to Pico's *Heptaplus*, a mystical explanation of the creation story in Genesis.</note>, devised by few men, the progress of things, the revealed hiding places of nature and God, and finally the secret riches of the Supreme Craftsman <term>Supreme Craftsman: "summi opificis", a Platonic way of referring to God as the Architect of the universe</term> now brought into the open. I know not if I have ever heard anything more admirable, or what I might have read that is deeper. 

Since among the philosophers and Moses—who were weaving the craftsmanship of the world by different paths—peace has now been entered into, and certain combined treaties of nature and God are understood without controversy. But I reserve this to be repeated more deeply and explained more wordily for another time. I come to you, my Robert, truly an excellent man, whom I love uniquely from your writings; though they are few, they show such a specimen of your virtue that they promise no less a harvest of genius to come than the most graceful hope of little flowers they now offer. Thus, know your Junianus to be yours; and if you give me anything further of your writings, know that I am no less a herald of your affairs than a lover of you for that very reason. Victorius <note>likely referring to a mutual friend or scholar in their circle</note> therefore proclaims the excellence of your genius and your learned refinement in these letters, so that he provokes me to desire and proclaim the same. One thing, however, I ask: that him whom Victorius [encourages] with flattering exhortations to lov— <meta>catchword: -dum (the beginning of "loving")</meta>

He [Pico] compared all their opinions, as well as those of the Latins, most diligently with the views of the Jewish and Chaldean <note>referring to Aramaic translations or Targums.</note> interpreters, sifting and weighing everything, so that the truth might be elicited, obscurity removed, faith strengthened, or impiety refuted.
