### Roberto Salviati to Lorenzo de' Medici, Greetings. <note>Roberto Salviati was a Florentine businessman and scholar; Lorenzo "the Magnificent" de' Medici (1449–1492) was the patron of the Florentine Renaissance.</note>

Since I was born with such a disposition, most illustrious Lorenzo, and was so naturally inclined that nothing is more important to me than to love, cherish, and venerate those who are either excellent in talent or singular in learning, I could not help but love your Pico of Mirandola above all others and admire a man truly most worthy of all admiration. Since he recently dedicated to you his book on the *Sevenfold Explanation of the Six Days of Genesis* <note>The *Heptaplus*, published in 1489, which applied mystical and philosophical methods to the biblical creation story.</note> as the first fruits of his studies—a work most excellent not only in my judgment but in the judgment of all—I wished to see to it that it was published in a corrected edition at my own expense. I have no doubt that I will simultaneously satisfy my love for him and the public benefit of scholarship. Furthermore, I hoped that I would be doing something pleasing to you if those physical and divine mysteries which he shared with you were finally made common to all through my efforts. Farewell.

<meta>This page marks the beginning of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s famous polemic against astrology. It follows the introductory testimonials from the previous pages, transitioning from praises of Pico’s character to his own intellectual crusade against what he considered a fraudulent science.</meta>

# OF GIOVANNI PICO
## Count of Mirandola and Concordia, [His] Disputations Against Astrology,
### P R E F A C E.

Homer and Caecilius <note>Caecilius Statius was a Roman comic poet of the 2nd century BCE.</note>, the most ancient poets, proclaim those to be the worst enemies who circumvent us under the guise of friends. No truer statement can be uttered, and no healthier precept can be taught. Yet why do we need the testimony of poets? Divine Truth <note>A reference to the teachings of Christ in the Gospels.</note>—the teacher of life and morals—has warned us to avoid wolves in sheep's clothing <note>A reference to Matthew 7:15: "Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves."</note> and not to judge by appearances. Indeed, there is this one kind of enemy which can neither be turned aside nor overthrown, and which we ourselves do not wish to overcome. Instead, we run to meet it, we freely kiss and welcome it, and we stand with it against our very selves, rather than against it as we ought. This is surely a <term>deception</term> <note>original: *praestigium*. This refers to an illusion or a trick of sleight-of-hand.</note> that, because it costs us dearly, ought to be looked into more deeply and examined longer; it should neither be admitted rashly nor driven away immediately. But once the fallacy is detected, it must be rejected all the more sharply, the more secretly it was gliding toward our destruction under the pretext of doing us good.

Nor should those evils be considered less significant which do not seem to be the worst simply because they are occasionally mixed with good things. In fact, they cause more fatal harm precisely because they are admitted more easily through the appearance and mixture of the good; once admitted, they occupy the mind more tenaciously and hold it more powerfully. In the same way, if poison is offered with pure wine, although pure wine is by its own nature most healthy, it nevertheless disguises the malice of the poison with its own flavor, and by its own vigor, drives the poison into the veins and innermost parts more quickly.

This must be observed in every part of life, but especially in the arts and disciplines. Among these, the most pernicious are those which, being deceptions or some other kind of vanities, have nevertheless held out the allure of a lie so that they have claimed the title of science or art for themselves. Perhaps that allure was sought from antiquity by inventing authors, or it was a lure for human curiosity and greed through great promises, or perhaps it came from some false coloring and appearance of probability. For, as Aristotle testifies <note>Pico likely refers to Aristotle's *Rhetoric* or *Poetics*, noting that a "plausible impossibility" is often more convincing than an "implausible truth."</note>, false things are sometimes more probable than true ones—especially to the common people and the multitude, who have not looked inside or explored the matter, and for whom it has always been characteristic to err, to be deceived, and to know nothing. What, however, is more fatal? What is more impregnable than when error insinuates itself into us under the title of "wisdom," so that we devote our labor to what that poet said: that we might "be insane with reason" <note>original: *cum ratione insaniamus*. This is a quote from Terence's play *The Eunuch*, describing the paradox of trying to handle the madness of love through logical calculation.</note>. This is nothing other than to dismiss the counsel and the mind—whose innate power was given to us solely for driving away falsehood—so that we might approve its lie even by the mind's own testimony...

<meta>catchword: more nobly [honestius],</meta>

<summary>In this preface, Pico della Mirandola introduces his attack on astrology by warning that the most dangerous errors are those that disguise themselves as science or wisdom. He compares astrology to a poison hidden in wine, arguing that its appearance of truth makes it more harmful to the mind.</summary>

--- Page 445 ---
<meta>This page continues Pico's preface, moving from general warnings about "wolves in sheep's clothing" to a specific attack on divinatory astrology. He establishes a sharp distinction between the legitimate science of astronomy and the "madness" of predictive astrology.</meta>

# OF GIOVANNI PICO
## Of Mirandola

...more honorable, more robust in power, and better protected. Furthermore, there is no further hope for health when nature itself aids the disease. <margin>-</margin> This happens, as I was saying a moment ago, through a madness that circulates and sells itself to the people under the guise of either art or science. It is no less a madness because it counterfeits wisdom on its outer surface; indeed, the more deceptive it is, the more ruinous it becomes. <margin>-</margin> Just as among physicians, none rave more insanely, so to speak, than those who put on a serious face while in their delirium. This is the peculiar blight of all superstitions, which profess nothing other than to hand down instructions for going mad.

But above all, astrology has claimed this title for itself, just as it holds the first place among those superstitions of which it is rightly considered both mother and nurse. When I speak of astrology, however, I do not mean that which measures the masses and motions of the stars by mathematical reasoning—a certain and noble art, most honorable in its own merits, and highly approved by the authority of the most learned men. Rather, I mean that which predicts future events from the stars: a fraud of mercenary lying, forbidden by both civil and pontifical laws <note>Pico refers to both Roman civil law (the *Codex Justinianus*) and Church Canon law, which frequently banned "judicial" or predictive astrology while allowing for astronomical study.</note>, kept alive by human curiosity, laughed at by philosophers, cultivated by charlatans, and suspected by every good and wise person. 

Its practitioners were once called by the pagan name <term>Chaldeans</term> <note>original: *Chaldæi*. In the ancient world, this ethnic name became synonymous with Babylonian astrologers and stargazers.</note>, or <term>Genethliacs</term> <note>original: *Genethliaci*. From the Greek word for "birthday," referring to those who cast horoscopes based on the moment of birth.</note> from their very profession. Soon, so that they might be honored by a shared name, they called themselves "mathematicians" and "astrologers," as if this too were one of the liberal disciplines that speaks of the stars with reason. They separated themselves from true mathematics only by this distinction: that the name "astronomy" was given to the former, and "astrology" to themselves. This was done with an excessively wicked zeal for usurping another's title, since "astrology" is actually the name of another art, as we shall explain. 

But as for this divining art, which always labors under the ambition of being named after the stars, we shall grant it both names, but in a different way: to match that art which deals with the motion of the stars, we shall call [it] astrology for astrology and astronomy for astronomy, quite fittingly and according to its merit. Regardless of how the naming is decided, I—supported both by reasons and by the judgments of the wisest men—would not hesitate to affirm that among the deceptive arts, there is none that more effectively cheats the gullible and the unskilled, nor any which, through its persuasion, causes more harm by its deception. It is more deadly than other superstitions in proportion to how closely it seems to approach the truth. 

For while other superstitions display the marks of their own madness and levity on their very face, and hardly deceive anyone except those who are completely blind, this one harbors madness in its heart and nourishes it in its core, while putting on the appearance and habit of wisdom. If you look at it from a distance or through a lattice, you are captivated by its form; but if you bring your eye closer, you see it is a mere shadow or like a mask, and in the open light, you would loathe the deception of its darkness. It is certainly so, and it shall become clearer than light through the most manifest reasons: there is no greater fallacy, none more ruinous. It displays the heavens and the planets from afar, from which you might easily believe that in such a sublime and bright spectacle, nothing could fail to be most truly [foretold]...

<summary>Pico distinguishes between mathematical astronomy, which he respects as a noble science, and divinatory astrology, which he denounces as a fraudulent superstition that masquerades as wisdom. He traces the names of its practitioners (Chaldeans, Genethliacs) and argues that its "seriousness" makes it more dangerous than other forms of madness.</summary>

# Preface to the Work on Astrology.

...to be foreseen. Soon, when you have considered it more closely, you see that it is a mirror so sublime that the images of earthly things do not ascend there, and so bright that our weakness is blinded by its glare. Then, when you approach nearer, you will see woven into its robe <term>peplum</term> <note>The 'peplum' was a traditional Greek garment; Pico uses it here as a metaphor for the "fabric" of the heavens draped over the world.</note>, instead of heavenly things, monstrous likenesses: stars transformed into animals, and a heaven full of fables—indeed, instead of the true heaven, a counterfeit heaven not made by God, but fabricated by astrologers. 

It seems so well-equipped with every support of proven dogma, carrying around books titled with great names, and offering so many reasons for its decrees. Besides these reasons, it offers "experiments" corroborated by such long-lasting observations, by such diligent annotations, and received through the use of so many centuries and the approval of so many ages. It is a wonder how, through these fogs and mists, it presents to eyes clouded by ignorance a beautiful, venerable image of itself, full of a succession of authority. 

When you have dispersed these shadows and illusions with the ray of reason and diligent treatment, you will see that in those books there is nothing balanced, in authors no authority, in reasons nothing rational, in experiments nothing consistent, nothing constant, nothing true, nothing credible, nothing solid. Instead, you will find things conflicting with each other—false, vain, and ridiculous—so that you would scarcely believe that those who wrote them had any faith in what they were writing. 

As for its claim to unity, you will not easily find anything that offers more hope to its followers <note>original: "aurarijs" — a term for those seeking quick wealth or "gold-seekers," used here sarcastically for the clients of astrologers.</note>, or promises greater and more desirable things. It makes itself the guardian of prudence, claiming to stabilize our conjectures about the future with certain foreknowledge. It even claims to be the guardian of philosophy, whose greatest part concerning the heavens (as they would have it) is perfectly resolved through celestial influence. 

There is no need to speak of medicine, of seafaring, or of agriculture, since astrology not only predicts the future for these fields, but even brings down the powers of the heavens to earthly things. It claims that through this, the works of all arts are most effectively achieved, and that the masters of all arts may easily attain what they desire. And indeed, it has persuaded not only the ancients but also the moderns that it brings much authority and benefit to religion—if the gods please—both to all religions in general and to the Christian faith. To say it all at once, having imitated its master <note>A reference to the Devil, who tempted Christ by offering the kingdoms of the world (Matthew 4:8-9).</note>, it promises the kingdoms of the world to those who worship it; and to those who taste its fruit, it promises a rivalry with divinity and the knowledge of good and evil <note>An allusion to the Serpent's promise to Eve in the Garden of Eden (Genesis 3:5).</note>. 

This practice is not only unhelpful for any use in life (despite its promises), but is the most pestilential fraud of all. Since it is that very thing, as we shall demonstrate, which corrupts all philosophy, adulterates medicine, weakens religion, gives birth to or strengthens superstitions, fosters idolatry, takes away prudence, pollutes morals, defames heaven, and makes men miserable, anxious, and restless. It turns free men into slaves and, in almost all matters to be done, it makes them plainly unfortunate. 

When I seemed to have explored and discovered this for myself, I thought I would be committing a crime <term>piaculum</term> <note>In ancient Roman religion, a 'piaculum' was a sin or an act that required an expiatory sacrifice to appease the gods.</note> that no victim could atone for, if I remained silent or if I dissembled. I felt I must try with all my might to wrench this poison from the hands of the credulous, especially in this age, when more than at any other time [people fall] toward this fraud...

Indeed, every age, rank, and sex is blinded. # JOHN PICO
## Of the Count of Mirandola and Concordia, Disputations against Astrology,
### BOOK ONE.

First of all, I want the reader to know that it was not our own invention or audacity to reject and refute astrology. Rather, since the earliest antiquity, it has always seemed to those of good judgment that this is not a profession which should bring so many inconveniences to man and so many insanities from every side under the pretext of science and utility. 

Hence, by the laws of the Caesars and the prudent, it is eliminated from cities as harmful to life. Hence, by the oracles of the Prophets, the sanctions of the Pontiffs <term>Pontiffs</term> <note>Here referring to both the high priests of ancient Rome and the Christian Popes who issued decrees against divination.</note>, and the voices and doctrines of the holiest men, it is condemned as a plague to morals and piety. Hence, by philosophers and mathematicians—whoever has learned to be wise from books rather than merely to talk—it is almost always either despised or refuted as false, useless, impossible, and unfriendly to philosophy. 

This fact—which we shall declare in this book, while others are either ignorant of it or deny it before the matter is argued by reason—is so that after such a long line of accusers, this accusation may not bring envy upon us. Instead, it may serve as a defense for the honor of men of integrity, should any choose to take it up. 

We shall indeed begin with the philosophers, whose authority is greater and more prudent, and sometimes more universally accepted than that of the Prophets. That Pythagoras did not grant credit to astrology is indicated both by Theodoret, and by Laërtius, as well as Diogenes and Plutarch. That famous saying of Democritus is often repeated: "No one looks at what is before their feet while they scrutinize the regions of heaven." <note>original: "ante pedes nemo spectat, coeli scrutantur plagas." This is a classic philosophical trope, often used to mock those who focus on abstract or celestial matters while ignoring the practical reality right in front of them.</note> Favorinus the Academic and Panaetius the Stoic attacked it; it is laughed at by Seneca and refuted by Cicero. And who is ignorant of Carneades disputing against it, or the philosopher Bion, who was hostile to diviners? If it indeed surpasses every madness, such that even a madman would not approach it,

<header>Against Astrology, Book I.</header>

## Against Astrology, Book I.

Orestes <note>A figure from Greek mythology often used by ancient authors as a symbol of extreme madness.</note>, how much insanity does astrology contain! Not even Epicurus, though he raved about many things, could agree with it. Plato and Aristotle, the princes of philosophy, thought it so unworthy that they did not speak a single word about it in their entire philosophical systems—condemning it more by their silence than anyone else could by voice or writing. For I ask those who feel otherwise to answer this: why, in the whole course of their commentaries—where they had to explain either the properties of the heavens or the causes of lower things to be sought from there—did they never bring in any astrological arguments? Did they think these matters did not concern the philosopher? These are the first and most noble parts of the universe: moving bodies that in turn move others, the most efficient causes, without which nothing in nature can happen or be known—if, that is, one believes the stars to be what the astrologers claim they are. To know the universal truths about these things (as the leaders of philosophy have written) is the mark of a philosopher; but if more specific details could be understood, it would be the duty of a philosopher, not an "imperfect philosopher," to grasp them.

Why, then, did Aristotle leave his books *On the Heavens* so empty? He could have said so many splendid things—and if he could, he certainly should have—regarding the stars and planets, indicating to us their efficiency, properties, and the knowledge we might gain from them. Why in his *Meteorology*, while searching for the causes of rains, comets, and winds, does he always forget astrological matters? Why in his books *On the Generation of Animals* does he not refer twins, nor monstrous and portentous births, nor the sex or number of offspring, nor their form or qualities, to the stars? Why does he not even mention in passing that such things *could* be referred to them? 

Why do Plato in the *Timaeus* and, before Plato, Timaeus the Pythagorean himself in his book *On Nature* (a supreme philosopher and astronomer alike, as Plato says) do the same? Why also Ocellus Lucanus <note>A Pythagorean philosopher whose work "On the Nature of the Universe" was highly regarded in the Renaissance, though now considered a later forgery.</note> in his book *On the World*, a man who by Plato’s own testimony was most eminent in philosophy? Did they despise these things as if they were small? If astrology were true, no matters could be greater. Or did they not despise them, but were simply ignorant? Did they spend time in Egypt and Babylon and yet fail to understand these things that were constantly repeated among those peoples and known even to the common man? Surely they did not think it was outside their profession (as we have said)—unless they were so ignorant of their own calling that they believed it a philosopher’s task to investigate the properties of bees and ants in minute detail, yet thought it unnecessary to do the same for Jupiter and Saturn. This is especially true if, as the astrological writers loudly claim, the truth of these matters is shown not only by observation but by reason itself. 

What else can be said, then, except that Plato and Aristotle held the opinion that the heavens are not the causes of the things astrologers claim? They believed that astrology is neither an art nor a science—otherwise, it would have been mentioned alongside the others. Rather, they saw it as one of those trifles, or rather the frauds of charlatans, in the same category as <term>geomancy</term> <note>Divination using patterns in the earth or soil.</note>, <term>hydromancy</term> <note>Divination using water.</note>, illusions, and incantations, none of which the ancient philosophers included among the sciences and arts. For if astrology were a true art, it would depend on natural science just as medicine does; for just as a physician learns from the philosopher the nature of shrubs, herbs, and animals...

<summary>Pico argues that the silence of great philosophers like Plato and Aristotle regarding astrological influences in their scientific works is proof that they viewed astrology as a fraudulent superstition rather than a legitimate field of study.</summary>

<page-num>416</page-num>
<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

...borrows <note>This sentence continues from the previous page, likely comparing how a physician borrows materials for healing.</note>, which he may use to bring health to bodies; in the same way, the astrologer should learn from the philosopher the powers and properties of the stars which he uses, and he himself should teach how to use them for predicting. For as to the person who thinks that the divinatory part of astrology is either a branch or the goal of mathematical astronomy—having more in common with it (if such a thing is thought to exist) than with natural philosophy—we shall declare later how far that person is mistaken. 

Now we only remind the learned of a matter placed beyond controversy: that it belongs to the philosopher to know whatever follows from the substance and order of the stars; that the measuring of their movements and masses is delegated to the astronomer; and that the predicting of future events from their state and position is for the astrologer—if, of course, any such craftsman as an "astrologer" is even conceded to exist. 

Therefore, the silence of Plato and Aristotle would be entirely too drowsy and inexcusable if they did not even indicate those things which they ought to have treated most exactly. This silence can be wondered at everywhere in the works of Plato—who deals with a miscellany <note>original: "Miscellaneam," referring to the wide-ranging, encyclopedic nature of Plato's dialogues.</note> and every kind of doctrine—and especially in Aristotle’s *Problems*. In that book, proposing questions about mathematics and about all arts and disciplines, and bringing forth solutions from every kind of dogma (even ancient ones), an "astrological word" is nevertheless found nowhere to be uttered; likewise in the *Eudemian Ethics* where he discussed good fortune. 

If we are not moved enough by this evidence, let us hear the disciples of both philosophers, who testify to us that same opinion which the masters speak to us through their silence.

<margin>—</margin> Plotinus is held to be of almost the first authority in the Platonic family. Porphyry writes <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) was the student and biographer of the Neoplatonist Plotinus.</note> that when Plotinus had given diligent work to astrology, he finally discovered the vanity and falsehood of the art, and he stripped all credit from astrological prediction. Therefore, in a book dedicated to the subject, titled *On the Influence of the Stars*, he resolutely laughed at and refuted the dogmas of the astrologers. 

Maternus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer who defended the practice.</note>, resenting this, tells many lies about Plotinus's death, as if Fate had taken punishment from him. That those claims are utterly false is easily understood from Porphyry himself, the disciple of Plotinus, who clearly and faithfully describes both the type of disease from which he died, the cause, and why he departed from Rome. 

Origen "the Adamantine" <note>Origen (c. 184–253 AD), an early Christian scholar nicknamed "Adamantius" for his unbreakable stamina.</note>, most eminent in the philosophical sect as in all disciplines, often and with many reasons ridiculed astrological vanity—unless perhaps superstitious men give his testimony less weight because he was also a Christian. But Eudoxus <note>Eudoxus of Cnidus (c. 390–337 BC), a Greek astronomer and student of Plato.</note> was not a Christian; he also listened to Plato, spent time in Egypt, and was considered the prince of astronomers in his time. Yet he left it written that nothing should be believed of astrologers who predict the fates of men from their births. 

Alexander of Aphrodisias <note>A celebrated commentator on Aristotle (c. 200 AD).</note>, the highest authority in Aristotelian philosophy, writing a book *On Fate* to the Emperors Severus first and his son Antoninus, both rejected the necessity of fate and remained silent regarding astrological matters—even though the mention of fate usually draws people in, even against their will.

# Against Astrology Book I.

Perhaps he <note>Likely referring to Alexander of Aphrodisias, a famous commentator on Aristotle mentioned in preceding sections.</note> had no other purpose in laboring over his commentary than to use philosophical reasoning to correct the mind of Severus Caesar, which was inclined toward this kind of superstition. Averroes, a famous philosopher of the same school and a weighty evaluator of natural things, everywhere tears apart, condemns, and attacks astrology. Indeed, in his *First Philosophy* <note>The *Metaphysics*.</note> he calls the opinion of the astrologers—regarding celestial images which they believe earthly animals of similar form are subject to—a "fable." If this is removed, the greatest part of astrological superstition collapses. The same man, when explaining the *Canticles* of Avicenna, says in one place that these dogmas are contrary to philosophy, and elsewhere that almost all the teachings of astrologers are false, and finally that the art itself is entirely vain and weak. Likewise, in his books against Al-Ghazali <note>referring to *The Incoherence of the Incoherence*.</note>, he asserted that the artificial images <note>Talismans or amulets designed to "capture" starlight.</note> into which astrologers think they can channel the powers of heaven are utterly ineffective. Avicenna, a great man in all disciplines, proved with many arguments in the last book of his *First Philosophy* that the future cannot be foreseen by astrologers, and therefore no faith should be placed in their predictions.

I pass over Henry of Hesse <note>original: "Henricum ex Asia"; Heinrich von Langenstein (c. 1325–1397), a theologian who wrote influential works against astrology.</note> and many illustrious moderns in the University of Paris who pursued this vanity in dedicated works, although the majority of philosophers have preferred to despise it rather than refute it—treating it like other itinerant arts, old wives' tales, and the delusions of charlatans.

But it is worthy of notice that the astronomers themselves also rejected that profession. This could not have happened except for the consciousness of discovered falsehood; for otherwise, so much knowledge, glory, and profit would have accrued to those most skilled in the celestial motions if astrology were granted any faith or authority. But that man whom we recently cited, Eudoxus of Cnidus, was supreme in mathematics, and Aristotle relies on his judgment in astronomical matters. Yet Eudoxus was a most prudent legislator—for he wrote laws for his citizens—as well as a distinguished physician under Philistion and a philosopher under Plato; he nevertheless warned us not to believe the astrologers and left this warning in writing. Thus, evidently, mathematical reason had demonstrated it to him, and his master Plato had persuaded him. Panaetius is the authority for the fact that Cassander and Archelaus, although they excelled in astronomy, never used this kind of prediction. Scylax of Halicarnassus, although most learned in all mathematics, rejected this whole kind of divining through the stars.

Let us come to the moderns. Nicole Oresme <note>A significant 14th-century philosopher and mathematician.</note>, both a most sharp philosopher and a most skilled mathematician, also attacks astrological superstition with indignation in a specific commentary. He believed nothing was more deceptive, nothing more detestable, and nothing more ruinous to all ranks of people, but especially to leading men. Giovanni Marliani, who in our age was and was considered the greatest in mathematics, not only always abstained from these predictions but had also begun to write about their falsehood in his final years; though he lived a long life, he was intercepted by death and did not complete it. He used to say—being a man not at all boastful—that he possessed most certain demonstrations against the astrologers.

demonstrations. This is what others, and especially our friend Luchinus <note>Possibly Luca Gaurico or another mathematician in Pico's circle.</note>, himself an excellent mathematician, have told me more than once. Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli <note>original: "Paulus Florentinus"; a famous Florentine mathematician and astronomer (1397–1482) who provided maps for early explorers.</note>, most learned in medicine but especially in Greek and Latin mathematics, whenever he was asked about that profession of astrology, he always asserted it was uncertain and deceptive. He cited, among other things, a clear experiment regarding himself: although he had already completed eighty-five years of life, he had found no "vital" constellation <note>A configuration of stars predicting long life.</note> in his own birth chart <term>genitura: a horoscope or natal chart</term> which he had examined most diligently. I could cite many of those still living, both philosophers and astronomers, who feel the same way, but I do not know if they wish to stir up ill-will against themselves from men who believe in the power of the heavens and fate. 

Furthermore, our Marsilio [Ficino] wrote against them openly, following in the footsteps of Plotinus <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who argued that stars are signs, not causes, of earthly events.</note>; in interpreting and explaining him, he greatly aided, expanded, and illuminated the Platonic cause. And if, while looking after people’s health, he sometimes requests certain aids from the heavens for himself, he wishes that it were possible rather than actually believing it. I can most faithfully testify to the man's mind, as I am his close friend; I have had no one who urged me more often or more effectively to expose this fallacy. Nor is there a more abundant occasion or harvest for laughter when we joke together than concerning the vanity of astrologers—especially if Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), a brilliant Renaissance humanist and poet.</note> joins us, who always intervenes as a wonderful mocker of all superstitions. 

Perhaps the judgment of our Niccolò Leoniceno <note>A famous medical humanist (1428–1524) known for correcting errors in ancient botanical and medical texts.</note> should not be concealed either: though he possesses a faithful grasp of mathematics, like all liberal sciences, he nevertheless judges this "prophesying" astrology so vain that he does not even think those who wrote about it—especially the more learned ones—placed any faith in what they were writing. If you ask the reason why they wrote it anyway, he answers that it was caused partly by greed and partly by the ignorance of princes. 

For, he says, when those excellent men labored day and night in measuring the motions and bodies of the stars—which is what mathematical astronomy does—there was no profit for them from the princes, who certainly did not care how large the stars were or with what speed they revolved through the spaces of heaven. When the astronomers saw this, so that they would not be destitute of earthly things while investigating heavenly ones, they devised a clever fallacy by which they might bind the minds of princes to themselves and make them lovers of their profession. Therefore, they fabricated the idea that everyone's fortunes depend on these stars, but especially those of princes—namely, children, life, empires, victories, and health. They claimed that for themselves, who had long observed the motions and natures of the stars, it was thoroughly known and explored what good they promised or what adversity they announced to each person. 

Moreover, they claimed to have remedies at hand by which foreseen evils could be repelled and good things confirmed. For if a "fortunate hour" <term>felix hora: an auspicious time determined by planetary positions</term> were noted, they claimed images could be cast from a material more akin to those celestial natures; through wonderful mechanisms, power drawn down from the stars into these objects would make men most happy and powerful in affairs. They claimed men could easily attain whatever they desired either by touching or wearing these objects. To gain more trust for all these things, they added that it had been revealed to them by divine—

->### On Astrology, Book I<-

...entirely the more secret mysteries of this art, just as it is said that Petosiris <note>A legendary Egyptian priest and early authority on astrology.</note> and Aesculapius received very many things from the most powerful divinity, Mercury. One reads in [Firmicus] Maternus <note>A 4th-century Roman senator and astrologer, author of the *Mathesis*.</note> how unlearned and curious princes—who were most greedy for the things the astrologers promised—were easily led to believe them, to support their practitioners, and to stimulate these studies more and more every day with rewards. Our friend [Niccolò] Leoniceno <note>A famous humanist physician and critic of traditional medicine and astrology.</note> speaks and feels this way seriously about astrologers, and he is not far from the truth.

However, we must first of all beware lest volumes of astrologers—falsely attributed to great authors—creep into our trust, a practice they share with every form of superstition. For since what they produce cannot be confirmed by reason, whether they believe those things to be true themselves or want them to be believed by others, they attribute books of such fables to the most famous and ancient men, hunting for credibility for their own error by using fabricated authors. From this class comes the book *On the Properties of the Elements* <note>A pseudo-Aristotelian work often cited by medieval astrologers.</note>, which treats of "great conjunctions" <term>conjunctionibus: the alignment of planets, thought to herald major historical shifts</term>, and the *Secrets* addressed to Alexander, which they attribute to Aristotle through no fault or demerit of that good philosopher. Likewise, they circulate books of Plato such as *On the Cow of the Mage* and those they call the *Institutions*, which are filled with cursed dreams and fictions; these are no less foreign to Plato than such wretched trifles are far removed from Plato's integrity and wisdom.

In the same way, the heretics called Gnostics once displayed books of Zoroaster to make their heresy venerable through Zoroaster’s antiquity; Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neopythagorean philosopher and critic of Christianity.</note> demonstrated with many arguments that these were new and fabricated, not written by Zoroaster. However, those who are unrefined in the "humane letters" <note>The *studia humanitatis*: grammar, rhetoric, history, poetry, and moral philosophy.</note>—even if they are otherwise learned—can easily be deceived and ensnared by these lies. For it is through these studies especially that we recognize the style and character of authors, and immediately distinguish the counterfeit from the legitimate. Nevertheless, the fictions of our own astrologers and the superstitious arts currently in circulation are so far removed from any semblance of truth that they would be obvious even to an ordinary person.

For who could be led to believe that the *De vetula* <note>original: "Ouidium de uetula"; a medieval poem falsely attributed to the Roman poet Ovid; it contained "prophecies" of Christ and astrological theories.</note> was actually by Ovid? In it, wonders regarding great conjunctions and the Christian law are proclaimed—to such an extent that Roger Bacon, that great patron of astrology, uses the testimony of no other writer more willingly. Unless, perhaps, he prefers Artephius <note>A legendary alchemist and astrologer.</note>, who reveals countless other secrets, such as this: that by inspecting not the stars, but the urine <note>original: "lotio"</note>, a man's life, character, circumstances, and indeed everything about him, can be known in advance. 

He [Bacon] also places great faith in Aethicus the philosopher, whose book *On Cosmography* is said to have been translated by [Saint] Jerome. The reading is so ridiculous that none could be more so, yet it is frequently cited by our Roger [Bacon] in his *Letter to [Pope] Clement* [IV]. He goes so far that he almost presents a certain booklet he composed titled *On the Errors of Students of Theology* <note>Refers to Bacon's *Compendium studii theologiae*.</note>. In that volume, he primarily accuses theologians of error because they confirm the mysteries of our religion using Aristotle and other philosophers rather than the authors we just named: Aethicus, Artephius, the *De vetula* of "Ovid," and similar "apish" poets <note>Imitative or false poets who mimic the style of others.</note>. A book is also attributed to Albert [Magnus], but most falsely, since he never...

...he mentioned these dreams in his theological writings, but he seems rightly to be referred to Bacon <note>Roger Bacon (c. 1219–1292), an English friar and philosopher who, despite his scientific contributions, was often associated with astrological and alchemical theories.</note>; whose other writings clearly show that he held that opinion, always overflowing with the testimonies and "observations" of those [unreliable] authors. If he was able to believe them, it is no wonder if he could also believe in astrology. Indeed, this superstitious class of men has acted with such shamelessness <note>literally: "rubbed their foreheads," a Latin idiom for behaving without shame.</note> that they even circulate books on **necromantic images** <term>necromanticis imaginibus: the creation of talismans or statues supposed to be animated by spirits or astral forces</term> under the title of **Thomas Aquinas**, so that it is now less surprising that they invent certain books by **Ptolemy** on "rings," and even astrological books addressed to Aristo which Ptolemy never wrote.

With similar recklessness or ignorance, many also attribute the little work of a certain **Yorkist** to Albert [the Great], and mention books by **Hippocrates** on the "prognosis of diseases from the course of the stars." I believe Hippocrates was ignorant of these when he wrote the books of *Prognostics*—which were explained by **Galen** and celebrated throughout all Greece—or if he did know them, he must have set them aside as secret matters only to be communicated to those properly initiated.

I pass over what **Al-Kindi** <note>A 9th-century Arab philosopher and astrologer.</note> and others record concerning rains and [astrological] "interrogations" as being Pythagorean or Aristotelian, and the book titled *On Governance*—attributed by them to **Aristotle**—which they say deals with the heavens. I wish they had not attributed such profane things even to holy men, and had not made **Saint Jerome** the translator of a certain book on incantations; although, if they have defamed the angels, they can easily do so to men, since they even say these "delusions" were handed down by the angel of **Adam**, others by the angel of **Solomon**, and others by the guardian of **Tobias** <note>Refers to the Archangel Raphael.</note>.

But let us return to the astrologers, leaving aside the Magi, to whom a shared error has led us as neighbors. **Aristotle** showed in a single word what he thought of this class of men when, in his *Problems*, he categorized the astrologer alongside the mime and the conjurer. But you will say: "Even if those [famous] philosophers did not write such things, those who *did* write them were nonetheless philosophers." Men like **Albumasar**, **Ptolemy**, **Haly Abenragel**, **Julius Firmicus**, and countless other authors of astrology—Latin, Greek, and "barbarian" <note>A term used by Renaissance humanists for non-Greek or non-Latin authors, particularly Arabic ones.</note>—who were men of the highest learning and talent.

My friend, you have timely reminded me not only to say that astrology was neglected by philosophers, but that whoever wrote about it either philosophized poorly or not at all. Therefore, leave to us—if it pleases the Gods—**Pythagoras**, **Plato**, and **Aristotle**, and keep for yourselves your **Abu Ma'shars**, your **Al-Qabisis**, your **Ibn Ezras**, and your **Abenragels**. How far they were from the philosophical mind will be openly demonstrated when we show that they stoop to the most fabulous stories, assert things that have no reason, say contradictory things, and openly overturn their own arguments. These traits are utterly alien to a philosopher, whose most particular duty is to believe nothing and affirm nothing that cannot be demonstrated by either evidence or reason.

But come, let us say something here to establish that the authors of astrology either philosophized too little or badly. Furthermore, they will easily grant that **Ptolemy** is the prince of the others, for he is the most learned of the astrologers and, regarding mathematics, a most ingenious man. However, regarding the **casters of birth-horoscopes** <term>genethliacos: astrologers who predict a person's fate based on the alignment of stars at their birth</term>, as is commonly said, the best...

# On Astrology, Book I

...he is considered the best of a bad lot. Therefore, he sufficiently indicated with what judgment he handled philosophical matters both in the prefaces of the "Great Composition" (which they call the *Almagest* <note>The most influential mathematical and astronomical treatise of antiquity, written by Claudius Ptolemy in the 2nd century AD.</note>) and in the books of the *Apotelesmaton* <note>original: "Apotelesmaton." This work is better known as the *Tetrabiblos*, Ptolemy's foundational text on the philosophy and practice of astrology.</note>. For, beginning his mathematical books, he divides "contemplative philosophy" into three types according to the opinion of **Aristotle**: the theological, the natural, and the mathematical. Then, explaining the reason for this division, he says that all things that exist consist of three parts: matter, form, and motion. These can be separated from one another by thought, but not in reality. From these three, therefore, those three types of philosophy are named: the "theological" from *motion* (since the cause of the first motion is nothing other than God), the "physical" from *matter*, and the "mathematical" from *form*. 

This is the opinion of **Ptolemy**, in which any person with even a little learning would not doubt that there are as many errors among good philosophers as there are words. For not all things consist of those three. If, by saying "all things," he understands only natural things, how then will philosophy itself be concerned with them if it is further divided into those three types: physical, divine, and mathematical? But even among natural things, nothing consists of motion, even if nothing is made or remains without motion; however, let us grant him this license of speech. But how will **Aristotle** himself—whom he approves of—grant him that the "theological" category arises from motion? For God himself, insofar as He is the author and cause of the first motion, is investigated not by the theologian <note>In this context, Pico refers to "theology" as a specific academic category of the time, distinct from general metaphysics.</note>, but by the philosopher. The rest of his points are also either false or easily seen to be produced by a man poorly skilled and knowledgeable in philosophy. 

Indeed, even more notable and evident errors can be found in the books of the *Apotelesmaton* (which they call the *Quadripartitus* <note>The "Four-Part" book, another name for the *Tetrabiblos*.</note>). In these, he believes the **Moon** is more "humble" <note>Here meaning "lower" in quality or position, or more susceptible to earthly influence.</note> because humid vapor rises from the earth to it, as it is closer to the earth than the other stars. By the same reasoning, he claims **Saturn** is dry because it is further removed from these vapors; but he also claims it is cold because it is far from the heat of the sun. He claims **Jupiter** is temperate because it is placed in the middle between icy **Saturn** and burning **Mars**. He includes many other things of this sort regarding the properties of the stars, which philosophers will hiss at rather than bother to refute. 

And although his **Arabic** commentator <note>Referring to Ali ibn Ridwan, known in the West as Avenrodan (c. 988–1061), who wrote a famous commentary on Ptolemy.</note>, blushing at the errors of his master, tries to twist Ptolemy's words into a different meaning, **Ptolemy** himself does not allow himself to be defended or excused. He asserts, affirms, and repeats these things so often that no doubt is left regarding his meaning. 

Indeed, learn the nature of them all from this one man, and judge the worse ones by the best. Almost the first after Ptolemy is held to be **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), one of the most famous Persian astrologers in the Islamic world, whose works were widely translated into Latin.</note>. He was neither a philosopher nor a logician, and was unskilled in mathematics. He was actually a professor of the art of grammar, and (as **Avenrodan** relates) he turned himself from writing histories to astrology. You may recognize how "true" he was in his own profession from the fact that he thought **Ptolemy** the astrologer was one of the **Kings of Egypt** who succeeded Alexander—as if more than five hundred years did not stand between those kings and him! For the Ptolemaic kings flourished four hundred years before Christ, while Ptolemy the astrologer wrote under **Hadrian** and **Antoninus** <note>Roman Emperors of the 2nd century AD.</note>. Behold this wonderful "investigator of the highest things" and "faithful observer," who in a matter so obvious possessed such sleepiness or sluggishness of mind! The same man in...

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

...later we will declare how much he erred in astrological matters, and how he persisted in such open and confessed lies as if they were truths. Why should I mention **Maternus** <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus (4th century AD), a Roman senator whose work *Mathesis* was a primary textbook for medieval astrologers.</note>, who hallucinates even in the basic elements of arithmetic? He writes about what **Mercury** decrees when it occupies the "midheaven" <note>The highest point in the sky that a celestial body reaches.</note> in a nocturnal birth, as if Mercury could ever be more than forty parts <note>Degrees.</note> or thereabouts away from the **Sun**, or as if the Sun were not always more than seventy parts away from the midheaven during the night. I pass over many other instances in which you will find him to be a man of much talk but little wisdom. 

Now as for **Manilius** <note>Marcus Manilius (1st century AD), author of the didactic poem *Astronomica*.</note>, good God, with what laughter would we pursue him if he were not a poet? He says that those celestial images he imagines were started with a few stars rather than completed, lest the world should burn with fire if more "fires" <note>Stars.</note> were lit there. 

I do not descend to the more recent men, common and uneducated, to whom almost the entire profession has devolved as if to its rightful owners. **Bonatti** <note>Guido Bonatti (13th century), the most famous professional astrologer of the Middle Ages.</note> is of the first authority among them; he is not only ignorant of philosophy, but he clearly raves and is delirious. Read his first book *On Judgments* in which he provides a preface to the work; I am lying if you do not judge the man worthy of hellebore <note>A plant used in antiquity as a treatment for madness.</note>. Where he is slightly less foolish, he constructs certain reasons by which he might prove astrology to be true—reasons I won’t just call false, but more childish and ridiculous than can be said. 

The one he thinks most effective is that the <term>quadrivium</term> <note>The "four ways": the mathematical sciences of arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy that formed the higher half of the seven liberal arts.</note> would be destroyed if astrology were removed, for it is one of the four mathematical arts. Do you see how he does not even know what this thing is that he professes? For this "divining" astrology which we are refuting differs as much from the astrology which is numbered among the mathematical sciences as light from darkness, and as truth differs from a lie. And indeed, this version which usurps the prediction of the future cannot stand if that prior and truer one <note>Mathematical astronomy.</note> is removed; but the logic does not flow back—if the "divining" part is taken away, the mathematical part is not also removed. This is so clear, even to those who have touched the first elements of these arts, that it is superfluous to declare it with more words. 

**Ptolemy** himself, in the introductions to the *Apotelesmaton* <note>original: "Apotelefmaton." This is the *Tetrabiblos*, Ptolemy's work on astrology.</note>, after he speaks of a "double astronomy," nevertheless refers his discourse to the prior and mathematical one, saying: 

-> "There are two things, **Syrus** <note>The person to whom Ptolemy addressed his works.</note>, by which one arrives at astronomical predictions. One is the primary and greatest, both in place and power, by which we apprehend the configurations of the movements of the Sun, Moon, and stars, both toward themselves and toward the earth. The other is that by which [we judge] concerning those configurations..." <-

And so on. But if by chance this profession has not occasionally displeased some good judges, it is not immediately "good" just because some good person did not disapprove of it. For even good men are not always good in every respect, and few achieve the prerogative of being learned in all accounts. And if something must be said: not all learned philosophers are always "philosophers." 

But it is also necessary to remember that there are certain truths which our desire resists, and others which [do not]. In the first category are all those things concerning morals and many theological matters; in the second is the greatest part of those things concerning physics and mathematics. Furthermore, look upon this truth which we are treating—concerning the vanity of astrology—as belonging to that first category...

<meta>This page continues Pico's argument regarding the psychological and historical reasons why people believe in astrology despite its lack of logic. He moves from the character of the practitioners to the nature of human curiosity and the confusion caused by historical names.</meta>

<page-num>423</page-num>
<header>on Astrology Book I.</header>

...it is clear to see, since the innate vice of curiosity in humans fights against [the truth]. Because this curiosity is the most powerful of all traits—being proper to man insofar as he is man—it sometimes causes many people to either lack the time to investigate this truth, or to unwillingly accept it even once it has been discovered. And just as many people, after hearing the most evident reasons given by philosophers against greed, still pant after the accumulation of wealth; so too many people, after it is established for them that what astrologers say could not possibly be true, find that their innate curiosity is only torn away from astrologers with great difficulty. If we are greedy for new things, we even listen to fables with pleasure; thus, being curious about the future, we feel pleasure even when we perceive that astrologers are lying to us. Added to this is the fact that an excessive self-love always infatuates us; this love easily hopes for whatever prosperous things pertain to us and fears the adverse. It solicits us with a blind desire to seek those things even when we know they cannot be found. 

What should we say of the fact that, by this long-standing common consensus, many people judge as a settled matter that astrology must be *something*? It never occurs to them to look deeper into what foundation this thing has, or how solid a firmament <note>Pico uses a pun here on "firmamentum," meaning both a logical foundation and the physical heavens.</note> lies beneath it. Therefore, you will find that almost everyone held by this vanity was either not enough of a philosopher, or certainly not enough of an astrologer; through the former, their errors might not be seen, and through the latter, they might not be judged. Finally, it may have pleased some when merely tasted, but it never satisfied the palate of a philosopher who truly drank of it. For it has something on its surface that allures, which seems great, plausible, and useful; but when you look deeper inside, you see that everything is false, uncertain, and fabulous, born of either no conjectures at all or only the weakest ones, about which we shall discourse abundantly and at length in the following books. 

Truly, this fact may have also deceived some: that since the names of certain philosophers and astrologers are similar, it might be thought that they were the same people who wrote both the philosophical and astrological works. For there is an **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a famous Persian astrologer whose works were highly influential in the Latin West.</note> among the philosophers, and likewise one among the astrologers; but although the Latin language has confused these names, they are recognized as distinct among the Arabs. For he who is the philosopher is called **Albumasar**, but the astrologer is called **Aboafar** <note>Pico is attempting a philological distinction here to distance respected philosophers from the "vanity" of astrologers.</note>. **Abubater** <note>Abu Bakr.</note> also wrote on the predictions of births, and another by the same name wrote philosophical works—especially the book on how one might become a philosopher by himself, which I translated last year from Hebrew into Latin <note>Pico is referring to the work *Hayy ibn Yaqdhan* by the Andalusian philosopher Ibn Tufayl (often called Abubacer in Latin). Pico’s translation was made for Lorenzo de' Medici.</note>. But that man was **Al-Tasibi**, while this one was the son of **Tophail**. In many cases, there is a similar affinity of names, even though there is a great discrepancy in both their times and their professions. 

And of the philosophers, enough has been said. Let us pass to the Prophets—that is, to the oracles of the Old and New Law—beginning with **Isaiah**. He, when he was threatening future destruction upon the Babylonians (among whom this sect flourished most, which is why astrologers were also called **Chaldeans**), and while he was rousing the trumpets against them—even calling **Cyrus**, the King of the Persians, by name as "the Anointed" two hundred years before he was born—addressed the city of the Chaldeans who were to be desolated in this way: "Stand now and let your au-

...figures of the sky, who gazed at the stars and calculated the months, so that they might announce what was to happen to you. Behold, they have become like stubble; the fire has consumed them, nor shall they deliver their own soul from the hand of the flame <note>Pico is quoting the Prophet Isaiah 47:13–14, a key text used by theologians to argue that astrologers are powerless before God's judgment.</note>. And a few verses before this, regarding this observation of the heavens, he had censured them thus: *This wisdom and your science shall deceive you; evil shall come upon you, and you shall not know its rising, and a calamity shall rush upon you which you shall not be able to ward off.* In these words, the divine Prophet accuses the astrologers of a double recklessness. The first is believing that they can foresee future events from the heavens; the second is the belief that, once foreseen, they can either drive away evils or secure good things. 

"Evil will come," he says, "whose rising you shall not know"—that is, which neither Mars nor the cold star of Saturn <note>In traditional astrology, Saturn was associated with coldness and misfortune, while Mars was associated with heat and conflict.</note> shall have signaled to you beforehand. Then, you will not be able to ward off the rushing calamity—that is, you cannot drive it away from you through the <term>election of hours</term> <note>The practice of choosing a specific moment when the stars are "favorable" to start a task or journey.</note>, astrological images, or other superstitious inventions.

It is worth noting that these points refute the responses of those who wish to be <term>Chaldeans</term> <note>A common Renaissance term for astrologers, referencing the ancient Mesopotamian origins of the practice.</note> and Christians at the same time. For they are accustomed to saying that astronomy is not simply condemned by the saints and prophets, but only insofar as they attribute either vices or virtues solely to the heavens, or bind the outcomes of human affairs to a fatal necessity. Therefore, since even "good" astrologers refute these errors, they argue that the prophets do not loathe the science of astrology, but only the mistakes of certain astrologers. 

Let them tell me then—both **Pierre d’Ailly** <note>original: "Petrus Alliacensis" (1351–1420), a famous French cardinal and scholar who tried to use astrology to predict major events in Church history.</note> and whoever else protects themselves with this defense—did it pertain to "morals" that the King of the Persians brought war upon the Assyrians? Even if it does not involve morals, why did the Prophet think that even the greatest astrologers could not foresee it? 

Moreover, if they had been in such error as to think that future things would come by necessity, they would not be charged with the fact that they could not "ward off" the coming calamity. For why would they hope to ward off something that they themselves believed would happen by necessity, as if it were an omen? 

Furthermore, good arts are not condemned by any right judgment simply because certain evil people misuse them. Otherwise, the reading of the Sacred Scriptures would have to be condemned first of all, since so many heresies and so many of their own insanities have been confirmed by certain unlearned and proud men. Likewise, philosophy would have to be condemned, because this philosopher says the soul is mortal, while that one says there is only one soul for all people. Some deny that God provides for men; others deny there is any religion at all. By this logic, all good things would be overturned, since there is nothing so good that the nature of men cannot abuse it. 

Therefore, those who defend themselves in this way are, in the meantime, indirectly but gravely slandering the judgment of the Church, which they are ashamed to openly despise. But they can be forced to either renounce that vanity or admit they have strayed to the left away from their elders—that is, the leaders of the Church. For by whatever reasoning those leaders condemned astrology, I ask you: did they condemn it justly or unjustly? They do not wish to say "unjustly"; but if it was "justly," why do you not also condemn it along with them? 

"But we do condemn," they will say, "those errors because of which astrology displeased them." To which I ask: why does it not displease you for the same reasons? For they did not forbid those astrological practices to a certain extent, but entirely... <meta>The text cuts off here as the catchword "nem" leads into the next page.</meta>

...to follow it <note>This continues the sentence from the previous page, likely referring to the practice of astrology</note>, it is clear that we detest it, as we will soon show. You contend that it was done because of certain errors—so be it—but answer this: is the whole thing rejected by a correct judgment because of those errors? If the judgment was correct, why do you not do the same? On the contrary: what they condemned, you approve; what they attacked, you defend; what they forbade, you spread; what they did not want known, you teach publicly. Or is it as <term>Alliacensis</term> <note>Pierre d'Ailly (1351–1420), a French cardinal and scholar who tried to reconcile astrology with theology by arguing it could be used to predict major religious shifts.</note> says: that while it could have hindered the growing faith—and therefore the first teachers of the nascent Church attacked it—now that the Church is adult, it does no harm, and indeed even profits us greatly? But this will be refuted later, for we shall clearly demonstrate that it is just as pestiferous now as it was then, as experience itself still shows. Nor was it merely the abuse of it that was to be condemned, but the thing itself. Why, then, did the philosophers not condemn philosophy, but only the impiety of certain philosophers, and yet they did not similarly condemn astrologers, but <term>astrology</term> itself? Surely it is because in philosophy, if any error occurs, it is the fault of the professor; in <term>astrology</term>, the profession itself is the fault. Following their authority along with reason, we too, when disputing against the impious, have refuted not philosophy, but the errors of philosophers. Here, however, we refute not <term>astrologers</term>, but <term>astrology</term>, because <term>astrology</term> itself is an error. But let us return to the testimonies of the Prophets: God speaks to us through <term>Moses</term> in this way:

> The nations listen to soothsayers and diviners, but you have been instructed otherwise by the Lord your God. <note>original: "Gentes augures, & diuinos audiunt, tu autem à Domino Deo aliter es institutus" — Deuteronomy 18:14.</note>

Where we read "soothsayers," the Hebrew has מעוננים <note>me'onanim</note>, through which <term>Achinnas</term> <note>Likely a reference to Rabbi Akiva or a similar Jewish authority cited in Renaissance polemics.</note>, the greatest teacher of the Hebrews, says those are understood who calculate times, and observe lucky and unlucky hours; for that word is derived from ענן <note>anan, meaning "cloud" or "to cover"</note>, which <term>Jerome</term> translated as "soothsayers," but we also see in <term>Isaiah</term> that <term>astrologers</term> are called "soothsayers." For the name <term>astrologer</term> is not used anywhere in the Sacred Scriptures. Indeed, it has various expressions, and that superstition has been allotted various names at various times. For formerly they were called <term>Chaldeans</term> and <term>Genethliacs</term> <note>Casters of birth-charts.</note>; in the time of <term>Augustine</term>, they were called <term>mathematicians</term> and <term>planetaries</term>; now they are commonly called <term>astrologers</term>. Moreover, what <term>Jerome</term> translated both in that place and elsewhere as "diviners," in the Hebrew is קסמים <note>kesamim</note>, which <term>Ibn Ezra</term> <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra (1089–1167), a Spanish Jewish scholar who was himself an astrologer, yet Pico cites him to define these terms.</note> himself, although an <term>astrologer</term>, says is a name common to all diviners, but is more properly the name of <term>astrologers</term>. Who is ignorant of that passage in <term>Jeremiah</term>?

> Do not fear the signs of heaven, which the nations fear. <note>original: "A signis cœli nolite timere, quę gentes timent" — Jeremiah 10:2.</note>

Why then does a Christian man either rejoice or grieve at the judgments of <term>astrologers</term>, from whom <term>Isaiah</term> and <term>Jeremiah</term> affirm nothing is to be hoped for and nothing is to be feared? Indeed, through both of them, divine truth affirms that this whole thing they profess, as <term>Ambrose</term> says, is absurd to seek, since what they promise is impossible. Hence the Ruler of heaven says in <term>Job</term>:

> Do you know the order of heaven, and can you set its law upon the earth? <note>original: "Nunquid nosti ordinem cœli, & pones rationem eius in terra?" — Job 38:33.</note>

and below:

> Who shall declare the logic of the heavens? <note>Job 38:37.</note>

For the error of <term>astrologers</term> is twofold: one, that they subject many things to the sky that do not depend upon it; the other, that even those things which the sky does effect cannot, as they think, be foreseen by them—which the words brought forth in the midst of <term>Job</term> show us.

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

And since the doctors of the church equally refute both positions, how can it be said that they only disapprove of astrology when it takes away the freedom of the will or introduces the necessity of fate? Does not **Augustine’s** reasoning regarding twins <note>original: "ratio illa de geminis"; Augustine famously argued that twins born almost simultaneously often have radically different lives, which he believed proved that the stars do not determine human destiny.</note> tend toward removing all foreknowledge of the future from the stars? Does he not also say in his *Enchiridion* <note>A "handbook" on Christian piety written by Augustine.</note> that the mere observation of times—thinking this hour is lucky and that one unlucky—pertains to a great sin? This is despite the fact that in this choice of hours and days we are exercising our freedom rather than losing it. 

But it is certainly true: they disliked astrology in every respect, though especially in that part which subjected religion and morals to the heavens. For this they cursed it; everywhere they refuted it. In this respect they judged it impious, everywhere vain, here blasphemous, everywhere superstitious, here abominable, and everywhere ridiculous. For this reason, **Augustine**, in his book *On Christian Doctrine*, said that those called <term>Genethliaci</term> <note>From the Greek 'genethlios,' referring to those who cast birth charts or nativities.</note> belong to a pernicious superstition, not only because they think our actions, but even the outcomes of those actions, proceed from the stars. 

And in his book of *Confessions*, speaking of the <term>Planetarii</term> <note>Literally "planetary-men," a derogatory term for astrologers.</note>—that is, the astrologers—he says that Christian and true piety expels and damns them. Explaining that passage of **Moses**: *Let the stars be placed for signs and times* <note>A reference to Genesis 1:14.</note>, he says they are not the kind of "signs" that it is vanity to observe, but rather signs necessary for the uses of life, such as those observed by sailors, farmers, and craftsmen of that sort. In the same place, **Basil** said astrology was a "most busy vanity." **Ambrose** called it useless and impossible. **Theodoret** noted it was even refuted by the philosophers. **Chrysostom** called it vain, false, and ridiculous. 

Let us read **Bardesanes**, **Eusebius**, **Didymus**, **Apollinaris**, **Tertullian**, and countless others, even the Apostolic men; what more is there to say? We see that Hebrews, heretics, and the gentiles alike have pursued this class of men with a censorious rod. Thus, **Augustine** wondered why, even though these testimonies rebuking astrologers were read with such fame in the churches, the small assemblies were nevertheless full of our own people who received "the times for things to be done" from the <term>mathematicians</term> <note>In the Roman and Medieval periods, the term "mathematicus" was frequently used as a synonym for "astrologer."</note>. 

When the same man was preaching to the people on the sixty-third Psalm, he brought forward a repentant "mathematician" who had renounced his profession, just as if some Jew or Pagan had received the bath of regeneration <note>i.e., Baptism.</note>. How beautifully the same author, interpreting **John**, warns us of our madness: we enter the astrologers' homes as free men only to leave as slaves, and we pay out our freedom to them for the price of purchased lies. 

Indeed, in his book *On the Nature of Demons*, he says expressly that after Christ, no one is permitted to interpret anyone’s nativity from the heavens. **Jerome** says that searching the courses of the stars and prying into the outcomes of the future from them is among the "reproaches of Egypt"—that is, the remnants of idolatry. **Severianus**, in the book he wrote *On the Seven Arts* (which **Roger** <note>Likely referring to Roger Bacon, who frequently cited scientific and pseudo-scientific authorities.</note> falsely cites as if it were by **Cassiodorus**), says after speaking of true astronomy: "Then those things which pertain to the foreseeing of the future ought to be so unknown that they do not even seem to have been written, for they are without doubt contrary to our faith." These are his words, verbatim. 

But if the opinion of such great and excellent men does nothing to move some...

If [reason] moves you, let at least the Papal authority deter you, which so strictly forbids this profession to our people that Pope Alexander III <note>Alexander III (reigned 1159–1181) was a significant lawyer-pope who expanded ecclesiastical law.</note> wished to suspend a certain priest from the ministry of the altar for an entire year because he had used an **astrolabe** <note>A handheld tool used by astronomers and navigators to solve problems relating to time and the position of the stars.</note> to investigate a theft from a certain church—even though, as the same Pope testifies, the priest had admitted no magic or other superstition there. In the synod of Pope Martin, it is written that true Christians do not observe the courses of the Moon or stars, nor the empty deception of the zodiac signs for the purpose of building a house or joining a marriage. Furthermore, under the name of <term>haruspices</term> <note>original: "aruspicum"; traditionally Roman diviners who read entrails, but here used as a general term for forbidden diviners.</note>, the <term>astrologer</term> is pronounced anathema <note>A formal curse or excommunication by the Church.</note> by a decree of Gregory the Younger <note>Pope Gregory II (reigned 715–731).</note>. And in the Council of Toledo, it is stated: if a priest or deacon himself practices this, let him be relegated to a monastery, there to pay the penalties of his crime through perpetual detention.

For as **Augustine** teaches in his book *On the Nature of Demons*, it is customary among our people to designate under the name of <term>haruspices</term> those who observe days and hours for the conduct of business and works. In this, that part of <term>astrology</term> known as <term>elections</term> <note>The practice of "electing" or choosing the most astrologically favorable moment to begin an undertaking.</note> seems especially noted. Who then, as a Christian—for I speak now to everyone—would dare to defend, follow, or extol <term>astrology</term>, which is prohibited by law, damned by prophets, ridiculed by the saints, and forbidden by Popes and holy synods?

If you should oppose me by citing **Albert the Great** <note>original: "Albertum"; a 13th-century Dominican friar and polymath often associated with the natural sciences.</note>, that most excellent theologian who was nevertheless a supporter of astrologers, I will remind you first that many things are attributed to Albert which are not his, a point we touched on above. Then, if you should perhaps object by citing the book *On Lawful and Unlawful* <note>Likely referring to the "Speculum Astronomiae," a controversial work defending astrology often attributed to Albert the Great.</note>, in which the author rejects magicians but approves of astronomical authors, I will respond that while many believe that work to be Albert's, neither Albert himself nor the title of the book consistently signifies this. For the author, whoever he finally was, deliberately and professedly concealed his name. Furthermore, many things are read in it that are unworthy of a learned man and a good Christian—such as the claim that astrological **images** <note>Astrological talismans or seals believed to capture the power of the stars.</note> can be made by which not just one man, but an entire city might be made unhappy or unfortunate. He also claims that magical books should not be discarded because they might someday be useful to the Church. This is plainly contrary to the judgment of the Church itself, which orders such books to be burned and utterly exterminated wherever they are found. For by what logic is it useful to preserve entire books that it would have been most useful never to have written? 

Either Albert did not write these things, or if he did, one must say with the Apostle: *in other things I praise him, but in this I do not praise him.* Just as it is the mark of envy to seek in great men something to condemn rather than extol, so it is the mark of madness, if they have failed somewhere, to prefer to imitate them rather than condemn their error. I will praise in **Peter d'Ailly** <note>original: "Petro Aliacen"; a French cardinal and scholar who famously attempted to align planetary cycles with major historical events.</note> his zeal for letters, his experience in affairs, his wide reading, and the fact that he wrote and treated certain theological matters with skill and subtlety. But as for his attempt to reconcile astrology with history in one booklet and with theology in another—so that he might prove astrology by history and history by astrology—I plainly do not praise it; I condemn, curse, and detest it.

...since we can maintain no position that is either more false or more hostile to religion. Because we will discuss this matter at length in the following books, nothing more needs to be said in this place. For there, we shall leave it abundantly proved, even to the supporters of these ideas, that those little books are both enemies to religion and full of so many historical and astrological errors that our common saying might be applied: "If you wish to remove the error, remove the book." We have spoken of the Philosophers and the Prophets; there remain the civil laws—that is, the commands and judgments of the Emperors and the wise <note>original: "prudentium," referring here to "jurisprudents" or legal experts</note>—whose purpose is chiefly to look after the benefits by which the life of men may be spent well and happily. Since life is most aided by the good arts and disturbed by harmful ones, these leaders took the greatest care so that the good arts might flourish and the harmful ones might not exist (as far as possible) within their cities. To achieve this, they decreed rewards and honors for the professors of the good arts, while for the harmful ones, they decreed public disgrace and punishments that were more severe the more harmful they deemed those arts to be. 

Therefore, no one who has read the legal codes of Emperor **Justinian** <note>Justinian I (reigned 527–565 AD), whose "Corpus Juris Civilis" formed the basis of Western civil law.</note> is ignorant of what the ancients thought about astrologers. In those codes, the "art of the **Mathematicians**" <note>original: "Mathematicorum." In Roman law, this was the technical term for astrologers who cast horoscopes, distinguishing them from simple arithmeticians.</note> (for so the astrologers used to call themselves) is forbidden as something abominable. The Emperor commanded that no one should consult a Mathematician, and that the "curiosity for divining" should be silenced forever for everyone. If anyone consults a Mathematician, the penalty of the head <note>The "capital penalty" or death sentence.</note> is pronounced against him. Surely, the most wise Emperor, who relied on the experience and judgment of so many wise men, would not have established this unless experience had demonstrated that this profession was not only useless to life but actually ruinous to mankind. 

The most fortunate **Justin** <note>Likely referring to Justin I or Justin II, emperors of the same dynasty as Justinian.</note> himself so abhorred this class of men that if any Mathematician were caught in his company, he would pay the penalty for his rashness with the most extreme tortures, even unto the **rack** <note>original: "eculeum," a wooden frame used to stretch the body during interrogation.</note>. Finally, speaking of this superstition, the Emperor pronounces that those who teach these things and those who learn them are partners in the same guilt. Even before Justinian, have we not often read that all "Mathematicians" were expelled from the city of Rome? We will clearly demonstrate this at the conclusion of these disputations. 

If all right reason is either ruled by prudence, perfected by philosophy, or illuminated by the rays of divine splendor, then astrology will surely be cast down by every right judgment; for the wisest Lawgivers have banished it, the most learned philosophers have refuted it, 
->and divine and most holy men<-
->have abominated it.<-
