# GIOVANNI PICO
## Of Mirandola’s Disputations against Astrology, Book II.

-> THAT THIS ART IS UNCERTAIN EVEN BY THE JUDGMENT <-
-> of its own leaders. Chapter I. <-

---

**B**UT lest we fight by authority alone, we shall demonstrate throughout this entire work, using certain reasons, that this superstition was rightly rejected by the holy fathers because it is so greatly opposed to religion, and was usefully forbidden by laws because it is useless for life—or rather, it is harmful and exceedingly so—and was rationally refuted by philosophers so that they might recognize it as false and uncertain. 

And although it seemed that we should begin by demonstrating it to be false (since that would immediately prove it useless), I nevertheless thought it necessary to proceed otherwise. Specifically, before I disputed its falsehood, I wanted to show the lovers of astrologers that even if this profession were exactly as they claim and affirm it to be, no benefit comes from it to the "outer man" <note>Referring to the physical or worldly life.</note>, while to the "inner man" <note>The soul or spiritual life.</note>, it brings not only the greatest damages but even fatal ones. 

Before we approach this, it is necessary to preface some things from which we may understand how much the supreme leaders of the astrologers themselves attribute to their own profession. Ptolemy, therefore, in the first book of the *Apotelesmatika* <note>The *Apotelesmatika*, better known as the *Tetrabiblos*, is the fundamental textbook of Western astrology written by Claudius Ptolemy in the 2nd century AD.</note>, after he said that the judgments of astrologers are often lies due to the fault of the practitioner, nevertheless adds these words exactly as we wished to translate them—for they are poorly rendered in the common translation, and worse in the translation of Avenrodan <note>Avenrodan is the Latinized name of Ibn Ridwan (c. 988–1061), an Egyptian physician and astrologer whose commentary on Ptolemy was a standard medieval text.</note>, and poorly explained by him. But once they have been faithfully translated, they will not need explanation. 

"But that point is clear: even if someone has tracked these disciplines properly, as far as can be done, it is still necessary that he should stumble as often as possible. This is not only because of those reasons we mentioned above, but rather because of the very nature of the matter, or because our own weakness is greater than our ability to be equal to the magnitude of such a great profession. For indeed, since every contemplation that deals with the qualities of matter seeks probabilities <note>original: "verisimilia," meaning things that are 'like the truth' or likely, rather than certainties.</note> rather than decreeing anything as absolute truth, then indeed this is especially characteristic of [astrology]. It is a discipline, as it were, confused from many things dissimilar to each other, and it depends upon the ancient configurations and aspects of the <term>wandering stars</term> <note>The "wandering stars" (*errantium siderum*) is the classical term for the planets, distinguished from the "fixed stars."</note>. For those things which were observed by the ancients regarding the outcomes of events, we adapt to our own age only when the situation holds in the same manner. But who does not see that it can happen that the configurations themselves and the aspects may be more or less similar to each other over long cycles of time? But that an entirely identical harmony of all things in heaven—especially if you also include the earth—should return..."

it follows <note>The text begins mid-sentence, completing the thought from the previous page.</note>, that it seems it should not even be hoped for, unless perhaps someone boasts vainly and gloriously of comprehending and knowing things which, by their own nature, cannot be fully grasped, or at least not within that span of time granted to human senses. Consequently, when presented with dissimilar examples, the practitioner may err in his predictions, even when observing those things that occur within the nature of the world surrounding us.

Moreover, there is nothing more difficult than in the case of births <note>Latin: "genituris," referring to the calculation of individual horoscopes based on birth time.</note> and in the private comparisons of individuals; small and slight causes arise by which each person's character is shaped. For the differences in biological potential <note>Latin: "seminum," literally "seeds," referring to the genetic or hereditary material of a species.</note> are very powerful regarding the property of a genus. Even if the surrounding atmosphere and the horizon remain the same, each "seed" carries great weight in the universal formation of its specific shape—for instance, in a human, a horse, and others. 

The locations of birth also bring no small difference. For if the genus of the seed is the same—such as the human race—and the state of the surrounding celestial body is the same, those who are born differ greatly in body and mind due to the diversity of regions. It also matters greatly for varying the actions of life, even if other things are equal, what foods a person eats or what customs they follow. Unless each of these factors is contained within the cause of the surrounding celestial body (which supposedly has this most powerful force), then these factors themselves must be a part of the cause of why things are as they are—which is largely the opposite of what astrologers claim. 

In this, those who think they can do everything might hesitate; for although the cases are not exactly the same, they claim to distinguish them solely from the motion of the heavenly bodies. So says Ptolemy there; and in the first statement of the other book entitled *The Fruit*—commonly called the *Centiloquium* <note>original: "Centiloquium," a collection of 100 astrological aphorisms attributed to Ptolemy, though modern scholars consider it a later medieval forgery.</note>—speaking of the science of astrology, he says: "Thus, it is impossible for one who is knowledgeable to predict the particular forms of things, just as the sense does not perceive a particular object but rather a general form of a sensible thing; it is necessary for the practitioner of these matters to use conjecture, for only those inspired by the divine predict particulars." These are his words exactly, although they are found otherwise—faulty and corrupted—in the common manuscripts.

But it is also the undisputed opinion of the Arabs and Hebrews who write on astrology that even if one's star has promised something, it may still not come to pass: either because the material is not suitable for receiving the influence, or because human affairs depend largely on our own free will <note>Latin: "arbitrio," referring to the theological and philosophical concept of free choice.</note>, or because a particular fate can be overcome by the power of a more universal opposing fate, or because divine providence—which is more powerful than fate and greater than the heavens—sometimes orders things differently than the ordinary revolution of the sky would have effected. While these points are scattered everywhere among the astrologers, you may read them all together

### THAT AUSPICES, WHICH THEY CALL ELECTIONS, ARE USELESS,
### according to the testimony of an astrologer, reason, and experience. Chapter II.

Now, if these things are true, let the astrologer show what benefit life gains from his predictions. He will perhaps answer that the benefit is twofold: first, that he speaks the truth, and we are taught the hour at which we should begin <note>original: "auspicari"</note> our actions so that what we are about to do happens successfully. Second, when he predicts what is to come, there is a benefit in that we might avoid those things in which we have learned we will be unlucky, and instead undertake those in which our birth hour promises us success. 

But come, let us examine both points, starting with the one he proposed first; and since our dispute is with the astrologers, let us use those very assumptions which are considered most true among them. Either the celestial birth constellation has made the heaven favorable to you in the matter you are about undertaking under an auspicious hour, or it has made it adverse. If it is adverse, an **election** <term>Election: the astrological practice of "electing" or choosing a specific time to start a project, marriage, or war to ensure a lucky outcome.</term> is of no use according to the opinion of Ptolemy; therefore, you will always undertake that matter unsuccessfully, and you will always successfully abstain from it. If the heaven is favorable, there is no need for an election of hours, for your own choice is sufficient, since you will undertake that matter most successfully when your own mind invites you to it. 

For to be "fortunate" (if anyone is indeed made fortunate by the heavens) is nothing other than our imaginative power—the servant of reason—being so moved by the heavens that we undertake each thing at the times and in the ways that our wish can be fulfilled as successfully as possible. Regarding this, Aristotle said that counsel is of no use to the fortunate man—that is, in the matter for which nature has formed him—lest perhaps deliberation distract and lead you away from where that established impulse of the mind was calling you. 

I pass over the fact that Haly <note>Ali ibn Ridwan (c. 988–1061), an Egyptian physician and astrologer who wrote a famous commentary on Ptolemy's Tetrabiblos.</note>, the interpreter of Ptolemy, says that this part of astrology concerning elections is frivolous and ineffective. I pass over the evidence of experience itself, than which nothing is more certain or more consistent; for it daily makes manifest that those who observe this vain distinction of times are especially unsuccessful in conducting their affairs. On the contrary, those who have rejected that superstition and use only choice and prudence as their guides are far more successful. 

For who in our age was more fortunate than Francesco Sforza <note>The mercenary captain who became Duke of Milan (1401–1466), known for his pragmatic and effective rule.</note>? Through military success, he secured for himself the large and flourishing domain of Lombardy <note>original: "Insubrium," the ancient name for the region around Milan.</note> and left it increased and strengthened for his descendants. Yet all astrologers were always either an object of hatred or contempt to him, let alone him employing them as advisors in his military or domestic affairs. Who among the ancients was more powerful in astrology, magic, and every superstition than Zoroaster? And yet Ninus—who was certainly neither an astrologer nor a mage—defeated and killed him in war. Pompey placed the greatest faith in the responses of diviners, while Caesar placed none; to the former fell adverse fortune, to the latter, happy and joyful luck. Who is ignorant that Justinian—the eradicator of astrologers, as we have seen—was most successful at home and in war? On the other hand, the Emperor Julian <note>Julian the Apostate (r. 361–363), known for his attempt to revive paganism and his reliance on omens and divination.</note>, an enemy of the Christian name and a most curious observer of all superstitions, how briefly and how unluckily did he lose both his life and his empire? I could, however, [mention] one...

...or another, even naming learned astrologers who were my friends, whose trust in that vanity <note>Pico consistently refers to astrology as "vanity" (*vanitas*), implying it is empty of substance and truth.</note>—according to which they had arranged their way of life—led either to their destruction or to no small loss. But I do not wish to dishonor men who were otherwise good, nor to violate the laws of sacred friendship in a matter that is, in truth, not entirely necessary. Yet I wish it had not taken away one man's inheritance, and from another his country and his life, nor made many people foolish and insane through vain hope, and many others wretched through fear. As I hope God may not look upon my sins, I have seen no one more lacking in those very things which astrology promises to its followers than those who have devoted themselves entirely to astrology and who hunt for the favor of heaven at every passing hour. 

A certain great man known to me changed his way of life, resulting in no small loss of his previous fortune based on this plan. He was prompted mostly by astrological hope, believing that in his new profession he would achieve great happiness through celestial favor. But when, in that new life, he experienced increasingly adverse fortune every day, he used to say that he had been deceived by Mars—unwilling to say what was more true: that he had been deceived by astrological vanity. That same man died a little later an even more miserable death, which he himself had not foreseen from the heavens. For he was preparing many things and striving for great goals, as one who had established for himself a long span of living yet to come. 

I could recount many instances of this kind, but my soul recoils from the narration of those things which I can hardly remember without tears; and since these events befell very dear friends, they demand compassion from me rather than criticism. But I hope that this reluctant refutation, while concealing the names of old friends, may benefit those friends still living. By all the rights of friendship that exist between me and them—by their fortunes and their hopes for happiness—I would warn and ask them again and again never to commit themselves to the counsel of that vanity in their affairs. Let them treat it (if they like) as a poetic fable over which they may laugh, play, and joke; let them not hold it as a leader or a mistress of life. 

Instead, when the health of the body must be considered, let them consult physicians; when external matters must be weighed, let them use the eyes of prudence and reason. Divine wisdom teaches us both of these: it says that the physician was created by the Most High for our necessity <note>A reference to the Biblical Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 38:1, which justifies the medical profession as divinely ordained.</note>, and it says that prudence must be kept by man so that he may be delivered from the evil way <note>A reference to the Book of Proverbs 2:11-12.</note>. 

We find nothing of the sort written about astrology. We have proved its profession to be so useless that we would grant it only as much as the astrologers themselves think should be granted. For when it is subsequently proved that it possesses no truth at all, it will be beyond all controversy—as we have endeavored to prove here—that it is most dangerous to entrust our affairs to the counsel of astrologers. If ever something happens correctly following their predictions, it should be attributed not to reason—which 

->does not exist among them, but to recklessness and chance.<-
->it must be referred.<-

<header>In Astrology, Book II.</header>

### THAT ASTROLOGY IS NOT USEFUL IN DECIDING what should be done and what should be avoided. Chapter III.

**A**nother supposed benefit of astrology can be imagined, as we were saying above: specifically, that we should pursue whatever course the astrologer commands and flee from those he forbids. We have demonstrated that this is either superfluous or harmful. For what the astrologer predicts pertains either to the body or to external and accidental matters. 

In these matters of the body, if they concern health, I ask: does the physician’s judgment agree with the astrologer’s, or is it rather different? If both think the same, the astrologer provides nothing that the physician could not provide alone. If they disagree, to which one, I ask, do you think you should listen? Surely, if you reject the physician and entrust yourself to the astrologer, you will pay the penalty for your madness. 

In practical affairs, I ask a similar question: does prudence <note>In the Renaissance, "prudence" (*prudentia*) was a technical term for practical wisdom and the ability to govern oneself through reason.</note> also advise doing what astrology suggests, or are these judgments entirely opposed to each other? If they are in harmony, why should we seek in the heavens, so far away, what is already within us? If they disagree, who could rightly or reasonably defend a choice where prudence is abandoned in the conduct of affairs? Prudence is nothing other than the "right reason" for doing things. 

But these matters will be clearer with examples. Suppose an astrologer predicts that Mars threatens you this year with a tertian fever <note>original: "tritæum"; a fever that occurs every third day, traditionally associated with the "hot and dry" influence of the planet Mars.</note>, because he will stir up bile through the power he holds in the annual revolution. Therefore, he claims you should use cooling remedies and organize your lifestyle against the heat of Mars. This very thing he predicts from the heavens will either be demonstrated by the physical signs found in your body—upon which the physician's diagnosis relies—or they will not be demonstrated. 

If they are demonstrated, this will be a sufficient sign for you to prevent future ill health. If they are not demonstrated, I ask: would you think it right to act when there are no signs of boiling bile? If your urine is pale and thick, your pulse sluggish, your face deformed by paleness, and your limbs lethargic—signs which physicians use to identify the dominance not of bile, but of phlegm <note>original: "pituitæ"; according to the theory of the four humors, phlegm is cold and wet, the opposite of the hot and dry bile associated with Mars.</note>—will you still purge the bile just because the astrologer has imagined Mars threatening you from the sky? 

What if the astrologer does not even advise you prudently? Even if he speaks truly about Mars, your natural temperament, the overall disposition of that year, or the lifestyle you have long followed could have turned you toward the opposite condition. In short, the astrologer sees only one cause that might produce this effect, and a remote and universal one at that. The physician judges not only from specific and immediate causes but perceives the matter itself through the senses. He grasps what results from the combination of all causes together, as the evidence of present nature demonstrates. I pass over the fact that even those who favor the judgments of astrologers are not so insane as to think they are less likely to be deceived than by the judgments of physicians. 

Let us propose a similar example in the handling of external affairs: suppose a mathematician <note>original: "mathematicus"; in this period, the term "mathematician" was often synonymous with "astrologer."</note> advises a prince not to enter into war with his enemies, because Mars...

...may God be favorable to them. I ask whether, at the time he gave this advice, the prince had no just cause for war, or if there were a cause for war, yet no opportunity or chance of victory. Or rather, was a just cause not lacking, and were all the instruments for victory at hand? If you grant the first case, he will not go to war by right, but guided by prudence alone, even if the mathematician <note>The term *mathematicus* was frequently used in the Renaissance to refer to astrologers.</note> remains entirely silent. If the second case is true, then not even the astrologer himself—unless it is in his own interest—would judge that he should abstain from war; and if he did abstain, what would that be other than to abandon sense and evidence in favor of [mere] reason and conjecture?

## THAT ASTROLOGY IS NOT USEFUL FOR RELIGION,
### as Roger Bacon and Pierre d'Ailly believed. Chapter IV.

**B**ut if it is useless for [practical] life, is it perhaps useful for religion? This is what both **Roger Bacon** <note>A 13th-century English Franciscan friar and philosopher who took a keen interest in the natural sciences and astrology.</note> and **Pierre d'Ailly** <note>A 14th-century French cardinal and theologian (Petrus Alliacensis) who wrote extensively on the "harmony" between astrology and history.</note> seem to have thought. They believed this for two main reasons: first, that from the astrological calculation of the <term>Great Conjunctions</term> <note>These are alignments of the planets Jupiter and Saturn, which medieval astrologers believed signaled major historical shifts, such as the rise of new religions or empires.</note>, the truth could be obtained regarding the number of years from Adam to Christ, a subject of great debate among ecclesiastical texts. Second, they believed the oracles of the Prophets could be confirmed if the testimony of astrological prediction were added to them. 

For they argue that since every truth is consistent with every other truth, the truth of astronomical science must necessarily be in accord with theological truth; indeed, they argue that more than all other sciences, it should serve theology like a handmaid to her mistress. Since "the invisible things of God are perceived through those visible things that have been made," and there is nothing among those things nobler than the heavens, they cite David: *The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands.* <note>original: "Cœli enarrãt gloriam Dei, & opera manuum eius annũciat firmamentũ." (Psalm 19:1)</note> 

As if to prove this opinion by his own hand, Pierre d'Ailly wrote a short book divided into twenty theorems, which he calls "Words," in which there are plainly as many errors as there are words. Its title is <term>On the Harmony of Astrology and Theology</term>, as if he had never read Paul exclaiming: *What fellowship has light with darkness? Or what part has Christ with Belial?* <note>2 Corinthians 6:14-15</note> He strives in that work to achieve the two things we were mentioning: namely, to show that what the Prophets predicted by divine inspiration was also foretold by the celestial constellations, and then to investigate the calculation of years from Adam to Christ from the dogmas of the astrologers. 

He adds to this another small work <term>On the Harmony of Astronomy and History</term>, in which, noting seven "Great Conjunctions" since the beginning of the world, he strives to relate them to those great and wonderful things gathered from histories in the intervening times. He does this to confirm the dogma of the astrologers, who maintain that great changes in human affairs, both in laws and kingdoms, are always brought about by those Great Conjunctions. 

And indeed, I could wish he had written things that I should praise rather than refute, since I love him for his talent for letters and I venerate the office he held in the Church. But perhaps I will even be doing him a service if I point out what was written too incautiously and...

...[accepted] that he would truly benefit the church, although his work is found to be both false and harmful without a doubt; by this just refutation, let it be wiped out as much as lies within our power. 

Moreover, ignorance of astronomy primarily led this otherwise learned man into this error. When he had begun to sample the art just a little as an old man—after his theological studies, in which he had exercised himself at the most famous University of Paris—he was enticed by that magnificent appearance of this art discussing the greatest matters, which human curiosity desires to know above all else. Before he had reached the point of detecting the weakness of the doctrine through deep examination, he wrote too hastily those two small works which he later retracted after becoming a little more skilled. Then, he wrote much in that book which he calls the <term>Elucidarium</term> <note>Full title: *Elucidarium astronomice concordie cum theologica et hystorica veritate* (The Elucidator of Astronomical Harmony with Theological and Historical Truth). It was Pierre d'Ailly's primary attempt to align the history of the Church with astrological cycles.</note>, although there are many shadows within it. 

If anyone unrefined in astronomy reads all these booklets, he will marvel at them the more, the less he understands. But anyone who has progressed even moderately in that art will judge him to have been a writer rather than an astrologer, and will say that whatever he wrote was merely read by him rather than understood to the core. Indeed, almost everything he writes is taken word-for-word from **Roger Bacon**, **Abraham the Jew** <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a Spanish Jewish scholar whose astrological works were widely translated into Latin.</note>, **Henry of Mechelen** <note>Henricus Bate of Mechelen (1246–c. 1310), a philosopher and astronomer who translated many Arabic astrological texts into Latin.</note>, **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a Persian astrologer whose *Greater Introduction to Astrology* was a fundamental text for medieval European practitioners.</note>, and some summary or other by a certain **Johannes Britannus** <note>Likely referring to John of Salisbury or another English scholar who summarized astrological tenets.</note>.

That he himself was only a listener and little skilled in astronomical matters can be recognized even from this: in the <term>Elucidarium</term> itself, which is his most corrected work, he says in chapter 11 that when he was writing those things—namely in the year 1404—we were in the **airy triplicity** <note>In astrology, the twelve zodiac signs are grouped into four "triplicities" based on elements: Fire, Earth, Air, and Water. Astrologers believed that "Great Conjunctions" (the meeting of Saturn and Jupiter) stayed within one element for about 200 years before shifting to the next.</note>, and that they would remain there for another sixty-one years, until the year 1465, at which time there would be a <term>Great Conjunction</term> <note>The alignment of the planets Saturn and Jupiter, considered the most significant marker of historical change in medieval astrology.</note> of **Saturn** and **Jupiter**, with a shift from the airy to the **watery triplicity**. 

In truth, that shift had already occurred nearly forty years earlier, namely in the year of Christ 1365, at which time on the twenty-ninth day of October, in the seventh degree of Scorpio <note>Scorpio is a Water sign, indicating the shift into the Water triplicity had already happened.</note>, Saturn and Jupiter were together; and thereafter they have always joined in watery signs until these times. But our man of **Ailly** was still waiting for something to happen in the future that had already occurred nearly a hundred years before his prediction's end-date.

As for the other utility which the same man thought would come from astrology—namely, determining the true number of years [for chronology]—we have abundantly refuted that in the book we wrote concerning the *True Calculation of Time* <note>Pico likely refers to a separate, possibly lost, treatise on chronology, or a different section of his ongoing arguments.</note>. Although, even if it did help the Christian commonwealth in this regard, astrology would not belong to that part which we are refuting here—which deals with the prediction of the future—but to true **astronomy**. Astronomy is one of the liberal arts, and its role is to calculate times and measure the motions of the stars by mathematical reasoning. 

But this is not the place to refute all his errors; we shall do that in the following books. For there, regarding the harmony of philosophy and theology, we shall show that things announced by the Prophets are neither caused nor signified by the heavens; and thus, even if astrology were true, the prediction of those things would not pertain to it. Those who exempt things from nature insofar as they are above nature...

from heaven; however, insofar as there is something natural in these events, they contend that they are both produced by heaven and foreseen through heaven. We shall show that these men say nothing at all, even though they seem to say something. Indeed, so far is it from being the case that prophetic oracles are usefully confirmed by the decrees of astrologers, that nothing could be done more powerfully and effectively to weaken religion. Furthermore, those who have attempted to do this have always been caught as liars, ignorant of astronomy, and straying far from the profession of history. 

In general, however, not only regarding what pertains to laws and divine miracles, but also to other changes in human affairs—which many have wished to predict from "great conjunctions" <note>A "great conjunction" refers to the meeting of the planets Jupiter and Saturn, which medieval astrologers believed signaled major historical and religious shifts.</note>, as they call them—we shall there expose the vanity and falsehood of their dogma. We shall do this where we must contend for the truth against **Albumasar** <note>original: "Albumasare"; Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a highly influential Persian astrologer whose works were translated into Latin and became foundational for Western medieval astrology.</note>, the author of that error, along with **Jerome** <note>original: "Hieron."; likely referring to the translator or commentator on Albumasar.</note> his interpreter, with **Abraham the Israelite** <note>original: "Abraham Israēlita"; referring to Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a Jewish polymath and astrologer.</note>, and with **John of Exeter**. 

As for the book of **Alliacensis** <note>Pierre d'Ailly (1350–1420), a French cardinal and theologian whose work "On the Concordance of Astrology with History" Pico is attacking here.</note> in which he wished to do the same—namely, concerning the "concordance of astrology and historical narrative"—we shall so thoroughly re-examine it from the beginning that, running through from that first conjunction he notes right up to the last, we shall show that he said nothing sound or close to the truth regarding either celestial or terrestrial matters. We will show that not one of those seven conjunctions he notes happened at the time he thinks, but that they differ greatly from the very narrative of times (that is, of deeds done) and from true calculation. 

But let us see if those things he later brought forward carry any weight: namely, that "all true things harmonize with one another," and "the heavens declare the glory of God" <note>original: "cœlos Dei gloriam enarrare"; a reference to Psalm 19:1.</note>. Certainly, that first point is most true; but it should have been concluded therefrom that, since astrology is false, it cannot harmonize with theological truth. As for the testimony of David, the **Apostle Paul** teaches that it should be referred to the celestial minds of the Apostles, who announced that glory of God about which it is later written: *The law of the Lord is immaculate, converting souls* <note>original: "Lex domini immaculata convertens animas"; Psalm 19:7. Pico is arguing that the "heavens" in the Psalm are an allegory for the Apostles, not a justification for astrology.</note>. 

But even if it were referred to the visible heaven, what kind of logic is this: "if the heavens declare the glory of God, then those things which astrologers fabricate about the glory of God from heaven must be favored"? "But his invisible things," he says, "and his power and Divinity are understood through visible things" <note>A paraphrase of Romans 1:20.</note>. This is true for the philosopher, whose proper role it is to ascend from the order, motion, and nature of heaven to the invisible, divine Creator of heaven. But the astrologer, if he sees the heaven at all, sees it unwillingly, and turns his eyes down from heaven to the earth; the philosopher alone contemplates invisible things from visible ones.

### HOW HARMFUL ASTROLOGY IS, AND HOW
### pestiferous to the Christian religion. Chapter V.

As I survey everything on all sides and scout the enemies of the church, I do not see from where more troops or more arms are supplied against the truth than from this profession. For from here, there is a headlong and very easy slide into impiety, into bad religion, into heresy, into vain superstition, into ruined morals and irrevocable malice. For from where else could one better [arm oneself] against...

...impiety will arm its weapons against religion, rather than allowing the divine miracles—by which all religion is chiefly confirmed—to be attributed to the heavens. If you point to the Martyrs who despised death, or the Apostles—who, though few, poor, and unlearned, subjected the world to the law of the Gospel—or even to those men recalled from the dead; if you point to these things which are too great to be human and too good to be the work of demons, these men will strip away their power, unless they can be attributed to the course of a star and celestial influence, which alone they recognize. If someone should say this, is it not like bringing an axe to the roots of religion? If he persuades others, does he not examine it only to utterly uproot it? Now, if you say that this is not a vice of the art itself, but of its practitioners who err in their own profession, I will admit that this is so. For I was not saying this was an error inherent to astrology, but rather that it is a facile lapse from it into this error. Nor, even if astrology were true, would I cease from this task of turning men away from that danger, since no truth is to be confirmed by lies; but since it is false, its falsehood is usefully exposed. For if it were thought to be true, it could generate such a grave pestilence in the minds of the unlearned—though if you see that all professors of an art hold the same vanities, the fault may as well be referred to the art itself.

Indeed, among the principal writers on astrology, I have read no one who does not subject religion and all laws, like other human affairs, to the constellations of the stars. **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer/astrologer of antiquity.</note>, in the second book of the *Apotelesmaton* <note>original: "Apoteleſmaton"; better known as the *Tetrabiblos*, Ptolemy's foundational work on astrology.</note>, understands that the fact that one deity is worshiped by one nation and another by a different one arises from no other source than the varying nature of the stars and their signs ruling over those peoples and nations. Not far from that passage, a certain Greek interpreter of **Ptolemy** says that the miracle of **Moses** <note>original: "Moſeos"</note>, who crossed the Red Sea with his people on dry land <note>original: "sicco pede"</note>, happened because he had observed the ebb and flow of the sea. As if the Hebrew people did not cross those same waters unharmed at the very moment that Pharaoh was drowned along with his own astrologers! Or as if **Joshua** <note>original: "Ioſue"</note> did not cross the Jordan on dry land, where no tide and no reciprocal motion of the waves can be imagined by them. But we have sufficiently refuted all these and similar trifles elsewhere.

**Albumasar** <note>original: "Albumaſar"; Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a Persian astrologer who claimed religions are born under specific planetary conjunctions.</note> the Arab derives the law of the Saracens, his own law, our law, and all laws equally from the sky, such that he pronounces from a constellation which one created which law, and how many years each is to endure. We shall later declare how little astrology and how little truth is found in these matters. His interpreter, **Henry of Mechelen** <note>original: "Henricus Macliuienſis"; a 13th-century Belgian astrologer and disciple of Albertus Magnus.</note>, raved to such an extent that he even "found" a ship in the sky <note>likely referring to the constellation Argo Navis.</note> after which **Noah** <note>original: "Noë"</note> was supposed to have modeled his ark—a thing which **Pierre d’Ailly** <note>original: "Alliacenſis"; (1350–1420), a French cardinal and scholar who attempted to reconcile astrology with theology.</note> admired greatly as if it were a divine discovery. Finally, it can be known from this that they reduce religious law to the rank of those things which happen by a natural course and celestial change: they wish to know from the heavens how many revolutions of years will occur from the "ascendant" of a law <note>The "ascendant" in astrology is the sign rising on the eastern horizon at a specific moment—here, the "birth" of a religion.</note> until its fall. And **Haly Abenragel** <note>original: "Haly Abenragel"; Abū l-Hasan 'Alī ibn Abī l-Rijāl (died c. 1037), a Moroccan astrologer.</note>, to say nothing of the others, pronounces the prosperity or sterility of a year from this, as if at the "ascendant" of the law the place of **Jupiter** or **Venus**...

[if the planet Venus] is applied, the year will be fertile; conversely, if she is in the positions of unlucky stars. Abraham the Jew <note>original: "Abraam Iudæus"; Pico refers here to the 12th-century scholar Abraham ibn Ezra, though he disputes the specific identity here</note>—not the one called Ibn Ezra, as d’Ailly <note>Pierre d’Ailly (1351–1420), a French cardinal and astrologer</note> falsely believed, but the one they call *Nasi* <note>A Hebrew title meaning "Prince" or "Patriarch"</note>, that is, the Patriarch—did he not attempt to refer the Mosaic law, the departure of the Jews from Egypt, and whatever happened to the people under the Law to various <term>conjunctions</term> <note>The meeting of two or more celestial bodies in the same area of the sky</note>, foolishly and even ridiculously? But would that only those we have mentioned had failed to see the light of this truth amidst the darkness of their false religion; would that our own people, in the splendor of the Gospel, were not so blind, and did not think worse of our religion and theirs than those others did. 

That madman Bonatti <note>Guido Bonatti (c. 1210–1296), the most famous Italian astrologer of the 13th century</note> says the Lord Jesus made use of the <term>selection of hours</term> <note>original: "horarum electione"; the astrological practice of choosing the most auspicious time to begin an action</note> when the Apostles advised Him not to return to Judea. He answered that there are twelve hours in a day. For He chose for Himself an hour, he says, in which they could not harm Him—as if He had not cast them down when He wished, and had not remained hidden among them while passing through in the light of day. I pass over how recklessly and blasphemously he speaks of the divine family of Francis <note>The Franciscan Order</note>, and fabulates that the miracle of Divine Love <note>Likely referring to the Stigmata of St. Francis</note> was the work of Mars. 

But why do we look for remote examples? In those things which are daily broadcast abroad in public prophecies concerning the year's events, do we not read that the Christian law is the perfected teaching of Christ and Mercury, and the religion of Jupiter, and that it receives its purity from a Virgin? <note>A reference to the constellation Virgo, often conflated by astrologers with the Virgin Mary</note> Thus Christian men read these things with their eyes and without indignation. And in the prefaces of I know not what theory, disputing much against Gerard, is it not also written—when the selection of a new Pope was being discussed—that one must devoutly pray that the star of Mercury might temper him with its holy ray? For they say our law is subject to Mercury, and for that reason he called Christ’s men "men of Mercury"—something I know not how any Christian man can hear with calm ears. 

Roger Bacon was carried so far that he did not hesitate to write that Christians err by not keeping holiday on the Sabbath and abstaining from work according to the Jewish rite, since that is the day of Saturn, a star considered little suited or lucky for conducting business. In these words, he not only accuses our people but Moses himself; indeed, he openly turns the Prophet into an astrologer, teaching that what Moses established regarding the Sabbath rest was based not on any divine mystery, but on astrological dogma. 

If anyone weighs all this with a correct judgment, he will see that the piety of true religion is offended by no error more than this; for it is equally impious to think there is no religion at all, and to derive it from the heavens by some fatal necessity. But if an astrologer were to take up a religion, to which would he be more inclined than to idolatry, so that he might worship and revere those gods especially from whom he thinks all good and evil comes to men? Now the Manichaean heresies <note>A dualistic religious movement that taught a struggle between light and darkness, often associated with determinism</note>, which take away the freedom of the will—from where do we think they emanated, if not from this false opinion of the astrologers regarding fate? Concerning superstitions, there is no controversy that they all proceed from astronomy <note>Pico uses "astronomia" here to mean astrology</note>, and Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a prolific Roman scholar</note> confirms that those superstitions are maintained by it as if they were its foster-children. All writers call <term>Geomancy</term> <note>A method of divination that interprets markings on the ground or the patterns formed by tossed handfuls of soil, rocks, or sand</note> the daughter of astrology. The Magi deemed the use of this art so necessary...

...[neces]sary, so much so that they think astrology is the key to magic. <term>Palm readers</term> <note>original: "Chiromantici"; those who practice chiromancy or palmistry</note> even fashion seven "mounts" in the palm of the hand to match the number of the planets, from which they claim to foresee the future based on the lines visible there. However, it is sufficiently clear from this that all these arts are born from her and cannot stand without her, because there is no superstition that does not make use of the <term>selection of days and hours</term> <note>The practice of "elections," picking a specific time for an action based on planetary positions</note>, a matter in which only astronomy <note>Pico often uses "astronomia" and "astrologia" interchangeably when citing others, though his work seeks to separate the two</note> provides them instruction. Thus, that phrase from <term>Ecclesiastes</term> <note>A book of the Old Testament</note> might be said of her: **Vanity of vanities, astrology, and every superstition is vanity.** <note>original: "Vanitas vanitatum astrologia, & omnis superstition vanitas"; a parody of Ecclesiastes 1:2, "Vanity of vanities, all is vanity"</note> It is not necessary to say more regarding morals, since it is clear enough that no greater protection can be given to vice than if the heavens are thought to be its author. There is nothing that makes us fear <term>Gehenna</term> <note>Hell</note> less or hope for happiness less than this belief. If these points are undoubtedly true, then even if this profession of theirs were accurate, wouldn't the truth be more usefully ignored? And since it is false, how much more usefully is its falsehood attacked? I only wish I could execute this task with as much success as I have embraced it with the desire to help religion and protect the truth.

---

### THAT THIS ART IS DECEPTIVE, IF IT EVEN EXISTS, BOTH BECAUSE OF MANY REASONS AND BECAUSE OF THE DISCREPANT OPINIONS OF ASTROLOGERS. Chapter VI.

Hitherto we have shown that it is useful to refute astrology, and that its patronage is unworthy of both a philosopher and a Christian. Now, before we engage hand-to-hand with the astrologers and begin our refutation, let us see how much the reality of the situation and the actual outcomes of their work repel their claims. For how many of the things they predict actually happen? Or if something does happen, why did it happen? I am usually amazed by those who, when arguing against this art, always object: "If their art is not true, then why are their predictions sometimes correct?" For an astrologer thinks he has done excellently for himself if, when we object to the falsehood of his predictions, he can satisfy us with even a few [correct ones]; he is far from thinking he can take an argument against us from this place.

We cited above the words of **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer/astrologer of antiquity</note> trying to resolve this question. In them, we saw him shift the blame for the lies of astrologers not only onto the astrologers themselves—as being insufficiently skilled or diligent—but also onto the art itself, which he claimed is uncertain and can be very deceptive. **Porphyry** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD)</note> himself said that the responses of oracles were discovered to be false; therefore, those spirits <note>original: "numina"; divine powers or deities</note> foretold things based on celestial causes which they had investigated. Yet, the foretelling that comes from those causes is deceptive. But if the <term>demons</term> <note>original: "dæmones"; in this context, intermediary spirits or fallen angels believed to have vast knowledge of the physical world</note> themselves, from whom nothing of celestial matters is hidden, are deceived when perceiving the future from there, what, I ask, shall we judge concerning men? Even those who are and were the most excellent in this art (if it is one) have never attained even a thousandth part of it. Finally, among all the arts—where it is the nature of all of them to fall away from the truth—I believe even the astrologers themselves will not deny that no judgment is more uncertain than theirs. For, they say, even the choice of a human being makes many things turn out differently...

He begins a formal refutation by pointing out that even great authorities like Ptolemy and Porphyry admitted the art's inherent uncertainty and frequent failures.</summary>

...and the flux and mobility of matter often frustrate the works of celestial actions, and one fate is turned aside or hindered by another. For if you examine human affairs diligently, you will find almost nothing in which some of these things we have mentioned—even an outcome truly foreseen from the heavens—is not changed. For it is characteristic of man to arrange his affairs by will and reason, and that which is everywhere attached and bound to matter is vehemently subject to its change. Then, since nothing is isolated, almost all men depend on one another in such a way that there is no one whose fortune cannot either harm or help another. 

Thus, a fortunate son will inherit the misfortune of an unhappy father—even an unhappy end—and a fortunate one will receive good fortune from a parent’s good fate. And a servant, though little favored by his own <term>nativity</term> <note>original: "genitura"; the configuration of the stars at the moment of one's birth</note>, will fare happily with a fortunate master. So the fate of the soldier will happen one way or another based on the fate of the general, and the fortune of the sick man from the doctor, and conversely, the doctor's from the sick man. From all this, it is declared how often it is necessary that what the <term>mathematician</term> <note>original: "mathematicus"; in the Renaissance, this term was frequently used to mean an astrologer</note> predicted for each person does not occur, even if that profession were true—let alone that the truth of the profession could be proven from the true predictions of its practitioners. 

What of the fact that there is such great disagreement among the authors of this art’s dogmas? It is necessary that either all or the greatest part of them speak lies about the future. They themselves greatly admire and venerate certain Egyptians, Persians, Indians, and Babylonians as if they were priests of celestial mysteries, and with puffed-out cheeks <note>A rhetorical image suggesting pomposity or boastfulness</note>, they daily sound their names like deities into the ears of the unskilled. 
<margin>•</margin>
But oh astrologers, you cannot speak the truths of that ancient discipline, you who possess only the books of the juniors which you imitate, differing everywhere from that ancient discipline. For Ptolemy, your father, everywhere censures and tears apart the astrology which was specifically that of the Egyptians, attacking it now as little consistent with reason, now with other reproaches, which is easily established by reading his books of the *Apotelesmaton* <note>The *Apotelesmatika*, better known as the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology by Claudius Ptolemy</note>. And truly, not only did Ptolemy differ from them, but they disagreed equally among themselves—the Indians from the Chaldeans, the Egyptians from both one another and from these others, and the Persians from all of them. 

Nor is Greek astrology any more harmonious within itself than the "barbarian" kind, since what Ptolemy rejects, Dorotheus embraces; and Paulus feels one thing, Hephaestion another, and others still more; nor will you find any among them who does not claim the reliability of their outcomes based on the "authority of experience." Do not the Arabs also fight among themselves and against the Greeks? Furthermore, just as Ptolemy rejected that ancient astrology, so <term>Albumasar</term> <note>The Latinized name for Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), a highly influential Persian astrologer</note> rejects the astrology of Ptolemy, to the point that he says nothing can be read in his books that is found to be consistent with either reason or experience. 

On the contrary, <term>Avenrodan</term> <note>Ali ibn Ridwan (c. 988–1061 AD), an Egyptian physician and astrologer who wrote a famous commentary on Ptolemy</note> says that no one has spoken with reason in astrology except Ptolemy. And if you inspect the sayings of others, you will find them far removed from the truth, while the sayings of Ptolemy can in no way be found false. The Hebrews too, and the first of the Hebrews, Abraham <term>Avenazra</term> <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167 AD), a famous Jewish scholar and astrologer</note>, disagrees with Ptolemy, and he often tore Albumasar apart—indeed, [he rejected] his whole book...

<summary>Pico argues that astrology is unreliable because human free will and the interconnectedness of people (like masters and servants) disrupt "fate," and he highlights the massive contradictions between major astrological authorities like Ptolemy, Albumasar, and Ibn Ezra.</summary>

...those who are regarded in Latin as experts on **great conjunctions** <term>great conjunctions</term> <note>The rare alignment of the planets Jupiter and Saturn, which medieval astrologers believed signaled major historical or religious shifts.</note> cast aside and reject them. If they are truly followers of **Ptolemy**, must they not admit that the ancient Arabs—who claimed to be his followers—were necessarily lying? And if those books, as these men boast, were admired by all because they revealed the truth, then must not both Ptolemy and **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), a highly influential Persian astrologer whose work blended Greek and Arabic traditions.</note> have necessarily been objects of ridicule in their own centuries? For they and others completely deviated from one another’s decrees. Yet you will find it has always been thus: in every nation and every age, there have always been men who claimed that true things were predicted by astrologers. This happened not through the truth of their doctrines, but by mere chance. Nor has there ever been a lack of those who held this fallacy in mockery and contempt, or even in hatred.

But whatever may be said of previous ages, in our own time the truth of the doctrine certainly cannot be confirmed by the "professors" of the art. Not only do they follow mostly bad authors and fail to understand the good ones, but they also perform their duties so negligently that they are ignorant of many things they ought to know. They omit even more things that should be considered, sparing themselves the labor and hurrying toward financial gain. If my purpose here were to teach astrology rather than to refute it, I would pour out my hand against the errors of the younger men professing this art, but that is not my intention. Nevertheless, it may be worthwhile to note a few things, so that it becomes more manifest that they cannot predict the truth, even if the doctrines of the astrologers were themselves entirely true.

-> ### ON THE IGNORANCE OF THE ASTROLOGERS OF <-
-> ### our age. Chapter VII. <-

These foretellings of men are either universal—as when they predict future goods or evils for the whole world from the **chart of the year** <term>chart of the year</term> <note>A horoscope cast for the moment the Sun enters Aries, used to predict world events.</note>, from an eclipse of the Sun or Moon, or from the meetings of the superior planets—or they are particular, such as when they divine something about a private individual's fate from his own personal **nativity** <term>nativity</term> <note>The specific configuration of the stars at the exact moment of a person's birth; a birth chart.</note>. In the first category, nothing is more effective than an eclipse of the **luminaries** <term>luminaries</term> <note>The Sun and the Moon.</note>, from which (as the most universal causes) the greatest universal changes in the lower world arise. In the second category, nothing carries more weight than the **equation** <note>A calculation used to determine the length of life and the timing of major life events in a horoscope.</note>, which is usually done regarding the span of life and the number of years.

In both of these, it is a wonder how much the modern and "barbarian" writers err—those whose authority and use are most significant among our astrologers. Ptolemy writes in the second book of his *Apotelesmaton* <note>Also known as the *Tetrabiblos*, Ptolemy's foundational 2nd-century work on the philosophy and practice of astrology.</note> that in an eclipse of the Sun, two things must be observed above all: the place in which the Sun is eclipsed, and the **angle** <term>angle</term> <note>The four most powerful points in a horoscope: the Rising (Ascendant), Midheaven, Setting (Descendant), and Lower Midheaven.</note> which immediately follows that place. For example, if the eclipse occurs in the ninth region of the heavens, the angle of the tenth place should be observed; if in the eleventh or twelfth, the angle of the East. However, because it is written there in Greek as <note>original: "ἑπομένον κέντρον"</note> **"the following center"**—that is, the following angle—the common translation instead has **"the preceding angle."** From this, a completely contrary meaning is derived, and an opportunity for error was given to the "barbarians." Thus, **John of Eschenden** <note>A 14th-century English astrologer. Pico refers to his major work, the *Summa Anglicana*, though the text here calls it the *Summa Angelica*.</note> in that work which they commonly call the *Summa Angelica*, which holds the highest authority among our people, after he had tormented himself with a long and argumentative questio—

...that finally, according to the opinion of **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity, whose *Tetrabiblos* was the standard textbook for the field.</note>, he defines that the angle to be observed is not the one that follows, but the one that precedes the place in which the defect of the luminary <note>A "defect of the luminary" refers to a solar or lunar eclipse.</note> occurred. That this is entirely contrary to Ptolemy’s actual opinion is clear from what we have already said—namely, why in the Greek it is written *following* <note>original: "ἐπομένου" (*hepomenou*)</note>, which means that which follows, and not *preceding* <note>original: "ἡγουμένου" (*hegoumenou*)</note>, which means that which leads. 

But because a little later, Ptolemy himself, explaining what these angles are, named the meridian of the Sun and the Eastern angle, the Greek interpreter warns us that the Western angle is omitted. This angle cannot follow the location of the eclipse unless the Sun is obscured beneath the earth; when that happens, they do not believe it has the power to effect future events. But if the preceding angle were the one to be observed, then the East should have been omitted by Ptolemy—as it cannot precede a failing Sun unless it is beneath the earth—and the West should have been included, which would always be found to run ahead and precede it, whether the eclipse happened in the eighth or ninth house of the heavens. 

From this error, the entire system of prediction is overturned. In forecasting, nothing is more important than the nature and state of the stars in relation to the location of the luminaries and the planets dominating that angle. Since one angle will be swapped for another, there will also be a different ruler of the chart. Thus, due to the different nature of the dominant star, the pronouncement regarding future events will always be various—or rather, completely contradictory.

I will show in a few words how these "petty diviners" see nothing at all regarding the prediction of the **span of life** <term>span of life</term> <note>The "length of life" calculation was one of the most complex and controversial parts of traditional astrology.</note>. **Haly Abenragel** <note>Abū l-Hasan 'Alī ibn Abī l-Rijāl (d. 1037), an influential Arab astrologer whose work was widely translated into Latin.</note>, the oracle of the astrologers of this age, says in the fourth part of his work that, according to Ptolemy’s opinion, there are five **Hilech** <term>Hilech</term> <note>Also known as the Hyleg or "Life-Giver," the planet or point in a birth chart thought to be responsible for the person’s vitality.</note>—for that is how they speak: the Sun, the Moon, the Ascendant, the Part of Fortune, and the place of the Full or New Moon immediately preceding birth. 

In addition to these five, he says the planets in those five places must be considered as holding law and authority. In the next chapter, speaking of that which they call the **Alchochoden** <term>Alchochoden</term> <note>Also known as the Alcocoden or "Giver of Years," the planet that determines the actual length of life based on its relationship to the Hyleg.</note>, which is the "giver of years," he says: "Ptolemy says the *Alchochoden* is the planet that has the most authority in the *Hilech*, whether it aspects it or does not aspect it." And so he repeats many things about this *Alchochoden* as being the opinion of Ptolemy; our astrologers, who follow this man and other barbarians, persist in the same error. 

They search through every birth chart to find who is the *Hilech* and who is the *Alchochoden* according to the "opinion of Ptolemy." Yet, in the works of Ptolemy himself, this *Alchochoden* is as much a non-entity as a **goat-stag** or a **chimera** <note>Pico uses these classical philosophical examples to describe things that do not exist in reality; a goat-stag (*hircocervus*) is a mythical beast that is part goat and part deer.</note>. Read all his books, read all the interpreters, read even the "barbarian" <note>By "barbarian," Pico usually refers to Arabic translations or medieval Latin versions he considers linguistically inferior to classical Greek.</note> translations, and you will not find that word, nor any word corresponding to it, in his writings. 

For that doctrine—which makes one thing the *Hilech* in a birth chart and another the giver of life and years (which they call the *Alchochoden*)—belongs to later authors. Neither Ptolemy nor those older than him ever held such an opinion. Ptolemy himself first enumerates the places he calls **Aphetic** <term>Aphetic</term> <note>From the Greek *aphetēs*, meaning "one who releases" or "sender."</note>, which the Arabs call *Hilech* and which we in Latin can call **dismissory** <note>original: "dimissoria"</note>. They are so named because the course of life is sent forth from there, as if starting from the starting gates of a race. These places are known to be above the earth, having some affinity with either the West or the Ascendant...

...connected by nature. Then he <note>Ptolemy</note> establishes the **Aphetae** <note>original: "Aphetas," from the Greek for "releasers." In astrology, these are points in a birth chart that determine life and vitality.</note>, that is, the "releasers" themselves, who from those locations—as if by their own breath of life (so to speak)—grant the impulse of life. He intends these to be the **Sun**, the **Moon**, the **Horoscope** <note>The Ascendant, or the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at birth.</note>, the **Part of Fortune** <note>A specific mathematical point in a chart calculated from the positions of the Sun, Moon, and Ascendant.</note>, and the wandering stars <note>The planets.</note> ruling in those places. 

Beyond these, by which all the **Hylechs** <note>The "Hylech" is the specific planet or point among the Aphetae that is chosen as the "Giver of Life."</note> are numbered, he makes no other distributor of years, although he thinks that what these aforementioned "releasers" grant can be increased or exhausted by the commerce of lucky or unlucky stars. However, the Barbarians <note>A term Pico uses for medieval Arabic astrologers and their followers.</note> and our own writers believe that, besides these **Aphetae** (whom they call the **Hylech**), there is another entity who decides the span of living, even claiming this is based on the opinion of Ptolemy. They call this the **Alchochoden** <note>A Persian-Arabic term for the "Giver of Years," a planet that "rules" the Hylech and determines the lifespan.</note>. Regarding this matter, as I was saying, Ptolemy himself says nothing anywhere; yet, based on his supposed opinion, they seek many things, argue, and define them. 

And they do not only err in this, upon which the entire sum of the matter depends, but also in the very numbering of the Hylechs. Among them, <term>Haly</term> <note>Haly Abenragel (c. 10th-11th century), a famous Arab astrologer.</note> says that the location of the preceding new moon or full moon should be included by the authority of Ptolemy. Yet Ptolemy judges that this should never be done, whether the birth occurs at night or by day. 

What of the fact that this Haly accuses Ptolemy of being inconsistent with himself? He boasts greatly over this assessment of Ptolemy—in which Haly claims no one has ever opposed him—and offers immense thanks to God, the "revealer of secrets." He says Ptolemy contradicts himself because he does not count the eighth house <note>The eighth house of the zodiac, traditionally associated with death.</note> among the <term>Hylechia</term> <note>Places in the sky capable of hosting a Hylech.</note> because it does not "behold" <note>An "aspect" or geometric relationship between points in the sky.</note> the Horoscope; yet in choosing the <term>Alchochoden</term>, Haly thinks it matters not at all whether it beholds the Hylech or not. 

Why are you so foolish, Barbarian? Or what are you dreaming? Where in Ptolemy have you read of the **Alchochoden**? I know what deceived him and the others: Ptolemy places the planets ruling in the remaining Hylechial places among the Hylechs themselves. These men, however, think the rulers are a different thing from the Hylechs. They think that while the other four—the **Sun**, **Moon**, **Horoscope**, and **Part of Fortune** (to which they falsely added the new and full moon)—should alone be considered Hylechs, the planets ruling those locations should determine the years. 

And since Ptolemy never said it was necessary for the ruling planets to behold the Hylechs, they wondered why he did not think those two things—which they themselves believe are two distinct things, namely the <term>Hylech</term> and the <term>Alchochoden</term>—should be joined by an aspect. Yet it is no fault of Ptolemy's if he did not seek a relationship of aspect between things that are actually one and the same. For in his system, whenever the Sun or Moon are Hylechial, there is no other planet besides them acting as the disposer of life. He only uses a "ruling planet" when the other Hylechs lack authority in granting years. When that occurs, the vital commerce can be left to one of the Hylechs, because besides that, clearly, none is found. 

I do not know how they failed to understand this from Ptolemy's words, or why no one caught it. But they have all gone off into this error in a flock, so that there is no one who does not go looking for an Alchochoden and a Hylech based on the "opinion" of Ptolemy. See how "true" the dogmas of the astrologers are, and how...

He argues that this fundamental misunderstanding of their own primary authority invalidates their methods for predicting the length of a person's life.</summary>

<meta>catchword: CONCERNING THE</meta>

...how can those men predict true things about the span of life, especially when the greatest errors are piled on top of the things we have already mentioned? They prescribe the number of years according to the opinion—or so they claim—of <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity.</note>, based on whichever planet is the "giver of life." They follow that common saying of theirs: that there are so many "greater," "lesser," and "middle" years for the Sun, so many for the Moon, so many for Mars, and so on for the other stars. Yet, Ptolemy actually rejects that Egyptian opinion, saying it has no basis in reason. 

And where he speaks of the span of life, he does not count the years based on the nature of the Planets, but from the number of parts of the equatorial circle, according to the "place of life"—that is, the divisor—and another "deadly" or "killing" place among the intercepted parts. It is at this point that the course of a life, already grown weary and faint, first seriously stumbles for the person born. Thus, when the <term>Aphetes</term> <note>The "releaser" or "giver of life," a specific point in a birth chart used to determine longevity.</note> is positioned between the horizon and the peak of heaven, that "walking through" is observed which the Greeks call <term>ἀκτινοϐολίαν</term> <note>original: "aktinobolian," meaning "projection of rays."</note>, which is to say, a radiant projection. However, when it has declined from the peak toward the setting point in either direction, we use the calculation they call <term>ὡριαίαν</term> <note>original: "hōriaian," meaning "hourly."</note>, which we can call "hourly." Our astrologers are so ignorant of all these matters that even if they were to read them, they would think they were hearing about monsters.

Indeed, I have no doubt of this; yet we are so miserably credulous of their predictions. While they promise us the old age of Nestor <note>A legendary King in Greek mythology known for his extreme longevity.</note>, we forget the Lord's voice commanding us to be ready, since we know neither the day nor the hour of our death. If they threaten us with a short life, we are tortured for twelve days and nights, and the word of a single astrological table strips away all the joy of life.

<term>Haly</term> <note>Likely Haly Abenragel, a 10th-century Arab astrologer whose works were widely translated into Latin.</note> says that if a fortunate planet is in the <term>horoscopo</term> <note>The Ascendant, or the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth.</note>, it adds its "lesser years" to the years of life according to the sentiment of Ptolemy. And yet, as I just said, in Ptolemy’s work there are no "years of the planets"—neither greater, middle, nor lesser. When Ptolemy speaks of adding years, he follows a completely different path, using a division of hours which I believe Haly did not understand. But I should not pursue every single point, otherwise this book would grow to an immense size.

Even in those very questions they call "interrogations" <note>Also known as horary astrology, where a chart is cast to answer a specific question.</note>, do they not err so remarkably that the entire method of answering is perverted by a single mistake? For it is a common axiom among them that the seventh place of the chart—the West—is assigned to the matter being asked about. And yet Ptolemy commands that this place be given neither to the person consulting nor the matter being consulted, but to the <term>Mathematico</term> <note>In the Renaissance, "mathematician" was often a synonym for an astrologer.</note> himself who is being consulted. This was also observed by the <term>Indorum</term> <note>Indian astrologers.</note> mathematicians, to the point that when the West and the "lord of the West" were in a bad state, they would not answer the question, fearing they would fall into error. 

I could list six hundred errors of this kind, were it not my primary goal to show that the entire profession is in error. For recently, when I compared the books of Ptolemy with the Barbarian <note>Pico's term for medieval Arabic and Persian sources.</note> and Latin authors, almost everything they wrote had to be pierced through with spits <note>original: "uerubus confodienda." A metaphor meaning the text was so full of errors it needed to be slashed or "skewered" by the critic's pen.</note>.

<summary>Pico criticizes modern astrologers for using "greater" and "lesser" planet years to predict lifespan—a system Ptolemy actually rejected—and argues that their ignorance of technical Greek methods and their disregard for religious humility makes their predictions both inaccurate and spiritually harmful.</summary>

# On Astrology Book II.

#### ON THE CARELESSNESS OF THE ASTROLOGERS OF OUR
#### age, which is so great that even if astrology were true, they
#### themselves could not be truthful. Chapter VIII.

---

Now truly, how great is the carelessness! You will find few even among those who have the skill for calculation (a skill which, nonetheless, the greatest part of them lacks) who do not flee to <term>ephemerides</term> <note>Tables showing the daily predicted positions of the sun, moon, and planets.</note> to find the true position of the stars. This is something <term>Bonatus</term> <note>Guido Bonatti (c. 1210–1296), one of the most famous medieval Italian astrologers, whose work Pico frequently critiques.</note> testifies to in a certain passage with these words: "The wise men of this art," he says, "use an <term>Almanach</term>," for that is what the Arabs call <term>ephemerides</term>. Those who do this, however, must necessarily speak incorrectly and omit many things, by which the entire truth of their predictions is weakened. 

For there is almost never any mention in those tables of the latitude of the Planets. If this is ignored, where will the astronomer not err? Where will he not lie? If we consider the true decrees of this art, they believe the stars have the greatest power when they are placed in the beginnings of the twelve houses of heaven, especially in the "cardinal" points. But a man will think a star is in those places when it is not, and think it is not there when it is, if he only observes its forward movement and fails to look at the star's declination to the side <note>Pico is arguing that astrologers ignore "latitude"—how far a planet is above or below the ecliptic—which changes when a planet actually rises or sets on the horizon.</note>.

For when a star veers toward either the north or the south, it both rises later and is always placed more quickly in that part of the zodiac sign in which it is located. Thus, you will sometimes think a planet is above the earth when it is actually below the earth, and you will think one has already set which will actually still appear visible above the horizon. 

While this births error in every prediction, it makes them fail even more when they investigate the hour of birth from the hour of conception. For if the Moon happens to be very close to the west, it might be thought to have already set when it is still actually above the earth; and conversely, it might be thought not to have dipped yet when it is hidden below the east. This causes a wandering away from the truth for many days, starting right from the hour of conception. 

Who could correctly determine the radiations <note>The "aspects" or angular relationships between planets that astrologers use to make predictions.</note> of the Planets if the latitude is unknown? Who will rightly measure the "walking" of a star—as it is called in Greek, though commonly named a <term>direction</term> <note>A calculation used to predict the timing of life events by moving a planet forward in the chart at a rate of roughly one degree per year.</note>? For every deviation of a star to either side of the Sun's path <note>The ecliptic.</note> makes the event of a matter occur either some years faster or slower. 

From this, how great a slip occurs even in arranging the fixed stars! They are commonly placed in that spot to which they are carried by a straight-line progression. But they do not consider at all with which part of the sky they set or rise in various regions, or when they shine upon the beginnings of the remaining houses. Furthermore, <term>ephemerides</term> often show the location of Planets with very little reliability—not only through the fault of the copyists, but often because of the author, who was either not diligent enough or not skilled enough. 

I pass over the fact that different astronomers use different tables, which are sometimes not exact; even when a man has made his own diary, they wander far from the truth, and in this current time, they wander greatly. Everyone now rejects the tables of <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>The astronomical data from Claudius Ptolemy (2nd century AD), which had become outdated by the 15th century due to the precession of the equinoxes.</note>. A large part of the more learned follow the <term>Alphonsine</term> tables <note>The Alfonsine Tables, updated in 13th-century Spain, were the standard for late medieval astronomy but were beginning to show inaccuracies.</note>, yet it is now established that there is evident falsehood in their foundational calculations. But no less sleepily...

<summary>Pico argues that even if astrology were a valid science, contemporary astrologers are too incompetent to practice it accurately. He specifically highlights their failure to account for planetary latitude and their reliance on outdated or flawed astronomical tables like the Alfonsine Tables.</summary>

if in selecting the <term>horoscope</term> <note>original: "horoscopo"; here referring to the Ascendant, the specific point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth.</note> and in taking up the twelve remaining positions of the celestial places. I have seen many, not mediocre in skill and even of good name in that profession, using I know not what table of their own for distributing the <term>12 houses</term> <note>The division of the sky into twelve sections, each governing different areas of life like wealth, health, or travel.</note> (as they call them), no matter under what sky the person whose birth they were to examine had been born. But if they occasionally wish to be diligent, noting the difference in climate—the only thing <term>Alphonso</term> <note>King Alfonso X of Castile, who sponsored the famous "Alphonsine Tables" used by medieval astronomers.</note> showed them—they will hardly investigate anything more exactly beyond that. Now, as for the <term>declinations</term> <note>The distance of a celestial body north or south of the celestial equator.</note> from the equator, and the circumferences of the Planets, and the various elevations in the shorter circle, or the changes of latitudinal motions in <term>eccentrics</term>, who observes these now when judging nativities? Regarding the <term>equation of days</term> <note>The correction required to convert apparent solar time (sundial time) into mean solar time (clock time).</note>, how much the younger ones do not know, and how many things they say incorrectly! We have said all this so that it might become manifest that this art of predicting cannot be confirmed by the reliability of its predictions; for even if it were most true in principle, yet by the fault of the practitioners—that is, either through ignorance or negligence—the truth about the future could not be known from them. So, if we cannot persuade people to abandon faith in astrology itself, let us at least persuade them, as it is said in the *epigram*, not to place their faith in *astrologers*.

## THAT WHAT ASTROLOGERS SAY RARELY COMES TO PASS,
### which he demonstrates through both external and domestic examples.
### Chapter IX.

If their arts were sound or true, even if not entirely so but in great measure, they would not only not have been cast out of cities and always held in mockery by every prudent person, but would have been held in the highest honor in every age and among all nations. For so great is the curiosity of men for foreknowing the future, especially those things which pertain to themselves, and so great by right is the opinion and esteem for those who provide this. And yet, we read of statues erected and public honors decreed for philosophers, physicians, poets, and commanders, but never for astrologers. Instead, we read of them being exiled, laughed at, and even turned into the subject of popular tales, so that the allegories of stories—which are usually told about common sense and life—contained a critique of this vanity among the ancients. For those who explain **Homer** allegorically say that by that story of **Icarus**—who, committing himself to the thin air with fashioned wings, was plunged into the sea—the astrologers are signified. They, raising themselves into the sky on the wings of a rash profession, fall into a sea of lies when they are about to predict what their celestial dogmas (by which they seem to be sublimated) actually are. And why do we need other testimonies or conjectures, when daily experience itself testifies this to us? This is especially true in a matter where, if astrology can excel anywhere, it ought to excel most: in predicting the truth of the air—namely, its changes—rain, drought, heat, cold, winds, hail, and earthquakes. In these things they are daily caught in such falsehood that the state of almost no single day ever corresponds to their predictions. I observed during this winter, in my suburban villa where we wrote these things, every notable change of the air on individual days
