change, having meanwhile placed the decrees of the astrologers before my eyes, so may the healthy sky favor me everywhere, that in a continuous observation of over one hundred and thirty days, I saw no more than six or seven such days as I had previously foreseen would occur according to their books. My friend **Pandolfo Collenuccio** <note>Pandolfo Collenuccio (1444–1504) was a famous Italian humanist, jurist, and historian.</note>, a man indeed learned in the law but most ingeniously erudite in all literature, still remembers, I think, how much a certain **mathematician** <note>original: "mathematicus"; in the Renaissance, this term was frequently used as a synonym for "astrologer."</note> in **Bologna** gave us cause for laughter regarding this matter. On a certain day, he commanded us to expect the most copious rains, yet the brightest Sun made that entire day most clear and serene. **Ambrose** <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 340–397 AD), the Bishop of Milan and a Doctor of the Church.</note> in his ***Hexameron*** <note>original: "Hexameron"; a series of homilies on the six days of creation. Pico cites this to show that skepticism of astrology has deep roots in Christian tradition.</note> says that when, some days earlier, there was talk of rain which was said to be perhaps useful, someone said, "Behold, the **new moon** <note>original: "neomenia"; the first appearance of the moon in its cycle.</note> will provide it." However, no rain was poured out until rain was finally granted through the prayers of the church to manifest that it should not be hoped for from the beginnings of the Moon, but from the providence and mercy of the Creator. These are his words. From them, both the vanity of astrology and the efficacy of religion are proven by the facts themselves.

Therefore, those who are less capable of reason, and who have enslaved their faith to these men, can assert their freedom in this way: let them repeatedly ask them about the state of the air. When they find that these men tell falsehoods almost always, they will easily realize that if these **scoundrels** <note>A pun in the original Latin "nebulones" (worthless people/scoundrels) which derives from "nebula" (cloud or mist). Pico is mocking them for lying about the clouds.</note> lie so much about the clouds, they will predict false things much more in judging the fates of men and nations. For in the latter case, they are predicting things that are less subject to the heavens and far more difficult and laborious to foresee. 

But if anyone examines what they fabricate daily for hire regarding human **horoscopes** <note>original: "genituris"; literally "births" or "nativities."</note>, they will see that they lie even more than when they answer regarding the quality of the air. Unless I feared bringing the fault of folly upon myself while pursuing the follies of others in too much detail, I could list many horoscopes of the living and the dead—unhappy predictions for the fortunate, and exceedingly fortunate predictions for the miserable. In this matter, I lie as little as I know that divine truth, for which this present expedition fights, neither needs nor delights in our lies.

But I will be content with certain domestic examples by which I wish especially to warn those who, having a promise of a long life from the astrologers, forget the Gospel voice warning us to watch lest the Day of the Lord seize us unprepared. To **Pino Ordelaffi** <note>Pino III Ordelaffi (1436–1480), the ruler of Forlì.</note>, prince of **Forlì**, whom my sister **Lucrezia** had married, the astrologer **Girolamo Manfredi**—a man remarkable in our age—had promised total safety of life in the very year he died. From Manfredi, however, it is no wonder that the deaths of others were poorly foreseen, since he did not even foresee his own. For although he died the following summer, in the public prophecy of that year (which was fatal to him), he promised more than once that he would say many wonderful things the following year. I do not know how he will redeem his pledged faith, unless perhaps he now looks down upon earthly things more truly from heaven than he once looked up at celestial things from the earth. **Pietro Attendolo**, an ingenious young man who had as his wife **Eleonora**, the daughter of my brother **Galeotto**...

...**Aemilia** <note>The previous page likely referred to a person from or named Aemilia.</note>, died this past year, killed by the distress of a sudden and unexpected illness, even though the astrologer—whom he believed most implicitly—had predicted no such thing for him, but had instead promised a safe life. Did not **Constantia**, the most loving wife of my brother **Antonio** <note>Antonio Maria Pico della Mirandola (1458–1501), Pico’s brother.</note>, who departed this life in **Rome** two years ago amid the public mourning of almost the entire city, testify to us the vanity of that art? In the very year she left us in longing for her, she had received from an astrologer a promise not only of prosperous health but of a most happy life. Not forgetting this, even as she was drawing her last breath, she held the hand of her weeping husband, by whom she was uniquely cherished. "Behold," she said, "how true are the prophecies of the astrologers." 

Conversely, for my brother **Antonio** himself, good God, what evils, what heaps of troubles, what great dangers did astrology threaten this year? And yet, having experienced no injury from the heavens, he has lived with his family safe, his affairs secure, and his health intact, tossed by no disturbance of misfortune or danger. And lest you think perhaps that only our modern astrologers lie, you should know that the same thing happened to the ancients. **Seneca** <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BC – 65 AD), a Stoic philosopher. Pico refers here to Seneca’s satire, the *Apocolocyntosis* (The Pumpkinification of Claudius).</note>, in a certain passage where he tears into the most wicked **Claudius Caesar**, introduces **Mercury** among the gods procuring his death; to strike down that vanity in passing, among other reasons by which **Mercury** persuades them of the Emperor's death, he says: "out of pity, you should do this for the **Chaldeans** <note>original: "Chaldaeorum"; a term used in antiquity to denote astrologers or soothsayers from the Babylonian tradition.</note> as well, who for so many years now have been 'burying' him." For the **mathematicians** <note>original: "mathematici"; in the Renaissance, this term was frequently used as a synonym for "astrologers."</note> were certainly predicting in every single year that **Claudius** would die, yet he did not die. When I read this, there came to my mind our own little diviners who also "bury" the **Roman Pontiff** <note>The Pope.</note> every single year. **Cicero** writes that it was predicted by the **Chaldeans** for **Pompey**, **Crassus**, and **Caesar** alike, that none of them would die except in old age, at home, and in glory. Wherefore that most prudent orator says it seems a wonder to him that anyone exists who believes those whose predictions he sees daily refuted by facts and events.

### WHY ASTROLOGERS SOMETIMES PREDICT THE 
### TRUTH. Chapter 10.

<insert>S</insert>ometimes, however, the things they predicted do come to pass; but since the things that do *not* happen are far more numerous, why should we not judge that they have stumbled upon the truth by chance? Consider that there is no "old wives' art," however full of vain superstition, which might not be proven true by the same argument—namely, because what was predicted from it occasionally happens. For there is no method that cannot achieve this, even one you might make up yourself at random and by luck. Therefore, let those who are moved by that reasoning tell me: do they think every art of divination is true, or rather that many are vain and false? If they say many are false, I shall prove those "true" by the same argument: because sometimes, of course, what they foretold happens. If they say all are true, I will demonstrate that they believe in contradictions, because different arts of divination do not give the same answer regarding the same matters. For I have often experienced, even a hundred times, when...

...regarding the same question, I had both drawn a geomantic figure and outlined an astrological chart, yet a different outcome appeared to me in the marks than in the stars. If someone perhaps does not believe this, let him try it for himself and consult a palm reader <term>Chiromantem</term>, an astrologer <term>Astrologum</term>, and a geomancer <term>Geomantem</term> about the fate of the same man; he will see that almost always, what is designated in the lines of the hands is not the same as what will be pronounced either from geomantic marks or from astrological planets. And if he considers the actual outcome of the matter, he will find the truth more often where he least expects it—either because chance has more power where there is less reason, or because spiritual wickedness <note>Pico often attributes the occasional success of divination to demonic interference intended to lead people astray rather than any natural law.</note> more willingly mocks us in those matters. 

A multifaceted deceit, however, aids the predictions of astrologers, explaining why they are not so much proven by the reliability of their outcomes <term>Apotelesmaton</term> <note>From the Greek *apotelesma*, meaning the "completion" or "effect" of the stars' influence.</note> as they seem to many to be proven. For if they must speak of past events to show that things happened exactly as the heavens signified, they lack nothing for ensnaring the minds of the unskilled; since there is no position of the stars, no birth chart, in which a complex constellation of both prosperous and adverse significance cannot be found. This is especially true since they themselves have invented no fewer things in the sky than the stars God formed there from the beginning. Therefore, they will always have grounds in past events to defend their positioning; for they will rarely find in the Planets what they want, yet they make them both happy and unhappy in many ways—having more jurisdiction in heavenly matters, of course, than in earthly ones. 

Thus, the location of the sky, or the goodness or malice of a sign, or the radiation of another star, or "love" with the Sun, or "hatred" or "friendship" with the ascendant, will always support them. Or if these eventually do not suffice, they will implore help from the "fixed" stars—in which they themselves never fail to wander <note>Pico is making a pun here on the Latin *erraticas* (wandering stars or planets) and *errant* (to be mistaken or to wander off course).</note>—or if even those do not satisfy, there will be ready for them either the "images of the Indians," or the "lots of the Egyptians," or the "shadow-projections" <term>antiscia</term> <note>A technique involving zodiacal points equidistant from the solstice points.</note> of Firmicus <term>Firmici</term> <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer.</note>, or the "twelfth-parts" <term>dodecathemoria</term> <note>A system dividing each zodiac sign into twelve smaller parts.</note> of the Chaldeans <term>Chaldæorum</term>, or something entirely fabricated by them, in which they glory all the more as if over some hidden dogma, the more false and fictional it is. 

In predicting the future, they have less opportunity for deception, though they do not lack it even here; for they guess many things, observing the earth <note>The Latin text reads *tetram*, likely a variant or error for *terram* (earth), used to contrast with *caelum* (heaven).</note> rather than the sky, following that saying of Euripides <term>Euripidis</term>: 
> He who guesses well, let him be the best prophet. <note>original: "Recordati bene, qui conijciet, is uates optimus esto." Pico translates a famous Greek fragment into Latin to show that astrology is mere guesswork.</note>

And they pronounce certain generalities that almost cannot fail to happen, or at least cannot be thought not to have happened; and they offer many things ambiguously, in the manner of oracles, always making some exception by which the prediction can be diminished, increased, or obstructed—so that if it happens, you cannot say it wasn't predicted, and if it doesn't happen, they are nonetheless considered truthful. You will rarely hear anything explicit, specific, or certain from them; and when they do dare such a thing, they are either proven right by chance (which is very rare) or refuted by experience (which is very frequent). 

But it happens as that man said of the temple of Apollo <term>Apollonis</term>: that successful predictions are celebrated and remembered, while no one records the errors; for those who favor them do not want these errors known, and those who despise them are entirely ignorant of both. However, one must not pass over what Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo, who famously argued against astrology in *The City of God*.</note> says, and what reason persuades us: that hidden demo[ns]...

...or by an inspiration <note>original: "afflatione"</note> which they experience without knowing it, through which they sometimes reach a truth they would not otherwise attain. This should be considered to happen if, by some miraculous prediction, they pronounce some specific deed or word to have occurred—a feat which even Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential ancient astronomer and author of the "Tetrabiblos," the foundational text of systematic astrology.</note> testified that the art of astrology itself cannot provide. But someone will wonder how they experience this without knowing it, and yet we think they predict those things through demonic inspiration <note>original: "afflatione dæmonica"</note>. Yet this can happen in many ways, regarding which I will warn the astrologers by a similar case. 

For it is admitted among them that one astronomer is more "fortunate" than another in attaining the truth, even when both have equal talent, learning, and diligence. So let them tell me what this "being fortunate" is, if they do not track the truth by any other way than the dogmas of the art? For he who holds these dogmas equally or even better will still not be equally fortunate in predicting the truth. Furthermore, this is nothing other than the fact that almost always concerning the same matter, various constellations occur—and conflicting ones over the same constellation—or the diverse opinions of authors arise. The mind of the predictor is moved from above <note>original: "flecti cœlitus," literally "bent from the heavens," suggesting a spiritual nudge.</note> so that, while attempting many things, he unintentionally <term>imprudenter</term> <note>Meaning "without foresight" or "unawares."</note> stumbles upon the truth in a correct judgment. 

This same thing can also be achieved by the occult and hidden inspiration of a demon, by whose drive a person may be moved without perceiving the agitation themselves. How this happens, when it happens, is not to be explained more extensively now. But divine power and wisdom do not only allow demons this capability, but also that they themselves—by fulfilling the deed—make true what had previously been falsely predicted. No punishment is more fittingly demanded by supreme justice than that those proud minds who do not submit themselves to divine truth should thereafter bind their faith and their freedom to the lies of a single scoundrel and sycophant. 

But I think we have said enough now as to why these triflers <note>original: "nugatores," meaning idlers or purveyors of nonsense.</note> sometimes seem to blurt out and spread some truths—although, as we were saying from the beginning, one should not labor greatly over this matter, since:

<header>On Astrology, Book III.</header>

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA’S Disputations Against Astrology, Book III.

### WHAT WAS DEALT WITH IN THE PRECEDING BOOK, AND *what is to be done hereafter, and in what order.* Chapter I.

We have addressed the question posed by the public, who constantly ask about astrologers: why is there such faith in their answers if there is no solid foundation to their profession? I mentioned that this is a question that more accurate and learned men <note>Pico often distinguishes between "the people" (vulgi), who are easily swayed by superstition, and the "learned" (doctiores), who demand rational proof.</note> do not ask, for they know that what astrologers say does not happen frequently, but rarely—as one might say, by accident. Nor, if their predictions do come true, must we conclude that the art is necessarily true—just as we shouldn't necessarily conclude it is false simply because they very often lie in their predictions. Indeed, false things can be pronounced even from true principles <note>original: "præceptis"</note>, not so much because of the absolute falsity of the art, but because of its speculative and conjectural uncertainty—to say nothing of the ignorance or negligence of the practitioner.

Conversely, truths may be pronounced from false premises, not through the truth of the doctrine, but through the cleverness of the predictor, or by luck, or chance, or the hidden prompting of spirits <note>original: "numinum"; Pico refers back to the idea from Book II that demons or spiritual forces might provide "lucky" guesses.</note> that foreknow what they predict, or by other causes which we sufficiently explained in the previous book. If anyone cannot be persuaded of this, let him recall how much we discussed just a little while ago—hopefully without causing offense or envy—regarding the negligence and errors of the astrologers of our own time. Unless he wishes to be deceived, he cannot be led to believe that whenever they hit upon the truth, it was discovered by their method <note>original: "inuentam"</note> rather than simply stumbled upon <note>original: "repertam"</note>.

The following treatise will settle this dispute entirely. In it, we will demonstrate that the things they predict about the heavens have no causes or signs there by which they are brought about or indicated. Or, if they do originate there, they happen in a way different from what astrologers believe. Or even if they did happen in that way, they do not stem from these specific causes in the heavens, nor from these origins <note>original: "primordijs"</note> of things on earth. Furthermore, even if all these things were granted, certainly neither these origins nor those causes could be grasped by human beings; or if they could perhaps be grasped, they have not yet been grasped. I believe that once all this has been demonstrated, it will be beyond controversy for any sharp mind that whenever an astrologer happens upon the truth, it can be attributed to no cause more truly than to anything *other* than the truth of his profession. For it will appear clearly that this profession is false for so many reasons, supported by no rational truth, but is instead a collection of fictions and deceptions, and therefore by its very nature a liar.

Therefore, let us now begin the refutation itself, examining first the core of the entire matter: whether the heavens actually bring about what these diviners pronounce from the heavens. This will be handled by us in such a way that in this specific book, we shall maintain that the heavens act upon us only through **motion and light**, <note>This is Pico’s core scientific argument: he rejects "occult" or "astrological" influences, arguing that the stars only affect the Earth through physical heat (light) and movement.</note>

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing from the previous page's discussion on empirical proof.</note>...ment, and that besides these it is in vain to imagine other more hidden influences <note>original: "occultiores afflatus"; Pico refers to the "breaths" or spiritual emanations astrologers claimed flowed from stars.</note>. Furthermore, from that light and motion of the stars, nothing else is communicated to the receiving matter except motion, light, and heat. I say heat, which both consumes bodies in its general flow and disposes those bodies capable of life toward life and its functions. This heat flows from all stars, although it is not universally admitted that the outflows of all the planets reach us. Truly, that the stars bestow anything besides these things upon lower things can neither be proven by reason, nor demonstrated by experiments, nor persuaded by the authority of the leaders of philosophy. Rather, all these things stand in the way of us understanding, in any way, that the power of the heavens reaches <term>sublunary bodies</term> <note>Bodies "below the moon," meaning everything on Earth, which was thought to be subject to change and decay unlike the "incorruptible" heavens.</note> beyond these common influences. Therefore, the peculiar properties of things—even physical ones, whether they follow the species or the particular thing—do not have their origin from the stars (except by way of a universal principle), but from the proper nature of the things themselves and their <term>proximate and related causes</term> <note>In Aristotelian logic, a "proximate cause" is the immediate, direct reason something happens, like a fire burning wood, as opposed to a "universal cause" like the Sun.</note>. And we shall prove this very opinion of ours to be probable and asserted by no other arguments more than those which the astrologers themselves use against us. 

When this has been sufficiently explained, let us nevertheless come to that treatise in the fourth book, so that even if we grant the astrologers that hidden powers exist in the rays beyond the effect of light and heat—from which humans and the rest of nature might uniquely receive various gifts and powers—we may yet prove, by the clearest reasons and the consensus of all the more illustrious philosophers and theologians, that those powers they imagine do not exist in them, nor are they the ones by which they divine from the sky. Once that is sufficiently finished and we have retracted each point they prophesy about the stars, let us add this and leave it most firmly attested: **that which is not caused by the heavens is not signified by the heavens.** That is, those things for which celestial bodies are not the causes are not necessarily their signs. Therefore, there is no reason why they can be foreseen from the sky. Now, about to perform what we first proposed, let us see with what arguments they attack us—those who contend that all things are led and governed as if bound to the stars—so that we may soon not only repel the same, but, relying on divine help, drive them back against the adversaries themselves with greater force than they arrived.

### FIVE REASONS BY WHICH ASTROLOGY 
### *seems to be strengthened. Chapter II.*

The arguments by which astrologers attempt to persuade us that all changes in the sublunary world—but also the diversities of all things, as well as fortuitous events, and human character and talents—depend on the stars, are chiefly these. There is one voice among theologians and philosophers: that the lower world is governed by God through the heavens. Aristotle teaches this in that most common sentiment: *This lower world is necessarily contiguous to the higher motions, so that all its power is governed from there.* <note>original: "Necessariò mundum hunc inferiorem superioribus motibus esse contiguum..." Pico quotes Aristotle's "Meteorology" 1.2.</note> Thus also the <insert>venerable</insert> Augustine said: *these grosser bodies are ruled and moved by the subtler bodies.* <note>original: "per corpora subtiliora grossiora hæc regi atq; moueri"</note> Who then, they ask, would doubt that any changes whatsoever in earthly things are caused by the motions of the higher bodies? ...experience, as the seasons of the year vary by the Sun's approach toward and departure from us <note>Pico refers to the solar cycle of solstices and equinoxes.</note>, from which the state and condition of all living things is also varied, while the sky tempers the fields, while it varies the fruits, giving and taking away. But even in its daily revolution, the Sun changes the qualities of the air, more or less, at noon, morning, and evening—heating, drying, and leaving the air to moisture and cold. As for the Moon, who is ignorant of how much power she has over all bodies, especially the more fluid ones? She causes the tides of the Ocean, rising and falling, moves the Sea <note>original: "Pontum"</note>, and sends it into and brings it onto the lands; but also the animals submerged in the straits, enclosed in the prisons of their shells, vary their bodies according to the motion of the Moon <note>A common ancient belief that shellfish grew and shrank in size according to the lunar phases.</note>. The <term>Critical Days</term> <note>original: "Crisimi," from the Greek "krisimos." These were specific days in the course of a disease when a physician expected a "crisis" or decisive change for better or worse.</note> observed by physicians follow the motions of the Moon and the Sun. We see that at the new Moon, the full Moon, and the half Moon, storms are very often stirred up, and the <term>humors</term> <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—believed to determine health and personality.</note> are agitated in bodies; hence many observations about the Moon’s motions have been accepted by shepherds, sailors, and farmers, and confirmed by manifold experience over many centuries. Why, then, if we perceive the more manifest impressions of the luminaries <note>The "luminaries" are the Sun and the Moon.</note> and their authority in changing lower things, should we believe the remaining stars to be idle and ineffective? Why should we not believe that their powers reach us, though more hidden, by which the bodies subject to them are affected in various ways? Those who are skilled and wise in these matters can foreknow certain more secret things regarding future events, more so than what doctors, shepherds, farmers, and sailors predict. Furthermore, no one would deny that the condition of the air and the storms vary according to the state and position of the stars, since heat, cold, dryness, moisture, and whatever impressions occur on high are generated by celestial motions and influences. For if dry breaths trapped in the bowels of the earth move the earth [cause earthquakes], if the causes in the air arise from the excess or defect of those four qualities, if excessive moisture or dryness causes the <term>high price of grain</term> <note>original: "caritatem annonæ." In the ancient and medieval world, the price of grain was the primary indicator of economic stability or famine.</note> when fruits are either gathered or sown, and in turn a moderate and timely state of the air creates fertility—who will deny that not only changes of storms and earthquakes, but also plagues and various kinds of diseases in men and cattle, the healthfulness of regions, and fertility or sterility proceed from the stars? Then, if we also consist of those same qualities and bodily <term>temperament</term> <note>The "complexio," or the specific balance of humors in an individual body.</note>, and our characters and wits are varied (yet with our freedom intact), why can it not be that inclinations in us toward anger, gentleness, and other good and bad effects are caused by the stars, either by stirring up or reining in the bile, blood, phlegm, and black bile—humors which those emotions for the most part accompany? Why can the dry and hot impressions of the heavens not likewise, by sharpening the bile within us, excite us to strife, brawls, insults, and enmities? From which wars, slaughters, and devastations arise, and by which empires and kingdoms are changed. After this, Ptolemy concludes thus: if the stars cause the diversity of the body and the soul, this is then derived to those things which are indeed extrinsic, but have an affinity with them—such as a wife has with the body, possessions and wealth, or as dignity and honors have with the soul...

This is the primary reasoning of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), whose *Tetrabiblos* was the most influential textbook on astrology in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note>, nor does he prove the power of the stars to be the cause of all things in any other way than through the production of **primary qualities** <term>primary qualities</term> <note>In ancient and medieval science, these were Heat, Cold, Moisture, and Dryness; all things were thought to be composed of these four.</note>, through which they might subsequently produce all other things as well. For this reason, he offers no other causes for why Saturn does this, Jupiter does that, or Mars performs those things, except that Jupiter is a planet that is hot and moist, Saturn is dry and cold, and Mars is more dry and burning. He holds this view concerning the **wandering stars** <note>The planets (from the Greek *planētēs*, "wanderer").</note> and the **non-wandering stars** <note>The "fixed" stars of the constellations.</note> alike, judging the non-wandering ones by the nature of the wandering ones, based on the nature of their primary qualities. 

But truly, others, having abandoned the primary qualities, might take refuge in **occult powers** <note>Hidden properties or "virtues" that cannot be explained by simple heating or cooling, often used to explain why a specific star affects a specific person's fate.</note> and more eminent forces, which it is not fitting to doubt exist in the celestial bodies in great number and efficacy. If we observe any singular and excellent gifts in earthly things, we are accustomed to think of them as gifts of the heavens—things which do not follow the elemental qualities from which those bodies coalesce, but rather follow a virtue infused into them from the heavens. How much more, then, will those most noble bodies—with such clear light, such vast bulk, and such rapid movement—not lack powers and properties of this kind? Or in what way, if they are transmitted to the earth along with motion and light, will they not be the cause of wonders among us? 

Finally, the course of human affairs (concerning which the astrologers' divination of the heavens and of fate seems to persuade people everywhere, even against their will) shows a familiar and very frequent variety. We see many things happen beyond the powers of our mortality, many things beyond reason and merit, and very many things beyond the order and established condition of the human state, which seem to have no possible causes elsewhere than in the heavens. 

This man is born suited for philosophy, that one for poetry; another, scorning letters, handles either civil business or arms more willingly and successfully. From where does this variety of talents come? There is one who counts riches as nothing; there is another who would sell his soul for profit. This man is sober, that one a scoundrel; this one bold, that one fearful. Whence comes such great dissimilarity in character? **Alexander the Great** <note>original: "Alexander Magnus"</note> conquered the East as quickly as he saw it; whence came the impulse of such great success? What force unlocked the secrets of nature for his teacher **Aristotle**? What force for **Plato**, or before them for **Pythagoras**, **Socrates**, and the rest? This reason is too great to be believed to have sprouted from the earth. 

On the other hand, who would not ascribe these things to the fortuitous paths of the stars: that an innocent man is condemned, a guilty man is gifted with rewards; that the industry, skill, talent, and learning of many men go begging, while the idleness and wickedness of others are enriched? That a pirate, bloodied by slaughters, amidst a thousand dangers of sea and land, finally dies at home among his own people and in old age, while a most gentle man—most ready to help—is butchered by the swords of those who did not even intend it? Then there are those portents of character, those "monsters" who either delight in foul things or, to put it simply, wander outside the laws of humanity—do they not seem to testify to a certain force and necessity of a fatal power within themselves? Since the life of mortals is full of these things, they persuade many that these changes of good and evil, deserved or undeserved, and such a great...

## THE FIRST REASON IS REFUTED AND IT IS SHOWN 
## that the heavens are a universal cause and the variety 
## of individuals should not be attributed to it. Chapter III.

**W**e <note>The original Latin begins with "Has," referring to "these reasons." The English translation adjusts for the decorative initial.</note> have striven not merely to weaken these reasons of the astrologers, but even to amplify them, lest anyone complain they were cheated of their due. First, however, we want the Reader to know that even if one were to concede these reasons, it does not therefore follow that any such thing as astrology could exist, as will be made clear in the following books. But we are so far from conceding them that we take strong arguments against the astrologers from those very same points. For as far as the first reason is concerned, as soon as the astrologers say that all lower motion depends on the motion of the heavens, they immediately contradict their own dogma. 

From this follows that principle well-worn among philosophers: that the heavens are the **universal cause** <term>universal cause</term> <note>In Scholastic philosophy, a universal cause (like the sun or the heavens) provides the general power for an effect to happen, but the specific result depends on the "particular" or "proximate" cause (like a specific seed or parent).</note> of lower effects. A universal cause, however, does not distinguish between effects; one does not ask of it why *this* happens or *that* happens, but rather one asks this of the **proximate causes** <term>proximate causes</term>, which are various and different according to the difference and variety of the effects. Since among these proximate causes one does one thing and another does something else, the universal cause does all things with all of them. 

Since this is clearly apparent in things of different nature and species, it is a wonder how they do not understand that the same must be much more believed regarding the variety of individuals. The more an individual is particular—deriving its origin largely from **matter** <note>In the Aristotelian tradition Pico follows, "matter" is the principle of individuation; it is what makes two things of the same species different from one another.</note>—the less it can be referred back to a cause that is supremely formal and universal. For who does not see that the heavens produce a horse with a horse, and a lion with a lion? Is there any position of the stars under which a lion is not born of a lion, or a horse from a horse? Why, by the same reasoning, should the heavens not produce different children from different parents, even under the same or a similar constellation? 

This is proven by experience itself: we sometimes see those born at the same hour, and under the same inclination of the heavens, who are nevertheless most different in fortune, character, and body. At this point, the astrologer cannot avoid the blow. For when the birth of twins is thrown in their faces, they are accustomed to flee to the **wheel of Nigidius** <note>original: "Nigidianam rotam." This refers to Nigidius Figulus, a Roman scholar who argued that just as a potter's wheel spins so fast that two drops of ink hit different spots even if applied nearly simultaneously, the heavens move so fast that twins born moments apart have different fates.</note>, in which it is impossible to mark the same spot twice with ink. But here too they explain themselves poorly, since they themselves cannot grasp that difference of a rapid moment, from which there nonetheless arises—as they would have it—so great a difference of fate. Therefore, while they try to defend the efficiency of the heavens, they fall into other snares, so that they are forced to confess against their will that they cannot possess knowledge of that efficiency. 

Furthermore, we do not only confront them with twins (where the small delay that intervenes as one comes out after the other offers them a tiny handle for responding). Rather, we point to those born at the same moment from different parents, yet within the same longitude and latitude of the same region. The astrologer must describe the same **theme of the heavens** <note>The "thema coeli" is the technical term for a horoscope or birth chart.</note> for these individuals and must pronounce the same things, both concerning what will happen after the hour of birth and what happened to them even within their mother's womb—for since they were born at the same hour, the astrologer must think they were conceived at the same hour. What, I ask, will the astrologer answer concerning these? Since...

<meta>Catchword: Which</meta>

...even if the constellation is exactly the same, will the fate of both individuals not appear different? Could anyone—unless they were insane—say anything other than that those celestial influences, though universal in their power and strength, are determined and distinguished by **proximate and secondary causes**? <term>proximate and secondary causes</term> <note>In the Aristotelian science used by Pico, a "proximate cause" is the immediate trigger for an event, like a parent's genetics or the quality of soil for a seed, whereas the heavens are a "universal cause" that provides the general energy for life to exist at all.</note> 

If this is so, how can the astrologers promise to provide the cause for the entire variety of individuals based on the hour of their birth? They claim the stars decide why this person is pale and that one is dark; why this one is short and that one tall; why this one is slow-witted and that one clever; why one is loved by all and another is a nuisance; why one is born for philosophy and another for trade; why one is rich and another poor; why one is short-lived and another long-lived. All this variety among individuals of the same species is far less a result of the heavens than is the diversity of different species under the same genus—such as why a lion is born now, then a human, then a donkey, or an elephant. Just as all these species follow the specific differences of their proximate causes, so too do individuals follow the differences of their "seeds" (if we consider bodily qualities or natural talent), or their education and free will (if we consider their animal or rational faculties), or their parents' own choices, prudence, and opportunities (if we consider external and fortuitous circumstances).

## HOW THE HEAVENS ACT BY MOTION AND LIGHT, 
## and are the universal cause of the meteorological elements, 
## minerals, and living things. Chapter IV.

**B**y as much as a universal cause is more divine and eminent than particular causes, we hold a view of the heavens that is as much truer as it is more honorable than that of the astrologers. To make the reason for this universal efficiency shine more brightly—and to explain more clearly what the heavens do and do not effect—we must begin from a deeper starting point concerning the nature of the heavens and their actions upon "lower" <note>In the pre-modern worldview, "lower" refers to the Earthly realm below the moon, which is subject to change and decay, unlike the "higher" unchanging heavens.</note> bodies. 

The heaven is a natural body, the most perfect of all natural bodies. As it is a natural body, it possesses both motion and a quality perceivable by the senses. Therefore, the most perfect motion and the most perfect sensible quality must belong to this most perfect of natural bodies. No motion is more perfect than the **circular** <note>original: "orbiculari"</note>, and no quality perceivable by the senses is more perfect than **light**. These, therefore, shall be the specific properties of the celestial body. Furthermore, the heaven is of an "unfading" or incorruptible substance, since its motion and quality have no contrary <note>In ancient physics, things decay because they are made of opposing elements (like hot vs. cold). Since circular motion has no "opposite" direction and light has no physical opposite, Pico argues the heavens do not decay.</note>. 

Because it is the most perfect body, it must also occupy the first place—that is, the highest—and to it, the "first motion" is owed. Now, that which is "first" in any category is the cause of all others contained in that series, even if they do not all relate to the cause in the same way. Therefore, because the heaven is moved by the first motion, it moves all other things that are moved; if that motion were to cease, the others would not move. This is just like in the **microcosm** <note>original: "minore mundo." The "lesser world" or microcosm refers to the human body, which was believed to reflect the structure of the entire universe (the macrocosm).</note>: if the motion of the heart ceases, it is necessary that all the motions of the living being perish. For this reason, Aristotle rightly said in the eighth book of the *Physics* <note>original: "Physicæ auscultationis," the standard Latin title for Aristotle's Physics.</note> that the motion of the first heaven is "life" to all things, since the most internal motion is the most evident and common operation of life. This, then, is the singular dignity and efficacy of the heavens toward our lower world: that by its tireless agitation, all other motions are both ordered and set in motion.

# On Astrology, Book III.
### Page 457

How universal this efficiency is—and how it does not distinguish between lower motions by this principle—is quite evident. For just as it cooperates with a falling **clod of earth**, so too does the one and the same celestial motion cooperate equally with a **flame** moving upward, and indeed with all other kinds of motion. 

The heavens possess another prerogative derived from **light**. For since light is the highest quality of bodies—and the first step of life for corporeal nature—and since the highest points of a lower order always reach toward the furthest reaches of a higher order, it follows necessarily that light possesses a certain **perfecting power** over bodies. <note>original: "consummatricem quandam... uirtutem"</note> Meanwhile, it also possesses something of a vital nature. This is not because light itself is alive or brings life directly, but because it best prepares and disposes a body capable of life to receive life. This is because a certain **heat** follows light as its own property—a heat that is not fiery, nor airy, but **celestial**, just as light is the proper quality of the heavens. 

I speak of a heat that is most effective and supremely healthy <note>original: "salutaris," implying life-giving or wholesome</note>, penetrating all things, fostering all things, and moderating all things. This is the primary gift of the heavens by which bodies are perfected and living things are prepared for life. This is in addition to the agitation of **circular motion**, which is necessary not only to carry that light and heat down to us and to impart it to the earth more or less through a wonderful timing of turns, but also so that we, being moved, might be made more cheerful by the heat which flows constantly from a body in perpetual motion. 

We perceive the power of this most beneficent heat throughout the entire **corruptible world**, <term>corruptible world</term> <note>In Renaissance science, the "corruptible world" refers to the Earth and everything below the moon, where things are born, change, and die, unlike the "incorruptible" stars.</note> in things both unfinished and complete, and in the inanimate as well as the animate. For it contains and preserves the elements just as their own location does, acting like their form and a kind of craftsman; it surrounds all things, yet also diffuses itself intimately through all things. 

Just as it is the privilege of the **First Motion** to turn all other motions (which cannot move without it), so too is it the privilege of the **first sensible quality** <note>Meaning light/heat</note> that no other qualities can act without it. Therefore, if they were deprived of celestial heat, coldness could not act as cold, nor could heat act as warmth. For that **sidereal heat** <note>Heat originating from the stars</note> is not the opposite of cold in the way that fiery or airy heat is; rather, it contains all elemental qualities within its simple excellence, just as the nature of the heavens contains every body, as circular motion contains all motions, and as light contains all heats. 

As the **Pythagoreans** would say: it is as **unity** contains all numbers. <note>The Pythagoreans believed that the number One (Unity) was the source of all things and contained the potential for all other numbers within it.</note> Thus, those who deny that cold elements can be preserved by the heavens are mistaken, unless they believe the stars also influence the world with "coldness" in addition to heat. They would have a point if the heavens preserved warm things with a heat of the same nature and principle as our own; but instead, the heavens preserve all things—hot, cold, moist, and dry—by this unique quality of theirs. While this quality is none of those four elemental qualities, it nonetheless encloses them all within itself—not as they exist in the elements, but as a "manifold" concluded within "unity." It does this through a principal virtue, through which it rules them in such a way that it unites each thing to itself by preserving it, governs the whole by moderating them all, and gives birth to other things by mixing them all together. 

However, the name "**heat**" is deceptive; when we hear it, we immediately understand something that is the opposite of cold. But while elemental heat is indeed closer in nature to that celestial heat than elemental cold is (just as it is more perfect), nothing prevents celestial heat from being exalted above the properties of both elements, possessing both powers...

<meta>This page continues Pico's argument regarding the "celestial heat" and its role as a universal cause. On the previous page, he established that celestial heat is a byproduct of light and motion, serving as a vitalizing force. Here, he addresses how this single "heat" can be responsible for contrary effects like cold or moisture.</meta>

## Giovanni Pico della Mirandola
### Page 458

...to embrace, just as we see brightness—when we speak of an opposite thing—in a dark or black color. Yet no one would deny that black color is both preserved and made effective by the brightness of light, no differently than white is; although the latter is closer to the nature of light, and even shares a common name, so that it is sometimes called "bright." Finally, if the substance of the heavens, as the primary body, most perfectly contains every body in both power and virtue, its own proper quality must necessarily contain every bodily quality in virtue and perfection. This is what we call **celestial heat**, the offspring of light. We call it "heat" both because it provides life-giving warmth, and because among all the properties of the elements, heat is most similar to it. Thus, even when it deviates from its celestial condition, it primarily exercises the operation of heat, as we shall explain later. 

Therefore, if this heat contains all the qualities of the lower bodies in its perfection and virtue—including all those qualities alongside their immediate causes—it will both generate and nourish them. This is much like **seminal heat** <note>The internal heat within seeds or embryos that Aristotelian biology believed drove the development of life.</note>, which, although it is called "heat," nevertheless governs, matures, preserves, forms, and regulates all the matter of the fetus, whether those parts are cold or hot.

For this reason, if anyone asks me whether the heavens produce coldness by their own nature <note>original: "per se"</note> or only incidentally <note>original: "ex accidenti"</note>, I will answer: if you are asking what the heavens produce by themselves with no intermediate cause, they produce only heat by their own nature, and other qualities incidentally—just as heat itself incidentally causes cooling, as we will explain in the following chapter. However, if you ask what they produce as a **universal cause** acting with secondary causes, they produce coldness just as much as heat, and dryness as much as moisture. In this way, the heavens are no less involved when water generates water than when fire generates fire; nor can water generate water without the heavens any more than fire can generate fire. When the heavens generate the substances of the elements, they also generate their corresponding properties; hence, with water they produce coldness, and with fire, heat. 

Indeed, if we were to deny that the heavens produce anything other than heat by their own nature, those absurdities mentioned by <term>Thomas</term> <note>Referring to St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential medieval theologian whose views on celestial influence Pico is analyzing and partially contesting.</note> would follow: that coldness, dryness, and moisture do not exist by their own nature in the universe, but only by accident; or that the substantial forms of the lower bodies are not contained within the power of the celestial bodies. These absurdities do not follow at all when we deny that the heavens—by themselves and from their own nature—cool the air or other lower bodies. Therefore, those arguments of <term>Thomas</term> do not prove what we deny, but rather what we assert.

We have seen what the heavens do to the elements, and we have first confirmed their universal efficiency here; let us now descend to other things that are made from the elements. That same heat—the son of light—raises vaporous exhalations from earthly bodies, thinning what is thick and dissolving what is dreg-like; it gives birth to those things that occur on high, varying according to the diversity of the material that is raised upward. For if vapor is raised from a fluid body, it creates moist impressions in the middle or lowest region of the air. But if a fiery evaporation is raised from dry and earthy material to the higher regions adjacent to the **ether** <note>The "fifth element" that makes up the heavens; the region above the air.</note>, it necessarily grows hot from the proximity of the motion and the fire. Therefore, that celestial heat works all these things, whether they be cold or hot, since they all come from vapors, which only heat can draw out...

<summary>Pico explains that celestial heat, as a universal cause, works with secondary elements to produce all physical qualities (heat, cold, moisture, dryness). He argues that while the heavens are inherently "hot," they are the necessary power behind all elemental generation, including meteorological phenomena like rain and fire.</summary>

## On Astrology, Book III

...heat and universally all things, since their distinction and variety arise not from the variety of the **constellation**—as the astrologers fabricate—but depend on the **matter** and the **place** in which they are generated. This is well known from Aristotle’s books on *Meteorology* and Plato’s *Timaeus*. Therefore, when Aristotle was about to treat this part of nature, he put forth that common saying: "the lower things are continuous with the upper things," <note>original: "continua superioribus esse inferiora"</note> so that all their power might be governed from there. 

Although this could truly be understood more universally—based on what we said regarding **celestial motion** and **heat**, by which all things are moved and nourished—it was nonetheless said by Aristotle specifically on account of <term>meteorological impressions</term> <note>In the 15th century, "impressions" referred to atmospheric phenomena like rain, wind, comets, or lightning caused by the interaction of celestial heat and earthly vapors.</note>, which he was primarily dealing with at that time. Wherefore, intending to prove or explain what he had said, he added that of all these things, the lower elements are the "matter," while the heavens are the "efficient cause." 

I wonder, however, that certain interpreters exhaust themselves to defend Aristotle from the charge that he said "every lower power is governed from the heavens," as if our **freedom** were also endangered by these words. They do not see from the context of the words that what is said pertains only to the **elements**. For there, when he uses the word "world" <note>original: "mundum"</note>, he is referring to the elementary bodies filling this **sublunary space**; he calls this "the world" without including the living things that inhabit that world. 

This is most evident from the sequence of the speech; for after he stated that he had determined in his earlier books that there are four bodies below the heavens—fire, air, water, and earth—he then adds:
> "Since therefore the world around the whole earth consists of these bodies, whose affections we are about to discuss: this world is by necessity continuous with the upper motions, so that all its power is governed from there." 

Therefore, the "world" whose every power he said is governed by the superior body is this very mass of the **four elements**. No other "world" is "continuous" with the upper motions in this sense, nor was he planning to discuss the "affections" of any other world in that book. Certainly, in that work there is no mention of plants or animals, but only of those things which occur in the elements—such as comets and other atmospheric phenomena—and whatever common experiences of air and water there are, as he himself states just before in the preface. 

Accordingly, let our **diviners** stop holding up this testimony of the Philosopher <note>A standard title for Aristotle in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> in their annual prophecies as if it were a decoration and strength for their fraud. In that very book, the most prudent Aristotle actually detracts from astrology, for he seeks the causes of neither rain, nor earthquakes, nor other effects of this kind in the stars, but in **matter**. He argues that the sun's heat affects things in different ways according to the variety of the material, not according to the diversity of the constellation. 

This, then, is how the matter stands regarding atmospheric phenomena. More perfect bodies devoid of life, such as **gems** and **metals**, coalesce from lower matter and are processed and formed by the force of that radiant heat. Nor does it stand in the way that we said this heat proceeds from light, even though light does not reach certain subterranean places in which those precious mixtures are generated. For even if one does not accept the opinion of certain Platonists—that light penetrates all bodies through their "transparency" <note>original: "diaphano"</note>, even if it is not seen when pressed into the densest bodies or dispersed through the thinnest—certainly it cannot be de... <note>catchword "gari" suggests the next word is "negari" (denied).</note>

<summary>Pico argues that Aristotle’s famous claim about the heavens "governing" the Earth refers strictly to physical elements and weather, not to human fate or specific astrological constellations. He contends that diversity in nature comes from the variety of earthly matter acted upon by a single celestial heat.</summary>

<keywords>Aristotle, Meteorology, celestial heat, sublunary world, four elements, astrological fraud, free will, gems and metals, Plato, Timaeus</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s argument from page 459. He is refuting the astrologers' claim that specific celestial configurations (the "stars") are the direct cause of earthly variety. Instead, he argues that the heavens provide a general, vitalizing heat, while the specific qualities of objects are determined by "secondary causes" (the nature of the matter itself).</meta>

<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

...it should not be denied that heat diffused from light can reach places where the light itself does not penetrate—just as the heat of a fire can be felt through a wall, even if the flame itself cannot be seen. Thus, there is nothing to prevent the light poured upon mountains and caverns from failing to enter within (being repelled by the opacity and density of the body, which are not suitable dispositions for receiving light), while nevertheless sending its heat inside. For although such bodies cannot be illuminated, they can still be heated—indeed, even more so than bodies that are thin and transparent. How the mixing of such things is brought about by the heavens, and how it is conversely brought about by <note>Secondary causes are the natural, earthly processes or physical laws that act as the immediate cause of an event, as opposed to the "First Cause" (God) or general celestial influence.</note> secondary causes, we shall explain in the solution to the fourth reason.

The remaining things are those that live by the breath of this heat. Indeed, as we gathered a little earlier, since this quality holds the highest rank in bodies, it serves to perfect those bodies—as we have described—in such a way that it is spread directly beneath life itself. It binds together, as if at the furthest edges, the life to the body and the body to the life. For this reason, in all living things, there is a medium between the soul (the fountain of life) and what is seen as the coarser dwelling-place [the body]. This medium we call the <term>spirit</term> <note>In Renaissance philosophy, the "spirit" (spiritus) was considered a subtle, vaporous substance that acted as a bridge, allowing the non-physical soul to communicate with and move the physical body.</note>. It is a most thin body, invisible to light, and most closely related to that celestial heat. Life is present primarily in this spirit, and through it, the soul unfolds and diffuses its powers into this visible body and back again. 

Likewise, this kind of spirit lies hidden in seminal matter. That more divine power—the architect of the works of life—uses the mystery of this spirit in place of the soul; it flows down like water, propagating the likeness of the generator into the matter it has occupied. However, these spirits are not useful for generating bodies, or preserving them, or performing the duties of the senses, if they are destitute of the help of the **celestial spirit** (that is, the heat we mentioned). Because the celestial spirit is more mobile, pure, and effective—and therefore closer to life—it strengthens the weakness of the lower spirit and, through its commerce, renders it more akin to the soul. 

Thus, it is no longer an argument that the **heavens are alive** simply because they nourish living things with their rays. For all these things live by their own souls, and are propagated by the power of the soul implanted in their seeds, with the heat of the heavens merely supporting them. It does not act as the direct giver of life, but rather as the most convenient and immediate disposer for life, for the reasons we have stated. No one would say that the power of seeing, which comes from the soul, is "in the light" or "comes through the light," even though we cannot see without light. Whether the life of the heavens can be proved by other reasons was discussed by us in our <term>Harmony of Plato and Aristotle</term> <note>original: "concordia Platonis & Aristot." This refers to a major, now-lost work by Pico where he intended to prove that the philosophies of Plato and Aristotle were fundamentally in agreement.</note>. Thus, it is clear that in the corporeal world, nothing indeed happens without the heavens; and yet, that *this* or *that* specific thing happens is not from the heavens, but from secondary causes. The heavens perform such things in cooperation with all these causes, according to what those causes were born to do, whether they pertain to the species or to the individual.

# THAT BEYOND THE COMMON INFLUENCE OF MOTION AND LIGHT
### no peculiar power belongs to the celestial
### bodies. Chapter V.

Now, this outpouring of heat is common to all stars, since it follows the entire celestial nature, just as light does. However, whether it applies to the <term>spheres</term> <note>In the cosmology of Pico's time, the planets and stars were thought to be embedded in transparent, concentric "spheres" or shells that rotated around the Earth.</note> themselves is a matter of doubt; for if they are not luminous, they cannot be propagators of this heat. If they are luminous, the question arises: could it be that due to their <term>rarity</term> <note>Original: *raritate*. This refers to the thinness or lack of density in the celestial substance.</note> their light is invisible and thus has little effect on us, as **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath and one of the most influential philosophers of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> writes in his book *On the Heavens*? Regarding the stars themselves, whatever comes under our sight cannot be doubted, unless we were to strip them of both their celestial nature and the gifts of light. Therefore, whatever comes forth besides motion and light is a life-giving heat born of that light. No experience shows—as we have seen and shall see more clearly in what follows—that any other influences descend to us from the stars, or that they possess other corporeal or effective qualities, since the heavens seem able to fulfill their duty everywhere sufficiently through motion and heat-producing light.

Thus **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher whose physics and cosmology formed the basis of medieval university education.</note> never said that we are affected by the heavens in any way other than by motion and heat—a view that **Averroes** <note>The 12th-century Andalusian philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> and **Plotinus** <note>A major Hellenistic philosopher and the founder of Neoplatonism.</note>, great men each in their own schools, most firmly asserted. Indeed, as far as "cooling influences" are concerned, reason seems strongly to deny them. For those who hold the opposite view, when they are convinced that all light is the producer of warmth, are accustomed to decide that while all stars that shine are indeed productive of heat by a certain general property common to all, they then possess their own specific powers, so that this one grants dryness, that one cold, and another moisture. Thus, they say nights during a full moon are warmer because the more abundant light provides more heat. Yet they claim this does not prevent the Moon, by its own influence, from either cooling or moistening the air.

I therefore ask them: this heat which they admit is common to all stars just like light—do they believe it is the kind we have described, containing within itself in an <term>eminent</term> <note>In Scholastic philosophy, to possess a quality "eminently" means to possess it in a higher, more perfect form that can produce all its lower effects.</note> way all <term>four qualities</term> <note>The traditional Aristotelian qualities: Hot, Cold, Moist, and Dry.</note> and therefore productive of all things when combined with secondary causes, while being in itself only a diffuser of itself? Or do they rather believe that the other qualities are not contained in it, but only heat, while cold (being a different thing from heat) flows from some other particular power of a specific star?

Whichever they choose, they fall, if I am not mistaken, into no small difficulties. If they answer the first, I will press them: a specific quality cannot belong to any star by its own particular nature if that quality is more imperfect than what belongs to it by its more universal nature—since a more specific distinction always adds a degree of perfection to a universal one. But a quality that contains every quality is more perfect than one which is only effective of cold. Therefore, if that [universal] quality is owed to the stars by the general condition common to all, a cooling influence cannot be owed to any star from its own specific nature. There remains, then, the second part of the division, in which they must necessarily become no less stuck: for if nothing belongs to a star from its own nature that is repugnant to...

<summary>Pico argues that stars influence the Earth solely through motion and light (which produces heat). He refutes the astrological belief that specific stars have inherent "powers" to create cold or moisture, arguing that the heavens provide a universal, life-giving heat instead.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s argument from page 461, where he asserts that celestial bodies act only through physical means—light and heat—rather than through hidden "influences." # Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

...common properties that agree with its general nature. For example, if it is appropriate for a man, insofar as he is an animal, to have senses, then numbness <note>Original: *stupiditas*. In this philosophical context, it refers to a lack of sensory perception or "insensitivity," rather than a lack of intelligence.</note> cannot be appropriate for him insofar as he is a man. Or, if it is appropriate for him to have a principle of internal motion insofar as he lives, it could not happen that, insofar as he is this or that living being, some principle of inanimate immobility would fit him. Rather, a specific degree distinguishes that which exists in the general principle. For example, if it belongs to a living being simply to be moved not just from the outside but from within, it follows necessarily that for the nature of an "animal"—which is a species of living thing—there is a principle of some internal operation; and for the "rational" being—which is another species—there is another internal operation. 

Therefore, by a similar example, if that life-giving heat follows from the celestial nature insofar as it is celestial, then the effective power of coldness and dryness—which are qualities contrary to life <note>In the physics of Pico's time, "heat" was associated with life and "cold/dry" with death or decay. Pico argues that since the heavens are the source of life, they cannot be inherently cold.</note>—will not follow from the specific nature of any particular star. This is how we argue against those [astrologers]. 

The arguments for the opposing opinion have been partly resolved, and the rest will be dismantled in their proper places later. For they thought it would follow that the cold elements <note>The elements of Water and Earth.</note> could not be preserved by the heavens, and that all other qualities in the universe would result from heat only by accident. Furthermore, they thought it would not be true (as is believed) that all the substantial forms of bodies are contained within the power of the celestial nature. We have already dismantled all these points in the preceding sections, as well as the claim that many things are generated in these places by celestial action, even though the light of heaven does not reach them. 

Two problems remain. One is that the air can be changed so suddenly from heat to cold—and indeed intense cold—as is observed by experience, unless this arriving cold is believed to be the work of a new constellation. The other is how the Moon, when it has passed beneath the earth and even to the very depths of the earth, moves the tides of the ocean—at which time the Lunar rays undoubtedly do not reach the water—unless the Moon performs this through an "influence" <note>Astrologers argued for a "secret influence" to explain how the Moon could move water it couldn't "see." Pico seeks a physical explanation instead.</note> that is separate from both light and the heat that follows light. 

These will indeed be resolved later: the first in Chapter 13, where the changes of the lower world caused by the Sun will be treated; the other where the cause of the ebb and flow of the ocean will be debated by us at length. Here, we will only satisfy those who ask how the Moon affects us during the <term>New Moon</term> <note>Original: *interlunium*. The period when the moon is between the earth and sun and is invisible to us.</note>, even though it does not illuminate us at all during that time. 

**Galen** <note>A famous Greek physician (c. 129–216 AD) whose work was the standard for medicine in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> asserts that just as the Moon does not illuminate us, so it does not affect us in any way during its <term>conjunction</term> <note>Original: *coitu*. The astronomical meeting of the Sun and Moon in the sky.</note>. For this reason, he calculates the [medical] month as 26 days and 12 hours—the number of days on which the light of the Moon reaches us with efficacy—since it lies hidden under the Sun's rays for about three days. However, the Moon *does* act upon us when it joins with the Sun, in the same way that one acts by "doing nothing." For by depriving bodies of its light, it harms them; but as it waxes <note>Original: *adolescens*.</note>, it nourishes them more fully and fills them with moisture. But if we believe that the Moon has its own light (even if it is very dark and thin, which is why it does not entirely vanish from sight during a conjunction), one could believe that it retains its efficacy, derived somewhat even from that faint light.

### THAT THE LIGHT OF THE MOON IS LIFE-GIVING JUST AS THAT OF THE SUN IS: and that neither causes cold or humidity except by accident. Chapter VI.

It is therefore (to bring everything together into one point) that celestial heat is the universal craftsman of bodily things. There is no reason for us to believe that different "breaths" <note>Original: *flatus*. In this context, Pico refers to the specific "influences" or "emanations" that astrologers claimed each star projected onto Earth.</note> are breathed from the stars into earthly bodies, lest we grant more to those higher bodies, or less to the lower ones, than is proper. Let the reader only keep this in mind: whatever a lower nature participates in from a better nature is necessarily altered. This happens because the influence leaves its source and is received according to the capacity of the recipient. One thing becomes worse because it departs from its primary origin; another becomes worse because it is mixed with a foreign and alien nature—specifically, a lower nature. Since this lower nature is affected by many different impressions from other sources, it necessarily stains and confuses what it had received from the better place with a "sludge" of many affections. Therefore, there is no doubt that this very thing happens to celestial heat: whenever it is received into the sublunary <note>The "sublunary" sphere refers to the Earth and its atmosphere, the region below the Moon where things are subject to change and decay.</note> mass, it fails to achieve its natural action and perfection.

This happens in two ways. First, although the heat is always healthy by its own nature, it sometimes turns out to be harmful because of the weakness of the recipient. Second, although celestial heat produces no elementary qualities <note>The "elementary qualities" are hot, cold, moist, and dry. Pico argues that celestial heat is a "quintessential" or higher heat that is fundamentally different from a common kitchen fire.</note> (being different from them by its own character), it "degenerates" within elementary nature into the actions of the elements—especially into the action of heat, which it resembles most in name and nature. Therefore, it often acts not so much as a celestial heat, but as an igneous and elementary heat usually does. That this happens not by the heat's own nature, but by a "vice" or defect in the matter, is clear from this evidence (to set aside theory for a moment): whenever this heat finds matter among sublunary bodies that is kindred to itself, it is always found to be beneficial, life-giving, and only healthily warming. 

Indeed, there is no better example of this than the <term>spirit</term> <note>The *spiritus* was thought to be a subtle, vaporous substance in the blood that linked the physical body to the soul. Pico explains its qualities in the following lines.</note>, and especially the human spirit, which is a thin, clear, and mobile bloody vapor. As Aristotle and Avicenna write, this spirit corresponds proportionally to the heavens. The heat of heaven always fosters and strengthens this spirit, such that the heat is to the spirit almost what the spirit itself is to the thicker body. If it occasionally causes harm, it does so for no other reason than the weakness of the recipient. A sign of this is that the very same ray of light can hurt a weak person and strengthen a robust one. Here the saying is true: *to him who has, shall be given; from him who has not, shall be taken even that which he has.* <note>A reference to the Gospel of Matthew (25:29). Pico uses the biblical logic to explain that a healthy body thrives under the sun, while a sickly one withers.</note> Therefore, the harm does not come from the Sun—since it would not have benefited the other person—but from the weakness of the matter, which collapses under the weight of such great goodness because of its own illness. 

Otherwise, things that are equal to the Sun's rays gain more life and vigor the more they are exposed to it. For this reason, no one should think that a "consuming heat" or a "dryness contrary to life" flows from the Sun, just as one should not think a "suffocating" or "overly fluid humidity" and a "numbing coldness" flow from the Moon. If this were so, the light of the waxing Moon would not assist the innate reproductive power in things by which bodies are nourished and grow along with the Moon itself. Nor would the full Moon [act] as Hippocrates writes in his book on...

...in an eight-month birth, <note>In ancient and Renaissance medicine, an "eight-month birth" was often considered less viable than a seven-month one; Pico argues that celestial light is necessary to foster life even in these difficult cases.</note> it would be useful for conceptions, making the female fertile and fertilizing the male. Nor would it be truly said by Aristotle <note>original: "Aristot."</note> that the Moon is, as it were, a second, smaller Sun, and that it contributes to all generations and perfections. For in what way could these things be true, if its light were not by its own nature nourishing, vital, and fecund, just like that of the Sun and other stars? For all of them have this property, just as the celestial property is common to all. 

But (as we were saying) this celestial heat, just as it may sometimes be excessive due to the weakness of the recipient, so because of the elemental nature into which it descends, it almost turns into elemental heat. Thus, you would not easily recognize it as celestial, except in those spiritual small bodies <note>Original: "corpusculis spiritalibus." Pico refers to the "vital spirits" or *pneuma*—a subtle substance in the body that acts as a bridge between the physical organs and the soul.</note> which we have declared to be most similar to heaven among all bodies. For when infused into these, it both perfects every mixture and serves everywhere in completing the works of the soul. 

Otherwise, when it falls upon hard, rough, thick, watery, or dreggy bodies, it degenerates from its celestial property and behaves almost exactly as elemental heat <note>Heat found in the four elements (fire, air, water, earth) as opposed to the "pure" heat of the stars.</note> is accustomed to do. This heat, if it is stronger, burns, dries out, and reduces things to ash. On the contrary, if it is thin and slight, it causes a flow and dissolves moisture. Thus, it happens to celestial heat according to the conditions of the matter it hits; from this, the opinion was born that the Sun causes dryness and the Moon increases humidity, simply because the Sun's heat is more burning, while the Moon's is more lukewarm. 

But in suitable and related subjects, neither will the Sun's ray dry out healthy moisture, nor will the Moon generate useless or harmful humidity. Instead, each star will perform the same work by its own nature, although the Moon effects more weakly what the Sun does more intensely. By accident <note>A technical term in Aristotelian logic meaning "incidentally" or "not by its primary nature."</note>, however, through the staining <note>Original: "infectionem." In this context, it means the way pure light is "contaminated" or altered by the quality of the matter it strikes.</note> of foreign matter, they appear to act differently: the Sun drying, and the Moon moistening. 

For the Sun's rays, when they are closer to us—as in the Northern signs—or when they touch us at more direct angles—as at noon—or when they gather together in concave, rough, and resistant places, being compressed and repulsed, they leap back. By the fiery property which they acquire through such violence or staining, they dry and parch the bodies they fall upon. In turn, the Moon, with that slight and thin heat of hers, if she touches any moist and fluid body, she loosens the moisture she finds in it and makes it more fluid. She does not bring that cold and watery humidity herself, but by her own heat she dissolves the humidity she finds in the watery and cold body, calling it forth and spreading it out. 

For this is the nature of heat: if it is stronger, it consumes the moistures it calls forth from bodies; if it is weaker, it calls them forth (because it is the same healing heat, after all), but because it is weak it fails in the attempt and does not consume what has been called forth any further. Thus, by accident, the Moon indeed moistens immoderately and the Sun dries, but both also cause cold by accident. For as Aristotle writes, both are principles of cold and heat, and the movement of these stars holds the limit of both the beginning and the end of those qualities. How this is to be understood, the same author declares elsewhere. For he says the Sun makes winter and summer through the whole year, and the Moon does the same through the month, but there is this difference that...
