<meta>This page continues Pico’s argument that the Moon’s influence on Earth is not due to an inherent "cold" or "wet" nature, as astrologers claim, but rather its vital heat. He is explaining that apparent cooling or moistening effects are secondary results of the Moon's light interacting with the environment, rather than its primary qualities.</meta>

<page-num>465</page-num>
->On Astrology, Book III.<-

These effects indeed come from the Sun through its approach and departure; from the Moon, they happen not in this way, but one occurs during the waxing light, and the other during the waning. Thus, just as the Sun, moving far away from us, leaves us to the cold and is so said to "make" cold, so the Moon, when its light is repeatedly stripped away at its conjunction <note>The New Moon, when the Moon is between the Earth and the Sun and its visible face is dark.</note>, is said to make things cold—not because it brings coldness itself, but because it protects us less from the nocturnal chill than it does at other times. 

Moreover, it is worth examining why <term>Aristotle</term> <note>original: "Aristot."</note>, in those same books—namely *On the Generation of Animals*—says that the times of the waning month are wetter and colder, even though it is commonly admitted that as the Moon "grows old," moistures dry up. I would solve the problem this way: when the Moon is waning, a moisture thrives that does not come from the Moon itself, but from the lower elements which the Moon resists less, being weakened in heat and hiding below the horizon <note>original: "sub finitorem"; the horizon line.</note> for the greatest part of the night. Wherefore that moisture is also watery, unhealthy, and excremental <note>Waste-like or surplus fluid not used by the body's vital processes.</note>; hence, as the New Moon approaches, many vapors rise, a "harvest" of rains occurs, and menstrual cycles usually flow more fully, as <term>Aristotle</term> <note>original: "Aristot."</note> writes in his *Histories* and *On the Generation of Animals*. 

However, when the Moon is growing [waxing], a moisture increases—either the kind already present in bodies which is made more fluid, or a more life-giving kind approaching by the benefit of lunar heat. For <term>Aristotle</term> <note>original: "Aristot."</note> believes that due to the lunar increases, sea urchins <note>original: "echinos"</note> and similar living things become fuller. This is for no other reason than because, since they are cold creatures lacking blood, they are warmed more vitally when touched by the Moon’s richer light; thus they digest <note>original: "concoquant"; the physiological process where internal heat matures nutrients into bodily substance.</note> better, which necessarily makes them juicier and more robust. 

Therefore, moistures flow both when the Moon is waxing and when it is waning, but they are of different kinds: good ones when waxing, bad ones when waning. From this it is most clearly evident that the Moon does not moisten because it is cold and damp (for such moisture increases when the Moon is waning), but because it is healthily and life-givingly warm; for under the abundance of its light, those bodies become wetter and stronger. Nor do they become wetter in any other way than by the force of heat assisting the nourishing power, and by what is characteristic of heat: calling forth humors <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to control health in ancient medicine.</note> from the innermost parts to the extremities. 

For this reason, bloodletting <note>original: "sanguinis missio"</note> is also most conveniently done then [during the waxing moon]. Thus the astrologer <term>Haly Hamec</term> <note>Likely referring to the medieval Arabic astrologer Albohali or Haly Abenragel, whom Pico frequently critiques for perceived errors in natural philosophy.</note> erred greatly, who said that veins should be cut when the Moon is waning. Therefore, let us conclude with certainty: the moisture that increases along with the Moon—and is therefore increased by its influence—is a most healthy moisture. It does not loosen the body with a "flux" or kill it with coldness, but makes it firmer and more vigorous. This is witnessed even by that experience proven by the testimony of all physicians: those who fall ill at the start of the month bear the onslaught of the disease more strongly; and those who have been given up for dead and are gasping their last breath can scarcely be abandoned by life while the Moon is ascending [waxing]. 

However, both the Sun and the Moon can "cool things down" not only by withholding their light from us, but also by affecting us (though this also happens by accident). The Sun, indeed, cools things when it either kills through excessive drying, or draws vital heat outward, or generates rains from watery sea-mists (which it raises more than it can dissolve), or by stirring up winds, or even for other reasons. The Moon, however, through its thin heat, opens and thins the pores more widely...

<summary>Pico argues that the Moon's influence is based on life-giving heat rather than inherent coldness, distinguishing between healthy moisture during the waxing moon and unhealthy "excremental" moisture during the waning moon. He critiques astrologers like Haly Hamec for recommending medical procedures during the waning phase, asserting that the Moon's light supports vitality and digestion.</summary>

they have also tested the body's nocturnal cold with its rays, letting it in more abundantly upon us. For this is the source of the error by which many think the Moon is cold; that numbness and coldness, I say, which affects those sleeping under the lunar rays—to which the weaker ray of the star makes a path into the body for the cold of the earth and water occupying the air through the night. In this way, the rays of the stars both cause cooling and—falling now upon hard bodies, now upon those dripping with watery thickness—they dry and moisten; by their own nature, they only warm healthily, but are sometimes harmful, not by their own fault, but by the weakness of the one receiving them.

### THE DOGMAS OF THE ASTROLOGERS CANNOT BE DEFENDED, as Ibn Ezra thought, if all stars are considered hot. Chapter VII.

But someone will say that it might be enough for the astrologers if, by this reasoning, this star produces dryness, that one moisture, and another different qualities. For even <term>Abraham Ibn Ezra</term> <note>original: "Abraam Auenazra"; a highly influential 12th-century Jewish polymath and astrologer.</note>, a great figure in the astrological profession, contended that the stars only produce heat, and that it could not be otherwise for bodies that are bright and in perpetual motion. However, he claimed that some stars are called "cold" because they do not impart as much heat to us as is sufficient for our constitution. Thus, <term>Saturn</term> is accused of coldness because, being positioned far from the Earth and smaller than <term>Jupiter</term>, it nourishes the lower nature more lukewarmly than it ought; and therefore, when it is the <term>lord of the birth</term> <note>The planet that holds the most influence over a person's horoscope based on its position at the moment of their birth.</note>, it signifies death not because of an imposed cold, but because of a lack of heat. 

I, however, praise Ibn Ezra for thinking correctly regarding the heat of the stars, but he loved his profession too much, so that he did not see how its dogmas necessarily conflict with that truth. For while his argument—that Saturn is considered cold because it is only slightly hot and thus causes death—might work for Saturn, this reasoning does not work for the others; nor does it even work completely for Saturn, since a planet that is only slightly hot moistens by accident (as we have explained) and does not dry things out; yet they [the astrologers] contend that Saturn is dry. 

Furthermore, would it not clearly follow that all the fixed stars, especially those below the first degree of magnitude, are colder than Saturn, since they are both smaller than it and farther from the Earth? And if stars are only "cold" because they are "slightly hot," then the <term>Heart of the Lion</term> <note>original: "cor Leonis"; the star we now call Regulus, the brightest in the constellation Leo.</note> would be a cold star, yet it is judged by astrologers to be most burning. Then, among the planets themselves, if we wish to examine which star warms us more or less according to this principle accepted by Ibn Ezra, we will find nothing at all consistent with the sayings of the astrologers. For three things generally create the intensity of heat: the magnitude of light, density, and proximity. It has not been clearly explored how much magnitude outweighs density, or density magnitude, or how much proximity itself outweighs one or both of them; wherefore the matter will remain uncertain for those wishing to reason it out; nor can our senses judge it, since they do not perceive the rays of the other stars besides the Sun and the Moon. And this is the first obstacle for the astrologers, whose...

<summary>Pico argues that while stars are naturally hot, their varying distances and sizes lead to different effects on Earth. He critiques Abraham Ibn Ezra’s attempt to reconcile this with astrology, noting that if heat were purely a matter of proximity and size, astrological classifications of "hot" and "cold" stars (like Regulus vs. Saturn) would fall apart.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s critique of astrological physical theories. Here, he focuses on the logical inconsistencies of planetary "temperatures" and then introduces a counter-argument (an "objection") that defenders of astrology might raise to save their system.</meta>

<page-num>467</page-num>
->on Astrology, Book III:<-

No science can exist if the powers of celestial rays remain ambiguous. Indeed, for those willing to follow mere guesswork, something entirely different will appear than what they themselves have determined. For if they consider the physical mass, the rays of <term>Mars</term> would be thought less hot than those of <term>Saturn</term> and <term>Jupiter</term>. But if they respond that Mars is hotter because its light comes from closer proximity and greater density, I would say it is in no way credible that these factors could achieve so much. Furthermore, consider the smallness of its <term>disc</term> <note>The "disc" refers to the visible circular face of a planet as seen from Earth.</note>: if Saturn, which is nearly fifty times larger, is numb with cold while Mars seethes with heat, then the smallness of the body must detract very little from the light's efficacy. If, however, proximity and abundance of light add so much power, we should be warmed more by <term>Venus</term> than by any other star except the Sun and Moon; for when that nurturing, heavenly <term>Cytherea</term> <note>original: "cytherea"; a poetic name for Venus, referring to the island of Cythera where she was said to have been born.</note> shines far and wide, smiling with nectar, she alone among all the stars casts a shadow. Nor is any star closer to the Earth—at least according to the common opinion that the sphere of Venus does not exceed the Earth's width—and yet most astrologers condemn her to coldness, just as they do not doubt that Jupiter and Mars far surpass her in heat. In this, if they refer back again to the imagination of the physical body, it will be done with little reason; for since Jupiter's disc does not exceed that of Venus by much (considering its vast size) nor is it much closer to the Earth than Saturn, they nevertheless define it so that Jupiter warms far more than Venus, and Saturn far less—indeed, they say Venus and Jupiter nurture bodies, while Saturn deadens them with cold.

---

### OBJECTION AGAINST THE THINGS THAT HAVE BEEN SAID. Chapter VIII.

**B**ut let it be, someone will say: perhaps the differences between rays are not known to astrologers, nor can they be known, but this pertains to another question. Now we must see whether such diversity can exist in rays that, although they are all hot by their own nature, and life-givingly hot, yet based on the abundance or lack of light—or its thinness or efficacy—one compared to another might be called "cold" and "contrary to life." One might be called "dry" and another "moist," whether this is caused by its own nature or by contact with elemental matter. For if this is so, what is to prevent it? Although the heavens are a <term>universal cause</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, a "universal cause" is a broad force (like the sun) that affects everything, while a "particular cause" is a specific local factor.</note>, yet because of their continuous motion, they behave in different ways. Depending on the various positions of the stars, they cooperate differently with those lower causes, so that not every variety of effect happens because of the lower things themselves, but also from the varying disposition of the universal cause itself. This is especially true if the stars differ from one another not only in the quality or quantity of light, but in their other gifts and peculiar properties, as the "fourth reason" <note>Pico is referring back to a specific numbered argument he addressed earlier in his treatise.</note> alleged against us. For then it seems possible that through motion and heat (which are common to all stars insofar as they are celestial), a common efficacy is owed to the heavens; but through the <term>influxes</term> <note>The "influx" (influentia) was the supposed invisible fluid or power flowing from the stars to the Earth.</note> which follow the particular natures of the stars, something more particular is produced by it, and likewise through the various [aspects] of the same star, both toward other stars and toward the hea— <meta>catchword: toward the heavens (ad cœlum)</meta>

<summary>Pico argues that astrologers are inconsistent, labeling Venus "cold" despite its brightness and proximity, while calling Jupiter "hot." He then presents an "objection" suggesting that stars might have unique, hidden "influxes" that produce specific effects on Earth beyond simple heat.</summary>

### THE OBJECTION IS RESOLVED, AND IT IS SHOWN THAT NEI-
### ther specific nor individual differences in things depend on the 
### motion of the heaven. Chapter IX.

<gloss>historiated initial</gloss> The objection that has arisen recalls many things which we might object against them—and it is almost always the case with a bad cause that the more it defends itself, the more it betrays itself. On the contrary, truth is like fire: the more it is shaken, the more it brightens. Therefore, we shall satisfy the inquiry in this way. We will first declare what diversity exists in celestial influence, whether due to the different nature of the many stars, or due to the various and rotating changes of the same star. We shall also say what evidence or natural reason prescribes regarding these by necessary demonstration. For how the adversaries err requires more effort than can be finished in passing; therefore, it will be treated in the following books. Here, since it will have been sufficiently explained how one constellation can differ from another, we will see how much authority that diversity has in varying lower effects. From this, what we ourselves wish will be confirmed: that the primary, substantial, and almost total distinction among things comes from secondary causes <note>By "secondary causes," Pico refers to earthly, material, or biological factors rather than the "primary" celestial influence</note>, and the fallacy of the astrologers—who profess a prediction of this kind of distinction from celestial causes—will be more clearly exposed. 

We have said that the heaven acts upon us through motion and light. Through motion, it is believed to do three things: to move, to heat, and to bring light. This third point must be discussed later, when light is treated. But as for their claim that it heats through motion, this is a difficult question and must be discussed separately in books of philosophy, for it pertains little to astrological practice. Certainly, we have explained above how it moves: namely, that all motions depend on the <term>first motion</term> <note>original: "primo motu"; in Aristotelian physics, the "Primum Mobile" or outermost sphere that imparts motion to all lower spheres</note>, just as the movements of an animal depend on the motion of the heart. 

Let us see, then, as far as motion is concerned, whether different stars move differently, and whether the same stars move differently at different times; then we shall look at light. The motions of the stars differ in three ways: First, that some are moved faster, others slower. Second, that some move with more motions, others with fewer. Third, according to the position of the region in which they move, because some occupy higher seats than others and traverse larger spaces. <term>Aristotle</term> does not think that the multitude or fewness of motions pertains to the diversity of the things affected or moved, but that it occurs according to the dignity of the movers—so that a more noble mover achieves with few motions what a less noble one can only achieve with many. 

Concerning their speed and slowness, nothing has been sufficiently explored. For <term>Aurelius Macrobius</term> <note>A 5th-century Roman writer whose work was a standard source for medieval cosmology</note>, imitating more ancient writers, asserts that all the planets proceed at an equal pace—a view supported by <term>Abraham ibn Ezra</term> <note>original: "Auenazra"; a prominent 12th-century Jewish scholar and astrologer</note>, who places the Sun, Venus, and Mercury in the same sphere, separated by the positions of their <term>epicycles</term> <note>original: "epicticiorum"; small circular paths used in ancient astronomy to explain the complex movements of planets</note>. However, those who claim they move at unequal speeds fight among themselves. For <term>Alpetragius</term> <note>original: "Alpetragius"; Al-Bitruji, a 12th-century astronomer who proposed an alternative to the Ptolemaic system</note>, [contends that] those which seem faster, those...

asserts that they are slower; on the other hand, others observe the time of their return. This must necessarily fail, unless someone has examined the proportion of delays and spaces more <note>original: "penificulatius," likely a variant of "peniculatius," meaning meticulously or thoroughly</note> meticulously. But however the matter stands, if indeed they heat through motion, they will heat more by faster motion. Regarding that primacy of motions which we were discussing, this can create no variety, since lower motions depend on the motion of the heaven. Insofar as that first and circular motion is such that it matters not whether it is slower or swifter: a stone would not move downward, nor fire upward, if the heaven were at rest; but the stone does not descend faster, nor the fire ascend more quickly, simply because the heaven revolves more rapidly. It derives only its capacity to be moved from there, just as it derives any vital growth from universal nature. It takes the type of motion from its own substance, but its easing or intensification from the mover, from impetus, from shape, and from other similar conditions. Therefore, Saturn will not move us differently just because it moves slower than Mars, which is considered faster. For as to what astrologers say—that slower planets bestow what they grant more belatedly—this will be refuted later. Now we maintain that nothing else is given by them through their motion except that we ourselves are also moved; which certainly does not happen differently from them, whether they are driven around more slowly or more swiftly. Furthermore, regarding the same planet, there is no reason to doubt that we are moved by it in different ways because it moves differently at different times; for it is a firm dogma of philosophers that celestial motions are always similar and equal to themselves, and that stars do not suppress their course or turn back, although it may appear so to us. This appearance is attributed by mathematicians to <term>eccentric circles</term> <note>circles whose centers are off-set from the Earth, used to explain why planets seem to change speed</note>, or to different motions striving against one another, or other things of that kind. The only possible diversity could be that those carried through the lowest parts of their <term>epicycles</term> <note>small circles on which planets were thought to revolve while simultaneously orbiting the Earth</note> might affect us more favorably as being closer; though this disagrees with the decrees of astrologers rather than agreeing with them, as will be explained more broadly in what follows. Regarding the dignity and rank of the <term>movers</term> <note>the spiritual or physical forces responsible for celestial rotation</note>, or the bodies that are moved, the question is whether they all do the same thing equally in those things which happen, or whether one mover does one thing and another something else. For there are those who think that everything which happens is caused by the immediate cause, and that the higher things do nothing else but move that very immediate cause to act. They believe so many intermediate causes are interposed by nature, not so that one does one thing and another another, but so that the thing is accomplished in its own order. Since an effect cannot be produced except by a related cause, and that cause is too ineffective due to the bonds of matter (by which lower things are more tightly bound) to move unless it is moved; and since it, in turn, cannot be moved directly by the most noble and supreme causes, it was necessary for as many intermediate ones to intervene as there were degrees of dignity in the order of causes. Therefore, these people believe things are made by just as many causes, not because one claims one part of the work and another another (since they are joined together with an essential connection), but because, so that they may do the same thing, one is necessarily moved by another in a <note>The "triple series" likely refers to the Neo-Platonic or Aristotelian hierarchy: the First Mover (God), the Celestial Orbs, and the sublunary (Earthly) world.</note> triple series. On the contrary, there are those who maintain that in the things that happen, the higher and lower causes do not do the same thing, but according to the degrees of perfection which the substance of the work contains, that substance also depends on causes separated by a gradual progression of order.

<summary>Pico argues that the varying speeds of planets like Saturn and Mars do not influence the specific nature of earthly events, as celestial motion is merely a general cause. He also discusses the hierarchy of causation, questioning whether higher causes act directly on Earth or only through a chain of intermediate steps.</summary>

In the previous page, he argued that the speed of celestial motion (like the slow movement of Saturn compared to Mars) does not dictate the timing or nature of events on Earth. He continues here by distinguishing between how the heavens affect us through motion versus how they affect us through light.</meta>

therefore, the more general principle in a shared work belongs to the more general cause—that is, in the act of bringing something about, just as a cause is more excellent, it is also more universal. Thus, things that are created receive the fact that they **exist** from God; they receive the fact that they are **substances** from the next cause in line; and again, they receive the fact that they are **bodies** from the cause that follows, until one arrives at the thing's own specific type and nature, which is referred to its own proper and most immediate cause. Whichever way we look at it, it is clear that not only the differences between individuals, but even the differences between species of things, do not come from the heavens, at least insofar as we are considering this "efficiency of motion" <note>the ability of motion to produce an effect</note>.

## OTHER STARS APART FROM THE SUN AND MOON ACT EITHER NOT AT ALL OR CERTAINLY LITTLE UPON US. Chapter 10.

We have spoken of motion; it remains to speak of light. But first, one ought to notice certain differences between the action the stars have on us through motion and that which happens through light. The power of motion comes more from the "moving soul" <note>In the physics of Pico's time, celestial spheres were believed to be moved by spiritual "intelligences" or souls</note> than from the moved body; whereas the power of light comes from the actual body of the Planet. The former is believed to belong to the spheres rather than the stars themselves; the latter to the stars rather than the spheres. In the case of motion, lower things depend on higher ones, since no one doubts that the Planets are subject to the motion of the "first heaven" <note>the *Primum Mobile*, the outermost sphere that drives the daily rotation of the sky</note>, and that the Sun is driven around along with the rest. Regarding light, on the contrary, it is thought—with nearly all philosophers agreeing—that not only the Moon, but all the other stars are illuminated by the Sun. Likewise, those things that are higher up move us more, since all other things are moved by their power. But regarding the light reaching us, all else being equal, the influence is more powerful from a closer location. 

Furthermore, it is not even clear (as we shall explain) whether the lights of the higher bodies act upon us at all, or whether only those of the Moon and Sun do, while the others do not reach us with any efficacy due to either the smallness or the distance of those shining bodies. Regarding motion, there is no doubt: in that realm (as we said), the higher things are more powerful. From all this, it can be gathered that what is said by philosophers—that a chain of causes is linked and hangs downward in a certain essential order—pertains mostly to this efficiency of motion. This is because this rank and order of causes is understood to exist in the "moving souls" more than in the physical bodies. It is the nature of this order that second things depend on the first, and a superior cause has more strength and power than any of the inferior ones—so much so that the inferior cannot act if the superior ceases. 

However, we do not deny that the heat of the Sun acts as a cause in an "essential superior order" <note>a primary, governing rank of causality</note> relative to "seminal heat" <note>original: "caloris seminalis," the vital heat found within living organisms or seeds that allows them to grow</note>, but that order does not extend any further. Therefore, there is not here that <note>original: "conspicatio," likely a variation of "conspiratio," meaning a "breathing together" or harmony</note> harmony of causes drawn from the first down to the lowest through intermediate steps that the astrologers talk about. Rather, such a thing is found more completely in the series of movers, insofar as they are movers. Yet in both cases one can observe nearly a four-fold progress. In motion, that sphere (or the universe itself) which revolves with a daily agitation holds the first place; from it, this motion is communicated to the others. There follows the choir of Planets running in the opposite direction over the poles of the zodiac <note>original: "signiferi," the "sign-bearer" or the belt of the zodiac</note>. Nor are there more degrees to be distinguished within that group, since they are neither moved by each other, nor do they move each other; wherefore they are as one mobile thing...

<summary>Pico distinguishes between celestial influence through motion (which is universal and governed by higher spheres/souls) and influence through light (which is physical and dominated by the Sun and Moon). He argues that while motion provides a general "push" for existence, it does not determine the specific nature of earthly things.</summary>

# Against Astrology, Book III.

just as each [sphere] is swept along by the <term>first mover</term><note>The *primum mobile*, the outermost sphere in the medieval geocentric model that carries all other spheres from east to west every 24 hours.</note>, so it moves by its own motion as well (which is called the "motion of diversity" by Plato). It moves the aether, I say, and the highest air. From there, through every fourth degree, motion reaches us and the lower bodies; while they are being nourished, all the particular motions of natural things arise from it. In terms of light—and when I say light, I always mean the heat flowing from light—the Sun is the fountain of the entire influence of the world. It illuminates the Moon; the Moon affects the air; and the air affects all bodies that live under and within the air. 

But regarding this diversity—that we are moved by the first mover through the Planets, and illuminated by the Sun differently than by the Moon—we recount all these things primarily so that, before a discussion is held on the difference of "astral flows" <note>original: "sideralium fluxuum"</note>, we may know it is not even established whether those higher influences, whatever they may be, actually reach our region. Rather, what is believed by astrologers about certain smaller stars could be believed about all of them, even the Planets, except for the Sun and the Moon. 

Because this opinion could be opposed primarily by the idea that celestial bodies are the "essential causes" of lower things—an order in which nothing can be inactive—I wanted to declare that this order pertains more to the "moving powers" <note>the spiritual or physical forces causing movement</note> than to the illuminating bodies. For the astrologers cannot say that God created the stars in vain if their "breaths" <note>original: "afflatus," referring to celestial influence</note> are not felt. They cannot say they are in vain, since they themselves freely admit that they do not know the purpose of many things. Otherwise, perhaps they do not think this sublime candelabrum, radiating with so many lights, was made primarily for this: that by bringing light to our nocturnal eyes, it might illuminate the dens inhabited by light-shunning moles. 

But why, you will ask, are there so many stars if the Sun and Moon alone are sufficient for us? This was appropriate to the celestial nature; the order of things and the perfection of the entire universe demanded it. Just because they do not all illuminate us, it does not follow that there cannot be some other use and benefit for us from them. <term>Averroes</term><note>original: "Auerodam," referring to the 12th-century philosopher Ibn Rushd</note> argues this way: The Sun and Moon act upon us, therefore the others do as well, since they are all of the same nature. This style of argument is pleasing and tastes of Aristotle, who also argues this way: The Moon does not move by its own motion, but with its sphere (as its spots declare); therefore, the same must be judged of the others, since the nature of all celestial things is one. 

Wherefore, following in these same footsteps, we shall conclude: The Sun heats, therefore the Moon heats, because they are all of the same nature. And we shall conclude correctly, because reason proves only this: that the conditions of all are the same insofar as they are considered absolutely in themselves. But when you compare them to other things, since they are not compared in the same way, the reasoning falters. For if the Sun, by its own nature, is going to do the same things as Saturn, it does not follow that both do the same thing toward us, because one is compared to us as a near neighbor, the other as one far remote. 

Thus, those who would say that only the Sun and Moon act upon us have reasons they may bring for their suspicion, even though the nature in all celestial bodies is the same. For three conditions of a shining body primarily make the action of light effective upon us: magnitude, density, and proximity. All these concur excellently in the Sun; for it is nearest to us, especially if it is placed above the Moon as the ancients and...

<summary>Pico argues that while the heavens move as a whole, the physical influence of light on Earth is dominated by the Sun and Moon due to their size and proximity. He mocks the idea that every star must have a direct effect on humans, suggesting they exist for the universe's overall perfection instead.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s systematic dismantling of astrological theory. Having previously argued that celestial motion is a universal force, he now focuses on the physical properties of the planets—their size, distance, and light—to argue that most stars are physically incapable of exerting the specific influences astrologers claim.</meta>

->### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola<-

[after the calculations of] Ptolemy, <term>Geber</term><note>Jabir ibn Aflah, a 12th-century Andalusian astronomer whose work "Correction of the Almagest" influenced European science.</note>, and <term>Theon</term><note>Theon of Alexandria, a 4th-century mathematician and commentator on Ptolemy.</note> contend; and with a body so vast that it exceeds the largest star by more than a <term>sesquialter ratio</term><note>A ratio of 3:2, meaning the Sun is more than one and a half times larger than the largest stars.</note>, it is seen with the densest light, the most brilliant of all. The Moon is so close to our regions that it cannot fail to affect even the things it touches; thus its light is necessarily effective, being nearly the same as solar light. You would not find these conditions in the other planets; therefore, what you grant concerning the Sun and Moon, you cannot be forced to grant regarding the rest.

But distance will perhaps stand in the way for the lights of the <term>eighth sphere</term><note>The sphere of the "fixed stars," which in the geocentric model sits beyond the planets.</note>, even the largest ones; the same distance will stand in the way for the stars of Saturn and Jupiter, which are closer to the Earth but also smaller. For they report that the largest fixed stars contain the mass of the Earth one hundred and seven times, while Jupiter contains it ninety-five times, and Saturn only ninety-one times. These figures were not stated with absolute precision, yet if we follow experience, we see that the rays of those fixed stars—though of such vast magnitude—are not felt at night, even if Saturn and Jupiter shine upon us from above the horizon along with them. Mars decreases in its physical power far more than it gains by being closer in position, for it has a proportion to the Earth only a little greater than one and a half; thus, a single Sun could contain nearly a hundred "Mars." Indeed, the Sun is one hundred and sixty-six times larger than the Earth.

Therefore, why should we listen to the absurdities of a man who, witnessing with his own senses the power of the Sun upon physical bodies, believes it possible for the powers of the star of Mars to reach us, despite it being so much smaller and more remote from the Earth? Let him believe the same concerning the star of Venus, which is perhaps even further from us than the Sun, and certainly far smaller than the Earth itself (of which it is thought to be not even a twentieth part). As for Mercury, it is smaller than the Moon and further from us. Why then is it a wonder that we feel so little from it? It is also rarely seen, yet astrologers are accustomed to attribute the greatest importance to it.

But Aristotle also seems to support those who think this way. Indeed, when he treats of motion, he mentions all the spheres, as in his book *On the Heavens*, and especially the "supreme motion," as in the final book of the *Physics*, because obviously all bodies are moved by these universal motions. But when he speaks of that life-giving heat that cherishes the generation of things and brings them to perfection, he makes mention either only of the Sun—as when he said <note>original: "a Sole & homine generari hominem"</note> "man is generated by the Sun and by man"—or of the Sun and the Moon, as in the books *On the Generation of Animals*. If anyone were to contend that this was Aristotle's true opinion, he could not be refuted by any of that philosopher's own words.

We assert not so much that [the stars have no effect], but rather this: whatever reaches down to us from the other stars is so thin and scant that if perhaps the air is softened slightly by the nightly lights of the stars, it is only to make it more suited for generation. However, if someone were to credit all generation to the Sun alone, he could conclude that what the Sun performs by its light during the day, it also performs at night through that light reflected to the Moon, as if by a mirror. From there it is reflected back to the Earth, with Nature arranging these turns most wisely; since Earthly weakness could not continually endure the direct rays of the Sun, at night it receives them through the Moon as weaker refractions <note>original: "fractiones imbecilliores"</note>. These are better suited to its own infirmity, so that things are neither completely abandoned by the vitalizing light, nor again placed under its full intensity...

<meta>catchword: ...intensity (plenitudinem)</meta>

He cites Aristotle to support the idea that only the Sun and Moon provide the "life-giving heat" necessary for the generation of life on Earth.</summary>

as if they were failing. In this way, the Sun returns to us more healthfully in early spring after being far away all winter, than if it had lived constantly and assiduously near us; indeed, our fragility is so pressed by the "goodness" of heaven—if it be too much—that not even the Moon herself always pours back all the solar rays to us, but now more sparingly, now more abundantly according to her <term>schematisms</term><note>The geometric relationships or phases of the Moon relative to the Sun.</note> relative to the Sun. Divine care so ordered them for that utility, since for that same reason it did not fill the star nearest to us <note>The Moon</note> with its own light. If you survey all of nature, you will see no sign given by it that lower things are fostered by any heat other than the Sun's. While we do not stubbornly defend this—and we do not refuse to admit the stars into a partnership of this duty, as many philosophers think—we nonetheless refute the astrologers who think that in some <term>nativity</term><note>original: "genitura"; a birth chart used to predict a person's fate.</note> (if the nativities of men pertain to the stars at all) the leadership should sometimes be owed to other planets, with the Sun or Moon being disregarded, whether it be a diurnal or nocturnal birth. They even think the Sun itself can be "oppressed" by the rays of others and badly affected, as if it were reduced to the ranks like just one of the crowd. But more on these things later; for now, we only advise that those who believe other stars have more power than the Sun in changing lower things are more refuted by the evidence of the senses than those who contend they can do almost nothing, attributing this entire illumination and <term>vegetation</term><note>The power of growth and life-force in the earthly world.</note> of the lower world to the <term>Phoebean lamp</term><note>A poetic reference to the Sun, named for Phoebus Apollo.</note>, from which the lunar lamp is also lit for us during the night.

### IN WHAT WAY THE SAME STARS CAN ACT UPON US
### DIFFERENTLY AT DIFFERENT TIMES. Chapter XI.

<term>B</term>ut let us grant the astrologers—and we ourselves do not greatly deny it—that something flows from all the stars into us; it remains to be examined, as their objection demanded, whether the same stars always grant the same things, or whether different stars also grant different things, so that if they are not the same, we may see whether the lower effects are also varied by that diversity. They argue that there are "proper powers" in each star, besides motion and light, in a <term>fourth manner</term><note>An additional category of influence beyond the three standard physical ones.</note>; they prove this from the "nobility" of the heavens and the powers of certain bodies thought to be from heaven; these, therefore, we shall dismantle there. They only bring forward the diversity of the stars themselves for their reasoning: since star differs from star, and light and motion are common to all, they must necessarily have certain proper qualities besides these by which they differ from one another. But <term>Paul</term><note>St. Paul, referencing 1 Corinthians 15:41: "For one star differs from another star in glory."</note> said "star differs from star in brightness"; what then if, just as circular motion is common to all, they differ in motion such that this one moves faster and that one slower? Although this itself might not be granted by all, let it be the same for light: that they agree in light, but differ in the conditions of light, as the light of one star may be more compact, more copious, more concentrated, or thinner than another. For there will be those who believe a star differs more from its own sphere than a star does from another star, yet they differ in no other way than by rarity and density. If this is accepted, it will consequently be thought that their action upon us varies in no other way than that those which are denser, larger, or closer [act more strongly]...

He begins to analyze whether stars possess unique powers or if their differences are merely physical traits like density and brightness.</summary>

-># Ioan. Pici Mirandulæ <-

<meta>Catchword: tur (completing the word "effunduntur" / they are poured out)</meta>

...[they] pour forth more of that light and more heat; those that are rarer, smaller, and more distant pour out less. Ultimately, the breath of warm light and bright heat is the same from all of them, providing health, life, and nourishment to bodies. They differ only in that the breath is thinner from some and more exuberant from others, inspired from some nearby and from others far off. 

But what shall we decide about the same star, given the perpetual revolution of its own motion? Furthermore, it is the opinion of the <term>Peripatetics</term><note>The followers of Aristotle, known for walking about while lecturing.</note> that stars do not change their quality, but only their location—except for the Moon, which, shining with borrowed light, is illuminated more or less according to its turns toward the Sun. Therefore, depending on the turning it has made from the Sun, it reflects light to us more abundantly or more sparingly, and with its light, its heat. Thus, it leaves us almost destitute at the <term>new moon</term><note>original: "nouilunio"</note> when the part facing us is deprived of light, but it fosters and warms us more at the <term>full moon</term><note>original: "plenilunio"</note>, just as it does more when waxing and less when waning. Such variety cannot exist in the stars that shine with a stable and proper light of their own. For this reason, if there is any celestial cause for nearly all the changes that frequently happen to bodies, it is usually attributed to the Moon, because she herself is changeable—not only in position, but she touches us most closely in quality.

For the other planets, change occurs only through the motion of their locations; hence, the variety of their influence is nothing more than that they affect us more intensely or more weakly, insofar as they become nearer or more remote to us while migrating here and there. Their motion is two-fold: universal and proper. The <term>universal motion</term><note>The daily rotation of the entire celestial sphere from East to West.</note> carries them to us daily, lifting them above the earth, and snatches them away daily, leading them toward the setting. From this arises the first diversity of action: they hurl the strongest rays from the summit because they fall more directly to the <term>perpendicular</term><note>The point directly overhead; the zenith.</note>. Therefore, the closer they approach the peak, the more powerfully they affect us; the more they descend from there, the more weakly. 

Whether they can affect us when sunk beneath the earth is a matter for discussion. For since they are not yet completely snatched from us when near the <term>horizon</term><note>original: "finitore"</note>, they can certainly do something, though very little, with rays still reaching us obliquely. However, when they are hidden deep within the hiding places of the earth and are taken further away from us—if I believe they can do nothing, my senses will support me, and reason will not oppose it. Indeed, how can it be believed otherwise? If it is true, as we have defended so far, that nothing reaches us from heaven except via the vehicle of light. This is what <term>Avicenna</term><note>An influential Persian physician and philosopher (c. 980–1037).</note> also said in his books on <term>Meteorology</term><note>original: "metheorologicis"</note>, calling light the vehicle of all celestial powers, and <term>Albertus</term><note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a scientist and philosopher who sought to reconcile Greek science with Christian thought.</note> confirmed it in his book *On Sleep and Waking*. Therefore, just as light does not reach us then, so too no power will reach us.

We shall say that the Sun alone is present to us even at night for this reason: that making his sister <note>The Moon</note> his deputy, he shines upon us through the splendor impressed upon her. Unless, perhaps, this could also be said: since this upper air is continuous with the lower air, the air itself is so fostered by the Sun's presence there that it would be colder if no Sun at all illuminated any part of the air. But how nearly that itself is nothing, if it be anything at all, our eyes and sense of touch will report. If the astrologers have dreamed up some powers for themselves against which the entire mass of the earth is no obstacle, let them at least not be so delirious in their sleep as to not concede that these powers are imprinted upon us more purely and effectively when they are poured into us through the surrounding air...

...than when the entire dense thickness of the brute earth must be perforated by them. If they do not concede this, who could defend them from insanity? For they think that the powers of the stars in the <term>twelfth place</term><note>The 12th House in an astrological chart, located just above the eastern horizon.</note>—which, rising nearest to the east above the horizon, is only one station away from the highest point—are sluggish, ceasing, and weak, yet they believe those same stars have the most vigor and efficacy when at the bottom of the earth <note>The *Imum Coeli* or 4th House, the lowest point of the chart, positioned directly "under" the earth from the observer's perspective.</note>. But we shall show their errors later; now we deal only with what ought to be decided by reason. 

We have spoken of universal motion. By their <term>proper motion</term><note>The independent movement of a planet through the zodiac, as opposed to the daily rotation of the sky.</note>, the planets are carried now toward the south, now toward the north—which the <term>fixed stars</term><note>original: "stellæ hærentes"; the stars that do not move relative to one another, unlike the "wandering" planets.</note> are also believed to do in the opinion of the younger [astronomers]. The Sun does the same, not because it deflects from the orbit it once occupied, but because that orbit is oblique, making it now closer to us, now more remote: closer in the north, more remote in the south. From this, another variety of influence arises, since there is greater efficacy in rays inclining toward us, and less in those receding toward the south. 

Beyond these or similar factors, whatever diversity is imagined in the action of the stars is utterly vain and irrational. Such is the case among astrologers, who think that the same star is affected differently and acquires the most diverse powers for influencing based on the <term>twelve places</term><note>The twelve astrological houses.</note>, the signs it passes through, or the fixed or wandering stars to which it is joined by certain calculated intervals—which they call <term>aspects</term><note>Specific angles between planets, such as a square (90°) or trine (120°).</note>. Against this error, the entire sixth book will be prepared. Here, by the skill of this chapter, we will merely cast against them the authority of the <term>Peripatetics</term><note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note>, who deny any change in the stars other than position—except in the Moon. For if they exclude only corrupting and harmful change, the Moon should not have been excluded, since she herself is not changed in that way by the Sun. Indeed, as we shall see, astrologers do not even free the stars from harmful changes, which weaken their powers and faculties if not their substance; but more on this later.

One might wonder about the Moon: does she receive the rays of other planets just as she does from the Sun? This appears probable because, by her nature, she seems to be a vessel for incident light rather than being luminous herself; and being the lowest of all, she seems uniquely prepared for this function. However, neither the authority of the ancestors nor the evidence of the senses supports this. For instance, when the Moon is in conjunction with the Sun, if she is then positioned opposite the rays of Jupiter or Mars—from which she ought to reflect their light to us more fully—she is nevertheless found to have no rays or light. 

We touch upon this question because if she did draw light from the others, the planets would become more effective toward us by being joined to the Moon, transmitting their power through her to us, which might perhaps reach here less effectively on its own. But if this were to happen, it would happen in a way entirely different from what astrologers think. They believe the Moon transmits the rays of whichever star she is currently found with. I, however, have no doubt that the further the Moon departs from a star, the more of that star's light is communicated to us through her; and the less they are distant, the less light is shared—minimal or certainly none when they are not distant at all. I am moved by evident experience: when joined to the Sun, she does not transmit the Sun's rays to us, the bulk of her body creating a great obstacle. How much less, therefore, would she transmit the rays of others, which are far thinner than solar rays, and...

<meta>This page continues Pico's argument that celestial influence is primarily physical (light and heat) rather than magical. He continues to dismantle the logic of astrological "aspects" by arguing that the Moon and the density of the Earth act as physical barriers to stellar rays.</meta>

<page-num>476</page-num>
<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

...farther from the Moon. See how greatly those are deceived who believe a day or a birth is fortunate when the Moon joins with **benefic** stars <note>In traditional astrology, Jupiter and Venus are labeled "benefic" (good-natured), while Mars and Saturn are "malefic" (harmful).</note>, and unfortunate when she joins with **malefic** ones; in reality, for the Moon to "join" them is nothing other than their influence being intercepted from us by the Moon’s density. Perhaps there is also logic in this: that in the changing of lower things, a **morning planet** <note>original: "Planeta matutinus"; a planet that rises before the sun in the dawn sky.</note> has some prerogative, and because it rises before the Sun, it claims the air for itself before the Sun completely occupies it. But if there is anything to this, it cannot have much weight. 

It remains to be examined whether a new power coalesces from a mixture of rays, acting as the cause of a new effect that individual rays would not produce on their own. **Plotinus** <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who argued that the stars are signs but not causes of human affairs.</note> denies that such a "tempering" can happen to rays—that a new virtue or a new form might spring forth from their union. I believe he thinks this because rays are not bodies like liquids, nor are they qualities fixed to bodies, in the manner of which they are received into bodies so as to be either infected or changed in any way from their own state. Therefore, it is likely for this philosopher that what happens to many qualities does not happen to rays: namely, that from some combination or mixture they are sometimes changed into another form coalescing from all of them—especially since this does not usually happen without the destruction of the simple and particular qualities flowing into the same thing, which one would not easily imagine happening in rays. 

But even if we grant to the astrologers that rays are mixed, or that heat flowing from rays is mixed, we assert this: all rays are always mixed, rather than being, so to speak, **un-allied** <note>original: "asymbolos"; here meaning rays that do not contribute to a common effect.</note>, as if they would not at all be joined with others through those configurations they now call **aspects** <note>Geometric relationships (like squares or trines) between planets that astrologers believe modify their influence.</note>. Therefore, the mixture of the present hour, moment, year, month, and day does not vary from the radiant mixture of another time, except for those reasons by which we have explained that the actions of the stars vary: namely, that there is one temperament of the night and another of the day, one when the stars recede to the south and another when they incline to the north, from which alone arises the strengthening and weakening of heat.

### WHAT VARIETY OF EFFECTS CAN BE ATTRIBUTED TO THE HEAVENS AND WHAT CANNOT. Chapter XII. ###

Let us consider the mixture of all rays in the air; in it there is something you might call **substantial**, and something **accidental**. What is **substantial** is that there is one light or one heat gathered or resulting from all the lights of heaven, and this is indeed perpetual and immutable. But that this specific ray is now more intense in it, or another is weaker, is **accidental**, and it changes repeatedly according to the constant movement of the celestial bodies. The reason for this distinction of ours is easily apparent. For in heaven, which we know to be the principle of this heat, something can be called "substantial," just as we say those things are substantial which follow the substance of a thing inseparably; such things are the incorruptible body, the circular figure (the first of all bodies), the motion in a circle, and the light that nourishes all things with its heat. And if indeed the stars have their own powers, those are also the substantial strengths of the stars. There is again something in heaven and...

<summary>Pico argues that planetary "aspects" are merely physical interceptions of light and that stellar rays do not form new "magical" qualities when they mix. He distinguishes between the "substantial" constant influence of the heavens (heat and light) and "accidental" variations caused by planetary positions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s argument regarding the physical nature of celestial influence. He is moving from the physical properties of light and rays to the philosophical distinction between "substantial" (essential) and "accidental" (incidental) causes in the generation of life.</meta>

<page-num>477</page-num>

...and stars is as variable as it is accidental, so that in all stars there is only a change of position, and in the Moon a change of light. Therefore, whatever in the mixture of rays follows from the **substantial** <note>In Scholastic philosophy, "substantial" refers to the essence of a thing—what makes it what it is (e.g., a human being's "human-ness").</note> properties of the heavens, we call substantial; what follows from the **accidental** <note>“Accidental” refers to non-essential qualities that can change, such as being hot, cold, or in a certain position, without changing the essence of the thing.</note> properties, we call accidental. For example, the mixture may encompass the **Saturnian** <note>original: "Saturniam"; relating to the planet Saturn.</note> power, and the **Jovian** <note>original: "Iouiam"; relating to the planet Jupiter.</note>, and the **Solar**, and the others likewise; this power is in the mixture substantially. But whether these powers are more intense or more relaxed, according to the variety of the rays, is said to be accidental. 

The Sun, therefore, aided by that superior virtue—which is certainly not a changeable virtue, for otherwise it would not always be present in the causes that drive all things, as it is observed to be—the Sun, I say, aided by it, generates man insofar as he is a man. And it generates *this* man, insofar as he is generated from *this* seed and from *this* matter. Therefore, if you look at the substantial condition, or the nature, or the individual character of this effect, any constellation is **indifferent** <note>Meaning the specific arrangement of stars has no effect on the fundamental "essence" or "species" of the creature being born.</note>. However, because of the diversity of the constellation—that is, the various states of the stars and their relationship to the earth—more or less heat is poured into the air, and from a different mixture of rays a new proportion and measure of warm light results; it is this "accidental" factor in the heavens that creates "accidental" diversity in the things produced. 

It is as if someone were to say that a better conception occurs during a full moon, or that a fetus grows more while the Moon is waxing, or that under a temperate state of the sky, a half-full moon is better affected, and therefore a better offspring of this kind is procreated. That diversity which can exist in the substances being generated due to the varying positions of the heavenly bodies, we call accidental and adventitious. This is because, as we have declared, the specific substantial mark of the conceived fetus depends on its own proximate principle and its own substantial matter. Furthermore, the accidents of the seed and the matter contribute more even to accidental properties—since they are more kindred, more proximate, and more intimate—than the outward disposition of the surrounding air. Daily experience makes this manifest: so much so that **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BCE) whose natural philosophy dominated medieval thought.</note> says that if a son does not take shape according to the seeds of the parents and does not draw his likeness from there, it should be counted among **monsters** <note>original: "monstris"; in a pre-modern biological sense, a "monster" was any birth that deviated significantly from the natural likeness of the parents.</note>. 

Hence, nothing prevents us from making the stars only universal causes. To those seeking a distinction of effects from a secondary cause, we say that the varying disposition of the stars can, through changes in the air, vary the disposition of bodies—whether already born or about to be born—in some way, since, as we have said, this change is external and very general. But those things which pertain to the substance, which draws its internal qualities more directly and closely from its own origins, can in no way be foreseen from the heavens. And this is indeed true in the case of physical bodies that are a "perfect substance," all of which have proximate efficient causes present, or what corresponds to them in proportion, as in those things generated from **putrefaction** <note>A reference to the theory of "spontaneous generation," where it was believed that simple organisms like insects or worms could arise from decaying matter without parents.</note> and inanimate mixtures, of which we shall speak in the solution to the fourth reason. 

Yet the sky can produce changes in the air toward heat and cold, moisture and dryness, without any mediating cause. It produces these universally, however, because while it is inherently and healthfully warming, it produces the rest accidentally, according to the condition of the matter, just as by one and the same heat...

<meta>This page continues Pico’s argument that celestial influence is a universal, general force rather than a specific, determining one. He distinguishes between how the Sun affects simple matter (like mud or wax) versus how "perfect substances" (living organisms) are governed by their own internal and proximate causes.</meta>

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola #

...the mud hardens and the wax melts, and under the same Sun, linens become white while they are being washed, yet the face of the one washing them is darkened in the meantime. Furthermore, since this is an **accidental change** <term>Accidental change: A change in non-essential qualities (like color or temperature) that does not change what the thing actually is.</term>, the most powerful factor in it is what we have called "accidental" in the celestial constellation—that is, the position and arrangement of the stars, from which the power of the rays is either intensified or relaxed. Because of this, heat grows stronger or weaker in the air; specifically, because of the various turnings of the Sun, the four seasons of the year vary, and the rising and setting, the ascending and descending, produce nearly the same four changes in the course of a day.

However, positioned between these primary qualities of bodies and inanimate mixtures are the **meteorological impressions** <note>These are atmospheric phenomena like rain, thunder, and clouds, which Renaissance thinkers believed were "impressed" upon the air by celestial heat.</note>, for which the heavens are also the efficient cause, while the lower elements are the matter. For this reason, their diversity depends more on the celestial disposition than do "perfect" bodies <note>“Perfect” here means fully formed living beings, like plants and animals.</note>. Just as thunder occurs mostly in spring and autumn, hail in summer, and snow and rain in winter—though these are less absolute than the four qualities themselves—it is because the solar ray, falling upon matter, creates the qualities by its own power, whereas the meteorological events are indeed moved by the ray but are formed out of the lower matter. Therefore, they vary mostly according to the condition of that matter, as we shall explain more fully in the treatise on the third reason.

But **perfect substances** <term>Perfect substances: Living organisms with their own internal blueprints (seeds/souls) that determine their growth.</term>, which have not only matter but also their own "efficient cause," receive whatever is substantial and proper to them from their own causes. They receive these from the heavens only as a "universal cooperating cause" through its unchanging influence. The heavens do produce a certain changeable, external, and very general mutation, but even about this, astrologers can say nothing. Indeed, this does not depend on the celestial causes they have imagined, nor on the hour of birth, but on other principles, as we shall demonstrate later; for now, we are only investigating what the heavens do and what they do not do.

Therefore, understanding these distinctions we have discussed, **Aurelius Augustine** <note>original: "Aurelius August."; referring to St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD).</note> said it could be thought "not altogether absurdly" that certain stellar influences have power over the differences of bodies alone. He did not assert that it is so, nor did he accuse those who thought otherwise; rather, he lessened the blame of those holding such an opinion, pronouncing it not so much an "absurd opinion" as one that is "not altogether absurd." However, he added an explanation of which physical differences should be understood: just as we see the seasons of the year vary with the Sun’s approach and retreat, and certain kinds of things increase or decrease with the wax and wane of the moon—such as **sea urchins and shellfish** <note>original: "echinnos & chonchas"</note> and the marvelous tides of the ocean. These are his words, in which you see nothing included that contributes to the generation of any perfect substance. Augustine immediately added a warning that their diversities, although mostly physical, ought not to be referred to the stars, but to proximate causes: "What is more physical than the sex of a body? And yet, under the same position of the stars, twins of different sexes could be conceived."

Confirmed a little earlier in the same passage, he had approved of **Hippocrates** <note>The famous Greek physician, often called the "Father of Medicine."</note>, who gave a reason based on proper and secondary causes for why two brothers would fall ill at the same time and recover at the same time. But he did not approve of **Posidonius** <note>A Stoic philosopher and astronomer who argued for "cosmic sympathy" and astrological influence.</note>, who attributed this to the equality of their constellation...

<summary>Pico argues that while stars affect the weather and simple biology (like tides or shellfish), they do not determine the essence of complex living beings. He cites St. Augustine to show that even physical traits like sex are determined by biological "proximate causes" rather than astrology.</summary>

referring it to this, he says, "A medical conjecture is much more acceptable, since parents, as they were affected in body while they lay together, so could the beginnings of those conceived be affected, so that, following the initial growth from the maternal body, they were born with equal health; then, being nourished in one house, with the same foods, where medicine testifies that the air, the position of the place, and wine and water have the greatest power for the body to be affected well or poorly, and accustomed to the same exercises, they bear such similar bodies that they are even moved similarly by the same causes to fall ill at the same time." <margin>P</margin>ressing the first argument of the astrologers back against them, we have declared through a long but necessary digression what the heaven does to us, and how the action of the celestial bodies is varied, whether we consider the stars themselves or the matter receiving their influence. From this it has been made clear that the heaven is a universal cause <term>Universal cause: A general force (like heat or light) that provides the necessary conditions for life, but does not determine specific individual outcomes, much like how a lamp allows everyone in a room to see without choosing what they look at.</term>, and that the distinction of effects—especially the primary and substantial ones—is not to be sought from there. Now, in a fitting order, having moved step-by-step through those things we have disputed, we shall set our hands to resolving the second reason: namely, since it is found that the dispositions of lower bodies vary according to the Sun and Moon's various relationships to us, they contended that the same should be believed concerning other things and planets. For they say that the cycles of the four seasons through the solar circuits, and the status of all bodies, are varied both by that succession and by the lunar increases and decreases. What then? Two things are thought to be gathered from these observations: First, just as we see sea urchins, shellfish, the ocean <note>A reference to the tides and the ancient belief that certain sea creatures grew or shrank in sync with the moon's phases.</note>, and the moisture of bodies change according to the cycles of the Moon, and generally the earthly mass changes according to the Sun’s annual and daily revolution, so we should agree concerning all other things that they are bound to the stars and governed by them. Second, that the manifest power of the Sun and Moon in changing sublunary matter <term>Sublunary matter: Any physical substance on Earth or in the atmosphere, located "below the moon" and therefore subject to change and decay.</term> forces us to believe the same about the rays of other stars—that is, that there is also in them some more hidden but nonetheless great power in changing things and affecting them in many ways. We shall make it clear that neither conclusion follows, as these very points they bring forward for themselves actually favor those who suspect otherwise. But before that happens, we will give the reason for all those observations from the principles already established, so that it may be clear that just as...

Pico argues that what astrologers call "celestial influence" is actually just the physical heat of the Sun changing with the seasons.</meta>

by arguments, so neither should we be led by experiments to feel anything regarding the efficiency of the stars and the change of celestial virtues other than what we have prescribed thus far, guided by natural reason itself. Nor meanwhile shall I cease to mock the many fallacies of the astrologers and their many errors encountered along the way. Let us begin, therefore, with the works of the Sun. The approach and retreat of the Sun varies the seasons of the year; this we would even assert under oath if necessary. But the tilt of the zodiac <note>The "obliquity of the ecliptic," or the 23.5-degree tilt of Earth's axis, which causes the Sun's path to appear higher or lower in the sky throughout the year.</note> causes this very thing, not the nature of the signs. That is to say, the Sun does not blaze in Leo because it is the "sign of the lion," or the "house of the Sun," or a "hot sign," as the astrologers fabricate, but because the Sun is positioned in that spot and is closer to our air, and having been closer for a month and a half <note>original: *sexquimensem*</note> before, it had already heated it. Otherwise, it is also most burning in Cancer, even though, even according to the astrologers, Cancer is not the house or the exaltation <term>exaltation: a specific position in the zodiac where a planet is thought to have its maximum power</term> of the Sun, nor is it a fiery sign, but a watery one.

In the same way, the Sun restores the world in Aries, calling forth flowers and increasing seeds, because then, first returning to us, it breathes a fertile and favorable warmth into bodies. But it is a fiction of the astrologers that Aries is the "exaltation" of the Sun—as if the Sun did not do the exact same thing for other peoples in Libra (which is opposite Aries) as it does for us in Aries. This happens, of course, while it recedes from here and approaches them. Therefore, the sole cause of the entire variety that occurs with the seasons is the greater or lesser distance of the Sun from the lands we inhabit, from which we participate in more or less of its heat.

From this also, thunder occurs in the spring, because when the Sun reaches Aries, the winter humidity is dissolved by the heat of the air; from this, evaporation lifts many things up into the air—namely, a harvest of clouds—from which thunder and lightning proceed. If the astrologers also understand this, what is this—be it sluggishness or a desire to deceive—that they define Aries as a sign that stirs up rain and thunder, as if the nature of that sign, that is, of the Ram, were at work? For this reason, they would never say that the Moon also produces thunder in Aries if they were able or willing to notice that this happens not because of any "fiery virtue" of the sign, but by the action of the Sun arriving at that sign. 

A similar fallacy was written by Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity.</note> in his books on *Judicial Astrology* <note>original: *apotelesmaton*; referring to Ptolemy's *Tetrabiblos*.</note>: that if the Moon in Aries causes disease, it especially causes vitiligo <note>A condition causing loss of skin pigment.</note>, which the Greeks call **alphos** <note>original: *ἀλφὸς*</note> and is commonly called *morphea*; in Cancer it causes *mentagra* <note>A bacterial infection of the beard area.</note>, which the Greeks call *lichenas* and is commonly called *impetigo*; in Libra, leprosy; in Capricorn, freckles. For this is actually drawn from the state of the air when the Sun is carried through those signs; that is, from the quality of spring, at which time the Sun is in Aries. It is drawn from summer when it is in Cancer, from autumn when in Libra, and from winter when it runs through the sign of Capricorn—provided that those types of diseases fit the conditions of these seasons. Vitiligo occurs in spring because it easily invades and occupies the surface of the skin then, on account of humors <note>In ancient medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) whose balance determined health.</note> overflowing especially at that time of year. *Mentagra* belongs to summer, as it arises from drier and sharper matter. Leprosy belongs to autumn, since it is thought to be an infection of black bile. Freckles belong to winter, as they are generated from colder and moister excesses. It is, therefore, the height of stupidity to attribute to the signs things that are caused by the Sun heating the air more or less according to the variety of its position, under which...

...[temperate] times the Sun is carried. Or if they understand this—though it is as if they do not—they think that other planets in the same signs produce the same effects. Let us conclude that the fixed variation in the seasons of the year occurs from nothing else than the approach and retreat of the Sun due to the obliquity of the zodiac <note>The "obliquity of the zodiac" refers to the tilt of the Earth's axis, which causes the Sun's path (the ecliptic) to appear at an angle, creating the seasons.</note>. If all summers are not equally hot, nor all winters equally freezing, this can happen because of the disposition of the physical matter, which has the greatest influence on the air—as proven by our senses and by Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential ancient astronomer and geographer, who despite being an astrologer, grounded much of his work in physical observation.</note>. It is not necessary to attribute this to the heavens, except as a universal cause of all bodily things, as one can learn from Aristotle’s books on *Meteorology* <note>original: *meteorologicis*</note>. 

Thus, if on certain days during the same summer the heat is more intense and on others more dull, the position of the Sun itself does not demand this. Rather, a change occurring lower down produces it—perhaps a wind stirred up somewhere, or a flooding of rain, or something else of this kind that can happen far away from us so that we do not see the cause itself, yet we nevertheless experience its force as its effect flows all the way to our own sky. If some planets are hotter than others, those that are less hot can—by chance, when humors <term>humors: in ancient physics, the qualities of hot, cold, wet, or dry that govern the state of matter and the human body</term> are dissolved but not consumed—generate rains and cover the sky with clouds, from which heat fails and cold intensifies. On the other hand, those that are hotter lead to dryness and heat. It is not contrary to our principles that the "dominion" of a various star might contribute something to the change of the air, provided we do not understand "dominion" here as anything other than the star illuminating us from a closer position or with more direct rays. 

Truly, since if anything reaches us from the higher stars, we suspect it to be altogether very thin, especially regarding those qualities we can perceive with our senses. Furthermore, the causes of storms, if sought in the heavens, are for the most part not found, whether we think about the stars according to the opinion of the astrologers or the philosophers, as we have defined it. It seems that this whole matter—which subtracts from or adds to the actions of the luminaries <note>The "luminaries" refer specifically to the Sun and the Moon.</note>—should be referred instead to the nature of the matter itself. Indeed, the luminaries themselves cause change: one [the Sun] by its position alone, and the other [the Moon] also by its changing light. Neither does so because of the "nature" of the signs they travel through, nor because of the places where they sit, nor because of the planets with which they are configured <term>configured: a technical term for "aspects," or specific angular relationships between planets that astrologers believe create influence</term>, as will be made manifest in the following arguments. 

For this reason, the fact that the Persian Sea is tossed by waves and surges when the Sun enters Virgo, and especially when it reaches Sagittarius, yet is again calm and navigable when the Sun is carried to Pisces, and especially to Gemini—while conversely the Indian Sea is tranquil under Virgo and Sagittarius, but navigable <note>The text suggests a contrast in navigability/storms between these two regions based on the Sun's position.</note> under Pisces and Gemini—this comes not from the quality of the signs, but from the position of the Sun and the condition of the material environment, which even the astrologers confess. Therefore, it would be a useful and not at all superstitious observation for sailors to track these times, taking into account the sea they are navigating; they even observe days on which they predict one must abstain from sailing. If these things have any cause from the heavens, they can have it from nowhere else but the Sun, since the observation of them is fixed and perpetual. Therefore, it can only be referred to the Sun—whose relationship to us is almost always exactly the same at the same times—and in no way to the other constellations, which are never found in the same place at the same times,
