# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

...are defined; for example, the days always suspected by sailors are the 1st, 7th, 15th, 17th, 19th, and 25th of March; the 6th of April; the 5th, 6th, 12th, and 20th of February; and the 12th, 15th, 17th, 19th, and 20th of the sixth month <note>original: *sextus*, referring to June</note>. They always use this unchanging observation and say that on these days, great changes in the sea usually occur, moving either toward calm or toward storm. Since the outcomes are uncertain, those who abstain from sailing will act more safely, lest the change perhaps turns toward the worse. This, therefore, cannot be reduced to the <term>astrological positions</term> <note>The specific geometric relationships and "houses" planets occupy in a horoscope.</note> that astrologers note and command us to observe, since those same planetary alignments do not return at the same times of the year, but are entirely different. An astrologer might pronounce those very days—always suspected by captains—to be harmless or even most fortunate for navigation, while labeling days that sailors do not particularly fear as the most dangerous, based on the varying state of the Sun and the mixed ranks of the planets they represent at that hour.

For this reason, a sailor will not approve of such rules, as they are most hostile to his own principles. Since these sailors' rules are proved daily by long experience and the practice of a sublime art, they provide the most abundant proof of the astrologers' vanity. These changes can have a twofold cause: one from the Sun and the other from the water. Just as the humors <note>In ancient medicine, the four fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that were thought to determine a person's health and temperament.</note> of our body have their own periods by which they are moved, so might the <term>ocean</term> <note>Pico uses the term "oceanus" to refer to the great body of water encompassing the world, which he treats as a living system with its own rhythms.</note>. It is known with evident certainty that the Sun, according to the moments of its approach to us or retreat from us, changes the disposition of both the sea and all physical bodies.

However, the reader ought to be warned that this variety of seasons is denoted by those who write on farming and sailing through the setting and rising of the "fixed stars," such as Arcturus, the <term>Pleiades</term> <note>original: *vergiliarum*. A prominent star cluster used since antiquity to mark the seasons for planting and sailing.</note>, the Hyades, and others. This is not because these stars themselves are the ones whose influence is feared or sought—otherwise, not even the astrologers would say this, as they hold that fixed stars are ineffective on their own unless they occupy the <term>pivots</term> <note>original: *cardines*. The four most powerful points in an astrological chart: the Ascendant, Descendant, Midheaven, and Imum Coeli.</note>. Rather, these stars serve as a visible sign for the masters of those arts, whether they are learned or uneducated, by which a specific time may be distinguished. No better sign could be found that is both perpetual and conspicuous than the emergence and setting of the stars. Furthermore, nothing else would secure more authority and observance among the unrefined common folk.

It is written by physicians that winter illnesses are sometimes resolved in summer, and summer ones in winter; those that attack in winter may leave in spring, and those that start in spring may depart toward autumn. Finally, those occurring at any time of year are ended at another, precisely because the quality of these times differs according to the Sun's proximity to or distance from the earth. What they say about the Moon regarding <term>critical days</term> <note>Days during an illness when a major change or "crisis" was expected; astrologers linked these to the Moon's phases.</note> is vain and irrational, but we shall discuss this later when we speak of the Moon. From these same progressions of the Sun comes the varied condition of all things, both those lacking life and all living beings, under the different inclinations of the heavens. Not all lands produce the same things, and the customs of peoples and the physical constitution of their bodies vary in different regions. Nor is it necessary for us to imagine other constellations, other signs, or other planets under which those places are subject, besides the Sun. The Sun is always carried between <term>Cancer and Capricorn</term> <note>The Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, which mark the northernmost and southernmost latitudes where the Sun can appear directly overhead.</note>. Therefore, whoever lives between the equator <note>original: *circulum aequidialem*</note> and the summer solstice necessarily inhabits a very hot...

### on Astrology Book III.

...inhabit the region, while those situated under the North <note>original: *aquilone*, referring to the north wind</note>, since they are furthest from the Sun, inhabit a very cold one; those in between have a temperate climate. And since the right part of the sky, the East, is more effective, the power of the Sun is greater there than in the West. From this, a reason can be given for all things, insofar as it pertains to the heavenly cause, which are driven by the property of things. For gems, spices, and others of this kind, which require more celestial heat, are produced toward the East and the South; likewise, lions, tigers, and elephants are produced in those same lands, along with other animals that require powerful heat to be generated, to live, and to remain in their vigor. Only man is born and preserved in every part of the earth, because of the ample <term>latitude</term> <note>In this context, "latitude" refers to the broad range of adaptability or the "span" of human nature.</note> of his nature under a multiform habit; although to some philosophers it has even suggested the suspicion that one man differs from another by a specific <term>essential difference</term> <note>The philosophical idea that different groups of humans might belong to different species, which Pico generally rejects in favor of human unity.</note>. Therefore, those who inhabit the southern part, the more they breathe hot air, the colder they are internally; for this reason they are timid, effeminate, and—as is proven by both ancient and modern experience—born for servitude. These things happen because immoderate heat so relaxes the body that it evokes and consumes the greatest part of the internal heat; hence, being drawn to the surface of the body and leaving the inner chambers, it leaves blackness on the skin and timidity in the heart. In contrast, those who live under a cold sky, toward the North, are high-spirited, strong, and fair-skinned, for the opposite reason. Yet both peoples—either those who are most under the Sun or those who are moved furthest from it—possess little "humanity" and are not very sociable, due to the exuberance of heat or cold, by which they depart from that moderate <term>temperament</term> <note>The "mean" or ideal balance of the four qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry) which was believed to foster civilization and reason.</note> in which our nature is primarily situated. Indeed, both peoples are monstrous and wild, both because of the common cause we have mentioned, and because one is fierce while the other is fearful.

Therefore, it is not as the Greek astrologers fabulate—that because the harmful planets **Saturn** and **Mars** dominate the extreme <term>climates</term> <note>Traditional geographical zones or latitudes used in ancient science.</note>, those peoples are therefore more monstrous; nor because **Saturn** rules the southerners are they therefore timid and short-lived; nor because **Mars** rules the northerners are they more warlike. This is a fiction, in which even the other astrologers do not agree, as they do not place **Mars** over the northerners, but the **Moon**. We, using neither **Mars** nor the **Moon**, have provided the proper reason for the condition of both peoples from the Sun; to dream up any other cause for oneself belongs to a trifler rather than a philosopher. As they say, **Saturn** also dominates in India, and yet they are long-lived there; why then are the southerners short-lived due to the exuberant coldness of **Saturn**? Why are they timid? For even there the most ferocious beasts are born, although <term>Aristotle</term> writes that all animals in the north are more "masculine." But the human "middle ground" <note>Humanity's ideal state of balance.</note> suffers the extremes most poorly; and by the same reasoning that stomachs are warmer in winter than in summer <note>A reference to the theory of *antiperistasis*, where internal heat is concentrated by external cold.</note>, so those people under excessive heat grow cold internally, and having scarcely completed their thirtieth year of life, they are worn out by old age, as <term>Avicenna</term> relates. Those in the North, under a frozen seat, boil most deeply in their principal members, with their heat enclosed and with much thicker blood; they are as much stronger than the southerners as the southerners turn out to be more ingenious due to the subtlety of their spirits and blood.

The middle nations, being neither dull from a lack of blood nor from a thickness of spirit, are just as much more prudent and wise as they are made for ruling; they are, so to speak, more fully human. This general variety of the earth's inhabitants comes from the <term>celestial circulation</term> <note>original: *cœlesti circulatione*; the regular movement of the sun and stars around the Earth</note>, to which are added many specific qualities from the <term>sublunary disposition</term> <note>original: *sublunari dispositione*; the physical arrangement of the environment below the moon, such as the local terrain and elements</note> of lands, air, and water. For instance, while one region is impassable due to swamps or half-withered by stagnant waters and repeatedly besieged by the gloomy nights of mists, another is open to the winds and their harshness, or elevated by mountains. But I have already held you on these matters longer than is proper.

These influences pass from the lands to the air, and the air itself has its own properties from within itself—that is, in different places, as <term>Panaetius</term> <note>A Stoic philosopher (c. 185–109 BCE) who argued that many human traits attributed to the stars were actually caused by climate and environment.</note> says—not sought from heaven, but held from its own principles. The extent to which these differences in the air can affect bodies is a matter of debate. That these factors immediately change the inhabitants by their very breaths is evident from the things they consume; for there is no one who does not know that these things become either harmful or healthy based solely on the condition of the water and air. 

Hence, the first diversity of bodies arises from the celestial impression made by the Sun, which is immediately followed by another diversity arising from diet. But the variety of intellects and morals depends both on the condition of the body and on education and the foundation of habit, which closely rivals the power of nature. Added to this are the laws, which carry the greatest weight in these matters; so much so that they can make wild nations very gentle, if they are rightly enacted, and conversely can weaken the strongest nations and turn the best into the worst if the laws are bad. From this, the freedom of choice is most clearly demonstrated against every necessity of nature.

The Gauls <note>original: *Galli*; the ancestors of the modern French</note> were once infamous for the love of boys, if we are to believe <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>The famous 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer and astrologer.</note> and <term>Aristotle</term>; yet now, by the benefit of <term>Christian law</term> and the most holy prince <term>King Louis</term> <note>Likely referring to Saint Louis IX of France (reigned 1226–1270), famous for his moral reforms.</note>, they abhor this crime so much that no nation under heaven does so more. Nor should we rely on the example of a single people, since the preaching of the Gospel has changed the morals and institutions of almost the entire world, replacing those that had been established from the beginning. 

Furthermore, the quality of a region can do much to encourage the pursuit of arts and mastery—depending on what a person first encounters—such as a city favorable to the sea causing one to devote oneself to trade and navigation, or a city near an academy to letters, or to military service if it is troubled by hostile neighbors or internal civil factions. There are those whom fertility and abundance make idle and pleasure-seeking, while scarcity and sterility make them hardworking, industrious, and diligent. 

"But indeed," some <term>astrologer</term> might perhaps say, "we do not deny these things; rather, we assert and proclaim them with you. However, we contend that there are other properties in places, namely from private influences and a peculiar <term>constellation</term>, according to the <term>trigon</term> <note>An astrological grouping of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element (fire, earth, air, or water).</note>, the planet, or the sign under which a region falls, or the disposition of the sky under which the foundations of a city were laid, or under which its empire, or king, or tyrant took power. Therefore, even if what you say is true, it does not follow that our claims cannot also be true." 

But, most excellent diviners, I do not think it follows from the things I have recounted that your fabrications *cannot* exist, but rather that we should understand that through what we have said, a cause can be clearly given for every kind of diversity and...

of places and nations, so that seeking other causes is not at all necessary. For the following pages will demonstrate that those causes which you astrologers introduced above are both false and fabulous. Truly, as we were disputing against those things to which you yourselves attribute the diversity of peoples and regions, it was likely that someone would ask: what, then, is the cause of such great variety? Therefore, before we overturned the false causes, it was necessary to demonstrate the true causes, so that from this, those unnecessary claims of yours might be understood—which will afterwards be refuted as fictions and impossibilities. Thus, we did not introduce that life-giving heat of the heaven, about which we have discussed so much above, nor the efficacy of the sun, in order to tear down your views; nor did we introduce the idea that rays are intensified or relaxed based on the distance or proximity of the stars to us. Rather, before we refuted your invented trifles and showed that a change of stellar power based on places, signs, and aspects is most absurdly imagined by you, I wished to make it known that whatever the force of the heaven effects in us—by the authority of philosophers, the testimony of the senses, and the judgment of reason—all of it can most sufficiently occur through the <term>common influx of light</term> <note>original: *communem influxum luminis*; the idea that the stars influence Earth through the physical properties of light rather than magical or symbolic "powers."</note>, which is wholesomely warm and continually emanating from a perpetually moving body. Therefore, to imagine other virtues or "stellar influxes" upon bodies is a mere outpouring, after which it would be more easily declared that believing in what you have imagined is no longer merely superfluous, but insane.

### HOW THE POWER OF THE MOON VARIES, and that certain days of the Moon are observed by vain superstition. Chapter 14.

<margin>THE MOON</margin>
<margin>Stars</margin>
**W**e have shown from the works of the Sun that the dogmas of the astrologers are proven unnecessary. The same must be done regarding the works of the Moon. **Ptolemy**, in his <term>Apotelesmata</term> <note>original: *apotelesmatis*; referring to Ptolemy’s *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology</note>, says that the Moon, from the <term>new moon</term> <note>original: *interlunium*; the period when the moon is between the earth and sun and invisible</note> until it becomes halved, is more effective at producing moisture; from then until the full moon, it produces heat; from the full moon until it is halved again, dryness; and then until the conjunction, coldness. Thus, he claims she has the nature of spring and air in her first quarter, summer and fire in the second, autumn and earth in the third, and winter and water in the fourth; and that she then most greatly excites the qualities of these seasons in bodies. That division is more "pretty" than it is natural or true, since the condition of heat is such that when it is weak, it does not move moisture (as it can scarcely be felt), but when it possesses some efficacy, it begins to dissolve; and once diffused, it dissolves more as it becomes more powerful, unless it grows so strong that it consumes the moisture it caused to flow—for then it dries out, rather than moistens. But the Moon's heat, being very thin, is never so intensified that it dries; rather, it grows within those limits by which it moistens bodies with heat, but does not parch them. Thus, it follows that the more light the Moon has, the more moisture it effects, just as it effects more heat; conversely, as it is deprived of light, it likewise both moistens and warms less. It would therefore be better to say she has the nature of spring...

<summary>Pico argues that the physical light and heat of the heavens are enough to explain celestial influence, dismissing complex astrological theories as "insane." He begins a specific critique of Ptolemy's theory that the Moon's phases correspond to the four seasons and their physical qualities.</summary>

...and its quality follows from the first quarter to the full moon, rather than from the <term>interlune</term> <note>The "interlune" or "interlunium" refers to the period of the New Moon when the moon is between the Earth and the Sun and invisible to us.</note> to that first quarter itself; for if the nature of spring is defined as moist, it cannot represent winter from the second quarter to the <term>conjunction</term> <note>The "coitus" or "conjunction" occurs at the New Moon, when the Moon and Sun are at the same celestial longitude.</note>, nor autumn from the full moon to that same quarter, since autumn is dry and winter is moist. 

In truth, after the Moon has been full, it provides moisture until it is half-full; from then until the conjunction, it dries out—that is, its moistening effect ceases—which is why timber that is meant to last is cut at that time. Therefore, <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer of antiquity.</note> himself spoke much more correctly in the *Book of One Hundred Enunciations* <note>original: "libro centum enunciatorum"; this refers to the *Centiloquium*, a collection of 100 astrological aphorisms traditionally attributed to Ptolemy, though now considered pseudo-Ptolemaic.</note> when he said that from the Moon’s first quarter (namely, from the point it moves away from its meeting with the Sun) the moisture of bodies flows until the second quarter [the full moon], but in the remaining times it decreases. 

This is confirmed not only by the reasoning we have stated, but also by experience itself; for as the Moon waxes, there is an addition of moisture, and as it wanes, there is a diminution. This is because it is not only the quality of the light that operates, but also its motion toward increase or decrease. Therefore, when it begins to rise after departing from the Sun until it is half illuminated, it moistens and warms more than when, possessing the same amount of light, it tends toward the conjunction during the second <term>dichotomy</term> <note>The "dichotomy" refers to the moon when it is exactly half-illuminated (the quarter phases).</note>; this is because in the former case the light is growing, while in the latter it is failing. 

This is the whole of lunar astrology, observed usefully and naturally by physicians, farmers, and sailors. For they have generally judged the time of the waxing Moon to be favorable for planting, because seeds, nourished by a more generous moisture, grow more rapidly themselves. Conversely, the time of the waning Moon is for cutting timber, since at that time all material is drier and thinner, and thus does not rot as easily or get consumed by decay. On the other hand, if any wood is cut while the Moon is increasing in light, it easily putrefies and is ruined because moisture is then overflowing. 

For this reason, <term>Hesiod</term> <note>An ancient Greek poet (c. 700 BC); his *Works and Days* contains much agricultural and lunar advice.</note> rightly praises the ninth day of the Moon for planting trees, as he does the thirteenth, because—as <term>Plutarch</term> <note>A Greek philosopher and biographer (c. 46–120 AD).</note> says—the power grafted into the roots is now more fully spread by the light. Yet he makes the same day unfavorable for casting seeds, because a cast seed desires rains more, so that it might rot and sprout. Furthermore, he says the sixteenth day is not suitable for planting, because the failing light does not sufficiently draw out the sprouts. 

Wherefore, what <term>Virgil</term> <note>The Roman poet (70–19 BC); this refers to a passage in the *Georgics* regarding lucky and unlucky days for farm work.</note> said—"the seventh after the tenth is lucky both for planting vines" and what follows—cannot be understood as meaning the seventeenth day; for that day is least lucky for planting vines due to the diminished light. Rather, he either judged the "first-seventh" which comes after the tenth to be better (that is, the fourteenth day, on which, as the Moon is full, vines are planted not unluckily), or—what is more consistent with reason—he praised two days: the seventh and the tenth, but the tenth more so; which is why he says the seventh *after* the tenth is lucky. For the matter stands thus: on the seventh day, the half-full Moon supplies enough heat and moisture to the roots of the plants, but the tenth day does the same even more abundantly. One could not denote the seventeenth day except through ignorance and error, since that day is suitable not for planting trees, but rather for cutting them, as Hesiod also [says]...

He reconciles classical advice from Ptolemy, Hesiod, Virgil, and Plutarch with his theory that the waxing moon promotes growth through moisture while the waning moon facilitates drying.</summary>

...[he] also records, clearly for the reason we mentioned: the decreasing moisture. For this reason, timber for building ships, which must last a long time, is prepared at that time <note>The waning moon, when moisture is thought to retreat, making the wood drier and less prone to rot.</note>. As for the fact that the Greek poet <note>Hesiod, the 8th-century BC author of *Works and Days*.</note> commands that crops be brought to the threshing floor then, Proclus <note>A 5th-century AD Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a commentary on Hesiod’s work.</note> writes this reason: that winds usually rise after the full moon, by which the grain itself may be distinguished from the chaff and the husk. 

Just as the cause and reason for the work on these days is easily understood, so other lunar days can be more suitable for certain tasks for reasons that are not so obvious, even though they arise from those same natural principles we have mentioned. Indeed, a portion of such great light can harmonize with something in a matching proportion, while it will clash with another. This is perhaps the nature of those instructions: Hesiod commands that lambs be castrated on the sixth day of the Moon, oxen and pigs on the eighth, and mules on the twelfth; and that the sixth and sixteenth days are more favorable for begetting males than females, but the tenth for females. However, he orders calves to be castrated in autumn during the waning Moon for a well-known reason: for those to be emasculated, they fear the flow of fluids; therefore, he requires both a dry season and a "dry" Moon <note>A waning moon was physically associated with dryness.</note>. For this reason, they also prevent them from drinking much during castration. 

Thus there is an evident reason why Hesiod says the sixth and sixteenth are more suitable for begetting males than females, but the fourteenth for females: because, as we have repeated quite often, moisture increases with the light. Therefore, at the full moon, the "excrements of generation" <note>original: "excrementa generationis"; in ancient biology, reproductive fluids like semen were categorized as a refined "surplus" or "excrement" of the body's nutrition.</note> will drip more moistly, from which offspring are more likely female than male. In this manner, you may reduce other things passed down by Hesiod to natural causes. Although he mixes in a few things—albeit very few—from ancient superstition, there is nothing anywhere that favors the [judicial] astrologers. 

Similarly, pilots <note>Referring to ship captains or navigators.</note> can usefully observe many days based on these changes of the Moon's reflected light without superstition, since that variation of light has great power in altering the state of the air. For this reason, they prudently abstain from sailing during the new moon and full moon, when storms are usually stirred up during these times. 

Physicians themselves also rightly advise the sick by observing the days during the Moon's increase and growth, lest the flowing humors, to a greater or lesser degree, escape their notice—especially in an afflicted body which, being destitute of its own strength, is more vulnerable to "foreign injury" <note>External harmful influences or physical imbalances caused by the environment.</note>. For example, to open a vein <term>bloodletting</term> while the Moon is waxing, but conversely to apply <term>cupping glasses</term> <note>original: "ventosare"; a medical practice where heated glass cups are used to create a vacuum on the skin to draw out "vices" or imbalanced humors.</note> while it is waning rather than waxing, perhaps has a reason, since the incision of a vein expels while the cupping glass attracts. Therefore, since the humors are boiling up and expanding toward the extremities of the body during the beginning of the month [the waxing moon], perhaps more of the attracted matter would be drawn out than is proper. Unless one says that the works of [medical] art are always more successful when they harmonize with the progression of nature. But let these matters be left to the judgment of physicians. Truly, whatever else they might observe beyond these things possesses a manifest vanity <note>In this context, "vanity" refers to empty or false superstitions that have no basis in physical reality.</note>, as will become clear in what follows.

### THE TIDES OF THE SEA CAN BE ATTRIBUTED TO A
### cause other than the Moon, and if they are so attributed,
### astrology derives no benefit from it. Chapter XV.

**D**E <note>The original text begins with a decorative woodcut initial 'D', common in 16th-century printing to mark the start of a major new section.</note> There is a complex question regarding the flow and ebb of the sea <note>The "flux and reflux," or the rising and falling of the tides.</note>, since it seems to everyone that this proceeds from the Moon. Adelard <note>original: "Adelandus"; likely referring to Adelard of Bath, a 12th-century English scholar who introduced many Arabic scientific concepts to the Latin West.</note>, following the opinion of the Saracens <note>original: "Saracenorum"; a medieval term for Muslims or Arabs, who were the leading astronomers and physicists of the Middle Ages.</note>, explains and proves this cause for the rising and falling of the sea as follows. For when, he says, the arms of the sea themselves—namely, those masses of water that are separated by the intervening land—rush to meet and flow together with a rapid force, it happens partly because of the mountains standing in the way, and partly because of the position of the land itself, that they are turned back from that same course when they fail, and they are called back by the positioning of that place to where their ancestral and natural motion impels them. 

The Moon, however, is not the cause; otherwise this same thing would happen in the seas closer to the torrid zone <note>The tropical regions of the Earth near the equator.</note>, since they are no further from the Moon—so that there is no reason they should not feel its power—nor are the waters there thought to be less moist in nature. And yet, there is no such reversal <note>reciprocation or ebb/flow</note> there, because the cause we mentioned is missing: the parts of the sea running together through the gaps in the mass of the earthly terrain. This opinion of his is not greatly different from the appearance of truth, since the parts of every element are carried by a natural inclination toward their own integrity <note>A common Aristotelian idea that elements seek to be "whole" or "united" with their own kind.</note>. What wonder is there, then? If the stretches of the ocean, separated by intervening lands, desire to rush together, they strike the shores as they approach, and having been repelled by the obstruction, they retreat in the same way. When this cause is removed (as happens in the southern sea), we see that these tides do not appear. So someone might say that this motion of approaching and receding is natural to the water—not insofar as it is simply water, but insofar as it consists of parts of the principal element <note>The universal sphere of the element of Water.</note> that have been divided and separated by the obstruction of the land's mass.

If this reasoning does not satisfy someone, let them hear another. Astrologers admit that such recurring flows do not happen in all waters, even sea waters, but only in those where the earth is deep, hard, rough with frequent disturbances, and uneven, while the water is abundant—water that neither increases with the addition of rivers nor decreases by flowing away, but which has taken up a long-lasting residence there with a thick density. Therefore, a reservoir is formed, a nurse of many vapors, neither thin nor easily blown away, which derive that well-known bitterness and saltiness <term>falsugo</term> <note>original: "falsuginem"; a term for the briny quality of seawater, which Pico suggests is caused by "vapors" trapped by the density of the sea and the heat of the sky.</note> from their parents—that is, the watery earth, the earthy water, and the heat of the sky. 

Since springs, rivers, and even some seas do not have these conditions and sources, they say these tides do not appear in them. From this, a sufficiently clear and sufficient cause for the sea's reversal might appear to anyone: since from such earth and water, vapors such as we described and winds are repeatedly stirred up, from which wind and turmoil arise in the water, especially because from that motion and impulse, and the mixture of vapors, it grows hot, and so it seeks a larger space in which to spread itself. There is also a third cause of motion: the reflection of winds lashing the surface of the water down to its lower parts, which blowing...

<summary>Pico argues that the tides of the sea are caused by physical geography, the movement of water masses, and internal vapors/heat rather than the mystical influence of the Moon. He uses these naturalistic explanations to undermine the necessity of astrology in explaining terrestrial phenomena.</summary>

entangled by the winds from there, they rush the waters forward in an upward attempt; then the waters necessarily overflow while they belch out, and they swell and are similarly thrown back and driven. Once turned back, they create their own rising flow. Again, when that force settles as the vapors are dissolved, they subside and are halted, and contracting into narrow places, they withdraw from the occupied locations. This generation of vapors and winds—according to the nature of the sea—just as it is almost perpetual, so too is its perpetual dissolution; it seems to be a sufficient cause for the continuous ebb and flow. From this, the water returns cold which previously had arrived warm. This is what Adelard <note>Adelard of Bath, a 12th-century scholar who translated Arabic scientific works into Latin.</note> points out to us. 

And those who hold this opinion can indeed give a reason why certain larger seas do not ebb and flow, even though both winds and exhalations are present. For the same effect certainly happens to them as well, but the vastness of the open sea and the distance of the shores removes the appearance of the rise and fall. Thus, it is more correctly said that the waters appear to do this, rather than alternating; that is, they exhibit a fluctuating swell rather than a reciprocating tide. If these things harmonize with natural reason and experiments, why should they be judged improbable? Or why is it necessary to add the motion of the Moon to these causes—claiming it drags the waters downward and even upward—especially since those factors do not correspond which would be necessary? For instance, tides should become more abundant when the Moon is increased in light, faster in its course, closer to the earth, declining north from the path of the Sun, or positioned in northern signs. On the contrary, the tides are weaker when the conditions are otherwise than what we have said. 

Furthermore, it does not seem that anything can be objected to those who feel this way, except for the harmony of the waters with the Moon in both their rising and falling. Which (if what Abu Ma'shar <note>original: "Aboafar"; Abu Ma'shar was a Persian astrologer whose "Great Introduction" was a standard textbook in the Middle Ages.</note> confesses is true) I do not know how it could even be used as an objection. For he writes that the beginnings of the flow and ebb are not the same everywhere, even where there is no difference in the horizon, but it sometimes happens that at the same time the waters recede in one place, they begin to flow in another. Nor does he himself hide the fact that this has given many people reason to suspect that these movements do not depend on the movements of the Moon. Although he tries to give a reason for this diversity to defend the idea that the Moon is nonetheless the cause, it follows that an argument for the Moon's influence cannot be drawn from it. From this, an opportunity for contradiction is rather provided; these views differ greatly among themselves—whether the cause of the tide is evidently confirmed by the Moon’s timing, or whether it is not evidently refuted by them. 

Al-Bitruji <note>original: "Alpetragius"; a 12th-century astronomer from Al-Andalus who proposed an alternative to Ptolemy's planetary system.</note> proposed a celestial cause for this motion, not from the Moon, but from the daily motion by which all things are moved. But lower things are moved less. For the sphere of fire is rotated in a circle; an uncoordinated motion occurs in the air, which in the water results in the flow and ebb. I discuss all these things more as a philosopher investigating the true cause of this effect, rather than just to contradict astrologers, since nothing is added to or taken away from astrological matters here, whether we attribute these ebbs and flows to the courses of other stars or to the Moon. Since this very thing is (as Favorinus <note>Phauorinus of Arles, a 2nd-century skeptic philosopher who argued against the validity of astrology.</note> most truly said) rather a fallacy of astrologers, who, when they see certain earthly things situated among men moved by the sense and guidance of celestial things, such as

The fact that the ocean, as if a companion of the Moon, grows old and young along with her, has clearly provided them with an argument to persuade us to believe that all human affairs, both the smallest and the greatest, are led and governed as if bound to the stars and constellations. For even if they are influenced by the Moon—which we ourselves freely and easily believe—what does that prove for the astrologers or against us? For it is not, as some think, to be understood from this that the stars act not only through motion and light, but through <term>occult influxes</term> <note>Hidden or supernatural "flows" of power from celestial bodies, a core concept in astrology that Pico argues against.</note>, especially since the Moon, when positioned beneath the bottom of the earth, might move the waters to which its light cannot then reach. Roger Bacon, in a letter to Pope <note original: "Clementem Quintum">The text mentions Clement V, though Roger Bacon famously addressed his major works to Pope Clement IV; Pico may be following a specific manuscript tradition or making a historical slip.</note> Clement V, wished to provide the cause based on light in this manner: For when, he says, the Moon rises over the sea of any region, the lunar rays fall at oblique angles and are therefore weaker; thus they stir up vapors from the depths of the sea which they cannot consume—vapors, I say, filling the waters with swelling tumors so that they are extended from their channels, just as a fire placed under a **cooking pot** causes the water to evaporate, from which the lips of the vessel foam over. For this reason, while this attraction of bubbling vapors lasts, the water flows from its seat. But when the Moon nears its summit, the rays likewise become straighter and therefore stronger the more she ascends; eventually, they become powerful enough to be equal to dissolving the vapors. On account of this, says Roger, the <term>flow</term> <note original: "accessus">The incoming tide.</note> becomes slower as the Moon nears the meridian; but when she declines, the waters immediately decline as well, just as in that same pot: when the heat has become more intense and the vapors are consumed, the liquid subsides and retreats to the bottom of the vessel. After this question has been proposed, he moves to consider by what means the Moon retains its power of moving while tending from the west to the bottom of the earth. For then the waters rise just as they do when the Moon is striving from its rising to the summit. And yet (as he confesses) no force of rays can penetrate through the middle of the earth. He therefore resolves it thus: The highest heaven, he says—whether it be the eighth or the ninth—is necessarily dense, since it terminates our sight, which is only terminated by something dense. Consequently, it is necessary for the lunar rays extended there to be reflected to the opposite part. Therefore, if the Moon is moved from the west to the bottom of the earth, its power will be active in the opposite quarter of the heavens, and by the reflected ray, it does what it was doing when proceeding from the east to the summit. This is Bacon's invention, in which he takes so much pleasure that he boasts that he was the first to give a reason for the <term>flow and retreat</term> <note original: "accessus atque recessus">The tides.</note> in opposite quarters, even though there are as many shameful errors in his words as there are words themselves. First, he contradicts—I will not say experience—but certainly <term>Abu Ma'shar</term> <note original: "Aboasari">The 9th-century Persian astrologer and astronomer whose work was central to medieval European astrology.</note>, whose interpreter he makes himself; for Abu Ma'shar teaches that the vigor of the flow occurs when the Moon reaches the summit of heaven, and is not relaxed until she begins to descend. Conversely, Bacon thinks the flow is relaxed the more the Moon nears the summit, because the vapors are dissolved by the hotter light. Nor did he see that the light of the Moon is never so intensified that it could consume maritime exhalations—not even stir up such great ones as are needed for moving the...

high tides. If he should stubbornly deny this, he must admit, even against his will, that for several days around the new moon there would be no ocean tides, since at that time there is either no lunar light or it is so thin that no amount of impudence could claim it is sufficient for generating so many vapors in the sea and then dissolving them. Finally, why are the rays of the descending Moon not stronger than those of the ascending? Why does the descending Moon call back the waters, while the ascending Moon pours them out? And why are the rays not weaker when slightly declining from the summit <note>The zenith, or the highest point in the sky.</note> than when first rising? Why does it cause a retreat there, and an advance here? For, as he himself feels, the vigor of the rays with more intense heat represses the tide, since their weakness increases it. Finally, who would believe that in the reflected rays of the Moon running beneath the earth, there is such great power that they can even consume the aroused vapors? Or if they cannot do that, what is the cause of the retreat, when the Moon is carried below the <term>horizon</term> <note original: "finitorem">Pico uses the term "finitor" to describe the boundary of the visible sky.</note> based on Bacon's foundation? Why, when the Moon departs, do those waters depart which were approaching as it rose?

Let Bacon therefore keep these inventions of his for himself; as for us, if such an effect pertains to the Moon, let us refer it to its motion, which the movement of the ocean imitates by a silent consensus of nature, wherefore it rises with the rising Moon and falls with the falling Moon. This indeed seems to have pleased Saint Thomas <note original: "Diuo Thomae">St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential scholastic philosopher and theologian.</note> in his book *On the Occult Works of Nature*. Nor should we think these tides are an increase or decrease of the volume of waters, but rather—as the words themselves express—an "access" and "recess," <note>Referring to the flow (access) and ebb (recess) of the tide.</note> not of added or diminished water, but of the sea extending itself by rising and contracting by falling. We say these things concerning the nightly and daily tide. 

For if there are any seas (as written by some) always positioned in high tide while the Moon's light increases—that is, from <term>conjunction</term> <note original: "coitu">The "meeting" of the sun and moon at the New Moon.</note> to full moon—and again in retreat when it diminishes from full moon back to conjunction, those seas do not follow the Moon's motion in its sphere, but rather the motion (so to speak) of the light in the Moon, as it decreases and increases in like manner; the variation of which can also somewhat vary the daily tide. But the observations handed down on this point do not agree. For both the Egyptians and those who sail to the west said that the high tide was invigorated from the noon of the first day of the lunar month until the eleventh day, and weakened from the eleventh to the eighteenth and part of the following day. Then from there it intensifies again until the twenty-sixth, and thereafter slackens until the beginning of the month. Moreover, whenever the high tide is greater, the low tide is smaller, and vice versa in a changed ratio. 

There are others who say this is truly perceived in the waters of rivers flowing from springs, which on the mentioned days are extended in some and contracted in others at their sources. But concerning the sea, it is reported differently by the Easterners, who do not even agree among themselves; for there are those who report that in the first and last <term>decan</term> <note>A ten-day period of the lunar month.</note> of the month, the high tides are diminished, but they grow in the middle. The reason for this seems to be that they grow with fuller light and decrease with failing light. Others say it is not a perpetual state for many days—that the tides either increase or fail—but that it happens on one or two days, whether they are intensifying or slackening. <term>Albumasar</term> <note original: "Aboasar">The Latinized name for Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a famous Persian astrologer whose work was a cornerstone of medieval European astrology.</note> makes four shifts in this manner: the first after conjunction, when it begins to recede...

The Moon, as long as it is half-full, then [he] says the <term>tide</term> <note original: "accessum">The "access" or rising of the sea.</note> is diminished in that proportion by which the Moon departs from the Sun, so that when it comes to the **quadrature** <note>An astrological aspect where two bodies are 90 degrees apart, such as the Moon when it is half-full.</note> they are weakest; second, from there until the full moon, at which time they are gradually intensified so that they reach their peak at the full Moon; third, from the full moon until it is again divided [half-full], the tide decreasing along with the light; fourth, from then until the <term>conjunction</term> <note original: "coitum">The meeting of the Sun and Moon at the New Moon.</note>. But then he claims the tides become progressively more violent, so that they are most violent when the Moon joins the Sun. 

But this can have no rational basis, seeing as this difference in light (as far as the proposal is concerned) is simply "much," "little," "increasing," or "decreasing." If the tide occurs when the light is either "much" or "increasing," the fourth observation is proven false. If when it is "little" or "decreasing," the second is false. If "much" but "decreasing," the third is false. If "little" but "increasing," the first is false. Yet, whichever of these traditions one might prefer to receive, it is clear that we are not compelled to devise any new "power" in the Moon—besides its motion and light—to explain why it moves the sea. For all the variations reported in the rising and falling of the tides can most evidently find their cause either in the diversity of the motion of the star as it climbs or declines, or in the losses and increments of its light.

## GALEN'S OPINION ON CRITICAL DAYS
### Refuting his attribution of them to the Moon. Chapter XVI.

Regarding <term>Crises</term> <note original: "Crisimos">Turning points in a disease where a patient either begins to recover or declines toward death.</note>, which in Latin you might call "judiciary days," I have no doubt that they are referred to the Moon as falsely as they are superstitiously—a point which must be declared more at length. Galen is the author among physicians of this opinion; in the third book of *On Critical Days*, he mentions a twofold lunar influence: one from the Sun, from which the Moon receives its light, and the other from the signs of the <term>oblique circle</term> <note original: "obliqui orbis">The Zodiac.</note>, which the Moon traverses by its own motion every month. Then he posits, according to the opinion of the astrologers and as if proven by experience, that great disturbances are excited by the Moon in opposite places and quadratures. He contends this is true both in its relationship to the Sun and also to the signs, even when no consideration is given to the Sun. 

Regarding the Sun, he claims that because the Moon is divided [half-full] (which occurs roughly at the quadrature points from the conjunction) and again when it is filled (which is in the opposite position), it changes the state of the air and the weather. Regarding the signs, he claims it works in this manner: whatever begins when the Moon is positioned, for example, in Taurus, a change in that matter will always occur when the Moon subsequently reaches Leo, Scorpio, or Aquarius—which are the places <term>quadrate</term> <note>90 degrees apart.</note> or opposite to Taurus. 

He confirms this by the authority of the Egyptians, who assert that if, in someone’s <term>nativity</term> <note original: "genitura">A birth chart or horoscope.</note>, fortunate stars were seated in Aries (to use an example), the person born will fare well whenever the Moon traverses either Taurus, the quadrate signs, or the opposite signs; conversely, they will fare poorly if unfortunate stars were there. From this, Galen thinks the cause of "critical days" becomes most evident. For the seventh and fourteenth days are especially critical. The Moon reaches the fourth sign from the one it held at the beginning of the illness on the seventh day, and the opposite sign on the fourteenth day, with its full cycle <note>The sidereal month of approx. 27.3 days.</note> taking twenty-seven days and nearly a third part of a day...

...completes its course. Since the Moon, therefore, in these positions—namely the <term>squares</term> <note>Quadratures, or 90-degree angles.</note> and <term>oppositions</term> <note>180-degree angles.</note>—stirs up disturbances, it causes diseases to undergo a crisis during these days (specifically the seventh and fourteenth) when those positions are reached. These crises are favorable for health or fatal for death.

However, because Galen thought the twentieth day was the <term>critical day</term> <note original: "dies creticus">A day when a disease reaches a turning point or "crisis," determining recovery or death.</note>, rather than the twenty-first as Archigenes <note>A Greek physician of the 1st/2nd century AD.</note> believed, he labored to provide a reason for how the twentieth day itself was actually the [end of the] third "seventh" day. First, he demonstrated this with a proof that was neither absurd nor difficult: for the Moon completes its course in [27] days and [8] hours <note>The OCR reads "7 days and 28 hours," but the mathematical logic that follows requires the standard sidereal month of approximately 27 days and 8 hours.</note>. If you divide this into four weeks, each week will consist of six days and twenty hours. Therefore, three weeks will consist of twenty days and twelve hours. For this reason, the twenty-first day—that is, the third week-day in the lunar course—will belong partly to the twentieth natural day and partly to the twenty-first. For twelve hours of it will finish the twentieth day, and the remaining hours will begin the twenty-first. Thus, the critical disturbance will happen on the twentieth day, as the Moon reaches its second square in the third week.

Again, the same reasoning applies if the crisis is delayed until the twenty-first natural day, which often happens in acute illnesses; just as in chronic illnesses, they run through cycles of even or odd numbers. After Galen had said this himself—which <term>the man of Abano</term> <note original: "Apponensis">Pietro d'Abano (c. 1257–1316), a famous medieval physician and astrologer often cited by Pico.</note> later reported as if it were his own discovery—Galen devised a new explanation. By this, he would not just share the credit with Archigenes by making the critical influence apply to both days, but would conclude that the twentieth day is entirely critical, and the twenty-first is not.

Thus he devised a time period in which the Moon returns to its <term>conjunction</term> <note original: "coitū">The meeting of the Sun and Moon at the New Moon.</note> with the Sun: 29 days and 12 hours, which is commonly called a month. Let us subtract the days in which the Moon does not appear, being overwhelmed by the Sun's rays, since it then has no power to change things below; there remain 26 days and 12 hours. For it is hidden for roughly three days. Let us add these days (the span of the shining Moon) to the days in which it traverses the signs, which he calculates as 24 days and 20 hours <note>This specific figure is part of Galen's idiosyncratic calculation to justify his medical observations.</note>; the sum will be 53 days and 20 hours, half of which is 26 days and 22 hours. Galen thought this span was a not irrational measure for the placement of critical days. He saw that only half the days in which the Moon travels the zodiac are also illuminated by the Sun, as if the power of lunar influence then doubled within itself—namely, the power from the zodiac signs and the power from the Sun—both of which likely cause disturbances in diseases.

This number was later called the <term>medical month</term> by his successors on Galen's authority, just as they call the 29-day cycle the month of "conjunction." The cycle of 26 days and 12 hours they call the month of "manifest vision," and the cycle of 27 and one-third days the month of "transit." From this discovery, Galen achieved what he wanted against Archigenes. For if the whole month is 26 days and 22 hours, each week of this month will be six days, seventeen hours, and a half-hour. Therefore, half the month is 13 days and 11 hours. Thus, from the first hour of the seventh natural day until the seventeenth...

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

...[the second week] will also look toward the seventh day of the medical month, and for that reason, they will be <term>critical days</term> <note original: "creticae">Days where a disease reaches a turning point or "crisis."</note>; the remainder of the day will belong to the eighth medical day. The fourteenth natural day will have only the first eleven hours from the latter part of the fourteenth medical day, while its preceding thirteen hours will be counted with the thirteenth natural day. However, regarding the third medical week—since any such week consists of six days and about eighteen hours and seven and a half minutes—it is clear that it terminates on the twentieth natural day, with four and a half hours remaining which are carried over into the twenty-first day.

And so, that which Galen especially desired is achieved, and for the sake of which this entire fiction <note original: "commentum">A fabrication or mental construct.</note> was manufactured: that the twentieth day should be considered critical far more than the twenty-first, according to the logic of the following week. Galen took this labor upon himself for nothing; for it was not necessary, since the twentieth day was already defended as critical by the duration of the Moon's transit through the <term>zodiac</term>, especially since he himself does not deny that the twenty-first is also critical, and indeed most often in acute diseases.

Nor have we recounted these things in order to act as a judge between Archigenes <note>A 1st-century Greek physician who disagreed with Galen on the timing of critical days.</note> and Galen, thereby overstepping our purpose. Rather, we do so lest—having demonstrated that critical days cannot be referred to the Moon (whether we consider the power the Moon receives from the Sun or from the signs of the zodiac)—someone might think the matter has not been fully satisfied because Galen introduced a sort of "mixed influence" that supposedly stirs up these critical days.

For perhaps Galen did not actually do this, or if he did, he could not have done so rationally. For if we say, with him, that the Moon stirs up disturbances when it is in <term>squares</term> <note original: "quadratis">An astrological aspect of 90 degrees, often considered tense or provocative.</note> or <term>oppositions</term> <note original: "oppositis">An astrological aspect of 180 degrees.</note> to some primordial position in the signs, and again when it is illuminated by the square or opposite rays of the Sun, we cannot expect these events from the Moon except at those times when it is positioned in one of those ways—if, that is, we expect the event to come from those causes. 

For if it produces such effects at both times, according to the condition and constellation of each time, are we to believe that the power of both constellations is mixed together at a time when neither of those constellations is actually found? We would have no other argument than that such a time is the midpoint of the sum of both times counted together—if so, then we do not know where we are, nor are we even among the madmen like Orestes. <note>Orestes is a figure from Greek tragedy often used as a proverb for madness. Pico is suggesting Galen's logic is so convoluted it borders on insanity.</note>

Therefore, if Galen thinks this "exciting force" exists in the weeks of this "medical month" of his and its midpoint, but not in the weeks or the midpoint of the month in which the Moon is illuminated by the Sun or passes through the signs of the zodiac, he brings upon us a problem: this force of his imagined month cannot be reduced to any astrological influences. That is, it corresponds neither to the squares or opposite signs, nor to the square or opposite configurations of the Moon with the Sun. For to claim that the power of these things is preserved and fused together at a time when they do not exist is, as I said, far too absurd and fabricated. Nor could those who wished to defend Galen, and simultaneously fit the critical days to the Moon's cycles, stand by their promises; instead, they defend now this point, now that, but never both at once. For it may be asked: why is the fourteenth day critical, returning as it does to the Moon's cycles and the month of its transit...

## on Astrology Book III.

...since on that day the Moon arrives at the opposite signs. This calculation fits the portion of the medical month. Indeed, its second week falls back into the 13th natural day, and there remain from it only 11 hours pertaining to the 14th day. For, as we have said, any week of Galen’s month <note>Galen was a 2nd-century Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a millennium.</note> consists of six days and ten and seven-and-a-half hours; therefore, the 13th day should be called more **critical** <note original: "cretica">A "critical day" in ancient medicine was the day a disease was expected to reach its "crisis" or turning point.</note> than the 14th, since the former has 13 critical hours, while the latter has only eleven. Here, therefore, having abandoned the power of the "mixture" and the artificial month, they will flee to the spaces traversed in the <term>zodiac</term> <note>The 360-degree belt of the heavens divided into twelve signs.</note>. 

Conversely, so that they may make the 21st day critical, they use Galen’s month, not the Moon's actual transit. But if someone should fall ill on the day before the Moon joins with the Sun, and has the 7th day as a critical day, how will that result from the influence of power received from the Sun <term>as much as</term> from the signs? For during the greatest part of those days, just as the Moon was not seen, so she affected us with solar power, according to Galen himself. It is necessary here also for them to turn toward the signs, whose influence alone, by the power of the "square" <note>An astrological aspect where two celestial bodies are 90 degrees apart, often considered stressful or significant.</note>, would have made that 7th day critical for the patient. 

I pass over the fact that Galen’s month is entirely artificial, nor is it struck from the "coinage of nature." For it is forged as if the Moon were always hidden by the Sun for three days. Yet sometimes she is seen in the morning before the Sun rises, and in the evening of that same day with a **razor-like face** <note original: "novaculari facie">Referring to the very thin crescent of a new moon.</note>. Both experience indicates this and Al-Farghani <note>A 9th-century Persian astronomer, known in the West as Alphraganus.</note> testifies to it. Furthermore, Galen determines the space of the lunar motion as if she always moved at the same pace, and not sometimes faster and sometimes slower, as is demonstrated in astronomical calculations. 

Therefore, let Galen keep his month to himself; lest he thrust it upon us too importunately, let us grant it to those whom Archigenes <note>A Greek physician from the 1st century AD who often disagreed with Galen on the timing of crises.</note> prefers, not rejecting that there are critical days. I firmly assert that these days are governed by no cycles of the Moon, whether we estimate the power as received from the Sun or from the signs. For that power which comes from the Sun is solid and natural (as we have declared), but critical days cannot pertain to it unless diseases always attacked us at the New Moon; otherwise, the 7th day would not correspond to the half-moon, nor the 14th to the full moon, in which the "quadrangular" <note>A 90-degree angle.</note> and opposite configurations of the Sun stir the humors. 

There remains the power which comes from the signs. This is actually non-existent, as following sections will declare; and even if there were any, it would in no way regard the critical days in the way they describe. For if they argue from experience that a "commotion" <note>A medical term for a sudden change or disturbance in the body's state.</note> occurs on the 7th day, and again on the 14th, and that during these days the Moon is in square signs or in opposite signs, they conclude that those commotions follow from this change of signs. We, on the contrary, argue thus: a commotion occurs on the 7th day, and again on the 14th, yet during these days the Moon is frequently *not* in square or opposite places; therefore, that commotion is not stirred up by this change of signs. 

Which side relies on truer assumptions is a doubt to no one to whom the lunar motions are not entirely unknown. For when the Moon is traveling through the lower parts of her <term>epicycle</term> <note>In the Ptolemaic system, an epicycle is a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; it was used to explain why planets seem to speed up or slow down.</note>, she moves more swiftly and reaches the square signs on the 6th day, and sometimes the opposite signs on the 13th. But when she is carried around the higher parts, she moves more slowly, and does not reach the quadrangular place before the 8th or 9th day. But if they should respond that for this cause...

For indeed, they might have something to say if those **critical days** <note original: "dies creticas">Days when a disease was expected to reach a turning point or "crisis."</note> occurred when the Moon's course is slow, so that the **humors** <note original: "humores">The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which ancient medicine believed governed health.</note> were stirred on the eighth or ninth day; and when the Moon is fast, on the sixth; and when it is in a middle state, on the seventh. But observation does not teach this. Instead, it frequently happens in practice that even when the Moon is slower, the seventh day—and sometimes even the sixth—brings the "judgment" of the disease. Conversely, when the Moon is moving more rapidly, the stirrings of the illness are delayed until the eighth or ninth day. Noting this, many physicians have flatly denied that this order observed by nature in diseases depends on the lunar cycles. 

Nothing led those who taught otherwise to their conclusion except either a love for astrological matters or the authority of Galen. We shall soon discuss how much weight these factors should carry in this matter. Furthermore, some of the **modern scholars** <note original: "neotericis">Referring to recent or contemporary Renaissance commentators.</note> falsely claim that Avicenna and Hippocrates held this opinion too. For Hippocrates never said a word about this. Rather, he likely traced this order of days back to **numbers** <note>Pythagorean-style numerology was often used to explain natural cycles.</note>, which nature tends to observe willingly, as Celsus and Asclepiades have noted. As for **Avicenna** <note>An influential 11th-century Persian physician and philosopher.</note>, when he recalled the opinion relating these things to the Moon, he said, "there is much ambiguity in these statements." He then rejected the question, as its investigation did not belong to the physician; indeed, he felt it was more of a hindrance to them. 

Therefore, let Galen’s authority be strong among us when we are deciding which days are critical and how the patient should be treated when these days appear or are foreseen. For this is the physician’s duty, and in this profession, we—along with the consensus of the learned—approve of and admire the truly "divine" Galen as preeminent. But when the *cause* of those days is investigated, since this is a task for a deeper philosophy, Galen's opinion should be granted no status as a legal precedent, nor even as a major testimony. 

For as **Maimonides** <note original: "Moses Aegyptius">The famous 12th-century Jewish philosopher and physician from Egypt.</note> and Avicenna—great men and great supporters of Galen in medicine—record, Galen clung more to the "branches" of the other sciences than to their "roots." Certainly, he is laughed at by logicians for his **fourth figure of syllogisms** <note original: "figura eius quarta syllogismorum">A specific form of logical argument that Galen was traditionally credited with adding to the Aristotelian system, often criticized as redundant.</note>. In philosophy, he is so often terrified and fails to perceive the most powerful reasons, such that many find a lack of philosophical judgment in him. He cannot understand how, if the soul survives and is immortal, it would cease its work when the body—which is often not even fully dissolved—stops functioning. He says he was "fatigued" by a certain Platonist on this question. This is as if a sailor, surviving a wrecked ship, did not "cease from navigation" <note>Pico’s point is that the soul (the sailor) still exists, but simply cannot "sail" without the instrument of the body (the ship).</note>. Nor does he understand what is demonstrated by philosophers: that universal notions of things are grasped only by our intellect, and not even by the talent of brute animals. 

It is not the time now to recount how he wavers in his understanding of **Time**. For we are not here to discuss Galen’s philosophy; we have only touched upon these points to confirm the judgment of Maimonides and Avicenna regarding him, and simultaneously to warn lest anyone be deceived by his authority into accepting superstition. For in this very subject under discussion—astrology—the calculation of the lunar motion shows that he was very little skilled. Nor does **Peter of Abano** <note original: "Apponensis">A 13th-century Italian physician and astrologer.</note> defend him in any other way than by saying that in Galen's age, the system of celestial motions had not yet been clearly explored. Therefore, while we may grant him the greatest possible trust in medicine, let us remember to act more cautiously with the man regarding other doctrines. He must be examined more diligently...

# On Astrology, Book III

Tt 3
<meta>catchword: gods</meta>

...let us more diligently examine what he <note>Galen, the influential 2nd-century physician whose works dominated medieval medicine.</note> handed down—whether they harmonize with experience, reason, or the opinions of others. And indeed, concerning what he put forward about **critical days** <note original: "creticis diebus">Specific days in the course of a disease when a "crisis" or turning point was expected to occur.</note>, we have proved that they do not agree with the facts themselves; it will also become clear to those who look into it that they do not even possess the color of reason. For what reason dictates that the Moon, when it reaches the fourth or seventh sign from the place it occupied when the disease struck, should stir up an agitation in the **humors**? <note original: "humoribus">The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that were thought to determine health and temperament.</note> Galen refuses to give a reason, but instead hides behind the authority of the Egyptians. We shall remind him of his own sixth book *On Simple Medicines*, in which he marks the Egyptians as "delirious." Why their authority wavers among us will be made clear in the final two books. For now, we should say this: the mutations of bodies according to these lunar courses could not have been faithfully observed by the Egyptians, because the lunar courses were not faithfully known to them. For Hipparchus, on the island of Rhodes, was the first to observe them with greater certainty, although even he did not reach the truth; Ptolemy later came closer to it, though he still did not satisfy the requirements of the **Spanish astronomers**. <note>Likely a reference to the Alfonsine Tables, a major set of astronomical data produced in 13th-century Toledo, Spain.</note>

The **modern scholars** <note original: "neoterici">Contemporary Renaissance commentators who attempted to reconcile astrology with medicine.</note> have devised a reason that is not only inconsistent with the truth, but also with the very position they defend and the words of Galen which they follow. It is as follows: **Square** <note original: "signa quadrata">Signs 90 degrees apart in the zodiac.</note> or **opposite** <note original: "opposita">Signs 180 degrees apart.</note> signs have contrary qualities. Square signs differ either in both qualities or at least in the "active" qualities. For instance, **Aries** <note original: "Aries">A Fire sign: hot and dry.</note> differs from **Cancer** <note original: "Cancro">A Water sign: cold and moist.</note> in both qualities, since Aries is a hot and dry sign, while Cancer is moist and cold. **Taurus** <note original: "Taurus">An Earth sign: cold and dry.</note> differs from **Leo** <note original: "Leone">A Fire sign: hot and dry.</note> but not in both, for they agree in dryness; however, they clash in the active quality, Taurus being cold and Leo being hot. Likewise, opposite signs always clash in at least one quality. Furthermore, they say it is a common refrain among astrologers that **quadrangular** and **diametrical radiations** <note original: "quadrangulas & diametras radiationes">The geometric "aspects" or angles—90 and 180 degrees—that planets make with one another.</note> are contrary and combative. These premises being established, they conclude that when the Moon reaches locations "enemy" to those it held when the disease struck, a battle necessarily arises between the disease and nature. 

But having granted their premises, we shall address them thus: you think this is the cause for why the Moon creates critical days—because if, for example, the disease occupied nature while the Moon was in Taurus, it must produce a contrary effect when it reaches a contrary location. Therefore, nature will rise up against the disease, leading to a struggle and a judgment as victory leans toward one side or the other. But it will be in a contrary location when it reaches Leo or **Scorpio** <note original: "Scorpiu">A Water sign: cold and moist.</note>. It will reach Leo on the seventh day and Scorpio on the fourteenth. Therefore, on these days, the Moon will sound the call to battle for the disease and nature. But why will it not do the same on the third day, when it reaches **Gemini** <note original: "geminos">An Air sign: hot and moist.</note>, which differs more from Taurus than Leo does? Why not on the twelfth or thirteenth day when it reaches **Libra** <note original: "Libra">An Air sign: hot and moist.</note>, with which Taurus agrees even less than with Scorpio? Why not the fifteenth day, entering **Sagittarius** <note original: "Sagittariū">A Fire sign: hot and dry.</note>, which is just as discordant with Taurus as Scorpio and Leo are? I know what they will answer: that there is no connection of **aspect** <note original: "aspectus">The specific geometric relationship between zodiac signs that astrologers believe transmits influence.</note> between these signs. But I did not wish to lead them elsewhere, not to object that this logic of aspects is non-existent (which we shall do in the sixth book), but to show that even if it were something, it does not serve the question at hand. For those aspects are observed between two planets, whose...

He is specifically addressing the "critical days" of illness—a concept from ancient medicine where certain days (like the 7th, 14th, or 21st) were thought to be turning points for a patient. Astrologers claimed these days were determined by the Moon’s position relative to where it was when the person first fell ill.</meta>

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

...astrologers do not think the planets can work together to complete an effect, whether they are in harmony or discord, unless they are configured with each other by specific intervals: the hexagon <note original: "exagono">The sextile aspect, 60 degrees apart.</note>, the trine <note original: "trigono">An aspect of 120 degrees, considered harmonious.</note>, the square <note original: "quadrangulari">The quartile aspect, 90 degrees apart, considered difficult.</note>, and the diameter <note original: "diametro">The opposition, 180 degrees apart.</note>. But in this case, we are not configuring the Moon to other planets; we are only noting whether it has moved to a place contrary to the one it occupied before. Even though astrologers would deny that a star positioned in Gemini and a star positioned in Taurus are linked by an aspect, they would not deny that the latter position is the contrary of the former. 

If the Moon produces an effect contrary to the initial one because it has reached a place of contrary quality, why is it that if it stirred up a disease while in a cold and dry sign <note>In ancient medicine, the zodiac signs were categorized by the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>, it does not stir up nature to fight the disease when it moves into hot and moist signs—regardless of whether that sign is the sixth, the second, or any other number you prefer to count? This is entirely ridiculous, and not something that should be said by a man seeking truth rather than merely defending a preconceived position. 

Furthermore, if they insist that the power resides in these specific aspects, they must logically concede that when the Moon reaches the "square" signs, it will strengthen the disease; for just as square signs are discordant, trine signs are concordant. Why then, if square signs provoke nature through a quality contrary to the sign of the illness, do trine signs not stir up the disease through harmony? Since the Moon reaches these [trine signs] on roughly the eleventh day, the eleventh day would have to be designated as harmful—yet physicians number it among the healthy **critical days** <note original: "creticas">Days of "crisis" or judgment in a disease's progress.</note>. 

Finally, it will be perfectly clear to anyone considering the observations of critical days handed down by physicians that they cannot be based on the Moon's motion. For they say that bad disturbances happen on these days: the sixth, eighth, twelfth, tenth, sixteenth, and eighteenth. Let them explain the reason for these from the Moon if they can! On the sixth and eighth days, it would be more fitting for good things to happen (as we were saying), since on these days the Moon reaches square aspects. But why are the tenth or twelfth days bad at all, given that the Moon is not in places linked by any aspect to the sign of the illness? Why are the seventeenth and thirtieth days counted as healthy? 

And what is the logic that gives the Moon power every four days before the twentieth day, but every seven days after the twentieth? For example, the twenty-seventh, thirty-fourth, and forty-first; and once you pass that, critical days are found every twenty days, such as the sixtieth, eightieth, then the hundred and twentieth? Why from there is the cycle measured in months and years? Just as these things have no cause from the Moon, so they can have none from the Sun, nor from any other constellation. These stars are not found in fixed, similar, or concordant positions on these set days; instead, they vary in a marvelous way and follow no order that could correspond to the order of disturbances in diseases, which is for the most part maintained by nature. 

It is truly a wonder that the <term>Man from Abano</term> <note original: "Apponenſem">Pietro d'Abano (c. 1257–1315), a famous philosopher and physician who tried to reconcile Greek medicine with Arabic astrology.</note>, who says the malice of the sixth day—which <term>Galen</term> <note>The most famous physician of the Roman Empire, whose theories on humors lasted for 1,500 years.</note> compares to a tyrant, just as he compares the seventh to a king—can be reduced to the fact that the Moon, in its swifter course, reaches the square aspect. He is too unmindful of himself, for he had previously said that illnesses become healthy on the seventh day due to the "square" nature...
