nature, which would obviously oppose the sign of the disease. How then does he now provide a reason for the "malice" of the sixth day based on a square aspect <note original: "ex quadrato">A 90-degree astrological aspect, usually considered unfavorable.</note> as well? It is clear, therefore, that all these things have other causes. But they were deceived because the crisis seemed to coincide on the seventh and fourteenth day—although even there, as we have said, it does not truly coincide with the Moon's positions. However, we see this progression by sevens observed elsewhere in the works of nature where there is no suspicion of the movement of the Moon or the Sun. For instance, in the periods of diseases themselves: just as acute diseases peak on the seventh day, so long-lasting ones—as <term>Avicenna</term><note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath and one of the most influential physicians of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> writes—are often accustomed to being terminated in the seventh month, the seventh year, the fourteenth, or the twenty-first. 

Yet I do not approve of those who superstitiously observe numbers in this matter. Rather, I say that the courses of nature are mostly fulfilled in this way, not because of the constellations appearing at these times (for astrologers do not actually find them to be consistent), but because of the hidden property and condition of those specific things. For we see nature so arranged that, as <term>Galen</term><note>Aelius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), the prominent Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medical science for over a millennium.</note> himself writes, acute diseases move through odd-numbered days, while the slower and longer-lasting ones move through even days. Attribute these to the Moon, or attribute them to the Sun and the stars if you can! Why then should we refer the commotion of the seventh day in acute diseases to <term>square signs</term><note original: "tetragona signa">Zodiac signs placed 90 degrees apart from the starting point.</note> through which the Moon might travel, especially since that rule is not universal? 

Furthermore, some of the younger writers, speaking against the opinion of Galen and others who flee to the Moon for explanations, say this: If someone takes to their bed while the Moon is positioned in **Aries**, they ought to have a <term>critical</term><note original: "cretica">From the Greek 'krisis,' meaning a turning point or judgment in a disease.</note> day on the eighth, because that is when the Moon would arrive at the square of **Cancer**. They answer that while this *ought* to happen based on lunar motion, the actual "commotion" or crisis happens on the seventh because of the nature of the disease itself, which, being acute, moves through odd days until the fourteenth day. 

Finally, the facts truly observed by medicine concerning critical days do not confirm the claims of astrology; instead, they weaken them. This serves as the greatest argument that the affections of our bodies do not depend on the causes introduced by astrologers. For if there were no fixed order in these days—if now this day were critical and now that one, or if among critical days one was harmful at one time and healthy at another—we would not be moved to investigate a cause, being satisfied by the shifting diversity of physical matter. But since certain days are—not always, but for the most part—critical, and some mostly lead to life while others lead to death, this order requires a cause that is certain and rarely changeable. 

To Galen, it seemed to follow that the cause must be in the heavenly bodies, because they are bodies that move in a rare and stable order and can therefore produce a fixed and stable effect. To me, on the contrary, it seems clear that the cause cannot be from the heavens. If it were, different days would be "critical" for different people, and the observed order would not be preserved. For if the Moon were joined to Mars or the Sun, the planetary influence would speed up the crisis; if joined to Saturn, it would delay it. Furthermore, the conjunction of the "luminaries" <note>The Sun and the Moon.</note> immediately preceding the start of the illness would have to be inspected; if the "Lord" of the place where they joined held the ascendant <note original: "orientem">The Eastern horizon or rising sign.</note>, the crisis would happen quickly; if it were in the west, it would happen late. Moreover, stars proceeding with direct motion or positioned in "movable" signs would sound the battle cry for the disease and nature more quickly, while those moving backward <note>Retrograde motion.</note> or located in "fixed" signs would do so more slowly. Yet these things do not happen to any sick person in such a way, even when they share these same constellations...

<summary>Pico argues that the "critical days" of an illness (like the 7th or 14th day) are caused by the internal nature of the disease and the human body rather than the Moon's transit. He points out that if astrology were responsible, the timing of medical crises would fluctuate wildly based on other planetary aspects, which is not what physicians observe.</summary>

...would coincide, but in different ways for different people according to the condition of their birth. I pass over the figure <note original: "figuram">An astrological chart or horoscope.</note> whose angles <term>Ptolemy</term><note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity.</note> instructs us to observe—whether they are derived from favorable or unfavorable rays—so that we may pronounce judgment on the disease; this is something which some most ignorant people believe pertains to <term>critical days</term><note>Days on which a disease was expected to take a decisive turn toward recovery or death.</note>. If physicians took all these things from astrologers, the critical days would not mostly be those which the medical art intends, but would vary from person to person. Nor would it be a fixed rule that the sixth day kills with "tyrannical cruelty," while the seventh liberates with "royal kindness." <note>This refers to a common medieval medical proverb: the 6th day of an acute fever was considered dangerous and 'tyrannical,' while the 7th was considered 'regal' and curative.</note> Instead, with harmful constellations, the seventh would be counted as the dangerous day, and with healthy ones, even the sixth would be beneficial. If such things happen occasionally, it should not be said to come from the heavens (where they seek a cause for something that happens in an orderly way and almost always), but rather it should be attributed to the matter and to some particular property of the suffering human.

### THE PERIODS OF THE HUMORS ARE NOT TO BE
### REFERRED TO THE MOVEMENTS OF THE STARS. Chapter XVII.

But let no one believe that the periods of the <term>humors</term><note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed in ancient medicine to determine health and temperament.</note> in fevers are to be referred to the movements of the stars; as if, for example, <term>black bile</term><note original: "bilis atra">Also known as melancholy.</note> rests for two days and is aroused on the fourth because it is under <term>Saturn</term>, whose motion is slower than others. For by what reasoning does blood—assigned to <term>Jupiter</term> by astrologers—continuously putrefy for no cause, since Jupiter is not the fastest of all? Indeed, if the time of its return <note original: "restitutionis">Its orbital period.</note> is considered, it is the slowest of all planets after Saturn. Why likewise is the movement of <term>red bile</term><note original: "rubræ bilis">Yellow bile or choler.</note> ascribed to <term>Mars</term>? Its movement is a little slower than that of black bile, for it rests six hours less; since the latter is dormant for forty-eight hours, while the former is quiet for thirty-six <note>Pico is comparing the cycles of different types of fevers (quartan vs. tertian) to planetary speeds.</note>—yet the star of Mars is much faster than Saturn. Furthermore, it is a decree of the astrologers that the works of stars with slow motion are more long-lasting the slower they are. Since, therefore, the movement of <term>phlegm</term><note original: "pituitæ">Also called pituita.</note> returns faster than red bile—for the former returns after six hours, the latter after thirty-six—because the Moon's motion exciting phlegm is faster than Mars' motion exciting <term>choler</term> <note original: "coleram">Yellow bile.</note>, why, I ask, if this is true, does the agitation of choler not affect the patient longer than phlegm? But the former lasts only twelve hours, while the latter lasts eighteen. For the works of Mars ought to be more long-lasting than those of the Moon, if indeed the Moon's are faster than Mars'. 

But if we wish to refer all these periods to the Moon alone, as though she were predominant over all humors, the astrological reasoning on which they lean will falter no less. For phlegm, they say, because of its kinship with the Moon and water, almost imitates the movement of the waters <note>Refers to the tides.</note>; those flow and ebb with a delay intervening between them, but a small one, such as necessarily falls between directed movements. Thus phlegm leaves only six whole hours. But this could better suit blood, in which a continuous surge is found just like water, in which the brief delay separating the flow from the ebb does not correspond well to a six-hour interval, by which that whole flow or ebb is driven. But in blood there could be a greater similarity, the interruption of whose motion by imperceptible delays the proponents of this opinion themselves do not deny. But let us pursue the rest...

<summary>Pico argues that the cycles of bodily humors and the timing of "critical days" in illness are caused by physical, human properties rather than the orbital speeds of planets like Saturn, Mars, or the Moon. He uses the varying durations of different fevers to show that they do not logically correspond to the astrological "speeds" of the planets they are supposedly linked to.</summary>

...[pursue] our argument. Therefore, the same judgment will hold for the humors when related to the elements: the movement of red bile <note>Choler.</note> ought to be more different from the movement of phlegm than that of black bile. 

Furthermore, none of the illustrious and ancient physicians traced the cycle of fevers back to these astrological causes. The first to attempt this was **Pietro d'Abano** <note>original: "Petrus Apponensis" (1250–1316), an Italian philosopher and astrologer known for attempting to reconcile Greek and Arabic medical science with astrology.</note>, a man born to collect many things rather than to digest them; indeed, the more unlearned a person is, the more they are usually inclined to admire him when he is talking nonsense.

### THAT THE UNLUCKINESS OF AN EIGHT-MONTH BIRTH IS NOT TO BE ASCRIBED TO SATURN. Chapter XVIII.
### ###

While we are discussing these matters, it comes to mind that astrologers are accustomed to attribute the misfortune of an **eight-month birth** <note>In antiquity and the Middle Ages, it was a common belief that a baby born at seven months would survive, but one born at eight months would not.</note> to **Saturn**. This must be discussed here, but briefly, lest by failing to refute it, we seem to be forced to concede—even against our will—that we are caught in the rays of hostile stars. While I am willing to concede that we are influenced by the heavens, I do not concede that we are gripped by them in such a way that we are held captive; for I perceive the heavens’ influence in such a way that I do not believe anything harmful proceeds from them. 

The gist of the matter is this: astrologers are mistaken if they believe that those born in the eighth month do not live because individual planets preside over the individual months of pregnancy. They claim that because **Saturn** rules the first month, he also rules the eighth—and being a "cold and dry" planet, he is contrary to the qualities of life. 

First of all, those "shifts" of planetary dominion handed down through the years have no basis in reason (as will be stated elsewhere in its proper place). Secondly, there is a completely different reason why an eight-month birth does not survive. There are those who believe the fetus tries to exit in the seventh month and is injured in the attempt; if it then exits in the eighth month, it is not yet restored to health and thus usually does not live. 

However, I agree more with **Hippocrates** <note>The ancient Greek "Father of Medicine."</note>, who, in the treatise he wrote *On the Eight-Month Birth*, says the reason it usually does not live is that the pregnancy becomes difficult in that month. At that time, pregnant women feel more heavily burdened, and the womb suffers certain heavy and uncomfortable things. If they give birth then, being overwhelmed by the double labor of birth and sickness, they become extremely weak; consequently, the fetus itself is made feebler and rarely lives long. 

This opinion is supported by the fact that if women are found who are more vigorous and strong, they often give birth in the eighth month to children who will live—such as those **Avicenna** <note>A famous Persian physician and philosopher (c. 980–1037).</note> writes are found in **Spain**, or **Aristotle** says are found in **Egypt**. I have added the words of Hippocrates himself on this matter below, so that—since this book is not commonly available—it will not be thought that I have made this up: 

*"Regarding the eight-month generation, I say these two things happen in a continuous series that the child cannot endure, and for that reason, eight-month babies do not survive..."* etc., as follows.

<summary>Pico refutes the astrological claim that Saturn causes the death of babies born in the eighth month, arguing instead that physical exhaustion and the health of the mother are the true factors, citing Hippocrates and Avicenna.</summary>

### WHY SAILORS, PHYSICIANS, AND FARMERS PREDICT THE TRUTH MORE
### often than astrologers. Chapter XIX.

There were roughly three objections in that second line of astrological reasoning. The first was based on the changes in lower things <note>Earthly or "sublunary" matters.</note> resulting from the courses of the Sun and Moon; from this, they inferred that the actions of other stars upon us and the changes of other things must also be predicted. The second was based on the testimony of the noble arts of **medicine**, **agriculture**, and **navigation**, which employ astrological observations in their work. Both of these we have already rejected in such a way that we turned their own weapons against them, showing—as I said a little earlier—that from the effects of the Sun and Moon and from the observations of those arts, one should conclude the opposite of what the astrologers claim. 

There remains the third objection, which was taken from the predictions of those same craftsmen and the common people themselves. It is as if we were being too unfair by granting no foreknowledge of the future to astrologers—who are skilled in the whole of the heavens—when even crude masters and anyone from the common crowd sometimes achieves it. Thus, we see many things concerning rains, diseases, livestock, and the **grain supply** <note>original: "annona," referring to the yearly harvest and the market price of food.</note> predicted daily by the common folk with reliable results. Why then, they ask, should those who have explored the celestial causes more accurately not be able to predict those same things more rightly, along with other more secret matters? 

This is what we must dissolve for the present—or rather, as is our habit, throw back at them. We shall explain this briefly with no trouble. For if true things are predicted by those common folk without any regard for the rules of astrology, who would not say that the astrologers' conjectures are either trivial, or that the things they omit are unnecessary, or that what they do not know is superfluous? Their "secrets" are not deeper, but more false; they are not doctrines, but fictions. 

But does **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity.</note> not say that those who are ignorant of astrology are sometimes mistaken? What of the fact that astrologers are mistaken even more often! It follows, therefore, that astrologers have less grasp of "astrological" matters than those who are not astrologers at all. For it cannot be denied that what physicians say about the sick, farmers about the harvest, sailors about storms, and shepherds about their flocks corresponds more closely to the truth than what is predicted about these same things by astrologers. 

The reason is immediately obvious: because the astrologer looks at **signs** which are not signs, and observes **causes** which are not causes; for this reason, he is deceived. He looks at the celestial arrangement, which is only a **universal cause** <note>A general influence that affects everything equally, like the heat of the sun, which cannot explain why one plant withers while another thrives.</note> and does not produce the variety of lower things except according to the condition of the matter and the specific **lower efficient causes** <note>The immediate, physical factors on Earth, such as soil quality or biological health.</note>. 

However, even that celestial arrangement he looks at is not real, but a fictional arrangement in the sky made by him through the most empty and made-up rules, established not by nature but by the whim of astrologers. As we shall demonstrate, that **Father of men and God of gods** <note>A poetic reference to the Creator.</note> did not create images, signs, parts, **antiscia** <note>term: Antiscia (points on the zodiac that are mirrored across the solstice axis, used in calculating planetary "shadows").</note>, **twelfth-parts** <note>original: "dodecathemoria," the division of each zodiac sign into twelve smaller segments.</note>, **houses** <note>The twelve divisions of the sky relative to the horizon at a specific time and place.</note>, and other such things which they use. Rather, it is the astrologer—the deceiver of men and slanderer of the gods—who has lied about these things being in the heaven. Therefore, it is no wonder if this art is unable to foreknow any future thing by any certain reasoning. The crafts-

Having established that practitioners like doctors and sailors are often successful in their predictions, Pico now argues that their success comes from observing nature directly—proximate causes—rather than the distant stars. He contrasts the practical experience of the "unlearned" with the "fictional" systems of astrologers.</meta>

<page-num>503</page-num>
<header>on Astrology, Book III.</header>

The [arti]fices <note>Experts or practitioners of specific crafts.</note> whom we have mentioned rely on true, natural, proper, and immediate causes and signs. For this reason, they rarely miss the truth; rather, through true foreknowledge of things to come, they build trust in their methods and practice their arts with success and good fortune. Read the books of **Prognostics** by **Hippocrates** <note>The famous Greek "Father of Medicine."</note>; you will never find him searching for the future condition of a sick man among the stars. He knew that these things are better sought from <term>urine</term> <note>original: "lotio." Uroscopy, or the diagnostic examination of urine, was a cornerstone of Hippocratic medicine.</note> than from a star, and are more certainly foreknown from the pulse of the veins than from the motion of the celestial spheres. 

Skilled navigators do not foresee storms by looking at **Jupiter**, **Saturn**, **Venus**, **Mars**, or **Mercury**, but by observing clouds, winds, and the general condition of the air. This expert discipline of theirs, confirmed everywhere by experience, understands an imminent storm from the breath of the slightest breeze or a barely visible cloudlet—signs of which no omen or trace was yet apparent to the eyes of others. Nor do they only understand that a storm is coming, but from which direction it is likely to be stirred up, how it can be avoided, and how it can be overcome. In the face of such practical knowledge, all the "wisdom" of the astrologers goes completely blind. 

In the same way, shepherds, farmers, and even the uneducated common folk themselves foreknow the state of the weather, not from the stars, but from the disposition of the air itself and from the impressions made in the upper atmosphere. This is why they rarely fail: they judge the air from the air itself, just as doctors judge the sick from the sick man—that is, from their own proper principles. They do not do what the astrologers do, who judge from remote and general universals, or worse, from fictional, imaginary, and mythical inventions. 

Therefore, let no one think that farming will be better, medicine more effective, or navigation safer if these matters are handled by men who are well-versed in and observant of astrology. On the contrary, this would be the wasting away and destruction of those arts; they would be led away from certain rules to uncertain ones, and from true methods to fabricated ones. By mixing in false dogmas, the solidity and truth of every experiment already discovered would be undermined. 

Even without yet understanding the rational arguments by which the vanity of astrology becomes known, one can be sufficiently persuaded by what we said at the beginning of this work: that the greatest masters of these arts, and those most successful in practicing them, not only did not apply astrological observations to their works, but either despised or even refuted them. **Columella** <note>Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella (4–70 AD), a Roman writer whose work on agriculture was a standard reference in the Renaissance.</note>, whom we have cited elsewhere—that most precise writer on agriculture—in the passage where he passes down the rules for observing the seasons, mentions his own "midnight studies" written against the astrologers. He says: "These things which we have treated with <term>plain common sense</term> <note>original: "pingui Minerva," a Latin idiom meaning a simple, practical approach without excessive or abstract theory.</note> are true; but those things which the **Chaldeans** <note>A common historical term for astrologers.</note> most impudently promise are false, and have been refuted by us elsewhere." 

Therefore, when **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the most famous ancient authority on both astronomy and astrology.</note> argues that because farmers foresee many things about the state of the air, he and his kind must foresee more and more certain things (since they excel farmers in their knowledge of celestial matters), Columella would deny that there is any truth in that conclusion. For this "astrological wisdom" by which they claim to surpass farmers is not wisdom, but folly. That is, they do not know more than the farmers, but they invent more, using the vast scale of the things they lie about as a screen to cover the mockery of their profession.

<summary>Pico argues that practical experts like doctors, sailors, and farmers succeed because they observe immediate natural signs rather than distant stars. He cites authorities like Hippocrates and Columella to show that true science rejects astrological interference as a "wasting away" of certain knowledge.</summary>

...which [astrology] would undoubtedly have received a most honorable place in life along with the others, if it made those good and necessary arts—farming, medicine, and navigation—any better. But its vanity and deceit, having been frequently detected by the wisest lawmakers, forced them to banish it from their cities with the severest prohibitions (as we declared in the first book), lest it infect both good minds and good arts with its hidden poisons. How much it is surpassed by those common arts we mentioned in the matter of foreseeing the future may be seen even from this: among sailors, farmers, and shepherds, there is a wonderful agreement in their prognostications; among astrologers, there is none at all. So much so that one does not hesitate to take the path of **Abofafa** <note>Probably a reference to the Persian mathematician and astronomer Abu al-Wafa' al-Buzjani, though here used to highlight the contradictory nature of astrological predictions.</note> without hesitation, on the very day that **Ptolemy** has announced a flood of waters.

### NOT ALL THINGS PREDICTED BY ASTROLOGERS
### DEPEND ON THE PRIMARY QUALITIES. CHAPTER 20.

We wish now to examine what things can depend on the <term>primary qualities</term> <note>The four basic physical states in ancient and medieval science: heat, cold, moisture, and dryness.</note>, since the third argument of the astrologers seemed to demand it. **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note> attempts to prove that whatever happens is caused by the stars in no other way [than through these qualities], as his <term>books on effects</term> <note>original: "apotelesmatici eius libri," referring to the *Tetrabiblos*.</note> declare. All astrologers always retreat to this point whenever they defend themselves by saying they claim nothing superstitious, nothing that does not follow the tracks of nature, or nothing for which a clear reason cannot be given. For they almost always take refuge in these qualities whenever they are asked why **Jupiter** does this, **Saturn** that, or another planet something else. In this, it will be shown in that part of the work where the reasons for astrological dogma are refuted, that they speak in a way that is consistent neither with themselves nor with the truth. 

Indeed, many things besides what we have already said clearly show that they prepare this refuge for themselves in vain. Among these, the first point that occurs is that in the allotment of fate, the <term>season of the year</term> <note>original: "anni tempus."</note> in which someone is born would have a greater effect than any other diversity of the constellation. This is because the season does more to increase or decrease the primary qualities than any position of the stars or mixture of rays. Thus, summer days are always hotter than winter ones, even if **Saturn** <note>Associated with cold and sluggishness.</note> is as stiff and numb as can be during the summer. Conversely, winter days are always colder than summer ones, even when **Mars** <note>Associated with heat and fire.</note> burns and rages in flames in the middle of the heavens. 

But if the difference in fate arises from cold and heat, dryness and moisture, being more or less vigorous, it follows that everyone born in winter would be condemned to an always "cold" fate compared to those born during summer—especially if (as they must necessarily defend) they follow this quality of the air, thus affected by the heavens, more than the condition of the seed and the immediate matter. Furthermore, if **Ptolemy** maintains this—which is for him the foundation of natural astrology—that the rays of the planets produce all other effects through the primary qualities, then he ought not to prophesy about human character or fortune from any other source than from that constellation which creates and demonstrates the condition of the body, since all things would follow from this. Likewise, in universal prophecies, only one thing would need to be inspected: what the future state of the air will be. Once this is inspected, the rest...

<margin>would be clear <note>original: "patea," matching the catchword.</note></margin>

<summary>Pico argues that astrology is a deceptive art unlike practical sciences, and refutes the idea that stars influence human fate through physical qualities like heat and cold, noting that seasons have a far greater impact on these qualities than planets do.</summary>

He now deepens this critique, arguing that even natural disasters like plagues and floods cannot be blamed on the heavens.</meta>

->On Astrology, Book III.<-

will be made clear. For indeed, all other things are arranged according to the measure of heat and cold, or dryness and moisture. But neither others nor **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note> himself act in this way, since what they say regarding character in a private <term>nativity</term> <note>A birth chart or horoscope.</note>, or regarding chance events, often does not correspond at all to the temperament of the body—at least not by the logic through which other things are usually referred to these qualities. Nor will those things they pronounce regarding the weather of the whole year, or regarding morals, plague, the grain supply, and wars, be consistent here; for they clearly seek these things out from the most diverse constellations. This will be easily established for anyone reading both the books of astrology and the prophecies of astrologers. Therefore, let them not hold up this facade and "honorary mask" of a **Natural Method** <note>The claim that astrology is a legitimate branch of physics/natural science because it deals with the "natural" influence of the stars on the air and body.</note> to cover their superstition, claiming they only subject human affairs to the stars insofar as the disposition of the air and the body depends on the <term>primary qualities</term> <note>The four basic building blocks of the physical world in ancient science: heat, cold, moisture, and dryness.</note> from heaven. For Ptolemy indeed spoke of this when entering into the art and asserting it to be possible, but in the process and explanation of his teachings, he neither observed it, nor could he have observed it while keeping his professional oaths intact. Otherwise, as I was saying, astrology would consist of very little, if it only had to speak about the disposition of the air and the condition of bodies. Anyone from the common crowd could guess the rest for themselves from these few given rules. But there are also innumerable things in the books of Ptolemy and others which can in no way take their origin from the <term>primary qualities</term> of matter.

***

### NEITHER THE HARMS OF THE ELEMENTS NOR THE DAMAGES
### TO OUR BODIES ARE FROM HEAVEN. CHAPTER XXI.

<insert>F</insert>rom those things we have just said, that point which was brought forward earlier in the third place as an assertion of astrology can easily be rejected. For when it is said: "If the changes of the air come from the stars, then so do plagues, floods, conflagrations, and the high price of grain." We deny this; for it does not follow. Indeed, whoever says this is ignorant of what heaven is. For what else is heaven in the whole of corporeal nature, if not—just as in any particular body—the very force that holds the whole together <note>original: "uis continens totū"</note> so that it does not flow away or dissolve? It is like the heart in an animal, the source of that power by which integrity and the order of the mixture are preserved, and the injury of invading members is repelled. Let him know, therefore, that he who credits the heavens for the excesses of the elements—from which fires and floods happen, and from which high prices, diseases, and plagues arise—is no less in error than someone who attributes the diseases, vices, and ailments of our body to the very power of nature that rules the body; for it is the role of that power to cure these things, not to cause them; to put them to rest, not to stir them up. If these things are true, it is clear that the <term>primary qualities</term> are one thing, while the failures and detriments of those qualities are another. To say these failures happen by the heavens is like denying that the laws and magistrates of a city are one thing, and the crimes committed against them (which do not take their origin from the work of a good prince) are another. Thus, while **the philosopher** <note>Likely referring to Aristotle, whose "natural philosophy" was the standard scientific framework of the time.</note> would grant that whatever is orderly and natural in the elements has heaven as its author, I do not know by what logic he would concede that the heavens also cause them to fail or to deviate from the prescription and laws of nature. On the contrary, it is the dogma of the philosophers that the elements remain within their boundaries and are content with their own laws, and do not cause trouble for the world—

<sig>V.u</sig>
<meta>catchword: cause trouble—</meta>

<summary>Pico argues that astrologers use the "natural" influence of heat and cold as a deceptive mask for their superstitious predictions. He asserts that the heavens act as a preserving, orderly force (like a heart or a good ruler) and therefore cannot be the cause of natural disasters or "failures" like plagues and floods.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s argument that celestial bodies are causes of order and perfection, not of chaos or "evil" on Earth. He is refuting the astrological idea that certain planets (like Saturn or Mars) are inherently "malefic" or responsible for disasters and diseases.</meta>

<page-num>506</page-num>

->**Of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola**<-

<meta>catchword: concinn (harmonious/fitting)</meta>

Far be it from the celestial nature—which rules and moderates the fluid and wandering number of corruptible things—to be the cause of such disorder. But, you will say: "Once you grant me that some stars produce cold and others heat, does it not follow that when cold stars predominate, the cold elements grow strong, and when hot stars lead, the hot elements do the same? And if this is said, might it not also happen that by a great convergence of cold constellations, the coldness of the waters might so overflow that the earth is submerged in floods? Conversely, with very powerful hot stars, might conflagrations not occur?"

The response is easy, and not just of one kind. First, regarding the "dominion" of planets and signs which the astrologers have dreamed up: it will be demonstrated later that these claims are false. Why, I ask, would any planet so command the heavens as to produce monstrosities in this world, especially evil ones? Since the work of heaven springs from the <term>conspiracy</term> <note>From the Latin *conspiratio*, meaning "breathing together" or "harmonious union," not a secret plot.</note> of all lights, that entire superior harmony is always tempered in such a way that, just as all things sound together within it, so through it nothing is ever out of tune in the inferior world. 

In this lower world, whenever something **clumsy**, **harsh**, or **discordant** is heard, let it not be referred to the touch of the heavens, but rather to those **four strings of the sublunary lyre** <note>A metaphor for the four elements (earth, air, fire, water) which make up the world below the moon.</note> which, being made of inordinate and impure matter, are sometimes found to be stubborn when touched by the **celestial plectrum** <note>A plectrum is a tool used to pluck a stringed instrument; Pico imagines God or the Heavens "playing" the physical world into motion.</note>, even though that plectrum always moves them toward rhythm and concord. 

After this, it must be considered more subtly: if various stars are set over various elements, they are set over them so that the elements themselves may be perfected. Therefore, any element will be that much more perfect as its presiding star is more powerful. Now, if the perfection of the parts does not conflict with the perfection of the whole—indeed, since the parts fail along with the whole—it will not belong to the perfection of an element for its nature to overstep its bounds and occupy the others. Rather, it will be perfect when it has deflected nothing from the order and course of nature; and it can certainly deflect from that order as much by exceeding it as by falling short. 

Therefore, if **Mars** presides over fire, since it is not fitting for anything to be done by a star to a subject quality that does not agree with the good order and laws of nature, it would be the office of the celestial prefecture to restrain the tumultuous just as much as to arouse the sluggish. It can therefore be granted that the <term>four primary qualities</term> <note>Heat, cold, moisture, and dryness.</note> come from heaven, yet their "crimes," transgressions, and tumults are not from heaven, but from the inordinate movements of matter, which does not everywhere obey the laws of celestial discipline. 

For this reason, I believe that neither **Plato** in the *Timaeus*, nor **Aristotle** in his *Meteorology*, ever referred these temporary "tyrannies" of the elements to any power of the constellations. Moreover, it is clear from what has been said that not only the harms caused by the elements, but by the same logic, the damages to our bodies and to other living creatures, do not have their causes in heaven. For heaven, which is the most eminent among all bodies and distinguished by its titles of order and beneficence, ought not to produce those things which are instead the works of tumultuous or failing matter. 

Therefore, what we have said concerning the elements, we may likewise say concerning the **humors** <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to control health and temperament.</note> in our body that correspond to them. If **Saturn** presides over <term>black bile</term> <note>Melancholy; traditionally associated with sadness and madness in astrology, but Pico argues Saturn's role is to keep it in check.</note> and **Mars** over <term>red bile</term> <note>Choler; associated with anger.</note>, and another planet over blood, and another over phlegm, the work of these planets is nothing other than to bridle these qualities and contain them under the laws of nature.

<summary>Pico argues that the heavens are a source of perfect harmony and that natural disasters or bodily illnesses are caused by the "stubbornness" of earthly matter, not by the stars. He redefines planetary influence as a restraining, perfecting force rather than a cause of elemental or "humoral" excess.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s argument that celestial bodies, as perfect and divine instruments, can only produce order and life. He specifically addresses the "malefic" planets Saturn and Mars, arguing that their influence on the human humors is naturally constructive, and that any "evil" or "monstrosity" observed on Earth is the fault of flawed matter, not the stars.</meta>

<page-num>507</page-num>

# on Astrology Book III.

...a **harmonious** disposition of life. Nor when **Saturn** is most powerful will **black bile** <term>atra bilis</term> <note>The humor associated with melancholy; astrologers blamed Saturn for its excess, leading to depression or madness.</note> be stirred up to destroy the rest and undermine the whole; rather, things will be more orderly, composed, and better arranged. The same must be said of **red bile** <note>Also known as "choler," the humor associated with anger and fire.</note> when **Mars** reigns, since their rays and their very nature are beneficial and health-giving. They do not act like a destructive fire, but rather like the **innate vegetative heat** within us, which works rightly by the hand of the soul toward a certain end for the well-being of the living creature. In the same way, those vital lights—the instruments of the mind and soul of the universe—never act toward destruction, but always for the benefit and well-being of the bodies subject to them. 

**Saturn**, if indeed he presides over **black bile**, will never influence it except in an orderly and life-giving way; therefore, he will not excite it toward the death of the animal, but will moderate it for its preservation. Nor do the humors receive from their stars a tendency to act more violently when those stars prevail, but rather to act more moderately and vigorously. **Death never comes from heaven**, but from matter with its own inherent flaw, where some quality has so degenerated that it cannot sustain the discipline of the presiding star, but either wanders off through excess or fails through deficiency. 

But our **diviners** <note>Pico’s term for astrologers, whom he views as superstitious rather than scientific.</note>, who make themselves the patrons and defenders of heaven just as they do its interpreters, refer not only diseases caused by the excessive irritation of the primary qualities to the stars, but even **vices**, **blindness**, and **deafness**. What is even more detestable, they even blame the stars for **monstrosities** <term>monstra</term> <note>In the Renaissance, "monsters" referred to any birth defect or biological anomaly that deviated from the natural "norm."</note>, than which nothing more absurd can be said or imagined. 

For what else are **monstrosities** but the **sins of nature**? No philosopher has ever referred these to an **efficient cause** <note>The "efficient cause" is the primary agent that brings something into being; for Pico, this is God or the Heavens, which cannot "sin."</note> (especially an unfailing one), but everyone attributes them to **matter**. No one has ever been so delirious as to say that monstrous births occur through the fault of the **forming power**—which, being moved by the hand of God, commits no error—but they blame the **matter** for being poorly shaped in its position, quantity, or quality, and for being stubborn and rebellious against its maker. 

Indeed, it is a far greater insanity to condemn the power of **heaven** than to condemn that of the **seed**. Heaven’s power is all the less able to err or fail as it is more potent than nature itself, being a mistress more closely joined to the Great Architect. It is from heaven, and through heaven alone, that this inferior seed-power is ruled and formed. It is therefore utterly absurd to think that the motions and configurations of the heavens (even if those configurations do vary the effectiveness of the planets) ever proceed or are composed in any way other than what the natural course and ordered tenor of lower things requires. 

Otherwise, where would that **order of nature** reside—the very order whose transgression constitutes a monstrosity? Where would it have its origin, if not in heaven? Or how can they hear their own voices? For they ascribe an evil thing, something disordered and unnatural whose origin is vice and infirmity, to the primary causes of nature, which are the best, most orderly, and most powerful of all. Truly, therefore, did **Averroes** <note>The 12th-century Andalusian philosopher known as "The Commentator" on Aristotle.</note> say that whoever believes that **Mars** or any other star, however it is positioned, can harm bodies, believes things that are foreign to all philosophy. 

But it is certainly so: no profession is more injurious to heaven than **astrological superstition**. Whatever we do beyond reason through the fault of our will, or whatever happens in matter beyond order through the vice of recklessness and unstable matter, this superstition attempts to impute entirely to the **stars**. It does not think their dignity is safe unless every most unworthy thing is credited to them.

### THAT THE VARIETY OF TALENTS AND MORALS DOES NOT
### entirely depend on the primary qualities. Chapter XXII.

**B**ut in truth, even if the stars do not cause harmful bodily conditions, they do at least cause the various differences in bodies—not those that are diseased, faulty, or pathological, but those within the bounds of natural integrity, differing from one another by the proportion of their balance. For it follows universally that if the stars are the authors of the four primary qualities <note>The four primary qualities in Aristotelian physics: heat, cold, moisture, and dryness.</note>, then bodies are born or conceived drier and colder under **Saturn**, hotter under **Mars**, wetter under **Venus**, and so on for the rest. This diversity of temperament is usually followed by a diversity of talents and mental dispositions—not those by which we are compelled, but those by which we are stirred. However, this topic will be treated more extensively later. But let us see whether the dissimilarity of talents and morals can truly arise from this. 

For while it is true in some way, it is nonetheless false in another. Indeed, the manner of the dominant qualities in the body results in certain dispositions: boiling bile <term>bilis</term> <note>Yellow bile, or "choler," associated with a fiery, irritable temperament.</note> makes people more prone to anger; phlegm <term>pituita</term> <note>The humor associated with a slow, calm, or "phlegmatic" nature.</note> makes them sluggish; blood makes them more cheerful; and black bile <term>atra bilis</term> <note>Melancholy; believed to cause sadness or deep thought.</note> makes them sad. But this is quite general and does not always match the evidence, nor does it satisfy certain more hidden and specific conditions of character. I said it does not always match the evidence because one can sometimes find people very similar in bodily temperament, yet very different in their pursuits—not by choice, but by natural inclination. I have seen wild brutality under a maidenly face, and a mild and lovable gentleness under a fierce and contemptible countenance. Others, who by the grace of their brow and the beauty of their face appear to carry perpetual joy, inwardly seethe with sorrows and are a burden to themselves. Others, whom you would judge to be plain slaves of **Saturn** <note>Meaning those with a dark, somber, or "saturnine" appearance.</note>, brighten everything with cheer and wit. There can be other powers following from the primary qualities—as is the consensus of almost all philosophers—that are neither the "daughters" nor the appendages of those first four qualities. We shall declare shortly that many things which astrologers prophesy regarding the diversity of morals cannot clearly be referred back to these qualities.

---

### THAT NEITHER WARS NOR EXTERNAL EVENTS
### depend on the primary qualities. Chapter XXIII.

**I**t is indeed quite ridiculous to suggest that if stars can make cold, heat, and other qualities, they can also cause wars and seditions, or that they can overturn cities and change empires. The reasoning for this position is no less ridiculous. For they say that when bile <term>bilis</term> is stirred up in the bodies of kings and princes, they become more eager to give or take offense through a burning heat of the mind. O blessed Italy, flourishing in perpetual peace, if only you were allowed to have phlegmatic <term>pituitosos</term> princes! This great and divine good could be bought for a small price: a single ounce of a chosen drug to purge the bile, if properly distributed to those princes who are more warlike, would bring peace to the whole world for us. Who would not mock these things rather than refute them? As if this were the only cause of wars, or as if there were no [others]...

<summary>Pico argues that human character and historical events like wars cannot be reduced to the "primary qualities" or humors influenced by stars, mocking the idea that purging a king's bile could prevent a war.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s critique of astrological reasoning. In the preceding section, he discussed how physical temperaments (the humors) relate to human character. Here, he argues that while astrologers might claim a link between humors and behavior, they fail to explain how the stars could possibly govern "external" fortunes like wealth, marriage, or the manner of one's death.</meta>

<page-num>509</page-num>
<header>On Astrology, Book III.</header>

## On Astrology, Book III.

[...not so much] avarice as anger, not greed, nor the opportunity or hope of gain <note>Pico is listing human motivations for war that are internal, rather than celestial.</note>. Nor is it rivalries and hatreds—which among the astrologers are attributed to **Saturn** rather than **Mars**. Nor does the love of justice itself sometimes stir up wars and tumults, as if the mind of kings were not more often God [acting] in place of the <term>bile</term> <note>original: *bile*; referring to the humor of yellow bile or "choler," which was thought to cause anger. Pico suggests God directs history through human passion.</note>. Now He exercises the good toward virtue, now He punishes the wicked through the ministry of the wicked, whom He employs as executioners in the worldly republic and as if they were visible demons. 

But here, although the astrologers say ridiculous things, they seem at least to be saying *something* [regarding the humors]. But how will they relate external things—which vary not at all according to our humors—to those four qualities? Such as exile, honors, riches, poverty, children, a wife, friends, or enemies? Ptolemy says: "They have an affinity with the soul and the body; for instance, honor and dignity with the soul, and a wife and riches with the body." What is this "affinity," O Ptolemy? That these chance events should follow the condition of the soul or the body? 

Or is it what you are accustomed to say: that if the influence of **Mars** makes someone bilious <note>Full of yellow bile; irritable or "choleric."</note>, it also inflicts wounds and a violent death upon him, since the heat of the bile incites one to brawls and to arms, where death itself dwells familiarly. But we usually consider it most clearly the work of the stars when a mild man, living in leisure, insulting no one, is nonetheless dragged into danger, into swords, into enmities by some fatal force as if against his will; likewise, a warlike man, a "stirrer of hornets" as they say, dies full of days and unharmed at home among his own. Why then does the former, lacking Martian heat, die by the sword—which is the work of **Mars**—while the latter dies in peace, though he himself is hotter than **Mars**? 

Furthermore, while certain internal states might display some connection with the things within us, and thus might be referred to the habit of the body, by what reasoning could things like a wife, riches, honors, and other things of this kind follow the differences of the body and soul? Truly, one cannot even dream of this. 

Wherefore Ptolemy himself, in the first chapter of his book <term>Apotelefmaton</term> <note>original: *Apotelefmaton*; the Greek title of Ptolemy's *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note>, where he builds his argument on the efficacy of the stars, concludes nothing other than that the diversity of the body—and of the soul insofar as it clings to the body—follows from the stars in some way. He adds nothing about chance events in that place. For he writes thus: "It is useful, therefore, for someone to say what the state of the surrounding air will be at any time. But he will also understand the specific habit and <term>temperament</term> <note>The "complexion" or specific mix of the four humors in an individual.</note> of any man by an argument drawn from the state of the air when he was being formed. Wherefore he will be able to say what kind of body and what kind of soul he would obtain. Then, how he will fare in the course of time, by foreseeing that the future disposition of the air—being suitable to such a temperament of the body—leads to his health, or, being discordant, provides the occasion for disease and sickness." 

These are the words of Ptolemy there, in which, as it appears, there is no mention of external things. But soon, in the next chapter, where he repeats his statements and links them to what follows, he also adds external things—as if he had proven something about them too—perhaps thinking he could deceive the reader, whose memory of the reasoning from which that conclusion was said to be derived and proven might have already slipped away. Therefore, even if we grant to Ptolemy that the primary qualities of matter are changed...

### THAT HIDDEN POWERS ARE NOT PRESENT IN CELESTIAL BODIES, THROUGH
### WHICH THEY MIGHT PRODUCE THE HIDDEN PROPERTIES OF LOWER THINGS, BUT ONLY
### HEAT AND LIFE-GIVING LIGHT. CHAPTER 24.

**I**t remains to be discussed whether, besides the effective power of these qualities, there are more hidden and eminent powers in the stars, through which they are able to do many things that they cannot do through those primary qualities—just as the magnet, by its own particular property, attracts iron, or the **peony** <note>original: *pœonia*; a plant highly valued in Renaissance medicine.</note> helps those suffering from epilepsy <term>falling sickness</term> <note>original: *caducis*; refers to the "falling sickness," an old term for epilepsy.</note>, and as other powers exist in other things, which are both nobler and more effective than the primary dispositions of matter. This was the contention of the fourth reason, asserting that it is impossible for the stars not to abound in virtues of this kind if (as is said by almost all philosophers) earthly things obtain such gifts by the benefit of the stars, especially since they are the most noble bodies and must necessarily be endowed with the noblest gifts. 

But neither the nobility of these bodies, nor the fact that the hidden and marvelous powers of earthly bodies are said to come from them, is an argument by which we are compelled to believe that such virtues—that is, some power in the celestial nature besides that which we called life-giving heat—exist. For, to address the last point first, they do not correctly understand what is said: that lower bodies obtain from heaven the powers by which they do those things that cannot be effected through the four primary qualities. Those gifts and powers flow from the innermost principles of the bodies themselves, that is, from their <term>forms</term> <note>In the Aristotelian tradition Pico follows, the "form" is the essential nature or "soul" of an object that gives it its specific properties.</note>, or if you prefer to say, their essences. Furthermore, just as heaven is said to have given the form which that motion follows, so it is said to give them such virtues. 

Yet the diversity of these powers arises from a diversity not of the constellation, but of the <term>mixture</term> <note>original: *mixtionis*; the specific combination of elements (earth, air, fire, water) in a physical object.</note>, from whose varying proportions different forms spring forth. And this very thing pertains to the dignity of the heavens: for whatever things are divided into a multitude in the lower order, the higher order possesses them through a single and more eminent act. Therefore, if this sublunary, so multifaceted, and so numerous crowd of perishable bodies—weak, tumultuous, particular, and narrow—is compared to the celestial body, which is eternal, unfailing, simple, vast, and universal, it is most consistent with reason that whatever power or perfection is cut into parts and distributed among lower things proceeds from that first body. 

However, the celestial bodies bestow all these things equally, though they are so various and manifold, through their own unique gift of light and heat. This gift, communicated more or less through the series of stars, creates an order among them rather than a diversity. Nor should we inquire further into what this gift or property is; we have said many times that it does not need a demonstrator, as it demonstrates itself and all other things with itself—namely, **light**, evident to everyone, which, flowing from a moving body and breathing forth heat, indicates to us the almost hidden <meta>The text cuts off here at the syllable "my-"; the catchword "sterium" indicates the next word is "mysterium" or mystery.</meta> my-

<summary>Pico argues that the stars do not possess "occult" magical powers; instead, the diverse properties of earthly objects (like magnets) result from their own internal physical "forms" and "mixtures," influenced only by the universal celestial gifts of light and heat.</summary>

# on Astrology, Book III.

<note>The large initial M is missing from the transcription, intended to be added later by a rubricator.</note>[The my]stery of divinity, and in its power of motion, it figures <note>or "represents"</note> wisdom in its light, and love in its heat. Through these, that first God—the first of all, I say—moves, illuminates, creates, perfects, and preserves all things, just as heaven is the first among all bodies. Beyond this prerogative of a threefold efficacy depending in a certain order upon one body, what more do we desire in heaven, or what do we feel is lacking for it to reach the highest perfection of bodily nature and the dominion over the lower world? To be marked and distinguished by multiple properties is a claim to dignity for an *imperfect* nature, but it actually detracts from a *perfect* one. For it is the property of a perfect nature, as I have said, to possess gathered together in one what lower things possess separately and in parts. 

If this privilege did not belong to the perpetual motion of the body and its heat-giving light, we would certainly have to search for something else in heaven which, by a simple act, might encompass and embrace the power of any corruptible bodies whatsoever. But if this is found fully within it, there is no need for the labor of mixing in other things. And it is found undoubtedly, since without it no bodily thing can generate, nor, once generated, can it carry out its operations. For take it away along with its heat, and the **peony** <note>original: *pœonia*; a plant used in traditional medicine.</note> will not help those with epilepsy <term>the falling sickness</term> <note>original: *caducis*; a historical term for epilepsy.</note>, nor will the **hyacinth** <note>original: *hyacinthus*; likely referring here to the gemstone, believed to have medicinal properties</note> stop blood, nor will **rhubarb** <note>original: *rheumbarbarum*</note> draw out bile. 

And just as the efficacy of whatever things act upon us would cease if it were not stirred by the fuel of our own internal heat, so too would the power of those bodies cease, as well as the heat of living things themselves, unless they were both separately nurtured and joined together by celestial heat. Therefore, the very act and perfection of the powers placed within earthly things is this heat-giving light—insofar as it is hot—just as the heat of all things is, in turn, their perfection insofar as it shines. And just as colors cannot be seen, nor eyes see, except by the benefit of this light: so neither can the gifts of any bodies either exist by themselves or affect each other if they are deprived of the help of that motion and heat. 

Wherefore, just as it pertains to the dignity and beauty of the heaven that it should gleam with the single splendor of its own native light despite such a great diversity of colors, so it belongs to its perfection to have possessed one single power in place of the manifold number of material virtues—and one more noble than all of them, just as light precedes all colors and is their perfect constitution, just as light is the perfect constitution of all colors. Nor should we think that anything is taken away from the dignity of heaven if we deny these particular gifts to the stars, any more than we believe heaven itself is not

### IF ITS OWN SPECIFIC POWER IS GRANTED TO EACH STAR, THAT POWER IS NEVERTHELESS UNIVERSAL. Chapter 25.

**E**ven if someone should contend that, besides this property of movement, light, and heat common to all, each star has its own specific **influence** <note>original: *influentia*; the flowing down of celestial power.</note>, I would not strongly resist them, although I could. But I would remind them that these various virtues by which the stars differ from one another still agree in this: they are all celestial virtues. Whatever is in the heavens, even if it is a particular part compared to the whole of the celestial realm, is nevertheless **universal** when referred to sublunary <note>The "sublunary" world refers to the Earth and its atmosphere, which, in the ancient worldview, was the region of change and decay below the moon.</note> things (even if that influence seems very narrow). When I say "universal," I wish it to be understood that it encloses within itself the perfection of the entire <term>corruptible</term> <note>Corruptible refers to anything made of matter that can break down, die, or change.</note> world; otherwise, it would not be celestial, as has been partly declared already and will soon be explained more fully. 

If this is granted, those peculiar gifts of the stars will not help the cause of astrology at all. There will indeed be one property for **Jupiter** and another for **Saturn**, but Jupiter will not, for that reason, produce a different effect among us than Saturn. Therefore, both will be able to perform all things equally through their own property. I will not deny that the Jovian virtue differs from the Saturnine. But there is no virtue of the lower bodies that the Jovian does not contain, generate, preserve, make effective, and perfect just as much as the Saturnine, and vice versa. I will first say why this is so, and then how this diversity of property and action stands alongside such commonality.

The nature of heaven does not seem capable of being explained more clearly and briefly than if you say that **heaven is the unity of all bodies**. Indeed, there is no multitude that does not depend on its own unity; there is nothing in the universe that does not derive from a single, as it were, **fountain-like head** <note>original: *fontali capite*</note>. And just as in an army every single legion refers to its own prefect, and the whole army to one General, so every series of things agreeing in a common genus has its own principle from which it is led, by which it is nourished, governed, and contained. Since there are many such principles, this manifold unity is ultimately reduced back to the simplest unity of the **First Principle**. 

But just as every number is in a certain way within unity, the whole city in the King, and the entire army in the General, so is every virtue and perfection within the principle of its own "herd," so to speak. Yet, what in that "herd-like" condition is divided, maimed, unfinished, and indeterminate, thrives in the "head" in a singular embrace of an indeterminate unity—pure, effective, and perfect. Thus it happens that one might say no part of the subsequent body is in the head, and yet again, that the whole body is in the head. So it is with the **Ineffable God**, who is the first among those things that are; He is none of the things that exist, and yet again, He is all things through a certain eminence of His primary nature and all-encompassing power. 

From what principle, then, shall the bodily genus depend, if not from the **First Body** in both place and dignity? This, moreover, is the **Heaven**. What we were saying is therefore true: Heaven will be the unity of all bodies, of which all things that belong to other bodies can be denied, and yet all things can also be affirmed. They are denied, certainly, because that which in lower bodies is formed has various limits—it is discrete, multiple, and imperfect—and such characters of **form** <note>original: *formæ*</note> are not in heaven...

forms, nor does it possess diversity in the same way. He concludes that all those things exist together, not by the potentiality of matter, but by the fullness of power and the loftiness of their original nature. If this is the nature of the heavens, it certainly belongs to every celestial body; nor should it be thought that while the whole heaven contains the total perfection of the lower bodies, one part contains only one part. That would be no privilege for the heavens; rather, any part of the heaven is the entire lower world, excluding those things which are *in* the world but not *of* the world. The **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who often used mathematical and allegorical symbols to explain the cosmos.</note> seem to have signified this by a certain allegorical opinion of theirs, by which they were accustomed to affirm that this entire **sublunary** <note>The region below the moon, consisting of the four changing elements: earth, water, air, and fire.</note> region is a single star, and that in every star of heaven there exist all the things seen in this region of ours. Thus, in the **Moon**, there are the distinctions of the four elements, as well as of valleys and mountains; and also the plants and whatever living creatures are found among us. The same would be true in **Venus**, **Mercury**, and the rest of the stars. 

By this symbol, they certainly declare nothing else to us than what we wished to prove: that there is no star in heaven that does not encompass the whole of what is beneath the Moon. Otherwise, they would not be of a celestial nature, if it were not a most true and proven principle that "celestial nature" is nothing other than the unity of bodily nature. Furthermore, this would be a privilege worthy of heaven: that with such vastness and an innumerable number of lights, it finally embraces the goods of our narrow sublunary space. Therefore, in the power of any star, there is every power of **perishable bodies** <note>original: *corporum caducorum*; bodies subject to decay and death.</note>. The powers of different stars do not differ in that some preside over certain things and others over others, since they all preside over all things. Nor does a higher star excel a lower one by a wider embrace (that is, of more things), but by a more noble one; it contains the same things that the lower one contains, but in a far more unified and eminent way than the lower star does. 

This same principle can be seen in **separated minds** <note>original: *mentibus ſeparatis*; a philosophical term for incorporeal beings or angels.</note> and in the cognition of living beings. For just as every body depends on the heavens, so every power that participates in cognition depends on the **Intellect**. I call "Intellect" not our own, which is called **reason**, but that of the **angels**, whom the philosophers call "minds" and "intellects." This Intellect is sufficient unto itself for understanding; it does not look at anything below itself, nor in anything below itself, to understand what it perceives; it is not deceived, and it does not toil. And that which, in every kind of cognition, is distributed among various powers, the Intellect possesses through a unified power far more excellently than it exists in those lower powers. It beholds truth within itself and touches it as present with the certainty of a sense. It holds within itself that which is in fleeting things through an **imaginary faculty** <note>The power to form mental images or "phantasms" of physical objects.</note>; it perceives the causes and species of things, both bodily and incorporeal, through **rational perspicacity**—not that the Intellect is rational, or sensory, or imaginary, but through an **intellectual property** <note>A characteristic nature unique to the higher intellect.</note> of a more noble condition, gathering what is perfect in those lower faculties and rejecting what is imperfect. 

For in us, **physical knowledge** is one thing, **mathematical** is another, and **divine** is another. For reason attains physical knowledge with the help of the senses; it attains mathematical knowledge with the **imagination** <note>original: *phantasia*; the faculty of the mind that deals with shapes and numbers independent of matter.</note>; and it attains divine knowledge with the mind and intellect. Furthermore, there is no mind, even the lowliest, that does not see all truth in its own light—the truth which we either certainly reach or at least pant after through those sciences and arts. Come then, let us compare these things to bodily things...

Are these arts and sciences within us, and are there various kinds of knowledge in the whole of knowing nature? It is just as it is in the multitude of bodies, where there are various privileges of different virtues. All knowledge is a certain participation in **intellectual light** <note>A Neoplatonic concept where human understanding is seen as a "spark" or "reflection" of a divine, universal intelligence.</note>, and every bodily virtue is a certain participation in celestial faculty. However, just as the former shines more clearly in reason, so the latter shines more perfectly in the **spirit of the heart** <note>In Renaissance physiology, the "vital spirit" (spiritus) was a fine substance that mediated between the soul and the body, centered in the heart.</note>. 

These things being established, come, let us see whether anyone has correctly said that if intellectual rays flow down from those minds, some will be those that make physicists and not mathematicians, others mathematicians and not divines, others divines rather than physicists or mathematicians. And so this light will exist, so that these studies depend on the diversity of the nature of the breathing minds, rather than from rays proceeding from the same mind by its own counsel and will. I think he will judge more rightly who believes there is nothing of this kind which any of those stars cannot give abundantly; and that they do not grant these things by their own freedom, in the manner of the stars, but by nature. 

And if it happens that this gift is received from there rather than that one, it should be said to be referred not to the giver, who is equally liberal toward all things, but to the **capacity and condition of the receiver** <note>A fundamental rule in Scholastic philosophy: "Whatever is received is received according to the mode of the receiver." Pico is arguing that the "influence" of a star is universal, but different objects on Earth react differently to it.</note>. 

For if, as we have said, the star stands in relation to the corruptible body (as far as our present purpose is concerned) just as the mind stands to failing knowledge, it must likewise be said that a star can give from itself anything whatever that a subject body, whatever it may be, is born to receive. Thus, the diversity of **hidden influence** <note>original: "afflatus occulti" – literally "hidden breathings," referring to the invisible emanations believed to flow from the stars.</note> is now caused not by the star that breathes—as the **astrologer** <term>astrologus (astrologer): in Pico's time, this often referred to those who practiced "judicial astrology," the prediction of human affairs based on planetary positions.</term> thinks—but by the diversity of the matter being breathed upon. 

I said "hidden influence," since the action of a star through light and heat can be diverse according to the intensity and weakening of the ray, as we explained above; but in these hidden properties through which the star propagates itself, as it were, and pours out its own (so to speak) **species and images** <note>In this context, "species" refers to the formal essence or "likeness" of a thing that was thought to be transmitted through space to produce effects elsewhere.</note>, just as that intensity and weakening does not appear in them, so we are not persuaded to posite any diversity of action. 

But you will say, the power of **Jupiter** and that diffused species is certainly different from the power of **Saturn**. I admit it, but I do not admit that they will therefore produce a different thing, since there is no thing in the **sublunary world** <note>The region below the moon, made of the four elements and subject to change and decay.</note> which either one could not produce. What then is the diversity of action? Each does the same thing, but one does the same thing in another way—the nobler star in a nobler and more eminent way. Although I do not know if we should so determine concerning these powers, whether perhaps an inferior power is more effective upon us, not because it is closer in location, but because it is more related in nature; but this inquiry belongs to another work. 

Here we only assert that if, besides light and heat, its own property is granted to each star, it can be defended that all are **universal** <note>In this context, "universal" means the stars have the power to influence all types of things, rather than being specialized "specialists" as astrologers claimed.</note>, so that they produce no diversity of the lower things from themselves. We could, however, grant them some particular force, by contracting, of course, the stellar power; and we could grant it in such a way that this would nonetheless help the astrologers not at all—as if we were to grant that all stars always work the same in all things, but not all things in all. To this example: Any bodies consist of **matter and form** <note>The "Hylomorphic" theory that all physical things are a combination of underlying matter and an organizing principle or "form."</note>; suppose, therefore, someone thinks the matter stands such that those things which pertain to matter, the three smaller stars...

...stars might perform their duties, with the Moon, Venus, and Mercury having divided offices, so that the Moon itself rules the matter, while it is arranged for form by Venus and Mercury: by Venus through quantity, establishing order, figure, composition, and the proper beauty in the parts; and by Mercury through quality, as it takes on appropriate affections for a form to be admired through its malleable mobility. Likewise, the permanence of form comes from the three superior stars in this manner: that it has its form from Saturn, that it gives being and life to those things which live from Jupiter, and that it moves and excites them internally to action from Mars. 

However, whatever a thing itself diffuses, and makes known or propagates through that diffusion, is referred mostly to the Sun, whose effect is seen to conquer the worked matter, from which it produces something like itself, which is both the generation and the manifestation. What if, then, the works of the planets differed? We grant this of our own accord, not forced by reason, nor by the faith of experiments, nor by the authority of Plato or Aristotle; yet every diversity of lower things would still be, not from the heavens, but from lower causes. The heaven acts in its own way always in all things, but the work is varied both by proximate causes and by the disposition of the matter. No reason persuades us to place particular virtues in the stars rather than universal ones. One could suspect otherwise regarding certain things without sin, and I do not deny this even with the authority of the learned; but as the following book will show, these influences are not of the kind the astrologers describe, nor are we affected by them in the manner they believe.

### EPILOGUE OF THIS BOOK, WITH A REJECTION
### of certain arguments of the astrologers against those 
### who debate them. Chapter XXVI.

We have examined all the natural changes of inferior things which seem to be the work of the heavens; as for the chance accidents of men, we shall speak of those in the solution of the fifth reason. We have found nothing in those changes that favors the astrologers; rather, the occasion was given to object to many things, so that they might regret having stirred up this **necessity** <note>original: "ἀνάγκην" (anankēn). In Greek philosophy, this refers to a blind, irresistible force of fate or cosmic compulsion.</note>. For what else do we conclude from this but that sublunary bodies are affected by the rays of the luminaries? But they are affected by no other influence than that of heat, and no other heat than vital heat, whose action would not change except according to the position of the star, radiating us more intensely either from nearby or directly. 

From these principles, we provide the reason for all effects, whichever ones they used to bring forward from the "faith of experience" as testimony for their dogma. In giving this account, it was clear that astrology was not confirmed by those observations but rather weakened, and where they were either deceiving or being deceived was everywhere uncovered. Thus, it appeared that they falsely believe the Sun has a drying power, or that the Moon has an unhealthy moistening and cold power. It is falsely imagined that there is an **occult power** <note>A "hidden" or non-physical force. Pico argues that the Moon moves the tides through its light and motion alone, not through a specialized "magical" property.</note> in the Moon besides motion and light which pulls and pours the sea. It is falsely claimed that Saturn is made the culprit for the harm of an **eight-month birth** <note>In ancient and medieval medicine, an eight-month fetus was thought to be under the influence of the "cold" planet Saturn and thus less likely to survive than a seven-month or nine-month fetus.</note>. It is falsely ascribed to the signs of the Zodiac as if they had different powers and virtues, when the ray of the Sun works only through variety. Finally, it is falsely claimed that **critical days** <note>The specific days during an illness (like a fever) when a patient was expected to either recover or take a turn for the worse.</note> and periods of fevers are referred to the motions of the Moon or other stars. Indeed, it was so far...

<meta>This page continues Pico's systematic dismantling of astrological reasoning. Having previously argued that celestial influence is universal light and heat rather than specialized "powers," he now addresses the specific observations of the Sun and Moon often used by astrologers to justify their claims about other planets.</meta>
