It has reached a point where an argument for the reliability of astrological decrees was being drawn from those changes caused by the Sun and the Moon, in such a way that astrology is brought into no small suspicion of falsehood. For they argued thus: if anyone lies out under the Moon, a numbness seizes their limbs, and <term>sea urchins</term><note>original: "echini." It was a common ancient belief, cited by Aristotle and Cicero, that the flesh of shellfish increased and decreased in size according to the phases of the moon.</note> are filled up in like manner; therefore, they say, the Moon cools and moistens. The senses attest that the Sun is scorching, therefore it is dry. 

We, on the other hand, press our case thus: the Moon fills the sea urchins, therefore it is warm; we have demonstrated this from **Aristotle**. People sleeping under it are numbed by the cold, therefore it is warm. We have explained this by clear reasoning, namely the manner in which it happens <note>Pico likely refers to the idea that the Moon's gentle heat draws internal warmth to the surface, leaving the inner body cold, or that it stirs up cold vapors.</note>. During the full moon, it favors conception, nourishes bodies, and as it waxes, it strengthens and quickens them; therefore, it is warm. We have proved this from **Hippocrates** and from evidence itself. 

Regarding the Sun, we likewise appeal to experience, through which it is clear that every spirit of life is vivified by its rays; truly, that is not the work of a "dry" power, but of a healthily warm one. Nor was it difficult to explain how the Sun—either by accident or by drying or by scorching—might even cause cooling, and why the Moon might be called the cause of cold and moisture, even though each star is, by its own nature, the author only of life-giving light and heat. 

They also gathered their evidence this way: we see our bodies clearly transformed by the Sun and the Moon, and therefore we should not doubt the influences of the other stars. But this very thing we see regarding the Sun and Moon draws us into doubt regarding the others. Specifically, we find that the dispositions of bodies vary because of them in such a way that we judge the remaining stars to be <term>non-contributing</term><note>original: "asymbolas." A Greek-derived term meaning "not throwing into the common fund," or having no share in the result.</note> rather than called to a share of the work. Indeed, when the light of the Moon decreases, moisture in bodies is always thinned; it always increases as the Moon waxes. 

Why then—if what the astrologers think about the efficiency of the other stars is true—why, I ask, do the other planets not occasionally compensate for the loss of lunar light when they are dominant? Why do they not increase moisture so that we might, by the benefit of the stars, sometimes dine on succulent oysters even during a new moon? Why, conversely, does that "dryness of Saturn" or the "law of Mars" never use the laws of the heavens to desiccate bodies when the Moon is full, or defend cut timber from rot? 

Therefore, these observations favor those who take away the power of the planets rather than those who affirm it; just as they favor those who attribute no efficacy to the <term>signs</term><note>The twelve signs of the Zodiac.</note> rather than those who attribute much. Otherwise, when the sea is moved by the Moon (as they claim and we do not deny), why does the Moon not move it more when positioned in "watery" signs than in "fiery" ones? And why is it no less moved in "dry" signs than in "moist" ones? Or why does the Moon not create more abundant tides when joined to "moist" planets than to "drying" ones? 

And if what they predict concerning the twelve places—which they call <term>houses</term><note>The twelve divisions of the celestial sphere in an astrological chart.</note>—is true, how does it harmonize with the fact that as the Moon climbs from its rising, the closer it approaches the summit, the more strongly it acts upon the Ocean? Thus, it acts more strongly from the **12th house** than from the **ascendant** <note>original: "horoscopo." The point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon.</note>, yet they claim that in that place [the 12th house], the power of all stars languishes and becomes weakest. Therefore, these experiments of ours stand against them, rather than arrogating authority to the opinions of astrologers—unless it is as **Favorinus** used to say (as we also touched upon above): that the Ocean, as a companion to the Moon, grows old and young along with it...

...[it is] a great argument to persuade us that all human affairs, both minor and major, are led and governed as if bound to the stars and constellations. But it is far different—and as that same author used to say when mocking astrologers—it is far too inept and absurd to think that, simply because the tides of the Ocean synchronize with the Moon’s cycle, a legal dispute someone might happen to have regarding a water duct <note>original: *aque ductu*; a channel or pipe for conveying water, often a source of property disputes in Roman and Renaissance law.</note> with his rivals before a judge should also be thought of as being governed by some rein from heaven.

## CHAPTER XXVII.

It remains for us to dissolve the final argument, which is taken from human events. In these events, some things so exceed our powers, or happen so contrary to merit and reason, that they seem to support the influence of a <term>fatal decree</term><note>Pico is addressing *fatum* (fate), the idea that human life follows a pre-written celestial script.</note> and celestial power. We shall resolve this for the present by showing that all these things have sufficient causes within ourselves, and that nothing appears in any of them that requires a heavenly author. That is to say, there is nothing in the course of human affairs from which a suspicion ought to arise that the deeds of men are ruled and governed by the fates. 

For at the beginning of the next book, no longer merely resolving the issue but actively arguing it, we will first teach that these things—in which those people seem to recognize the power of fate—could in no way be produced by the heavens. These events are divided into two great categories: the great and the bad. Let us speak first of the great, whether they pertain to the mind or to external circumstances. For in this way, they used to throw in our faces both the "good fortune" of **Alexander** <note>Alexander the Great (356–323 BCE). Astrologers often claimed his rapid conquest of the known world was due to a lucky birth chart.</note> and the genius and learning of the **Teacher** <note>Referring to Aristotle, often called "The Philosopher" or "The Teacher" in medieval and Renaissance texts.</note>. 

Let us begin, then, with those things which pertain to the mind. You admire the consummate knowledge of natural things in **Aristotle**; I admire it along with you. You say the cause is heaven and the constellation under which he was born. I do not agree—and not just for the common reason that many people were born under the same star who did not become Aristotles, but because, beyond the heaven (under which, as a universal cause, both the <term>pigs of Boeotia</term><note>original: *Boëtiae sues*. In antiquity, the inhabitants of Boeotia were proverbially stereotyped as dull-witted and "swinish," contrasting with the "Attic" wit of the Athenians.</note> and the <term>Attic philosophers</term><note>original: *philosophi actici*; referring to the intellectual brilliance of Athens.</note> sprout equally), there are proximate causes proper and peculiar to **Aristotle** himself, to which we may attribute his singular progress. 

First, certainly (as he himself said), he was allotted a good soul; and this surely did not come from heaven, since the soul is immortal and incorporeal, as he himself demonstrated. Nor do the astrologers deny this. Then, he was allotted a body suitable to serve such a soul; and this too came not from heaven (except as a common cause), but from his parents. He chose to practice philosophy. This was the work of the principles we mentioned—that is, of the mind and the body—and of his own free will. He made progress in philosophy; this was the fruit of his adopted purpose and his own industry. 

But, you say, many others practiced philosophy with equal zeal and labor. In his case, the cause was the teaching of his master <note>Plato, who was Aristotle's teacher for twenty years.</note> and the good fortune of the age in which he was brought forth, an age full of the writings of the ancients, though they were not yet perfected; thus, he lacked neither the labor of beginning and finishing the liberal arts nor the material with which to do so. Yet he progressed far more than his contemporaries and his disciples. He was allotted not a better star, but a better genius <note>original: *ingenium*; referring to innate talent or natural capacity.</note>. Nor is genius from a star, since it is incorporeal, but from God—just as the body is from the father, not from heaven.

He mocks the idea that specific human events like lawsuits are governed by the same celestial forces that move the tides.</summary>

of which we speak with as much more honor than the astrologers do, as a universal cause is more divine and eminent than particular causes. But if this exceeded the grasp of the human intellect, whether that of Aristotle or any other philosopher, it will be because the cause is not altogether inferior—such as every body is, even a celestial one—but rather better, which is to say divine. Just as Socrates, who in my opinion was the greatest of all philosophers, attributed the wisdom he received not to his birth stars, but to a <term>guiding spirit</term><note>original: *assistenti numini*; Pico refers to the *daimonion* of Socrates, an inner divine voice he claimed warned him against mistakes.</note>. Therefore, we give more to heaven than is proper if we lower the divinity of our souls to those bodily rays; yet we give too little if we attribute bodily differences, which are received from private matters, to heaven as if it were a particular cause.

It is, however, altogether less than is fitting when we ascribe our very deformities and the stains of our minds to the stars. This is one of the main reasons people are moved to take refuge in the stars: because there appear in many men certain <term>inharmonious desires</term><note>original: *abasonæ quædam appetitiones*; desires that seem "out of tune" with normal human nature.</note>, contrary to the laws of humanity, which seem to have not an intrinsic (that is, human) cause, but an extrinsic one—and because it is a powerful cause, they assume it is celestial. 

But I would ask them: why does a pregnant woman more gladly eat earth and coals than every kind of exquisite food? And if they find the cause of that monstrous craving to be the fetus rather than a star, I will likewise advise them that the cause of those things which they marvel at should be sought in the <term>temperament</term><note>original: *temperatura*; in Renaissance medicine, this refers to the specific balance of the four "humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) in an individual’s body.</note> of the body rather than in heaven. I might say it is also found among wicked demons, but that would lead them away from bodily causes. 

Certainly, besides the habit of the body, I can declare by a most true example how much <term>custom</term><note>original: *consuetudo*; Pico argues that behavior is learned and reinforced through habituation rather than being innate or fated.</note> contributes to such portentous affections. There is still living a man known to me of a prodigious and unheard-of lust. For he is never kindled toward Venus <note>A common euphemism for sexual arousal or desire.</note> unless he is beaten; and yet he contemplates this crime in such a way, and so desires the raging blows, that he scolds the one whipping him if she acts too slowly with him. He is not fully in possession of his wish unless blood breaks out, and the more violent lash leaves the limbs of this most guilty man (who is otherwise innocent) <note>Pico likely means the man is not a criminal in other aspects of life, despite this "guilty" or shameful fetish.</note>. That wretched man demands this service with the highest prayers always from the woman he approaches, and he offers a whip, which he has hardened the day before for this duty by soaking it in vinegar. As a suppliant, he begs to be beaten by the prostitute; the harder he is struck by her, the more fervently he catches fire, and he hastens at an equal pace toward pleasure and pain—a man discovered to be unique, who finds bodily delights in the midst of torture. 

Since he is not otherwise a bad man, he recognizes and hates his disease; and because he has been familiar to me for many years now, he freely revealed what he suffered. When I diligently inquired from him the cause of such an unusual plague, he said: "I became accustomed to it this way since I was a boy." And when I asked again for the cause of that custom, he said he was raised with most wicked boys, among whom it had been agreed that by this license of beating—as if for a price—they would sell their mutual shame to one another in a shameful alternation. 

I have not suppressed this fact, though it may be heavy for refined ears to hear, so that we might recognize by the evidence itself how much power custom has over those affections. We must not immediately accuse heaven as if such things could have no earthly cause. For indeed...

Indeed, if an astrologer were to hear of such things, he would say that Venus was "condemned" in that man’s birth-chart, and perhaps lashed by the hostile or otherwise threatening rays of Mars. Let us come to external matters, in which Alexander the Great was preeminent. It was often asked where such a great and sudden success had its origin, if not from heaven? The answer is easy: it came from the virtues of Alexander, of which he possessed many that are necessary for a commander—fortitude, generosity, endurance of labor, skill in military affairs, excellent learning, and others which it is not necessary to list here. It came from the army he acquired, which had been highly trained under his father Philip, and was most warlike due to the nature of the region, and most devoted to him because of his generosity and his own example of virtue. It came from the cowardice of the peoples he overcame, which is why his uncle said that Alexander had "fought against women." 

But what of Fortune, which dominates so much in matters of war? When I say "Fortune," I do not mean heaven, but that cause which Aristotle mentions in the second book of his *Physics* <note>Aristotle defines "fortune" (*tyche*) and "chance" as accidental causes that occur in things done for the sake of an end, but which are not the intended result.</note>, and which we commonly call fortune, and are accustomed to express with these words: "so luck brought it," "so it happened," "so the matter fell out." It is by this that it happens that those playing with dice either throw what they want or what they do not want; this is that so-called "blind" goddess who—besides those causes we have mentioned and similar ones—made the Caesars, the Syllas, the Augustuses, and the Alexanders. 

This Fortune does not, in itself, depend on heaven, nor is it the same thing as Fate, nor does it detract from divine providence. What it finally might or might not be—since it must be discussed at length in the next book—it is not appropriate to say here, where we shall overwhelm the astrologers with no greater weapons than those of Thomas Aquinas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274) was a major theologian whom astrologers often tried to claim as a supporter, but Pico intends to use Aquinas’s emphasis on free will and secondary causes to refute them.</note>, whom these men think favors them most highly. 

As for what is primarily being treated here, I deny that anything on earth is so great, or appears so, as to deserve heaven as its author. For the miracles of the soul (as we have said) are greater than heaven; but the things of fortune and the body, however great they may be, are found to be tiny when compared to heaven. As Favorinus <note>A Roman-era philosopher and orator.</note> rightly said: *"Nothing is great on earth except man; nothing is great in man except the mind and the soul."* If you ascend to this, you transcend heaven; but if you incline toward the body and look up at heaven, you see yourself as a fly, and something less than a fly. 

Consider that black line of ants: there are some that surpass others in strength or size; there are victories, wars, peaces, duties, labors, poverty, and riches among them. To us watching, all these things are tiny and, without distinction, are as nothing. In the same way, our little bodies, our fortunes, our kings, our provinces, wars, treaties, and marriages—if compared to heaven—are absolutely nothing. Compared to heaven, the entire earth (of which men divide one tiny portion among themselves with fire and sword) is but an indivisible point. 

Therefore, the magnitude of earthly things is not such that they could only be the work of heaven. And if those things that we consider "worthy" are not worthy of the stars' attention, how much more unworthy will be those things we do shamefully? Such as wicked men being raised to high dignity, or Socrates perishing by the judgment of a <term>stargazer</term><note>original: *stellicatoris*; a mocking term Pico uses for those who follow astrology rather than reason.</note>, and many enormous things of that kind which we see and suffer daily. In which matters, especially—

<meta>This page concludes Book III of Pico’s massive critique of astrology and begins Book IV. Having previously argued that individual success (like that of Alexander the Great) is due to human virtue and earthly circumstances, he now addresses the "problem of evil"—why the good suffer and the wicked prosper—concluding that these outcomes are the result of human agency or luck, not the stars. He then transitions to a discussion of his debating methodology.</meta>

->520<-

Maternus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer who wrote the *Mathesis*, a primary textbook for ancient astrology.</note> says that fate shines forth, and along with it, the necessity of the celestial decree. I would gladly ask him, along with other astrologers, why they are so eager to attribute our errors to the stars, and why, when we ourselves sin, they would rather accuse heaven than us—as if it were a wonder that we, who have been prone to evil since our youth, should err, or as if those heavenly bodies, which serve the unchangeable orders of the most high God in a constant cycle, could ever stray. 

The innocent are condemned, they say, while the wicked are bestowed with rewards. By which leaders, I ask: by the just or the unjust? If by the just, then even heaven will not suffice to explain such a miracle; if by the unjust, what need is there for heaven, when the malice of man, which despises heaven, is explanation enough? Aristotle asks in his *Problems*: "Why is it that the good and the poor are almost always the same people?" And although he brings forward many causes—both true and witty—he brings forward none from the heavens, as one who surely knew that the earth, not the sky, germinates thorns and thistles. 

But does the cautious and prudent man often run into the very danger he most avoided, while another escapes a peril to which he had recklessly exposed himself? Why should we wonder? Indeed, we should find it more a miracle if such things never happened than if they happen often. When these things occur, a cause must be sought, first the most immediate one; if that is lacking, a more remote and hidden one. For rare and fortuitous events, no other cause need be investigated, provided we remember well what the most wise Aristotle left written for us in the second book of his <term>Physics</term> <note>original: "physicæ auscultationis"; Aristotle’s lectures on natural philosophy, specifically discussing chance and luck.</note> and the sixth book of his <term>First Philosophy</term> <note>original: "primæ philosophiæ"; better known today as the *Metaphysics*.</note>.

# GIOVANNI PICO
## della Mirandola’s Disputations against
## Astrology, Book IV.

### THE METHOD OBSERVED IN DISPUTATION HITHERTO AND TO BE
### observed hereafter; and that even if we grant the astrologers their 
### greatest claim, astrology is nonetheless nothing. Chapter I.

Our custom in debating is generally this: if an adversary proposes something that can both be granted without impiety and reasonably denied, we prefer to deny it rather than grant it, even if granting it would not help him achieve what he intends. By proceeding in this order toward his greatest possible demand, we may show that even if we grant what we rightly declared could be denied, it by no means follows what he thinks. In this way, the whole matter under debate is explored more particularly through its individual parts, and the opponent understands how many things he takes for granted, and how little and how absur—

<header>On Astrology, Book IV.</header>

# On Astrology, Book IV.

...to maintain a certain opinion which is false in many respects, or at the very least doubtful. Yet, however things may stand, it is impossible for that opinion not to be entirely false. Keeping to this custom when dealing with astrologers, we first defended the view that only the rays of the **Sun** and the **Moon** possess the power to transform lower <note>In the medieval worldview, the "lower" or sublunary world refers to Earth, which is subject to change and decay, unlike the "higher" unchanging heavens.</note> things, and that the other stars have no influence on us due to either their distance or the weakness of their rays. 

Secondly, if it were granted to them—not because they forced the point, but as a concession—that something flows down from all the stars into us, we showed that this influence differs from all of them only in terms of its intensity or weakness <note>original: "intentione tantum remissionęq;"—This refers to the scholastic concept of the "intension and remission of forms," describing how a quality like heat can vary in degree.</note>. This means that light flows out along with life-giving heat, but that cold, moisture, and dryness do not emanate from them. 

Thirdly, even if the stars did produce these four primary qualities <note>The "four qualities" are hot, cold, moist, and dry, which were thought to compose all physical matter.</note>, it would not follow that the diversity of impressions made in the upper atmosphere <note>original: "in sublimi"—referring to meteorological phenomena.</note> originates from them; or, if it did, it still would not mean that plagues, cataclysms, or great fires are caused by them. Much less would it follow that, by the power of those four primary qualities, external affairs and matters subject to chance and fortune are governed by the stars. 

Fourthly, even if the stars were believed to be the authors of these primary affections—that is, if they had the power of heating, cooling, moistening, and drying—no other gifts should be attributed to them through which they might accomplish many things that cannot be done by the force of those qualities alone. 

Finally, whatever virtues and properties the stars might have, we argued that they are so universal that there is no condition or power of the lower bodies which they do not encompass. Therefore, all stars act upon all things, which is the defining characteristic of a **universal cause**. However, the diversity of what actually happens or what they imagine to happen takes its origin entirely from **proximate causes**, whether they be free, natural, or accidental.

We undertook to defend all these points with the intention that astrologers might understand that when they think and assert otherwise, they are not speaking of things that are self-evident or manifest. Rather, their claims are confirmed neither by certain reasoning, nor by evident experience, nor by the authority of **Plato** or **Aristotle**; instead, they are placed in ambiguity, and just as they are defended by some, they are attacked by many. 

If all of astrology relied on these points and did not place itself on even more unreliable foundations, I would not consider it utterly ruined, but merely wavering; that is, my opinion of it would be as likely to fall as it would be to stumble. But even if we grant the astrologers as much as **St. Thomas Aquinas**, many other theologians, and philosophers contend can be granted—without reason being greatly opposed—they would still receive far less than is necessary for astrology to be defended as a science, not only among us but by its own nature and in the minds of the angels themselves. 

For Thomas will grant them the greatest thing that can be granted without an open slander of the truth: namely, that the "out-flowings" of all the **Planets** reach us with power, and that different stars have different properties—not only of heating, cooling, moistening, and drying, but also more **occult** <note>In this context, "occult" means "hidden" or "not immediately observable by the senses," referring to subtle physical properties rather than magic.</note> ones. From these, the crowd of earthly things might obtain various gifts, so that not every property possessed by humans and other lower physical natures is derived from their own proximate causes, but some are also derived from the heavenly bodies. All of this we also...

<meta>catchword: cause</meta>

...even if we grant this to the astrologers as a concession, we will show that this art is nevertheless empty. This is because it prophesies using the stars primarily about things that cannot be caused or even indicated by them—even if all the things we previously mentioned were true. Thus, having already shaken astrology or even brought it to the brink of ruin in the previous book, the present discussion will utterly overthrow it, leaving no hope for peace or leniency.

### CHANCE EVENTS DO NOT COME FROM HEAVEN. CHAPTER II.

**F**ortuitous matters—those by whose good or bad outcome we call men "fortunate" or "unfortunate"—are the very things that are chiefly thought to be fated and dependent upon a celestial decree. As such, they constitute the largest part and most significant subject matter of astrological predictions. For things that possess their own <term>immediate causes</term><note>In Scholastic philosophy, a "proximate" or immediate cause is the direct reason something happens (like fire causing heat), whereas a "remote" cause is further back in the chain of events.</note>, such as the conditions of the mind and body, do not seem to require a higher and more hidden cause as much as those things which we say happen by "blind luck" or "chance." These appear to happen without an immediate cause. Such events include: sailing or traveling successfully or unsuccessfully; conducting trade; finding treasure while digging the earth; encountering bandits or wild beasts; pleasing a king; escaping danger; obtaining good or bad servants; or entering a house that is just about to collapse. These, and other things of this kind, happen to wretched and truly weary mortals beyond any plan or expectation. Regarding these matters, since they are entirely out of our hands and come upon us from the outside, we most desire to hear the opinion of the astrologers. After all, a person can learn the condition of their body from a mirror or a doctor, just as they know the quality of their own mind from themselves—provided they actually possess a mind! But what we call "fortuitous" events are exactly what human curiosity most seeks out through the divining arts. Therefore, we shall prove before all else that these can in no way be foreseen by the heavens. We will use no other reasoning than that used by **Thomas Aquinas** <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the most influential medieval theologian. Pico is citing him to show that even the great Church authorities argue against the idea that the stars control random human luck.</note>, specifically in that passage which [ironically] seems to favor the opinion of the astrologers: namely, in the third book of *Against the Gentiles* <note>original: "contra Gentes"</note>, where he seems to say that men are made both fortunate and unfortunate by heaven. His reasoning is as follows: 

The power of a celestial body does not act through intellect or choice, but acts in the same way that nature acts. It is the property of Nature to aim toward a single, specific end. Therefore, an effect that is not "one" <note>In this philosophical context, "one" refers to a unified, single result intended by a specific cause.</note> cannot come from a natural cause <term>in itself</term> <note>original: "per se"—meaning directly or by its own nature.</note>. But things that occur by accident and happen to meet each other are not truly "one," but only "one by accident" <note>original: "per accidens"—meaning a coincidence of two unrelated chains of events.</note>. Therefore, a coincidence of this kind, which we are accustomed to calling "fortuitous," can have no natural cause <term>in itself</term>; but the celestial cause is a natural cause, as we were saying. And thus, it cannot be the cause of such fortuitous things <term>in themselves</term>. 

To these points, Aquinas adds an example by which he simultaneously explains how heaven is not the cause of these outcomes directly, but only <term>by accident</term>. "Suppose," he says, "someone is urged by the heaven to dig a grave. It happens <note>original: "accidit"—it is an accident.</note> that there is treasure in that spot. Thus, while digging the grave, he finds the treasure. It was not caused by heaven that he should find treasure, except <term>by accident</term>." For it is merely an accident that the same location is both a grave and a place for treasure. Indeed, to urge a man to dig a grave in which treasure is hidden specifically so that he might find the treasure...

<summary>Pico argues that astrology cannot predict "luck" or "chance" because the heavens act as a natural, uniform force, whereas chance events are the accidental collision of unrelated causes. He uses the logic of Thomas Aquinas to demonstrate that a celestial impulse to perform one action (like digging) does not mean the stars intended the accidental result (finding treasure).</summary>

...belongs to a rational and intelligent cause, whose proper nature is to relate and order one thing to another; it does not belong to a natural cause, which is directed only toward one thing, as we have said, and no one will deny that the celestial ray is such a cause.

### HOW GOD IS THE CAUSE OF FORTUITOUS THINGS,
### how angels are, how heaven is, how we are,
### and how fortune is. Chapter III.

**W**hen mention is made of fortuitous things <note>original: "fortuitis rebus"; refers to events occurring by chance or luck.</note>, it will be worthwhile to explain more deeply what their causes are according to philosophers and theologians. For from what we have said so far, it might be thought that we are merely attributing those things to chance and recklessness. One might think we should not condemn the astrologers who try to maintain order and certain causes even in these extraordinary matters, so that nothing in nature happens recklessly or without a legitimate cause. If any such cause must be considered, that one seems most likely to be chosen which the astrologers accept—namely the heavens—since no other power below the heavens is judged capable of governing all the things that happen here. Nor do they say any power above the heavens does so, since many things seem to happen unworthily, beyond merit and reason; these events would seem to argue for the necessity of a physical cause rather than the <term>providence</term><margin>through providence</margin> of an intelligent chooser.

Therefore, so that we may remove these doubts, it will be useful to discuss these matters more extensively. Now that we have shown that these things cannot be governed by the heavens, let us now reveal from where and how they are governed. We say that "fortuitous" things are those which happen beyond the intention of the agent. For this reason, fortune is spoken of only in human affairs, as they are the only things done with counsel and reason. Take the example we used earlier: a farmer set out to dig the earth, thinking of cultivating the soil, not of finding treasure. It happens that he finds treasure; we say it was done by chance, nor do we give any other cause for the found treasure than "fortune." By "fortune," however, we do not mean a divinity, or nature, or any specific thing that is a cause of such an event; rather, we exclude these, saying it happened only by fortune, as if we were to say "it happened so by chance and not from some specific cause." For the digging of the earth cannot be called the cause of finding the treasure; the earth, insofar as it is a place, is not the cause, but it happens that the same place is simultaneously both soil for farming and a hiding place for treasure.

Therefore, if you ask by what cause it happened that he dug up that treasure, there is none to bring forward, since not one cause, but a fortuitous meeting of many causes brought this about. Therefore, those who denied that fortune exists in things were in error, an opinion which Aristotle shatters in the second book of the *Physics* <note>original: "phisicæ auscultationis"</note> and the sixth book of the *First Philosophy* <note>original: "primæ philosophiæ"; this refers to Aristotle's *Metaphysics*.</note>. They were in error, however, not because they thought that what is unforeseen and fortuitous to us could be known and foreseen by higher minds—for which reason nothing is "fortune" in an absolute and simple sense—but because they thought events of this kind necessarily have a proximate cause in themselves. They did not understand how that which is <term>one by accident</term><note>An "accidental" unity (per accidens) refers to two things occurring together by chance (like a man being both a musician and a soldier) without a single direct cause making them so.</note> does not require a single cause in itself. For example, there is no single cause for a man being both a musician and a warrior at once; otherwise, if they were together because of some cause, they would have a mutual order arising from that cause. But things which happen to one another recklessly, like being a warrior...

<summary>Pico explains that "fortune" refers to the accidental intersection of unrelated causes, particularly in human affairs. He argues that while events may seem random to us, they are not caused by the stars, as natural causes cannot coordinate the complex coincidences that define chance.</summary>

...for a warrior to be a musician, or for a musician to be a warrior, it is clear that these roles have an order between them; however, this pairing has no active cause in itself, but happens only by accident. In this way, the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> rightly defend the existence of <term>chance</term> and <term>fortune</term> in things, thereby excluding absolute necessity. But some among them err more detestably than those who do away with chance entirely; namely, those who deny that these things happen in any way other than by fluke—that is, with no plan from a higher cause and no <term>providence</term>. For this most foul error sprouts from the root of impiety, by which it is believed either that human affairs are not known by the powers above, or if they are known, they are not cared for. This error will be refuted with logic elsewhere, in the dispute against the impious philosophers. For now, let it be rejected as a judged falsehood upon the authority of all <term>theologians</term>, the entire family of philosophers, and <term>Aristotle</term>, the prince of the Peripatetics, in his <term>Moral Books</term> <note>Referring to the *Nicomachean Ethics*.</note>. Both where he discussed happiness and where he discussed good fortune, he most clearly asserted that men are a care to the Gods (especially the wise), and that all things, past and future, are known to God through his senses, and that we are directed by him in these matters. He also confirmed this in the book *On the Universe* <note>original: "de Mundo"; a treatise once attributed to Aristotle, though now considered by many to be by a later author.</note>, a book certainly worthy of Aristotle’s wisdom, which he concluded with that Platonic sentiment regarding divine justice as if with a crowning oracular statement. 

If, therefore, the Gods care for human affairs—for we speak in this way so as to include the <term>guardian angels</term> and the servant-order of intelligent causes who wait upon the counsel and providence of the true God—if, I say, this is true, no one will doubt that men, prompted by them, often do things that are unforeseen and unknown to the person, yet are arranged by those beings with the wisest foreknowledge. A very common example is that of servants sent to the same place by a Master so that they might meet, yet they are unaware of the Master's will; their meeting and collision is unexpected and fortuitous to the servants themselves, but was foreseen and pre-arranged by the Master. Likewise, a guardian angel, looking out for the benefit of a poor farmer, can invite him through hidden impulses to dig in that spot where the angel knows a treasure to be; thus, what was "fortune" to the poor man was "counsel" to the angel. 

Regarding this, <term>Aurelius Augustine</term> says in the fifth book of <term>The City of God</term>: "We do not say that the causes called fortuitous (from which fortune takes its name) are non-existent, but rather that they are hidden; and we attribute them either to the will of the true God or to that of any spirits whatsoever." He said "any spirits whatsoever" because this can be done by good angels as well as by evil ones, though the evil ones cannot do everything the good can, nor is their end the same. For the good, the goal is the common good of men, but for the evil, it is harm—though the divine goodness frustrates their malice, since God orders and reduces toward the good whatever they have perpetrated with an evil will. 

But more on these things elsewhere. <term>Proclus the Platonist</term> in his commentaries on the <term>Timaeus</term> <note>A famous dialogue by Plato concerning the nature of the physical world.</note>, using the same reasoning for which <term>Augustine</term> also defined fortune, called it a "daemonic power" <note>In the Platonic sense, "daemonic" refers to a mediating spiritual power, not necessarily an evil "demon."</note> that brings together causes that were otherwise separate from one another. This does not differ from the Peripatetic definition, which says that fortune exists in human choice as a cause effecting something by accident; the only difference is that the former looks at a more remote and hidden cause, while the latter...

<summary>Pico argues that what humans perceive as "chance" or "fortune" is actually the result of divine providence or the intervention of angels. He refutes the idea that the universe is governed by blind luck, citing Aristotle, Augustine, and Proclus to show that "accidents" are often part of a higher, intelligent plan.</summary>

<page-num>525</page-num>
<header>On Astrology, Book IV.</header>

...the other looked at what is nearest and most known. For <term>Proclus</term> <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on the hierarchy of spiritual beings.</note> said that the <term>Platonists</term> call "daemonic power" <note>In this context, "daemonic" refers to *daimons*—intermediary spirits or guardians—rather than evil demons.</note> those minds placed among men and superior intellects that are removed from the specific and immediate knowledge of our affairs. Let us illustrate with examples how these things happen, so that we may understand what the heavens do in these matters. 

Lucius was at home, and he had no reason to go out; however, the thought of leaving settled in his mind. As soon as he left the house, the house collapsed. You would call him fortunate for having escaped imminent danger in such a way. If you ask a wicked—and indeed a poor—philosopher the cause of this, he will respond that it happened by chance, and that no other cause should be sought. If you ask an Astrologer, he refers this to some beneficial radiation from a "fortunate" Planet, by whose help Lucius was defended from the ruin. 

However, the Astrologer is mistaken for the reason explained above: because inciting Lucius to go out so he would not perish in the collapse is a matter of an intelligent agent acting with plan and reason. No radiation from Jupiter or any other star could be so great from the sky that Lucius’s mind would be more inclined to leave than to stay still—unless this also could have come from the very habit of the body (from which some men are more sedentary and others are walkers). If any constellation were the cause of this good outcome, it would be from those stars that make us vigorous and more active, which they call "Martian" <note>Influenced by the planet Mars, associated with action and movement.</note>, rather than some beneficial and defensive power against evils, as we often point out. 

For it is necessary to arrange these things in turn: a planetary ray cannot [specifically intend] an exit and protection from a collapse. Just as it is accidental to Lucius—who chose to go out for the sake of walking—that by leaving he escapes the danger of death, so too it is entirely accidental to a constellation (if we even believe one acts thus) that by helping him to move, it happens to free him from the ruin. Thus, an astrologer, even if he knows what the heavens are influencing at that time, knows nothing more than that Lucius will be eager for movement and walking. But neither the <term>horoscope</term> <note>original: "thema"; the arrangement of the stars at a specific moment.</note> nor any logic agrees that he could foresee that Lucius would escape both the house and the danger simultaneously. 

Therefore, only one cause remains for which this could be a matter of foresight and not chance: namely, a divine power nudging Lucius's mind from within and instigating him to leave, so that he would not perish under the house that was about to fall. This same divinity understands both that the house will fall and can coordinate Lucius's exit to that end. None of this can be said of a physical planetary ray. For this reason, no philosopher has ever defined "fortune" as the decree of a celestial constitution, or a product of a birth-chart, or any such thing drawn from the dogma of astrologers. Instead, they referred either to chance itself and the unexpected clashing of causes, or to intellectual causes that reconcile things by their own counsel, which escape the limits of our own providence. 

Thus, that great leader of philosophers, <term>Aristotle</term>, while discussing at great length what is good fortune, what is bad, and what it means to be fortunate or unfortunate, does not even mention celestial constellations in his judgment, nor even in his inquiry or debate. He did not think this opinion of the <term>Genethliacs</term> <note>Astrologers who cast birth charts to predict a person's fate.</note> was even worthy of a philosopher's doubt, but regarded it rather like the other ravings of charlatans...

He asserts that stars might influence a general desire to move, but they lack the intelligent foresight to coordinate a specific rescue, a view he claims aligns with Aristotle.</summary>

<page-num>526</page-num>
<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

...it should be numbered among fables and illusions rather than among the controversies of philosophy. Therefore, Aristotle himself, in that treatise <note>Pico refers to Aristotle’s discussion of "Good Fortune" (*Eutychia*), likely in the *Eudemian Ethics* or the *Magna Moralia*.</note> after a diligent examination of the whole question, defines it thus: When something happens well for us by chance, it usually occurs in two ways: either by us falling entirely without foresight into that which produces a good outcome, or—even if not by deliberate plan and reflection—by being led toward it by an impulse of the mind. We are so ignorant of the reason for this impulse that we descend as if by a swift oar <note>original: "remo ueloci," a metaphor for moving quickly with a current or driving force.</note> toward wherever it most persistently carries itself. 

The first case, he thinks, should be attributed to chance. The second he attributes to <term>divine motion</term> <note>The idea that God can directly influence the human will or "nudge" the soul.</note> by which the will itself is inclined by hidden impulses. Those who have experienced this are accustomed to saying: "The mind has a premonition of I know not what," or "I cannot wish otherwise," or "I am being swept here," or "The mind does not agree with other thoughts." And so, although they can give no account of their own plan, they nevertheless assert that it was their pleasure, or that their mind was so stubbornly predisposed. In this passage, the philosopher Aristotle affirms both that all things are known to God (as we said above) and that nothing is more sublime than God, by whom our will can be moved—which he asserts is a great argument for immortality. 

From all of this, it can be gathered that some human affairs happen by chance, some by nature, some by choice, and some by divine counsel. For although nothing happens outside of God’s counsel, we categorize things so that we say those things happen "divinely" which human minds, if left to themselves, would not achieve, but which they do achieve when moved by a specific impulse of the <term>divinity</term> <note>original: "numinis," referring to divine power or a presiding spirit.</note>. This is distinct from that general assistance of the Supreme Power which supports everyone, and without which nothing—not even the smallest thing—can exist or happen. Thus, although it is characteristic of a human to act by choice, he is nevertheless sometimes ruled by nature; when he is enslaved to the movements of bodily passions, he does not wait for the judgment of reason.

This is explained by a single example. A king declares war on his neighbors. Perhaps the cause lies in the king’s nature, which is warlike, greedy, and restless. Perhaps he is led not so much by passion as by reason, or by the right of reclaiming what is his, or of repaying an injury, or for other reasons. Beyond all these, a special counsel of God can intervene—always just, always rational—even if its justice or reason is not always open to everyone. It is the counsel of God, I say, both of the one stirred up to take up war, and of the one so liberated for victory. This is the way the prophet <term>Jeremiah</term> speaks:

> Behold, I will send and take all the families of the north, and Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and will bring them against this land, and against its inhabitants, and against all the nations that are round about it. <note>Jeremiah 25:9</note>

And in <term>Isaiah</term>:

> Woe to Assyria, the rod of my anger and the staff in whose hand is my indignation! I will send him against a deceitful nation, and against the people of my wrath I will command him, to take the spoil, and to seize the prey, and to tread them down like the mire of the streets. But he himself will not think so, and his heart will not imagine it. <note>Isaiah 10:5-7</note>

# THAT WE SHOULD NOT REFER TO THE HEAVENS IF ANYTHING IS DONE BY
## us that seems to exceed our powers, but rather either to the angels
## or to God. And therein many things regarding how divine 
## providence certainly does not take away
### our freedom. Chapter IV.

WHEN, however, something is done by a man that seems to exceed his powers, our mortal nature is usually shaken by unusual and admirable events. Overcome by the magnitude of the matter, we suspect the force of a more powerful cause acting within the man, and through the man, which exceeds the human capacity of faculty. And indeed, by this suspicion, those who have only eyes of flesh <note>original: "carneos tantum oculos," meaning those who only perceive the physical world.</note> are carried away to the heavens, than which they themselves see nothing greater nor feel anything more powerful. They are so poorly in control of their minds that they refer this to a mindless cause <note>Pico argues the stars are "mindless" or "irrational bodies" compared to the human soul.</note> and one devoid of cognition—a cause they do not even believe is sufficient for the total counsel of the human mind. 

But if they respond that those things are indeed disposed and ordained by God, but fulfilled by God through the heavens and stars (whose virtue and efficacy are so great), they are proven to speak quite absurdly. If these intermediate causes between God and us are lower than God, they ought to be higher than men. It is not fitting for things that are carried out through reason and counsel—such as our own affairs—to be disposed by the First Author through irrational bodies. Instead, just as He rules and moderates the elementary mass (which is inferior) through the celestial body (which is superior), so it is fitting for human affairs to be governed not by the mystery of bodies, but of <term>angels</term> <note>In the celestial hierarchy, angels are spiritual beings with intellect, making them "higher" than the physical stars.</note>, who by nature and dignity mediate between us and God. Therefore, when you descend from God to the earth, descend through the heavens; but when you descend from God to men, descend through the angels. 

Thus we read in the prophets of the angels of the Persians, Greeks, and Hebrews providing for their own peoples; and in Plato and all the Platonists, we find mention of "local gods" set over cities, kingdoms, and men. Aristotle also made mention of these, and the elder Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville, an influential early medieval scholar.</note>, and after Isidore, Clement of Alexandria in his *Miscellanies* <note>original: "Stromatis," referring to the *Stromata*.</note>. Nor should it disturb us that certain things sometimes seem to us to be done unworthily and unjustly, so that we might more willingly recur to a cause acting by natural necessity rather than by counsel. For it would certainly be ridiculous if the lowlier slaves of a city presumed to judge the counsels of the prince; how much more is our rashness either ridiculous or rather sacrilegious, when it claims for itself the judgment of the first order and of divine wisdom! This wisdom extends the eye of providence and the ray of its goodness not to the utility of one man, one family, or one city, but of the whole world—not for the present age, but for all ages alike. 

Do we—little men, or rather little owls, moles, truly donkeys, truly oxen, and indeed judging while lying on our backs—call God back to an examination? We, who more often judge not with what little judgment we have, but rather with a disease of the soul, complain that whatever happens is "unjustly done" simply because we did not want it to happen. And who would not have insistently cried out that God was dozing when the righteous Joseph was sold by his brothers? Who would not even have said there is no God, when that same man was given prison as a reward for his <insert>chastity</insert>? <note>Referring to the biblical story of Joseph, who was imprisoned after refusing the advances of Potiphar's wife.</note>

<summary>Pico argues that superhuman human actions should be attributed to God or Angels rather than the stars, as rational human affairs must be governed by rational spiritual beings. He also defends Divine Providence against those who blame "fate" or "stars" for perceived earthly injustices.</summary>

<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

...was it not for his **chastity** that he received his reward? See him shortly afterward in Egypt as king, or second only to the king. See him redeeming his father and his entire family from famine. See him noble in his gift of prophecy; you cannot deny that those earlier events were orchestrated by God, through which he eventually arrived at these honors in their proper order. 

But if you look even higher, you will understand how that matter was led from such a wicked sale <note>referring to Joseph being sold into slavery by his brothers</note> to the point where the entire people descended into Egypt. After being worn down there for a long time by the Egyptian kings, they were gloriously claimed for liberty by Moses. This power of God was confirmed by so many portents and manifested by so many oracles—in Pharaoh, in Egypt, and among the Hebrew people—through the Law and through so many miracles of divine majesty. Sometimes this was shown through beneficence, other times through justice, all of which prefigured those ineffable mysteries of the divine incarnation that were to come under **Jesus**.

Truly, even a madman could not be brought to suspect that anything in human affairs happens without reason. Therefore, you should not believe that the world is governed by an evil demon (as the **Manichaeans** do), or by the necessity of celestial revolutions (as the **astrologers** do), or by random chance and rashness (as a few bad philosophers do). Instead, believe it is governed by God, the best and wisest. 

Whenever you hear of wars being stirred up, slaughters, the devastation of cities, and the overthrow of kingdoms, do not imagine the cause to be the "mixing of two rays" <note>An astrological term referring to the alignment or "aspect" of planets</note> or the Moon positioning itself in its natural course between the Sun and the Earth, as these charlatans do. Rather, consider it the **counsel of God**, either punishing the wicked or testing the good. 

This is why one was called the "Scourge of God" <note>Attila the Hun (d. 453 AD), known as *Flagellum Dei*</note>, and another, very close to our own age <note>Likely referring to Tamerlane (d. 1405), who was also called the Scourge of God in the 15th century</note>, said of himself that he was not a man, but the "wrath of God and the desolation of the world." 

The wise Persian in the writings of **Herodotus** spoke rightly. While reclining at a banquet in Thebes, he revealed the future slaughter of his own race, which he had foreknown by some premonition. When the Theban urged him to report this to the commander of the army and discourage him from an undertaking that would have such an unhappy end, he replied that what God has ordained to happen is inevitable for man. Therefore, his words would not be believed—even if he warned the commander—since God had so decreed it. Consequently, he and **Mardonius** <note>The Persian general at the Battle of Plataea, 479 BC</note> followed because they were bound by necessity. 

It is pleasing that he spoke of a necessity not of the stars, but of **divine counsel**. If anyone calls this "Fate," **Augustine** says they think more correctly than they speak <note>Augustine argued in *The City of God* that if "Fate" means the Will of God, the concept is acceptable, though the word is dangerous due to its pagan associations</note>. 

However, as can be gathered from the monuments of the ancients, this name of "**Fate**" <term>Fatum: a Latin term for destiny, literally "that which has been spoken"</term> is accepted in a fourfold sense:
1. Fate as **Nature** itself.
2. Fate as a **series and order of causes** producing all things by a necessary connection.
3. Fate as the **constitution of the stars** at the moment someone is born, conceived, or begins a task.
4. Fate as the certain and inevitable execution of **divine counsel**.

The first definition is accepted by **Alexander of Aphrodisias** <note>A famous commentator on Aristotle (c. 200 AD)</note> in his book *On Fate* dedicated to the emperors Severus and Antoninus. He grants that "fates" exist in the sense that Fate is nature itself; this principle is distinct from free choice. Thus, by "fate," fire heats, water is wet, and the Sun illuminates. Furthermore, when someone dies because the balance of their body has failed, they die by fate. But if they are thrown from a horse or killed by swords, they do not die by fate. It is in this manner that **Virgil** writes of **Dido**:

<note>original: "Sed misera ante diem..." — "But the unhappy woman died before her day." Virgil implies Dido's suicide was not her "fated" natural end.</note>

<summary>Pico argues that historical upheavals and personal fortunes (like Joseph's) are governed by Divine Providence rather than astrological necessity or chance. He clarifies the definition of "Fate," distinguishing between natural necessity and the supreme counsel of God.</summary>

<page-num>529</page-num>
<header>On Astrology, Book IV.</header>

...speaking of one preparing death for herself by force. "But because she perished neither by fate nor by a death she had earned." <note>Pico is quoting Virgil’s Aeneid (Book 4), describing the suicide of Dido. The poet suggests her death was "extra-fatal"—not what was meant to happen.</note> <term>Astrologers</term>, however, would have most certainly attributed that kind of death to fate. Thus says <term>Demosthenes</term>. And indeed, in this sense, no one would deny that <term>fate</term> <note>original: fatum</note> exists, just as no one denies nature. 

In this way, <term>Aristotle</term> also spoke in the fifth book of his *Physical Lectures* <note>original: physicæ auscultationis; the standard title for Aristotle’s Physics</note> of "fatal generations"—that is, those things which come to be according to nature. Nor is there any doubt that when we understand fate in this manner, we recognize that many things happen *outside* of fate, just as many things happen *outside* of nature, whether by chance, or by our own choice, or (as <term>Alexander of Aphrodisias</term> <note>A famous 2nd-century commentator on Aristotle who defended human free will against Stoic determinism.</note> says in that same passage) by the Counsel of the Gods. 

But those who introduced the second opinion believed that nothing happens in nature that is not necessary, provided one could grasp all the causes at once. For those who say many things happen outside of necessity defend their view in two areas: in natural things and in matters of choice. In natural things, they argue that not everything that happens naturally happens by necessity, since the work of nature can be hindered. In matters of choice, they argue that our selection and judgment are free. 

The opponents press back: they say that in natural things, if something is hindered, it is hindered by necessity, because that very hindrance comes from a natural cause, which must eventually be traced back to the supreme nature—the heavens. They claim the heavens act by necessity. But they are mistaken; for even if a natural cause acted as a hindrance, it was still a cause that itself could have either not existed or been hindered while it was acting. Therefore, that hindrance was <term>contingent</term> <note>In philosophy, "contingent" means something that happens but could have happened otherwise; the opposite of "necessary."</note> and not necessary. 

And if you press us further regarding that hindrance—claiming it must have a natural cause which will itself be hindered either naturally or necessarily—I respond: if you believe the world is eternal, you will progress infinitely from one contingent cause to another contingent cause. Between these, the order is always accidental, and you will never reach a single, first, "necessary" cause from which necessity is forced upon all following things. No such cause exists among natural things, not even the heavens, whose works are easily obstructed by the meeting of lower causes and matter. 

If, however, you agree with the theological truth regarding the **creation of the world**, you will arrive (through that tireless backtracking) at the first contingent institution of things. From this, necessity is removed, not confirmed. Regarding our choices, they introduce necessity even more irrationally, claiming the will chooses nothing that has not been prejudiced by reason, and that it is not in our power to will or judge in such a way. But they rely on false assumptions, as has been shown by others elsewhere and will be shown by us. 

For these matters require their own separate treatments and do not greatly pertain to the refutation of the astrologers. It is their **third definition of fate** that must be refuted throughout this whole work. This differs from the first opinion because it makes the celestial nature itself the origin not only of natural things, but also of <term>fortuitous</term> <note>accidental or chance events</note> things, as we have seen. This view thinks poorly of lower causes, but worst of all regarding the heavenly ones. For although the heavens are a part of nature, those "constellations" they invent from the positions of stars—using places, signs, houses, and other such things—are not natural causes at all. They are **fictitious**. The operation of the heavens does not depend on a single initial moment <note>referring to the moment of birth or a "horoscope"</note>, nor are they responsible for things that properly belong to lower causes.

as we have already declared, and as what follows will declare even more. There remains a fourth theological meaning of <term>fate</term> <note>original: fatum</note>, just as that first one was more physical, but both are true. This fourth meaning denotes the series and order of causes hanging from Divine Counsel. Under this order, our freedom is in no danger, since we ourselves are also among these causes. In this <term>dance of fate</term> <note>original: chorea fati; a vivid metaphor suggesting humans are active participants in the cosmic order, not just passive observers</note>, we do not merely suffer [passively], but we act. Therefore, whether you consider God's foreknowledge or His providence—that is, whether you consider His mind foreknowing all things, or His will disposing all things according to His pleasure—there is no prejudice against our free actions.

For if we consider foreknowledge, why do I not do freely what God foresaw I would do? For if that which He foresaw will come to pass, surely I will do freely what He foresaw I would do freely. And because it will be what He willed—and He willed me to be free—I shall act freely in whatever I do, unless He Himself takes my freedom from me. And certainly God not only foreknew our wills, but also preordained them. When <term>Gregory of Nyssa</term> <note>A 4th-century bishop and theologian known for his works on the soul and resurrection.</note> and <term>Damascene</term> <note>St. John of Damascus, an 8th-century monk and theologian who wrote extensively on the "Orthodox Faith."</note> seemed to deny this, they did so only to offer a warning: that while other things are disposed purely through the Divine will, our choices are disposed through that Divine will along with our own will. 

Yet this is so even though not only the outcomes of our thoughts, but even the thoughts themselves, the counsels, and the purposes—not only of kings, as it is written, but the hearts of all—are in the hand of God, who alone moderates all things. He inclines the will wherever He pleases in matters that pertain neither to vice nor to virtue, if the fulfillment of one of His decrees requires it. At times, He starts virtues in us, working with us to perfect what has been started; at other times, He turns those who have moved from virtue to vice back to the path of justice. He may apply the teacher’s rod out of mercy, or crush [the wicked] as if they were in a daze for the sake of justice. He always makes all things either good, or certainly opportunities for good.

Let us have said this much about fate, providence, and the government of human affairs. These things are useful to know in themselves and necessary for tearing down the <term>vanity of astrology</term>. When we see something happen that appears too great or too orderly to be attributed to mere chance or human effort, we should understand it not as the force of physical rays <note>Referring to the "influence" of light and energy that astrologers believed radiated from the stars to control earthly events.</note>, but as the care and power of Divine Counsel and angelic ministry combined with human freedom. 

It is clear from what we have said how future events can be both foreseen and—if they are bad—avoided by us. For if human affairs happened only by chance, no foreknowledge of the future could exist. But since they happen by human and Divine counsel, human reason can conjecture somewhat about them, but only those inspired by the Divine Spirit can foresee them with absolute certainty. This is confirmed by the predictions and oracles of the Prophets; and wise men are close to the prophets, though at a very great distance. As <term>Euripides</term> said: *The one who guesses well, let him be the best prophet.* <note>original: "Qui bene coniectauerit is uates optimus eſto." This is a Latin translation of a famous fragment from the Greek playwright Euripides.</note> 

Thus, in ensuring the happy success of things and avoiding misfortunes, the most important thing is to make God favorable to oneself through purity of soul, pious works, and most holy vows. After this, man himself should look out for himself with his own prudence, for

Although fortune is powerful in many matters, and indeed the disposition of the divine will is the most powerful or rather everything in all things, it is nonetheless necessary that the right way of living itself carries great weight in these affairs, unless we are to say that this gift was bestowed upon us by God in vain. Therefore, he spoke rightly who said: *No divine power is absent if there is prudence, but it is we who make Fortune a goddess and place her in heaven.* <note>original: "nullum abesse numen si sit prudentia, sed nos facere fortunam Deam cœloq́; locare." This is a famous quote from the Roman satirist Juvenal, suggesting that human wisdom, not luck, governs our lives.</note> Because of this, Plato, in his letter to the Syracusans, recalled that saying of Homer: *The gods took away his mind,* <note>original: "Dij mentem abstulerunt." A reference to the Iliad, where the gods are blamed for human folly.</note> because men themselves had rather cast away the mind that was given to them; this is confirmed by the sentence of Euripides, who said that *Fortune is the daughter of a brave soul.* <note>original: "fortem animæ filiam esse dixit." Pico likely refers to a fragment where Euripides links success to courage rather than stars.</note> Therefore, by arranging our life prudently through natural reason, and then by preparing divine benevolence for ourselves through pious religion, let us avoid all superstitious vanity. Otherwise, anyone who hopes to either foresee the future or avoid evils through astrological observations will hear Isaiah saying to him: *Evil shall come upon you, and you will not know its origin; and calamity shall fall upon you, which you will not be able to expiate.* <note>Isaiah 47:11. Pico uses scripture to warn that astrology provides no protection against divine judgment.</note>

### CHAPTER V. NEITHER THE PAST NOR MATTERS PERTAINING TO OTHERS CAN BE FORESEEN FROM ANY CONSTELLATION.

**B**ut if they should happen to have some answer regarding chance events—though they can have nothing true or even plausible—what, I ask, will they answer about those things that precede the hour of birth? That is, in what way will they think that an efficient cause can be later than its own effects? What likewise of those things that are not only prior, but also foreign to the individual? These things possess their causes elsewhere, and not in the constellation of this specific birth—such as when they pronounce judgments on the natures and fortunes of parents, ancestors, and older brothers based on the hour in which a son is born. For these things are both prior to that constellation and foreign to it, as they have the order and dependence of their own fate from their own long-past constellations (if indeed we were to think that there is any fate from the heavens). Likewise, in the one who is being born, how does the birth constellation cause that which he received many days before his birthday? For they predict from the birth chart whether the one being born is male or female, maimed or whole, beautiful or deformed, and other such physical conditions, regarding all of which the die was cast <note>original: "iacta alea erat." A reference to Caesar's "the die is cast," meaning the outcome was already determined.</note> before the infant was committed from the mother’s "purse," as <term>Lucilius</term> <note>Gaius Lucilius, a Roman satirist. He uses the word "bulga" (purse/bag) as a slang or metaphorical term for the womb.</note> says. By what logic do astrologers claim the prediction of all these things for themselves? Neither is a cause later than its effect, nor can things be foreseen from the sky in any other way than the way an effect is known in advance from its cause. <term>Haly Auenrodam</term> <note>Also known as Ali ibn Ridwan, an 11th-century Arabic physician and astrologer who wrote famous commentaries on Ptolemy.</note>, in his commentary on the astrological books of <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note>, wishing as it were to solve this question of ours, tried to show how the fates of parents could be foreseen from the birth of a brother or from the births of children. He says that a woman does not conceive every time she joins with a man, but only when that hour occurs whose constellation matches the constellation of the parents; and since things that agree with another thing must also agree with each other, if they agree...

[If] the horoscopes <term>geniturae|An individual's birth chart or the specific configuration of the stars at the moment of birth.</term> of all the children align with the constellations of their parents, then they will also be in harmony with one another. Therefore, they will mutually signify each other’s fates; thus, the nature and fortune of the parents are shown from the horoscope of the brothers, or from the horoscope of the son. 

Truly, in this astrological "subtlety," I do not know what I should refute first or what I should mock. A woman does not conceive, they say, unless the position of the stars at that hour matches the stars of the parents. If that is so, then the parents' deeds ought to be foreseen not from the hour the boy is born, but from the hour he is conceived. But since the father was born under one sky and the mother under another, how can a single constellation correspond to such diverse constellations? Or, if they think this can happen through some diversity of the stars, how will the charts <term>themata|Astrological birth charts or horoscopes.</term> of so many children correspond to the charts of the father and mother at the same time? 

Since the significance of the parents in all cases must be sought from the same stars and the same regions of the sky. The lot of the father and mother is investigated by them from the fourth and tenth places of the sky, and likewise from the Sun, Saturn, Venus, and the Moon. The arrangement of these in the charts of births is almost always varied and manifold, according to the variety of the children. Do you think all that variety can avoid differing from the constellations of the parents? It is as if something could agree with another thing when it first disagrees with itself—or as if it were not the case that the same father must necessarily be both fortunate and unfortunate, simply because one of his sons has the "fourth place" illuminated by happy rays, while the other has it besieged by unhappy ones. 

To avoid this, the common crowd of astrologers is accustomed to say that the fates of parents are foreseen not from the horoscopes of all the children, but only from the firstborn. But that refuge is immediately taken away from them by the horoscopes of the brothers, which they used to show were in agreement with each other precisely because all of them harmonized equally with the constellations of the parents. 

But why is it necessary to laboriously refute a thing so evidently frivolous? For by what reasoning is it defended? They say a woman does not conceive unless the child being conceived is then destined to be born at an hour whose constellation will be of such a kind that it can signify the lot and nature of the parents to the astrologer. It is as if the heavens and all of nature serve them! <note>original: "scilicet illis cœlum & tota natura deseruit." Pico is being sarcastic here, suggesting astrologers arrogantly believe the entire universe rearranges its physical laws just so they can make a prediction.</note> As if nothing can happen in the universe unless it happens in a way that allows an astrologer to divine it. 

Furthermore, how do they solve the point where the whole force of our argument lies: that something which happened long ago to the parents cannot be caused by the hour in which an infant is born? For we will later refute the opinion of those who said that things are not caused by this, but are only signified by the stars. For now, we are disputing against those who believe that heaven is the cause of those things which are predicted from the sky—which

# FUTURE EVENTS LONG AFTER THE PRESENT
# constellation cannot be produced. Chapter VI.

[Woodcut initial Q] What about the fact that not only past events, but if we consider it rightly, not even those things which are far in the future can be produced by the current constellation? Yet, this is a very common and familiar claim in the predictions of astrologers. For where does one not read among them that a planet in the east <term>orientalem|A planet rising before the sun or located in the eastern hemisphere of the chart, associated by astrologers with the first period of life.</term> provides what it promises in the first part of life, while one in the west <term>occidentalem|A planet setting after the sun or in the western hemisphere, associated with the later years of life.</term> does so in the last part? They claim that whichever planet occupies the horoscope <term>horoscopum|In this period, 'horoscope' specifically refers to the Ascendant—the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth.</term>, or is the ruler of the horoscope, quickly gives what it has to offer. Shortly thereafter follows the planet which possesses the rights of the tenth place <term>decimi loci|The 'Medium Coeli' or Midheaven, the highest point of the chart, usually associated with career and public life.</term>; then, he who is either present in or presides over the west gives his gifts late; and latest of all is the planet located in the lowest heaven <term>imo cœlo|The 'Imum Coeli,' the lowest point of the chart (the fourth house), associated with the end of life and hidden things.</term>. There are countless other claims of this kind. 

Ultimately, these claims testify that what the constellations are going to do is not done when they are actually constellations <note>Pico means the effect happens long after the physical alignment of stars has dissolved.</note>, but rather many years after they have ceased to be. Truly, an example of this marvel appears in no other power or natural action (and they admit celestial influence is natural); it suggests that a power is thought to be more effective when it does not exist than when it does. Furthermore, celestial influence <term>influxus|The 'flowing in' of power from the stars into the physical world, a central concept in medieval and Renaissance science.</term> does not remain in the body like a medicine. 

But perhaps they will respond that even if that position of the stars has passed, the power infused into us from it nevertheless endures, which will eventually bring its effects to light in its own time, according to the nature of the acting agent and the suitability of the matter. 

To this, regarding the nature of the "agent" <note>In Aristotelian terms, the 'agent' is the cause that produces a change (the stars), while the 'matter' is the subject being changed (the human).</note>, I object as I did before: the nature and condition of an effect do indeed vary according to the condition of the agents and their various powers. But it is equally common to all causes that they perform what they are going to do more effectively when they *are*, rather than when they have already ceased to be for a long time. 

Regarding the "matter," if they say a newborn does not immediately become a king or a philosopher even if the sky promises it—because his age is an obstacle—that might seem not to be absurd. But when his age *is* capable of those gifts which the birth-stars promised, why does the event still not happen, since the sufficient cause has already preceded it and the material is now ready and suitable? 

Instead, they say the effect is delayed for as many years as the planet was distant from such-and-such a place by "parts of the signs" <term>signorum partibus|Degrees of the zodiac. Astrologers used a system where one degree of planetary movement equaled one year of life.</term>. They claim a planet cannot provide its benefits except late because it held such a place in the birth chart. This belongs to a rational nature—one that dispenses its gifts at whatever time it wishes by its own choice and will. It is not, nor can it be, the mark of a natural cause. 

Furthermore, if the sky indeed gave what it promised immediately, but the "disposition of the matter" <note>The physical state or readiness of the person.</note> causes the delay, then it will not be the business of the astrologer (who looks at the sky) to foreknow the timing of events. Rather, it would be the business of one who understands the state and condition of the matter. Thus, he would hear from the astrologer *what* is going to happen, but he himself would show the astrologer *when* it is going to happen. 

As for their response that the force derived from the sky is preserved after the constellation passes, I should like to know from them: where is it preserved? Certainly either in the matter, or in lower and secondary causes. Whichever of these they prefer, let them know that in the flux and reflux of changing matter, and in such a varied and shifting...
