### ON THE TAKING OF AUSPICES WHICH THEY CALL ELECTIONS,
### how vain and impossible the opinion of the astrologers is. Chapter VII.

**I** am also inclined to inquire of them about that part of astrology which is thought to be most useful in life, which concerns the taking of auspices—commonly called **elections** <term>electiones|The astrological practice of 'electing' or choosing the most favorable moment to begin an undertaking, such as a journey, a marriage, or a war.</term>—that is, in what way they understand it to happen through the heavens, that what we undertake to do at this particular hour is done successfully, while what is done at another hour is done unsuccessfully by us. For while all these things are easily said and have a surface appearance of probability, yet when they are examined more diligently, they are found to be vain and impossible. If someone (they say) sets out on a journey under such a heavenly constellation, he will have a comfortable travel, be kindly received by the king, and increase his family property. On the contrary, if at another hour he mounts his horse or boards a ship, he will experience difficult paths and a dangerous voyage, and in the end will not achieve the purpose for which he undertook the journey or voyage. I confess I do not see how all these things are caused by the heavens; let them teach me if they can. Suppose Jupiter should cast his rays upon the earth from the ninth region of heaven <note>The ninth 'house' of an astrological chart was traditionally associated with long-distance travel and religion.</note>; they would call it a lucky constellation for setting out on a journey. I ask them: does that fortunate outflow and breath <term>afflatuſque|A 'breath' or spiritual influence flowing from the stars to the earth.</term> affect the people themselves who are about to seize the journey, or rather the very action of the people traveling? That is, does it affect the mounting of the horse, the exit from the house, or some such thing that is a necessary beginning of a journey? 

If they answer the first—that the people are affected—then those people would be inspired by the benefit of the star even if they do not then first take the journey, as often as the intention of seizing the journey was proposed to them, especially since according to their opinion, the constellation does not provide what it promises most when it is present, but often after a long interval of time. If they answer the second—that the action itself is affected—they will certainly be forced to rave many things to protect their position, while they explain to us in what way that "Jovian" mounting of the horse both spreads a soft path under the feet, drives robbers from the road, and makes the sky peaceful with diffused light once the clouds are driven away. And they will have no small trouble in maintaining that "outflow" while a journey of perhaps many days is being completed, since there must be no small suspicion that the power does not descend from heaven upon that man mounting his horse in such a reciprocal way that when he gets down from it, that power ascends back into heaven, and the traveler always needs a new "Jupiter" whenever he must leap onto his horse. For to dream of some primordial force consisting nowhere, rooted in nothing, which completes the whole journey softly and happily for you, belongs to men raving even in their sleep, who, considering nothing of what they speak, produce a futile sound without a mind. Let us see again whether they fall into the same difficulties in those things which are our works <term>opera|Physical objects or completed projects, such as a building or a city.</term> rather than our operations <term>operationes|The active process or the performance of an action.</term>. It is the opinion of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential ancient authority on astronomy and astrology.</note> that if Mars occupies the middle of heaven at the founding of a city, the princes of that state will mostly perish by the sword. Where, pray tell, is that bloody radiation of Mars received, which is destined to kill so many princes in succession by the sword over the course of time? If [the astrologer] wishes it to be received in the prince who is then building the city, I shall ask in what way those stones, cast and buried in the earth at the prince's command—the foundations of the city, of course—might bend and derive those celestial rays, which are turning elsewhere, toward that prince. In what way do they descend to his descendants and successors of the kingdom by a kind of hereditary right, this harmful power whose vessel has perished and whose origin has passed? Truly, I do not see what he could answer to us when we ask such things without blushing.

He will say, perhaps, that it is received not in the prince himself, the founder of the city, but rather in the city itself, in those very first stones upon which it is to be raised; as if by some pestilential breath of Mars, it will breathe upon all the princes of that city. A fine invention, surely, to be confirmed even by the testimony of Moses, who once showed us the expiation of a leprous house through prophetic inspiration <note>A reference to the laws in Leviticus 14 regarding "leprosy" (likely mold or plague) in the walls of a house, which required ritual cleansing or demolition. Pico is being sarcastic, comparing astrological "influence" to a house-plague.</note>. But I fear lest the earth piled on top and trampled upon the nearest stones would not prevent that martial sickness <note>original: "nephritim illam martiam," a medical metaphor likening the celestial influence to a disease or "stone" ailment.</note>; or if it should exhale at all, would it not rather invade the needy and the poor, who are more susceptible to pestilence, than the prince of the city himself? He who happens to live in some suburban villa will, I believe, not perish by the sword, especially if it is distant from the city by more miles than that Martian vapor—meanwhile suffocated on all sides by lime, rubble, and scrapings—could reach there whole and effective. 

But for philosophers, this will endanger the glory of **Plato**, the Academy, and **Aristotle**, who in their books on the Republic—where they perceived so many things concerning the founding and successful governing of a city and state—left us nothing written about such a useful and necessary caution. If we weigh all these things seriously and not as a joke, we shall see that Haly <term>Haly|Ali ibn Ridwan (c. 988–1061), an Egyptian physician and astrologer famous for his commentary on Ptolemy's Quadripartitum.</term>, the interpreter of Ptolemy, although a supreme astrologer, rightly judged this part of astrology concerning **elections** <term>elections|The practice of "electing" or choosing a favorable time to begin an endeavor based on the position of the stars.</term> to be frivolous and ineffective.

### THAT ASTROLOGERS SUBJECT OUR MIND TO THE HEAVENS,
### ALTHOUGH THEY ARE CLEVER AND TRY TO DISGUISE IT. Chapter VIII.

**H**itherto it has been demonstrated that nothing among physical and temporary things, over which the heavens are thought to have the greatest jurisdiction, depends upon the heavens in the way that astrologers imagine. For neither those things which are accidental, nor those which pertain to others, nor those which are either past or future after a long time—nor, indeed, the greatest part of those things which are begun under the observation of certain hours so that they may happen successfully—[depend on the stars]. If the heavens do not cause these things in such a way that they can be foreseen from the sky, how much less those things which are incorporeal? Concerning which, however, astrological superstition does not blush to pronounce. For in this category are contained the diversities of morals and character, and whatever works and properties of our soul; those which pertain to demons, to superior minds, to God, to the efficacy of prayers, to the secrets of conscience,

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

...to the state of the future life, and other things of this kind pertain, concerning all of which this arrogant and reckless race of men publishes a thousand dogmas of nonsense. Indeed, I would begin with character, which they think varies among men according to the variety of the birth constellation. But when they are pressed on this point, they are accustomed to hide what they truly feel; pouring out many words about the freedom of the will, they instruct us to be careful not to think our freedom is coerced by the stars, from which they claim we have only a certain propensity or invitation, which it is in our choice either to follow or decline. I will therefore first uncover the fraud of this defense, bringing forward many of their own dogmas from which it may be clear that they subject the mind itself to the heavens, even where it does not depend on the body. Afterwards, I shall declare that the diversity of morals and talents cannot be referred to celestial causes even in the way they describe. 

Therefore, if they think the differences of the human mind come from the state and position of the stars in no other way than this—that the body being affected in one way or another, the operation of the mind is also somewhat changed—how can they contend that from Mars being "happily" positioned in the ninth region of the sky <note>The "ninth region" refers to the Ninth House in an astrological chart, traditionally associated with religion, philosophy, and divinity.</note>, so much power can be granted to us that we may expel demons from possessed bodies by our presence alone? This is not merely an act of a soul inclining toward the body, but of a soul living in the body in such a way that, full of God and inhabiting the inner chambers of the mind, it does not feel itself to be living in the body at all. 

Likewise, how do they presume they can judge, based on the position of the Sun, concerning the secrets of the conscience of the one born toward gods and men? In those secrets, nothing is placed outside the hand of the mind and our own freedom—they are not even open to angelic knowledge <note>In medieval theology, it was a standard belief that only God can know the "secrets of the heart" or the inner conscience; even angels and demons could only guess based on external signs.</note>, nor are they subjected to any external power. Finally, if the companionship of the body is what links the soul to the heavens, how can they pronounce upon the soul's state when it is placed *outside* the body, based on a celestial constellation? 

For it is a common saying among them that there are two planets who are the authors of happiness: Venus and Jupiter, but with different duties: Venus bestows the happiness of the present life, and Jupiter that of the future. Maternus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer whose work *Mathesis* was a primary source for medieval and Renaissance astrology.</note>, after he recounted many of these things which are provided by Saturn when positioned in Leo, then adds this: "But when they have attained all these things, they shall die at a great age, and their soul shall pass to heaven, joined to the Gods. For Saturn placed in Leo recalls the souls of those who have been so situated on earth, freed from innumerable straits, to heaven and to the beginnings of their origin." Thus he writes. 

From this, I wish it to be understood not only how far this astrological superstition spreads itself—even to the point of being suspected of impiety—but also how little faith can be placed in the writers of this art. It is as if they had committed to writing only things tested and proven by experience, when we know without doubt that when they were writing, they had no experience of the future life. For if they perhaps learned these things from their dead followers, they might rather have understood what constellation sends one to the world below rather than the world above. For although they think that by praying at a certain hour they can obtain what they want from God, I would not easily believe—unless they changed their dogma—that they will obtain eternal happiness from Him, and...

...and they certainly believe what we have said. For that most fable-spinning **Albumasar** <note>Albumasar (Abu Ma'shar, 787–886 AD) was a highly influential Persian astrologer whose works were widely read in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> writes that whoever supplicates God when the **Moon is joined to Jupiter at the head of the dragon** <note>The "head of the dragon" refers to the ascending lunar node, a point where the moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic. It was considered an auspicious point in astrological calculations.</note> will obtain from God whatever he asks. And yet there will still be philosophers and theologians who are pleased by these things, and who think that they and the astrologers they follow still sufficiently understand what God is and what prayer is. Such insanity, in this place, is not so much to be refuted as to be cursed, since it has been sufficiently refuted by those things we have disputed elsewhere regarding prayer against the impious. But as for **Pietro d'Abano** <note>Pietro d'Abano (c. 1250–1316) was an Italian physician and astrologer who attempted to reconcile Greek and Arabic medicine with philosophy.</note>, whenever I read his writings, that saying of **Heraclitus** comes to mind: **"Much learning does not teach wisdom"** <note>original: "πόλιμα θεία γόου οὐ φερὲ," a corrupted transcription of the Greek "πολυμαθίη νόον οὐ διδάσκει."</note>. He himself, I say, writes that at that hour of which we were speaking, he sought knowledge from God and that after that day he progressed greatly in it. It is not my place to measure how much this "new Solomon" <note>A sarcastic reference to King Solomon, famous for his wisdom granted by God.</note> progressed in it; I certainly believe that whatever progress he made was no more than what can be accomplished by human effort. But however the matter stands, I would advise this Pietro to credit everything he achieved to his own industry and talent rather than to that supplication of his to Jupiter. But—lest he stubbornly defend that claim—good judgment must force them to deny that he progressed at all in good letters, rather than having them assent to such a vain superstition. I would likewise advise all astrologers in common that, since Jupiter is so favorable to them, they should acquire so much wealth and resources for themselves by a single supplication at a lucky hour that, no longer needing our money, they might finally stop tricking the minds of the unlearned with so many daily lies for the sake of **milking them for money** <note>original: "emungendae pecuniae," literally "wiping the nose of money," a Latin idiom for cheating someone out of their cash.</note>.

### HUMAN CHARACTER IS NOT FORMED BY THE HEAVENS. CHAPTER IX.

Let us see concerning character, whether it can be defended by right reason that the cause of these things also exists in some way in the sky. For perhaps if we think that the rational part of the mind does not suffer force from the heavens, nor that our freedom is coerced, there will be no reason why either philosophy or piety should deny that the various pursuits of men and the manifold properties of their talents proceed from different celestial influences—since even the habit of the body does this, while the dignity of the mind and the freedom of choice remain safe. But he who thinks so is far mistaken; for the idea that the sensual part itself and alone is so affected by the Sun that it has a propensity toward some disgrace is both contrary to reason and greatly adverse to piety. For whatever things happen from natural causes—especially those which keep the laws prescribed for them by the founder of nature immutably—must be referred both to the author of nature who so instituted them and to nature itself. Moreover, whatever virtue or property the stars are endowed with, by the consensus of both philosophers and theologians, God, the principle of nature, bestowed upon them. Even the foolish hardly deny that God is most good and most wise; but what kind of goodness or most powerful wisdom would this be: to bend a man—who, though free, is nevertheless weak—by the hand of the heavens toward that side to which he ought least to decline? And then to make the best servants <note>Pico refers to the stars as "servants" of God's natural order.</note> the authors and ministers of evil, so that...

## Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

Since the stars themselves never transgress the King’s commands, why are they the ones who most invite and drive others to transgression? Finally, what order of nature is this, what consensus, what wise institution? That what nature's own reason would not wish to happen is nonetheless diligently procured by those parts of nature that are great, powerful, excellent, and principal? Furthermore, one who sins does not truly *act*, but rather *fails* <note>original: "non facit qui peccat aliquid imò deficit." Pico relies on the Scholastic philosophical idea that sin is not a positive creation, but a "privation" or a failure of a good action.</note>; therefore, he who invites one to sin invites them to fail—which is not fitting for "superior efficient causes" <note>The stars and celestial bodies, seen as the primary drivers of physical change on Earth.</note> which always act, and never fail.

It is, therefore, a most absurd dogma of the astrologers to think that we have from one position of the stars an inclination toward theft, and from another toward incest, fraud, or homicide. All of nature, especially the higher parts joined closest to the Divine Mind, can perhaps favor the observation of natural and divine law, but can in no way oppose or hinder it. Let them, therefore, silence their profane mouths! Let them not say that **Venus** joined to **Mars** calls us to adultery, or that those same planets, when placed in masculine signs, incite us to "nefarious intercourse between males" <note>original: "masculorū nepharios concubitus." A standard Renaissance reference to sodomy or homosexual acts, then considered a grave sin.</note>. Nor should they say that **Mars**, when occupying the **ninth part of the sky** <term>the Ninth House</term> <note>In astrology, the 9th House governs religion and philosophy; Mars’ presence there was traditionally thought to cause atheism or impiety.</note>, makes people irreligious, or that other constellations entirely irritate us toward other crimes. Let them blame their crimes on themselves, not on the heavens, nor on "filthy matter"; and let them not think the filth of an unjust soul emanates from the purest fountains of nature.

Truly, this objection could perhaps be resolved if (as some think) we were to say that the powers of all stars are good and salutary, but when they are received in us, they degenerate through the vice of matter; thus, the breaths of influence that were beneficial sometimes turn out to be harmful and malicious. In this view, **Mars** provides fortitude of soul and "Herculean efficacy," but—either through a defect of the body in which red bile excessively seethes, or the fault of a soul abusing a celestial gift—those impulses are sometimes bent toward cruelty and injustice. In the same way, from **Saturn**, height of mind, depth of counsel, investigation of hidden things, and love of contemplation are poured in; yet because these things find a sluggish vessel <note>Referring to a dull human mind or a heavy physical temperament.</note>, or through the fault of the will in the one receiving them, they make the soul deceitful, filthy, uncultured, superstitious, and imaginative even to the danger of **frenzy** <note>original: "limphationis." This refers to "lymphation," a state of being "water-struck" or driven to madness/hallucinations.</note>. 

So too from **Venus** we are made prone to cheerfulness, benevolence, and civil elegance, yet we abuse that instinct toward wickedness, luxury, and dishonesty. We are incited by the **Sun** to magnanimity, but we abuse that impulse for ambition—and so on for the rest.

However, someone who says these things is more a *defender* of astrology than an *astrologer*. For among the very first and most confessed axioms of the astrologers is this: that some planets are good, and others are evil. If what was just said were true, then all planets would be called equally good by their nature, and all equally evil by the same logic. For there is no "breath of influence" so salutary that the matter and condition of the receiver cannot infect, change, or disturb it. But if even the astrologers do not want any planet to be so evil that great goods cannot also come from it, nor any so good that great evils cannot

For this reason, they say that if **Saturn** occupies its own <term>house</term><note>The zodiac sign where a planet is said to have its greatest influence.</note>, its own <term>exaltation</term><note>original: "altitudinem." A specific degree in the zodiac where a planet's power is heightened.</note>, or its own <term>bounds</term><note>original: "fines." Subdivisions of zodiac signs that supposedly belong to specific planets.</note>, and if it is mixed with favorable <term>aspects</term><note>original: "radiationibus." The geometric angles between planets.</note>, and if the birth occurred during the day, it makes men contemplative, pious, and wise. 

But if it is received in a less favorable position, they say this same planet degenerates into a bad condition; if it is poorly placed, joined to **Mars**, or in bad configurations with the **Sun**, it makes men demonic, filthy, envious, and liars. They contend that when **Saturn** is so situated in the heavens, nothing good can ever be expected from it. Therefore, anyone who defends astrology in this way clearly does not understand what he is defending. 

For what we have said of **Saturn** should be understood as said of all the planets. For they are also accustomed to say that **Mars**, when not fortunately positioned, incites men to ambition, to lack of self-control, and to the lust for tyranny—not because the vital spirit of the one being born is excessively hot or cold (thereby making the good fire of heaven either sluggish or consuming), but because **Saturn**, **Mars**, and the **Sun**, when they are so situated in the sky, pour such evils into those being born by their own nature and property. 

This is what the astrologers write and believe. Nor does anyone defend astrology any better by denying this, for he "corrects the book with a sponge"<note>A classical metaphor (from Augustus) meaning to erase or destroy the work entirely rather than fixing it. Pico argues that if you remove this deterministic influence, you destroy the very foundation of astrology.</note> and, as we have shown, does away with both the dogma and the truth of every prediction, if it does not depend on the observation of celestial influx, or if the disposition of matter does not merely diminish or increase that influx, but entirely changes and transforms it.

### CHAPTER X. THAT NEITHER BAD NOR GOOD LAWS ARE SUBJECT TO THE HEAVENS.

Hence the opinion is refuted of those who deny that good laws are subject to the heaven (arguing they depend on divine power), but concede this for bad laws, since they believe nothing in them exceeds the powers and capacity of nature. But just as the "sublimity of error" in good things prevents them from being subjected to physical causes, so too does the wickedness of bad things prevent them from being referred to the highest causes which are most obedient to the best God. 

Indeed, experience itself sufficiently demonstrates that, in general, religions—both good and bad—do not depend on the heavens. For some refer the origin and variety of religions to the stars which, as they believe, rule over cities and provinces by their own right. Others refer them to what they call the <term>Great Conjunctions</term><note>The meeting of the outer planets, Saturn and Jupiter, which occurred every 20 years and was believed to signal major historical and religious shifts.</note> of the superior planets, especially **Saturn** and **Jupiter**; this is the opinion followed by the <note>original: "Arabes & Latini." Referring to medieval Islamic astrologers like Abu Ma'shar and the European Scholastic writers who followed them.</note>Arabs and the Latins who walk in the footsteps of the Arabs. 

**Ptolemy** seems to have approached this view, although (as we shall show later) he never made mention of those "Great Conjunctions." Instead, in the second book of his *Apotelesmatika*<note>original: "Apoteleſmaton." Also known as the Tetrabiblos, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note>, he says that those among the Asians who lean toward the east and south worship **Venus** and **Saturn**, because they fall under the "dry <term>triplicity</term><note>A group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element (in this case, Earth).</note>," that is, **Virgo**, **Taurus**, and **Capricorn**, which he believes are ruled by **Saturn** and **Venus**.

Having previously argued against the moral influence of planets, he now turns to the historical and geographical arguments used by astrologers like Ptolemy, pointing out the logical inconsistencies in their theories about the "lifespan" of religions.</meta>

<page-num>540</page-num>
->Giovanni Pico della Mirandola<-

Again, [he claims] that those who live between the south and the west have **Venus** and **Mars** as their deities because they are subject to the humid <term>triplicity</term><note>In astrology, a "triplicity" is a group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element—Fire, Earth, Air, or Water.</note>, over which he places **Mercury** and **Venus** along with **Mars**. Both opinions, however, are refuted by the evidence of the facts and the outcomes themselves, as we were saying. For if a religion is born by the power of some great <term>conjunction</term><note>A "conjunction" occurs when two or more celestial bodies appear near each other in the sky; astrologers believed these alignments triggered major historical shifts.</note>, then when that power is abolished, that religion ought to be abolished as well.

But there is no conjunction of the stars whose power is imagined—even by astrologers—to last for as many years as the worship of idols, the Mosaic religion, and the Christian religion have lasted. The world was darkened by the worship of idols for about five thousand years. What conjunction, I ask? What "great year" of any star claims such a span of years for itself? The rites and observances of the Mosaic law still flourish among the Hebrews today, and they have flourished for a thousand years or more already. What constellation is so strong, so long-lasting? What extinction of empire allows a religion to persist regardless? 

The theologian will give the true causes of these things, consistent with his own dogma; the astrologer can give none from the heavens. If this variety of religions were derived from the stars, we would see them vary daily and change more frequently. Indeed, the astrologers themselves, sensing this and gathering it from the principles of their own science, predefined limits for every religion; but when those religions crossed those limits, they demonstrated by the evidence of the fact itself that they depend on something other than the stars.

Now, that opinion of **Ptolemy**<note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity.</note>—which thinks that just as different stars dominate different places and nations, so there are different religious rites in those places—is even more thoroughly refuted by experience. Since the same stars preside over those provinces lying between the east and the south as used to preside over them, yet **Venus** and **Saturn** are no longer worshiped there as they once were. For why did these deities once dominate them? Certainly, as Ptolemy himself writes, because the earthly triplicity (consisting of **Taurus**, **Virgo**, and **Capricorn**) presides over those regions, and **Venus** and **Saturn** preside over that triplicity—or so he believed. 

But this partition of the world and its regions, distributed under various triplicities, is perpetual, not temporary; therefore, the influence should always be the same as it once was. Why then, O Ptolemy, does the same religion not endure in those same places today? Finally, let us conclude this entire dispute by asking Ptolemy himself: if other stars were formerly worshiped among other nations because of the varying presidency of the stars, by what star's force and power is it brought about that almost no stars are worshiped today in any region of the whole world?

But not even that can be caused by a birth constellation, since a child has the habit and form of the body which he carries with him from the womb before he even leaves <unclear>it</unclear>. ### Against Astrology, Book 4

This must also be numbered among those matters of which we spoke in the fifth chapter: that a prediction cannot be made using the time of birth which they employ, because these traits precede the birth. For this reason, they should rather be predicted through the <term>conception</term><note>The moment of fertilization. Pico argues that since physical traits begin developing at conception, a "birth chart" created nine months later is logically irrelevant to a person's physical makeup.</note> or the arrangement of the seed. But the seed is not created at that moment [of birth]. Therefore, the constellation under which the seed was created ought to be considered instead—but we will deal with this later. If, therefore, the disposition of the body can be foreseen and announced, it could surely be done more effectively from the hour of conception than from the hour of birth, from which it can be done in no way at all; however, whether it is even possible from the former will be examined in the following books.

Now it is demonstrated that astrologers err when they pronounce—based on the hour of <term>birth</term><note>original: *geniturae*</note>—whether the person being born will have a short body or a tall one, be fat or lean, strong or weak, maimed or whole, normal or <term>deformed</term><note>original: *monstruoso*. In the 15th century, "monstrous" births referred to any significant congenital disability or physical anomaly.</note>. For the person acquires all these conditions long before they are formed, perfected, and sent out from the mother's womb into the public. Therefore, just as these traits are not created by that constellation which they clearly preceded long ago, so too they cannot be predicted by an <term>astrologer</term><note>original: *mathematico*. In this period, the term "mathematician" was frequently used to refer specifically to practitioners of judicial astrology.</note> through the observation of that constellation. 

We shall dispute the timing of conception later; for now, we wish the reader to know that the greatest astrologers—such as **Haly** <note>Ali ibn Ridwan, an 11th-century Egyptian physician and astrologer often cited in medieval texts.</note>—believed that things pertaining to the body's <term>temperament</term><note>The balance of the four "humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to govern human health and personality.</note> depend on God through proximate causes lower than heaven. Thus, as **Haly** writes, they asked that they be forgiven if they fell short of the truth in predicting the disposition of the body. 

Let us therefore summarize the entire dispute concerning the efficiency of heaven. If heaven is a universal cause, it cannot be the cause of the variety and distinction of particular things. And even if we grant that there are powers in heaven capable of producing particular properties, they are nonetheless not of the kind that astrologers prophesy from the sky. For chance events cannot be traced to natural causes, nor can things that are "evil" be traced to the most perfect authors <note>Pico implies that if God or the heavens are "perfect," they cannot be the direct cause of earthly "evils" or defects.</note>. Nor can things which proceed from reason and choice be traced to principles acting by natural necessity. Nor can incorporeal rays be traced to bodies, nor things already past or far in the future be traced to a present constellation. Nor can things pertaining to others be referred to our own birth-hour by any logic. 

Furthermore, it is utterly absurd and most foreign to all philosophy to see the proper, manifest, and sufficient causes for things right here among us—in the powers of lower bodies, in the diversity of minds, in emotion, choice, opportunity, and habit, and in the various coincidences of things and causes flowing together from every side—and yet seek their origin in the stars. Such an origin is neither there, nor is it permitted to be there by the nature and condition of either the things being made or the "efficient" power of heaven. 

Hinc factum <margin>Hence it happens</margin>, that all philosophers (whose labor and study are occupied with scrutinizing the causes of things) borrow the true causes of things from medicine, mathematics, or any other art and science, yet they never use astrological causes. To pass over **Favorinus**, **Carneades**, **Posidonius**, **Timaeus**, and **Pythagoras**, we declared at the beginning of this work that this was the practice of **Aristotle** himself, of **Plato**, **Plotinus**, **Averroes**, **Avicenna**, and the good followers of both their schools.

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

### THAT THE HEAVENS CANNOT BE A SIGN OF A THING 
#### for which it is not the cause. Chapter 12.

**B**ut perhaps someone will say that even if it is granted that these variations and outcomes of human affairs are not produced by the stars, it does not immediately follow that they cannot be foreseen and predicted from the heavens. This is because things that the stars do not cause at all, they might nevertheless signify and portend. For there are those who have held this opinion: namely, that lower matters are not produced by the power of the heavens—except in matters of general influence—but that since these events depend on their own immediate and proper causes, they are nevertheless indicated by the heavens before they happen. And they believe that through the transit, <term>station</term><note>A point where a planet appears to stand still in the sky before changing direction (retrograde motion).</note>, and retreat of the planets, future things can be known, just as **birds**—whether by flying past or by standing still—signify future things by their wings or their voices, without even knowing it themselves.

But in truth, neither have famous astrologers themselves ever believed this, nor does any reason allow us to believe it. For whatever is a sign of something by nature (and not by human institution) and is a physical body, it must be either the **cause** of the thing it signifies, or the **effect**, or both the sign and the thing signified must proceed from the same common cause. If anyone thinks something should be added to this—as if different from what we have said—such as that the sign is necessarily and inseparably connected to the cause, he is greatly and far mistaken. This is because such a connection and accompaniment cannot happen in any other way than that either the cause produces the sign from itself before it effects the other thing, or that whatever stirs that cause into action also rouses this sign at the same time; thus we concede that both are referred back to a common cause.

Come then, let us see which of these more properly fits the heavens, if future events are signified by the heavens. Certainly, the motions and dispositions of the heavens are not the **effects** of lower things; and the astrologers themselves deny they are the **causes**. It remains, then, for the state and disposition of the heaven, and that which is believed to be indicated by it, to be said to proceed from the same cause—just as the <term>iris</term><note>original: *iris*. Here referring to a rainbow, traditionally seen as a natural sign of changing weather.</note> sometimes portends clear weather, not because it creates clear weather, but because the cause of the rainbow is also the cause of the clear weather. 

But no physical cause will be found that is superior to the heavens and that therefore produces the dispositions of both the heavens and the lower world simultaneously. Will there then remain an incorporeal cause? For perhaps it might seem possible to say that human events are brought about by the <term>divine minds</term><note>original: *divinis mentibus*. In Neoplatonic and Aristotelian thought, these are the "Intelligences" or angelic beings believed to move the celestial spheres.</note> themselves, who revolve the celestial bodies; and while these events are happening, they are indicated to us by the very state and position of the heaven they move, as if by certain nods of the head. 

Truly, whoever says this—which is indeed very close to the fables of the poets—how will he avoid this absurdity: that those things are brought about by divine minds which men themselves cannot do without the guilt of a <term>shameful crime</term><note>original: *flagitij*. Pico is arguing that if God or angels used the stars to "signal" a murder, they would be complicit in the sin.</note>? For it would mean they urge and impel this man to homicide, that one to adultery, and another to theft. I set aside how much all philosophy finds it offensive for physical things to be produced by incorporeal causes without a physical cause intervening as a medium. Furthermore, why are those born at different hours born with a different fate, if the cause and author of fate is not the position of the heaven (which varies by the hour), but the immobile **Author** of the heaven, who is always equal to Himself and like Himself?

## Against Astrology, Book IV.

<sig>Zz 2</sig>

...considered to be? Finally, as **Thomas Aquinas** argues: Since the effects of the same cause indicate one another from the same principle and proceed in the same manner, yet the motions of the heavens and the disposition of lower bodies and affairs do not proceed from superior causes in the same way—for the former follow an immutable and necessary order, while the latter follow a variable order that falls contingently <term>contingently</term><note>In philosophy, "contingent" refers to things that happen by chance or free will and could have happened differently, as opposed to "necessary" things which must happen.</note> into either side, according to the nature of the things being moved and governed. Divine principles do not change this nature but preserve it; otherwise, they would not be guiding nature, but destroying it. 

Therefore, the heavens cannot signify lower things except insofar as a cause indicates its own effect. Consequently, those who are defeated by reason and admit the heavens are not the cause, yet still contend they are a "sign," do not understand their own words. This is what **Thomas Aquinas**—a man of the weightiest judgment who was not accustomed to asserting anything rashly—firmly pronounces in his *Theological Summa* <note>original: *theologica summa*; referring to the *Summa Theologica*, the massive compendium of theology written in the 13th century</note>. 

This "sign" argument might be applied to **comets**, to **meteors** <note>original: *traiectionibus*; literally "throwings across," referring to shooting stars</note>, and to other things of this kind that occur in the upper air. These might be stirred up by the stars as effects of some underlying cause, so that they do not *cause* the event, but merely *signify* what their own cause is about to do. But this can in no way be said of the stars themselves, since, as we have said, no superior corporeal cause can be found above them. 

Furthermore, those who hold this opinion [that stars are signs] introduce the necessity of **Fate**, even if they do not wish to. If the stars are the *causes* of lower things, it is possible for the intended effect of their influence to fail—either because the physical matter resists it, or because a particular cause diverts the general influence elsewhere. If, however, they are *signs* established by nature for the purpose of signifying, then their significance will be as true as their very nature is true. Otherwise, why would they be established by **God** for signifying? Are His works perfect if they deceive or lie? If they do not lie, then whatever future they signify must necessarily happen. 

Finally, if the stars are numbered among causes, it is not contrary to their condition to be in that order of causes which can be hindered, changed, or overcome. But if they are considered signs, they cannot be held as lies; otherwise, the one who inscribed the notes and "letters" of the future in the celestial volume (as they call it) would be either a deceiver or ignorant. 

Lastly, if the heavens do not indicate things by *doing* them, but indicate things they do *not* do, it must be that they indicate what *other* causes are doing. Either they indicate what all causes do, or only what some do. Why, I ask, would they indicate the works of these causes and not those? If they indicate all equally, then no other causes remain by which the predicted outcome could be prevented; therefore, what was portended will happen by necessity. 

If we say this, however, we shall oppose not only the truth (as we have shown elsewhere), but also the astrologers themselves. For the **Egyptians**, **Ptolemy**, and every most celebrated astrologer has always denied the necessity of fate. They declare this especially in their treatises on "interrogations" <note>The branch of astrology that answers specific questions based on the time the question is asked.</note>. Since they say that not every question is legitimate—only those that proceed from an impulse of the soul moved by the heavens—and since they admit many questions are *not* of this type (those arising from our own reason and counsel), they clearly declare that they do not admit the necessity of fate. Yet, if such necessity were introduced, all astrology...

## WHETHER THE STARS ARE SIGNS OR CAUSES, that part of astrology which concerns interrogations is of no account. Chapter 14.

Whichever opinion the astrologers might prefer—that is, whether they want the stars to be the causes of lower things, or merely signs and not causes—the part concerning "interrogations" <term>interrogations</term><note>Also known as horary astrology, where an astrologer answers a specific question by casting a chart for the exact moment the question is asked.</note> (which they use the most) will necessarily be fundamentally abolished. For the foundation of this part is that our minds are moved by a celestial constellation, at least in the imaginative part; and when the mind is prompted from there to desire to know something, if it then consults an astrologer, [it is claimed] that from the configuration of the heavens at the hour of consultation, what the inquirer desired to know can be portended. Thus, the astrologer is supposedly able to give true answers to those questioning him about all matters. 

Let us ask those who think they can resolve every question: are the stars only signs of lower things, or are they also causes, signifying by acting? If they are only signs, then the impulse of our desire does not come from the stars. Instead, just as those who hold this opinion say other things happen by their own causes (even if indicated by stars), so too the movement of desire would take as its origin and cause not a celestial constellation, but the imaginative power itself, our own choice, the appetitive power of the soul, and those things from without that stir the sense and mind. 

If they respond that they are causes and that lower things are signified by them (just as effects are demonstrated from a cause), in what way will they defend the idea that the configuration of the heavens appearing at the hour of consultation is the cause of those things about which the astrologer answers the inquirer? For since some things have happened long ago, or others will never happen, they ought to have no cause [at that specific moment]. Surely **Mars** will be in the west <note>In traditional astrology, Mars in the "descendant" or western horizon could be interpreted as a sign of deception or failure in the consultation.</note>, which will not permit true answers to be given by them. 

But if they could obtain from him [Mars] that they might even hear the truth, I will respond to those who do not even ask, with very great truth concerning these questions. It seemed to astrologers that too little glory and—what pressed them more—too little profit was gained if they pronounced each person's fate only from the time of birth <term>geniture</term><note>The casting of a natal horoscope based on the moment of birth.</note> or the turning of the year. For to understand these things, it was necessary for a client to visit them either once in a whole lifetime or only once a year. However, since our curiosity desires to know many things daily about which they could provide no answer—which took much authority away from their art among the unlearned <term>idiotas</term><note>original: *idiotas*; referring here to the general public or those not educated in the sciences, rather than a slur on intelligence.</note> and much money from the practitioners—they persuaded themselves or at least others that they could clearly foresee whatever was asked based on the hour of the question, provided that the one asking acted with a natural im-

## Against Astrology, Book IV.

...by the impulse <note>The text begins mid-word with "petu," completing "impetu" from the previous page.</note> of a celestial motion, and not by their own choice, that they were moved to ask a question. In this way, they cleverly rescue themselves from the infamy of falsehood. For if the answer they gave was refuted by the actual facts, they would say it was not that the astrologer was false, but that the question was not "effective" <note>In this context, an "effective" (efficax) question is one prompted by a genuine, star-driven impulse rather than idle curiosity.</note>; yet if the answers matched the outcomes, what would then stand in the way of regarding them as oracles on earth? With these tricks and fallacies, this trifling race of men mocks the unlearned, for nothing more dissonant from reason can be said or thought than what they have devised regarding this fallacy of "interrogations."

For even if I were to grant them that my desire to know about an absent person (for example) comes from the heavens, what possible logic follows that the very hour I explain this desire to an astrologer, the configuration of the heavens must be such that it reveals the status of that absent person to me? Whence comes this alliance or "federation" between our desire and the very thing we wish to know? 

If they happen to answer that the same celestial force which brings about that event far away from us also "twitches" our mind at the same time, warning us of the thing that is happening—well, first, it would follow that these desires would only strike us at the exact moment the event occurs. And yet, they believe that "effective" interrogations can be made about things that happened long ago, or will happen far in the future, or things that will never happen at all. 

Furthermore, if we were to say this, we should not look at the configuration of the heavens at the hour we ask the astrologer, but at the first moment the desire to ask seized us. For it would be that same (or a similar) constellation <term>constellation</term><note>A specific arrangement of planets and stars at a given moment.</note> that both produces the event and stirs the desire to know it within us. If one must be "rationally insane," it would be far more rational to say that than what the astrologers claim: that we must observe the time of the inquiry <note>original: "sciscitationis"</note>, rather than the moment the concern first troubled us. 

Then, as we were saying, if there can be any kinship or consensus between these things, it can only exist if both the event that occurred and our desire seem to refer to the same or a similar constellation. Furthermore, the hour at which we actually consult the astrologer can vary for a thousand reasons: we might meet the astrologer sooner or later if his house is far away, or if someone delays us on the road, or other such random interruptions. These things change the hour of the question, and therefore change the configuration of the heavens upon which the astrologer will base his answer. But the astrologers care for none of this—

### DIVINE MIRACLES ARE NEITHER BROUGHT ABOUT NOR
### SIGNIFIED BY THE HEAVENS, BUT MIRACLES ARE INDICATED BY MIRACLES, JUST AS NATURAL THINGS ARE INDICATED BY NATURAL THINGS. Chapter XIV.

**B**ut if only they were insane only to this extent, and did not also think that divine miracles—those which exceed the power of all nature—were nevertheless produced by the natural rays of the superior bodies <note>The "superior bodies" refer to the planets and stars in the Aristotelian cosmos.</note>. For we have shown above that they are entangled in this error, demonstrating that they attribute divine religion to the power of the stars—both that which God once promulgated through Moses to the Hebrew people, and that which Christ later promulgated through the Apostles to the world. Thus, they have also ascribed that flooding of the whole world under Noah, and other divine miracles of this kind recorded in sacred history, to their own constellations.

In this matter, they undoubtedly seem more insane than those who simply do not concede that these things ever happened at all; for the astrologer believes these things happened exactly as they are narrated, yet claims they were produced by natural causes. No greater insanity can be imagined than to think something done *above* nature was done by the powers *of* nature. Now, in disputing against the impious, we have proven that the divine law exists from those things which exceed the powers of nature. The same can easily be demonstrated concerning the universal cataclysm <note>The Great Flood of Noah.</note>, since nothing is more contrary to nature than for nature itself to plot its own destruction. Therefore, nature would never inflict such an injury upon herself, from which she could not deliver herself by her own power. 

If it could not happen by a natural course that when the waters surpassed the peaks of all mountains by fifteen cubits, Noah—with his family and every kind of animal, enclosed within a single ark for twelve months—escaped that shipwreck, then it was also not nature's purpose to submerge the whole earth in a flood of waters for the destruction of all living things. And if these things are not done by the heaven, they cannot even be foreseen from the heaven. For what the heaven does not do, it also does not signify, as we proved a little while ago. 

Although they have this specific reason why miracles are not portended by the stars, even if we were to grant that other things (which do not exceed the capacity of nature) are either done or indicated by the heaven: for, as we have declared elsewhere, the order of things established by God for the natural course is so enclosed within its own boundaries and separated from those things which are done by divine power and will beyond nature, that if all these supernatural things were removed, nothing would be missing from the nature of things, nor would anything be superfluous. But the heaven, and whatever happens in the heaven in its common course, are among those things that are *according to nature* <note>original: "secundum naturam"</note>. Therefore, if the motion or arrangement of the stars (which is due to them from their natural condition) signifies something future, this significance and indication must be held and numbered among natural things. 

If we say that some of these signs portend things that will happen *above* nature, this absurdity will follow: if God leaves nature to its own conditions and does not do anything above it, nature itself will then be found false and lying—and in nature, God would have established something in vain and superfluously, since there would still be signs in the stars for future events [that never occur].

<summary>Pico argues that divine miracles like Noah's Flood cannot be attributed to or predicted by astrology, as they exist outside the "natural order" that the stars govern. He asserts that nature would never naturally seek its own destruction, meaning the Flood must have been a purely supernatural act of God.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s argument that miracles and divine events operate entirely outside the rules of astrology. He argues that while nature follows a predictable order, God’s interventions—like the Flood or the birth of Christ—are marked by signs that break natural laws, rather than following them.</meta>

...rare, which nevertheless will not exist, since the things being signified are matters beyond nature which we supposed were taken away. The signs themselves are things according to nature; if the supernatural elements are removed, it must be said that these signs are neither taken away nor deprived of any perfection due to them. Therefore, if God disposed for some miracle to be performed through someone, He did not insert the signs of that miracle into natural things in such a way that the meaning belonged to the logic of their nature. Instead, He willed for miracles to be signified by natural signs preceding miracles. 

The cataclysm <note>The Great Flood of Noah.</note> that would occur by the miracle of divine justice was signified to the world by Noah—who was divinely inspired and divinely to be saved. The leading of the Hebrews out of Egypt and the giving of the Law to them were attested to the Egyptians and their astrologers by the miracles performed through the divine rod of Moses. The conquest of the Promised Land by the people of God, and the wonders God was to work in it beyond the laws of nature, were indicated not by some natural configuration of the heavens, but by the most rapid motion of the Sun being restrained by the hand of the Creator <note>A reference to the Book of Joshua, where the sun is said to have stood still during a battle.</note>—to say nothing of the crossing of the Jordan on dry feet and the walls of the city being destroyed by the sound of trumpets. 

That the life of Hezekiah was prolonged by divine power was demonstrated not by the benign irradiation of Jupiter <note>Astrologers associated the planet Jupiter with health and longevity; Pico argues it was a miracle, not a planetary alignment.</note> running its spaces in the right order, but by the miracle of the Sun moving backward. When the oracles of minds divinely inspired beyond the nature of the human mind announced the wonder of the Word made flesh and the Virgin’s childbirth, a thousand wonders were then attested in the celestial and earthly bodies themselves: that immense new star arose for the Lord; and later, when He was dying on the cross, the Sun failed while the Moon was full—contrary to the order of nature <note>A solar eclipse cannot naturally occur during a full moon; Pico uses this to show the event was a miracle, not an astronomical event.</note>. By these signs, divine miracles are both demonstrated and confirmed; such miracles can neither be produced by the natural state of things nor is it appropriate for them to be indicated by it.

### THAT THE STAR OF THE MAGI CANNOT BE UNDERSTOOD AS
### any constellation, and an explanation of certain scriptures
### which might seem to support astrology to the 
### unskilled. Chapter XV.

**N**ow, since we have come to the mention of the star that showed the newborn Jesus to the Magi, it would not be out of place to have warned the reader lest they perhaps suspect this star favors the opinion of the astrologers. It is as if that star were nothing other than a celestial constellation indicating a born prophet, known and investigated by those Magi from the East who were, as is thought, exceedingly skilled in celestial science. 

However, the very letter of the Gospel most evidently leads us away from this error, for speaking of this star it says: *And behold, the star which they had seen in the East went before them until it came and stood over where the child was.* <note>Matthew 2:9.</note> No one, unless they are insane, will think this is to be understood as referring to the natural stars and configurations of the heavens. That star was therefore artificial and temporary, not a perpetual and natural star created for that duty by the Creator, so that the birth of the King of the Jews might be signified through it. The Magi understood this perhaps in the same way they later understood in their dreams that they should avoid Herod, and other things which...

He specifically refutes the idea that the Star of the Magi was a natural planetary alignment, noting its movement was contrary to the behavior of real stars.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s polemic against astrology. On the preceding page, he argued that miraculous events like the Star of Bethlehem or the stopping of the sun for Joshua were signs from God, not products of natural celestial cycles. He now addresses specific biblical phrases that astrologers often misinterpret as supporting their craft.</meta>

<page-num>548</page-num>
...had come, they were to return to their own country by another way. But we must equally take care that we are not disturbed by certain expressions in the Scriptures, such as when we read in Paul that the Son of God was sent in the "fullness of time," and in the Gospel where the Lord says: *Now is your hour and the power of darkness*, and elsewhere, *My hour has not yet come*. For the superstitious man will think that constellations of hours and times are being signified. 

But you should ask him: when he is hungry, does he think it is the time for eating because of whatever the arrangement of the heavens might be at that time? And when he has labored enough, is it time to care for the body? And when he has slept enough, is it the time for waking? If he says that all these things have their own "time," he does not mean it is because of the constellation of that time, but because of the nature of the thing itself which is being done, and because of the occasion and opportunity for doing it. 

In the same way, other things which God does above nature, and which men do by their own freedom, although they require no constellations in order to happen, they must necessarily happen at some time; and it is more fitting and more convenient that they happen at this time rather than that one. It was fitting for the Son of God to be sent at the time he was sent; before then, it was not fitting. The cause is not in the heavens, but in the purpose of God and the "exigency of things" <note>The requirements or needs of the historical situation.</note> about which theologians write much, insofar as they were permitted to penetrate the secret of divine counsel through the clues of the Scriptures. 

It was likewise fitting that after He was born He was not killed immediately, but at the time it was expedient, He permitted Himself to be in the hands of the wicked, and that was the "hour and the power of darkness." The same must be understood in other matters, which is clearly declared to us from one place in the Book of Genesis. There, when God promises the land of promise (so called from the event) to <term>Abraham</term> <note>original: "Abrae"</note>, He then says: *Know that your seed shall be a stranger in a land not their own, where they shall be afflicted for four hundred years, but in the fourth generation they shall return here.* 

If only this much had been written, the astrologer would boast that the divine promise could not be fulfilled until, after the passage of so many years, a certain disposition of the heavens was reached which would bring about that event. But look at what the prophet adds from the person of God: *For the iniquities of the <term>Amorites</term> are not yet full up to the present time.* <note>Genesis 15:16. Pico uses this to show that the "timing" was based on a moral threshold (sin), not a celestial one.</note> 

See, therefore, what was being waited for? Not a conjunction, namely of Jupiter and Saturn, or any other sidereal constellation, but the fullness of iniquity among the Amorites. Through this, divine justice—by whose laws human affairs are governed, not by fatal necessity—would both justly expel them and introduce the seed of the faithful <term>Abraham</term> into that place.

could they be signified by the stars from that perspective? For instance, if no constellation could indicate God's incarnation, could a law-giving man, about to promulgate good laws, nonetheless be shown? I answered that even in this way, those things cannot be signified by the stars, nor can they happen in the way Alliacensis <note>Pierre d'Ailly (1351–1420), a French cardinal and scholar who famously tried to harmonize astrology with theology.</note> thought. For he thought there was no other way to defend from the charge of impiety those who seek the causes of such wondrous and divine things in the stars, except by saying that these things depend on heaven—not insofar as they are above nature, but insofar as there is something natural in them. 

But whoever says this says nothing, just as he says nothing who claims a man is made by a constellation, yet his rational nature is not made by it; for if the constellation does not produce that which is rational in a man, there is no reason why it should be said to produce a man any more than a lion. If, therefore, you take away from divine miracles that which is unique to them, and leave only those things which they have in common with countless other things, there is no reason for you to search so studiously in the heavens for the singular cause of that effect. 

But indeed, those who investigate the nativity <note>original: "Genesim," here referring to the astrological birth chart</note> of Jesus do not strive to know why he was in the womb for nine months like other men, or why he was in good bodily health, or why he had long hair, or why he was poor, or why he was a Jew, since the life of all mortals abounds in these conditions. Rather, they seek the cause of those things that were exceptional and singular in him in the stars, which they believe to be both exceptional and singular. 

Yet those things are the works of God above nature, not of the heavens: that he was born of a virgin, that he was both man and God, that he was Lord in his homeland and a pilgrim in the flesh, that he was the worker of wondrous deeds, the rightful Lord of the world, the judge of the living and the dead, the author and dispenser of divine grace, the expeller of idolatry, the conqueror of demons, the author of virtues, the driver out of vices, the peace of the world, and the manifester of truth. If you do not seek these things, you seek nothing; if you do seek them, you seek impiously. 

Therefore, there is no refuge provided for astrologers by Alliacensis in saying that divine miracles happen because of heaven, though not insofar as they are miracles. These things cannot be signified by the stars for that reason (as our friend Jerome <note>Likely Girolamo Savonarola, the influential friar and Pico's close friend, who encouraged this work.</note> was asking us); for if the order of things which proceed from God above nature is removed, those celestial indications will remain, pointing toward those effects in some part (as we were saying), but the effect will no longer exist; those signs, therefore, are

# GIOVANNI PICO OF
## Mirandola’s Disputations against
### Astrology, Book V.

#### That the decrees of astrologers concerning great conjunctions are usefully refuted, and how deceitful those have been found to be who wished to judge great changes in earthly affairs through them. Chapter I.

**MANY** people are led away from the truth by the fallacy of astrologers who persuade the unskilled that there has never been a change of laws, no arrival of prophets, nor any wonderful event in human affairs that a <term>Great Conjunction<note>A rare alignment of the planets Saturn and Jupiter. Medieval astrologers believed these events, occurring roughly every 20 years and shifting through zodiacal "triplicities" every 200–240 years, signaled the birth of new religions or the collapse of kingdoms.</note></term> of the superior stars—especially Saturn and Jupiter—did not precede. When these astrologers discuss this matter in person, either with their followers or with the more uneducated, they treat it as a certain and conceded fact in their charts. They run through many thousands of years and say: "this is the constellation that caused the Flood," "this one gave birth to Moses," "that one preceded the arrival of Jesus," and "this one preceded the law of Muhammad." There is hardly anyone who is not moved by this, and is not forced either to descend into their opinion or at least to harbor some doubt. 

Therefore, since this profession harms religion most in this regard, I wish to confront this pestilence before we tear up the very foundations of the whole art. For astrologers err so greatly in this place that, even if they were correct in other matters, they still could not be defended here. This is not only because they predict things which undoubtedly do not fall under the power of heaven, but because the very rules they use in predicting contain the most manifest errors in both history and astronomy. Before we show this through reasoning, experience itself can provide enough certainty to those who do not fully perceive the force of logic; for all those who wished to divine anything concerning the change or success of sects and laws from these constellations have been caught as liars and deceivers. 

In the past, when the faith of Christ began to sprout, the <term>mathematicians<note>In this context, "mathematicians" refers to astrologers, as the terms were often synonymous in the ancient and medieval world.</note></term> said it would not last more than * <note>The number is missing or marked with an asterisk in the original; typically, critics of Christianity like Porphyry cited a 365-year astrological limit for the religion.</note> years; yet from its beginning, the one thousand four hundred and ninety-fourth year is now passing. <term>Albumasar<note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), a Persian astrologer whose works were the primary source for "Great Conjunction" theory in Europe.</note></term>, either the author or the inventor of this error, said that this same law (that is, ours) would endure for 1,460 years, because that is the number of years they call the "Greatest Years of the Sun." Those years have passed, and the law has not passed away, for truly "Heaven and earth shall pass away, but the words of the Lord shall not pass away" <note>original: "Cœlum & terra præteribunt, Verba autem Domini non præteribunt"; a reference to the Gospel of Matthew 24:35.</note>. Nor did he predict more truly concerning his own law—that of Muhammad. <term>Abraham the Jew<note>Likely referring to Abraham bar Hiyya or Abraham Zacuto, Jewish scholars who used astrology to calculate the arrival of the Messiah.</note></term> said that in the year of Christ 1464, their Messiah would come, based on astrological observation; for he claimed that the position of the stars under which Moses once led the people out of Egypt was then first due to return.

and had given the law to those he led out <note>original: "eductis dederat legem." Referring to Moses leading the Israelites out of Egypt.</note>. Having been born in the year immediately before him, and since I am now in my thirtieth year <note>Pico was born in 1463; this puts the composition of this passage around 1493, shortly before his death.</note>, I have learned through experience the falsity of that prediction. <margin>12</margin> Arnald of Villanova <note>original: "Arnaldus Hispanus." A famous 13th-century physician and alchemist who turned to apocalyptic prophecy.</note>, a noble physician indeed but a little too inclined toward superstitions, threatened us with the coming of the **Antichrist** in the year of grace 1345, based on astrological vanity and many other additions. One hundred and forty-eight years have now flowed by since that time, and no Antichrist has appeared yet, except for the many who were already present in the time of the Apostles. How often have younger men announced to us the arrival of a "false prophet" based on some conjunction of the superior planets? Especially from that conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn in **Scorpio** ten years ago; yet no false prophet has appeared to the world since then. <margin>13</margin> Pierre d’Ailly <note>original: "Alliacensis." A 14th-century cardinal and theologian who tried to reconcile astrology with theology.</note> himself writes that in the year the General Council of Constance <note>Held 1414–1418 to resolve the Great Western Schism.</note> was celebrated, astrologers predicted there would be no peace in the Church, but rather the destruction of religion and the marking of great dissensions within it. They based this on Jupiter being retrograde in the "first house" <note>The first house in an astrological chart represents the "life" or beginning of an entity.</note> in the figure of the year. And yet, that <term>Great Schism<note>A 40-year period (1378–1417) when there were two, then three, simultaneous claimants to the papacy.</note></term>, than which none was ever greater or more long-lasting in the Church, having been confirmed for forty years, was first extinguished in that very year, and the customary peace and tranquility was restored to the Church. This certainly could have moved d’Ailly himself not to place any further faith in that vanity—he who, perhaps persuaded by them, feared that the schism would bring us the Antichrist shortly thereafter. There were other predictions of theirs about laws and sects that I could recount, which were later contradicted by the actual outcome, but I think these suffice, since there are no others in that art of such great authority as those whose predictions I have shown to be refuted by experience itself. Now, let us descend to the reasons.

## ->BY WHAT WAYS ASTROLOGERS PASS JUDGMENT<-
### ->on greater matters, and the rejection of<-
### ->the Great Orbs. Chapter II.<-

**ASTROLOGERS** are accustomed to investigate the great changes of inferior things <note>Earthly affairs.</note> in four main ways through the superior planets—especially **Jupiter** and **Saturn** when they are together, which they call a <term>Great Conjunction<note>The meeting of the two outermost planets known in the Renaissance. They were believed to reset the "clock" of world history.</note></term>—as well as through **Great Orbs**, through Saturnian revolutions, and through the "accession and recession" <note>An astronomical theory called "trepidation," which suggested the stars moved back and forth rather than in a continuous precession.</note> of the eighth sphere. We shall show all these ways to be irrational, false, and impassable. From this, we shall not only achieve what we first sought here—that their impious and reckless claims about religion and laws be proven false—but every judgment regarding the great changes of the world will be weakened. I will begin with a refutation of the **Great Orbs** and the revolutions they call "Saturnian," so that once these are rejected, the entire dispute of this present book can then range freely against the Great Conjunctions. They imagine that each of the planets, and likewise each of the signs, holds empire over the world for **three hundred and sixty years**. When these have passed, they say a new **Great Orb** begins, over which the planet next to the previous one, and...

When a new **Great Cycle** <note>original: "orbis," referring to a "Great Year" or a long astrological period governing human history.</note> begins, they claim many things are renewed in the lower world, and the condition of our affairs is always changed according to the nature of the celestial ruler. 

Then, if someone asks them where we are, or in what "cycle" we are living now—that is, under which ruler—they respond: under **Leo** and the **Moon**. They prove it in this way: **Aoniar** <note>Likely a reference to the Persian astrologer Abu Ma'shar, often cited under various names in the Middle Ages.</note> writes in his *Book of Nativities* that a new Great Cycle began at the time of that conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn which they believe foretold the Great Flood <note>original: "cataclifmum." Aoniar claims that among the planets, **Saturn** ruled this cycle, and among the signs, **Cancer**—which **Abu Ma'shar** <note>original: "Albumafar." The Latinized name of Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), one of the most influential astrologers in the Latin West.</note> also said in the first book of his *Great Conjunctions*, in the first distinction. 

Therefore, taking this as the hinge of their entire calculation, they conclude from the number of years he provided that the Lord **Jesus** was born when the one hundred and forty-first year was turning in that cycle. This cycle was the fifteenth from the one we mentioned (the one under which the Flood occurred), and it is ruled among the signs by **Leo**, and among the planets by the **Moon**; it is destined to end in the year of grace **1659**. 

This is the universal opinion of the astrologers; you will not see anyone who, in public prophecies of the years, if he mentions a Great Cycle, does not appoint Leo and the Moon as the rulers and governors of the world. 

I could object here to how flimsy a conjecture moves them to call a span of as many years as they have imagined parts of the heavens a "Great Cycle," and how it can be said with no reason that the governing power of a single planet lasts through so many years—especially an inferior planet <note>The Moon was considered the "lowest" or "closest" planet to Earth in the geocentric model, and thus deemed less powerful than the "superior" planets like Saturn.</note>. Nevertheless, such a thing was never devised by **Ptolemy** <note>The most famous ancient astronomer/astrologer; Pico uses him as a standard for "purer" science compared to later medieval additions.</note> nor by any of the ancients, but is a fiction of the more recent Arabs. 

But putting these things aside, let us first press them with necessary arguments—ones they cannot avoid if they wish to stand by their own principles and not renounce their dogma. Let them tell me, then: if these Great Cycles are to be established, do they make the start of a new cycle coincide with the very first constitution of the world (upon which everyone agrees), or do they not? If they say they do not, what could be more absurd? If they say they do, I shall now tear apart by mathematical deduction whatever they determined above regarding Great Cycles, showing that it is impossible for those things they were saying to be true if the beginnings of a new cycle started with the creation of the world. 

For **Abu Ma'shar**, who is the chief authority they rely upon, counts two thousand two hundred and twenty-eight full years from the beginning of the world to the Flood; although the calculation of **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century bishop whose *Chronicon* was the standard for historical dating in the Middle Ages.</note> exceeds this number by sixteen years. But it makes no difference what we say, since when disputing with astrologers, we should primarily use their own opinions. Let the number of years from **Adam** to the Flood be established according to the opinion of Abu Ma'shar, against whom we are disputing. It is clear that from the conjunction which they say pre-signified the Flood—and with which a new cycle simultaneously began—there are one thousand nine hundred and for-
