It will be clear that it consists of five whole great cycles, with a remainder of one hundred and forty-seven undivided years. Therefore, the beginning of the great cycle is necessarily fixed in the year of the world 1408. If this number of years is part of another preceding cycle, it must necessarily be said that two hundred and thirteen years of a cycle passed before there were any years at all—that is, before the very beginnings of the world itself. It is sufficiently obvious that nothing more delusional could be said. 

But so it is: certainly nothing is more reckless than that class of men, nothing more prone by nature or profession to lying and deceiving. They invent something for themselves to cultivate their dogma and perform deceptions for the unskilled—which is a mark of their malice and vanity—but the force of truth always ensures that something either false, or entirely impossible, or repugnant to their own sayings and dogmas follows from it. Being quite unobservant, they bring this about, yet these liars and forgetful men spread their claims anyway, which is surely a vice of ignorance and sluggishness. 

A clear example is at hand in the matter we are discussing. For, in order to persuade others by whatever reason they could that the great inundation of the world through the **cataclysm** <note>original: "cataclysmum," the Great Flood of Noah.</note> was accomplished by the heavens, they added a childish fiction of a **great conjunction** <note>original: "magnae coniunctionis," a rare alignment of Jupiter and Saturn.</note> and claimed a new cycle began with it, under which the world was to be renewed. To ensure nothing was missing from the deception, they put **Saturn** and **Cancer** in charge of that cycle, as the former among the planets and the latter among the signs are considered the authors of humidity and coldness. 

And this indeed, as I said, is a product of their malice and vanity. But their stupidity, sluggishness, and ignorance also appear: first, because they do not see the delusions that follow—such as when a "new" cycle would not actually have the start of a new cycle—and second, because if Saturn and Cancer presided over that cycle, we necessarily conclude that **Mars** and **Aquarius** presided over the very first entire cycle of the world. Why the empire of the world should have its auspices from these two, they could never defend by any reason. For if they said this of the **Moon**, they might offer something (as it is closer to the earth); or if from **Saturn**, the eminence of the cycle; if from the **Sun**, the power of virtue; if from **Jupiter** or **Venus**, the beneficence of nature. But in Mars they find nothing why it should deserve the first governorship of the world. Likewise in Aquarius, since it has no initial prerogative, such as **Cancer**, **Libra**, and **Capricorn** are thought to possess <note>These signs mark the solstices and equinoxes, the "corners" of the year.</note>. 

But why do we wander further? One may see plainly and clearly from this how they are equally liars and forgetful. For they say, as we have shown, that Cancer and Saturn presided over that cycle before the event of the flood, because this confirms their dogma that a great inundation of waters proceeded from a humid and cold planet. Yet again, because it seems harmonious that we should begin the government of the world from the **Sun** among the planets and from **Aries** among the signs, they say the planet of the world was the Sun, and the sign was Aries. For **Haly Abenragel** <note>Abū l-Hasan 'Alī ibn Abī l-Rijāl, an 11th-century Arab astrologer.</note> writes these things, as does **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar, the 9th-century Persian astrologer whose "Book of Great Conjunctions" was a standard text.</note> himself in his book...

...first concerning the great conjunctions <note>original: "magnis cõiunctionibus," the rare alignments of Jupiter and Saturn that astrologers used to predict major historical shifts.</note>, and yet these things conflict with each other so much that they cannot be true at the same time. For since there are five complete great cycles <note>term: "great cycles" (magni orbes) — in mundane astrology, these are 360-year periods assigned to a zodiac sign and a planet to track the rise and fall of religions and empires.</note> before the cycle of the flood reaching back to the beginnings of the world—or rather six incomplete ones, whether we count five or rather six—it cannot happen that if Aries rules the first cycle, Cancer rules the fifth or sixth. Or if the solar star <note>The Sun.</note> ruled the first cycle, that Saturn should be set over the cycle of the flood. For if Aries and the Sun presided over the first, then Taurus and Venus presided over the second, Mercury with Gemini over the third, and the Moon with Cancer over the fourth. But in neither the fifth nor the sixth was it Cancer and Saturn; rather, it would be Saturn with Leo, and after this Jupiter with Virgo. How then do they not blush to leave these writings to posterity—the most manifest testimonies of either such ignorance or such stupidity?

But nearly all authors of astrology are of this character. Thus, a certain Ocliaton <note>A likely reference to a medieval astrological authority, sometimes identified with a source used by Leopold of Austria or a corruption of an Arabic name.</note>, inventing other "great cycles" for himself, wanted to bring it about that both the creation of the world and the birth of Jesus would mark the beginnings of a new cycle, and that the same sign—that is, Aries, the head of the zodiac—would be set over both. Since this would not otherwise work for his math, he said that 4,320 years ought to be counted from Adam to Christ. If we count that many, it will clearly be exactly what he wanted. 

But no history accepts that number; rather, it differs from Greek and Latin writers by nearly nine hundred years, from the Hebrew records by five hundred, and from other astronomers even by one thousand one hundred. But he preferred that what was true should not be, rather than renounce his own beautiful fiction. He is just like those ancients whom Aristotle records, who, once they had established that all things are distributed according to the number ten, yet could find no more than nine spheres in the universe, said that there must necessarily be "another earth" <note>The "Counter-Earth" or *Antichthon*, a hypothetical body invented by some Pythagoreans to bring the number of celestial bodies up to the "perfect" number ten.</note>, so that their number ten might be filled—in a certain imitation of divine wisdom, which does not shape itself to things, but shapes the truth of things to itself.

Finally, it must not be overlooked that even if those great cycles were necessarily a real thing, what the astrologers say through them would still have to be false, since they err greatly in calculating them. For they think that the cycle which is now revolving—the 195th year of which they claim is currently passing—is the nineteenth cycle from the first, and the fourteenth from the one under which the flood occurred; and for this reason, they set Leo and the Moon over it. But this cannot be unless we count 6,838 years from the creation of the world to our own time, which exceeds the true calculation of years by more than 1,400 years, as we have proven in our treatise *On the True Calculation of Times* <note>Pico refers to his own chronological research, where he attempted to reconcile biblical history with secular records.</note>. But even if we follow other histories—namely the other Latin authors who compute more years—we will still find fewer years than those which these men scrape together to complete their cycles. For no history exceeds about 6,700 years in that count, to which they are nevertheless caught adding nearly 140 years just to defend their own arrangement of cycles. I think this has been sufficiently refuted even for those without expertise.

# On Astrology, Book V.

->SATURNIAN REVOLUTIONS, THE DISCOVERY OF ALBUMASAR,<-
->WHICH IS OPPOSED TO BOTH HISTORY AND REASON. Chapter III.<-

**T**here remains the matter of <term>Saturnian revolutions</term> <note>These are "planetary years" or cycles based on the orbital period of Saturn, which takes roughly 30 years to return to the same point in the zodiac.</note>. Indeed, Albumasar <note>original: "Albumasar," the Latinized name of Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), a highly influential Persian astrologer whose works were foundational to medieval European astrology.</note> seems to have been the only one to invent these, and those after him do not use them much. But let us see what they are, what motivated Albumasar, and how greatly he has wandered from the truth in these matters, as is his habit in others. When Saturn has completed ten periods, which are finished in nearly three hundred years, he believes that great events then occur in human affairs. He was moved by this conjecture because in his other histories he occasionally found that something remarkable happened after this number of years; from this, he established the dogma that ten revolutions of Saturn bring about a change in lower <note>earthly</note> things. 

But look at how much he erred in this very first historical conjecture. For he says that three hundred years after Alexander, Aielasor <note>A figure mentioned in medieval translations of Abu Ma'shar, possibly referring to an Artaxerxes or a Persian ruler.</note> the son of Bel appeared and crushed the Persians; and after another equal number of years, Jesus appeared, who is our leader. By this reasoning, therefore, there would be six hundred years from Jesus to Alexander, which is established beyond all controversy to be most false. For no history counts as many as four hundred years from Christ back to Alexander, and Alfonso <note>original: "Alphonsus," referring to King Alfonso X of Castile and the "Alphonsine Tables," the standard astronomical data of the late Middle Ages.</note> himself, in his astronomical tables, counts no more than three hundred and eleven. Let us now see how these principal authors of astrology support their miraculous dogmas with such foundations! 

The same Albumasar says that after Jesus, when ten Saturnian revolutions were completed, a law arose which is halfway between the Nazarenes and the Pagans <note>original: "Nazarenos & Paganos" — Pico uses "Nazarenes" for Christians and "Pagans" or "Gentiles" for non-Abrahamic peoples.</note> (for so they call the nations). But we certainly know that no law arose after Christ and before Muhammad; but I think those Arabs meant the sect of the Manichaeans <note>Manichaeism was a major dualist religion founded by the prophet Mani.</note>, who are also called <term>Minin</term> <note>original: "Minin" — a Hebrew term used in the Talmud to refer to heretics or sectarians, often applied to early Jewish-Christians or Manichaeans.</note> among the Talmudists; indeed, that heresy became powerful not only after ten revolutions were completed, but even before the ninth Saturnian revolution was finished. 

Even if he had brought these facts from faithful history, a dogma should not have been made from it—that ten periods of Saturn produce such results—otherwise I could devise a thousand such dogmas for myself. For the Hebrews say that the first temple built by Solomon lasted for four hundred years or a little more. Then, that the second, built under Darius, lasted no more than ten years beyond that—that is, four hundred and ten—and from its desolation for nearly as many years they devised their laws in Babylonia. From this, let us make a dogma: that every fourteenth Saturnian revolution brings a great change to the Saturnine race of the Jews <note>Saturn was traditionally associated with the Jewish people in medieval astrological thought.</note>. We would be saying things more probable than Albumasar, who chose the number ten for himself. 

I would also like to ask him: from where, by nature's law, do these revolutions begin? And under which part of the heaven will he start that period? I ask that he provide a reason why he preferred that starting point over the others. But we must not labor any longer in refuting these trifles, especially since they seem to have little satisfied other astrologers besides Albumasar; indeed, even Pierre d'Ailly <note>original: "Alliacensis," referring to Cardinal Pierre d’Ailly (1351–1420), who attempted to reconcile astrology with theology and history.</note>, who in his treatise *On the Concordance of History*...

history and astrology, and had used these things greatly, confessed in his *Elucidarium* <note>An "Elucidarium" is a type of explanatory handbook; Pico refers to an author who eventually admitted his astrological works were baseless.</note> that they have no foundation, and with a reversed pen <note>original: "everso stylo," a Latin idiom meaning to retract or rewrite one's previous opinions</note>, he corroded a great part of his own book with a newly discovered critique.

### THE ORDER OF THINGS TO BE DISCUSSED, AND THE
### disagreeing opinions of astrologers regarding great
### conjunctions. Chapter IV.

**I**t remains to discuss the approach and retreat of the eighth sphere and the ninth sphere <note>These refer to the celestial shells in the Ptolemaic model of the universe; the eighth sphere contains the fixed stars, and the ninth was often added to account for the wobbling movement called precession.</note>; it remains to discuss the great conjunctions, but let that former matter be examined in the following book. For now, let us turn to the great conjunctions. However, it would be worthwhile to first present what they themselves think about these things, so that what we bring forward in refutation may be more easily understood. This narration itself will not be without the benefit of refutation, as we shall see them disagree on these matters to such an extent that it is not yet clear among astrologers which is the greatest conjunction, which is the greater, and which is the middle. In this matter, the controversy is not merely about a name; from this arises a great diversity of predictions, as some command that events be expected from the greatest, others from the middle, and others from the minor conjunctions.

Therefore, the common opinion which Alchabitius <note>Al-Qabisi, a 10th-century Arab astrologer.</note> and Leopold <note>Leopold of Austria, a 13th-century astronomer and astrologer.</note> hand down, and before them Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar, the most influential Persian astrologer of the Middle Ages.</note>, is of this kind: a **Great Conjunction** occurs when Jupiter and Saturn are joined together, which happens every twenty years. A **Greater Conjunction**, however, occurs when a migration is made from one <term>triplicity</term> <note>The twelve signs of the zodiac are divided into four "triplicities" based on the elements: Fire, Earth, Air, and Water. A conjunction "migrates" when it shifts from one group of signs to another.</note> into another, meeting at the boundaries of a new triplicity; they say this happens approximately every two hundred and forty years. For within the limits of one <term>trigon</term> <note>Another term for a triplicity, forming a triangle on the zodiac wheel.</note>, the passage of the pairs occurs twelve times before moving to the sign of the next trigon—not the first, but the second from the one in which they joined. For example, if both departed from Capricorn, they do not first receive each other in Libra, but in Aquarius within that triplicity. 

The **Middle Conjunction** between these is said to be that which is completed every thirtieth year by Saturn and Mars in Cancer. The **Greatest Conjunction** of all is that of Jupiter and Saturn in Aries, which occurs after nine hundred and sixty years. Messahalla <note>Masha'allah ibn Athari (c. 740–815), a Persian-Jewish astrologer and astronomer.</note>, disagreeing with these men in his book on conjunctions, says that the **Greatest Conjunction** is that which consists of the three superior planets <note>The "superiors" are the planets further from the Sun than Earth: Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>—that is, Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars. From this, he expects the change of religious sects, the transfer of kingdoms, and the arrival of prophets, and not from that conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn in Aries which the common crowd of astrologers believes in. He makes the next conjunction after this that of Jupiter and Saturn; the third, Saturn and Mars; the fourth, Jupiter and Mars. Let us see now:
->how much each position errs.<-

<header>On Astrology, Book V.</header>

### THAT PLANETS JOINED IN GREAT CONJUNCTIONS
#### have no more power than when they are separate, and that these
#### great conjunctions are a new invention poorly 
#### understood from Ptolemy. Chapter V.

**F**irst, I would like to know from them why they think Jupiter and Saturn do more when they are together than when they are separate, since each performs and exercises their own individual powers. For while the mixing of rays of various natures does indeed create something new that a separate and individual influence would not, we cannot find a reason why it should be considered "greater." On the contrary, we are more inclined to believe that something lesser is produced than if each planet acted separately. For if the planets coming together were of the same property and had powers productive of the same effects, then surely by the addition of a double ray, the effect would also be doubled. But since they are of contrary and opposing natures—such as Jupiter and Saturn—one necessarily hinders the other. While they mutually restrain and bind their powers by the diversity of the mixture, it follows that we can expect nothing from them but the mediocre, just as all things are that result from the mixing of extremes. 

This is much like what the astrologers themselves are accustomed to say when Saturn and Mars are together: even though both are harmful and both become <term>malefic</term> <note>original: "maleficus"; in ancient astrology, planets like Saturn and Mars were classified as "malefic" because they were thought to cause harm or imbalance.</note>, because they have different ways of harming, no greater or extraordinary evil arises from their conjunction. Instead, the powers of one are broken and weakened by the other, so that neither can harm effectively while both strive to harm according to their own specific nature. Therefore, it is not at all certain—even if earthly events were subject to the heavens—that greater and more lasting things happen when the superior planets are joined than when one of them, while the others are weakened, perhaps gains a bit more strength and power than usual. 

Even if we were to grant them that planets joined do more than when separate regarding the great changes of this world, we will still not grant that this should be attributed to the conjunction of Jupiter, Saturn, or Mars. Instead, we will prove by both reason and the authority of the greatest astrologers that other stars possess the primary power in these matters. For none of the ancients ever judged universal changes in the world through these things which they call "great conjunctions." Maternus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer.</note> says nothing of them, though he was a most diligent investigator of astrology; neither does Paulus <note>Paulus Alexandrinus, a 4th-century author of an introductory work on astrology.</note>, nor Hephaistio <note>Hephaistio of Thebes, a 5th-century astrologer.</note>, nor Theophilus <note>Theophilus of Edessa, an 8th-century scholar and astrologer.</note>, nor Astaxarchus, nor Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the most influential astronomer and geographer of antiquity.</note> himself, whose testimony here will be enough for us, lest we use witnesses unknown to them. He, therefore, in the second book of his *Apotelesmaton* <note>Better known as the *Tetrabiblos*, Ptolemy's foundational work on the effects of the stars.</note>, teaching the way general and world changes are foreseen, refers them all solely to the <term>eclipses</term> <note>original: "defectus"; literally "failings" or "deficiencies" of the Sun and Moon.</note> of the Sun and Moon. Nothing more reasonable can be said, for universal and great effects ought to be referred to those causes which are the greatest, most universal, and most effective. It is admitted by all among...

...only two planets possess <term>universal efficiency</term> <note>original: "efficientiæ uniuersalis"; this refers to the power to cause general effects across the entire earth, rather than specific effects on individuals</note>, namely the Sun and the Moon; the Moon’s light is nothing other than the light of the Sun, brought down to earth through her as if through a mirror, so to speak. Therefore, if any celestial power ought to be considered the origin and cause of great and universal effects, none should be considered more so than these two luminaries. As for what <term>Masha'allah</term> <note>original: "Mesafalla"; an influential 8th-century Persian Jewish astrologer and astronomer</note> says—that great things are brought about by Jupiter and Saturn because they move more slowly—this actually proves the opposite of what he affirms. For it is the unanimous opinion of all that a swifter motion is owed to a nobler and more powerful body. On this point, those who defend the status and dignity of the higher stars—lest they be thought weaker because they return to their place in the zodiac more slowly—are accustomed to argue from the proportion of the circles they traverse. They claim these planets are actually swifter than many others, even though they appear slower due to the long duration of their orbits. 

But I know what they will say about <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the "Tetrabiblos," the foundational text of Western astrology</note>: that this was omitted by him in his book *Apotelesmaton* <note>original: "Apotelesmaton"; another name for Ptolemy's "Tetrabiblos"</note> so as not to betray the "mystery." This is what his commentator <term>Haly</term> <note>likely referring to Haly Abenragel or Ali ibn Ridwan, famous Arabic commentators on Ptolemy</note> writes. They claim that in the *Centiloquium* <note>original: "centiloquio"; literally "The Hundred Sayings," a collection of 100 astrological aphorisms falsely attributed to Ptolemy in the Middle Ages</note>, he provided many proofs of this matter. In the fiftieth aphorism of that book, he commands us not to forget the <term>conjunctions</term> <note>the alignment of two or more planets in the same degree of the zodiac</note> of the planets, in which there is great efficacy. Likewise, in both the fifty-eighth and sixty-fourth aphorisms, he warns us of the same things, handing down great precepts concerning them and distinguishing between the "greatest," "middle," and "least" conjunctions. 

I, however, would want nothing more than for them to answer for this, so that it might become clear to everyone that whatever of their dogmas seem greater and more admirable have sprouted either from vain opinions or from a false understanding of ancient authors. For as to their claim that Ptolemy remained silent about this in the *Apotelesmaton* so as not to betray a mystery: I do not deny he was silent, but I do not believe he betrayed any such thing in the *Centiloquium* either. Certainly, he spoke no more of those conjunctions there than he did of the death of Priam or the Trojan War. We shall reveal later how they have perverted many of that author’s pronouncements and how many subsequent errors have been propagated from a single mistake. 

Ptolemy’s fiftieth aphorism, as it appears among them (that is, in the common <note>Latin</note> edition), says: *Do not forget that there are one hundred and twenty conjunctions among the wandering stars <note>the planets</note>; for in them is the greatest knowledge of things that happen in this world, which experience increase and decrease.* In the <note>original</note> **Greek**, it is written thus: *Let us not overlook the one hundred and nineteen conjunctions. For in these is placed the union of those things which occur in the world of generation and corruption.* <note>original: "generationis & corruptionis"; a standard Aristotelian phrase for the physical world where things are born, change, and die</note> 

First of all, the "barbaric" <note>Arabic/Latin</note> translation attributes more to these conjunctions than Ptolemy does; in his version, it is not said that there is no "greater knowledge" of worldly events than what comes from them. Furthermore, setting that aside, the meaning of the statement is simply that we should not look at the property of a single star alone. Rather, we should know that various powers, producing various things, arise from their conjunction—a fact that no one denies and which is agreed upon by all **astrologers**.

...we must yield, but <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the foundational astrological text, the *Tetrabiblos*</note> certainly did not say that we should attribute the greatest changes in lower things primarily to the conjunctions of the higher stars. Indeed, if his words are read and understood correctly, they will indicate to us the opposite opinion. For he did not say there are one hundred and twenty of these conjunctions (as is commonly read), but only one hundred and nineteen. This is because he does not count the <term>conjunction of the Sun and Moon</term> among them; since these have peculiar privileges and a unique prerogative in great and universal changes, he groups all the rest together into a numbered order, as if none among them were superior to another by any special condition. 

The <term>barbarian expositors</term> <note>original: "barbari expositores"; Pico’s dismissive term for medieval Arabic and Latin commentators who did not work from the original Greek</note>, not noticing this and assuming it was an omission caused by a scribe's error, added the <term>conjunction of the Sun and Moon</term> back in. They believed the text should read "one hundred and twenty" rather than "one hundred and nineteen," which is what all the Greek manuscripts actually have. Thus, not content with corrupting the meaning, they also falsified the physical text.

Let us move on to other matters. <term>Ptolemy</term> writes in Aphorism 58 <note>original: "uerbo. 58"; referring to the *Centiloquium*, a collection of 100 astrological sayings long attributed to Ptolemy, though Pico is skeptical of its transmission</note> in this manner: "Look at the place of the conjunction, and in what place it falls relative to the Ascendant of the year; for when the <term>profection</term> <note>an astrological technique where a point, like the Ascendant, is moved forward through the zodiac at a set rate to determine the timing of events</note> reaches that place, then will be the time [of the event]." And in Aphorism 64: "In the smallest conjunction is the difference of the mean conjunction, and in the mean is the difference of the greatest conjunction." 

The <term>Arabs</term> and <term>Latins</term> <note>referring to the medieval Islamic and Western European astrological traditions</note> think that in both instances, <term>Ptolemy</term> means the conjunction of <term>Saturn</term> and <term>Jupiter</term>. But no one would be so deceived if they had ever read the Greek astrological authors—and especially <term>Ptolemy</term>—with open eyes. For what we call a "conjunction," in Greek is <term>synodos</term> <note>original: "σύνοδος"</note>. When this word is used on its own, it is always understood to mean the union of the <term>Sun</term> and <term>Moon</term>, unless it is specified which conjunction it is, such as <term>Venus</term> and <term>Mercury</term>, <term>Jupiter</term> and <term>Saturn</term>, or other planets. 

Therefore, since <term>Ptolemy</term> used the word <term>synodos</term> <note>conjunction</note> on its own in both statements without adding anything further, it is perfectly obvious to anyone not entirely unfamiliar with reading Greek that <term>Ptolemy</term> is speaking of the <term>conjunction of the luminaries</term> <note>the Sun and the Moon</note>, and not of the other stars. 

And so, the meaning of the first statement (the 58th aphorism) is this: once the sign and place where the <term>conjunction of the Sun and Moon</term> occurred in the revolution of the year has been carefully observed, we should expect the effect when the "profection" of the year (distributed by the months of the year, through which one sign succeeds another in power according to the order of the zodiac) reaches that place. This is because the <term>conjunction of the Sun and Moon</term> that preceded the year's turning signifies the events to us. Indeed, <term>Ptolemy</term> uses these meetings of the luminaries above all else to investigate the outcome of the entire year, as anyone knows who has turned the pages of his <term>Apotelefmaticos</term> <note>original: "Apotelefmaticos"; another name for Ptolemy's *Tetrabiblos* or *Four Books*</note>. 

However, in the translation of this aphorism, many things have been added, omitted, and altered. For they read "minor conjunction" for "conjunction," even though no distinction between "greater" or "minor" is added in the Greek manuscripts; and they extend the term of the "profection" to several years, even though there is nothing about this in <term>Ptolemy</term>, who (as we were saying) only mentions the events of a single year—though the text seems to favor them more [in their view]. Finally, that statement where the "greatest conjunctions"...

...are distinguished as middle and smallest. Many do not understand this distinction regarding the <term>conjunction of the luminaries</term> <note>The "luminaries" are the Sun and the Moon.</note>, but it is easy and clear to those who have occasionally stayed awake by the lamp of <term>Ptolemy</term> without yawning. For since he, as we said, attributes everything to the conjunctions of the Sun and Moon, he distinguishes them into three types and orders.

For those which cause an <term>eclipse</term> <note>original: "defectum"; literally a failure or lack of light.</note> of either luminary, they place in the first rank; through these, the events of not just one year, but sometimes of many years, can be foreseen. We shall call these the **greatest** [conjunctions] because the stars are most closely joined then—differing in neither <term>longitude</term> nor <term>latitude</term>—and they portend the most distant future events.

On the other hand, the **smallest** for him are those that occur every month, which indicate to us the disposition of only a single month.

The **middle** ones between these are those which immediately precede the Sun’s entry into the four <term>tropical signs</term>: **Aries, Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn**. From these, the entire following season of the year is indicated to us—be it spring, summer, autumn, or winter. 

Therefore, since the following particular disposition distinguishes and determines what the universal disposition indicates, he said that the **middle** conjunction is the **variation** of the **greatest**, and the **smallest** is the variation of the **middle**. For example, if a conjunction of the Moon and Sun immediately preceding the spring equinox shows us the coming quality of spring, we should know that this whole quality is both diminished and increased according to the nature of the conjunctions that occur in each following month in their fixed revolution. And whatever relationship these monthly conjunctions have to those four seasonal conjunctions, those three-month conjunctions have the same relationship to the **greatest** and rare meetings and unions of the eclipsing stars. 

This is Ptolemy’s opinion on the **greatest, middle, and smallest conjunctions**. Not understanding this, those <term>barbarians</term> <note>Pico's term for medieval Arabic and Latin astrologers like Albumasar.</note> have fabricated beautiful dreams for themselves about the **conjunctions of Saturn and Jupiter**. They claim the **greatest** of these return after 960 years, the **middle** after 240, and the **smallest** after 20 years. 

This cannot even agree with what has been stated, because for them, the "greatest" conjunction encompasses the middle and smallest ones; therefore, the effect of the greatest conjunction cannot be determined by those smaller ones through which it is carried out over many revolutions of the centuries. Why then did Ptolemy say the **middle** is the **variation** of the **greatest**, and the **smallest** the variation of the **middle**? 

This is that fiction, born from the false understanding of a single author, which these men boast of so much. It is the basis upon which they boastfully consider that **every religion is bound to the stars**. By this, they subject the most holy laws, the coming of prophets, and divine miracles to the powers of the stars and the fates. Certainly, in no other place do they show themselves to be more childish, or are they found to be more ignorant and ridiculous.

## THAT THE PRINCIPAL ASTROLOGERS USED MEAN
## CONJUNCTIONS RATHER THAN TRUE ONES, AND OTHER ERRORS
## OF THEIRS CONCERNING THE SAME. CHAPTER VI.

But perhaps one of the astrologers will say: "Suppose we did not understand Ptolemy. What if, just as a storm sometimes drives a ship into harbor <note>original: "uelut tempeftas nauem aliquando agit in portū"</note>, this very error of ours has led us to the truth?" They argue that whatever Ptolemy or others may have thought, experience confirms that no great change in laws or kingdoms has ever occurred that was not preceded by a conjunction of the **superior stars** <note>The "superior stars" refers to the planets further from the Sun than Earth: Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>, nor has any such conjunction ever occurred without such changes in earthly affairs following afterward. It is well if they recognize the "storm"; we shall soon see if they are actually in that "harbor." For even if they have raved about great matters, they have not yet attempted to show how well these lowest things stand up to the test of experience. 

We shall first declare this in general, and then we will show more clearly than the sun that every "great conjunction" any astrologer has ever marked—and linked to wonderful events—is false, falsely calculated, and falsely related to its effects. To begin with, all authors of this doctrine do not use true conjunctions, but "mean" ones—that is, fictional and imaginary ones. So that everyone may understand this plainly, I will explain what "true motion" is and what "mean motion" is. <term>Wandering stars</term> <note>original: "Erraticæ ftellæ"; the planets.</note> do not travel through the Zodiac at a steady pace; that is, they do not always cross equal parts of it in equal intervals of time. Therefore, those who wished to measure their movements and reduce them to numbers invented a uniform motion for each planet. They did this so that from this fictional, uniform motion, they might more easily track that unequal, true motion. 

<term>Ptolemy</term> calls this fictional motion "periodic," while more recent writers call it <term>mean</term> motion, because they use it as a "middle way" to investigate the truth. When we search for a planet's location through calculation, we sometimes use this mean motion—not because that "mean" location shows us where the planet actually stands, but so that we may seek its true seat from there by an easier method and logic. For a planet is never actually where it is found to be through mean motion; it never moves in such a way. As I said, this was devised by astronomers so they could reach the truth with more certain order. 

I was saying, therefore, that those who judge the future by <term>great conjunctions</term> use these mean conjunctions, not true ones. For when they say that **Jupiter and Saturn** are joined after 20 years, or that they meet at the beginning of the <term>triplicities</term> <note>A "triplicity" is a group of three Zodiac signs associated with one of the four elements: Fire, Earth, Air, or Water.</note> after 200 years, or finally that they meet at the borders of **Aries** after 860 years—this is utterly false if we look at their true movements. It is only true (though not exactly so) if we look at those "means"—that is, those fictional and false motions which were devised by mathematicians solely for the ease of teaching, but which have no reality. Moreover, what the mean motion says is so different from what we reach through the true motion that even the Zodiac sign of the conjunction may change. For example, a conjunction might be assigned to **Pisces** when it actually occurred in **Aquarius**; and the time varies so much that if we are discussing events that happen after 240 years...

conjunctions, the true one sometimes precedes the <term>mean</term><note>In pre-modern astronomy, the "mean" position is a mathematical average of a planet's speed, while the "true" position is its actual location in the sky at a specific moment.</note> one by as much as a hundred years. It appears from the astronomical tables to anyone calculating correctly that in the year of grace 1226, Jupiter and Saturn, migrating from the <term>earthly triplicity</term><note>A "triplicity" is a group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element. The "earthly" signs are Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn; "aerial" are Gemini, Libra, and Aquarius.</note> to the aerial one, met in Aquarius. According to the logic of mean motion, they were supposed to remain in that same element for two hundred and forty years; and yet, after about a hundred and forty years—that is, in the year of grace 1345—they met in Scorpio, having made a shift from the aerial to the <term>watery triplicity</term><note>The watery signs are Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces.</note>. Having been found together always in watery signs thereafter, they did not return to the aerial ones. 

What insanity is this, then, to fight against the open truth and to use things so shamelessly false and fictional? With blind recklessness, they refer the events of human affairs to a constellation that they cannot even agree upon. To think that something which is not, nor was, nor ever will be, is the cause of things that actually exist—certainly nothing is more delusional than that vanity. Yet all the principal authors of astrology have fallen into it. 

**Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), a highly influential Persian astrologer.</note>, the prince of this doctrine, in that book titled *On the Great Conjunctions* <note>original: "de magnis coniunctionibus"</note>—which is much celebrated among astrologers—always used mean conjunctions and never true ones. **Abraham** <note>Likely Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a Jewish polymath and astrologer.</note>, moreover, in that work titled *Redemption* <note>original: "Redemptio"</note>, though he might investigate one or two conjunctions based on true motion, always flees back to the mean ones, making no mention of the true ones at all. **Alliacensis** <note>Pierre d’Ailly (1350–1420), a French cardinal who attempted to reconcile astrology with biblical history.</note>, in his treatise *On the Concordance of History and Astrology* <note>original: "de concordia historiæ & Astrologiæ"</note>, although he cites seven "greatest conjunctions," cites them all as mean and none as true. Many others do the same, always suffering from this same disease, whom we shall discuss individually later. 

And indeed, these points could suffice for us to show that their claims are worthless, since the very constellation from which they predict does not exist. However, since these mean positions—which is to say, non-existent ones—do not correspond to the truth (that is, they do not fall at the times the astrologers would most like), they engineer another refuge for themselves, defending their prior insanity with a new stupidity. 

For they have imagined that what they portend does not follow immediately after those conjunctions; rather, they say it happens not quickly, but after many years—a hundred, two hundred, or even more. See how greatly they are deceived in this: for it is not the nature of a powerful and effective cause to start what it is going to do so late. It should end late, certainly, but it should begin either immediately or quickly. Therefore, the power of these conjunctions is either effective or weak. If it is effective, it cannot cease from acting for a long time; if it is weak, it cannot last long enough to act late. A great force tames and overcomes whatever prohibits or resists it; a weak force vanishes and dissolves its own thinness over a long stretch of time. 

Furthermore, in this interval of time, new conjunctions always intervene. Their nature, as the astrologers themselves say, is to obliterate the previous ones, since a succeeding constellation destroys the preceding one. This is why, if an eclipse of the luminaries occurs at an uncertain time of the year, they are accustomed to say that the fate which was received from the beginnings of the annual revolution has ceased. Why, therefore, should the same not happen with a following conjunction, especially...

...especially since it ceases because of a different property and nature? Why would it not wipe out that first one? Yet to that first conjunction they want to attribute effects which follow even three hundred years later, through so many various intervening middle constellations. No one would say this—neither a philosopher nor even a man not of the extreme sluggishness <note>Pico uses "tarditatis" to imply a slow-witted or dull person.</note> of mind. This error is increased in a wonderful way by another inexpiable error: for in the calculation of times itself, they err so remarkably that a conjunction they sometimes think preceded some event by, for example, two hundred years, actually preceded the time of that deed by one thousand four hundred years—as will be demonstrated in the following chapters of this book. In these matters indeed they are caught as liars, unlearned, and ignorant. 

But see also how clever these fine diviners are; for lest the opportunity for deceiving ever fail them, they have so linked their doctrines that at whatever time something a bit more wonderful happened, they could refer it back to some preceding conjunction. For they said, so as to achieve this, that the power of one conjunction lasts right up to the hour of the next; and thus whatever occurs in the middle can always be referred to some conjunction as its cause. Nor did they see their own ruin in this fallacy: because if they hold that there is no great effect without a great conjunction, and no great conjunction appears without an effect, while they maintain this so that such causes are never missing from such events, they necessarily make it so that such causes are often exhausted without any such events. This is because great and wonderful things do not always happen from them; indeed, those things they claim happen from "great conjunctions" do not even occur frequently. And yet, as they themselves wish, the power that produces these effects remains always uninterrupted through the succession of time. These arguments are directed generally against those who speak of future events from these great conjunctions with impious recklessness; now let us examine everything individually.

## WHAT ORDER IS TO BE OBSERVED, AND THAT D'AILLY HELD DIFFERENT OPINIONS AT DIFFERENT TIMES. Chapter VII.

**L**et us begin from the greatest conjunctions which <term>Pierre d’Ailly</term><note>Latin: *Alliacensis* (1351–1420). A French cardinal and influential scholar who sought to harmonize astrology with theology and history.</note> collects in his treatise on the <term>Concordance of History and Astrology</term>. From this, he intended to confirm that the conjunctions described by astrologers never occur without a great change in the affairs of the world below. And indeed, he himself disagrees with all this "concordance" of his in his <term>Elucidarium</term><note>Latin: *Elucidarium astronomicae concordiae*. A later work where d'Ailly attempted to clarify or revise his earlier astrological-historical theories.</note>; for although in that work he makes use of both Saturnian revolutions <note>The cycle of the planet Saturn, often used in medieval astrology to time major political or religious shifts.</note> and the "greatest conjunctions," he openly confesses—just once—that the former have no foundation and the latter were not calculated by him. 

This makes it all the more surprising that he has a praiser in a matter which he himself did not approve of. But because he sometimes raised arguments against himself that were hardly true (since some are not necessary and several are poorly expressed), let us collect a few but effective points by which that entire treatise may be clearly dismantled; then we shall approach...

...we shall proceed to refute the other conjunctions <term>conjunctions<gloss>the alignment of two or more planets in the same sign of the zodiac</gloss></term> which Abraham <note>likely Abraham Avenezra</note>, Albumasar, and many others—and following them, d'Ailly himself in his *Elucidarium*—have put forward. But since we must often speak regarding the calculation of times, I thought it necessary to preface certain things. From these, it may first be shown that when the timing of events is in doubt, it is not (as d'Ailly thinks) within the judgment of astrologers to decide the matter, but rather within the domain of history. Furthermore, when there is a discrepancy among historical writers, we must determine which of them should most rightfully be followed. We will touch upon these matters briefly and in passing here, since we have discussed them extensively in a special work we wrote on the *True Calculation of Times*.

### THE TIMING OF EVENTS IS TO BE SOUGHT NOT FROM ASTROLOGY, AS
### d'Ailly thought, BUT FROM HISTORY. Chapter VIII.

**A**lliacensis <note>Pierre d'Ailly (1350–1420), a French Cardinal and scholar who attempted to harmonize astrology with theology</note> in his book *On the Concordance of Astrology and Theology* thinks the number of years from the beginning of the world to our own times can be discovered and brought to the truth by astrological reasoning—even those dates which various sacred or foreign histories have reported differently. For he says that if you have the birth chart <term>thema<gloss>a horoscope or map of the heavens at a specific moment</gloss></term> of the world itself fully investigated, you will be able to gather by calculation the first conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter from the world's beginning. If you then search for another conjunction closest to your own years, the interval of time that falls in the middle between that first and last conjunction will be drawn out from the calculation of the intervening conjunctions. 

He indeed held these views at that time, but in his *Elucidarium* <note>The *Elucidarium Astronomice Concordie*, a later work by d'Ailly</note> he plainly confessed that there is no astrological way for us to find anything certain regarding a doubtful number of years. Therefore, he notes that not even the greatest astrologers ever attempted this or promised it from their art. But since he says this, I do not know why he persists again in that opinion: that the supreme question concerning the reckoning of times should be referred to astrologers, and that whatever is found in histories concerning the age of the world that differs from them ought to be amended and corrected according to their opinion. 

We shall briefly show that this can be defended by no logic. For an astronomer can indeed—if he has one true position of the stars from the past and another recent one—determine by most certain reasoning how much time must necessarily have passed between them. But how will this help him? Is it not the timing <margin>}</margin> of the actual historical event that is uncertain? For suppose someone says three thousand years have flowed from Christ to us, and another says 1400 years. In settling this dispute, what will be the duty of the astronomer? You will say he will show that between the position of the stars under which Christ was born and the position held now, three thousand years could not have passed, but only one thousand four hundred. 

But what slowness of mind is this? What dullness, that you do not see that you are taking as a certainty the very thing which is under question? For the astrologer does not know the position of the stars under which Christ was born unless he first receives from history the time at which He was born. Let us move on to more remote times.

<summary>Pico argues that astrology cannot be used to determine or correct historical dates, as astrologers rely on historical records to know when past celestial configurations occurred. He specifically critiques Pierre d'Ailly's shifting stance on whether astrology can calculate the age of the world.</summary>

## on Astrology, Book V.

Alfonso <note>Alfonso X of Castile (1221–1284), sponsor of the "Alfonsine Tables" used for astronomical calculations</note> counts three thousand one hundred and two years from the Deluge <note>the Great Flood of Noah</note> to Christ. Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a highly influential Persian astrologer</note>, whom Alfonso followed, holds the same view. All of history contradicts this number, yet d'Ailly <note>Pierre d’Ailly (Alliacensis)</note> thinks all histories err rather than the astrologers. By what reasoning, I ask? Is it because the time between the conjunction <term>conjunction<gloss>the meeting of planets in the same part of the sky</gloss></term> that preceded the Deluge and the birth of Christ spans that many years? No one denies them that calculation, but from where did they learn that this conjunction occurred exactly as many years before the Deluge as they think? Could they have known this from any source other than history? Truly, this is so manifest that unless I had seen d’Ailly’s error here, I would think I was wasting words on a superfluous matter. 

For how ridiculous was the opinion of those who said we could be made certain about the years of the world from the first conjunction at the beginning of the world! They derived that "first conjunction" from the horoscope of the world <note>original: "mundi genitura," a theoretical birth-chart for the universe</note> as if we could doubt the age of the world—we who have found out not only in what year, but even at what hour it began! <note>Pico refers here to the biblical account of Creation</note> Therefore, no one should doubt that the timing of events must be sought from history, the "mistress of things"; in this matter, Astronomy, her disciple, cannot be the judge. 

For I will grant Alfonso that so many thousands of years before Christ there was such a position of the stars as appears from his tables; but I will not grant that a cataclysm <note>the Flood</note> or any other historical deed occurred at those times, unless a faithful history demonstrates this to me. All astronomers have erred vehemently in this calculation of times (which will become more manifest in its own place), and this could have happened to them for no other reason than that they adhered to false histories. For Latin astronomers followed the Arabs, and they are the most prone to fables. If the Arabs received any histories from Greek or Latin writers, foreign translation violated most of them. This happens easily in every subject among barbarians who abhor literature, but it happens most easily in the notation of numbers, where even the most accurate diligence of scribes almost always hallucinates to some degree. 

Therefore, one must use true and faithful histories, among which no Christian will doubt that the Sacred history <note>the Bible</note> is to be preferred to others. Indeed, neither would a Hebrew nor a Saracen <note>a term used in the Renaissance for Muslims</note> doubt this. Furthermore, regarding those things which happened before the cataclysm, the nations will have either this Mosaic history or no history at all to follow, since among other peoples nothing regarding those times has been handed down in writing. 

But if in the sacred volumes the Greek edition <note>the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> disagrees with the Hebrew truth <note>original: "Hebraica veritate," a term used by scholars like Jerome to argue for the priority of the original Hebrew text over translations</note> in this measurement of years, no one of right judgment can prefer the reliability of the translator over the author himself. This is especially true since not only does Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420), who translated the Latin Vulgate from the Hebrew</note> side with the Hebrew number, but even Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430)</note> thinks one should side with them. Although Augustine willingly follows and approves the old translation, nevertheless, where he mentions this varying counting of years, he says that the reliability of historical deeds must be sought from that language from which our version was translated. And so, just as Augustine wishes, he might consider what is different in the "Seventy" <note>the 70 translators of the Septuagint</note> to be a mystery rather than an error, yet he does not doubt that the truth of the history—that is, the literal word—is found among the Hebrews.

<summary>Pico argues that astrology is dependent on history for its data, refuting the idea that planetary cycles can "correct" historical dates. He asserts that the Hebrew biblical text is the only reliable source for early human chronology, dismissing the calculations of Arab astronomers and their Latin followers.</summary>

# SUMMARY OF THE OPINION OF D'AILLY IN THE BOOK WHICH HE TITLED "ON THE CONCORDANCE OF ASTROLOGY AND HISTORY." CHAPTER IX.

Now that we have briefly laid these foundations regarding the true calculation of time, let us come to those "greatest conjunctions" <term>greatest conjunctions<gloss>The rare meeting of Saturn and Jupiter that occurs roughly every 960 years, believed by astrologers to signal major historical shifts</gloss></term> of the astrologers—or rather, to their greatest follies. We shall begin with those which d'Ailly <note>Pierre d'Ailly (1351–1420), a French cardinal and influential scholar who tried to reconcile astrology with Christian history</note> collected in his treatise *On the Concordance of History and Astrology*. In that work, he followed this order: he assumes two principles, one regarding the number of years from Adam to Christ, and the other regarding the <term>horoscope of the world<gloss>original: "themate genituræ ipsius mundi," a theoretical birth chart calculated for the moment of creation</gloss></term>. He says that 5,344 years passed from Adam to Jesus; specifically, 2,242 years from Adam to the Deluge <note>the Great Flood of Noah</note>, and 3,102 years from the Deluge to Jesus. 

In the first constitution of the world, he claims the stars were positioned in the heavens thus: the <term>ascendant<gloss>the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon; original: "horoscopum"</gloss></term> was the first degree of Cancer, while the highest peak of heaven <note>the Midheaven</note> possessed the first degree of Aries. Mercury was in the 15th degree of Gemini in the twelfth house of heaven; Venus occupied the eleventh house in Taurus; both luminaries <note>the Sun and Moon</note> were also placed: the nocturnal one <note>the Moon</note> in Taurus, and the diurnal one <note>the Sun</note> shone at the 19th degree of Aries in the middle and highest point of heaven. Saturn was in Aquarius in the house of death <note>the 8th house</note>; Jupiter held the ninth place of heaven in Pisces; Mars stayed in Scorpio in the fifth house from the ascendant. In that same place, but in Sagittarius, was the Dragon's Tail <note>the South Node of the Moon, traditionally considered a point of negative influence</note>. You can visualize this entire arrangement for yourself as a drawn figure. 

With these points established, he concludes with no effort that the first "greatest conjunction" of Saturn and Jupiter since the beginning of the world occurred at the start of Aries after 320 years. After this, he enumerates six others with intervals of 960 years between them (due to the error of mean motion). Thus, he follows that the seventh greatest conjunction since the beginning of the world occurred in the year of grace 735. After that, the eighth will follow in the year 1693. Having distributed them this way, he gathers from histories the headings of the most memorable events that occurred in those middle spaces of time—that is, the 960 years required between one greatest conjunction and another. In this interval of time, whatever notable or memorable thing happened, he thinks it must be referred back to the preceding conjunction. And because he always finds some great and memorable deed performed in this span of years, he considers it confirmed that these greatest conjunctions do not happen without a very great change in earthly affairs. He believes he has fulfilled what he promised in another book: to show that the truth of history harmonizes with astrological truth. This is the summary of the whole book, this its order, and this its foundation.

# THAT D'AILLY ERRED IN MANY WAYS, AND EVEN IF EVERYTHING HE SUPPOSES WERE GRANTED, HE STILL DOES NOT ACHIEVE WHAT HE INTENDS. CHAPTER X.

At the start, even if we allow that it is so regarding the conjunctions, the timing of events and deeds, the birth-chart of the world—and even if we finally grant him everything he demands—what kind of "confirmation of astrology through history" is this, pray tell? Especially if we show that those 960 years never passed...

[and] sixty <note>referring to the 960-year cycle of the "greatest conjunctions" of Saturn and Jupiter mentioned on the previous page</note>, without the world having seen some great mutation of created things or a change in the human condition. Describe this span of years, I ask you, from other starting points; for instance, do not start from the year of the world 320 (which was the time of the first conjunction), but from the year 500 of the world, and count those nine hundred years which revolve from one conjunction to another. You will find just as many various wars, and laws, and prophets, and pestilences, and a diverse and varied kind of events occurring in that long stretch of time. Why did you not always trace the series of these actions back through intervals of two hundred years from the time of that conjunction of yours?

This is a far too **clumsy effort** <note>original: "pinguis hic nimis Minerva," a Latin idiom meaning a crude or unrefined approach lacking intellectual subtlety</note> if we are to harmonize astrology with history in this way. But neither were those conjunctions "true," but "mean"—that is, false and non-existent <note>"True" conjunctions are the actual visual meetings of planets; "mean" conjunctions are theoretical averages used in older astronomical tables that did not always match reality</note>; and even if we were to accept them as "mean," they should not be applied to those times. Nor is the number of years from Adam to Christ what he thought it was, but it exceeds the true calculation by more than one thousand four hundred years; nor did those deeds or events occur at the times he thought they did. Moreover, the <term>birth chart of the world<gloss>original: "mundi genituram," a horoscope cast for the moment of creation</gloss></term> which he describes is not only doubtful or false, but is clearly demonstrated to be impossible by astrological reasoning.

For this reason, that entire little book could be corrected with a single strike of the pen. No one is ignorant—nor does he himself deny—that those conjunctions were "mean" rather than "true." But if the world's birth chart, from which all others are derived, is necessarily impossible, and if that chart is calculated falsely even according to "mean" motion—well, we would like **Mercury** to interpret for you whether that is impossible! For in that figure <note>the horoscope of the world</note>, Mercury is placed fifty-six degrees away from the **Sun**; yet Mercury would swear by all the gods and goddesses that he has never strayed even a finger's breadth beyond twenty-nine degrees from the Sun <note>In reality, Mercury is never seen more than about 28 degrees from the Sun; d'Ailly's chart is physically impossible according to the laws of astronomy</note>. This is an error all too evident and unpardonable.

He also considers that to be the primordial figure of the world which **d'Ailly** <note>Pierre d'Ailly (1351–1420), referred to here by his Latin name Alliacensis</note> presents in his *Elucidarium*, a work burdened with marvelous illusions. For he attributes it to the **Chaldeans** and **Ishmaelites**, whom he claims Divinity made privy to this mystery. In that chart, **Mercury** is placed in the first part of **Gemini**, and the **Sun** in the first part of **Aries**; thus it happens that Mercury is separated from the Sun by sixty degrees, which no astronomer will deny is plainly impossible.

But let us return to those conjunctions which (as I was saying) are found to be false and impossible under that broad first figure of heaven from which all were gathered. To this is added the fact that even after nine hundred years there is no conjunction in **Aries**, as **Abraham the Spaniard** <note>Abraham bar Hiyya (c. 1070–1136), a Jewish mathematician and astronomer</note> teaches in his sixth book, the title of which is *The Redemption of Israel* <note>original: "Redemptio Israël"</note>. Furthermore, the events he relates to those times did not happen when he thinks they did. For from the beginning of the world to the Deluge there were not two thousand two hundred and forty-two years, as he reports, but one thousand six hundred and fifty-six, as will be shown later. Therefore, that third "greatest conjunction"—which he says preceded the Deluge by two years, occurring 2,240 years from the constitution of the world—actually took place six hundred and eighty-four years *after* the Deluge itself. Likewise, in the nine hundred and forty-second year after the Deluge, the fourth...

...he notes the greatest conjunction, and says that the patriarch Abraham was born sixteen years before it. From this number, even the Latin historians who calculated the most years still fell short of that lesser number by more than one hundred and forty years.

In reality, their heresy arose nearly in the three-hundredth year of grace, and by the year 600, it no longer existed. Regarding these matters, I believe we have argued using sufficiently, and if I am not mistaken, evident testimonies.

### On Astrology, Book V.

Jupiter and Saturn were in the fourteenth degree of Cancer, while the beginning of Aries was in the horoscope <note>the ascendant, or the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</note>, with both stars placed together in the fourth region of the sky <note>the fourth astrological house, associated with the depths of the earth and the end of things</note>. Aoniar wrote this in his *Book of Nativities*, and the common crowd of later writers for the most part followed his opinion. Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar, a 9th-century Persian astrologer</note> noted this conjunction eight years earlier—that is, two hundred and eighty-seven years before the Flood—and Henry, his interpreter, also followed this. However, since the same Albumasar says that this conjunction preceded the conjunction signifying the "sect of the Arabs" <note>the rise of Islam</note> by three thousand nine hundred and fifty-eight years, Henry contradicts him, relying on the Machlivian tables <note>likely referring to tables by Al-Majriti or a similar Arabic source</note>. By the numbers in these tables, Henry says he discovered that in the year Albumasar claimed they were joined, there was actually an interval of four signs between Saturn and Jupiter. But calculating more carefully, he says he found that conjunction occurred three thousand nine hundred and fifty-one years before the "Arabian constellation." Furthermore, while this Henry says they were joined in the fourth degree of Cancer, others using the Alfonsine tables <note>astronomical tables compiled in Toledo under King Alfonso X</note> contend they were joined in the fourteenth degree of that sign.

But let us dismiss these disagreements and show how they all equally depart from the truth. For whether we use the tables of King Alfonso or those Machlivian ones, when we calculate backward from the time of Christ to explain the beginnings of celestial motions, we find that this conjunction occurred in the year (as Henry says) 3,352 before Christ—a number from which others vary by only a few months. We, however, demonstrated in the previous chapter that a true calculation shows there are a little more than two thousand three hundred years from the Flood to Christ. Therefore, that conjunction preceded the Cataclysm <note>the Great Flood</note> not by two hundred and eighty years, as they claim, but by one thousand and eighty-two years. What, then, does that conjunction have to do with the Cataclysm? For I do not think they would extend the influence of that conjunction over so many years.

But let us grant them that it preceded the Flood by no more years than they wish, and at the very times they think the Flood occurred; do you believe they will achieve what they intend? Even if we grant them these points, they are nonetheless false, empty, and ridiculous. For even if Saturn and Jupiter were joined in Cancer, did the world perish submerged in a flood of waters for that reason? Yet more than ten times since then they have been together in the same sign, and the world did not perish; indeed, not even a single region was submerged in water because of it, let alone the entire world. It is a rare event, great and admirable, but what, I ask, does the conjunction itself have of such a nature? For it returned more often afterwards (as I was saying), and whether we agree with the opinion of Messahala <note>Ma'shallah ibn Athari, a prominent 8th-century Persian-Jewish astrologer</note> or others, it would not be counted among the "greatest" nor even the "greater" conjunctions. Since only two stars are joined in it, and not at the beginning of the signs (that is, in Aries), nor at the start of any triplicity <note>a group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element, such as water or fire</note>, why then should it be considered unique? Why should it be thought the cause of such a wonderful effect, never seen since, and surpassing all belief?

<summary>Pico exposes the chronological and astronomical inconsistencies among astrologers like Albumasar and Henry regarding the planetary conjunction supposed to have caused the Great Flood. He argues that since such conjunctions happen regularly without causing global disasters, they cannot be the cause of the biblical Deluge.</summary>

<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

...is thought. Why, and for what reason, should its power be considered to have lasted so long—that is, for two hundred and seventy-nine years? For if you say that events occurring at the beginning of a <term>triplicity</term> <note>In astrology, a 'triplicity' is a group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element: Fire, Earth, Air, or Water.</note> have an influence that lasts until the beginning of the next one, you are saying something false and already disproved by us above; yet, it is perhaps consistent with your own dogmas. But to say this about a conjunction that happens in the middle of a sign agrees neither with our truth nor even with your own vanity, since you usually derive their power and significance for no more than twenty years. 

Furthermore, since that conjunction occurred almost in the middle of Cancer <note>a water sign</note>, there still remained 120 years (calculating by the ratio of mean motion) before Saturn and Jupiter would turn from the watery triplicity to the fiery one. Therefore, if that coupling in Cancer preceded the flood by so many years—that is, by two hundred and seventy-nine—it follows that the inundation of the world occurred in the middle of a fiery triplicity. The superior stars <note>Saturn and Jupiter</note> had migrated into this fiery triplicity one hundred and fifty-nine years before the cataclysm, and they would remain in it for 120 years after the submersion of the world.

However, if we use the **Alfonsine Tables** <note>The *Tabulae Alphonsinae*, a set of astronomical tables providing data for computing the positions of the sun, moon, and planets, extremely influential in the Middle Ages.</note> and resolve the years from our own time back to the beginning of the world, we can calculate from the time of Christ back to the Flood. According to their opinion, we find three thousand one hundred and ten years. In that period, we find a "mean conjunction" of Jupiter and Saturn in the nineteenth degree of Sagittarius <note>a fire sign</note> two years and twenty-one days before the Flood. Before that, there was a "true conjunction" in the fourteenth degree of the same sign, twenty-one years and three hundred and thirty-seven days before the Flood. 

Likewise, we find a mean conjunction of the same planets in the tenth degree of Aries <note>another fire sign</note>, with the corresponding true conjunction occurring nearly fifty-three days before that mean one, in the sixth degree of that sign. This was twenty-two years and twenty-five days before the Flood. Why, then, did these conjunctions—which were both true and chronologically closer, and occurred in the full strength of their own triplicity—not produce a <term>conflagration</term> <note>original Greek: ἐμπύρωσιν (*ekpyrosin*), a term used by Stoic philosophers to describe the periodic destruction of the cosmos by fire.</note> instead? That is to say, why did they not cause the consumption of the age by fire, rather than that single, false conjunction in Cancer causing a cataclysm? I call it false because it was calculated only by "mean motion" <note>an idealized, average speed of a planet, rather than its actual observable position</note> and preceded the event by so many years. Furthermore, it was followed by so many subsequent conjunctions of a completely different and opposing nature due to the change in their triplicity.

I do not doubt that there is no astronomer (provided he does not wish to deceive himself) who would not admit that these things are the trifles of delusional men. They invent such nonsense according to their own will and lust, provided they can confirm their decreed errors and insanities by whatever reasoning they can find. It is clear, therefore, that at the time of the universal Flood, there was no such conjunction as these men imagine. Even if we grant them the number of years they want, the constellations during those times were of the sort from which fire and 
->burnings, rather than floods of water, were to be expected.<-

## ON THE CONJUNCTION CONCERNING MOSES AND THE
## PROPHECY OF THE MESSIAH: HOW DELIRIOUS ABRAHAM THE
## JEW WAS. CHAPTER XII.

<insert>A</insert>braham the Prince <note>likely referring to Abraham bar Hiyya, a 12th-century mathematician and astrologer often called "Nasi" or Prince</note> (as he is titled among the Hebrews), whose student was Abraham ibn Ezra <note>original: "Abraam Auenazre"</note>, composed a book which he titled *On the Redemption of Israel* <note>original: "de Redemptione Israël"</note>. His purpose in this work was to use the methods of astrology to investigate the time of the coming Messiah. He began, therefore, with the birth of Moses, imagining for himself a certain arrangement of the stars—of which we have already spoken—involving a <term>conjunction</term> <note>A meeting of two or more planets in the same degree of the zodiac, thought by astrologers to signal major historical shifts.</note> of Saturn and Jupiter. To this alignment he attributes the life of Moses, the kingdom of Israel, and the giving of the Law to the Jewish people. He does this even though (as these authors often do, using very religious language to protect their books from being burned) he himself constantly denies that he is saying what he is actually saying.

Having established this celestial configuration under which the kingdom and Law of the Hebrews supposedly arose, he found a similar alignment occurring two thousand, eight hundred and fifty-nine years after the time of Moses (according to his own calculations). This corresponds to the year of Christ 1464, at which time he commanded the Messiah should be expected. In that year, Saturn and Jupiter were together in the sign of Pisces; and twenty years prior to the others—that is, in the year 1444—they were together in the sign of Cancer. Following either of these conjunctions, he pronounced with astrological certainty that the arrival of the Messiah would occur, along with all those wonders they expect the Messiah to perform.

However, this claim has now been sufficiently disproved by reality itself. Since fifty years have already passed from the first conjunction <note>1444</note> and thirty from the second <note>1464</note>, his fables concerning Moses can also be weakened by this evidence. We should not believe that a constellation granted them a kingdom in the past when, upon the return of that same constellation, their kingdom failed to return at all. Nor does it seem that the stars produced Moses; for when those same celestial forces returned to us, they brought no prophet with them.

Furthermore, not only did the Hebrew people fail to experience better fortune after those conjunctions, but they were overwhelmed by calamities nearly as great as those suffered under the Emperors Titus or Hadrian. I refer to the recent expulsion of all Jews from the whole of Spain by that **most Christian King** <note>Ferdinand II of Aragon, who signed the decree of expulsion in 1492</note>, who can certainly never be praised enough. In that land, they were formerly very powerful in number, wealth, and authority. They themselves do not deny that they have never suffered anything more somber or bitter than this ejection: many were lost to shipwreck, a great many to pestilence, and the largest part consumed by extreme hunger. Even to us Christians, while the glory of divine justice in this event was pleasing, the sight of them suffering such extremes nevertheless moved us to compassion and grief.

This is the "Messiah," this is that "Redemption" which Abraham promised them based on the Mosaic constellation! Lest anyone believe he divined past events any better than future ones, let us look at how plainly false and ridiculous he is regarding that conjunction to which he traced the coming of Moses; for that conjunction, through which he believed Moses was born,

occurred many years after the death of Moses; and even if we were to grant him the timeline, it still signified nothing of the sort that he imagines. Let us look at the dates. But first, one must know that in this year of Christ 1493, the Hebrews reckon five thousand two hundred and fifty-three years from the constitution of the world <note>The Hebrew calendar year 5253 AM (Anno Mundi) corresponds to 1492–1493 AD.</note>; therefore, they themselves calculate three thousand seven hundred and sixty years from the world’s beginning to Christ. Since he [Abraham] says that the <term>conjunction</term> <note>The alignment of Saturn and Jupiter, which astrologers believed triggered major historical shifts.</note> occurred in the year of the world 2365—claiming Moses was born three years later—it follows that it would have happened 1395 years before the time of Christ. 

But in truth, by a correct calculation, one finds one thousand five hundred and nine years from Moses to Christ; therefore, that conjunction actually occurred one hundred and thirty years *after* the birth of Moses. The number of years itself demonstrates this: for from Moses to the first building of the Temple (according to the Third Book of Kingdoms, which they call the First Book of Samuel <note>Pico is referencing the historical books of the Bible; in the Vulgate, the books of Samuel and Kings were often titled 1–4 Kingdoms.</note>), 479 years are gathered. The sum of all these is what I stated: namely, 1509 years. 

That conjunction, however, preceded Christ by 1,395 years, and thus it occurred 130 years after Moses was first born. But that constellation was not so miraculous or prophetic that we must fight much over its timing. "Jupiter and Saturn," he says, "were joined in the year of the world 2365, on the 25th day of the month of Adar <note>original: "Idar"</note> (that is, February), in the first part of Pisces by <term>mean motion</term> <note>The theoretical average position of a planet, as opposed to its actual observed position.</note>; but in the same year by <term>true motion</term> <note>The actual, observed position of a planet in the sky.</note>, they were together in the twenty-fourth part of Aquarius."

Let him first explain, then, which conjunction he prefers to choose as the one to which he chiefly refers the kingdom of the Jews and the Mosaic Law: the "mean" one in Pisces, or this "true" one in Aquarius? If he says the true one, he will contradict himself and other astrologers, for that was a "minor" conjunction, since it did not happen at the beginning of a <term>triplicity</term> <note>A group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element (Fire, Earth, Air, or Water). A "Great Conjunction" occurs when the planets shift into a new triplicity, supposedly marking the rise of new empires or religions.</note>. Such conjunctions, as he himself writes in the same place, do not signify changes in laws or the arrival of prophets; rather, they signify either a fertile harvest or a scarcity, or perhaps a transfer of power—but only among relatives or within the fortunes of a single nation; indeed, they keep themselves within the boundaries of the same family. 

Furthermore, in the <term>theme</term> <note>A horoscope or celestial map of a specific moment.</note> of the conjunction he describes, Aquarius (in which Jupiter and Saturn were located) filled the seventh house of the sky, not the ninth or tenth, which are the houses where kingdoms, laws, and the beginnings of new wisdom are signified.
