...the world was created. But Abraham [bar Hiyya] does not seem to have especially noted that <term>conjunction</term> <note>The alignment of Saturn and Jupiter, believed by astrologers to signal major historical changes.</note> which occurred in Aquarius, but rather the conjunction of the Jewish kingdom and the Mosaic law. For he called the one that was in Pisces [the Mosaic conjunction], and for that reason, he identifies it with the one that occurs 2,859 years after it, also in Pisces, from which he commanded that the Messiah be expected as a second Moses. 

Why do we bother refuting this at length? It is based on what they call "mean" motions <note>Mean motion is a mathematical average of a planet's speed, rather than its actual, observed position in the sky.</note>—that is, positions that are nothing in reality, but are fictitious and imaginary constructions of our own. I can never sufficiently marvel at this madness of astrologers, which I have so often mocked and censured, who profess to refer the events of the lower world to these as if they were true causes, when they are nothing, and have never been, nor ever will be. 

I do not know why Abraham ibn Ezra, who says no faith should be placed in Albumasar because he uses mean conjunctions, did not say the same of this teacher of his [Abraham bar Hiyya], who throughout his entire booklet always deals with mean conjunctions. These occur after 238 years when a migration from one <term>triplicity</term> <note>A group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element: fire, earth, air, or water.</note> to another takes place. In that initial "prophetic" conjunction of his, it is unbelievable how ridiculous he is. 

He describes the <term>theme of the heavens</term> <note>A birth chart or astrological map of the sky at a specific moment.</note> for that hour in which Leo holds the <term>horoscope</term> <note>In traditional astrology, the 'horoscope' refers specifically to the Ascendant, or the sign rising on the eastern horizon.</note>; Saturn and Jupiter are guests in the seventh house, in Aquarius; and the Sun runs through the Midheaven <note>The highest point in the sky at a given moment, associated with power and career.</note> in Aries. Pisces occupies the ninth region. Since all significance regarding laws and prophets is sought from that ninth house, it was turning out poorly for him that no planet was found in it. But being a man of "admirable subtlety," the astrologer transported the Sun from the tenth house and Jupiter and Saturn from the seventh house into the ninth. 

"For," he says, "by mean motion Jupiter and Saturn were in Pisces, and Pisces is in the ninth house. Therefore, Jupiter, Saturn, and the Sun—although the Sun is in the tenth by the division of the houses—will be in the ninth if we consider the number and sequence of the signs. For Aries is the fifth sign from Leo, and the ninth house is the fifth from the horoscope." Do we think anything could be more "subtle" than these fabrications? I do not know whether to answer with indignation at such stupidity and madness, or rather to grieve for the loss of simpler minds who hand these things down as scripture because they are not understood. Such people often move from error to superstition, and from superstition, they gradually slide into infidelity. 

Tell me, I pray, "admirable" Abraham: at what hour were Saturn and Jupiter in Aquarius, and were they also in Pisces? "By mean motion," you say <note>original: "medio inquis motu"</note>. But what is this other than saying they were *not* there? And if the Sun promised imperial power from the tenth house, how could it simultaneously indicate the brilliance of the law from the ninth? For neither can the ninth be turned into the tenth, nor the tenth into the ninth, nor can the same planet be in both places at once.

### THAT THE CHRISTIAN LAW IS ASCRIBED BY VARIOUS MEN TO VARIOUS MEAN CONJUNCTIONS, AND WITHOUT ANY ASTROLOGICAL REASON. CHAPTER XIII.

Up to now, I have seen no one who refers the Christian law to any true <term>conjunction</term> <note>The alignment of two or more planets in the same sign of the zodiac. Astrologers believed the meeting of Jupiter and Saturn signaled major historical and religious shifts.</note> but only to "mean" ones. Some refer it to that which was in the sixth part of <term>Aries</term> <note>The sign of the Ram.</note> six years before <term>Jesus</term> was born; others to that which occurred in the last part of <term>Cancer</term> <note>The sign of the Crab.</note> twenty years prior to the first one. There would be much here with which I could trouble them—for instance, if I were to show that <term>Jesus</term> was born not under a fire or water sign, but under an earth sign, which could be proven both by reason and by the authority of <term>Abraxas</term> <note>A term often found in Gnostic and magical papyri, here likely referring to an ancient chronological or mystical source used by Pico's opponents.</note> and others. Furthermore, that conjunction in <term>Cancer</term> was not signaled by the prophets, since it was neither among the "greatest" nor even the "major" ones. 

Seeing this, one author says: "What if one were to say it belongs to <term>Leo</term>?" For the end of <term>Cancer</term> and the beginning of <term>Leo</term> are adjacent, and thus it would be the start of the <term>fire triplicity</term> <note>The group of three zodiac signs—Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius—associated with the element of fire. Great changes were supposedly triggered when conjunctions moved into this group.</note>. This is surely a clever invention! Since those locations are not even five "fingers" apart, this "migration" can be claimed with almost no effort. But I think we have laughed enough and sufficiently refuted these mean <term>conjunctions</term> <note>Calculations based on the average speed of planets rather than their actual, observable positions.</note>. Since we have now entirely removed them from the field, there is no reason to spend more effort against them. It has been clearly enough declared that what are called "mean" conjunctions are no different than if we said they were nothing at all. And that which does not exist certainly cannot act, nor can it indicate things that do. 

If, however, they bring forward some true <term>conjunction</term> after the birth of <term>Christ</term>, I shall wonder at nothing further unless we are to believe that the heavens stood still after He was brought into the light. Otherwise, it was necessary for <term>Jupiter</term>, <term>Saturn</term>, and the other <term>planets</term> to meet and move away from each other frequently. But no astrologer has ever said that these conjunctions have power over things that have already passed; rather, they precede their effects by many years, but never follow them. This is said reasonably: for if they are causes, the cause cannot come after the effect; if they are signs, it is pointless for the celestial signs to signify that which has already happened.

### THAT THE COMMONLY CIRCULATED BIRTH CHART OF JESUS IS NOT TRUE, NOR DOES IT INDICATE THAT HE WOULD DIE A VIOLENT DEATH OR BE A GREAT PROPHET. CHAPTER XIV.

Some people are usually moved by the trifles these <term>petty diviners</term> <note>original: "diuinaculi"</note> babble regarding the <term>birth chart</term> <note>original: "genitura"</note> of <term>Jesus</term> Himself. For He was born, they say, while the first face of the <term>Virgin</term> (for so they call the <term>decans</term> <note>A 10-degree subdivision of a zodiac sign; each sign has three "faces" or decans.</note>) was ascending. Of this, <term>Albumasar</term> <note>The Latinized name of Abu Ma'shar, a famous 9th-century Persian astrologer whose works were highly influential in Europe.</note> writes that in it there is a beautiful <term>Virgin</term> carrying two ears of grain in her hand and nursing a boy, whom a certain nation calls <term>Jesus</term>. Thus they think the miracle of the Word made flesh is confirmed by the science of <term>Astrology</term>, which finds the <term>Virgin and Jesus</term> among the images of the heavens. Here, I am not particularly angry with them, since they are accustomed to confirming their own dogmas with such testimonies; therefore they think we will also gladly receive these things to corroborate our own doctrines.

He also begins to dismantle specific astrological myths about Christ's birth chart, such as the claim by Abu Ma'shar that the constellation Virgo literally depicts the Virgin and Child.</summary>

...we [reject these things], for Christian truth does not need these fables and dreams; indeed, in the presence of that truth, even the serious matters of the philosophers are almost fables. Who has seen these images? To whom has a more hidden reason indicated them when the senses were silent? Where did either <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity.</note> or any ancient author ever make mention of them? They are the purest trifles and figments of the Arabs, although they attribute them to the Indians <note>Pico often refers to "Indians" or "Arabs" when discussing medieval astrological traditions that he considers corruptions of Greek science.</note>, against which we shall dispute more broadly in the following book.

But neither was the Lord Jesus born with that <term>Virgin</term> <note>the constellation/sign Virgo</note> (as they say) ascending; otherwise, He would have appeared into the light almost two hours before midnight, whom we have received from church tradition as born at midnight. Therefore, not the third part of <term>Libra</term> <note>the sign of the Scales</note> (as someone says), but rather the tenth part occupied the <term>horoscope</term> <note>the Ascendant, or the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth</note> when the most desired of all those born was arising. 

From this, it is also shown to be false what they spread with a blasphemous voice: that in that <term>nativity</term> <note>original: "genitura," referring to the birth chart</note> Mars was in the <term>house of death</term> <note>The 8th House in a birth chart, traditionally associated with the manner of death.</note>, from which He would have had to die by the punishment of the cross. For Mars could not have been in that place unless we make the Virgin the ascendant, which we have declared to be greatly different from the hour of His birth. 

But someone will insist that if we remove Mars from that part of the sky, we will place him in the West <note>the 7th House, associated with open enemies and conflict</note>, where he might also threaten dangers of a violent death. I, however, departing not at all from their own decrees, will show that a violent death was not pre-signified from that nativity. For although Mars in the seventh house brings the newborn into danger of life, <term>Maternus</term> <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer.</note> nevertheless writes that this misfortune is diminished if the birth was at night; likewise if Mars was in his own house, or his "terms," or his "exaltation." Furthermore, even if he were found in the eighth house (from which no clearer indication of death comes), the benevolence of Jupiter nevertheless resists the malignancy of Mars if Jupiter was in the ascendant, and the ascendant itself is in the house of Jupiter or Venus, which prosperous star [Venus] joins herself to Jupiter by an aspect <note>original: "radiatione," the "rays" or geometric angles between planets</note>.

Of these conditions, however, not one or two, but clearly all are found in the nativity of Jesus. For He was born at night, not by day; and Mars was in <term>Aries</term> <note>the sign of the Ram</note>, which is to say he was in his own home. And the ascendant was Libra, the house of Venus, which Jupiter nevertheless illuminated almost <term>exactly</term> <note>original: "partiliter," meaning an aspect calculated by the specific degree rather than just the sign</note>. Then he joined Venus, located in <term>Aquarius</term>, in a friendly fellowship by a <term>trine aspect</term> <note>original: "trigoni radij," an aspect of 120 degrees, considered the most harmonious in astrology.</note>. To these things you may also add that the Moon—which rules the night in a nocturnal birth—being fortunately placed, held the house of death. You will see that a "good death" must necessarily be pronounced from that position of the stars; for she was in <term>Taurus</term>, that is, in her own <term>exaltation</term> <note>original: "sublimitate," a sign where a planet's influence is strengthened</note>, and increased in light, and in the place where she rejoices—that is, the eighth—flowing away from a most happy sight of the Sun toward Venus, with whom she was staying as a guest. She was infested by no rays of either Mars or Saturn, neither departing from them nor going toward them; that is, bound to them by no bond of association. 

Add that Venus, mistress of both the house of death and the ascendant, was struck by no hostile aspect of Mars or Saturn, but was cherished by the rays of Jupiter, promising a good end for herself. He was offered, therefore, because He willed it, not because the fury of the heavens drove Him to the punishments of the cross. But an occasion for some chattering can never be lacking for rash men of no shame. For imagine Mars was in any place whatever, they will have a pretext...

<header>John Pico of Mirandola</header>

...they will appear to be doing nothing less than raving in some way. For if it is established in the <term>horoscope</term> <note>original: "horoscopo"; the Ascendant or the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at birth</note> that a face is shown here as slapped by palms, struck by fists, and defiled with blood, they will say that even that "Martian" man <note>A person born under the strong influence of Mars.</note> brought the swords of destruction upon himself. If it is in the second place from the <term>horoscope</term> <note>the "Second House," traditionally associated with wealth and possessions</note>, it brings poverty and a lack of all things; if in the third, no brothers; if in the fourth, no patrimony <note>inheritance</note>, so that he who was the Son of David nonetheless did not obtain even the temporary kingdom of David. 

If in the fifth, no children; if in the sixth, all his servants are put to death; if you look at the seventh and eighth places, you know what they would say. But if in the ninth—oh, blessed astrologers!—since Maternus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer.</note> says that whoever has Mars in its own house in the ninth region of heaven will be a terror to good spirits <note>original: "daemonibus," which in a Neoplatonic context could mean spirits or guardian divinities</note>, and from his arrival the spirits of evil demons flee, and he frees men laboring under them not by a word, but by his mere appearance. With what great shouts and applause do you believe the astrologers would celebrate and spread these things if the star of Mars had happened to be positioned there at the birth of the Lord? 

But if it had held the heights of heaven <note>the Midheaven or 10th house, associated with career and public life</note>, they would immediately proclaim an empire subject to his laws, especially if Jupiter occupied the first pivot <note>the Ascendant</note>. If they had found him in the eleventh place, they would have brought forward the "Charleses" and "Constantines" <note>Referring to Great Christian emperors like Charlemagne and Constantine the Great.</note> and however many Emperors fought for the church of Christ. If in the twelfth, they would complain about the snares of enemies, among whom they would even find themselves; for as it is said, there is always an occasion for the insane to rage. 

But hear also what they say about Saturn. For it was in the ninth region of heaven in the <term>sign of Gemini</term>. But, they say, it makes prophets and priests—what about the fact that it is in retrograde? <note>Appearing to move backward in the sky, usually considered a weakening or debilitating influence in traditional astrology.</note> This ought to entirely diminish those promises. It would therefore make a prophet, but it could not make one who is "more than a prophet" like John the Baptist. Could it then make the divine inspirer of all prophets? 

Saturn was positioned in the same place and in the same sign when Eleanor, the daughter of my brother Galeotto, was born <note>Eleanor Pico (1478–1529). Pico uses his own niece's birth chart to prove that identical planetary positions do not produce identical destinies.</note>—a girl indeed modest and of most upright character, but neither an Anna, nor a Deborah, nor a Cassandra <note>Biblical prophetesses and the famous Trojan seeress.</note>. But persist, I pray, you "admirable" astrologers, in your proposed dogma, and let us see what Saturn signified there in His [Christ’s] birth. Your Abraham <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a prominent Jewish scholar and astrologer often cited by Pico.</note> writes in his *Book of Nativities* that whoever has Saturn placed thus (that is, in the ninth region of heaven), will be a "bad Christian." 

You see how beautifully he has confirmed your dogma! For who would dare call Christ a "bad Christian," who was not even a Christian <note>Pico points out the logical absurdity: Christ is the source of Christianity, not a follower of it.</note>? O ridiculous men, surely never mocked enough! That superstitious man of Ascoli <note>Cecco d’Ascoli (1257–1327), an astrologer and poet who was burned at the stake for heresy, partly for attempting to explain Christ's life through astrology.</note>, who is called a Magician, says: "Jesus was born in a stable because <term>Capricorn</term> held the bottom of heaven <note>the "Imum Coeli," the lowest point of the chart</note>," and "He was another king of the Jews because the <term>horoscope</term> was <term>Libra</term>." For the Hebrews belong to Saturn, and the kingdom of Saturn is <term>Libra</term> <note>In astrology, Libra is the "exaltation" of Saturn.</note>—as if many people were not born every single month under these same conditions who are neither born in stables, nor recorded as kings of the Jews.

<header>Against Astrology, Book V.</header>

### THAT WHAT ALBUMASAR SAID ABOUT MUHAMMAD HAS BEEN FOUND FALSE BY EXPERIENCE. Chapter 15.

**Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), a Persian astrologer whose works were highly influential in medieval Europe.</note> the Arab attributes the arrival of his **Muhammad** and that law of the **Saracens** <note>A common medieval term for Muslims.</note> to a <term>conjunction</term> <note>When two celestial bodies appear in the same area of the sky.</note> of Jupiter and Saturn which occurred in Scorpio fifty-two years before the publication of that law. He does not need much refuting, since the very prophecies he made from that same constellation regarding that law have already been proven false by experience. 

Finally, as we have said above, at whatever time prophets—whether good or evil—may come, a conjunction cannot be lacking to which their arrival might be attributed. This is because, as stated before, Saturn and Jupiter always meet after twenty years. However, the fact that such meetings are neither a sign nor a cause for why prophets of this kind appear is sufficiently proven by this: often at other times, similar or even more powerful <term>constellations</term> <note>The relative positions of stars and planets at a specific time.</note> return for the same effect, yet after them no prophet, no new law, and no change of religion follows. 

Muhammad, they say, came after Jupiter and Saturn were joined in Scorpio; why then did another Muhammad not arrive after the year of grace 1065? At that time, Jupiter and Saturn were together under similar conditions, and even the <term>triplicity</term> <note>In astrology, the zodiac is divided into four "triplicities" based on elements (Fire, Earth, Air, Water). A change in triplicity was thought to signal massive historical shifts.</note> had changed. Furthermore, something that did not happen in that conjunction of Muhammad occurred then: in that same year, Mars joined them by bodily <term>application</term> <note>When a faster planet moves toward an exact alignment with a slower one.</note> in the same sign. Yet, if we leaf through the histories, we will read of no institution of a new religion through those times which drew nearly a third of the world into its laws.

### THAT IN THE PROPHECY OF THE ANTICHRIST SOME HAVE ALREADY APPEARED AS LIARS, AND OTHERS WILL BE LIARS IN THE FUTURE. Chapter 16.

If we have found these scoundrels to be false, vain, and ridiculous in what they have said concerning past religions, we ought not to think that any more faith should be granted to their trifles when they speak with a certain "prophetic authority" about the **Antichrist**, the end of the world, and other future matters of this kind. 

For reality has already rejected certain outcomes: for instance, **Arnaldus** <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a physician and reformer who predicted the end of the world based on astrology.</note> and several others who said that in the year of our Lord 1345, because of that conjunction of the three superior planets in Aquarius, or in the year 1464, because of Jupiter and Saturn joined in Pisces, the **Messiah Abraham** <note>Likely a reference to Jewish messianic expectations or specific astrological predictions circulating in the 15th century.</note> would appear; others threatened us with the Antichrist. I do not doubt that others who have pushed these dates further into the future will be refuted by posterity with the same argument, because reality itself will refute their prophecy. This will continue until that day arrives which is unknown even to the angels. When the Lord Jesus denied that knowing this day was our business, he—as **Augustine** says—"loosed the fingers" <note>original: "digitos... resoluit"; a metaphor for stopping people from calculating or counting years on their fingers.</note> of all bold men with a single word.

Having discussed Muhammad on the previous page, he now examines a popular medieval theory that categorized all world religions into six types based on the alignment of Jupiter with other planets.</meta>

<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

## HOW WEAKLY THE ASTROLOGERS PROVE
## that there can be only six religions: and that the law of the Hebrews
## should be called Jovial or Solar rather than Saturnine. Chapter 17.

**B**ut hear with what a fine fiction they gather all past religions, and that which is to come under the Antichrist, into one (so to speak) bundle. Jupiter, they say, signifies religion, but one or another depending on its embrace <note>original: "complexu"; referring to an astrological conjunction where two planets appear to meet.</note> with various other stars. There are six planets besides Jupiter; therefore, there are also six species of religions, and there will be neither more nor fewer than these.

Jupiter with Saturn makes the religion of the **Jews**; with Mars, that of the **Chaldeans** <note>An ancient people of Mesopotamia, often associated by medieval writers with star-worship and magic.</note> who worship fire; with the Sun, that of the **Egyptians**, who worship the "host of heaven," that is, the stars; with Venus, the **Saracen** <note>A medieval term for Muslims.</note> religion; with Mercury, the **Christian**; and with the Moon, that religion which is to be the last of all under the **Antichrist**. 

This is that subtle and profound invention which, although many others use it, <term>Roger Bacon</term> <note>A 13th-century English philosopher and friar who famously attempted to use astrology to explain history and theology.</note> uses most notably in his letter to Clement, and which <term>Pierre d’Ailly</term> <note>A French cardinal and scholar (1351–1420) who wrote "On the Concordance of Astrology and Theology."</note> also used in his treatise on the *Concordance of Astrology and Theology*. 

In this, I first marvel that they have so forgotten their own dogma. Those who were always accustomed to saying that religions are created or signified only by the meeting of the "superior stars"—specifically Saturn and Jupiter—now descend all the way to the Moon to have her give birth to some Antichrist for us. 

Furthermore, if they wish to count the species of religions according to the number of the planets, they must either remove one planet from the sky or beg for several more elsewhere; otherwise, the number will not match. For they either accept **idolatry** as a single religion, or they wish to count every single type of idolatry separately in that number, according to the various rites and cults of those who served idols. 

If they prefer the first option, they must remove one planet from the middle, since there would not be one religion for the Egyptians and another for the Chaldeans, but one and the same—that is, idolatry. Thus, there would only be five religions: the Idolatrous, the Mosaic <note>The law of Moses; Judaism.</note>, the Christian, the Muhammadan, and, so to speak, the Antichristian. 

If, however, they command that the types of idolatry be taken separately, there are scarcely as many stars in the sky as there are religions on earth. But if they think these others can be reduced to those "heads"—where one is the worship of fire and the other the worship of heaven—they would rightly deserve great evil from the demons, who would be indignant at being left out of that partition, since they are the ones principally (and almost exclusively) worshipped in idolatry. For "all the gods of the Gentiles are demons" <note>A quote from Psalm 96:5 (or 95:5 in the Vulgate).</note>; therefore, they must necessarily make at least three species of idolatry: of the heavens, of demons, and of the elements. 

They will be forced to seek one "error" from their friends—I meant to say "errant star" <note>A pun on the Latin "errorem" (error) and "erronem" (wanderer/planet).</note>, that is, a planet—so that eight might be found to match the number of religions. 

But they are always poorly skilled in all the matters of which they speak. For the worship of the celestial bodies was characteristic of the Chaldeans, as <term>Iamblichus</term> <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on the Egyptian mysteries.</note> writes, while the Egyptians were more occupied with the worship of demons. Therefore, they should give the Sun to Mars [and vice versa]...

<summary>Pico ridicules the astrological theory that ties the world's major religions to the conjunctions of Jupiter with the other six planets. He argues the system is mathematically inconsistent and historically inaccurate regarding the religious practices of the Egyptians and Chaldeans.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Book V of Pico della Mirandola’s "Disputations Against Astrology." Picking up from the previous page, Pico continues to mock the specific planetary associations that medieval astrologers—like Roger Bacon and Albumasar—assigned to different world religions.</meta>

<page-num>579</page-num>
<header>Against Astrology, Book V. 579</header>
<sig>CC 2 IOAN.</sig>

...to the Chaldeans, and meanwhile provide some diabolical planet for the Egyptians. It would be easy to show that they fight against the truth everywhere, as they have always been little friends with it. But why do they so often disagree with themselves? For if they consulted their own dogmas sufficiently, they would find no reason why the Law of the Hebrews should be Saturnine <note>Related to the planet Saturn, traditionally associated with melancholy, old age, and restriction.</note> rather than Christian; instead, the former should be referred to the Sun or to Jupiter, and ours [Christianity] to Saturn.

For Saturn, as some say, does not bestow bodily goods but takes them away; instead, it gives spiritual things and those which are not seen. The Mosaic Law both promised and bestowed bodily goods, whereas our law [the Gospel] takes them away rather than offering them, and it promises and provides spiritual things that are not seen. Saturn does not produce kings of the people, commanders of armies, rich men, or nobles with many offspring who are by nature womanizers—such as all the leaders of the Hebrew religion were, like Abraham, Jacob, Moses, Joshua, Solomon, and David. Rather, Saturn makes men ignoble, poor, hermits, haters of pleasures, those who meditate on eternal things and despise bodily ones. Such a person—if he is to be numbered among others—is our leader and commander Christ Jesus, and such were the apostles, martyrs, monks, and Christians, by whose life, doctrine, and blood our religion was born, grew, and was confirmed.

Therefore, if one were to speak in accordance with the astrologers' own decrees, we should be called Saturnine, and the Hebrews should be called Solar or Jovial <note>Related to Jupiter.</note>. But what drew them into that opinion was the worship of the Sabbath; since that day is considered the day of Saturn among them, it seemed most obvious to them to say that they were a "Saturnine people" because they venerated the day of Saturn above others. Guided by this same conjecture, they are also accustomed to say that our religion is Solar, because we observe the Day of the Sun, which we call the Lord's Day.

But why should we not rather be assigned to the Day of Mercury, since they also subject us to Mercury? For they gave the Sun to the Egyptians and Mercury to us. And <term>Albumasar</term> <note>An influential 9th-century Persian astrologer whose works were foundational to medieval European astrology.</note> says that Jupiter with Mercury signifies the Christian law, although he also said the same about the Sun. For it is no vice either to err or to change one's opinion among those who are so diligent in the "errors" and motions of the planets; in that rapid dizziness of inspecting the heavens, they are so stunned that they can hardly ever stand firmly on their own feet.

But however it may be, they have marvelous reasons with which to confirm these inventions of theirs. For they did not refer us to Mercury by chance, but because—says <term>Rog. Bac.</term> <note>Roger Bacon, the 13th-century English friar who sought to use astrology to explain the history of religions.</note>—Mercury has multiple motions that are difficult to know, and so he claims for himself the Christian religion, whose dogmas are found to be almost incredible and most difficult to recognize. Other younger astrologers have thought up I-don't-know-what: because Mercury is the scribe <note>original: "Librarius"; meaning a copyist or librarian.</note> of the gods, and there is a great abundance of books among Christians, they say this religion should rightly be considered Mercurial. This is the "admirable wisdom" of the astrologers! They have clearly forgotten the libraries of the pagans, and they have seen almost none of the books of the Arabs and Hebrews yet.

<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

# GIOVANNI PICO MI-
# randola’s Disputations against Astro-
# logy, Book VI.

->IN WHICH ORDER WE SHOULD PROCEED IN OVERTUR-<-
->ning the foundations of the Astrologers: Also, that it is impossible for all<-
->the stars to ever be restored to the same positions in<-
->which they once were. Chapter I.<-

**WE HAVE EXCEEDED** the planned order and method of our commentary. In this work, the roots of the astrologers ought to have been torn up before we cut down those lofty peaks of the <term>great conjunctions</term> <note>Alignments of major planets, particularly Jupiter and Saturn, which medieval astrologers believed signaled major historical shifts like the birth of prophets or the fall of empires.</note>, the great orbits, and other things of that kind; for once those roots were removed, those peaks would necessarily have collapsed. For who would put faith in those who pronounce the change of kingdoms and religions through great conjunctions? It will be established that those signs—Aries, Leo, Cancer, and Sagittarius, in which they think Jupiter and Saturn meet to produce these effects—are nothing; or if they are something of this sort, they are not in that part of the heavens where they are calculated to be. Furthermore, it will be shown that Saturn, Jupiter, and the rest of the planets do not cause events or the shifting fortunes of lower <note>Meaning earthly or "sublunary" affairs.</note> things. Even if they did cause them, nothing has been discovered through either reason or experience regarding their efficacy, nature, or specific properties. Since different results come from different conjunctions (if indeed they come from them at all), this cannot be judged by men among whom even the very first principles of that art are still in doubt. 

For we shall see in the discussions that follow that it is not yet agreed upon which hour should be considered the time of a conjunction: whether it is the beginning of the year in which it occurred, or rather the specific turning point when the stars themselves meet. Furthermore, we will see that they cannot accurately determine either of these times, which is why the <term>horoscope</term> <note>In this context, the "horoscope" refers to the Ascendant or the exact configuration of the heavens at a specific moment.</note> of the conjunction is left in doubt. Likewise, even if the horoscope were established, nothing is yet certain regarding the method of arranging the <term>theme</term> <note>The "theme" (thematos) refers to the astrological chart or figure.</note>; it remains uncertain where the beginnings of the twelve "places" are rightly established. And even when those are established, the power of the place itself—what is the beginning, middle, or end—is not clear to them. Since they are ignorant of the region of the sky in which the stars are joined, they cannot know what the conjunction will produce, since almost every variety of what is signified is reduced to the nature and property of those places they call <term>houses</term> <note>Original: "domos." The twelve divisions of the sky in an astrological chart, each supposedly governing a different area of human life, such as wealth, travel, or death.</note>. And because in these conjunctions they usually observe which planet is <term>exalted</term> <note>Original: "exaltatio." A "dignity" or state in which a planet is thought to have its most powerful influence when located in a specific zodiac sign.</note> above the other, we will see that they do not yet know what this "exaltation" (which they commonly call "elevation") actually is. It also matters greatly which planet primarily rules that place, whether it be the coupling of the higher stars or the eclipse of the sun or moon.

He asserts that if the basic principles are in doubt, their grand predictions about the fate of kingdoms are baseless.</summary>

[...deter]mine. We shall see that all those rights, empires, and authorities of the planets are so controversial that there is almost no part of any sign for which the astrologers have anything certain regarding its prince and lord. But it is not necessary to enumerate here the foundations of that art which will be overturned later. Along with these foundations (as I said before), everything they dare to pronounce about divine miracles through **great conjunctions** <note>The alignment of major planets, particularly Jupiter and Saturn, which astrologers believed heralded the birth of prophets or the collapse of empires.</note> and other such things must also fall.

Indeed, since this part of their theory especially offended the nature of religion, every delay in removing this plague seemed too long—especially since the whole field of astrology seemed most effectively refuted if this part concerning the great conjunctions was proven false, even if the rest remained unshaken; for where they seem greatest and strongest, they should rather be defeated. Now, returning to where we digressed, we shall proceed to root out the primary foundations of that art in their proper order.

Nor indeed should we pass over in silence a common error among astrologers, into which **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a Persian astrologer whose works were the primary source for the theory of "Great Conjunctions" in the Latin West.</note> and many others fell, thinking that eventually all the stars would be restored to the same positions, so that a completely similar arrangement of the heavens and the position and relationship of all celestial bodies to each other would be found just as it once was. From this they think it would follow that the same things would happen among us as before: the same men, the same events, the same animals, and absolutely the same condition for all lower things. 

Certain "astrologomists" <note>A derogatory term Pico uses for those who attempt to blend astrology with theology or heresy.</note>, examining this more deeply, are accustomed to whisper in the ears of their followers: "this is that resurrection of the Christians, which the Hebrews and Muslims also hope for." They say those prophets were certainly the greatest astronomers, but they hid these mysteries from the common people and the uneducated. For they thought there was a common number of years and days for the world with which the locations of the planets and stars could be certified, and when that number is completed, all stars will have returned to that very same point, and because of this, all things will return exactly as they were. 

But it is not necessary for us to refute this madness at length, since **Haly** <note>Ali ibn Ridwan (c. 988–1061), an Egyptian physician and astrologer.</note> himself, in his commentary on the first book of the <term>apotelesmata</term> <note>original: "apotelesmatum"; This refers to Ptolemy's *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational textbook of astrology. The Greek term "apotelesma" refers to the "completion" or "influence" of the stars.</note>, following the opinion of **Ptolemy** himself who said the same, indignantly rebukes it. He says there is no one skilled in arithmetic to whom this error is not obvious. 

Then after him, **Nicole Oresme** <note>A 14th-century French polymath who argued that the movements of the planets are likely "incommensurable" (like irrational numbers), meaning they will never perfectly repeat the same alignment.</note>, a most sharp philosopher and diligent mathematician, in his treatise *On the Ratios of Ratios*, demonstrated by mathematical reasoning that the opinion is false and impossible—namely, the belief that the same position of the heavens and stars that once existed could ever return. Since he has sufficiently fulfilled this task,

### BY WHAT MEANS ASTROLOGERS CLAIM THE INFLUENCES OF THE 
### stars vary, and how these claims are altogether absurd. Chapter 11.

**M**any, unless I am mistaken—or to speak more truly, all—the foundations of Astrology have been removed if it has been sufficiently proved that nothing is caused by the heavens, nor indicated by those things for which astrologers profess a prediction based on celestial observation. Among the reasons we used against them, there was one especially powerful argument concerning the <term>momentary change</term> <note>original: "momentanea... mutatione"; the idea that celestial power shifts instantly as a planet moves a fraction of a degree.</note> of celestial virtues which they imagine. We touched upon this in the previous discussion, but we rightly postponed its full explanation until this point. Indeed, it requires its own specific treatment and carries great weight in overturning Astrology. This is because it confirms not only what has been proven so far—namely, that the stars do not cause particular changes in lower things—but also that if such things did proceed from heaven, they would proceed in a manner far different from how they might be grasped or signified by any celestial observation.

This, then, is what the astrologers say: that the virtue and power of the stars and planets is different at every hour and moment, depending on whether they are in other parts of the heaven, which the <term>later astrologers</term> <note>original: "neoterici"; Pico often refers to Medieval and Arabic astrologers as "moderns" or "later" compared to classical sources.</note> call **houses**, or in other signs (of which they imagine twelve are found), or because the planets themselves, being separated from one another by a certain distance of space, are joined by various reciprocal radiations, which are commonly called the **aspects** of the planets. These are the primary ways (to omit certain more recent inventions) by which they think the flow and virtue of the celestial bodies is changed: namely, the house, the sign, and the diversity of the aspect.

Unless they defend these things, they cannot uphold the dogma of the efficiency of the stars—that is, the idea that every change and diversity of lower things originates from the stars. For if those stars always possessed the same and unchangeable virtue (as we believe of all things except the **Moon** <note>In the Aristotelian worldview Pico operated within, the Moon was the boundary between the changing "sublunary" world and the perfect, unchanging "superlunary" heavens.</note>), then the same or similar effects would necessarily always proceed from them. They cannot attribute the diversity of effects to "lower causes" (as we do) without also admitting with us that they can divine nothing from heaven regarding that diversity, since the heaven is held by them to be our author and cause. 

Therefore, it is necessary for them to find as much diversity among the causes in heaven as there is variety in the effects of lower things. In this matter, the multitude of stars does not help them at all, since no matter how many stars and planets there are, they are all present to every person at birth. For this reason, no logic could be offered as to why they would bestow things differently upon different people, rather than the same things upon everyone, unless they invented something whereby the virtue and efficiency of the stars would be one thing at one time and another at another. From this, it could then easily be gathered that things which happen or arise at different times receive a different condition from heaven, according to whatever the state of the stars was then—a condition which those who have investigated and known the state of the stars at any time might be able to predict. This is what we shall refute in the present book, since nothing can be thought more absurd or more removed from all reason than to imagine there is such inconstancy and mutability in the nature of the higher bodies—the likes of which is not even seen in lower things.

<header>Against Astrology, Book VI.</header>

...although in their own nature they are extremely fluid and changeable. For what is this shape-shifting mutation and chameleon-like inconstancy, so that in a short interval of time those most divine bodies are never found to be similar to themselves or endowed with the same gifts? I ask them to say what they think those properties of stellar <term>influxes</term> <note>original: "defluxuum"; the supposed flowing down of celestial influence onto the earthly realm.</note> are: do they proceed from the nature and substance of the stars themselves? Or rather from some force introduced from the outside—whether drawn from the twelve places of the heaven, from the signs, or from their mutual radiations [aspects]? If they answer the first, they cannot change those properties unless the substance of the stars is also changed—which even they (I believe) will not grant. If they prefer the second, the celestial bodies will be the most ignoble of all bodies, doing almost nothing from their own nature, but everything according to a force and affect attacking from the outside; whereas a physical substance is more perfect the more its resulting operation proceeds from the innermost substance of the actor. 

And these things indeed we have said in general terms; for the madness of this opinion will shine forth most clearly when we examine in detail the ways they think the virtues of the stars are changed. In examining these, we shall maintain the order of their errors and fables. Let us now proceed to do this, starting from the twelve houses of heaven, according to whose diversity they most fabulously devise that the influx of both signs and stars is not only intensified and weakened, but rendered entirely and utterly different.

## THE HOUSES OF THE ASTROLOGERS: HOW THEY ARE RESTING UPON NO FOUNDATION, and how astrologers fight among themselves in explaining their powers. CHAPTER III.

**N**o one who is not entirely ignorant of that art is unaware of the twelve houses celebrated among astrologers; to these, it seems to me, almost every significance and property of the influxes is finally referred by them. For if you ask about the nature of any planet—what it might effect, or of what thing it is considered the giver and author—they will respond with nothing definite or certain, except according to the nature of the house in which the planet is found. Thus, almost everything they are accustomed to say in general about the properties of the planets seems to fall under those things which have a manifold meaning under a common name. For what is more general in the nature of a planet than whether it is "good" or "bad"—that is, the author of happiness or unhappiness? 

And yet even this is not firm and always the same in the stars; rather, a "good" planet does harm in a "bad place," and a "bad" one is thought by them to be beneficial in a "good" place. Finally, to mention one example for all, **Jupiter** placed in the <term>ascendant</term> <note>original: "oriente"; the eastern horizon or the 1st House, considered the most powerful point in a horoscope.</note> differs as much from himself when he has moved a little above the ascendant into what they call the twelfth place of heaven, as fire differs from air or water, or a hare from a donkey, or a donkey from an elephant. For in the ascendant he always decrees the greatest goods; in the twelfth house, which is adjacent to the ascendant, he often decrees great evils. It is the most characteristic work of **Jupiter** to bestow wealth; yet when placed in the third or eighth [house], he frequently dissipates an inheritance, even though by his own nature he makes men noble and wise. If he holds the eighth place, he will make them ignoble and those whose "madness turns to insanity," as *Maternus* <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman author whose work "Mathesis" was a primary source for Renaissance astrologers.</note> says. Finally, what is more characteristic of Jupiter...

...more properly as a beneficent star, since it is called both the "greater of the fortunate planets" and the "great happiness of heaven." <note>Pico is likely referring to Jupiter, which in traditional astrology is the "Greater Benefic."</note> But positioned in the third place <note>The Third House, traditionally associated with siblings and short journeys, often considered "cadent" or weaker.</note>, Maternus says it is neither good nor bad. Also, when placed in the sixth place <note>The Sixth House, traditionally the house of illness, slavery, and misfortune.</note>, it decrees the greatest evils. Giving a reason for this, Maternus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century author of the *Mathesis*, a major astrological compendium.</note> adds: "For the sixth place has the specific prerogative of malice, and whatever star is in that place—that is, the sixth—will borrow the greatest power for decreeing evils from the vice of the location." Thus he says. 

Let us ask the astrologers, then, from where such a great, sudden, and perpetual division arises in these divine bodies [the planets], which ought rightly to be believed to be most tenacious of their own nature and always similar to themselves, due to the firmness and immutability of their substance. Truly, only two ways can be imagined by which this happens: One, that we understand various powers and forces to be implanted in those locations, which they pour into the stars placed within them, as the quoted words of Maternus seem to indicate. The other, that we believe the planet itself neither receives anything from elsewhere nor is affected in different ways, but just as the projection of its rays varies according to the different positioning of the star relative to the earth, we should also believe the force and efficacy of the rays vary accordingly. 

Whichever they choose to say, they will be convicted of madness. For if they answer that powers of this kind flow from the location to the planets, we will ask what they think about "location": is it, as some of the ancients held, a naked space separated from bodies? Or, as Aristotle held, the outermost surface of the surrounding body? <note>Aristotle defined "place" not as a vacuum, but as the boundary where one thing touches what surrounds it.</note> If it is space and interval, let them admit along with those same philosophers that such an interval has no virtues or properties, since natural forms follow the physical substance, not mere dimensions and a naked gap. 

If it is the outermost surface of a surrounding body, some force could indeed be in this location, such as belongs to the body whose surface it is—a surface by which the surrounded body might then be affected. But what are these bodies? Which of them will be considered the location of the stars? Certainly, whatever they are called—whether the outermost sphere of all, or the one joined and nearest to each star—there will be no part of such bodies that does not circle the East, the West, the highest point of heaven, the lowest, and the other places in the revolution of a single day. Therefore, if the power comes from those parts, the power of the East will not always be the same, nor will that of the West; but according to the nature of that body currently positioned there, the power itself will also change. 

Finally, they cannot say this, because the twelve signs—which are said to be in the houses, just as the planets are in the houses and the signs—are described by them as being in the highest sphere of all. These signs themselves, just like the planets, are said to borrow their powers and nature from the house in which they are located. For they say that Aries <note>The first sign of the Zodiac.</note> does not do the same things in the East that it does in the West, and the same for the other signs which are located in the eighth sphere (if there is none higher) or in that which is considered the highest sphere. <gloss>original: "exiſtimatur"</gloss> Since these [the highest spheres] are surrounded by no other body, there is nowhere for us to imagine this power of the houses to be, except in immobile space and the interval occupied by bodies. But that is either nothing...

<page-num>585</page-num>
<header>On Astrology, Book VI.</header>

## On Astrology, Book VI.

If we follow the teachings of Aristotle <note>Aristotle (384–322 BCE) argued that the "ether" or celestial matter was uniform and unchanging; therefore, specific "spots" in the sky shouldn't have different magical properties.</note>—or even if we grant that celestial space is something in itself—it possesses no inherent power or specific character of its own. Therefore, to imagine that different powers exist in those locations (that is, in the various positions of the signs and planets), and that stars are affected by being placed there, is entirely removed from all reason.

Nor will their arguments be any less absurd or ridiculous if they use the other side of their defense: namely, that because of the difference in position, the planets look at us with a "different face" and their rays are sent down to the earth differently, and that this creates a variety of effects. Anyone who has even tasted the basics of optical philosophy <note>In the Renaissance, "optics" (or *perspectiva*) was a branch of physics. Pico argues that the angle of light changes its strength, but not what it fundamentally is.</note> will easily understand how absurd this is. For everyone knows that the quality of an effect is distinguished by the quality of the ray and the nature of the body emitting that ray—not by the different "circulation" or angle of the ray itself.

This angle can be the reason why a thing becomes more or less intense. A ray of the Sun, in whatever way or position it is cast upon us, always heats and always illuminates. It is true that when it is closest or directly overhead, it illuminates and heats more. But when it is slanted, or refracted, or descends from a more remote place, it does the same things as the direct or close ray, just less so. No other variation in effect can occur except that which follows the actual strengthening or weakening of heat and light.

Therefore, the dogma of the astrologers is insane. They think that the twelve signs of the heaven and the planets, when positioned in one spot, can bless us as "brothers" or make us miserable; yet, when they have moved just a little bit further, they have no power or meaning over brothers, but instead either give or snatch away riches, or in another place win us friends, and in another stir up enemies against us. All this, they say, happens with nothing changed in the nature of the sign or the planet, but solely by a change in position!

Now, as we have said, whether this position makes the rays closer to us, or pulls them more powerfully to the earth, or joins or separates them from the rising horizon, or mixes them more or less with the vapors of the earth—it can perhaps sharpen or dull the force of the ray, but it certainly cannot change its nature. Therefore, the thing that the ray acts upon does not change its type of effect. Instead, without changing the nature of the effect, it will perhaps work with some different disposition—more firmly and effectively, or perhaps more weakly. For powers and properties (whether they are like those of the elements <note>The four elements: Earth, Air, Fire, Water.</note> or more hidden "occult" ones) follow the nature and species of the thing. Thus, if the nature of the star is not changed into something else, the effects themselves cannot be changed into entirely different things.

However, if they were to respond that they have "experienced" it to be so, they might perhaps be believed—either if an experiment could be prepared on these matters (which will be refuted below), or if they all agreed among themselves on the same opinion. But since different astrologers assign different properties to the same locations, they strip their own observations of any authority as faithful testimony. 

The Arabs—and even the Latin writers following in the footsteps of the Arabs <note>Medieval European astrologers relied heavily on Arabic translations and commentaries, such as those by Albumasar or Al-Qabisi.</note>—contend that the quality of servants is indicated by the **sixth place**. But the Egyptians and Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 CE), the most influential ancient authority on astrology and astronomy.</note> look to the place furthest from the sixth—that is, the **twelfth**—for adverse health, whether it be a defect or a disease. Ptolemy does not seek this from the sixth place so much as from the **seventh**...

...tenth and first, since he <note>Pico is referring to Ptolemy, the most authoritative astronomer of antiquity.</note> never uses that house in his <term>apotelematics</term> <note>From the Greek *apotelesma*, meaning the "outcome" or "judgment" of a horoscope; the practice of making predictions.</note>, but he uses these others, always contrary to the common crowd of astrologers. Setting those aside, when others seek every indication of what kind of children a person will have from the sixth house, the Arabs and the Latins make their pronouncements from the fifth house. **Ptolemy** judges from the tenth and eleventh, and when a person’s life is not expected to be long, he uses the fifth and fourth equally. **Paul of Alexandria** <note>A 4th-century astrologer whose *Introductory Matters* was a standard textbook.</note> observes the same. **Mallius** <note>Marcus Manilius (1st century CE), author of the astrological poem *Astronomica*. Pico refers to him as "Mallius."</note> makes the fortune of children and the prayers of parents depend on the East <note>The ascendant or 1st house.</note>. **Porphyry** <note>The Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 CE), who also wrote on astrology.</note> says that children are signified chiefly by the tenth, because souls are sent down into bodies from that part of the sky—and so, quite beautifully, one myth confirms another.

Regarding the fortune of parents, **Ptolemy** accepts it from no specific house. The Arabs take it from the fourth; **Heliodorus** <note>A later Greek astrological writer, often associated with commentaries on Paul of Alexandria.</note> takes it from the sixth. Others, as **Abenragel** <note>Haly Abenragel (Al-Rijal), an 11th-century Arab astrologer highly influential in the Latin West.</note> reports, even take it from the ninth. The second house, for the Alexandrian <note>Paul of Alexandria.</note>, signifies especially <gloss>the matter of sale</gloss> <note>original: "περι πράσεως λόγον" (peri praseos logon)</note> and sudden hopes; among the younger astrologers, it signifies almost none of these things, but rather wealth. Yet **Ptolemy** in his *Apotelematics* offers no judgment on wealth from the second house, nor from any other of the twelve houses; meanwhile, **Heliodorus** would take the indication for those things even from the third house.

Regarding marriage, almost all predict from the West <note>The 7th house, where stars set.</note>; **Heliodorus** also judges from the *Midheaven* <note>The 10th house or the highest point of the sun's path.</note>; **Ptolemy** ignores both. They judge foreign travels from the ninth and third regions. **Heliodorus** also uses the seventh; but **Ptolemy**, when he goes to investigate these matters, treats both this house and those others with equal contempt. Regarding the parent, **Heliodorus** judges from the fourth house, **Maternus** <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer.</note> from the tenth; **Ptolemy** judges from neither. They foresee friends in the eleventh, **Heliodorus** also in the third; **Ptolemy** uses neither the eleventh nor the tenth. The rest take religion from the ninth. 

Likewise, **Mallius** <note>Manilius.</note> takes it from the seventh, which he also calls the "Port of Pluto," a name given to the second house among the Egyptians. The same author places Saturn in charge of the fourth house, contrary to the opinion of others who assign the twelve rulers. If we unroll the works of **Mallius**—who says he occasionally imitated the dogma of the ancients, and than whom no older narrator of celestial matters (or, to speak more truly, of myths) exists among the Latins—we find the matter of the **12 houses** to be so different from every opinion currently reported that the entire method of prediction is utterly changed. For he placed Mars in the setting <note>The 7th house.</note>, while others decreed the first seat below the setting for him. What of those other **12 houses of heaven** handed down by **Mallius**? Are they not different from all the astrology currently in use? Do they not vary every reason for predicting?

> First (he says) is given the lot of Fortune;
> It is designated by this title in the art, because it holds
> Within it the nearest foundations of the home, and all that belongs to it:
> The management of slaves, the harmony of the fields,
> And how much power is granted to construct great works,
> Just as the wandering stars of the shining heaven harmonize.
> After this is the place of military service, where whatever is gathered
> In arms, and among those traveling through foreign cities,
> Is encompassed under a single title.

<header>Book VI Against Astrology</header>

# Book VI Against Astrology

The third <term>station</term> <note>Original: *statio*. In this context, Manilius uses this to mean an astrological "house" or region of the sky.</note> must be counted for city labors.
This too is a type of military service within civil acts.
Established, it holds the bonds of obedience and faith;
It shapes friendships, and how great the rewards 
Reaching duties and service—often performed in vain—might be,
It teaches, when the world harmonizes with the stars placed near.
Nature placed the work of judgments <note>That is, the law courts and legal trials.</note> in the fourth,
And the fortune of the forum, the advocate pouring out words,
The defendant hanging on his tongue, and the words of those presiding
Set over the people, baring the established laws,
And settling disputes with their own furrowed brow.
When the judge calls upon nothing more than himself,
Whatever eloquence accomplishes among the proposed laws:
It yields this whole matter into one part <note>The 4th house.</note>.
And however the dominant stars behave, so it flows.
The fifth step is dedicated to marriage through the signs,
And it holds allies and companions, and is joined
With the guest, a treaty uniting similar friends.
In the sixth seat, a rich abundance is numbered,
And the health of things is joined to it; of which the one
Advises how much use occurs, the other how lasting,
As the stars incline their strengths and govern the <term>temples</term> <note>Original: *templa*. Another term used by Manilius for the astrological houses.</note>.
The seventh is deemed dreadful for its cruel dangers,
If the stars located through the signs subscribe poorly.
Nobility holds the eighth, in which consists the condition
Of honor, the measure of fame, and lineage, and grace
Under a beautiful pretext. The ninth place occupies all
The doubtful lot of the Fates, and the fears of fathers,
And all the mixed nourishing words of those entering.
Neighboring this will be the house containing the action of life <note>The 10th house.</note>,
In which the character of slaves is found, and by what examples
The whole house is formed, and by what certain order
The slaves, arranged for their own duties, depart.
The eleventh part is placed in a special lot,
Which always governs the sum and the strengths of our body.
Whether health stands now free from diseases
Or oppressed, the stars and the world warn of everything—
Not in other seats, nor at another time or manner of healing
Which it might demand for itself, or at what time it might offer
Aid, and to mix the healthful juices of life.
The last, concluding the whole sum in order...

Thus far **Manilius** <note>Pico writes "Mallius," but he is quoting the Roman poet Marcus Manilius, author of the *Astronomica*.</note>, whose opinion clearly differs from all astrology currently in use. Yet I believe he has been understood by none of those who claim to be Manilius’s interpreters and followers. In such a great variety of opinions, then, what faith can be placed in experience? Especially since another greater problem is added: the manner in which the beginnings and boundaries of the "houses" <note>The twelve divisions of the sky in a horoscope.</note> ought to be divided has not yet been established, but different people think differently, as we shall declare in another book. This is something that ought to have been fully investigated *before* any observation regarding their properties was established for the sake of making an experiment. So far are these things from being certain that no observation can be even pretended which would compel us with true and persuasive reasons to agree. Whatever **Ptolemy** <note>The 2nd-century mathematician and astronomer whose *Tetrabiblos* was the foundation of Western astrology.</note> and the rest believed, we conclude—driven by the evidence of reason—that it is ridiculous and false to claim either that these locations possess any inherent properties, or that the flow and efficacy of the planets are changed by their diversity.

### CONCERNING THE TWELVE SIGNS, THAT THEY WERE DEVISED BY MATHEMATICIANS <note>In the Renaissance, "mathematicians" (*mathematici*) often specifically referred to astrologers or those who calculated horoscopes.</note> FOR EASE OF CALCULATION: ALSO THAT ASTROLOGERS HAVE ERRED IN MANY WAYS CONCERNING THEM. Chapter IV.

**I**ndeed, they observe this division and the boundaries of the signs as if they were prescribed by the laws of nature. They think two planets have more of a connection even if they are twenty degrees apart, provided they are placed in the same sign, than if one holds the final degrees of **Aries** and the other is found in the beginning of **Taurus**. This is despite the fact that the former are separated by a vast space, while between the latter there does not fall even the width of a finger. 

But if someone should contend that this number of signs is from nature—not devised by mathematicians for ease of calculation, but established by philosophical reason, such as that offered by **Abu Ma'shar** <note>Original: *Albumasar*, a 9th-century Persian astrologer.</note>, who claims there are twelve signs because there are four elements, each of which is divided into three parts (middle, first, and last)—I could respond that this reason is no less ridiculous and frivolous than the mathematical one. But that the authors of this division were not moved by such conjectures at all, as we have declared above by the testimony of **Haly** <note>Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer.</note> and **Ibn Ezra** <note>Original: *Auenazre*, the 12th-century Jewish scholar and astrologer Abraham ibn Ezra.</note>, can be easily demonstrated by reason. For even if that conjecture were to hold for the signs, what about the...

<meta>This page continues Pico’s critique of the mathematical divisions of the zodiac. He moves from questioning the boundaries of the twelve houses to questioning the very division of the signs into degrees and minutes, arguing that these are arbitrary human inventions for calculation rather than natural divisions with physical influence.</meta>

<page-num>589</page-num>
<header>Against Astrology, Book VI.</header>

...concerning the distribution into thirty parts <note>The thirty degrees that make up each of the twelve zodiac signs.</note>: what shall be said of the division of these parts into sixty minutes? What philosophical reason will they offer for these? Or how will they justify the fact that these were created by mathematicians <note>In this context, "mathematicians" refers to astronomers or those who calculate planetary positions, rather than abstract theorists.</note> who believed there were no natural properties in those divisions, but were merely seeking numbers more convenient for calculation?

From this arises an error for astrologers, or a certain opportunity for deception, when they judge these divisions as if they possessed entirely separate powers, and as if nature, rather than human choice, had divided them from one another. For it is well known that they ascribe various properties to different parts and even to the individual minutes of the same sign. Hence they preach that some parts are "bright," others "dark," some related to the **Sun**, some to **Mars**, and others to various other planets. They even tell fables about the minutes themselves, just as **Aesculapius** <note>A legendary figure to whom many early astrological and medical texts were attributed.</note> wrote the *Myriogenesis* <note>Original: *Miriogeneſim*; a lost astrological work supposedly detailing the influence of every single minute of the zodiac.</note>, which **Maternus** <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman astrologer and author of the *Mathesis*.</note> concealed as if it were a sacred mystery. In that work, he supposedly revealed the specific property of every minute of the celestial flow, as well as its secondary division.

Just as the mere will of those performing calculations created these divisions, so too the principal division of the entire zodiac into twelve signs received its origin from nowhere else. However one understands their division, we have already declared that they possess no efficacy. Thus, the insanity of the astrologers may be refuted here—those who think that a planet is transformed according to the condition of the sign through which it travels. 

For they establish the "houses" and the exaltations <note>Original: *altitudines*; the specific signs where a planet's influence is said to be strongest.</note> of the planets according to these signs, and not according to the constellations <note>Original: *imagines*; the actual groups of stars in the sky. Pico distinguishes between the mathematical "sign" and the physical "constellation."</note>, which we showed in the previous book can only be imagined and have no physical solidity. It is perhaps for this reason that the **Chaldeans**, who did not use these signs, also established no "houses" for the planets. Among them, **Leo** was not the domicile of the **Sun**, nor **Cancer** of the **Moon**, nor **Libra** and **Taurus** of **Venus**, nor **Pisces** and **Sagittarius** of **Jupiter**, and so on for the rest. 

Instead, they observe only the exaltations of the stars, not in relation to the signs, but to the constellations. Thus, among the Chaldeans, **Saturn** possesses nothing in **Capricorn** and nothing in **Aquarius**, but holds authority only in **Libra** and **Scorpio**. For although these are two signs, they are judged as a single constellation among the Chaldeans <note>In ancient astronomy, the stars of Libra were often seen as the "Claws" of the Scorpion.</note>. Otherwise, if **Ptolemy** and others were to refer the houses of the planets to the constellations (which they do not do), their logic would not hold. For **Mars** has the greatest affinity with the stars that constitute the constellation of **Taurus**—more so than any other planet—yet in astrology, he is said to be "in detriment" <note>Original: *deijci*; literally "cast down," referring to a planet being in a sign opposite its home where its power is weakened.</note> when in the sign of **Taurus**.

Therefore, they derive the houses, exaltations, bounds <term>fines: specific segments of a sign ruled by different planets</term>, triplicities <term>triangulariates: the grouping of signs by the four elements</term>, monomoiria <term>monomirias: the individual influence of each single degree</term>, decans <term>decanos: ten-degree subdivisions of a sign</term>, faces <note>Original: *hydrofoſopias*; likely a corruption of *prosopa*, the Greek term for planetary faces or decanic appearances.</note>, and other such planetary affinities with the parts of the zodiac from these signs. Since it has been sufficiently proven, I think, that no power can pass to the planets if these divisions are entirely imaginary, not natural, and not effective, one must wonder at those who try to bolster astrological opinion with an analogy. 

They say that the planets "smell of" <note>Original: *redolere*; to emit a scent or reflect a quality.</note> the qualities of the zodiac sign in which the "seeds of things" are dispersed, just as plants reflect the flavor of the soil they grow in. But this analogy is very flawed. Plants are nourished by the earth, and for that reason, they reflect its flavor. The planets are not nourished by the zodiac, even though every kind of "animal" <note>A pun on *zodiakos*, the "circle of animals."</note> shines there. The planets are not attached to the zodiac like the roots and shoots of plants are to the earth; rather, they are separated from it by an immense chasm...

<summary>Pico argues that the mathematical divisions of the zodiac (degrees, minutes, houses) are arbitrary human inventions for calculation rather than natural phenomena with physical power. He highlights contradictions between the "Chaldean" and "Ptolemaic" systems to prove that astrological properties like "houses" and "exaltations" lack a consistent or natural basis.</summary>

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

->...proximity and<- distance. For this reason especially, **Panaetius** and **Plotinus** <note>Panaetius (c. 185–109 BC) was a Stoic philosopher who doubted astrology; Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism and argued that stars are signs, not causes.</note> mock those who think that an influence <note>Original: *contagionem*, literally "contagion" or "infection," used here to describe the supposed physical transmission of power from stars to Earth.</note> can travel from the zodiac to the stars across such a vast interval of space. We are moved not so much by the space that lies immensely between them, as by the nature of the things themselves: for real and natural bodies cannot be affected by imaginary ones, nor can glowing stars be changed by things that do not glow (not to say by things that are nothing at all). 

But it is easy to see what deceived them here: for since the **Sun**, when positioned in **Leo**, heats the lands more violently, and when coming to **Aries** it as if restores the world, it seemed to them that the **Sun** had a kinship with **Leo** and **Aries**, because in traversing those signs it is rendered stronger and we experience its power more greatly every year. From this they established **Leo** as the "domicile" of the **Sun**, and **Aries** as its "kingdom" <note>In astrology, a "domicile" (home) is the sign where a planet has most harmony; a "kingdom" (exaltation) is where its influence is most intense.</note>. Led by this conjecture regarding the **Sun**, they thought a similar thing should be decided for the other signs—that a planet might have more power in one sign and less in another. 

Indeed, by a very "fine" reasoning, they distributed two houses to each planet except for the **Sun** and the **Moon**, for whom one royal seat each would be enough. For when they had decided, for the reason given above, that the **Sun** should receive **Leo** as its home (where in the burning heat it might best exercise its powers), it seemed reasonable that the house next to it should be thought to belong to the **Moon**, as she approaches us more closely. Indeed, her circle is the one closest to us; therefore, they assigned **Cancer** as the domicile of the **Moon**. However, according to the position of the spheres in which the planets are carried, they distributed two houses to each of the others—one on either side, as follows:

*   To **Mercury**, who is believed to be adjacent to the **Moon**: **Gemini** on one side, **Virgo** on the other.
*   To **Venus**: **Taurus** on one side, **Libra** on the other.
*   To **Mars**: **Aries** on one side, **Scorpio** on the other.
*   To **Jupiter**: **Pisces** and **Sagittarius**.
*   To **Saturn**: **Aquarius** and **Capricorn**.

With these persuasions—which do not even have the weight of <term>rhetorical probability</term> <note>Meaning the arguments wouldn't even pass a basic test of logic in a debate, let alone scientific proof.</note>—they founded their dogmas, handed down by posterity with such authority that they are accepted almost as if they were great oracles. 

In these matters, first look at what else remains; see how criminal it is, and how full of both ignorance and dullness. For the fact that the **Sun** in **Leo** heats us more is not due to the nature of the sign it traverses, but happens because of its position and placement—because from that place it strikes the earth more directly in our regions which are closest to it. Otherwise, if a quality received from the "sign" caused this, it would do the same among all nations, since the same signs are present for everyone. But in truth, at the same time the **Sun** scorches the lands situated to the North when it is in **Leo**, it is cold among those who inhabit the South; among them, it is hot when the **Sun** comes to **Aquarius**, under which it pours out ice and watery rain upon us. This is because the more it approaches us, the further it moves from them, and conversely, it turns its path toward them whenever it departs from us. 

But if they contend that they were led not so much by that logic as by other experiments, by which a planet was observed to have more or less power elsewhere: perhaps there would be some faith in this, if the true founders of the art had handed down consistent things on these matters. I speak of the **Chaldeans** <note>The ancient Babylonians, traditionally regarded by Renaissance thinkers as the "masters" and inventors of astrology.</note>, the masters for the new professors, who they claim observed the heavens for many thousands of years in the open plains; yet they [the Chaldeans] placed no faith in these "houses," as we were saying above. Why then, with such diligent and long-lasting observations, did they...

He mocks the idea that imaginary mathematical divisions could physically influence real celestial bodies.</summary>
