->Against Astrology, Book VI.<-

...they have never discovered **Mars** to be strong in **Scorpio** or weak in **Taurus**, nor **Saturn** powerful in **Capricorn** or weak in **Cancer**? The same should be understood for what is said of the rest. And since the same sign is divided into so many <term>terms<note>Original: *finibus*. These are sub-sections of a zodiac sign, usually 5-7 degrees long, where a planet other than the sign-ruler is said to have influence.</note></term>, into so many <term>decans<note>Original: *decanis*. 10-degree segments of a sign, totaling 36 in the zodiac.</note></term>, and furthermore into so many <term>monomoiria<note>Original: *monomiriis*. A system where every single degree of a sign is assigned to a specific planet.</note></term> among the Egyptians, or <term>dodecatemoria<note>Original: *dodecathemorijs*. "Twelfth-parts"; the division of a single 30-degree sign into twelve smaller segments of 2.5 degrees each.</note></term> among the Chaldeans—and since there is no agreement among them regarding the "terms," and **Ptolemy** ignores the "decans" (which the Indians and Egyptians divide differently), and the **Arabs** are ignorant of the "monomoiria" while the **Greeks** mock them (though the **Egyptians** use them in every prediction). I pass over the use of "dodecatemoria" which is very frequent among the **Chaldeans**. Yet, as **Maternus** <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer who wrote the "Mathesis."</note> writes, a planet provides in its own "terms" what it provides in its "domicile," and in its "decan" what it grants in its "terms" and "house," or certainly things very close and similar to these. 

Since these things are so, I ask: what reliable and consistent experience can there be regarding which part of the zodiac a planet travels through or where it is "exiled," or whether it is found powerful or weak? Add to this the various opinions about the signs when they are referred either to the ninth sphere or rather described in the eighth, and one person wants **Saturn** to rule the same part, another **Jupiter**, and another another of the planets. Some use these signs which they think move, others those that do not move. Regarding these opinions, nothing has been so decreed or prejudged that **Abraham** <note>Likely Abraham Ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a renowned Jewish scholar and astrologer whose works were widely read in the Renaissance.</note> in his *Book of Nativities* commanded that a double chart be made: one for the moving signs and another for the fixed ones. By this variety of charts, the entire logic of predictions is varied. Thus all authority of experiment is weakened, because it will be demonstrated later that no experience can be had regarding these matters, or if it could be had, it has not yet been obtained.

### WHAT THE OPINION OF ASTROLOGERS IS CONCERNING ASPECTS, and how little rational it is. Chapter V.

We have already refuted the opinion of astrologers regarding the twelve signs and the twelve houses of the sky; there remains the third way in which they fabulate that powers and "outpourings" <note>Original: *defluxus*. The supposed physical or spiritual influence flowing from a star to Earth.</note> are exchanged, which is commonly called **aspects**. For they think that if **Saturn**, for example, is distant from **Jupiter** by 60 degrees—that is, by two whole signs—it affects and moves the lower world differently than if it were distant from the same star by 90 degrees, which is an interval of three signs. In the first distance, they say **Saturn** "looks at" **Jupiter** with a **hexagonal radiation**, which they call a **sextile aspect**, because the space between them is a sixth part of the zodiac. In the other, they say they behold each other from a **square** <note>Original: *quadrato*. The "square" aspect (90 degrees) was traditionally considered difficult or "malefic."</note>, because they are separated by a fourth part of the zodiac. Similarly, there are other properties of both stars if one is 120 degrees from the other, from which a **trigonal radiation** arises—that is, a **trine aspect**. Still others if they are simultaneously opposed across the diameter, or meet in the same position or place. And what we have said of **Jupiter** and **Saturn** should be understood as said of all: that their power and effectiveness are changed according to their varying distance from each other. And they are changed to such an extent that when they are distant by certain intervals—that is, by a trine or a sextile—their entire "outpouring" is good and healthy. On the other hand, when positioned at another certain distance...

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

...situated, that is, either in a square or in opposition, they possess the most harmful powers in their rays, or at least are always minimally beneficial; and likewise, that from this diversity of distances, not only the goodness or malice of the <term>influx<note>Original: *defluxus*. The "flow" of celestial influence down to the Earthly realm.</note></term> changes, but also the very appearance and method of their operation. These are the delusions of astrologers concerning the **aspects** of the planets, which a philosopher, upon hearing them, will immediately condemn even without a counter-argument. For it can be defended by no reason that the nature and property of two causes working toward the same end could be so transformed solely by the diversity of the distance and interval between them.

First, I ask this of them: do they intend for these things they say about **aspects** to refer to the planets themselves, or only to the effects of the planets? That is, when they say that **Jupiter** is "provoked" by **Mars** with square rays, or that **Venus** is "fostered" by the trine radiation of **Jupiter**, do they mean that the actual bodies of the planets are moved by these kinds of good or bad <term>affections<note>In this context, "affections" refers to being affected or changed by an external force.</note></term>, or do the planets themselves suffer nothing from one another and feel nothing of such changes? Do they instead mean that these terms merely signify what the planets do toward us, and in what way they move the physical bodies below? 

For whether they answer one way or the other, they fall into a thousand snares and a thousand straits from every side. If they think the planets are moved by each other—exercising friendships and hatreds, now fostering each other in a friendly embrace, now pursuing and invading each other in a hostile manner with the points of their rays—not only will the divine **Job** cry out (with whom we read that God "makes peace in his high places"), <note>Job 25:2. Pico uses this to argue that there is no "warfare" or "hostility" between celestial bodies.</note> but so will the entire family of the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note> along with their leader **Aristotle**. Among them, it is certain that the higher bodies are changed only by their variety of location, and that those qualities found below the **Moon** neither arrive there [in the heavens] nor depart from it. 

But if they wish to grant those qualities entirely—certainly as far as harmful qualities are concerned—they seem worthy of being exploded from every assembly of philosophers. They appear to be entirely ignorant of the nature of the celestial homeland, thinking there is something in it that can do or suffer injury. Therefore, if any **passion** <note>Original: *passio*. In Aristotelian philosophy, "passion" refers to the act of being acted upon or undergoing change, the opposite of "action."</note> is to be admitted in the stars, it is none other than what should be called perfection rather than "passion." For example, when the **Moon** is illuminated by the **Sun**, she "suffers" from him then in no other way than a person "suffers" who receives a benefit. 

Therefore, for a star to be hurt by another star, or besieged, or infected, or made weaker or worse—or to be turned from beneficial to harmful, or from powerful to weak—is as far removed from all truth as the nature of the celestial beings is removed from all evil. 

Furthermore, if the stars *could* suffer injury, surely those that are more noble and perfect ought not to suffer it from the less noble. Thus, it should at least be concluded that not all things can be mutually affected and moved by all things, but rather certain things by certain others, so that some only act, while others only suffer. Otherwise, how do they not blush at this: to reduce the **Sun**—the ruler and king of the planets, the highest celestial fountain of light and power—into such a rank and order that he too, overcome by the rays of others, should either languish or become unhealthful? This, despite the fact that every virtue of the planets is derived from him as if from his own...

<summary>Pico argues that astrological "aspects" are logically impossible because celestial bodies are immutable and cannot harm or "provoke" one another. He uses Aristotelian physics and scripture to assert that the heavens are a place of peace and perfection, not physical conflict.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s critique of the astrological "aspects." On the previous page, he questioned whether the planets themselves are affected by these geometric relationships or if only their influence on Earth changes. He now points out the logical absurdity of planets being "unconnected" when near each other but "connected" when further apart.</meta>

# On Astrology, Book VI.

...it is usually said) suffer from a weapon. But let us set aside all these things which perhaps do not seem absurd to them, and let us establish (as they wish) that the planets are affected and moved. Let them answer this: what reason do they have that stars which are very close to one another do not move each other at all, yet when those same stars become more distant, they begin to perceive and mutually affect one another? For this is how they usually define **aspects**. For if **Jupiter** occupies **Cancer** and **Mars** occupies **Leo**, they say these stars are <term>unconnected<note>Original: *asyndeta*. From the Greek for "unlinked." In astrology, planets in adjacent signs were thought to be unable to "see" or aspect one another.</note></term> because no sign lies between them—that is, they are joined by no coupling of rays or aspects. But then, when **Mars** has moved further away from **Jupiter** and traveled into **Virgo**, they will consider that **Mars** participates in **Jupiter**, and **Jupiter** in **Mars**.

What could be said that is more absurd than this, or further removed from all philosophy? For it is a most common principle that everything which acts upon another does so more effectively the closer it is to the <term>patient<note>The "patient" is the philosophical term for the object being acted upon by an "agent."</note></term>. Therefore, if this thing which the younger astrologers call an **aspect** is nothing other than **radiation**—as it was also named by the ancients—that is, the propagation of its own light and power onto another, and (so to speak) a certain shedding of light, how can it be that there is no effect on things that are closest, yet it will be effective on things that are very remote? What on earth persuades them that a ray is poured out from a more distant or a closer range in such a way that it turns out to be of one nature or another? Since (if we follow true reason) no other diversity can arise from this except that the ray is impressed upon the "patient" planet more weakly or more strongly. 

But why its very property should be changed, no cause can be imagined or devised. For even if the number of intervening parts varies due to the difference in interval, or the planets themselves obtain a different geometric figure of position among themselves, that power of natural things does not vary according to the diversity of numbers and figures. This is because **natural virtues** do not arise from numbers and figures, but from natural forms; it is according to the diversity of these forms that the figures themselves—those that are stable and innate, not the accidental ones that arise from motion—are moved and varied.

Nor indeed do fewer difficulties arise if they think the diversity of radiation should be considered not in the bodies of the planets, but in their effect. That is, if they say the stars suffer nothing from each other, but that the logic of the distance between them causes the flowing rays to be mixed differently, and therefore various effects arise from the diversities of the mixture. For if they answer this, we could first object on the authority of **Plotinus** <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism. Pico frequently cites him to argue that celestial influences are simple and incorporeal, and therefore cannot "mix" like physical liquids.</note> that rays flowing down from heaven cannot be so mixed with one another that a new power or form arises. This is because they are neither bodies, nor liquids, nor qualities fixed to bodies; they are not received into bodies in the manner of such things, so as to be "infected" by them, or to be changed in some way from their own state according to the condition of the substance. Therefore, to that philosopher, it seemed quite probable that what happens to many qualities does not happen to rays: namely, that from some concrete bonding or mixture they are sometimes changed into another form coalescing from all of them—which also does not happen without the destruction of the simple and particular parts flowing together into the same thing.

...it is usually said to happen, since no one will easily think of this occurring in rays. But let us grant them that the rays are mixed, provided they demonstrate to us how the rays are mixed differently when they flow together from the stars when they are at various different distances from one another. For only this diversity (as we said above) can arise from this: that those rays which emanate from bodies that are closer and more joined will be mixed better and more intimately, while conversely, those that proceed from separated and more remote bodies will cohere with more difficulty. Yet this does not please those who allow no commerce between the rays of planets located in <term>adjacent signs<note>Original: *attiguis signis*. In traditional astrology, planets in signs next to each other (like Aries and Taurus) were thought to be "inconjunct" or unable to "see" each other.</note></term>, but allow the greatest commerce between those that have emanated from stars separated by a vast and immense region of the sky. Furthermore, if the ratio of the diameter of opposition, or the quadrangular [square] or triangular [trine] figure creates a difference in the property of the rays, this cannot be defended unless we say the bodies of the planets change their condition based on that variety of figures—since the power and property of a ray comes from nowhere else than the nature of the radiating body. Nor is that variety of figures located anywhere else than between the bodies themselves, from which the rays descend to us. The further those rays recede from their source, the less they preserve that relationship of figures between themselves, until, touching the earth, they come together into a cone; thus, those rays which flowed forth from opposite sources flow together into a unified mass here with us. Therefore, when they are mixed, they are no longer entangled in triangular or quadrangular <term>schemes<note>Original: *schematis*. From the Greek *schema*, referring to the geometric configurations or "aspects" formed by the planets.</note></term>. Thus, the nature of the mixing cannot be changed by that variety of schemes. Instead, astrologers will have to resort to saying that there is such a property in the rays because the stars from which they emanated were arranged among themselves in such a relationship of figures. In the end, they will either have to say that the stars vary their own nature according to the variety of their <term>configurations<note>Original: *configurationum*.</note></term>—which has already been refuted—or, if the stars themselves do not vary, they will be forced to admit that the power of the rays flowing from them is also the same and unchanged.

### VARIOUS REASONS FOR THE ASPECTS ARE RECITED
### and refuted. Chapter VI.

The <term>ancients<note>Specifically referring to Hellenistic and Roman astrologers.</note></term>, whom <term>Maternus<note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman official and astrologer who wrote the *Mathesis*, a major compendium of ancient astrology.</note></term> imitates, brought forward a reason for the **aspects** based on numbers. They said that separate stars were "joined" by that number of degrees between them which, when multiplied, would count out the total parts of the sky <note>The 360 degrees of the zodiac.</note>. Therefore, they say an <term>opposition<note>Original: *diametram radiationem*. A 180-degree aspect.</note></term> occurs at an interval of one hundred and eighty degrees, because this number doubled makes the full number of three hundred and sixty degrees. Likewise, a <term>trine<note>Original: *trigonum*. A 120-degree aspect.</note></term> consists of 120 degrees, because if you triple these parts, you again complete all the parts of the sky. A <term>square<note>Original: *quadrata radiatio*. A 90-degree aspect.</note></term> radiation requires ninety degrees, which if you doubled <note>Original: *duplicaueris*. Mathematically, 90 must be quadrupled to reach 360; Pico may be highlighting a slip in the astrologers' logic or referencing a different calculation method.</note> you would gather the sum of three hundred and sixty; the <term>sextile<note>Original: *hexagonus*. A 60-degree aspect.</note></term> is calculated at 60 degrees, which are the sixth part of all the parts. But this reasoning is far too drowsy and far too lazy: for the same...

He begins refuting the ancient Pythagorean-style justification that these angles are significant because they are factors of the 360-degree circle.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's systematic critique of the mathematical and "natural" justifications for astrological aspects. ### Against Astrology, Book VI.

...by the same reasoning, they form an aspect at seventy-two degrees, since multiplied five times they complete three hundred and sixty degrees; let them do the same for forty-five, since this number is an eighth part of all the degrees of the heaven. But (says <term>Abu Ma'shar<note>Original: *Aboasar*. A 9th-century Persian astrologer and philosopher whose works were influential in medieval Europe.</note></term>) those numbers have another prerogative, since when multiplied they count not only the parts of the heaven but also the number of the signs. For in a <term>hexagon<note>Original: *hexagono*. In modern astrology, this 60-degree angle (1/6 of a circle) is called a sextile.</note></term> two signs are counted, in a <term>trigon<note>Original: *trigono*. A 120-degree angle (1/3 of a circle), commonly called a trine.</note></term> four, in a <term>tetragon<note>Original: *tetragono*. A 90-degree angle (1/4 of a circle), commonly called a square.</note></term> three, and in a <term>diameter<note>Original: *diametro*. A 180-degree angle (1/2 of a circle), commonly called an opposition.</note></term> six are computed. For twice six, three times four, four times three, and six times two make up the number of twelve signs. 

But this confirmation is also frivolous; for by similar reasoning, stars that were separated by thirty degrees would be configured toward each other, because if you look at the number of degrees, you will have a twelfth part of the heaven's degrees, and if you look at the signs, a twelfth portion of them as well. Finally, the reasons brought by <term>Ptolemy<note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note></term> from geometric figures do not conclude the proposition, given that these harmonies of figures do not produce different properties in natural things. Instead, those who use them incur that error condemned by <term>Aristotle<note>The Greek philosopher warned against applying the methods of one discipline (like mathematics) to the subject matter of another (like physics) without considering their different natures.</note></term>: treating physical things mathematically. Seeing this perhaps, <term>Ibn Ridwan<note>Original: *Auenrodan*. An 11th-century Egyptian physician and astrologer who wrote a famous commentary on Ptolemy.</note></term> says that Ptolemy, after the mathematical reason brought concerning aspects, brought another from nature.

The reason he brings is of this sort: that the hexagonal and trigonal radiation are beneficial because they are from signs of the same kind, either masculine or feminine. That is, the planets tied together by those patterns are so disposed that if one is in a feminine sign, the other is also in a feminine one; if one is in a masculine, the other is likewise in a masculine. Conversely, the square and opposite radiations are harmful because they emerge from signs of different kinds. 

This is Ptolemy's reason—not only weak but self-defeating. First, because those signs truly are nothing (as we will reveal in the following books); second, if they are something, they are nevertheless not marked by those notes of quality or sex, such that these could be called masculine, those feminine, others fiery, others airy—which has already been sufficiently proven above. Finally, whatever their condition may be, the planets cannot be changed by them, as we will demonstrate below. 

Now let us make no quarrel over these things, but let us most evidently demonstrate how these, like all their claims, fight against themselves. For if what is assumed is true, the opposite radiation [the opposition]—which is considered the most harmful—should be numbered among the good, since it too occurs nowhere else than in signs of the same kind. For Aries and Libra are of the same kind; likewise Cancer and Capricorn, and all others that look at each other from across the diameter. 

It is truly quite strange that Ptolemy did not see this—that a man otherwise so ingenious should hallucinate in a matter so open and manifest. If he had remembered what he said elsewhere, he would have seen that the reasoning does not proceed but is contrary to his own precepts. For in the third book of the same work, he himself thinks that between signs not only of the same sex but also of the same quality, there is sometimes not a hexagon [sextile]—which is good—but a tetragon [square]—which is bad...

...configuration, so that when they are oblique—that is, of "short times"—three of those which are of a different kind are equal; they do not have a square affinity, but rather a hexagonal one. Thus, in that composite radiation, Gemini and Aquarius would form a square, but Taurus and Aquarius would form a hexagon. If this is true, how can the goodness or malice of configurations arise from the affinity or discord of the signs? This is a difficulty that must be faced by all those who measure the spaces of radiations not by the parts of the zodiac, but by the parts of the equator—a practice observed by the majority of astrologers. Yet all of them (as they are wonderfully inconsistent) when they must give a reason for the malice or goodness of the aspects, reason from no other source more than from that very kinship or diversity of the signs.

<term>Abu Ma'shar<note>Original: *Aboafar*. 9th-century Persian astrologer.</note></term> brings forward another reason which he considers "natural" regarding the aspects. He says that the **opposition** is confirmed by the fullness of light which the Moon attains when it is opposite the Sun. He claims the **square** power appears in the motion of the planets from their <term>apsis<note>The point in a planet's orbit where it is nearest to or furthest from the Earth.</note></term>, for when they are ninety degrees distant from it, they change their course. The **trine** is seen in the superior planets, which, when removed from the Sun by one hundred and twenty degrees, move backward if they were previously moving forward, or move forward if they were previously retrograde. The quantity of the **hexagon**, he says, corresponds to half the diameter of the circle, as well as to the distance of the houses of Venus from the houses of the <term>luminaries<note>The Sun and the Moon.</note></term>. 

Thus has he poorly stitched together a single patchwork quilt from a thousand scraps. He seeks the opposition from the Moon, the square from the apsis, the trine from the superior planets, and the hexagon from Venus—and all of them poorly from everyone. For what reason is it that, because the Moon is filled with the Sun's light through the diameter, all planets should be coupled at this distance, not only to the Sun but also among themselves? And if the superior planets change their course at a trine from the Sun, why should this interval have the power of changing the strengths of the planets—not only the superior ones but also the inferior ones—and not just toward the Sun, but even when taken between the planets themselves? 

Furthermore, even that observation is not constant among the superior planets. For Mars, as <term>Paulus<note>Paulus Alexandrinus, a 4th-century astrological author.</note></term> and <term>Porphyry<note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on astrology.</note></term> write, sometimes halts itself to go retrograde when it is only eighty-four degrees distant from the Sun in the preceding signs, not waiting for the expected trine, but having only completed a <term>tetragon<note>A 90-degree square aspect.</note></term>. But if they gathered the power of the trine from that change of the superior planets in a trine to the Sun, it ought to be numbered among the "bad" radiations rather than the "good" ones, since every superior planet is unhappy in a trine to the Sun, if we believe Paulus and <term>Heliodorus<note>An 8th-century commentator on Paulus Alexandrinus.</note></term>. For they say all <note>original: *ἀστερὰς ἀστάτους κακοποιοὺς*</note> **unsteady stars are evildoers**—that is, that all stationary planets are bad and unhappy, whether they are in their first station or their second. <margin>†</margin> But all these things are of such obvious triviality that to refute them further is unnecessary.

Finally, another reason has been devised by certain "moderns" concerning musical consonances, from which they hand down that the rays of the planets sometimes harmonize with each other and sometimes clash through a certain similarity to musical harmonies. For they say it is proven among musicians by both reason and experience that the third and fifth voices harmonize with the first, but the fourth and seventh by no means do so. What if, therefore, those stars distant from each other by equal spaces now well...

<meta>This page continues Pico’s refutation of the justifications for astrological "aspects" (the specific angles between planets). ...find these to be poorly tuned? The hexagonal radiation <note>The sextile aspect, 60 degrees</note> corresponds to the third note, the trine <note>120 degrees</note> to the fifth, and the square <note>90 degrees</note> to the fourth, since there are as many signs mediating between them as there are intervals between the notes. But these are surely pretty things, and they have an appearance of probability to those who have only "greeted philosophy from the doorstep" <note>A Latin idiom meaning to have only a superficial or amateur understanding</note>. But for our part, to omit these similarities among such different kinds of things, we shall declare that they have no efficacy or reason, and that the calculation and similarity do not hold up. 

For among musicians, a note either harmonizes or is dissonant with any other note; among astrologers, many spaces are (as I might say) "mute" to one another—that is, they neither harmonize nor are they dissonant. For example, the second note is counted among the dissonant ones by musicians no less than the fourth, seventh, or eleventh. But among astrologers, the second sign does not discord with the first, but rather emits no voice at all. The fifth and seventh signs emit some voice, but not a concordant one. Furthermore, there is that even greater difference: the sixth note among musicians harmonizes just as the third does, yet among astrologers, the sixth sign is utterly distinct from the first. Then, in music, the eighth note <note>the octave</note> harmonizes as if it were the same note, but the eighth sign does not recognize the first, nor can the eighth note reflect the kind of conjunction that notes of the same tone represent. Therefore, in this so-called "pretty similarity," <margin>*</margin> there is found altogether more dissimilarity than similarity.

### WHAT DECEIVED THEM: NOR IS THERE ANY EXPERIENCE REGARDING ASPECTS. Chapter VII.

**I**n truth, those who first invented that dogma were not led even by reasons of this kind, but a certain conjecture regarding the Moon deceived them more. For when they observed that the Moon, borrowing light from the Sun, varied its shape according to its different position relative to the Sun—whether it was closer or receding—they transferred this same idea to the rest of the planets: that all of them, according to their different distance not only from the Sun but also from each other, would change their condition and state. You may easily notice that they were led to this opinion from nowhere else by the fact that they established neither more nor fewer, nor any other configurations of the planets among themselves, than those which the Moon is found to undergo relative to the Sun within the diversity of the signs. 

There are, however, five celebrated "schematisms" <note>patterns or configurations</note> of the Moon relative to the Sun: when it is seen either joined with the Sun <note>the New Moon</note>, or crescent-shaped, or halved, or bulging <note>gibbous</note>, or full. To these, as many configurations devised by them among the planets correspond. For they are seen either together, or in a hexagonal, or quadrangular, or triangular, or opposite radiation. For conjunction corresponds to conjunction; then the hexagonal radiation <note>sextile</note> corresponds to the crescent-shaped figure, which is first seen in the Moon when it is 60 degrees distant from the Sun, and is called by the Greeks <term>menoeidēs<note>Original: μηνοειδής. Crescent-shaped or moon-like.</note></term>. By the number of these same degrees, they also established the hexagonal radiation among the planets. Likewise, the Moon is halved—called <term>dichotomos<note>Original: διχότομος. Cut in two; the first or last quarter phase.</note></term> in Greek—when between it...

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

->[Page 598]<-

...and the Sun, ninety degrees lie between them. When the stars themselves are separated by this same distance, they are said by astrologers to be joined in a **square** configuration. They derived the **trine** radiation <note>The "trine" is an aspect where planets are 120 degrees apart</note> from the "pre-swollen" appearance of the Moon; this is the shape she is first seen to take when she is removed 120 degrees from the Sun. It is called *amphikyrtos* <note>original: "ἀμφίκυρτος"</note> by the Greeks, which we may call "pre-swollen" or "gibbous." Everyone understands that the **opposition** aspect corresponds to the full moon itself. 

Furthermore, because the Moon is accustomed to changing physical bodies in different ways according to the diversity of her shape <note>i.e., her phases</note>, they established the same rule for all the planets: namely, that according to this variety of intervals between them, they would also affect lower things <note>Earthly matters</note> in various ways. If they were led to this conclusion by a conjecture of logical consequence (as I suspect), one can easily understand how much they are deceived. It is true that the Moon, due to her varying distance from the Sun, changes both her shape and the properties of her influence, because she receives her light from the Sun. She is illuminated more or less by the Sun in that part which faces us, depending on the condition of her position and her relationship to him. 

From this, it follows by natural reason that—due to the increases or decreases of light—the Moon not only represents herself to us in a different image, but also changes the physical qualities of our bodies and those of other things in a different manner. For who does not know that the moisture of bodies is dissolved by heat? Or who, in turn, does not know that light is the cause of heat? From this, it is clearly gathered that the more light the Moon has, the more the bodies of lower things (to which she is closest) are heated; and by a consequent reason, the moisture within them more greatly melts and resolves. In this way, that statement of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century foundational authority on astronomy and astrology</note> will be true: that from the first quarter of the Moon until the second <note>from the first quarter to the full moon</note>, the moisture of bodies flows out, clearly because during that time the parts of the Moon facing the Earth enjoy a more abundant light. 

Hence come those experiments <note>term: *experimēta* (observations or practical trials)</note> proven by the labors of farmers: that timber cut when the Moon is filling with light quickly rots, whereas, on the contrary, timber cut when the Moon is waning is believed to be preserved from decay and the vice of putrefaction. This is because moisture is the most opportune condition for putrefaction, and as I have said, this moisture increases and decreases in bodies in step with the increase and decrease of the Moon’s light. 

But truly, to transfer these changes of the Moon—which alone is subject to this kind of change in light—to the other planets (which shine always with their own and immovable light) is utterly insane. On the contrary, one might argue from the opposite perspective: if the Moon changes us in different ways according to the measure of her light because she is illuminated more or less by her change in position, it should follow that the planets' property of influence does *not* change, just as their light does not change. By reason of their varying distance, whether to the Sun or to each other, they are neither impoverished of light nor enriched, but they always look upon us and other earthly things in the same way. 

Therefore, whether they were led into this opinion by these reasons (as we suspect), or by the conjectures we first attacked, it is clear they rely on the flimsiest and most ridiculous arguments. If they perhaps lack confidence in these and allege the "certainty of experience"—which is the sole refuge for those destitute of reason—we can equally appeal to experience, which...

their astrological outcomes <term>apotelesmata: the results or predictions derived from an astrological chart</term> are refuted every day. But let them answer this one thing: what true and reliable experiments have been held concerning these matters, about which there is such great controversy among them, that where one has established a **square** <note>An aspect of 90 degrees</note>, another contends it is a **trine** <note>An aspect of 120 degrees</note>? And what this one makes a **hexagon** <note>A sextile aspect of 60 degrees</note>, let there be someone who wants it to be a **tetragon** <note>A square aspect</note>; indeed, let it be a trine to one person, which nevertheless will be a **diameter** <note>An opposition aspect of 180 degrees</note> to others. Since this matter will be discussed at length below, we refer the reader to that place, now merely warning that they differ not only in prescribing the boundaries of the radiations, but also in many things regarding their very nature. This is so much the case that Paulus and Heliodorus <note>Paul of Alexandria (4th century) and Heliodorus (6th century), influential astrological writers</note> write that a hexagon that is not between signs of equal distance from either the equinoxes or the tropics has the nature of an opposition. Furthermore, they claim that even the opposition is not malicious, but mediates between good and bad aspects; likewise, Ptolemy thinks that neither is the square bad nor the trine good. Thus, it is clear enough that no authority of experience supports them, even though each master contends that such support favors him, despite their diverse opinions held with equal faith and equal authority.

### WHAT IS SAID ABOUT OBSESSION CONFLICTS WITH THESE
->regarding the aspects. CHAPTER VIII.<-

**T**here are <note>The Latin text 'Vnt' is a decorative typographical error for 'Sunt' (They are)</note>, however, besides those figures and aspects which we have mentioned, other positions of the stars both among themselves and in relation to the Sun, by which they think the powers are affected and the properties of things are changed. Among these are those that seem to contradict those prior rules. For they say a planet is **obsessed** whenever the rays of evil stars surround it on both sides. This condition the Greeks call *emperischesis* <note>original: "ἐμπερίσχεσιν," meaning encirclement or being hemmed in</note>. For example, if Jupiter occupies Libra, Mars occupies Virgo, and Saturn occupies Scorpio—or even with Jupiter placed there, if Mars hurls rays from Taurus into Virgo and Scorpio—then they will call Jupiter "obsessed."

I therefore ask them: do planets move or affect one another when located in joined and neighboring signs? If they say no, then "obsession" <note>original: "ἐμπερίσχεσις"</note> is abolished, since a ray reaching Virgo will not harm a star placed in Libra, just as one sent to Scorpio will not, because Scorpio and Virgo are the signs adjacent to Libra. If they concede it, then the whole logic of aspects is nothing, for that logic depends entirely on the idea that planets affect each other at certain intervals and suffer nothing from one another at others. But if they respond that it happens differently in "obsession" because there are rays on both sides, they say the very thing by which their insanity is made manifest. It is as if they think (as usually happens to men) that a pursuing enemy from behind does not harm a fleeing man so long as a free field lies open in front for escape, yet he is nonetheless caught by the pursuer if someone else stands opposite, blocking the path of flight. To use this example: if Mars occupies Virgo, he does not reach Jupiter placed in Libra, yet he will reach him from there if Saturn stands in Scorpio opposite Jupiter. What kind of self-consistent discipline is this, where you call neighboring signs "unconnected" <note>original: "asindetæ apostrophæ"</note> so that the stars placed in them have no communion with each other, and nothing flows from one into the other, and yet you say the planet is obsessed...

### THAT PLANETS POSITIONED UNDER THE SUN'S RAYS
### are not badly affected or, as astrologers say,
### "combust." Chapter IX.

**D**o they not also rave regarding the planets compared to the Sun? They claim that those positioned under its rays are ineffective and ill-affected, as if the stars could not bear the light of the Sun, or as if their heads were rather weak and they fall ill if they stay in the sun too long. And yet, all celestial light—and especially solar light—is beneficial. If it is sometimes harmful to earthly things, this happens only through a defect in the matter [receiving it]; however, there is no such defect of matter in the stars. Therefore, the more they enjoy the light of the Sun, the more vigorous and effective they become, especially since the Sun, compared to the stars, holds the status of a universal cause, whose nature is not to undermine the specific nature of particular things, but to confirm it. 

If the "silent" Moon <note>The New Moon, when it is invisible from Earth</note> appears to be deprived of its benefit for the lower regions, that is for another reason: because on the side facing us, it is joined to the Sun and stripped of light. This does not happen to the other planets, which shine with their own light, so that for that reason, when they are surrounded by the rays of the Sun, they should not be less capable of altering lower things. 

But if they stubbornly defend this—that the power of the stars is oppressed and exhausted—this ought to happen more the more powerful they are, and the closer the planets are to the Sun; both of which they usually deny. For if a planet joins the Sun <term>partiliter: an exact conjunction to the same degree and minute</term> and in the very same minutes, they claim it becomes most effective. <note>This refers to the concept of 'Cazimi' or being 'in the heart of the Sun,' which astrologers paradoxically viewed as a position of great strength despite it being the peak of 'combustion.'</note> Furthermore, they claim the Sun does not harm a star occupied by its rays in **Aries** or **Leo**—places where they nonetheless decree the Sun is most powerful. For, they say, it "receives" the star into its own home, since **Aries** is the Sun's exaltation and **Leo** is its house, and no good man brings harm to a guest. As if (the error they commit everywhere) these celestial matters were handled in a human fashion, and as if the Sun poured out light and heat beyond itself not by natural necessity, but by some sort of choice.

### authority of certain astrologers, retrograde planets
### would seem stronger than

<header>Against Astrology, Book VI.</header>

with mere and arbitrary inventions, such as those they hand down concerning the "images" <note>Referring to the constellations or specific degrees of the zodiac assigned symbolic forms.</note> about which we shall discuss below, or by taking the occasion of certain mathematical positions—which mathematicians use correctly— and perversely transferring them to this profession of divining birth-charts. In this, they have erred most greatly regarding the division of the zodiac. But concerning this division, it will be discussed in its proper place later. Now, this belongs to that category of error: they think the efficacy of the planets is either diminished or strengthened, and even that the very nature of the effects varies, according to those diversities of motion which mathematicians devise. For instance, sometimes they proceed in a **direct course**, sometimes they move **backward** <note>original: "retrogradiantur"</note>, and sometimes they stand still in **stationary slowness**. They claim a planet acts weakly when it moves backward, and effectively when it proceeds forward. Furthermore, they say a planet is sometimes favorable when it moves forward, but the very same planet is harmful if it moves backward. In this matter, you see what could be said against the astrologers. Heliodorus <note>Heliodorus of Alexandria (6th century AD), an astronomical commentator.</note> raised a question against himself in his book of commentaries on Paulus Alexandrinus <note>A 4th-century author of an influential introductory text on astrology.</note>, which I shall explain using no other words than his own, adding the solution by which he thought he could resolve the question, though he actually increases it instead. His words in Greek are these:

* We have translated them into English <note>original: "Latinum"</note> rendering them almost word for word. *Furthermore, it is necessary to know that although the planets are said to move unequally, in truth there is nothing unequal or disordered in the heavens; rather, all order and all equality are found within them. But this happens according to our perception, so that they appear to move unequally and sometimes even to stand still; for in reality, they neither stand still nor ever slow down or move backward. But it happens that they appear to do so because of the position of the **eccentrics** and **epicycles** <note>In the Ptolemaic system, an "epicycle" is a small circle on which a planet moves, while that circle's center moves along a larger circle (the "deferent"). An "eccentric" is a circular path whose center is not the Earth.</note> upon which they move, as Ptolemy taught us in his composition. And if anyone should object: "How then are the <term>apotelesmata</term> <note>original: "apotelesmata" (Greek: ἀποτελέσματα) meaning the completion or outcome of a planetary influence; astrological predictions.</note> different? Does something either increase or decrease because of their motion, or because they are said to stand still, given that they truly neither stand still nor move unequally?" We respond that the <term>apotelesmata</term>—that is, the responses of the astrologers—do not happen properly because of that inequality or station of the motions, but because it then happens that the planets, carried on their epicycles, either become closer to the Earth or are moved further away from the Earth.* This is what Heliodorus says, from whom we accept not only a concession but a testimony and confirmation: that the stations of the planets effect nothing insofar as they are stations—that is, they do not change the efficacy of the planets at all. Likewise, neither do the backward movements nor the forward directions insofar as they are such things. Rather, different outcomes are pronounced because it happens during these differences of motion that the planets either approach the Earth or move further away. It is as if he had said that this has a natural reason: that they affect us one way when they are close, and another way when they are distant. This, certainly, we also concede; however, if they observe direct, stationary, and backward-moving planets for that reason, then a contrary dogma ought to be established: namely, that backward-moving planets should be more effective than when they are carried in a direct course, and weaker when they are direct, if indeed...

<summary>Pico critiques the astrological belief that a planet's "retrograde" or "stationary" motion affects its power, citing Heliodorus to argue that these are mere optical illusions caused by orbital geometry. He points out a logical contradiction: if closeness to Earth grants power, retrograde planets (which are closer) should be stronger, not weaker as astrologers claim.</summary>

...only a greater or lesser distance from the earth is observed in these motions. For, as Haly <note>Haly Abenragel (11th century), an Arab astrologer whose commentaries on Ptolemy were standard textbooks in the Renaissance.</note> writes when explaining Ptolemy, every principle certainly testifies that the closer a planet is to the earth, the more strongly it changes us and the more powerfully it affects us. Furthermore, every planet, when it moves backward <note>original: "retrocedit"; referring to retrograde motion where a planet appears to move in reverse from Earth's perspective.</note>, draws closer to the earth; on the contrary, when moving in a straight path, it becomes more distant from the earth. Therefore, a planet moving backward ought to have been considered stronger, not—as they themselves have decreed—weak and infirm.

### CHAPTER XI. THAT THE HEAD AND TAIL ARE INTERSECTIONS OF 
### imaginary circles endowed with no natural power; the ancients 
### did not use them in predicting, nor do the moderns 
### agree on their powers.

Who does not see that the **Head of the Dragon** and the **Tail** <note>These are the Lunar Nodes (Caput and Cauda Draconis), the points where the Moon’s orbit intersects the Ecliptic (the Sun's apparent path).</note>, to which the crowd of astrologers attributes so much, are empty and fictitious things? But as we said before, the astrologers often slide into error from this: whatever they find noted by mathematicians as necessary methods for measuring motions, they abuse all these things for predicting, as if they were equally natural and endowed with a power of influence. 

Yet the matter is far different, since those mathematicians devise and invent many things in the heavens that serve mathematical numbers and measurements, but which are otherwise founded on no stability of nature. We showed this regarding the signs which Ptolemy considers non-mobile, intercepted by the solstices and equinoxes; we shall show it in the definition of the parts and minutes of the signs. Now, the same will appear in the "Head" and "Tail," for they are nothing other than the intersections of two circles—mere points, a joining of two lines conceived in the mind—introduced by mathematicians so they might discern the locations of eclipses. There is, however, no power there, no quality or natural efficacy that could be transferred to the practice of <term>genethlialogy</term> <note>The branch of astrology concerned with casting birth charts (horoscopes).</note>. Certainly, they can do nothing more than this: that a planet placed there might, due to the convenience or inconvenience of the place, decree something better or worse. But these points, noted by themselves and separately, can have no power of ruling or changing physical bodies. 

This was also seen by the distinguished astrologer **Abraham Ibn Ezra** <note>original: "Abraam Auenazra," a 12th-century Jewish polymath and astrologer.</note>, who in the first book of his *Reasons of Astrology* writes as follows: *They also said the Head of the Dragon is exalted in Gemini, and the Tail in Sagittarius. But this is empty, since the Head and Tail signify neither good nor evil. For they are connections of two circles; however, the Moon is observed when she is in them because, when placed in the Head, she is more invigorated for that reason—because she is closer to us—whereas she is weaker in the Tail, because in that position, turning toward the south, she is further away from us.* The same happens to the remaining planets when they are found in the Head and Tail, except for the Sun, which has no declination toward either side. *When, however, you read the Head and Tail noted separately in the tables, know that they neither harm nor profit, although many think otherwise.* So says he. 

But neither does Ptolemy ever use them in predicting, nor will you find that the ancients used them according to **Maternus** <note>Firmicus Maternus (4th century), author of the *Mathesis*, the most extensive Latin handbook on astrology from antiquity.</note>, in whose work there is no mention of the cause...

<meta>The catchword "tio cau" indicates the sentence continues on the next page with "causation" or "caution."</meta>

<summary>Pico argues that the Lunar Nodes (Head and Tail of the Dragon) are merely mathematical points used for calculating eclipses and possess no physical or "natural" influence on human affairs. He cites the astronomer Abraham Ibn Ezra to support his claim that these points are "empty" and "fictitious" constructs.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s critique of the "Head and Tail of the Dragon" (the Lunar Nodes). He argues that these are merely mathematical points of intersection where the Moon's path crosses the Sun's path, rather than physical bodies with their own power.</meta>

<page-num>603</page-num>
<header>On Astrology, Book VI.</header>

...mention of the head and tail of the dragon. If the ancients ever speak of them, it is no different than speaking of a certain place or position. Hence, there was a different opinion among them, since both places seemed evil to the older writers because of the ecliptic—that is, the path <note>The "ecliptic" is the Sun's apparent path; the "nodes" are where eclipses occur, which the ancients often viewed as omens of doom.</note>—and therefore they established both equally among the unlucky places. 

Heliodorus in his treatise *On Children* <note>original Greek: περὶ τέκνων</note> says: "If the places signifying children are free from the unfortunate planets and the ecliptic nodes—that is, the head and the tail—the outcome is happy." The more recent astrologers, if the "head" should be in the place of children, will announce that children will be "like young olive plants around the table" <note>A reference to Psalm 128:3, which astrologers used to signify a fruitful family.</note>, a deduced conjecture which we reported above from Avenazra <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar and astrologer.</note>: namely, that at the "head," the planets closer to us are more effective. Indeed, that reasoning holds when some planet is *at* the head, although a planet moving toward us before reaching the head ought to be considered stronger by that same reasoning. 

But when no star is found in that spot, what can it either give or take? For it is designated by us only by the mind <note>Pico is emphasizing that the nodes are imaginary points in space, not physical objects like planets.</note>. As for what some suspect—that a certain power is left there by the Moon—no astrologer has said this; furthermore, it is not physical if you consider the nature and light of the celestial bodies, nor is it astrological, since the Moon traverses the tail equally. 

It is therefore only a site and mere position, about which, however, both the Arabs and the Latins have finally decreed as if it were a certain star. They go so far as to think this "head" adds years to a person's life, and governs a certain part of one's age, and is "exalted" in Gemini, and possesses the nature of **Venus** and **Jupiter**; conversely, they say the "tail" has the nature of **Mars** and **Saturn**. In this matter, we see how much they disagree with the truth itself. But it is also a wonder how much they disagree with themselves, since they have called it the knot and bond, as it were, of all celestial happiness. 

Elsewhere, however, they say it is "good with the good and evil with the evil," and that it increases whatever it finds. Elsewhere they speak of it as if it were entirely evil. For Alchabitius <note>Al-Qabisi (10th century), whose "Introduction to the Art of Judgments of the Stars" was a standard textbook.</note>, among whose writings are the laws we just reported, commemorates this also among the misfortunes of the planets: if they should be with their own "heads" (for every planet has its own head and its own tail, called <term>Genzauar</term> <note>The Arabic term *al-jawzahar*, referring to the nodes of any planet's orbit.</note> among the Arabs), or if they should be with the "head" or "tail" of the dragon—which is the specific name for the head and tail of the Moon—in which cases they behave as badly as if they were in the "head." 

The same author, in his book *On Nativities*, makes a <term>climacteric</term> <note>A critical point in life, such as the 7th or 63rd year, thought to be dangerous.</note> application to the head of the Moon; and among the principal places of life, he counts this head and tail equally. Abraham, as we reported, affirms that the Moon is strengthened when placed in the "head." We saw Heliodorus above count them among the unfortunate stars. The same man, in his treatise *On the Climacteric*, counts them alongside the Sun, Moon, horoscope, and Part of Fortune. Thus, what they have brought forth about this "head," they seem to have brought forth with "no head"—or certainly no heart. Everywhere, however, they maliciously call it the "head of the dragon," so that it might sound in the ears of the credulous with greater reverence and, as it were, with the authority of a divinity.

### THE ORIGIN OF ANTISCIA, AND THAT PTOLEMY DID NOT USE
### THEM IN PREDICTION, AND HOW MUCH MATERNUS
### AND HALY ERRED IN THESE MATTERS. CHAPTER XII.

**O**n the occasion of a certain mathematician's saying, they likewise erred regarding antiscia <note>From the Greek "anti" (opposite) and "skia" (shadow). In astrology, antiscia are points mirrored across the solstice axis (the Cancer-Capricorn line).</note>. For since there are degrees in which, when the Sun is positioned there, the days are equal to days and the nights to nights [in length], Hipparchus and the ancients called these "antiscia" from the corresponding equality of days and nights on both sides, as if you said "equal from the opposite side." Our so-called "diviners" <note>Pico's mocking term for astrologers.</note> claimed these degrees were equal in virtue and power—an act of supine ignorance that anyone can recognize—so that from the equality of light occurring when the Sun traverses them, they transferred themselves to an equality of [astrological] power. 

But I wish to accuse Maternus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer who wrote the "Mathesis."</note> above all others as the propagator of this error; though, as a man most ignorant of all mathematics, he should be pardoned. He says that Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer and geographer of antiquity.</note> attributes the highest weight of judgments to antiscia. I am not surprised by this claim, for though I have read all of Maternus’s work diligently, he never gave me any indication that he had actually read Ptolemy himself. 

As for what pertains to antiscia in judging and pronouncing predictions, Ptolemy never uses them, whether you look in his *Hundred Sayings* <note>Known as the *Centiloquium*, a collection of astrological aphorisms formerly attributed to Ptolemy.</note> or his *Apotelesmata* <note>The *Tetrabiblos*, Ptolemy's foundational work on astrology.</note>. Only in the first book of the *Apotelesmata*, where he recounts the opinions of others <term>concerning the affinity and consensus of the signs</term> <note>original Greek: περὶ τῆς συμπάθειας τῶν ζῳδίων (peri tēs sumpatheias tōn zōidiōn)</note> among the foundational principles, did he use these words: "Again, they say those signs are of equal power which are equally distant from either of the tropics, because the Sun positioned in them makes days equal to days and nights to nights." Once he had said this, as if forgetting it afterward—as one who clearly did not approve of it—he never brings it up again. He never mentions not only the name "antiscia" (which is nowhere found in his work), but not even the thing itself—that is, the supposed affinity and consensus of parts equally remote from the tropics. 

For as for what he says in a certain place in the *Hundred Sayings*—that a planet often extends its powers where it is not—to want to apply this to antiscia and <term>dodecathemoria</term> <note>The division of each 30-degree zodiac sign into twelve smaller 2.5-degree segments.</note> is too forced and reckless. This is especially true since in all his teaching, Ptolemy laughs at the one (the *dodecathemoria* and other things of that kind) and neglects the other (these antiscia we are talking about). 

By that precept, he wished to indicate nothing to us other than <term>the appearance of the configuration</term> <note>original Greek: σχήματὸς φάσιν (schēmatos phasin)</note>, that is, the power of the geometric alignment and radiation. Through these, according to the opinion of astrologers and especially Ptolemy, planets do many things effectively in places where they are not physically present. For he himself observes almost nothing else in the constellations except "phases" and "configurations," or certainly nothing else more so. 

But our Maternus did not even understand what antiscia were supposed to mean; he promised to explain their hidden logic elsewhere, as if it were a matter not already explained to any mathematician, or something that could not be explained in three words. You may detect his ignorance from this: that he uses the very manner of speaking too unskillfully, [saying] that Mars, positioned at the fifth degree in Gemini, sends an "antiscium" into Cancer—he would not speak in such a way if he knew what that "antiscium" actually was.

<summary>Pico critiques the concept of "antiscia" (astrological mirror points), arguing that they are a misinterpretation of seasonal day-length equality and that major authorities like Ptolemy never actually used them for predictions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's critique of "antiscia" (shadow points). He transitions from mocking the imprecise terminology used by medieval astrologers like Abenragel to introducing a related error regarding "commanding" and "obeying" signs, which astrologers mistakenly believe influence a person's social status based on nothing more than the length of daylight.</meta>

<page-num>605</page-num>
<header>Against Astrology, Book VI.</header>

understood this. For it is neither a ray nor a light that sends an antiscium <note>The "shadow" point mirrored across the solstice axis.</note>, nor is it anything else to say that an antiscium is "sent" by one of the planets than to say that the degree which it occupies is sent into its equal degree. Therefore, experts would rather speak thus: "the epoch of Mars—that is, the part it occupies—is the antiscium to such a part of Gemini," or, what amounts to the same thing, "Mars is in the antiscia of Gemini." But he who says that Mars "hurls" an antiscium into Gemini will be hissed at and mocked by mathematicians. 

But Abenragel <note>Al-Hassan 'Ali ibn Abi l-Rijal (died c. 1037), a famous Arab astrologer whose "Book of the Skilled in the Judgments of the Stars" was a standard Latin text.</note> also slipped in many ways; in the first book of his commentaries, while explaining certain aphorisms, he writes that degrees equally distant from the equinoxes are of equal power, just as those which are equally distant from the tropics—namely Cancer and Capricorn. Yet this was not said by the ancients regarding distance from the equinoxes, but only from the tropics, to which the name of antiscia was given. Nor should Abenragel have failed to see this, since the circles described on both sides of the equinoxes are indeed equal. For it is necessary that parallels equally distant from them be equal to each other, but not that the half-circles <note>hemicyclia</note> be equal to each other, which occurs in points equally remote from the tropics; hence that "agreement" of the antiscia. 

He also errs, along with many others, in counting the relationship of a degree to its antiscium degree among those which he calls <term>aspects</term> <note>Geometrical angles between planets, like a square or trine, thought to indicate their influence on one another.</note>; hence they conclude that a star placed in one of them has power also in the other, just as it does in hexagonal, tetragonal, trigonal, and opposite positions. This error was born from the fact that what the Greeks call <term>schemata</term> <note>original: σχήματα, meaning "figures" or "shapes."</note>—that is, figures—the barbarians and our own people call "aspects." Among the Greeks, signs are said to "look at" each other, not because they are configured to one another (which is what our people mean by "aspects"), but because—to use the Greek phrase—they "emerge and set from the same points" <note>original: ἐκ τῶν φθανουμένων</note>. Because this happens in signs equally separated from the tropics (for they are on the same parallel), the majority of astrologers call those signs which are antiscia "seeing" <note>original: βλέποντα (*bleponta*)</note>. The Arabs, and later the Latins, then accepted this in the sense in which they misuse the name of "aspect." And so it happens: often an error in words gives birth to an error in facts. Thus it has been sufficiently declared how varied the observation of antiscia is among astrologers in explaining fates (if we were to grant any fates at all), and how much both the Arabs and the Latins have dreamed up regarding these things, contrary to the opinion of the ancients.

For mathematicians called those signs in which the Sun is positioned when it makes the days longer than the nights <term>commanding</term> <note>original: προστάττοντα (*prostattonta*)</note>, when compared to signs in which light is overcome by darkness in equal proportion. Those which conversely portend darkness over day, they called <term>obeying</term> <note>original: ὑπακούοντα (*hypakouonta*)</note>.

### REFUTATION OF THE REASONS WHICH CERTAIN ASTROLOGERS ASSIGNED CONCERNING THE EXALTATIONS OF THE PLANETS. Chapter XIV.

But as to where that opinion concerning the heights or **exaltations** of the Planets emanated from, and how they likewise rushed headlong into this through a certain mathematical occasion, I was reminded by that most diligent writer of natural history, to whom all antiquity and all posterity is indebted—who rescued the former from barbarism and the latter from death <note>Pico is praising Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), whose *Natural History* preserved a vast amount of ancient knowledge.</note>. He, therefore, in his second book, treating the question of why the same stars seem higher at some times and lower at others, adds the following after certain other points: "Another cause for the heights <note>original: "sublimitatum"</note> is that they have their highest <term>apsides</term> <note>original: "absidas"; the point in an orbit farthest from the center of the earth (apogee).</note> from their own center in those signs: **Saturn** in the twentieth part of **Libra**, **Jupiter** in the fifteenth of **Cancer**, **Mars** in the twenty-eighth of **Capricorn**, the **Sun** in the nineteenth of **Aries**, **Venus** in the twenty-sixth of **Pisces**, **Mercury** in the fifteenth of **Virgo**, and the **Moon** in the fourth of **Taurus**." Thus he wrote. From this, even one who is not the slowest of mind may easily gather either that it was once so, or that it was thought so by those then devoted to the science of the stars: that the stars placed in the aforementioned parts were truly at the highest point of the height from the center of their apsides; for which reason those degrees or parts were called the "heights" of the Planets. From this, the <term>Genethliaci</term> <note>Astrologers who cast birth charts to predict a person's fate.</note> took the opportunity to preserve the name of "height" [exaltation], yet they abused it as if it were not a height of *place*, but of *nature and power*. For astrologers do not say the Planets are "exalted" in any other parts than in those where we have shown they were thought, according to ancient astronomy, to be most distant from their centers. However, the reader ought to know that a flaw is found in the common manuscripts of **Pliny**, and the words which are placed thereafter have grown distorted by swapped numbers, such as when the mark of ten due to **Venus** was transferred to the **Sun**, so that in the **Sun** the twenty-ninth part is read wrongly instead of the nineteenth, and in **Venus** the sixteenth instead of the twenty-sixth. For there is also a fault in **Maternus** <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman astrologer.</note>, where we read that **Venus** is exalted in the twenty-seventh part of **Pisces**. For it should be written "twenty-sixth" according to **Porphyry** <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), a Neoplatonic philosopher who wrote on astrology.</note>. There is also some variation in that ancient astrology assigns the fourth part of **Taurus** to the **Moon**, while the following age assigned the third—whether there is a diversity of opinion or the fault of scribes, who very often hallucinate in the notation of numbers. Similarly, in **Saturn**, it should be read as the twentieth, not the twenty-first, on the authority of the same **Porphyry**. Nor do I now doubt that it has been made clear to sound minds how the **exaltations** of the Planets crept into divinatory astrology. But when the dogma reached later generations, and that original reason for the dogma had become obsolete due to changes in the theoretical discipline of the stars, posterity devised other reasons for themselves by which they thought the earlier ones had been persuaded—some one way, others another, as often happens with a lie—but they are trivial and ridiculous. **Ptolemy** in...

He is currently dismantling the arguments of Ptolemy and other ancient authorities by pointing out that their reasoning relies on local seasonal changes rather than universal celestial laws.</meta>

<header>on Astrology, Book VI.</header>
<sig>EE 4</sig>

In **Aries**, he <note>Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer and astrologer.</note> says, the **Sun** is **exaltated** <note>In astrology, "exaltation" is a sign where a planet is thought to have its maximum power, distinct from its "home" sign.</note>, because when he reaches it, his power begins to appear more clearly. But (as we said above when speaking of the houses) it is not the quality or nature of the sign that effects this, but the position. It is not because he travels through **Aries** that he begins to be stronger, but because he begins to approach us <note>Pico notes that the Sun's "strength" in spring is simply a matter of the Earth's tilt/proximity in the Northern Hemisphere, not the zodiac sign itself.</note>; wherefore, if he pours warmth into your gardens, arriving at that sign, it is to be hoped that he might even raise one to a kingdom—since he is placed in his own height, in which he would certainly be dried out in other regions from which he happens to be more distant in **Aries** and closer under **Libra**. 

But let us also look at the remaining planets. The height of the **Moon** is **Taurus**, because if she is joined with the **Sun** in **Aries**, her power will first appear in **Taurus**. O most effective reasoning! As if, if she were to meet the **Sun** in **Taurus**, the same would not happen in **Gemini**; and if she met in **Gemini**, the same in **Cancer**; and if in **Cancer**, the same under **Leo**; and so on for all the rest, so that one may marvel at **Ptolemy**, who was not ashamed to write such things. 

But there are also other reasons: because the **Moon** is closest to the **Sun**, and the Moon’s <term>trine</term> <note>original: "trigonum"; an astrological aspect where two points are 120 degrees apart, considered harmonious.</note> is lateral. But **Ptolemy** does not think the **Moon** is closest to the **Sun**, nor ought we to guess the height from the trine, nor from the house, nor the trine, nor the altitude, nor the <term>terms</term> <note>original: "terminos"; specific degrees within a sign ruled by different planets.</note> or the <term>decan</term> <note>original: "decanum"; a subdivision of a zodiac sign into ten-degree segments.</note> from any of them, because these things are unmixed, so that to each one its own authority in its own proper matter is due. 

Furthermore, if the argument of the trine moves him, why will **Mercury** not be exalted in **Gemini** rather than in **Virgo**? Where also this would fit: that he would be closest to the exaltation of the **Sun**, from whom he is usually not far distant. This is what **Aboasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), a highly influential Persian astrologer whose works were standard in the Middle Ages.</note> also tries to maintain in the reasoning of these exaltations. But (says **Ptolemy**) **Virgo** suits **Mercury** because it is dry, and under **Virgo** the autumnal dryness appears. But we have already said concerning the nature of the signs that this change of the four seasons does not proceed from them; wherefore the **Sun** placed in **Virgo** will do to other regions what it does to us when placed in **Taurus**. 

Furthermore, if this was observed, why did he not decide that **Mars** should reign in **Cancer**? Under which, evidently, the world swelters, just as under **Virgo** it now withers. For **Mars** is a most fervent planet, yet they want him to be exalted in **Capricorn**, under which we are constrained by cold, frost, and ice. But (they say) **Capricorn** turns toward the south, and the southern part is warmer. This is what we object to you, astrologers: namely, that levity and inconstancy of your reasons (if indeed those are to be called reasons); for concerning the same sign, for your convenience and according to your whim, you discourse now as if it were hot, now as if it were cold, and soon you will call the same neither hot nor cold, but rather moist or dry. In the partition of the signs, you make **Capricorn** earthy, and therefore dry; when it is transferred to **Mars**, it is counted among the fervent things; and when it is called the domicile of **Saturn**, namely the most frigid star, snows and rains are remembered to occur under it. But if **Capricorn** is granted to **Mars** as if it were a hot sign, by similar reasoning **Cancer** ought to be numbered as the most frigid; wherefore it certainly will not have **Jupiter** as king, who is most powerful in life-giving heat, as they say.

<summary>Pico attacks the internal inconsistencies of astrological "exaltations," arguing that the qualities assigned to signs (like heat or dryness) are arbitrary and based on local European seasons rather than universal principles.</summary>

He is currently refuting the logic of Ptolemy and other astrologers who attempt to justify these assignments through seasonal weather or geometric relationships between the signs.</meta>

->**Of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola**<-

But there is a hiding place ready for them to retreat into. For **Jupiter** (says **Ptolemy**) stirs up true northern winds, wherefore a sign positioned in the north suits him. But first, other astrologers cannot flee here, who deny that winds of this kind are stirred up by **Jupiter**. Furthermore, even **Ptolemy** is not excused, who by similar reasoning ought to have sent **Mars** to the west, not to the south, since he thinks western winds, not southern ones, are excited by **Mars**. I pass over the fact that **Gemini** and **Leo** incline toward the North; why therefore is **Leo** not rather the exaltation of **Jupiter**? 

The heat of **Leo** (says Averroes <note>original: "Auenrodam"; Pico likely refers to the commentator Ibn Rushd, known as Averroes, or a specific astrological authority from that tradition.</note>) does not suit **Jupiter**; on the contrary, it suits him more than the coldness of **Cancer**. Add that **Leo** is a trine <note>original: "trigonum"; a trine is an astrological aspect where planets are 120 degrees apart, usually considered harmonious.</note> sign of **Jupiter**, diurnal and masculine; **Jupiter** likewise is Masculine and diurnal. **Cancer** is designated among the feminine, nocturnal, aquatic signs, all of which are removed from the nature of **Jupiter**; therefore **Leo** suits him altogether more than **Cancer**. 

Concerning **Venus** and **Saturn**, they rave no less, saying that **Libra** is the height of **Saturn** because **Saturn** is contrary to the **Sun**, and that **Venus** is exalted in **Pisces** because she is moist, and the moisture of spring begins under **Pisces**. But indeed we have already often said that those qualities of the seasons do not follow the nature of the signs, but rather the position of the **Sun** as it approaches and recedes. Regarding **Saturn**, they speak as usual for their own convenience. For here indeed they make him opposite to the **Sun**, yet elsewhere they preach that they <term>agree in sound</term> <note>original: "συμφωνεῖν" (symphōnein); meaning to be in harmony or of a similar condition.</note>, that is, that they are of the same condition, wherefore a part is signified by both, and both are oriental. But both are masculine, both diurnal. 

But we would surely have too much to say if we pursued all other such things in detail; little trusting in these, others have devised a new reasoning, shorter indeed, but entirely ineffective: namely, that the exaltations for the planets are in the trine <note>original: "triquetra"</note> or sextile <note>original: "hexagona"; a 60-degree aspect.</note> of their houses, except in **Mercury**. But if you ask why they preferred the sextile for the **Moon**, **Venus**, and **Mars**, and the trine for the others, they reply that the trine suits the diurnal and more powerful planets better, while for the nocturnal ones, which are of the "sect" <note>original: "haeresi"</note> of the **Moon**—which the Arabs call <term>hayz</term> <note>original: "aiz"; an Arabic astrological term referring to a planet being in a sign and hemisphere that matches its own nature.</note>—the sextile [is chosen] <term>on account of the weakness of the ray</term> <note>original: "διὰ τὸ ἀσθενὲς τῆς ἀκτῖνος" (dia to asthenes tēs aktinos)</note>, that is, because of the feebleness of the beam. 

But they are mistaken regarding **Mars**; for he is not counted among the nocturnal because he is weak, but rather so that the vigor and efficacy of the **Martial** ray might be restrained by the nocturnal cold. Nor can he be said to be of the **Moon’s** sect, since he is a masculine planet, and both his qualities disagree with the **Moon**, and he is considered nocturnal for a reason entirely contrary to that of the **Moon**; for she is so because of similarity of nature, but **Mars** because of dissimilarity, being opposed to the **Lunar** [sign] and **Cancer** in **Capricorn**, just as he is opposite to **Taurus** in **Scorpio**. 

But let that conjecture proceed; let them answer this: why a right-handed <note>original: "dextra"; in astrology, a "dexter" aspect moves against the order of the signs.</note> trine rather than a left-handed <note>original: "sinistra"; a "sinister" aspect moves with the order of the signs.</note> one? Why a left rather than a right? Indeed, why for **Jupiter** a left one, but for **Saturn** and the **Sun** a right one? And since the planets have two houses, why is the trine taken from one rather than the other? For instance, since **Jupiter** resides in **Sagittarius** and **Pisces**, why should he be exalted in **Cancer** rather than in **Leo**? Especially since he has more affinity with **Sagittarius**, as the astrologers say, and also more (as we were saying before) and far more than

Having dismissed the specific cases of Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn, he now argues that the entire system of exaltations is based on outdated astronomical measurements of the planets' distances from Earth (apogees), which have since changed, rendering the old rules obsolete even by the astrologers' own logic. He then transitions to a new attack on "triplicities" (grouping signs by elements).</meta>
