<header>on Astrology, Book VI.</header>

**Cancer** and **Leo** would suit him. Finally, so that you may understand that all conjectures of this kind were invented by those who came later, and that those who first established this dogma laid no foundation for them at all, you may know it from this: they can give no reason why a Planet is said to be exalted not just in a particular sign, but in a particular *degree* of that sign. We have shown the cause of this above from the perspective of ancient astronomy. For this reason, **Abu Ma'shar** <note>original: "Aboasar"; a famous 9th-century Persian astrologer whose works were foundational to Western astrology.</note> says it was difficult for the whole community of astrologers to find this out; and he himself, so as not to seem entirely silent, anxiously twisted many things regarding this perverse matter with a legendary and fabled subtlety. Therefore, it is undoubtedly clear that by the occasion we mentioned—namely, the ancient discipline which thought that Planets are at their greatest distance from their centers in these specific degrees—this dogma about the "heights" <term>altitudinibus: here meaning planetary apogees, the points furthest from Earth</term> of the Planets was accepted by the casters of birth charts. Everyone now understands how vain the observation of these heights is, not only because they transferred what was merely a name for a location and position to a planet's nature and power, but also because ancient astronomy was perhaps mistaken in that matter, being far too deceptive and poorly investigated in its infancy. Even if they had decreed true things back then, that reasoning does not fit for posterity, since the apsides <note>The points in an orbit closest to or furthest from the center.</note> and what are called the "apogees" of the wandering stars have since shifted.

## THE REASONS OF THE ASTROLOGERS CONCERNING THE TRINES AND 
## THE RULERS OF THE TRINES, AND INCIDENTALLY CONCERNING 
## THE GENDER OF THE SIGNS, ARE REFUTED. Chapter XV.

Nor should we think that the astrologers rave only when they have seized an opportunity; they are too "keen-sighted" to be able to stray without a leader. They transgress most often precisely where there is no one to lead them astray. For regarding those mathematical "exaltations," they almost owe it to the mathematicians that they are mad, although they owe it more to themselves (lest we cheat them of any of their own credit). But as for what they commonly call **trines** <note>original: "trigona"; also known as triplicities, these are groups of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element.</note> or **triplicities**, they sired these themselves. In this area, mathematics did not help them, though the matter depends on it; for since they make some signs fiery, some earthy, some airy, and some watery, we shall first compel them to give an account of these things, and we shall examine how they define this as the trine of this Planet, and that as the trine of another.

Tell us, therefore, O most wise men and interpreters of the heavens: by what reasoning did you distribute those qualities of the elements to the signs in the sky? **Ibn Ridwan** <note>original: "Auenrodan"; likely referring to the 11th-century Egyptian astrologer and commentator on Ptolemy.</note>, a great figure in your discipline, refers the nature of the signs either to the **Sun** or to the stars. To the **Sun**, so that the nature of such a sign is said to be whatever the effect of the **Sun** is while passing through that sign—in which way the "movable" signs are called equinoctial or solstitial, and the rest are called "fixed" or "common." If it is referred to the stars, the virtues of the stars residing there are attributed to the sign. I see neither reason fitting your partition. For if we follow the works of the **Sun**, **Cancer** will be fiery, not watery <note>Because Cancer occurs during the heat of midsummer.</note>, just as **Sagittarius** would be watery rather than fiery <note>Because Sagittarius occurs during the rainy/cold winter.</note>; **Aries** would not be fiery but airy <note>Associated with the moist, temperate heat of spring.</note>, and **Taurus** would abound with moisture and heat rather than cold and dryness; thus the condition of almost all the signs would change, nor would they be perpetual (as you wish them to be). If it is referred to the stars, they are constantly migrating from their seats. Or do you think the reasoning of **Al-Kindi** <note>original: "Alchindi"; a 9th-century Arab philosopher known as the "Philosopher of the Arabs."</note> is better, since in the Zodiac there are four...

<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

[They claim] there are four principal signs, two equinoctial and two solstitial, and to these four they assign the four primary qualities of the elements: Fire to Aries, Water to Cancer, Air to Libra, and Earth to Capricorn. Furthermore, because trigonal radiation <note>A "trine" or "trigonal radiation" occurs when signs are 120 degrees apart, forming a triangle within the zodiac circle; astrologers group these into "triplicities" of the same element.</note> falls upon corresponding places, the three signs on either side of any given sign are rightly judged to have been allotted a similar nature. 

But this reasoning does not square either. In referring the four properties of the elements to the signs, there could have been two ways of ordering them: one based on the kinship between a sign and an element, and the other based on the position of the elements themselves, so that the first is attributed to the first, the second to the second, and so on. 

If they followed the first rule—that hot should correspond to hot and cold to cold—they should have given Fire to Cancer <note>Cancer represents the summer solstice, the hottest time of year in the northern hemisphere.</note> and Air to Aries, as I have said. If they followed the second rule—assigning Air to Cancer, which is second after Fire—then (says <term>Alchindus</term> <note>original: "Alchindus"; Al-Kindi (c. 801–873 AD), a famous Arab philosopher and astrologer.</note>) heat and cold must be distributed accordingly. Therefore, to the sign of the second season—that is, Cancer—or rather to Libra, which is opposite Aries, [a different quality belongs]. If they say that Water should be placed before Air because it is more "effective," they are making themselves out to be wiser than nature itself. 

Furthermore, if an active quality like coldness, rather than a passive quality like moisture, belongs to Cancer, how is it ranked by them among the feminine and nocturnal signs? Why not rather among the diurnal and masculine? They observe this even in the Planets, recognizing sex in the heavenly bodies for no more rational reason than the presence of active and passive qualities. Because of this, they called Jupiter, the Sun, and Mars "masculine" (in which heat excels), and Saturn (in which cold excels) masculine as well; but they called the Moon and Venus "feminine" because they are moist. 

Thus, Water and Fire were also called masculine by the Egyptians for the reason mentioned, while Air and Water were feminine. Therefore, the astrologers should have numbered the signs they established as "watery" among the masculine, not the feminine. Yet they did this equally for all of them—namely Cancer, Pisces, and Scorpio. Conversely, they decreed the "airy" signs to be masculine, even though moisture is the proper quality of Air. In these matters, therefore, <term>astrology</term> fights against itself and overturns its own foundations, as it is delusional everywhere. 

For—lest we wander from the subject at hand, though not pointlessly—consider these most trivial trifles about discerning sex in the heavens. They were moved by such a conjecture to establish six masculine signs and six feminine ones, so that the first is male, the following female, and thus by turns always one man and one woman. If this had to be done, it should have been done according to the nature of the signs, not by a fated and vain consequence of "first" and "second" and so on. Listen to the reasoning <term>Ptolemæus</term> <note>original: "Ptolemæus"; Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity.</note> has for this:

> Night, he says, follows day, and women cling to men; therefore, a feminine sign must be placed next to a masculine sign.

One should not argue against such reasoning, but laugh at it—unless, perhaps, it is a serious matter to consider whether night follows day or day follows night. Perhaps the nocturnal signs should have been placed first, since day follows night more than night follows day. For it is written: *and the evening and the morning were one day* <note>original: "factum est vespere & mane dies unus"; a reference to the Book of Genesis 1:5.</note>. For this reason, the Hebrews established the beginnings of time from the night. But we are too busy for it to be permitted to trifle with many words. Although, in his own [writings]...

->### On Astrology, Book VI.<-

Even **Ptolemy** himself holds that this diversity of sexes is of great importance; he reports that it matters no small amount whether planets are found in **masculine** or **feminine** signs. But if he contends that this dogma is proven by experiments, I ask: by whose? His own, or those of the ancients? If they are his own, they lack the "gray hairs" <note>An idiom meaning they lack the authority of age and long-standing tradition.</note> to command such great authority; if they are from the ancients, a large part of the ancients thought otherwise. Many established the order starting from the **horoscope** <note>The "horoscope" here refers to the Ascendant, the sign rising on the eastern horizon at a specific moment.</note>, so that the rising sign was always masculine and diurnal, and the remaining signs were divided by turns in the following order. Others made four signs diurnal: **Aries, Cancer, Leo, and Sagittarius**. They made four nocturnal: **Gemini, Libra, Capricorn, and Aquarius**. And four they called "promiscuous" <note>Meaning neutral, common, or mixed in gender/sect.</note>: **Taurus, Virgo, Pisces, and Scorpio**. Indeed, antiquity itself used to explode <note>In the Latin sense of *explodere*: to drive off the stage or reject with hissed disapproval.</note> the received opinion. Whence this passage from the old astrology:

> There are those who prefer that those which rise as masculine be diurnal,
> And that the feminine ones rejoice in the night with its broad shadows;
> These people say many things to themselves, with no one to guide them.

In this passage, it is a wonder how much a certain trivial interpreter of that poet raves. Likewise, that man was far more reasonable (if indeed one must occasionally be insane with reason) who called all signs equally "fiery" and "watery" **diurnal**, and the remaining six **nocturnal**—namely the "earthy" and "airy" ones. Also, if what pleases Ptolemy is true—that masculine and diurnal properties follow one another—then those will be masculine and these will be feminine. Thus he <note>Likely referring to a poetic source like Manilius or a similar astronomical poet.</note> sang:

> For the sign of **Sagittarius** and of the swift **Leo**,
> And the one looking back at its own back with the golden fleece, <note>original: "aurato uellere"; referring to Aries, the Ram.</note>
> Then **Pisces**, **Cancer**, and the **Scorpion's** sting,
> Whether neighboring in place or at equal parts,
> All are said to be diurnal under a similar lot;
> The others, neither sharing in number nor in turn of the bond,
> Interspersed in their places, are said to be just as many nocturnal ones.

There were also those who thought otherwise, wherefore he adds:

> Furthermore, they said that six continuous turns of **Castor** <note>original: "Castoris"; referring to the constellation Gemini.</note> are diurnal,
> Which start from the leading sign of the **Wool-bearer**, <note>original: "Lanigeri"; another reference to Aries.</note>
> And that six starting from the **Scales** <note>original: "Libris"; the sign of Libra.</note> are seen as nocturnal.

Let them cease, therefore, to allege the "faith of ancient observations," from which they so often disagree, just as all astrology disagrees with the truth. But this could also be objected: if they judged that a masculine sign must be established in the first place, it remains uncertain which sign is the "first" and "masculine" one—just as it is uncertain which sign is the initial one of the whole zodiac, as we declared above. For to some **Cancer**, and to others **Capricorn**, seemed to be the first; yet both of these are considered feminine among these astrologers. But perhaps it was not necessary to mock these fables with so many arguments, although it was worthwhile to refute this fable in passing—the dividing of celestial signs by sex. We diverted into this topic specifically to show that in the case of **Cancer**, they contradict themselves: they make it "watery" and "feminine," even though they also claim it is "cold," and coldness is listed among the **active** qualities, not the passive ones. <note>In Aristotelian physics, which astrologers used, Heat and Cold were "active" qualities, while Moisture and Dryness were "passive." Pico points out the logical inconsistency of calling a "cold" sign "feminine" if feminine is associated with passivity.</note>

<summary>Pico highlights the internal contradictions and lack of consensus among ancient astrologers regarding the gender and diurnal/nocturnal status of zodiac signs. He argues that if these "rules" were based on observation, there would not be so many competing systems.</summary>

The division given to them in the tropical and equinoctial signs will not hold up in other signs; for they use circular reasoning—which is a logical disgrace—since when they prove here that <term>trigonal</term> <note>Signs forming a triangle, also known as triplicities.</note> signs are of the same nature, they take as an argument that the trigonal radiation belongs to places that agree with each other. Conversely, when they are about to prove that the trigonal radiation is harmonious, they assume that it falls upon places of the same nature. Let <term>Al-Kindi</term> <note>Alchindus; a 9th-century Arab philosopher and astrologer known as the "Philosopher of the Arabs."</note> be silent now. What remains is the opinion of <term>Abraham Ibn Ezra</term> <note>Abraam Auenazra; a prominent 12th-century Jewish polymath whose astrological works were widely translated into Latin.</note>, who derives the reason for these qualities from the figures of the constellations and the properties of the animals depicted there. For example, <term>Pisces</term>, <term>Cancer</term>, and <term>Scorpio</term> are called "cold" because they represent the names and images of aquatic creatures. The sign of <term>Leo</term> is called "hot" because of the nature of the Lion, and so on for the rest. 

But this reasoning is either void (if there are no images, as we have demonstrated) or false (if there are images, in which the images are confused with the signs—a point we also refuted above). Finally, since the figures change their location <note>Pico refers here to the "precession of the equinoxes," where the physical stars move relative to the fixed calendar of the zodiac signs over centuries.</note>, this distinction of the signs would be temporary, not immobile and perpetual as all astrologers want—including Ibn Ezra himself. Nor will <term>Aries</term> be a fiery sign in our time, when almost the entire image of Pisces has occupied it, the image of Aries having already been moved into its twenty-fifth part.

If there are no triplicities, there are also no <term>trigonocrators</term> <note>From the Greek, meaning "rulers of the triangles."</note>, that is, the lords of what they call the <term>triplicities</term>. Yet even if those are granted, they still define things regarding them beyond all reason, as is their custom. For they will not deny that if a sign is good for some planet, it must be bad in the sign diametrically opposed to it; this is evident in the <term>houses</term> <note>The zodiac signs where a planet is said to have its "domicile" or home and greatest strength.</note> of the planets and in their <term>exaltations</term> <note>Specific signs where a planet's influence is said to be heightened.</note>. 

Since this is most fully confessed among them, how have they forgotten their own astrological dogma and willed that the same three planets should rule in opposite triplicities? Namely, in the Earthly and Watery ones, they place <term>Mars</term>, <term>Venus</term>, and the <term>Moon</term>. Yet <term>Taurus</term> is opposed to <term>Scorpio</term>, <term>Virgo</term> is set against <term>Pisces</term>, and <term>Capricorn</term> resides in the region across from <term>Cancer</term>. Nevertheless, those who dominate in Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn all rule with triplicity power in Cancer, Pisces, and Scorpio. Nor, if you should ask the astrologers why Mars is <term>cast down</term> <note>original: *deijciatur*; referring to a planet's "fall," the sign where it is at its weakest.</note> in Cancer, will they answer otherwise than because it is exalted in Capricorn; and why it is harmful in Taurus, they will say because it has its house in Scorpio. Therefore, all these things fight against each other and prove themselves false through mutual contradiction. 

Add to this that in the first triplicity, <term>Albumasar</term> <note>Abu Ma'shar, an influential 9th-century Persian astrologer.</note>, <term>Al-Qabisi</term> <note>Alchabitius; a 10th-century Arab astrologer.</note>, and all the Latin authors decree that <term>Saturn</term> dominates along with <term>Jupiter</term> and the <term>Sun</term>. Yet in that triplicity, Saturn is an exile; he is cast down in Leo, and in Aries and Sagittarius he recognizes nothing of his own. "But," they say, "he is diurnal just like Jupiter and the Sun." But he is also cold, while both of those are considered hot. And if, when dealing with exaltations, they assigned <term>Libra</term> to Saturn only for the reason that it was opposite to the nature of the Sun, why then is his kingdom in Aries? Why, in the lord of the triplicity, does he associate with the Sun against the very nature of those signs, as if he were most in harmony with the Sun's nature? There are more things of this kind, but to pursue each one might be superfluous; certainly the custom

...that you are bothersome and nauseating to me; but if you look here at the reliability of the evidence, I return once again to the discord of such experiments. For the Egyptians establish only two <term>trigonocratores</term> <note>rulers of the triplicities; planets that govern a group of three signs</note>, as can be understood from the <term>monomoiria</term> <note>the assignment of individual degrees of the zodiac to specific planets</note>, while others establish three, who then disagree among themselves. For in the first triangle, **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar, a 9th-century Persian astrologer</note>, **Alchabitius** <note>Al-Qabisi, a 10th-century Arab astrologer</note>, and the **Latins** want **Saturn** to dominate, while **Ptolemy** prefers **Mars**. Conversely, in the second triangle, Ptolemy makes Saturn the ruler, while almost all the Arabs and Latins make it Mars. In the fourth triangle, Ptolemy makes Mars the ruler, with two subordinates or secondary rulers: the **Moon** by night and **Venus** by day. Others equate Mars with Venus in leadership, and do not want Mars to rule except at night, and Venus by day; then the secondary authority of the Moon by night and day is held among these more recent authors. They say the opinion of the Arabs and Latins is confirmed by experiments, while **Ali ibn Ridwan** <note>Auenrodan; an 11th-century Egyptian physician and astrologer</note> himself (not to mention the Greeks) affirms that all observed effects agree with the opinion of Ptolemy. I pass over the many points on which they clash over these same triangles, since they were discussed above; it is clear, however, from this that even the **great conjunctions** <note>rare alignments of Jupiter and Saturn that astrologers used to predict major historical shifts</note> are invalidated, insofar as they depend on the <term>trigonal migration</term> <note>the movement of these conjunctions through the four elemental triangles</note>, not to mention other dogmas of the astrologers that derive their credit and origin mostly from these triangles.

# ON THE FACES, TERMS, AND THE <term>DODECATHEMORIA</term> <note>the division of each zodiac sign into twelve 2.5-degree segments</note> OF THE BABYLONIANS, and on the nine-fold divisions, and how little they are consistent, even by the testimony of Ptolemy himself. Chapter XVI.

**R**emaining now is the task of refuting the **faces** <note>also called decans; 10-degree divisions of a sign</note> and the **bounds** <note>uneven divisions of a sign assigned to planets</note>, so that everything regarding the signs' affinity with the planets may be addressed. For we have already overturned the **houses**, cast down the **exaltations**, and wiped out the **triangles**; there is now no difficulty in refuting these, for there are no "faces," even according to Ptolemy. So it is also with the **Greeks**, who also call them <term>decans</term>. But these are decans of the signs, yet faces of the planets. Ptolemy scorns these faces, thinking them unworthy of mention or of ever being used in **astrological judgments** <note>original: apotelesmatis</note>. Since they can support these with no reasons, they might perhaps claim experience as a pretext, were it not that consistency fails them in this area as well. For at one time the **Indians**, at another the **Babylonians** (whom the Arabs imitate), and at another **Maternus** <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman author</note>, claim different planets to be the faces. The first decan of **Taurus**, according to the Babylonians, bears the face of **Mercury**; according to the Indians, of **Venus**; according to Maternus, of **Jupiter**. The second, for some, belongs to the **Moon**; for others, to Mercury; for others, to **Mars**. The first decan of **Gemini** belongs to **Jupiter** for the **Chaldeans**, to Mercury for the Indians, and to Mars for Maternus. Not to follow every one of them in detail, the Babylonians followed this method: they gave the first decan (the beginning of **Aries**) to Mars, because that is the house of Mars; however, following the order of the spheres, they gave the first ten-degree segment of any sign to the "head of the family"—that is, the lord of the house—and the remaining two to the lords of the signs of that triangle. The invention of Maternus is entirely arbitrary; he merely pretends to an ancient tradition, which, when one weighs it, also recognizes...

## Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

...recognize that they established these dogmas not through true observations or the reliability of experiments, but through weak and flimsy conjectures of this sort—conjectures they substituted for the reliability of experience. We shall later dispute these very "experiments" at great length below. Just as the **Egyptians** devised <term>decans</term> <note>divisions of a zodiac sign into three parts of ten degrees each</note> by dividing a sign into three parts, so the **Babylonians** dissected a sign into twelve parts, using the **twelfth-parts** <note>original: "dodecathemoria"</note>. They did not use the system that **Maternus** <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Latin astrologer</note> ascribes to them, according to the authors **Mallius** and **Porphyry**; **Ptolemy** also mentions this, but in mockery, noting that these twelfth-parts are called <term>places</term> <note>original: "τόπους" (topous)</note>. Likewise, **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar, a 9th-century Persian astrologer</note>, **Avenezra** <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a 12th-century Jewish scholar</note>, and **John of Seville** <note>Hispalensis</note> mention only this twelfth-part system, not the one handed down by Maternus, **Alchabitius**, and **Heliodorus**, which we shall discuss in its proper place later. **John of Saxony** <note>Saxoniensis</note>, deceived by the similarity of the names in his commentaries on Alchabitius, confuses the two.

The **Indians**, inventing their own fictions, divided each sign into nine parts. They established that the first part belongs to the lord of the sign that is "movable" within that <term>triplicity</term> <note>a group of three signs associated with an element</note>. For example, the first ninth-part of Aries belongs to **Mars**, because Aries is a movable sign; but the first part of Leo also belongs to Mars, because Aries is the movable sign of the "fiery triplicity." They then assign the following parts according to the sequence of the following signs: if the first belongs to Mars (whose house is Aries), the second belongs to **Venus**, and the third to **Mercury**, because Venus owns Taurus and Mercury owns Gemini.

The **Egyptians**, again, numbered every single degree, which they called <term>monomoiria</term> <note>individual degrees of a sign, each assigned to a planet</note>. They assigned these to the planets by the order of the triplicities. Thus, the first degree of any sign would be the <term>monomoiria</term> of the planet that rules that triplicity—the nocturnal ruler if the birth is at night, or the diurnal ruler if by day. The second degree belongs to the second ruler of that same triplicity, and the third degree to the ruler of the next sign's triplicity, and so on. They did this in such a way that the same planet would not obtain a degree twice in one sequence.

I shall refute all these "anatomies" and "dissections" of the signs using no words other than those of **Ptolemy** himself, who said that all these things have <term>a physical-sounding but empty argument</term> <note>original: "φυσικὸν ἀλλὰ κενόδοξον λόγον" (physikon alla kenodoxon logon)</note>. That is to say, they have no basis in the laws of nature, but are merely for **vain ostentation**. He could not have defined them more correctly; for the more these things are fashioned with audacity and excessive license, the more wonderful and significant they seem to the unrefined and unskilled. There was no other reason why **Abu Ma'shar** was considered a "great man" in astrology—though otherwise ignorant of mathematics—than because nothing seemed too irrational to him. He piled up the fables of everyone at once, rejecting and despising nothing. Consequently, he seems to have revealed more "secrets" than others, simply because he recorded more myths.

It remains to speak of the <term>bounds</term> <note>original: "finibus"; specific segments of a sign ruled by different planets</note>, which I shall refute just as briefly by pointing to the discord among those still arguing over them. For **Ptolemy** prescribes some, the **Egyptians** others, the **Babylonians** others, the **Indians** others, and some other astrologer mentioned by **Albumasar** others still. According to the opinion promised in his *Great Introduction*, the younger astrologers side with the Egyptians, while the Greeks follow Ptolemy, as does **Ali ibn Ridwan** <note>Auenrodan</note>, while others have their own followers. Therefore, not only the signs...

He cites Ptolemy's dismissal of these methods as "vain ostentation" and argues that their complexity only serves to deceive the unlearned.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s critique of the internal inconsistencies of astrology. Having previously discussed larger divisions like the "triplicities," he now moves into the specific hierarchies of planetary "dignities" (the power a planet has in a certain location) and the even smaller subdivisions of the zodiac signs, such as individual degrees.</meta>

<page-num>615</page-num>
<header>Against Astrology, Book VI.</header>

The system itself is nothing; but even if these associations of the planets with the signs were meaningful—where one planet has its **home** <note>The "house" or "domicile," the sign a planet is said to rule</note> here, its **kingdom** <note>Original: *regnum*, usually referring to exaltation</note> there, or its **bounds** <note>The "terms" or "fines," specific degrees within a sign assigned to different planets</note> elsewhere—they are frivolous, mythical, contradictory, and fabricated. Not only do the Latin authors disagree on these matters, but they clash when their systems are compared to one another. For instance, the common crowd gives the first importance to the **house**, the second to the **exaltation**, the third to the **bounds**, the fourth to the **triplicity**, and the fifth to the **face** <note>Divisions of 10 degrees, also called decans</note>. **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century foundational authority on astronomy and astrology</note> places the house in the first rank, the triplicity in the second (as **Haly** <note>Likely the commentator Ibn Ridwan</note> agrees), the exaltation in the third, and the term in the fourth, while he ignores the "face" entirely. The **Chaldeans** <note>Ancient Mesopotamian astronomers/astrologers</note> do not use houses at all; the **Egyptians** add <term>monomírias</term> <note>Systems assigning a specific planet to every single one of the 30 degrees in a sign</note> to all of them; the **Indians** use ninths; the **Babylonians** use <term>twelfth-parts</term> <note>Original: *dodecathemoria*; 2.5-degree subdivisions</note> and do not include triplicities with the houses. **Maternus** <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman astrologer</note> grants more weight to "height" <note>Exaltation</note> than to the bounds, and more to the bounds than the houses. For he says, "The stars rejoice when placed in a princely location in their height; secondarily in their bounds; thirdly in their houses." Therefore, these dogmas of the astrologers are utterly vain, for they neither support them with reason nor with experiments; when they are not babbling in the former, they are disagreeing in the latter.

---

### ON FEMININE, BRIGHT, AND DARK DEGREES, AND OTHERS OF THAT KIND; HOW PTOLEMY DISREGARDED THEM, AND HOW OTHER ASTROLOGERS DO NOT AGREE ON THEM. CHAPTER XVII.

We have already refuted those divisions of the signs which they attribute to the planets—how Mars may be exalted here, and the Sun there; or that this is one planet’s **face**, and that another’s; or this one's <term>monomíria</term> <note>single-degree division</note> and that one's another. Likewise for **triangles** <note>triplicities</note>, **bounds**, **ninths**, and **twelfth-parts**. Now we must address those things which they have taught regarding the degrees themselves in an absolute sense: how some are **bright**, others **dark**, others **fortunate**, others (as they say) **Pitted** <note>Original: *Puteales*; degrees thought to swallow up a planet's luck like a well or pit</note>, others **sickly** <note>Original: *alzemena*; from the Arabic for "debilitated" or "chronically ill"</note>, some **masculine**, and others **feminine**. But as we have already satisfied most of this above, we shall now add this: Ptolemy disregarded all of these as well. His commentator, **Avenrodan** <note>Ibn Ridwan, an 11th-century Egyptian physician and astrologer</note>, seems to concede only so much as to say they should be observed *if* truth is found in them through experience. But what trust can be placed in "experience" when there are six different opinions regarding masculine and feminine degrees? For you will read them described one way in **Firmicus**, another in **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar, a 9th-century Persian astrologer</note>, another in **Avenrodan**, and another in **Alchabitius** <note>Al-Qabisi, a 10th-century Arab astrologer</note>. **Abraham** <note>Ibn Ezra, a 12th-century Jewish polymath</note> varies in many points; then those who make the twelfth part of every sign alternately masculine and feminine—setting the first parts based on the gender of the sign—discord completely with all of these. I pass over those who place twelve degrees out of thirty in the gender of the sign, the next twelve in the opposite, and then divide the remaining six into equal portions. Regarding **bright**, **dark**, and **obscure** degrees, another opinion first arose among the ancients based on the position of the stars; they called a degree "bright" if a star was located there. They believed this was permanent because they thought the stars did not move—and in this they were wrong. If we agree with **Hipparchus**, **Ptolemy**, and the rest—though the later astrologers do not look into the origin of the dogma—even while they argue that the stars *do* move <note>Referring to the precession of the equinoxes, which shifts the stars' positions relative to the zodiac degrees over centuries</note>, they still define the same degrees as "bright" and "dark" that the ancients determined. What great confusion has been born among them in this matter!

The confusion and the great perversity of matters and terms has been explained above, showing that nothing could be further from the truth than their so-called "experience" in these things. We have also declared their error regarding the degrees they call **"increasing fortune,"** which you will find recorded one way in the works of **Alchabitius** <note>A 10th-century Arab astrologer and mathematician</note>, another way in **Albumasar** <note>Also known as Aboasar; a 9th-century Persian astrologer whose works were foundational to European astrology</note>, and yet another in **Avenezra** <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra, a 12th-century Jewish scholar and astrologer</note>. 

The same diversity is found in the **"pits"** <note>Original: *putealibus*, also known as "deep" or "lame" degrees, thought to cause misfortune or disabilities if a planet falls in them</note>, which none of the ancients established. Albumasar cannot help but lie when he claims to follow the opinion of the Egyptians in describing them; for many of those degrees which Albumasar designates as "pits," **Hephaestio of Thebes** <note>A 5th-century astrologer who synthesized Egyptian and Greek traditions</note>—an expert in all Egyptian astrology—counts among the **"bright degrees"** <note>Degrees associated with luck or clarity</note>. Such examples include the sixth degree of Aries, the fifth of Taurus, the thirtieth of Gemini, the twenty-second of Cancer, and many others in different signs. 

Furthermore, what of a certain **Dorian astrologer** <note>Likely Dorotheus of Sidon, a 1st-century poet-astrologer</note>, who called himself an "investigator" of these properties of degrees? He holds a completely different view from all the ancients, and for his own dogma he alleges nothing other than the "certainty of experience"—claiming that events do not correspond to the sayings of the ancients, but rather to his own. Therefore, this observation of various degrees is vain, unreliable, and inconsistent; it is condemned not only by us, but by **Ptolemy** as well.

### THE LOTS: FROM WHERE THEY ARISE AND HOW MUCH 
### astrologers conflict with one another in measuring them. Chapter XVIII.

Now, as for the **"lots"** <note>Original: *partes*. These are mathematical points in the zodiac calculated by the distance between two planets, then projected from the Ascendant. The most famous is the "Lot of Fortune"</note> which they use in every prediction: are they not a mere fiction, a vain thing, and a baseless dogma? "Count," they say, "the degrees intercepted between this planet and that one, and when you have counted the same number of degrees from the <term>horoscopus</term> <note>The Ascendant, or the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth</note>, where that number ends, there shall be a 'lot' that signifies some matter." They say this point must be observed no differently than a planet or a star. 

What could be imagined more delusional than this instruction? Not only because a natural power in heaven exists where there is no star, no light, and no other natural quality—as is certainly the case at the specific degree where that calculation ends—but because this counting is also devised according to whim and can have no physical reason. The most trifling Albumasar wished to provide a cause for these sorts of lots, which none of the ancients had done. But even so, he said things in such a way that, in his extreme wordiness, he says nothing at all. 

For the sum of his words is finally this: when there are two planets signifying the same thing, the distance between them also has the power of signifying, but it must be measured from the ascendant. He claims that because coming goods or evils are known once the place where the "signifier" of one's affairs has arrived from the ascendant is known. For example: since the Sun and Saturn are the stars of **parents**, the interval by which they are separated from each other must be counted from the ascendant; at the degree where that number falls, there will be the future significance regarding parents, as if the power of the Sun and Saturn were somehow joined in that place. This is the "subtlety" of Albumasar, in which that which is denied is instead assumed—and which we primarily mock: namely, that such a distance has a power such that the end of a similar interval drawn from the...

<page-num>617</page-num>

...if the ascending degree has any power of producing an effect, he ought to have provided the reason for this power. Since he fails to do so, his view is not a reasoned opinion, but a mere story, which, as we have seen, is ineffective because it proves nothing regarding the matter in question. Moreover, it is a false narrative that contradicts the principles of the astrologers themselves; for the original authors of the "parts" <note>The "Arabic Parts" or "Lots" are specific points on the zodiac calculated by the mathematical distance between two planets or points, then added to the Ascendant</note> (as we just mentioned) made the **Planets** themselves the primary factors, rather than the things and events themselves—that was a later invention devised by their successors. 

In the matter of the "parts" of the Planets, consider the logic of **Abu Ma'shar** <note>original: *Aboasaris*, a 9th-century Persian astrologer</note>, who says that parts are taken from the interval between two planets signifying the same thing. This is especially problematic because, according to **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of Hermeticism and astrology</note>—who was the first author of these parts in that book he titled *The All-Virtuous* <note>original: $\pi\alpha\nu\alpha\rho\acute{\epsilon}\tau\omega$ (*Panaretos*)</note>—the distance of no Planet except for the Sun and Moon is taken by itself. Rather, it is taken from the Planet whose "part" is sought and a part of one of the two luminaries. For instance, he takes the Part of Venus from the distance between the Sun and Venus; here, as we noted in the first book, **Abu Ma'shar** and **Alchabitius** <note>A 10th-century Arab astrologer</note> were deceived. The Part of Mercury is taken from the Part of Fortune <note>original: *parte Lunae quae fortunae dicitur*</note> and Mercury itself, where those men also went astray. The Part of Mars is from Mars and the Part of Fortune; the Part of Jupiter from the Part of the Sun and Jupiter; and those of the Sun and Moon from each other, as is manifest to everyone. 

Nor does he intend for any things to be signified by these "parts" other than what each Planet, whose part it is said to be, signifies. Add to this that the parts of specific things are not taken from the Planets that signify those things among the astrologers. For example, **Mars** signifies "brothers" according to all of them, and yet the "Part of Brothers" is taken from Jupiter and Saturn, and never from Mars. Furthermore, all the ancients derive the "Part of Marriage" <note>original: *partem coniugij*</note> from **Saturn**, even though they maintained that this Planet has no connection to weddings or marriage. 

Therefore, that commentary of Abu Ma'shar is not only flimsy and trifling—since it assumes the very point under dispute—but it is also alienated from the opinions of the authors of this dogma. Those original authors were moved by something other than what this trifler dreamed up so many centuries later. For the first occasion of this error was as follows: it seemed to the ancients that the rising degree—that is, the **horoscope** <note>The Ascendant, or the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth</note>—corresponded to the Sun. Therefore, since the Moon is thought to be secondary to the Sun, they wanted there to be another horoscope responding proportionally to the Moon. They judged that it should be placed in no other location than one that was as far from the eastern horizon as the Sun was from the Moon in any given birth chart <note>term: *genitura* (nativity or birth chart)</note>. They called this place the **Lot of Fortune** <note>original: $\kappa\lambda\tilde{\eta}\rho o\nu ~ \tau\acute{\upsilon}\chi\eta\varsigma$ (*kleron tyches*)</note>, for a reason we shall mention shortly. 

**Ptolemy** himself teaches this in the third book of his *Apotelesmatika* <note>Known today as the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology</note>, reminding us that all antiquity agreed that the Part of Fortune should be as distant from the horoscope as the Moon is from the Sun. Nor did the opinion of those who, in nocturnal birth charts, calculate from the Moon to the Sun vary from this; for they simply turn from the ascendant toward the preceding signs, and thus they end up in the same place as those who, calculating from the Sun to the Moon, count according to the sequence of the signs. I suspect the reason for the name is this: since they had made two "horoscopes," as it were—one for the Sun and one for the Moon—they assigned the lot of the body and soul to the true and Solar one, but to this Lunar and adventitious one, they assigned the **Lot of Fortunes**; that is, of those things which are outside of us...

<meta>This page continues Pico's systematic debunking of the "Lots" or "Parts" in astrology. He moves from a critique of Abu Ma'shar to a historical overview of how these arbitrary mathematical points—such as the Part of Fortune—were multiplied by later authors like Hermes and Paulus Alexandrinus until they reached the point of absurdity, assigning "parts" even to kitchen vegetables.</meta>

<page-num>618</page-num>
# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola #

...are established so that from the first we might obtain ourselves, and from the second our possessions might obtain their fate. This is why the lunar horoscope is called the **"Lot of Fortune,"** and **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the influential 2nd-century astronomer and astrologer</note> judges concerning fortunes from no other thing more than from this. For commonly these lots are called **"parts,"** but in the works of **Maternus** <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer</note> they are called "places." 

When this concept had already been accepted, a certain **Hermes the Egyptian** <note>Referring to the legendary Hermes Trismegistus</note>—having poorly considered the reasoning of the earlier system—thought that "lots" should be created for all the Planets by a similar example. Thus, he established lots for Saturn and the rest in the book titled <term>The All-Virtuous</term> <note>original: παναρετὸν (*Panaretos*)</note>. He called the part of the Sun the <term>Good Spirit</term> <note>original: ἀγαθὸν δαίμονα (*agathon daimona*), often interpreted as "Good Divinity"</note>; that of Jupiter, <term>Victory</term> <note>original: νίκην (*niken*)</note>; that of Mercury, <term>Necessity</term> <note>original: ἀνάγκην (*ananken*)</note>; that of Venus, <term>Love</term> <note>original: ἔροτα (*erota*)</note>; that of Mars, <term>Audacity</term> <note>original: τόλμαν (*tolman*)</note>; and that of Saturn, <term>Nemesis</term> <note>original: νέμεσιν (*nemesin*)</note>. 

In organizing these, he observed this method: he took each part from the distance of the Planet itself to which the part belongs, to a part of either the Sun or the Moon. Specifically, he used the Sun for Venus and Jupiter, and the Moon for the others. Where the Sun’s part was to be used, the calculation was made from the Sun in a daytime birth <note>genitura</note>, but in a nighttime birth from the Planet to the part. The opposite was done where the part of Fortune was used. Furthermore, he ordered that the total number for all of them be calculated from the **horoscope** <note>In ancient astrology, the "horoscope" refers specifically to the Ascendant, the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</note>, because he saw that this was done by the ancients for the Part of Fortune. Using that as his example, he devised the rest, paying little attention to the fact that the reasoning (whatever it may be) which moved the ancients to establish a lot for the Moon does not apply to the remaining Planets. These other planets do not share the same parity or kinship with the Sun that would make it necessary for them to correspond to the horoscope in the same way the rising Sun corresponds to the East.

But would that this license for invention had stayed within those limits! For **Paulus Alexandrinus** <note>A 4th-century astrological author</note>, several centuries younger than the Hermes we mentioned, added four more parts to the parts of the Planets—no longer for the stars, but for human affairs: namely for **parents, children, brothers, and marriage.** This invention provided the opportunity for such further raving that, by devising an infinite number, they designated a "part" for almost every scrap of trash in the sky. For you can read of parts for **chickpeas, beans, lentils, barley, onions,** and a thousand things of this sort in all the **Arabic** and **Latin** authors. 

I am not so much inclined to believe that the **Chaldeans** <note>The Babylonian astrologers, often considered the "purest" source by Renaissance thinkers</note> used no parts simply because they were an Egyptian invention, but rather because **Porphyry** <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note>, when writing his *Apotelesmatic Institutions* according to the opinion of the Chaldeans, never mentions parts. **Ptolemy**, except for the Part of Fortune, abominates all the others—though he would have done even better to despise that one as well, since a "horoscope of the Moon" and whatever they devise within it is vain and arbitrary. But his error seems pardonable when one looks at the things which, following the example of a single "part," have collapsed into the futile temerity and license of the astrologers. 

The reason why they take the distances of two Planets and count them from the horoscope is now clear: namely, because they found it done that way for the Part of Fortune. The ancients did it there because a "secondary horoscope" was being sought; therefore, it had to be placed at that distance from the East <note>the Ascendant</note> which the Sun had moved from the Moon. Later, being ignorant of the origin of this dogma, they made up their own fables there, such as those told by **Abu Ma'shar** <note>original: *Aboasar*, the famous 9th-century Persian astrologer</note>. If they had been moved by experiments rather than by [flawed] reason...

He argues that these calculations are arbitrary imitations of the Moon's Part of Fortune and lack any true physical or philosophical basis.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's critique of the mathematical "Lots" or "Parts" in astrology. Having previously discussed their arbitrary origins, he now demonstrates the internal contradictions among the greatest astrological authorities, arguing that because they cannot agree on how to calculate these points, the system lacks any empirical validity.</meta>

<page-num>619</page-num>
<header>Against Astrology, Book VI.</header>

## Against Astrology, Book VI.

If they say they are moved by experience, I will respond as I have always done: there is no authority in experiences about which men of equal authority do not agree. And this occurs in the matter of the **parts**, just as in every dogma of the astrologers. First, almost every author places the **Part of Fortune** <note>A mathematical point in a birth chart calculated from the positions of the Sun, Moon, and Ascendant</note> in a different location. For **Ptolemy**—whether the birth was by day or night—commands it to be calculated from the Sun to the Moon. Others affirm that in a nocturnal birth, it must be calculated from the Moon to the Sun—this being the **Part of Venus**. **Heliodorus** and **Maternus** calculate from the **Part of the Demon** <note>original: *parte dæmonis*; also known as the Part of Spirit</note> to Venus by day, and the opposite by night. **Alchabitius**, following **Abu Ma'shar**, calculates from the Part of Fortune to the Part of the Demon by night, and from the Demon to Fortune by day. **Abenragel** <note>The Arab astrologer Albohazen Haly</note> takes it from Venus to Fortune, both by day and night alike. 

Regarding the **Part of Parents**, the Arabs take it from the Sun to Saturn in a day birth, and from Saturn to the Sun in a nocturnal birth. **Heliodorus** says that if Saturn is hidden by the Sun's rays, whether it be night or day, the calculation goes from Mars to Jupiter. Concerning the **Part of Siblings**, **Maternus** calculates from Jupiter to Saturn at night; the Greeks do so at night as well, but by day they calculate from Saturn to Jupiter.

Regarding marriage, they disagree in a marvelous way. For if you seek the **Lot of the Husband**, **Alchabitius** always counts from the Sun to Venus. **Heliodorus** also counts to Venus, but starts from Saturn. **Maternus**, following the opinion of the ancients, commands that by day we go from Saturn to Venus, but by night we begin from Venus. He further testifies that he himself—as others also teach—has proven in many birth charts that it should always be calculated from the Sun to the Moon in both day and night births. 

But if we examine the birth chart of a woman, **Maternus** commands the calculation be made from Mars to Venus by day, and from Venus to Mars by night. Others always calculate from Venus to Saturn; **Abenragel** says this was the opinion of **Vettius Valens** and **Hermes**. **Abenragel** himself approves that it should always be taken from the Moon to Mars, while others say always from the Sun to Mars. They disagree in the remaining parts in the same way, but it would be tedious to pursue them all. 

The **Part of Travel** <note>original: *peregrinationis*</note> is taken by the Arabs from the Lord of the Ninth House to its first minutes; the Greeks take it from the Sun to Mars. The **Part of Inheritances** the former take from Saturn to the Moon, but the latter from Saturn to Venus. The **Part of Servants** the former take from Mercury to the Moon, the latter from Mars to the Moon. The **Part of the Mother** is calculated by all the ancients from Saturn to the Moon, then counting the number from the <term>horoscope</term> <note>Here referring to the Ascendant, the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</note>, as the ancients were accustomed to do in all things. The Arabs seek it from the Moon to the first minute of the eighth house, and they add as many degrees as Saturn has traveled through the sign in which he is located, and whatever total the calculation produces, they count that much from the beginning of the sign in which Saturn is, through the following signs. 

But we are not so idle as to record all their fables. This much certainly can be clear to anyone: these are nothing but dogmas which each man

-> has fabricated for himself at his own whim, <-
-> rather than through faithful experiments. <-

### THE DOCTRINE OF THE TWELFTHFOLDS IS REJECTED, AND THEIR AUTHORS
### the Egyptians, along with their climacteric years, are cast aside. Chapter XIX.

**P**arallel to the madness of the Twelfthfolds <note>Greek: *dodekatemorion*; a technique where a single zodiac sign is subdivided into twelve smaller parts, effectively projecting a miniature version of the entire zodiac within each sign</note>, and by the same reasoning, these parts are to be hissed off the stage. I do not mean that Twelfthfold we mentioned above, which is simply the twelfth part of any sign—a span of two and a half degrees—but rather the one handed down by **Maternus** <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer</note> and Greek writers in the following manner: whichever star’s Twelfthfold you wish to find, they say, multiply its degree by twelve. Whether that planet is in the tenth degree, the fifth, or any other number of the sign it occupies, you take the total sum of that multiplication and divide it among the individual signs, allotting thirty degrees to each. However, you must begin the count from the start of the sign in which the star is located; the sign where the final number falls reveals the Twelfthfold part to you.

Consider this example: the Sun is at 5 degrees and 5 minutes of Aries. If you multiply five by twelve, the result is 60 degrees; the 5 minutes, when multiplied, make one additional degree, so the total is 61 degrees. You give thirty degrees to Aries (where we said the Sun was), thirty to Taurus, and thus the Twelfthfold will be found in the first degree of Gemini. Now that this has been found, what could be imagined more vain or futile? For through these numbers, no power of the planet and no quality is actually transmitted into that part of the zodiac.

If it is claimed that observations have shown these results to correspond to reality, I shall bring forward **Paul of Alexandria**, a most weighty author among the Egyptians (whose invention this primarily was). He testifies that such observations were found to be false, for he himself introduced a new method against the opinion of all the ancients. He argued that those degrees should not be multiplied by twelve, but by thirteen. Clearly, the ancient calculation did not work for him, being false and fabricated. And because multiplying by thirteen occasionally yielded the result he sought, he established a dogma from a single success, after the manner of astrologers. 

These are those "mysteries" of the Egyptians, whose opinions the superstitious common folk adore like oracles. Their doctrine not only lacks any divinity, but is ridiculous even to the semi-educated. If there were such a thing as true astrology, the Egyptians would be the last to deserve the name of astrologers. As we shall discuss later, they were ignorant of the true and natural things in the heavens—that is, the actual motions of the constellations and stars—and in their predictions they relied more on these fallacious dreams than on the stars and planets themselves. 

**Heliodorus** writes that **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure perceived as the founder of astrology and alchemy</note>, who first discovered the degrees of the planets, opened a path whereby one could pronounce judgment on all individual degrees and Twelfthfolds by looking at those parts alone, without regarding anything else. It is a wonder how much weight they gave to this in every prediction. Because of this, **Ptolemy**, the most prudent of astrologers, notes them indirectly. He says he will hand down his own dogmas <note>original: μὴ διὰ κλήρων κὰι ἀριθμῶν ἀναιτιολογήτων... περιττὰ ὑπὸ πολλῶν φλυαρόμενα κὰι μὴ πιθανὸν ἔχοντα λόγον</note> "not through lots and numbers that lack a cause," all of which are "superfluous things chattered about by many, and having no persuasive reason." When he speaks of "numbers," and those which he censures...

<summary>Pico attacks the astrological "Twelfthfolds" (Dodecathemoria), arguing that the mathematical formula used to calculate them is physically meaningless and that even the "ancient" authorities like Paul of Alexandria and Ptolemy disagreed on how to use them.</summary>

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA
## Mirandola’s Disputations Against Astro-
### logy, Book VII.

#### WHAT HAS BEEN DEBATED THUS FAR, AND WHAT IS TO BE
#### debated in this book. Chapter I.

**H**ITHERTO <note>A decorative woodcut initial 'H' appears here, depicting a landscape with figures.</note> it was demonstrated that astrology is nothing if the causal power of the stars is removed, which we showed could be rationally asserted based on philosophy, the dignity of the stars, the condition of inferior things, and the evidence of experience. Then, if they [the stars] do effect what the astrologers believe, we proved that why these things nonetheless happen differently than they have devised, no knowledge of that efficacy, and consequently of future events, is possible for them. Now we must act so that even if we grant that these things occur through the heavens, and in the manner they have established—that is, that all things receive their fates from the sky at their primordial hour <note>the exact moment of a thing's beginning or birth</note>—we may declare that it is impossible for them to know what the fate of any particular thing is. For this is first necessary for them if they are to succeed: they must have determined with absolute certainty which hour is fatal <note>destined</note> for each person, which we will teach in the disputation of the present book can neither be known nor has been certainly known by them. And since various beginnings are established for various things, we shall first dispute regarding the beginning of man, declaring that it is ambiguous, and that whatever it may be, it is certainly not what the astrologers think.

#### THAT THE FATAL HOUR IS AMBIGUOUS, IF ANY SUCH EXISTS,
#### in all things which are completed not in a moment but over time,
#### and especially in men, in whom the nativity
#### seems to have little strength. Chapter II.

**E**XISTING <note>A decorative woodcut initial 'E' appears here, depicting a seated figure.</note> however, in determining the beginning of any thing which is not completed in a moment but over time, there is an inextricable question: whether that time is fatal to it in which the maker <note>original: *opifex*; the creator or craftsman</note> first sets about making it, whatever the cause...

<meta>This page continues Pico's philosophical investigation into the "fatal moment"—the precise instant when the stars are supposed to exert their influence. He continues a sentence from the previous page regarding whether a thing obtains its efficient power from the stars at the start or end of its creation.</meta>

<page-num>622</page-num>
<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

obtains its efficient power. Or is it rather when the work is finished? Or, since the whole is not required all at once, but rather in parts, are the fates of the different parts also different? For whatever we might say, there is a reason to support it. For if the craftsman’s hand is applied **successfully**, how can the work be **unsuccessful** if the craftsman works successfully? Since the success of both the worker and the operation consists ultimately in this: that the work turns out both well and according to the worker’s wish. 

Then, if fate is an efficient cause from the stars and not merely a sign, when ought a thing to receive its fate more than when the stars effect it through other intervening causes? It seems, therefore, that the deed depends on that hour in which the craftsman first begins to undertake the work. 

On the other hand, how will a thing receive its fate before it exists? Or how shall we say it exists when it first begins to be made, so that it might eventually exist? Finally, a thing is what it is by its species <note>original: *specie*; the essential nature or "form" of a thing in Aristotelian philosophy</note> and by the form which arrives at the final moment of its constitution. What "fatal moment," therefore, is more likely than that in which it first begins to be what it is? At that point, separate from the cause by which it was being made, it can stand by its own nature and stability. We will not, therefore, reasonably look for the fates of things from the hour they begin to be *made*, but from the hour they begin to *be*.

Again, if different parts are completed at different times, why does each part not obtain the decree of its own fortune from its own time? This is especially true since it is proven by experience that things happen differently to various parts of the same thing. For even in the body of the same man, sometimes some members will be healthy while others are ill; and one part of a city will be subject to ruins and fires, while nothing of the sort happens to the remaining parts. Why then is it not more reasonable for each part to be moved and governed by its own constellation, rather than subsequent events drawing the condition of fate from some past and perhaps abolished beginning? 

And let these things indeed be said in general about all things; now let us examine the same specifically in man, concerning whose "fatal origin" (if any such thing exists) much inescapable ambiguity necessarily arises. For what shall we establish as the primary moment, since so many beginnings are seen, and all of them are worthy of primacy? 
* Do we think that "fatal point" of time is the moment when the man first joins with the woman? 
* Or is it not that, but rather when the seed from the male increases in the womb? 
* Or are these perhaps merely preludes and necessary antecedents? 

Shall we instead establish the first beginning of human formation when the seminal power itself attacks the purest part of the female discharge and constitutes it—that is, drives it into a fetus—just as milk is united and thickened by rennet? <note>This was a common ancient analogy for conception, comparing the action of male seed on female blood to rennet curdling milk into cheese.</note> Or is it not yet the beginning of a human even then, but rather when all parts of the body are present in potential within the conception? Or when it is already wrapped around by the small membranes or afterbirth? Or does nature begin the human being when the heart is first distinguished in actuality? For by the heart’s power, that which is produced—now like a son emancipated <note>original: *emancipatus*; a legal term for a child released from their father’s authority to become an independent agent</note> from his father—begins to be governed by itself, as Aristotle, the interpreter of nature, taught. Indeed, great authority and power are owed to this beginning, since the heart is the first thing formed, and in the distinguishing of the other parts, both the movement of all and the growth are distributed from the heart.

<summary>Pico questions when the "fatal hour" of astrology actually occurs—at the start of a project, its completion, or during the development of its individual parts. He applies this problem to human biology, asking whether destiny is fixed at conception, during the formation of the fetus, or when the heart first begins to beat.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's critique of the "fatal hour," specifically addressing the various "beginnings" of a human life—conception, the formation of organs, the infusion of the soul (animation), and birth—and questioning why astrologers fixate on the moment of birth despite its lack of biological or metaphysical priority.</meta>

# Against Astrology, Book VII.

...[continued] so that (if we must trade fables with the astrologers), just as the power implanted in the heart subsequently unfolds the whole man as other parts cooperate, so the **Solar virtue** <note>The "Solar virtue" refers to the perceived life-giving influence of the Sun, which ancient and Renaissance thinkers often associated with the vital heat of the heart.</note> first received in the heart might then unfold the entire power of fate. 

Or is it rather that the primary fate of the heart and of life comes from this moment, but the disposition of each individual limb depends most of all on the hour in which it is shaped, thereby coming under the condition of its own private fate? For to those who consider and weigh all things correctly, it seems very reasonable that if, for example, the "lights" (as they call them) <note>original: *luminaria*; the Sun and the Moon</note> preside over the eyes, the condition and mixture of the eyes depends more on the disposition of the Sun and Moon at the time the eyes are being formed, rather than on what preceded it when the seed filled the womb, or what follows later when the infant is about to come forth from the mother's womb with the eyes already finished—and let it be understood that the same reasoning applies to the other limbs. 

But if, setting aside all these things we have said, a more excellent beginning in terms of authority and efficacy is sought, what more reasonable one can we offer than the moment when the soul is shared with the fetus? For it is then that a human begins to be, having attained the full rationale of substance; then the person consists of their own matter and form. And if fate proceeds from the hour in which a thing first exists, no hour would surely be thought more of a "fatal hour" for a human than this. 

However, if we must move away from that opinion, there is great probability in this: that things of the body are referred to the seminal principle <note>original: *seminale principium*; the moment of conception</note>, things of the soul to animation itself, and external matters of fortune to that chance moment when the person first enters this world—where fortune plays its game—having left the enclosures of the womb. 

Finally, from this so varied and knotty ambiguity concerning the human beginning, perhaps those who are divinely inspired will extricate themselves; philosophy, which relies only on reason, can in no way rightly explain itself. Yet if philosophy is to affirm anything, it will affirm nothing more than what the astrologers have decreed: that the fates of the newborn depend on the hour of birth. Yet this is an opinion to which the astrologers were not led by reason. Rather, because they saw they could track this beginning more easily <note>Birth is a public, observable event, whereas conception and the "infusion of the soul" are hidden.</note>, they granted it the primary role. Therefore, after birth, they are also accustomed to give some weight to conception, since they hope that something can sometimes be known about it. 

The other principles, which are certainly the most powerful—especially the moment the fetus is animated—they have rejected completely <note>original: *ex asse*; literally "from the as," a Roman coin unit, meaning "entirely" or "totally"</note>, because these are entirely unknown to them. Nor, if they admitted that human fates depend on that, would they be able to claim for themselves any power of divining fate. 

But to skip the rest, by what reasoning do they prefer birth over conception and the animation of the fetus? Since, if we give the primary role in establishing fate to that beginning which is first in time, there is no earlier beginning than the seminal principle <note>conception</note> from which all other things proceed. If a beginning is preferred not for being first in time, but rather for efficacy and dignity, then the time of the fetus being animated <note>The "animation" of the fetus refers to the traditional Aristotelian and theological belief that the rational soul enters the body at a specific point during pregnancy.</note> must be preferred above all. Birth is both the latest of all events and has little or no efficacy; it does not start the human, nor make him, nor complete him, but only shows the one who was already started and completed.

-> Ioannes Pico della Mirandola <-

### THAT PTOLEMY ASCRIBED MORE TO CONCEPTION THAN TO BIRTH, 
### ALTHOUGH PTOLEMY’S OWN REASONING CONVINCES US THAT NOTHING 
### SHOULD BE ASCRIBED TO EITHER. Chapter III.

If the words of **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity, whose works were the foundation of the field in Pico's time.</note> himself are weighed seriously, we will see that he was led by the force of reason to grant more to *conception* than to *birth*, even though, to favor his own profession, he attempted to assert much regarding the efficacy of the moment of birth. His words in the third book of the *Apotelesmatika* <note>original: "Apoteleſmatum"; better known today as the "Tetrabiblos," Ptolemy's foundational textbook on astrology.</note> are as follows: 

"When some temporal beginning of a man is established, by nature that beginning will be when the seed is admitted into the genital womb; however, potentially and according to accident, it is the hour of birth when the infant emerges. Therefore, he who has grasped the hour of the admission of the seed, whether by chance or by observation, ought rather to follow that hour in discerning the properties of body and soul, after considering the configurations of the stars active at that time. For since the seed is once disposed with a certain quality from the beginning by the state of the surrounding air—even if it is varied through the times of subsequent formation—since it naturally adopts only such matter as is proper and related to itself, when it has reached completion, it will be even more assimilated to the disposition of its first quality." 

These are Ptolemy’s words verbatim. Here it seems to me that he pronounces, most expressively and assertively, without any particle of doubt interjected, that the first, natural, and most effective principle of a man is the **admission of the seed**, and that one must cling to this most of all when it is known, for the foreknowledge of human vicissitudes, both those pertaining to the body and those pertaining to the soul. And where he asserted this, he then accurately and anxiously resolved the objections that could be raised about the change of the seed. 

But because he knew that his art was in danger if he denied the possibility of pronouncing on human fate from any other source, he added to what we have said in this manner: "But those who are ignorant of the hour of the seminal beginning—which is mostly ignored—for them it is **necessary** to follow the beginning of the birth." Let us weigh these words before we add others, in which he says only the hour of birth should be used when the hour of conception is unknown. Regarding the hour of conception, he said it *is fitting* to adhere to it—for in Greek it is written <term>prosekei</term> <note>original: "προσήκει"; meaning it is appropriate, right, or natural.</note>—but regarding the hour of birth, he did not say it was fitting, but <term>anankaion</term> <note>original: "ἀναγκαῖον"; meaning necessary by force or compulsion.</note>, that is, it is "necessary." 

It is as if for those who do not know the hour of a man’s conception, but still wish to divine his fate, they must necessarily take refuge in the birth, so that it appears clearer than light that Ptolemy did not descend to this opinion willingly, but was driven by necessity. Thus, the hour of birth is used like a **second plank after a shipwreck** <note>original: "ſecunda poſt naufragium tabula"; a classical idiom for a desperate last resort or a backup plan when the primary option has failed.</note>. Up to this point he has spoken according to reason; but soon, lest he desert his profession, he tries as much as he can to demonstrate that this principle of birth is also valid. Therefore, he adds this about it: "And this is also a very great principle, and falling short of the first only in this: that from conception those things can also be foreknown which happen before birth. Furthermore, if anyone should call this the principle, while the other..."

<summary>Pico analyzes the writings of Ptolemy to show that the "father of astrology" actually considered the moment of conception to be the true biological beginning, only using the birth chart as a "necessary" backup because conception times are usually unknown.</summary>

<margin>*</margin> <note>The marginal mark corresponds to the discussion of the "temporal beginning."</note> a temporal <term>beginning</term> <note>original Greek: "αρχην" (archēn). Pico is discussing the philosophical definition of a starting point.</note>, that is, after the first principle; it will indeed be secondary to this time, but perhaps more perfect in potential. For almost by right, this [conception] will not be denied as the generation of the human seed, while that other [birth] is the generation of a human being, since the infant then receives many things which it did not have before while in the womb, and those things are proper to human nature. Furthermore, even though it seems that what surrounds us at the hour of birth contributes nothing to making the newborn "this way or that," it nonetheless causes the infant to come into the light under a configuration of the surroundings that is related to the one before it. This is because nature, after perfecting the infant, gives the impulse to exit only when the disposition [of the stars] is similar to that figure which formed the fetus at the beginning. Thus, it is reasonable that the disposition of the stars at the hour of birth also carries significance for these things—not because it is the cause of them, but because by necessity and according to nature, its power is similar to that which caused them. 

These words of **Ptolemy** have been faithfully recited by us. In them, the first thing to observe is that what the interpreter **Avenrodan** <note>Ali ibn Ridwan (c. 988–1061), an Egyptian physician and astrologer who wrote an influential commentary on Ptolemy's Tetrabiblos.</note> says is entirely false: he claims that **Ptolemy** speaks hesitantly in the earlier words where he discusses the efficacy of <term>conception</term> <note>The technical term for the moment of fertilization.</note>, and assertively in these final words where he demonstrates that the hour of birth has the power of signifying. On the contrary, in the former case, **Ptolemy** affirms everything, excluding nothing and doubting nothing; whereas here, he says nothing without adding a particle of doubt, interposing now "almost," now "perhaps." Finally, when he is about to conclude his entire dispute, he has no other reason to defend the hour of birth as a signifier of fate than to suggest that it is similar to the seminal beginning. 

So far is he from denying that the authority for deciding what the future person will be like resides in the <term>conception</term>, that he grants no more to the birth chart regarding this matter than that it be found similar to and in agreement with the conception. For that opinion common among astrologers—also believed by the interpreter of **Ptolemy**—that the hour of <term>conception</term> signifies only what happens to the fetus in the mother’s womb, is easily understood to be born from a false interpretation of **Ptolemy’s** words. **Ptolemy** did not say that only those things are signified by conception, but also those things which a birth chart cannot capture. 

*Ptolemy says,* he writes, *that conception excels the birth chart in this: that through it, even those things which occur before birth can be foreseen.* Now, if it only signified those things, he would never have added that the first principle [conception] should not be considered superior to the second [birth] for that reason; for the span of an entire life is far greater than governing the first stages of a nature that is still crude and unformed. Therefore, if **Ptolemy** trusts in those words uttered so hesitantly and waveringly—that the power of the second principle is "perhaps" more effective than the first, and that this is "almost" the beginning of the human being while the other is merely the beginning of the seed—he clearly disagrees not only with reason, but with himself. 

He disagrees with himself because, as I was saying, he could not defend the authority of fate at the beginning of birth unless he devised an affinity between birth and the seminal beginning. Furthermore, when he later hands down rules for foreseeing the sex and other conditions of the newborn, he says these are better known from the conception than from the birth. He disagrees with reason both for many things we have said above, and because it is utterly beyond reason that conception, the beginning of the seed...
