<page-num>626</page-num>
<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

...should we call birth the **beginning** of a human being? For once the seed has filled the womb, it does not "become" itself, but rather begins to be abolished when nature applies its hands to the task of fabricating a human. Therefore, just as that moment is the principle of generating a human, it is also the principle of the destruction of the seed. But if you call birth the beginning of a man because he then possesses many things for the first time which he did not have in the womb, those things do not actually pertain to his **substance**—which is already completed and finished—but only to the exercise of certain functions. These functions are not even unique to humans <note>Pico means these are basic biological functions shared with animals, rather than the unique human capacity for reason.</note>. If we were to date a man's fate from the start of his unique human functions, fate would begin much later than birth; it would start when the infant begins to think, deliberate, and reason. For immediately upon being born, he has nothing uniquely human except his wailing.

Therefore **Ptolemy**, the most prudent of astrologers, would not have insisted on these false and frivolous points, though he offered them hesitantly <note>original: "dubitanter"</note> so that he might not be seen as an absolute deserter and betrayer of his profession. Nor, indeed, can those arguments which prioritize the birth over the conception (or which add some force to birth in decreeing fate) hold much weight. For the sum of their entire argument rests on a "consensus" <note>A presumed harmony or mathematical relationship.</note> that is said to exist between the birth and the conception. 

But what is this "consensus"? What is the similarity? **Haly** <note>Ali ibn Ridwan (c. 988–1061), a famous Egyptian physician and astrologer who commented on Ptolemy.</note> responds that the Sun at the hour of birth is always found in a sign that is either the seventh, ninth, or tenth from the sign it was in at the hour of conception. Is this, then, that "similarity"? **O ridiculous vanity!** As if any time, by this logic, would not "agree" with another time, since the Sun at any given moment must necessarily be at a distance of *some* number of signs from where it was at another time! 

Or is the claim regarding the Moon more probable? They say the Moon's position when we are born was the **horoscope** <term>Ascendant</term> <note>The "horoscope" here refers to the specific degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon.</note> at the time of conception, and the Moon's position at conception becomes the Ascendant at birth. It will be demonstrated later that this is false and a fabrication by astrologers. Even **Haly Avenrodan**, in explaining **Ptolemy** in a treatise on this very question, says he has found this to be sometimes true and sometimes false. 

But come now: even if it were true, that "fictional consensus" between the two hours would be even more clearly refuted by another path. For if you investigate the hour of conception according to that rule of the astrologers and set up a <term>thematic chart</term> <note>An astrological birth chart or figure.</note> for that time, you will find the disposition of the heavens and stars to be entirely different from—and signifying completely different things than—what appears to those calculating the hour of birth. But why do we waste more words in refuting such trifles? **Haly**, a distinguished astrologer, in the book he wrote *On Elections*, openly confesses that the power of discerning fate lies in the hour of conception; but because this hour is unknown, astrologers have fled to the hour of birth. 

Furthermore, when they are pressed on the birth of **Twins** <note>A classic skeptical argument: if twins are born nearly simultaneously under the same stars, why do they have different lives?</note> whose fortunes are vastly different, they are often forced to say that a difference in their *conceptions* varies their fortune. However, if the hour of conception only determines what happens inside the womb, it would follow that those whose conception was different could have a similar fortune, but their birth could in no way be the cause.

<sig>VNI</sig>

<summary>Pico mocks the astrological "rules" that try to link birth times to conception times, calling them mathematically arbitrary. He argues that if fate is real, it must begin at conception or even later at the dawn of reason, rather than at birth.</summary>

# UNIVERSAL FATES: BY WHAT PATHS ASTROLOGERS
# investigate them and how little they are based on reason. Chapter IV.

We have spoken of the beginning of individual fate, how uncertain it is and by what false reasoning it is established by astrologers; it remains to speak of universal fate—that is, from whence the fates of cities, nations, kingdoms, and the world in general are pronounced. For this too (even if one were to concede that such a thing exists) remains ambiguous and uncertain, and has been incorrectly defined by our astrologers. Now, they are accustomed to proceed by three main paths to predict universal changes: either from the "great conjunctions" of the superior stars or eclipses of the luminaries <note>the Sun and Moon</note>; or from the disposition of the heavens when the Sun enters the first minute of **Aries**, which they have established as the beginning of the year; or from the peculiar origins of cities, kingdoms, and nations—that is, from the hour in which a city was built, a kingdom instituted, or a law given to a people by which they live and are governed.

That all of these methods are for the most part frivolous has been shown above, not only where the entire influence of the stars was refuted, but also when we weakened the whole system of predicting from great conjunctions. We have declared it a vain thing to expect an effect either from those conjunctions or from the failures <note>eclipses</note> of the luminaries a long time after they have occurred. Furthermore, we have exposed the impiety and madness of astrologers who subject the law of heaven to fate, and nations to the fate of their own law. We have also shown how vain it is to decree a "birthday" for the building of a city or the acceptance of a kingdom as if it were a natural thing. 

Now, even if we were to grant that there is such a thing as the fate of all things, we are going to show that nothing certain regarding the fatal principle of these matters can be defined, nor has it been defined by astrologers thus far. First of all, in taking omens for the fate of a city from the "throwing of the first stone," by what reason are they moved? Since they are now scrutinizing the fates of the *community* rather than the *physical city*, that moment should rather be observed when the built city began to be inhabited and to be ruled and contained by its own laws. Regarding the fortune of a king, there is likewise great discord among them: some think it depends on the hour in which the king is instituted or chosen; others think the "taking of the throne" or the coronation should rather be inspected. But let us pass over these as if they were minor details, since even **Haly** <note>Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer whose "Book of the Skilled in the Judgments of the Stars" was a standard textbook.</note> believes the fates of nations, cities, and kingdoms depend not so much on these very things we were mentioning, but rather on the principles of great and universal constellations—concerning which we shall soon dispute with them at close quarters <note>original: "collato pede," a military term for hand-to-hand combat</note>.

---

# THAT THE ASTROLOGER CANNOT PREDICT IN WHICH
# region of the world a certain fate will occur, since among them it is uncertain which region lies under which sign or planet. Chapter V.

Even if the "great conjunctions" (as they call them) and the eclipses of the Sun and Moon produced such great changes as the astrologers fabricate, I now contend that nothing can truly be predicted about them by astrologers. This is not even considering those objections that can be thrown at them: that the horoscope of a great conjunction is uncertain; whether it is the specific one or that of the year in which it happens to turn; and that they arbitrarily observe the beginning and the middle in an eclipse of the luminaries...

<summary>Pico argues that astrological methods for predicting the fates of nations and cities—such as great conjunctions or foundation charts—are logically inconsistent and lack a defined starting point. He specifically questions whether a city's "fate" begins with its construction, its first inhabitants, or its first laws.</summary>

## Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

Therefore, even if we disregard other times and consider only the beginning of an event, let us grant them all these points and not fight over them; we can press them more effectively elsewhere to demonstrate the total uncertainty of these kinds of predictions. For there are four main points to them: first, what is predicted to happen; second, what kind of thing it is; third, at what time; and fourth, among which people and in which places and regions. 

If there is almost no change in human affairs, no event—whether prosperous or adverse—that does not happen in some part of the world among some people at whatever time it may come, then every prediction of this kind will be vain and futile unless they have explored this last point: namely, in what place or part of the earth those remarkable changes are going to occur. Regarding this, they define it such that the event is expected in those regions that are subject to the sign in which such a conjunction of stars or eclipse of the luminaries <note>The Sun or Moon</note> occurred—and not only those under the exact same sign, but either the same sign or at least a sign of the same triplicity <note>triplicity: a group of three zodiac signs associated with one of the four elements (fire, earth, air, water)</note>. This is the undisputed opinion of all astrologers on this matter. 

From this, it follows that nothing can be truly predicted about the fate of any region unless it is first established which planet that region is subject to. Just as a person's fate cannot be predicted if the time of birth is unknown. But if the distribution of lands under different signs and planets is entirely uncertain among astrologers, it is most clearly evident that their predictions about such things will necessarily be highly uncertain. Truly, anyone who reads the books of **Ptolemy** and **Albumasar** <note>original: "Albumasaris," the Latinized name for the Persian astrologer Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD)</note> accurately will easily understand that there is no doctrine in which astrology is less consistent with itself.

**Ptolemy**, in his book *Apotelesmatum* <note>original: "Apotelesmatum," referring to the *Tetrabiblos*, Ptolemy's foundational 2nd-century work on astrology</note>, says that the fire triplicity rules the north, the earth triplicity the south, the air triplicity the east, and the water triplicity the west. This was followed by **Julius Firmicus** <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer</note>, an emulator of ancient opinions. Yet the same **Ptolemy**, in the second book of that same work, seems to either explain differently or change that partition somewhat; he assigns the fire triplicity not so much to the north as to those lands situated between the north and the west; earth to those between the east and the south; air to those between the east and the north; and he places water between the west and the south. 

What **Albumasar** writes is as distant from all of these as the east is from the west. For in the sixth book of his *Great Introductory*, he wanted the fire triplicity to rule the east, not the north as **Ptolemy** did. To the north itself—to which **Ptolemy** assigned fire—he [Albumasar] contends that water rules; and the air triplicity, which **Ptolemy** assigned to the east, he instead assigns to the west. **Paul of Alexandria** holds the same in his *Institutions of the Art of Astrology*. 

But this same **Albumasar**, as if forgetting himself, writes things in his first book *On Great Conjunctions* that are as different from what he had written in his *Introductory* as those were from the doctrine of **Ptolemy**. For in that same place, he assigns the air triplicity—not fire like the Greeks with **Ptolemy** and **Maternus**, nor water like he does elsewhere and many Arabs—but the air triplici- [ty]...

<summary>Pico argues that astrological predictions are useless without knowing exactly where an event will occur, then points out that major authorities like Ptolemy and Abu Ma'shar completely contradict each other on which zodiac signs govern which geographic regions.</summary>

[triplici]ty <note>This completes the word "triplicity" from the previous page.</note>, and the watery nature which he had assigned there to the north, he then assigns to the opposite region—that is, the south. For the west, he claims it is governed neither by the watery nature (as Ptolemy does) nor by the airy nature (as he himself does elsewhere), but by the earthy. What could be more contradictory than these opinions? Who shall make themselves the judge of them? For neither logic can prevail here, nor can experience demonstrate the truth. Henry of Mechelen <note>A 14th-century astronomer and commentator on the "Speculum Astronomiae."</note> says that this last opinion of 

<margin>Albumazar <note>The influential Persian astrologer Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD).</note></margin>

is the truest and is confirmed by a great many experiments. On the other hand, Alchabitius, Sahl ibn Bishr, Abraham Ibn Ezra, Jafar in his introductory works, Masha'allah, and Haly <note>Referring to Al-Qabisi, Sahl ibn Bishr, the Jewish scholar Ibn Ezra, and the Arab astrologers Abu l-Hasan 'Ali ibn Abi l-Rijal and Masha'allah.</note> all approve of the view written in the *Introductory* of Haly. Ibn Ridwan, rejecting both, prefers the opinion of Ptolemy above all others. I shall pass over how the ancients themselves disagreed on these matters—the Egyptians from Hipparchus, and Ptolemy from Hipparchus. I will illustrate this with a few examples. For Aries <note>The first sign of the zodiac.</note>, the Egyptians assigned ancient Babylon and Arabia bordering Egypt; Ptolemy subjected Britain, Gaul, Germany, Bastarnia <note>A region in Eastern Europe near the Carpathian Mountains.</note>, and Palestine to it. Hipparchus and the most ancient astrologers used a more exact method, subjecting different regions to different parts of the sign. Thus, to the left shoulder of Aries they assigned Babylonia; to the right, Thrace <gloss>of the east <note>original Greek: της εωα</note></gloss>; to the <gloss>sides <note>original Greek: τ' πλευραις</note></gloss> of Armenia, the Arabia bordering Egypt; <gloss>looking from the north <note>original Greek: της απ' αρκτ' βλεπ'ω</note></gloss> they assigned Persia, Cappadocia, Mesopotamia, Syria, and the Red Sea. And so there is discord in all the other signs: the Egyptians, Hipparchus, and Ptolemy disagree no less than Abu Ma'shar disagrees with Ptolemy or even with himself. From this, it is clearer than light that nothing certain can be pronounced by astrologers as to where among nations and lands a particular event is going to happen, since they have nothing certain or proven regarding the very division of nations and lands under the signs.

---

### THAT A SINGLE BEGINNING CANNOT BE ESTABLISHED UPON WHICH
the fates of the entire year depend; then, that various beginnings of the year
are established by various people, and according to the Hebrews the year
begins in autumn rather than spring. Chapter VI.

**R**EGARDING what remains, let us speak of the beginning of the year. Ptolemy himself expressly confirms that a single beginning cannot be established from which the state of the whole year is predicted; indeed, I shall prove this with no one's words rather than his own. In the second book of his *Apotelesmatika* <note>Commonly known as the *Tetrabiblos*, Ptolemy's foundational work on astrology.</note>, he writes as follows: *In a circle, no one can simply conceive of a beginning; however, in the Zodiac, one would rightly establish those beginnings which are determined by the equinoxes and solstices, of which there are four: namely, two equinoctial and two solstitial. But here there is room for hesitation as to which of these four should be preferred. For if you look at the nature of the circle itself simply, none of them will obtain the privilege of being the singular beginning. However, those who have written on these matters use different suppositions, each moved by one of those four as a beginning, based on their own reasoning and natural consensus; for each of those parts has something peculiar and excellent about it, from which they seem to claim for themselves the authority of a beginning and a new year.*

...matter, so that the vernal equinox <note>The spring equinox, around March 21st, when day and night are equal.</note> is chosen because then the day first begins to become longer than the night, and because that time of year abounds in moisture. This quality and nature (as we said above) is most present in every beginning of things being generated. The privilege of the summer solstice <note>The longest day of the year, around June 21st.</note> is this: that then the day is extended to its greatest height and completion; furthermore, among the Egyptians, the Nile then overflows and the Dog Star <note>original: *Canicula*, referring to the star Sirius, whose rising coincided with the Nile's flooding.</note> rises. In the autumnal equinox <note>Around September 23rd.</note>, all fruits are gathered and the seeds of the earth are sown. In the winter solstice <note>The shortest day of the year, around December 21st.</note>, after the decrease of light, the day then first begins to increase. 

However, what seems more suitable to me and more in harmony with nature is this: that in the observation of the events of the year, we should use those four turning points, observing those conjunctions or oppositions of the Sun and Moon—especially the eclipses—that occur immediately before them. Thus, from the beginning taken from Aries <note>The sign associated with Spring.</note>, we may foresee what the spring will be like; from Cancer, the summer; from Libra, the autumn; and from Capricorn, the winter. 

These are the words of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century foundational authority on astronomy and astrology.</note> verbatim. From these it appears he both believed and proved that no single "true" beginning can be established from which the fate of the entire year may be foreseen. Thus, I cannot sufficiently wonder at Ibn Ridwan <note>original: *Auenrodan*, an 11th-century Egyptian physician and astrologer who commented on Ptolemy.</note>, his interpreter, and the younger astrologers who repeatedly claim that Ptolemy attributes more importance to the vernal equinox in starting the year than to the beginning of autumn or the solstice. For just as he says the vernal equinox has certain reasons why it might deserve the privilege of being the "beginning," he does exactly the same for the others. After showing that all four have initial authority, he determines that one does not have more weight than the other, but that all must be observed equally. He asserts this is more suitable and in harmony with natural laws than choosing only one and neglecting the rest. 

Indeed, each one has its own reason why it is rightly considered a beginning of the year. This is why different nations began their year from different points. The Egyptians started from the summer solstice, the Romans from the winter, and others from the autumnal equinox—that is, from the Sun's entry into Libra. These latter groups even observed the hour when the Sun traversed the twentieth part of Scorpio, believing that moment had the most efficacy for predicting the state and changes of the air; this was a practice followed by Saphar and Aoniar <note>Likely referring to the Arabic astrologers Zael (Sahl ibn Bishr) and Al-Anwari.</note>. 

Some, following the opinion of the Egyptians, want all four beginnings to be considered, but not so that everything is observed in all of them. Instead, when the Sun enters Aries, they consider the state of the Sun itself; when it enters Cancer, they look to Jupiter; when Libra, to Saturn; and when Capricorn, to Mars—because these planets are thought to "rule" in those signs. 

Albumazar <note>Abu Ma'shar, a famous Persian astrologer.</note> dreamed up another fiction: that if the Sun enters the first minutes of Aries and the ascendant <note>term: *horoscopus* — the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at a specific moment.</note> is found to be in a "fixed" sign, the celestial arrangement of that hour allows one to predict correctly for the whole year. If it is in a "common" sign, two beginnings for the year are established; if it is in a "movable" sign, four. These ideas are utterly empty and arbitrary; they are supported neither by reason, nor by the authority of the ancients, nor by experience. But if someone, perhaps from the creation of the world, should form an opi—

...opinion of astrologers he wishes to confirm, so that the future fortune might be known from the entry of the Sun into **Aries** <note>The first sign of the zodiac, marking the spring equinox.</note> because God created the world at that time—meaning that the annual turnings of the years are nothing other than the recurring cycles of the world’s original birth chart—he will truly be refuted very easily and immediately. Since, if we follow the world’s birth chart, the beginning of the year to be established will be just as uncertain as the time of year in which the world was first instituted is uncertain. For even among the Hebrews, from whom we received the account of the world's creation, nothing on this matter is certain or defined; rather, some contend the world began in the spring, others in the autumn. And if one opinion is to be preferred, they lean more toward believing it was founded in autumn. 

As for what is written—that the same month in which the <term>Passover</term> <note>original: *phase*. The Jewish festival commemorating the Exodus from Egypt.</note> was celebrated would be the first month among the months of the year—they maintain this was said for the sake of celebrating religious festivals. Therefore, that was the greatest, first, and foremost solemnity, from which their exit from Egypt (the first of God’s benefits to that people) and all other things followed. But in all other matters, they began the year from September, which seems to be proved both by many expressions in the sacred scriptures and by the ancient customs of the Jews. For it is written in <term>Exodus</term> that <term>Scenopegia</term> <note>original: *scenophegia*. The Feast of Tabernacles or Booths (*Sukkot*), a harvest festival.</note>, that is, the Feast of Tabernacles, is celebrated at the end of the year, and those were celebrated in mid-September. 

And in the book of <term>Nehemiah</term> it is written: "and it happened in the month of <term>Kislev</term>" <note>original: *Casleu*.</note> (which is the month of December for us) in the twentieth year; then it happened in the month of <term>Nisan</term> (which is April) in the twentieth year. If the month of Nisan, that is April, were the "head" or start of the year, it should have been written not as the twentieth year, but as the twenty-first. Furthermore, since the Law provided that in the seventh year—which was the <term>Sabbath of years</term> <note>The *Shmita* year, a biblical command to let the land rest from farming every seven years.</note>—they should neither reap the fields nor sow: if the head of the year were April, it followed that what they had sown in October of the sixth year, they would not be allowed to reap the following summer. This is because that summer would belong to the seventh year if its beginning was taken from the spring. If that were the case, the seeds entrusted to the earth in the sixth year would perish—a disadvantage that did not occur for those establishing the year from September. 

I pass over what <term>Helperic</term> <note>original: *Lersiensis*. Likely referring to Helperic of Auxerre, a 9th-century monk and leading authority on the *computus* (the calculation of dates).</note> wrote in his computation, and <term>Bede</term> <note>Bede the Venerable (d. 735), a famous English monk and scholar of time-keeping.</note> in his *Book of Times*, and <term>Josephus</term> in the first book of *Antiquities*, and <term>Jerome</term> in his letter on Solemnities, who, even in explaining <term>Ezekiel</term>, says that October is the first month and January the fourth. ## ON DIRECTIONS AND OTHER WAYS BY WHICH
### they define the times of future events; how little consistency they have, and
### how much astrologers differ among themselves on these matters. Chapter VII.

**J**ust as they err in predicting the fates of years (if any prediction of fate be granted), so too do they err in defining the time at which that which the initial hour promised is to occur. For in this matter also they use frivolous, false, and vain suppositions that in no way agree with natural methods. Among these, the first and most powerful is the theory of **directions** <note>In astrology, "direction" is a technique where the positions of planets are progressed forward in time to predict future events.</note> of the Planets and the parts of the Zodiac (for so it pleases them to call them), so that we may be better understood by those with whom we are disputing. We shall, therefore, briefly reveal upon what false and ridiculous foundations these directions rest, after first explaining the opinion of the astrologers according to their own purpose.

Let there be, for example, a birth chart <note>original: *geniturae*</note> with a **horoscope** <note>The "horoscope" here refers specifically to the Ascendant, or the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth.</note> at the fifteenth degree of **Leo**. Let **Saturn** be placed at the sixth degree of **Virgo**. It is clear that Saturn is joined to the horoscope neither by aspect nor by any other thing; therefore, it ought not to harm it. Nevertheless, they believe that the horoscope will eventually reach Saturn through "direction," and in the year it reaches that point, a danger of disease from Saturn threatens the native. They say it reaches that point by this reasoning: because for every year of our lives, individual degrees of the signs are attributed to us, though according to the proportion of the **ascensions** <note>original: *anaphorarum*. This refers to the varying speeds at which different zodiac signs rise over the horizon.</note>—but this is irrelevant to the matter at hand.

They say, therefore, that in the first year of life, the degree in which the horoscope sits is assigned to us. Thus, if a good Planet is in that degree, either by its body or its rays <note>A "ray" refers to an astrological aspect or influence cast from one degree to another.</note>, it bestows its benefits in that year; conversely, if a bad one is there, it bestows evils. In the second year, the second degree from the first corresponds; in the third, the third, and so on. Therefore, if Saturn (for example) occupies the twenty-first degree from the horoscope, since that degree corresponds to the twenty-first year of age, that year will be infested by the rays of Saturn.

Thus, when they wish to foresee whether something good or bad will happen to a person in a given year, they measure the degrees between the principal places of the birth chart and the body or rays of a good or bad star intercepted between them. According to the number of degrees, they prescribe the number of years after which that event ought to be expected. This is their position on directions, from which both **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity.</note> and the whole crowd of astrologers pronounce the span of life and all the accidents and turns of fortune.

What could be more frivolous than these things? What could be imagined more irrationally? For first, that distribution of degrees to years—can it be anything other than a product of whim? It is conceived with no foundation of science or reason, especially since they say these degrees sometimes indicate years and sometimes days (depending on what suits them). And this might perhaps have some probability if the partition of degrees itself were from nature. However, that partition depends entirely on choice; the mathematicians divide the signs into thirty parts rather than twenty for no other reason than that the number thirty is more convenient for arithmetic divisions—as will be demonstrated by the testimony of the astrologers themselves in our next book. But how can Saturn in the sixth part of Virgo harm me (just as...

<meta>catchword: star</meta>

...was received) found when I was being born, even if we grant them that its influence pertains to me in the twenty-first year of my life; for when **Saturn** pertains to me, it will not be in that place, and when Saturn is in that place, that part of the sky will not pertain to me. 

If they should perhaps say—just as clothes infected by a plague do not lose their poison for some time—that the same happens to the regions of the heavens, so that they retain for a long time the contagion received from a malignant star <note>original: "malo sidere"</note>, and therefore that degree, which was already infected by Saturn when I was born, pours that harmful power back into me even after many years: they would be defending their position quite beautifully and subtly. However, if this conversation were with philosophers, I would bid them remember that the affection of light does not stick to the subject, but departs along with the body from which it is diffused. Furthermore, of all celestial impressions (as **Avicenna** <note>The influential Persian polymath (980–1037 AD) whose works on "Meteorology" and natural philosophy were standard in medieval universities.</note> says in his *Meteorology*), light is both the vehicle and the nourishment. 

But let them answer me this: since the paths of other **Planets** have crossed that same degree during so many intervening years, do they think that ingrown virus could be abolished or diminished by the arrival of beneficial lights? <note>Referring to the "good" influence of planets like Jupiter or Venus crossing the same spot.</note> Moreover, if the qualities received and taken up from the Planets endure in the regions of heaven and are not preserved for only a brief span of time, then in judging events one must not only observe which Planet is found in which place of heaven during the revolving year or at the hour of birth, but also which planets traveled through those same places in all the preceding years.

Finally, that invention of **directing** <note>A technique where the positions of planets are progressed forward through the zodiac to predict the timing of future events.</note> is nothing other than subjecting things not only to those constellations which exist, but to those which *could* exist. For what else is it to say that the **Moon**, which at my birth was struck by <term>hexagonal rays</term> <note>Now commonly called a "sextile" aspect (60 degrees), usually considered harmonious.</note> from the **Sun**, will nevertheless eventually produce misfortune in that same spot from a <term>square aspect</term> <note>An aspect of 90 degrees, traditionally considered challenging or harmful in astrology.</note> of the Sun? She was certainly not under that aspect when I was born, but she would have been if she had been positioned further from the Sun by several degrees of the sky; and yet they claim that when she has traversed those degrees—from which she was distant from that square radiation—that calamity will be inflicted by her after so many years. But that constellation did not exist at my birth, and if it is to exist sometime later, it is nothing to me; for if there is any fate for me, the past disposition of the heavens gave it. 

It is clear, therefore, how absurd, how false, and how inconsistent is the theory of directing. The astrologers who use it daily have not yet, I think, even considered or examined the foundation from which it is derived. In addition to directions, they also use the **rulership of the Planets** in predicting the times of events, which they have devised to take up the empire of life in a certain order. From this come the "centers" of the **Chaldeans**, the <term>fridaria</term> <note>A Persian system of "time-lords" where planets rule over specific periods of a person's life.</note> of the **Persians**, the "nines" <note>original: "nouenae." Likely referring to the Navamsha or ninefold divisions used in Indian astrology.</note> of the **Indians**, the <term>tecates</term> of **Ptolemy**, and the "departures" and "recruiters" <note>original: "aphoriaq; occursorq;"</note>; from here come the "decades" of the **Egyptians**, the <term>chronocrators</term> <note>The OCR reads "crancocratores," likely a typo for "chronocratores," the "lords of time" who rule specific ages of a human life.</note> of the **Arabs**, and whatever other dreams of this kind different men have dreamt according to their own whims. All of these err in this inconsistency: they define the stars such that one Planet rules us for a certain number of years, and when that time is consumed, it hands over the rudders of government—as if by hand—to the succeeding Planet, according to the order of the spheres or the climate; and this successor, having administered his jurisdiction for the time granted to him, yields to the

<meta>This page continues Pico’s critique of the arbitrary nature of astrological systems. Having previously argued against the "contagion" of the stars in specific degrees of the sky, he now turns his attention to the systems used to divide a person's life into planetary periods, arguing that these systems lack natural logic and contradict one another.</meta>

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

...that the right and power of the nearest star <note>original: "fideri [sideri] proximo ius & potestatem"</note> is established, which is indeed entirely alien to all natural reason. For why this star rather than another should dominate those things below at this specific time, no cause can be reasonably assigned other than either the disposition of the matter being more suited to the impressions of this star rather than another, or a more effective relationship of the star itself to us—such as its being carried above the earth while others are placed below it, or its turning toward the northern regions making it closer to us, or its casting more direct rays upon the earth. Even if we were to agree with the astrologers about the good or bad condition of things based on the diversity of locations, signs, and radiations of that **Planet** which holds more authority and power in the heavens at that time—this is the only thing that can be said following a natural method.

But the rest are fictions and fables: for instance, saying that **Jupiter** now presides over earthly affairs because **Saturn** presided in the preceding years (whom Jupiter follows in the order of the spheres), or that **Taurus** dominates this year because **Aries** dominated the last, as if the rotations of earthly offices and magistracies <note>Pico is mocking the idea that planets take turns holding office like human politicians.</note> were found among the stars. 

If they were to say that this has been proven by experience, there might be some faith in it if they agreed among themselves on this distribution of times. But when one man attributes the same years to the **Moon**, another to **Mars**, and another to **Jupiter**, should not the reliability of "experience" be stripped from all of them equally? For each man claims it for his own opinion amidst such a great variety of views. 

The **Egyptians**, whom **Firmicus** <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer who wrote the "Matheseos libri octo."</note> follows, give the administration of life to each of the stars in an equal partition of 10 years and 9 months. They do so in this order: in a daytime birth <note>original: "diurna genitura"</note> the **Sun** receives the first decade; in a nighttime birth, the **Moon**. After that decade, the star that was found in the second place in the birth chart through the course of the signs takes over; then the third star after the second, and the others in a similar way. But whoever has been allotted the decade, although he is the lord of the whole period, he nevertheless divides the entire substance of the decade among all the stars, beginning with himself and handing it over to those placed in order after him—first to whoever was found second in the theme <note>The "theme" or "themate" refers to the natal horoscope or chart layout.</note>. The sum of the years moderated by the seven **Planets** is, according to their opinion, seventy-five years with three months added; when these are completed, there is a return again to the first Planet. 

The **Persians** indeed collect the same number of years and similarly begin from the Sun if someone was born during the day, or from the Moon if by night. They also make one star the principal lord of the times but make others participants in the lordship by a vicarious succession. This distribution they call the <term>fridaria</term> <note>Also known as "firdaria," a system of planetary periods where each planet rules a specific number of years in a fixed sequence.</note>, from which comes that common phrase among the younger astrologers: "someone is a participant in the *fridaria* of Jupiter." 

However, they differ greatly from the Egyptians; for in the succession of the Planets, they do not observe the locations of the birth chart's theme, but rather the order of the spheres <note>The traditional Aristotelian/Ptolemaic order of the planets from the Earth outward: Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn.</note>, placing the Sun in the middle. Furthermore, they do not assign an equal time to each Planet, but rather:
*   To the **Sun**: 10 years
*   To **Venus**: 8 years
*   To **Mercury**: 13 years
*   To **Moon**: 9 years
*   To **Saturn**: 11 years
*   To **Jupiter**: 12 years
*   To **Mars**: 7 years
*   To the **Head** <note>The "Head of the Dragon" (Caput Draconis), or the North Node of the Moon.</note>: 3 years
*   To the **Tail** <note>The "Tail of the Dragon" (Cauda Draconis), or the South Node of the Moon.</note>: 2 years

As to what reason this could possibly have, even **Avenazra** <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar and astrologer whose works Pico studied deeply.</note> himself, in his book on astrological matters...

He argues that since astrologers cannot agree on these cycles and they follow no natural physical laws, the systems are merely "fictions and fables."</summary>

# On Astrology, Book VII.

...he confesses he does not know. Conversely, in the ascending order of shared lordship, the Persians give an equal portion to any of the **Planets**, so that the leading **Planet** governs the first seventh part of its time alone, the second part with the second **Planet**, and the third with the third. The Egyptians, however, make this an unequal distribution, decreeing nineteen months to the **Sun**, thirty to **Saturn**, twelve to **Jupiter**, fifteen to **Mars**, eight to **Venus**, twenty to **Mercury**, and twenty-five to the **Moon**. They then subdivide these; for example, from his thirty months, **Saturn** imparts six days to the remaining **Planets**, and the others do the same with their own months, as Hephaestion <note>Hephaestion of Thebes, a 4th-century Hellenistic astrologer who synthesized Egyptian and Greek methods.</note> teaches and Maternus <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman author of the *Mathesis*, a major astrological compendium.</note> was ignorant of. But there was a constant difference between the Persians and Egyptians: the Persians include the Head and Tail <note>original: "caput & caudam." These are the North and South Nodes of the Moon, imaginary points where the Moon’s path crosses the ecliptic.</note> among the <term>chronocrators</term> <note>Time-lords: planets or points assigned to rule over specific periods of a person's life.</note>, while the Egyptians do not. From all of this, it is clear that after the first decade, it will be rare for the governor of the years to be the same among the Persians and the Egyptians.

Ptolemy dissents from both, making the planets lords of specific ages: the **Moon** governs the first four years, **Mercury** the following ten, then in sequential order **Venus** governs eight, the **Sun** nine, **Mars** fifteen, **Jupiter** twelve, and **Saturn** the remainder of life. However, when he seeks the exact and particular distribution of times for each individual birth, he adds annual, monthly, and daily rulers to those principal <term>chronocrators</term>. But the hinge of the entire fate according to Ptolemy turns on this: he censures those who make only one <term>chronocrator</term> of a life—alluding to the Egyptians and Dorotheus <note>Dorotheus of Sidon, a 1st-century poet and astrologer whose work influenced later Persian and Arabic systems.</note>. If anyone should follow Ptolemy’s opinion, they will define the distribution of times very differently from the Egyptians and Persians. This makes it all the more pleasant to mock the astrologers of our age who, not understanding that Ptolemy’s <term>tecates</term> <note>From the Greek word for "tenths," a system of dividing life into ten-year periods.</note> and <term>chronocrators</term> belong to the same category as the Persian <term>fridaria</term> <note>A system of planetary periods used primarily in Persian and Medieval astrology.</note> and the Egyptian <term>decennials</term> <note>The "ten-year" periods mentioned earlier.</note>, have wanted to use all of these at once, as if they were not diverse and contrary systems regarding the same matter. But regarding different matters, their opinions are least of all in agreement.

Indian astrology knows neither <term>fridaria</term>, nor <term>decennials</term>, nor <term>tecates</term>, nor <term>chronocrators</term>, but divides a single life not into seven parts as the others do, but into nine members. Regarding these, it pronounces based on the order and arrangement of the "themes" of the houses: so that the first part of the years is ruled by the constellations belonging to the twelfth house, the second by those at the horoscope <note>The first house or the rising sign.</note>, the third by those at the second house, the fourth by those at the ninth, the fifth by those at the tenth, the sixth by those at the eleventh, the seventh by those at the sixth, the eighth by those at the seventh, and the ninth by those at the eighth. 

They disagree with others not only in this dispensation of times, but in the very partition of the houses, dividing them by the degrees of the zodiac (which they call equal). The Arabs, imitating Andrugazar <note>Abu’l-Anbār, a Sassanid Persian astrologer known in Latin as Andruzagar.</note>, judge the three parts of life through the <term>trigonocrators</term>—which you might call "triangulators," that is, the lords of the triplicities <note>The four groups of three zodiac signs associated with the elements: fire, earth, air, and water.</note>. Thus, regarding the matters signified by each of the twelve houses, one judges the state of the first and future things from the first lord of the triplicity, the middle state from the second, and the final state from the third. But if there are only two lords for one triplicity, as we said in another book, or only one...

<summary>Pico details the irreconcilable differences between Persian, Egyptian, Greek, Indian, and Arabic astrological systems for dividing a person's life into time-periods. He argues that since these systems contradict each other, the entire practice of "time-lord" astrology is a fraudulent human invention rather than a natural science.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s critique of the internal contradictions between various astrological traditions. Having previously discussed the conflicting systems of the Persians and Egyptians regarding "time-lords," he now turns to the Chaldeans and several individual medieval authorities to show that their methods for dividing a person’s life are entirely arbitrary.</meta>

<page-num>636</page-num>
->Ioan. Pico della Mirandola<-

Perhaps there is one <term>disposer</term> <note>original: "dispositor," a planet that rules another point or planet by being the ruler of the sign it occupies.</note> of the birth, though if one rules in the day and another in the night, a large part of life will be left without a governor. But those <term>trigon-rulers</term> <note>original: "trigonocratores." These are planets that rule over the four "triplicities" or groups of three zodiac signs associated with the elements (Fire, Earth, Air, Water).</note> do not exist at all, and even if three thousand of them were granted, that system of "substitute succession" in the ruling of a life is utterly ridiculous.

But the inventions of the Chaldeans <note>Ancient Mesopotamian astrologers often cited as the founders of the craft.</note> differ greatly from all of these. They use neither houses, nor decades, nor <term>fridaria</term> <note>A system of planetary periods used in medieval astrology to determine which planet is "ruling" a specific number of years.</note>, nor the "nines" of the Indians, nor the trigon-rulers, but rather the <term>angles</term> <note>original: "cardinibus," the four most powerful points in a chart: the Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, and Imum Coeli.</note> of the birth. They sought the first part of life from the first angle [the Ascendant], the middle part from the peak of the highest heaven [the Midheaven], and the final part from the west [the Descendant]; then, they pronounced judgment on death, and even on those things that happen after death, from the fourth place of the <term>theme</term> <note>original: "thematis," meaning the astrological chart or horoscope.</note> [the Imum Coeli].

Furthermore, they subdivided that earlier three-part division again, such that the <term>decline</term> <note>original: "apoclima," refers to the houses "falling away" from the angles (the 3rd, 6th, 9th, and 12th houses).</note> of the horoscope—as if you were to say the "slope"—indicated the pains of labor and what happens to the mother while she carries the child in her womb; the <term>horoscope</term> <note>original: "horoscopus," here used in its original sense to mean the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon.</note> itself indicated the birth and the very first years; and from that <term>succession</term> <note>original: "epanophora," the houses that "follow" the angles (the 2nd, 5th, 8th, and 11th houses).</note> of the horoscope came the final remainder of the first age. Again, the decline of the Midheaven governed the first parts of middle life, the Midheaven itself the middle, and its succession the final parts. They did similarly in the fourth house: the declining house indicated the events immediately preceding death, the fourth house itself indicated death, and the succession indicated what might happen after death. 

I have set out to explain these opinions so that the contradictions between them might be recognized, showing that there is no trust to be found in "experience," and so that the vanity of these arbitrary dogmas, resting on the flimsiest conjectures, might be exposed. For why should we give the first part of life to the east and the middle to the highest heaven? Since middle age follows the first age, the Midheaven does not follow the east, but rather precedes it <note>Pico is pointing out a logical flaw: in the sky's daily rotation, a star reaches the Midheaven *before* it reaches the Ascendant (east) from the perspective of the house order.</note>. But one must not labor in refuting these opinions which refute and shatter themselves. 

If I were to proceed in recounting the dreams of every astrologer, there would hardly be any end. Messahala <note>Masha'allah ibn Athari (c. 740–815 AD), an influential Persian-Jewish astrologer.</note> governs the first half of life by the eastern Sun and the second by the western Sun. Hemus says otherwise: he gives the first half to the **Planets** located in the upper hemisphere—whether they be eastern or western—and the second half to all those under the earth. Vellius <note>Vettius Valens, a 2nd-century Greek astrologer.</note>, in another fiction, ascribes the first part to the **Moon** and the other to the ruler of the second house. Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), the most famous Persian astrologer of the Middle Ages.</note>, the most legendary teller of tales, says the first part refers to the <term>Part of Fortune</term> <note>An Arabic Part or mathematical point in the chart representing prosperity.</note> and the second to the ruler of that Part. Others say still other things, but it is not necessary to pursue them all; read Hephaestion <note>Hephaestion of Thebes.</note> in his book on the *Apotelesmata* <note>original: "Apotelesmatum," meaning the "Effects" or "Outcomes" of the stars.</note> of Ptolemy. Read Abenragel <note>Albohazen Haly Abenragel (11th century), an Arab astrologer.</note>, and besides those we have recounted, you will find many other conflicting opinions on this matter there; for each man composes his own fable according to his whim.

In the end, by being too credulous of these things—as if they were oracles and responses of prophets—and by entrusting our faith to these most trifling and deceitful charlatans, we hand over our hopes, fears, anxieties, joys, and (what is more destructive) the very direction and steering of our entire life.

# JUST AS THEY ADOPT USELESS THINGS, SO THEY OMIT
## necessary ones, and how much they err regarding the fixed stars. Chapter VIII.

Just as they adopt many imaginary things, such as those we have mentioned—which have no natural existence and therefore no influence, namely the <term>houses</term> of the signs, the <term>constellations</term> <note>original: "imagines," referring to the traditional figures like the Bear or the Lion.</note>, the <term>head and tail</term> <note>original: "caudam & caput," the nodes of the Moon's orbit.</note>, the <term>lots</term> <note>original: "partes," mathematical points like the "Part of Fortune."</note>, the <term>twelfth-parts</term> <note>original: "dodecathemoria," 2.5-degree divisions of a zodiac sign.</note>, the <term>ninths</term> <note>original: "nouenaria," 3.33-degree divisions.</note>, and other things of this sort—so they overlook many things that are primarily necessary, and they decree many false and conflicting things regarding those they do use. For just as things lacking light are ineffective, so no light in the heavens is ineffective. Yet, while almost innumerable stars shine in the **eighth sphere** <note>In the ancient model, the sphere of the "fixed" stars beyond the planets.</note>, they only use **one thousand and twenty-two**. When this is thrown back at them, different men offer different solutions.

**Petrus Aponensis** <note>Pietro d'Abano (c. 1250–1316), an influential physician and astrologer.</note> says in his *Elucidarium* that this merely shows the "difficulty of the art," but does not prove it is impossible. In responding this way, he seems to concede that those stars are indeed necessary to understand if a "fatal constellation" <note>A birth chart supposedly determining one's fate.</note> is to be perfectly grasped. Since this is difficult, he admits the art is difficult; but we contend that it is both impossible for all of them to be identified, and even if it were possible, astrologers who have not yet done so will not truly predict the future from the heavens.

Others, hiding themselves in a safer refuge, say that those stars they omit are "ineffective." They claim that all the larger stars—those with the power to decree fate—have been investigated by astrologers, while the rest were passed over because, due to the smallness of their bodies, they have almost no importance. But they are easily dragged out of these hiding places. For if they have never observed these stars, how can they assert anything about their nature—whether they act or do not act, whether they change things or do not change them?

And if they reply that they are convinced by the "smallness" of the bodies, what body in the heavens will be considered small when compared to the Earth? Or, to put it more correctly, compared to those things located on Earth which are thought to be governed by the heavens? If you compare the nature of celestial and earthly bodies, in one there is nothing that is not sublime, powerful, and great; in the other, nothing that is not humble, weak, and tiny. Furthermore, many of these stars which they say are neglected due to smallness are perhaps not surpassed in size by the globe of **Mercury** or the **Moon**. Indeed, some are thought to be larger than **Mars** and **Venera** (Venus) among those they *do* observe.

Moreover, if perhaps individual smaller stars do not possess great power, nevertheless a gathering and assembly of many of that kind will have the greatest power—just as those stars which make up the **Milky Way** <note>original: "lacteum orbem."</note>, so thick with many lights; though individual stars may do little, they all act together, and how can they then be thought to have little power? Often in music, if one tiny note is withdrawn, the harmony is destroyed; while that note by itself might hardly be heard, it makes all the others be heard more melodiously. The entire ornament of the heavens, interconnected and harmonious, has nothing that is idle, nothing superfluous, nothing useless. Therefore, whatever part you take away, even the smallest, that which the whole integrity produced is immediately lost. Among **haulers** <note>original: "helciarios," men who tow boats with ropes.</note>, even a man who is not strong adds to the pull...

He rejects the excuse that "small" stars have no influence, noting that their collective power (like the Milky Way) is essential to the harmony of the heavens.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's critique of the incompleteness of astrological knowledge. On the previous page, he noted that astrologers ignore the vast majority of stars, focusing only on a small fraction (1,022). Here, he addresses the defense offered by the famous 13th-century astrologer Guido Bonatti and uses a medical analogy to show why partial knowledge in astrology is equivalent to no knowledge at all.</meta>

<page-num>638</page-num>

# Ioan. Pici Mirandulæ

Just as a chain cannot be pulled if a single link is missing, so can the ignorance of even one star undermine the truth of fate; much less should they be permitted to omit an almost infinite number of stars without it being a sin against their art. **Bonatti** <note>Guido Bonatti (c. 1210 – c. 1296), the most famous Italian astrologer of the 13th century, whom Pico often targets.</note> perhaps fearing these points (if he even perceived them), said: "The <term>Astrologer</term>," he says, "uses all the stars although he does not explain them all by name, for he uses the twelve signs under which almost all the stars are contained." But who would say this—not just an astrologer, but even a madman? For the twelve signs, as they are called, have a specific width in degrees, outside of which there are innumerable stars on both sides. And if he should reply that those stars which are co-extended with any sign between those same lines possess the same power, I will first ask: how can he assert anything about unknown things?

If he says that this habit of making assertions is typical of astrologers, I will not argue; instead, I will appeal to the astrologers themselves. Among them, the **figures** <note>original: "imagines," referring to the constellations like Orion or the Great Bear.</note> rising along with the signs claim one set of effects, while the signs with which they rise claim another. Otherwise, the signs they use are immobile, while the figures change their location <note>Pico is referring to the precession of the equinoxes, where the physical constellations and the mathematical zodiac signs have drifted apart over time.</note>. Therefore, the nature of the same figure will be different at different times, corresponding to different locations and signs.

But I think **Bonatti** himself, noticing the insanity of his response, immediately digressed elsewhere. Since he saw it could not be denied that knowledge of all the stars is relevant to the astrological business—yet astrologers do not possess knowledge of them all—he said: "What does it matter if we do not know the whole of astrology? Christian preachers do not know all divine things, yet they preach about them daily to the people."

Observe in this matter how little our "good" **Bonatti** is deceived <note>Pico is being sarcastic here, suggesting Bonatti's analogy is intentionally misleading.</note>. For if someone investigates the nature of the stars for the sake of knowledge—which is the role of the <term>philosopher</term>—by knowing even one star, he has achieved something. But if he professes what the astrologer does—seeking not so much the knowledge of the stars as the knowledge of the future through the stars—he will have accomplished nothing at all unless he possesses knowledge of those stars from which the future can be foreseen. But futures are foreseen from the things by which they are made; they are made from all the stars, therefore they must be foreseen from all of them. Thus, he who does not know all of them—though he might know some—will never foresee the future from the stars.

Take an example from <term>medicine</term> and philosophy. The philosopher seeks the powers of herbs so that he may understand them. The physician seeks them so that he may cure diseases by their virtue. If a philosopher understands even one herb, he is a philosopher, albeit an imperfect one, because he possesses some of the knowledge he seeks. But let us suppose there are ten species of herbs so necessary for driving away all diseases that if one is missing, no bodily ailment can be cured. If someone is skilled in nine of them but ignorant of one, he will not only be an incomplete physician, but no physician at all; for while he has some knowledge, he can provide no cure, which is what a physician professes.

Likewise, he cannot be called an <term>astrologer</term> who cannot speak of the fate of even one man after inspecting his <term>nativity</term> <note>original: "genitura," the configuration of the heavens at the moment of birth.</note>. For if fate is composed of the combined influence <note>original: "afflatione," literally a breathing-upon or inspiration.</note> of all the stars, how will he foresee it if he knows neither what each individual star effects nor what the combined temperament of them all produces? Regarding <term>Theology</term>, however, the reasoning is different...

<summary>Pico refutes Guido Bonatti's defense of astrology, arguing that because the "influence" of the heavens depends on every star, an astrologer who ignores most of them is like a doctor who lacks a necessary ingredient for a cure—useless.</summary>

## THE DOGMAS OF ASTROLOGERS CONCERNING THE FIXED
## STARS CLASH BOTH WITH EACH OTHER AND WITH THE TRUTH. Chapter IX.

**S**ed—But astrologers do not only err in this, that they are ignorant of most stars; they have also established the most contradictory and false dogmas concerning those stars which they believe they have fully investigated. For there are times (as I shall demonstrate) when they judge the stars to be more effective than the Planets, and times when they judge them to be less powerful and effective. In this matter, they both clash with themselves and disagree with the truth on both counts. They promise "ordinary" happiness (if I may call it that) based on the capacity and condition of the person being born from a favorable alignment of the Planets; but from the fixed stars (which do not wander), as **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity.</note> says, they expect <term>παραλόγους ἀτυχίας</term> <note>original: "paralogous atychias" — misfortunes beyond all reason or expectation.</note>, which is to say, successes greater than any expectation.

I, however, contend that greater things can be provided by the Planets than by the fixed stars, following both **Proclus** <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> in his commentary on **Plato's Timaeus** and the dictates of reason. For a higher seat in the heavens does not necessarily indicate a higher nature for the non-wandering stars, since the **Sun**, the moderator of all things, certainly has many stars positioned above himself—including all except the **Moon**. Furthermore, an argument for why we should judge the Planets to be superior to the fixed stars is this: while many spheres serve a single Planet, only one sphere serves the multitude of fixed stars; thus, while the entire army of those stars might surpass the power of a single heavenly body, individual stars cannot surpass individual Planets.

If you look at the size of their bodies, the **Sun** is without controversy larger than all; likewise, **Jupiter** and **Saturn** are larger than all others, if you except a few of the most principal stars—though a greater power is not necessarily understood by the vastness of their bodies. For it has not been proven that **Jupiter** is more powerful than **Saturn** simply because he is larger; and although **Mercury** is the smallest of all the heavenly bodies, he nevertheless possesses (as they themselves claim) the most power in every <term>genitura</term> <note>A birth chart or horoscope.</note>. Nor do they rank **Venus** below the **Moon**, even though she is exceeded by the Moon's physical bulk. 

Finally, that bright star located at the "Heart of the Lion," which is called the **Queen** <note>original: "Regina"</note> by the Latins and <term>Basiliscus</term> <note>The star Regulus; the name means "Little King."</note> by the Greeks—although it is not of the first magnitude in size, it is nevertheless considered by them to be of the first authority and power. They certainly make it more noble because it does not deflect from the path of the **Sun** <note>The ecliptic.</note>; but by that same reasoning, the Planets are more noble than the stars, as they deviate even less from that same path in either direction. 

Added to this is the testimony of antiquity, which called the Planets <term>cosmocratoras</term> <note>original: "cosmocratoras" — world-rulers.</note>, as if to say "rulers of the world," a title they did not deign to give to the fixed stars. But I wish they would at least maintain their own dogma, and not speak of those same stars—which they claim are the workers of miraculous effects—as if they were weak and feeble. For they say the stars effect nothing unless they occupy the <term>cardines</term> <note>The "angles" or four most powerful points of an astrological chart: the Ascendant, Descendant, Midheaven, and Imum Coeli.</note>, or at least the beginnings of the "houses," or are joined to one of the two <term>luminaries</term> <note>The Sun and the Moon.</note>. And so, to a star to which they attribute so much...

...while they previously attributed too much to them, here they detract so much from their power that they claim the stars accomplish nothing on their own unless they are supported by the vigor of their position or the assistance of a most powerful planet. For this claim, they offer neither a cause nor any probable reason, but perhaps they have stumbled due to a false understanding of a certain ancient saying. For the ancients (as <term>Maternus</term> <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer whose work *Mathesis* was a primary source for medieval astrology.</note> teaches) used to say regarding the signs that when they were found bare of stars, they had no effectiveness except for those occupying the four <term>cardines</term> <note>The four "hinges" or angles of an astrological chart: the Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, and Imum Coeli. These were considered the most powerful points in a horoscope.</note>. These men transferred what was said about the signs, the mansions, and the "lodgings" of the stars to individual stars as well—unless, instead, they shrewdly established this dogma so that they would not be tortured by a wretched and inextricable labor if the logic of fate had to be explained by every single star. They would never have been able to persuade the gullible that such a task could be overcome by a human; otherwise, what is the reason for their opinion? Is it because they are in a more remote location? But how much closer to us is <term>Saturn</term>? Or what is so great a prerogative of the "cardine" that in it they do not merely act, but perform wonders, despite the vastness of the distance? Yet as soon as they have declined a little from it, or have not yet reached it, they do nothing at all, even though the eleventh house, rising toward the heights of heaven, seems more powerful for action than the fourth house, located beneath the middle of the earth. 

But it is certainly as we were saying: the labor deterred them, and they did not want the art to appear so difficult that it might easily be judged impossible. As for the "slowness of motion" they usually cite, this slowness supports nothing; for the ray of a star is fixed all the more strongly and clings more constantly the longer the star itself lingers in the place from which it is emitted. What of the fact that these claims also fight amongst themselves? For the dogma concerning a slower planet is that it gives whatever it gives late, but that its gifts endure and remain for a long time. On the contrary, concerning the <term>fixed stars</term> <note>original: *non erraticis*, meaning the stars that do not "wander" like planets.</note>, they decide that although they move with the slowest motion, they are accustomed to say they bring the greatest happiness, but end at last in calamities. Therefore, the gifts do not linger long, nor are they long preserved; but just as they always differ from variety, so they disagree with themselves everywhere—though we are not pursuing every point. 

For someone might also ask them why they do not consider the intervals and aspects between the fixed stars themselves, just as they do between the planets? Noticing this, <term>Regiomontanus</term> <note>original: *Ioannes de Regio Monte* (1436–1476), a major Renaissance mathematician and astronomer whose work Pico often used to critique judicial astrology.</note> says that the aspects of the fixed stars might perhaps be more perfect than those of the planets, because they are not fleeting and momentary like the planets, but rather stable and perpetual. Other objections could be raised on these points, but let us run through the consequences.

...distance, according to the condition of the signs, according to the <term>schematisms</term> <note>In astrology, these are "aspects"—the specific angular relationships (like a square or trine) between planets that supposedly alter their influence.</note>, and the manifold relationship of all things among themselves, and according to the various names given to their movements—whether they are stationary, proceeding forward, or stepping backward—all of which, unless I am mistaken, I have most clearly shown to be far from all truth, far from reason, and far from the dignity and nature of celestial things. 

We also critique the fact that they claim the Planets and those twelve signs alike dominate in turns, prescribing "empires" over different things and times as if they were administrative duties handed over by a legal right of succession. In doing so, they are clearly not so much *measuring* <note>original: "metientes"</note> the celestial bodies based on human affairs as they are *lying* <note>original: "mentientes"; Pico is using a play on words here between measuring and lying.</note> about them. 

Moreover, we have laughed and, along with <term>Plotinus</term> <note>A major Greek-speaking philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) and the founder of Neoplatonism, who argued that stars might be "signs" but were not "causes" of human destiny.</note> and his contemporaries, we have struck out their claim that one must wait for a Planet's effect for as many years as it was distant in degrees from some point in a sign. They invent a thousand such falsehoods, conceived without any foundation of knowledge. 

Therefore, let us summarize this entire preceding dispute: it seems indeed that astrologers say plausible things when they claim that lower things are governed by celestial ones; however, they are soon caught out as false, vain, and detestable—that is, neither pious nor philosophers—when they believe, preach, and assert that particular things can be produced from universal causes: 
*   evil from good, 
*   the tiny from the great, 
*   the reckless from the orderly, 
*   the incorporeal from the physical, 
*   the arbitrary from the necessary, 
*   the artificial from the natural, 
*   and things already past from things present, or things present from the past.

Even if all these things were caused by the heavens, the astrologers nonetheless assign causes that are anything but celestial. They remain silent about the actual powers of the true constellations and stars in the sky, yet they adopt many properties from things that do not exist. And since they possess only a small part of the truth, they personally add many fabricated things, such as those we mentioned in the preceding book: "places," "houses," "images," <term>nodes</term> <note>The points where a planet's orbit intersects the ecliptic.</note>, <term>antiscia</term> <note>Points in the zodiac that are equidistant from the solstice points; astrologers believed they "mirrored" a planet's power.</note>, "parts," and <term>dodecathemoria</term> <note>The further division of each zodiac sign into twelve 2.5-degree sub-sections.</note>. These are fictitious, ineffective, and imaginary things with no solidity in nature. If a wise

### CHAPTER 1. THAT THE NUMBER OF CELESTIAL BODIES,
### IN WHOSE POWER THE DECREEING OF FATE LIES 
### ACCORDING TO ASTROLOGERS, IS UNCERTAIN.

<term>AMONG</term> <note>original: "INTER"; this marks the start of the text with a decorative initial.</note> all the things that he who professes the science of the stars ought to know, the task we were just debating—judging the fatal hour of any given thing—can be considered almost the easiest. If astrologers have neither achieved this, nor are able to achieve it, how can they hope for even more difficult things? For it is a much more difficult and laborious task to fully comprehend the total number of celestial bodies from which fate reaches us, so that in describing a "fatal constellation," nothing imaginary is added and nothing true or effective is omitted. We shall reveal in the discussions of this present book that this knowledge is both useful and necessary for them, yet impossible to obtain. Thus, not only are their predictions unable to be true because they do not see the movements and positions of the stars clearly, and have not fully explored all of them (as we shall argue in the following books), but also because it is not yet established for them which bodies these are whose positions must be inspected and whose properties must be investigated. So far are they from achieving everything their profession promises, that they do not even know what those things are, the knowledge of which is necessary to them.

For if they say we are mistaken or that we raise these objections out of malice, I will challenge them with a divine voice and ask them to tell me something about the number of the stars. When I question them, I realize not only that the stars cannot be counted by them even from those that are visible, but that it is not even certain whether there are other stars in heaven besides those we see, which escape both our senses and our reason. 

The philosopher <term>Favorinus</term> <note>A Roman-era philosopher (c. 80–160 AD) known for his skepticism; his speech against "genethliacs" (horoscope-casters) is preserved by the writer Aulus Gellius.</note>, in that elegant oration of his against the <term>genethliacs</term> <note>Castors of birth-horoscopes.</note> found in <term>Gellius</term>, said he wondered how it could be clear to anyone as a fixed rule that the <term>Planets</term>—which <term>Nigidius</term> <note>Nigidius Figulus, a Roman scholar and contemporary of Cicero, known for his interest in the occult and astrology.</note> calls "wanderers" <note>original: "errones"</note>—are no more numerous than the common people believe. For it could happen that there are certain other Planets of equal power which humans cannot see, due to an excess of either brilliance or distance. 

Certainly if, as <term>Alpetragius</term> <note>Nur ad-Din al-Bitruji (d. 1204), an influential astronomer from Islamic Spain who challenged Ptolemaic models.</note> says—a man most wise in celestial matters—there is still movement in the heavens that remains unknown, there can also be a body there to which that movement most specifically belongs, which has not yet been detected by any scientific observation. This is attested to by the many and various movements of the superior bodies devised by more recent astronomers, which were unknown to the ancients (as they themselves believe) and were finally detected through long-term, daily observations. ...it is manifest that other motions also, either due to their slowness, their obscurity, or some other aspect, may still lie hidden from mathematicians, which posterity itself will one day come to know through longer observations. I do not wish to speak of <term>epicycles</term> <note>Small circles whose centers move around the circumference of a larger one, used in ancient astronomy to explain planetary motion.</note> and <term>eccentrics</term> <note>Circular orbits whose center is not the Earth, used to explain why planets seem to change speed.</note>, nor of the multitude of spheres serving the planets, which remains uncertain among all astronomers; for perhaps they [the astrologers] will deny that the power to decree fate lies within these bodies. 

Regarding the spheres above the planets, how great the ambiguity is, and how uncertain that divining astrology is rendered by it, must by no means be kept silent. For some make the eighth orb—which is illuminated by the non-wandering stars <note>The "fixed" stars as opposed to the "wandering" planets.</note>—the outermost; others have placed a ninth above it, and some even a tenth. 

The astronomers of the Egyptians and Chaldeans thought there was nothing above the eighth orb; they were followed by Plato, Aristotle, Hipparchus, and Ptolemy. Perhaps more recent thinkers did not believe this, but such is the fact. There is no ninth sphere in Ptolemy, which can easily be understood from his *Great Composition* <note>original: "Magna compositione," refers to the "Almagest," Ptolemy's definitive work on astronomy.</note>. Many, however, are deceived because they think everyone who has discovered that the eighth sphere moves from west to east <note>A reference to the precession of the equinoxes.</note> must necessarily fall into the opinion of a ninth orb. Therefore, since both Ptolemy and Hipparchus admit this motion, they [the critics] do not doubt that the invention of the ninth orb belonged even to those by whom that motion was first noted. 

Added to this is the fact that Ptolemy uses both mobile and immobile signs, since he makes the images <note>constellations</note> of the eighth sphere mobile, and refers the locations of the planets to immobile signs. Therefore, it seems undoubtedly certain to them that besides the signs of the eighth sphere which move, there are other signs in Ptolemy which do not move (except by the motion of the whole world), and that these are conceived nowhere else than in a ninth sphere above the eighth. 

But they are far and most greatly deceived; for even the motion of the stars from west to east does not necessarily lead to the opinion of a ninth orb. And as for what he says regarding immobile signs, it is most clearly declared by this: that Ptolemy was content with only the eighth orb—which I marvel was not noticed and understood by those men. For Ptolemy describes these immobile signs in the eighth sphere itself, which he would not do if he had devised another higher one. His words in the second book of the *Great Composition* are these:

> We shall use the names of the signs in the twelve parts of the oblique circle <note>The ecliptic, the sun's apparent path.</note> itself, and as if their beginnings were taken from the tropical and equinoctial points. Thus, the <term>dodecathemorion</term> <note>original: "dodecathemorion," literally a "twelfth part," referring to a 30-degree sign of the zodiac.</note> (that is, the twelfth part) which is from the vernal equinox toward the following parts of the whole sphere, we shall call Aries; the second, Taurus; and so on in order according to the sequence of the twelve signs handed down by us.

So says Ptolemy, who also teaches the same in the first book of the *Apotelesmatika* <note>original: "Apotelesmatum," Ptolemy's astrological work, also known as the "Tetrabiblos."</note>: that the parts of the zodiac to which the planets are referred are begun and determined as primary by the solstices and equinoxes. Since these four points are fixed and unmoved, the partition of the signs established by them is itself fixed and immobile, even though the images <note>The actual star patterns/constellations</note> from which those names were transferred move continually, and in the course of time their boundaries and beginnings are found in different places.

He uses Ptolemy’s own writings to show that the distinction between moving constellations and fixed zodiac signs does not require a ninth sphere, thereby highlighting the uncertainty of astronomical foundations.</summary>
