Therefore, these signs are not immovable in a higher sphere according to Ptolemy, but are described by four fixed and immovable points of the eighth sphere; if he had conceived of any other sphere above it, he would never have remained silent about this great discovery in his **Great Composition** <note>original: *Magna compositione*, referring to the *Almagest*, Ptolemy’s most influential astronomical work.</note>. I am inclined, however, to mock John of Saxony <note>A 14th-century astronomer and prominent commentator on astrological texts.</note>, who in his expositions on Alchabitius <note>A 10th-century Arab astrologer whose work was a standard textbook in medieval universities.</note> strives to prove that the signs of the ninth sphere should be used according to the opinion of Ptolemy. To confirm his opinion, he cites certain words of Haly <note>Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer and commentator.</note>, the interpreter of Ptolemy, regarding "bright" and "dark" degrees; John believed these to be the words of Ptolemy himself, rather than Haly’s. However, these are the words of the commentator, not the author, as anyone can easily understand not only from the Greek manuscripts but also from the common translation. See what trust can be placed in such men regarding the heavens, when they are found to be so sleepy-eyed and half-blind in the examination of their own authors. 

Furthermore, not only Ptolemy, but no one who followed him for more than a thousand years is found to have used a ninth orb. <margin>[passage marked with marginal bracket]</margin> Alfonso <note>Alfonso X of Castile, who commissioned the *Alfonsine Tables* in the 13th century, which integrated the idea of a ninth sphere to account for the movement of the stars.</note> was the first to calculate the locations of the planets according to a new sphere, a practice which all the modern thinkers have followed. The ancients used only the eighth sphere, which even Leo Hebraeus <note>Levi ben Gershon (Gersonides), a 14th-century Jewish polymath and astronomer.</note> and Proclus the Platonist <note>A 5th-century philosopher who wrote extensively on the structure of the cosmos.</note>—most excellent mathematicians—contend to be the supreme orb of all. 

From this opinion, various more recent thinkers disagree, asserting by a far from empty conjecture that there is another orb superior to the eighth. They argue this because two motions toward completely opposite directions cannot exist within the same physical body by themselves. Therefore, since it has been discovered through true observation that the fixed stars <note>original: *non erraticas stellas*, referring to the stars that do not change position relative to one another, unlike planets.</note> move from west to east <note>This refers to the phenomenon of precession, where the positions of the stars shift slowly over centuries.</note>, and yet that sphere, along with the others, is turned from east to west, they believe it must necessarily follow that the former motion—which is completed in a single cycle over many thousands of years—belongs to the nature of the sphere of stars itself. The other motion, which is completed in the space of one day, is communicated to the eighth sphere by another and therefore higher globe, just as it is to the "wanderers" <note>The planets.</note>. This higher globe sweeps everything with it from east to west, including the stars that are carried from west to east by their own specific motions. 

This suspicion, which was not born from nothing, is nevertheless refuted by others in many ways. For there are those who deny that the stars move from west to east—though there are certainly both observant men and mathematicians who say that the **diurnal motion** <note>The daily rotation of the sky.</note> belongs to the **ether** <note>The "fifth element" or substance of the heavens.</note>, which is one and not divided into spheres but continuous. They claim that all stars, both fixed and wandering, are carried from west to east by their own motions. Leo Hebraeus attributes that motion to a certain lower sphere rather than a higher one. Others, considering the whole heaven as a kind of animal composed of all the spheres as if they were limbs, say that there is one motion belonging to the whole heaven from a certain universal motor, and other motions belonging to individual spheres according to their diversity, which are owed to their own distinct motors. <margin>[passage marked with marginal bracket]</margin> Therefore, that motion which we call diurnal, since it is common to the other spheres, does not belong to the eighth or to any other more than the rest; rather, it arises from a certain common motor of the celestial whole. For this reason, there is no need to imagine another orb to which that motion specifically belongs, nor does it follow that the same sphere...

of the same sphere there are two proper motions, since one is derived from what is common with the remaining parts of heaven, and the other is attributed to its own nature by a different motor <note>A "motor" or "mover" in Aristotelian physics is the spiritual or divine entity responsible for keeping a celestial sphere in motion.</note>. Let us place all these matters before us, asserting only this: that nothing indubitable or certain can be asserted about them. Instead, the entire dispute returns to probable and metaphorical arguments, which, because they are numerous and ambiguous on both sides, ultimately leave us in uncertainty. For if we think we must concede to the reasoning by which a ninth orb is confirmed, we must also agree with those who devised a tenth above the ninth, since the logic for both dogmas is almost the same. For the former, in order to stubbornly defend the idea that no more than one motion belongs to a single sphere by itself, introduced a ninth because they had detected that the eighth sphere was turned by a double motion; the latter, having detected a triple motion and led by the same conjecture, introduce a tenth. This was believed by Alfonso <note>Alfonso X of Castile, who sponsored the Alfonsine Tables.</note>, Campanus <note>Campanus of Novara, a 13th-century mathematician and astronomer.</note>, Leopold <note>Leopold of Austria, a 13th-century astronomer.</note>, and Messahala <note>Masha'allah ibn Athari, an 8th-century Persian-Jewish astrologer.</note>, who also refer this opinion (albeit falsely, as Albert <note>Albertus Magnus, the 13th-century polymath.</note> did after them) to Ptolemy.

## CHAPTER II. IF THERE IS ANOTHER SPHERE ABOVE THE EIGHTH, ANCIENT
## astrology is false; if there is none, modern astrology is false; and even if it exists, the
## ninth must necessarily collapse.

**FROM** this so varied and manifold variety of opinions, it is easy to perceive how uncertain divinatory astrology is rendered. For if there are two other spheres above the eighth, all ancient astrology is false, as they relied on useless and imperfect observations while being ignorant of the most powerful parts of heaven. This is because those higher spheres cannot be ineffective, as the supreme one excels the others in the rapidity of its motion, and both excel in the sublimity of their location and the vastness of their mass. If, on the other hand, there is no sphere besides the eighth, then all the astrology of the younger generation <note>Pico refers to medieval and Renaissance astrologers as "the younger" compared to the ancients.</note> is nothing, for it describes the twelve signs in a ninth orb; if that orb is non-existent, what authority will it have in decreeing fate? Furthermore, whether there is a ninth sphere or not, all the astrology of our age is known to waver, and not only to speak with inconsistency, but with controversial and clashing claims.

For let them answer me this: do they think that influences <note>original: *afflatus*, literally "breath" or "blasts," referring to the flow of power from the stars to Earth.</note> reach us from the entire heaven? Or only from those parts that flash with conspicuous light? If they concede the first, then by that reasoning not only the planets but the orbs that carry the planets will be included in the sharing of the fatal decree; yet they do not observe these orbs, as if they believe there is no efficacy in them for changing things in the lower world. If they answer the second—namely, that a power of this kind, like that of the Sun, exists in stars shining with a ray of conspicuous light—it must also be conceded to them that no flows from the ninth sphere reach here. For that sphere is endowed with either no light or an invisible light, and is distinguished neither by stellar rays nor by any variety of lights; rather, it is either entirely transparent <note>original: *diaphana*</note> (whence it is called the watery and crystalline heaven <note>The "crystalline heaven" was a theoretical sphere of clear, water-like substance added to the cosmos to account for biblical descriptions and astronomical motions.</note>) or is infused with a thin and rare light, such as can and is thought by many to exist in the other globes. Therefore, either every sphere must be observed, or that ninth one as well [must be ignored]...

Therefore, these signs are not immovable in a superior sphere according to Ptolemy, but are described by four fixed and immovable points of the eighth sphere <note>In traditional cosmology, the eighth sphere is the firmament of the fixed stars.</note>; if he had conceived of any other sphere above it, he would never have remained silent about such a great discovery in his *Great Composition* <note>original: "Magna sua compositione", referring to the *Almagest*, Ptolemy’s foundational work on astronomy.</note>. One cannot help but mock John of Saxony <note>A 14th-century astronomer known for his commentary on the Alfonsine Tables.</note>, who in his expositions on Alchabitius <note>A 10th-century Arab astrologer and mathematician.</note> strives to prove that the signs of the ninth sphere must be used according to the opinion of Ptolemy. To confirm his opinion, he cites certain words of Haly <note>Ali ibn Ridwan, an 11th-century commentator on Ptolemy.</note>, the interpreter of Ptolemy, regarding "bright and dark degrees." John thought these were the words of Ptolemy himself, rather than Haly’s; however, they are the words of the commentator, not the author. This is something anyone can easily understand, not only from the Greek manuscripts but even from the common translation. See what faith can be placed in those men regarding celestial matters, who are caught examining their own authors with such sleepy and blinking eyes!

<margin>☞</margin> Furthermore, not only Ptolemy, but no one following him for more than a thousand years is found to have used a ninth orb. Alfonso <note>Alfonso X of Castile, sponsor of the Alfonsine Tables in the 13th century.</note> was the first to calculate the locations of the planets according to a ninth sphere, and all the moderns have adhered to him. The ancients used only the eighth, which even Leo the Hebrew <note>Levi ben Gerson (Gersonides), a 14th-century Jewish philosopher and astronomer.</note> and Proclus the Platonist <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note>—most excellent mathematicians—contend is the supreme sphere of all. Departing from this view, younger thinkers argue by a not entirely vain conjecture that another orb is superior to the eighth, because two motions in diametrically opposite directions cannot exist in the same body by itself. Therefore, since it has been discovered by true observation that the "wandering stars" <note>The planets, though here referring to the movement of the fixed stars in the context of precession.</note> move from west to east, and again that this sphere revolves with the others from east to west, they think it necessarily follows that the former motion—which is completed in one revolution over many thousands of years—follows the proper nature of the sphere of stars; the other motion, which is completed in the space of one day, is communicated to the eighth sphere from another and therefore higher globe (just as it is to the wanderers), which sweeps everything with it from east to west, including the stars that are carried from west to east by their own proper motions. This suspicion, which was not born from nothing, is nevertheless refuted in many ways by others. For there are those who deny that the stars move from west to east, although there are certainly observant men and mathematicians who say the diurnal motion belongs to the ether, because it is one and not divided into spheres but perpetual; they claim all stars, both fixed and wandering, are carried from west to east by their own proper motions.

<margin>⌜</margin> Leo the Hebrew attributes that motion to a certain inferior sphere, not a superior one. Others, viewing the entire heaven as a kind of animal <note>The "World Soul" or organic view of the universe common in Platonic thought.</note> composed of all the spheres as if they were limbs, say that there is one motion owed to the whole heaven by a certain universal motor, and other motions owed to individual spheres according to their diversity, distinct from their own specific motors. Therefore, that motion which we call diurnal, since it is common to the other spheres, belongs no more to the eighth than to any other, but exists from a common motor of the celestial universe. For that reason, it is not necessary to invent another orb to which that motion properly belongs, nor does it follow that the same sphere...

### IF ABOVE THE EIGHTH SPHERE THERE BE ANOTHER,
### ancient astrology is false; if none, the new is false; even if it
### exists, the ninth must necessarily ruin everything. Chapter II.

From this so varied and manifold variety of opinions, it is easy to perceive how uncertain <term>divinatory astrology</term> <note>The practice of predicting human affairs and earthly events through the positions of celestial bodies</note> is rendered. For if there are two other spheres above the eighth, all ancient astrology is false, as they relied on useless and imperfect observations, having been ignorant of the most powerful parts of heaven. Since those spheres cannot be ineffective, the highest of them surpasses the others in the swiftness of its motion, and both in the sublimity of their position and the vastness of their mass. If, on the other hand, there is no sphere besides the eighth—none of the newer ones—then all [modern] astrology, which describes the twelve signs in a ninth orb, will have what authority in discerning fate, if that orb is non-existent? 

Indeed, whether there is some ninth sphere or none at all, all the astrology of our age is known to waver, speaking not only with inconsistency but with controversial and clashing claims. For let them answer me this: do they think that influences <note>original: "afflatus," meaning the "breath" or celestial flow of power from the stars</note> reach us from the entire heaven? Or only from those parts that flash with conspicuous light? If they concede the first, then by that reasoning not only the planets, but the very orbs that carry the planets, will be included in the sharing of the <term>fatal decree</term> <note>The predetermined destiny supposedly written in the stars</note>; yet they do not observe these orbs, as if they think there is no efficacy in them for changing things below. 

If they answer the second—namely, that such power of the Sun is present in the stars shining with a ray of conspicuous light—it must also be conceded to them that no flows from the ninth sphere reach here. For it is endowed with either no light or invisible light, and is distinguished neither by stellar rays nor by any variety of lights. Instead, it is either entirely transparent—whence it is called the <term>aqueous and crystalline heaven</term> <note>A term from medieval cosmology for a sphere made of a clear, water-like substance, often associated with the biblical "waters above the firmament"</note>—or it is spread with a thin and rare light, such as can be and is thought by many to be present in the remaining globes. Therefore, either every sphere must be observed, or that ninth one also...

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

If any sphere should be disregarded, as <term>Bonatti</term> <note>Guido Bonatti was a famous 13th-century Italian astrologer often cited and criticized by Pico.</note> believed, you assert that nothing placed above the <term>eighth sphere</term> <note>In the ancient model of the universe, the eighth sphere was the "Firmament" where the fixed stars were located.</note> pertains to the astrologer. And yet, the twelve signs are described by everyone within it—signs which possess not just some, but the most powerful authority over the year’s constellation, not only for what they bestow by their own powers, but because the primary role in modifying the powers of the Planets is assigned to them by all authorities. Therefore, whichever way the astrologer turns, he falls into inexplicable snares: for they either omit many spheres that should not be omitted, or by admitting one that is ineffective, they corrupt the truth of the entire constellation. 

But even if they could somehow extricate themselves from this, they would be held entirely by an inescapable bond. Even if we were to grant that as much power and efficacy as you wish resides in the <term>ninth sphere</term> <note>The "ninth sphere" was a theoretical addition to the celestial model, placed outside the stars to account for the slow wobbling of the Earth's axis (precession).</note>, and no other dispute were raised regarding the other spheres, the predictions of the more recent astrologers would still be proven utterly false. It cannot be denied that the power and properties of that sphere are distinct from the influences of the eighth; yet these men, treating them as if they were the same, have taught nothing regarding the signs of the <term>ninth</term> other than what was taught by the ancients regarding the signs of the eighth. 

This is certainly due to either great dullness or malice—either they failed to see that different spheres cannot have the same nature, or, seeing this, they wished to persuade others otherwise. It seems likely enough that they managed to deceive others because, once the <term>ninth sphere</term> was devised, if they had to deal with the influence of a different orb, their profession would have had to cease for many ages. This is because the nature of the newly discovered orb would first have to be confirmed by many experiments—something that more boastful and ambitious men could by no means endure. 

Therefore, they transferred the same names to the parts of the ninth sphere that the ancients had used for the parts of the eighth—as if the nature itself were communicated along with the name—and they put forth the exact same dogmas about them that their predecessors had produced regarding the eighth. Thus, they describe <term>Aries</term>, <term>Taurus</term>, <term>Gemini</term>, <term>Cancer</term>, and the rest of the signs in the <term>ninth sphere</term>, and they claim these signs do the same things that the ancients wrote were done by signs of the same name, but in a different sphere. They defend this entire imposture solely by the association of names. 

In this matter, if they are deceiving us, it is a crime; if they are themselves deceived, it is madness. They err no differently than if they were to transfer the name of <term>Jupiter</term> to <term>Saturn</term>, and then believe that Saturn had become Jupiter—proceeding to pronounce those prophecies for Saturn which the ancients taught were portended by Jupiter. For the difference between the eighth and ninth orbs should be considered no less than the difference between Jupiter and Saturn, if we evaluate their motions and the quality of their light, by which celestial bodies are primarily distinguished. Between those two planets, the only apparent difference is that one is slower than the other, and the light of one is either darker or brighter than the light of the other. 

But how much greater is the distance between those two higher orbs! Here, one is moved by its nature with the slowest motion, while the other is moved with the swiftest of all. One is radiant and conspicuous with a manifold army of stars, while the other, having either no light or an invisible light, does not fall under our gaze or eyes. Finally, if of its parts—

...of the same sphere, and they even claim a very different efficacy for its smallest parts; in what way then will the efficacy of different spheres be the same? And if two spheres have the same nature, did not God, the maker of nature, create the second one in vain? And if, as I have said, they do not agree in motion, nor in light, nor in position, nor in mass, what other communion of nature is there between them? Let the machine of the universe be looked at from every side, and in all the globes of the elements or the heavens, a clear diversity will always appear. Therefore, if a ninth sphere exists (an idea not thought of by others), it is necessarily of a different nature from the eighth; and thus, what <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the Greco-Egyptian mathematician and astronomer whose works were the foundation of medieval astronomy and astrology.</note> and other ancients taught about the signs and parts of the eighth sphere cannot be assigned to or agree with the signs of the ninth. Because the younger astrologers do this anyway, their prophecies—even if they claim to follow a true art—can only hit upon the truth by mere chance.

### HOW THE CONSTELLATIONS DIFFER FROM THE SIGNS, ALTHOUGH THEY SHARE THE SAME NAMES. Chapter III.

**B**ut indeed, whatever may be decided about the number of spheres, we shall briefly demonstrate that those twelve signs—to which both the ancients and moderns attribute so much that the main turning point of all astrological prediction rests upon them—are fictional and non-existent. Furthermore, even if they were real, the astrologers have handed down false and conflicting doctrines about them; for which reason the divinations that depend on them (and all of them do) are entirely deceptive. 

But it is necessary to first warn the reader that <term>signs</term> <note>In technical astrology, a "sign" is a mathematical division of 30 degrees on the ecliptic, starting from the point of the spring equinox.</note> are one thing, and <term>images</term> <note>Pico uses "images" to refer to the actual constellations—the visible groups of stars in the sky.</note> [constellations] are another, although they agree in name and number. I say these are entirely different, even among those who—either ignoring or neglecting the ninth sphere—make the same division of signs in which the forms of the images are also imagined. For <term>signs</term> are established as immovable and fixed, marked out by the <term>equinoxes</term> and <term>solstices</term>, so that the beginnings of <term>Aries</term>, which is a sign, are always taken from the <term>vernal equinox</term>. However, the beginnings of the <term>Aries</term> which is an image [the constellation] are calculated elsewhere at another time, just as the stars from which it is formed are continually carried from the west to the east <note>This refers to the phenomenon of precession, where the stars appear to move slowly against the backdrop of the seasons over centuries.</note>. 

In this matter, a large part of the astrologers have erred, thinking that those who refer the <term>Planets</term> to the eighth sphere must necessarily use moving signs. Nor have they understood the words of <term>Ptolemy</term> in the first book of the <term>Apotelefmatum</term> <note>original: "Apoteleſmatum"; this refers to Ptolemy's *Tetrabiblos*, his foundational work on the effects of the stars.</note> teaching the contrary, which are as follows: "Let us not pass over that which is worthy of note: that it is reasonable to establish the beginnings of the boundaries or terms of the <term>dodecathemoira</term> <note>original: "dodecathemorum"; a Greek term for the twelve signs or "twelve-parts" of the zodiac.</note> (that is, the twelve signs) from the tropical and <term>equinoctial</term> points, which the writers also most strongly indicated. For from what we have said above, it is clear that their natures, powers, and relationships have their cause from the <term>tropical</term> and equinoctial principles, and not from any other. Therefore, whether we establish other principles or not, we will be forced either to use their natures in predictions or, by using them, to fall away from the truth of the <term>zodiac's</term> intervals, from which their powers proceed."

...having been omitted and changed. This is the view of <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the influential Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose work Pico is scrutinizing.</note>, whose opinion had to be explained before it was refuted, since it has been little understood or noticed by very many. It is clear, therefore, that the first difference between the <term>constellations</term> <note>original: *imagines*; the actual groups of stars forming patterns like Leo or Scorpio.</note> and the <term>signs</term> <note>original: *signa*; the twelve equal 30-degree mathematical divisions of the zodiac.</note> is that the former move, while the latter do not move; and even if they are described as being in the eighth sphere, another difference is very obvious: the constellations have unequal sizes, while the signs are equal to one another. For each of the signs contains thirty parts, but some constellations extend through fewer spaces and others through more.

Since, therefore, signs are one thing and constellations another, we shall refute both with their own specific arguments. And first, regarding the signs, we shall ask what reasoning showed them that there are twelve distinct natures there, distinguished by powers and properties, and neither more nor fewer than these. <term>Abraham Ibn Ezra</term> <note>original: *Abraam Auenazra*; a famous 12th-century Jewish scholar and astrologer.</note> says at the beginning of his *Book of Astrological Reasons*: "Some things are said about the signs which are proven; some things you declare immediately by choice." When he asks which of these are most especially brought forward arbitrarily, he mentions the division of the zodiac. For he says: why are the divisions of the signs only into three hundred and sixty parts? Because this number is more convenient for divisions.

<term>Ali ibn Ridwan</term> <note>original: *Haly Auenrodan*; an 11th-century commentator on Ptolemy.</note> also writes the same while explaining the *Apotelesmatika* <note>Ptolemy's *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of western astrology.</note> of Ptolemy: "We have divided the circle into twelve parts called signs, and each of the signs into thirty parts called degrees, and any thirtieth part into sixty minutes, because these numbers are found to be more suitable for mathematical divisions."

With whose words, then, rather than their own, should I refute them? They are so ignorant of the nature of things and logical consequence that, because those who measure the movements of the stars divided the circle into twelve parts for the convenience of calculation, they then established a dogma that those twelve parts have different powers and properties—as if their distinction arose not from the choice of mathematicians, but from the nature of the heavens! And it happens that if they are described in the eighth sphere (as Ptolemy, the Egyptians, and all the masters of signs intended), no physical reality or natural solidity corresponds to them; they can only be thought of and conceived in the mind.

For this reason, <term>Origen</term> <note>A 3rd-century Christian theologian.</note>, steeped in the doctrine of the Egyptians, called these signs "intelligible" and perceivable only by reason. For there is no part of the eighth sphere where an equinox or solstice always occurs; rather, it happens in different parts if (as they think) that sphere carries itself from west to east by its own motion. Therefore, the points where we understand the equinox or solstice to always occur depend on no physical thing, but on our thought alone. These can certainly serve mathematicians for finding motions and calculating the positions of the planets, but they cannot be established as the origins of virtues or the principles of any physical influences.

Perhaps the <term>Chaldeans</term> <note>A term often used for ancient Babylonian astrologers.</note> considered this, as they used only constellations and not signs in their predictions. From this, the great weakness and inconsistency of this art is clearly recognized: when those things which the consensus of astrologers considers its first and strongest foundations are nevertheless rejected by the Chaldean practitioners and...

<meta>This page continues Pico's argument that the twelve signs of the zodiac are arbitrary mathematical constructs rather than physical entities with inherent power. He uses the commentary of the medieval astrologer Ali ibn Ridwan to show that even prominent astrologers inadvertently admit that the "power" of a sign actually comes from the Sun's seasonal position or the stars temporarily residing within it, rather than the space itself.</meta>

<page-num>649</page-num>
<header>On Astrology, Book VIII.</header>

Those most famous in the prediction of the future have considered these signs to be of no consequence. <term>Ali ibn Ridwan</term> <note>original: *Haly Abenrodan*; an 11th-century Egyptian physician and astrologer whose commentary on Ptolemy's *Tetrabiblos* was a standard textbook.</note>, noticing these things in part, said: "The signs are merely mansions <note>dwellings or stations</note> that perform no work of their own; rather, it is the <term>fixed stars</term> <note>stars that appear to maintain a permanent position relative to each other, unlike the "wandering" planets.</note> within them that act." He adds that the signs receive their names because the Sun travels through all of them each year, and they take their names from the effects the Sun produces while situated in them. Furthermore, because the fixed stars—which move one degree every hundred years according to the ancients, or every seventy years according to more recent observers <note>Pico is referring to the "precession of the equinoxes," the slow shift of the stars relative to the calendar.</note>—stay in the same part of a sign for a long time, the power of that sign is considered the same as the power of the star dwelling there; if the star were moved to another part, its power would likewise be transferred to that new part.

This was his opinion, as recognized both from the words cited and from his other writings elsewhere: that the parts of the <term>zodiac</term> <note>the belt of the heavens divided into twelve equal signs.</note> themselves have no power to produce effects if the influence of the stars is excluded. When astrologers say that one sign has one property and another sign has a different influence, he argues this is true for two reasons: either because the stars meeting in that part of the sign at that time possess such power—meaning the "guest" (the star) gives efficacy to the "lodging" (the sign)—or because the Sun produces such effects upon reaching that sign. In this way, the <term>equinoctial</term> and <term>solstitial</term> signs—namely **Aries**, **Cancer**, **Libra**, and **Capricorn**—are called "movable" <note>also called "cardinal" signs because they mark the start of the four seasons.</note>, because the Sun, when positioned in them, changes the season of the year. Conversely, those signs next to them are called "fixed," because during the time of year the Sun traverses them, the state and quality of the air does not change.

Similarly, <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>The most influential astronomer of antiquity.</note> says that **Aries** causes thunder and lightning, not because of some inherent power located in that part of the zodiac, but because when the Sun is in Aries, it is the <term>vernal equinox</term> <note>the first day of Spring.</note>. That season, by its very nature, stirs up these kinds of atmospheric changes. For the Sun's heat, as it approaches us closely, dissolves the moisture left over from the preceding winter and lifts up many vapors; when the resulting thick clouds collide with one another as they rush together, they emit flashes of lightning.

This is Ali ibn Ridwan’s opinion on the power of the signs, and it could not more strongly confirm what we wanted to prove: that the parts of the zodiac marked by the equinoxes and solstices—in which Ptolemy says the primary power resides, and which all astrologers (except the Chaldeans) use—have no power to produce effects. For while ibn Ridwan desires to explain and clarify Ptolemy’s opinion, he obliterates and erases it—perhaps even against his own will—with a pen dipped, so to speak, in the river of truth. He asserts that the parts of the circle effect nothing, and that what is thought to be done by them is actually triggered by the operation of either the Sun or the stars acting in those parts.

But the Egyptians, Ptolemy, and the whole crowd of astrologers assign permanent and immobile properties to the signs, which do not fade or change even when the Sun or stars depart. Otherwise, Ptolemy should have passed down different information about the nature of the signs than what had been produced long ago by the Egyptians. Furthermore, later writers should have written differently than Ptolemy if the power of the signs changed as the stars shifted. Yet they pass down the same descriptions of the signs' natures, syllable for syllable, as those who wrote before them—even those found in the works of <term>Petosiris</term> <note>a legendary ancient Egyptian priest to whom early astrological texts were attributed.</note>...

...and the path of the eclipses. Yet it ought to happen that the properties which once belonged to Aries should at some time become the properties of Taurus, and those which were of Scorpio should eventually belong to Sagittarius, and so on for the rest. This is because the stars that formerly ran their course in Aries have now passed forward into Taurus, and those which once occupied Scorpio will, in the passage of time, migrate into Sagittarius. 

Now, regarding what is said about the Sun—good Jesus, how empty and trifling it is!—an attribute is assigned to a sign which, when the Sun is located there, actually proceeds from the power of the Sun and not from the sign. This is almost the same as if people were to say that a chair breathes forth the power of debating because a philosopher is accustomed to dispute while sitting in it, or likewise that one should seek <term>syllogisms</term> <note>A form of logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises.</note> from a stool because those sitting on it formulate them. They claim this, for instance, because the Sun, when positioned in Aries, stirs up thunder and changes the winter frost into the mildness of spring. 

The <term>astrologers</term> <note>original: *Planetarii*; literally "those concerned with the planets."</note> decree that when the Moon is in Aries, thunder is to be expected, and that Aries is the author of mobility in all things. They do not notice that if thunder occurs while the Sun is in Aries, the same does not follow for the Moon and the other planets. This is because that effect comes not from the nature of the sign, but from the heat of the Sun lifting watery vapors into the heights—the material for clouds—from which thunder and other such things are later produced. Since this power of heat is not present in the other stars, what is produced by the Sun will not be produced by them, even though they are located in the same sign. 

Furthermore, the fact that the Sun does this more in Aries than in Aquarius is not due to the properties of the signs, but the position of the place; namely, that in Aries the Sun is closer to us <note>Pico is referring to the northern hemisphere's spring equinox, when the Sun appears to move higher in the sky and the days grow longer.</note>. Therefore, the things near us are more affected by its rays during that time. For this reason, the Sun, when placed in the same sign, produces different effects in different regions at that same time. 

But these men are ignorant of the first rudiments of <term>logic</term> <note>original: *dialectices*.</note>, in which we are taught to distinguish that which is "essential" from that which is "accidental" <note>original: *per se* from *ex accidenti*. In logic, an essential property is what makes a thing what it is; an accidental property is a coincidence of timing or location.</note>. I only wish they were merely bad at logic, and did not simply rave like children. For who would not call it insanity rather than error to think that—because the season of the year changes when the Sun is in Aries (not to depart from that example)—whatever you begin while the Moon is positioned there will not be stable or firm, but fluid and changeable? 

And because the quality of the air does not change but remains the same while the Sun occupies Leo (namely, in the middle of summer), they think Leo is a "fixed" sign, and therefore whatever one starts under it will be long-lasting and immovable. From this comes that wonderful dogma: that when the Moon is traveling through Leo, one should neither put on new clothes for the first time nor cut them. They claim that, due to the quality of a "fixed" sign, those clothes are destined to last for a very long time—a significance which seems to imply either a disease or some other bad cause because of which you would be unable to wear them. 

Since the clothes you actually use cannot help but be consumed and cannot last forever, who, upon hearing this, could not think these things were either invented by storytellers for a laugh or are the ravings of madmen? By what skills can these men be moved from their errors, when such things can appear to them not only not absurd, but true? Philosophers, when they dispute with those who feel no shame and resist even the most basic principles at first glance, are accustomed to force them to their own destruction; that is, to...

Here, he exposes a fundamental contradiction: astrologers apply traits derived from the *shapes* of constellations (the "images") to the fixed *locations* in the sky (the "signs"), even though these two have drifted apart over time due to the precession of the equinoxes.</meta>

...that what they say does not so much firmly prove their point as contradict it. We shall therefore attack them by that same path. Since it does not seem absurd to them that Aries possesses the power of making things mobile simply because the Sun, upon approaching it, changes the season of the year, let us at least obtain this one thing from them: that they do not move from their position like those born under Aries, but rather hold fast to and defend their own dogma. For if they do so, we shall question them thus: Are these signs—which they call <term>mobile, fixed, and double</term> <note>These are the three "modalities" of the zodiac: Cardinal (mobile), Fixed, and Mutable (double). They describe how a season begins, peaks, and transitions.</note>—immobile, or do they move along with the <term>images</term>? <note>original: *imaginibus*; referring to the actual constellations or star patterns as opposed to the mathematical "signs."</note> 

If they answer that they are mobile, then they themselves are moved from their own signs; for the initiation of summer, autumn, winter, and spring belongs not to moving signs but to immobile ones. The properties they give to the signs—that they be mobile, fixed, or double—are derived from the aforementioned variety of the seasons. Therefore, these properties belong to no other signs than those which are conceived as forever unmoved in their places within the circle. 

But if they say the signs are immobile, it follows that they do not coincide with the location of the <term>images</term>, which (along with their stars) have repeatedly changed their position. If this is so, by what logic are properties derived solely from the *shape* of the images attributed to these other signs? They call Aries "mobile," "equinoctial," and "of short duration"—which are conditions of an immobile sign—but then immediately call it "four-legged," "with drooping eyes," and "lustful," which are traits not of the sign (the space) but of the image (the ram), having the same name but differing in nature, location, and properties.

And not to pursue every detail individually: the whole crowd of astrologers, when they partition the signs, claim that some are common, some fixed, some mobile; and again, some are <term>straight</term> and others <term>oblique</term>, <note>Refers to the "signs of long and short ascension," describing how signs rise over the horizon at different angles and speeds.</note> which are (as I have said) conditions of immobile signs. Likewise, they use distinctions such as some being human, others wild, others aquatic, others earthy, others mute, others vocal, these sterile, those fertile—all of which belong to the *images* and not the *signs*, because these follow no position of the circle, but rather the nature, form, and figure of the image. 

What is this great sluggishness or sleepiness, that they seem not to see how they mix and confound diverse things, deceived solely by the sharing of names and not of nature? For that other classification—whereby this sign is "hot," that one "earthy," another "airy," and another "watery"—is also taken from the images and transferred to the signs with the same recklessness. 

For if the state of the circle is considered from immobile points, Aries should rather be judged as "airy"—that is, hot and moist—rather than "fiery" (hot and dry), since the spring opens with it, a season of hot and moist quality. Indeed, even <term>Ptolemy</term>, <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity.</note> giving the reason why we are accustomed to take the beginning of the year from Aries in a circle that has no actual beginning, answers that in the "first age" of all things, humidity abounds, which is the quality of the spring that we begin from Aries. 

So then, O Ptolemy, if Aries is the first sign because humidity is owed to the first age, do you think the sign is dry or humid? If it is dry, then it is not the first; if it is humid, why is it called "fiery" by you? Finally, these distinctions (as I wished to prove) of cold, dry, hot, and moist...

...ties <note>The text begins mid-word, continuing "proprietates" (properties) from the previous page.</note> distributed to the signs seem to be taken from the condition of the **images** <term>images</term> <note>original: *imaginum*; Pico uses this to refer to the actual constellations or shapes of stars, as opposed to the mathematical "signs" of the zodiac.</note> rather than from the signs themselves, which even **Ibn Ezra** <note>original: *Auenazra*; referring to Abraham Ibn Ezra, a 12th-century Jewish scholar and astrologer.</note> confesses in his *Book of Reasons*. For in this way they established that **Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces** are cold, having weighed the nature of the animals whose names they bear; they established **Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius** as hot for the same reason. They held **Gemini and Aquarius** to be airy because of their human likeness, as that quality is most dominant in man; likewise, they held **Taurus, Capricorn, and Virgo** to be earthy, both because of the power of their sex and, in the case of Virgo, by reason of the **ear of corn** <note>original: *spicæ*; referring to the star Spica, which represents the grain held by the maiden in the constellation Virgo.</note> which she carries in her hand. Therefore, they attributed this power, taken from the diverse properties of the images, to the signs. In this matter, the good **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century foundational authority for Western astrology and astronomy.</note> not only nods off but wanders quite sluggishly, so that in the same context he transfers his argument from the sign to the image. This I shall clearly demonstrate, along with the inexpiable error of **Haly** <note>Likely Ali ibn Ridwan or Haly Abenragel, famous medieval commentators on Ptolemy.</note> in explaining Ptolemy’s words.

His words in the second book of the *Apotelesmaton* <note>Ptolemy’s *Tetrabiblos*, the most famous ancient textbook on astrology.</note> are these: "The **twelfth-part of Aries** (for so he calls the signs) is universally **thundery and hailing** <note>original Greek: βροντῶδες καὶ χαλαζῶδες</note>; but in its parts, more or less, according to the **property of the fixed stars** <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τῆς κατὰ τὰς ἀπλανῶν ἀστέρων ἰδιότητος</note> [contained in it]." And he adds: "for its preceding parts produce rains and winds; the middle parts a temperate air; the final parts heat and plague. Furthermore, the parts that turn toward the north produce heat and corruption, while those toward the south are icy and somewhat cold." I understand these words of Ptolemy such that what he pronounces regarding Aries in general refers to the **immobile sign** <term>immobile sign</term> <note>The fixed 30-degree division of the zodiac where the spring equinox occurs, regardless of which stars are currently located there.</note>; this cannot be denied, since that is where the equinox occurs. For that reason, Ptolemy said it was "thundery and hailing," because it usually stirs up all these things before the springtime—and then he adds his consequences regarding the differing efficacy of its parts according to the nature of the stars existing therein.

Indeed, Haly believes this refers even to the parts of the sign by day, as I shall soon declare; but I will show more clearly than light itself from Ptolemy that this was said of the **image** (the constellation). And as much as Ptolemy errs in establishing the dogma, Haly errs just as much in explaining Ptolemy. For Haly thinks Ptolemy’s words should be understood to mean that the stars he says are in those parts were in those parts of the sign at the time he was writing; and thus, that the property belonged to the sign then, but with the passage of time and the movement of the stars to another place, that property would be transferred elsewhere. This interpretation by Haly would appear plausible if Ptolemy had done for other signs what he does for Aries. And he would have brought forth no names for the stars which he places in those parts; but when he explains certain stars in **Taurus**, he makes manifest both his own error and that of his interpreter by naming them. This is because those stars were not in that part of the sign where he places them during Ptolemy’s own time, but rather in the part of the **image**—where, of course, they are, and will be, and have been. 

His words concerning Taurus are these: "The sign of Taurus universally brings both qualities of the air, yet it is inclined toward heat; however, its preceding parts, especially where the **Pleiades** <note>A famous star cluster in the constellation Taurus.</note> are, bring earthquakes, winds,

...and clouds, they awaken; and following where the **Hyades** <note>A star cluster in the constellation Taurus, traditionally associated with rain.</note> are, they produce flashes of lightning and thunderbolts. Come then, who does not see that these things were said by **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century authority on astronomy.</note> regarding the **image** <term>image</term> <note>original: *imagine*; Pico distinguishes between the "image" (the actual group of stars) and the "sign" (the 30-degree mathematical division of the zodiac).</note>? In its leading parts are the **Pleiades**, which our people call the *Vergiliae*; in the following parts are the Hyades, for which in the common translation one reads **Aldebaran** <note>The brightest star in Taurus; Pico notes that "Aldebaran" is sometimes used loosely to refer to the whole Hyades cluster in medieval translations from Arabic.</note>. For although the Hyades are in the crown, the horns, and the whole head, while the Pleiades are between the boundary of its body and the tail of **Aries**, which they call the "place of cutting off" <note>original: *locum abscissionis*; a technical term for the point where one constellation figure is separated from the next.</note>, nevertheless the former occupy the following parts and the latter the leading parts, since the Bull sets and rises backward. 

But truly, if these things are referred to the **signs** <term>signs</term> <note>The fixed 30-degree segments of the ecliptic used in horoscopes.</note>, there will be no truth in the statements; since in Ptolemy's time the Pleiades were not in the sign of Taurus, but in Aries, as is easy to recognize from his *Great Composition* <note>original: *magna eius compositione*; better known by its Arabic-derived name, the *Almagest*.</note>. Since **Haly** <note>Ali ibn Ridwan, an 11th-century Egyptian physician and astrologer who wrote famous commentaries on Ptolemy.</note> ought to have read this, and should not have doubted that the author of both works was the same, I cannot sufficiently marvel at the hallucination in so clear a matter: that he explained Ptolemy’s sayings concerning the places of stars within the signs, yet left it written that the Pleiades at that time were in the first parts of Taurus. This error was followed by Haly, and **Leopold** <note>Leopold of Austria, a 13th-century astrologer.</note>, and **Eschenden** <note>original: *Ascadensis*; referring to John Eschenden, a 14th-century English astrologer known for his *Summa judicialis de accidentibus mundi*, often called the "English Summa" (*Summa Anglicana*).</note> in the work they call the *English Summa*, and finally by later writers like **Bonatti** <note>Guido Bonatti, the most famous Italian astrologer of the 13th century.</note>. 

But the greater error of these men is that they follow Haly's claim that Ptolemy spoke of stars placed in those specific parts of the sign, and yet they do not change them; they say the same thing Ptolemy said, even though since that time the stars have moved by more than twenty degrees <note>Due to the precession of the equinoxes, the actual stars move about 1 degree every 72 years relative to the spring equinox point.</note>. It is clear, therefore, what we wished to prove: that astrologers imprudently contradict themselves, mixing the properties of signs and images (if they have any) as if they did not differ in location, nature, or parts.

**C**ome now, even if we grant there is no power in the signs, are the **images** <term>images</term> <note>Constellations.</note> themselves anything? For perhaps here the astrologers will not seem to rave, nor to lean on fictional and arbitrary things; for who will deny that those images, each with its own lights, stars, and rays, have the greatest power according to the nature of the stars? 

But I truly have no doubt that the astrologers are raving here as well. For even if the stars from which the images are constructed are both true and natural, nevertheless the very arrangement of those stars into "images" is neither true nor natural. It is false, fashioned entirely by the imagination according to the whim of those who made them, and without any appearance of probability. For who would not immediately judge that if the power of one star is great, the power of many "conspiring" <note>original: *conspirantium*; here meaning "breathing together" or acting in unison.</note> together into one would be even greater? But reason, returning to itself, sees that there is no "conspiracy" of stars there except for what we have imagined; for certainly there is no mixture through physical union there.

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola #

How, then, do many stars—distinct in nature and separated by the immense vastness of great distances—combine into a single property? I know what they will answer: that they meet in the likeness of a single image, which is evidence of some hidden affinity. Just as a figure is outlined from a single form, they say there is one native property in these stars derived from all of them together. But truly, this might perhaps amount to something (though not achieving what they wish) if those images appeared there expressed and completed with very real markings. However, since they are imagined according to our whim (as I shall show), and it is no more necessary for dogs and hares to be there (as they wish) than tigers and elephants—for anyone may form whatever is convenient for himself—it is clear that the argument taken from the figure is, like the rest of the <term>astrologers’</term> <note>original: *astrologorum*; in Pico's time, "astrologer" and "astronomer" were often used interchangeably, but here he specifically targets those who draw mystical meanings from the stars.</note> claims, vain, arbitrary, and mythical. 

If they contend that those figures exist there not by the whim of the onlookers but by nature, I will appeal not so much to the evidence of experience as to the arguments and testimonies of the <term>astrologers</term> themselves. For **Abraham Ibn Ezra** <note>original: *Abraam Auenazra*; a 12th-century Jewish polymath and influential astrologer.</note>, an author of great authority among them, in his second edition on <term>astrological</term> arguments (for he wrote two books on the same subject), being about to give an account of these images, writes in these very words:

> <gloss>*</gloss> <note>original: *Quæ nos ita ad sensum uertimus in latinum* / "Which we have thus translated into Latin according to the sense:"</note>
> **Ptolemy** <note>The 2nd-century Alexandrian astronomer whose *Almagest* defined the 48 classical constellations.</note> calls the "Falling Vulture" the **Lyre**; this is no wonder, since just as anyone can change the shape for himself, so can he change the name. For the sky is spherical, wherefore there is no reason why you should establish the beginning of anything in this place rather than another. But just as some stars are joined to others according to the whim of the eyes, so different images are created; we, therefore, shall recount them in the way they have been handed down. These are his words.

No one can confirm my opinion more truly or effectively. Since there is no beginning or end in the parts of a circle, you can begin an image for yourself from whatever star you prefer, and end it in whichever you wish. There is no doubt that, due to the diversity of the beginnings and endings you prescribe for yourself, and the number of stars you either include or exclude, you will fashion various images from them. This is especially true since different people represent different forms to themselves from these same stars, as **Ibn Ezra** declared regarding the Vulture and the Lyre; and you can demonstrate the same in other cases. 

Indeed, they have not even agreed on the number of the most famous images of the **zodiac** <term>zodiac</term>. While others made twelve, the **Chaldeans** <note>A term often used for ancient Babylonian astronomers/astrologers.</note> made them eleven, constituting one image out of **Libra** and **Scorpio**. <note>In ancient Greek astronomy, the "Claws" of the Scorpion were later separated to form the constellation Libra (the Scales).</note> For what prevents anyone—since an equal power of seeing whatever they wish in this celestial painting is granted to all? Even **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar, a 9th-century Persian astrologer whose works were foundational to European medieval astrology.</note> himself, who professes that he will provide the reasons for the dogmas of <term>astrology</term> in all things, when he came to the images, brought no other reason than that **Aratus** <note>A 3rd-century BC Greek poet whose poem *Phaenomena* described the constellations.</note> described them so. It is as if Aratus were not the most mythical of writers—who, as **Cicero** says, wrote about <term>astrology</term> while being utterly ignorant of <term>astrology</term>. <note>Pico quotes Cicero's *De Oratore*, where it is noted that Aratus wrote a brilliant poem on stars without being a mathematician.</note> Furthermore, if you compare the sphere of Aratus with the "Barbaric sphere," <note>original: *Barbarica sphæra*; this refers to the non-Greek constellations (often Egyptian, Persian, or Indian) documented in ancient texts.</note> you will find that they frequently disagree and are discordant...

<summary>Pico argues that constellations are arbitrary human constructs rather than natural groups of stars. He supports this by citing astrological authorities like Ibn Ezra and Albumasar, who admit that the names and shapes of constellations are based on tradition and the observer's perspective rather than objective reality.</summary>

<header>Against Astrology, Book VIII.</header>

# Against Astrology, Book VIII.

...you will see those things, namely why they were fashioned for lust and rest on no solidity of learning or reason. The Hebrew masters, just like the <term>astrologers</term> <note>Those who study the influence of stars on human affairs.</note> with their images, strive to find their own **alphabet** <note>original: *alephbetarium*</note>—that is, the marks and elements of their language—in the stars. If they find credulous eyes, they can persuade people of this with no less probability than the astrologers do with their images. What more is needed? Every form and every likeness is there, and yet no forms and no likenesses are there; they exist entirely by the power and will of men, and not at all by the act of nature or truth. 

If our little <term>diviners</term> <note>original: *divinaculi*; a diminutive, mocking term for those who claim to predict the future.</note> had at least fashioned some images of august and more sublime things there, I might be more easily persuaded to see them as the works of God rather than their own works against nature. But when I consider His counsel and wisdom, I do not see why He could not or would not have adorned that temple of divinity, those halls of heaven, with better images than those of irrational animals, monsters, or even lifeless things. For what is there besides **bears**, **dragons**, **hares**, **dogs**, and things that are inanimate, such as **arrows**, **ships**, and **triangles**? Add to this **severed heads** <note>A reference to the head of Medusa held by the constellation Perseus.</note> dripping with decay and gore, and a **maiden** <note>Andromeda.</note> banished to punishment—to say nothing of the **hydra** and the **centaur**. If nature does not allow these things on earth, why would she describe their patterns for herself in heaven?

Indeed, I think it is beyond all madness to be led to believe that these were formed there by the institution of nature and divine counsel. A good priest or a high-minded king would be ashamed not to have better paintings in his temple or palace. Otherwise, what was nature's purpose in establishing these things? Was it so that she might govern inferior bodies of the same kind through these superior images? That through the heavenly **Lyre** she might provide musical melody to whichever men she wished? That through the animals that are there, she might generate and preserve those which are among us, which are born and die every day? Or are **monsters** <note>Pico is mocking the idea that mythical creatures like the Centaur or Hydra in the sky are necessary to govern nature.</note> appropriate there, even though they do not exist in nature? Why are countless animals not depicted there? For what is the special privilege of **dogs** and **bears**, that they should have two rulers or priests in heaven, while **elephants**, **tigers**, and countless species of animals have no divinity in heaven by which they may be ruled? 

But I have said too much about these things, which are not only shameful for a philosopher to believe, but even unworthy to refute. Yet if someone should ask me why, in this license for imagining, the supporters of astrology descended to these images rather than others, I will answer that he asks a question of reason, which is sought in vain in these matters that were established by no reason. However, it is easy to see what led them on in most cases. For I think the names of the images assigned to parts of the **zodiac** were derived from the works of the **Sun**, which occur most frequently when the Sun is found in those parts. For example: the name of the **Crab** <note>original: *Cancri*</note> was given to that part of the <term>zodiac</term> <note>The belt of the heavens divided into twelve signs.</note> in which the Sun, being placed, begins to move backward in the manner of a crab...

<summary>Pico argues that constellations are arbitrary human inventions, mocking the idea that God would fill the heavens with "ugly" images like monsters and severed heads while excluding noble animals like elephants.</summary>

Here, he explains that the names of the zodiac signs (like Leo or Aries) were originally agricultural or seasonal metaphors that superstitious astrologers eventually mistook for actual celestial forces.</meta>

<page-num>656</page-num>
<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

...[the part] which is closest is called **Leo** <note>The Lion</note> on account of the excess of immoderate heat, just as another part is named **Taurus** <note>The Bull</note> because when the Sun reaches it, the earth is plowed by oxen. **Gemini** <note>The Twins</note> follows, where all things are then doubled <note>original: *geminando*; likely referring to the doubling of vegetation or the abundance of twin births in livestock during late spring</note>. Under **Virgo** <note>The Virgin</note>, the earth, scorched by the Sun’s heat, brings forth nothing; and under **Aries** <note>The Ram</note>, the fields are clothed in a fleece of flowers—for which reason they even set that animal over the head because of the similarity to hair <note>Pico suggests the "Ram" was chosen because the blossoming fields looked like wool, and the sign governs the "head" because flowers are like the hair of the earth</note>. **Libra** <note>The Scales</note> balances nights and days against each other as if weighed in a scale <note>original: *librili*; referring to the Autumn Equinox</note>. When the Sun reaches **Scorpio** <note>The Scorpion</note>, the air first stings with cold; soon under **Sagittarius** <note>The Archer</note>, it provokes us with the stings of both more violent cold and winds. In **Capricorn** <note>The Horned Goat</note>, the reason is clear: for from that point, the Sun begins to ascend again like a climbing goat. In **Aquarius** <note>The Water-Bearer</note> and **Pisces** <note>The Fish</note>, rain is poured out in abundance for the fish. Led by such similarities, those [ancients] were able to manufacture these images rather than others in various parts of the sky, easily drawing the stars into the likeness of that nature whose name they intended to impose on that part for some reason. 

The fictions of the poets were added, many things being devised either for pleasure or for favor—just as **Conon of Egypt**, the mathematician, first "saw" monsters and the lock of hair from **Berenice’s head** <note>original: *Beroniceo vertice cæsariem*; a reference to the constellation Coma Berenices, which Conon "discovered" to flatter Queen Berenice II after her hair went missing from a temple</note>. But it is not worth the effort to scrutinize more diligently and explore the insanities of others, as it is more than sufficiently clear to those who refuse to be delusional that these are not the works of nature, but the trifles of those who imagine them, or the delusions of dreamers. Thus, let me finally define these inventions correctly: they arose from corrupt philosophy and the fables of poets. Yet all <term>astrologers</term> <note>Those who claim to predict the future via the stars</note> attribute so much to them, as if they were the truest things and formed (so to speak) by the finger of God, that it is scarcely believable into what superstitions this madness has led them. 

"Take medicine," they say, "when the **Moon is placed in Taurus**, because that animal ruminates <note>Chews its cud</note>; therefore, the moon will cause the medicine to be vomited back up." "When you build a house, beware lest **Scorpio** occupy the fourth house, because many scorpions will abound in that house." He who is procreated while the **Crown** <note>The constellation Corona Borealis</note> is rising will be a king; he who is born under the **Lyre** will be a musician—and a thousand other things of this kind. From these, you can see how deeply they are persuaded that the true likenesses and natures of all these things are in the sky, from which powers flow down to us in a wonderful way for the deciding of fate. 

Finally, that whole superstition of fabricating images <note>Astrological talismans or amulets</note> sprouted from that madness: they think that by fashioning a similar image in some metal, a virtue from that celestial image is breathed into the metal. Yet these things are not in the sky; nor, if they were, would they descend from there just because an image was carved here; and even if they did descend, they would be of no benefit to us, as **Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd, the 12th-century philosopher</note> proves against **Al-Ghazali** <note>original: *Algazelem*; the 11th-century Persian theologian</note>. But we will discuss these matters more extensively later in a specific treatise.

Here, he mocks the complex and contradictory visual descriptions that medieval astrologers assigned to these subdivisions, treating them as literal, invisible entities rather than poetic symbols.</meta>

<page-num>657</page-num>
<header>On Astrology, Book VIII</header>
<meta>catchword: we?</meta>

...and that for each **decan** <term>decan: a subdivision of a zodiac sign covering ten degrees, also known as a "face"</term> or face of any sign there are certain images—invisible, to be sure, but consisting of the solidity of a most true nature. Those who hear of these cannot help but burst into laughter. For they are of this sort: in the first face of **Cancer** <note>The Crab</note>, they say, there rises a handsome young man, well-clothed, but with some crookedness in his face and fingers; his remaining body is like a horse and an elephant, with white feet, and he hangs various types of grain and tree leaves above himself. In the first face of **Leo** <note>The Lion</note> there rises a tree with very deep roots, in whose branches a dog sits; there is also a man dressed in clothes that are noble but filthy, weeping and mourning for his parents. Other images similar to these are described by them for the other decans of the signs. **Albumasar** <note>Latin name for the 9th-century Persian astronomer Abu Ma'shar</note> mentions all of these as things of the highest efficacy in the sixth book of his *Great Introduction*. **Avenazar** <note>The 12th-century scholar Abraham ibn Ezra</note> mentions them in the book he titled *The Beginning of Wisdom* <note>original: *Initium sapientiae*</note>. **Peter of Abano**, **Michael Scot**, and many Arabic and Latin astrologers also mention them. 

When I had heard something of these matters long ago, I thought that by these images they were indicating what the decan of each sign produced—not that they actually believed there were figures there in the heavens. But upon consulting their books, I recognized it was far otherwise. For they think, assert, and contend that these images in those decans are most real, and are the effectors of marvelous works among us. Indeed, **Albumasar** says: "Sometimes they produce things similar to their own forms, but often they produce other things entirely different." 

Truly, if these men were **lynxes** <note>Proverbially believed in the Renaissance to have sight so sharp they could see through walls</note>, I might be led in some way to suspect that things which escape our gaze were open to their eyes. But I find no reason to give credit to these men who proclaim such "admirable mysteries," since they have no eyes other than those humans usually have. Yet humans do not see these things, nor do we read that they were seen even by the **Apostle** <note>Saint Paul, who was famously "caught up to the third heaven"</note> when he was snatched up into heaven; nor could any reason demonstrate these things to those situated on earth. 

Those who call themselves philosophers should blush! They are not ashamed to write down such trifles, which a storytelling old woman could barely persuade a two-year-old child to believe. Add to this that they do not even imagine the same images, but different ones. Here, one says that in the first face of **Aries** <note>The Ram</note>, a woman rises, resplendent with brightness and the tail of a sea-fish. Another says there is no beautiful woman there, nor a fish, but a **Black man** <note>original: *aethiope*</note>, though there is some doubt about his eyes—whether they are black or red; he is of tall stature and wrapped in a cloak. In the third face of **Gemini** <note>The Twins</note>, some say there arises a golden pipe, a barking dog, and a dolphin. Others contend that none of these are there, but rather a man seeking weapons to put on, protected by a shield and equipped with a quiver. In the third face of **Scorpio** <note>The Scorpion</note>, the Arabs say there is a horse and a hare. The **Indians** <note>referring to Indian astrological traditions which often differed from the Arabic-Latin system</note> say there is neither a horse nor a hare, but a dog, a boar, and a leopard. Others see no beast, but a man bent on his knees—perhaps (if one may interpret the mysteries) he is praying to God on behalf of the astrologers, that He might eventually restore their minds and free them from this insanity. For what else are they but insane?

He points out the absurdity and lack of visual evidence for these invisible monsters, noting the blatant contradictions between Arabic, Indian, and Latin sources.</summary>

...who would believe us, or agree with us, if we were to devote ourselves to such deceptive and impossible nonsense? Seeing these things, **Abraham the Jew** <note>original: *Abraham Iudæus*; referring to the 12th-century scholar Abraham ibn Ezra</note>, an astrologer himself, confesses in his book *On Nativities* <note>original: *de Natiuitatibus*</note> that these images are ridiculous rather than true. Indeed, I find no one who has placed any faith in them except for the Arabs—a people always most prone to fables—and those Latins who have followed them. 

The Egyptians wrote nothing of them, nor did the Chaldeans, the Greeks, or the ancient Latin writers of astrology. As for **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar, a 9th-century Persian astrologer</note> claiming that the Indians, Egyptians, and Babylonians handed these things down, he is easily caught in a lie. For regarding the Egyptians and Chaldeans, we have the means to understand that no such delusions existed among them. From this, it can be conjectured that he lies equally about the Indians, although it is not as easy to refute him on that point, since no monuments of the Indians have been handed down to us by trustworthy authors. But this is a peculiar habit of the Arabs: whatever commentaries they invent themselves, they sign with the names of illustrious authors, many of whom we have recounted in the first book of these disputations. 

Since there still exist certain works of **Petosiris** <note>A legendary Egyptian priest-astrologer</note>, a master of astrology among the Egyptians; and since there exist—besides **Maternus** <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman astrologer</note>—**Hephaestion**, **Thebanus** the commentator, and **Paulus of Alexandria**, all of whom are interpreters of astrology, it is easily recognized from their works that no mention of these images was made in Egypt. 

The same is evident regarding the Chaldeans on the authority of **Teucer of Babylon** <note>original: *Tenrus Babylonio*</note>, who wrote on the *Apotelesmata* <term>Apotelesmata: the "effects" or "outcomes" of the stars</term> of the **decans** <note>subdivisions of ten degrees in a zodiac sign</note> and the images that rise alongside them. It is also evident from the testimony of **Porphyry**, who wrote astrological institutions based on the opinions of the Chaldeans—not to mention **Manilius** <note>original: *Mallium*</note> and **Maternus**. 

In any case, regarding those who report the dogmas of the Chaldeans to us, only those who have not read the Greek authors can have any doubt; for nowhere in any Greek writer is there mention of those "invisible" images. Thus, we must greatly blame **Haly** <note>Ali ibn Ridwan, an 11th-century Egyptian physician and astrologer</note>, who attributed this error to **Ptolemy**. For in the ninety-fifth aphorism of the book titled *The Fruit* <note>original: *Fructus*; also known as the *Centiloquium*, a collection of 100 astrological sayings</note>, Ptolemy says: 

-> "It is likely that the things rising alongside each decan reveal the disposition of the one being born" <-
<note>original Greek: *κινδυνευέτω παρανατέλλοντα ἑκάστω δεκανῶ δηλοῦν τὴν προαίρεσιν τοῦ γινομένου*</note>

and what kind of profession he will practice. The commentator **Haly** thinks that by "co-rising images" <note>original: *coorientes imagines*</note> these invisible things we have been discussing are meant. He was ignorant of what the Greeks meant by "co-rising" <note>original: *παρανατέλλοντα* / *paranatellonta*</note>. For among the Greeks, this name is given to those thirty-six images outside the zodiac, of which fifteen incline toward the south and twenty-one toward the north. **Ptolemy** writes about their properties and nature in the first book of his *Apotelesmata* <note>Known today as the *Tetrabiblos*</note>. Neither in that place nor anywhere else does he ever mention any other images except those fashioned from **visible stars**, against which we argued in the previous chapter. He uses the same word in the following passage when he says that in the eclipses of the luminaries, one must consider the "co-rising" stars; he discusses this same sentiment in the second book of the *Apotelesmata*...

...from which category are those stars called "co-rising" <note>original: *coorientia*; stars or constellations that rise at the same time as a specific degree of the zodiac</note>. When he says that the will and the profession of the newborn are indicated by these, he teaches what **Manilius** <note>original: *Mallius*; a 1st-century Roman poet and astrologer</note>, **Firmicus Maternus**, and the Greek writers explained: that he who is born while the Ship <note>the constellation Argo Navis</note> is co-rising will be a sailor; he born under the Lyre will be a musician; he under the Charioteer <note>original: *Emotho*, likely a corruption of the Greek *Heniochus*</note> a driver, and so on for the rest. Furthermore, **Porphyry** <note>a 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> says in his *Introduction* that the "type"—that is, the figure and form <gloss>of the zodiac animals</gloss> <gloss>of the zodiac animals</gloss>—that is, the animals which are in the zodiac <gloss>co-rising</gloss> <gloss>co-rising</gloss>, that is, he says they consist of a composition of stars. From this, we understand that these so-called "co-rising" things are no other images than those formed by the stars themselves. I have been more long-winded in declaring this because I hear that **George of Trebizond** <note>a 15th-century Greek scholar and rival of Pico’s circle</note>, a Greek man (for his book has not reached us), followed the exposition of **Haly** <note>Ali ibn Ridwan, an 11th-century Egyptian physician and astrologer</note> in his commentaries on the *Centiloquium* of Ptolemy. From this error, even the barbarian **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar, a 9th-century Persian astrologer</note> could have steered them away; he affirms that, according to the opinion of Ptolemy, no images except those visible and constituted from stars located to the south and north rise with the decans.

It is pleasing, however, to recall to mind what we said in the fifth book against those who say that the Lord **Jesus** was born while the first "face" <note>the first 10 degrees of a zodiac sign</note> of Virgo was rising, in which there is a Virgin nursing a boy called Jesus. For it is certain that this image of a Virgin nursing a boy is among those fabulous images which we have mocked—although the Indians do not even devise such an image there, but another kind, as Albumasar relates. Whoever considers in his mind how vain and ridiculous this invention is will be ashamed to ever want to confirm the truth of the Gospels with these astrological ravings. This was procured by the devil for no other reason than that this plague <note>astrology</note> might be received as if it were a friend and patroness of religion. But let them keep their own trifles to themselves; by summoning such things, the Christian truth is not confirmed,
