# GIOVANNI PICO OF
## Mirandola’s Disputations against
## Astrology, Book IX.

### A SUMMARY OF WHAT HAS BEEN CONCLUDED SO FAR,
### and what must be done in the following books, and where we should
### begin. Chapter I.

IT HAS BEEN DEMONSTRATED so far that astrology is a nullity, because the things about which it makes pronouncements do not depend on the heavens, except by accident, or as if from a remote and universal cause—neither of which produces specific knowledge of events. It has likewise been declared that even if those events were caused by the heavens, they would not occur as astrologers imagine: that is, starting from a specific initial moment. Furthermore, even if this were granted, they certainly do not arise from the causes astrologers use in their predictions, none of which (if we examine them strictly) is true or natural. For although they use stars and planets, they increase, diminish, or change their influence according to locations, signs, intervals, and other such factors, which we have shown to be false and ineffective. Therefore, they either introduce bad causes—that is, mythical ones—or they corrupt good causes by mixing them with bad ones.

Now our task is to declare that, even if all those premises stood firm, these matters are of such a nature that they cannot be known by astrologers; or if they could be known, that knowledge has not yet been obtained. Three things are necessary to know if true predictions about future events are to be made. First: that the initial hour <note>the exact moment of a beginning, such as a birth or the founding of a city</note> of any thing be faithfully recorded. Second: that we exactly comprehend the state of the heavens and the position of the stars at that hour. Finally: that we understand, through true reasoning or observations made through unfailing experiments, what that position of the heavens and stars actually signifies. In the following two books, we will reveal that none of these things can be known, or at least that no one has yet emerged who has known them. We shall begin with the primordial hour, the knowledge of which is primary and necessary; nothing else can be correctly established if there is any ambiguity or error in that timing. This applies either to the "births" <note>original: *geniturarum*; the casting of individual natal horoscopes</note> of men, or to the foundations of cities and kingdoms, or to the constellations marking the start of a year. Let us begin with births.

---

### THAT AN ASTROLOGER CAN NEITHER ALWAYS
### know the certain hour of birth, nor investigate it
### through a true rule. Chapter II.

An astrologer cannot have the exact moment at which someone is born well-investigated, unless perhaps he stands ready with an astrolabe <note>a handheld instrument used to measure the altitude of stars to tell time or determine latitude</note> to measure the celestial bodies at the very instant the infant comes forth. But this happens very rarely, nor can it always happen even when we wish it—such as at night, in cloudy weather, or when no mathematician is present. Indeed, it is also very easy to make a mistake, as **Avenrodan** <note>original: *Auenrodan*; the Latinized name for Ali ibn Ridwan, an 11th-century Egyptian physician and astrologer</note> testifies in his commentaries on **Ptolemy** <note>the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology</note>. For if the instrument is not of the utmost precision...

<meta>catchword: then,</meta>

<summary>Pico begins Book IX by outlining the three practical requirements for a horoscope—the exact time of birth, the exact positions of stars, and a proven system of interpretation—and argues that the first is nearly impossible to obtain. He notes that unless a mathematician is present with precise tools at the exact moment of birth, human error and environmental factors like clouds make accuracy impossible.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's argument from the previous page regarding the practical impossibility of obtaining an accurate birth time. He is specifically addressing the "estimated hour" and the astrologers' attempts to "rectify" or correct it using artificial methods.</meta>

<page-num>661</page-num>
->On Astrology, Book IX.<-
KK

...which perhaps never happens, so that an inspection at the exact moment of birth <note>literally "the moment of egress," i.e., leaving the womb</note> corresponds clearly to the reality, then the calculation of the specific degree of the <term>horoscope</term> <note>In this context, the "horoscope" refers specifically to the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth.</note> will waver. Indeed, for there to be a true investigation of the hour by means of an <term>astrolabe</term> <note>An ancient instrument used to determine the positions of celestial bodies and tell time.</note> happens, as we were saying, very rarely. What is frequent—nearly constant—is that the parents or the master of the <term>geniture</term> <note>The birth or the casting of the birth chart.</note> tells the astrologer what the hour of birth was. Even astrologers do not deny that these people are not to be trusted, for they are mostly deceptive. This is why they call it the "estimated" or "suspected" hour, about which there is no certainty. For sundials lie, and even if water-clocks <note>Latin: *horologia*</note> do not fail at all, they nevertheless do not show the intervals that fall between the middle of the hours. 

Furthermore, the "common hours" do not begin from sunset, as the reasoning of the mathematicians <note>At this time, "mathematicians" often referred specifically to astronomers and astrologers.</note> requires, but rather when the air begins to grow dark. This happens when the Sun has already been submerged below the <term>horizon</term> <note>Latin: *finitorem*</note> for some time, especially when the Sun is placed in "oblique signs." Since these signs linger longer in the west, the night may sometimes have already claimed an hour before the air grows dark. Finally, the astrologers admit this along with us, but they apply a remedy so that their divination is not endangered. For even if that which they call the "estimated hour" is not the true one, they claim that unless it differs greatly from the truth, they have a method for finding the true hour; therefore, they say that earlier uncertainty is no obstacle. 

To this we would object—if those men were capable of wisdom—that no art or science can be given by which it may be known whether a particular thing has happened or not. Therefore, there is no method by which we can be made certain of the exact moment that John or Paul was brought into the light. But these things do not seem absurd to them. Nor, perhaps, does it seem absurd that there are many small particles of time in any given day or hour during which no one can be born in a certain region; yet this is very easily demonstrated to follow from their logic. 

For if I am said by my parents to have been born at the first hour of the night, and the astrologer denies that this hour fits his "method," I ask: Why was I born later or earlier? Could no one else have been born at that first hour of the night under that same inclination of the heavens? If they deny that this could happen, it follows (as I was saying) that there are many parts of any hour in which a human being cannot be born in certain places. I say "many parts of any hour" because almost no birth time given by those consulting the astrologers fits their rules; instead, it is always changed by them to a different part, either preceding or following the hour. 

Suppose they concede that someone else *could* have been born during that time in that region, even though I myself was not born then. Let us say Antonius is said to have been born at the first hour of the night. I ask: if Antonius provides the astrologer with what we now establish as the *true* hour of his birth, will the astrologer judge it to be true or false? If he judges it true, he ought by the same reasoning to have judged mine true when it was offered, since it fits his method no better now than when John offered it. If he judges it false, yet it was established that Antonius was truly born at that hour, then the dogma is false through which a most true hour is rejected as if it were false. Furthermore, those who have handed down this kind of instruction say that the zodiac sign shown by the estimated hour must not be changed, but that the specific part <note>i.e., the degree</note> of that sign is to be declared by their method...

<summary>Pico argues that astrologers cannot accurately determine the exact moment of birth because clocks are imprecise and human testimony is unreliable. He mocks the "methods" (rectification) astrologers use to correct these times, noting that such methods logically imply that people can only be born at specific intervals, which is an absurdity.</summary>

...is most certain in the <term>horoscope</term> <note>The exact degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon.</note>. Truly, the estimated hour often lies regarding the sign; especially when a person is born while the very last or first parts of a sign are ascending, then the method will not amend the error but confirm it. It is clear by these reasons that there is no way of tracking the horoscope when it is uncertain. Now let us show that if any method could perhaps be devised, those which the astrologers have passed down are most clearly deceptive.

## THE DOCTRINE OF PTOLEMY WHICH THEY CALL ALMUSELI OR ANIMODAR, is refuted by both authorities and reasons. Chapter III.

**P**tolemy, in the third book of his *Apoteleismatics* <note>This refers to the *Tetrabiblos*, Ptolemy's foundational 2nd-century work on astrology; "Apoteleismatics" refers to the study of the stars' effects.</note>, passes down a doctrine of this kind: He instructs one to observe the New Moon or Full Moon immediately preceding the <term>geniture</term> <note>The birth or the casting of the birth chart.</note>. Then, one looks for the Planet having the most authority <note>This refers to "essential dignities," a system where planets have more power in certain degrees of the zodiac.</note> in the place where that conjunction or opposition occurred. Finally, with the chart already laid out, to whichever <term>cardinal point</term> <note>The four most powerful points in a chart: the Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, and Imum Coeli.</note> that Planet is closer, that place is set to the number of degrees which that ruling Planet held in its own sign. They fashion this cardinal point as the basis of the entire birth; all astrologers decree this as the foundation of the entire study of astrological effects. This is that decree which they call *Almuseli*, and sometimes *Animodar* <note>Technical terms derived from Arabic astrological traditions for "rectifying" a birth time.</note>. In this, the younger astrologers err greatly by wrongly understanding the opinion of Ptolemy, as mentioned above. 

Now Ptolemy himself is examined, against whom I can first oppose great masses of authorities. For Abraham the Jew <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar and astrologer whose work Pico respected but used selectively.</note> says that he observed many births with the most exact <term>astrolabes</term> in those regions whose longitude and latitude were admitted and explored, yet he never found any of the Planets whose degrees and minutes (within the signs they occupied) corresponded to the degrees and minutes of the East <note>The Ascendant.</note> or the Midheaven; nor did they vary by more than half an hour from the birth time already discovered to be most true by the senses. Truly ridiculous are those who say that Ibn Ezra <note>original: "Auenazrā"</note> did not write these things from a judged conviction of mind—as if he were contending with Ptolemy for a kingdom!—given that he lived nine hundred years later, and in determining the year, the giver of years, and many other things, he does not prefer the opinion of others over Ptolemy. 

But even Alchabitius <note>Al-Qabisi, a 10th-century Arabian astrologer.</note> writes in his own commentary that he has demonstrated that the true rising degree can in no way be found through that reasoning. Henry Bate <note>Henry Bate of Mechelen (1246–1310), a scientist and astrologer.</note>, a disciple of Albert the Great, examining his own birth chart—though hiding his name and calling himself "a servant of God"—says, "let us dismiss the *Animodar* of Ptolemy, which has been rejected by the wise." Others do not strike out the doctrine but "correct" it, like Aoniar <note>Likely referring to another Arabic source or a specific commentator.</note>, who disagrees somewhat with Ptolemy. Others fight over the understanding of it. And when it is asked to which place a Planet is closer, there are those who wish for discrete quantity to be observed, and those who wish for continuous quantity, such as Antonio de Monte Ulmo <note>A 14th-century Italian astrologer known for his complex mathematical approaches.</note>. 

But, setting aside the authorities of those opposing Ptolemy, I am accustomed to declare the falsehood of the doctrine in this way: Suppose Lucius is born in Rome, and Fabius in Florence at the same hour and the same moment. It is clear to astrologers that they will not have the same horoscope...

<summary>Pico critiques Ptolemy's "Animodar" method for rectifying birth times, citing various historical astrologers like Ibn Ezra and Al-Qabisi who found the method mathematically and observationally inconsistent.</summary>

...horoscope of each, because of the different inclination of the heaven under which they are born. And yet, if we enter into a calculation according to Ptolemy’s precepts, we will make the <term>horoscope</term> <note>The degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth.</note> of each the same, since the preceding full moon or new moon occurred in the same part of the heaven for both regions. Therefore, the same ruler who holds the same degree of a sign in the chart for both will define the <term>cardinal points</term> <note>The four critical angles of a chart: Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, and Imum Coeli.</note> by the same numbers in both <term>genitures</term> <note>The birth charts or the moments of birth.</note>. But this is refuted by the evidence of the matter and the senses. Therefore, the doctrine is false, and I wonder that Ptolemy, that greatest mathematician, did not see through it.

### THE INVESTIGATION OF THE EXACT HOROSCOPE
### through conception—falsely attributed to Ptolemy by the Arabs—is irrational and rejected by many astrologers. Chapter IV.

**A**mong the more recent astrologers, another method of tracking the horoscope from the hour of conception has been found, to which they attribute much importance. It is of this sort: they assume it as if it were an admitted fact from the tradition of the ancients, and especially from the fifty-first aphorism of Ptolemy’s *Book of a Hundred Sayings* <note>The *Centiloquium*, a collection of 100 astrological aphorisms. While traditionally attributed to Ptolemy, Pico and later scholars recognized it as a later medieval or Arabic compilation.</note>, that the position of the Moon at birth was the horoscope at conception. Conversely, they hold that the position of the Moon at conception is the horoscope of birth. Having established this, they pass down a method by which they think the position of the Moon can be discovered at the moment the seed filled the womb; once this is found, they conclude that a similar degree must ascend at the hour of birth. 

However, the occasion of their error was a faulty translation of Ptolemy's books, since he nowhere wrote about this specific degree, but only about the sign. His words in the place mentioned above are these: <note>original Greek: ἐνθα ἐστὶν ἐν τῷ καιρῷ τῆς γεννήσεως ἡ σελήνη, ἐκεῖνο τὸ ζῴδιον ἐμ τῆ σπορᾷ ὡροσκόπησον, καὶ ἔνθα πῶι τῆς σπορᾶς ἔτυχεν, ἐκεῖνο, ἐμ τῇ ἀποκυήσει ὡροσκόπησον, ἢ τὸ τούτο κατὰ διάμετρον.</note> "In whatever sign the Moon is at the time of birth, set that sign as the horoscope at the sowing [conception], and wherever it happened to be at the time of sowing, set that as the horoscope at the delivery [birth], or the sign opposite to it."

Therefore, Ptolemy did not think that the horoscope could be found <term>partially</term> <note>In this context, "partially" refers to finding the exact *part* or degree of a sign, rather than just the sign itself.</note> by this way. This is why in his books of the *Apoteleismatics* <note>The *Tetrabiblos*, Ptolemy's major work on the influence of the stars.</note>, where he investigates this matter, he makes no mention of this opinion. Otherwise, if he had understood it to refer to the specific degree—which we have shown to be false from his own words—he would also have thought it easiest to find the hour of conception. Today, the "modern" astrologers provide this hour with no great trouble to anyone who desires it, using the method they claim belongs to Ptolemy. 

How then does Ptolemy himself, in the third book of the *Apoteleismatics*, say that the <term>seminal principle</term> <note>The moment of conception.</note> is <term>for the most part</term> <note>original: ἐπίπλεον (*epipleon*)</note>—that is, usually or in most cases—unknown? And when knowledge of it is attained, he says it happens either <term>by chance</term> <note>original: σύμπτωματι (*symptomati*)</note>—that is, accidentally and by luck—or by observation? He certainly ought to have added "or <term>by art</term>" <note>original: ἐν τεχνῶς (*en technos*)</note>—that is, skillfully—if indeed he believed that this could be detected by some art or method. But how he says it is known by chance or observation, he declares...

<summary>Pico refutes the "Trutine of Hermes" (a method to find the birth horoscope based on the time of conception), arguing that it is based on a mistranslation of Ptolemy and that Ptolemy himself admitted the time of conception is usually unknowable.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's critique of the "Trutine of Hermes" or the method of correcting a birth chart based on the moment of conception. He argues that even ancient authorities like Porphyry and Hephaestion acknowledged the limitations and rough nature of these calculations, which later Arabic and Latin translators misinterpreted as precise science.</meta>

<page-num>664</page-num>
-> Giovanni Pico della Mirandola <-

The Greek interpreter says that if it happens by chance that a woman feels the sensation of the seed being received—as Cleopatra <note>Likely referring to Cleopatra the Physician, an author of medical texts on women's health in antiquity, rather than the famous queen.</note> teaches—it is by observation if the man deliberately notes that time when he has coupled once with the woman and subsequently abstains; then the months would declare that the coupling was successful. Besides these, no one among the ancients has handed down another way of exploring that time with clarity, let alone wishing to investigate the hour of birth from it. For what the Arabs say, that Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many foundational astrological and alchemical texts were attributed.</note> commanded this, is a fable; just as they refer many other things to the same author most lyingly (as we noted in the first book). For what the Egyptians handed down on this matter, Hephaestion <note>Hephaestion of Thebes, a 4th-century astrologer.</note> relates, as does Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote an introduction to Ptolemy’s astrology.</note>, who say that this very precept read in Ptolemy was the discovery of Petosiris the Egyptian <note>Petosiris was a legendary priest-astrologer of ancient Egypt; his works were foundational to Hellenistic astrology.</note> in these words: "The [discourse] concerning the seed" <note>original: "ὁ δὲ περὶ σπορᾶς"</note> and what follows.

<margin>*</margin>
Petosiris, however, says that the sign in which the Moon was at the time of conception is the <term>horoscope</term> <note>The degree or sign rising on the eastern horizon.</note> at birth, or its opposite; and what the Moon occupied at the time of birth was the horoscope of conception. But in the same place, Porphyry relates two other ways—from the opinion of Antiochus and certain others—of tracking the sign in which the Moon was at the hour of sexual union, with no mention ever made of the *degree*; indeed, the very chapter in which these things are written is titled: "On the feminine sign of the Moon," because they designate that whatever sign the Moon held when the seed was admitted into the <term>genital place</term>. Hephaestion of Thebes also narrates three other methods of the Egyptians, different from these mentioned by Porphyry, by which they might investigate this same thing: namely, what sign was ascending at the hour of union. Where, in express words, Hephaestion warns us that one does not arrive at a precise <note>original: "partilem," meaning down to the specific degree.</note> horoscope through those ways, but that it is tracked "roughly" <note>original: "παχυλῶς" (pachylōs)</note>; that is, with a "thick-witted Minerva" <note>original: "crassa Minerva." A Latin idiom meaning a rough, unrefined estimate rather than a subtle or precise one.</note> as the saying goes. Truly, he says there is only one method for determining the degrees, which Ptolemy handed down in the third book of the *Mathematical Effects* <note>Pico is referring to Ptolemy's *Tetrabiblos* (also known as the *Apotelesmatika*).</note>. It is, however, the one we refuted in the previous chapter.

But as we have said, the younger astrologers have fallen into error because, in the Arabic translation which the Latins follow, the interpreters wrongly put "degree" in place of "sign." Furthermore, whatever the authors may have written, what is the reasoning for this dogma, or by what observation could this be detected? They respond that the calculation "answers" [the question], since from the place of the Moon at the hour of birth, it is understood how many days the infant was in the womb until the hour of birth; if you count these backward, you arrive at the hour of conception, and through that time you will find the place of the Moon to be the one which ascends at the time of birth. But I ask this: who teaches us to define the time of stay in the womb from the place of the Moon? Neither Ptolemy, nor any of the ancients, nor even your Hermes handed this down. There is no other answer you can give than that those stays must be defined in such a way *if* the dogma about the exchange of the ascendant and the Moon's place in conception and birth is true. Therefore, you are demonstrating in a circle, proving the truth of the dogma because it happens that way when the stays are observed, and that the stays ought to be observed that way because otherwise the dogma will not be true. Clearly, in this way, it becomes easy for anyone to confirm their dogmas.

<summary>Pico argues that the astrological method for finding a birth time based on the moment of conception (the Trutine of Hermes) is based on a translation error and circular reasoning. He cites ancient authorities like Hephaestion to show that these were always meant to be rough estimates, not precise degree-based calculations.</summary>

Moreover, if you perhaps dare to assert this by experiment—simultaneously observing and comparing the time of birth and conception—you may lie with impunity, as the act was done without witnesses. But even those among your own ranks who most strongly claim to be experienced deny that the rule corresponds to the truth. ## MASHA'ALLAH’S FICTION IS REFUTED ALONG WITH FIVE
## OTHER METHODS FOR EXAMINING THE ASCENDANT
## RECORDED BY PAUL OF ALEXANDRIA.

### Chapter V.

**T**hese are roughly the methods most accepted by astrologers. Masha'allah <note>original: "Messalla," an 8th-century Persian-Jewish astrologer who was a primary source for Western medieval astrology.</note> devises another fiction, but it is rejected by everyone and is of clearly proven vanity. For he commanded that the time of the Moon from the new moon to the full moon, or conversely from the full moon to the dark moon, should be considered as if it were one hour. Then, whichever of those preceded the birth, the space that fell between it and the time of birth should be compared to the total distance of the Moon's waxing and waning; and whatever the proportion of the intervals was, that part of the temporal hour should be taken—provided, however, that we observe this: that no male should ever be born in an even hour, nor a female in an odd one. The age that followed laughed at this, discovering by experience that males and females are born in the same hour. For my part, I do not think so much of the vanity of this one decree as I judge the whole of Masha'allah by it. For while it is characteristic of a human to slip, err, and be deceived, nevertheless, to write things so shameful, to rely on ridiculous things, to present fables as dogmas, and to say things which the universal evidence of reality refutes—this is certainly not the mark of a human, if reason is man's specific gift. But I do not judge Masha'allah alone so much as I judge all astrologers by Masha'allah, among whom he is of the first rank; nor will you easily find wiser men in that family. For the Egyptians, those wonderful high priests of this sacred discipline—what great fables [they told] on this matter...

<meta>This page continues Pico’s critique of the "Trutine of Hermes" and other ancient methods for rectifying a birth chart. Having dismissed the reliability of earlier techniques, he now examines five specific methods recorded by Paul of Alexandria, arguing that they are scientifically groundless and contradict the basic principles of geography and astronomy.</meta>

<page-num>666</page-num>
<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

...were invented. Paul of Alexandria <note>original: "Paulus Alexandrinus," a 4th-century astrological writer whose *Introductory Matters* was a standard textbook.</note> reports five different methods—beyond the three already mentioned—which they use to track down the exact degree of the horoscope <term>horoscopus: the "Ascendant," or the specific degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth</term>. Good God, how vain, crude, futile, and false they are!

The **first** is of this kind: "Look," they say, "at the position of the Sun in a daytime birth, and the Moon in a nighttime birth; whichever planet holds the individual degree <term>monomiria: a system where each of the 30 degrees of a zodiac sign is assigned to a specific planet</term>, make the individual degree of that same planet that is nearest to the suspected degree the true horoscope." 

The **second** looks only at the position of the Moon, whether it be day or night, but is otherwise similar. 

The **third**, which provided Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the most influential astrological text of antiquity.</note> with the occasion for his own doctrine, considers the Full Moon or New Moon nearest to the birth; then it looks at the "lord of the house" <note>original: "despotem," from the Greek *despotes*</note> in which it occurs, and the "ruler of the bounds" <note>original: "onocratorem," likely a corruption of the Greek *horokratōr*, referring to the planet ruling the specific "terms" or "bounds" of a zodiac sign</note>, and sees which is stronger in the birth constellation and which possesses more authority in it; from that, it calculates the ascending degree. 

The **fourth** merely looks at the supreme lord of the degree in which the Sun and Moon either join or oppose one another after the infant comes forth from the womb; however many "bounds" that planet possessed in the ascending sign, they think that many degrees of that same sign have already appeared in the east. 

The **last** method observes not only the birth, but the conception—that is, which time, either Full Moon or New Moon, preceded it. Then it orders the twelfth-parts <term>dodecathemoria: the division of a zodiac sign into twelve equal parts of 2.5 degrees each</term> of the degrees in which those occurred to be calculated and observed, to see which of the planets' individual degrees they fall into; whichever planet is better positioned in the chart is given the judgment for measuring the horoscope. 

Heliodorus, writing on how they might investigate the time of conception, says they "counted back nine months from the birth," as if the time of carrying a child in the womb were always equal! Thus, these "most divine" Egyptians are found to be the most ignorant everywhere. I could, however, object to many things in which these particular dogmas fail. But one single reason is enough for those of us striving for brevity, by which we also rejected Ptolemy's doctrine: for whatever method we follow from the aforementioned, we will always conclude that for those who

## THE ORIGINS OF CITIES, KINGDOMS, FACTIONS, AND LAWS
## are unknown, and astrologers have handed down no art by which 
## they can be investigated. Chapter VI.

It is clear from these points that the hour of birth is never known to us with absolute clarity, except by pure chance. Furthermore, because the time deviates, it cannot be restored by any technical art; and when the time is not true, the truth of the prediction cannot stand. Therefore, nothing true can be said by the **Genethliaci** <term>Genethliaci: astrologers who specialize in casting "genitures" or individual birth charts</term>, who with one voice testify that the precise degree of the horoscope—the pivot of the birth, the framework of all fate, and the foundation of the entire **Apotelesmatic** <term>Apotelesmatica: the study of the effects of stars on human life; astrological forecasting</term> art—is essential. Nor, indeed, is there any better reliability in the origins of cities and kingdoms, for which the knowledge is far more difficult to scrutinize than individual births. For who recorded these? What historian observed them? If the reliability and diligence of history should yield the exact day a city was restored or founded, it would certainly be considered a great achievement by the high-minded. It was the custom for the birthday of Rome to be celebrated, but astrologers know nothing more from it than that the Moon was "at its start" <note>original: "in imp.," likely an abbreviation for "in impetu" (at its onset) or "in imis" (at its lowest point), referring to a specific lunar position</note>—that is, in Libra—when the city was being founded. In the notebooks <note>original: "opisthographis," literally manuscripts written on the back of the leaf</note> of **Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli** <note>original: "Pauli Florentini," the renowned Florentine physician, mathematician, and cartographer (1397–1482)</note>, I found two different times noted for the restoration of the city of Florence: one in the year of grace 801, and the other in 802. From these, the arrangement of the stars would be entirely different. I am inclined to believe that many of the city constellations commonly circulated are actually forgeries based on the *Apotelesmata* <note>prognostications made after the fact to fit known history</note>, just as **Julius Firmicus** <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer who wrote the *Mathesis*</note> invents those of the ancients—Paris, Plato, and others—and as he himself testifies concerning the "birth chart of the world" which he puts forward.

Furthermore, they claim that the moment is of great importance when a new faction begins to prevail in a state, when a tyrant occupies a city, when a sedition occurs among the common people, when civil discord is born, when a foreign nation invades a kingdom, or when new laws are established and new decrees are promulgated. Who but a soothsayer could provide the horoscope for these things? Yet it is necessary to have these moments before we can begin to divine. Finally, even if some moments of these historical events could be obtained, they certainly will not deny that they would be less exact and less certain than individual birth charts. Therefore, if they think those birth charts need correction—and cannot be trusted otherwise—this is much more necessary for these political events. Yet they teach no method for correcting them; for the methods we mentioned are applied only to the birth charts of men.

Therefore, all their prognostications regarding the fates of cities and kingdoms will be crippled and deceptive, since they want these to depend on those primordial moments which they either completely ignore or have received from sources that are not sufficiently reliable or precise. Therefore, let men no longer fear death, exile, and poverty, nor cities fear destruction or plague, when these most audacious triflers threaten such things in their annual pamphlets published everywhere.

<summary>Pico argues that astrological predictions for cities and kingdoms are groundless because their founding moments are historically uncertain. He highlights discrepancies in the founding dates of Florence and dismisses political astrology as a collection of fabrications.</summary>

...they have devised. Paulus Alexandrinus <note>A 4th-century astrologer whose *Introductory Matters* was a standard textbook.</note> reports five different methods—in addition to the three already mentioned—which they use to investigate the truth of the horoscope in detail. Good God, how vain, crude, futile, and false they are! 

The first is of this sort: "Look," they say, "at the **epoch** <term>Epoch: the specific position of a celestial body at a given moment in time</term> of the Sun in a birth by day, or the Moon in a birth by night; and whichever planet's **monomiria** <term>Monomiria: a system where each single degree of a zodiac sign is assigned to a specific planetary ruler</term> it falls under, make the **monomiria** of that same planet that is closest to the suspected degree the true horoscope." 

The second method looks only at the **epoch** of the Moon, whether it be day or night, but is otherwise similar. 

The third method—which gave Ptolemy the occasion for his own doctrine—considers the full moon or the new moon closest to the birth. It then looks for the **despot** <note>original: "despotem," meaning the ruler or "lord" of a zodiac sign</note> (that is, the lord of the house in which the moon's phase occurred) and the **onocrator** <note>original: "onocratorem," referring to the lord of the "bounds" or specific subdivisions of a sign</note> (that is, the ruler of the boundaries). It checks which one is stronger in the birth constellation and which possesses more authority within it, and from that, it calculates the ascending degree. 

The fourth method merely looks at the highest lord of the degree in which the Sun and Moon either join or oppose after the infant leaves the womb. However many **bounds** <term>Bounds: unequal subdivisions of a zodiac sign, each ruled by a different planet</term> that planet possessed in the ascending sign, they believe that many degrees of that same sign have already appeared in the east. 

The last method observes not only the birth but the conception—specifically, whichever time (either the full moon or new moon) preceded it. Then it orders the **dodecathemoria** <term>Dodecathemoria: the division of a zodiac sign into twelve equal parts of 2.5 degrees each</term> of the degrees where those occurred to be calculated and observed, noting which planet's **monomiria** they fall into. The planet that is better positioned in the chart is given the judgment for measuring the horoscope. 

Heliodorus <note>An Alchemical and astrological writer, often confused with the novelist or the philosopher of the same name.</note>, writing on how they investigated the time of conception, says: "They would go back nine months from the birth," as if the time of carrying a child in the womb were always equal! Thus, these "most divine" Egyptians are found to be the crudest thinkers everywhere. 

I could object to many things in which these dogmas specifically fail. But that one reason is enough for those of us striving for brevity, by which we also rejected Ptolemy's doctrine: for whichever method of those mentioned above we follow, we will always find that for those who were

->born at the same time,<-
->but in a different region, we would make<-
->the same horoscope, although it is established<-
->among all mathematicians beyond<-
->any controversy<-
->that it is<-
->different.<-

<header>Against Astrology, Book IX.</header>

### THE ORIGINS OF CITIES, KINGDOMS, FACTIONS, AND
### laws are unknown, and astrologers have provided no art by which
### they can be investigated. Chapter VI.

**I**t is clear from these points that a birth hour is never known with complete clarity except by chance. Furthermore, because it is impossible to restore a wandering <note>In this context, "wandering" refers to an inaccurate or "off" birth time.</note> hour through any technical art, once that hour is not the true one, the truth of any prediction cannot be established. Therefore, nothing of truth can be said by the **Genethliacs** <term>Genethliacs: Astrologers who specialize in casting horoscopes based on the moment of birth</term>, who testify with one voice that the exact degree of the horoscope is the pivot of the birth, the framework of all fate, and the foundation of the whole **Apotelesmatic** <term>Apotelesmatic: The branch of astrology focused on predicting the effects or outcomes of celestial positions</term> art. 

Nor, indeed, is there any better reliability in the origins of cities and kingdoms, the minute knowledge of which is far more difficult than that of individual births. For who has handed these down? Which historian has observed them? If the reliability and diligence of a historian should record the day of a city's restoration or foundation, he would certainly be considered most high-minded. It was the custom to celebrate the "birthday" of Rome, but no more is certain to astrologers from that than that the Moon was in its midpoint <note>original: "m̄p." likely an abbreviation for "medium punctum" or a similar astronomical notation</note>, that is, in Libra, when the city was founded. 

In the notebooks <note>original: "opisthographis," referring to manuscripts or notes written on the back of pages</note> of **Paulus the Florentine** <note>Referring to Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli (1397–1482), a famous Florentine physician, mathematician, and astronomer</note>, a physician and mathematician, I found a double recorded time for the restoration of the city of Florence: one in the year of grace 801, and the other in 802, which results in an entirely different arrangement of the stars. I would even believe that many of the city constellations commonly cited are varied—fictional creations based on the observed outcomes <note>Pico argues that astrologers look at a city's history and then work backward to invent a "fitting" birth chart</note>, just as **Julius Firmicus** <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century lawyer and astrologer who wrote the "Mathesis"</note> invents them for Paris, Plato, and others—something he himself testifies regarding the birth chart he provides for the world itself.

Furthermore, they claim that the specific moment when a new faction began to prevail in a state is of great importance: the moment a tyrant occupied a city, when a riot occurred among the commoners, when civil discord was born, when a foreign nation invaded a kingdom, or when new laws and decrees were promulgated. Who but a diviner could provide the horoscope for such things? Yet one must have these times in hand before we can even begin to divine. 

Finally, even if some moments of those times could be obtained, they certainly will not deny that they would be less exact and less certain than those of individual birth charts. Therefore, if they believe that birth charts require "correction" <note>The technical process of adjusting an uncertain birth time to match major life events</note> and cannot be trusted otherwise, this is much more necessary for these historical events. Yet they teach no method for "correcting" these, for the methods we mentioned are applied only to the births of men. Therefore, every one of their pronouncements about the fates of cities and kingdoms will be crippled and deceptive, since they want these things to depend on those primordial moments which they either completely ignore or have received from records that are not sufficiently faithful or precise. 

Therefore, let men no longer fear death, exile, or poverty, and let cities not fear destruction or pestilence, simply because these most audacious triflers threaten such things in their annual booklets published everywhere.

# IT IS STILL UNCERTAIN AMONG ASTROLOGERS
## how the houses are to be divided, how far their powers extend, and which signs are to be used.
### Chapter VII

**I**t remains to speak about the beginnings of the year, great conjunctions, and eclipses <note>The "Great Conjunctions" of Jupiter and Saturn were historically believed to signal major political and religious shifts.</note>; for by observing the moment at which they occur, astrologers prophesy the fates of public and universal affairs. It must therefore be declared that such times cannot be apprehended by them without falling into error; however, this will become clear from what follows, when we show that the motions of the planets are still uncertain and have not been grasped by blameless calculation. Thus far, therefore, we have said how uncertain the "fatal hour" is for any thing—if indeed there are fatal hours for things, as astrologers especially believe; for we demonstrated above that there are no fatal hours, and if there are any, they are other than what they think. Now we will make it clear that even if they should obtain the times for undertaking a prediction, they still cannot know what the position of the stars or the state of the heavens was at that hour.

First, therefore, is the task of arranging the **theme** <term>theme: Here meaning a 'thema' or horoscope chart.</term>, with the twelve predetermined places which they call **houses** <term>houses: Twelve divisions of the celestial sphere in astrology, each representing different areas of life (wealth, health, etc.).</term>. No one who has touched the books of the mathematicians <note>In the Renaissance, "mathematicians" often referred to astrologers and astronomers.</note> is ignorant of how much darkness astrologers are poured into here, and how much they clash with one another, the matter being entirely unproven. Some distinguish these places by six circles, one of which, rotated through the point of the East, makes the seventh **pivot** <term>pivot: A 'cardinal point' or 'angle' of the horoscope, such as the Ascendant or Midheaven.</term> and the **horoscope** <term>horoscope: Specifically the Ascendant, or the degree rising on the eastern horizon at a specific moment.</term>; another, the meridian itself, outlines the highest and lowest points of the ether. Others are said to be caught in the four middle places by four points and marks of the arcs of division, the semi-diurnal and semi-nocturnal arcs, divided into three equal portions. But all these circles also pass through the poles of the world. This commonly accepted opinion we were refuting above.

**Abraham Avenazra** <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a renowned Jewish scholar and astrologer whose works were highly influential in Latin translation.</note> teaches in his work on the construction of the astrolabe, and elsewhere too, to partition the houses so that we delineate six circles, one of which is the horizon, another the meridian itself, by which the four pivots are immediately established. He orders the other four to be drawn through the marks of the intersection of the horizon and the meridian, and of the division of the parts of the equator falling between the East and the meridian—and of the division, I say, into three equal portions. **Johannes of Regiomontanus** <note>Johannes Müller von Königsberg (1436–1476), the most famous astronomer of the 15th century, who proposed a "Rational" method of house division.</note>, the most learned mathematician of our age and a man of high standing, strongly approves of this method (though he suppressed the author's name). However, he did not satisfy **Campanus** <note>Campanus of Novara (c. 1220–1296), a mathematician whose system of house division competed with Regiomontanus'.</note>, who himself also brought a new reason for this partition, similar in other respects to Avenazra, but very different in this: that instead of the equator, he uses a certain artificial circle which he called the **vertical circle** <term>vertical circle: Known today as the prime vertical.</term>, from which another measurement and other boundaries of the places emerge. Johannes of Regiomontanus wrote a copious confirmation of his own dogma, relying on many authorities, both mathematicians and ancient astrologers. Others partition them in yet other ways, and our own **Ludovico the Hermit** <note>Ludovico de Regio, a contemporary and acquaintance of Pico.</note>, a diligent and most exact calculator, was accustomed to prove that none of the methods we have mentioned agree with the sayings of **Alchabitius** <note>Al-Qabisi (10th century), an Arab astrologer whose introduction to astrology was a standard textbook in European universities.</note>.

<summary>Pico argues that astrology is foundationless because practitioners cannot agree on the basic geometry of the heavens, specifically how to divide the twelve astrological houses. He cites conflicting methods from major authorities like Ibn Ezra, Regiomontanus, and Campanus to illustrate this internal scientific chaos.</summary>

# On Astrology, Book IX.

What of the fact that many believe these same places should be divided by equal degrees of the zodiac, either using this method alone (which we noted above the Indians <note>Pico frequently cites Indian astrology as a source of alternative technical methods that contradict the Greco-Roman tradition.</note> often did) or by accepting both types of division equally: that which varies according to the rising times <note>original: "anaphoris"</note> at the equator, and that which looks only to the degrees of the zodiac <term>zodiac: original "signiferi," the "sign-bearer" or circle of constellations.</term>. This is what Abraham the Spaniard, the teacher of Avenezra <note>Abraham bar Hiyya, a 12th-century Jewish philosopher and mathematician who influenced Abraham ibn Ezra (Avenezra).</note>, and Henry of Valois observe, pronouncing judgment no less from the place in which a planet is located when the distribution is made by equal degrees, than when the divisions are noted in the common manner. Furthermore, even if it were established where the beginnings and ends of these places are to be set, there remains another doubt which once again calls everything into uncertainty, since they do not agree whether the power and efficacy of a place are confined within the boundaries of the designated area.

But Ptolemy begins that power five degrees before the cusp into the preceding parts of the signs; others extend it by only three parts. The wise men of the Egyptians wanted the beginning of a place, which they commonly call the **cusp** <term>cusp: The boundary line marking the beginning of an astrological house.</term>, to be not the beginning, but the middle and a sort of center of its power; for this reason, they believed its influence diffused fifteen degrees above that point and just as many below it. If we notice that all these varieties of opinion are supported by almost equal reasons or authorities, we must confess that by this uncertainty alone, the entire system of pronouncing judgment through the stars (if such a system even exists) is left in ambiguity. 

For when the divisions of the places are varied, the entire constellation is varied, since (as we were criticizing above) the stars change their nature, influence, and properties according to the astrologers’ shifting of the place. What is most significant is that they assign primarily clashing and contrary conditions to those places which are joined and contiguous in position. For what can be more different than the first house and the twelfth, which follow one after the other? Or what of the sixth and seventh, or again the fifth and sixth? Likewise the eleventh and twelfth? Or the ninth and eighth? And so it goes for the rest. Frequently, one mathematician will place a planet in the sixth house, while another contends it is in the fifth, which will utterly change the entire prediction; and one whom someone decrees to be in the ninth, another will say belongs to the eighth. Therefore, this entire distribution of places, the very root and foundation of all **predictive astrology** <term>predictive astrology: original "Apotelefmaticæ," from the Greek term for the study of the effects of the stars.</term>, remains in uncertainty.

There follows the concern regarding the signs: namely, which ones ought we to use? Here arises a complex and inexplicable question concerning the "movable" and "immobile" signs, and concerning the eighth, ninth, and tenth spheres <note>This refers to the problem of the Precession of the Equinoxes, where the physical constellations no longer align with the mathematical zodiac used by astrologers.</note>, about which we need not speak here, as it has been treated abundantly above. Abraham the Jew <note>Likely referring again to Abraham ibn Ezra.</note> commanded that a **double theme** <term>theme: A horoscope chart or map of the heavens at a specific moment.</term> be made, as if he did not believe the controversy could be settled. It will be uncertain from this doubt which signs are owed to the planets, and from that which we treated before, which places are theirs. But every astrological

->judgment hangs from this: therefore every judgment is doubtful,<-
->uncertain, and unexplored.<-

# THAT ATTAINING THE TRUE LOCATIONS OF THE PLANETS IS MOST
## LABORIOUS, AND ON THE FALLACY OF INSTRUMENTS.
### Chapter VIII.

**O**nce the places have been divided and the signs distributed, there remains the task of establishing the epochs <term>epochs: reference points in time used for calculating celestial positions</term> of the constellations and stars; that is, indicating at which degrees and minutes both the fixed and the wandering stars <term>wandering stars: the planets, from the Greek "planētēs"</term> may be found. This is a task which the unrefined and unskilled believe they can perform very easily, yet the most learned men hesitate and distrust it. To the latter, it is well known how great the difficulty is in truly attaining the locations of the planets—a feat judged by many to be not merely laborious, but impossible. Andreas Summarius <note>Likely referring to a contemporary mathematician or a specific commentary; the name implies a "maker of summaries" or compendiums.</note>, a serious mathematician, begins his book thus: "Whether the motions of the stars can be known, I do not know; that they have not yet been known, I hold as most certain." 

He offers such a reason for his opinion: because those who measure the motions of the constellations must necessarily first define the location of the constellation where they observe it with the help of an instrument. Once the location of the star is obtained, they use it as a sort of supposition <note>A working assumption or starting hypothesis.</note> upon which to direct their calculation of its course. If the location is truly apprehended, the future calculation of the motion will be true, for they rely on mathematical reasoning, which is never deceived. However, the reliable apprehension of the location is not possible everywhere, simply because the instrument is deficient. For no matter the vastness of a mechanical instrument, it cannot be sufficient for divisions that are perceptible to the action and the senses, which are necessary to avoid error—especially if one considers the distance of any star from the observer’s location, and the proportion by which the circuit of the entire universe exceeds the circuit of the instrument. Therefore, since the senses cannot grasp the relationship of the parts of an instrument—which is a very tiny body—to the parts of the whole universe, which are immense, the location of a constellation cannot be observed without deception. 

Perhaps the error will remain hidden at first, but with the passage of time it will become more evident, as the constellation recedes further from its true location with every single revolution. Ptolemy confirms this; for this reason, regarding the fallacy of instruments, he commands that astronomical numbers be restored every two hundred years, because in that stretch of time the fault of the old observation is uncovered. Therefore, it must be corrected by new observations, which will not themselves be blameless, but will at least be free of the error that can then be detected by the senses. When these, in turn, stray significantly after many completed cycles, they shall again be reduced to the truth by a new correction, as much as is possible. 

Thus the tables of Ptolemy, the prince of astrologers, were considered useless many years ago. Indeed, the studies of more recent men constantly correct these observations because, as we said before, no construction of any instrument is so skillful or so subtle, and no size is so vast, that it can report the location of a star with blameless faith. Abraham the Jew <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar whose astronomical and astrological works were widely translated into Latin.</note> reports in his book on the use of tables regarding two astrolabes <term>astrolabe: a complex hand-held instrument used to solve problems related to time and the position of the Sun and stars</term> made with the highest reasoning and of such great size that the diameter of each extended nine palms <note>Roughly 6 to 7 feet, an enormous size for a portable instrument of that era.</note>. When the two Bersechit brothers <note>Likely a reference to the Banu Musa brothers, 9th-century scholars in Baghdad known for their mechanical and astronomical works.</note>, the makers of the instruments, were observing the altitude of the Sun together at the moment it entered Aries, they did not find the same...

<meta>The text breaks off as the author prepares to describe how even these two identical, masterfully crafted instruments produced different results.</meta>

both instruments were produced, but they varied from each other by two minutes. Henry Baten of Mechelen <note>A 13th-century astronomer and philosopher known for his work on the astrolabe.</note>, preeminent in this art as in all mathematics—for he wrote a noble treatise on the construction of the astrolabe—thinks it either impossible, or as he says, nearly impossible, for an instrument to be made that is in no way deceptive. He reports that while he was in Paris, he saw two very large quadrants <term>quadrant: an instrument used to measure the altitudes of celestial bodies</term> arranged with wonderful skill to observe the maximum height of the sun at noon (specifically at the summer solstice). By one instrument, the height was found to be sixty-four degrees and forty-two minutes; by the other, the same number of degrees but zero minutes. Therefore, there was an error in one or the other of forty-two minutes. 

See how easily even those who determine the horoscope of a birth by an instrument can be deceived—a point on which we have testified above that we were also warned by Avenrodam <note>Likely referring to the Andalusian scholar Ibn Rushd (Averroes) or his successors.</note>. Likewise, the same Baten whom we just cited proves in his *Mirror of Natural Things*, across many thousands of verses, that neither Ptolemy, nor Geber <note>Jabir ibn Aflah, a 12th-century Spanish-Arab astronomer.</note>, nor Albategni <note>Al-Battani, a major 9th-century astronomer whose observations corrected some of Ptolemy's data.</note> could track the size of the diameters of the Sun and Moon more certainly than through eclipses <term>defectus: eclipses or "failings" of light</term>, for the reliability of instruments on that matter would be suspect. I pass over how many ways Ptolemy in the *Great Composition* <note>Better known by its Arabic title, the *Almagest*.</note> and Alhazen <note>Ibn al-Haytham, the "father of optics."</note> in his seventh book on vision teach that the eyes can be deceived in observing the locations of stars. For even if the air is held to be clear and cloudless, what prevents a wind from blowing that is not felt? Yet the philosopher Aristotle writes that when the East Wind <term>Eurus: the southeast or east wind</term> blows, the stars appear larger. Leo Hebraeus <note>Levi ben Gershon, also known as Gersonides (1288–1344), a Jewish polymath who invented the Jacob's Staff.</note>, a distinguished man and famous mathematician, as if trusting the ancients too little, devised a new instrument, whose mathematical rules <term>canons: instructions or tables for use</term> we have seen to excel in subtlety. Nevertheless, when he had observed two fixed stars twice in the same year with it, he says the first observation differed from the second by two degrees, which he thinks should be attributed to the state of the atmosphere.

<page-num>672</page-num>

# X. Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

<meta>The "X" in the header likely refers to a book or section number in this edition, though the content continues the arguments of Book IX.</meta>

from his observations, he [Hipparchus] <note>Pico refers to Hipparchus (c. 190–120 BCE), the Greek astronomer who discovered the precession of the equinoxes.</note> calculated that less than a quarter part of a day should be added <note>Original Latin: *minus quarta parte diei*. This refers to the fraction over 365 days; a "quarter part" is 6 hours, as in the Julian year of 365.25 days.</note>, but he did not determine exactly how much was lacking for a perfect calculation. Two hundred and eighty-five years after him, **Ptolemy** defined that missing portion as the three-hundredth part of a day. **Al-Battani**, observing the heavens 743 years after Ptolemy, found the motion of the Sun to be faster, because it fell short of that quarter part by a one-hundredth and sixth part of a day. **Thabit** <note>Thabit ibn Qurra, a 9th-century mathematician and astronomer.</note> said the year consists of 365 days, 6 hours, 9 minutes, and 12 seconds. Then there is that great disagreement: some think all years are equal in length, such as Ptolemy and **Alfonso** <note>Referring to the Alfonsine Tables commissioned by King Alfonso X of Castile.</note>; others think they are unequal, such as **Arzachel**, **Baten**, and **Isaac the Israelite**, who are followed by others among the more recent scholars. These men believe that the Sun returns to the point from which it departed sometimes sooner and sometimes later. They claim the cause of this inequality is that the **eighth sphere** <term>eighth sphere: the firmament of fixed stars, which in the geocentric model was believed to rotate around the Earth.</term> is not always carried from West to East (as Ptolemy and many others think), but is sometimes carried from East to West. Therefore, when its motion is in the same direction toward which the Sun returns, the Sun's motion appears faster; when it moves in the opposite direction, the Sun appears slower. Hence, at different times, the year has been observed to be now longer, now shorter. 

And the Isaac whom we cited, in that book titled *Yesod Olam*—which is to say, *The Foundation of the World* <note>original: "Ieſodolam"</note>—wrote in his own time (specifically in the year of grace 1310, which was the year of the world 5700 <note>Note: The year 1310 AD corresponds to 5070-71 in the Hebrew calendar; the OCR "5700" is likely a transcription error or a typo in the original manuscript.</note> for the Hebrews) that he thought the years were at their shortest, such that they could not be shortened further; but he believed the time was now appearing when, by the motion of the eighth sphere, they would begin to gradually lengthen. Between the year that could be the longest and that which, conversely, is the shortest, he claimed the median duration is 365 days and 5 hours; then, dividing the hour into 1,080 parts, it has 996 of those parts; and finally 48 "scruples" or small minutes, each of which is the 76th part of one of those 1,080 parts. I remember reading this same meticulous calculation in a very ancient Hebrew writer, **Rabbi Adda bar Ahaba**, the son of Rabbi Abba. 

Finally, solar eclipses show just how much the motion of the Sun is in doubt; they often precede the time noted in the astronomical tables by more than half an hour. This is reported by **Andreas the Summarizer**, and is declared daily by the evidence of the senses. **Henry Baten of Mechelen**, in the book he titled *The Mirror of Natural Things*, asserts that in detecting eclipses—whether you look at the location, the hour, or the magnitude—anyone who follows the numerical motions of either Ptolemy or Al-Battani will fall into error. **Paolo the Florentine** <note>Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli (1397–1482), a famous Italian mathematician and astronomer.</note>, a distinguished mathematician, when he had observed the entry of the Sun into Aries <note>The spring equinox.</note> with the most diligent annotations, found it to be faster than the time defined in the tables by a third of an hour. **Pierre d'Ailly** also reports in his *Elucidarium* that when the Sun's entry into the vernal equinox was observed in Paris in the year of our Lord 1364, it was discovered that the **Alfonsine Tables** <note>The standard astronomical tables of the late Middle Ages.</note> fell away from the truth. 

Now, if they are blind in such broad daylight—that is, in the motion of the Sun, which is the most manifest of all, and where an error in one part makes an error in the rest inevitable—what will become of the motion of **Mercury**? That planet almost never shows itself to mortal eyes. **Sosigenes**, the teacher of Alexander of Aphrodisias, stated that it is never more than twenty-two degrees...

He highlights how even the most basic solar movements and eclipses regularly deviate from the "authoritative" astronomical tables.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s argument regarding the lack of consensus among astronomers. Having previously discussed the length of the year, he now focuses on the conflicting measurements of planetary positions and the tilt of the Earth's axis, leading into his main argument: if the mathematics are uncertain, the predictions must be false.</meta>

<page-num>673</page-num>
<header>Against Astrology, Book IX.</header>

Theon, Paulus, Heliodorus, and Porphyry <note>A group of late antique commentators and astrologers.</note> record that it <note>Likely referring to the planet Mercury, whose proximity to the sun makes its measurement difficult.</note> is able to be distant from the sun by twenty-three degrees; whereas Ptolemy says twenty-eight. Furthermore, concerning the motion of this planet, a certain distinguished mathematician confessed that he had discovered nothing for certain. Moreover, [he noted] that Mars was slower by almost one degree and thirty minutes than was previously thought—a thing he had discovered himself, though he remarked that in this matter the diligence of later scholars should be more exactly watchful. He likewise reported that the maximum declination of the sun from the equator <note>The "obliquity of the ecliptic," or the tilt of the Earth's axis.</note> observed by him was 23 degrees and 30 minutes, whereas Ptolemy recorded the same degrees but 51 minutes. Al-Battani <note>Latin: Albategni, a 9th-century Arab astronomer.</note> recorded 23 degrees, 36 minutes, and 30 seconds. Arzachel <note>Latin: Archazel, also known as Al-Zarqali, an 11th-century mathematician.</note> put forth a measurement of more than twenty-three degrees. Finally, Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>Latin: Abraam Auenazra, a prominent 12th-century Jewish polymath.</note>, the greatest mathematician, affirms in the sixth book of his *On Revolutions* that the degree that is in the "horoscope" <term>horoscopo — the "ascendant" or the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</term> cannot be found when the sun enters the first part of Aries. This is because the exact time when it reaches Aries can be grasped clearly neither by certain calculation of motion, nor by any kind of instrument. Averroes, in explaining Ptolemy, openly confesses this as well. The same Ibn Ezra, so often cited, whenever he was about to calculate anything by refined reason, used three types of canons <note>Standard astronomical tables.</note>: those of Ptolemy, the Persians, and the Indians, because they all varied from one another and determined the planets at different locations. Plutarch—who lived after Ptolemy and was a contemporary of the great Roman mathematician Aemilius under the Emperor Trajan—says in his *Roman Questions*: "Even at this time, when the highest peak of astrology has been reached, the inequality of times has nevertheless conquered the skill of the mathematicians, and very often escapes and deceives their numbers and calculations."

->THE ERROR OF A SINGLE DEGREE, OR EVEN OF A SINGLE MINUTE,<-
->SOMETIMES BREEDS MANY ERRORS; NEITHER THROUGH REVOLUTIONS OF<-
->YEARS OR NATAL CHARTS, NOR THROUGH GREAT CONJUNCTIONS,<-
->CAN THE ASTROLOGER JUDGE. Chapter 10.<-

**F**rom this uncertainty of the celestial motions, who does not see that the entire art of divinatory astrology is undermined? If it slips by a single degree, it is necessary that it fall away from all truth. For if the part of the sign in which a star is found is changed, the "bounds" <note>Original: *fines*. In astrology, these are subdivisions of zodiac signs ruled by different planets.</note> are often changed. All astrologers admit these bounds have equal power to the "houses," and some say more, and some the most. Occasionally the "exaltations" <note>Specific degrees where a planet's influence is said to be most powerful.</note>, which they have prescribed for determined parts, will certainly vary in the *monomoiria* <term>monomyriæ — a system where every single degree of the 360 in the zodiac is assigned to a specific planetary ruler</term>, and sometimes even at the borders of the "decans." And if a planet holds the last parts of a sign, it can happen that an error of one part transfers it from sign to sign; thus the Moon, which should have been in Taurus, might be in Gemini. Yet it would be fortunate in Taurus, but unfortunate in Gemini. Furthermore, it would be changed from a masculine part to a feminine one, from bright to dim, from dim to dark, from a "pit" <note>Original: *puteo*. Specific degrees considered "pitted" or "deep," which were thought to swallow a planet's strength.</note> to a height, from full degrees to empty ones, from sickly ones to the most fortunate. Finally, since among astrologers there is a different property for every single degree—and indeed even for the minutes, the distinct properties of which Aesculapius <note>Referring to a Hermetic text titled *Myriogenesis*, often attributed to the mythical Hermes Trismegistus or Aesculapius.</note> handed down in the *Myriogenesis*—how can the astrologer be far from error when the location of a planet varies by a degree or even by minutes?

He argues that because astrology relies on precise calculations of degrees and minutes, even a tiny mathematical discrepancy renders an entire astrological prediction false and contradictory.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s critique of astronomical precision. While the previous page focused on discrepancies in measuring the tilt of the earth and the distance of Mercury, this page argues that these small mathematical errors create massive failures in astrological predictions, particularly regarding the "Great Conjunctions" of Jupiter and Saturn.</meta>

<page-num>674</page-num>
<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

Will not the power of the star and its influence <note>original: "virtus sideris & influxus"</note> change? And just as an error in the degree sometimes changes the sign, so an error in minutes sometimes changes the degree. Indeed, even the "places" <note>Astrological "houses," twelve divisions of the sky.</note> will occasionally be deceptive due to a slip of a single degree; for example, a planet that should be in the west might be placed beneath the earth, and one that belongs to the ascendant <term>horoscopum — the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</term> might be pushed back into the darkness of the 12th house.

In the calculation of **dodecathemories** <term>dodecathemoriis — a system where each 30-degree zodiac sign is subdivided into twelve smaller parts of 2.5 degrees each</term>, an error of one degree will cause a wandering of twelve degrees; nor, if the starting point <note>original: "epocha"</note> of a star is held incorrectly, will any of the so-called **Lots** <term>sortium — mathematical points like the "Part of Fortune" calculated from the distances between planets and the ascendant</term> be correctly established. Add to this the deception in the "radiations" <note>The "aspects" or angles planets make with one another.</note> resulting from a variation of only one part; for a radiation does one thing if it is **partile** <note>exact to the same degree</note>, another if it is **applying** <note>moving toward an exact aspect</note>, and another if it is **separating** <note>moving away from an aspect</note>. 

Add the most serious error of all in **directing** <term>dirigendis — "primary directions," a complex calculation used to predict the timing of major life events</term> the rays of the planets as they ought to be: if the astrologer slips by one part, an error of one whole year will result. But these are merely the highest and greatest—nearly outrageous—failures in that profession. Yet, if you compare them to other errors, they will seem small. 

For it is necessary that they fall into these errors when they take the "initial hours" from the movements of the planets—a point we deferred discussing earlier. Suppose, then, the beginning of the year is to be established at the sun’s entry <note>the solar ingress</note> into the first minutes of Aries. Furthermore, if (as we have seen) they are mistaken there by more than half an hour, the constellation <note>the overall chart or arrangement of stars</note> will be entirely different, so great a variation will occur. 

The same will happen no less if they do not begin the year from the sun’s entry into Aries, but from the full moon or new moon preceding the year. And I do not see why **Ibn Ezra** <note>Latin: Auenazra</note> and **Averroes** <note>Latin: Auenrodan</note> think that error can be avoided in the former case, but not in the latter, since the hour of their meeting <note>the "coitus" or conjunction of sun and moon</note> cannot be clearly grasped unless the motion of both stars is correctly held. **Maclivanensis** <note>Likely a reference to a specific medieval commentator or a corrupted name of a known astronomer.</note> also objects to this. 

Likewise, regarding the annual revolutions of birth charts <note>solar returns</note>, when they are organized from the return of the sun to the same place: how will they not define them wrongly if the time of that restoration is unexplored? How will they correctly establish the ascendants of the **Great Conjunctions** <term>magnarum conjunctionum — the rare meeting of Jupiter and Saturn, believed to signal major historical or religious shifts</term> without having exactly comprehended the motions of Jupiter and Saturn? **Abraham** <note>Ibn Ezra</note> thinks we are so far from a perfect knowledge of these two that he pronounces it a great achievement if we even know the *day* on which they ought to be found together. **Joannes de Saxonia** <note>Latin: Saxonienis, a 14th-century astronomer.</note> agrees with this opinion; he says it is for this reason that the ascendant of a Great Conjunction is not considered to be what was rising at the hour of the conjunction itself, but rather what was rising at the beginning of the turning year in which it happened. 

Thus they defend error with error. But the ascendant of a conjunction does not cease to be what it is simply because it is unknown to us. Therefore, it should rather have been said that we *cannot* know what a conjunction will do because the horoscope cannot be known—rather than feigning another, false horoscope because the true one is unknown. For what does a conjunction have to do with the horoscope of a year that perhaps began many months earlier? Or what is the logic that we should observe the ascendant for eclipses of the luminaries, but not for conjunctions? 

Finally, even if it were granted that the ascendant of the year has power over the conjunction, they still will not deny that the conjunction's *own* ascendant is of equal or greater importance. Since an entirely different constellation arises from that unknown ascendant, they must necessarily waver in predicting the effects of the conjunction. I pass over the fact that the ascendant of the year is equally uncertain, according to the same author, Ibn Ezra. From all of which a shameful error is evident...

<header>Against Astrology, Book IX.</header>

Abu Ma'shar <note>original: "Aboasaris," the famous 9th-century Persian astrologer</note>, who in the first book of his *Greater Introduction* said it does not matter if an astrologer errs by one degree, showed by this statement that he plainly did not understand the astrology he was defending. Thus, it is no longer true to say—as many do—that astrology is accused only out of ignorance; rather, it is not condemned unless it is thoroughly inspected, not understood unless it is pursued, and not loved unless it is greeted only from a distance and from the threshold.

->DIFFERING OPINIONS ON THE MOVEMENTS OF THE EIGHTH<-
->sphere; the distance of the head of Aries of the eighth from the head of Aries<-
->of the ninth, and the apogee of the Sun. Chapter XI.<-

You see <note>The Latin text begins with a decorative initial 'V' for 'Vides' (You see), depicting a scholar observing the stars.</note> that so far we were speaking only of the movement of the planets, which are perhaps better understood; but who can faithfully report the movement of the "clinging" stars <note>The fixed stars, so called because they were thought to be fixed to the celestial sphere</note>? All astrology confesses that these stars possess great, indeed primary and wonderful power. Who, I ask, will correctly place the fixed stars in a birth chart? Or who will deny that an error of even one degree is of immense consequence? This is especially true when there is only one degree in which they are believed to be effective—that is, either at the angles <note>The cardinal points of a chart: Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, and Imum Coeli</note> or with the luminaries <note>The Sun and the Moon</note>. "But," they say, "we have them all in astrolabes and in tables of numbers described everywhere and by everyone." This, in fact, is what I was warning about when we began to dispute these things: that these matters seem easiest to the trivial astrologers, whose entire learning comes from a few small pamphlets, but they are inextricable puzzles to the teachers and experts. When the experts consult slightly more remote literature, they see that masters of equal authority disagree on these matters as much as the east is distant from the west.

The Egyptians, the Chaldeans, and indeed every ancient opinion, thought that the wandering stars <note>The planets</note> moved by only one motion, which we call the diurnal <note>The daily rotation of the sky from East to West</note>. Hipparchus <note>A Greek astronomer of the 2nd century BCE, credited with discovering the precession of the equinoxes</note> introduced another motion, by which they would be carried, like the planets, from west to east. Let this, therefore, be the first controversy: whether they move by their own motion or not. More recent writers will say there is no controversy, since it is not surprising that things were observed by the younger astronomers that the ancients could not yet have detected.

But there are also those among the more recent writers who defend the opinion of the ancients, and who do not doubt that those who thought otherwise were deceived. Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher and mathematician</note>, who lived long after Ptolemy, was most skilled in all mathematics, as is easily declared both by his astrological suppositions and his treatises on the sphere and the composition of the astrolabe, his commentaries on Euclid, and many other things he wrote. In his commentaries on the *Timaeus* <note>Plato's dialogue regarding the creation of the universe</note>, as he also does elsewhere, he rebukes Hipparchus and Ptolemy for thinking that the non-wandering stars revolve toward the east around the poles of the zodiac, completing one degree every hundred years. Instead, he argues that we should follow the Egyptians and Chaldeans, who produced nothing of this kind in their long-term observations—especially since our senses testify to the ancient tradition in such a way that Ptolemy could not disagree unless he were blind <note>original: "exoculatus"</note>. For if they move, he says, upon the poles of the zodiac, as Hipparchus and Ptolemy think, it would have been necessary in these places for the Bear <note>The constellation Ursa Major</note> to tilt not a little toward its setting—which, however, has been called "unsetting" <note>original: "inoccidua," or circumpolar stars that never drop below the horizon</note> since the time of Homer—and it would be necessary that Canopus <note>The second brightest star in the sky</note> should no longer be seen, although that star is visible to those living in the third climate <note>Historical geographic divisions of the earth based on latitude</note>...

<meta>This page continues Pico’s argument regarding the Eighth Sphere—the celestial vault containing the "fixed stars."
