<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

...completes a brief period above the horizon <note>original: "finitorem"</note>, but to those who inhabit Rhodes, it provides a rising, as Posidonius <note>A Greek Stoic philosopher and astronomer</note> writes. Since, therefore, the Bear <note>Ursa Major or Minor</note> appears today as non-setting just as it always appeared so many centuries ago, and Canopus has maintained the same position, it is detected by the evidence of the senses that the movement of the "clinging" <note>fixed</note> stars introduced by more recent thinkers is false.

If they should perhaps object that the calculations of the movements of the planets are correctly gathered by the testimony of the senses by those who, in arranging numbers and in the exposition of the astronomical tables <note>original: "canonis"</note>, assume the movement of the fixed stars, he says the objection is dissolved in two ways: First, because even those who omit that movement of the fixed stars when calculating the movements of the planets must establish tables regarding the revolutions of the stars that are consistent with appearances; although they mistakenly make them immobile, they nevertheless arrive at a result that fits the most true reasoning. Secondly, it is well known that the truth can be gathered from false calculations; therefore, the fact that the result corresponds to the senses does not prove the truth of the underlying assumptions.

That most learned philosopher and mathematician **Abraham Ibn Ezra** <note>original: "Abraam Auenaz," a 12th-century Jewish scholar</note>, though he often mentions both opinions—one making the non-wandering stars mobile and the other making them immobile (which he ascribes to the Indians)—never judges between them beforehand. Instead, he leaves the matter undecided, so that in his *Book of Nativities* he commands that a double birth chart be made: one as if the stars moved, and the other as if they did not move. 

And although I define nothing regarding these matters except this one thing—that nothing certain can be defined—it is nevertheless very true that the following favors the opinion of the ancients: the supporters of the opposite dogma agree on nothing among themselves. For **Ptolemy**, following **Hipparchus**, thinks they always move from the west toward the east. **Arzachel the Moor** <note>Al-Zarqali, an 11th-century Arab astronomer from Toledo</note> says that when they have proceeded a certain distance, they return from the east toward the west—an opinion followed by **Isaac the Israelite**, who says it was observed with the most certain experiences. **Thabit ibn Qurra** <note>original: "Thebit benchorath," a 9th-century Sabian astronomer</note> strikes out this movement and devises another that turns toward the south and the north. More recent thinkers, approving of Thabit's discovery, also admit Ptolemy’s opinion, tearing the Eighth Sphere apart with a triple motion. 

Furthermore, those who agree with Ptolemy that the stars progress toward the east and do not change their course still fight among themselves over the speed of that course, thinking it false that one degree is completed in one hundred years. For **Averroes** <note>original: "Auen."</note>, **Moses the Egyptian** <note>Maimonides</note>, and **Ibn Ezra** teach that the space of one degree is crossed every 70 years. **Albategni** <note>Al-Battani, a 9th-century astronomer</note> says after 66 years, making them faster than Ptolemy by nearly a ratio of six to four. **Paolo of Florence** <note>Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli, the famous 15th-century cosmographer</note> used to assert that they rolled even more swiftly than Albategni had said. 

Who will judge between these opinions? "We younger men," they say, "have detected their locations with faithful instruments, so we cannot be deceived." What then? Did it deceive those ancients, who did not lack instruments, nor had less skill in the art than you? It is commonly said in this time that the mobile **Aries** <note>The "first point of Aries" used as a reference for the zodiac</note> is distant from the immobile Aries by twenty-five degrees. But Ibn Ezra, in a certain book titled *On the Eight Parts of Astrology*, records what the distance was when he was writing; for he wrote in the year of human salvation 1153. Therefore, he preceded our times by about 340 years, more or less. Accordingly, if the movement which Albategni...

<meta>This page continues Pico's critique of astronomical precision. Having previously discussed the visibility of constellations like Canopus, he now moves to the mathematical discrepancies between various historical authorities regarding the "Precession of the Equinoxes"—the slow shift of the stars relative to the spring equinox.</meta>

<page-num>677</page-num>
<header>Against Astrology, Book IX.</header>

...which is swifter than the rest, let us follow him. Not more years have passed since the time of **Ibn Ezra** <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra, a 12th-century Spanish Jewish scholar and astronomer</note> to our own day than would allow the stars to have advanced five degrees; therefore, the distance today would not be 25 degrees (as some say), but thirteen. Was Ibn Ezra therefore mistaken? For he possessed both reason and the proper instruments. **Moses the Egyptian** <note>Moses Maimonides, the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher</note>—in that book titled *Mishneh Torah* <note>original: "Mis-methora," meaning "Repetition of the Law"</note>, which you might call in Greek *Deuterosis* <note>original: "δευτερωσιν"</note> and in Latin *the Second Law*—says at the beginning of the first part: at the time of the Great Flood, the "moving" Aries <note>the point in the sky marking the start of spring</note> coincided with the "immobile" Aries <note>the actual constellation of stars in the physical vault of heaven</note>. After that time, the **eighth sphere** <note>the celestial sphere containing the fixed stars</note> has always moved toward the east at a rate of one degree every seventy years. Since the waters flooded the earth in the year 1,656 from the creation of the world <note>Anno Mundi</note>, and now (according to more accurate calculations) nearly 5,300 years have passed since the world's beginning—for it does not matter here to demand a perfectly exact figure—there are nearly 3,600 years or thereabouts from the Flood to our time. Therefore, the eighth sphere would have moved more or less fifty-two degrees in those years, which would be the distance separating the moving Aries from the immobile one.

**Isaac the Israelite** <note>Isaac Israeli ben Joseph, a 14th-century astronomer</note> writes that both signs coincided in the year 560 after the birth of Christ. **Pierre d’Ailly** <note>Petrus Alliacensis, a French bishop and theologian</note> records in his *Elucidarium* that this occurred in the year 260 AD, a calculation that disagrees with the former by three hundred years. **Angelo of Mantua** and many more recent authors contend that this occurred in the fifteenth year of Grace <note>AD 15</note>, with a few months added. Isarith reports the same, noting that a certain younger scholar, when he had calculated the positions of the Sun and Moon in relation to the eighth sphere, found a New Moon in the month of March—after 5,224 years had passed since the creation of the world—nearly at the fourteenth part <note>degree</note> of Pisces. But he found that Angelo, calculating that same New Moon relative to the immobile signs (since he was using the tables of **Emanuel** which he titled *Baal Cuaphim*), found it at the twenty-eighth degree of Pisces; if he followed the **Alfonsine Tables** <note>astronomical tables commissioned by King Alfonso X of Castile</note>, he found it at twenty-seven degrees and fourteen minutes. From this, it would be concluded that the moving signs were thirteen or fourteen degrees distant from the immobile ones.

Now, this man wrote a few years before our own age, which is why he says it is a marvel to him that the **Oxford Tables** <note>original: "Ozonienses tabulae"</note> record the star situated between the horns of Aries—which is the beginning of the moving Aries—as being removed from the immobile Aries in the year of Grace 1360 by twenty-four degrees and fifty-seven minutes. During that time, I find that both that Isaac and **Roger Bacon** <note>the 13th-century English philosopher and scientist</note> flourished nearly forty years earlier, both of whom thought the immobile Aries varied from the moving one by no more than ten degrees in their lifetime. For both followed **al-Zarqali** <note>original: "Azerchelem," an 11th-century Arab mathematician</note>, who thought the maximum distance that could occur between them was ten degrees; Isaac recorded that this limit had been reached in his own time. Therefore, the time was approaching for them to start moving back again toward the west in a reversed motion <note>Pico is referring to "trepidation," a defunct theory that the stars oscillated back and forth rather than moving in a continuous circle</note>. Let us therefore conclude: either the mathematical instruments do not fail, or they do. If they do not fail, how is it that Isaac and Roger, observing the stars of the moving Aries, did not...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s systematic dismantling of astrology’s claims to precision. On the previous page, he cited historical discrepancies regarding the movement of the stars (precession). Here, he focuses on the internal disagreements between major astronomical authorities concerning the position of the sun and the mathematical methods for calculating "directions"—the techniques used to predict the timing of future events in a person's life.</meta>

<page-num>678</page-num>
<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

...they judged that the stars had moved more than ten parts <note>degrees</note> from the equinox. However, if the true opinion of the Oxford Tables <note>The 14th-century astronomical tables calculated at Merton College, Oxford</note>, or that of more recent scholars, is correct, they moved more than twenty-three parts from that point—making an error of thirteen degrees evident. If these men are mistaken, how can our own astrologers know they themselves are not mistaken, when the leading men in this art disagree with such a vast variety of opinions? Among these, if anyone thinks he can reach a judgment, he does so by brute impulse rather than by a method capable of judging the heavens. Therefore, whoever offers an opinion on the locations of the fixed stars <note>original: "non erraticarum," referring to the "fixed" stars as opposed to "wandering" planets</note> might perhaps avoid error by chance, but he will certainly not achieve it through reason. 

Nor should we overlook the fact that **Proclus** <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> and **Ptolemy** <note>The 2nd-century author of the *Almagest*, the most influential astronomical text of the Middle Ages</note> deny that the <term>apogee</term> <note>the point in an orbit farthest from Earth</note> and <term>perigee</term> <note>the point in an orbit closest to Earth</note> of the Sun move at all. Yet there is a point which they call by the barbaric name <term>augen</term> <note>from the Arabic *auj*, referring to the solar apogee</note> and its opposite, which more recent scholars claim does move; these scholars are rebuked by **Leo the Hebrew** <note>Levi ben Gershom, also known as Gersonides, a 14th-century Jewish polymath</note>, who defends the true opinion of Ptolemy. I will pass over how little they know and how fiercely they clash regarding the <term>equation of days</term> <note>the correction needed to account for the Sun's irregular apparent motion</note>, which leads to the greatest uncertainty in casting a <term>horoscope</term> <note>specifically referring to the "Ascendant" or the exact point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</note>.

### ON DIRECTIONS, HOW MANIFOLD
->the opinions of astrologers. Chapter XII.<-

**B**eyond all these issues remains the inextricable task of calculating "rays" <note>astrological aspects or angles between planets</note> and those points which Ptolemy calls <term>apheses</term> <note>original: "αφέσεις," meaning "releasors" or starting points for life-span calculations</note> and are commonly called <term>directions</term> <note>original: "peripachos," a corruption of the Greek for "circuits"</note>. For the mathematicians stab each other with mutual wounds on both sides; they cannot rely on any equal authority, nor could they settle any matter through the experience of so many ages. 

The opinion of more recent scholars is that the most exact "radiation" <note>the projection of astrological influence</note> is composed from <term>ascensions</term> <note>original: "anaphoras," the time it takes for a sign to rise over the horizon</note> that are right, oblique, or mixed, according to the variety of locations. But this leads to the following: if someone is born in a region where the <term>zenith</term> <note>the point directly overhead</note> is 48 degrees above the horizon, and the first part of Capricorn is in the horoscope, the <term>trine</term> <note>a 120-degree aspect</note> radiation would be in the parts of Cancer—which, however, we know is diametrically opposite to Capricorn <note>a 180-degree opposition, not a trine</note>. 

**Henry Baten** <note>Henry Baten of Mechelen, a 13th-century astronomer</note> observes the configuration of planets based on their physical locations, so that a trine is formed by whatever occupies the fifth house relative to the horoscope, regardless of the zodiac sign; and so on for the others. **Albategni** <note>Al-Battani, a 9th-century Arab astronomer</note> counts the intervals by the degrees of the zodiac, which they call "equal" unless a star declines to one side or the other, although the number varies little because of that—not more than thirty minutes even if it declines by ten degrees. This was the method followed and handed down by **Johannes Regiomontanus** <note>The most famous 15th-century German mathematician and astronomer</note>, and by **Abraham** <note>Ibn Ezra</note>, the prince and teacher of **Ibn Ezra**. 

But if you say that experience has shown that these charts should be composed through "ascensions," Ibn Ezra will resist; he will say that through many observations it has been noted infinitely many times that they must be established by equal degrees. There are some who always use "right ascensions," which we have already shown above was falsely attributed to Ptolemy. Furthermore, Ptolemy does not observe <term>latitude</term> <note>the distance of a planet north or south of the ecliptic</note> except in the case of planets in conjunction. **Abenragel** <note>Ibn Abi al-Rijal, an 11th-century Arab astrologer</note> observes it in every radiation except the diameter <note>opposition</note>. **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar, a 9th-century Persian astrologer</note> observes it even in the diameter, for which they criticize him. I pass over how much they disagree on how far the power of a "ray" extends: there are those who say three degrees, those who prefer five; for the Moon, some say up to twelve parts, and some even thirteen, as **Porphyry** <note>A 3rd-century scholar and astrologer</note> says. A similar question, and an inexplicable disagreement among mathematicians, exists regarding directions (as they call them)...

<summary>Pico highlights the massive discrepancies (up to thirteen degrees) between various astronomical tables and authorities like Ptolemy, Al-Battani, and Regiomontanus. He argues that if these "leading men" cannot agree on basic measurements or the correct way to calculate astrological "directions," the entire practice of astrology is based on guesswork rather than science.</summary>

Having previously discussed the inaccuracies in measuring the positions of the sun and stars, Pico now highlights the fundamental lack of consensus among the greatest astronomical authorities regarding "directions"—the mathematical methods used to calculate the timing of events in a human life.</meta>

<page-num>679</page-num>
<header>Against Astrology, Book IX.</header>

...let us speak further) For the Egyptians indeed always used the <term>anaphorae</term> <note>rising times of the signs of the zodiac</note> of the region. Dorotheus <note>Dorotheus of Sidon, a 1st-century astrologer</note>, in directing the first part, always used "right" qualities <note>referring to right ascensions</note>, which Abraham <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra</note> testifies corresponds most frequently to experience. Ptolemy and almost all later authors, when a star is positioned in the east or west, [direct] through the <term>ascensions</term> <note>the time it takes for a sign to rise over the horizon</note> of the region; when they are placed in the fourth or tenth house <note>the Lower and Upper Midheavens</note>, they use the equator; but in the middle locations, they use a mixture of both. The same is felt by Al-Ma'mun <note>An 8th-century Caliph and patron of astronomy</note> in the seventh chapter of the fourth treatise on directions. Abu Ma'shar <note>A famous 9th-century Persian astrologer</note> directs by the degrees of the zodiac; for thus, in the eighth "difference" of the second treatise of his book *On Great Conjunctions*, he directs the Moon to the place of the conjunction of the "unfortunate" stars <note>the "malefics" Saturn and Mars</note>. Abraham Ibn Ezra thinks the same in the book titled <term>The Beginning of Wisdom</term> <note>original: "initia sapientiae"</note>, confirming it also by the authority of Al-Battani <note>A 9th-century Arab astronomer</note>. There are those who think both ways: that the "rays" <note>astrological aspects</note> should be extended and the stars directed through both the degrees of the zodiac and the proportion of the <term>anaphorae</term>, which John of Seville <note>A 12th-century translator of Arabic science</note> seems to have intended in his <term>Isagoge</term> <note>Introduction</note>. For in the second part of his <term>Quadripartitum</term> <note>Four-part work</note>, in the chapter on the first house, he performed the same. Others indeed extend the rays through the degrees of the zodiac but direct by ascensions, which Ibn Ridwan <note>An 11th-century Egyptian physician and astrologer</note> seems to have ascribed to Mashallah <note>An 8th-century Persian Jewish astrologer</note> and also to Ptolemy. On the contrary, Abraham the Jew <note>Ibn Ezra</note> brings the same reasoning to both tasks: that the charts should be composed by equal degrees, and directions should be made through them. I will omit how much they disagree on which direction a planet should be led—one can see where Ptolemy differs from others in his <term>Apotelesmata</term> <note>The "Tetrabiblos," his foundational astrological work</note>, with Ibn Ridwan explaining some of it—but we will not discuss here how great a difficulty exists for those who think mixed ascensions must be used in executing these teachings. For the most learned have judged that Ptolemy taught this with little correctness or sufficiency. Paul the German <note>Paul of Middelburg, a contemporary of Pico and future bishop</note>, a distinguished mathematician who now lives with Guidobaldo, the Duke of Urbino—a most learned prince—wrote once that he had never seen anyone who correctly directed a star to a trine aspect <note>original: "locum triangulum," a 120-degree relationship between planets</note>; moreover (as should have been said above), he denies that the circulating tables for the latitudes of the planets are reliable. From all these things—whether in determining the initial hours of births, of cities, or of constellations; then in arranging the "theme" <note>the birth chart</note>, whether the "angles" <note>the four primary points of a chart</note> are established, or the houses are defined, or the signs are divided, or seats are assigned to stars (either fixed or wandering), or charts are composed, or <term>apheses</term> <note>techniques for "releasing" time-periods to predict life events</note> are counted—how great a door stands open to errors, since until now, the truth and mathematical certainty concerning these things lies hidden and unexplored in the cave of Heraclitus <note>A reference to the philosopher Heraclitus's famous saying that "Nature loves to hide" and that truth is found in the depths</note>.

->THE END OF BOOK IX OF THE DISPUTATIONS OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA<-
->Against Astrology.<-

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA 
## Mirandola’s Disputations Against 
## Astrology, Book X.

### EPILOGUE OF WHAT HAS BEEN ACCOMPLISHED SO FAR,
### and what must be done in the following books. Chapter 1.

**W**e have already cast down the matter of astrology by many steps. We have shown that the fates of all lower things neither hang from the heavens nor are signified by them. We also argued that even if they did depend upon the heavens, it would not be in any way other than through a natural kinship <note>Pico means physical influence like heat or light, rather than mystical "fate."</note>. Both of these points were confirmed by the perpetual and stable condition of the celestial bodies, which are always equal and similar to themselves; they do not change like a chameleon—as astrologers imagine—based on the power of their locations or distances.

Next, we denied that what the heavens might do or indicate could be understood by us. This is partly because our human weakness cannot know which hours are truly "fatal" <note>original: "horas illas fatales," referring to the exact moment of birth or beginning</note>, nor can we know to whom in the "celestial chorus" the power of decreeing fate has been assigned. Certainly, whatever the astrologers have handed down on these matters wanders entirely away from reason. They have turned things into "origins" which are not origins at all, while omitting the true ones. Either through ignorance or negligence of the most powerful celestial factors, they use invented and fabulous causes in their predictions. These causes possess no inherent truth, and therefore no power to actually effect anything.

Thirdly, it was declared that even if the astrologers found no fault in what we have said, they have still not achieved what they hoped. Instead, it has been revealed that the task they must complete is impenetrable and impassable to human footsteps: namely, to track down the initial hours of birth and to grasp every state and position of their invented celestial causes at every single moment. In the previous book, we argued that neither of these can be known.

But even if they had accomplished all these things, they would still be so far from fulfilling their duty that they would not have even begun their task. For the labor proper to the astrologer is this: once the <term>theme</term> <note>original: "themate," referring to the horoscope or birth chart</note> has been established—which is the work of a mathematician—he must investigate what that specific constellation actually *does*. This is the most difficult task of all. If these claims were proven to stand by reason, astrology would be a science; if they stood by experiments, it would be an art. But if they stand by neither reason nor experiment, then it is certainly neither an art nor a science, but rather rashness, an unstable trickery, and the most fabulous fiction of charlatans. First, therefore, we shall strip from the astrologers the authority of reason, and then the reliability of experiment.

<meta>catchword: Reason</meta>

->THE REASONS OF THE ASTROLOGERS ARE EMPTY AND<-
->ridiculous. Chapter II.<-

**A**ristotle, **Plato**, and the other philosophers, relying on reason, have handed down certain general truths about the stars—their eternal substance, their circular motion, and other things of that kind—but they never produced the specific properties of the stars. Reason indicates nothing about them that could be called "physical." In contrast, we know the peculiar gifts of the corruptible things we deal with, which we feel closely and know intimately, only through their outcomes and effects. However, the reasons that astrologers have fashioned to prove their dogmas are so far removed from reason that nothing more irrational could be imagined. Not only are they non-demonstrative or inferior even to the rhetorical shortcuts known as enthymemes <note>An "enthymeme" is a logical argument where one premise is implied rather than stated; Pico is saying astrologers' logic is even weaker than a simple persuasive speech.</note>, but they are false, futile, conflicting, flawed, and ridiculous—as we shall make clear by examining them each in order.

->THE DOUBLE PRINCIPLE BY WHICH ASTROLOGERS DECIDE<-
->WHICH HOUSE IS STRONGER IS FALSE; AND EVEN IF IT WERE TRUE,<-
->WHAT THEY DESIRE DOES NOT FOLLOW FROM IT. Chapter III.<-

**W**e shall begin with the reasons by which they prove the properties of the "places" <note>In astrology, "places" refers to the twelve Houses of a birth chart.</note>; yet we have already declared above that these places have no properties and that their boundaries cannot be known. First, we will deal with the quantity of power in these places. Second, we will deal with their quality, declaring that the principles they rely on are everywhere false; and even if they were true, what the astrologers want cannot be concluded from them. There is a kind of double "preamble" by which they define who is stronger or weaker in which place. One is that those places prevail which are connected to the ascendant <term>horoscope: here used in the technical sense of the "Ascendant," the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth</term> by an affinity of radiation, namely the trine <note>original: "trigona," an aspect of 120 degrees</note>, the square <note>original: "quadrangula," an aspect of 90 degrees</note>, or the sextile <note>original: "sexangula," an aspect of 60 degrees</note>. On the other hand, the "lazy" or "dejected" places are those which are not so joined. The second principle is that the "hinges"—which they call the angles—are of the first power; in the second place are those houses following the angles <note>known as "succedent" houses</note>; and third are those which decline from them, which in Greek are called *apoclimata* and the barbarians call "cadent" <note>original: "cadentia." Pico often refers to medieval Arabic sources as "the barbarians."</note>. First, then, these principles are false; or if they are granted, the things they understand from them are mostly repugnant both to each other and to these very principles. 

The falsehood of the principles is demonstrated thus: the efficacy of the places cannot be referred to anything other than the relationship of the place above the horizon <term>finitor: the horizon line that bounds our vision</term>, so that a star is thought more effective in that position where, being placed above us, it acts more strongly. A philosopher, persuaded by natural reason, will grant this immediately, and the astrologer is forced to grant it as well. For this power of the places is sought either from the nature of the space itself or from that relationship to us which we mentioned. It cannot be derived from the space itself—not only because there is no natural force in that space, as we showed above—but because if I were to say that, the ascendant and the division of places would remain the same regardless of what region was established. Indeed, if defined parts of space had their own properties by which they affected the stars placed therein, they would not vary according to the sky, but would be the same for everyone. But this is entirely repugnant to the whole of astrology, which decrees that the same star placed in the same part of space...

<meta>The text cuts off here at the catchword "ascens," which likely leads into "ascensio" (ascension) or "ascendente" (ascendant) on the next page.</meta>

<summary>Pico begins Book X by attacking the logical foundations of astrological "houses," arguing that the methods astrologers use to determine which parts of the sky are powerful are mathematically inconsistent and physically impossible.</summary>

<page-num>682</page-num>
<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

## Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

...with one ascending, for others in the second place, for others in the twelfth, for others in the third, for others in the eleventh, according to the various inclinations of the sky. This <note>The "inclination" or angle of the sky.</note> should not be the focus; rather, we should look at the nature of the space from which these properties would result, not its relationship to us. For while the slope of the sky never changes, this relationship to us is always changing. But if a place is granted to be more effective because a planet's position there acts more strongly upon us, then those foundations concerning the "angles" and the horoscope <note>The "angles" are the four most important points in a chart: the Ascendant, Descendant, Midheaven, and Lower Midheaven.</note> immediately collapse. First, any place beneath the earth would be weaker than all those above the earth; neither the fifth nor the fourth place would be preferred over the twelfth or eighth. Furthermore, among those above the earth, whichever rises higher above the horizon <note>original: "finitorem"</note> would be judged more powerful; therefore, the twelfth house would prevail over the first.

John of Eschenden <note>original: "Aschedensis"; a 14th-century English astrologer and physician.</note>, an astrological author of a "Summa" which he calls "English," conceded this point, trusting in an entirely indissoluble reason rather than the authority of all other astrologers. But Ptolemy also saw this reason, and mostly followed it in the first book of his *Judicial Astrology* <note>original: "apotelefmaton"; referring to the *Tetrabiblos*.</note>. He established that the strongest place of all is the Midheaven <note>original: "medium coeli"</note>, because the rays of the planets positioned there affect us most powerfully. The next place in power is the eleventh, for the same reason, while those planets are weakest which are midway between the west and the bottom of the earth. 

However, these claims conflict with other astrologers, the majority of whom place the East <note>The Ascendant.</note> above all other places—such as Messahala, Firmicus, and Abu Ma'shar <note>original: "Aboafar"</note>. Nevertheless, Abraham ibn Ezra <note>original: "Auenazra"</note> agrees with Ptolemy; for this reason, he does not make all the "angles" <note>The four cardinal houses.</note> primary, but prefers the eleventh place to all others except the highest <note>The Midheaven.</note>. Finally, if these sayings are maintained, they make a planet in the fifth place the weakest, since it is halfway between the fourth and seventh places. 

Yet in his third book, when speaking about the span of years, Ptolemy prefers everything above the earth to those things below the earth; but forgetting what he had said before, he prefers the East to the eleventh place. Then, following the other astrologers, he rejects the twelfth house for a reason that is certainly too futile and false: because, he says, a thicker and dark vapor of the earth, exhaling from moisture, disturbs and weakens the power descending from those stars. 

Certainly, if this reasoning holds, a person born in foggy weather would always be born unlucky, as all his planets would be under darkness, as if they were placed in the twelfth house. Furthermore, why would a star positioned in the East not suffer this more? Or could the light already created above not yet dissipate the many vapors and smoky fumes it was able to lift? Truly, perhaps this occurs with the sun; but at noon, what star residing in the twelfth place will be hindered by vaporous air? 

Therefore, he more correctly observed in his first book only that the Midheaven would be the most powerful among other places, being more or less intense depending on how much it approached or receded from the summit. This is the only thing that can be said naturally, if we weigh only the efficacy of natural forces. For perhaps a place below the West could have a property of some influence that the Midheaven does not have (if such differences even exist). But as for a planet acting strongly, what other cause could there be than its power to diffuse rays toward the horizon? It is therefore quite foolish to claim a fixed star is powerful in the fourth place—that is, hiding beneath the bottom of the earth—even if it should shine...

<summary>Pico critiques the contradictory theories of famous astrologers like Ptolemy and Ibn Ezra regarding which "houses" of the sky are most powerful. He mocks Ptolemy’s idea that the 12th house is weak due to "earthly vapors," pointing out the logical absurdity of such a physical explanation for a symbolic system.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s critique of the astrological "houses." On the previous page, he argued that the power of these houses should logically depend on their physical position in the sky relative to the observer; here, he points out that the traditional meanings assigned to these houses by astrologers frequently contradict their own geometric and physical principles.</meta>

<page-num>683</page-num>
<header>on Astrology, Book X</header>

...even at the very highest point of the sky, if it does not reach the pivot <note>The "pivot" or "angle" refers to the four most powerful points in a chart: the Midheaven, Ascendant, Descendant, and Lower Midheaven.</note> in those parts, it will be considered to have no strength. No one will ever persuade any person that a planet in the twelfth house is not "vital" <note>In traditional astrology, the 12th house was associated with hidden enemies and confinement, often considered "weak" or "malefic."</note> while one placed in the fifth is, when the fifth house could much more reasonably be called the "seat of darkness" than the twelfth. No one can be persuaded that we are more strongly affected by the Sun when it is still 25 degrees away from the east than when, having slipped by a single degree, it is submerged into the west—even though in the first case it belongs to the Ascendant, and in the second, to the sixth house. Much less will they persuade anyone (unless they lack all common sense) that a planet is more powerful in the fourth house—that is, at the dead of night—than if it occupied the eighth or twelfth house. For the "trine connection" <note>A "trine" is a harmonious astrological aspect where planets are 120 degrees apart.</note> with the horoscope <note>The "horoscope" here refers specifically to the Ascendant or the first house.</note> is rejected based on what was said above regarding the intervals of rays; if we wish to follow right reason, the **rising** <note>original: "anaphora"</note> of the horoscope is more relevant to its power than "Good Fortune" <note>The 11th house was traditionally named "Good Fortune."</note> which is distant by so many spaces.

But if such a connection carries weight, why would a place joined to a better pivot not be more powerful? Reason teaches, and various astrologers agree, that the "highest pivot" <note>The Midheaven (MC), the highest point in the sky.</note> is the best of all. Therefore, the sixth house, which is triangular <note>In a trine aspect.</note> to that point, ought to be numbered among the "good" houses, for the same reason the ninth is linked to the Ascendant. So much for the falsehood of their principles; now let us see how their decrees disagree with those very principles. For the eighth house is not always "bad" if it is supposedly bad because it is disconnected from the Ascendant; a planet located there often supports the east with a "trine ray." Similarly, in the second house, a **hexagonal radiation** <note>A "sextile" aspect (60 degrees), usually considered harmonious.</note> sometimes reaches the horoscope. Therefore, what they conclude is not universally true unless the places are divided by the degrees of the zodiac; but they do not accept this, and thus their conclusions amount to nothing. 

Let them also answer this: since an affinity with the Ascendant and the "angle" makes a place good, is one of these privileges enough, or are both required? If one is enough, then the eighth house (succeeding the west) would be good; if both are required, then the second house (separated from the Ascendant) would be bad. Heliodorus also writes, following the opinion of Paul <note>Likely Paul of Alexandria, a 4th-century astrologer.</note> and others, that "evil" and "unfortunate" planets cause more intense harm and injury when they are in "declines" <note>Cadent houses (3rd, 6th, 9th, 12th), which "fall away" from the angles.</note>; but if the lowest place, by its very nature, is meant to <gloss>resist</gloss> <note>original: "ἀντιπᾶν"</note>, then it ought to dull the rays of "bad" planets just as much as it does the "good" ones.

---

### THE ARGUMENTS OF ASTROLOGERS BY WHICH THEY
### STRENGTHEN THEIR DOGMAS CAN BE REDUCED TO ABOUT FIVE 
### KINDS, WHICH ARE WEAK AND INEFFECTIVE. Chapter IV.

Let us now examine the errors by which they prove the properties of the houses: that this one signifies brothers, another parents, another friends, this one death, and another enemies. However, to avoid refuting the same things repeatedly, I will first strike down certain **types of argument** that astrologers use whenever they intend to prove anything. Then, as we overturn the foundations of each specific dogma, we will simply point out which category of the already-censured arguments it belongs to. We shall do this in the appropriate places, so that once the principles and the form of their reasoning are granted, we can show that the conclusions they expect do not actually follow. There are roughly five headings to which you may reduce all astrological proof. The first may be called the argument from the **order of numbers**; the second, from **parabolic similarity**; the third, from **mathematical reasons**...

<meta>The text continues on the next page with the fourth and fifth types of arguments.</meta>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s systematic dismantling of the logical foundations of astrology. Having previously discussed the physical positions of the "houses," he now moves to the fourth and fifth arguments, which concern the symbolic order of numbers and the principles of logic (dialectics).</meta>

<page-num>684</page-num>
<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

## Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

...the fourth from astrological principles, the fifth from dialectical <note>In this context, "dialectical" refers to the formal rules of logic and debate used in universities.</note> ones. From the order of numbers, they argue as follows: the first climate <note>In ancient geography, "climates" were latitudinal zones of the earth, each supposedly ruled by a planet.</note> is subject to Saturn, the second to Jupiter, the third to Mars, because Saturn is the first of the planets, Jupiter the second, and Mars the third. There are 12 places <note>The twelve "houses" of an astrological chart.</note> and 12 signs. Therefore, the first sign corresponds to the first place, the second to the second, and so on. But the third sign is Gemini; therefore, the third place signifies brothers, as if they were twins <note>original: "geminos"</note>. Similarly, the first planet corresponds to the first place, the second to the second, and the third to the third. But Jupiter, the second star, signifies riches. Therefore, there will be a signification over riches in the second place. This method derived from numbers is easily refuted. Indeed, if one were speaking with philosophers or logicians, this argument not only fails to compel, but it does not even follow; it not only fails to persuade, it does not even encourage belief. 

First, it is a futile and quite insane supposition that the "first" in one category must agree by some natural kinship with the "first" of another category. Fire is the first element, and Saturn is the first of the planets; yet what is more different from fire, according to the astrologers themselves, than Saturn <note>Astrologers traditionally defined Saturn as cold and dry, the opposite of fire's heat.</note>? Mars is the third of the planets, and water the third element; does Mars not differ from water as much as fire differs from water? Aries is the first sign, and Saturn is the first planet, yet for astrologers, Aries has no proportion with Saturn; Saturn does not rule in it, nor does he dominate there—on the contrary, he is "depressed" <note>In astrology, a planet is "depressed" or "in fall" in a sign where its influence is weakened. Saturn is in its fall in Aries.</note> there. 

Therefore, it is a deceptive supposition, crude and unskillful, which, even if it were true, would be no less uncertain. This is not just because it is uncertain whether one should ascend from the Moon toward Saturn, or rather descend from Saturn toward the Moon—since any planet can be "first" in the order depending on one's reasoning—but because the position and order of the middle planets is entirely ambiguous. For that ancient dispute still remains "under the judge" <note>original: "sub iudice lis antiqua," a legal metaphor meaning the case is still undecided.</note>: whether the Sun is second from the Moon or rather in the middle. It was believed by the Egyptians to be closest to the Moon, but by the Chaldeans to be in the middle; Ptolemy and a crowd of more recent authors also think it is in the middle. 

However, not only Jabir <note>original: "Ieber"; referring to Jabir ibn Aflah, a 12th-century Spanish-Muslim astronomer who criticized Ptolemy.</note>, the most acute mathematician, but also Theon himself (the Greek interpreter of Ptolemy), disagreeing with his master, thinks the Sun should be placed immediately above the Moon. Plato and Aristotle also affirmed this. It is no wonder that the greatest authors disagree on this matter, about which there are many metaphorical or conventional arguments on both sides, but no certain one can be conceived. For when you remove "parallax" <note>original: "parallelares"; referring to the difference in the apparent position of a celestial body viewed from different points, used to measure distance.</note>—that is, the differences in sight—mathematics indicates nothing about which of two stars is higher. 

Nor is there ambiguity only regarding the Sun, but also regarding Venus and Mercury. As for Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, it is established—says the Summary—that all are above the Sun; however, in what order they stand is neither known nor can it be known. This is because there is much "diversity of aspect" <note>A technical term for the varying ways planets appear to observers on Earth.</note> (as they call it). Furthermore, whatever arguments you make from common principles will be vain and merely logical <note>original: "dialectica"</note>, not certain and mathematical ones derived from their own properties. Such is that argument of Ptolemy's: that the Sun is conveniently placed in the middle among the planets because some are removed from it by a great distance—as Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars are—while others always follow it, like Venus and Mercury. This is a frivolous conjecture that does not hold up, since the Moon departs from the Sun just as much as the "superior" planets do. Therefore, the Sun is not the middle point between those departing from it and...

He highlights the scientific uncertainty of his era regarding the true orbital order of the planets, specifically the position of the Sun relative to Venus, Mercury, and the Moon.</summary>

## Against Astrology, Book X.

...to that point and not departing from it. The reasoning of Alpetragius <note>original: "Alpetragij"; refers to al-Bitruji, a 12th-century Spanish-Arab astronomer who challenged the Ptolemaic system.</note> is equally weak in suggesting that the lower planets are faster in motion, although he attempts to prove that those who appear faster are actually slower. According to this, the position of Venus would be higher than that of the Sun and Mercury, because not all planets resist movement equally. The reasoning of the ancients, who determined the Sun to be closest to the Moon, seems to rely more on evidence, since the Sun is never hidden from us by the intervention of Venus or Mercury. 

But this objection is also resolved in many ways: for instance, what happens with Mercury might be due to its small size, while with Venus, it may be because it is occupied and intercepted by being so close to the Sun's rays. Therefore, it cannot block the path of the rays descending to us, whereas the more distant Moon can. Furthermore, what if they are perhaps thin and—lacking the earthy density of the Moon—do not block the rays? Likewise, they might possess their own light, so that when they return it in place of the Sun’s light that has been taken away, they do not remove the light but simply change it; therefore, no eclipse or deficiency is perceived. 

Averroes <note>The 12th-century philosopher Ibn Rushd.</note>, in his commentary on Ptolemy’s *Great Composition* <note>original: "Magnæ compositionis"; better known as the Almagest, the definitive astronomical manual of the Middle Ages.</note>, says that he once noted two blackish spots on the Sun, and when he had calculated the figures, Mercury was found at that time to be positioned opposite the Sun's rays. Correctly, therefore, did Moses the Egyptian <note>original: "Moses Aegyptius"; the Jewish philosopher Moses Maimonides.</note>—following also the testimony of Abubacher <note>original: "Abubachesis"; refers to the philosopher Ibn Tufail.</note>—pronounce the position and order of the planets to be uncertain. 

For we know that the Moon is lower than all others, the very threshold of heaven, because of its greater parallax <term>parallax: Pico uses "aspectus diversitatem" (diversity of aspect), the shift in the apparent position of a celestial body when viewed from different points on Earth; a larger shift means the object is closer.</term>, which necessarily indicates a smaller relationship of the earth's radius to the sphere's radius. But how the other three—the Sun, Venus, and Mercury—relate to one other is uncertain. Similarly, it is known that these four stars <note>The Moon, Sun, Mercury, and Venus.</note> are closer to us than the other three <note>Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>, but reason does not demonstrate the position and order of those three among themselves.

When, therefore, the practitioners of horoscopes <term>genethliaci: astrologers who cast birth charts to predict a person's life.</term> rely on an order of this kind as a starting point for their conclusions, they rely first on something false, and even if it were true, it would be uncertain. One may also object to the same thing regarding the signs, since (as we have sufficiently demonstrated) there is either no starting point in the zodiac, or there are four equally valid ones.

Having spoken of the first kind of argument, they attempt to prove their case from parabolic similarity as follows: the tenth house is open at the high summit of heaven, while the fourth house is hidden in the depths of the earth. Since, therefore, everyone knows more for certain about their mother than their father, they claim it is fitting that the mother be judged through the tenth house and the father through the fourth. <note>In traditional astrology, the 10th house (the Midheaven) often represents the mother or public life because it is visible, while the 4th house (the Bottom of the Sky) represents the father or hidden origins, playing on the legal maxim that "maternity is a matter of fact, paternity a matter of opinion."</note> This method needs no other refutation than its own title. 

For whatever arguments are sought from these similarities are not only unworthy of philosophers who teach, but are not even fit or useful for logicians in debate; indeed, they are not even suitable for the persuasions of rhetoricians. They present themselves more as the play of empty poetry than as any series of proof with proper authority. I said they argue from "mathematics" when they wrongly turn the sound decrees of mathematicians toward their own predictions, such as what we said above regarding the division of the zodiac into signs, signs into parts, and parts into minutes. Likewise, when they call some signs "straight" and others "oblique" because of unequal delays in their rising, they transfer this to the nature of "rectitude" and "obliquity" in character and movements. They gather from astrological matters whenever they make some astrological dogma the principle of another...

He also mocks the use of poetic metaphors, such as linking the "hidden" nature of the father to the "hidden" bottom of the zodiac.</summary>

to confirm their dogma, they use dialectics <note>The formal art of logical reasoning and debate.</note> if they ever adopt certain common and probable propositions from nature or first philosophy. But that is exceedingly rare; indeed, I do not remember reading any reasoning among them that brought the credibility of dialectical probability.

### ARGUMENTS DERIVED FROM SYMBOLIC ANALOGY <note>original: "parabolica similitudine"</note>
### by which they prove the properties of the houses, are refuted. Chapter V.

**W**e have said these things in general; now let us descend to recounting the fables in detail (for I would more truly call them that than "arguments") by which they assert the properties of the "places" <note>original: "locorum"; in astrology, these are the twelve "houses" representing different areas of life.</note>, beginning with those taken from the position and conditions of the signs. Their method of "symbolic analogy" works in this way: a father loves his sons, and the fifth house is joined by a friendly radiation because it connects in a triangle <note>original: "triangula"; the trine aspect (120 degrees), considered harmonious.</note> to the ascendant <note>original: "horoscopo"; the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon.</note>; therefore, the fifth house signifies sons. So that we may show this method of arguing—which is clearly ridiculous—is no good, let us demonstrate that what they claim is not correctly gathered. 

The first house, they say, signifies the person being born, because it "comes forth from darkness into light." Likewise the ascendant—behold the symbolic analogy!—for which they also give a reason why the same place represents short journeys, such as when one goes from one district of the same city to another, from the city to the suburb, or from the house to the boundary <note>original: "pomerium"; the open space or sacred boundary line just outside a city's walls.</note>. For they want the cause of these movements to be in the stars, which are portended by the disposition of the first house, as Bonatti <note>Guido Bonatti, a famous 13th-century Italian astrologer.</note> says. 

Furthermore, let us see if the analogy holds in the remaining houses. The property of the second house concerns riches, because they say nothing is "closer" to a man; therefore, the second house, being attached to the first, will signify wealth. This is a "necessary" reason for those to whom nothing is more important than wealth, but in truth, many things are closer and more intimate to a man—for example, the gifts of the mind and body, wisdom and health. Therefore, these ought to have been signified by the second house rather than by the sixth or the ninth. What of the fact that among external things, parents, a wife, friends, sons, glory, and money are often preferred as more important and "closer," except perhaps among one class of men who call themselves astrologers? Then, why does the same house also denote letters/epistles, as Sahl the Israelite <note>original: "Zaël Israëlita"; Sahl ibn Bishr, a 9th-century Jewish astrologer and mathematician.</note> says, unless perhaps it is noted in the birth charts of notaries, to whom the pen and writing tablets always cling? 

Now let us proceed to the rest. They want brothers to be indicated by the third house and sons by the fifth. We have mentioned the reason for sons; the reasoning for brothers is similar, because the third house is joined to the ascendant by a hexagonal radiation <note>original: "hexagona radiatione"; the sextile aspect (60 degrees).</note>. Since the hexagonal connection is friendly, but the triangular one is better, the latter is given to sons, whom we love more, and the former to brothers. For the same reason, the eleventh house is for friends, which the ascendant likewise regards from a hexagon. But I ask them: why does the ninth house not signify sons, since it is also triangular to the ascendant? They will answer: "Because it falls" <note>original: "cadit"; referring to a "cadent" house, which was considered weaker in traditional astrology.</note>. I ask again, then: is the third house better or the eleventh? It is clear by the same reasoning that the eleventh is to be preferred because the third "falls." Why then were friends not in the third and brothers in the eleventh? Unless, perverting the order of nature, they think friends should be preferred to brothers.

<header>on Astrology, Book X.</header>

That point about children is also disturbed by another saying: for parents ought to be judged by the fourth house, but between the fourth and the ascendant <note>original: "ascendentem"; the first house or the point rising on the eastern horizon.</note> there is a square aspect <note>original: "tetragonus aspectus"; an angle of 90 degrees, traditionally considered a "hard" or hostile aspect.</note>, than which no aspect is a greater judge of enmity. How then do they connect the newborn and his children with a friendly radiation <note>Referring to the "trine" aspect (120 degrees) between the first and fifth houses mentioned on the previous page.</note>, yet connect the same newborn with his own parents by an unfriendly one? Furthermore, it pleases Ptolemy, all the Greeks, and Ibn Ridwan <note>original: "Auenrodan"; Ali ibn Ridwan, a prominent 11th-century Egyptian astrologer and physician.</note> that children should be judged from the tenth house rather than the fifth—which Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on astrology.</note> proves is correct for this reason: because from there souls are sent down into bodies. 

But we can oppose a fable to Porphyry’s fable: for it is held that souls slide downward through Cancer and ascend through Capricorn. However, Cancer is a northern sign, to which corresponds, according to Ptolemy, the "bottom of the sky" <note>original: "imum terrae" or "imum caeli"; the fourth house, representing the lowest point of the meridian.</note>, not the top; yet they also start predictions about children from the fourth and eleventh houses alike. What of the fact that Al-Qabisi <note>original: "Alchabitius"; a 10th-century Arab astrologer.</note> and the Hebrew Andruzagar <note>original: "Andragazar"; likely referring to a source in the Persian-Hebrew tradition of astrology.</note> want "ambassadors" to belong to the fifth house? And what Vettius Valens <note>original: "Vellius"; a 2nd-century astrologer.</note> calls "rumors and messengers," they add "fame after death," and what Adla writes as "clothing"—by what reasoning, then? For they provide none. 

It is also highly irrational that they attribute the sixth house—which they call <term>aprakton</term> <note>original: ἀπρακτον; literally "idle," "ineffective," or "unproductive."</note>, as if you were to say torpid, ceasing, inert, or ineffective—to slaves, whose labor and industry nevertheless nourish the leisure and laziness of their masters. But see the most "beautiful" reason Ibn Ridwan makes regarding this dogma: "The seventh house," he says, "signifies equals, but subjects are distanced from equals" (these are his own words) "by as much as the sixth house is distanced from the seventh." Therefore they placed the sixth house as the house of subjects. Thus says he: things which are to be laughed at rather than refuted, lest we be too strictly rebuked by Aristotle <note>Pico implies that the logic is so poor it violates the basic principles of Aristotelian reasoning.</note>. 

For concerning what they say about the seventh house signifying "equals," see how they themselves consider these things least truthful and least consistent; for they refer to the same place the wife, partners, and open enemies—and what is more contradictory than these? But Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>original: "Abraam"; a 12th-century Jewish polymath and astrologer.</note> defends it in this manner: because the seventh house is opposite the first, he says, it signifies lawsuits and wars; but because it sets while the horoscope <note>The "horoscopus" here refers to the ascending degree of the first house.</note> rises, it signifies the wife. Finally, because the duration of its setting <note>The time it takes for a sign to descend below the western horizon.</note> is equal to the time of the ascensions of the first house—which is a certain agreement—it therefore signifies equals and partners. In this way, everything will be easily confirmed, since there is nothing that cannot be imagined as both similar and dissimilar to any other thing by some argument of analogy of this sort. 

For where does it not succeed? If indications are given for opposite things by the same house as if they agreed. But they "agree," he will say, by this reasoning: that the times of emergence in the ascendant and falling in the west are equal. I confess it is well said—if you also concede, by the same example, that water is similar to fire, because water possesses as many parts of coldness as fire has parts of heat. For I think perhaps setting and rising are as opposed (though this is not said most precisely) as heat and cold. Does a wife not more certainly belong to the second house, being closest to the man, always following him as a near-equal and a second, especially since they even want one of the signs to be male and the other female, since, as he says...

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note> says that women cling to men [in the seventh house]. But let them also give an account of why the same house signifies thieves and fugitives (as Vettius Valens <note>original: "Vellio"; Vettius Valens was a 2nd-century Greek astrologer whose *Anthology* was a major source for later practitioners.</note> prefers), as well as buying and selling; and why others hand down that it signifies moderately long journeys, while Bonatti <note>Guido Bonatti, the most famous Italian astrologer of the 13th century.</note> writes that it signifies the worship of pure divinity and foreknowledge of the future. Certainly, death was more rightly owed to this place than to the eighth house, since here one equally descends from light into darkness, just as in the ascendant <note>The first house, or the point rising on the eastern horizon.</note> one goes from darkness into light. But this did not please them, says Ibn Ezra <note>original: "Auenazra"; Abraham ibn Ezra, a 12th-century Jewish polymath and astrologer.</note>, because it is somewhat similar to the ascendant—by such a similarity, I suppose, as that by which we proved water is similar to fire. Yet Dorotheus <note>Dorotheus of Sidon, a 1st-century astrologer.</note> also judged death from this house rather than the eighth, observing the lord of the house for that purpose. 

Likewise, let them answer why the eighth house signifies wars according to Abu ‘Ali <note>original: "Aboali"; Abu 'Ali al-Khayyat, a 9th-century student of Mashallah.</note>, and what Al-Khayyat <note>original: "Alchainil"; likely another reference to Abu 'Ali al-Khayyat or a corruption of a similar name.</note> writes: farm management <note>original: "uillicationem"; the duties of a farm steward or bailiff.</note>. Others want it to signify usury, and inheritances should also be foreseen from here. I do not see how the heir and the dead man agree; it would have been better if the eighth house judged death and the ninth signified inheritance, which follows the eighth. But inheritances are related to the eighth, says Ibn Ezra, because it corresponds proportionally to the second house, to which assets belong. This is that "harmony of opposite things" that I have already mocked so often; for what similarity will there be in opposite places except for dissimilarity? 

If they always spoke of these things as being similar, their error might perhaps be forgiven; but now they use them sometimes as similar, and sometimes as maximally dissimilar and truly opposite, just so it might suit their needs. Thus, houses are taken as opposites when the second house portends the things by which we are nourished and preserve life, while the eighth signifies death and exile; yet soon the same house signifies inheritances and wealth, as if it were similar and related to the second. Altogether, those who die *make* heirs; they do not *become* them—unless perhaps they become heirs of heaven, which is certainly not subject to the sky. There would be other objections to make, but I fear that by stitching together trifles, I too might become a trifler. 

However, what they say about the ninth house cannot be omitted by any means; from it the reader has so much to laugh at that the weariness of their long-windedness might be somewhat relieved. The ninth house, they say, signifies long journeys. Hear the reason: because the Sun, positioned in the tenth house, moves by descending to the ninth. Ibn Ezra wrote this in the first and second books of his *Book of Reasons* <note>original: "lib. Rationum"; Ibn Ezra's *Sefer ha-Te'amim*, which attempted to provide the "why" behind astrological rules.</note>, where there is a need for loud mocking laughter <note>original: "cachinnis"</note> rather than syllogisms—as if the Sun does not move when passing from any one house to any other! Furthermore, since the Sun descends with that motion, I suppose the ninth house will not signify journeys by which we climb mountains and high places? For who would not joke when arguing with such ridiculous people? 

Add also that fable about the twelfth house: that through it are signified the animals on which we ride <note>original: "animalia quibus uehimur"</note>, because it is joined to the ascendant whenever the same zodiac sign extends through both houses. Elsewhere, however, they say that darkness and prisons are portended by the same house because it is most distant from the ascendant (from which it is the twelfth). Thus, mindful of neither themselves nor the truth, they measure things in whatever way they please. But if a house ought to be "joined" to the horoscope <note>The ascendant or first house.</note> when the same sign occupies both seats, and "disjoined" when the signs are different, it follows that neither the animals we ride,

# REFUTATION OF THE REASONS OF AVENRODAN CONCERNING THE
## properties of the signs which are taken from the order and sequence
### of the signs. Chapter VI.

<margin>Avenrodan, Book 1 of the *Apotelesmaton* <note>Ibn Ridwan (c. 988–1061), an Egyptian physician and astrologer known in the West as Avenrodan. His *Apotelesmaton* is a commentary on Ptolemy’s work.</note></margin>
**T**hese are arguments drawn from the position and condition of places by a kind of parabolic similarity. Avenrodan, in the first book of his *Apotelesmaton*, argues from the order and sequence of the signs, so that the first sign corresponds to the first place <note>The "places" or "houses" are the twelve divisions of the sky in a horoscope.</note>, the second to the second, and the nature of a place is judged according to the nature of the lord of the corresponding sign. Thus, he claims brothers and short journeys are judged through the third place, because Gemini is also the third sign, and its lord is Mercury. Likewise, he says that Mercury has influence over mixed matters—which is why it signifies brothers—and it always stays closest to the course of the Sun, which is why short journeys belong to it. But no other astrologer, nor even Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the primary authority for medieval and Renaissance astrology.</note> whom he follows, makes Mercury the significator of brothers. Nor is there any reason why it should preside over short journeys just because it imitates the course of the Sun. For if it were because it revolves with a swift motion, this would pertain no more to Mercury than to the Sun and Venus, since the courses of all of them are roughly equal.

Let us come to the fourth house, to which Cancer corresponds; he says it signifies the father because the Sun presides over fathers, and the power of the Sun appears in Cancer. See how vain, how frivolous are the conjectures they accept! For while in other cases the house always employs its own lord, here he flees to one who has no authority in that sign. For the Sun in Cancer has neither its kingdom <note>A planet's "home" or "domicile" sign.</note>, nor its lodging, nor its triplicity <note>A group of three signs associated with an element.</note>, nor its decan <note>A ten-degree subdivision of a sign.</note>. Because neither the mistress of the house, the Moon, nor the king of the sign, Jupiter, served the signification of fathers, he turned himself to the Sun, because when positioned in Cancer it is at its hottest. As we have already said many times, this happens not from the nature of the sign, but from the relationship of the Sun to the Earth; otherwise, what kinship does the Sun have (if we follow the principles of the astrologers) with a sign that is moist, cold, and feminine, in which—as we pointed out a little while ago—the Sun has no prerogative of any dignity? 

Furthermore, since Saturn rules in that same place, as Avenrodan says there, how can the Sun also rule? They consider the natures of these two to be opposites, and they even make their houses and palaces opposites. Or how does this other point he makes harmonize: that the nature of Saturn corresponds to that place, and therefore they extend it to inheritances and hidden things? Yet the sign of Cancer belongs to that place as the fourth house, in which Saturn suffers <term>exile</term> <note>original: *exilium*; also known as "detriment," this occurs when a planet is in the sign opposite the one it rules, supposedly weakening its power.</note> far from its home. Regarding the eighth and ninth places, he devises no less false and conflicting things. Scorpio, he says, is the eighth sign, whose lord is Mars, because it signifies death—not the kind of death Mars produces according to the astrologers, but rather Saturn; for as they say, it signifies poisons and sluggishness and...

...the place is called the house of darkness <note>The 12th House, traditionally associated with hidden enemies, prisons, and sorrow.</note>, and what could be more opposed to Venus than these? Yet certain men have devised a most "beautiful" defense: for since repentance usually follows pleasures, they claim both states should be assigned to Venus—namely, both joy and sorrow. I suppose they will defend it equally this way: that since death follows life, both are signified by the same planet. And I do not doubt that, by the same logic, they will say war and peace pertain to Mars, since peace always follows war, just as clear skies follow rain, and rain follows clear skies.

But, lest they think they must always mourn outside of all joy simply to avoid mourning eventually, I wish to remind them that sorrow is not the companion of *all* joy, but only of that which has been beyond measure and reason. However, they will not say these sorrows are signified by the fifth place <note>The 5th House, associated with pleasure and children.</note> if they are the sorrows of their own principles; for these things are referred to the fifth house because they help, cherish, and revive, just as the fifth house is joined to the ascendant <note>The 1st House, signifying the beginning of life.</note>, through which the life of the person being born is signified. Truly, immoderate pleasure, which repentance and pain follow, is not a nourishment of life but its destruction. 

But we speak too seriously in refuting such trifles. Concerning Mars, let us look at the reasoning of Aboafar <note>Abū Maʿshar (787–886), a Persian astrologer known in the West as Albumasar or Aboafar.</note> and we shall make an end of it. He says Mars signifies brothers and sisters because they are from the same parents. The reasoning for this dogma is this: because Saturn is assigned to the first place where the lord of the birth is judged, Jupiter is second (being the second planet), and Mars is third, according to the order of the spheres. But Mars and Saturn are of the same kind, because both are evil and harmful. Therefore, the third place will signify things that are of the same kind as the one who is born—which is why it signifies brothers and sisters. Thus says our Aboafar; who, if he did not write this while drunk, certainly wrote it while insane. For who among the planets is more dissimilar than Mars and Saturn? That one is fire, this one is earth; that one rages with heat, this one is sluggish with cold; that one is nocturnal, this one is diurnal; and if you run through them all, you will find no influence of Mars that agrees with the influences of Saturn. 

Furthermore, since children are also similar to their parents, either they should not have been signified by the fifth house (to which Venus is assigned), or it will have to be said that Saturn also agrees with Venus. 

We have recounted the reasons of the astrologers by which they "prove" the properties of the houses, perhaps more to be blamed for having examined them too diligently than for having described them untruly; they are drawn from a certain thin similarity of things. But although they are refuted with no effort, they nevertheless possess an authority from the tradition of the ancients and the testimonies of writers that should be refuted rather than ignored.

## THE JOYS OF THE PLANETS WITH THE HOUSES
## collapse. Chapter VIII.

**H**ere all things concerning the "joys" of the planets are overturned, since they are denoted by the properties of the houses <note>In astrology, "Joy" (gaudium) is a dignity where a planet is said to be particularly powerful or "happy" in a specific house (e.g., Mercury in the 1st house).</note>; for they want each planet to "rejoice" in that place whose property is similar to the property of the planet. Thus, they place Venus in the fifth house, because it signifies joys, children, and pleasures, just as Venus does. So too with the others in other places by the same reasoning, as may be understood from Avenazra’s <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (1089–1167), a Jewish scholar and astrologer.</note> third *Book of Reasons* and Aboafar’s *Introductory*.

Although, if we were to follow this line of reasoning, the third or sixth place <note>The "places" refer to the twelve astrological houses.</note> would have been more suitable for Mercury than the ascendant <note>The 1st House, where the sun rises.</note>. For the Moon, the ascendant or the descendant <note>The 7th House, where the sun sets.</note> would be more fitting than the third house. For the Sun, the tenth house <note>The Midheaven, the highest point in the sky.</note> would be more appropriate than the ninth. For Jupiter, the ninth or even the second house would be better than the eleventh. For Mars, the seventh rather than the sixth. For Saturn, the fourth rather than the twelfth. Anyone who compares the functions of these places with the conditions of the planets can observe this for themselves. **Abenragel** <note>Albohazen Haly filius Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer whose work was a standard textbook in the Renaissance.</note> says that of any sign, some parts are hot and dry, others cold and moist, others cold and dry, others hot and moist, and others are middling or mixed; therefore, any planet is strengthened by the parts that match its own nature. He claims that the "middling" or "mixed" parts suit Mercury. However, Ptolemy and others would not accept this reasoning, as they maintain that Venus is hot and moist; thus, the cold and moist parts would suit no planet at all. Furthermore, since Mars possesses only five parts <note>Pico is referring to the "terms" or "bounds," which are unequal divisions of a zodiac sign assigned to different planets.</note> in Aries, it would mean that if Abenragel is correct, only five parts in Aries are hot and dry, while the remaining parts would have a different condition and a nature diverse from the sign itself—even though the whole sign is judged to be hot and dry by nature. Similarly, in Taurus, there would be far more "airy" parts than "earthy" ones, and the same would happen in the other signs. Therefore, Abenragel's reasoning is deceptive; and even if it were true, it still does not explain our question, because it remains uncertain which parts are hot and which are cold, since it cannot be determined with certainty which parts ought to be assigned to which planet.

### THE REASONS OF PTOLEMY CONCERNING THE HOUSES OF THE 
### PLANETS ARE DESTROYED. Chapter IX.

We must now deal with the signs, and indeed we have already overturned many of their reasons regarding these—such as those by which they try to prove there are twelve signs, and neither more nor fewer. Nevertheless, the starting point of the signs is established at **Aries**; furthermore, there is that division into watery, earthy, fiery, and airy elements. We must also ask why this specific thing is considered the <term>exaltation</term> <note>A specific sign where a planet is thought to have its maximum power.</note> or <term>triplicity</term> <note>A group of three signs belonging to the same element (fire, earth, air, or water).</note> of one planet and why another belongs to a different one. There remain other matters of which we shall now speak, beginning with the houses of the planets. For even if it were granted that the planets have an affinity of this sort with various signs—so that a planet placed under one sign is weakened, while under another it becomes stronger—we still could not grasp the distinction between these signs through any reason. This is because it cannot happen otherwise than according to the nature of the stars and the nature of that sign, as we said above. But reason does not demonstrate the nature of the stars to us. Therefore, it does not demonstrate the affinity of the signs with the stars. If this affinity is said to follow the spaces of the heavens rather than the stars themselves, it will be no less impossible to explore through <term>syllogism</term> <note>A form of logical reasoning.</note> than the hidden properties of all other things. **Ptolemy**, concerning the houses of the Sun and Moon, relies on only one reason; concerning the houses of the rest, he relies on three. The first is taken from the nature of the signs. The second concerns the proportion of the configuration to the houses of the "luminaries" <note>The Sun and the Moon.</note>. The third concerns the number and sequence of the spheres. Let us examine the first one first. It is as follows: Capricorn and Aquarius are winter signs because they are cold; Saturn is also a cold planet; therefore, they are rightly suited to him. But this argument fails in many ways. First, because one must look at the nature of the sign in terms of how it is
