# Against Astrology, Book X.

One should consider what is suitable by its own nature rather than what is accidental. Indeed, coldness belongs to those signs <note>Specifically the winter signs like Capricorn and Aquarius.</note> only by accident; they are called cold for no other reason than that the Sun, when positioned in them, causes cold accidentally, namely while it is moving further away from us. However, when these signs are judged according to their own nature by the astrologers themselves, one is earthy and the other is airy. This latter quality <note>Air, which is hot and moist.</note> is more suitable for Jupiter than for **Saturn**, who is cold and dry and thus opposed to all the qualities of **Aquarius**. Furthermore, when astrologers associate various things with various stars, they are accustomed—if the stars are "malefic" <note>In astrology, Saturn and Mars are considered 'malefics' or bringers of bad fortune.</note>—to give them things that differ from their nature rather than things that agree with it. They do this so that the planet's evil nature might be tempered by a mixture of its opposite. Thus, they make Saturn a "diurnal" planet and Mars a "nocturnal" one, even though the cold night does not agree with the heat of Mars, nor does the hot day agree with the cold of Saturn. They do this so that the harmful quality of each may be restrained: the fire in Mars and the sluggishness in Saturn. Let them say, then: in assigning signs to a "malefic" planet, do they wish to follow this same reasoning? Or rather the opposite? Indeed, **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note> seems to follow the opposite opinion here, abandoning the method he preserved above in defining the nocturnal and diurnal planets. But let him be permitted to disagree with himself in different places, provided he does not contradict himself within the same sequence of words. If he makes a sign that is harmonious with Saturn's nature its "house," then Aquarius is excluded; if he makes a discordant one its house, then **Capricorn** is cast out. Ptolemy will say that he looks to those qualities of the signs which are owed to the operations of the Sun; thus, both the signs of the Goat <note>Capricorn.</note> and the Water-Bearer <note>Aquarius.</note> are numbered among the cold signs, which accords with Saturn’s quality. We contend that this is done without reason, but let us admit it for now, and let us show that what he thinks cannot even be concluded from it. For perhaps he will answer this regarding Saturn, but it will not succeed regarding the other planets. For the houses of **Venus** are **Libra** and **Taurus**. Libra is an autumnal sign, and is therefore dry and cold, just as Aquarius is a cold winter sign. Therefore, Libra is repugnant to Venus, who is defined by most as hot, and by everyone as moist. Nor am I little amazed at Ptolemy, who said these signs suit Venus because she is "generative" and "most fertile." For while this might be said of Taurus, it can in no way be said of Libra. In what way does the logic square for **Jupiter**? He has no community with **Pisces** and **Sagittarius**. Since the time of year is estimated under those signs, one finishes the winter and the other is the end of autumn. Therefore, the former will resist Jupiter through its coldness, and the latter through its dryness; moreover, the watery moisture of Pisces does not suit the vital humor of Jupiter. Ptolemy refers to this "concordance" by claiming that both of them create winds and also possess a "generative" power, which is why the temperate planet Jupiter harmonizes with them. While I refute these things, I would think I was performing a useless task, were it not that Ptolemy—whose authority can easily impose itself on the unlearned—had put them forth. Otherwise, these claims are like things that educated men sometimes say in jest while playing among themselves: "they stir up winds, therefore they are like Jupiter." **Auenrodan** <note>Also known as Ibn Ridwan, an 11th-century Arabic commentator on Ptolemy.</note> gives the reason: because Jupiter presides over the generation and the seeds of living things, and their vapors and breaths are not unlike winds. Oh, what marvelous wisdom, by which they can

<meta>This page continues Pico’s systematic debunking of the "domiciles" or "houses" of the planets. Having previously critiqued the assignment of Saturn and Mars to specific signs, he now turns his attention to the Sun and Moon (the "luminaries") and the inconsistencies in the logic used by various astrological authorities like Ptolemy and Abu Ma'shar.</meta>

### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

...[they claim] that even dry things are defended by similar humid things. For philosophers (unless I am mistaken) make all winds dry, contrary to all humid generation; and yet they also designate "fecund signs," because when the **Sun** is positioned in them, seeds germinate and things arise. Oh, if only they could have attributed human seed to **Aries**, it would have happened much more conveniently for them! But they could not give it to **Jupiter**, because **Mars** had already occupied it—though entirely by injustice. For what does Mars have to do with the first light of spring? His scorched dryness shares nothing with the spring's gentle heat and its prolific, genital moisture. With equal audacity, and with no right at all, he [Mars] invaded **Scorpio**, which is a cold and autumnal sign. Therefore, if we follow that reasoning, this partition of the "houses" <note>In astrology, a 'house' or domicile is the zodiac sign over which a planet is said to have rulership.</note> is hardly equitable. 

Let us examine other reasons taken from the configurations of the luminaries <note>The Sun and Moon.</note> and from the number of the celestial spheres. But since they gather these through their relationship to the houses of the luminaries, we must first examine the reasoning by which the houses of the luminaries themselves are established. 

The reasoning which **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the famous 2nd-century astronomer and astrologer.</note> brings forward is of this kind: **Cancer** and **Leo** are the two signs among the twelve that incline most toward the north, and they come closest to our zenith <note>The point in the sky directly above an observer.</note>; for that reason, they were given to the two greatest and principal stars—that is, the luminaries. **Leo** was given to the **Sun** because it is a masculine sign, and **Cancer** to the **Moon** because it is feminine. 

First, the assumption itself is false: for the signs closest to us are **Cancer** and **Gemini**, not **Cancer** and **Leo**. Secondly, even if it were true, what logic teaches us that the signs closest to us should suit the greater stars? The ancients could have said this using the following comparison: that those stars [the luminaries] are also the ones closest to us among the planets. But Ptolemy cannot say this, as he places the Sun in the middle of all the planets. 

Was it done, then, because the Sun heats more when in **Leo**? Truly, it has been said many times that this happens because of the Sun's position <note>The angle of the sun during summer in the northern hemisphere.</note>, not from any property of the sign itself; hence, for other nations <note>People in the southern hemisphere.</note>, the Sun does in **Libra** what it does for us in **Leo**. If we had senses and reasoning as true for the powers of the other stars as we have for the Solar heat, we would experience the same thing regarding the rest as we do with the Sun: that we are affected more by them as they approach **Leo**, not because of the sign, but because they are found far from us in other signs. 

Does the **Sun** then harmonize with **Leo** for other reasons? Certainly, the fact that it is a hot and dry sign, and likewise masculine, is not unique to **Leo**, but is shared with **Aries** and **Sagittarius**. One condition remains which that most serious author **Aboafar** <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), a highly influential Persian astrologer known in the West as Albumasar.</note> mentions: "For just as," he says, "the Sun is the middle of the planets, so Leo is the middle sign of summer." Unless he bound it by this reasoning, I would not have conceded that **Phoebus** <note>A poetic name for the Sun or Apollo.</note> is better hosted by **Leo** than by any other beasts of the sky. 

But I was persuaded by **Aboafar**, truly the protector and sweet glory of astrologers, who also thought of a most beautiful thing regarding the kinship of the **Moon** with **Taurus**. For Ptolemy cited the distance, noting that among the signs closest to us, it [Cancer] is feminine. Not content with this, **Aboafar** added another reason: that the Moon signifies the beginnings of things, and **Cancer** is the beginning of summer. To such a demonstration, who would not concede? **Auenrodan** <note>Ali ibn Ridwan (c. 988–1061), an Egyptian physician and astrologer known for his commentary on Ptolemy.</note> did not see this; he used another reason, namely that the house of the Moon is deservedly placed next to the house of the Sun, because the Moon always follows the Sun.

But... <margin>catchword: Sed</margin>

# Against Astrology, Book X.

But let one see how much more correctly this might be said concerning **Venus** and **Mercury**, whose houses nature even made closest to the **Sun**, if we believe **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note>, whose interpreter is **Avenrodan** <note>Ali ibn Ridwan, a medieval Egyptian physician and astrologer who wrote famous commentaries on Ptolemy.</note>, whom we have cited. Furthermore, granted that those are the houses of the luminaries <note>The Sun and Moon.</note>, **Ptolemy** brings forward this reason above all for distributing the others: so that the houses of the evil stars, such as **Mars** and **Saturn**, should look upon the houses of the luminaries with a hostile radiation <note>An "aspect" or angle in astrology; "hostile" refers to the square and opposition angles, believed to cause tension.</note>, while the houses of the good ones, such as **Jupiter** and **Venus**, should be established as friendly, and **Mercury** placed next to them. Thus, he claims it was right that **Scorpio** and **Aries** were given to **Mars**, being quadrangular <note>A "square" aspect of 90 degrees.</note> to **Cancer** and **Leo**; to **Saturn** were given **Capricorn** and **Aquarius**, being opposite to them; to **Jupiter** the triangular signs <note>A "trine" aspect of 120 degrees, considered very harmonious.</note>, **Pisces** and **Sagittarius**; to **Venus** the hexagonal signs <note>A "sextile" aspect of 60 degrees.</note>, **Libra** and **Taurus**; and to **Mercury** the signs closest to them, **Gemini** and **Virgo**. 

But what is assumed is neither true, nor does he correctly conclude from those assumptions. For we say a house is reasonably established as that in which a positioned Planet fares well; but the quadrangular radiation of those signs is equally harmful to **Mars** and the **Sun**, and likewise the opposition is harmful to **Saturn**, both because of the adversity of the opposition and because of retrograde motion. Furthermore, if that which **Ptolemy** himself hands down were true—that all Planets are happy at that distance removed from the **Sun** in which their houses are distant from the houses of the **Sun**, which the Greeks call <note>original: "ὑποποιοποιίην"</note> *subjection* and the Arabs call <term>almugea</term> <note>A complex planetary dignity involving the planet's distance from the Sun or Moon matching the distance between their respective signs.</note>—it would follow that both **Saturn** being opposite the luminaries and **Mars** being square to them would be happy. This contradicts the opinion of all astrologers, who decree great misfortunes and calamities from such configurations. 

Finally, it is evident that what he concludes does not square with the principle. For when they say these or those houses are triangular or quadrangular to the houses [of the luminaries], they take them in such a way that they are compared to **Leo** for those signs following in order between it and **Capricorn**, and in reverse order for those between **Cancer** and **Aquarius**. For this reason, one half is called the empire of the **Sun** and the other of the **Moon**. Otherwise, the houses of **Venus** could be called both quadrangular and triangular, since **Libra** is square to **Cancer**, and **Taurus** to **Leo**; and the houses of **Mars** would be triangular, **Scorpio** to **Cancer**, and **Aries** to **Leo**. Therefore, the collateral house, located as if under the star's jurisdiction, ought to be compared to the house of each luminary. If this is done, it will be found most false that the houses of **Saturn** are opposed to the luminaries, as **Ptolemy** says, since neither is **Aquarius** opposed to **Cancer**, nor **Capricorn** to **Leo**. Wherefore no one would call these the houses of **Saturn** since the luminaries would behold them diagonally, because they hold either the sixth place from the **Sun** or the eighth from the **Moon**, which **Avenrodan** also confesses. 

Another reason is taken from the number of the spheres: once **Leo** and **Cancer** were defined, then the houses closest to them were assigned to the Planets closest to the **Sun** and **Moon** in the order of the spheres. Thus they establish that **Gemini** is given to **Mercury** on one side and **Virgo** on the other; then follow those for **Venus**, then those closest for **Mars**, next for **Jupiter**, and the last for **Saturn**. We have already declared all these arguments drawn from the sequence of the spheres to be false, and even if they were true, to be uncertain. Correct, therefore, is **Avenazra** <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra, a 12th-century Jewish polymath and astrologer.</note> in the second book of his *Reasons*: "I have searched," he says, "in the books of the wise for the reasons for the signs of the houses, and I have not found in them anything good; it is only held by faith..."

...they turn to experiments. Thus says he. In this book we shall undermine the reasons, and in the next, we shall undermine the experiments of the astrologers.

### THAT THE REASONS FOR FACES AND BOUNDS HAVE ALREADY BEEN
### REJECTED. Chapter 10.

The **Faces** <note>Also known as decans, these are ten-degree subdivisions of a zodiac sign (30 degrees total per sign, thus three "faces" each).</note> of the Planets, which everyone uses, they likewise divide according to the sequence of the celestial spheres. For assigning the first parts to **Aries**, they give them to the lord of the house; the following parts they give to the following planets according to the order of their position and spheres—namely, after **Mars**, they give the first to the **Sun**, the second to **Venus**, and so on. The **Indians** gave the first to the lord of the house, and the other two to the lords of the signs of the same **triplicity** <note>original: "trigoni"; a group of three signs belonging to the same element (Fire, Earth, Air, or Water).</note>. But since we have sufficiently refuted triplicities and those who argue based on the number of the spheres, there is no need for new arguments against these sorts of reasons.

Concerning **Bounds** <note>original: "fines"; also known as "terms." These are irregular subdivisions of a zodiac sign where different planets are said to have influence.</note>, they disagree so much that they have produced five different opinions on them; for this reason, one person’s logic is argued against and ridiculed by another. Indeed, they are all so weak and frail that each person, by some new law of his own, changes his own neighbors and invades the territory of others. From the order of the triplicities, the **Chaldeans** arranged their bounds so that the signs of the triplicities were divided similarly. The method of partition, however, would be that the lord of the triplicity occupied the first parts, then those who have power over the triplicity in the following signs, with the numbers always decreasing from eight down to four.

The **Egyptians**, as **Ptolemy** <term>Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD): The most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity.</term> objects against them, maintain no consistent method; now they approach triplicities, now "kings," now "heads of the family," starting occasionally from those who possess no authority in the sign—such as starting from **Mercury** in **Capricorn**. **Ptolemy** approves another division, the reasoning for which is available for anyone to read in the first book of the *Apotelesmatics* <note>original: "Apotelesmaton"; better known today as the "Tetrabiblos," Ptolemy’s foundational work on astrology.</note>. It depends, however, on the lords of the house, of **exaltation** <note>A specific degree in a sign where a planet is thought to be at its maximum strength.</note>, and of the triplicity. Yet **Ptolemy** ought not to have approved this unless he were refuting himself, since the author of that division prefers exaltation to triplicity, and triplicity to the house. **Ptolemy**, however, prefers the house above all, and makes exaltation the very last, though in that division it is preferred to all others.

The **Indians** divide masculine signs similarly through all things, and feminine signs likewise by the same example, but no logic for the example is recognized in either. **Asotol** <note>Likely a reference to an Arabic astrological source, possibly a corruption of a name like Al-Sufi or a specific school of practitioners.</note> even gave bounds to the **luminaries** <note>The Sun and the Moon.</note>, and as many parts to each Planet, but the first parts to the lord of the house in the "order of the prophets," and the rest to the others.

Since we have now removed this foundation—and likewise **houses**, **exaltations**, and **triplicities**—or have proven them to be a matter of uncertainty, every logic for defining bounds collapses (if indeed any bounds are to be granted at all). Furthermore, even if the truth concerning triplicities, houses, and elevations <note>Another term for exaltations.</note> were fully explored, it is still not established that bounds should be decided in this way rather than that; hence the variety of opinions was born, while one thing seemed more probable to some than to others.

## THAT WHICH SIGN RULES OVER WHICH BODY PART IS DETERMINED DIFFERENTLY
### by various authors, and by all of them with very little reason. Chapter 11.

That they likewise subject the head to <term>Aries</term> <note>The Ram</note>, the neck to <term>Taurus</term> <note>The Bull</note>, and other limbs to other signs, they also derive from that often-criticized order of numbers; namely, so that the first sign is placed over the first part of the body, the second over the second, and the third over the third. Yet they also err in this partition, not so much because they make <term>Aries</term> the first of the signs—which is an ambiguous if not outright false thing to take for granted—but because no logic can persuade us that there are exactly twelve principal parts of the body. Aristotle identified seven parts; Nicomachus <note>Nicomachus of Gerasa, a mathematician who emphasized the mystical properties of numbers.</note> identified ten. Let the astrologers themselves provide the reason why there should be twelve. 

They see an even more absurd thing: that they force the shoulders, arms, and hands into a single part subject to one sign, yet they treat the feet, shins, knees, and thighs as four large parts to be subjected to four different signs. Furthermore, if one were to make such a distribution, hot parts should have been compared to hot signs, and cold to cold, rather than just matching the second sign to the second part and the third to the third. In this, a shared nature ought to be observed rather than a mere counting of position and order. Perhaps they would not be laughed at for subjecting the feet to <term>Pisces</term> <note>The Fish</note> if Pisces were not the only ones among the heavenly figures who actually lack feet. 

Therefore, let doctors beware lest, being persuaded at some point by such a futile dogma, they fear to lance a vein in the arms if the situation requires it, simply because the Moon is traveling through <term>Gemini</term> <note>The Twins</note>—on the grounds that <term>Gemini</term> rules the arms. Let them not delay a life-saving remedy because they are led by vain superstition. Neither Hippocrates, nor Galen, nor Avicenna, nor Paul <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine physician.</note>, nor Oribasius either did this themselves or established that others should do it. Nor have those who, in our own time (as we have said elsewhere), practiced this art successfully and prudently. Therefore, let all insane superstition of this kind cease; for if it is proven to have no basis in reason, it cannot have the strength of experimental evidence either. This is true both because no truth harmonizes with a lie, and because of the many things we shall prove in the following book, and also because of the sheer contradiction among those who propose these things. 

For Avenazra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a 12th-century Jewish scholar and astrologer.</note> gives the testicles to <term>Sagittarius</term>, while Aboafar <note>Abu Ma'shar, a famous Persian astrologer.</note> gives them to <term>Scorpio</term>. Alchabitius <note>An 10th-century Arab astrologer.</note> gives the <term>diaphragm</term> to <term>Virgo</term>, which in Latin is called the <term>transverse septum</term> <note>original: "septum transversum"</note>. Porphyry gives it to <term>Leo</term>, to whom he also assigns the belly, which the Arabs assign to <term>Virgo</term>. There are some who assign the knees to <term>Sagittarius</term>, which both the Arabs and Latins assign to <term>Capricorn</term>. Heliazer of Guérande <note>original: "Heliazer Garnozensis," likely a reference to a Jewish scholar.</note>, a Hebrew man, in his book *On the Soul*, assigns the hands and feet to <term>Cancer</term>, even though others give the hands to <term>Gemini</term> and the feet to <term>Pisces</term>. That same man again subjects the legs and feet to <term>Libra</term>, though for a different reason than he did for <term>Cancer</term>; for he subjects them to <term>Cancer</term> insofar as they fulfill the function of walking, but to <term>Libra</term> <note>The Scales</note> because of a perceived similarity: because while one is walking, the limbs are raised and lowered like the pans of a scale. Others say no such thing of <term>Libra</term>, but subject the legs to <term>Aquarius</term> and the feet to <term>Pisces</term>, while subjecting both the buttocks, kidneys, and loins to <term>Libra</term>. Heliazer says the bile corresponds to <term>Scorpio</term> and the "nature" <note>likely referring to the genitals or reproductive essence</note> to <term>Sagittarius</term>, but others give the private parts to <term>Scorpio</term>. But if anyone should say that it has been observed by astrologers that it is never safe to apply the blade...

### THE REASONS OF THE ASTROLOGERS BY WHICH PROPERTIES
### are assigned absolutely to the signs, and why the
### aforementioned reasons are rejected. Chapter 12.

**W**e have spoken of the properties by which the signs are related to us and to the planets; there remain those which belong to them simply and absolutely, which they [the astrologers] derive from a threefold kind of proof. The first is drawn from that affinity with the planets which we have already refuted. The second is from the figure of the animal for which the sign is named. The third is from the effects produced by the Sun when it is positioned under them. From the affinity with the planets, they argue that the nature of a sign is the same as that of the planet which rules it; for instance, when they say <term>Aries</term> <note>The Ram</note> signifies the hiding places of thieves and wicked men because it is the "house" of <term>Mars</term>, who signifies that class of people. From the work of the Sun, they decree which signs are "movable," "fixed," and "common," <note>In modern astrology, these are called Cardinal, Fixed, and Mutable signs.</note> based on whether the Sun, being in that sign, changes the season, confirms it, or tempers it with a mixed quality. From the figure [of the constellation], they say some signs breathe mild manners and others wild ones into those being born, because these bear the image of all things: some are human, like <term>Aquarius</term>, <term>Gemini</term>, and <term>Virgo</term>; others are of beasts, like <term>Leo</term>, <term>Taurus</term>, and <term>Capricorn</term>. Likewise, they say some are beautiful and others deformed; for they call "beautiful" whichever are conceived under a human likeness, such as <term>Aquarius</term>—simply because it is the home of old <term>Saturn</term>, as if an old and deformed man could not either need or delight in a beautiful home! Similarly, they call those with brute appearances, like <term>Taurus</term> and the like, "semi-vocal"; they call the human ones "vocal," and the "mute" ones are those which reflect the likeness of aquatic creatures, because that kind of living thing has no voice. Again, the aquatic ones are said to have many offspring, while those of human likeness are sterile. They establish the rest as being of a middle condition, according to the nature of the animals whose images they are believed to be. 

The arguments we disputed above have sufficiently overturned these modes of classification. For when they make a conjecture from the houses and character of a planet, they argue from astrological principles which we refuted a little while ago. When they argue from the work of the Sun, we have shown how much they either deceive or are deceived, since the nature of a sign should not be judged by the work of the Sun located in that sign; that work is not due to the sign's nature, but to the Sun's position and distance relative to the Earth. Furthermore, what happens in the seasons and atmospheric changes is, by a most fallacious inference, transferred to other things. For example, they claim that because <term>Aries</term> is a "movable" sign and changes the weather, it must also make the character of one born under it "movable" or inconstant—better suited for starting things than for finishing them. Nor do they only err regarding the quality of the air...

in Astrology, Book X

...they turn their natural abilities toward various outcomes and properties; but it is thought that in the very changes of the air, what is observed in the Sun also happens in other stars. For example, because the Sun, when positioned in <term>Aries</term> <note>The first sign of the zodiac, associated with the start of spring.</note>, creates the vernal equinox and rouses lightning and thunder, we are led to think that the Moon positioned in Aries would do the same. Nor have they fallen into any other error than this: they attribute to the nature of the sign what actually results from the variation of the Sun’s position. Regarding the shapes of the images <note>original: "figuris imaginum"; referring to the constellations like the Ram or the Bull.</note>, we have said abundantly in the eighth book how they are non-existent, empty, and fictitious. They are not the works of God, but of men; they did not proceed from the reason of nature, but were fashioned by the recklessness of the poetic mind. But as has been most truly said, astrologers are never more false than when they derive the properties of the signs from these images, seeing as the images differ from the signs—as we demonstrated extensively above—even in the eighth sphere, not only in position and movement, but also in the measurement and quantity of their moving parts. Finally, they resist with an all too sluggish, futile, and indolent slowness when they seek the condition of these same signs from both the work of the Sun and from the image: for clearly, by their own common consent, those traits belong to the immobile signs, while these others agree with the mobile ones.

->PTOLEMY IS CRITICIZED FOR SPEAKING OF THE PLANETS AS IF THEY WERE COMPOSED OF THE ELEMENTS, AND THE REASONS OF OTHERS BY WHICH THEY PROVE THE QUALITIES OF THE PLANETS ARE LIKEWISE REFUTED. Chapter 13.<-

**H**itherto we have spoken of the reasons for the signs and how remarkably irrational they are; in the planets, there is the same falsehood—indeed, a greater one, and a greater recklessness. Intending to show above that Ptolemy philosophized poorly regarding errors, we pointed out those things especially by which he investigates the nature of the planets. For he speaks of them as if the planets consisted of the elements, or consisted of the passions of the elements—not only as if they were changing one another through heat or cold, but as if they were even changed by the vapors of the Earth. Ptolemy says the Moon is humid because, being closest to the Earth, it becomes moist from the Earth's vapors ascending toward it. The star of <term>Saturn</term> is cold and moderately dry; it is cold because it is positioned far from the Sun, and it becomes parched because it is raised far from the vapors of the Earth. <term>Mars</term>, by its proximity to the Sun, is scorched and dried out. <term>Jupiter</term>, being in the middle between the cold of Saturn and the heat of Mars, turns out temperate; but because it is carried above the hot spheres of Mars and the Sun, it primarily provides heat. <term>Venus</term> is humid just like the Moon, for by the abundance of its light it draws many vapors of the Earth to itself; likewise, it has a power of heating from the Sun, to which it is close. <term>Mercury</term> has the property of drying from the Sun, to which it always clings, and the power of moistening from its proximity to the Earth and its border with the Moon. Thus Ptolemy reasons in the first book of the <term>Apotelesmaton</term> <note>original: "Apotelesmaton"; the Greek title for Ptolemy's "Tetrabiblos," the foundational text of Western astrology.</note>. Even if he cannot be persuaded by the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle, who taught that the celestial bodies were made of a perfect "fifth element" (aether) and were not subject to earthly change or elemental qualities.</note> that the heavens are free from these affections, let him at least understand from the number of things he himself demonstrated: the Earth is further from the Moon than would allow the vapors and breaths of the Earth to reach it. These are thought by physicists to be raised no more than sixteen <term>stadia</term> <note>An ancient unit of distance; 16 stadia is roughly 2 miles or 3 kilometers.</note> upward, let alone reaching the Moon, Venus, or Mercury intact...

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

...are raised up. Consider **Venus**: because of its proximity to the Sun, it should be drier than it is humid from the vapors of the earth, especially since it is closer to the Sun than to the earth, and the power of the Sun cannot be compared to the strength of earthly moisture. Consider also **Mercury**: being closer to the earth and therefore more distant from the Sun, they claim it is more dry than humid. How then does <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity, whose work *Tetrabiblos* defined these planetary qualities.</note> remain consistent with himself when he compares the humidity of Venus to the Lunar fire <note>Referring to the "sphere of fire" thought to exist just below the Moon.</note> which is so nearby and yet heats so little that many consider it cold? And if **Saturn** is frozen because it is quite far from the Sun, wouldn't the entire multitude of fixed stars, being even more distant from the sun, be paralyzed by the ice of torpid cold? Yet many declare that there are many of a fiery nature among them. Therefore, the reasoning of <term>Ptolemy</term> is not only false but inconsistent with itself, as usually happens with false arguments.

Others argue based on the colors of the planets, a point which <term>Ptolemy</term> also touched upon regarding **Mars**. These people say that philosophers are lying when they think the elements possess no color or flavor. They claim instead that white color and sweetness among flavors belong to water. To the earth, they assign a dark color and a bitter taste—though others deny this, contending it is rather sweet, for if the earth were bitter, nothing would sprout from it. You admit no flavor in fire, but a red color. They say the air is devoid of both color and flavor, but that it accepts various foreign colors. They say that in the planets themselves there are indeed no flavors, but there are multiple colors, from which we can easily explore their natures.

For they say that the darkness in **Saturn** shows an earthly property, corresponding to <term>black bile</term> <note>original: "atræ bili"; one of the four humors, associated with a melancholic and "earthy" temperament.</note>. In **Mars**, the redness testifies to a fiery quality and <term>red bile</term> <note>original: "bilis rubræ"; also called yellow bile, associated with a "fiery" or choleric temperament.</note>. **Venus**, radiating with yellow and white: from the yellow she is understood to be hot, and from the white, humid; since these qualities are not equal, they indicate a <term>temperament</term> <note>A "temperamentum" in Renaissance medicine was a specific balance of the four primary qualities: hot, cold, wet, and dry.</note> of nature, like the condition <term>of air and blood</term> <note>original: "aëris sanguinisq;"; associated with the sanguine temperament, which was considered the most balanced and healthy.</note>. A similar conjecture is made about **Jupiter**. In the **Moon**, the fact that it shines white shows humidity, while the fact that it has some darkness shows it to be cold. The color of **Mercury** is indeed changed repeatedly; now it seems green, now dark, now it turns to another appearance, but it is more fond of darkness, which is why it is rendered more like earthly dryness.

Thus they reason, quite beyond reason indeed; for colors follow the mixture of elements, of which there is none in the celestial bodies. Nor are the celestial things said by <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The Greek philosopher who argued that the heavens were made of a "fifth element" (aether) and were not subject to the same laws as the four terrestrial elements.</note> to participate in color, except insofar as light is a kind of color. Truly, if color indicates some property of a mixture, light will also indicate the nature of the shining body—if indeed a conjecture is made from color, which is thought to emerge from a variety of mixtures. Therefore, since color will be nothing other than the evidence of light, more or less bright, flowing not from a composite but from a simple body, it will give us no indication of the body that illuminates. What’s more, there would be no certain investigation for us in exploring the celestial bodies from their colors, even if they were endowed with true colors, because the intervention of such a vast and—what is more disturbing—so manifold a space would completely strip away the reliability of the color. And I did not want to object to them that <term>Plato</term> <note>The Greek philosopher; Pico is likely referring to Plato’s views on the deceptive nature of sensory perception or the purity of the celestial realm.</note> wrote...

### Against Astrology, Book X.

...having <note>The Latin word "bentem" is the end of "habentem" (having) from the previous page.</note> in the <term>Phaedo</term> <note>A dialogue by Plato concerning the soul and the nature of the true Earth and heavens.</note>, that what we see are not the actual bodies of the stars, but certain reflections of rays in the air that mirror the appearance of the stars. It is much like how fish living in the deep see, on the upper surface of the water, not the stars themselves, but the images of the stars—what I might call radiant shadows. 

But whether we are looking at these reflections or the stars themselves, no one initiated into the sacred mysteries of philosophy is unaware that colors vary in a marvelous way and that things appear differently due to the intervention of many-shaped bodies. Furthermore, there is a dispute among physicians: <term>Galen</term> <note>A Greek physician and philosopher (c. 129–216 AD) whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note> believes that the powers and properties of herbs can be known from their smell, color, taste, and touch, but it has been demonstrated that this is false, both by the reasoning of <term>Averroes</term> <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), a medieval Andalusian polymath who commented extensively on Aristotle.</note> and through experiments. 

Moreover, no one has even suspected that we can grasp the nature of things from color alone—even for those objects which we can keep right before our eyes and under our gaze for entire days, where neither movement, nor distance, nor a vast amount of light interrupts our diligent study. Who, then, would dare to promise this regarding the heavenly bodies? This is true even if the colors of those bodies are reported back to us as unmixed, sincere, and pure. The whiteness of **lime** is hardly surpassed by that of **snow**, yet in lime there is a great deal of heat, while in snow there is a great deal of cold. 

<term>Avenrodan</term> <note>Ali ibn Ridwan (c. 988–1061), an Egyptian Muslim physician and astrologer known for his commentaries on Ptolemy.</note> errs too shamelessly when he believes that while we are indeed deceived by color in earthly things, we are not deceived in heavenly ones. He argues this because earthly things are mixed from the elements, whereas heavenly things are not. On the contrary, it is precisely from this that we know we should not trust colors regarding the nature of the heavens; since they are not mixed from elements, color can only indicate the nature of a body in so far as it shows us the manner of its mixture. 

Furthermore (as we were just saying), a multitude of bodies intervening across such a vast region cannot fail to pervert or interrupt whatever colors might be imagined there. This is proven by the very variety of opinions that have arisen regarding those colors. For **Aboafar** <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), one of the most influential Persian astrologers of the Middle Ages.</note> denies that the celestial colors of the **Planets** are such as we described above, which were believed by those who judged the stars by their colors. He claims that the star of **Saturn** reflects the color of lead rather than one representing the darkness of the earth; that there is no whiteness in **Jupiter**, nor is a particular brightness proper to **Venus**. 

Again, if **Mars** is called "hot" because it is red, then a red color should be much more due to the **Sun**, which is hotter than **Mars**. As for the **Moon**, no one who is not lacking eyes would think it is white. In the "Natural History," the accounts of the colors of the **Planets** handed down from the records of the ancients appear somewhat different: there **Saturn** is described as white, **Jupiter** as clear, **Venus** as "glowing" when called <term>Lucifer</term> <note>The Morning Star.</note> and "shining" when it has the name <term>Vesper</term> <note>The Evening Star.</note>, **Mercury** as radiating, and the **Moon** with a mild color. 

In general, what is said about **Mercury**—that it varies in color, and is therefore of a multiform and changeable nature—arises from a deceptive appearance. This does not happen because **Mercury** is actually like this, but because it is always seen very close to the **Sun** and largely near the <term>horizon</term> <note>Original: "finitorem".</note>. In that part of the sky (as <term>Ptolemy</term> testifies), the many vapors and earthly moistures create shifting appearances and colors for the stars...

represent the many wandering rays. Therefore, that entire commentary of <term>Aboafar</term> <note>Also known as Albumasar (787–886 AD), a Persian astrologer whose works were highly influential in medieval Europe.</note> concerning colors is not colored by any shred of probability—though the whole universe of astrologers depends upon it. Aboafar himself, rejecting the aforementioned reasons, thinks the nature of the planets can be known from the <term>primary qualities</term> <note>The four basic building blocks of matter in ancient physics: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> they produce, just as <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most famous astronomer of antiquity, whose "Tetrabiblos" was the foundational text for astrology.</note> advised. For this reason, he claims Saturn is found by experience to be the author of cold and dryness; for these qualities flourish in bodies when Saturn is the <term>governor of the year</term> <note>In astrology, the planet that "rules" or has the most influence over a particular year's events and weather.</note>. The same has been observed for Mars and the rest—whatever elementary influence each one breathes into physical bodies. From these effects, he conjectures about the entire nature of the planet: since the works of Saturn (cold and dryness) are hostile to life, the star of Saturn is judged to be <term>malefic</term> <note>An astrological term meaning "evil-doing" or producing negative outcomes.</note> and unlucky. Mars is also judged malefic because of its parching heat and immoderate dryness. Conversely, Jupiter and Venus are <term>benefic</term> <note>Producing good or favorable outcomes.</note> stars because of their hot and moist nature, which are the qualities by which life is preserved. He argues similarly for the others. Finally, he refers everything to those four qualities: cold, moisture, heat, and dryness.

However, this kind of reasoning depends entirely on experiments. He does not prove by reason that Saturn is the cause of cold rather than heat (as those I just refuted were trying to do), but treats it as if it were a fact discovered by the evidence of the senses. Yet many philosophers think this is utterly false, asserting that no star is a producer of cold and dryness. Nor is there any agreement among them as to which star produces which quality—something that is especially ambiguous regarding the Moon and Venus. For both <term>Abenragel</term> <note>Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer.</note> and <term>Alchabitius</term> <note>Al-Qabisi, a 10th-century Arab astrologer and mathematician.</note> consider Venus to be cold, while Aboafar and Ptolemy think she is hot. Ptolemy thinks the Moon is hot; others say she is cold. They do not even agree on Mercury. Furthermore, if the observation is based on the planet governing the year (as Aboafar wants), how can they agree on the result when there is such an ambiguity of opinions regarding how to choose the "Lord of the Year"? There are almost as many future "lords" as there are astrologers to pronounce them.

### IF WE GRANT THAT PLANETS PRODUCE THE PRIMARY 
### qualities, it must not be granted for that reason that some 
### are harmful and others beneficial. Chapter XIV.

Furthermore, whether we are led by such experiments or by the first reasons mentioned, even if we grant what they say about the qualities, nothing more is achieved than the discovery that the influence of the stars alters the state of the air. It does not follow that the stars themselves possess these primary dispositions, nor that some are beneficial and others harmful, nor can the unique and peculiar gifts of the stars be gathered from this. First, if the star of Saturn represents the nature of Earth, and Mars represents Fire, why is one "evil" and the other "evil"? Neither Earth nor Fire is evil; they have countless uses for life, and nature could not exist without them. Even in the bodies of living creatures, <term>black and red bile</term> <note>Two of the four "humors" or bodily fluids (melancholy and choler) thought to control health and temperament.</note> are not harmful but necessary; they are no less useful for performing certain duties than blood or phlegm. If they are said to cause harm by excess, then [even blood...]

# Against Astrology, Book X.

...in that way, blood and <term>phlegm</term> <note>one of the four "humors" or bodily fluids in ancient medicine; associated with cold and moisture.</note> behave if they grow beyond measure. But if the logic of the "particular world"—which we call man—rightly investigates the universal world, we will recognize that it is a mistake to ascribe the excess of any quality in the human body to the stars. For we believe it is the task of the celestial nature to rule and moderate the flowing and wandering matter of corruptible things, so that the <term>elements</term> <note>The four basic building blocks: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</note> stay within their boundaries and remain content with their prescribed laws, not causing trouble for the world’s business. 

Why, then, by the same logic, should it not rather be the heavens' role to contain and restrain the qualities in our body throughout the continuous arrangement of life, rather than for the heavens to destroy the whole and undermine everything by the excessive provocation of one part? Therefore, if Saturn presides over <term>black bile</term> <note>original: "atra bilis"; also known as the humor of melancholy. Astrologers associated it with Saturn's supposed cold and dry nature.</note>—since nothing emanates from the heavens that is not orderly and life-giving—he will not excite it to the destruction of the living creature, but will moderate it for its preservation. Nor will black bile receive from its star a reason to act more violently, but rather a reason to act more moderately and vigorously. For the matter of these things is a certain heap of elements, while the heaven is the <term>efficient cause</term> <note>The primary agent that brings something into being.</note>. This cause forces the things being mixed into a unity, and tempers all things under the peace of a single community, moving one thing by one part of the heaven and another by another (if those things are subject to different stars), yet with all stars breathing together toward the harmony of the whole in unison with the heaven. 

Therefore, let no one be deceived into suspecting that, when they hear Saturn is set over <term>red bile</term> <note>Usually associated with Mars, though Pico is discussing the general principle of planetary "prefectures" over bodily fluids.</note>, anything is done by the star to the quality subject to it which does not agree with the good order of life. For the duty of the celestial government should be understood as much to restrain what is tumultuous as to stir up what is sluggish. 

Death does not come from the heavens, but from nature, when each quality has so degenerated by its own vice that it cannot sustain the discipline of the presiding star, but either wanders out of bounds or, having slackened, fails. This is why I have warned the reader once and again: there is no profession more injurious to the heavens than astrological superstition. Whatever we do that is contrary to reason, it blames on the fault of the will; whatever happens to nature contrary to order, it blames on the vice of reckless and failing matter—yet astrology strives to blame all of this on the stars. It does not think the dignity of the stars is safe unless we credit them with every most unworthy thing. 

Therefore, the logic should be gathered thus: the four qualities do not harm bodies but benefit them when they are moderate and tempered, and they proceed from the stars in no other way [than tempered]. Thus, just because they proceed from them, the stars cannot be called harmful. In the first place, neither Mars nor Saturn can be called "evil" because one stirs up black bile and the other red in our bodies, since neither bile is harmful to life if it does not exceed its limits—on the contrary, they are necessary. Indeed, far from overflowing to a fatal degree by the authority of the heavens, these fluids are contained within their prescribed limit by no other source. I have spoken abundantly on this matter in the third book, where we proved that the evils of the body do not proceed from the heavens. 

But if the heavens did invigorate qualities of this sort even beyond measure, it would not immediately follow that Mars and Saturn are "evil planets" for everyone; rather, these excesses would be healthy for some people. For the rays of Mars would temper "cold seed," and a body that is becoming too hot would be brought back to a proper balance by the cold of Saturn. Therefore, an astrologer could not [judge] him whose...

He is currently arguing that the "primary qualities" (heat, cold, moisture, dryness) which astrologers attribute to planets do not logically align with the actual effects those planets are said to have on human health and fortune. He is specifically dismantling the idea that certain planets are inherently "evil" because they correspond to certain bodily humors.</meta>

-># Giovanni Pico della Mirandola<-

...if [the astrologer] had seen in a birth chart that powerful Saturn assigned the troubles of <term>black bile</term> <note>original: "atra bilis"; the humor associated with melancholy and Saturn's cold, dry nature.</note>, he would not pronounce anyone subject to the heats of <term>yellow bile</term> <note>original: "choleræ"; the humor associated with fire and Mars.</note> because Mars had breathed upon them more than others, unless nature had already written these traits for those people, or experience had explored them. Since the astrologer neither knows this nor investigates it, but only examines "good" and "bad" fortune based on those excesses of qualities, it is clear he will always be wandering in doubt. 

It is also clear that what they say—that a "lucky" planet is sometimes changed into an "unlucky" one, and an "unlucky" one into a "lucky" one—happens only because of the condition of the physical matter, not because of the variety of locations, distances, and zodiac signs. If these placements were the cause of such changes, the astrologers' decrees on the matter would be very poorly founded, since they maintain their position based on the primary qualities <note>The four basic qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>. 

For instance, Mars in Aries—as it will heat more intensely—should also cause more harm; yet the astrologers flatly deny this. For they say, "Mars does not overthrow his own house." Indeed, universally, they consider any star to be "happy" when it occupies its own house, term, or exaltation. But who would doubt that Mars heats more in Aries? Since Aries is, as they wish it, a fire sign. By the same token, Saturn in Capricorn would be harmful, but in Aries he would have to be considered lucky, contrary to their opinion; for in Capricorn, Saturn's coldness and dryness (by which he is thought to cause harm) are intensified, whereas the heat of Aries would moderate his cold rigor. 

Furthermore, Saturn would be "luckier" when moving in <term>retrograde</term> <note>The apparent backward motion of a planet in the sky.</note>—which they do not believe—than when moving in a direct course, because as <term>Al-Kindi</term> <note>original: "Alchindus"; a 9th-century Arab philosopher and astrologer known as the "Philosopher of the Arabs."</note> says, when a planet regresses, it heats more. By the same logic, Mercury in Virgo will harm us with excessive dryness, and the Sun's heat will invade us more violently than is proper when combined with the heat of Leo; it would be more moderately healthy only when its rays are spread upon us tempered by the mixture of a "cold" sign. 

Thus, this theory of "primary qualities" is taken in so many conflicting ways that it contradicts not only the truth but the very dogmas of the astrologers. For besides what we have said, there are still many things we might object to: for example, why is there no star ruling over <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: "pituitæ"; the cold, moist humor.</note>, just as Saturn commands black bile, Mars commands red bile, and Jupiter commands the blood? If they should say that the Moon or Venus rules it, then Venus and the Moon would have to be numbered among the "unlucky" <note>malefic</note> planets, since an excess of phlegm harms life no less than black or red bile does. 

Furthermore, if the Moon is such as she is defined by <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>original: "Ptol."; Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note>, she will seem to have the character of the most "unhappy" star of all. For she is (as he likes to say) of little heat but much moisture, and nothing is more subject to putrefaction than such a temperature. Therefore, if a planet is judged to be harmful or healthy based on the influence of its primary qualities, the Moon—as the producer of a dissolving and corrupting mixture—will be harmful, and far more harmful than Mars or Saturn. For even if those two do not infuse the "best" natural qualities, they at least infuse qualities that only harm when they are not moderated. But what descends from the Moon is, by its very nature, immoderate: due to the weakness of its heat, the flowing moisture is neither sufficiently "cooked" nor "refined." Yet <term>Ptolemy</term> himself counts the Moon among the "lucky" <note>benefic</note> stars, leaning on the authority of the ancients, and...

He uses the examples of Mars in Aries and the Moon's moisture to show that astrologers ignore their own physical rules in favor of arbitrary symbolic traditions.</summary>

->### Against Astrology, Book X.<-

...and <term>Aboafar</term> <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a highly influential Persian astrologer known in the Latin West as Albumasar.</note> even contends that the **Sun** is more fortunate than **Jupiter**. One might gladly ask him why this is so, since the **Sun** is hotter than **Mars**, and when that heat is joined with dryness, **Mars** is considered "unfortunate," yet the **Sun** is judged the first among the "fortunate" stars. For this is how **Aboafar** defines it: he grants the **Sun** the primary place among the authors of good fortune, the **Moon** second, **Jupiter** third, **Venus** fourth, and **Mercury** fifth. He even seems to disagree with himself regarding **Mercury**, since he wants its nature to be dry and to taste more of the nature of the earth than the other planets. Therefore, if he followed his own principles, he ought to count **Mercury** among the harmful planets. 

However, other authors disagree not only with each other but also significantly with **Aboafar** himself. A large portion of them treat the **Moon**, the **Sun**, and **Mercury** as "neutral" <note>original: "medios"; meaning they can be either good or bad depending on their placement.</note> between the harmful and the beneficial planets; yet, as we have seen, **Aboafar** makes them all beneficial. <term>Heliodorus and Paulus</term> <note>Heliodorus and Paulus Alexandrinus were prominent Greek astrological writers whose works formed the basis of many medieval theories.</note> also number **Mercury** among the healthy planets. <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>The 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, considered the "bible" of traditional astrology.</note> makes the **Moon** healthy, but he makes **Mercury** and the **Sun** of a neutral condition. Thus, this discord among them over these matters significantly overthrows their theory and lays bare the uncertainty of their art. 

Furthermore, if that supposition regarding the "primary qualities" <note>The four basic building blocks of the physical world: heat, cold, moisture, and dryness.</note> were true, it would follow—beyond any controversy—that out of the twelve celestial signs, six would be "unlucky" and "unfortunate." Specifically, all the fire signs and all the earth signs would be so, because they abound in those qualities for which **Mars** and **Saturn** are accused of causing misfortune. Indeed, nine signs would be unlucky rather than six, since in the water signs there is also a "deadly moisture" (as they think), combined with coldness. This moisture is not like the moisture in the air signs, or like that found in **Jupiter**, **Venus**, and the "airy" planets—which is vital and prolific—but is instead a "watery" and "leaking" moisture. 

This leads to an absurdity for two reasons: first, the heavens—the most beneficial of all bodies—would be condemned in their greatest part; and second, "unfortunate" signs would serve as the houses for "fortunate" stars. For example, **Pisces** and **Sagittarius** serve as houses for **Jupiter**, and **Taurus** for **Venus**; yet these ought to be distributed according to a kinship of nature. 

Finally, if they call these planets "fortunes" and those others "misfortunes" because vital qualities proceed more from the former while corrupting and harmful qualities come from the latter, this would (to settle the matter most generously with them) affect nothing more than the condition of the physical body. After all, the body is tempered and organized by those primary qualities. But how will they defend the idea that this influence extends to external affairs and "accidental successes"? Their defense would be weakest of all, as we have shown in the arguments above. 

Lastly, even if everything we have said so far amounted to nothing, there is no doubt that those who wish to explain the influence of the stars solely through these primary qualities are acting with too little skill and consideration. Yet there is no astrologer who does not do this; even those who boast that they can provide "natural causes" for the dogmas of this art turn eventually to nothing other than these elemental dispositions. But in truth, if there are any breaths of influence <note>original: "afflatus"; a divine or celestial breath or inspiration.</note> that are proper and particular to the stars, these do not follow such elemental qualities. Rather, they follow the "occult" and truly celestial properties of each individual star. In earthly things, people are accustomed to refer to these same types of properties whenever they see effects that rise above elemental nature, yet remain within the boundaries of the physical body...

...while we see gifts and virtues that not only do not arise from the mixture of elemental qualities, but even disagree with them. For example, <term>myrobalans</term> <note>Astringent plum-like fruits used in medieval medicine, believed to purge the body of "black bile" and extend life.</note>, possessing a cold and dry temperament, would seem to contribute more toward death than toward life; yet, by the privilege of a more secret nature, their efficacy is believed to be wonderful for prolonging and revitalizing life. Much more so do **Jupiter**, **Saturn**, and all superior nature—if what the astrologers believe is true—influence us. Even if this planet is judged cold and dry <note>Saturn</note> and that one hot and moist <note>Jupiter</note>, we must think that they perform many of their most important works not through these qualities, but through other hidden powers of their rays. This is true partly because such works are more consistent with their nature, and partly because the effects attributed to them by astrologers cannot (as we have demonstrated) be traced back to those physical qualities and conditions. If this is the case, it is clear by reason that those qualities cannot be detected [by their effects], which is what we undertook to prove in this section. There remains the path of experience, about which we will dispute extensively in the following book.

### THAT THE REASONS OF ASTROLOGERS CONCERNING THE RULERS OF DAYS AND HOURS, AND THE YEARS OF THE PLANETS, ARE INEFFECTIVE, AND THAT ASTROLOGERS OFTEN USE CIRCULAR REASONING. Chapter 15.

**C**onfuted now is every method by which they trust they can prove the universal properties of the planets—whether from the locations of the spheres and the position of the earth, or from the colors of the stars, or the influence of the four primary conditions. There remain arguments by which they gather certain more specific conditions of the planets. These are elicited either from a parabolic similarity, or from astrological principles, or from the order of the spheres. They argue from the spheres as they do regarding the lordship of days and hours: for example, giving the first hour of the day to the **Sun**, they give the remaining hours to the **Planets** which follow in succession based on the position of the spheres. From this, the distribution of the days is born, so that a day is ascribed to that Planet which happens to fall on the first hour of the day when the hourly division is made through the preceding order. 

However, these things are amply refuted by what was said above, where we declared how futile this mode of arguing is, and how the order of the orbs is placed in ambiguity; and how the idea of a "succession of command" in the heavens is a vain imagination. Beyond this, we can also ask the astrologers: what reason showed the **Chaldeans** and **Egyptians** (the authors of this superstition) the very first day of all time? For they cannot use the authority of the **Mosaic Law** <note>The Law of Moses/The Torah.</note>, unless they believe that astrologers, along with every other diviner, should be utterly exterminated. 

They reason from astrological principles when they say a certain Planet grants so many years of life because it possesses that many <term>bounds</term> <note>original: "fines"; specific segments of a zodiac sign traditionally ruled by different planets.</note> in the **zodiac**. Yet what they assume about the "bounds" is just as uncertain as the very "years" they are trying to prove by them. Furthermore, even if what they claim about the bounds were true, according to <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity.</note> there is no logical reason why our lifespans should be determined by that number. Moreover, they often sin in these matters by using circular reasoning: in one place they derive the number of bounds from the number of years, and in another, they derive the years from the bounds...

He specifically critiques the circular logic used to determine human lifespans based on astrological "bounds."</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Book X of Pico’s "Disputations Against Divinatory Astrology." Having previously critiqued the physical attributes assigned to planets, Pico here mocks the circular logic and symbolic leaps—such as associating body parts with planets based on height or visual similarity—that astrologers use to justify their systems.</meta>

->## Against Astrology, Book X. <-

...collecting these points. They begin the year from **Aries**, since it is the first of the signs; however, they usually demonstrate that it is first in a continuous circle by arguing that we begin our reckoning of time from it. In the same way, they argue both that the second place <note>The "second house" in an astrological chart, often associated with wealth and resources.</note> corresponds to **Jupiter** because he makes and portends wealth, and that **Jupiter** makes and portends wealth because he corresponds to the second place. 

You will find many examples of this kind in their books, but some are far more ridiculous, especially if you happen upon the books of <term>Abu Ma'shar</term> <note>original: "Aboasaris." A famous 9th-century Persian astrologer whose works were central to medieval European astrology.</note>. I was recently reading in his work that the **Moon** grants one hundred and eight years, while the **Sun** grants one hundred and twenty. His reason is that the **Moon** falls short of the **Sun's** life by twelve years, because she has no power until she has moved twelve degrees away from the **Sun** <note>This refers to the "combust" phase in astrology, where a planet close to the Sun is thought to be weakened by its heat.</note>. Thus, it is no wonder that <term>Abu Ma'shar</term> boasts of having given a full rational account of astrological dogma, since there is nothing so irrational that he does not consider it "reason." 

There is a similar insanity when they say the shorter years of the **Sun** are nineteen, because the luminaries <note>The Sun and Moon.</note> are joined by their mean motion through this number <note>The Metonic cycle of 19 years, after which the phases of the moon recur on the same days of the year.</note>. Here there is nothing at all in common, nothing connected, and no logical sequence between the premises and the conclusion; yet they argue that because the **Sun** and **Moon** meet after this number of years in their mean motion, the **Sun** therefore "gives" that many years, even though it is the smallest number it grants. 

It is just as if one were to say: "A man is born with two eyes, therefore he is also born from two parents." They use symbolic similarities in this way: "The **Moon** is the door of heaven, therefore it signifies the mouth," for a door is essentially the "mouth" of a house, and the mouth is the "door" for food and speech. Likewise, the beard belongs to the same star because it is renewed again and again, just like the **Moon**. 

The ears, however, are assigned to **Saturn**, because they occupy the high parts of the head, just as <term>Saturn</term> himself is high in the heavens. By that same logic—namely, because he is the highest—he produces tall men, even though this does not fit his nature at all, since he is judged to be dry and cold <note>In Aristotelian physics, heat and moisture are required for growth and height; Saturn's cold, dry nature should logically result in stunted growth.</note>. 

These are the "reasons" of the astrologers by which their celestial dogmas are supported. I would not call them reasons, but rather opportunities for wandering or joking. Once heard, the vanity of their dogma is as obvious as the firmness of truth usually becomes when it is heard. Therefore, it would have been better for them to cover these things with a veil or a chest, like secret rites <note>original: "orgia." Referring to the mystery cults of antiquity where rituals were kept hidden from the uninitiated.</note>, leaving behind a suspicion of mystery, rather than trying to appear rational. By offering these reasons, they sign the indictment of their own case with their own hand; for to hear these explanations is nothing other than to understand exactly what led the astrologers into error.

Having spent the previous books dismantling the logical and physical "reasons" astrologers provide for their system, Pico now turns his critique toward their claim of "experience"—the idea that their predictions are based on centuries of recorded empirical observation.</meta>

# GIOVANNI PICO 
# della Mirandola’s Disputations Against 
# Astrology, Book XI.

->FROM THE MATTERS PROVEN HITHERTO, IT IS CLEAR<-
->that astrology has not been verified by experiments, and<-
->that this is also proven by many reasons. Chapter 1.<-

If they have been unable to grasp the nature of the heavenly bodies through reason, as we have demonstrated, could they have done so through experience? And although they may be ignorant of *why* something happens, have they nonetheless learned *that* it happens through observations? If so, even if astrology cannot claim the name of a science <note>In the medieval sense, a "science" (*scientia*) required knowledge of the underlying causes, not just the results.</note>, it might still hold the prerogative of both an art and a true tradition. Therefore, it might also predict the truth, whether it has achieved this through <term>syllogisms</term> <note>Formal logical arguments where a conclusion is drawn from two premises.</note> or through experiments; for it matters little to the act of divining how the result was reached, provided it *was* reached. 

However, astrologers—as is common with every prodigious art—are accustomed to defending themselves largely under the title of "experience." This is the cunning refuge they retreat into whenever they say or promise things beyond belief and beyond reason, thinking they can immediately extricate themselves from the snares of all logical arguments if they simply say they have "experienced" it so. We shall therefore take away this refuge from them—a refuge which those who are more accustomed to speaking with their lips and hearing with their ears than with their hearts imagine to be something substantial. 

For if anyone has thoroughly explored and meditated upon what "experience" actually is, and the ways in which it might be acquired regarding the influence of the stars, he will certainly not doubt that the peculiar powers and specific operations of the stars are as inscrutable to experiments as they are to reason. Indeed, this can be made clear enough from the preceding books: if there is either no fate directed from heaven at all, or if fate—if it exists—depends not on the initial hour but on the knowledge of the matter <note>Pico argues that the physical makeup of a person (matter) matters more than the alignment of stars at their birth.</note>, it is obvious that no path is left for experiments. Since it will be as uncertain to you when each star first breathed upon a person as the specific condition of that original matter is entirely unknown. 

Furthermore, even if someone makes the "seminal hour" <note>The moment of conception.</note> the hour of fate, the astrologers themselves will not deny that the opportunity for observing it would be far too hidden. But even granted that the time of the birth <note>original: "genituræ"</note> were sufficiently observed, how could that observation be faithful? For it has not been established (as we have declared) how many and which celestial causes must be observed. Nor can they determine with any reliability, at every single moment, the form, the condition, or the position of those causes they *do* think they have grasped. Finally, they neither possess an exact birth hour from the "lord of the birth" <note>The planet thought to rule over the specific moment of a person's birth.</note>, nor can they correct any errors by some other method. Furthermore, if they fail in any of these points (and we have shown they always fail), the authority of the entire observation must necessarily collapse. Now, even if they do not fail in those matters, the fact remains that experiments regarding the heavens... <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page.</note>

<summary>Pico begins Book XI by challenging the astrologer's last line of defense: "experience" or empirical observation. He argues that since the exact moment of conception or birth is impossible to record with precision, and the variables of the heavens are too numerous, astrology cannot claim to be based on experimental evidence.</summary>

<meta>On the previous page, Pico began his critique of "experience"—the empirical claim that astrology is based on thousands of years of observation. He argued that if astrologers cannot understand the heavens through reason, they certainly cannot claim to have mastered them through experience, especially since they use this "experience" as a shield to deflect logical scrutiny.</meta>

<page-num>709</page-num>
<header>On Astrology, Book XI.</header>

...we shall show that nothing of the sort is possible. Let us therefore grant the <term>natal astrologers</term> <note>original: *genethliacis*; those who cast charts based on the moment of birth</note> that they faithfully record the hour of birth, and as accurately as possible the state of the heavens at that hour. I ask: by what means do they think they will determine through experience what "decree" of heaven such a constellation makes or signifies? After all, experience is gathered from the manifold and frequently repeated observation of the same thing. Yet the same <term>constellation</term> <margin>--</margin> either never returns (as the more learned prove) or, as the ancients believed, it will not return until after many thousands of ages.

Perhaps they will respond that particular configurations of stars return and are repeated more often, even if the restoration of the whole and absolute constellation does not occur. They might argue that they can therefore obtain knowledge of those particulars through repeated observations, and from these, once the experiments are gathered, future events may be predicted with confidence. This might be explained by an example: someone is born with <term>Aries</term> <note>The Ram, the first sign of the Zodiac</note> rising on the horizon, with the star of <term>Mars</term> placed there, and with <term>Saturn</term> occupying the seventh <term>angle</term> <note>original: *cardinem*; the "hinges" or most powerful points of a chart, such as the Ascendant or Descendant</note>. Then, while the other stars are arranged in their own ways, another person is born; their birth chart (<term>genitura</term>) is different in all other respects, but similar regarding Mars and Saturn. The <term>astrologer</term> will be able to make an observation of that specific part twice, even if he cannot observe the whole constellation. They may defend themselves by saying that when this happens frequently, the repeated observation creates an "experiment."

But they speak with little truth and little consistency, even with their own principles. Firstly, that same particular configuration works differently within a different "whole." Secondly, the substance of the entire "decree" does not arise from individual parts so much as from the whole—that is, from the harmony of all the parts together producing something unique and specific, which no part produces on its own, nor even all the parts simply added together. For all the parts are one thing, but that which springs forth from the proportion of the mixture of them all is quite another. 

Therefore, such an observation, by which they gather their "experiments," will be imperfect. For an observation is imperfect if it ignores the whole, and it is deceptive if it considers the same part but not within the same whole. This reasoning draws its strength from none other than the precepts of the astrologers themselves, who assert that everything happens according to the mixtures of the stars, and that the <term>allotment of fate</term> <note>original: *fati sortitionem*</note> does not come from their individual powers, but from the combined embrace of them all and the union of their fellowship. 

Therefore, if in one or two birth charts you see the subject of the chart torn apart by calamities when <term>Mars</term> and <term>Saturn</term> look upon each other from opposite angles, you cannot—as if an "experiment" had been proven—announce calamities just because the same thing happens another time. For there is nothing to prevent that configuration, under a different tempering of the other stars, from combining in such a way that it either does no harm, or perhaps produces something entirely different than what it had done in other birth charts through various mixtures of rays—at least, if we were to agree with the astrologers that human affairs happen by fate. To this we might add what is discovered daily through experience: that the birth charts of the most miserable people are often the most "fortunate," and conversely, those of the fortunate are the most "miserable." This is because, although particular configurations might seem to portend either a good or bad lot based on past observations...

Here, he examines the tension between ancient astrologers who focused on specific cases and Ptolemy, who attempted to create a systematic, rule-based approach.</meta>
