<header>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</header>

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

...the harmony of the total temperament itself—never before seen, never known, never explored—can now produce an effect different from what those stars portended elsewhere, whether individually or in a different mixture. Observing this, the most ancient astrologers handed down the dogmas of this art in no other way than by setting out, in detail, individual <term>birth charts</term> <note>original: *genituras*; the specific configuration of stars at a person's birth</note> they had observed, and finally comparing them with the actual outcomes. They did this so that they might indicate not just what <term>Saturn</term> or <term>Jupiter</term> produced, but what such a complete constellation brought forth. <term>Maternus</term> <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer</note>, following the example of the Egyptians, achieved this in some way in the sixth book of his commentaries.

However, <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity</note> accuses those ancients of failing to reduce the art to a systematic method, and of pursuing a matter that is infinite and incomprehensible. Therefore, he turned himself toward explaining universal rules and the simple powers of the stars, believing that once these were known, a <term>natal astrologer</term> <note>original: *genethliacum*; one who predicts a person's fate from their birth chart</note> could finally judge a specific mixture by his own conjecture. 

But although he rightly accuses the ancient astrologers, he himself is no less rightly to be accused. For those ancients saw correctly what needed to be done, but they erred in thinking it was something that *could* be done; since the matter is infinite, it can be reduced neither to an art nor a method. Furthermore, there is no use for it, since the same constellation is never restored. Thus, Ptolemy, considering what *could* be done rather than what *ought* to be done, wandered too far if he thought that true predictions could be made from those simplified rules. Perhaps this is why <term>Avenazra</term> <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a medieval Jewish scholar and astrologer</note> writes that Ptolemy's rules never agree with actual outcomes and experiments. Yet Ptolemy is less to be blamed because, as we showed in the second book, he clearly confessed that this art is based on opinion, conjecture, doubt, and deception.

Therefore, with the subject now brought into the open, let us challenge the natal astrologer. Here is something, O Astrologer, that is powerful and primary in producing an effect (if all else were granted to you): namely, the specific effect of the *entire* harmony, upon which the fortune of the newborn most properly depends. Since neither reason nor observation has given you knowledge of this harmony, how can you explain the truth of fate? For you are deceived if you think the power of the whole is nothing more than a collection of the effects of the individual parts. This would only be true in the case of objects or qualities that are merely heaped together and clinging to one another, but not where they are mixed and grow together into another form—which is what all astrology believes happens with the stars. 

Just as one has not truly experienced the property of <term>theriac</term> <note>original: *theriacæ*; a famous ancient "universal" medicinal compound made of dozens of ingredients, including snake flesh</note> who has merely observed the individual powers of the ingredients from which it is composed, so too the person who has experienced the parts of the heavens separately does not understand what the present army of the sky will achieve. For it is not only the relationship of part to part (that is, star to star) that produces the outcome, but the status and condition of *all* the stars together among themselves. This is what is unique to the person being born—just as their own individual nature is not born from a mere flood of accidental qualities, but is an incommunicable and peculiar substance, a private allotment of fate. What of the fact that not even a single star...

<summary>Pico argues that astrology fails because the "total harmony" of a constellation is a unique mixture that cannot be understood by simply adding up the known effects of individual planets. He compares this to a complex medicine (theriac), where the final product has properties that its individual ingredients do not possess.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's systematic dismantling of astrology. On the previous page, he argued that because celestial configurations never repeat exactly, astrologers cannot claim to have a body of "experimental evidence." Here, he addresses the problem of causality: since stars always act in combination, it is impossible to isolate the specific influence of a single planet.</meta>

<page-num>511</page-num>
<header>Against Astrology, Book XI.</header>

...[no one] can attain knowledge of the stars through experiment, since nothing acts in isolation, but everything always operates in conjunction with others. This means not only that any given star can only be defined by its relationship to others, but that it is utterly impossible to discern a star’s influence through knowledge separated from the rest. For you will indeed see a series of a certain kind of life and certain events proceed from a total constellation; however, since all the stars are acting upon all those things, you will not be able to know which star was the author of which specific event, unless you have first grasped the nature of each star separately, either through reason or some other prior path. 

But if you say that you will observe in this way: that when you see men with similar fates, you will argue that the outcome arises primarily from that part where their <term>birth charts</term> <note>original: *decreta*; refers here to the "decrees" of the stars at birth</note> harmonize—and that you will reach this conclusion through frequent observation.

I respond that this way of conjecturing is far too fallacious. This is because a similar state of a star can produce a different result when in a different mixture, and a dissimilar state can produce the same result. Furthermore, the same chance event may not have the same cause, since according to the opinion of astrologers, the causes in the heavens for the same effect are almost innumerable. 

This will all be clearer with an example: Peter is born with **Jupiter** placed in **Pisces**; Paul is born with **Jupiter** similarly situated, but with the rest of the constellation being entirely different. They live with disparate lots in terms of character, talent, and health, yet they share an equal fortune in accumulating wealth. Is it permitted from this to conjecture that Jupiter, placed in the <term>second house</term> <note>original: *loco secundo*; in astrology, the "second house" of a chart governs personal finances and wealth</note> in Pisces, is the giver of riches? 

Certainly it is not permitted. For what was common to them in fate—namely, the abundance of riches—could have proceeded from different celestial causes, not from common ones. For example, in one man's <term>nativity</term> <note>original: *genitura*; the configuration of the stars at the moment of birth</note>, the <term>Lord of the Horoscope</term> <note>original: *dominus horoscopi*; the planet that rules the sign rising on the eastern horizon</note> might have bestowed power upon the Sun occupying an <term>angle</term> <note>original: *cardinem*; one of the four most powerful points in a chart: the East, West, Zenith, or Nadir</note>. Meanwhile, for the other man coming into the light, the <term>Lot of Fortune</term> <note>original: *pars fortunae*; a mathematical point in a chart used to predict prosperity</note> might have held the East, joined to its own lord by a favorable aspect. Or perhaps in one birth a <term>benefic planet</term> <note>original: *Planeta fortunator*; a "lucky" planet, usually Jupiter or Venus</note> shone in the first angle, while in the other, **Mercury**—situated in that same place—had its nature changed by a lucky and angular planet. Or even if **Venus** was residing in the fifth house at Peter's birth but held power in the first, while at Paul's birth the <term>luminaries</term> <note>The Sun and the Moon</note>, weakened by no <term>debilities</term> <note>original: *humilitatibus*; positions where a planet's power is diminished</note>, looked upon each other amicably. 

According to the opinion of the astrologers, the same fortune of riches for both men would result not from the same "face" of the stars, but from different causes. Various chances can lead to the same result, even if the star that supposedly "crafted" that result was in a similar position in both births. 

Furthermore, the condition of a single star cannot be exactly the same unless the entire constellation is fundamentally the same. Also, a contrary force could have been present in the other person's <term>theme</term> <note>original: *themate*; another word for a horoscope or birth chart</note>, with the power of a star there either overwhelming or dulling the effectiveness of the planet in question. It is clear, therefore, that from the joined and <term>indiscriminate</term> <note>original: *promisscuoq*; meaning mixed together without distinction</note> influence of the stars, we cannot discern by any observation whatsoever what any star primarily bestows. Therefore, neither the powers nor the natures of the stars can be defined by known experiments. 

There is another reason for this invincible difficulty: even if each individual star did act separately, the condition of another star could still invert, interrupt, or frustrate those effects...

<summary>Pico argues that because stars always act in combination, it is logically impossible to isolate the influence of a single planet through observation. He uses the example of two wealthy men (Peter and Paul) to show that identical outcomes can stem from entirely different astrological causes.</summary>

...or by the multiplicity of lower and surrounding causes, no one—unless they are reckless and hasty in judgment—would assert that these things happen because a star is in such a state, and that therefore when it is in that state again, a similar outcome is to be expected. For perhaps that star was by its own nature going to produce a different result, but the outcome was changed by a person's private fate, or the universal fate of the region or the year, or of a prince, or city, or family, or household. It could even be changed by the precedent of parents, grandparents, or great-grandparents, or the free will of the person born, or the disposition of the air through which celestial <term>influences</term> <note>original: *influxus*; the "flowing in" of power from the stars</note> are transmitted to us, or by "stubborn matter," or a nearby cause that is not suitable or fit for the higher motions of the heavens. Since all these things can—as the astrologers themselves admit—change the efficiency of the stars, how can an argument be sound if we interpret the nature of the stars solely by what happens? This is especially true since the factors we mentioned are always so closely linked to the operations of the stars that an event we have observed frequently cannot be traced back to a star as its sole origin. 

In this matter, they seem to be irredeemably mistaken: they think that observations made by the **Egyptians**, the **Chaldeans**, or the **Arabs** in their own regions can be held as universal dogma. That is to say, they believe these rules will be equally valid in every region, when in fact it is necessary for things to happen entirely differently—if indeed there is any truth in what they teach and what experience itself demonstrates. For in the changes of the weather, we see quite clearly that the same constellation stirs up different storms in different places: here it is calm, there it is violent; here there is snow, there it is clear; in one place winds, in another rain. It is therefore completely inconsistent to think that in the birthing of human bodies or the success of business affairs (if indeed these things come from heaven) the stars would not operate differently due to the different curvature of the heavens in different locations, even if the stars themselves are the same. 

**Favorinus** <note>A Roman-era skeptical philosopher</note> also raised these objections against them, which we shall confirm with the authority of **Paul of Alexandria**. In his *Introduction to Astrological Effects* <note>original: *isagogis Apotelesmaton*</note>, he writes that births in **Egypt** are especially fortunate when **Aquarius** is in a principal position and well-disposed, because the region of Egypt is subject to Aquarius. From this, perhaps, comes the idea that **Mercury** in Aquarius breathes favorably upon the talents of the Egyptians; and yet, it has been recorded by **Maternus** <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century astrological writer</note> that Mercury is debased and fares poorly in every <term>house of Saturn</term> <note>In traditional astrology, Saturn "rules" the signs of Capricorn and Aquarius; Pico is pointing out a contradiction between different authorities</note>. It is clear, therefore, by the testimony of a singular astrologer, that the same observations will not be valid in every region alike (even if it were possible for any reliable observations to be made in a specific region, which we have already shown to be impossible for many reasons). And if **Hippocrates**, the father of physicians, said that in medicine "experience is deceptive,"

## IF ANY EXPERIENCE OF ASTROLOGICAL
## dogmas can be had, it has not yet been obtained. Chapter II.

**W**e have been arguing up to this point that no length of time, and no amount of industry or learning by any men, could provide a reliable experiment regarding the more secret powers of the stars. Now, even if that has perhaps not yet been fully persuasive, we shall at least demonstrate most clearly this: if any such experience could be obtained, it has certainly not been obtained yet. For by our previous arguments, it was established that knowledge of all such things is extremely difficult, and cannot be perfected except through many revolutions of the ages. Therefore, we first refuted those lies of the astrologers by which they—neither as good Christians, nor skilled scholars, nor truthful men—proclaim that they possess observations spanning so many thousands of years. Next, we shall declare that whatever observations they do have are, by their own words, deceptive.

The philosopher Favorinus <note>A Roman philosopher and orator (c. 80–160 AD) who was a skeptic regarding astrology.</note>, as quoted in the works of Gellius <note>Aulus Gellius, author of *Attic Nights*, a collection of notes on grammar, philosophy, and history.</note>, says: "That discipline of the **Chaldeans** <term>Chaldeans</term> <note>original: *Chaldæorum*; a term often used in antiquity to refer to Babylonian astrologers and mathematicians.</note> is not of such great antiquity as they wish it to appear." And Cicero, following the authority of Panaetius, says: "For as to their claim that the **Babylonians** spent four hundred and seventy thousand years in testing and examining whatever children were born, they are lying; for we have no author who says it could be done or knows that it was done." So says Cicero. 

We, beginning from a deeper point, shall prove their impudence. Whether the world is eternal (as some philosophers believe) or created in time (as the divine truth teaches), let us leave this as a well-attested fact: no observations older than four thousand years could have reached those who handed down the science of the stars. For it is certain even to those philosophers who believed in the eternity of the world that through great changes of the <term>elements</term> <note>The four elements: earth, water, air, and fire, which were believed to shift and cause cataclysms.</note>, the seas dry up and the lands are flooded; the dwellings of lands and men are exchanged, so that the ocean comes to be where there was land, and land where the ocean once was. Not only the sacred historians, but also the philosopher **Plato** and foreign writers have often mentioned such <term>deluges</term> <note>original: *eluuionum*; massive floods like that of Noah or Deucalion.</note> and conflagrations. It matters little whether the novelty of the world or the total change of things robs us of the memory of the past. 

Let us therefore examine from history how old these celestial observations could truly be. **Varro**, the most learned of the Romans, when he set out to compile the oldest possible history, began from the kingdom of the Sicyonians. Trogus <note>Gnaeus Pompeius Trogus, a Roman historian of the 1st century BC.</note>, either slightly earlier or a contemporary, began his work with **Ninus** himself, who fought against **Zoroaster** and lived only a few years before the Patriarch **Abraham**. Hence, those who write that **Zoroaster** flourished five thousand years before the **Trojan War** are caught in a fiction, since not even that many years are counted from **Abraham** to our own times. What reason, then, could there be for both Trogus and Varro—who professed to write the most ancient histories—not to start from an earlier point, except for the novelty of some things in the world, or at least their total renewal? Or...

...none, or they have been entirely obliterated. For although those ancients wished to write, and even wrote the very first histories, they nevertheless wished to write true ones, not fables like those of Herodotus <note>Herodotus (c. 484–425 BC), often called the "Father of History," but also frequently criticized by later writers for including myths and legends.</note> and Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BC.</note>. The most shameless storytellers are accustomed to bolstering their observations of so many thousands of ages with the words of these authors—as if Diodorus, by his own title, and Herodotus, by the consensus of all literature, were not considered the most prolific of fabulists. But let us *pass over* these things; there is in our matter the most evident testimony of Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD).</note>. He says that those notes on the stars which Callisthenes <note>The nephew of Aristotle who accompanied Alexander the Great on his conquests.</note> sent to Greece from Babylon, in the times of Aristotle and Alexander, contained observations of only one thousand nine hundred and three years. If you count those years back from the time of Alexander, you will find they end in the times of the patriarch **Abraham**, or only slightly before.

Hipparchus and Ptolemy <note>The two most influential astronomers of the ancient world; their work formed the basis of Western astronomy for over a millennium.</note>, the princes of astronomy, when they bring forward the observations of the ancients to establish a dogma, bring none older than those which existed under King **Nebuchadnezzar** <note>original: Nabuchodonosor; the Babylonian king who reigned c. 605–562 BC.</note> among the Egyptians or Babylonians. Hipparchus flourished nearly six hundred years after that king's reign, and from his time to our own, no more than one thousand six hundred years or thereabouts have passed. Therefore, they boast falsely and fabulously that they possess observations from so many ages; and it is easily demonstrated that those they do have are necessarily false.

For either these observations began in the time of Ptolemy, or they fell away from those who preceded Ptolemy. Since the record of these observations began after Ptolemy, there has not been enough time to perfect the science—which they themselves will not deny. If, however, the science relies on the experiments of the ancients, which either the Egyptians or the **Chaldeans** <term>Chaldeans</term> <note>original: Chaldaei; a people of Mesopotamia famed for their early developments in astronomy and astrology.</note> handed down, who would doubt that it is deceptive? For there can be no faithful observation of the heavens among those who do not correctly grasp the motions of the stars. Everyone who has touched the books of the mathematicians knows that in these matters the Chaldeans and Egyptians alike erred greatly. Ptolemy censures them everywhere in his *Great Composition* <note>original: *Magna compositione*; better known by its Arabic-derived name, the *Almagest*.</note>, and Hipparchus censures them as well.

Nor could anyone easily believe how late in the life of the world men began to know anything correct about the movements of the heavens. Thales <note>Thales of Miletus (c. 624–548 BC), often regarded as the first Greek philosopher.</note> was the first to predict an eclipse of the sun, according to Eudemus; and Callimachus says he was the first discoverer of the Little Bear <note>Ursa Minor, the constellation containing the North Star.</note> by which the Phoenicians sail. He also divided the year into three hundred and sixty-five days. Plutarch asserts that the obliquity of the Zodiac <note>The "tilt" of the Earth's path relative to the celestial equator, which causes the seasons.</note>—the very first rudiment of stellar science—was thought out by **Pythagoras**, although a certain Euripides of Chios, younger than Pythagoras, boasted that it was first discovered by himself. Before Solon flourished in Greece—and he flourished nearly six hundred years before the time of Christ—everyone thought the lunar month was exactly thirty days. Solon was the first to correct this error, as Proclus writes in his commentary on Plato's *Timaeus*. If they were erring so significantly in the motion of the Moon, which is so easy and familiar to us, what must be thought of the motions of the other stars, which are more hidden and slower? But there is no need here for conjecture. Let the book of Ptolemy be read, the title of which is...

...the title <note>The OCR "tulus" completes the word "titulus" (title) from the previous page's catchword. It refers to Ptolemy’s *Great Composition*, better known as the *Almagest*.</note> **Great Composition**, it will be clear—without any doubt—that all the ancients were "as wide of the mark as the whole heaven" <note>original: *toto ut dicitur cœlo*; a Latin idiom meaning to be completely and utterly wrong.</note> regarding the motions of the celestial bodies. Regarding the motion of the nearer star <note>Referring to the Moon.</note> which we were discussing, you will learn there that the ancients grasped nothing that was true, nor even close to the truth. 

<margin>*</margin>Hipparchus was the first, on the island of Rhodes about two hundred years before Christ, to observe the course of the Moon more accurately; yet even he did not attain perfect clarity. For this reason, he was corrected by Ptolemy, who indeed came closer to the truth than Hipparchus, but still did not quite reach it. It was later corrected by Spanish astronomers. Regarding the motion of the Sun, by which they measure all other things, they are even now still "groping in the dark" <note>original: *cæcutiunt*; literally "they are blind" or "blinking."</note>; antiquity certainly never mastered it. 

But the Egyptians went far too far astray, thinking the Sun's return occurred after three hundred and sixty-five days and a quarter, with an additional <margin>*</margin> thirtieth part <note>Pico is criticizing the Egyptian calendar's inaccuracy compared to later observations which showed the solar year is slightly shorter than 365.25 days.</note>; for later, truer observations taught that even the quarter-day is not fully completed. How, then, could the wisdom of the Egyptians have performed reliable experiments on the "fate of the year" when they were so mistaken about its very beginning? They were also ridiculous in that they inaugurated the year, as Theophilus <note>Possibly Theophilus of Alexandria, a 4th-century bishop and computerist of Easter.</note> relates, at the very moment the Nile first flooded Egypt. 

Anaximander <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher (c. 610–546 BC).</note>, as Favorinus writes in his *Universal History*, was the first to invent the **Gnomon** <note>A vertical rod used in a sundial to measure the sun's altitude and direction.</note>, with which he might note the solstices and equinoxes. No one who has read his books is unaware that the **Astrolabe** was Ptolemy’s invention. Pythagoras was the first to say that the Evening Star and the Morning Star <note>original: *vesperum atq. luciferum*; both are the planet Venus.</note> were the same celestial body, on the authority of Parmenides; Pythagoras did not precede Christ by even five hundred years. 

But let us return to the motions of the stars, which were so little understood by the ancients that Hipparchus said there were so few surviving observations by the ancients regarding the motions of the five planets (excluding the Sun and Moon) that he could not affirm anything he himself discovered about them with any degree of certainty. Ptolemy was the first who seemed to say something certain about them, although the succeeding age, by the benefit of time, has corrected him in many places. 

In counting the rising times of the zodiac signs, which the Greeks call <term>anaphoras</term> <note>The time it takes for a sign of the zodiac to rise above the horizon.</note>, the extent to which those who practiced divination by the stars in Egypt fell away from the truth is testified both in the first book of Ptolemy's <term>Apotelesmaton</term> <note>The *Tetrabiblos*, Ptolemy's foundational work on the "effects" or "prognostications" of the stars.</note> and by Apollinarius in his commentaries. <margin>*</margin> Furthermore, Apollonius of Laodicea, in a work dedicated to the subject in five books, attacked their errors. 

Who, then, considering these things, could doubt? No true experiment regarding the influences of the stars could be held by the Egyptians or Chaldeans, since they had mastered neither the risings of the signs—upon which the greatest part of this art depends—nor the motions of the planets. It is as if they could reliably test what a planet did in a certain place, when the planets were actually never in the place where those men thought they were! This is not even mentioning the "erratic stars" <note>The planets.</note> whose motions, if we believe Ptolemy, were entirely unknown to them. But if they erred, as is undoubtedly clear, then the Greeks err who follow them, the Arabs err who follow the Greeks, and the Latins err who follow the Arabs and Greeks, pronouncing what will happen based on rules derived from these "experiments."

For they do not believe they can set forth anything with greater authority than what they confirm by the authority of the **Chaldeans** and **Egyptians**. From this source, they scatter names like **Aesculapius**, **Hermes**, **Nechepso**, and **Petosiris** <note>These were legendary or mythical figures traditionally cited by astrologers as the "founding fathers" of their craft. Nechepso and Petosiris were purportedly an Egyptian king and priest to whom many early astrological texts were falsely attributed.</note>—completely empty names—before their readers like mists, as if these men were not utterly ignorant of the very science they professed. If **Hipparchus** and **Ptolemy**, the chief authors of astrology, handed down the truth to us, why then did Ptolemy, in the first book of his *Apotelesmaton* <note>original: *Apotelesmaton*; better known as the *Tetrabiblos*, Ptolemy's foundational work on the philosophy and practice of astrology.</note>, turn to the "experiments of the ancients" as if to give credit to his words? He himself, in his own time, could scarcely establish the truth of these things through celestial science. 

When these matters were first investigated with some degree of success, **Peter of Abano** <note>original: *Petrus Aponensis*; a 13th-century Italian philosopher and physician who attempted to reconcile Greek and Arabic science.</note> excused **Galen** <note>The most famous physician of the Roman Empire, whose medical theories dominated Europe for 1,500 years.</note> (who went astray regarding the motions of the Moon) in this way: "Galen did not write these things with exactness, for they were not yet fully understood." And yet Galen was not prior to Ptolemy, but rather his contemporary. Therefore, let us conclude the entire dispute in this way: if the astrology that has been written down relies on the experiments of the ancients, it is fallacious, because they lacked a systematic method. Since even among the moderns <note>original: *neotericis*; referring to scholars of the late Middle Ages and early Renaissance.</note> these matters remain in doubt (as we have shown above), they were certainly not manifest to antiquity. If astrology relies on the work of more recent writers, it is even more fallacious, for they lacked both the proper method and the necessary time for observation.

<header>Against Astrology, Book XII.</header>

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA 
## Mirandola’s Disputations Against Astro- 
## logy, Book XII.

### THAT NO FAITH SHOULD BE PLACED IN ASTRO-
### logy as if it were a revealed truth. Chapter 1.

If neither reason supports the fables of the astrologers, nor can any trust be derived from practical experience, what reason remains for a wise man to surrender to them? Will they be treated as oracles? And should we accept as divine those things which we have already refuted for being irrational? Are we to imitate the astrologers who, whenever humans do something irrational, blame it on the stars? Shall we then, by a similar example, attribute the delusions of men to the Gods? 

Yet if this persuasion has seized anyone, let him know it profits him nothing to believe in "divine revelations" of this kind. As we have seen, there is such great disagreement in the decrees of astrology that it remains unclear which version was "revealed"—whether it be the astrology of the **Chaldeans**, the **Egyptians**, the **Jews**, **Ptolemy**, or the **Arabs**—and which of these the Gods allegedly breathed upon us as a singular gift for our merit. Therefore, this supposed divine benevolence does us no good as long as that "most true wisdom received from heaven" remains hidden in a cesspool of our own lies. Nor has any Lydian stone <note>original: *Lydius lapis*; a touchstone used in antiquity to test the purity of gold. Pico is saying there is no "litmus test" to tell true astrology from false.</note> been sent down from heaven by which the legitimate might be discerned from the counterfeit. 

What if I were to speak with Christians? I would ask whether they think this art was revealed by God, or rather by a demon. It cannot be said to be from God, for the Sacred Scriptures, which interpret the divine voice, forbid it. If they answer "by a demon," then no faith is due to a demon, whom God called the "father of lies." 

From this, the insanity of those people is refuted who fabricate the story that this science, like all others, was conferred by divine gift upon **Adam**, from whose hands it passed down to **Noah**. They claim that **Methodius** <note>Pico refers to "Pseudo-Methodius," a popular medieval text that claimed Noah had a fourth son born after the Flood.</note> records that Noah’s son **Ionichus** <note>A legendary figure in medieval tradition, often credited with being the first to study the stars and the founder of kingship.</note> predicted many future events through this art. They say it then passed through the sons of Noah who survived the Great Flood to the Patriarch **Abraham**, who (according to the testimony of **Josephus** <note>Titus Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Jewish historian who wrote that Abraham taught the Egyptians arithmetic and astronomy.</note>) taught it to the **Egyptians**. From the Egyptians, they say, it devolved to the **Greeks**, and from the Greeks to the **Latins** <note>The Romans/Western Europeans.</note>. 

In this way, these people devise a very pretty "succession" for themselves—one well-suited for ensnaring the unrefined, but which is everywhere recognized as false and deceitful by the more learned. For regarding what they say about Adam: unless this too was "revealed" to them, by what evidence do they prove it? Just because we believe that Adam, by God’s gift, was a master of all sciences, does it follow that he knew this one as well? It would certainly follow if this were actually a science, and not something vain, false, ridiculous, and contrary to the principles of true doctrine—unworthy not only of God, as we have said, but even of a human inventor. Let us now turn to Ionichus.

Methodius indeed writes about this, but he is a hardly suitable author; for he is not the one mentioned among illustrious men by the blessed Jerome—that man was from Patara <note>original: "Parcharensis"; referring to Methodius of Patara, a 3rd-century Church Father.</note>—but this is another altogether, frequently cited by Peter Comestor <note>original: "Petro Commestore"; a 12th-century author known for his *Historia Scholastica*. Pico is being dismissive of the quality of sources Comestor uses.</note>, in whom no person of even moderate learning would fail to notice a lack of discernment in choosing good authors.
But not even Methodius says that he predicted anything; furthermore, what weight can the authority of an ignoble writer have regarding that "Ionicus"? <note>A legendary fourth son of Noah often mentioned in medieval chronologies but rejected by Pico as unbiblical.</note> Especially since Moses himself, the Prophet, counts only three sons of Noah: Shem, Ham, and Japheth; nor does Josephus name any others besides these, nor does Philo, nor any Hebrew person, whether a writer of annals or an expositor of the Mosaic Law. 
We might believe Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Jewish historian.</note> that Abraham passed on astrology to the Egyptians, but not that superstitious divining-art, which was more frequent among idolaters than among the worshipers of the true God. This God of Abraham, so named by Moses and the Prophets, condemned that art, yet they still professed to follow the tradition and precepts of Abraham. 
Rather, it was that mathematical science concerning the movements and magnitudes of the stars, the use of which was frequent and necessary for the Hebrews for the sake of observing the fixed times of ceremonies; and it has been handed down in the Hebrew records that the tribe of Issachar <note>One of the twelve tribes of Israel, traditionally associated with scholarly pursuits and "understanding the times."</note> was delegated to this study. This cannot be learned without arithmetic, since it consists almost entirely of numbers and measurements; Josephus writes that Abraham demonstrated this along with astrology to the Egyptians. 
If Josephus had intended that divining-art instead, he would have been entirely mistaken, since he says the Egyptians received from the Chaldeans this astrology which Abraham had first judged for the Egyptians. However, it is clear from earlier discussions that the Egyptians created their own astrology for predicting the future, which has almost nothing in common with the dogmas of the Chaldeans; but in that part which concerns the motions of the stars, Ptolemy teaches in his *Great Composition* <note>original: "Magna compositione"; known today by its Arabic-derived title, the *Almagest*.</note> that few Chaldeans practiced it, and from them it flowed to others. Therefore, Josephus understood no other astrology than this mathematical one. 
As for Abu Ma'shar <note>original: "Aboasar"; a famous 9th-century Persian astrologer and astronomer.</note>, he is to be mocked; for in his own place, he says that the sons of Noah disseminated this science when they came into Chaldea. He claims it was received from heaven, yet he himself rejects the Chaldean opinion regarding the "bounds" <note>term: "bounds" (termini); specific degrees of a zodiac sign assigned to a particular planet in ancient astrology.</note> of the planets. 
But it was not worth spending so much effort in refuting these trifles, since anyone but the most dull-witted understands that these are the deliriums of men, so enslaving their faith to their own dreams that they confirm things they have brought forth without any reason by claiming an authority traced back to Adam. 
For let them answer this: why did other arts and sciences not come down to us through that same succession, but were instead thought out by the talents of later men and brought to perfection by the diligent study that followed? Or did we receive this gift of divine providence only in astrology, as if it were more useful? 
In truth, that Providence (which is not accustomed to doing so) would have to have been dozing off, failing to notice that this divining-art is preserved for us in vain unless the mathematical science were also preserved, without which we cannot use the other correctly. For it is of no use to have the powers and natures of the stars discovered, unless you can note by exact calculation the sin... <note>The text cuts off mid-word "singulis" (individual [degrees/moments]), matching the catchword "gulis" noted in the metadata.</note>

...at every hour the state, shape, and position of the stars. Since only <term>mathematics</term> <note>original: "mathematica"; in this period, the term "mathematics" often referred specifically to astronomy and the calculation of planetary movements.</note> provides this, it ought to have been passed down to us from the first father through hereditary tradition, if divine providence had not wished for the use of such a beneficial divination to be missing from our lives.

### OF WHAT SORT WERE THE EGYPTIANS AND CHALDEANS
### among whom astrology was born. Chapter II.

Here are rejected those who worship these trifles—so unworthy of heaven, so falsely fabricated—as if they were nevertheless held from heaven. When someone reads these things and looks closely, they see the nature of it so clearly that no suspicion of celestial inspiration remains. This, I think, is evident enough even to the dullest person from what has already been said. Nevertheless, Reader, it will not be useless to consider under a single view how this plague was born and spread through the world—that is, by which authors it originated, by which persuasions it was received, by what authority it was confirmed, by what nourishments it grew, and how it has persisted to this day. For this will also be not entirely ineffective for abolishing faith in it and exposing its vanity. It was born, therefore, from Chaldean and Egyptian parents, about whom something must be said before we speak of those vanities of theirs. 

Both nations were, above all, devoted to and skilled in two things: idolatrous religion and mathematics. They were invited to the latter by the suitability of their location, for they inhabited open fields and broad plains, from which the view of the stars is easy and more accurate. As for the former—that is, in vain and superstitious ceremonies—why they were occupied with and honored for them more than other nations was due to antiquity. Because of this, they were the first to practice the worship of the gods, acting as parents to others and, by necessity, teachers of religion. 

Furthermore, as we have shown elsewhere, it was due to their lack of skill in physical wisdom <note>original: "sapientiae phisicaeque rationis"; referring to natural philosophy or the scientific understanding of the natural world.</note> and reasoning, and the rudeness of their minds. For mathematics indeed does not make men wise—which is why among the ancients it was a study for boys. Rather, while it paves the way for philosophy if tasted moderately and with reason, if someone gives themselves entirely to it alone, it gives rise to the greatest occasions for error in philosophy, as Aristotle testifies <note>Aristotle, the Greek philosopher, often argued that the abstract nature of mathematics could lead to errors if applied incorrectly to the physical world.</note>. Therefore, as far as I can gather by conjecture, the Egyptians and Chaldeans had minds little suited for wisdom. This is still seen today in the people of those regions; even if the accident of cultural study were taken away from them, it should not have taken away their nature. 

Nor indeed should we be deceived by what once deceived me as a young man: the celebrated wisdom of the Egyptians and Chaldeans mentioned by the ancients, including Plato. It is recorded in memory that Pythagoras, Democritus, Eudoxus, Plato, and many others visited them for no other reason than to acquire wisdom. For they claimed that famous and divine name of wisdom for themselves solely from their knowledge of ceremonies and worshiping the gods. Among all nations, and even among all good philosophers, there was always this persuasion: that the highest wisdom consists in religion.

Therefore Plato, Pythagoras, and many others—rightly seeing that the truest philosophy lies in the knowledge of divine things—traveled down to the Egyptians because their reputation was that they were especially skilled in this. They went with an eagerness for learning whatever seemed more hidden and sacred among them. They also traveled down to learn <term>mathematics</term> <note>original: "mathematicam"; in the Renaissance, this term encompassed geometry, arithmetic, music, and especially astronomy/astrology.</note>, which those we just mentioned—the famous Pythagoras, Democritus, and Eudoxus—eagerly absorbed. Nevertheless, that title of wisdom and the privilege of "secret discipline" came to the Chaldeans and Egyptians from nowhere else than from their mastery and teaching of how to worship the gods. Whether those good philosophers approved of what they heard from them or not, we have spoken of elsewhere; here we only assert that concerning the <term>primeval natural philosophy</term> <note>The study of the physical world and its origins based on reason rather than myth.</note> which is demonstrated by logic, the Greek philosophers (whoever among them philosophized correctly) received nothing from the Egyptians. Instead, they received only what pertained to ceremonies and mathematics, for which even this serves as an argument: 

Whenever the subject is mathematics or "mysteries," we see the Chaldeans and Egyptians cited, and their opinions are always brought forward; yet in the rational arguments of philosophy found in Plato and Aristotle, their names do not appear at all. Now, if you say that <term>Thales</term> <note>Thales of Miletus (c. 624–548 BCE), often called the first Greek philosopher.</note> philosophized in Egypt, I will not deny it, as he even learned from them that "water is the beginning of all things." I believe the Egyptians were led to this opinion for no other reason than that they saw their region blessed and made fertile by the flooding of the Nile, from whose departure through Egypt they also inaugurated their year. 

They were indeed of very crude intellect, and therefore well-suited for superstitions. Nothing rejects and scorns such things more than the lively force of the mind when joined with learning. Thus, they were easily led even by demons to every kind of madness. If they had any religion at all, it was nothing <unclear>other than</unclear> superstition—a fact <term>Iamblichus</term> <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 CE) who wrote extensively on Egyptian mysteries and "theurgy" (rituals to contact the divine).</note> largely confesses, confirming that they were entirely occupied with the worship of evil demons. It follows that since their reputation for wisdom was based on the reputation of their religion, the "wiser" they were said to be, the more foolish they actually were. However, as was said above, the dealings of the Greek philosophers with them were always more focused on mathematics than on their superstitions. 

Thales, in a letter to Pherecydes, says: "I went down to Egypt with Solon so that we might see the priests and astronomers," but he says nothing of philosophy. Likewise, he says he learned geometry from them. Demetrius says that Democritus went to the Egyptians to learn geometry. Sometimes Democritus—and even Pythagoras—were called "monstrous" <note>original: "monstrosus"; here meaning strange, unnatural, or obsessed with omens/prodigies.</note> by Plato and other prudent men. But Plato, exhibiting that blameless character of his, gave only as much honor to antiquity and the "title of religion" as was necessary for his age; otherwise, he never defiled his own substance with the <term>leaven of Egypt</term> <note>A metaphor for corrupting or foreign influences.</note>. And so Eudoxus also followed the Egyptians in true astronomy, but in the "divining art," he did not agree with them. 

But lest we digress further, we thus conclude that the Egyptians and Chaldeans were very busy in idolatrous superstition and most dedicated to mathematics, [but] in the rest of philosophy...

...that they practiced it very little. Rather, he speaks from that opinion which, believing in the eternity of the world, claims that these arts have been both abolished and restored an infinite number of times among various nations. Nor did Abraham himself obtain his privilege through nature so much as through divine grace. But let us return to astrology, in which matter it is easy to see what led the Egyptians and Chaldeans astray, now that we have said enough about their studies and character.

### WHAT LED THE CHALDEANS AND EGYPTIANS TO THE OPINION 
### that human fates are created and can be 
### foreseen by the stars. Chapter III.

It is the habit of those who have completely immersed themselves in any one discipline to refer everything to it most willingly—not so much out of ambition, so that they might seem to know everything through it, but because it simply appears that way to them. This happens to them just as it does to those traveling through the snow: everything else begins to look white to them too, for once the habit of whiteness has been received into the eyes, it transforms everything else into itself. Likewise, for those desperately in love, whatever they encounter reflects the face of the beloved, or at least relates something back to the rule of that one image, the entire imaginative faculty of the lover having been surrendered to it. He who is a <term>Theologian</term> <note>One who studies the nature of God and religious belief.</note>, and nothing but a theologian, refers all things to divine causes; the Physician to the condition of the body; the <term>Physicist</term> <note>In this period, a "physicist" (physicus) was someone who studied "physics" in the Aristotelian sense—the natural laws of the physical world.</note> to the natural principles of things; the Mathematician to shapes and numbers (as the <term>Pythagoreans</term> <note>Followers of Pythagoras who believed that the universe was fundamentally composed of numbers.</note> used to do). By this same logic, since the ancient Chaldeans were constantly diligent in measuring the celestial motions and observing the courses of the stars, and nothing else occupied their minds more, to them, all things were "stars." That is, they willingly referred everything to the stars—and the same should be understood regarding what is said of the Egyptians.

Therefore, when to this professional inclination were added the conjectures which we recounted and refuted in the third book—such as the idea that lower bodies are moved by higher ones, that the stars must have the greatest power to exert influence, and what is seen in the Sun and Moon regarding how much they dominate our bodies and the air—when similar ideas occurred to minds already leaning in that direction, they were easily led to believe that whatever happened to men, whether of the body, the soul, or of fortune, proceeded from celestial causes. They believed that once these causes were known and explored, the future outcomes of all things could be foreknown. For their understanding of <term>physics</term> <note>The study of natural causes and effects.</note> was not so deep as to recognize that a universal cause...

<meta>This page continues Pico's argument from page 721, where he discussed why the ancient Egyptians and Chaldeans were susceptible to the errors of astrology despite their reputation for wisdom. He concludes the word from the previous page's catchword "philosophiae" (philosophy).</meta>

<header>John Pico of Mirandola</header>

...[the universal cause of] philosophy differed from particular ones, and what the duty of that universal cause and these particular ones was, they would have sufficiently understood what was suitable for a celestial substance and what was contrary to it. They would have known what is termed "in itself" <note>original: "per se." In Scholastic logic, this refers to essential properties that belong to a thing by its very nature.</note> among the <term>logicians</term> and what is "by accident," and how great a difference there is between the works of nature and the works of art. They would have understood how one thing could be a sign of another without being its cause. 

Thus, prompted by these reasons, they would not have attributed particular differences to a common cause—as if the immediate causes were idle—nor would they have imputed their own faults to the stars (as if God and the heavens were insufficiently good), deriving both the evils of the soul and the body from there. Nor would they have behaved as if a physical body possessed intellect, or as if the meeting of causes occurring randomly at the same time could be referred back to it. Nor would they have believed that new powers flow from the heaven into works of art <note>Pico is likely referring to the practice of creating "astrological images" or talismans believed to capture celestial influence through craftsmanship.</note>, as if the artist's craft could penetrate to the innermost substance of a thing. Even if these effects were not produced by the heaven, they would not have believed they could be signified by it, especially since they were not related to one another as effects or causes, and did not originate from the same source in the same way. 

Since those people were ignorant of all these things—philosophy being as yet imperfect and insufficiently investigated by them—it is no wonder that with so many factors pulling them toward error, they were first led by the conjectures we have mentioned. These were indeed ineffective, but to the common people and those unrefined in great philosophy, they carried much probability. This was combined with that constant observation of the stars—a kind of familiarity—to which was added the innate curiosity in humans for knowing the future. For what we desire to happen, we easily believe is possible. 

Added to this was the vice of the age, and a persuasion toward <term>divination</term> <note>The practice of seeking knowledge of the future or the unknown by supernatural means.</note> that was deeply rooted in men's minds during that time. They greedily pursued a thousand modes and types of divination far less probable than astrology and containing more madness: such as <term>pyromancy</term> <note>Divination by fire.</note>, <term>geomancy</term> <note>Divination by interpreting markings on the ground or patterns formed by tossed handfuls of soil, rocks, or sand.</note>, <term>astragalomancy</term> <note>Divination using dice or knucklebones.</note>, and other such old wives' trifles, amidst which the error of the astrologers could be regarded as the highest wisdom. 

Furthermore, astrology agreed marvelously with the <term>idolatry</term> to which they were subject; they considered the gods they worshiped to be the authors of all things, not only the good but also the bad. For it was also part of idolatrous teaching that some gods were beneficial and others harmful. Thus, even here, contrary to the reason of philosophy, they came to believe that some stars were good and others evil. 

Add to this the opportunity for glory and profit that astronomers saw ready for themselves, if—after the great labor but perhaps small reward of investigating the courses of the heavens—they were thought to foresee the future. To these factors, add the frauds of wicked <term>demons</term> <note>In the Renaissance worldview, demons were active agents capable of manipulating the physical world and human perception to lead people into error.</note>, who then ruled the world most powerfully. Finding people inclined toward this error for the reasons mentioned, the demons pushed their minds further with hidden instigations. They did this by perverting the judgments of minds entirely enslaved to them, and sometimes by confirming their predictions—either moving them to predict what was going to happen anyway, or bringing about what they had predicted. 

I have no doubt that all these things together were the reason why the practice first began among the Egyptians and Chaldeans—men devoted to superstitions and idolatry, and most intensely occupied with the motions of the heavenly bodies—that phi...

among those poorly skilled in philosophy, the opinion arose that future events could be seen in advance from the state of the stars. The age readily accepted this opinion because of curiosity and ignorance, and astronomers most gladly confirmed it in the hope of acquiring profit and glory.

### ->ON HOW THEY FELL INTO THE OBSERVATIONS ESTABLISHED FOR PREDICTIONS. Chapter IV.<-

We have seen among which nations and in what manner this error first was born—that human affairs are caused or indicated by the heavens—and it is easy to see how they arrived at these astrological dogmas which they use in predicting. For as we have demonstrated, they were not led to these by true reasons; for how could they be? Since there is no true reason for a lie. Furthermore, we do not explore the properties of the conjunctions of things, in both place and nature, except through their operations. Nor were they led by experiments. Otherwise, they would have had to cease from predicting for many ages, since experiments of this kind are perfected beyond controversy only by long-lasting observations and frequently repeated trials. 

What, then, did they follow? Conjectures, partly taken from the <term>mathematics</term> <note>In the Renaissance, "mathematics" often referred specifically to the calculation of planetary positions for astrological purposes.</note> they were focused on, and partly from certain symbolic analogies <note>original: "parabolicis similitudinibus." These are metaphorical or symbolic comparisons, such as saying Mars causes war because it is red like blood.</note>, than which nothing more fallacious could be imagined. But they themselves either deceived those unskilled in philosophy and logic, or they thought the ignorant common folk could be deceived. To those rushing toward the profit and glory of divination, the path that was easier and more ready was more satisfying than the one that was more likely true. 

Thus they first established that the fates of men depend on that hour of birth, both because it generally seems to the common people that a man "becomes" when he is born, and because other principles—whether of the conception of the fetus or the moment of animation—were more uncertain than could be observed for predicting. From the mathematicians they took this: first, because in measuring the motions of the stars they divided the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>original: "obliquum orbem," the "diagonal circle" or path the sun appears to follow through the stars.</note> into twelve parts for ease of counting, and by that same reasoning they took up the division of each part into thirty [degrees], and every thirtieth into sixty [minutes], as if this division were made by nature and not by human choice. And because they themselves had fashioned these parts, they decreed for themselves that there were as many different powers and properties of "influences." 

Then, according to the number of the twelve signs, they divided twelve "places" <note>These are the twelve "Houses" of a horoscope, which relate the signs of the Zodiac to the local horizon.</note>, six above the <term>horizon</term> <note>original: "finitorem," the boundary line.</note> and six below, just as six signs are always revolving below the earth and six above. Thus, by a great error, it was determined that the primary thing to be observed was in what place and under what sign a planet was located; for they claimed planets acquired different powers for "influencing" according to the variety of the place and sign. 

After this, whatever diversities they noted in the motions [of the planets], they judged those were also to be noted in the operations of the stars, as if the force and type of their efficiency were varied by it. Thus they decreed a planet does one thing when it moves in a straight line <note>Direct motion.</note>, another when it moves backward <note>Retrograde motion.</note>, and another when it stands still <note>Stationary.</note>. Then, they claimed different things happen because of either the conjunction or the distance of the stars from one another. They primarily observed certain distances which they measured by the motions...

perceived, such as the <term>trine</term> interval <note>An aspect where two planets are 120 degrees apart, forming a triangle.</note>, because in it Saturn and Jupiter, when configured to the Sun, always appeared to move backward, just as Mars sometimes does in the <term>square</term> <note>An aspect where planets are 90 degrees apart.</note>; likewise they saw that Mercury and Venus are never removed from the Sun beyond the <term>sextile</term> <note>An aspect where planets are 60 degrees apart.</note>. They thought, therefore, that these distances of the stars were to be observed when they were placed in a trine, sextile, or square radiation with each other, and also in opposition. The reason for this is evident, especially because in these configurations they observed the phases of the Moon change in relation to the Sun: becoming crescent-shaped in the sextile, half-full in the square, gibbous in the trine, and full in the <term>diameter</term> <note>The "diameter" refers to opposition, or 180 degrees, when the Moon is opposite the Sun.</note>. Just as they had also imagined the intersections of certain circles with the path of the Sun—a thing necessary for measuring motions, but useless for determining "influences"—so they also applied these to the decrees of fate. They call these the <term>Head and Tail</term> <note>original: "caput caudamque." These are the lunar nodes, the points where the moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic. In astrology, they were called the Head and Tail of the Dragon.</note>, as if, finally, the powers and "breaths" of the rays followed these mathematical quantities, positions, locations, points, and distances, rather than following the qualities and natures of the rays themselves. But they neither noticed this error due to their ignorance of <term>physics</term> <note>In the Renaissance, "physics" meant the study of nature and natural causes.</note>, nor could they avoid it if they wanted there to be different constellations in the sky at every single moment, which would vary the life, fortune, character, and talents of people being born at the same time.

### ->BY WHICH CONJECTURES THEY DEFINED WHAT THOSE<-
### ->OBSERVATIONS INDICATED. Chapter V.<-

Here they received from the mathematicians what should be observed, though with a perverse intention. This was (if we believe Aristotle) also the occasion of error for the ancients: judging natural things as if they were mathematical. After this, it remained to investigate what these signs, stars, motions, and aspects themselves signified or brought about, when they were found arranged in this or that way. Here they acted based on the lightest and most fallacious conjectures, which we shall recount. Concerning the signs, they first devised this: it was an undisputed fact to the Egyptians that everything consists of four elements. When, therefore, they had already received twelve signs by the occasion we mentioned, a division seemed very beautiful and convenient to them: that these too should be distinguished by the four elements, which, when repeated three times, completed the number of the signs. And since they believed the first bodies to have been fire and earth—as if they were the center and the circumference—for fire was the highest body to them, and then air and water came between them as mediums, as Plato also shows in the *Timaeus*. Therefore, they established the first sign as fiery, the second as earthy, the third as airy, and the fourth as watery. Then returning in a similar sequence, the fifth was fiery, the sixth earthy, and so on. From this it followed that those signs which were distant by a trine interval (that is, with three signs intercepted between them) were judged to be of the same nature, because the fifth sign returned to the nature of the first. Those, however, in the sextile aspect were partly related and partly discordant, but more related, since the first...

# Against Astrology, Book XII.
->PP 3<-

[...the first was] fiery, the third was airy. Regarding those which are diametrically opposed in a square—if fire and water are completely discordant—they fashioned a fiction that a <term>trine</term> <note>A 120-degree aspect.</note> radiation would be good, a <term>square</term> <note>A 90-degree aspect.</note> bad, and a hexagonal <note>The sextile aspect, 60 degrees.</note> truly middle-ground; but they held the square to be better than the <term>opposition</term> <note>A 180-degree aspect.</note>, which would also be bad because stars so positioned look at each other from directly across. Some, however, wish this middle-ground to also depend on the qualities of the signs, looking at them in this aspect just as they do in others. For there are some signs which agree in one quality but disagree in another. 

It is clear from this how these dogmas gave birth to one another; while they leave a suspicion of some underlying reason when heard in isolation, they immediately become contemptible once their origin is revealed. For if that first foundation is tottering and weak—namely, the number of the twelve signs, introduced by the mere judgment of those calculating (as astrologers themselves confess)—then all things built upon it are ruinous. Yet there are many things sprouting from that one root; for from it come the trines which claim a great part of <term>astrology</term> for themselves. From these come the <term>lords of the triplicities</term> <note>original: "trigonocratores." These are planets that rule a group of three signs belonging to the same element.</note>, as they call them, from whom the later *Chaldæans* received their reasoning about "bounds." The *Egyptians* derived the <term>individual degrees</term> <note>original: "monomirias" (monomoiriai). A system assigning a specific planetary ruler to every single degree of the zodiac.</note>, and the *Arabs* derived their greatest dogmas from the great conjunctions. *Ptolemy* and all others (though some in different ways) derived the distribution of the world's regions under the signs, so that they might assign this trine to the East, that one to the West, another to the South, and another to the North. From this, predictions about the year's fate greatly depend, so that we might know what will happen in which region. 

But let us return to the other properties of the signs, for we have sufficiently uncovered the mystery of their division into elements; having pulled back the veil, we found nothing but the purest nonsense. They devised other properties from what the *Sun*, gliding beneath the signs, performs in them, dividing them into <term>fixed, movable, and common</term> <note>These are now known as Fixed, Cardinal, and Mutable signs.</note>. Others they took from the names of the parts of the circle, as if those signs were similar to those things not only in image but in powers and nature. Hence they called some signs "human" and others "brute" [animal-like], because the sign of *Aquarius* was figured as a young man, and that other was called *Aries* [the Ram]. Thus almost all dogmas about the signs were born either from the work of the *Sun*, or the names of the constellations, or the division by elements—all of which are immediately judged as worthless once they have been refuted. 

They also judged the nature of the planets from their colors, as *Abu Ma'shar* <note>original: "Aboasar." A famous 9th-century Persian astrologer.</note> testifies, saying this is a conjecture held by the whole community of astrologers; and they applied this even to the fixed stars. For they said all reddish stars were of the nature of *Mars*, such as the Eye of *Taurus* <note>The star Aldebaran.</note> and the Heart of *Scorpio* <note>The star Antares.</note>; however, it has already been sufficiently demonstrated how irrational and false those claims are. They gradually introduced the affinities of the <term>Planets</term> with the signs in this way: "exaltations" were first invented, I believe, among the *Chaldæans* (about which we wrote in Book 8), based on the idea that when stars were positioned in those degrees, they were furthest from the centers of their <term>apsides</term> <note>The points in a planet's orbit where it is at its maximum or minimum distance from the center.</note>. The *Egyptians* added the "houses," a conjecture first taken from *Leo*, under which the power of the *Sun* seemed to grow; making a beginning from that sign, they divided the remaining signs among the other planets according to the order of the celestial spheres, as we have seen. We have already said what introduced the trines; next, the terms...

...and the **decans** <note>Subdivisions of a zodiac sign into three parts of 10 degrees each.</note>, **dodecathemoria** <note>Divisions of a sign into twelve parts of 2.5 degrees each.</note>, **ninths**, and **monomoiriai** <note>Individual degree-by-degree divisions.</note> were created by the division of the signs. Because these signs seemed too vast to be granted to the rule of only one planet while excluding others, they mapped them out into various parts in many ways. They wanted these specific **bounds** <note>term: bounds (original: *fines*). These are specific segments of a sign where a planet other than the sign's main ruler is said to have influence.</note> to belong to one star, and those to another. Since everyone decided this based on a different guess, five different opinions about these "bounds" arose, over which they are still fighting without end. 

Some divided the signs into **decans** (that is, into three parts), others into nine, others into twelve—but all did so according to their own whim, with no rational basis. For who could call it "rational" to say a sign must be divided into twelve parts simply because there are twelve signs? Or into three parts for the sake of the "perfection of the number three"? Or into nine because the ninth sign agrees in quality with the first—namely, *Sagittarius* with *Aries*, *Capricorn* with *Taurus*, and so on for the rest? Even **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity.</note>, although an astrologer himself, laughed when he read these things. Yet those "divine" men—the **Egyptians**, **Indians**, and **Chaldeans**—embraced them as if they were "First Philosophy" <note>A term for metaphysics, the highest form of knowledge.</note>.

Let us come to the **places** <note>term: places (original: *loca*). In astrology, these are the twelve "houses" that represent different areas of life like wealth, travel, or death.</note>, whose properties they defined based on certain similarities. For example, because the "Midheaven" is a high place, they said it signifies things thought to be "high"—empires, kingdoms, and powers—as if a human being does not descend inward rather than ascend. They said the East [the Ascendant] indicates the newborn emerging from the womb; the seventh place indicates adversaries because it is opposite the first; the twelfth indicates prisons and darkness because, when the Sun reaches that place, the air grows dark as if from vapors that have been stirred up but not yet dissolved. 

But there is no need to follow up on everything we mentioned above; it is enough to recall to memory how the oracles of this "sidereal" and "celestial" discipline emerged step by step. These ideas are marvelously connected to one another, with one fable everywhere extending a hand to the next fable. 

Thus, when they determined that the **trine** and **sextile** <note>Aspects of 120 and 60 degrees, respectively.</note> intervals were good, and likewise that the planets **Venus** and **Jupiter** (and also the **Sun** and **Moon**) were good, they said that "good ones rejoice in good things." They claimed **Jupiter** rejoices in the 11th house and the **Sun** in the 9th, because one is a sextile and the other a trine from the horoscope <note>The Ascendant or 1st house.</note>. They placed the **Moon** in the 3rd and **Venus** in the 5th, which are distant from the Ascendant by similar intervals. They gave the better and more powerful places—those above the earth—to the better ones, namely **Jupiter** and the **Sun**; but to the weaker ones, they gave those below the earth. 

By the same reasoning, they wanted **Mars** to rejoice in the 6th place and **Saturn** in the 12th, because these are "bad" places, just as those planets are "bad." Nor do I doubt that many properties were then assigned to these places based on the nature of these planets: such as prophecies to the 9th (which the **Sun** is believed to give); short journeys to the 3rd (just as the **Moon** circles a space more briefly than all other stars); sorrow and secret enemies to the 12th (matching the condition of **Saturn**); and slaves and diseases to the 6th (due to the nature of a harmful but effective and active planet [Mars]). 

To the 5th house, they gave joys, children, and pleasures because of **Venus**. They established her as the ruler of these things no more by rational judgment than by the brightness, rays, and beauty of the star. From this comes that poetic image of her: *the nourishing one laughing nectarean from above* <note>original: "alma superne nectareum ridens." Pico suggests that Venus's astrological role is based on her visual beauty and poetic myths rather than science.</note>, which is why she was believed by the ancients to be the Goddess of elegance and beauty. Using such demonstrations...

-># On Astrology, Book XII.<-

...with these explanations, they have woven a deceptive web, like the threads of a spider. If you look from afar, it deceives by the false size of the threads and the allure of the weave and the charm of its novelty. If you look closely, you despise it; if you touch it with your hand, you break and dissolve it. The descendants increased the invention of their fathers, and the more ancient the fiction, the stronger it became, with the fraud of its origin hidden more deeply—an effect that always happens as age wins authority.

We have not said everything, but have only shown the method of invention—that is, the slipperiness of the error. All the rest are based on that example: very light conjectures and thin similarities to earthly things. Examples of such things are: that **Planets** <term>Planets (original: *Planetas*). In ancient astrology, this included the Sun and Moon, referring to 'wandering stars'.</term> are lucky when they move forward and unlucky when they move backward, and even when they are believed to stand still. It is as if they were saying that those moving backward deny what they had promised, those moving forward expedite what they pledge, and those staying still delay what they bestow.

They claim that the failing **Sun** <note>original: *Solem*</note> and **Moon** <note>original: *Lunam*</note> [eclipses] produce great calamities. For these things terrify especially because the cause is unknown, as if the Gods were either abandoning or rejecting us. They say a person born when stars are in **apogee** <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Earth.</note> is exalted, since that place is also the highest. As for who introduced the "Parts" of the Moon, then of other stars, and finally even of oats and beans—that error was explained in Book Eight. 

After they founded these dogmas on such conjectures, they began to observe the **horoscopes** <term>horoscopes (original: *geneses*). Literally 'births' or nativities.</term> of those being born. If once or twice by chance the dogmas responded <note>matched reality</note>, no further faith or authority was needed for the "experiment." For example, if someone born while **Mars** <note>original: *Marte*</note> occupied **Scorpio** <note>original: *Scorpium*</note> became famous in war, it was held as an indubitable fact that Scorpio was the domicile of Mars. It was as if there were not a far different reason for Mars to be so positioned than for a warlike person to be born, or as if they could faithfully "test" anything in the celestial motions while failing so greatly in their logic, as we have said. 

Therefore, they also noted what had happened to the subject of any birth-chart <note>original: *thematæ*</note> and from there established rules and canons. Since this was not the path of true experiments, but chance and recklessness served as their reason, it happened differently for different people, and even for the same people observing at other times. Thus, almost as many versions of **astrology** <note>original: *astrologiæ*</note> emerged as there were observers, leading to that confusion and conflict of opinions which we followed at length in the previous book.

### BY WHAT INCITEMENTS IT INCREASED AND HOW IT WAS PROPAGATED. Chapter VI.

**S**o, having arisen from trifling conjectures, it grew through deceptive experiments, fostered by the vice of the age and nourished by human curiosity. There is no one not eager to know the future concerning themselves, and to seek it most truly from heaven. For how few of the common people, or even the learned, know how wrongly these things are sought from heaven? To this was added the zeal of princes, who believed everything because of ignorance and hoped for everything because of greed. If ever happiness was pronounced for them from heaven (and it was always pronounced), they were unwilling...

...rather than astrology being overturned, even that [false] "good fortune" was preserved. They <note>The demons or ancient practitioners</note> predicted true things at times—now by chance, now by cunning, and now with the support of a demon, in the ways we have explained. For who would not succeed [occasionally] when predicting many things? Yet, while the true hits brought applause and acclamations, a thousand lies were immediately buried in oblivion. Moreover, they gained much faith and authority from oracles, which not only approved of this art but actively practiced it. When **Apollo** <note>The Greek god of prophecy and the sun.</note> was asked whether a male or female child would be born, he replied "a female," because at the moment of conception, the **Moon** <note>original: *Luna*</note> was moving toward **Venus** <note>original: *Venerem*</note>. What greater testimony could there be for a profession than to have the gods as its authors? 

Clearly, those wicked demons—named as such not only by our own [Christian] writers but also by the **Platonists** <note>Followers of Plato, who often discussed "daemons" as intermediary spirits.</note>—knew how much poison they were offering the world under the guise of a single superstition. Once this poison penetrated deep into the veins, it first stripped away faith from religion (the highest good of humanity), as if everything depended on a fatal necessity hanging from the sky. It made it seem as if there were no miracles and no divine foreknowledge of the future, but that all things happened by the force of the constellations. Then, it provided a defense for vices, claiming they descend upon us from the heavens; and finally, it infected the good arts of medicine and philosophy. While it could not completely overturn them (any more than it could overturn theology), it nonetheless contaminated them. It turned philosophy from true reasoning toward fables, and medicine from natural and effective remedies toward vain observations and the "delirious ravings of old women" <note>original: *anilia deliramenta*</note>. Thus, it became a single plague of perverse superstition, fatal to both body and soul at once. 

They saw prudence perish; for now, astrology was consulted on what should be done, at what time, and by what method. A most foolish vanity sat at the helm of life, holding the tiller in its hand. Finally, they hoped for what actually came to pass: that this one art, which seized authority from heaven through mathematical calculations, would provide a cover for other superstitions whose fraud was less disguised and whose weakness was less painted over. No superstition would be thought vain if it appeared as an "appendix" or "nursling" of celestial doctrine. Indeed, as we showed in Book I, there is no superstition that does not acknowledge astrology as either its partner, its parent, or its leader. 

Is it not, therefore, a worthy cause for the most harmful demons to make themselves into astrologers and to provide everything necessary so that this pestilential persuasion might daily take possession of human senses and studies? Who, even among the followers of **Porphyry** <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who was often critical of popular religion while still believing in spirits.</note>, would doubt that demons used the rules of astrologers in their oracles for no other reason than to deceive—that is, to give credibility to a fallacy? For Porphyry himself says that the oracles lied when they gave responses based on astrological dogmas. This would not have happened if the art were true and a real indicator of the future, since the demons—who are most skilled in natural things—could not have been ignorant of it. 

Nurtured by these encouragements and many protections, astrology fully occupied the Egyptians and **Chaldeans** <note>Ancient inhabitants of Mesopotamia, famous for their astronomical observations and star-gazing.</note>, and immediately gave birth to a superstitious form of medicine among them. For **Nechepso** <note>original: *Necipsus*. An Egyptian king and priest to whom many early astrological and medical texts were attributed.</note> wrote in Egypt about which **decan** <term>Decan (original: *decanus*). A division of the zodiac into ten-degree segments (three per sign), which ancient astrologers associated with specific spirits and bodily ailments.</term> caused which disease, and which decan’s power was required to cure it...
