## HOW ASTROLOGY PASSED FROM THE EGYPTIANS TO OTHERS. Chapter VII.

**A**strology passed from the Egyptians and Chaldeans to the Greeks, but through authors of no reputation. For, except in the houses of street-performers, it did not enter the **Lyceum** or the **Academy**, nor even the **Porch** <note>These refer to the major schools of Greek philosophy: the Lyceum (Aristotle), the Academy (Plato), and the Porch or Stoa (Stoicism).</note>; and although it was harmoniously admitted by **Thales**, even **Epicurus**—who was able to believe in atoms and the void—could not bring himself to believe in astrology. The first to cultivate it with a good reputation in literature was **Ptolemy**, in the one hundred and fortieth year after Christ. However, he did so more sparingly than the others, so that he seems not so much to favor that insanity as to wish to set a limit upon it. Nevertheless, the authority of this one man (always a mathematician, rarely a philosopher) collapses when weighed against so many opposing judgments of the most famous men in both mathematics and philosophy. 

The name of Ptolemy pulled some Greeks into error who were otherwise inclined toward superstition, such as **Porphyry**, whose excessive labor in the worship of demons and care for superstitions was condemned by both his teacher **Plotinus** and his disciple **Iamblichus**. From the Greeks, it passed to the Arabs with even greater authority; they marveled at whatever they found written by the Greeks and looked up to that vain appearance of antiquity in the names of the Egyptians and Chaldeans. 

But just as the most prudent of astrologers, Ptolemy, purged and trimmed that art as he received it from the "Barbarians" <note>In this context, "Barbarians" refers to non-Greek peoples like the Egyptians and Chaldeans.</note> to the best of his ability, so a certain grammarian and historian named **Abu Ma'shar** <note>original: *Aboasar*. A famous Persian astrologer (787–886 AD) whose works were highly influential in the Middle Ages.</note> took it from the Greeks and filled it with innumerable trifles and fables. He made astrology almost as much worse than Ptolemy’s astrology as astrology itself is worse than the "good arts" <note>The *bonae artes* or liberal arts.</note>. He was a man made for empty loquacity, almost entirely ignorant not only of philosophy but also of astronomy. He is mocked by every learned astrologer but welcomed by the masses, among whom he is considered great who says the most, not he who says the best. 

However, during those times, the study of mathematics grew, as did all philosophy and all disciplines in Spain. There, while **Alfonso** <note>Alfonso X of Castile (reigned 1252–1284), known as "The Wise," who sponsored the Alfonsine Tables of planetary movement.</note> reigned—a man most diligent in mathematical numbers and the calculation of celestial motions—he also loved this divinatory vanity, though he was otherwise untrained in the studies of philosophy. For his sake, many monuments of that art from the Arabs and Greeks reached us, primarily through **John of Seville** and **Michael Scot** <note>A 13th-century scholar and translator known for his interest in the occult.</note>, a writer of no weight but of much superstition. **Albert** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a prominent theologian who sought to reconcile Aristotelian science with Christian faith.</note> first embraced these things because they were new, having been born during those times, but I think...

## Giovanni Pico della Mirandola

...he did not approve of it as an old man as much as he did as a youth; just as he published works on magic as a young man, but in his mature age detested them, living a most holy and blameless life in a monastery. <note>Pico is likely referring to a specific historical authority or perhaps reflecting on his own intellectual journey, as he famously moved from youthful interest in "natural magic" to a rigorous defense of orthodox piety.</note> However, as time passed, due to both the long duration of the tradition and the sheer volume of writings—and because of a certain affinity in name and subject matter with mathematical astronomy—the matter reached the point where it was debated: was this a science without deception, or was it merely superstition? Truly, although it was accepted for so many centuries by the masses (who naturally lack wisdom) and cultivated by the superstitious (whose "knowledge" is actually delusion) and sought after by the curious who lacked judgment; nevertheless, as we warned in the first book, it was always mocked, refuted, and driven away by the prudent, by philosophers, and by the holiest of men.

For in the time when the cult of idols was growing in Egypt and Chaldea, along with the insanity of all vanities, it was condemned by the Hebrews—the worshippers of the true God—through **Moses**, **Isaiah**, **Jeremiah**, and other prophets, both in speech and writing. When it came to Greece, it did not please **Pythagoras**; according to the authority of both **Diogenes** and **Theodoret**, the Platonists and Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note> did not even think it worthy of being discussed, considering it among the <term>peddling arts</term> <note>original: "artes circulatrices" — refers to the "arts" practiced by wandering charlatans or street-performers.</note>. **Eudoxus of Cnidus**, a most prudent lawmaker (for he wrote the laws for his fellow citizens), who was also a great philosopher under **Plato** and, by universal consent, the leading mathematician of his age, affirmed that astrologers were in no way to be believed, and he left this in writing. **Cassander** and **Archelaus**, distinguished mathematicians, did the same some years later; as did **Panaetius** and **Carneades**, weighty and true philosophers.

As often as those diviners came to Rome, whether from Egypt or Babylonia, that famous Roman providence removed them from the city with the strictest laws. Thus under **Tiberius**, **Vitellius**, **Diocletian**, **Constantine**, **Gratian**, **Valentinian**, and **Theodosius**, they were forced either to abandon their profession or suffer the penalties of practicing it. Why **Hadrian** was delighted by their deceptions is clear enough: by a certain natural inclination, he loved Egypt so much that nothing Egyptian could fail to please him; yet even then, **Favorinus** openly and **Plutarch** indirectly attacked it with the judgment of most serious men.

Soon after, under **Ptolemy**, when it seemed to gain a little respectability, it was immediately discredited by the judgments of **Plotinus** the great Platonist, **Alexander of Aphrodisias** the distinguished Peripatetic, and **Origen**, who was eminent in all disciplines. When it reached the Arabs, it did indeed hold the attention of **Abenragel** <note>Ibn Abi al-Rijal, an 11th-century Arab astrologer.</note> and **Aboafares**, who were neither logicians nor philosophers; but it did not hold **Averroes** or **Avicenna**. Indeed, when it first appeared at the University of Paris, it was barely prevented by the curious from being utterly destroyed and hidden under the flames. And when, some years later, **Roger Bacon** and certain others tried to give it respectability, they were resisted by most learned men: **William of Auvergne**, Bishop of Paris, and after him **Nicole Oresme**, an excellent mathematician, and **Henry**...

### THE END OF THE TWELVE BOOKS OF THE DISPUTATIONS
### OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA AGAINST ASTROLOGY.

## GIANFRANCESCO PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA to the most 
## sacred father Oliviero Carafa, Bishop of Sabina and 
## Cardinal of Naples, Greetings.

**W**e read, most distinguished father, that while **Apollonius of Tyana** <note>A Greek Neopythagorean philosopher and teacher from the 1st century AD</note> was about to undertake that journey for the sake of acquiring learning which **Philostratus** <note>The author of the "Life of Apollonius of Tyana"</note> later made famous, he wished that he might both find and recognize good men, and he even sought with many prayers that this might be granted to him by the Sun. This vow, indeed, cannot be praised enough without fault, just as the prayer to the Sun itself cannot but be criticized; for both the learned and the unlearned masses proclaim this everywhere by the innate light of knowing the truth—to omit the most powerful reasons and the testimonies of divine eloquence. But if that gift is to be wished for and demanded from God the Best and Greatest, then those must undoubtedly rejoice most greatly who have happened not only to recognize good men, but even to find these very men within their own family and bound to them by the bond of blood, rather than merely "finding" them abroad; and from this, to attain some of those fruits which the friendship of good men produces. 

I do not deny, nor do I hide the fact, that this divine benevolence has happened to me, since I discovered within my own domestic walls **Giovanni Pico della Mirandola**, the brother of my father **Galeotto**—a man truly worthy of being eagerly sought out by Apollonius beyond the Caucasus and the Brahmins <note>original: "Brachmanas"; referring to the ancient Indian philosophers Apollonius famously visited</note>, even to the opposite side of the world—and I have emerged enriched by many benefits from him. While he was living with us, I judged that I should return like for like as far as I could; and now that he is deceased, I have decided that I ought all the more to repay the duties I undertook. This is because both his glory and the usefulness of his studies were at risk, and the Church was suffering no small loss. 

For this reason, I have more than once committed his works to writing, and through long and anxious investigation of his labors, I have taken care to have them transcribed into many copies. I have labored most intensely in restoring the books that utterly overthrow all divinatory astrology, since they had been sketched out in such characters <note>Referring to Giovanni Pico's notoriously difficult handwriting</note> (which was the man's custom) because of the speed of his writing and dictating, that they seemed to present the appearance of any language other than Latin; so many interlin...

# BIAGIO BONACCORSI,
## To his most beloved friend, Girolamo Benivieni.
## Greetings. <note>original: "S.", an abbreviation for "Salutem"</note>

Doubtless, most beloved Girolamo, all the scholars of our times, and those yet to come, should continually mourn the untimely death of that admirable young man, **Giovanni Pico, Prince of Mirandola**. Considering his many excellent virtues, they must realize how great a loss they have suffered, especially regarding the benefit they might have hoped for and promised themselves from his life. This loss has been shared not only by those who desire philosophical matters—particularly those of **Plato**—but also by all lovers and professors of Holy Scripture. He had already satisfied the former group in large part with many most excellent works which he had not yet published; and he was seeking, with the greatest utility and glory to the Christian religion, to satisfy the latter group when he was hindered by his unexpected and lamentable death. However, I believe that the aforementioned scholars and men of letters endure this patiently, considering that Almighty God performs nothing except with the greatest mystery and divine providence.

I believe that this same providence has now moved the spirits of our printers to publish, through their art, the learned and elegant commentary of the late Prince upon one of your learned and graceful **Songs** <note>original: "Cãzone"; a lyric poem</note> composed on Divine Love according to the mind and opinion of the **Platonists** <note>Followers of the philosophy of Plato, who in the Renaissance sought to reconcile ancient Greek thought with Christian theology</note>. This is so that this work, like many of his others, does not remain neglected and forgotten by men, and so that all the literate and lovers of his name may have the convenience of enjoying it, gathering that fruit which they cannot take from his other works that have not been brought to light.

Having in my possession a transcript of the said Song and commentary, and being requested with great urgency by certain of our printers, I was somewhat hesitant as to whether I should grant it or not. On one hand, I was held back by knowing how much the publication of such a work was contrary to your mind and to that of the author, for the reasons understood by you. On the other hand, I was incited by the urgency of these printers, the desire of many people, and the utility and convenience that seemed to me would result from such a publication. Therefore, having finally been overcome by the comforts and prayers of friends, I chose to make a copy of this transcript of mine for the printers—even if it is against your will—rather than withholding it and defrauding the desire of many. I weighed most heavily that my fault should be all the more excusable as a private offense is less grave than a public one; for this, beyond the common good, also has the private good of a friend as its end.

Furthermore, since I am aware of several transcripts of this work being read and disseminated in various places and by many hands, I judged it utterly impossible that it would not one day be published in the same manner. This would have happened with much greater displeasure to you and to all lovers of the Count's <note>Referring to Pico della Mirandola, who held the title Count of Concordia</note> works, because such transcripts are imperfect and filled with many errors. I believe that this copy of mine is purged of these, if not entirely, then at least for the most part. And if you recognize any fault of mine in this, excuse me to yourself and to the happy memory of the author of this Commentary. Beyond that love which knows no restraint or law, all those who read it will easily recognize—if my judgment does not deceive me—that if the Count had written of love in a **Christian** manner, as was his intention, he would have done so with even greater happiness, just as truly divine doctrine surpasses and excels that of Plato and all other philosophers. Farewell.

# GIROLAMO BENIVIENI,
## citizen of Florence,
## to the Reader.

Giovanni Pico, Prince of Mirandola—a man truly admirable in every respect—was reading, as happens among friends, a Song of mine. In this poem, invited by the most pleasant reading of the learned commentaries of our **Marsilio Ficino** <note>A leading philosopher of the Italian Renaissance who translated Plato's works into Latin</note> upon Plato’s *Symposium*, I had restricted into a few verses what Marsilio describes most elegantly across many pages. It pleased Pico to illustrate this Song with an interpretation no less learned and elegant than it was copious. He was moved, I believe, not so much by the merits of the work itself as by a tender and singular affection that he, beyond all belief, always held for me and my works.

However, when later revising this Song and commentary—that spirit and fervor which had led me to compose it and him to interpret it having already partially faded—there arose in our minds some shadow of doubt. We wondered if it was appropriate for a professor of the Law of Christ, wishing to treat of Love (especially celestial and divine Love), to treat of it as a <term>Platonico</term> <note>A Platonist; someone following the philosophical system of Plato</note> and not as a Christian. We thought it best to suspend the publication of such a work, at least until we saw if, through some reformation, it could change from Platonic to Christian.

Shortly after this deliberation, there occurred the untimely and—above all other calamities of these times—damaging and lamentable death of the said Giovanni Pico. Due to his unexpected passing, remaining as if without any sense and full of confusion and weariness regarding the things of the world, I thought to leave this <term>canzona</term> <note>A song or lyric poem of high literary style</note> and commentary, together with many of my other verses, to the judgment of the dust, and to suppress it forever.

Although this was observed by me until these times, the study and desire of others to bring this work to light has nevertheless had more power than my own scruple and diligence in withholding it. Meanwhile, it having already come into the power of some who were more curious—through the indulgence and permission of those who held his original draft along with the other books and commentaries of the said Giovanni Pico—it was first given into the hands of our printers and put into production before I even had notice of it. Since I could not honestly resist this, and on the other hand, recognizing no fault of my own in the publication of such a work, I thought to "let it go to the benefit of nature," as they say.

I trust especially in the prudence, goodness, and learning of those who persuaded me to do so. I now pray that whoever reads this, in all those places where this Song or Commentary, following the doctrine of <term>Platone</term> <note>Plato, the ancient Greek philosopher</note>, departs in any way from Christian truth, let the authority of Christ and his saints have more power over them than the opinion of a pagan man. This is in addition to the irrefragable reasons of our theologians—especially the Angelic Doctor, **St. Thomas Aquinas**—brought to the contrary. Excuse our error (if it can be called an error) as simply reciting, without any approval, the opinion of others, even if it is not true. I say this because of the inscription or title placed before this Song and commentary, which openly states that we wish to treat of Love, not according to the Catholic truth, but according to the mind and opinion of the **Platonists**.

In the execution of this matter, even if there may be many other errors besides the one mentioned, this benefit and utility cannot be taken away: that students of Plato and his doctrine, reading attentively, will find in this commentary many lights. Through these, the eye of their intention may more easily, and perhaps with another gaze, penetrate the innermost marrow of some of the more remote meanings of such a great Philosopher.

->BOOK<-

# COMMENTARY OF THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS LORD
## Count Giovanni Pico della Mirandola on a Song of Love, composed by Girolamo Benivieni, a Florentine Citizen, according to the mind and opinion of the Platonists.

*That every created thing has being in three ways: Causal, Formal, and Participated.*

### CHAPTER ONE.

The Platonists <note>Followers of the ancient Greek philosopher Plato, who believed in a world of ideal "Forms" beyond our physical reality.</note> set down as their dogma and principal foundation that every created thing has its being in three ways. Although these are named differently by different people, they all converge toward the same meaning, and for now we may name them thus: **Causal being**, **Formal being**, and **Participated being**. This distinction cannot be expressed by more accurate terms, but let it be made manifest by an example. According to the philosophers, there is no heat in the Sun, because heat is an <term>elemental quality</term> <note>A property belonging to the four physical elements (earth, air, fire, water) rather than the "higher" celestial matter of the stars.</note> and not of a celestial nature; nevertheless, the sun is the cause and source of all heat. Fire is hot, and it is hot by its own nature and by its own proper form. A piece of wood is not hot in itself, but it can certainly be heated by fire, "participating" in the aforementioned quality from it. Therefore, this thing called heat has **causal being** in the sun, **formal being** in the fire, and **participated being** in the wood or other similar matter.

Of these three modes of being, the most noble and the most perfect is **causal being**. Therefore, the Platonists—and indeed every perfection that is conceded to exist in God—wish for it to be in Him according to this mode of being. Because of this, they will say that nothing exists in God, but rather that He is the cause of all things. Similarly, they say that there is no intellect in God, but that He is the source and principle of every intellect. These sayings, because their foundation is not understood, cause no small trouble for modern Platonists. I remember that once a great Platonist told me he marveled much at a saying of <term>Plotinus</term> <note>A major Hellenistic philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) and the founder of Neoplatonism.</note> where he says that God understands and knows nothing. But perhaps it is more to be wondered how that man did not understand in what way Plotinus means that God does not "understand"—which is nothing other than his desire that this perfection of "understanding" be in God according to that **causal being** and not according to the **formal**. This is not to deny understanding to God, but to attribute it to Him according to a more perfect and excellent mode. That this is so can be clearly understood from <term>Dionysius the Areopagite</term> <note>The "Prince of Christian Theologians," a 5th-century writer who integrated Neoplatonic philosophy with Christian doctrine.</note>, the prince of Christian theologians. He maintains that God knows not only Himself, but even every smallest and particular thing; yet he uses the same mode of speaking used by Plotinus, saying: "God is not an intellectual or intelligent nature, but is ineffably elevated above every intellect and cognition." This distinction is therefore to be noted diligently, because we will use it often, and it offers the greatest light for the understanding of Platonic matters.

*That all creatures are distinct in three ranks.*

### CHAPTER II.

The Platonists distinguish every creature into three ranks, of which there are two extremes. Under the first is comprised every corporal and visible creature, such as the Heavens, the elements, plants, animals, and everything composed of the elements. Under the other is understood every invisible creature—not only incorporeal, but even entirely free and separated from every body—which is properly called **intellectual nature**, and by our theologians is called **Angelic nature**. In the middle of these two extremes is a middle nature, which, although it is incorporeal, invisible, and immortal, is nonetheless a mover of bodies and bound to this service; and this is called the **rational soul**. It is placed below the Angelic nature and above the corporal; subject to the former, and patron of the latter. Above these three ranks is God Himself, the author and principle of every creature. All of these have their "causal" being of divinity in their source [God], and proceeding from Him, they have their second being—that is, "formal"—immediately in the Angelic nature. Finally, in the rational soul, it shines by being participated from the Angelic nature to her. Thus the Platonists say that divinity consists in three natures: that is, in God, in the Angel, and in the rational soul. Below these, no nature can be attributed this divine name, except abusively. One could make a more explicit mention and more detailed division of these natures, dividing bodies into various natures, and similarly souls, declaring which are called "animals" <note>Living beings with sensory perception.</note> and which are "animated" <note>Possessing a soul or life-force but not necessarily animal senses.</note> but not animals (since the world is called an "animated animal" by Plato in the *Timaeus*). However, we will reserve this discussion for the proper places, and let what is necessary for the knowledge of this treatise on love suffice here.

*How the Platonists prove that God cannot be multiplied, but that there is only one God, the principle and cause of every other divinity.*

### CHAPTER III.

Regarding these three natures—that is: God, the Angelic nature, and the rational nature—the Platonists, the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note>, and our theologians prove through most evident reasons (which would be superfluous to recite in this place) that the first, which is God, cannot be multiplied, but is the one and only God, the principle and cause of every other divinity. Regarding the other nature—that is, the Angelic and intellectual—there is discord among the Platonists. Some, such as **Proclus**, **Hermias**, **Syrianus**, and many others, place between God and the rational soul a great number of creatures which they call part "intelligible" and part "intellectual" (terms which Plato sometimes confuses, as in the *Phaedo* when speaking of the soul). **Plotinus**, **Porphyry**, and commonly the most perfect Platonists place only a single creature between God and the soul of the world, which they call the **Son of God**, because it is produced immediately by God. The first opinion is more in conformity with **Dionysius the Areopagite** and with Christian theologians, who posit a nearly infinite number of Angels. The second is more philosophical and more in conformity with **Aristotle** and **Plato**, and is followed by all the Peripatetics and the best Platonists. Therefore, since we propose to speak of that which we believe to be the common opinion of Plato and Aristotle, leaving aside the first view (although it alone is true in itself), we follow this second path.

*That God produced from eternity a single incorporeal and intellectual creature, as perfect as could be.*

### CHAPTER IIII.

Following, then, the opinion of **Plotinus**, followed not only by the best Platonists but also by **Aristotle** and all the Arabs—and especially by **Avicenna** <note>An influential 11th-century Persian philosopher and physician.</note>—I say that God produced from eternity <note>original: "ab eterno"</note> a creature of an incorporeal and intellectual nature, as perfect as it is possible for a created thing to be. Therefore, besides this one, He produced nothing else, because from a most perfect cause there cannot proceed anything but a most perfect effect. And that which is most perfect cannot be more than one; just as, for example, the most perfect color among all colors cannot be more than one. For if there were two or more, it would be necessary for one of them to be more or less perfect than the other; otherwise, one would be the same as the other, and thus they would not be many, but one. That which is less perfect than the other, therefore, will not be the most perfect. Similarly, if God had produced another creature besides this Mind, it would not

<summary>Pico establishes the Neoplatonic hierarchy of being (Causal, Formal, and Participated) and the three ranks of creation (Angelic, Rational Soul, and Body). He argues for the existence of a single, most-perfect "First Mind" or "Son of God" produced immediately by the Creator.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s exploration of the Neoplatonic hierarchy of being. Having previously introduced the modes of being (Causal, Formal, Participated), he now discusses the "First Mind" or "Angelic Mind" produced immediately by God, and how this relates to the physical world and ancient mythology.</meta>

->FIRST<-

it would not have been the most perfect, because it would have been less perfect than that. I am used to offering this reason in confirmation of this opinion, and it seems more effective to me than the one used by **Avicenna** <note>A Persian polymath (c. 980–1037) whose philosophical works deeply influenced Western medieval and Renaissance thought.</note>, which is based on this principle: that from a single cause, insofar as it is one, no more than one effect can proceed. But since these matters are introduced only for the understanding of our main purpose, we should not linger on them with a more exact examination. Let it suffice to know that according to these philosophers, no other creature proceeds from God immediately except this first one. I say "immediately" because even of every effect produced afterward by this Mind and every other secondary cause, God is said to be the cause, but a mediated and remote one. This first created Mind is called by **Plato**, and likewise by the ancient philosophers, **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the synthesis of Greek and Egyptian wisdom.</note>, and **Zoroaster**, sometimes the "Son of God," sometimes "Mind," sometimes "Wisdom," and sometimes "Divine Reason." Some also interpret this as the "Word." <note>original: "uerbo"</note> And let everyone be diligently careful not to believe that this is the same as what our Theologians call the "Son of God." For we understand the Son of God to be of the same essence as the Father, equal to Him in all things, finally a Creator and not a creature; but what the Platonists call the "Son of God" must be compared to the first and most noble angel produced by God.

# Of two modes of being, Ideal and Formal.
## CHAPTER V.

**F**or the declaration, then, of what will follow, it must be known that every cause that works an effect through art and intellect first has within itself the form of that thing which it wishes to produce. Just as an architect has within himself and in his soul the form of the building he wishes to construct, and looking to that as his model <note>original: "essempio"</note>, he produces and composes his work in imitation of it. This such form the Platonists call **Idea** and **Exemplar**. They maintain that the form of the building which the craftsman has in his mind has a more perfect and truer being than the building later produced by that craftsman in suitable matter—that is, of stone, wood, or other similar things. That first being, they call **Ideal being**, or rather **Intelligible being**. The other they call **Material and Sensible being**. Thus, if a craftsman builds a house, they will say there are two houses: one intelligible, which the craftsman has in his mind, and another sensible, which is the one composed by the craftsman out of marble, stones, or something else, expressing as much as he can in that matter the form he has conceived within himself. This is what our poet **Dante** touches upon in one of his songs, where he says: *He who paints a figure, if he cannot be it, cannot portray it.* <note>Dante Alighieri, the famous Italian poet. The quote emphasizes that the artist must possess the "idea" or essence of the subject internally before creating it.</note> The Platonists say, therefore, that although God produced only one creature, he nonetheless produced everything, because in that one he produced the ideas and forms of all things. There is, therefore, in that Mind the idea of the Sun, the Moon, of men, of all animals, plants, stones, elements, and universally of every creature. Since the idea of the Sun is a "truer" sun than the sensible Sun itself—and so with every other creature—it follows not only that He has produced everything, but that He has produced it in the truest and most perfect mode of being possible: that is, in their **Ideal and Intelligible being**. For this reason, they call this Mind the **Intelligible World**.

# How this world was caused and produced from eternity by that first mind, and how it is animated by a soul most perfect above every other soul.
## CHAPTER VI.

**F**rom this Mind they hold that this sensible world was caused, which is an image and a likeness <note>original: "simulachro"</note> of the intelligible one. Since the model in imitation of which it was manufactured is the most perfect of all created things, it follows that this world is also as perfect as its nature allows. However, since every animated thing is more perfect than inanimate things—and especially those that have a rational and intelligent soul compared to those animated by an irrational soul—it is necessary to grant that the world is animated by a soul most perfect above all other souls. This is the first **rational soul**, which, although it is incorporeal and immaterial, is nonetheless bound to this ministry of governing and moving the corporeal nature. Therefore, it is not as free and separate from the body as that Mind from which this soul was produced from eternity—just as that Mind was from God. From this, a most evident argument is drawn: that according to Plato, the world cannot but be eternal, as all the Platonists also agree. Therefore, since the **World Soul** <note>term: World Soul (Anima Mundi) — an intrinsic connection between all living things on the planet, which relates to our world in much the same way as the human soul is connected to the human body.</note> is eternal, and since it cannot exist without the body (as they maintain), it is also necessary that this worldly body existed from eternity, and likewise the celestial motion. For the soul, according to the Platonists, cannot exist without moving. We have said that all Platonists agree on this: that the world is eternal. For even Atticus and Plutarch, and others who hold that this present order of the world had a beginning, do not hold that before this there was nothing but God (as our Catholic Church posits), but they believe that before this orderly motion of the heavens and the present disposition of worldly things, there was an unordered and tumultuous motion, governed by an unformed and depraved soul. Thus, they would concede that there have been infinite worlds, because infinite times the world emerged from the confusion of **Chaos** into order, and infinite times it returned to it. With this, the opinion of the **Talmudists** <note>Scholars of Jewish civil and ceremonial law.</note> seems to agree, who ask what God was doing from eternity, and they answer that He was creating worlds and then destroying them; although, following the opinion of the **Cabalists** <note>Followers of Kabbalah, a school of thought in Jewish mysticism.</note>, a truer and more fitting sense can be given to their words. **Aristotle** attributes this opinion to Plato, and therefore sometimes says that he alone makes time anew, and sometimes—as in the 12th book of the *Metaphysics*—confesses that according to Plato, motion was eternal.

# How the three aforementioned natures—God, the angelic nature, and the rational nature—are signified by these three names, Caelus, Jupiter, and Saturn, and what is meant by them.
## CHAPTER VII.

**T**hese three first natures—that is, **God**, that **First Mind**, and the **World Soul**—are denoted by these three names by the ancient theologians of the gentiles, who covered their mysteries under poetic veils: **Caelus**, **Saturn**, and **Jupiter**. **Caelus** <note>The Roman god of the sky, equivalent to the Greek Uranus.</note> is God Himself, who produces the first mind called **Saturn**, and from Saturn is generated **Jupiter**, who is the World Soul. And because these three names are sometimes found confused—that is, the first will be called Jupiter, and the World Soul Saturn, and that Mind Jupiter—we will declare the foundation and the reason for these names. Once understood, we will comprehend that all that variety and those changes, which seem to be made at pleasure and licentiously, proceed concordantly from one and the same foundation. They say, then, that this name **Caelus** is significant of every first thing and everything excellent above others, just as the first heaven (the firmament) is the first and supereminent over all corporeal things. **Saturn** is significant of the intellectual nature, which only attends to and is turned toward understanding and contemplating. **Jupiter** is significant of the active life, which consists in ruling, administering, and moving with its command the things subject and inferior to it. These two properties are found in the planets signified by these same names—that is, Saturn and Jupiter—because, as they say, Saturn makes men contemplative, while Jupiter gives them kingdoms, governments, and the administration of peoples. And because the contemplative life is concerned with things superior to the one who contemplates...

### On the variation of these three names, Coelus, Saturn, and Jove; and why and how they suit the three aforementioned natures.

#### CHAPTER VIII.

**I**n the first, that is, God, it cannot be understood that He contemplates, because this is a property of an intellectual creature, of which God Himself is the principle and cause; therefore He cannot be called Saturn. Instead, only this is understood of Him: that is, being the principle of every thing, in which intellect two things are included. The first is His super-eminence and excellence, which every cause has over its effect, and for this He is called Coelus <note>original: "Celio"; the personification of the Sky or Heavens.</note>. The second is the production of that which proceeds from Him, in which is understood a turning toward things inferior to Him while He produces them, which we said above is a likeness of the active life; and for this, in some way, the name of Jove <note>original: "Gioue"; Jupiter.</note> suits Him, especially with the addition of supreme perfection, as in saying: Jupiter the Best and Greatest <note>original: "Gioue ottimo maſſimo"; a translation of the Latin title 'Iuppiter Optimus Maximus'.</note>. To the first angelic mind, more names are suited, because it is less simple than God, and more diversity is seen within it. And first, it must be known that every creature is composed of two natures. One of these is called *potentiality* <term>Potentiality: The capacity for being or becoming; unformed matter or possibility.</term> or *unformed nature*. The other is called *act* <term>Act: The actualization or 'form' that makes a thing what it is.</term> or *form*; and Plato in the *Philebus* <margin>Philebus</margin> calls the first *infinite*, and the second *limit* and *end*. By Avicebron <margin>Avicebron</margin> <note>Solomon ibn Gabirol, an 11th-century Jewish philosopher.</note> and many others, they are called *matter* and *form*. And although among philosophers there is a difference of opinion as to whether this unformed matter is one and the same in all creatures and of one same reason, or whether it is found differently in different degrees of nature, nevertheless all agree in this: that every thing that is between God and matter is first mixed of *act* and *potentiality*; and this suffices for us, nor does it matter for our purpose in what way this might be, whether a mixture or a composition. Therefore, in a similar way, this first mind is composed of these two parts, and every imperfection that is in it comes in respect to that part called *potentiality*, just as every perfection comes through the other. In this mind, three operations can be considered. One concerning things superior to itself. The other concerning itself. The third concerning things inferior to itself. The first is nothing other than turning to contemplate its father. And similarly, the second is nothing other than knowing itself. The last is turning toward the production and care of this sensible world which, as we said above, is produced by it. These three operations are understood to proceed from that mind in such a way that, by virtue of that part called *act* which is in it, it turns toward the father; by virtue of the other called *potentiality*, it descends to the workmanship of inferior things; and by virtue of both, it remains fixed within itself. For the first two operations, it shall be called Saturn, because both are contemplation; for the third, Jove. And because this act of producing worldly things suits it through 그at nature called *potentiality*, that part in it shall principally be called Jove—which is to be observed for what we shall say in the second book when explaining what the orders of Jove are. By the same foundation, the World Soul, insofar as it contemplates itself or things superior to it, can be called Saturn. Insofar as it is occupied with the movement and governance of bodies and worldly actions, it is called Jove. And because this operation of governing the corporeal world principally suits it, just as contemplation principally suits that [Angelic] mind, it is therefore *absolutely* called Jove, just as that mind is called Saturn; although that mind, whenever one speaks of it as the craftsman of the world, is always called Jove for the reason stated above. This is the true property of these names.

### On the composition, division, and order of this sensible world, and the reason why it is said to be divided among the three sons of Saturn.

#### CHAPTER IX.

<margin>Timaeus</margin>
**T**herefore, this world—produced by that mind in the image of the intelligible world produced within it by the first father—is composed, like every animal, of its soul and its body. The worldly body is everything that appears to our eyes, made, as is written in the *Timaeus*, of four elements: Fire, Water, Air, and Earth. And for a true understanding of this, one must remember the foundation we laid in the first chapter of this treatise: that every thing has three states of being: *Causal*, *Formal*, and *Participated*, as we declared in that chapter. It is necessary, then, that these four elements also have a triple mode of being. The first, that is, the causal being, they have in the celestial bodies, because the substance of those bodies is not composed of this Fire, Air, Water, and Earth that are from the Moon downward (commonly called elements), but contains them all within itself as every cause contains its effect; for in the celestial bodies there is a power productive of inferior bodies. Nor can it be understood in any way that the body of heaven is a substance mixed of these elements, as are the other mixed bodies among us; for it would follow (besides the other reasons cited by others) that this part of the world from the Moon downward was made before the superior celestial part, because the being of the elements in their simple state is understood first, and then through their joining together, that which is mixed of them is caused. Therefore, the elements have a causal being in the Heavens, as Plato <margin>Aristotle</margin> maintains, and not a formal being, as Aristotle rightly denies; and of this we shall speak more at length elsewhere. They have their formal being from the Moon down to the earth, and the third being—that is, participated, imperfect, and diminished—they have in the subterranean parts. That this is the truth—namely, that in the bowels of the earth are found fire, air, and water—experience demonstrates, and natural philosophers prove it, and ancient theologians confirm it, designating those enigmatically through the four infernal rivers:

Acheron, Cocytus, Styx, and Phlegethon. We can therefore divide the worldly body into three parts: *Celestial*, *Worldly*, and *Infernal*, using these latter two names according to common usage of speech, also adopted by the ancients, which is to call this part from the Moon downward properly the "world." Wherefore John the Evangelist, speaking of souls that are infused by God into bodies, says: "every soul that comes into this world," and so it is found observed in many other places as well. Similarly, they call this subterranean part "Hell," designated as a place of punishment for guilty souls. From this, one can understand for what reason the kingdom of Saturn is said by the Poets to be divided among his three sons: Jove, Neptune, and Pluto; for it denotes nothing other than the triple variation of this corporeal world—both as to the body in the manner described, and also as to the World Soul, according to how we understand these three parts to be animated. The kingdom of Saturn is the intelligible and exemplary world of this one; which, while it remains Saturn's—that is, while it remains in its ideal and intelligible being—remains one and undivided, and consequently firmer and more powerful. But after it has come into the hands of the sons—that is, when it is transmuted to this corporeal being, and divided by them into three parts through the variation of that triple being of bodies—it becomes weaker...

much less powerful than it was before, degenerating from the first as much as every corporeal thing degenerates from the spiritual. They say the first part, that is, the celestial, belonged to Jove <note>Jupiter</note>; the last and lowest, to Pluto; and that of the middle to Neptune. And because this part is where every generation and corruption <note>The cycle of birth and death in the physical world.</note> primarily occurs, it is symbolized by theologians as water and as the sea, which is in a continuous flux and reflux. From this—and from Heraclitus—this continuous motion of things that can be generated and corrupted is compared to the motion of a most rapid torrent. For this reason, the Poets say the kingdom of the sea fell to Neptune. By "Neptune," the pagan theologians in their mysteries understand that power or deity who presides over generation. 

However, we should not understand this to mean there are three different souls that inform and rule these three parts of the world; since the world is one, it must also have only one soul. When this soul animates and gives life to the subterranean parts of the world, it is called Pluto; insofar as it gives life to the parts below the Moon, it is called Neptune; and insofar as it gives life to the celestial parts, it is called Jove. Therefore, Plato says in the *Philebus* that by Jove one understands a "royal soul," that is, that part of the World Soul which is the principal one and rules and dominates the others. And although this division among these three sons of Saturn is made differently by others, I have wanted only to recite that which is my own opinion and which I consider to be truer, setting aside the explanations brought by the Greeks, of which we shall make a more complete examination elsewhere. 

For a more perfect knowledge of the things said—namely, the nature of celestial, worldly, and elemental bodies—I must remember that according to most Platonists, celestial bodies are composed of matter and form like other bodies, though of a more perfect matter and of a different nature.

# That the souls of the eight celestial spheres together with the soul of the world are the nine Muses.
## CHAPTER X.

**A**fter the World Soul, the Platonists place many other rational souls, among which there are eight principal ones: the souls of the celestial spheres. According to the ancients, there are no more than eight of these—namely, the seven planets and the starry sphere. These are the nine Muses so celebrated by the Poets, among whom the first is Calliope, who is the universal World Soul; the other eight are distributed in order, each to its own sphere.

# On the universal soul of the world, and on all other rational souls, and on the correspondence that man has with all parts of the world.
## CHAPTER XI.

**P**lato writes in the *Timaeus* that the Maker of the world fashioned the worldly soul and all other rational souls in the same vessel and from the same elements. Among these, just as the universal World Soul is the most perfect, so ours is the last and the least perfect. We shall note a summary division of its parts. The nature of man, being as it were the "link and knot of the world," is placed in the middle rank of the universe. And as every middle part participates in the extremes, so man, through his various parts, has communion and correspondence with all parts of the world. For this reason, he is usually called the <term>Microcosm</term>, which means "little world." 

In the world, we first see corporeal nature, and this is twofold: one eternal, which is the substance of the heavens; the other corruptible, such as the elements and every nature composed of them, like stones, metals, and similar things. Then come the plants; above these in the third degree are the brute animals; in the fourth, rational animals; in the fifth, the angelic minds; above which is God Himself, the source and principle of every created being. Similarly, in man there are two bodies, as we shall prove in our assembly: one eternal, called by the Platonists the <term>Celestial Vehicle</term>, which is immediately vivified by the rational soul; the other corruptible, which we see with our bodily eyes, composed of the four elements. Then there is within him the vegetative power, by which this corruptible body is generated, nourished, and grows, while that eternal one lives a perpetual life. Third, there is the sensitive and motive part, through which he has correspondence with irrational animals. Fourth, there is the rational part, which is proper to man and rational animals; the Latin Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note> believe this to be the last and most noble part of our soul. Nonetheless, above it is the intellectual and angelic part, through which man corresponds with the Angels just as he corresponds with beasts through the sensitive part. The summit of this intellectual part the Platonists call the "unity of the soul," and they maintain it is that through which man is immediately joined with God and almost corresponds with Him, just as he corresponds with plants through the vegetative part. 

Among the Platonists, there is disagreement over which of these parts of the soul are immortal and which are mortal. Proclus and Porphyry maintain that only the rational part is immortal, and all the others are corruptible. Xenocrates and Speusippus maintain that, in addition to this, the sensitive part is also immortal. Numenius and Plotinus, adding the vegetative part to these as well, conclude that every soul is immortal.

# On the Ideas, and on their triple being.
## CHAPTER XII. AND THE LAST OF THE FIRST BOOK.

**T**he subject of the Ideas celebrated by the Platonists is perhaps the most useful and the most difficult for us among all questions of philosophy, because upon it depends the knowledge of the angels, of our soul, and of the celestial soul. In our assembly and in the commentary on Plato's *Symposium*, we shall speak of it exactly. Regarding this matter, because the Greek Platonists—I mean those who have come into our hands—speak of it obscurely and briefly, our work will perhaps not be useless to students of Platonic matters if, insofar as it serves our purpose, we note certain of their concise sayings. First, let us bring an end to this present introductory book to the following treatise on love. 

We must therefore remember the first foundation laid by us in the first chapter: namely, how everything has a triple way of being—causal, formal, and participated. It must follow, then, that the same is true of the Ideas, which in God will have a "causal" being, in the Angel a "formal" being, and in the rational soul a "participated" being. In God, therefore, according to the Platonists, there are no Ideas, but He is the cause and principle of all Ideas, which He primarily produces in the angelic nature, as is also clearly found written in the *Chaldean Oracles*. The rational soul is made a participant in them by that angel. Therefore, when our soul turns toward its intellectual and angelic part, it is illuminated by it, participating in the true forms of things which, just as they are called "Ideas" in the intellect, are later called "reasons" <note>original: "ragione"; meaning rational principles or logoi.</note> and not Ideas in the soul. 

In this, the souls of corruptible bodies, like ours and those of certain demons according to the Platonists, are different from celestial souls. Because of their administration of the body, celestial souls do not depart from the intellectual part, but always turned toward it and joined together, they exercise both duties: that of contemplating and that of governing bodies. For this reason, the Platonists will say that bodies ascend to them, and they do not descend to bodies. Others, dedicated to the care of falling and earthly bodies, become occupied in this and deprive themselves of intellectual contemplation; they beg for knowledge of things from the senses, to which they are entirely inclined. Therefore, they are always full of many errors and false opinions, from which prison and misery we shall see below there is a most powerful [remedy]...

## Regarding the aforementioned song; that whenever the name of a proposed thing is ambiguous, one must first establish what is signified by that name.

### CHAPTER ONE

**P**lato says in many places, and after him Aristotle, and universally all schools of Philosophers, that at the beginning of treating any subject, one must first establish what the name of the thing to be disputed signifies. To execute this, they command us that whenever such a name is <term>equivocal</term> <note>A word that has multiple, distinct meanings.</note>—that is, signifying various and diverse things—we must distinguish those meanings and declare for which one we principally intend to use the name. Otherwise, every dispute is always confused, disordered, and vain. Nor did the errors of those Sophists, whom Plato reproves in so many of his dialogues, proceed from anything other than not knowing this rule of distinguishing equivocal and ambiguous terms. Eudemus <note>Eudemus of Rhodes, a pupil of Aristotle.</note> claimed that Plato was the first inventor of this rule. Therefore, whoever approaches the works of the Philosophers, and especially the Platonists, without <term>logic</term> <note>The formal study of reasoning and definitions.</note> (in which the aforementioned method is learned), is bound to fill himself and anyone else who listens to his words with infinite errors and the greatest confusion. Since this name, "Love," as we shall see in the following chapter, is commonly used to signify diverse things, it is necessary before we speak of love to declare what is meant by this name, excluding everything else that it might imply.

->On this word "Love," and its various meanings.<-

### CHAPTER TWO

**J**ust as the cognitive virtues of the soul turn toward the true and the false, so the desiring virtues turn toward the good and the evil. The virtue that knows assents to what it judges to be true and dissents from what it judges to be false; that assent is called "affirmation" by philosophers, and that dissent is called "negation." Similarly, the virtue of the soul that desires inclines toward what presents itself with the face of the "good," and flees or withdraws from what shows itself with the face of "evil." That inclination is called "love"; that flight and withdrawal is called "hate." This is the broadest and most common meaning of this word "Love" that can be understood. Under this are many species which are distinguished according to the diversity of "goods" toward which our desire inclines. For example, if this Love concerns property—and especially if it is immoderate—it will be called "avarice"; if it concerns honors, "ambition." Similarly, if it concerns God or someone superior to us, it will be called "piety"; if it concerns an equal, "friendship." 

Excluding, therefore, this and all other meanings, we are to understand only that which is the desire to possess what is, or what appears to us to be, beautiful. Thus, in Plato’s *Symposium*, it is defined: "Love is the desire for beauty." And just as the Poets—among the Greeks meaning Homer and among our own meaning Virgil, due to their excellence among all poets—say "Love" absolutely <note>To use a word "absolutely" means to use it in its highest or most specific sense without further qualification.</note> to mean the love of beauty, they do so because it excels and surpasses every desire for any other created thing. This is similarly observed in the Latin language, in which, although one properly says "this man loves God," "this man his brother," or "this man money," nevertheless, when they say absolutely "this man loves," it is understood that he is seized by this desire for the beauty of someone, which is commonly called being "in love." 

And because among all the desires of love, this desire for beauty is the most vehement, Plato says in the *Phaedrus* that Love is named from the word <note>original: "Romis," referring to the Greek *rhōmē* (ῥώμη), meaning strength or might.</note> which among the Greeks signifies what we call "strength" and "vehemence." For this reason, whenever we want to signify that some other love or desire is vehement, we denote it by this name, as when it is said that someone is "in love" with letters, or with arms, and so with other things. Both Plato in the *Symposium* and the *Phaedrus*, and our Poet in the present song, speak of that love by which he who is seized is commonly said to be "in love." This is nothing other than the desire to possess and enjoy the beauty of another. 

From this, it is concluded that the love with which God loves his creatures, and that which is properly called friendship, and many other similar loves, are different from this love of which we speak. For now, let it suffice to say that since the love we are discussing is the desire to possess the beauty of another, and since God has no desire for anything outside of Himself (as He is entirely perfect and lacks nothing), this love cannot be attributed to Him. For the love with which He loves creatures arises from the exactly opposite reason. In our love, the one who loves has need of the thing loved and receives his perfection from the beloved. In Divine Love, the beloved has need of the Lover, and receives from Him. Similarly, that love called friendship has a property opposite to our love. In friendship, reciprocity is always necessary—that is, that one loves the other in the same way and for the same reason. This is an agreement, as Plato says in many places, which is not necessary in our love, for he who loves may not be beautiful, and consequently is not fit to move the beloved to a mutual desire for his beauty. 

Love, then, of which we are to speak, can be defined as Plato defines it: "the desire for beauty." "Desire" is placed there as the generic and common nature, by which love agrees with all other desires, just as man, insofar as he is an animal, agrees with all beasts. Then "for beauty" is added, which specifies the proper nature of love and distinguishes it from every other desire, just as being "rational" and "mortal" distinguishes man from other animals. If, then, we perfectly understand the parts of this definition, we shall perfectly understand love. Beginning with the first, I say that desire is nothing other than an inclination and impetus of the desirer toward that which truly is, or which he estimates to be, suitable for him. Such a thing is called "good." Therefore, the object of desire is the good, whether real or apparent. And just as there are different species of goods, so different species of desires arise—such as in our case, Love, which is a species of desire concerning a species of good called "the beautiful." From this, it is concluded that the beautiful is different from the good, as a species differs from its genus, and not as something extrinsic from something intrinsic. 

Desire can be divided by its primary division into "natural desire" and "desire with cognition." To fully understand what natural desire is, one must understand that since the object of desire is the good, and since every creature has some perfection proper to itself through participation in goodness...

divine goodness, from which everything proceeded, as Moses writes <note>Referring to Genesis 1:31, where God sees that His creation is "very good."</note>, it was exceedingly good. It must have a certain end in which that degree of happiness of which it is capable is found, and toward that it naturally directs and turns itself, like every heavy thing toward its center. This inclination in creatures that lack cognition is called "natural desire," a great testimony to divine providence, by which such creatures have been directed to their end, like an arrow from the archer to its target—which is not known by the arrow, but by him who moves it toward that goal with the eye of most wise providence. By this desire, God is desired by all creatures, because since every particular good is a vestige and a participation in the first good, which is God himself, in every good that is desired, He is the first thing desired. The "good" of stones and plants is nothing other than that of which they are capable of participating in divine goodness. And according to whether a nature is capable of participating more or less, it is ordered to a more or less noble end. Thus, the end of all creatures is one: namely, to enjoy God in the manner possible for them, and to taste as much as they can of the sweetness of His goodness. But according to whether they can attain more or less, their ends are diversified. From this, you can understand how God is that "good" of which Aristotle speaks at the beginning of the *Ethics* <note>original: "Arist. lib. 1 Ethic." Referring to the opening of the Nicomachean Ethics: "The good is that at which all things aim."</note>, saying that all things desire it. From what has been said, one can know in what way they desire it even though it is not known, and in what way they do not desire a thing impossible for them. How far from the truth is the exposition of those who have interpreted Aristotle otherwise in that passage, we shall declare elsewhere with most evident reasons. Turning toward Him with this natural desire, every creature praises and adores Him, as the Hebrew prophets sing; and all turn and offer themselves to Him as if supplicating, as the great Platonist Theodore <note>Likely Theodore of Asine, a Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> writes.

### Regarding desire in general, and how, of its own nature, it is always turned toward the good.

#### CHAPTER III.

<margin>Aristotle, Book 1 of the Ethics.</margin>
**T**he other species of desire concerns only things known by the one who desires. It is established by nature that to every knowing power there is joined an appetitive power; that which the knowing power judges to be good, the appetitive power loves and embraces; that which it judges to be evil, it hates and refuses. Insofar as it follows its own nature, it is always turned toward the good, nor was there ever anyone who desired to be miserable. But because the power that knows often errs in judgment and judges that to be good which in truth is evil, it happens that sometimes evil is desired by the appetitive power—which in itself is blind and does not know. On one hand, it can be said that it does this voluntarily, because no one can do violence to it; on the other hand, it can be said it does it involuntarily, because it does it deceived by the judgment of its companion <note>The cognitive faculty.</note>, for of itself it would never desire evil. This is what Plato means in the *Timaeus* when he says that no one sins voluntarily.
<margin>In the Timaeus.</margin>

### That to know things is to possess them.

#### CHAPTER IIII.

**A** common property follows every desiring power: he who desires always partly possesses the thing desired and partly does not; for if he were entirely deprived of its possession, he would never desire it. This is verified in two ways. The first is because, as we said in the preceding chapter, one does not desire a thing unless it is first known. It is subtly declared by philosophers how "to know things is to possess them," whence follows the common saying of Aristotle, that our soul is all things because it knows all things <note>A famous dictum from Aristotle’s *De Anima* (3.8.431b): "The soul is in a way all existing things."</note>. Likewise, Asaph the Hebrew poet says, "O God, all things are mine because I know them all" <margin>Psalm 49.</margin> <note>original: "Ps. 49." In the Vulgate numbering (Ps 50 in modern Bibles), verse 11: "I know all the fowls of the mountains..." Pico interprets "knowing" as a form of divine possession.</note>, although, just as there is a vast difference between His knowing and ours, so there is an equal difference in the possessing. The other way is that there always exists a suitability and similarity between the desirer and the desired thing. Every thing is preserved by what is most conformed to it by kinship of nature; by what is dissimilar and contrary to it, it is saddened and corrupted. Therefore, love does not fall between dissimilars, and the repugnance of two opposite natures is nothing other than a natural hatred, just as love is nothing other than a similarity with cognition. From this, it evidently follows that it is necessary for the nature of the desired thing to be found in some way in the desirer; otherwise, there would be no similarity between them. Yet it must be found there imperfectly, for it would be vain to seek that which one possesses in full.

### That different appetitive natures are attached to different knowing natures.

#### CHAPTER V.

**J**ust as desire in general follows cognition in general, so different appetitive natures are attached to different knowing natures. For now, it is enough to distinguish the cognitive powers into three levels: sense, reason, and intellect. Similarly, three levels of desiring nature follow these, which can be called <term>appetite</term>, <term>choice</term> <note>original: "elettione." In Renaissance psychology, this refers to the rational faculty of making decisions.</note>, and <term>will</term>. Appetite follows sense; choice follows reason; will follows intellect. Appetite is in brute animals; choice is in men <gloss>men</gloss> and in every other creature that is found between us and the angels; will is in the angels. And just as sense knows only corporeal and sensible things, so appetite desires only corporeal and sensible things. Just as the angelic intellect is intent and turned only toward the contemplation of spiritual concepts and does not incline toward material things (except insofar as they become immaterial and spiritual by being absolutely freed from matter), so their will feeds only on the good of eternal and spiritual things. Rational nature, placed between these two as a middle point between extremes—now inclined toward one side, namely sense, and now rising toward the other, namely intellect—can approach the desires of one or the other through its own choice. From all the aforementioned things, one can conclude that whenever the desired thing is corporeal and sensible, the desire for it must be either the appetite that follows sense or a choice of reason inclined toward sense. Whenever the thing is spiritual and incorporeal, it must be either angelic intellectual will or a choice of reason assumed and elevated to the sublimity of the intellect. Let Love, then, be desire; and having declared what desire is, to know what kind of desire Love is—whether it be sensitive, rational, or intellectual (which is to say, bestial, human, or angelic desire)—one must see what beauty is, which is the object of desire. Once this is known, we will have the definition of Love, and consequently an absolute knowledge of it.

### Regarding common beauty.

#### CHAPTER VI.

**T**his word "beauty" can be taken according to a broad and common significance, or it can be taken properly. According to the first way, whenever several different things concur in the constitution of a third, which is born from the proper mixture and temperament made of those various things, that decorum and that harmony or that temperance which results from that proportioned mixture is called beauty. And since every created thing is composed, and is composed with as much proper reason and proportion as is possible for the nature of that thing, one can, according to the aforementioned second way, call every created thing beautiful, since beauty itself is nothing other than that temperament which is the cause that those natures, though diverse and various, yet [unite]...

<summary>Pico defines desire as a universal movement toward the Good (God) and distinguishes three levels of desire—appetite, choice, and will—corresponding to the soul's hierarchy. He concludes that to understand Love, one must first define its object: Beauty.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the Neoplatonic hierarchy of being. Having previously defined desire as a natural inclination toward the "Good," the text now shifts to define "Beauty" not as a simple quality, but as a harmonious resolution of opposing forces. It bridges the gap between general metaphysical desire and the specific experience of Love.</meta>

-> BOOK <-

they come together and agree to compose a single nature. According to this reasoning, no simple thing can be beautiful; from which it follows that in God there is no beauty <note>In Neoplatonic thought, God is the "One"—pure simplicity—whereas beauty requires the relationship between different parts.</note>. Beauty begins after God, because that is where contrariety begins, without which no created thing can exist (otherwise there would be only God himself). Yet this contrariety and discord of diverse natures is not enough to constitute a creature unless, through a proper tempering, that contrariety becomes unified and the discord becomes concordant. This can be assigned as the true definition of beauty: namely, that it is nothing other than a friendly enmity and a concordant discord <note>original: "amica inimicitia" and "concorde discordia"</note>. For this reason, <term>Heraclitus</term> <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher known for the idea that "strife is justice."</note> said that war and concord were the father and mother of all things; and according to <term>Homer</term>, whoever curses contention is said to have blasphemed nature. But <term>Empedocles</term> spoke more perfectly, placing not discord by itself, but discord together with concord as the principle of things—understanding by discord the variety of natures of which things are composed, and by concord, their union. Therefore, he said that only in God is there no discord, because in Him there is no union of diverse natures; rather, He is simple unity itself without any composition. And because in the constitution of a creature it is necessary for union to overcome contrariety (otherwise the thing would dissolve, as its principles would separate from one another), the Poets say that <term>Venus</term> <note>The goddess of love and beauty.</note> loves <term>Mars</term> <note>The god of war and strife.</note>. This is because that beauty which we call <term>Venus</term> (as we shall say below) does not exist without that contrariety. When it is said that <term>Venus</term> tames and mitigates <term>Mars</term>, it means nothing else than that this tempering mitigates, clears, and blunts the battle and the hatred that exists between those contrary natures. Similarly, among the ancient Astrologers—whose opinions <term>Plato</term> and <term>Aristotle</term> follow, and as Alexander the Spaniard and even Moses write—<term>Venus</term> was placed in the middle of the sky next to <term>Mars</term>, so that she might tame his impulse, which is by nature corruptive and destructive, just as <term>Jupiter</term> tames the malice of <term>Saturn</term>. And if <term>Mars</term> were always subjected to <term>Venus</term>—that is, if the contrariety of the component principles were always subject to their proper tempering—nothing would ever decay.

### Of beauty properly understood.

### CHAPTER VII.

**T**his is the broad and common meaning of beauty, a meaning shared with the word <term>Harmony</term> <note>original: "Harmonia"</note>. Hence it is said that God composed the whole world with a musical and harmonic tempering. But just as "Harmony" can generally be taken as the proper tempering of any composed thing, but properly signifies only the tempering of several voices coming together into a melody, so too, although "beauty" can be said of any properly composed thing, its proper meaning applies only to visible things. Just as Harmony applies to audible things, beauty applies to visible things; and this beauty is that, the desire for which is called <term>Love</term>. Therefore, <term>Love</term> is born from a single cognitive power: namely, from sight. This was celebrated by <term>Musaeus</term> and <term>Propertius</term>, and universally by all the Greek and Latin poets. Because of this, <term>Plotinus</term> <note>The foundational philosopher of Neoplatonism.</note> is moved to believe that *Eros*—which in Greek means <term>Love</term>—derives from the word *Oresis* <note>Greek for "vision" or "appetite/striving." The author connects sight with the impulse of desire.</note>, which signifies vision. But one might ask: if beauty is only in those things which the sight perceives, how can it be attributed to the "Ideas," which are entirely invisible by nature? To clarify this doubt, upon which the foundation of this matter depends, it must be noted that there are two "sights": one corporal, the other incorporal. The first is what we commonly call the face or sight, which <term>Aristotle</term> says is loved by us above all other senses. The other is that power of the soul by which (as was said in the penultimate chapter of the first book) we have a kinship with the Angels. This power is called "sight" by the Platonists, and this corporal sight is nothing other than an image of it. <term>Aristotle</term> in his *Ethics* and in many other places says that the intellect has the same proportion to the soul as sight has to the body. Hence <term>Pallas</term> <note>Pallas Athena, goddess of wisdom.</note>, who signifies intellectual wisdom, is praised throughout <term>Homer</term> for the beauty of her eyes. With this sight, Moses saw, Paul saw, and many other elect saw the face of God; and this is what our theologians call intellectual cognition or intuitive cognition. With this sight, <term>John</term> the Evangelist says we are rightly destined to see the supreme God, and that this is our entire reward.

### That beauties properly understood are two: namely, corporal beauty and intelligible beauty.

### CHAPTER VIII.

**T**here being, therefore, beauty in visible things, and there being two sights (one corporal, the other incorporal), there will also be two visible objects and, consequently, two beauties. These are the two <term>Venuses</term> celebrated by <term>Plato</term> and by our Poet: namely, corporal and sensible beauty, called the "Vulgar Venus," and intelligible beauty which is in the <term>Ideas</term> <note>The perfect, eternal forms or archetypes of all things.</note>. This intelligible beauty, as we demonstrated above, is the object of the intellect just as colors are the object of physical sight, and it is called the "Celestial Venus." It follows that since <term>Love</term> is the appetite for beauty, and since there are two beauties, there must also necessarily be two Loves: Vulgar and Celestial. Just as the former desires vulgar and sensible beauty, the latter desires celestial and intelligible beauty. Therefore <term>Plato</term> said in the *Symposium* that as many Venuses as there are, there must necessarily be as many Loves.

### For what reason it is said that Venus, namely beauty, is the mother of Love.

### CHAPTER IX.

**T**hus, <term>Venus</term> is not a power of the soul, but beauty itself. Since <term>Love</term> is generated from beauty, beauty is deservedly called its mother. For beauty is the cause of Love, not as the productive principle of the act of loving, but as its object. According to the Platonists, the soul itself is the efficient cause of its own acts, while objects are like the "matter" concerning which the soul produces those acts. In this way, beauty becomes the "material cause" of Love and is said to be its mother, because philosophers compare the material cause to a mother, and the efficient cause to a father.

### Brief Epilogue of Venus, of love, and of the Ideas.

### CHAPTER X.

**V**enus, therefore, shall be that beauty which generates <term>Love</term>. The celestial and ideal beauty generates celestial love, which shall be defined thus: Celestial <term>Love</term> is the intellectual desire for ideal beauty. We explained above what desire is and what intellectual appetite is. The <term>Ideas</term> were discussed in the fifth chapter of the first book; to put it briefly, they are nothing other than the exemplary forms of the natures of things. Every intellect is full of them, and through them it understands. It is written in the *Book of Causes* <note>A significant medieval philosophical text often attributed to Aristotle but actually based on Proclus.</note> that every intelligence is full of forms. It was demonstrated in the final chapter of the first book that these forms are called <term>Ideas</term> in God himself, as in their source and principle; they exist essentially in the angelic mind, in which they are first produced by God; and finally, through participation, they exist in the rational soul. Just as the soul participates in the substance of the intellect, so it participates in these ideas and, consequently, in their beauty. From this we can conclude that the <term>Love</term> of the beauty of the soul is not yet perfectly "celestial love," but a perfect and close image of it. The first and truest love is found where there is an appetite for the ideal...
