...possesses beauty, which is necessarily in the first mind <note>The "Angelic Mind," which in Neoplatonism is the first created being, containing all the Platonic Ideas.</note>, which God, without any intermediary, clothes and adorns with the beauty of the Ideas.

-> ## On the birth of Love, and what is meant by the gardens of Jove, by Porus, and by Penia, and by the birth of Venus. <-

### CHAPTER XI.

<margin>Plato.</margin>
Plato says that Love was born in the gardens of Jove, at the birth of Venus, after Porus <note>Original: "Poro," meaning Plenty or Resourcefulness.</note> coupled with Penia <note>Original: "Penia," meaning Poverty or Want.</note>, and while all the Gods were gathered at a banquet; this Porus, the son of Counsel, was drunk with nectar. We must first presuppose that God himself is uncreated and the creator of all things. Next, we must understand that formless nature which, when formed by God, becomes the Angelic Mind, as was said above. The form that God gives to the Angelic Mind is nothing other than the Ideas themselves, which we call the primary beauty. These Ideas descend into the Angel from God; and because everything that moves away from its source and principle, mixing with a contrary nature, becomes more imperfect, these Ideas—as they move away from God, their source, and join with that formless nature which is entirely different and alien to their form—must necessarily become imperfect. 

Thus, the Angel then possesses the beauty of the Ideas within himself, but it is imperfect and darkened by the opacity of his own substance. Because of this, a desire to possess their perfection must necessarily follow within him. This desire, being a desire for beauty, is that very desire which we call Love. This Love would not be born if the Ideas were not in the Angel, or if they were already perfect there; for as we explained in the fourth chapter of this book, the thing desired is partly possessed and partly not. If the lover were entirely deprived of the beloved thing, there would be no similarity between them, and similarity is the cause of Love. 

<margin>Porus and Penia.</margin>
Therefore, this Love is born when **Porus** (which signifies abundance, that is, the affluence of these Ideas) mixes with that formless nature called **Penia**, which is poor and begging because it is deprived of all being and every act. Strictly speaking, Penia is not the essence of that formless nature itself, but rather its state of want and imperfection. In the eighth chapter of the first book, we explained that this formless nature is called Jove <margin>Jove.</margin>; it is called the **Gardens of Jove** because the Ideas are planted within it, just like trees in a garden. 

From this, it follows that the Angelic Mind, already adorned with these Ideas, was called **Paradise** by the ancients <margin>Paradise.</margin>—which is a Greek word meaning what we call a garden. Those who live entirely in the intellectual life, elevated above human nature and made similar to the angels, nourish themselves through contemplation and are said to be in Paradise. Toward this contemplative life and eternal happiness, <term>Zoroaster</term> <note>Ficino refers to the "Chaldean Oracles" attributed to Zoroaster, which were highly influential in Renaissance Neoplatonism.</note> exclaims: "Seek, seek paradise." This term was later adopted by our theologians to also signify a physical place—the highest heaven, which is the dwelling and home of blessed souls, whose bliss consists in that contemplation and in the perfection of the intellect, as Plato clearly states in the *Philebus* and the *Epinomis*. 

The Gardens of Jove are therefore that formless essence; and in it, from the mixture of the perfection of the Ideas (which is Porus) with their imperfection and the need for perfect being (which arises from the imperfect nature of that essence), Love was born—that is, the desire for perfection. Love was not born before the birth of Venus <margin>Venus.</margin>; that is, not before Ideal beauty, however imperfect, was born in the Angelic Mind. To say "at the birth of Venus" is the same as saying that Venus was then like an imperfect child in swaddling clothes, different from the adult who has reached a perfect age. 

And as for all the Gods being seated at the table: remember what was said in the sixth chapter of the first book—that everything, besides its natural being, has another being called "ideal," according to which it was produced by God in the first mind. Therefore, by **Saturn** <margin>Saturn.</margin> one can understand either the planet Saturn or the *Idea* of Saturn, and similarly for all the others. Here, by "Gods," we must understand the Ideas of all the Gods. In this, Plato follows the manner of speaking of the Pythagorean <term>Parmenides</term>, who always calls these Ideas "Gods." The Gods, then, are the Ideas, which precede Venus, because she is that beauty and grace resulting from the variety of those Ideas. It is said they were at a banquet and at the table because their father then fed them with ambrosia and nectar. 

To understand this, one must know that the ancient pagan theologians (as Hesiod writes and Aristotle confirms) say that all those things which God fed at his table with nectar and ambrosia are eternal; those that are not eternal were not at that banquet. Since the Ideas of the Angelic Mind are both primary and truly eternal, Plato intends for them to have been at that celestial banquet, where they were fed with ambrosia and nectar. He expressed this even more clearly by saying that **Porus** <margin>Porus.</margin> (the universal affluence of the Ideas) had become drunk with Nectar. And although the Ideas of other [mortal] things were there, he does not say they were accepted at the banquet, because the gift of immortality was not granted to them. I believe it has been sufficiently explained how Love was born in the gardens of Jove, from the union of Porus and Penia, at the birth of Venus, at the banquet where the Gods were seated and eating.

-> ## For what reason Love is placed by Orpheus in the bosom of Chaos. <-

### CHAPTER XII.

<margin>Orpheus.</margin>
From the things explained above, it is clear why **Orpheus** places Love in the bosom of Chaos before all the other Gods. Chaos <margin>Chaos.</margin> signifies nothing other than matter full of all forms, but confused and imperfect. When the Angelic Mind was already full of all the Ideas, but they were still imperfect and almost indistinct and confused, it could be called Chaos; and in that Chaos, Love was born—that is, the desire for their perfection.

-> ## To which natures, and for what reason, the name of the "Circle" belongs. <-

### CHAPTER XIII.

That Angel, therefore, desires to make those Ideas perfect. It is reasonable that their perfection arises from a cause opposite to that which caused their imperfection. Imperfection came from two causes: one is moving away from the source and principle, and the other is joining with a dissimilar and contrary nature. Therefore, their perfection will arise both from removing and separating themselves from that dissimilar nature, and by returning to where they first proceeded—to their Principle—reuniting themselves as entirely as possible. 

Thus Love—the desire to acquire this beauty—perfectly moves and stimulates the Angelic Mind to turn toward God and to join with Him as much as it can. Each thing acquires its perfection insofar as it joins with its Principle. This is the first **Circle** <margin>Circle.</margin>: the Angelic Mind, proceeding from the indivisible unity of God and, through the circular motion of its internal intelligence, returning perfectly to Him. Every nature capable of doing this is called a "circle," because a circular figure returns to the same point from which it first began. This property is found in only two natures: the Angelic and the Rational [human]. For this very reason, only these two natures are capable of happiness; for happiness is nothing other than reaching one’s supreme good and final end—and that same final end of every thing is its first principle. Therefore, those natures that can [return] to the...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Angelic Mind" and the "Rational Soul" as they relate to the concept of the "Circle." Ficino is explaining how spiritual beings return to their divine source, a process that defines their perfection and happiness, unlike material things which cannot "reflect" back to their origin.</meta>

BOOK TWO

...to return to its first principle, they can still achieve happiness; and such are only the immortal substances, because corporeal and material nature does not have—as all Peripatetic <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note> and Platonic philosophers concede—this power that they call reflexive, by means of which they might revolve either within themselves or back to their principle. Therefore, they proceed only from their cause and participate in that good which is communicated to them by their cause. Since they cannot reunite this good to its principle, it cannot achieve absolute perfection; rather, their good always remains imperfect, and thus they do not possess happiness, or they have it so imperfectly that it cannot properly be called happiness. There being, then, only two natures—namely the angelic and the rational—that can return to their principle, only these two can be called circles, and they should be called intelligible circles because they are immaterial. Similarly, among bodies, according to our theologians, there are two circles that are the image and likeness of those: namely, the tenth heaven <note>The Empyrean or the highest, unmoving part of the physical universe in medieval cosmology.</note>, which is a corporeal and immobile circle, an image of the intelligible circle which is the angelic mind; the other circle is the moving celestial body, an image of the circle which is the rational soul. Of the first, the Platonists make no mention, and they would perhaps say that since the angelic nature is entirely separate and diverse from corporeal nature, having no respect or relation to it, it is not represented by any corporeal thing. Of the second, Plato in the *Timaeus* makes express mention, showing how all the circles of the moving celestial body—which is divided, according to him, into the non-erratic sphere <note>The sphere of the fixed stars.</note> and the seven planets—are likenesses of as many immaterial circles that are in the rational soul. 

Some attribute to God himself the name of the "circle," and it seems to be an opinion of the ancient gentile theologians who call him "Heaven," as if he were a sphere containing all things within himself, just as the last Heaven contains all corporeal things. Nor is it inappropriate for the name of the circle to be proper to him according to one reason, and repugnant to him according to another. Understanding then, as we explained above, a circle to be a nature that, starting from an indivisible point, returns to the same, it is entirely repugnant to God himself, who in this way is not a circle because he does not have a beginning from elsewhere, but is himself that indivisible point from which all circles begin and to which they return. So, as far as this property is concerned, the "circle" is repugnant to God, because he has neither beginning nor end. It is also repugnant to material things because, although they begin from a principle, they cannot return to it; thus, it remains that the circle is proper to the mind and the soul. 

According to many other properties, it suits God: first, because it is the most perfect figure of all others, as God is of all things; and only to this figure of the circle can nothing be added, which demonstrates it to be absolutely perfect. Beyond this, there is another reason which I believe to be most powerful, and this is that the last sphere is the "place" of every located thing. The Platonists subtly prove this of God himself, declaring—as Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> does among others—that the soul is not in the body, as it seems to the common people (which Plato also notes in the *Timaeus*), but on the contrary, the body is in the soul; and for the same reason, the soul is in the angelic mind, and the angelic mind is in God, the ultimate place of all places. This can be understood in the mysteries of the Hebrews, who among the most sacred names of God place this one: namely, "Place" <note>Original: "Luogo." This refers to the Hebrew name *Ha-Maqom*, meaning "The Place," implying God's omnipresence.</note>, and it is thus called many times in the sacred scriptures. For this reason then—to sufficiently declare which would require more words, but would be outside our purpose—and for the aforementioned reasons, God is called a circle. This was deservedly observed in the theology of the Ismaelites <note>Original: "Smaeliti," likely referring to an esoteric tradition Ficino associated with ancient Near Eastern wisdom.</note> by Parmenides <note>A Greek philosopher; Ficino is interpreting Parmenides's "Being" as a sphere.</note>—no, although many believe it, we will prove elsewhere that what he calls the "intelligible sphere" is not God himself but the intelligible world produced immediately by God.

### *Brief summary of the birth of Love.*

### CHAPTER XIV.

**S**ummarizing briefly, then, I say that at the birth of Venus—that is, when the beauty of the Ideas first descended into the angelic mind—this mind being newly born (that is, not yet mature, which is to say that beauty was still imperfect), Love was born. That is, there was born in the angel a desire to possess that beauty perfectly, which it already possessed in some way; and stimulated by this love, it turned toward God and received from him the perfection of that ideal beauty. Once it held that beauty perfectly within itself, it was then the mature Venus, having reached her perfection.

### On the three Graces who follow Venus, and their names.

### CHAPTER XV.

**T**he poets say that this Venus has as her followers, and almost as handmaidens, the Graces, whose names in the common tongue sound as Viridity, Joy, and Splendor. These three Graces are nothing other than three properties resulting from that ideal beauty. First, to be "green" <note>Original: "Viridità," meaning greenness or vitality.</note> is nothing other than for a thing to remain and endure in its being, whole and without any decay. Nor is youth called "green" for any other reason than because man is then in his whole and perfect being, from which vigor and integrity he later loses more and more with the years until he is entirely nullified. Since every composite thing lasts in its being as long as that due proportion lasts which unites its parts into a unity, and since Venus is nothing other than this proportion, deservedly this Viridity is nothing other than a property resulting from Venus. Therefore, where the first and true Venus is—that is, in the ideal world—there is also found true viridity, because every intelligible nature is unchangeable in the integrity of its being and entirely insensible <note>Immune to the decay of the physical senses.</note>. This property derives to sensible things insofar as they can participate in Venus, because as long as that proportion lasts in them, they last and maintain themselves "green." The other two properties of ideal beauty are to illuminate the intellect and to move the will to desire it, filling the will when it is possessed with ineffable joy. And because being, that durability and permanence, is not a reflexive act, one of the Graces is painted with her face toward us, as proceeding and not returning. The other two, because they belong to the intellect and the will—the operation of which is reflexive—are painted with their faces turned away, as if returning; for things are said to come to us from the Gods, and from us to the Gods to return.

### On the birth of Venus described by poets under a fabled veil.

### CHAPTER XVI.

**P**lato saying that Love was born at the birth of Venus, it is necessary at this point to understand how Venus herself was born. Plato in the *Symposium* says nothing other than that she was the daughter of Coelus <note>Uranus.</note>. The ancient gentile theologians declare the manner in which she was born from him under a fabled veil, saying that Saturn castrated Coelus, his father, and threw the testicles into the sea, and that from their seed Venus was born. For the declaration of this mystery, it must first be presupposed that matter—that is, that formless nature of which we have said every creature is composed—is many times signified by theologians as water, because water is in continuous flux and easily receptive to every form. It would be long if I wished to bring forth all the passages from the sacred scriptures of Moses and the Gospels...

It also begins an allegorical explanation of the birth of Venus from the castration of Coelus, representing the descent of divine form into matter.</summary>

SECOND [BOOK]

<margin>❦</margin> Regarding the sacred scriptures of the Gentiles <note>The author refers to the works of Platonic and Hermetic philosophers as "sacred letters of the Gentiles."</note>, where this unformed nature is signified by water, I wish only to add this: because this unformed nature is found first in the Angel—as the first creature—the Angels are signified by the name of "waters." Nothing else is to be understood by the "waters that are above the heavens" (of which David says they continually praise God) than these very Angelic minds. Origen Adamantius <note>A prominent early Christian theologian (c. 184–253 AD); "Adamantius" was a nickname meaning "man of steel."</note> agrees that this is so. Furthermore, there are some among the Platonists who claim that the Ocean, called by Homer the "father of gods and men," is nothing other than that Angelic mind, which we declared above to be the principle and source of every other creature found after it. For this reason, George Gemistus <note>George Gemistus Pletho (c. 1355–1452), a Byzantine scholar who was instrumental in the revival of Greek learning in Renaissance Italy.</note>, a most esteemed Platonist, calls this first mind "Neptune," as the ruler of all waters—that is, of all other minds, both Angelic and human. These are those waters; this is that living fountain from which he who drinks shall never thirst again. These are the waters and seas upon which, as David says, God has founded the universal world.

## Exposition of the Fable of Saturn.
### CHAPTER XVII.

**A**fter this knowledge, one must learn the reason why the poets say that Saturn castrated his father Caelus. It was declared in the first part of the present work how the God who is called Caelus <note>Latin for "Sky" or "Heaven," corresponding to the Greek Uranus.</note>, according to the Platonists, produced the first Angel, whom they call the Divine Mind and the poets call Saturn. It was also declared that this God produced no other creature but this one, from which the rest of the world was then produced. If, therefore, one who remains sterile and can no longer generate can deservedly be called castrated, then—since the first Angelic mind was created to have communicated to it all that can be communicated by the first God, and so thoroughly communicated that He remains no longer productive of any other thing—it is not without great reason that the poets say Saturn castrated Caelus, his father.

Saturn, then, castrates Caelus, but Jupiter does not castrate Saturn; rather, he deprives him of his kingdom. This is because once that Mind has produced the Soul of the World (which is Jupiter), it does not remain sterile as Caelus did after producing Saturn. Instead, it produces after that all the heavens, the elements, and rational souls. But because the administration of these worldly things is carried out by means of the heavens and the rational soul—which move inferior things together—and since (as we declared above) the World Soul is the principle of all motion and that Mind is entirely immobile, the poets say Saturn is "bound," as one who does not move. The empire and administration of the world is said to belong to Jupiter. However, Jupiter would not govern the world well if he were not helped by the counsels of his old father; that is, the Soul would not move the Heaven in an orderly way, nor rightly dispose other things, if it did not participate in the paternal, intellectual wisdom. This is fully declared by Plato in the *Laws* <note>Plato’s final and longest dialogue, discussing the nature of law and the cosmos.</note> to anyone who reads them with a sound mind; for his words in that place, poorly understood by some Platonists or by all the Manichaeans <note>Followers of a dualistic religion that saw a struggle between a good spiritual world of light and an evil material world of darkness.</note>, were the cause of great errors.

It is therefore manifest why Saturn castrates Caelus, and Jupiter binds Saturn and takes his empire. Following the exposition we have brought forward, we must say that everything Caelus communicates to Saturn—that is, the fullness of the Ideas <note>In Platonic thought, "Ideas" or "Forms" are the eternal, perfect patterns of all things.</note> which descends from God into the Mind—are the "testicles" of Caelus. Once these are separated from him, he remains sterile and is no longer generative. These testicles fall into the sea—that is, into the unformed Angelic nature—where, as soon as they are joined with it, Venus is born. Venus, as has been said, is that beauty, that ornament, and that grace resulting from the variety of those Ideas. Because those Ideas would not have that variety and distinction in themselves if they were not mixed with that unformed nature, and since without that variety there can be no beauty, it follows deservedly that Venus could not be born except by the falling of Caelus's testicles into the maritime waters.

## Concerning Porus, and Why He Is Called the Son of Counsel.
### CHAPTER XVIII.

**I**t remains to declare for what reason Porus <note>Greek: *Poros*, meaning "Resource" or "Plenty."</note> is called the son of Counsel. Since Porus is the abundance of those Ideas proceeding from the true God, he is called the son of Counsel by Plato, who was an imitator of the sacred letters of the Hebrews. In those letters, God Himself is called by the same name, which is why Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A Christian theologian and philosopher of the late 5th to early 6th century, often conflated with a convert of St. Paul.</note> says Jesus Christ is called the "Angel of Counsel"—meaning the messenger of God—understanding "Counsel" to be none other than the first Father, God. Imitating this, Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath and influential philosopher in the Islamic Golden Age.</note> called the First Cause the "Counseling Cause." This is to demonstrate that the Mind does not have the Ideas and the reason of things from itself, but from God; for counseling someone is nothing other than giving them the knowledge and the reason for what they must do. Having produced the Mind, which was to be the fabricator of this visible world, God "counseled" it—that is, He taught and instructed it in the work it had to do, forming that Mind with the most perfect Idea of this worldly artifice.

## In What Way One Must Understand Love to Be Both the Youngest and Oldest of All the Gods.
### CHAPTER XIX.

**H**aving explained the words about the birth of Love spoken by Diotima <note>The female philosopher in Plato's *Symposium* who teaches Socrates about Love.</note>, and demonstrated that the words of Orpheus (who says Love was born in the womb of Chaos before all other gods) conform to the meaning of Plato, it remains to demonstrate how this does not contradict what Agathon says: namely, that Love is younger than all the other gods. This seems to clearly contradict Orpheus, who says Love is more ancient than all the others.

For the understanding of the true solution, one must remember what was said above: just as a house has two "beings"—one in its Idea in the mind of the architect, and the other in the matter, such as stones, wood, and similar things—and the first is called "Ideal being" and the second "natural being," so it is with all other things which have their Ideal being in that first Mind and their natural being outside of it. Jupiter, Saturn, and all the other gods can therefore be signified either by the Idea of Saturn or Jupiter, or by the "natural" Saturn and Jupiter (not the Ideal).

I say, then, that the first god in his natural and perfect being was Love; and before him, there was no other god who had a natural being—that is, a perfect being. He was the cause of giving this to all the other gods. That this is so is manifest from what was said above, because Love was born when the Ideas descended into the Angelic mind. Since these Ideas are the substance of that Mind, the substance of that Mind was not perfect until they were perfect, which did not happen until after Love was born. If, then, that Angelic mind did not have a perfect natural being before Love was born, Love was the cause of giving it to him, insofar as those Ideas were made perfect through the conversion <note>The Platonic concept of *conversio*, where a created being turns back toward its source to achieve completion.</note> performed by Love toward God. This can be said much more strongly of the other gods who are posterior to that Mind; that is, Love existed before they had their perfect natural being, despite the fact that they existed before him according to their imperfect Ideal being. For this reason, Love comes to be both younger than all the others and most beautiful, because those Ideas were immediately joined to that unformed nature, and he was not born in it until after it was formed by the Ideas, however imperfectly.

## *How it is understood that the kingdom of necessity*
## *existed before love.*

### *CHAPTER XX.*

**F**rom the same foundation, one can easily understand what Agathon <note>A tragic poet appearing in Plato's *Symposium*; his speech praises Love as young and beautiful, contrasting with older views.</note> says: that the kingdom of necessity existed before the kingdom of love. To understand this, one must know that Plato, in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s famous dialogue regarding the creation of the universe.</note>, calls that unformed nature "necessity." Although elsewhere he uses "necessity" to mean fate itself, in this context he means necessity in the first sense—that is, as unformed nature. It must be known that every creature is composed of two natures: one is material and the other formal; one is imperfect and the other the cause of perfection. Whenever one of them participates more in the nature of the other, it is said to be subject to that one, and the other is said to predominate over it. For these reasons, because in lower creatures there is more of the imperfect part than the perfect, matter is said to predominate in them. When, therefore, the Ideas were still imperfect and disordered—because that unformed and material nature is the cause of all imperfection—theologians say that "necessity" then reigned. Every imperfection found in a creature proceeds from that unformed nature. For this reason, Agathon says that all things said of the Ideas that denote some imperfection occurred while necessity reigned, just as all perfections followed once love began to reign; for when the mind was turned toward God through love, that which was previously imperfect became perfect within it.

## *For what reason Venus is said to command the*
## *three Fates.*

### *CHAPTER XXI.*

**I**t will not be out of place, then, to explain why Orpheus says Venus commands all three Fates <note>The *Parcae* in Latin mythology: Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos, who spin, measure, and cut the thread of life.</note>, which will be made manifest through the foundations declared above. As we have said at other times, the Platonists posit two worlds: this sensible world and another intelligible world which is the exemplar of this one. In this world, we see a very great order, with everything chained together and depending on one another in a friendly concurrence to form a single whole. This order, this series of causes and effects, is called "Fate" by philosophers. Since these worldly things are images of those Ideas in the intelligible world and depend upon them, being subject to them, it follows that the order of the former depends on the order of the latter. That higher order is called "Providence," just as this lower one is called "Fate." Therefore, the Platonists place Providence—which consists in the order of the Ideas—in that first Mind. This Providence, or order, depends on God Himself as the ultimate end of this order. Nor does the law of Providence, which orders things toward their end, direct them anywhere else but toward attaining that ultimate and infinite Good. If, then, Venus is nothing other than the order of those Ideas upon which the worldly order called Fate depends, it follows that Venus dominates Fate. This Fate is divided into three parts and designated by the names of the three Fates: Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos. This is because what is united in Providence and measured by the indivisible measure of eternity, once turned into temporal Fate, is divided into three parts: namely, present, past, and future. However, it can also be divided differently according to the three kingdoms divided among the sons of Saturn, as was declared by us in the first book. Others wish for Atropos to be attributed to the fixed stars, Clotho to the seven planets, and Lachesis to the things below the moon; but treating this matter requires its own specific place. From this, it can be understood that only temporal things are subject to Fate, and these are things that are corporeal. Therefore, the rational <gloss>soul</gloss> being incorporeal is not subject to Fate; rather, it dominates it. But it is certainly subject to Providence and serves it. This service is true liberty, because if our will obeys the law of Providence, it is guided most wisely toward the execution of its desired end. Whenever it wishes to free itself from this servitude, it truly makes itself a servant instead of being free, and makes itself a slave to Fate, of which it was previously the master. For to deviate from the law of Providence is nothing other than to leave reason and follow the senses and irrational appetite, which is subject to Fate by being corporeal in nature. Therefore, whoever submits to appetite makes himself a servant to that which is itself a servant. But of this, we shall speak another time.

## *Of Angelic and Human Love, and of their*
## *objects.*

### *CHAPTER XXII.*

**I** believe enough has been said of this celestial Love and of Venus its mother. It is true that if I wished to pursue all the questions that could be moved concerning the perfect knowledge of the Ideas in this place, a longer treatise would be needed; but here it would be superfluous, and it is our intention to speak of it copiously elsewhere. Leaving this matter for another time, and having dispatched what was to be understood of celestial and angelic Love, we will move on to declare the nature of that Love which is properly an image of this one. Just as the Ideas descend from heaven—that is, from God—into the angelic mind, and because of this, the Love of intellectual beauty is born in it, so the same Ideas descend from the angelic mind into the rational soul. These are as much more imperfect than those in the angelic mind as the soul and rational nature are more imperfect than the Angel and the intellectual nature; thus they change either nature or name, as was declared in the first book. That same thing which was said of Saturn in respect to Caelus <note>The Greek Uranus (Sky), father of Saturn (Cronus/Mind).</note> is also true of Jove <note>Jupiter, representing the Soul of the World or the Rational Soul.</note> in respect to Saturn. And note that Plotinus <note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 204–270 AD).</note>, in his book on Love, does not speak of the first celestial Love, but only of this one; and similarly, he does not speak of that first Venus, but of this second one—that is, not of the beauty of the Ideas descending from Caelus into Saturn, but of that which descends from Saturn into Jove, which is the soul of the world. He clearly declares this, because that celestial Venus of whom he speaks is not said to be born of Caelus, as Plato says, but of Saturn. Anyone who does not pay diligent attention to this would judge Plato and Plotinus to be in disagreement, whereas anyone who observes them correctly knows that total and absolute knowledge of celestial Love is had from both together: for Plato treats that which is the first and true celestial Love, and Plotinus treats the second, which is its image. Venus, therefore, the mother of this love, is born of Saturn and unites with Jove, just as that first one is born of Caelus and unites with Saturn. For the same reason that Plotinus maintains that the Ideas (which are the first Venus) are not accidental but substantial to the angelic mind, he also maintains that these specific "reasons" <note>The "logoi" or formative principles that exist within the soul.</note> which are in the soul, just as Ideas are in the Mind, are substantial to the soul. For this reason, Plotinus will sometimes say that the celestial Venus is that first rational and divine soul. And so as not to give anyone cause for error who might be moved by these words to believe that the nature of the soul—insofar as it is the nature of a rational spirit—is Venus, he adds below that this soul is called Venus insofar as there is within it a certain splendid and beautiful love, designating by this those specific "reasons" of which we have spoken. Returning to this, I say that just as that first love which is in the mind is called angelic and divine, so this other one which is in the rational soul is called human love, because rational nature is the principal part of the nature of man.

# On vulgar love, and on sensible beauty, which is its object.
## CHAPTER XXIII.

**H**aving now dispatched what is necessary concerning celestial love and its image, we shall pass on to treat of vulgar love <note>original: "amore uolgare"; referring to common or earthly love, as opposed to divine or "celestial" love.</note>, which is nothing other than the appetite for sensible beauty <note>Beauty that can be perceived through the physical senses, particularly sight.</note> through the sense of sight, as may be clear from the things said above. This beauty—just like intelligible beauty <note>Beauty perceived by the mind or intellect, consisting of divine ideas.</note> and like every nature universally—has three modes of being: namely, Causal, Essential, and truly Formal and Participated. Its cause is the sensible Heaven animated by that power which moves it, just as the cause of beauty and the Intelligible Venus <note>In Platonic thought, "Intelligible Venus" represents the divine beauty found in the cosmic intellect.</note> was that first and true intelligible God. This motive power of the Heaven is the lowest power of the celestial soul, according to which power it is joined to the body of the heaven, just as our own motive and progressive power is joined to muscles and nerves, which it uses as instruments and organs to execute its operation, which is motion; so the motive power of the soul of the heaven finds a body and organ suited to the circular and everlasting celestial motion, just as feet are suited to the motion of walking in animals. By means of this body of the heaven, it transmutes this lower matter and forms it into all the forms that are within it, no differently than the hand of the craftsman, by means of the brush, forms his material into this or that artificial shape. The cause, then, of this Vulgar Venus <note>The goddess representing physical, earthly attraction and the beauty of material forms.</note>, which is the beauty of these sensible material forms, is that motive power of the celestial soul, and in that, this Venus has her causal being. Her formal and essential being is in those colors illuminated by the light of the visible sun, just as the Ideas are illuminated by the light of that first invisible sun. Her participated being is in the quantitative disposition of the beautiful thing—that is, in its figure, which consists of a certain order of parts; and this can be called beauty by participation because, as was declared above, beauty is the moving object of sight. And since this quantity is not suited to move the sight except insofar as it participates in colors and light, it deservedly does not have the quality of being beauty and the procreator of love by the benefit of its own nature, but by participation and the merit of others, which of themselves and by their own nature are suited to move the sight and generate Love for the thing seen in the soul of the viewer.

# Following on celestial, human, and bestial Love.
## CHAPTER XXIIII.

**V**ulgar love, then, is nothing other than the desire to possess such beauty. And just as soon as intelligible beauty (which are the Ideas) descended into the Angelic intellect, there was born in the will of the Angel a desire to possess 그 beauty, and to achieve this it strove to draw near to Him from whom such beauty had come to it; so, as soon as the species <note>A philosophical term for the mental image or "form" of an object perceived by the senses.</note> and the image of this sensible beauty reaches the eye, there is immediately born in the sensitive appetite—which, as we declared above, follows the knowledge of the sense, just as the will follows the knowledge of the intellect—there is born, I say, a desire to fully enjoy that beauty. From here, two loves can be born: one is bestial, and the other is human and rational. For there is no doubt that, in seeking to fully serve this beauty, one must unite with that which is its principle and source, and from which it first proceeds. And if we follow the judgment of the sense—which the brutes and irrational animals follow—we will judge the source of this beauty to be in that material body in which we see it placed; and from this will be born in us the appetite for coitus, which is nothing other than joining with that body in the most intimate way possible. To dwell longer upon this matter would be to profane the chaste love-mysteries of Plato. But returning to our purpose, I say that the sense judges that beauty to have its origin in that body, and therefore the end of the Love of all brutes is coitus. But reason, by an opposite judgment, knows that material body not only not to be the source and principle of beauty, but to be a nature entirely different and corruptive of it; and it knows that the more it is separated from that body and considered in itself, the more it possesses of its own nature and proper dignity and presence. Therefore, one certainly must not pass from that species received in the eyes to the body itself, but must purify this species as much as possible if one sees any infection of a corporeal and material nature remaining in it. And because "man" can be understood as the rational soul placed in its perfect nature, and can also be understood as the rational soul already united and bound to the body: according to the first way, Human Love is properly that which was said above to be the image of Celestial Love. According to this other way, Human Love is that of which we speak—that is, Love of sensible beauty, which is already separated from the body by the soul and made intellectual, as much as its nature allows. Many are those who do not ascend any higher, and this is the case for the majority of men. Some more perfect ones, remembering a more perfect beauty which their soul once saw before it was immersed in the body, are then kindled with an incredible desire to see it again. To achieve this intent, they separate themselves as much as they can from the body, so that the soul returns to its pristine dignity, made entirely the master of the body and in no way subject to it; and then the soul is in that love which is the image of celestial love. This can be called the love of a perfect human nature, and that other the Love of a falling or almost imperfect human nature. From this Love, if one then goes on growing from perfection to perfection, man reaches such a degree that, uniting his soul entirely with the intellect, he is turned from a man into an Angel. Being all inflamed by that angelic Love—like an earth kindled by fire and converted into flame, rising to the highest part from the lower world—so he, purged of all the filth and stains of the earthly body, and transformed into a spiritual flame by the power of love, flying even unto the intelligible heaven, rests happily in the arms of the first father.

# In which souls vulgar love is found, and in which angelic, and why celestial souls are signified by Janus.
## CHAPTER XXV.

**B**y what we have said of Vulgar Love, it follows necessarily that this vulgar love can only fall into those souls which are immersed in matter, or in some way overcome by the body, or at least hindered, and finally in those souls that are not free from the disturbances of the affections but are subjected to passions; which, according to the Platonists, are both our souls and those of demons—either all of them, as some wish, or the lower ones closer to our nature. In other souls, such as our own [higher parts], it is necessary that that angelic Love be found eternally, just as the intellect of our soul is eternal; nevertheless, few men use it, as their memory has almost turned its back to the intellect, turning its eyes and converting them to sensible things and the care of the body. For a full understanding of this passage, it is to be understood that the celestial souls have in themselves such perfection (as all the Platonists say) that they can satisfy both of their duties together: that is, both to rule and administer their body, and by this not to be severed from the intellectual contemplation of higher things. These souls were signified by many Poets as Janus with two faces <note>original: "Iano bifronte"; the Roman god of beginnings and transitions, usually depicted with two faces looking in opposite directions.</note>, because, like him, being eyed on the front and back parts, they can see intelligible things and provide for sensible things at the same time. But other, more imperfect souls, which do not have eyes except in one part of them, must necessarily turn themselves with that part by which they see toward the body, so that the other part, which is without eyes, remains turned toward the intellect, and thus they remain deprived of the vision of...

<summary>This page defines Vulgar Love as the desire for physical beauty perceived through the senses, distinguishing it from Celestial Love. It describes the soul's journey from bestial desire to rational human love, using the metaphor of Janus to explain how celestial souls can look toward both divine and material realms simultaneously.</summary>

It introduces the "two-faced" nature of the soul and concludes with the opening of Girolamo Benivieni’s poem, which this entire treatise serves to explain.</meta>

...of intellectual things. Similarly, if they turn their eyes toward the intellect, they can no longer provide for the body, and it is necessary that they leave the care of it. For these reasons, divine providence has bound these souls—who are forced by the care of the body to leave the goodness of the intellect—to fleeting and corruptible bodies. Once released from these, they may in a short time (if they do not fail on their part) return to their intellectual happiness. Those other souls who are not hindered by the care of the body from the goodness of the intellect, providence has bound to eternal and incorruptible bodies. From this foundation, you can draw the solution to an argument by Aristotle in the first book of *On the Soul*, where he says that if being in the body is an evil for the soul, as Plato often says, it follows that celestial souls would be more unhappy than ours, which are sometimes separated from the body. 

And you can draw another foundation: that if we assume all demons <note>In the Platonic sense, "demons" or "daemons" are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily evil beings.</note> are subject to passion, we must assume they are all mortal. Therefore, the definition of Apuleius—that is, that Demons are of a passible <term>passible: capable of feeling emotion or suffering</term> soul but eternal—must be understood to mean they are eternal because their souls are eternal, but not that the separation of the soul from the body does not occur in them, just as it also occurs in us. 

Returning then to our purpose, I say that celestial souls (which are depicted by poets as Janus <note>Janus is the Roman god of beginnings, gates, and transitions, usually depicted with two faces looking in opposite directions.</note>, since they are the beginning of time through their motion) have two eyes to look upon that Ideal beauty in the intellect which they love continually. They have other eyes to look at inferior and sensible things, not to love or desire their beauty, but to communicate beauty to them and make them participants in it. 

Our souls, before they are bound to the body, are in the same way like Janus: that is, they have two faces. This is because, as Plato says in the *Phaedrus*, every soul—meaning every rational soul established in its nature—has care of the whole corporal universe. Thus, our souls finally have two faces before they fall into this earthly body, meaning they can simultaneously gaze at intellectual things and provide for sensible ones. But when they descend into the body, it happens to them just as if they were divided in half, and of the two faces, only one remained. Because of this, whenever they turn that one remaining face toward sensible beauty, they are deprived of the vision of the other. 

From this, it arises that no one can possess both vulgar love and celestial love at the same time. Therefore Zoroaster, encouraging us toward the vision of that supernal beauty, exclaims: "Raise your eyes and direct them upward." Of this, there is good testimony: many, for the same cause that snatched them away to the vision of intellectual beauty, have been blinded in their physical eyes with which one sees sensible beauty. This is signified by the fable of Tiresias <note>A famous blind prophet of Apollo in Thebes, known for being transformed into a woman and for his longevity.</note> sung by Callimachus. Tiresias, for having seen Pallas naked <note>original: "Pallade nuda"; Pallas refers to the goddess Athena. In this context, her nakedness represents pure, unmediated wisdom.</note>—which signifies nothing other than that Ideal beauty from which all pure wisdom proceeds, unclouded or covered by matter—immediately became blind. By that same Pallas, he was made a prophet, so that she who closed his physical eyes opened the eyes of his intellect, with which he could see future things no less than present ones. 

Homer, by the shadow of Achilles—from whom he was inspired by that poetic fury which contains within itself every intellectual contemplation—was also blinded in his physical eyes. Paul the Apostle was not caught up to the third heaven <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 12:2, where Paul describes being caught up to the "third heaven" or Paradise.</note> before his eyes were made blind to sensible things by the vision of divine things; perhaps we shall speak of his rapture another time. 

But returning to the main matter: I say that while our soul is turned toward sensible things, it cannot enjoy the vision of intellectual beauty. Therefore, although that celestial love lives eternally within the intellect of every soul, nonetheless only those few use it who, entirely removed from the care of the body, can say with Paul that they do not know if they are in the body or out of it. A man sometimes reaches this state, but stays there only briefly; these we call the Ecstatics <note>original: "Estatici"; referring to those in a state of religious or philosophical trance.</note>. Regarding the cause of this separation, there would be many things to say, which we shall discuss extensively in our commentary on Plato’s *Symposium* <note>original: "conuiuio"</note>, for I have not yet read anyone else who has written on it sufficiently.

# How there can be many loves in us.
## CHAPTER XXVI.

There will be, therefore, one eternal and substantial love in us—that which is in the intellect, which is Angelic and not human. Then, in our soul (which is by nature free and can turn either to sensible beauty or intelligible beauty), three loves can be born. 

1.  **Bestial Love:** If the soul loves sensible beauty and desires to be united to it corporally. This desire proceeds from irrational judgment—that is, judging that beauty originates from the body where it is placed—and is called bestial and irrational love.
2.  **Human or Rational Love:** If the soul desires to be united to beauty with the mind—that is, by preserving within itself the species <note>The mental image or essence of a thing.</note> and image of that beauty, and uniting it to itself through continuous thoughts and fixed intention. This love is called human or rational because it arises from rational judgment, knowing that beauty does not have its origin in that material body, but rather loses its perfection and dignity by being mixed with it, and recovers it when it is separated from that matter by the power of the soul. Most men revolve around these two loves.
3.  **Angelic Love:** But those whose intellect is purified and illuminated by philosophical study know this sensible beauty to be the image of another more perfect beauty. Leaving the love of the former, they begin to desire to see that celestial beauty. This is that third love which already tastes a part of that celestial beauty through memory. 

If they persevere in such elevation of mind, they finally attain that angelic and intellectual love which, although it was in them before, they did not notice because they were occupied with other things. Of these people, it can rightfully be said that "the light shone in the darkness and they did not comprehend it" <note>A quote from the Gospel of John 1:5.</note>. 

We shall speak largely of this act in the exposition of the final stanza of the present song <note>original: "canzona"</note>, to the narration of which we shall pass, provided we first remind the reader that some light on the fable of Aristophanes found in Plato’s *Symposium* can be found in what we said in the second chapter of this treatise. And since our Poet does not touch upon anything pertaining to it, it is not our duty to interpret it at present.

->The Song Follows.<-

### LOVE SONG COMPOSED
#### by Girolamo Benivieni, Florentine Citizen, according to the mind and opinion of the Platonists.

#### Stanza I.

> Love, from whose hands the suspended rein
> Hangs from my heart, and in whose sacred kingdom
> To be nourished, he did not disdain.
> The flame that was once lit in it by him
> Moves my tongue, forces my wit
> To speak of him, that which the burning breast
> Encloses; but the heart fails
> And the tongue recoils from such a great task.
> Nor can what is in me speak or make defense.
> And yet it is fitting that I express my concept;
> Force against a greater force does not prevail.
> But because to my sluggish wit, Love has promised
> Those wings with which he first descended
> Into my heart, though I believe his feathers
> Are at the summit, never to depart.

### PARTICULAR COMMENTARY.
### THIRD AND FINAL BOOK of the same Count Giovanni Pico della Mirandola regarding the particular exposition of the subject Song by Girolamo Benivieni.

### To which sciences it belongs to treat both celestial and vulgar love.

### CHAPTER I.

Treating the one and the other love belongs to different sciences. Regarding **vulgar love** <note>Also known as "earthly" or "sensual" love, directed toward physical beauty.</note>, the natural philosopher and the moral philosopher treat it. Regarding **divine love**, the theologian treats it, and if one wishes to speak in the manner of the **Peripatetics** <note>original: "paripathetici"; followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy.</note>, the Metaphysician treats it. Solomon speaks excellently of both; of the vulgar in **Ecclesiastes** as a natural philosopher, and in **Proverbs** as a moral one; of the divine and celestial in his **Song of Songs**, and therefore they say that among all the songs of the sacred scripture, this is the most sacred and most divine. Of these two loves, two poets have treated specifically in the Tuscan language. Regarding vulgar love, **Guido Cavalcanti** <note>A famous Florentine poet and friend of Dante Alighieri.</note> in one of his songs. Regarding the other—that is, the celestial—our Poet [Benivieni] in the present work, in which although he treats both, he nevertheless primarily treats the celestial, and speaks of the other only insofar as it is a weak image of that one.

### Of the differences that appear to be between the Author of the present Song and Guido Cavalcanti.

### CHAPTER II.

*Love from whose hands the Reins are suspended*, and after many verses he adds, *it moves my tongue and forces my intellect*. This is the beginning of the present Song by our Poet. The other composed by Guido begins, *A Lady begs me because I wish to say*, and by his expositors it is said that by that "Lady," love is understood. In these beginnings, I note three differences between the two poets. The first is that Guido says that love *begs* him, and our Poet says that love *forces* him. The second is that here love is called by its own proper name, which Guido did not wish to do. The third is that the former depicts it as a Lady, and this one does not, but uses the customary name of Love, which sounds like a male name. These differences arise neither from error by either of them, nor from discordant opinions, but both speak appropriately according to the nature of the love that is the subject of their poem. I said in the preceding chapter that Guido treated vulgar love, and our Poet, the celestial. The rational soul should not be subject to vulgar love, but rather should dominate it, because it is located in the inferior sensory appetite and is subject to the rational part of the soul; therefore, speaking of it, Guido says that *Love begs him* and does not force him, to declare that the sensory appetite cannot do violence to reason. Many, in excuse of their vices, say they cannot resist the impulse of the sensory part with human reason, which can indeed beg reason and invite and entice it to its desires—to which, when they are moderate, reason can condescend and consent without error, but it cannot force it in any way. The contrary is true of celestial love which, being placed in the intellectual part (as we declared in the second treatise), the rational part—which is inferior—must deservedly be subject to it. The inferior nature never retains its liberty except when it is internally a **servant** <note>original: "strua"; likely "serua" (servant or subject).</note> to the nature superior to itself; therefore, our Poet appropriately submits himself to the violence of celestial love, knowing in it the greatest liberty. The reason for the other diversity—namely, that Guido does not call love by its proper name—is because vulgar love is not true love; just as sensible beauty is not true beauty but an image of it, so too is it a simulacrum and a shadow of celestial love. The celestial alone properly claims and attributes to itself the most holy name of Love; it does not suit the other except in the way one is accustomed to call a statue of Hercules "Hercules," or the face of **Helen** <margin>Helen.</margin> painted or sculpted "Helen."

### Solution to the third diversity.
### CHAPTER III.

The cause of the third diversity—namely, that by Guido, love is signified by a female name, and by our Poet by a male name—is because vulgar love has the proportion to celestial love of an imperfect thing to a perfect thing. By the **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of the philosopher Pythagoras, who associated the "Limited/Perfect" with male and the "Unlimited/Imperfect" with female.</note>, the imperfect nature was signified by the female, and the perfect by the male. Nor will I refrain from adding to this that vulgar love—that is, of corporal beauty—is more appropriately regarding women than regarding males; the celestial is the opposite, as is written in the speech of Pausania in **Plato's Symposium** <note>original: "conuiuio"; Plato's dialogue on the nature of love.</note>. Because the vulgar, being a passion of the sensory soul, is very prone to let itself fall into the act of coitus, because that part of the soul is more irrational than rational; to which act, when indeed man falls overcome by fragility, it is less inappropriate in the female sex than in the other. The opposite is true in celestial love, in which there is no such danger, but everything tends and directs itself to the spiritual beauty of the soul and the intellect, which is found much more perfectly in males than in women, as is seen in every other perfection. Therefore, all those who have been inflamed by this love have for the most part loved some youth of generous nature, whose virtue was all the more pleasing to others the more it was in a beautiful body; they did not effeminate themselves following a herd of prostitutes, who not only do not lead man to any degree of spiritual perfection but, like **Circe** <note>The sorceress from the Odyssey who turned men into swine.</note>, transform him entirely into a beast. Socrates loved with this chaste love not only Alcibiades, but almost all the most talented and graceful of the youth of Athens; so too was Zeno loved by Parmenides; Musaeus by Orpheus; Nicomachus by Theophrastus; and Clinia by Xenophon. None of these desired anything filthy with their beloveds, as many believe who measure the celestial thoughts of others by the measure of their own shameful desires; but they sought only to be excited by external corporal beauty to regard that of the soul, from which the corporal emanated and arrived. And that of the soul being a participation in **angelic beauty** <term>Angelic beauty: In Neoplatonism, the pure, non-material beauty found in the higher realm of Intellect.</term>, rising further up, they might elevate themselves to a more sublime degree of contemplation until one reaches the first source of all beauty, which is God. This is the fruit that Plato sought from his love, and not that shameful one that Dicaearchus imputes to him. Socrates often achieved this; he, many times excited by the beauty of Phaedrus near the river Ilissus, sang the highest mysteries of Theology.

<margin>
Of the order placed by divine wisdom in created things.
</margin>

### CHAPTER IIII.
#### First Stanza.

**L**ove, from whose hands the suspended rein <note>original: "Amor dalle cui man sosp' es' il freno"; This image of the "rein" or "bridle" refers to the governance of the soul's desires, a common theme in Platonic philosophy.</note> of my heart hangs. Among the other orders of divine wisdom placed in created things, this principal one is seen: that every inferior nature is governed by the superior nature immediately above it. As long as it obeys that superior nature, the inferior is defended from every evil and is led to its determined happiness without any impediment. But if, through loving its own liberty too much and preferring a licentious life to a more useful one, it abandons obedience to the superior, it strikes now against this rock, now against that one, without hope of a harbor. The other result is that it loses its command over the other natures placed beneath it, just as it was placed beneath the one from which it rebels. So that this may be more manifest, we shall explain it through examples repeated from the sacred mysteries of the **Theologians** <note>In this context, "Theologians" often refers to ancient mystical writers like Dionysius or the authors of scripture.</note>. 

Irrational nature is governed by the providence of another, and through its own imperfection, it is not fit for the governance of any creature. Just as God, through his ineffable excellence, provides for everything and has no need for the providence of any other. Between God and the brute animals, as if two extremes, are the nature of **Angels** and the nature of **rational souls**, which are governed by others and have others under their own governance. The first Angels, immediately illuminated and, as it were, instructed by God, admonish and counsel the inferior Angels, as is read in the prophet David and explained more diffusely by **Dionysius the Areopagite** <note>A Christian theologian and philosopher (c. 5th–6th century) known for his work *The Celestial Hierarchy*, which describes the ranking of angels.</note>. 

The last order of Angels is immediate to us, called **Demons** by the Platonists and Pythagoreans, and by the Hebrews **Issim** <note>original: "Issim", from the Hebrew *Ishim*, meaning "men-like" or "individuals."</note>, which is derived from *Is* <note>original: "Is", transliterated from the Hebrew *Ish* (man).</note> which signifies man; they are as it were guardians and shepherds of men, deputed to our governance just as we are to the governance of all irrational nature. Truly and rightly David says that men are but little diminished from the angelic nature, and that under their feet are placed the flocks, the fish, the birds, and all the irrational beasts. By these words it is also to be noted how much more distant the beasts are from our perfection than we are from the Angelic, which he signifies by saying the brutes are under our feet, while we are but little diminished from Angelic dignity. 

Therefore, as long as the first Angels submit themselves to the yoke of divine power, they retain their own dignity, command, and authority over other creatures. But when, through an immoderate love of their own excellence, they aspire to such equality with God that they wish to preserve themselves by their own strength without other help—an error into which they can no longer fall because they are now confirmed by the gift of grace—but when **Lucifer** and his followers fell, they were then precipitated from their beatitude into the abyss of extreme misery, and every command over other creatures was taken from them. This happened to Lucifer, who, seeing us now free and loosed from his command, enviously lies in wait for our goods at every hour. 

Similarly, as long as **Adam** submitted to the obedience of his superiors and did not rebel against the divine precept and counsel, he was both most happy and the ruler of all other animals. He lost both when, through the desire to liken himself to God through the knowledge of good and evil—and as if to free himself from His governance by this path as if he had no more need of it—he tasted the forbidden fruit and deviated from the divine commandment. 

This same order is seen in the **small world** <note>term: "piccolo mondo" (Microcosm). The human being viewed as a miniature reflection of the entire universe.</note>, that is, in our soul, in which the inferior powers are corrected and administered by the superior, and while they believe in them, they proceed without error in all their works. The **imagination** <note>original: "imaginatiua"</note> often corrects the errors of the external senses, and **reason** <note>original: "ragione"</note> is illuminated by the **intellect** <note>original: "intelletto"</note>. No error ever falls upon us except when either the imagination, being too stubborn, does not lend faith to reason, or when reason, being adverse to the intellect, trusts too much in its own strengths. Likewise in the appetitive powers, the **sensory appetite** <note>term: "appetito sensitiuo", the part of the soul that desires physical or worldly things.</note> is governed by the **rational appetite**, and the rational by the intellect, which our Poet subtly touches upon by saying:

> Love, from whose hands the suspended rein of my heart hangs.

We declared in the second book that celestial love is an **intellectual appetite** <note>term: "appetito intellettuale", the soul's desire for spiritual truth and divine beauty.</note>; therefore, in every well-composed soul, every other appetite must be governed by that one. This governance is denoted here by the "rein," imitating the speech of the **Phaedrus** <note>A dialogue by Plato that uses the allegory of a charioteer (reason) controlling two horses (appetites).</note>. He says, therefore, that his heart is restrained by love—that is, that every desire of his depends on it. He says "heart" because commonly, as observed by philosophers and also in sacred scripture, the operations of the cognitive powers of the soul are attributed to the head, and those of the appetitive powers to the heart. *And in whose sacred kingdom.* A man who expects a new benefit from another cannot provoke that person's liberality toward himself by a better means than by showing himself grateful for the benefits first received from him. Therefore, our poet, expecting help from Love for the present undertaking, makes a demonstration of a most grateful spirit; for he refers the loving flame, by which the poet's wit has been elevated to the supernal intellectual beauty, neither to its beginning nor to its increase, nor to his own merits or strengths, but humbly calls it a gift, of which he is unworthy, born and nourished in him by the clemency of Love. *But the heart fails.* Having shown how he is led to this undertaking by the force and commandment of Love, in the rest of this first stanza he declares two things: that by his own strengths he cannot hope to bear such a weight, but with the help of Love, he hopes for every desired effect. *And the tongue resists such an undertaking.* The same weakness that makes the tongue an inept and insufficient minister for such an undertaking also makes it powerless to resist and oppose the greater force of the one who moves it to speak.

<margin>
That the descent of any superior virtue into us is a drawing of us to itself.
</margin>

### CHAPTER V.

**B**ut because to the sluggish wit Love has promised those wings, with which into my heart he first descended. The poet touches in this place upon a solemn saying of the **Theologians and Metaphysicians**, which is: whenever it is said that some superior virtue descends into us, it should not be understood that it, descending from its sublimity, places itself in a lower position to join with us; rather, it draws us to itself by its virtue. Its descending to us is a making us ascend to it. Otherwise, from such a conjunction, imperfection would result for that virtue, and not perfection for the one who receives it. What deceives the common imagination of the vulgar is the conceiving of the conjunction of spiritual things as being similar to that of physical things, which are joined by proximity of site and place. Thus they also believe that the intellectual light cannot join itself to our soul unless it, as a resident of a superior place, descends as if from heaven to earth to couple with us. This is what our poet signifies by saying the same wings with which Love descended into him are those with which he hopes to elevate himself to the sublime contemplation of the amorous mysteries. *Though at the top, I believe, never to depart, he makes a nest of his feathers.* Here the poet demonstrates two things:

### CHAPTER VI.
#### Second Stanza.

**I shall tell how love from the divine fountain.** In this second 
stanza the author does two things. First, he briefly
proposes what he has to say of love; then, as if
moved by the recent commemoration of the greatness of
the matter which he proposes to treat, he returns to the invocation, 
invoking Apollo together with Love to aid him to
say what pertains to the first part. **I shall tell how love from the di-**
**vine fountain of uncreated good pours down here below.**
<note>original: "Io dirò com’ amor dal diuin fonte dell’ increato ben qua giù s’infonde"</note>
That is, from the fountain of divine goodness, the first principle, as we 
have declared, of every beauty, and consequently of 
love which is born from it, it pours down here below. That is, into 
our souls, where such influence ultimately terminates. He says, furthermore, 
that he will say (which he does in the following stanza): **When**
**first born and from where.** <note>original: "Quando in pria nato & donde"</note> That is, how it first was born
in the angelic mind <term>angelic mind: in Neoplatonism, the first and highest created intellect, which contains the "Ideas" or blueprints of all things</term> at the birth of Venus, that is, of ideal beauty, of which in the second book three principal things were
said. The first, that the due order of those ideas
which we experience is to be noted by "Venus," and the order of 
providence by which this inferior world is ruled and governed.
The second is that the ideal splendor, through the liberal participation 
of the angelic mind, is shared with the rational soul,
by which ultimately, through an amorous conversion <note>In Neoplatonism, "conversion" is the process by which a created thing turns back toward its source to be perfected.</note> 
from the perfect mind, the celestial bodies are moved. Of these 
three things the poet promises to speak, and therefore says he will tell
**When first born and from where [it] moves the heaven,**
**informs souls, and governs the world.** <note>original: "Quando in pria nato et don de muou’ el ciel l’alme informa, e’ l mōdo regge"</note> He begins with the movement 
of heaven, which is the final effect, and from that in an orderly way
ascends to the first, which is to govern the world with the right reason 
of providence; although in executing the promised 
declaration he follows a retrograde order. This is done by the 
poet to signify that, although in the inquiry into any 
truth (when the intellect has only an obscure light and confused 
knowledge of it), it seems a convenient and necessary order—as 
Aristotle declares—to proceed from inferior things, as more 
proximate and more known to us, to the superior; nevertheless, 
after the truth has already been found, one who has scientific 
knowledge of it—and as Plato everywhere observes, speaks 
divinely—must in his writing preserve the order of the 
nature of things themselves. That is, just as from superior 
things the inferior emanate and proceed, so also from 
the knowledge of those things, one should descend to the 
knowledge of these in a scientific order. Of these three effects 
the poet speaks universally throughout the whole song, as 
the place requires. And it is to be understood that love is the cause 
of these effects, but not the efficient cause <term>efficient cause: the direct agent that brings something into being</term>; for it is 
not love that produces the ideas in the angelic mind (which God does), 
nor that illuminates the soul with ideal splendor (which the mind does), 
nor that moves the heaven (which has no other motor than its own 
soul). But love is the cause of them because without it, the 
aforesaid effects would not follow from their principal causes. 
For if the mind did not turn to God, and the soul to the mind—of 
which conversion love is the cause—neither the ideas would descend 
into the former, nor those specific reasons into the latter. And 
if the soul were not perfected and illuminated by these, it 
would not be a fit cause to extract these sensible forms 
through the motion of the heaven from the descent of inferior matter. 
The poet will therefore declare how love is the 
cause of these effects; then, finally, he will say how men 
are forced by the virtue of celestial love to elevate themselves 
from the earth (that is, from sensible things) to heaven (that is, 
to spiritual things). And he will say by what law and in what 
way there lives in us now that celestial love which turns us 
to heaven, now that vulgar love which bends us to the earth, 
and now places us in a middle state between these two 
extremes, as he will touch upon in the final stanzas, and as 
was diffusely declared by us in the preceding book. And it 
is to be noted that under "celestial love" are comprised the 
fifth and sixth grades of love; and under "vulgar love," the 
first, second, and third; and by the "middle state" is understood 
the fourth grade, of which there is no need to speak at present, 
because at the beginning of the 5th, 6th, and 7th stanzas, where 
the poet speaks of them diffusely, we shall treat of them. 
As to the second part, a doubt remains to be declared: for what 
reason are Love and Apollo invoked by our poet for his 
succor? Regarding this, it should be known that for anyone 
who has to speak of any matter, two things are necessary. 
First, to conceive its nature profoundly; and according to 
one's powers, to express that concept in an elegant manner, 
either by writing or speaking. As a consequence of the 
first, it is necessary not only to have good knowledge of that 
thing in the mind, but to transform oneself entirely into it. No 
one will ever treat a sad case well who does not first clothe 
his own soul within with sadness; and he who must write 
of a martial act, such as a war, the simple knowledge 
of it is not enough; but he must—wishing to depict and 
express it with his speech—first compose himself within into 
a similar disposition. And so it is in every other matter. 
Therefore, he who has to speak of love must be transformed 
into love. Who can transform water into fire, if not fire itself? 
Who can transform us into love, if not love itself? It is 
necessary then for one who writes of love to have the succor 
of love, since he cannot write of it if he does not first 
become love. As a consequence of the second, the aid of 
him from whom the gift of eloquence can come to us 
is necessary; and this by the ancients is attributed to the 
Muses and to Apollo. For this reason, then, Apollo and Love 
are invoked by our poet; just as one who writes of weddings 
or of war, besides the invocation of the givers of 
eloquence, invokes Mars for the latter and Hymen for 
the former. This matter we shall declare much more diffusely 
in the first book of our *Poetic Theology* <note>original: "poetica Thelogia"; This refers to Pico's projected (but never completed) work exploring the hidden theological truths within pagan myths.</note>. Here, in the 
present exposition, let what we have said suffice, adding 
this as well: just as conceiving the thing comes before 
explaining it, so also it was rightly necessary—as our poet 
has done—that the invocation of love made in the first 
stanza should precede the invocation of Apollo, which 
he does now in the second. Nor is it without reason that 
the invocation of love was alone, while that of Apollo was 
not without an appropriate repetition adding that of love. 
For one can well conceive the truth of a thing and understand 
it perfectly without speaking or writing of it; but one cannot 
speak or write well of it without first having well 
conceived and understood it. Therefore, the aid and benefit 
of love in us cannot exist regarding this by itself, without 
having with it the aid of Apollo; nor can that of Apollo 
in any way stand without the aid of love.

### CHAPTER VII.
#### Third Stanza.

**W**hen, turned from the true heaven, it descends.
In this third stanza our poet declares most
elegantly where Love is first born, and how...
