<meta>This page continues the commentary on the second stanza of Girolamo Benivieni’s poem, specifically analyzing the philosophical and theological mechanics of how divine love is born within the "Angelic Mind"—the first created intellect—through the interaction of divine light and the "Ideas."</meta>

<page-num>91</page-num>
<header>BOOK THREE</header>

is born in me, and that which in the end is love; and because this matter was treated by us extensively in the second book, a simple exposition of the words will suffice here. The summary meaning of the entire stanza is this: when the abundance of Ideas <note>In Platonic philosophy, "Ideas" are the perfect, eternal forms of all things, existing in the divine mind.</note> descends from God into the mind of the angel—the first offspring, that is, the first creature of God—the angel, desiring the perfection of those Ideas, turns toward God and obtains from Him full possession of what he desires. The more fully he possesses this within himself, the more ardently he loves Him. He concludes, finally, that this desire—which is born from the mind insofar as it is obscure in itself, and from the Ideas received within it—is that love spoken of in the present stanza.

I say, therefore: **when from the true heaven**—that is, from God, who is first among all things just as the physical heaven is first among all bodily things. He says "true" because the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who believed that numbers and spiritual realities were the only true existence.</note> and the ancient theologians generally esteemed intelligible and spiritual things to be the only true things, and sensible things to be the image and shadow of those—differing from them almost as alchemical gold, made by art in imitation of true and natural gold. And because there is the same difference between the Philosopher and the Sophist—for the Philosopher seeks the truth, while the Sophist seeks the appearance—the ancient Platonists called the maker of sensible things a "Sophist."

However, so as not to give anyone cause or occasion for error, it should be noted that God is not called the "true and intelligible heaven" as if He were the Idea of this sensible heaven. As was declared in the first book, the Ideas are primarily in that [Angelic Mind] produced by God. Rather, He is called Heaven by way of similitude and metaphor; for just as the physical heaven, which is the supreme part of the world, contains and preserves all other worldly things within itself, so God, in the infinite circuit of His indivisible and simplest unity, encloses and conserves every created thing.

**The divine sun descends**—that is, the light of the Ideas emanating from God, the author of every spiritual light, just as the celestial sun is the author of every sensible light. And the sun is said to "descend" where its light and power descend into the **angelic mind**. "Mind" and "intellect" are the same thing here. **Which [sun] illustrates and informs**, because, as was declared above, those Ideas are the substantial form of the Angel. Therefore, it was not enough to say "illustrates" (which would only show accidental perfection), but "informs." 

**Its first offspring**—that is, the angel, the first creature of God. **Under the living fronds**—that is, under the ornament of those Ideas. The reason why "fronds" [leaves] is used by the Poet will be clear to anyone who remembers what was said in the second book: that the unformed essence of the Angel is signified by Plato as the "Gardens of Jove," in which the Ideas are planted by God like ever-green and leafy trees. And he says "living" because a thing is called "living" when it has within itself an intrinsic principle to carry out its operation (which is sometimes called "intrinsic motion" in a broad sense). From this it follows that the angel, having through those Ideas an intrinsic principle to execute his operation (which is understanding), can rightly be said to have life from them—a life certainly noble and worthy. Of this life, David says to God: <note>original: "dammi intelletto & uiuero"</note> **"Give me understanding and I shall live"** <note>Psalm 119:144.</note>, considering anyone who lives without it to be more dead than alive. Whoever participates in it lives a perfect, lovable, and eternal life, which the contemplative philosophers taste as much as one can in this world. 

Furthermore, our author wished to give the epithet of "life" to the Ideas to follow John the Evangelist, who, wishing to signify that everything created by God first existed in Him according to "ideal being," said: <note>original: "et tutte le cose fatte in lui, erano uita"</note> **"And all things made in him were life."** <note>John 1:3-4. Modern translations usually punctuate this differently, but Pico follows an ancient tradition connecting "what was made" to "life" in the Word.</note> The sacred mysteries of the Hebrews also accord with this; to the second <term>Sephiroth</term>—that is, the enumeration that proceeds from the first Father and is in itself the first "Ideal Wisdom"—they attribute the name of "Life."

**She who seeks and wants her first good.** The light both illuminates and warms; but first it illuminates, and then it warms. And once it has warmed, it illuminates more perfectly than before. This is because the recipient, once inflamed by heat, is made more similar to the nature of light and becomes much more fit to be "informed" by it. Thus, as the Ideal light descends into the Angelic mind, it first illuminates it, but not perfectly. But after the light is given, there is born in the mind a heat of most ardent and unquenchable thirst to satisfy itself at the fountain of said light. Carried by such ardor, like a chariot of fire, it reaches the place where, through the infinite liberality of the first Father—that is, God Himself, in whom no envy dwells—so much of the desired light overflows into it (like a most sweet nectar) as the mind is capable of receiving. 

And because the more it drinks, the more it desires (since it tastes more of its sweetness), the poet adds: **Hence the first desire that transforms her.** That is, the desire to possess that ideal beauty perfectly. This desire (which is love) transforms the lover into the beloved at that moment—namely, when it receives more of the divine splendor within itself by moving closer to the **living sun of uncreated light**, which is God Himself. At that moment, it **marvelously catches fire and flames through innate desire.**

Someone might ask why he says "innate," since that desire is born in the mind from the received Ideas, which the mind does not possess of itself but which come from without. To this, one must answer: even though the mind receives the Ideas (the origin of this desire) from elsewhere, it does not receive them as something accidental and distinct from its substance, but as its first intrinsic and substantial act. To denote this, and to give no occasion for the error of believing these Ideas descend into the Angel as things distinct and external to his substance, the Poet called that ardor, that fire, and that flame an "innate"—that is, natural and not accidental—desire.

What the Poet adds next was sufficiently declared in the second book: how the desire to possess ideal beauty—which is born both from the angelic mind (which is obscure in itself) and from the first light (received but still imperfect)—is the first love in the world and the truest, just as the beauty it loves is the truest beauty that can be imagined. And from the same things said above, it is clear how love is **born from want** (that is, poverty) **and from wealth**, which are called <term>Penia</term> and <term>Poros</term> by Plato. Similarly, it is born when **heaven made her whom Cyprus honors**—that is, when Venus (whom Cyprus honors) is produced by heaven. 

Note that the Poet in this place preferred, with poetic grace, to signify both *Poros* and *Penia* with feminine names—namely "Wealth" and "Want"—rather than following Plato’s words by figuring one as a female and the other as a male. He did this because want and wealth (possessing the beloved thing in some way, and being deprived of it in another) are not the principal and efficient cause of love (which we said above was signified by the father), but are that species of cause which philosophers call "that without which the effect does not follow." And because the Platonists say this reduces to the species and mode of the "material cause" (as being less principal and less worthy, signified by matter), the poet wished to signify both by feminine names.

**These, because in the amorous arms.** The perfect knowledge of everything consists in understanding both its own nature and all its own...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical commentary on Girolamo Benivieni’s poem about divine love. The previous page discussed how divine light and the "Ideas" create love within the Angelic Mind. This page shifts to how this love manifests in human experience, moving from physical beauty to the "celestial beauty" of the intellect.</meta>

<header>BOOK</header>

...among which follow from that, sometimes through properties known to us, we investigate the nature of a thing; and sometimes, by the opposite process, from the knowledge of nature itself, we arrive at the knowledge of its properties. This latter way is the most perfect, and it is the one our Poet has followed here. Having declared the nature of love in the third stanza, he declares its properties in the present one, and from those, he assigns the reason for the most noble effects that love works within us. Because he assigns the first property of love—with its reasoning—to the "arms of love," and since this is the first and true love upon which every other love depends, born of ideal beauty (which is called **Cypris** <note>Cypris is a title for the goddess Venus, referring to her legendary birth on the island of Cyprus.</note>, that is, **Venus**, for the reason mentioned above), it follows that every love must turn toward beauty and be directed toward it. Therefore, no desire for a deformed or foul thing can be attributed to the most holy name of love: **from here arose the first desire that lay within us**. 

The second effect of love is this: through it, the desire for that celestial and intelligible beauty is excited within us. The soul, oppressed by the body, had forgotten this beauty, and every desire for it remained dormant and asleep within us. But, being excited anew by love, it awakens. Love leads us from the sensible beauty of bodies to the beauty of the soul by a **noble path** <note>original: "honorata traccia"</note>, ultimately conducting us into the bosom of that very divinity, the first fountain of all beauty. From him, the fire of admirable and secret mysteries of love is contained in the five verses that follow, and principally where he speaks of the fire of love being kindled within us—in which fire the heart burns as it dies, and by burning, that love continues to grow. 

He certainly conceals a most profound meaning beneath very brief words, which is this: when our soul is most effectively fixed in the exercise of one of its powers or virtues, the operations of the others remain weaker. When it is entirely converted to one, the others fail completely, except for that one in which the living soul of man consists. To make this clearer with an example: if someone is strongly fixed in their imagination, the operations of the external sensory virtues fail. We see by experience that some people, while deeply fixed in thought, neither hear those who speak to them nor see what is placed before their eyes. Likewise, he who is entirely turned to the rational part thinks and understands with the **pure eye of reason** <term>pure eye of reason: a Neoplatonic concept referring to the intellect's ability to perceive truth directly, without the distraction of physical senses</term> without having any act of the imagination in his company. Similarly, for he who reaches the exercise of the intellectual part, the acts and operations of reason and every other inferior cognitive virtue fail. 

And because (as was said in the first book) the rational part is proper to man, while through the intellectual part he communicates with the angels, such a person no longer lives a human life, but an angelic one. Dead to the sensible world, he is reborn in the intelligible world to a more perfect life. Motion and operation are the signs of life; the deprivation of these is the sign of death. Therefore, when no human operation appears in a man, he is truly dead regarding his human being; and if he passes from that to an intellectual being, he is transformed by the death of a man into an angel. Nor should we otherwise understand the saying of the wise **Cabalists** <note>Followers of the Kabbalah, a tradition of Jewish mysticism that influenced many Renaissance thinkers.</note> when they speak of **Enoch** being transformed into **Metatron** <note>original: "Matrathon." In Jewish tradition, Enoch was a patriarch who was taken by God and transformed into the highest of angels, Metatron.</note>, the angel of divinity, or universally of any other man being transformed into an angel. 

Therefore, if the divine and celestial love of which the author speaks is an intellectual desire (as was declared in the second book), and one cannot pass to such a state of being unless one first dies to the human part of the soul, the poet rightly says that while the heart—that is, the human soul that dwells in the heart—burns in the fire of love, it dies through that heat. But in that dying, it does not fail; rather, it grows. For that fire, like a most holy **holocaust** <note>A "holocaust" here refers to its original meaning of a religious animal sacrifice that is completely consumed by fire.</note>, being entirely burned and sacrificed to the First Father, the fountain of beauty, is happily led by ineffable grace to the **Temple of Solomon**—adorned with every spiritual wealth, the true dwelling place of divinity. This is the inestimable gift of love that makes men equal to angels; an admirable virtue that gives us life through death. 

From this, you can understand the mystery with which Plato, in the *Symposium* and in the speech of Phaedrus, placed the fable of **Alcestis** and **Orpheus**. We shall look at only one **anagogical** <term>anagogical: a method of interpretation that finds a spiritual or mystical hidden meaning in a text</term> sense of this fable, conforming to our aforementioned exposition, through which we will perfectly declare both the mind of Plato and the depth of this matter. 

It is, therefore, Plato's intention to demonstrate how there is no way to hope to reach the enjoyment of intellectual beauty unless one first abandons the inferior powers and the human life along with them. One does not love perfectly—that is, one does not die of love (I mean perfect love)—unless one does this. For that love which we said in the second book is an image of celestial love can still dwell in one who is a man, since it resides in the rational part. But of that love which is pure and sincerely intellectual (the antiquity and dignity of which is set forth by Phaedrus), no one can clothe themselves unless they first strip off this life—separating not the body from the soul, but the soul from the body. Therefore Alcestis loved perfectly, for she wished to go to her beloved as one dead; and dying for love, she was called back to life by the grace of the Gods—that is, regenerated into life, not through a physical, but through a spiritual regeneration. 

But whoever believes they can join themselves to the perfect ideal sublimity (the object of our love) without detaching themselves entirely from the sensible world, but still living within it, errs greatly. This is because the **Ideas** in themselves and in their true being cannot be seen except by the eye of the intellectual virtue, which does not suffer the company of any act of an inferior virtue. Whenever it is excited, it burns and consumes whoever approaches it, converting them into itself like a most vivid fire. In the other inferior powers—whether rational or imaginary—one does not see the Ideas themselves, but their image and likeness. This is more perfect in the reason (called the **possible intellect** <note>A philosophical term for the human mind's capacity to receive and process universal truths.</note> by the Peripatetics) than in the fancy or imagination, just as reason is closer to the intellect. 

Plato could not have declared this more gracefully or subtly than through the example he brought of **Orpheus**. He says that Orpheus, desiring to go and see his beloved **Eurydice**, did not wish to go to her through death (being made soft and effeminate by his music), but sought a way to go there alive. Therefore, Plato says that he could not obtain the true Eurydice, but only a shadow or a phantom of her was shown to him. No different is the fate of those who hope to reach the true knowledge of intellectual Ideas without detaching themselves from the operation of the imagination and even from the rational part; for they do not see the Ideas in themselves and in their true being, but only some phantom or likeness of them reflecting in either the possible intellect or the imagination. 

This meaning, although both subtle and high, is nonetheless so conforming to the matter that it seems a marvel to me. For when I read the *Symposium*, I had no sooner finished reading his words in that passage than this truth appeared in my mind—which we shall declare more diffusely in our commentary on the *Banquet* and in our *Poetic Theology*. I wish to loosen this knot for the reader: that the same serpent who deprived Orpheus of Eurydice taught him music and prohibited him from regaining his beloved through his own death. I do not wish to uncover this secret any further. But for a more sufficient declaration of this matter, one must know further that sometimes the soul is said to be separated from the body, but not the body from it; and this is when each of the powers of the soul, except that which...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how the soul ascends to divine beauty. It elaborates on the concept of "two deaths" (mystical separation from the body) and introduces the Kabbalistic concept of the "Death of a Kiss" to explain the soul's ultimate union with the Divine.</meta>

-> **BOOK THREE** <-
<page-num>517</page-num>

...body, which is called the vegetative <term>vegetative soul</term><note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "vegetative soul" is the lowest level of the soul, responsible for basic biological functions like nutrition and growth.</note> power, it is bound and does not operate as if it were not there at all. This, as we said, happens when the intellectual part—the queen of the soul—is in action and operating; she, by her dignity, does not allow the act of any other power to coexist with her, except for that of the nutritive power. Because of its great distance from the intellect, the nutritive operations are not entirely canceled by it, though they are greatly weakened. But if the intellectual operation is strongly fortified or prolonged, it is necessary that even this last vegetative part of the soul should separate, so that both she is separated from the body and the body from her.

Therefore, through the **first death**—which is only the separation of the soul from the body and not the opposite—the lover can see the beloved **Celestial Venus** and, face to face with her, reasoning with her divine image, happily feed his purified eyes. But he who wishes to possess her even more intimately, and is not content with seeing and hearing her but wishes to be deemed worthy of her intimate embraces and panting kisses, must separate himself from the body through total separation via the **second death**. Then, he not only sees and hears the Celestial Venus, but embraces her with an indissoluble knot. By transfusing their souls into one another with kisses, they do not so much change souls as they unify themselves so perfectly together that each of them can be called two souls, and both of them a single soul.

<margin>
Note that the most perfect and intimate union that the lover can have with the celestial beloved is denoted by the **union of the kiss**. This is because any other congress or copula used in physical love is not permitted in any way, even by metaphor, to be used for this holy and most sacred love. 

And because the wise <term>Cabalists</term><note>Followers of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah), whose ideas Pico della Mirandola integrated into Christian philosophy.</note> maintain that many of the ancient fathers died in such a rapture of the intellect, you will find among them those who died of **Binshika** <note>original: "Binfica," a corruption of the Hebrew *Binshika* (נשיקה), meaning "by a kiss."</note>, which in our language means **the death of a kiss**. They say this of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Aaron, Mary, and others. He who does not understand our aforementioned foundation will never perfectly understand their intention, nor will you read anything else in their books except that *Binshika*—that is, the death of a kiss—is when the soul, through an intellectual act, joins itself to separate things <note>Non-material or divine realities.</note> so completely that, elevated from the body, it abandons it entirely. But why such a name is appropriate for such a death has not been explained by others, as far as I have read until now. 

This is what our divine Solomon exclaims in his Canticle: **Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth** <note>Song of Songs 1:2.</note>. Solomon shows in the first verse the total intention of the book and the ultimate end of his love; we will never see Solomon, nor Plato, nor anyone else speaking of celestial love, go further than the kiss. 

**From him the fire through which from him derives / whatever lives in him is kindled in us / and where it burns, the heart / dying while burning, grows.** We have explained above how the heart, burning in the amorous fire, dies, and how through such a death it grows into a more sublime life. The explanation of the other part—that is, how through this fire of love that which lives in him derives into others—we shall have fully in the exposition of the next text. 

**Through him the immortal fountain overflows / whence issues that which then the heavens / forming here below, moves.** By the **immortal fountain**, he means God; this is a name also attributed to Him by the ancient Cabalists. If love did not exist, the inestimable abundance of living waters would not descend from this fountain. These waters are first received in the Angelic Mind, and from there, purely through love, they rain into the soul. From the soul, through the movement of the heavens, is produced whatever is newly generated among us in the sensible world. The Angel would not receive the influence of divine goodness if he did not turn toward it, and he turns only through love, as was said above. Nor would the soul participate in the angelic light if she did not likewise turn toward it through amorous desire. 

Love, therefore, is the cause of the production of everything that proceeds from God. This does not mean love exists *within* Him, understanding love to be what Plato and our Poet mean (because that would imply imperfection in Him), but rather through the love of creatures toward Him, as we have declared, and in the manner described. **Whatever lives in him derives from him.** That is, whatever lives in that Mind; and to clarify that this love is not an accident or a quality in that Mind, but is substantial to it, the Poet says that what is in the Mind is in that very love. By the merits of this love, and the perfection of the Ideas within the Mind, love proceeds from the Mind into the Soul of the World, and consequently, the production and adornment of all that is contained in the sensible world follows. What follows in the present stanza is clear from the things said above and needs no other exposition, because we demonstrated quite openly in the first and second books what that eternal love is, with which our soul burns continually—even though no sense of such heat reaches us, frozen as we are in the cold of matter. 

Wherefore we may deservedly grieve along with David, saying: **The waters have entered into the depths of our soul.** And blessed is he who can say: **The great multitude of waters of this my corporeal abyss has not been able to entirely extinguish the fire of the celestial love within me.**
</margin>

### CHAPTER IX. Fifth Stanza.

**A**s from the first Good the eternal mind is, lives, and understands. In the present stanza, the poet demonstrates how the **Vulgar Venus** <note>The "Common" or "Earthly" Venus, representing physical beauty in the material world, as opposed to the "Celestial Venus" of the intellect.</note> is born—that is, sensible beauty. Because we treated this matter sufficiently in the second book, a simple exposition of the author’s words will suffice here. 

Just as the Angelic Mind has its being, living, and understanding from God Himself, so the rational soul (which is produced by that Mind) has from it its understanding, moving, and fashioning. For the rational soul understands itself and other incorporeal things; it moves the corporeal things that are eternal (such as the celestial circles it fashions); and it fashions the corruptible corporeal things through the motion of the eternal bodies. By moving them, as the author adds, it depicts in the lower matter those forms of things which it has conceived within itself. The soul is illuminated by these forms, which are rays of the intelligible sun; and just as she receives them from the Angelic Mind, so too she communicates them to matter. In this way, she diffuses what she contains within herself, producing every other particular nature found after her. 

And because the sensitive and motive soul of the body is produced by the rational soul, as is the vegetative soul (as proved in the **Timaeus** <note>A dialogue by Plato concerning the nature of the physical world and human beings.</note>), the Poet therefore adds: **And that which then moves and feels / is through her admirably moved, feels, lives, and works / every effect of its own.** For all these operations come from her. From this soul, then—that is, from the soul that moves the heavens, called **Jupiter** by Plato in the *Symposium*—is born here below (that is, in the lower matter, signified by Plato as **Dione**) **Venus**: that is, the sensible beauty of bodies. This is just as the other Venus, which is celestial beauty, is born in the intellect (the Angelic Mind) from Heaven (that is, from God). 

**The other who mirrors herself within the sun / in the shadow of that which, through her / grows accustomed to contemplation.** The author concludes the end of this stanza with the briefest words containing the highest meanings of corporeal beauty, drawn from the marrow of the secret mysteries of the ancient philosophers and theologians. To understand these, one must know that—as we proved in the second book—beauty is the object of sight. Since every visible thing is visible through light, it follows that the act, the formed liveliness, and the efficacy of every beauty come from light—either corporeal light, if the beauty is in bodies, or intelligible and spiritual light, if the beauty is spiritual. 

When the Ideas first descended into the unformed essence of the Angel, their being was like the being of colors and visible figures at night, before the splendor of the sun's rays descends upon them. It is like one who, by the nocturnal light of the moon, sees a body and desires to see it in the clearer light of day to be able to enjoy it more fully...

...beauty, which is not granted to it in the opaque and shadowed light of night. Thus, the <term>angelic mind</term><note>In Neoplatonism, the "Angelic Mind" is the first and highest created being, containing the "Ideas" or blueprints of all things.</note> sees within itself the **ideal beauty**, but it is opaque and shadowy; it cannot see clearly in the night of its own imperfection and the darkness of its nature. Just as the moon does not shine by itself, so too if the mind does not turn toward the <term>First Father</term><note>A common Neoplatonic term for God as the source of all being.</note>, it possesses no perfection. It desires, with an amorous longing, to turn toward the **paternal sun**, and once clothed in his copious light, to make its own beauty more perfect and to illuminate its intellectual eye in such a way that it can fully enjoy the beloved beauty. 

Thus it turned, and as it turned, God said: <note>original: "Fiat lux"</note> **"Let there be light,"** and there was light—spiritual and intelligible light—which makes the face of the **Celestial Venus** within itself most beautiful, and makes her clearly visible to the eye of the first mind. That mind, thanking the paternal generosity, turns to Him and sings: <note>original: "signatum est super nos lumen vultus tui"</note> **"The light of your face is sealed upon us."** You are the fountain of true life, and **"in your light we shall see light."** 

In no different a manner, we must consider two things in **sensible beauty** <note>Beauty that can be perceived by the five senses.</note>. The first is the object itself that is seen, which in its primary substance is the same at midnight as it is at midday. The other is the daylight which, by joining with the object, is to it almost like the soul is to the body. Having presupposed this, our Poet imagines that just as the first part of sensible beauty proceeds from the first part of intelligible beauty—that is, corporate forms from those **ideal forms**—so too this sensible light proceeds and emanates from that intelligible light which descends upon the Ideas. This was the opinion of the **Phoenician theologians**, later approved by **Iamblichus** and **Julian the Platonists**. 

Therefore the Poet says: *The other who mirrors herself within the sun,* meaning the **Celestial Venus**, who continually mirrors herself in the **Divine Sun**. He says *within the sun* to demonstrate that this mind, turning toward God with all its effort, unites itself with Him as intimately as possible. And he says that *she mirrors herself in the shadow of that which grows accustomed to contemplation through her*, meaning in the shadow of the **Angel’s essence**. Because that essence, through its own formlessness, makes that ideal light somewhat opaque and dark, the Poet calls it a "shadow." And because through those Ideas the essence of the Angel becomes intellectual, the Poet says that she, by means of this Venus, *grows accustomed to contemplation*, as was fully declared above. Just as she takes all her wealth from the **living sun** that shines within her—as the Celestial Venus takes all her wealth (that is, her divine splendor) from the living sun, which is God—so her light **indulges**, meaning she gives, communicates, and shares that light of hers with this other beauty, the sensible beauty. From this sensible beauty, **vulgar love** is born in the same way that **celestial love** is born from the other. And just as the former always pursues the vulgar, so this latter love always yearns for, follows, and desires the celestial, as was declared above. And thus our author adds: *And as celestial love hangs upon her, so vulgar love always hangs upon this one.*

### CHAPTER X. Stanza
### Six.

**W**hen first formed by the divine face. Before I descend to the exposition of this stanza—because it deals with how the particular beauty of a body ignites the fire of love in the soul of another—it will be useful to give some light and knowledge regarding the aforementioned beauty of bodies. 

It is therefore to be considered that in the beauty of bodies which manifests to us in the light of day, two things appear to those who consider them well. The first is the **material disposition** of the body, which consists of the proper quantity of its parts and its suitable quality. **Quantity** consists in the size of the limbs (if they are appropriate according to the proportion of the whole) and in their placement and distance from one another. **Quality** consists in the shape and the color. 

The second thing is a certain quality which cannot be called by a more proper name than **Grace**. This quality appears and shines in beautiful things, and it seems to me that this is what is properly attributed to and claims the name of **Venus**—that is, beauty—because this alone is what ignites the amorous fire in human hearts. Many wish to claim that this quality arises and results from the first disposition of the body (that is, that from the placement, shape, and colors of the limbs, this grace results in the whole). However, in my judgment, experience alone should be enough to counter this opinion. For many times we see a body that is irreproachable from every angle and most perfect in every part regarding all the conditions mentioned above, and yet we see it deprived of all grace. Conversely, one will sometimes see a body which, in its shape and colors, could be much better proportioned, yet in which a **miraculous grace** appears. **Catullus** declares this very well in one of his epigrams where he says:

> Quintia seems beautiful to many, and in my eyes
> She is fair, tall, and straight; I confess
> Each of these parts is found in her.
> But I deny that the whole, gathered into one
> Form, is beautiful; for in such a large body
> Not a single grain of salt <note>original: "salso." Catullus uses "mica salis" (a grain of salt) to mean wit, charm, or "zing."</note> shines with any grace.

The Poet concedes that Quintia possesses the quality of color through her fairness, shape through being straight, and the quantity required for beauty, which is tallness; and yet, he in no way concedes that she can be called beautiful, because she lacked that Venus and that grace we spoke of above, which is to bodily beauty as salt is to every dish. 

What then shall we say is the cause for one body being endowed with such grace and another being entirely deprived of it? I will say what I think of it, submitting my judgment to any better opinion. I believe that since such an effect does not proceed from the body, it must necessarily be attributed to the **soul**. When the soul is very perfect and lucid in itself, I believe it pours some rays of its splendor even into the earthly body. All the ancient philosophers and theologians agree on this: when **Moses** descended from the mountain and from the divine vision, his face was so illustrious that the eyes of the people could not endure it. Thus it was necessary for him to speak to them with his face veiled. **Porphyry** writes that every hour the soul of **Plotinus** was raised in some sublime contemplation, a miraculous splendor appeared in his face. And this is what Plotinus himself writes: that no beautiful person was ever evil. Plotinus intends this beauty—that is, this grace that often appears in a body of less than mediocre beauty in stature or color—to be a most certain sign of the **intrinsic perfection of the soul**. Speaking of this perfection, **Solomon** says in the Proverbs: *The wisdom of a man illuminates his face.* I believe this sentiment was most perfectly verified in the three observed characters of the sacred name of the <term>first-formed</term><note>original: "protoplausto." From the Greek "protoplastos," referring to Adam as the first human created from clay.</note> **Adam**; let him who can understand this secret, understand it. 

A Platonist would add to this that souls descending from the **Sphere of Venus** have, above all others, the power to cause such an effect in their bodies. *When first formed by the divine face.* The order of the universe is that inferior things proceed from separate and intelligible things, and these, turning as much as they can toward their causes, return to them. I see that in the present Song, this is wonderfully observed by the Poet, who, having to treat beauty and love, first...

But he began from celestial beauty and celestial love, the nature, origin, and properties of which were sufficiently declared in the third and fourth stanzas; and in the fifth, he then narrated how sensible beauty and the love for it proceeded from that source. Now, in the remainder of the present Song, he shows how one ascends by ordered steps from sensible beauty to **intelligible beauty**; having reached this, the author ends his work, as it is there that every amorous desire must end. No more subtle, ordered, or sufficient method can be observed by anyone treating any subject than this, which we see has been observed by our Poet in the present song—a method understood and known by few. This is what Plato in the *Philebus* calls **leading the one into the multitude** and reducing the multitude back to its unity. He who knows how to observe this order and method well, as Plato writes, deserves to be followed almost as if he were a god; such a man is certainly divine and an earthly angel, fit to ascend and descend according to his will by **Jacob’s Ladder** <note>A biblical reference used here as a metaphor for the Neoplatonic scale of being, where the soul climbs toward God and descends toward matter.</note> in the company of the other contemplative angels. We shall treat this order extensively in the *Commentary on the Symposium*.

Following this order of ours, the author shows how man is happily led through six steps from the beauty of matter to the first fountain of beauty. To the soul turned toward the senses, the particular beauty of Alcibiades, Phaedrus, or some other beautiful body is first represented through the eyes. The soul inclines toward it and delights in that particular form, and in stopping there, it is in the first and most imperfect and most material degree. The poet assigns the cause of this effect at the beginning of the present stanza—namely, why it happens that one is more quickly affectionate toward one person than another.

The **Second Step** is when the soul, with its interior power—yet still material and <term>phantastic</term><note>Relating to the "phantasy" or imagination, which creates mental images from sensory data.</note>—describes that image received through the eyes within itself. It makes that image more perfect as it makes it more spiritual, and as it separates it from matter, it draws it closer to **ideal beauty**, though it is still very far from it.

The **Third Step** is when our soul, with the light of the <term>active intellect</term><note>A technical term for the part of the mind that abstracts universal concepts from particular sensory images.</note>, considers the proper nature of corporal beauty in itself, separating the received form from all particularity. It no longer turns to the specific image of one body, but to the **universal beauty** of all bodies together. This is the final step reached by the soul turned toward the senses; for although in this last step it regards beauty in itself and not as restricted to the womb of any matter, it nevertheless receives such knowledge from the senses and from particular mental images. 

From this it arises that whoever reaches the knowledge of the nature of things only by this path cannot see them clearly and without the veil of great ambiguity. Many <term>Peripatetics</term><note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note>, and especially the Latins, have believed and still believe that our soul, while united to the body, cannot ascend to a more perfect knowledge; in our Council <note>Likely referring to a specific philosophical gathering or a planned treatise.</note>, we shall demonstrate that this is greatly alien to the mind of Aristotle and nearly all the Arabian and Greek Peripatetics.

The **Fourth Step** is when the soul, considering its own operation, sees that it knows the nature of beauty universally and not restricted to any particular. It knows that everything founded in matter is particular; from this, it concludes that such universality proceeds not from the external sensible object, but from its own intrinsic light and power. It says within itself: "If those shadowed mirrors of material images represent this beauty to me by the vigor of my light, it is certainly reasonable that by looking into the mirror of my own substance, stripped of every material cloud, I should see every similar thing much more clearly." And thus, turned within itself, it sees the image of ideal beauty shared with it by the intellect, as was declared in the second book. This is the fourth perfect step, an image of **celestial love**, as was said above.

Then, ascending from itself to its own intellect, it is in the **Fifth Step**, where the **Celestial Venus** reveals herself in her own form and not as an image—though not with the total fullness of her beauty, which a particular intellect cannot contain. The soul, greedy and thirsty, seeks to join its own particular intellect to the **Universal and First Mind**, the first among all creatures and the universal home of ideal beauty.

And reaching that, the soul, in the **Sixth Step**, ends its journey. It is not permitted for it to move further in the seventh, which is like the **Sabbath of celestial love**; but there, as in its final goal, it must happily rest beside the First Father, the fountain of all beauty. This is the ladder of amorous steps by which one ascends to the true, complete, and distinct knowledge of this matter of love. I do not know if these steps, and how one ascends from one to the other, could be written with more grace of verse or with more order and doctrine than our poet describes them in the 5th, 6th, 7th, and 8th stanzas. 

But before he descends to that, at the beginning of the 6th stanza, he assigns the reason why one person is more drawn to the love of this person than that other. This reason, although it is entirely founded upon the principles of the ancient Platonists, I nonetheless do not remember ever having read in others. For the understanding of this, it must first be known that according to the Platonists, among human souls, some are of the nature of **Saturn**, some of the nature of **Jove**, and so with the other planets. By this they mean that one soul will have more knowledge and more conformity with the soul of the heaven of Saturn than with the soul of the heaven of Jove, and vice versa. This is for no other reason than that this soul is of such a nature and that one of another; no other intrinsic cause can be assigned for this, other than the extrinsic and effective cause who produces these souls—namely God. Plato says of Him in the *Timaeus* that He scattered seeds, some souls into the moon, some into the other planets and stars, which he calls "instruments of time."

Secondly, it must be known that—as was also said in the first book to be the mind of the Platonists—the soul joins itself immediately to the <term>celestial vehicle</term><note>A Neoplatonic concept of a "star-body" or spiritual carriage that carries the soul from the heavens down into the physical body.</note>, and through that to the earthly and corruptible body. Some, whose opinion our author follows in this place, hold that the rational soul, descending from its star, forms that earthly body itself, which it must afterwards govern. Founding himself on these principles, the Poet imagines that in the vehicle of the soul which descends—which is vivified by the power with which it then forms the earthly body—there is infused by its star a **formative virtue** of the corruptible body. According to which star it descends from, it receives a differently formative virtue. Because of this, <term>physiognomists</term><note>People who judge character or destiny from physical features.</note> say that such a man has a Lunar face, another Solar, another Martial, another Venereal, another Jovial, another Saturnine, another Mercurial; and from the face, they judge the soul of that person to be of a similar nature, which is very much in agreement with our Poet’s opinion. 

But because inferior matter is not always obedient to the one who forms and stamps it, the power of the soul cannot always express the face it would wish in the earthly body. From this it arises that there can be two "Jovial" people who appear dissimilar in form, because the matter of the conception of one was differently disposed to receive that figure of the soul than the other; nevertheless, what is perfect in one is like something begun and not completed in the other. Our Poet, therefore, holds that the shared appearance of the figures of two bodies, formed by the power of the same star, generates an intense love between them due to such conformity. ...first from the divine face—either immediately, as the Catholics hold, or mediately, according to Plato. To descend down here, the soul departs from the most sublime part that the sun inhabits and imprints itself into the human heart. Because the heart is the most appropriate room for the soul, which by its nature is the fountain of life and heat; through its continuous motion, it has great conformity with the heavens, from whence it descends. *From the most sublime part that the sun inhabits.* That is, from the sign of <term>Cancer</term> <note>The summer solstice sign, traditionally considered the "Gate of Men" through which souls descend into generation.</note>, which among all twelve signs of the <term>Zodiac</term> is the most sublime above our upper hemisphere—that is, the most elevated. This is the opinion of the Platonists, who say the soul descends through Cancer and ascends through <term>Capricorn</term> <note>The winter solstice sign, known as the "Gate of Gods," through which souls return to the heavens.</note>. I believe their reasoning is that Cancer is the house of the Moon, whose power dominates most strongly over the vegetative, life-giving part of bodies; and Capricorn is the house of <term>Saturn</term>, who presides over contemplation, to which the soul, once loosed from the body, can freely attend. *Where*, that is, in human earthly bodies. *Expressing.* This soul—with marvelous art, certainly a divine and admirable art derived from the paternal will through the intellectual wisdom and reason infused into the soul's celestial nature—expresses itself. *That value then which it has taken from its star, and which, gathered in its lap, lives of its first celestial garments.* That is, that formative virtue of the elementary body, which then lives and settles in the lap of its first celestial garments—that is, its celestial vehicle—and which thereafter expresses the figure contained within such a quasi-seminal virtue. *As much as its "files" can do in the human seed, it forms its dwelling in that fabric and stamp.* That is, it forms this sensible organic body in which the soul dwells in this world, within that human seed. *Which now more, now less, resists divine worship.* As was declared above. *Thence.* That is, from that body shaped by such a soul. *Whenever from the sun.* That is, from the splendor of that beauty which is sculpted within her. *The infused stamp descends into the heart of another.* Referring to the figure imprinted within itself; and this means that whenever that specific likeness is seen by any other person: *If it is conforming.* That is, if it is a figure produced by stars conforming to the star of the one who looks upon it. *The soul catches fire.* With that amorous flame, as we showed above regarding the first degree. *For once it dwells within, the soul portrays it much more beautifully by the divine rays of its own virtue.* 

Here are contained the second and third degrees indistinctly. It should be noted that the Poet, at the end of the sixth stanza and the beginning of the seventh, narrows down and generally touches upon the ascent from the first degree to the last, hinting at their distinction but not expressing it fully, following in this the order instituted by the philosophers, and especially the Peripatetics in the preface to the *Physics* of <term>Aristotle</term> <note>original: "Aristotile"</note>: namely, that the confused and indistinct cognition of a thing precedes its detailed explanation. Our Poet has observed this here; for after he has given some light through a tangled compendium of the knowledge of these degrees, he then follows through in that place. *Through three shining mirrors.* He explains distinctly what he briefly touched upon in the preceding verses. Nor is it without mystery that our Poet joins these three stanzas together in such a way that the meaning of the end of the sixth is signified in the beginning of the seventh, and the end of that in the beginning of the eighth. To one who did not consider further, this might perhaps seem contrary to the rule of the *canzona* <note>A traditional Italian song structure.</note>, in which it seems appropriate that every stanza should have its own finished meaning—as the poet observes in the first five and the last stanzas. But he wished by this to denote that man should not stop at any degree preceding the last, nor propose it as the end of his love, but should always have one as the ladder to the other. 

It is not laudable to delight in the form of a beautiful youth if you do not use this as a step to regard that proportion and conforming quality of that figure even outside of that gross and material body in which you first saw it. Nor can the occupation of the <term>imaginative faculty</term> in considering the figure of a body be anything but a vain labor if you stop there and do not use it as an instrument to contemplate, through reason, the universal beauty of all bodies. Nor can the soul be anything but weak and infirm if it is always prostrate upon the body, never dividing itself from it, and—revolving within itself—does not recognize its own treasures. But as <term>Asaph</term> <note>A reference to the biblical psalmist; specifically Psalm 49:20.</note> says, being placed in dignity and honor, the soul does not know them, and becomes like the witless beasts which do not have the power to return into themselves. Nor can the soul, in itself or by itself, sufficiently possess that light of beauty which it does not have from itself, but only as a gift and communication from another, if it does not return to Him who made the soul a participant in that beauty. Since He is the primary sea, if the soul wishes to quench its thirst entirely, it must be led to that first sea of beauty emanating immediately from that source. Our poet imitates this, for beginning in the sixth stanza to arrange the steps of this ladder upon which one ascends from earth to heaven, he did not end his verses until he reached the First Good. *Informed by whose living and sole light, the soul, loving, beautifully knows itself, the world, and what is in it.* 

Therefore, in truth, there are no more than seven stanzas in the present Song, although it is divided into nine, because none of these three stanzas is finished by itself, but one result comes from all of them together. Thus, in the perfect sixth stanza, the poet stops—as every lover does at his sixth degree—and being about to proceed further, he feels Love pulling the reins. By this, he denotes to us that he who reaches the sixth degree is not permitted to walk any further, because that is the limit of the amorous path; although one may go further by way of another love, and that is the love with which one loves God in Himself, and not merely as the author of ideal beauty. But this does not fit with the love of which we are presently speaking, because that is not a desire for beauty—which, according to the Platonists, is not found in God because of His simplicity, as was declared in the first books. 

Now returning to the exposition of the text, the poet says, encompassing the second and third degrees together: *That after the soul houses within itself the figure received through the eyes, it portrays, fashions, and forms it much more beautifully by the divine rays of its virtue.* That is, by the <term>phantastic</term> <note>Relating to the "phantasia" or imagination.</note> or <term>cogitative</term> virtue, and the <term>rational</term> virtue. *And from this it arises that the heart, loving, feeds on a sweet error.* Here the author shows how, through his words, one can understand why it happens—many times and almost always—that the beloved appears much more beautiful to the lover than they are in themselves. This proceeds because the lover regards the beloved in the image that the soul has fashioned within itself, made so much more beautiful the more it has been separated from matter (the principle of all deformity). Furthermore, besides the fact that the figure formed by the soul shows itself to be more beautiful than the outward appearance because it truly is more beautiful, there is the added fact that this image is generated and made by the soul; thus, the soul delights in it more as its own thing, and prizes it more than it is in itself and in its own proper being. Therefore, the author adds: *The heart feeds on a sweet error, looking at the beloved object within itself as its own offspring*; that is, as its own work and its own creature, made and generated by it. *Sometimes then reforming.* Here the author shows how one reaches the last degree from the fourth, omitting the explicit declaration of the middle ones—that is, the fifth and sixth degrees—which he nonetheless hints at...

<page-num>521</page-num>

...mentions where it says *From step to step, and by which one reaches the final step.* He says, therefore, that sometimes the soul reforms that universal image <note>original: *spetie uniuersale*</note> according to the divine light that is imprinted within it—that is, to the light of ideal beauty shared with it. **A rare and celestial gift**; truly rare and celestial, because few are those who reach this degree, and these are highly perfected. Indeed, they are so rare that, as we said above, many judged it impossible for man to reach this step; therefore he rightly said, **Rare and celestial gift.** From here—that is, from the aforementioned reformation which is the fourth degree—*Elevating itself from step to step*, that is, from the fifth degree (which is one's own particular intellect) to the sixth degree of union with the first and universal intellect, *it returns to the uncreated sun*, which is God Himself, from whence it was formed, and which is expressed in the beloved object. From this God—though through many intermediaries, as he immediately adds—is formed that light of beauty which appears in the beloved body. For one alone—that is, a single light emanating from the divine face—passing as if through three mirrors, the mind (the angelic nature), the spirit 
<margin>the rational nature, the mind, that is, the sensible world, adorns every beauty</margin>
(the body, which is the sensible world), adorns every beauty. From here, the eyes. Now our Poet 
<margin>our Poet explains and declares the aforementioned six degrees in an orderly fashion, of which we spoke quite distinctly.</margin>
explains and declares the aforementioned six degrees in an orderly fashion, of which we spoke quite distinctly at the beginning of the sixth stanza. He says, therefore, beginning from the first and lowest degree, that from here, that is, from the body, **The eyes receive the adorned spoils** <note>original: *spoglie*; refers to the visual images or "raiment" of the beloved's form</note> of that person—namely, the images of beauty taken from that body. This, as we said above, is the first and most material degree. Then he adds: **And through the eyes where she resides**, where he declares how this image of the object, having reached the eyes, passes from the visual power of the eyes (which is an external sense) to the imaginative power (which is an internal sense). This imagination he calls **Her other handmaid** <note>original: *anilla*, an archaic form of *ancella*</note>, meaning of the heart; understanding by "the heart" the substance of the rational soul, which the sensory powers serve and minister to, both internal and external, as all philosophers harmoniously declare. Now, these "spoils"—that is, those images conceived by the imagination—the poet says are by her **Sometimes then reformed, yet not fully expressed**. Because the imagination, being a higher and more noble power than the external sense, makes that image more spiritual, and consequently detaches and separates it more from the deformity of matter (which cannot endure the true form and <term>Venus</term> <note>Here used to signify the principle of Beauty.</note> within itself). However, because the imagination is still a purely material and organic power, it cannot yet reduce that image to perfect immateriality. Therefore, he says that it reforms them but does not "express" them [perfectly], and this is the second degree. Although this is still the love of a particular body, the lover no longer loves that particular beauty in that coarse and corporeal person, but rather in that image which has already been formed in his soul. And just as this degree is more perfect than the first, so it is also happier, because the lover enjoys it no less in the beloved's absence than in their presence; he always has them with him, always sees them, always hears them, and converses with them familiarly at all hours. He who is in the first degree is only as happy as the beloved is present—a condition that is, in any case, much better than that bestial fury (not love), whose goodness can only last a short time and leaves nothing behind but long-lasting bitterness and the greatest penance. This should certainly be a sufficient stimulus for everyone to remove themselves from this execrable pleasure and hasten with the swiftest course toward that celestial love, where no trace of misery is found, but every fullness of happiness. Nor should anyone be enticed to this miserable pleasure by the fact that many men celebrated for their prudence and learning have been gripped by it; rather, this should serve as a most effective reason to show that it must be entirely fled with every skill. For if this evil is so pestiferous and poisonous that it could generate an almost incurable illness in such perfect and strong souls, everyone must undoubtedly be persuaded that it will give birth to an entirely lethal and death-bearing disease in their own. From this, one can rightfully conclude that whoever falls into such a precipice through themselves and their own ill-composed thoughts receives correction and fatherly punishment from God, and perhaps no less compassion than blame from men. Now returning to the words of the Poet, after he has spoken of the first and second degrees, coming to the third he says: **Then from various and many beauties, loosed from the body, she forms one concept, in which she paints and figures in one that which nature has divided among all.** This is when the soul, rising above the first and second degrees (in both of which it considers beauty particularly and does not strip it from matter), considers nature itself in a universal concept. It reduces the multitude of all beautiful particular bodies into the unity of beauty within itself, which is the proper work of one who ascends from below to above—that is, one who reduces multitude into unity, as was said above. From here, love **Delights the soul, and in this, the heart; it still wanders in her as if in its own offspring; for while it yearns for the true, it sees it like a sunbeam under water.** In this universal cognition, the soul delights as if in something manufactured by itself, as we also said a little while ago. And in it, it sees the light of true beauty as one sees the light of the sun under water. Because the soul—that is, the water—reaches that light through two intermediate degrees (fire and air), so from God (the first intelligible heaven and fountain of the light of beauty) the light shines in the universal image abstracted from the senses, as if through the two intermediate degrees of the ideal intellect and the region participated by the soul (acting as the air and fire). Yet **I know not what divine thing flashes in him, which, though shadowed, entices the pious heart from this to a more perfect beauty that sits proudly atop that one.** This is the ascent from the third degree to the fourth—that is, to the Ideas shared with the soul, where there is no longer a shadow of beauty, but true beauty is seen, though not essential, but participated. From here, **while the pious heart follows the soul's vestiges, it sees it inserted within its own mind.** This is the ascent from the fourth degree to the fifth—that is, to the soul's own particular intellect, which he declares by saying, **He sees it inserted within his mind.** He then adds: **Then, drawn to a clearer and more open light, it flies suspended near that sun.** This is the ascent from the fifth degree to the sixth, in which one's own particular intellect joins with the universal and first mind, which is much more open and clear than ours; that mind is immediate and proximate to God, the first and intelligible sun, and therefore he said: **It flies suspended near that sun**, by whose living and sole light the mind, the soul, and the world are made beautiful, as has been shown at length above.

### CHAPTER XI. Ninth Stanza.

**Song, I feel love pulling back the reins.** It was the opinion of the ancient <term>theologians</term> <note>Here referring to the "divine" poets and philosophers like Orpheus or Plato.</note> that one should not rashly publish divine things and secret mysteries, except as much as was permitted from above. Therefore the poet feigns that, as he was prepared to speak further, he was pulled back by love and commanded to show only the "bark" or "husk" <note>The outer, literal layer of a text.</note> of the amorous mysteries to the common people, reserving the "marrow" of the true sense for the more elevated and perfect intellects—a rule observed by whoever wrote of divine things among the ancients. Origen writes that Jesus Christ revealed many mysteries to the disciples which they did not want to write down, but communicated only by word of mouth to those they deemed worthy. Dionysius the Areopagite confirms that our priests later observed this...

It concludes by emphasizing the traditional necessity of keeping such high mysteries hidden from the uninitiated.</summary>

one from the other, they received understanding of those secrets which it was not permitted to write down. Thus Dionysius, <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian and philosopher.</note> in explaining the names of God and the angelic and ecclesiastical hierarchy to Timothy, reveals many profound meanings but commands him to keep the book hidden and not to share it except with the few who are worthy of such knowledge. This order was most holily observed among the ancient Hebrews, and for this reason, their science—which contains the exposition of the abstruse and hidden mysteries of the law—is called <term>Cabala</term> <note>Kabbalah, from the Hebrew word meaning "reception" or "tradition."</note>, which signifies "reception." This is because they received it not through writing, but by succession from mouth to ear, one from another. This is certainly a divine science, worthy of being shared with only a few, and it is a most great foundation of our faith. The desire for this science moved me to the assiduous study of the Hebrew and Chaldean languages, without which it is entirely impossible to reach a knowledge of it. There is no need to mention how the same style was observed by the <term>Pythagoreans</term> <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras, known for their secrecy.</note>; the letter of Lysis to Hipparchus provides full evidence of this. Nor for any other reason did the <term>Egyptians</term> carve <term>Sphinxes</term> before their temples, if not to declare that divine things, even when they are written down, must be covered under enigmatic veils. As we have declared, our poet has done the same in the present song, according to our strength, and we shall declare in the book of our poetic philosophy that the same was observed by other poets, both Greek and Latin.

### GIROLAMO BENIVIENI TO
### LUCA DELLA ROBBIA.
### SALUTATIONS.

**I**t was certainly enough for me to have once, and perhaps even recklessly, permitted that of all my amorous verses only these should appear in public:

> Who, to the sweet sound of the celestial lyre
> Singing of love frequently,
> Converts and draws the soul to its first good,

without me now being invited by your loving persuasions and warned by the errors of my youth, to weary the mind of the reader once more with the explanation of the follies of that same youth. Of these follies—truly childish follies—since it pleased God to illuminate the darkness of my blindness in some way with the light of His grace, I have always considered, and still consider, the following <term>Bucolica</term> <note>A collection of pastoral poems, usually featuring shepherds.</note> to be no small part. I ought to have, and not undeservedly if it had been permitted to me, made a sacrifice to Vulcan <note>original: *uno sacrificio à Vulcano*; meaning to burn the manuscripts.</note> of this work, just as I did with my other childish follies. But because this work had already been printed several times and disseminated in many copies and various places, it was and is impossible. Therefore, for my own satisfaction, I now yield to your loving persuasions. Since the power to suppress it at any time has been taken from me, I am all the more stimulated by the memory of some of its concepts—chaste, certainly, but woven so incautiously due to the ardor of that age—that they might have been misunderstood. Furthermore, if the truth of their meanings were not uncovered, they could provide a weak occasion for some scandal. This is because the Introduction we placed at the beginning to guide the reader, and the previously published Preface of our *Bucolica*, do not open—as experience has shown me—nor do they sufficiently clear the path to penetrate the truth of our concepts, which were poorly shadowed in that work.

Therefore, being stirred by you and by the stimulus of the aforementioned memory to provide a remedy for this, I have added some other, somewhat broader and more direct arguments to what was said in the Preface. Distributing these in their proper places for the greater clarity and convenience of the reader, I have given each Eclogue its own [summary]. Since it pleases you, I permit that our *Bucolica*, now instructed and accompanied in this way, appear in public once more. This is so that, by means of these arguments thus placed and distributed, anyone who previously fell into some wrong opinion while reading may rise again, or anyone reading in the future may easily and without offense penetrate the true sense of our hidden concepts. For the veil of words—which are certainly in some places tender and licentious—under which this sense (though pure in itself) is hidden, may have until now appeared to your eyes and to others like a chaste matron in the dress and habit of a prostitute. I pray then to the reader that, for their own caution and my satisfaction, they do not find it troublesome to read the argument placed immediately before each Eclogue before descending to the reading of the Eclogue itself. Thus, through these warnings and the memory of them, they may penetrate the intimate, pure, and naked truth of our concepts, freeing and absolving themselves from any occasion of scandal and me from any fault. If they do not learn from the useful lessons of our Eclogues (which are few) the good that one should happily seek in this life, let them at least learn from the errors and the character of my youth described therein (which are many) what one should wisely flee. Farewell.

***

### ELEGY OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA
### Mirandola, distinguished youth, to Flor-
### ence, in praise of Girolamo Benivieni, 
### its citizen, who as a youth 
### recently published a 
### Bucolic 
### poem.

**I**o! I rejoice for you, Tyrrhenian Florence,
Let every friend present cry out "Io Paean!" <note>A Greek hymn of praise or triumph.</note>
What honor, what fame, what glory rises for you!
Lift up your head; lift up your proud Libyan manes.
He was born within your fields and your walls,
And grew to adulthood amidst the clear waters of your lands.
Since a divine power dwells in his sacred breast,
How well he derives his name from that "Sacred Name." <note>A play on the name Hieronymo, derived from the Greek *Hieros* (Sacred) and *Onoma* (Name).</note>
He, I say, has already begun to be read everywhere with frequent applause,
Already he is read with much honor.
His Sicilian Muse <note>original: *Sicelis musa*; a reference to the pastoral style of Virgil and Theocritus.</note> through the cities of Italy
Carries her famous, bright foot with great praise.
Whoever reads him envies his fatherland
And wishes for such names for his own country.
Rejoice, rejoice again, marked by such great beauty,
And you, blessed land, applaud your poet.
Bind your crowned hair with vernal flowers;
Flowery garlands befit your title. <note>A pun on the name of Florence (*Florentia*) and flowers (*flores*).</note>
Let the crossroads be scattered everywhere with Persian perfume,
And many lilies along the scented paths.
Behold, the Benivieni line has brought forth into our breezes
One who carries the wisdom of an ancient sage in a learned mouth.
Set aside now, people of Tuscany, the funeral cypresses
Which Laura gave when she was snatched by cruel death. <note>A reference to Petrarch's Laura; Pico suggests Benivieni's poetry revives the spirit of poetic love.</note>
Let plaintive weeping be banished; behold, Laura has lived again;
She breathes, and knows how to speak eloquently as before.
Indeed, she is more snow-white than usual, and a greater grace,
Through some unknown refinement, comes from her face than before.
Your Hieronymus has restored her to us, the praise of our city,
And granted the power to traverse the infernal lakes again.
But certainly (let the wicked be far from here)
Now she sounds more grandly with a weightier lyre. <note>original: *Chely*; a Greek term for a lyre.</note>
O gods above! He modulates so sublimely that now
The Tuscan tongue is equal to the Roman sound.
Yet he does not toss about leafy, empty winds;
The inner meaning holds more than the surface promises.
Why should I mention how smoothly it goes, how the verses
Run in their numbers joined in a flat order?
So I remember often having seen sacred waters
Flow where no force of the rain-bearing south wind is noted.

But who would marvel at his practiced works: such great
Beauty in his song, when he sings unpracticed things just as well?
Who would not swear this man was Apollo <note>original: "Phoebus," the god of light and music</note> if only his bow were hanging there?
Who would deny he was the god Bacchus <note>original: "Bromius," a title for Bacchus, often depicted with horns in ancient art</note> if he had horns?
How often have I heard him sing to the curved lyre;
He immediately carried my senses away.
And what could those speaking fingers not soothe?
With these, he could stop the great rivers of the rushing Po.
He could fix the chariot of Apollo <note>original: "Phaebeos," the sun chariot</note> in the middle of the sky,
And stop the painted oxen of the Moon on their axle.
He could call back terrible Mars from his savage weapons,
He could soften the goddess <note>likely Venus</note> and the scythe-bearing old man <note>Saturn, the god of time</note>.
And those whom once Orpheus of Thrace <note>original: "rhodopeius Orpheus"</note> could not

### THE SAME ELEGY FOLLOWS, BUT TRANSLATED FROM
### Latin into the Florentine language.

**R**ejoice, Florence, and every heart that with me
Loves your well-being, play and call upon Apollo,
And let yourself be glad now for such an honor of yours.
For such an honor, with which your fierce Lion <note>the Marzocco, the heraldic lion and symbol of Florence</note>
May well be satisfied; lift up your brow,
Lift up your proud and maned neck.
How great a boon is this, your new Phaethon <note>The son of Apollo who drove the sun chariot; here used as a metaphor for a brilliant new light</note>,
This your new sun, born and nourished
In your pious breast within your horizon.
How great a boon, I say, since carved within himself
He carries the divine light; from a sacred name
He has likewise obtained his own name <note>Girolamo, or "Hieronymus," which translates to "Sacred Name"</note>.
This is he, of whom I say, that just as
Not without grace, and not without frequent acclaim,
So not without the honor of his locks <note>Refers to being crowned with the poet's laurel</note>
Is he read at all times, not only in you, Florence,
But outside you, whereby his Sicilian
Muse <note>A reference to the pastoral style of poetry associated with Sicily</note> makes Italy as happy with her presence
As she is distant from it.
Italy, which in every place hangs
Upon the sweet sound of his smooth voice.
And whoever understands the fatherland of such an author
Longs for his own country to have such an honor,
Not without envy, and is kindled with sweet zeal.
Rejoice, and let everyone who seeks and loves your good
Applaud, O blessed fatherland, your poet,
Applaud your glory and your fame.
Gird his honest and happy brow with lovely flowers,
For such an honor is well-suited
To your name, Florence; nor does heaven forbid it to you.
Let your streets be decorated and filled for you
With Oriental spice, and with white lilies,
And with roses, in testimony of such a great blessing.
Behold among your most dear and graceful sons,
Born in Florence, in you, he who alone
Resembles himself and your learned old man.
Your learned old man <note>Likely a reference to Petrarch or Dante</note> who with his flight
Covered his people, and with his glory extended
His wings at last from one pole to the other.
Whereby, weeping then for ancient offenses,
His faults, his deceptions, and the vain sorrow
That nourished the fire with which his heart was kindled.
Of his first youthful error <note>An allusion to the opening of Petrarch's *Canzoniere*: "primo giovenile errore"</note>
He hopes to find pity as well as pardon
Wherever there is someone who knows love through experience.
Now, although death extinguished such a happy sound
In you, Florence, put an end to your weeping,
Since heaven has prepared a greater gift.
Behold now, behold him whom you once so greatly
Lamented as left dead, he returns to life,
And you can well recognize the voice and the song.
The voice and the song, in which happy grace
And love reside, from which proceeds
The honor that adorns both one and the other brow.
This Girolamo <note>original: "Hieronimo" (Girolamo Benivieni)</note> yields and grants to you,
Florence: a crown, honor, and glory,
Whereby your name excels.
And certainly (if this may now be said without memory,
And not just without presence or envy,
Of you or of any of your blind victories)
The sound of this lyre is no less grave,
No less sweet, and no less perfect
Than that which once adorned the sacred breast of your old poet.
Ah, with what a voice and with what notes he breathes!
Certainly with such that, for his sake, the Tuscan tongue
Aspires to the Roman language <note>Latin</note> with equal wings.
And if there is a mind that weighs and distinguishes well,
It will see how he does not just with flowers and leaves
Adorn such a great good, and nourish and enrich it,
But that the light hidden within
Their lovely breast is greater than that which,
Exposed on the surface, meets our eyes.
What shall I say of the other fruits and flowers
Of this plant, and how sweetly
His grave and sonorous verses run?
They run, certainly, just as I have often
Seen rain already falling to the earth from heaven
Quite peacefully, without any wind.
But who, where talent and time allow,
Can conceive within himself the marvel
Of what lodges within his sacred breast,
When that which the time or the heart counsels,
Is no sooner born and pushed forth,
Than it resembles his other works and nothing else?
Let his breast be decorated and girded
With an unbending bow, or his head adorned
With a new garland divided into two horns.
Who will not say, seeing the bow around
His shoulders, that he is Apollo <note>Phoebus</note>,
Or Bacchus, seeing one and the other horn?
How many times have we heard his Muse, Thalia,
Singing to the sound of the honored lyre?
So much did he then draw my soul to himself.
And what can he not do? What does his voice
And his song not obtain? He would make the Po
Stand still like an immovable stone, if nothing else.
He would put a bridle on the lovely steeds of the Sun
With his verses, and the chariot of the Moon
Would stand still in the middle of the sky for him.
Mars would not be able to make any resistance
Against his song; and he would make Saturn
And the King of the lowest abyss <note>Pluto, god of the underworld</note>
Placid and benign; and those whom the Thracian swan <note>Orpheus</note>
Could not stop, though moved by a more malignant spirit
With his sweet song,
I believe this new Orpheus would make them stop.
